[Saint Hilary.]

[Col. 000I]

# Maffei’s Preface to the Edition

[Col. 000IA] Since it was recently discovered that the works of St. Hilary of Poitiers were lacking in very many libraries and were scarcely to be found for sale anywhere in all Italy, the distinguished body of the Canons of Verona—and especially its Archpriest, Giovanni Francesco Muselli, a most ardent patron of learning and an unwearied promoter of pious and outstanding undertakings—resolved that the writings of that illustrious Father should again be committed to the press in this city. They hoped that, through their very ancient capitular manuscripts, a new edition might either be enlarged or greatly elucidated.

When it pleased them to entrust this task to me, I saw to it that this edition should suffer no loss; indeed, if by renewed study and repeated care we might be permitted to surpass all preceding editions, I determined that this should by no means be neglected. I therefore applied myself chiefly to the latest edition, that prepared by the Benedictine monks of the Maurist Congregation: not merely to inspect it, but, insofar as the slightness of my ability allowed, also to examine and weigh it.

Yet I found that edition so learnedly, diligently, and zealously prepared, and so complete in every respect, that I judged it by no means proper to depart from it, and considered it almost sacrilegious to insert anything of my own or in any way to lay hands upon the praiseworthy industry of those editors. I therefore proposed that the Paris edition should simply be reprinted; but that, at the same time, whatever could be extracted from our manuscripts for its adornment should be most carefully selected and published for the common good.

For I certainly could not approve the adoption in this city too of the practice of those printers who, hunting profit from paper wares, concern themselves solely with ink and cartloads of paper, and who, ignorant that the book trade depends upon learned men, reprint editions made elsewhere without effort and without judgment. Such men do not even think of adding a little preface, much less strive to illuminate by fresh labour and enlarge the works of ancient writers. Indeed, when they are obliged to produce from their own resources two or three words for a title, they themselves append them, and sometimes adorn and distinguish the front of a book with some solecism—if God so please—or with some clever or ridiculous formula.

This lamentable and almost fatal evil to the Italian name would surely not spread so widely, if those who immediately buy books without discrimination, merely upon hearing the authors’ names, would exercise a little caution, and would not receive with the same indulgence what is done in this field rashly and ignorantly and what is produced with care and usefulness.

[Col. 000ID] Now, since there are especially two codices of St. Hilary in the capitular archives, to which I should be unwilling to prefer many remnants of this kind surviving in whatever library, I proceed to provide a description of them, in compliance with the taste of the learned age.

[Col. 00IIA] One of them contains the work *On the Trinity*. It is a book of the largest format, displaying singular magnificence alike in its letters and in its parchment: square in shape, with smooth paper [i.e. parchment], generally thin; ink tending toward yellow; a two-column script untouched by the injuries of time; and broad white margins around the edges. You see a specimen of an entire page.

The same hand, departing in no respect from this grandeur and majesty of script, continues to the very end. Three or four leaves are missing near the conclusion; for this reason there remains neither a note of the copyist nor of the date. Yet every indication persuades us that the codex was written in the fifth or sixth century.

Thus our codex does not yield the glory of antiquity to that very celebrated manuscript kept in the archive of the Vatican Basilica and proclaimed, as though uniquely, the most ancient surviving to this day. For Father Mabillon said that it was written near the end of the fourth century or at the beginning of the fifth; Father Coustant repeats those words in his preface. But it is evident that these most learned men let them slip by a mere and unintended error, since they assign its collation to the year five hundred and ten. Accordingly, it should have been stated that it was written near the end of the fifth century or at the beginning of the sixth (*De Re Diplomatica*, book V, p. 350).

[Col. 00IIB] Nevertheless, I do not conceal my strong suspicion that some mistake or error lies hidden in the judgment hitherto passed upon that codex. For although Mabillon’s specimen shows the book’s extraordinary antiquity, it does not show antiquity of such a kind that, according to the observations commonly applied, it can be assigned to so early a date. I appeal as witnesses to all who have devoted more than superficial labour to examining and handling ancient codices.

The book in question is written in that script into which the Roman uncial gradually declined in a later age, with the letter *N* alone retaining its larger and ancient form. Many manuscripts written in this manner are found in many places; yet no one has ever assigned any of them to such great antiquity.

But what are we to say of the appended date? The following words are said to stand at the end: “I collated [this] in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, while stationed at Kasulis, in the fourteenth year of King Trasamund.” Mabillon calls these words the subscription of a certain scholar; but in truth they were added by the person who collated and corrected the codex, according to custom.

Thus Rufius Apronianus noted at the end of the Medicean Virgil: “I read and punctuated,” etc.; then, “I punctuated while correcting,” etc. Therefore, when Holstenius read “the fourteenth year of King Trasamund” in the subscription of the Hilary codex, all subsequently agreed that it had been written at least in the year of Christ 500.

[Col. 00IIC] This opinion must nevertheless be greatly weakened when we observe that the word represented in the specimen cannot be read either as *Trasamundi* or as *Trasamund*. Where, indeed, is the *m*? Where the double *a*? Where the *u*? I therefore fear that some other name is hidden there; but concerning this, since I have not seen the codex, I spare conjectures.

Likewise, the word which Holstenius took as *Putzalis*, and which Mabillon gives as *Kasulis*, explaining it as Casula, a city of the province of Byzacena, is highly uncertain. For the sons of diplomatic scholarship would not accept the first letter, as depicted there, as a kappa. And it may seem strange that manuscripts of Augustine, Cyprian, and Tertullian written in Africa should not be found there, while manuscripts of Hilary of Poitiers should be.

But let each believe what he pleases about these matters. I determine nothing obstinately, nor is anything else presently relevant to our purpose except that, from a comparison of the specimens of the two codices, the learned reader may recognize that the Veronese codex is to be preferred in the praise of antiquity.

[Col. 0IIIB] Even if it were in no way superior in age, it is abundantly superior in correction and fidelity. For Coustant observed that errors abound in the Vatican codex; whereas they occur very rarely in the Veronese, so that I have seen few codices less corrupted by scribal mistakes. It is also commended by its use of ancient orthography. Thus, for example, where the printed editions read *attingimus* (“we attain”; this edition, col. 34), the manuscript has *adtingimus*; where col. 225 reads, “that he may attain the thing under discussion,” the manuscript reads *adsequamur* (“that we may attain”). By these readings the sense also is restored.

Many enigmas have been introduced into ancient authors because copyists, following the soft popular pronunciation, departed from this correct norm of writing. Who can explain, for example, that verse of Horace as it is commonly read?

> *Cum ridentibus arrident, cum flentibus adsunt.*  
> “They smile with those who smile; they are present with those who weep.”

But anyone who knows that the poet wrote *adrident* immediately understands that the corresponding word is *adflent*; once that is restored, the sentence proceeds perfectly.

Still, I would not have this rule pressed in every case, so that we should be obliged to write *exsilium* (“exile”), although certain ancient grammarians prescribe it. This was indeed done in the latest edition of St. Hilary, though our most ancient books give it no support.

Our codex also has the archaic form *thensaurus* (“treasure”) more than once; and, in the comparable manuscript shortly to be described which contains the Treatises on the Psalms, *formonsa sum* (“I am beautiful”). For I remember observing *Formonsum* in the Medicean Virgil.

[Col. 0IIIC] It is remarkable how the populace, perpetually inclined to deform the words of every language, is carried toward mutually conflicting corruptions. Those who, wrongly inserting *n*, pronounced *thensaurum* and *formonsum*, when uttering other words unjustly expelled that same letter. I recently observed traces of this pronunciation on a coin of Vespasian, which bears *Roma Resurges* instead of *Resurgens*. Indeed, *freques* for *frequens*, and other forms of this kind, occur very often not only in manuscripts but in every sort of monument.

Yet it is greatly to be regretted that, by some evil fate, the first leaf and the last alike have been cut from our codex. Thus neither the author’s name—which there was no lack of persons to call into doubt—nor the title of the work appears; and that title has been variously given. From the mutilation of the manuscript we do not know whether the work *On the Faith of the Orientals* was likewise joined to the twelve books, whence Cassiodorus mentions thirteen books of blessed Hilary *On the Holy Trinity*.

The books appear to be divided into chapters, but the chapters are very long. Authorities cited are marked in closer-set lines. If any words had been omitted, they are seen added above in smaller letters, but everywhere in the same style and shape as the larger script.

[Col. 0IIID] Many years ago—for this labour is neither “of yesterday” (*ἐχθεσινός*) nor of this present year—when I first encountered this splendid codex, I was moved by a certain impulse to inspect the celebrated passage in the second book, chapter twenty-seven in the latest edition. For from that passage arose the sharpest controversies of the eighth and ninth centuries, and at that very time renewed disputes among learned men were fervently being debated.

I thought that the part of the controversy depending on ancient manuscripts would be decided above all others by this exceedingly ancient and outstanding codex. Yet, remarkably, I discovered that it too leaves us still uncertain.

The question is whether, at the end of the aforesaid chapter, one ought to read *dum carnis humilitas adoratur* (“while the lowliness of the flesh is adored”), or rather *dum carnis humilitas adoptatur* (“while the lowliness of the flesh is adopted”); and, because not only printed books but manuscripts also disagree at this point, which reading should be preferred and which proceeded from the author himself.

This was not at all a matter requiring so many disputes, since an orthodox meaning follows from either reading. For it is evident that the word *adoptatur* is to be understood of the humanity assumed by the Son, not of humanity adopted by the Father.

[Col. 00IVA] Yet the interests of history required that the truth of the matter should be discovered, especially insofar as it concerned Felix, bishop of Urgel. I forbear to explain this, since it is sufficiently well known and is fully and elegantly presented and discussed by recent writers. I shall faithfully report what our codex contains.

First, then, let it be accepted as established that *ADORATUR* is written in this book, with no trace of erasure and no suspicion of overwriting. But since a new line begins after that word, *ADOPTATUR* was added in the blank space which remained, either by the same hand or by a slightly later one.

No injury was indeed done to the first word; but lines placed above it and an *R* written in the upper margin indicate, in the customary manner, that the added word ought to be substituted for the earlier one—although still more certain testimony must be sought from other codices. In this book, as in others, doubtful passages are also occasionally marked in Greek, with *R* appended for *require* and *Z* for *ζήτει*, “seek” or “investigate.”

In the word *adoptatur*, the form of the letters and the colour of the ink are exactly the same; yet it is apparent that someone long ago tried with a light knife to remove and erase both the letters and the lines placed above them.

[Col. 00IVB] All these things lead me to the following conjectures. First, the copyist clearly and without hesitation wrote *adoratur*. But whether he himself later consulted other exemplars, or someone else did so, *adoptatur* was added, together with an indication that *adoratur* should be deleted. Then came another person to whom the second reading was displeasing; for this reason he attempted to remove the word *adoptatur*, as the cloudy traces of erasure sufficiently testify.

From this it may be inferred that *adoratur* was indeed once read willingly, but that this reading had also been doubted in ancient times, and long before Felix of Urgel. Nor can we suppose that this codex was one of those upon which Felix or his supporters laid hands, since *adoratur* has not been erased. Hence, in the Vatican codex too, as I hear, the disputed word was altered by a second pen.

It came about from this that Hincmar and Alcuin read *adoratur*, while Agobard of Lyons read *adoptatur*. Since the latter refuted Felix and was thoroughly acquainted with all that had preceded, he must be thought to have sufficiently guarded himself against every fraud.

It therefore seems quite probable that Felix did not first devise the reading *adoptatur*, but found it in some codex; and because he regarded it as favourable to himself and, as often happens with those seized by a certain prejudice, wrongly imagined it to support his error, he deceitfully introduced it into the codices at Aachen.

[Col. 00IVC] Perhaps the Catholics afterwards disliked that reading for the very reason that Felix attempted to build his error upon it; for, after the Arian heresy, the word “adoption” was otherwise sufficiently suspect to them.

“These things did not occur by adoption—far be it!” Thus, in another capitular codex containing the Council of Ephesus, the words of St. Athanasius in his Letter to Epictetus are rendered in Latin:

> *οὐ θέσει δὲ ταῦτα ἐγένετο, μὴ γένοιτο·*  
> “But these things did not come about by appointment [or adoption]; may it never be!”

The version printed in the Councils twists this wrongly. Cassiodorus, on Psalm I, writes: “because of the lowliness of the assumed flesh.” Hence Alcuin says to Felix: “You say, most perversely, *adoptatur*.” Yet the words themselves were not perverse, but rather the interpretation.

All this has been said in order to show how ancient the double transcription of that passage in the books is, and why it occurred. But as to what Hilary himself wrote, it seems to me altogether easy to determine. For anyone running through the context will immediately see that the word *adoratur* does not at all fit the rhetorical elegance which the author there pursues:

> “A virgin gives birth: the birth is from God. The infant cries: praising angels are heard. The swaddling-clothes are defiled: God is adored. Thus the dignity of power is not lost while the lowliness of the flesh is adored.”

[Col. 00IVD] The immediately successive clauses do not aptly end twice with the same word; nor does that wonderful effect which Hilary seeks from opposites arise at all if he whose dignity is not lost is adored. But it arises most fittingly if he whose dignity is not lost adopts the lowliness of the flesh.

Why Felix did not repel the charge of falsification by producing some old codex containing *adoptatur*, or at least lessen the odium against himself, I truly do not understand. Hilary certainly employed the same sense in his exposition of Psalm CXXVII, writing *per adoptionem corporis*, “through the adoption of the body.”

But an ingenious man conjectured in vain that one should read *per adeptionem* (“through acquisition”), though the Erasmian edition supports it (*De veteribus Haeresibus*, etc., p. 460). For *adoptionem* is given by the most excellent of all the books of our chapter, the second manuscript, whose description we now undertake.

[Col. 00VIA] You will find few manuscripts, especially ecclesiastical ones, which can compete with this in antiquity and which, by their very appearance and aspect, lay claim to still greater age. It contains St. Hilary’s Treatises on the Psalms, written copies of which occur very rarely.

Our manuscript confirms the presence of the treatises on Psalms IX, XIII, and XCI, which until this day had been found only in the Vatican manuscript. The book is of medium and oblong format, lest only a square format should be prized. Where it is undamaged, the parchment is white, and so delicate and thin that certain leaves seem to escape the touch. The ink is yellowish-brown and pale. The writing is divided into two columns, as you see in the specimen, carefully made indeed, although it does not adequately convey the appearance of the codex and the elegance of its letters.

When Greek words occur, they are written without accents or breathings. Whatever citations are brought forward, whether taken from other Psalms or from elsewhere, are set apart as in the example, with the first line also rubricated. The rubricated words retain in places traces of gold once laid over them.

[Col. 00VIB] The style of writing resembles the Medicean Virgil—poorly represented by the published specimens—chiefly in this: the letters are alike of medium size and written with a finer pen; *P* and *Q* never descend or extend below; and the cross-stroke of *T* is scarcely visible, as are the lower strokes of *G* and *L*. Our codex, however, is written more skilfully, distinctly, and evenly. To keep the hand from departing from a straight line in writing the verses, the path of the pen is visibly marked with a stylus.

The book is also generally commendable for its correction. Therefore we shall deservedly recall to human memory the name of its copyist, which we encountered, contrary to expectation, where it was least to be expected: namely, in the alphabetical Psalm CXVIII. After the words, “Letter IV ends; Letter V happily begins,” one reads below, in small but, as we call them, capital-shaped characters:

> “The antiquary Eutalius writes: let the letters *N T* be joined in this way.”

This kind of abbreviation has the flavour of usage on ancient inscriptions. In the same Psalm, after the tenth letter, appears within a circle the monogram of Christ at the top, together with:

> “Life to the writer; learning to the reader.”

[Col. 00VIC] The law of Valens, enacted in the year 372, adequately describes the office of *antiquarii*, of whom ancient writers frequently make mention:

> “We order that four Greeks and three Latins skilled in writing be chosen as antiquaries, to compile or, because of age, to repair the books of the library.”  
> (*Codex Theodosianus*, *On Antiquaries*, law II.)

Isidore thinks they were so called because they copied only ancient works (*Origins*, book VI). But the authority of our Eutalius opposes this view, for he calls himself an *antiquarius* while transcribing Hilary’s commentaries, which were by no means then old, but perhaps still fresh and warm.

I believe that this title was especially given among copyists to those who professed to produce codices not in cursive or rapid writing—which are commonly designated by barbarous names, with a remarkable and universal error—but in larger and carefully formed letters, with singular diligence. The Greek term *καλλιγράφος* (“beautiful writer”) teaches this, for in ancient glossaries it is rendered *antiquarius*.

The emperor Constantine commanded, in a letter reported by Theodoret in his *Ecclesiastical History* (book I, chapter 16), that fifty parchment codices of the Holy Scriptures should be made for the use of the many churches of his city,

> *ὑπὸ τεχνιτῶν καλλιγράφων, καὶ ἀκριβῶς τὴν τέχνην ἐπισταμένων*,  
> “by craftsmen who write beautifully and know the art perfectly.”

Epiphanius Scholasticus translates this in the *Tripartite History*: “by antiquary craftsmen, and men perfectly skilled in the art” (book II, chapter 6).

[Col. 00VID] For this reason Augustine says in his Sermon on the Words of the Lord: “He who sees letters in a finely written codex and cannot read praises the hand of the antiquary, admiring the beauty of the characters.”

I think that in a later age this name adhered to copyists who wrote codices in letters of larger form because, imitating the ancients, they preserved the original shape of the letters. For neither in the first nor the second age of the Latin language was *antiquarius* used in this sense, but rather for a lover of antiquity. Thus the author of the *Dialogue on Orators* says, “we shall accuse you of being an antiquary”; and in the same book, “nor do I think anyone so antiquarian,” etc. Juvenal and Suetonius use the word in the same sense.

But although our antiquary bears a Greek name, we should not suppose that he was Greek, since he worked on Latin books and wrote *Eutalius* for *Euthalius*—a name derived from *εὐθαλεῖν*, “to flourish.”

In the blank space left at the end of Psalm CXXI, a later hand, in an entirely different writing and more recent ink, added these apparently playful words:

> “In the name of the Lord: under King Aripert there was true and sincere justice . . . . . Then Builius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Thomas the Apostle, whose name is Pineolo.”

[Col. 0VIIC] The church and convent of St. Thomas, now occupied by Carmelite Fathers, are situated by the bridge called Pignolo to this day. No one had known that there had once been a monastery there, or that monks had lived there with their abbot.

You see how closely the Italian language was already being anticipated from that period. For what we now say as *Abate del Monasterio* (“abbot of the monastery”) was popularly written *Abbas de Monastirium*. Since popular pronunciation often changed *um* into *o*, as I have likewise learned from manuscripts—and as appears here also, for *vocapolo* stands for *vocabulum*—these words differ little from the vernacular language.

There was no lack of persons who argued from this note that the codex had been written under King Aripert. But the shape of the letters and the very appearance of this addition sufficiently show that it is much later. Indeed, unless this book long antedates the age of both Ariperts, no confidence should be placed in conjectures, and we must henceforth bid farewell to whatever surer indications there may be. For those words do not refer to the codex itself or its scribe; rather, as is wholly clear from their place and manner, they were the diversion either of Abbot Builius or of some idle person abusing that blank space—which sometimes occurs even in many printed books.

[Col. 0VIID] Conversely, I have heard others mistakenly think that the words had been added recently because their ink is black, almost as in modern writing. Thus all who do not weigh every consideration and make their judgment in such matters on the strength of a single argument are continually prone to error.

[Col. VIIIA] Now, in order that everything which the two codices could contribute to cleansing and enlarging Hilary might be available to view, Joseph Blanchini, canon and librarian of the Church of Verona, a young man of the greatest promise and worthy heir of his celebrated uncle, collated them thoroughly with the Benedictine edition. He noted every variant reading with the utmost diligence and fidelity, and gathered them distinctly and in order.

The outstanding priest Domenico Vallarsi likewise bestowed much learned effort upon them, as did Father Alexander Bonifacio of the Congregation of the Oratory, which was established in this city a few years ago to the great benefit of piety and learning alike.

To distinguish our variants more easily from the others placed beneath the text, we mark them with numerical notes. Yet we have not presented absolutely all of them: for what utility is there if an obvious error has crept into a codex, or if matters of no importance are reported? Some are nevertheless occasionally included even if they were likewise listed by the preceding editor, so that it may be known to which various readings the authority of these exceptionally fine parchments lends its support.

[Col. VIIIB] We admitted into the text only those readings which plainly repair it or safely restore it. This we were able to do at many passages, especially in the Treatises on the Psalms; nevertheless, the earlier readings are always placed alongside, so that judgment may remain whole and free to every reader.

I did precisely the same when I first published Cassiodorus’s *Complexions*. From its preface, so that the method employed in this recension too may be sufficiently clear, allow me to transcribe two sentences:

> “Where it is worthwhile, I shall point out the emendations, which I have made rarely, so that they too may be corrected by others. If critics had done this in former times, we should know the writings of the ancients somewhat better; for, repairing innumerable passages according to their own judgment, they have deprived us of the readings of ancient manuscripts.”

Hilary himself, whom Cassiodorus calls a most learned Father, teaches that slender and minute observations are not blameworthy or contemptible in such matters. For he rebukes Arian impiety because it equipped itself for fraud by adding a syllable which is not present in the books.

I had selected from the whole collection those variants which seemed to me fit for publication, and had added a few notes at only a few passages. However, since I had to go abroad before the individual items were delivered to the press and was absent during printing, those who supervised the work and its correction, being unable to make out the complicated script of the autograph sheets I had supplied, were compelled to omit some things and alter others somewhat.

[Col. VIIIC] Although this is of little importance, some people compel me to set out here the following items among those omitted or interpolated. I had therefore written:

Col. 15, no. 1. Since the first quire of the Veronese book has been cut away, the first variant reading encountered is *tenet* (“holds”) for *tenuit* (“held”), as occurs a little earlier: “The fourth book begins.” Our manuscript now begins from the words “not accepted by his own people,” at the end of the tenth paragraph.

Col. 17, no. 2. I had admitted *piae doctrinae* (“of pious doctrine”) into the text, noting below: “Thus our manuscript; whereas the earlier edition has *pietati doctrinae*.” No. 6: *divinitatem*, without adding anything. No. 7: in the earlier edition, *natum et ex Deo* (“born and from God”).

Col. 19, no. 1. Our book reads: *necesse est in professione absoluta adversandi calumnia videatur*. This is somewhat better than the reading in the Erasmian and other editions: *et cesset*, etc. We shall, I think, completely restore the passage if we read: *at necesse est*, etc., *calumnia caveatur* (“but it is necessary … that calumny be guarded against”).

Col. 21, no. 1. In the earlier edition, in place of *ab eo*, which Erasmus also reads, there was *aut illud*, which does not suit the sense.

Col. 32, no. 7. “Whatever the Father has, he gave to the Son.” These words are presented in the printed editions, but do not appear in our manuscript, nor can it be discovered whence they were taken.

[Col. 00IXA] Col. 34, no. 9. I had admitted into the text *manibus lino occupatis, pedibus limo oblitis* (“with hands occupied with flax, feet smeared with mud”); but through ignorance I listed it among the variants.

Col. 35, no. 3. The Veronese book reads: “and he will take for himself what is free. For if the word is released from time, it seems to follow that he will take for himself what is free, that is, that he will obey no one. This is immediately dissolved by the words of the Apostle appended below, and likewise because he who is absent from time is not absent from the author.” Thus our manuscript; whereas the earlier edition reads: “he who is absent from the time of knowledge.” The codex also has *erans* in place of the Greek *ὁ ἦν*, “he who was.”

Col. 39, no. 1. I inserted *odiosa* (“hateful”) into the text, because the manuscript gives it and because the fraud of heretics shouting on every side was certainly not *otiosa* (“idle”).

Col. 59, no. 1. We added from our book, as Erasmus also has, 1 Corinthians 15:8: “he was seen also by me.”

Col. 63, no. 2. “Of your salvation” (*salutaris tui*).

Col. 165, no. 2. We added *Deus* (“God”), not merely by conjecture but on the authority of our codex, which is older than the others. The Greek text likewise has *ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεός*, “the true God.”

Col. 169, no. 1. “That the synagogue lacks itself.” For in this codex occur *caret Patrem* (“lacks the Father”), *careat virtutem* (“may lack power”); and on Psalm LXVI, *substantiam non carebunt* (“they shall not lack substance”), following Greek usage, among whom *τί ὑστερῶ;* means “what do I lack?” Plautus also uses it in Latin in the *Curculio*: *id quod amo, careo*, “I lack that which I love.”

Col. 243, no. 2. *Aeternam* (“eternal”) is absent from ours as well.

Col. 246. “Christ’s second efforts.”

[Col. 00IXC] Col. 251, no. 1. “All the fullness of divinity,” *πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα*. So likewise below: “but all the fullness of divinity bodily.”

Col. 271, no. 3. “In him.” Thereafter: “of irreligious union.” Here the conjecture of the most learned Benedictine editor is confirmed; at note 36 to Book VIII, he suspected that the noun *unionis* was masculine in gender for Hilary. This noun was of the same gender among all writers when used to mean a pearl.

Col. 284, no. 5. *Ecferret*. In other places too, *ecferre* for *efferre*.

Col. 296, no. 3. *Mandando* (“by commanding”) for *manendo* (“by remaining”).

Col. 385, no. 1. “Above your companions.” In the other codex containing the Treatises on the Psalms: “above your associates.” At the end of the preface to the *Complexions* of Cassiodorus published at Florence, we observed that unlearned copyists sometimes fall into barbarisms of this sort through the habit of common speech. For this reason Petronius Arbiter makes Trimalchio and his companions speak in this way, in order to seek comic effect even from vulgar language: “We know that you are foolish beyond [your] letters.”

[Col. 00IXD] Col. 420, no. 6. “Unless it consists of both.”

Col. 440, no. 1. “Therefore he alone”: and the capitular codex goes no further, being diminished by the loss of its final leaf.

There is no point in observing that some words are occasionally added and placed beneath the text for which I am not to be credited, and that certain variants are supplied in proof of diligence which I had passed over: for example, *genum* for *genu*; *precem eguit* for *prece eguit*; *saltim* for *saltem*; similarly, *profane*, where the printed editions correctly have *profanae*; *far*, where wheat is ground into flour; *figens*, where *fingens*; *neque*, where *nempe*; *exteriorque*, where *eritque*; *crura vulnera*, where it was *cruda*.

There was much less variation concerning the Treatises on the Psalms, especially where I had added or noted something, because the writing of the autograph exemplar was clearer. These matters, however, were omitted:

Col. 24, no. 6. *Coelestis* (“heavenly”) is absent, as it is also from several Greek manuscripts.

Col. 26, no. 4. *Non mutilentur* (“may they not be mutilated”): a somewhat better reading, but still mutilated.

[Col. 000XA] Col. 27, no. 3. “In judgment.”

Col. 39, no. 2. In the manuscript, *jus libertatis* (“the right of liberty”); thereafter *artatum est* (“it was constrained”). Since copyists did not distinguish the letter *i* when it had a dot above it, the reading was very frequently ambiguous. There were some who likewise read “force and power” where jurists wrote “right and power.” Hence we do not know whether we should write *Liutprand* or *Luitprand*.

Col. 40, no. 6. *Convertimini* (“turn yourselves”). The excellent psalter codex of the Veronese chapter has *convertamini*.

Col. 64, no. 1. In the earlier edition: “as often as those who have titles.” Moreover, this codex habitually gives *quotiensque* for *quotiescumque* (“whenever”).

Col. 68, no. 4. In the manuscript: *civitate eversa* (“with the city overthrown”). We reject the first word and accept the second; shortly before, the book gives *eversam*. The codex confirms the Benedictine editor’s correct reading, *captivitas apellitur* [“captivity is driven away”]: for it comes from the Greek verb *ἀπέλλω*, “I drive away, reject,” although I do not recall another author who used it in Latin. Those who substituted *appellatur* (“is called”) conjectured unsuccessfully.

[Col. 000XB] Col. 68, no. 5. “Psalm of David XIIII,” as the ancients wrote, not “Psalm XIV.” So below: “Psalm XIIII ends; Psalm LI begins.”

Col. 73, no. 3. We restored *alia* (“other things”) in place of *alta* (“high things”) from the codex and from the context of the words.

Col. 74, no. 5. “What he confirms by the foregoing, the Prophet added, saying.”

Col. 78, no. 1.

> “For the end; an understanding of David, when Doeg the Idumean came and reported to Saul, and said to him: David has come into the house of Abimelech.”

*Abimelech* occurs consistently in our most ancient book; the Septuagint likewise wrote *Ἀβιμέλεχ*. The Hebrew text has *Achimelech*. The reason for this difference is that, in ancient Hebrew books, this name was not written with *heth*—or, as we may say, *cheth*—as in later books, but with *caph*. Since this letter bears a very great resemblance to *beth*, their interchange was extremely easy.

I learned this for certain from an ancient author of a Breviary on the Psalms once attributed to St. Jerome, who writes thus on this passage:

> “In the Book of Kingdoms and in the Hebrew Psalter itself, *Abimelech* is written. But because *beth* and *caph* are letters distinguished among the Hebrews by a slight stroke, error crept in more easily.”

[Col. 000XC] Col. 107, no. 4. Beyond the matters reported, I had added: “Sedulius and Tertullian use the word. As here *salvifica* stands for *salvum me fac* (‘save me’), so elsewhere [Hilary] uses *lucificat* (‘makes light’); and in Psalm CXLV Hilary reads, ‘The Lord makes the blind wise,’ where the Vulgate has ‘enlightens.’ I scarcely doubt that the present readings entered through St. Jerome’s corrections, while Hilary adopted the former readings from the Old Latin version.”

Col. 127, no. 1. Our book does not contain the treatises on this Psalm and the following one, but has at the end of the preceding [treatise]: “Psalm LIV ends; Psalm LVII begins.”

Col. 152, on no. 2. *Inmutantur* (“they are changed”).

Col. 155, no. 1. “And he prepared him, and in him he prepared,” exactly as in the Greek:

> *καὶ ἡτοίμασεν αὐτό, καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ ἡτοίμασεν.*  
> “And he prepared him, and in him he prepared.”

C. 247, 2. “By which he is tempted by Zabulus.” Thus it is written in the manuscript, and it frequently occurs in manuscripts. The same book gives “the vanquisher of Zabulus” near the end of the Sermon on Psalm LXIII [Col. 000XD]. We read “the offspring of Zabulus,” “the power of Zabulus,” “that he might be tempted by Zabulus,” in Hilary’s Commentary on Matthew, in Erasmus; Guillaume Cave, in his notice on Commodian, considers *Zabulus* and *Zacones* for *Diacones* (“deacons”) to be words peculiar to Africans. But in fact these words are neither different nor more remotely derived; rather, their occasional spelling in this way was caused by a certain softness of pronunciation, which I have often noticed among modern Greeks pronouncing ζ for δ, and ζιά for διά. Ancient books testify to the sound they had from antiquity, frequently giving *Zabulus*, as we have seen; and Photius strikingly confirms this when he observes that Philostorgius, in his Ecclesiastical History, wrote *Nadiandus* for *Nazianzus*: “He calls him both Nadiandus and Nazianzus” (Ναδιανδὸν δὲ καὶ Ναζιανζὸν ἐξωνομάζει).

C. 256, 4. The passage intended is Isaiah 53:5: “he suffers pain for us, and we considered him to be in pains.”

C. 256, 5. “In the heavens,” as in the Greek.

[Col. 00XIA] C. 285, 1. I had noted nothing here.

C. 329, 1. “The oil of exultation.”

C. 367, 5. “Unlawful.”

C. 383, 3. “It is sought.”

C. 395, 2. “Morning manna”; a little below, “heavenly manna”: thus Hilary has “Pascha,” etc., as Erasmus observed in his preface.

C. 400, 6. In the manuscript, *iniqui* (“of the wicked”), as in the Roman Psalter; nor does Jerome mean otherwise by “pursuers of wickedness,” that is, wicked persons. Plautus too used “one pursuing disgraceful conduct” for a lover of disgraceful conduct, or a disgraceful person.

C. 450, 3. The earlier edition had *mentis* (“of the mind”), a word which the Erasmian edition does not have, nor does our manuscript.

C. 517, 1. At this point the manuscript, collapsing under the weight of so many centuries, fails us: its final leaves have been wholly eaten away or wretchedly torn apart.

“*I have raised a monument more troublesome than a fever*”—thus, in the very heat of writing, I had added below, slightly twisting Horace’s line—as though congratulating myself that I had at last been relieved of so great a labour. For to compare variant readings against one another, pursue fleeing letters, catch at the minutest marks of manuscripts, and contend with the astonishing blunders of scribes, is a task unbelievably full of vexation and beset with dangers on every side. As I ran through the learned notes of the preceding editor himself, I pointed out to him some errors of the Parisian printer, however diligent, in our copy, so that he might guard against them; for example, on p. 175, where a passage of Cicero is cited with the negative adverb omitted. I now see that our printer corrected this on p. 197, but overlooked another word. For it should read: “And anyone who doubts this, I certainly do not understand why he cannot likewise doubt whether the sun exists or does not exist.”

[Col. 00XIC] Nevertheless, besides the variant readings presented here and beneath the text, our manuscript preserves several of Hilary’s treatises on the Psalms which differ from the published versions many times, and not merely in a few words or a single verse or two. We have transcribed and set them forth together exactly as they stand; we have only removed certain errors and rendered such forms as *profeta*, *filosofus*, *centensimus*, etc., into common usage. The chief ground of the variation is that these versions of ours are much shorter: either the written book cuts out several periods or whole pages, or the published texts insert them. What judgment ought to be made about such a difference the learned reader will decide.

I had first considered whether a shorthand writer, taking them down from the speaker’s mouth but unable to keep pace with the speed of his voice, might have supplied them in an abridged form [Col. 00XID], just as Augustus thought that a certain speech of Caesar which was circulating had been taken down by stenographers who poorly followed the speaker’s words (Suetonius, *Caesar*, ch. 55). But the continuity of the discourse opposes this theory, as do words sometimes added and the frequently altered texture of the composition. For example, where the published texts read: “From prophetic and apostolic teachings we have come to know the year of God’s kindness” (*On Psalm* LXV), and shortly afterward: “For this is the year of the Lord’s goodness, in which those unwearied times of gracious recompense will begin. Therefore the most delightful and pleasant fruit of the visited and watered earth will bless the crown of this year of God. For this is Christ’s victory: the corruption of our bodies having been driven away and the power of death destroyed”—the manuscript reads [Col. 0XIIA]: “Without doubt he declares the year of that eternal and blessed age, because this is the year of the Lord’s goodness. The crown of this year is blessed; for the visited earth will be a most delightful and pleasant year. For this is Christ’s victory in power.”

It is more likely that Hilary himself first composed it thus, then expanded it through later revision and brought it into a fuller form. Perhaps he first drafted them as sermons to be delivered to the people, and afterward transferred them into commentaries. Accordingly, on Psalm LXV the manuscript passes over all that pertains to Greek usage and is drawn from readings of the Greek text. Yet we do not rest fully content with this conjecture. For the exposition is generally too fragmentary, and it skips several verses of the Psalms which the sense sometimes shows that the interpreter treated in the passages now missing.

Certain things are also added that do not appear to be Hilary’s, such as, on Psalm LXIV, no. 4: “The Church, not yet enlightened by Christ’s coming, was at one time subject to empty superstitions, when Gentile precepts,” etc. In the published text this is said concerning the whole human race, which our author never designated by the name of the Church. Nor should I believe that the following is his on Psalm CXXIV: “Here ‘round about the people’ signifies the Gospel.” Nor are there lacking passages mutilated less aptly and connected less elegantly. One may therefore suspect that these epitomes proceeded from another hand and that someone adapted these commentaries in this fashion for personal use.

Indeed, the suspicion sometimes arose whether anything extraneous and foreign had been inserted into the commentaries we possess [Col. 0XIIC], such as those matters in the exposition of Psalm LXV derived from the particular meaning and force of Greek expressions. For Hilary had acquired only a slight smattering of Greek letters, if Jerome is to be believed in his Letter to Marcella. On weighing the matter, however, we rejected this suspicion. But let the judgment of learned persons be given on these matters.

The copyist indicates, by a space left blank, that something is missing at the very beginning; hence the exposition begins with verse seven. You will also recognize that Psalm CXXXII is mutilated near its end. Where the published text, column 188 of our edition, reads: “The girding on of power is fitted to the body which needed it. For power itself is not girded on, but in the power of God the man whom the Lord assumed is girded on”—the manuscript explains it much better: “For power itself is not girded on, but the power of the man is in the power of God; that is, it is fitted to the body which was lacking. Therefore the power of that man whom God assumed is girded on in power.” But now, dear reader, we delay you no longer, and place before your eyes the Treatises themselves, as they appear in the manuscript—whether you prefer to call them sermons or outlines of sermons.

## PSALM LXIII BEGINS. FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID.

“Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication to you; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy. They have searched out iniquities; those who search with searching have failed.”

The prophetic Spirit, speaking through David, hearing all things and knowing all things, declares in this passage that not only the malicious conspiracy of the Jews, but also the vain learning of philosophers and the perverse obstinacy of heretics, will at last fail. This is shown in this section when he says:

> They have searched out iniquities;  
> Those who search with searching have failed.

Therefore the intellectual powers of all evil people fail, as the Prophet shows. For the philosopher attacks the rule of the world, now assigning the name of God to waters, now to earth, now to heaven; while the heretic falsifies the doctrine of faith. Against them all he fought with wakeful vigilance and continual prayer to the Lord. Therefore the Prophet said: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication to you.”

We must therefore keep watch in prayer to God, so that, when the soul begins to grow weary amid afflictions, God, always invoked, may hear us and deliver us from the things we fear. For in what follows he says:

> Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.

For God is not to be prayed to only when the things feared have happened. He must always be invoked with unwearied prayers, that he may deliver us from fear of those whose power we fear. Therefore the Prophet, not ignorant of what was to happen, ever anxious amid imminent tribulations and watchful against every fear of the enemy, prays to God regarding what he fears, that he may be heard when in tribulation. For it is not our fear, but faith, that earns God’s mercy. And he added:

> You have sheltered me from the assembly of evildoers, from the multitude of those who work iniquity; who sharpened their tongues like a sword, bent the bow—a bitter thing—that they might shoot the blameless in secret.

But the bow of the murderer’s tongue is always drawn, and the sharp edge of his tongue’s sword is ready. His deadly arrows fly; and there is no doubt what they accomplish, for this is what they seek: “that they might shoot the blameless in secret.” The malicious person seeks to kill the blameless person—the one to whom remission of former sins has been granted through baptism, but who has not yet been instructed in spiritual teachings. Simple and tender in the infancy of new birth, he is sought out for wounding by the drawn bow through ignorance of realities. For he says:

> Suddenly they will shoot at him, and they will not fear.

They seek to deceive a simple and blameless nature; they spread hidden snares before such a person, that by concealed ambushes they may kill the innocent. For it follows:

> They have strengthened for themselves an evil word; they have plotted to hide snares; they have said: “Who will see them?”

They are always ready in themselves against the faith; and therefore it was said: “They have hidden snares and said, ‘Who will see them?’” If a heretic attempts to pervert the faith, it is incredible with how great ingenuity he strives to overthrow it. If philosophy attacks our hope of eternity, it astonishingly places every good of present life in the body, so that heavenly teaching may seem capable of being overthrown by the power of its intellect. Therefore both those who search fail, in accordance with the same Prophet: “Those who search with searching have failed.” But what is human perversity to God? What is the ingenuity of the work against its Maker? Though it displays all its cleverness with every argument to overthrow truth, the assertion of falsehood will nevertheless fail against truth. Therefore it follows:

> They have searched out iniquities; those who search with searching have failed.

Though they investigate every secret of natural causes, they nevertheless fail in the very purpose of their undertaking, refuted by spiritual teachings. For those who teach . . . all things will hear from us of the God of eternal power. And if the heretic attempts to destroy the faith, he will learn that the Son of God has always existed, separated from the Father by no interval of time. He will learn that he is the power and wisdom of God, the Creator of humankind; that he washed away the first sins of the world by the flood; that he gave the law to Moses; that he was in the Prophets; that through the weakness of flesh he renewed the glory of flesh. Those who search will therefore fail against these things.

After this he says:

> A human being will approach a lofty heart, and God will be exalted.

For one is instructed through the power of God’s teaching; and to the person whose heart is set on high, these proclamations of divine action will be presented, so that God may be praised by the confession of those very persons who hear them. This, then, is: “A human being will approach a lofty heart, and God will be exalted.” Once the failure of those who search has been recognized, and the person of lofty heart approaches, the magnificence of God is known. For who would not magnify God when he knows him as the Maker of this world? Who would not fear him when he knows him as judge? Who would not desire to be reborn into innocence, when receiving forgiveness of sins through new birth? Who, once reborn, would not cease from sinning and remain in the innocence of a little child, knowing that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such persons? This profession of ours weakens the ingenuity of those who search; these missiles of doctrine, which are the arrows of little children, wound foolish disputations. For once God’s works have been proclaimed, then his deeds will begin to be understood; then the righteous will rejoice in them; then all the upright in heart will praise him [Col. 0XIVB]. In these is the joy of the saints; in these their most steadfast hope. For these things, those who are upright in heart will praise God, knowing him to be the forgiver of sins, the destroyer of death, the vanquisher of Zabulus, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages.

## PSALM LXIV BEGINS. FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID.

> Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and a vow shall be rendered to you in Jerusalem.

This psalm is properly spoken with reference to the end and the gathering of the nations who are to praise God. At its beginning, according to his custom, the prophet directs the whole prayer to the Lord.

> Praise is fitting for you, Lord God, in Zion, and a vow shall be rendered to you in Jerusalem.

Zion is indeed a mountain adjoining Jerusalem; but here the name of the mountain and the city signifies the Church [Col. 0XIVC], which is the body of Christ our Lord, as he himself says: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain.” Thus this hymn is fitting for God when it is in the Church—innocent in spiritual song and sweet with God’s praises—because what follows is:

> Hear my prayer; all flesh shall come to you.

For it does not say “my,” so that the person of the speaker might be understood. Although many have added this as though it were missing, it is not found in the authentic copies. For the Prophet speaks these things not from his own understanding but by inspiration, and he added: “All flesh shall come to you.” For the Church, not yet enlightened by Christ’s coming, was at one time subject to empty superstitions, when Gentile precepts imbued all people with devotion to impiety, proclaiming God in wood and stone. But knowing that its former sins must be propitiated before God, all flesh will therefore come to him. He says:

> The words of the wicked have prevailed against us, and you will be propitious toward our impieties.

For how beneficial it is to have abandoned Gentile error and rejected impious teaching, he shows below, saying:

> Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken up, that he may dwell in your tabernacles.

For all flesh will come to God; that is, people will be gathered from every human race. But blessed is whoever has been chosen; for, according to the Gospel, many are called but few are chosen. Those chosen are splendid in their wedding garment and also in the pure and unblemished body of new birth. We should understand why the one chosen has been chosen: namely, for that which follows, “that he may dwell in the tabernacles of God.” Thus every perfection of good things is in the repose of heavenly dwelling [supplying *habitationis*]. For the Lord testifies that there are many dwellings in heaven; but in the Gospel he prays to the Father that the Apostles may remain where he himself is, saying: “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be with me where I am” (John 17:4). Therefore, from among the many dwellings, he shares with his Apostles that one which is his own.

The Prophet knows what great blessedness lies in the tabernacles of God. Elsewhere he says: “My soul desired and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83:3). Then, when one has been chosen, this follows:

> We shall be filled with the good things of your house; your temple is holy, wonderful in righteousness.

What the good things of the house are we can recognize: namely, the gifts of the Church, which Christ bestowed according to the multiplicity of their fruit, since the Church itself is, according to the Apostle, the house of God. Thus this Church bears fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. It will be filled with these good things of God’s house, which meanwhile is adorned through the distribution of gifts, as it is written: “To one is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12:8). But there are other full gifts of God’s house which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor have they arisen in the human heart—those which God has prepared for those who love him [Col. 0XVB] (1 Corinthians 2:9). Therefore the psalm continues: “Your temple is holy, wonderful in righteousness.”

For the Apostle teaches that the bodies of all believers are the temple of God, saying: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:16). Therefore this temple of God must be adorned in holiness and righteousness, through prayers and actions, that it may be filled with the good things of God’s house, so that we may be his holy and wonderful temple. After this the psalm continues:

> Hear us, O God our Saviour, hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far away in the sea.

Christ, therefore, is the hope of all, on sea and land. Why he is the hope of all, it teaches in what follows:

> Preparing the mountains in your strength, girded with power, and troubling the depth of the sea, the sound of its waves.

Here this discourse is not extended to the nature of earthly mountains; another prophet shows who these mountains are: “Hear, all peoples, and let the earth attend, and all who dwell in it; and the Lord God shall be a witness to you, the Lord God from his holy house. Therefore behold, God will come down from his place; he will descend upon the high places of the earth, crush the mountains beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire, because of Jacob’s impiety” (Micah 1:2).

For in another psalm it is shown written thus: “The earth was shaken and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because God was angry with them. Smoke rose from his wrath, and fire will blaze from before his face, and coals were kindled by him; he bowed the heaven and came down, and darkness was beneath his feet. He sent arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and troubled them” (Psalm 17:8).

In these words, so far as the reading teaches, the Holy Spirit shows through the Prophet the Lord’s coming from heaven: the terror of the earth and the trembling of the mountains, because God is angry with them, smoke having risen from his wrath and then fire being kindled from before him [Col. 0XVD]. The smoke which rises belongs to past time; in the fire, because it blazes from before his face, is contained the indication of future time. Thus arrows will scatter these mountains, and multiplied lightnings will trouble them: namely, every power set on high. Whoever presents himself as exalted against God will be subjected to God’s wrath. Therefore God the Word, descending and girding with power the human being assumed by him, first cast down these heights of the mountains: he crushed the excellence of the Devil, whom he prepared for the punishment of judgment.

For this reason the Prophet preserved this order, saying:

> Preparing the mountains in your strength, girded with power.

For power itself is not girded on; rather, the power of the man is in God’s power—that is, it is fitted to the body which was lacking. Therefore the power of that man whom God assumed is girded on in power.

Then he says:

> Who troubles the depth of the sea, the sound of its waves.

He does not trouble the sea, but the sea’s depth. In another psalm, however, prophetic discourse uses “sea” and calls it the world, as it says: “This sea is great and broad; there the dragon rests whom you formed to sport with him” (Psalm 103:25). Therefore the mountains—that is, all adversaries—are prepared for the punishment of judgment, and the foundations of the sea will be troubled. For the world stood in confidence in them; once the Devil is troubled, every ministry of its error will be troubled.

Let us remember, moreover, the murmurings and the frenzied clamour, and that the world once rang with the singing of all profane rites. But now, when the Lord Christ is preached, all things are silent and tremble: the maddened priests of temples are subjected to the power of believers; they are tortured by the words of the righteous, torn, burned, and punished. By these things, therefore, they are now prepared for judgment; and understand what this preparation accomplishes.

> The nations will be troubled, he says, and they will fear.

Seeing, then, their gods mute and groaning aloud at the laying on of our hands. But after the troubling of the nations, those also who inhabit the ends will fear. The end is the final time, in which the thing itself fails. Let us therefore see why those who inhabit the ends will fear and whence fear will come upon them. For it follows: “And they will fear because of your signs.” Thus all fear arises from signs. But what signs will these be?

> You will delight the outgoings of morning and evening.

For after the sea’s depth has been troubled, the greatest sign of God is the day expressed in prayers. The day begins with hymns to God; it is closed according to what was said: “The lifting up of hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140:11). This following sign succeeds:

> You have visited the earth and made it drunk.

God visited the earth—that is, the birth of the human race—and made it drunk, once visited, through the Holy Spirit. Multiplied by God’s gifts, it becomes rich, as the Apostle says: “In everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1:5). For we are filled with these good things daily and are made drunk. And he says in what follows what the fruit of this intoxication is:

> The river of God is full of water.

For in the Gospel he says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). He said this, therefore, concerning the Holy Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive. Thus this river of God is filled with water; it is inundated with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and from that fountain of life the river of God, filled with water, is poured into us. We also have food prepared. Let us see what this food is. But that he might teach that all these things are future, he says:

> Make its streams drunk; multiply its generations; in its drops it will rejoice when it springs up.

The earth, however, has been visited and made drunk; how then are its streams now made drunk? We ourselves are made drunk when we receive the Holy Spirit. Then the Prophet prays that he may make these same streams drunk, that our generations may be multiplied: that is, that the good earth, receiving the seed of the word according to the Gospel comparison, may be enriched with thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit; that after the joy of baptism understanding of the sacrament may enter into us, knowledge of prophecy, a word of wisdom, gifts of healing, and demons may be subjected to us. For these penetrate us like drops, which, beginning little by little, abound in manifold fruit. Therefore, when the earth springs up amid these drops, it will rejoice. But the drops multiply so that they may become streams; the streams are made drunk so that they may become rivers. After these things the psalm continues:

> You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.

Without doubt he declares the year of that eternal and blessed age, because this is the year of the Lord’s goodness. The crown of this year is blessed; for the visited earth will be a most delightful and pleasant year. For this is Christ’s victory in power; this crown of the Lord is blessed in flower, glorious in the choir of his saints. Then the fields will be filled with abundance; then the borders of the desert will grow fat; then the hills will be girded with exultation; then the rams will be clothed with sheep. For then is the time of recompense. In the fields, which are useful for cultivation, those works which have been under God’s law and cultivation will receive abundance. Where the desert borders grow fat, the people of the Church, once deserted, are again enriched with the fruit of promise. In the hills girded with exultation, the glorious joys of martyrs are announced; for they stand higher than other people. When the rams are clothed with sheep, the eternal and blessed garment of the patriarchs, prophets, and Apostles—who are leaders of the holy flock—is shown. Therefore the rams will be clothed with this garment of sheep, and they are arrayed in this attire of glorious immortality.

> And the valleys, he says, will abound with grain.

That is, humbler people and those of good works will obtain the fruit of life. They will not be filled with abundance like the fields, nor girded with exultation like the mountains, but will only abound with grain; that is, they will not lack the sustenance of life. For these fields, these deserts, these hills, these rams, and these valleys will cry aloud and sing a hymn; and, because of these different rewards of recompense, they will proclaim God’s power in unwearied and mighty voices [Col. XVIIB].

## PSALM LXV BEGINS.

> Make joyful noise to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name.

First, therefore, he instructs us to make joyful noise to God; second, to sing a psalm to his name; then to give glory to his praise; then to say to the Lord God, “How terrible are your works!” Finally, to confess: “In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you.” But to explain briefly the meaning and order of this discourse, it is necessary to resolve the point which causes difficulty.

In Latin manuscripts we read:

> Make joyful noise to God, all the earth.

But so far as the usage of our language is concerned, we call *jubilum* the sound of a pastoral and rustic cry, when in solitary places the drawn-out sound of a voice is heard, either answering or seeking. In Greek books, which are closest to the Hebrew, *alalagmus* (ἀλαλαγμός), which Latin writers render *jubilum*, has this meaning: it signifies the cry of an army fighting—or, alternatively, trampling down—in battle against the enemy, or testifying by a cry of exultation to the success of victory. The voice of exultation differs from *jubilum*. We too have been set in the battles of this life and in this contest of our flesh and blood, fighting against the Devil and his army with spiritual weapons. Therefore we are instructed to make joyful noise to God with the voice of exultation. Every profane hearer must be overborne by the speech of our confession; against the Devil and his weapons we must fight with the sound of our prayers, and the victory of our warfare must be displayed with the voice of exultation.

Let anyone standing outside the Church hear the voice of the praying people and receive the celebrated sounds of hymns with the devout responsive confession: every adversary must be terrified when he hears the victorious voices of our exultation resounding in glory: “Give glory to his praise.” For when the nations behold our works amid such praise, they will magnify our Father who is in heaven and give glory to his name.

> Say to God: How terrible are your works!

For who would not tremble before the majesty of him who established the ages, created the world, measured out time in its cycles, adorned heaven with stars, filled earth with fruits, enclosed the sea with boundaries, and chose humankind either to use these things or to rule them? Through all these signs of power, the eternity of his might is known. These things make the Creator’s name terrible. Therefore God must be proclaimed by us as the Creator of these works and confessed by all others.

> In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you.

That is, through the multitude of God’s power, the empty names of false gods are made vain; and because enemies will lie, what all must do is taught thus:

> Let all the earth worship you and sing to you; let them sing a psalm to your name, O Most High. Come, he says, and see the works of God.

This is the word of one inviting. For he has placed God’s teaching as though near at hand. “And when he came,” he says, “he preached peace to those far off and peace to those near” (Ephesians 2:17). For many who dwelt near, by reason of the law, believed; but the Prophet’s proclamation summons all from the distant Gentiles to behold God’s works. Yet not those works which lie before everyone’s eyes—the sky, air, earth, and sea—for everyone sees these; but those works known only through the earnest pursuit of believers: how with immense and wondrous power he crushed Pharaoh, for the deserts of his impiety, as an example of human fear; how the sea was dried; how the people entered the Jordan on foot. Thus the Prophet summons the nations to behold this God’s works, saying:

> Come and see the works of the Lord, terrible in counsels over the children of men. He turned the sea into dry land; they shall pass through the river on foot.

But what benefit does the Jordan then dried bring to the salvation of the whole earth so long afterward? Let us see. First, cleansing from sins was granted in its waters when John preached repentance. Through this river there had been a way for the people into the land of promise; now also through it the way of the heavenly kingdom is shown to us, the waters themselves having been consecrated by the Lord’s baptism.

“We shall rejoice in him,” the Prophet added, saying:

> He who shall rule in his power forever.

For the only-begotten Son of God, although he has always reigned, has not always reigned in a body. For this passage shows the time when, after the body has been glorified to God’s glory, both the name of God and kingship are given to it.

> For you have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined by fire.

This is an analogy by comparison. The sole purpose of assaying silver is that impurities adhering from its first earthly substance may be melted away, and that, if elements of another metal’s nature have been mixed with it, they may be purified.

Therefore God examines believers in him, not as one ignorant, but, according to the Apostle, he brings proof through temptations. Believers are thus examined so that, purified by fire and cleansed of the admixture of fleshly vices, they may shine in the tested brightness of innocence. Considering the kinds of temptations and the different victories of martyrs, we know in what ways souls are set in life. Some glory in prison chains; others rejoice when beaten with lashes; others happily submit their necks to the power that cuts off blessed heads. Many run to the constructed pyres, and, while the ministers of punishment tremble, leap into the fire with the devoted haste of a jump. Others, sinking into the deep, fall not into waters that kill but into the eternal refreshment of blessedness, offering their whole bodies to God as victims, like whole burnt offerings.

The prophetic discourse therefore runs through these kinds of sufferings in the person of Apostles and martyrs, saying:

> You have examined us by fire, as silver is examined by fire; you brought us into a snare—that is, into chains of custody; you placed tribulations on our back, namely, the punishments of blows, in which the Apostle Peter rejoices and Paul exults; you placed men over our heads; we passed through fire and water.

One is not dissolved in these things, but is led through them into something else, when it says: “We passed through fire and water.” And the Prophet is not ignorant where one is led, saying: “You brought us into refreshment.” He means the day of resurrection, in which, after the time of this death, there is no weeping, no sinning, and one lives.

> I shall enter your house with whole burnt offerings; I shall render to you my vows, which my lips have uttered.

These, then, are first the vows of martyrs in tribulation; afterward, that from us they may consume rich whole burnt offerings. The rams are clothed with sheep: here the rams with the incense of sheep are understood as martyrs, as leaders of flocks [Col. 0XIXA]. Yet not only rams with incense will be offered, but oxen also will be offered with goats; that is, animals of obstinate nature are tamed for the worship of God—those who have been instructed in a moment of time. Thus he does not speak about cattle, but in oxen the figure of a person of the Church is shown: namely, those whom the storm of persecution brought forth into the glory of martyrs.

For we know that many, through ignorance, ran to martyrdom following the example of martyrs and attained glory through martyrdom of faith. Such was that one of the thieves who was crucified with the Lord and, in his very condemnation, confessed God, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). God answered him thus: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise.” After the prophetic Spirit had shown the person of Apostles, martyrs, and prophets, it states in what ways souls were set in life, saying:

> How great things he has done for my soul.

For he set this soul in life; he brought it into refreshment; it entered God’s house in whole burnt offerings. Good, therefore, was the soul that cried to God with its mouth—not merely on its tongue, but under its tongue; that is, in secret it confessed God with its tongue. Therefore it is said in the person of martyrs:

> If I have regarded injustice in my heart, may God not hear me. Therefore God heard me; he attended to the voice of my prayer.

Contracting no vice within the heart, such a person was worthy to be heard. His soul was set in life; his feet were not moved; he was brought into refreshment; he entered God’s house; and he paid the vows which his lips had uttered, saying:

> Blessed be God, who has not removed my supplication and his mercy from me.

Having begun the Psalm with praise to God, at its end he confessed God, to whom is glory for ages of ages.

## PSALM CXIX BEGINS. A SONG OF ASCENTS.

[Col. 0XIXC]

> To you, O Lord, I cried when I was troubled, and you heard me.

The titles of the Psalms, as is shown in the Psalms themselves, have their own proper meanings, briefly containing the rationale and subject matter of the writings beneath them; there is no need to discuss them now. For this must be done when each Psalm is treated. But now we take up the “Song of Ascents,” whose inscription is continuous and uniform. In very many Psalms, however, we read that much is inserted into their superscriptions according to history and chronological order: as when David fled from the face of his son Absalom; when he changed his appearance before Abimelech; when, after Bathsheba, he was reproved by Nathan the Prophet; and elsewhere wherever the historical truth of events is contained in the titles of the Psalms themselves. Yet we must remember that the Psalms of the same author are not for that reason all to be understood literally; rather, our spiritual understanding must be aroused beneath this commemoration of events.

Therefore, we must see whether, according to the superscribed titles, this Psalm contains anything historical. For in the book of Isaiah, while Hezekiah was praying, a sign was set for him upon the steps, signifying the prolongation of his life. There were ten steps in his house, which the sun ascended when its light advanced beyond its appointed course of time; and, as the light of that same time withdrew on the day of his death, it descended again. But there is no similarity of this history to the Psalms. Nevertheless, this sign given to Hezekiah plainly shows that the light of God approaches those to whom, according to their merits, the blessedness of the life to come is granted, but withdraws from those to whom it is denied.

History has also told us that there were fifteen steps in the Temple, and that ranks were arranged so that a certain precedence, as it were, belonged to those placed before others: the Levites stood first, then the Israelites, then the proselytes, and thereafter the rest. For the Psalms do not announce only matters belonging to the time in which they were written; the word of God has provided for all who would enter into life. Let us therefore seek these steps of the Songs, by which we may ascend to the places of the Saints. For the ascent to them is steep and the way narrow. Therefore David the Prophet says:

> To thee, O Lord, when I was troubled I cried, and thou didst hear me.

For when anyone rightly cries to the Lord in supplication, he will immediately hear Him saying to him: “Behold, I am present.” And because He is present, He must again be entreated:

> O Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue.

A deceitful tongue is a deceptive work which, through the hope of temporal life, leads into death. Such too are the falsehoods of heretics: to hand down and teach everything otherwise than it has been written. From these, therefore, we are delivered through the mercy of God when we pray; and amid their afflictions, crying to God, we shall be heard. The following comes after this:

> What shall be given to thee, and what shall be added to thee, against the deceitful tongue?

That is, what aid may be brought to you against its falsehood? The answer is:

> Sharp, mighty arrows, with desolating coals.

Isaiah shows that the Arrow is the Lord Himself, saying in this way: “He made me as a chosen arrow, and hid me in his quiver, and said: It is a great thing for thee to be called my servant” (Isa. 49:2). Let these arrows, then, be understood in either sense: either as punishment for the wicked, or as wounding the sin of holy bodies. And let the coal be either devastating or cleansing; it cleanses those who confess, unto perfect innocence.

> Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged.

For after the arrows of the Lord and those desolating coals, he desires the glory of that blessed kingdom. Nor does he merely desire it, but hates every delay, saying:

> Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged!

This saying is like that in which we ask in the Gospel: “Thy kingdom come; thy will be done” (Matt. 6:10). Therefore, the prophetic spirit, placed in this body, complains that its sojourning here is far too prolonged, hastening to depart from earthly things and dwell in heavenly ones; so that, leaving present things behind, it may attain the invisible and eternal. Therefore he says:

> Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged: I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar.

Kedar is a people of the Ishmaelites inhabiting the desert, whose boundaries extend as far as the Medes and Persians. For Kedar was a son of Ishmael, as Genesis testifies: “The firstborn of Ishmael,” it says, “was Nebaioth, and Kedar” (1 Chron. 1:29). These are now called Saracens. Those, therefore, who thought these Psalms were to be understood with an earthly mind intend that the Prophet complained in the person of the captive people because that people’s sojourning had been long in the dwellings of Kedar. But we must not understand the force of the word in this way. For *Kedar*, according to the Hebrew language as it is pronounced among us, means “darkness.” That bride in the Song of Songs recalls this tent when she says: “I am black and beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem, like the tent of Kedar.”

Therefore the Prophet, because he hated the association of the wicked and their dwelling in darkness, says:

> My soul has long been a sojourner; with those who hated peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.

The Prophet indeed was peaceable with the enemies of peace; but they hated his preaching and were stirred up by the teaching of God. The Prophet, therefore, restrained these men in peace by his gentleness; and so he does not cease to preach peace, but the enemies of peace attack the preacher of peace.

## PSALM 120 BEGINS. A SONG OF ASCENTS.

> I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me.

The nature of the human mind is such that, if we contemplate something in thought, every image presents itself to us in the manner in which we have fashioned it by thinking. For wherever we direct the eyes of our mind, they bring that very thing on which they are fixed before our perception. Therefore the Prophet lifted his eyes to the mountains. What eyes? Surely those of which it is written: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall know the wonders of thy law” (Ps. 118:18). Thus the eyes are not to be unveiled for what is seen, but for what is desired to be understood in the law.

The Prophet lifted the eyes of his mind to the mountains. To what mountains? Certainly not to those which human sight beholds; rather, we understand by the mountains the prophetic books raised from earth to on high, through which ascent to higher things is made. We may also understand the mountains as the Gospel mysteries, and the powers and virtues of heaven, by whose ministry ascent to heaven is granted to us. Raising the eyes of his heart, then, to these mountains, and directing the light of his understanding toward them, the Prophet comprehended in his mind all that he had beheld in thought, knowing whence help would come, and saying:

> Whence help shall come to me.

And immediately he answers himself in a blessed confession:

> My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

This is happy faith; this is true confession; this is hope worthy of the gifts of eternal heavenly blessing. Then he says:

> My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth; therefore he says: Give heed to the movement of thy foot, and he who keeps thee shall not sleep.

The foot is that part of the body which carries the whole body about to perform and accomplish its actions. Under the name of the foot are signified the movements and course of our mind; and in the Gospels the Lord, signifying another kind of feet, commanded the offending right foot to be cut off, saying: “And if thy right foot causes thee to stumble, cut it off” (Mark 9:44). Thus, as the eyes of the mind, so also its feet are to be understood, possessing in themselves both the sight of understanding and the movement of the will. And he adds:
