> He who keeps thee shall not sleep.

Therefore, while the Lord abides in us, there is watchful guardianship and unfailing protection. But if through lukewarmness of faith we sleep, He too sleeps with us. For there is no sleep in God, whose Angels are watchful both in name and in nature; but because, according to our faith, the help of God with us will be either awake or asleep, He is therefore frequently signified as both awake and asleep.

> The Lord is thy protection upon thy right hand.

Scripture always shows the right side as the better and more useful; and by the hand we understand the effect of every work. Thus it is also said through the Prophet: “Deliver my only one from the mouth of the lion and from the hand of the dog” (Ps. 21:21). He prays to be delivered from works of wickedness. Therefore God’s watchful protection is promised over the hand of the right side, so that the works of good will may continue in us undefiled; and while these remain in us, after every infirmity has been wiped away, we shall enjoy the kingdom of that eternal and blessed time. For the prophetic Spirit also promises us what follows, saying:

> By day the sun shall not burn thee, nor the moon by night.

For the prophetic Spirit knows that blessedness of the times in which every change arising from bodily infirmity shall depart from us; in which there shall be neither cold nor heat, nor night, but eternal day and blessed mildness, while the sun of righteousness rules over us. The Lord already foreshadowed the repose of that time in the wilderness, tempering for his people the heat of day by a pillar of cloud, and the cold and darkness of night by a pillar of fire. Therefore, whoever has deserved the Lord’s guardianship in this protection of eternal times shall remain, lest he be burned by the frost of the moon or the heat of the sun; but, set free from the injuries of this age, he shall in the eternal and blessed kingdom receive for his body a firm and unchangeable nature.

Then follows:

> The Lord shall keep thee from every evil.

The Lord preserves the faithful mind from every evil: that the Devil may not corrupt it, the thief creep upon it, the wolf tear it, or the lion ravage it. For these are the Devil’s ministries: to consume through vices, to steal in through enticements, to tear apart through slanders, and to devastate with the whole force of his power. From all this evil, then, protection must be expected. Accordingly it follows:

> The Lord shall keep thy soul.

That none of so many evils may have power over it.

> The Lord shall keep thy going out and thy coming in, from this time forth and for ever.

For when, upon leaving the body, all the faithful are kept by the Lord’s protection for that entrance into the kingdom of heaven, they will meanwhile be placed in Abraham’s bosom, until the time comes for entering again into the kingdom of heaven. The Lord shall preserve the going out; He shall preserve the coming in. For He is the one who says: “I am the door,” and, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 10:7; 14:6). He is the Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever.

## PSALM 121 BEGINS. HAPPILY, A SONG OF ASCENTS.

> I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord.

Whoever is held by the hope of heavenly desire will find nothing obscure in this Psalm of the Spirit. For when he remembers that it is written that he is a co-heir, like the Angels, to be renewed by resurrection, and to become a dweller in the heavenly city built of living stones—of which Paul speaks: “Now you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the Saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the Apostles” (Eph. 2:19)—and when he reads that the things now partially announced were fashioned by Angels in the law, expounded by Prophets, and preached by Apostles, then he himself must necessarily cry out, following the example of the Prophet:

> I rejoiced at the things that were said to me.

But what are those things said in which joy was received? Surely that which follows:

> We shall go into the house of the Lord.

Therefore, because these things were said before, he rejoices and is glad that we are to go into the house of the Lord. What the house of the Lord is, he declares in another Psalm, saying: “For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has chosen her beforehand as a habitation for himself. This is my rest for ever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen her beforehand” (Ps. 131:13). Certainly not that earthly Jerusalem, which killed the Prophets and stoned them, but that free and heavenly Jerusalem. Lest anyone suppose that we go into that house in vain, he adds:

> Our feet stood in thy courts, O Jerusalem.

They announce no uncertainties; they promise no unknown things. We have recognized this house as desirable and beloved by many. For in another Psalm he says:

> One thing I have asked of God; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life. (Ps. 26:4)

This house is desirable: its foundation is composed of twelve living gems, and its stones are living stones, built and hewn. The first work of this building was in Moses through the law, in the Prophets through their sufferings, and in the Apostles through their martyrdoms. These are the builders; this is the city; here stand the feet of the Saints. The Apostles are the guardians of this house, to whom the keys were given, as it was said: “To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” This is Jerusalem, which is built as a city; for it is being built until the day of consummation, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters into it, whose participation is in itself. For whoever separates himself from the assembly of the Saints and from the body of the Church shall not have a share in this holy house. For the participation of this city is in itself; all who are of one mind shall be in it:

> The tribes, the tribes of the Lord, went up.

For there are those who are not the Lord’s, to whom it was said: “You are the children of the Devil.” The tribes that are the Lord’s, therefore, shall ascend: that is, those who, according to the testimony of God, enter the holy city.

> To confess, he says, his name.

But this confession is judgment. For judgment is exercised through those to whom it was said: “You shall sit upon twelve tribunals, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Not only these shall judge, but also the Queen of the South shall judge, and the Ninevites shall condemn, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah the Prophet, and because the Queen of the South, coming from the uttermost parts of the earth, heard Solomon’s wisdom. In that queen is a figure of the Church, which, though foreign and unknown, believed in repentance and desired to hear wisdom.

> For there sat seats for judgment, seats over the house of David.

For just as in other places the name of God is derived from the body, so here too Scripture calls God Himself David, taking his name from the parent of his flesh.

> Ask for the things that pertain to the peace of Jerusalem.

“Ask” is not a word of prayer but of inquiry: to learn peace belongs to the will of those who hear. For when they have asked about its peace, then they shall rejoice; then they shall be able confidently to say: “We shall go into the house of God.” Then follows: “Peace in thy strength, and abundance in thy towers.” The peace and strength of this house are mutually connected. But in every kind of city, nothing is either firmer, more useful, or more exalted than towers. Therefore, when peace in strength had been mentioned, he assigned the abundance of perfect blessedness to the princes of the peoples of this city, as to its strongest and weightiest towers, saying:

> And abundance in thy towers.

By this it is understood that this abundance is not promised indiscriminately to all, but only to the faithful and holy men who rise above others like the towers of buildings: namely, the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, and Martyrs. Of these the Lord says in the Gospel: “Father, I pray for these, that all may be one” (John 17:21). This is our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever.

## PSALM 124 BEGINS. HAPPILY, A SONG OF ASCENTS.

> Those who trust in the Lord are as Mount Zion: he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever; mountains are round about her, and the Lord round about his people.

For Mount Zion rises over the city of Jerusalem; and that city is situated so that several mountains are around it. Whoever trusts in the Lord, therefore, shall make such progress as to be like Mount Zion. For Jerusalem itself did not confer holiness upon its inhabitants, so that its dwelling might be established for ever. From it came sacrileges, the slaughter of Prophets, the judgment of death against God, the flight of the Apostles, and the scandal of the Cross. How often were those dwelling in it taken captive? How often killed? At last that very city was utterly destroyed. Thus Jerusalem was overthrown and its people were exterminated. Today it has neither priest, nor prophet, nor ruler. How then shall its dwelling not be moved for ever, and how shall the Lord be round about his people?

But since on this mountain there is no fruit of prophecy, Isaiah teaches what ought to be understood by the mountain, signifying the lofty mountain of the Lord to which the nations would come: “Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a splendid, chosen, precious cornerstone; and he who believes in him shall not be confounded” (Isa. 28:16). In this place he signifies Christ as the foundation; through him that blessed Church seems to be understood which the Apostle calls Jerusalem under another name, saying: “The Jerusalem which now is is in bondage with her children” (Gal. 4:25); but “the Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother.”

Therefore we have the Lord’s Mount Zion, and we have the city of God, Jerusalem; and the interpretation of the mountain’s name is “watching” or “contemplation.” Let us therefore follow the Apostle, follow the Gospel, follow the Prophets. Let us trust in the Lord, who has been called the mountain; let us dwell now in the Church, Jerusalem, which shall not be moved for ever.

> And the Lord is round about his people from this time forth and for ever.

In this place “round about his people” signifies the Gospel. For when the Lord said to Moses: “Behold, my Angel shall go before thee,” he replied: “Unless thou go with me, do not drive me out from here” (Exod. 32:34; 33:15). The protection of an Angel is indeed good, but that of the Lord is better. For our soul is assailed by many snares, and many weapons fight against us. Therefore, knowing that our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against the power of this world, the Lord says at the conclusion of the Gospels: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

> Who does not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands unto iniquity.

By the rod we should understand power. Moses received a rod by which he could perform signs; Aaron too had a rod; Pharaoh had a rod; Nebuchadnezzar had a rod. Therefore God guards us round about, lest the rod of sinners be left over our portion. Tribulations indeed come, but they do not remain; persecutions come, but they do not persist. For the rod of the sinner is not left over our lot, since the Lord is round about his people for ever. Then follows, concerning the recompense deserved from God by one who has kept his hands from every iniquity:

> Do good, O Lord, to the good and to those upright in heart.

For recompense is not lacking either for the good or for the evil, as follows:

> But those who turn aside unto crooked ways the Lord shall lead away with those who work iniquity.

For one who works iniquity is outside the law; one who turns aside from the law is a transgressor of the law. Our mind, therefore, must be kept apart from these, lest a person be led away with those who work iniquity. Whoever observes all these things as a peaceable person does not leave the rod of the sinner over himself, but remains in perfect faith for ever, and according to his merits shall hear it said to him:

> Peace be upon Israel.

For He is our peace, who made both one—our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever.

## PSALM 132 BEGINS.

> Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.

It is good and pleasant for brethren to dwell together in unity. When they dwell in unity, they are gathered in the assembly of the Church; when they are called brethren, they are united in harmony by the love of a single will. For we read that at the first preaching of the Apostles this great commandment was fulfilled, as it is said: “For the heart and soul of all who believed were one” (Acts 4:32). This, therefore, befits the people of God: to be brethren under one Father, to be one under one Spirit, to walk in harmony under one household, to be members of one body under one Body. It is pleasant and good for brethren to dwell together in unity. The Prophet establishes a comparison for this good and pleasant thing, saying:

> Like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which descends to the edge of his garment.

Aaron’s ointment was a compound of fragrances, by which he was anointed as priest. This consecration first pleased God for his priest. Our Lord too was invisibly anointed above his companions. This anointing is not earthly: He was not anointed from a horn, as kings were, but with the oil of gladness. Finally, after this anointing of Aaron . . . . .

[Col. 0009]

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE OF THE BENEDICTINE EDITION TO THE MOST EMINENT LORD LORD CÉSAR D’ESTRÉES, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH.

Among the chief patrons and supporters of our studies—indeed, of our whole Congregation—since we have long regarded you as foremost, MOST EMINENT LORD, no one should find it surprising that we dedicate and offer to Your Eminence the works of St Hilary, newly revised through our labours and, so far as lies within our power, elucidated, now once more issued to the public. For after so many honourable testimonies by which you have deigned to approve, before the Supreme Pontiffs, the Sacred College, and the whole Roman Curia, not only our entire body, but also the labours of certain of our brethren—both in revising the writings of the holy Fathers and in bringing to light the monuments of venerable antiquity—it would certainly have been wrong for so inclined a benevolence and kindness toward us to be deprived of the acknowledgement due from grateful hearts. To prevent this, as justice opposed it, nothing could have occurred to us more fitting or more suitable than this new edition of the works of the great Hilary, which, if it shall not prove unworthy in the eyes of present and future generations, will render that beneficence immortal.

Nor indeed, as we hope, will you refuse so good and suitable a surety on our behalf, MOST EMINENT LORD—one who is not unequal to payment and who will be a debtor neither troublesome nor ungrateful, such as you certainly might have wished for. For if you seek distinction of lineage, he himself was an eminent glory of the illustrious house of Estrées. As we learn from Fortunatus, he was not obscure among Gallic families in the radiance of nobility (Fortunatus, book I, *Life of St Hilary*; Jerome, preface to book II of the *Commentary on Galatians*). If you love sincerity and generosity of heart, which are gifts of your own spirit, he too was adorned with the grace of nobility and the brilliance of heart. But perhaps, most eloquent man, you further desire eloquence: Jerome calls him the Rhône of eloquence. Does freedom of speech please you, such as you have frequently displayed in those Roman assemblies? No one was freer or more steadfast than Hilary in speech, as even the Emperor Constantius testified. Finally, if you approve ardent love for the Catholic faith—as you certainly show that you do by what you recently accomplished with your most eminent colleagues, to expose and crush at its very birth a wicked heresy—Hilary was a pillar of religion, supporting the wavering Church. Through his benefit Gaul had no monsters, having been freed by him from the peril of heresy. He traversed the world infected by the evil of unbelief, in order to recall all persons to amendment and repentance. Hence, at the Council of Seleucia, he was asked what the faith of the Gauls was, and there he was brought forth as a spectacle to the world.

But you too, repeatedly brought forth upon the theatre of Europe, have defended the faith of the Gallican Church and the rights of the kingdom: first in those public disputations by which you prepared yourself for the doctoral laurel, which, after publishing a remarkable demonstration of learning, you attained amid universal applause before completing your twenty-first year; then in various proceedings you have asserted them with such zeal, success, and skill that no unexpected occasion ever found you unprepared, nor any matter, however difficult and arduous, made you disturbed or anxious.

Moreover, with what reverence will you regard the great Prelate of the Gallican Church, the vigilant and indefatigable watchman of the house of God, when you yourself, placed at the head of the Church of Laon by the king’s nomination—regard being had more to your merits than to your years—have shown, by your continual visitation of parishes, your diligence in conducting ordinations, and your frequent administration to your people of the sacrament of confirmation, in which you have marked with holy anointing an almost incredible number of persons to whom the age and infirmity of your predecessor had denied this benefit; by ordering throughout the whole diocese recurring conferences at fixed times concerning ecclesiastical practice and doctrine; by recalling the clergy to stricter discipline; by erecting from its foundations a seminary; by founding, for the use of needy persons of both sexes, children, old people, and the infirm, a hospital for the city and the entire diocese; and by your admonitions, exhortations, and edicts—what becomes ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, whom the Holy Spirit has appointed bishops to govern the Church of God?

And when summoned to Rome and enrolled in the sacred college of Cardinals, you had sustained the affairs of Church and kingdom for many years; lest so many right institutions in the diocese of Laon should be worn away by your prolonged absence, with the king’s consent you chose from your own family a successor who could not only preserve but complete what you had so excellently accomplished and established—a participant in your counsels and not merely your follower, but your rival in good works. In this matter divine goodness neither abandoned you nor did the outcome disappoint you. Moreover, when controversies which had arisen had invaded very many dioceses of Gaul and the bishops themselves seemed likely to be drawn into opposing parties, you, free from party spirit and a lover of truth and submission, provided for the Church of Laon with such fairness and prudence that it always remained peaceful, free, and secure from these storms. Nor did you devote yourself only to the tranquillity of your private church. When means were being considered for settling so great a matter and calming the contentions that might have broken into open discord, summoned by the king, acceptable to the Pope, suspected by no one—who does not know how nobly and successfully you laboured to restore peace to the Gallican Church, a peace which still flourishes and has struck such deep roots that we hope it will always live and endure?

And what wonder is it that you administer with such ease the greatest affairs entrusted to your fidelity, when, while still almost a boy, you were trained for more difficult business by the words and examples of your most illustrious father as he vigorously conducted the affairs of Gaul in the Roman embassy? Indeed, your descent from a most eminent family, renowned for the offices of peace and war, and your education in the city of Rome, foretold that you were born both for the purple and for every great undertaking.

That this omen was not vain is attested by the various embassies which you conducted in Germany, Portugal, and Italy, but especially in the city of Rome itself. You discharged these with such diligence when acting alone that you were never lacking for any business; and with such conscientiousness and charity when acting with others that, through any rivalry for praise, you did not deviate even a nail’s breadth from diligent performance of duty. But what is especially praiseworthy in an ecclesiastical man is that, although immersed in the weightiest affairs, you retained with no less zeal as you advanced in years the love for letters and learned men which you had conceived in youth; and as you never neglected the former, so you have always embraced the latter with singular benevolence.

What shall I say of the royal alliances which, while serving the interests of the kingdom, you joined to the house of Estrées, long adorned with so many titles? Yet, to crown your praises, the gracious, vigorous, and steadfast patronage bestowed by the greatest of all kings to obtain the purple for you is sufficient. You confirmed his judgment of you—so lofty and honourable that it was not inferior to the purple itself—by a notable example of fidelity and submission, when with equal constancy you refused the dignity offered upon a condition which seemed less consonant with the royal commands. We do not speak of unknown things. Distinguished witnesses of so splendid an act still live, and its memory shall always flourish among posterity. We do not wonder, therefore, that the glory of your deeds follows you everywhere. May it reach posterity in such a way that it is inscribed in that eternal remembrance in which nothing is lost; just as Hilary’s fame, not contained within the bounds of Gaul, filled foreign nations also, indeed even heaven itself, as the merit of his works spread abroad and made the glory of the most holy Pontiff illustrious in both worlds.

As we conclude with these wishes, we have regard for your modesty, MOST EMINENT PRINCE OF THE CHURCH, which neither permits itself to be burdened with excessive praises nor permits you to be compared with the great Hilary. In him, indeed, you behold many things worthy of imitation—rather, of admiration: fearless zeal for Catholic truth and for justice; powerful apologies for religion; long exile; and other illustrious deeds which won for him the glorious title of Confessor of Christ. You rightly judge that this one title is more illustrious than any panegyrics whatever.

As we entrust the works of so great a Doctor and Pontiff to your patronage, MOST EMINENT MAN, we seek from you protection not for Hilary himself, but for ourselves and our studies. Since you have granted it before, though we were undeserving, you will not, as we may hope from your kindness, deny it in the future, with Hilary pleading for us. We, for our part, shall render you immortal thanks because you permit yourself to be so easily entreated; and singular thanks to Hilary, through whose benefit it has come about that we are not ungrateful. This edition of his works shall be a perpetual monument of our respect toward you, and indeed of our grateful heart. Thus vow

To Your Eminence,

Your most devoted and most obedient

Monks of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur.

[Col. 0011]

## GENERAL PREFACE.

To love the Church sincerely and not cherish with the highest reverence Hilary, her illustrious defender, is very difficult. While he lived, I know not what marks of dignity together with kindness he displayed, such that, although he was the leader of Catholics and the terror of heretics, he won from both not admiration only but reverence. Some indeed attacked him by deceit, but no one ever dared resist him openly. Torn away from the West by their stratagems, he seemed not so much taken from that region as given to the East, so that no region of the world might fail to enjoy his light. For then the churches of the West did not cease to seek his counsel in order to be governed by his wisdom, and the bishops of the East gradually grew accustomed to obey him.

Consequently, the dark heresy which held sway in those regions, unable any longer to endure the arrival of so great a star, and foreseeing that it must either yield to him or drive Hilary from those territories, restored him to Gaul with new splendour, though it thought it could extinguish his light. What a blameless man—against whom his adversaries, skilled in the art of calumny, were then unable to devise any charge by which to destroy him! The sole charge brought against him was a happy one: that heresy, while he was present, was allowed to enjoy no peace and undertake nothing. Indeed, at his return, whatever it had previously attempted in Italy, Illyricum, and Gaul came to nothing; and it was agreed by all that our Gauls in particular had been freed from the stain of heresy through the benefit of Hilary alone. (Sulpicius Severus, book II, *Sacred History*.)

2. Whoever carefully considers these and the other deeds of that most valiant confessor will readily agree that he was given to the Church so that the gates of hell might not prevail against her; nor will he deny that his teaching deserves to be received with the highest veneration by Catholics, since he was so formidable to heretics. And so, that everyone might apply himself to it more conveniently and profitably, we have not declined to direct to the revision of his writings our modest work, which some have declared worthy of their favour and approval in editions of other Fathers. Certainly we acknowledge that we owe him this service on many grounds.

For while we venerate him with all the children of the Church as a father and teacher, and especially embrace him with the Gauls as the glory and ornament of our Gauls, he ought yet to be especially dear to us because he laid the first foundations of monasteries in Gaul. Finally, if we consider not our own interest but that of the Church, who can deny that it matters so much the more for her to possess Hilary’s writings pure and uncorrupted, because they carry greater authority for establishing her faith? For while the Church derives her faith from Christ and the Apostles, those witnesses are weightier in proportion as they are nearer to apostolic times. There are not many Latin Fathers to enumerate who preceded Hilary in age. For after Tertullian, Lactantius, and Cyprian, scarcely one writer of any standing can be found more ancient than he. Yet he has almost as many heralds as God has given us Doctors of the faith after him.

3. First, by the whole Council of Paris he was called a “faithful preacher of the name of the Lord”; shortly afterwards Augustine described him as “the Catholic Church’s most vigorous defender against heretics,” “a Catholic and distinguished doctor of the Catholic Church,” and “a man of no slight authority in the treatment of the Scriptures and in the defence of the faith” (Augustine, *Against Julian*, I.3; II.7; and *On the Trinity*, VI.10). Then Cassian praised him (Book VII, *On the Incarnation*, ch. 2; Book X, ch. 5; and Book I, ch. 4) as “Master of the Churches,” and Facundus of Hermiane now as the Arians’ most powerful and strenuous assailant, now as a most learned bishop and a most courageous confessor. Yet all other encomia are surpassed by that in which the same Facundus (*Against Mocianus*) calls him a wise and moderate governor of the Church: as though he had undertaken, and wisely steered, the helm not of one Church but of the whole Church.

But among Jerome, to pass over the rest, how great was his authority? Jerome thinks himself sufficiently cleared once he has shown that Hilary’s example guided him: “If this is a crime,” he says in Epistle 75, “let the confessor Hilary also be accused”; and in Epistle 62: “I did not do this alone, but the confessor Hilary did so too.” Finally, in Epistle 101, although he had examples of many men by which to defend himself, he offered this one alone: “For the present it is enough to have named Hilary the confessor.”

4. Even the Greeks, though exceedingly sparing in their praise of Latins, nevertheless did not refrain from praising him. Socrates, III.10; Sozomen, III.14 and 15, and V.13; and Nicephorus Callistus, X.17, commend him highly both for holiness of life and for excellence in learning and eloquence. Theodoret, *Dialogue* 2, and Ephraem of Theopolis in Photius, p. 807—where he is falsely called bishop of Gabala—also support their own statements by his testimonies. Indeed, the Council of Chalcedon not only, in Act I, p. 310, and Act II, p. 340, reckons him among those from whose teaching its decree concerning the mystery of the Incarnation ought to be expounded; but also, in Act II, p. 357, places first the extracts taken from his writings. Let us now see what has been accomplished in their various editions.

## I. On the Various Editions of the Works of St Hilary

5. From Robert Fortunatus of Saint-Malo’s preface to the edition of Badius, we learn that the books *On the Trinity*, *To Constantius*, *Against Constantius*, *Against Auxentius*, and *On the Synods* first came to light through the efforts of the priest George Cribellus; then that the Commentaries explaining the Psalms were rescued from neglect and squalor by John Solidus of Cracow, at the urging of Jacques Lefèvre of Étaples; and finally that, in 1510, Badius Ascensius, having received from Guillaume Petit, confessor to the king, the *Treatise on Matthew* together with the Letter to Abra, recovered from the monastery of St Benignus at Dijon, committed them to his press at Paris and published them together with the aforementioned works of Hilary. It would have been desirable for this edition to emerge not only free from spurious works, but also corrected of its innumerable errors.

6. Thirteen years later Erasmus applied himself chiefly to correcting the books *On the Trinity*. He generally either entirely neglected the other treatises or, owing to the scarcity of old manuscripts, was unable to correct them. Yet he would have earned praise by his labour had he refrained from his declamatory preface, which rightly appeared worthy of censure both to the Roman Sacred Inquisition and to the Faculty of Theology at Paris.

> [Note: Col. 0014D: It is listed among books marked for censure from 1544 to 1556.]

For in that preface, to use Gillot’s words, “through utterly vain and insulting digressions, which he wraps in flattering excuses,” Erasmus interprets many of Hilary’s words and deeds in an unfavourable sense, so that he seems to have wished to make a reputation for himself through an excessively free licence in criticizing the holy man. At one moment he excuses the Arians in order to attack the devout bishop more sharply; at another he attributes to vice what breathes virtue in him. Where Hilary strives to demonstrate his supreme moderation from the fact that throughout the whole period of his exile he wrote and said nothing inflammatory against the Arian party, Erasmus even invents as the cause of so prolonged a silence that, amid such a great conflict of the world, Hilary’s mind was somewhat uncertain as to what the true faith was (*On the Trinity*, VI.21). As though a man could be thought to have doubted the faith in the slightest degree when he both declared that he could die together with it in defending it, and that he could by no means be torn away from it, and most evidently demonstrated that he spoke truly through so long and protracted an exile and through many other splendid actions.

And what of this: although Hilary testifies that Christ’s cause alone moved him to break silence (*To Constantius*, 2 and 3), Erasmus maintains that this was done through impatience with exile? By these and other things he showed that he had never sufficiently understood the mind of this most courageous confessor, and that he handled his works hastily—works in which Hilary everywhere vividly recorded the fearless constancy of his faith. Hence Erasmus’s selection of readings was insufficiently careful and often even negligent. Hence his premature and usually false judgments concerning our Doctor’s writings, teaching, actions, and character. We willingly excuse the errors of a man occupied with many matters; indeed, we should ourselves have passed them over in silence, had not certain opinions insulting to Hilary thereby sunk deeply into the minds of many. Yet no one can readily excuse him for having been so facile and rash in delivering judgment on matters of the greatest importance. For who would not condemn him for applying to Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, everything Jerome wrote against Hilary, the Luciferian deacon, although Erasmus later admits that he is uncertain whether Jerome’s statements ought to be understood as directed against Hilary himself? For, to pass over the fact that the understanding of this matter was not especially obscure, a suspicion of obstinate heresy ought by no means to have been cast, on an uncertain basis, upon a Catholic Doctor and defender of the Church.

Froben printed this edition of Erasmus at Basel in 1523; there it was reprinted in 1535, with the pseudo-treatise *On the Unity of the Father and the Son* added.

7. Louis de Miraeus greatly praised Erasmus’s labour, but surpassed him in diligence. For, after carefully collating manuscript copies, he recorded with no less care everything he found in them differing from the Froben edition. He testifies that he consulted many manuscripts of remarkable antiquity, calling some of them Victorine; these, certainly, are far surpassed by many others in the claim of antiquity. From the same library of St Victor he brought forth the book *On the Essence of the Father and the Son*, two letters to Augustine, and the *Verse on Genesis*. These he arranged to be printed at Paris in 1544, by the widow Charlotte Guillard, together with Hilary’s genuine works.

8. Although in our judgment Miraeus’s edition is more corrected than all those published before and after it, it is nevertheless so rare that, after examining many Parisian libraries, we had already despaired of discovering it when we came upon it in the great convent of the Carmelites. Yet this edition was neglected, indeed not even mentioned; and Hilary’s works, as Erasmus had produced them, were published a third time at Basel by Froben in 1550, most diligently collated and revised from several copies by Dr Martin Lipsius. Lipsius’s vigilance in removing typographical errors cannot be denied; but in seeking out and examining manuscripts he seems to have exercised far less care than in devising conjectures, in which he was not always—indeed, rarely—successful.

9. Until then no one had thought to prefix a life of Hilary to his works. John Jacob Grinaeus was the first to undertake this task, and in 1570 gave it to Eusebius Episcopius of Basel to be printed at the front of the holy Doctor’s writings. But how meagre, dry, incomplete, and false is his account! He scarcely ever assigns dates correctly, omits many of Hilary’s deeds, imports falsehoods from elsewhere, and, to please the rising heresy, adds several exceedingly childish fables. This life was chiefly compiled from what Jerome wrote in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians* against Hilary the deacon, who would not receive the baptism of heretics. Grinaeus indeed noticed that it might be objected to him that Jerome there marks out a Hilary who had served as a deacon and never reached the episcopate; but he has a brief and ready answer: an error has crept into Jerome’s books.

No less significant is his assertion in the same Life that there were some members of St Hilary’s college—those whom they call canons—who said that they were permitted, by Hilary’s institution, to contract honourable marriage, because he had written no law of celibacy for his own. Hear the amusing proof of so grave an assertion: “as the most illustrious man, Gaspar Hervagius, a most learned doctor of both laws and my friend, told me.” We shall refrain from refuting such absurdities and recounting others.

10. As soon as Gillot read such a Life and Erasmus’s preface attached to it, he judged both works, as insulting to the most holy bishop and very harmful to Catholic piety, to be rejected by Christian readers. Having attained his better wish, he substituted a dissertation in which he first presents material bearing on Hilary’s history, collected from Hilary’s own writings and those of other ancient authors; then discusses his style and writings; and finally notes suspicious passages and interprets them as favourably as possible. It was a work refined and worthy of praise for its age, although very much in it may somewhat offend those accustomed to history now more polished and exact.

To this dissertation he added several encomia of Hilary, a Life by Jerome from the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, accounts by Fortunatus and Gregory of Tours, and Peter Damian’s sermon on the translation of St Hilary. But he suppressed the books *On the Essence* and *On the Unity of the Father and the Son*, having merely noted the centos from which they consist. Finally, he demonstrated his diligence in identifying most passages of Scripture; but he left Hilary’s text wholly untouched, and not a few errors entered into it through the carelessness of Nivelle, who produced this edition in 1572 in elegant type but with a less careful hand.

11. At last, that the purer and clearer streams of this Rhône of Latin eloquence might flow, the Parisian printers turned their attention to the matter in 1605. Let us now hear what they accomplished in it.

“First,” they say, “we took care that Hilary’s works should be collated with the best manuscript codices by the man accustomed to prepare books for the press and see them printed. These were kindly and generously supplied from their very rich libraries by men most illustrious and learned: Nicholas Faber for the books *On the Trinity*, Jacques Bongars for the Treatises on the Psalms, and Paul Petau, councillor of Paris, for revising the Commentaries on Matthew. Then, since a certain most learned man had not denied us his labour in writing various readings in the margin, so that, after selecting those which seemed preferable to the readings already received, he might strike out the others, it seemed proper to obtain from another man also that he should collect at the end of the book those readings tolerated in earlier editions, lest you perhaps should desire these too—either because some testimonies cited elsewhere might occur in their wording, or because you might wish to consider by your own judgment whether they should be set aside in favour of these new readings. Moreover, we added the Fragments from the historical work which P. Pithou, a distinguished man, published in 1598 through the labour of Nicolas Faber at Ambroise Drouart’s press, and the Treatises on Psalms 13, 14, 149, and 150 copied from the same manuscripts.”

12. Yet, after the labours expended by so many and such diverse persons upon this edition, the writings of that most eloquent Doctor did not emerge much purer. For the man who applied his labour to selecting variant readings, whether his judgment was not particularly refined or whether, as often happens in work done under another’s name, he performed the task perfunctorily, very often altered what should have been retained and, conversely, retained what should have been altered. Hence the person who, in the edition of 1631, placed in their proper locations and entered in the margin the variant readings that had first been relegated to the end, more than once restored readings which had prevailed in earlier editions.

The Parisian printers too, who borrowed from elsewhere what did not belong to their craft, so neglected what did belong to their diligence that, because of the multitude of errors, the Basel editions seem easily preferable to theirs. That edition was reprinted at Cologne in 1617, and again at Paris in 1631 and 1652.

13. Even from this simple account it is clear that nothing ever accomplished in publishing Hilary’s writings was complete in every respect. Badius’s edition abounds in countless errors. Erasmus scarcely revised any works other than the books *On the Trinity* against manuscript authority, and even those he corrected without much critical examination. Miraeus was more diligent, but had neither a large number of manuscripts nor manuscripts for all Hilary’s treatises, and placed rather too much trust in his predecessor’s ingenuity and conjectures. Then Martin Lipsius, while devising new readings from his own resources, corrupts individual books of Hilary in more places than he corrects. Yet those who assisted the Parisian printers followed him most closely; after them no one undertook further polishing of the same works.

## II. On Manuscript Codices

14. Not only from the time when the art of printing was invented, but also in earlier centuries, there were repeatedly men who showed their diligence in revising Hilary’s works. Yet because of his more recondite meanings, these men sometimes substituted readings of their own, adding clearer wording to obscure words which they did not sufficiently understand; and these additions subsequently tended alone to prevail in later copies. An example is supplied by the codex formerly of Fleury, now manuscript 1194 in the Colbert Library, copied about seven hundred years ago from a very ancient manuscript of the church of Chartres. In it are seen only those readings which were added in a second revision to the Chartres manuscript, although the first readings are generally better.

The activity of revisers appears even more clearly in the copy formerly at Aachen, later at Corbie, and now in the Library of Saint-Germain. Since several copies were later made from it, the earlier readings were everywhere set aside—indeed, they gave way to the later ones. Therefore Hilary’s writings could not be faithfully reproduced from one or two codices, especially if they were comparatively recent.

15. No manuscript seems likely to be older than that preserved in the archive of the Vatican church. For, to transcribe here the words of our Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, plate 6:

> “The codex was written, if one excepts the first leaves in a later hand, at the end of the fourth century or the beginning of the fifth, as is understood from an inscription added at the end of the book *To Constantius*, by a certain student, which I render thus: ‘I collated [it], in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, while staying at Kasulis, in the fourteenth year of King Thrasamund.’ The man who arranged the catalogue of the aforesaid archive read, instead of *aput Kasulis*, ‘Putzalis’: ‘This,’ he says, ‘is in Africa, in the region of Numidia or Barbary; it is commonly called Putrazzio and is situated between Tunis and the fortress of Goletta.’ If I understand the characters of the codex correctly, I do not doubt that it should be read *apud Kasulis*, a city of the province of Byzacena, called Antonio Casula; whose bishop Quintianus is read in the *Notitia of Africa* as ‘Quintianus of Casulis-Carianum.’ For the interchange of *d* and *t* is easy, as in the words *haut*, *set*, and others of that kind which occur not infrequently in manuscripts. Holstenius wrote in his own hand in the margin of this note that the fourteenth year of Thrasamund’s reign corresponds to A.D. 510.”

Thus far Mabillon. But it cannot be denied that this ancient codex contains ancient errors, which recall what Jerome warns Lucinius in Epistle 28:

> “I gave my little works to your men to copy, and I saw them copied into paper codices; and I repeatedly warned them to collate and correct them more carefully. For I was unable to reread so many volumes because of the constant crowds of visitors and travellers. Therefore, if you find corrupt readings or passages copied imperfectly which impede the reader’s understanding, you must not attribute this to me, but to your men and to the inexperience of copyists and the negligence of scribes. They write not what they find, but what they understand; and while they strive to correct other men’s errors, they display their own.”

For this reason we attribute nothing rashly to the antiquity of this codex, granting it only this reverence: that we carefully noted almost all readings in which it differs from the others. Our brethren living at Rome copied these readings for us from a collection made by Giovanni Battista Bendini, canon of St Peter’s Basilica, when he was preparing a new edition of Hilary; and, by carefully revising several works themselves, they confirmed the diligence of the praised canon.

16. Second in antiquity after the codex of St Peter, but easily first in integrity, is manuscript 825, formerly of the abbey of St Denis near Paris and now in the Colbert Library. Stephen Baluze, keeper of the same library, whom no praise could sufficiently equal for his kindness, most generously supplied it to us with many others. Although this codex is not free of errors such as often befall unskilled copyists, it has none which one might suspect to have been introduced by shallow pedants.

This is noteworthy in the manuscript: although Hilary’s name is placed at the end of each book, it nowhere occurs except bare and deprived of every honorific title—for example, “The first book of Hilary ends”; “The second book of Hilary ends”—and never “saint.” Yet he is designated by that title both by Jerome, Augustine, and others, and in the aforementioned manuscript of the Vatican basilica. This proves that it was copied with the greatest fidelity either from Hilary’s own autograph or from another copy written while Hilary was still alive.

17. It would be long, and perhaps superfluous, to discuss the remaining manuscripts individually. This at least may be asserted: we left nothing undone to obtain more and better manuscripts, and spared neither labour nor time in deciding what should prevail in them and in the printed editions. Concerning the books *On the Trinity*, the distinguished codex of the church of St Martin at Tours, copied about a thousand years ago, confirmed that there seemed to be nothing more for us to desire. For when its variant readings were sent after those books had been prepared and corrected, though not yet sent to press, not one reading was found preferable to those already printed which we had not already restored from other manuscripts.

18. Germans, Britons, and Italians testify to the zeal with which we sought manuscript copies everywhere; through their assistance we examined the libraries of those foreign regions. We considered this necessary, not only so that we might restore Hilary’s published writings to their original integrity, but also so that we might bring forth from hiding places works not yet published. For it is entirely certain that many lie hidden.

That he expounded, if not all the Psalms, certainly far more than those for which treatises survive, will be demonstrated by the special preface to the same treatises. Cassian and Alcuin besides praise his preface to the Commentary on Matthew. Jerome, moreover, in his list of Hilary’s works, records a book addressed to the prefect Sallustius, or *Against Dioscorus*; a book of hymns; another on mysteries; a book *Against Ursacius and Valens*; treatises on Job, which he translated freely from Origen’s Greek; letters to various persons; and, as he had heard from some, books on the Song of Songs. Of the books *Against Ursacius and Valens* only a fragment survives; of the rest, nothing or almost nothing. Yet it will be useful to make some observations on each, so that anyone may be able either to recognize works offered to him or reject works falsely masked under Hilary’s name.

## III. On Hilary’s Lost Works

19. Jerome, Epistle 84 to Magnus, explains what sort of book Hilary’s work to Sallustius was, and what Dioscorus’s position was, in these words:

> “In the short book which he wrote against Dioscorus the physician, he showed what he could accomplish in literature.”

If you add to this what Theodoret relates of Sallustius in *Ecclesiastical History*, III.11—that although a pagan, he nevertheless, so far as lay in his power, deterred Julian from torturing Christians, and finally persuaded him by skill and ingenuity of what he had at first been unable to accomplish by words—you will readily agree that this book ought not to be titled *Against Sallustius*, as in the printed Jerome, but, as in the Corbie manuscript written in Merovingian letters, *To Sallustius*. Hilary would have fled for protection to Sallustius, a man naturally gentle and humane, against the wickedness of Dioscorus, who perhaps carried out Julian’s commands more cruelly and eagerly. From this it also follows that the same short work was written while Julian held power.

20. The Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 13, briefly indicates what subject his Hymns treated:

> “It is known that certain hymns were composed by human effort in praise of God and of the triumphs of the Apostles and Martyrs, such as those which the most blessed doctors Hilary and Ambrose published.”

Jerome, in the preface to Book II of his Commentary on Galatians, gives only this indication about them: that Hilary, the Rhône of Latin eloquence, himself a Gaul and born at Poitiers, calls the Gauls “unteachable” in a hymn. But when Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, I.6, gives him this praise, that he was the first to become illustrious in hymn-writing, he must be understood to be referring only to the Latins. For long before Hilary those ascetics of whom Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, II.17, reports the following from Philo, had been distinguished in this genre:

> “They not only devote themselves to contemplation, but also compose songs and hymns in praise of God, in every kind of metre and melody.”

The famous *Thalia* of Arius also testifies that hymn-singing had been customary among the Arians from their very beginning. In it Athanasius, *Oration against the Arians* I, p. 310, records that Arius inserted his perverse inventions. The disciples imitated their master, singing alternately hymns fitted to their heresy. When, under the Emperor Arcadius, relying on the influence of Gainas, they did this publicly and with complete licence, Chrysostom feared that some of the simpler people might be drawn away from the Church by such songs. He therefore set against them certain members of the Catholic people, who surpassed the Arians’ activity by singing hymns with greater splendour and display.

If the words of Socrates and Sozomen, from whom we have received these matters (Socrates, VI.8; Sozomen, VIII.8), are considered, one may easily conclude that the custom of public supplications or processions, used on feast days and Sundays, arose from this. Nevertheless Ambrose calls such a rite already ancient in what is now Epistle 40 to Theodosius, §16, where he recounts that Valentinian had forbidden monks to take the route by which, according to a very old custom, they proceeded singing psalms to the celebration of the Maccabean martyrs.

Having noted these matters in passing, let us return to Hilary. Perhaps he too, while banished among the Arians, judged the use of hymns—by which they abused them to insinuate their heresy—most suitable for instilling and fostering true faith and piety in the minds of believers, and thus applied himself to writing hymns.

21. It is highly probable that at least some of them were adopted into ecclesiastical offices. Erasmus conjectures that the hymns concerning St John the Baptist and the Cross are Hilary’s; but he provides no proof for this conjecture, and it is established that the hymns on the Cross are specifically Fortunatus’s. Alcuin as commonly printed, *On the Divine Offices*, 40; Remigius of Auxerre, I, *On the Celebration of the Mass*; Hugh of St Victor, *On the Sacraments*, II.9.9; and Honorius of Autun, *The Jewel of the Soul*, I.87, state that he enlarged and completed the hymn *Gloria in excelsis*. Innocent III, *On the Mysteries of the Mass*, II.20, admits that many think so, although he himself assigns this *Gloria* to Telesphorus.

Indeed, Anastasius the Librarian in Telesphorus’s Life, Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, 22, Amalarius Fortunatus, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, III.8, and Alcuin as commonly printed, *On the Divine Offices*, 39, wrote that Pope Telesphorus instituted the singing of the angelic hymn in the Mass. But these testimonies can easily be reconciled with the preceding ones by saying that Telesphorus instituted the singing in the Mass of the angels’ words—as in fact they are spoken three times in the Liturgy of St James—but that Hilary authored the remainder.

Nor does anything establish the contrary opinion from the book *On Virginity* attributed to Athanasius, in which this hymn is mentioned entire, or from Book VII, chapter 47, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, where it is fully set out. For it is established that the latter was enlarged later by several additions, while it is by no means certain that the former is Athanasius’s. Yet neither is there authority sufficiently ancient for us to attribute to Hilary the hymn which the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 13, states indefinitely to have been composed by ecclesiastical authors. The Rule of St Caesarius of Arles, chapter 21, mentions the hymn itself, but not its author.

22. No less diverse are opinions concerning the author of the hymn *Te Deum*. The person who supposed that it had been composed by some disciple of our holy father Benedict, because his Rule, chapter 9, orders that it be sung every Sunday, is refuted by the Rule of Caesarius, Benedict’s contemporary and indeed somewhat earlier, in which the same hymn is mentioned in chapter 21. The popular opinion which makes Ambrose and Augustine its authors rests solely on the pseudo-Chronicle of Dacius, I.10. We have seen the hymn in a manuscript written four hundred years ago assigned to Ambrose alone; Smaragdus supports this in his commentary on Benedict’s Rule, chapter 11, where he calls it the Ambrosian hymn.

But Abbo of Fleury, in an epistle preserved in the Pithou manuscript in which he explains certain grammatical rules, treats it as a known and established fact that our Hilary was its author. “In the *palinodia* [recantation-song] to God,” he says, “which Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, composed, one should read not *suscepisti* [‘you undertook’], according to the error of certain ignorant persons, but rather *suscepturus* [‘being about to undertake’]: *Tu ad liberandum suscepturus hominem*, etc. [‘You, being about to undertake the liberation of humankind,’ etc.].”

23. Of the Book of Mysteries nothing remains to us except the title indicated by Jerome. Yet what we said concerning the hymns may equally be conjectured concerning this book: that it became incorporated into ecclesiastical offices. For it happens that, as the solemnities of ecclesiastical offices increase day by day, they cannot long retain the name of the person by whom they were arranged; rather, they become the property of the Churches which, according to times and places, arrange, regulate, and complete each item through their own members. A famous example is provided by Gregory’s Sacramentary, which individual churches adapted to their own uses in such a way that you will scarcely find one copy which you can wholly attribute to Gregory.

24. The words of Sulpicius Severus imply that Hilary’s letters had been collected into a single volume. In Book II, after testifying that Hosius fell when more than a hundred years old, he adds: “as St Hilary relates in his letters.” Some traces still remain in Hilary’s works from which one may discover when, to whom, and on what matters he wrote.

Anyone who grants that he was the author of the decree issued in 355, by which, as he declares in *To Constantius*, §2, he separated himself with the Gallican bishops from communion with Saturninus, Ursacius, and Valens, will not deny that he immediately communicated this decree to the holy confessors, whose authority he had left it to confirm. More explicitly, in *On the Synods*, §4, he recalls that from the time when he was driven into exile he sent many letters from various cities of the Roman provinces, informing the Westerners of the condition of the Eastern churches and of the progress of the Arian heresy. As the Council of Paris, Fragment II, §4, testifies, at the beginning of 360 he notified the same persons of how the Easterners had behaved after returning to Constantinople with the legates from Rimini.

From such information as this one may rightly conclude that he wrote to Catholics as often as anything occurred which he judged it important for the Church to know. For most of Hilary’s letters are Catholic letters, addressed to Catholics and to whole churches, not to private persons. His works both *On the Synods and the Faith of the Easterners*, *Against Constantius*, and *Against Auxentius* have indeed been called books; properly speaking, however, they are letters sent to churches. Thus, although he says that he wrote from various parts of the Roman provinces, one hears the name of no bishop to whom he privately sent letters. The whole Council of Paris, not an individual bishop, writes back that he had informed it of what was being done with the Easterners.

Nevertheless, it must not be denied, as we heard above from Jerome, that he also wrote to various individuals. And certainly it is probable that the Apology attached to the book *On the Synods*, now for the first time brought forth from manuscripts, was sent with a letter to Lucifer of Cagliari—unless the discourse addressed once and again to Lucifer is figurative in that work.

25. More celebrated than all these works are the treatises on Job, so often commended by the testimonies of Augustine and Jerome. We sought them with the greater desire because their genuineness can more easily be judged even from Augustine’s passage, *Against Julian*, II.8. From this one criterion is refuted the opinion, reported by Possevino in the *Sacred Apparatus* under “Hilary,” of those who doubted whether the three books on Job published under Origen’s name, with a preface beginning *Peritorum mos est medicorum* (“It is the custom of skilled physicians”), were Hilary’s.

For although in a manuscript of the monastery of Padolirone they are titled “books which Bishop Hilary translated from Greek into Latin,” the words cited by Augustine from Hilary’s Treatises on Job do not occur in them. Nor do these books, as Mabillon warned in his *Italian Journey*, p. 208, bear the flavour of so great a Doctor’s style or genius. Still less do they agree with his faith. The illustrious Daniel Huet, in the Appendix to Book III of the *Origeniana*, §2, proves that their author adhered to Arius from the fact that in them *homoousion* is rejected and Lucian is celebrated with praises—the Lucian whose disciples the first Arians gloried in calling themselves. Thus Arius himself, writing to Eusebius of Nicomedia in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, I.5, calls him a Collucianist.

Perhaps Licinianus also—called by Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, bishop of Carthagena in Spain—had been deceived by the false title when he wrote to Pope Gregory (*Spicilegium*, VII, p. 369): “We certainly possess six little books of St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, which he translated from Origen’s Greek into Latin. But he did not explain everything in the book of holy Job in order.” For Jerome nowhere mentions Hilary’s “little books on Job,” but in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* speaks of “Treatises on Job,” while in the *Apology against Rufinus*, Epistle 101 to Pammachius, and elsewhere he speaks of “homilies on Job”; Augustine too cites them under that name in *Against Julian*.

A further reason for doubting the genuineness of the little books which Licinianus possessed presents itself; but we shall consider it more conveniently below. This work of Hilary may be assigned to his exile. For the treatment of this book was especially suited to an exile, since in it God set before us a most rare example of patience.

26. Another work of Hilary is noted in the printed text of Jerome’s Epistle 50 to Pammachius. After listing Fathers who treated the odd number, it adds: “Of these, Hilary, discoursing on the number seven—that is, the odd number—said what things, and how great things, is attested by his book *To Fortunatus*.” There is no doubt that Jerome here indicates Cyprian’s book *To Fortunatus, On Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 11. For this reason Marianus thinks it must absolutely be assigned to Hilary, but in vain. For not only is that book’s style far more consonant with Cyprian’s genius than with Hilary’s, but when several manuscripts of the best quality were examined at the cited passage of Jerome, not one had “of these, Hilary”; all, with great agreement, had “of these, Cyprian.” As for Marianus’s assertion that Fortunatus was Hilary’s friend, it would not readily be approved; but even if approved, what, pray, would follow from it?

27. A more plausible ground for doubt would be whether Hilary wrote on the Epistles of Paul. For the Second Council of Seville, canon 12, quotes words of his from an exposition of the Epistle to Timothy as follows: “Therefore Saint Hilary, in his exposition of the Epistle to Timothy, speaks thus: ‘For when Scripture says,’ etc.” That fragment, which we shall arrange to print with others at the end of his works, entirely bears the character of our Hilary. Augustine also, in Book IV against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, chapter 4, adduces a passage under the name of Saint Hilary [Col. 0024A] in which Paul’s words at Romans 5:12 are explained: “Thus Saint Hilary understood it: ‘In whom all sinned.’ For he says: ‘In whom,’ that is, ‘in Adam all sinned.’” Since these words occur in the Commentaries commonly published under Ambrose’s name, which are very remote from the style of our Hilary, many suppose that Augustine was misled by the name Hilary, and that those Commentaries should be assigned to Hilary the deacon, a supporter of the Luciferians’ schism. But they cannot easily extricate themselves from the objection that their author was in communion with the Roman pontiff and refuted the errors of those who rebaptized, whereas Hilary the deacon, according to Jerome’s testimony in the Dialogue against the Luciferians, persisted in error and schism. Yet, whether Augustine was deceived or not, it does not necessarily follow either from his testimony or from that of the Council of Seville that Hilary published Commentaries on Paul’s Epistles; it follows only that, [Col. 0024B] in works whose loss we know and regret, he expounded certain passages from them. Though it must be admitted that the words of the Council of Seville seem to suggest something else.

28. We have thought it proper to say this beforehand concerning Hilary’s lost works, both to encourage everyone to seek them out and to teach them not to trust every title. In the Colbert manuscript 5079 there is a sermon entitled, “Of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, concerning the tree in which was the knowledge of knowing good and evil.” It contains nothing Hilarian beyond the name prefixed in the title. Nor does a homily on the beginning of Matthew, ascribed to him in Vatican manuscript 1267 and beginning, “With great anxiety and trembling I undertake to explain why the most holy Matthew used [Col. 0024C] such a beginning,” agree any more with his manner of expression; it ends with these words: “But the manner in which this generation was stirred up through the Apostles, I think, has been sufficiently discussed and shown in the question of the genealogies.” We do not repeat what has been observed concerning the books on Job wrongly ascribed to him.

29. If anyone wonders how so many works of so great a man have perished, besides the general reason that time wears away and consumes all things, two further reasons come to mind. The first is that he was called both an imitator and a translator of Origen, whose name was odious and whose doctrine condemned. Nor does any other cause seem to account for the loss of the greater number of his Treatises on the Psalms, the rarity of copies of the remainder, and the complete disappearance of his homilies on Job. Certainly Licinianus, who thought that he possessed this work [Col. 0024D] of Hilary, declares by the following words how little—and why little—he valued it: “I am greatly astonished that so learned and holy a man should translate Origen’s nonsense about the stars.” Those good men, plainly, did not observe what Jerome repeatedly says concerning Hilary’s scrupulous care in imitating Origen; in explicit terms, in Epistle 62 to Theophilus, Jerome says: “Cutting away everything harmful, he translated what was useful.” Accordingly, what Rufinus asserts of Jerome himself concerning the books *Periarchon* [*On First Principles*]—“Although certain stumbling-blocks are found in the Greek [Origen], he so polished and purified everything that the Latin reader finds in them nothing at variance with our faith”—may aptly be said of Hilary as well, especially since Jerome everywhere professes himself Hilary’s imitator in this method [Col. 0025A] of translation: “I have not done this alone,” he says in Epistle 62, “but Confessor Hilary has done it also.” Jerome was so convinced that Hilary’s writings were free from Origen’s errors that, in Epistle 7 to Laeta, when he commands that her daughter read the holy Fathers in such a manner as to judge rather than follow them, he nevertheless excepts Hilary’s books, which she may run through “with unoffended foot.” That these books had been especially cleansed of the things Origen dreamed concerning the stars is plainly established from Jerome’s Epistle 75. There, defending himself for having, in imitation of what Hilary had done in his homilies on Job, translated what was good and either cut away, corrected, or passed over what was bad, he immediately reproaches Vigilantius because he possesses copies of Origen’s Treatises on Job, in which, disputing against the devil and concerning the stars and heaven, Origen said certain things which the Church does not receive. [Col. 0025B] Hence we did not without reason warn in no. 25 that it is highly uncertain whether Licinianus came upon Hilary’s genuine work on Job. How far Hilary was an imitator of Origen we shall explain more suitably at the beginning of his Treatises on the Psalms.

30. A second reason why Hilary’s writings were not received and preserved with the zeal they deserved may be drawn from their obscurity, which can sometimes present an appearance of error to the unwary. Indeed, had they encountered many persons like a certain John, nothing of them would have reached us except bare titles, or at most those fragments transmitted to us by Jerome, Augustine, Leo, Theodoret, the Councils of Chalcedon and Seville, and others. At page 94 of Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance of the Premonstratensian Order, [Col. 0025C] this John says of Hilary’s books on the Trinity:

> Although in many matters he thinks well concerning consubstantiality and the distinction of persons—for no false doctrine exists that does not mingle some truth—yet in more matters he argues in a most perplexing manner, and in some even stubbornly proclaims error; so that for this reason he ought altogether to be rejected by those who chew the cud.

Then, at page 95, he dismisses Hilary’s Commentaries on Matthew with no less contempt: “For the books abound in simple matters; thus, on account of the offense, the scrupulous passages ought rightly to be avoided.” If this principle held good, a great part of sacred literature would be entirely lost to us.

31. An abbot, far more equitable and wise, could never approve so unjust a judgment of a man, even though he was a friend. “Must,” he asks in Epistle 6, [Col. 0025D] “those things also which are perplexing and subtle be avoided; or perhaps, when read but not understood, be condemned by an unconsidered judgment, and their very difficulty and subtlety be imputed to them as a fault, rather than be honored all the more and with much greater reverence on that account?” In Epistle 5 he candidly confesses that in those books he found very many things which he could not understand, either because of the obscurity of the language or because of the corruption of the manuscript; and that he encountered other things which did not sufficiently please him because of a certain novelty about them. At first he refrained from delivering judgment, lest, he says, “by rashly condemning things at which my blindness stumbles, I should deservedly lose the rest which my understanding in some measure grasps.” Then he declares that, by more attentive reading, he attained what he had at first been unable to apprehend, in these terms: [Col. 0026A] “Reading those very passages again more carefully, I at last seemed to myself to find what sense their obscurity appeared to conceal.” Had the Centuriators, Erasmus, Scultetus, and their like read Hilary in the spirit of that praiseworthy Philip, the alleged errors and blemishes which they supposed they had discovered in him would doubtless have vanished on the same principle. We must now disclose how cautiously we have weighed every one of his statements and what we have done to assist the reader, after saying something first concerning the causes of his obscurity.

## IV. The causes of obscurity in Hilary’s style; what has been accomplished in this edition

32. The obscurity of Hilary’s style arises from more than one [Col. 0026B] source. Jerome seems to attribute it to the Gallic temperament. For although in Epistle 4 to Rusticus he ascribes richness and elegance to the speech of the Gauls, he nevertheless writes of their style, and specifically of Hilary’s, in Epistle 13 to Paulinus: “Saint Hilary rises on the Gallic buskin; and though adorned with the flowers of Greece, he is sometimes entangled in long periods and is remote from the reading of simpler brethren.” And although his periods are long, their thoughts are dense; ellipses are frequent; and where a word ought to be repeated in two clauses, it is so placed between them as to answer to both. Thus an easy and fertile genius hastens to bring forth what it has conceived abundantly in the mind. Some transpositions of words are also sometimes troublesome to the reader, since words which, by the nature of the language, ought to cohere with those nearest them [Col. 0026C] must often be referred to words lying at a greater distance. More rarely, but still at times, grammatical rules are neglected.

33. The sublimity of the matters discussed by Hilary also produces obscurity. For he is occupied almost wholly either in drawing out the more hidden meanings of Scripture or in maintaining both the consubstantiality and the distinction of the Father and the Son; and nothing can be conceived more abstruse or more sublime than this.

34. To this must be added that, in the subjects he treated, no Latin author whom he could imitate had gone before him. By universal consent he was the first among Latin writers to draw the sword against the Arians—indeed, the first [Col. 0026D] to declare war upon them; hence Jerome, in Book II against Rufinus, rightly called him “the trumpet of Latin speech against the Arians.” That he was also the first Latin writer of hymns has been proved above from Isidore. Further, that none of the books of Scripture he undertook to expound had been explained before him by any Latin writer, at least so far as he knew, is indicated by the fact that, in explaining Matthew, he deliberately passed over the Lord’s Prayer because he had learned that it had been expounded by Tertullian and Cyprian. Finally, near the end of the book *On the Synods*, with a certain modest preface, he admits that in that work he spoke of matters hidden and, up to his own age, unattempted and unspoken of. Since Latin words were not yet sufficiently fitted to the divine subjects of which he had to speak, he labored all the more to find suitable ones because the Latin language was narrower and less copious than Greek. Hence Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 21, no. 46, reports that disputes were frequent at that time “because the Latin language is narrow and poor in terms [Col. 0027A]” (*dia stenotēta tēs para tois Italois glōttēs kai onomatōn penian*).

35. In the same Gregory, Oration 26, no. 2, observes that a threefold danger confronts those who speak of God: in the mind, in speech, and in hearing. “For,” he says, “it is difficult to comprehend divine things with the mind, exceedingly difficult to explain them in words, and a task of greater labor and difficulty to find ears purified [to hear them].” Hilary experienced and feared this threefold danger. Hence, in Book II, no. 2, he laments his plight: because of the fault of blaspheming heretics he is compelled “to do unlawful things, climb steep heights, utter what cannot be spoken, and presume what is not permitted,” so that matters which ought to have been contained in the reverent restraint of minds are brought forth into the peril of human speech. Then, [Col. 0027B] at no. 5, he expresses the heat and anxiety of a mind unable to explain its own perceptions in these words: “For myself, in answering these things, there is fever in my cares, failure in my understanding, stupor in my intelligence; and in speech I shall confess not merely weakness, but silence.” For, as he says in *On the Synods*, no. 5, “it is most difficult to bring forth in speech the very sense of my own faith according to the inclination of inward understanding.” Finally, he fears the hearing of others when, at no. 65 of the same book, he says: “Remember that it is not understanding that I lack, but words. Perhaps in this I shall blame my nature, yet I shall not blame my will; and I pardon nature if it cannot speak of what it wills.” Conscious that, in divine matters, the meaning of words was still narrower than understanding, he feared offending ears all the more because [Col. 0027C] people had not yet agreed sufficiently concerning the force of each term; for they were often, as he himself says in *On the Synods*, no. 8, “fighting one another fiercely over an unknown meaning of words.” For, says Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 21, no. 97, when some small matter arose daily that occasioned annoyance, affairs were finally brought to such a point that there was danger lest the ends of the world should be torn asunder together with the syllables.

36. Therefore, when about to speak of God, Hilary humbly implored God’s own aid, that the difficulty of thinking and speaking rightly might be made level for him. “I have set forth, beloved,” he says in *On the Synods*, no. 65, “as far as the custom of human speech allowed; and the Lord, always entreated by me as he himself knows, granted me the consciousness of the common faith.” Likewise, that others might more easily grasp what he had conceived, [Col. 0027D] he explained it in various ways, so that matters obscure to someone by one method might become clearer by another. For this reason, displaying the powers of his eloquence, he very often demonstrated by remarkable examples how loftily he thought concerning God. “For,” he says in the same work, no. 62, “the infinite and immeasurable God could not be understood or defended by the brief utterances of human speech; for brevity of speech often deceives both hearers and teachers.” Since, therefore, Hilary, fearing that he might deceive by brevity, pursued fullness of expression, he rightly and deservedly warns the reader in *On the Synods*, no. 6, not to think that he should be judged from the beginnings of his writing before its discourse is completed.

37. Since he repeats this request at no. 66 and urges it again in Fragment I, no. 7, no one will deny that he ought to be granted [Col. 0028A] what Eulogius of Alexandria, quoted by Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 215, enjoins also in reading the other Fathers:

> The teaching of the saints who were teachers of the Church in particular times must be read through in its entirety; their opinions must not be drawn forth in part, and from them a conjecture concerning their entire mind must not be made without danger … since the whole piety of a writer cannot be shown from one saying, letter, or composition.

Moreover, Hilary’s words should not always be measured by our modes of speaking. Many expressions which usage later introduced or sanctioned, especially through Augustine’s teaching, were either unheard of in Hilary’s age or not yet sufficiently established. Thus Ambrose rightly said in Epistle 48 to Sabinus, no. 4: [Col. 0028B] “If I offend in a word, inquire into the power of my confession.” The same writer adds at no. 6: “If words disturb, they do not prejudge the faith. For a mind that is not doubtful overshadows speech and guards it against error.” Thus no one will be disturbed by the word *person* when it is taken in the sense now expressed by the term *nature*; or when one encounters *to use God* (*uti Deo*) in the sense of *to enjoy God* (*frui Deo*); and by other such expressions, which would take too long to enumerate. Finally, since Hilary had no Latin authors whom he could imitate in the matters he treated, it must be observed that he rendered many things according to the thought of the Greeks, whose writings were familiar to him. From this observation, as from the former one, it follows that his language should be compared with that of Greek Fathers, or at least Latin Fathers who preceded him, not with those who followed him. Had those who marked many opinions and modes of expression in him as singular done so, they would have found that he had scarcely either thought or spoken singularly in any matter.

38. The more difficult Hilary’s writings have hitherto been judged, the more laboriously we have thought it necessary to strive to lessen that difficulty. [Col. 0028C] For this purpose we prefixed to each work particular notices or prefaces, in which we have explained, to the best of our ability, whatever concerns the occasion, date, purpose, authenticity, and similar matters of the work. To these we have sometimes appended a synopsis of the entire work; this seemed in some fashion necessary especially for the books *On the Trinity*. Then, to make the reader’s labor lighter in grasping Hilary’s meaning, we have taken care to set forth his principal arguments, as far as the margin of the book permitted, in brief summaries. Further, that the reader might have a place to rest when wearied by the length [Col. 0028D] of the periods, the individual treatises have been divided into various numbered sections. In this way provision has also been made for the convenience of citation, so that those wishing to identify a few verses need not turn through whole books.

39. But our chief care and effort have been devoted to restoring the text, whose corruption for the most part created the obscurity. Although we altered very many things, we altered nothing without previous careful and deliberate consideration.
