In this task we gave particular weight to the antiquity, accuracy, and number of manuscript copies agreeing in a single reading, especially if they otherwise disagreed in corrupt places. For truth commonly reconciles those whom falsehood makes disagree. [Col. 0029A] As we perceived the antiquity of manuscripts from their writing and script, so we established their accuracy from a certain consistency in preserving modes of expression which, because of their unusual character, were often altered in other copies. We have reproduced everything with such scrupulous fidelity to their text that we have restored even the order of words from them. Yet if anything has been corrected which ought not to have been, nothing has been taken from the reader; in the margin he will find, for selection according to his own judgment, whatever of importance occurs in earlier editions and manuscripts.

40. Frequent little notes are certainly intrusive and somewhat distract the reader’s attention from the author. Yet most readers wish to know by what right or authority an earlier reading has been changed; and no one [Col. 0029B] who is pleased by the author’s words alone is prevented from passing over notes placed separately from them. Thus, even where certain points of apparently lesser importance have been noted, this has been done sparingly, and for the sake of those who judge that nothing is to be neglected in an ancient and difficult doctor of the Church, treating a matter in which heresy often arises from words set forth without order. In other passages of greater importance, the changes made have been demonstrated not only by manuscript authority but also, in as few words as possible, by argument. We judged this especially necessary whenever those who had previously edited Hilary, having departed from his true meaning, substituted false readings that bore a certain appearance of truth. By the same notes unusual expressions, involved [Col. 0029C] phrases, and distinctive statements are illustrated and explained. For our purpose has been to present Hilary’s writings not merely free from errors and complete, but also easier to read; and, having attained the sense of certain passages only with labor, we judged it our duty to make this labor lighter for others. For the same reason we have not hesitated to select from the works of learned men anything that might facilitate knowledge of the events Hilary touches upon. Finally, we have endeavored to reconcile those things in him that appear contradictory and to vindicate them from every error—not by vain or externally borrowed arguments, but from his own words. Examining such passages either from their contexts or by comparing them with clearer ones, we discovered how rightly Hilary, secure not so much in his phrasing as in his faith, warned and earnestly asked that [Col. 0029D] he not be judged before his discourse was finished. It will be useful to treat certain of these more celebrated and difficult passages from the very beginning, since it is more convenient here than in a margin to assemble what he says in different places concerning one and the same matter; by the mutual comparison of several passages his true meaning will appear more clearly. And indeed it seemed expedient that the writings of so great a man should not be offered until the chief mists of suspicion had been wholly dispersed. In these discussions we have sometimes interwoven sayings of other Fathers, so that Hilary may be shown to agree not only with himself but also with the ancients. Let us begin with the mysteries of Christ, the first of which is his conception by the holy Virgin, [Col. 0030A] concerning which he is accused of having written certain things contrary to the received faith of the Church.

## §I. The sound faith of Saint Hilary concerning Christ’s conception is demonstrated

41. The provost John, in repeated letters to Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, contends that Hilary, in Book X *On the Trinity*, asserts that our Lord did not receive the beginning of his body from Mary, but, as it were, from the Holy Spirit. Yet, he says, the Catholic Church holds to the contrary that, in the conception of the Lord Jesus, the Holy Spirit was not the material cause but the efficient cause, whereas the flesh of the holy Virgin was the material cause. Therefore, if John is not mistaken, Hilary committed a twofold error in explaining Christ’s conception: first, in denying that Mary was the material cause of that [Col. 0030B] flesh; second, in believing that Christ took his flesh from the substance of the Holy Spirit. It follows that he embraced that absurd opinion which for some time had circulated among the Corinthians and which Athanasius sharply attacked in his Letter to Epictetus: namely, that Christ’s flesh is consubstantial with the divine nature.

42. John’s criticism might perhaps seem of slight importance, since he was a man occupied with many matters and lacking leisure not only for writing but even scarcely for reflection; there was no basis on which he could be judged to have delivered a sufficiently weighty opinion. But who could persuade himself that this judgment was false or rash when he reads in Erasmus’s preface: “In the third book, but especially in the tenth, he speaks of Christ’s body in such a manner as to seem to think that the Virgin Mary contributed nothing of her own beyond the [Col. 0030C] service of conceiving, carrying, and giving birth”? This is especially so since Scultetus concurs and says: “He seems to hold that Christ did not receive flesh from the Blessed Virgin.” For it cannot be thought that these men had read through Hilary’s writings only in part or hastily.

43. Therefore the Catholic bishop will hear that he is the author of an impiety which, when Saint Leo learned that it was proclaimed by Eutyches, he abhorred as destructive of the truth of all our mysteries. For if Hilary thought that Christ did not receive flesh from the Blessed Virgin, Eutyches taught nothing new when he said: “The body of the Lord, which was made from Mary, is not of our substance nor of human mixture; it is indeed called human, but is not consubstantial with us nor, according to the flesh, with his mother.” Yet [Col. 0030D] Flavian, in Leo’s new edition, p. 474, denounces this teaching as novel and impious. Leo himself, in his Letter to Julian of Cos, formerly no. 11 and now no. 25, states not only that Eutyches proclaims the Only-begotten Son of God to have been born from the womb of the Blessed Virgin in such a way that he bore the appearance of a human body, but that the reality of human flesh was not united to the Word; Leo also calls this opinion a prodigy of falsehood, from which innumerable monstrous notions are born and the errors of Valentinus, Manichaeus, and Apollinaris are revived—none of whom believed that Christ possessed the reality of human flesh. If this is not accepted, our faith concerning the passion, death, resurrection, and so forth of the only-begotten Son of God is denied. Accordingly, this opinion seemed so absurd [Col. 0031A] to the same pope that in his Letter, formerly no. 13 and now no. 27, to Pulcheria, chapter 4, he writes that it could only have been the offspring of ignorance, and that Eutyches would have been far removed from it “if he had wished to receive with a pure and simple heart the fullness of the Creed.” For, he says a little earlier, “the question is not about some small portion of our faith that has been expressed less clearly; rather, this most foolish objection dares to attack what our Lord willed no one in the Church, of either sex, to be ignorant of.”

44. From these and other words of Leo, in which he repeatedly condemns the stupidity of Eutychian impiety, the rashness of those who did not fear to cast suspicion of so senseless a doctrine upon a most holy and learned doctor of the Church is sufficiently evident. The Council of Chalcedon had left no place [Col. 0031B] for this insult to Hilary, when in Act 1 it listed him among the few other Fathers from whose doctrine a decree of faith against Eutyches concerning the mystery of the Incarnation was to be framed. Later, moreover, Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance of the Premonstratensian Order, so vigorously repelled in three letters the injury inflicted by a friend upon the holy confessor that John was finally forced to admit that these words of Hilary, Book X *On the Trinity*, no. 17—“For by calling him man, the Apostle taught birth from the Virgin, who, performing a mother’s office, carried out the nature of her sex in the conception and birth of the man”—do not at all apply to one who denied that Christ received the beginning of his body from Mary. Yet such is the power of preconceived opinion and human self-love that John preferred to answer that Hilary was self-contradictory rather than that he himself had spoken rashly.

[Col. 0031C]

45. Therefore, although before fairer-minded persons it would have been easy, by one or two testimonies in which Hilary plainly and clearly teaches that Christ took his flesh from the flesh of the Virgin Mary, to vindicate his faith from every suspicion, we have nevertheless thought it necessary to do so by many testimonies: both that the constancy of his doctrine may become clearer, and that everyone may understand from this beginning how highly to value the judgment of those who count blemishes in Hilary rather than establish them. Nor will it be enough to demonstrate that his faith concerning Christ’s conception is sound and orthodox. We must also explain and set forth why John thought Christ’s flesh conceived from the Holy Spirit as though from a material cause, and why both John and Erasmus and Scultetus seemed to find that Hilary denied it was assumed from Mary’s flesh.

[Col. 0031D]

### I. Hilary repeatedly teaches that Christ’s flesh was assumed from Mary’s flesh

46. In one Treatise on Psalm 138, Hilary simultaneously rejects all heretics who denied that Christ’s flesh was conceived from Mary. For not only does he say at no. 2: “Whatever may seem fitting and appropriate to that man whom he assumed from the womb of the holy Virgin, and in whom he who was God willed to be born as man, must be treated with the dignity due to his heavenly—that is, divine—nature”; he also adds at no. 3: “He did not assume a man of an alien or simulated nature.” For they would have it either that Christ bore the appearance, not the reality, of flesh; or that his body was brought down from [Col. 0032A] heaven; or at least that it passed through Mary rather than having been received from her. But the first opinion is contradicted by the assertion that Christ’s flesh was not of a simulated nature; the second, by the assertion that it was not of an alien nature; and the last, by the affirmation that it was assumed in the womb and from the womb of the holy Virgin.

47. But it will be useful to remove these suspicions from Book X *On the Trinity*, from which they are said especially to arise. What does this statement at no. 17 mean: “The Blessed Virgin, performing a mother’s office, carried out the nature of her sex in the conception and birth of the man,” except that the Blessed Virgin, in the conception of Christ’s body, supplied from her own flesh what other mothers ordinarily supply? He says this still more expressly at no. 15, where he declares that, in Christ’s conception, the Word—which we shall shortly show [Col. 0032B] must be understood under the designation “Spirit”—supplied by his own power the office of a man, while the Virgin nonetheless fulfilled a mother’s role:

> For the Virgin did not give birth to what she gave birth except from her own holy Spirit; and although she contributed from herself to the birth of the flesh only as much as women contribute from themselves to the origins of bodies brought forth once conception has taken place, nevertheless Jesus Christ did not grow together through the nature of human conception.

What does “she contributed from herself” mean but “from her own flesh”? Hence he immediately adds: “In the birth of the man, he retained what belongs to a mother.” And a little earlier one may read: “If, therefore, flesh was assumed by him for himself from the Virgin”; likewise, in chapter 16 on Matthew, no. 8: “For the salvation of humankind Christ is in the body which he assumed from a human being.”

48. For this reason he is accustomed [Col. 0032C] sometimes to call Christ’s body “flesh assumed from the Virgin,” and sometimes “the flesh of our flesh” or “the flesh of our body.” Thus, in Psalm 65, no. 12, he says: “The nature of the flesh assumed from the Virgin is transferred into his eternal glory”; and in Book I *On the Trinity*, no. 11: “And lest the Word made flesh should be either something other than God the Word or not the flesh of our body, he dwelt in us—as it were, in what is ours—so that, while he dwelt, he might remain nothing other than God; but while he dwelt in us, God might be made flesh of nothing other than our flesh.” For, he says in Book II, no. 16, “through that Word made flesh which dwells in us, God is in the reality of our body.”

49. Whoever wants further evidence should hear him say in Book IX, no. 7: “Born as a man of our body, he spoke according to the custom of our nature”; and in Psalm 118, [Col. 0032D] letter 14, no. 8: “Therefore the only-begotten Son of God, assuming for himself from the Virgin a body of our nature,” and so forth. And when he reads again in Psalm 68, no. 13, that Christ reconciled all things “in the blood of our body,” he must admit that Hilary could scarcely have shown himself more plainly alien from those who thought that Christ received nothing from Mary.

50. Nor indeed did Hilary assert only that Christ’s flesh was produced from Mary, [Col. 0033A] but also that it was produced from Mary’s ancestors. Thus Christ is proclaimed in Psalm 67, no. 28, to be from the stock of Judah, and in Psalm 68, no. 19, from David’s womb. Hence in Psalm 118, letter 5, no. 5, David is praised as worthy to have Jesus Christ for his son. And when in Psalm 131, no. 2, as elsewhere, Hilary teaches that Christ is often signified by the name David, he gives this one reason: that Christ was born from David’s line. “He,” he says, “who received the name of his parent according to the origin of the flesh, took the name of him from whose family he took his body also.” Indeed, he writes that the flesh of our Savior was received from the very people of Moab through Ruth; and therefore that its rawness and impurity, before it was assumed, had been boiled and cleansed through various generations, as it were through a pot. “For,” he says in Psalm 59, no. 11, “since the assumption of our flesh had to be entered upon by this Holy One of God not only from this line of holy persons, but also from the origin of sinners—because God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh—therefore Moab is the pot of his hope.” Then, having mentioned the curse upon the people of Moab and its purification through successive generations, [Col. 0033B] he adds: “And this Holy One, taking his origin from Judah and Moab, after the rawness of the flesh had been boiled as though through a pot, is signified under the form of everlasting food, since his flesh is truly the food of life.” But how does our Lord, the Holy One of God, take his origin from Judah and Moab if he received nothing from Mary? In Psalm 68 Hilary traces Christ’s origin still higher. For at no. 23 he affirms that the nature of the body of the first Adam was assumed by Christ; and at no. 10 he calls human beings Christ’s kinsmen according to the flesh.

51. Hilary so strongly held that Christ’s flesh was propagated from Adam and sinful descendants that he does not hesitate to call it both “sinful flesh” and “sin.” “He received sinful flesh,” he says in Book I *On the Trinity*, no. 13, “in order by the assumption of our flesh to forgive sins, becoming its participant by assumption, not by guilt.” Other Fathers [Col. 0033C] indeed interpret the statement that Christ was made sin to mean that he was made an offering for sin. But Hilary understood Christ’s body to be called the body of our sin and sin not so much because it was offered for sin, but because it was begotten from sinners. For that reason, in Book IX *On the Trinity*, no. 13, commenting on Paul’s words, “For in that he died, he died unto sin,” he adds, ascribing death unto sin—that is, to our body; and shortly afterward: “He who assumed the body of our sin now lives wholly to God.” Tertullian said with the same reference: “We maintain that not sinful flesh was emptied out in Christ, but the sin of the flesh; not the matter, but the nature; not the substance, but the fault.” Likewise Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 51, no. 18, testifies that condemned flesh was assumed by Christ. Nor does Hilary contradict himself when he says of the same [Col. 0033D] flesh of Christ, in Book X *On the Trinity*, no. 25: “Nor was that flesh sinful flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh.” For when here he denies that it was sinful flesh in order to show that it was free from the ruling vices of our flesh, there he rightly affirms it in order to establish the reality of the flesh received from human beings.

52. If we turn to the arguments by which the holy Fathers proved that the reality of our flesh existed in Christ, we shall be convinced that Hilary illustrated them no less clearly. Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 32, rests especially upon this argument against heretics: Christ could not truly be called Son of Man unless he had truly received the substance of his body from a human being: “If he did not receive the substance of flesh from a human being, [Col. 0034A] he neither became man nor [became] Son of Man.” Ferrandus the deacon presses the same argument against Eutyches in his Letter to Anatolius. Hilary, however, insists on nothing more frequently than that we remember Christ to be both Son of God and Son of Man. We select one passage out of many, drawn from Book X, which by itself is adequate to dispel all the clouds of suspicion raised from that book. At no. 15 he writes: [Col. 0034B]

> How will the Son of God be born as the Son of Man, or, while remaining in the form of God, have received the form of a servant, unless the powerful Word, God, is able from himself both to assume flesh within the Virgin and to give a soul to the flesh, so that Christ Jesus is born a perfect man for the redemption of our soul and body; and unless he has assumed a body in such a way that, conceived from the Virgin, it made him to be in the form of a servant, etc.?

For in this passage he maintains that Christ would falsely be called Son of Man unless, first, he were a perfect man, consisting of our soul and body; second, unless he possessed this not by merely any assumption, but through birth, so that he was born a perfect man; and finally, as though this were not sufficient, he wishes the body to have been assumed by him in such a manner that it was conceived from the Virgin.

53. Moreover, when, in affirming that Christ was born a perfect man, he adds “for the redemption of our soul and our body,” he touches upon another argument commonly employed by the Fathers against heretics who denied Christ the integrity of human nature. For, as Gregory Nazianzen says, Oration 51, no. 13: “What has not been assumed is without healing; but what has been united to God likewise obtains salvation.” If Adam fell only in [Col. 0034C] part, then that which is assumed and obtains salvation must likewise be only partial. Thus Fulgentius, Book I to Thrasimund, ch. 13: “If the whole man was held by the bond of captivity, the whole man needed the Liberator’s aid. But if divine mercy ought to liberate the whole, divine majesty ought to assume the whole.” Nor, I think, without reason does Hilary again, in his Commentary on Matthew, ch. X, no. 18, call Christ not simply the redeemer of man, but “the redeemer of body and soul.”

54. By a closely similar argument, against Apelles, who maintained that the Lord’s body consisted of stellar matter, not maternal substance, Tertullian concludes in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, no. 2, that the hope of resurrection is vain if the Lord did not receive the substance of His mother: “For it follows,” he says, “that they exclude salvation from that substance [Col. 0034D] whose fellowship with Christ they deny.” To this pertains what Irenaeus says, Book V, ch. 1: “Vain, therefore, are those who, being of Valentinus, maintain this doctrine”—namely, that Christ received nothing from Mary—“in order to exclude the salvation of the flesh.” But Hilary, because of that fellowship which Christ has with us, confirms that resurrection is not merely to be hoped for by us, but has already in some measure been granted to us; so that we may contemplate our flesh as already raised in Him, in whom, as he says in his Commentary on Psalm CXXIV, no. 4, “we behold ourselves through the assumption of our flesh and body. For in Him we are, contemplating our resurrection in the resurrection of our body in Him.”

55. Shall we return to Leo’s twenty-fifth epistle, already cited above? There Eutyches is charged with denying that Christ is [Col. 0035A] mediator, as though anyone who denies Him the substance of His mother thereby deprives Him of that title. So too Fulgentius, Book I to Thrasimund, ch. 15, teaches that Christ is vainly called the mediator of God and men unless He contains in Himself, as wholly and truly God born of God, so also wholly and truly man born of man. Whenever Hilary explains this same designation of Christ, he never explains it otherwise than by saying that Christ, possessing flesh from us and divinity from God, unites God and man in His one person. Hence, in his Commentary on Psalm LXVII, no. 37, considering that office of Christ as mediator, he declares that we are to be assumed into the unity of the Father’s majesty, since indeed the Father is in Him by nature, and He in turn is in us through fellowship in the flesh.

[Col. 0035B]

56. Book X of *On the Trinity* supplies many further arguments. There, from no. 16 onwards, Hilary expressly refutes heretics who asserted either that Christ’s human nature existed before it was assumed, or that His body had been brought down from heaven. He steadfastly requires assent to the words of the Creed: “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary.” In accordance with these, he concludes the whole argument thus: “For the Virgin brought forth from herself a body; but one conceived from the Spirit; possessing indeed in itself the reality of her own body, but not possessing the weakness of nature.” This being so, everyone must wonder that he has seemed to some to hold that Christ did not receive flesh from the Blessed Virgin. We must now examine whence that thought occurred to them.

## II. What Hilary meant by the term “Holy Spirit” was not understood by his critics

[Col. 0035C]

57. John’s occasion for error plainly arose from this: when he read in Book X of *On the Trinity*, and elsewhere, that Christ’s body was not only formed but also assumed by the Holy Spirit, he supposed that by “Holy Spirit,” according to our usage, the third person of the most holy Trinity was meant, whereas Hilary understood the second person. Certainly, in these words from Book II, no. 27—“The Holy Spirit coming down from above … mingled Himself with the nature of human flesh”—Hilary does not mean, as John imagined, that the Holy Spirit was the material cause of the flesh assumed by the Word, but that the Word Himself intimately joined human nature to Himself. For the Angel’s words to the Blessed Virgin, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee,” are for him equivalent to: “The Word and Wisdom of the Father shall descend into thee and shall adapt to Himself a body from thee.”

58. Nor should this interpretation seem unheard of or peculiar to him. Tertullian interprets the Angel’s same words in no other way in *Against Praxeas*, no. 26. Nor does another passage of the same writer, *On the Flesh of Christ*, no. 18, aim at anything else: “Thus finally man is with God, while the flesh of man is with the Spirit of God.” Lactantius, Book IV, ch. 12, likewise expresses the descent of the Word into the Virgin’s womb when he says: “Therefore that holy Spirit, descending from heaven, chose the holy Virgin, into whose womb He might enter.” To these may be added the *Shepherd*, Book III, Similitude 5, where it says of Christ’s body: “This, therefore, is the body into which the Holy Spirit was introduced”; [Col. 0036A] especially since a little earlier in the same place it had stated: “But the Son is the Holy Spirit.” Nor should Irenaeus’s statement, Book V, ch. 1, “The Holy Spirit came upon Mary,” be understood otherwise, if one considers what he immediately adds: “The Word of the Father and Spirit of God, united to the ancient substance of Adam’s formation, made man living and perfect.” Justin’s meaning is more explicit in his *Second Apology*, where he first declares the Son to be God’s power and might in these words: “The first power and might after God, the Father and Lord of all, is also the Son, even the Word, who in some manner became flesh and became man.” A little later he adds: “The power of God, coming upon the Virgin, overshadowed her and caused the Virgin to become pregnant.” Finally, joining both propositions, he concludes: “Therefore it is impious to understand the Spirit and power of God as anything other than the Word, who is also the first-begotten, as Moses the prophet whom we mentioned indicated; and He, by His coming to the Virgin and His overshadowing, not by intercourse but by power, made her pregnant.”

[Col. 0036B]

59. What are we to think of Cyprian? In the treatise *On the Vanity of Idols* one presently reads: “He enters into the Virgin and, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, puts on flesh.” But in place of this, an ancient German manuscript of excellent authority presents: “He enters into the Virgin; the Holy Spirit puts on flesh in her”; and Pamelius testifies that he found this reading in four manuscripts. This reading is certainly the less open to suspicion of corruption the further it departs from our customary manner of speaking. [Col. 0036C] An ancient author supports Cyprian’s words thus corrected, an author whom Augustine, Epistle 148, no. 10, very probably cites under the name of the holy eastern bishop Gregory. This writer, in the appendix to Ambrose, vol. II of the new edition, p. 354, says: “When He entered into Mary, when He filled the Virgin’s womb, something other than that which had come was born from her.” More plainly, on p. 356: “The Spirit of God shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee. Therefore the holy thing which shall be born from thee shall be called the Son of God. You see then that the Spirit Himself—that is, the Son of God—came to the Virgin, and from her proceeded the Son of God and of man.”

60. If you understand Athanasius to have had in view the same evangelical words in the same sense, you will readily see why, in *On the Incarnation*, p. 72, he says: “Therefore, when He first came to us, He formed for Himself a body [Col. 0036D] from the Virgin, so that He might furnish us with no slight proof of His divinity: namely, that He who had formed this body for Himself was also the Creator and Former of other bodies.” For since the Fathers named by us think that the Angel’s words to the Virgin declare the Son of God’s first coming to us, in order that He might form for Himself a body in the Virgin and from the Virgin, it rightly follows that He is the Creator of our bodies, and consequently God, whom the Gospels signify to us as the former of His own body. But if Athanasius had something else in view, whence, I ask, was he convinced that the Son of God, when He first came to us, formed a body for Himself, so that from this he might infer that He likewise created other bodies and is God? Certainly Athanasius did not doubt that the Word is at times denoted in Scripture by the term “Holy Spirit”; for in his fourth letter to Serapion, vol. I, p. 970, he interprets blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as that which denies Christ’s divinity.

[Col. 0037A]

61. Rufinus adds his testimony in his exposition of the Creed. Though he understands the preceding words, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee,” in our customary sense, as spoken of the third person of the holy Trinity, he nevertheless judges that the following words indicate the Son: “And what,” he asks, “is the Power of the Most High, unless it be Christ Himself, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God?” Maximinus also, according to Augustine’s testimony, though Augustine disagreed with him, referred the preceding words to the Holy Spirit but the latter to the Word. “You were trying to maintain,” says Augustine in Book II *Against Maximinus*, ch. 17, no. 2, “that the Holy Spirit came first, in order to command and sanctify the Virgin Mary, and then the Power of the Most High came—that is, the Wisdom of God, which is Christ—and that she herself, as it is written, built herself a house; that is, she herself created flesh for herself, not the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 0037B]

62. If you ask whence Hilary agreed with the ancient Fathers in this way of understanding, an answer will not be lacking. First, no one familiar with the reading of the ancients will deny that the term “Spirit,” or “Holy Spirit,” was among them not the exclusive name of one person, but common to the whole divine nature, and was indiscriminately attributed by them to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Examples of this occur everywhere in the Epistle of Barnabas, ch. 9; in the *Shepherd*, Book III, Similitude 5; and in Irenaeus, Book V, ch. 1. [Col. 0037C] Theophilus of Antioch, in his work to Autolycus, lists this term as though proper to the Son, thus: “The Father employed the Word as minister of His works, and through Him made all things. This is called the Beginning, because it has primacy and dominion over all things made through Him. Therefore, being the Spirit of God, and Beginning, and Wisdom, and Power of the Most High, He descended into the prophets.” The same term denotes the divine nature in these words of Athenagoras, p. 10: “The Father and the Son are one, the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son by unity and power of Spirit”; or when Tertullian says in *Against Praxeas*, no. 27: “They call the Son flesh—that is, man—that is, Jesus; but the Father Spirit—that is, God.” Clement speaks in the same sense in Epistle 2, ch. 9: “Jesus Christ our Lord, who saved us, though He was first Spirit, became flesh.” To this belongs Augustine’s statement in Epistle 140 to Honoratus, no. 11: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us; make the return, and become spirit, and dwell in Him.”

[Col. 0037D]

63. Still more relevant is this rule of Athanasius (*Letter to Serapion*, p. 980): “In the Gospel discourse, as I have often mentioned, when Christ says that He is the Son of Man, by that very fact He displays His humanity; just as, when He makes mention of the Spirit, He declares that it is His Holy Spirit in which He did all things.” “For,” he says in *On the Incarnation of Christ*, “the Word God is Spirit.” So too the author of the work *On the Common Essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*: “Therefore Christ Himself calls the divinity of the Word the Holy Spirit, and conversely called His humanity the Son [Col. 0038A] of Man.” Hence Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 42, no. 19, teaches that Christ consists of two opposites, namely flesh and Spirit, “of which the one gave divinity and the other received it.” You have also, in the Commentary on Romans 1:3 once attributed to Ambrose: “He who was the Son of God according to the Holy Spirit, that is, according to God—for God is spirit and undoubtedly holy—is said to have become, according to the flesh, the Son of God from the seed of David.” And in the *Treatise on the Orthodox Faith* in the same Ambrose: “When Christ deigned to put on manhood, He did not introduce a blemish into eternity by changing Spirit into flesh.” To return to our Hilary: we pass over the fact that, whereas we are accustomed to distinguish in Christ God and man, he is accustomed to distinguish Spirit and man: “Christ remaining Spirit,” he says in Book IX of *On the Trinity*, no. 14, “the same Christ was [Col. 0038B] man.” But we must not pass over the fact that he himself, expressly, in Book VIII, no. 25, demonstrates from examples drawn from Scripture that the word “Spirit” is common to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This shows why the term was so familiar both to him and to the other Fathers for signifying divinity.

64. This being so, it had to be judged from the context which of the three persons was more suitably indicated by the Angel’s words, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee.” The Angel added: “And the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee.” From this the thought easily arose that His entire speech concerned the Son of God. For the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 1:24, calls the Son of God “power”; and it seems especially proper that He should be the Power of the Most High, through whom the Father, who is the Most High, created all things.

[Col. 0038C]

65. This interpretation was considerably confirmed by Solomon’s prophecy, Proverbs 9:1: “Wisdom has built herself a house.” Since the Fathers commonly interpret this of the Word’s assumption of flesh, it will suffice to cite one passage from Leo’s celebrated letter to Flavian: “Wisdom building herself a house, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” that is, in that flesh which He assumed in man. Hilary was so persuaded by the authority of this prophecy that the Son Himself formed and adapted a body for Himself that, on its account, he says he doubts whether Christ can be said to have been formed by the Father according to the form of a servant: “And I do not know whether the fact that He was formed in the form of a servant can be referred to the Father, so that He was formed by Him; for Wisdom itself built herself a house, that she might dwell in us.” [Col. 0038D] Yet this doubt of his is not to be understood as if he did not think Christ’s body the work of the Father and Holy Spirit; rather, he judges it to have been created and formed by the Son in some special manner not applicable to the Father or the Holy Spirit—just as we attribute the title of Wisdom to the Son alone, although we believe that the wisdom of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. Otherwise, he defends with such devoted zeal the truth that every work of the Son is also a work of the Father that there can be no doubt that he believed the works of the Trinity to be inseparable.

66. But whatever may have moved Hilary to understand the Spirit coming upon the Virgin as the Son, it is certainly established that, when treating of Christ’s conception from the Virgin, he regarded the terms “Spirit” and “Word” as synonymous. If anyone wishes to test this for himself, let him compare nearby passages in the same Book X. At no. 15 he will read that “every cause of Christ’s birth was introduced through the Spirit”; [Col. 0039A] and no. 16 explains its meaning: “The flesh had no origin other than from the Word.” Again, if he is troubled by the statement there: “For the Virgin begot what she begot only from her own Holy Spirit,” and by the assertion in no. 17 that the origin of the Son of Man was from the entrance of the Holy Spirit coming upon the Virgin, his difficulty will be removed by no. 18, where Hilary affirms concerning Christ: “For He Himself is the origin of His own body,” since, he says, He subsists in the form of our body by the power of His own might; or when, shortly after, he declares that Christ is free from our defects through the power of an origin proceeding from Himself.

[Col. 0039B]

67. Nor should Philip’s reply to John here be passed over. When John had imagined blasphemy in those words of Hilary, Book II of *On the Trinity*: “The Holy Spirit … mingled Himself with the nature of human flesh,” the abbot, much wiser, prudently replied in Epistle 5: “Therefore, when it is said either that the Virgin conceived from the Spirit or that Christ received the origin of His flesh, it is not understood that the divine substance passed into flesh or became the material cause of this conception; rather, His coming into the Virgin and the wonderful operation by which the Virgin gives birth and Christ is born are indicated.” He was right indeed, provided that by “His coming into the Virgin” he understood the coming of the Word, not of the Holy Spirit.

68. Perhaps this discussion has already proceeded too far in explaining the term “Holy Spirit.” But since a most celebrated heterodox writer of our [Col. 0039C] age has asserted that the first Fathers of the Church erred in many things, and particularly that they were accustomed to confuse the Son and the Holy Spirit, something must necessarily be added to our observations, lest anyone suppose that they confirm such an imprudent assertion. It is one thing for the first Fathers to employ indifferently, in expressing the second and third persons of the Trinity, a term which by the passage of time became proper to the third; it is another for them to confuse the personal properties of each. After several centuries had passed, “Holy Spirit,” which the earliest Fathers had understood as common to the whole Trinity, came to be considered proper to the third person. But nowhere among the Fathers is one to find the persons of Son and Holy Spirit confused and undistinguished; for example, that, in interpreting the Gospel phrase “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” they confused Son and Holy [Col. 0039D] Spirit or did not distinguish them according to their mode of subsistence. That they referred to the Son “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee,” and other like passages now referred to the Holy Spirit, was done without error and without any danger to faith. For in these words either the person who created the body assumed by the Word, or the person who assumed it, is signified. If the person who created it is meant, the faith remains sound to whichever person they are referred; but if the person who assumed it is meant, Hilary’s and the other Fathers’ interpretation must be restored. Therefore, without any confusion of the divine persons, Hilary said that the Spirit of God, the power of God, the wisdom of God, the Son of God, and the only-begotten God, was born man for the forgiveness of sin and the condemnation of sin in the Law, since by all these various titles he understood the one Son of God. This difficulty, then, which had been a great stumbling-block to John, having been removed, let us briefly [Col. 0040A] explain what else moved some to say that Hilary thought Christ received nothing from Mary.

## III. Several passages in which Hilary seemed to deny that Christ took flesh from His mother are explained

69. Since there was no controversy over Christ’s generation from the Virgin’s flesh, Hilary did not labour much to establish it. Indeed, since his opponents freely granted this and endeavoured, from Christ’s lowly birth from Mary, to diminish and weaken His divinity, he had especially to demonstrate that Christ possessed divine as well as human nature, and to refute the argument drawn from His humble birth from Mary. To accomplish this, he shows that Mary, remaining a virgin, bore Christ not by natural power but beyond the common law; and that the Holy Spirit—that is, the very Son of God—coming upon her, by His divine power formed and assumed His own body from the Virgin’s flesh.

[Col. 0040B]

70. Whoever observes this will readily understand why the statement in Book X, no. 16, which so greatly disturbed John—“For Mary did not give origin to the body” (Erasmus, against the manuscripts, added “from herself”)—was made: namely, because Mary did not give Christ’s body its origin and beginning by her own natural power. For, as Leo says in the cited letter to Flavian, ch. 2, “the Virgin’s conception was the work of God; therefore the flesh of the one conceived was not from the nature of the [Col. 0040C] conceiving woman.” Nor will he judge, with John, that Hilary contradicts himself; rather, he will see Hilary carefully distinguishing in Christ’s conception what belongs to God and what belongs to the mother, when immediately after the words “Mary did not give origin to the body,” he reads: “although she supplied all that belongs to her sex for the growth and birth of the body.” Or, if these things conflict, let Leo’s statement in the passage just cited conflict as well, where he seems to express Hilary’s thought in different words only: “For the Holy Spirit gave fruitfulness to the Virgin, but the reality of the body was taken from her body.” Let there also be conflict with [Col. 0040D] what Gregory Nazianzen writes, Oration 36, no. 93: that Mary was Christ’s mother according to, and not according to, the law of generation—*nomō kai ou nomō gennēseōs* [“by law and not by law of generation”]; or with what he defends in Epistle 1 to Cledonius: namely, that Christ was formed in Mary divinely, because without a man’s intervention, and humanly, because according to the law of procreation. Finally, let this statement of Tertullian concerning the Virgin’s wondrous conception contradict itself: “She gave birth, and did not give birth: she gave birth, because [He was] from her own flesh; and did not give birth, because [He was] not from a man’s seed but from the power of the Word.” Certainly, since Christ’s body would never have been conceived in the Virgin unless the Spirit coming upon her had given her fruitfulness, not the Virgin herself but the Spirit must be said to have supplied the origin of Christ’s body. Hilary therefore rightly said at no. 16: “For Mary did not supply origin to the body”; and no less truly added at no. 18: “For He Himself is the origin of His own body.”

71. To prove that Hilary seemed to deny Christ’s flesh from Mary, Scultetus cites this single passage from Book X: “It is the appearance of a man, not the origin of a man.” [Col. 0041A] We searched the entire book in vain for it. Yet we suspect that he intended to indicate the words just explained from no. 16: “For Mary did not give origin to the body”; to which he may have attached these words from no. 25: “That appearance was not as of a man, but as man … while the appearance of flesh is in the reality of birth.” Thus, as he contributes nothing new, nothing new is required from us here. Only the reliability of this man in reporting the Fathers’ words, and a certain inclination to undermine the reputation of their faith, must be noted. For in no. 25 alone, from which he sewed together the words, “It is the appearance of a man,” Hilary repeats in three different ways that Christ is true man because of His true birth from a human being; and in the following section he insists upon this more than once. Yet with what zeal does he everywhere defend the truth that a birth is not genuine if it has not received the proper substance of the one from whom it arises?

[Col. 0041B]

72. From that divine Spirit, by whose power the Virgin conceived, Hilary, Book X, no. 35, calls Christ’s conception “spiritual”: “For that body is the reality of body which is generated from the Virgin; and that which took its beginning from a spiritual conception is outside the weakness of our body.” For the same reason Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, no. 19, calls Christ’s flesh “spiritual”; and Pope Leo, Sermon 5 *On the Nativity of the Lord*, ch. 5, uses precisely the phrase “spiritual conception.”

73. Others call the same body of Christ “heavenly” because of its heavenly union, the natures and likewise the names being intermingled, and, because of their most intimate conjunction, [Col. 0041C] passing reciprocally into one another, as Gregory Nazianzen says, Oration 51, no. 12, in agreement with Augustine, *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, ch. 8. Leo thus transcribes Augustine’s words in his letter to Flavian, ch. 5: “Because of this unity of person, to be understood in both natures, the Son of Man is read to have descended from heaven, when the Son of God assumed flesh from the Virgin from whom He was born.” But Hilary explains this designation chiefly from the fact that the sacred body is the work of the Word descending from heaven. “That flesh,” he says, Book X, no. 23, “that is, that bread, is from heaven”; and at no. 18: “So that, because He is bread descending from heaven, the origin of the body might be judged not to be from human conception, but from the Spirit coming down from heaven, while the body is shown to be heavenly.” Yet since he posits no interval between the formation of the body and [Col. 0041D] its assumption, but indicates that it was one and the same moment when the Holy Spirit coming down from above sanctified the Virgin’s inward parts and when He mingled Himself with the nature of human flesh and, by His might and power, took to Himself that which was alien from Him (Book II, *On the Trinity*, no. 26), his explanation does not differ greatly from that of the others. It moreover confirms the doctrine received by common faith, which Leo, in the same letter, again imitating Augustine from the same passage, states thus: “Our nature was not so assumed that it was first created and afterwards assumed, but that it was created by the very assumption.”

74. Erasmus was further moved by this statement in Book III, no. 19: “And certainly [Mary] did not receive what she brought forth; [Col. 0042A] but flesh advanced flesh without the shame of our elements.” There is no other passage in the whole third book that favours his suspicion. Yet if the final words are obscure, the earlier ones supply light. For if Mary did not receive from elsewhere what she brought forth, she must herself have supplied her own substance. What, then, is “the shame of our elements,” without which she advanced Christ’s flesh? It is precisely what Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 35, no. 26, signifies as shameful to say in ordinary human generation, when he says: “This generation of the Word would not be great if it could be comprehended by you, who do not even know your own generation, or at least understand only some small part of it—and how ashamed you are to speak of it.” Nor does Hilary mean anything else by saying that Christ’s flesh advanced without the shame of our elements than Leo means when he says, Sermon 5 *On the Nativity of the Lord*, ch. 4, that no contamination of earthly seed was mingled in the spiritual [Col. 0042B] conception. Hilary himself makes his meaning entirely unambiguous in Book XII of *On the Trinity*, no. 50. Raising the question why the Apostle called Christ “made of a woman,” he keenly answers that the Apostle did not speak irrationally in calling Him made of a woman, whom he knew to have been born; and that he often spoke thus so that both the birth might show the reality of the generation and the making of one from one might attest the birth, because the term “making” excludes conception through human intercourse, when He who was known without doubt rather to have been born was learned to have been made from the Virgin. By what means, I ask, could the distinctive mode of Christ’s conception from the Virgin be explained more clearly so as to affirm both His true birth from a true mother? Who does not see that, when Hilary excludes the shame of our elements from Christ’s conception in Book III, he denies not the substance of maternal flesh, but only conception through human intercourse, and asserts the birth of one from one?

[Col. 0042C]

75. Therefore, “our elements” mean for him exactly what “our beginnings” mean; and by these terms he explains not so much the substance of the thing conceived as the manner in which it is conceived. This is illustrated by no. 35 of Book VI of *On the Trinity*, where we are warned thus not to imagine the ineffable mode of eternal generation according to our manner of birth: “For God from God is not born according to the custom of human childbirth, nor is He brought forth as man from man through the elements of our origin.” This also removes what John, as appears from Hunald’s letter quoted by Philip, p. 97, objected from Book X of *On the Trinity*, no. 35:

> “For although the form of our body was in the Lord, yet He was not in the body of our defective weakness; He was not in origin [Col. 0042D] that which the Virgin brought forth from the conception of the Holy Spirit. Although she generated Him by the function of her sex, she did not generate Him by the elements of earthly conception. For she brought forth from herself a body, but one conceived from the Spirit, possessing indeed in itself the reality of her own body, but not possessing the weakness of nature. For that body is the reality of body which is generated from the Virgin; and that which took its beginning from a spiritual conception is outside the weakness of our body.”

[Col. 0043A] Perhaps no one will fail to wonder at the foolishness—indeed, not to say injustice—of Hilary’s critics, who could not reproach even one passage in which he did not expressly assert something other than what they wished him to think. For what is more unjust, not to repeat what has been said above, than to seize upon the final words—“She did not generate by the elements of earthly conception”—while either disregarding or failing to notice what immediately precedes, “although she generated by the function of her sex,” and what follows at once, “for she brought forth from herself a body”? Yet Cyril suffered the same injustice long before. [Col. 0043B] In his Letter to John, p. 106, vol. V, he complains that his opponents accused him of saying that Christ’s holy body was not taken from the holy Virgin: “Whereas,” he says, “they ought to have understood that almost our whole struggle for the faith has been undertaken in order that we may steadfastly affirm that the holy Virgin is Mother of God. But if we assert that the holy body of Christ, the Savior of us all, was not born from the Virgin but brought down from heaven, how shall we understand her to be Mother of God?”

## §II.—ON THE NATURAL UNITY OF HUMAN BEINGS WITH CHRIST, AND THROUGH HIM WITH THE FATHER; IN WHICH HILARY’S TRUE DOCTRINE OF THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST IS DEFENDED AGAINST SCULTETUS’S FALSE INTERPRETATIONS

76. Among the opinions of Hilary which Erasmus lists in his preface as suspect is this: that, both elsewhere and especially in Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, Hilary argues with great vigour that we too are one with Father and Son by nature, not by adoption or agreement. In this criticism Erasmus chiefly errs in two ways: first, because, without attending to Hilary’s definition of being “one by nature,” he judges these expressions by our usage; secondly, because he does not distinguish in what manner [Col. 0043C] Hilary understood us to be one by nature with the Father, and in what manner with the Son. But since Hilary proves that we are one by nature with the Son principally because He assumed the very nature of our flesh, how could that view of Hilary have been clear to Erasmus, to whom Hilary seemed to deny Christ the substance of our flesh? From this everyone sees how closely this discussion is connected with the preceding one. Its necessity is shown by this: whoever does not know Hilary’s view on this subject must necessarily struggle greatly with the whole of Book VIII of *On the Trinity* and with many passages elsewhere. We willingly undertake to lighten this labour for some.

77. First, then, it will be useful to observe that Hilary does not say we are one by nature with Father and Son in one and the same way, but directly with the Son, and with the Father [Col. 0043D] only through the Son, as will be clear from what follows. Secondly, since definitions of words depend upon human choice, we must attend to how he defines “one by nature.” That these terms have a wider meaning for him than for us is evident from the fact that in Book VIII, no. 9, he says generally: “Those who are one through the same thing are one by nature, not merely by will.” From this he concludes in no. 7 that believers, who are one through the one faith, are not one merely by agreement. “Therefore,” he says, “if all were one through faith, that is, through the nature of one faith, how do you not understand a natural unity in those who are one through the nature of one faith?” Again, in no. 8, he confirms the natural unity of these same persons because baptism is one for those who have put on the one Christ: “That they are one amid such diversity of nations, conditions, and sexes—is this from consent of will, or from unity of sacrament, because baptism is one for them and all have put on one Christ?” So, in no. 9, he concludes that both the one who waters and the one [Col. 0044A] who plants are one because they have been reborn in one baptism and are one administration of the baptism of the one who regenerates; and shortly afterwards because they have become the same thing, so that they are ministers of the same thing and operation. It is as though he said: those who water and plant are one because they are one instrument for bringing about one effect, namely the bestowal of baptism. Finally, in no. 12, he indicates that those who receive one honor are one by nature, because honor is either a kind, a form, or a dignity of nature. But let us examine more closely in what sense he wished us to be one by nature with Christ.

[Col. 0044B]

78. A man to be admired no less for keenness of intellect than for piety thinks that the natural bond by which Hilary wishes us to be joined to Christ is the Spirit of God, who is, as it were, the soul of Christian souls, giving them life and motion; and therefore all believers are not improperly called by blessed Peter “of one mind.” For this is why, just as the individual members of each person are joined with the soul to make one body, so individual believers are joined with the Spirit of Christ by a natural bond to make the one body of Christ, which is the Church. This interpretation is supported by the passage just cited from Book VIII of *On the Trinity*: that all, amid however great a diversity, are one by nature because all have put on the one Christ. Gregory Nazianzen says in no other sense, Oration 26, no. 17, after first stating that in the Church some rule and preside while others obey and are [Col. 0044C] governed: “Yet both become one in the one Christ, joined and fitted together by the same Spirit” (*amphotera hen eis hena Christon hypo tou autou synarmologoumena kai syntithemena pneumatos*). To this pertains Augustine’s statement, Sermon 268, no. 2: “What our spirit—that is, our soul—is to our members, the Holy Spirit is to the members of Christ, to the body of Christ, which is the Church”; and Sermon 267, no. 4: “The Holy Spirit does in the whole Church what the soul does in all the members of one body.”

79. Yet Hilary relates this matter less to the Spirit than to the body of Christ when he considers that natural unity of human beings with Christ. And just as Christ’s body is, in a manner, threefold—namely, the natural body which he took from the Virgin; the sacramental body which he left to us in the Eucharist; and the glorious body which he bore back to heaven—so, from this threefold source, he shows that we are one with Christ by nature: since he takes our nature in the Incarnation; we receive his true flesh in the sacrament of the Eucharist; and finally, in the restoration of our bodies, he repays to us the same glory that he received from the Father. Each of these three unities must be treated separately.

## I. The unity of human beings with Christ by reason of the nature assumed by him

80. The ancient philosophers, Cicero testifies in Book I of the *Academic Questions* [Col. 0045A], held that a human being is, as it were, a certain part of the commonwealth and of the whole human race, and is joined to other human beings by a certain human fellowship. Hilary is not far from this opinion when, on Psalm LIV, no. 9, he says of Christ’s incorporation: “He was made the flesh of our whole race”; and on Psalm LI, no. 16: “That the Son of Man might also be the Son of God, he assumed into himself the nature of all flesh; through this he became the true vine and holds within himself the stock of all offspring”; and, at no. 17: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us,” that is, assuming into himself the nature of the entire human race.

He signifies the same thing in many other places. But especially clear is the passage in chapter 4 on Matthew, no. 12, where he interprets the city set on a mountain as the flesh assumed by the Son of God, in these terms: “By the city [Col. 0045B] he means the flesh which he assumed; for as a city consists of a diverse and numerous body of inhabitants, so in him, through the nature of the body he assumed, there is contained a certain gathering together of the entire human race. Thus he too, from our gathering together into himself, becomes a city; and we, through participation in his flesh, are the habitation of the city.”

With reasoning not unlike this, Gregory of Nyssa speaks of Christ at the beginning of tome II, on 1 Corinthians XV.8: “His body is the entire human nature with which he is mingled.” Likewise Cyprian, in *On the Lord’s Prayer*, says of the same Lord: “He bore all in himself as one.” “Making us,” Augustine says on Psalm LXXXV, no. 1, “one human being—head and body.” Athanasius plainly agrees with them in his Fourth Oration against the Arians, where he interprets Christ’s words, “That they all may be one, as thou, Father, art in me and I in thee,” thus: “That, as though all borne by me, [Col. 0045C] they may all be one body and one spirit, and come unto a perfect man.” What else does Cyril of Alexandria mean when he says, *Dialogue* 1, p. 407: “All of us human beings are bound together by a natural bond into identity”? We shall show in Book II of *On the Trinity*, p. 800, no. g, that Leo, Ambrose, and the commonly received Titus of Bostra also used the same manner of speaking.

81. Because of these expressions, those holy Fathers might appear to have thought that Christ assumed not an individual but the universal nature of the human race. Yet their meaning was rather that, in assuming one individual nature, he contained the whole in it. Hilary’s opinion on this point is not obscure, when, in Book II of *On the Trinity*, no. 25, he says: “We needed God to become flesh, that is, by the assumption of one flesh he might dwell inwardly within all flesh.” Nor does he assign to Christ alone the privilege that all exist in him. He says the same also of Adam and Abraham: of Adam, indeed, in chapter 8 on Matthew, no. 5: “In the one Adam sins are forgiven to all nations”; and of Abraham, in chapter 18, no. 6: “For we are all in the one Abraham, and through us, who are all one, the number destined for heavenly glory must be completed.”

From this it is clear that, in the view of Hilary and the other Fathers, all who share human nature are joined by a natural unity. Indeed, they are united in that mass from which all alike derive their origin, and from which Christ himself did not refuse to take the substance of his flesh.

82. [Col. 0046A] Our bishop means nothing else when, in Book VIII, no. 13, he addresses the heretics who admitted no unity between us and Christ except one of agreement: “I ask whether Christ is in us today through the reality of nature.” He then continues: “For if the Word truly became flesh . . . how is he not to be believed to remain in us naturally, he who, having been born a human being, assumed the nature of our flesh, now inseparable from himself?”

In agreement with this, Ambrose writes in Book IV *On the Faith*, chapter 10: “As I confess that there is unity of heavenly life in the Father and the Son through the unity of the divine substance, so, with the privilege of the divine nature and of the Lord’s Incarnation excepted, I profess that in the Son there is fellowship with us in spiritual life through unity of human nature: ‘As is the heavenly one, such also are the heavenly ones.’ Finally, just as we sit at the [Col. 0046B] right hand of the Father in him—not because we sit with him, but because we sit in Christ’s body—so, I say, we sit in Christ through unity of body, and live in Christ through unity of body.” See also his Letter 76 to Irenaeus, no. 8.

83. Because of this natural unity of the human race with the flesh assumed by Christ, Hilary teaches, on Psalm LI, nos. 16 and 17, that a right to the kingdom of God has been given to the whole human nature. No one falls from it unless, either through unbelief or through barrenness, he is uprooted from Christ, in whom he is already, as it were, engrafted—not ever prevented from being in him, because through the assumption of nature he has been received as an indweller, but judged unworthy of fellowship in nature because of the crime of unbelief. So also, on Psalm CXLIII, no. 18, he writes that the nations already behold the salvation of their flesh in contemplating Christ’s resurrection. “For,” he says on Psalm CXXIV, no. 4, “we are in him, contemplating our resurrection in the resurrection of our body in him.”

These passages confirm what we think we have abundantly demonstrated in the foregoing discussion: that Hilary did not deny that Christ assumed flesh from the substance of Mary, since he affirmed that human beings are united to Christ by nature because he assumed that very nature and substance of flesh of which we consist. But since he denies the glory of this natural unity to no human being, it is clear, as we said, that he had regard less to the Spirit of Christ—by whom believers and good persons alone are united with God—than to his body.

## II. The unity of human beings with Christ through receiving his flesh in the Eucharist

84. [Col. 0046D] A second mode of explaining this same unity is drawn from the communion of Christ’s flesh, which we receive in the sacrament of the Eucharist. Hilary does not separate this second argument from the first; rather, combining both into one, he explains our natural unity with Christ thus, in Book VIII, no. 13: “For if the Word truly became flesh, and we truly receive the Word’s flesh as food from the Lord, how is he not to be thought to remain in us naturally, he who, having been born a human being, assumed the nature of our flesh, now inseparable from himself, and mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity under the sacrament of flesh to be communicated?”

85. It is astonishing how greatly Scultetus torments himself in his analysis of this passage in order to evade the force of the argument at issue. For, while he endeavors to twist what is clear concerning the communication of Christ’s flesh in the sacrament of the Eucharist into a sharing in Christ’s glory, his discourse becomes so entangled that the falsity of the interpretation is apparent even from its convoluted form. For he explains the cited words as follows:

“Human nature in Christ is joined to divinity in this supremely mystical manner: Christ’s very flesh is also communicated to us; that is, we are one in nature with it, partakers of the immortality and glory of resurrection which it enjoys. This is what Hilary’s words mean when he says, ‘He mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity’; he adds, ‘under the sacrament of flesh communicated to us.’ Here he does not speak of the symbol of the supper; for Hilary uses the word *sacrament* otherwise. Rather, he teaches that, by the humility of the Son of God in assuming our flesh, there is commended to us [Col. 0047B] the sacrament—that is, the hidden truth—that he communicated his own nature to us, so that we too might become immortal.”

86. Many replies to this tortuous, unfaithful, and inept interpretation are readily available. First, in the passage explained, he finds not a word about the Son’s humility. Secondly, in place of *communicandae* (“to be communicated”) he substitutes *communicatae* (“communicated”), contrary to the testimony of all manuscripts and printed copies. But with what face does he deny that Hilary speaks of the Eucharist because, by the word *sacrament*, Hilary signifies not what it commonly signifies but something hidden?

Is baptism not called “the sacrament of human salvation” at the beginning of Book II? Or in this very Book VIII does *sacrament* mean anything other than it does among us, where he says: “That they are one amid so great a diversity of nations and sexes—is this from agreement of will, or from unity of sacrament, since their baptism too is one?” And, according to Scultetus, what does this statement in no. 15 mean: that Christ, when we drink his blood and eat his flesh, is in us “through the mystery of the sacraments,” except that Christ is in us through the mystery of mysteries? And, not to accumulate more here, let Scultetus consult the *Treatise on Psalm* CXXXI, no. 23, and there hear the heavenly Jerusalem defined as “the harmonious assembly of the faithful, and souls sanctified by the sacraments of the Church.”

87. Moreover, Scultetus trifles and plays false with the word *eternity*. For since the divine nature alone claims eternity as its own by proper right—as is taught in chapter 23 on Matthew, no. 5—he either did not notice, or pretended not to notice, that Hilary calls it “eternal” or “eternity” without qualification. Certainly, when, against heretics who maintained that sorrow on our account could befall God, he says in chapter 31 on Matthew, no. 2: “As though eternity had taken on a nature of frailty,” and afterwards, “as though eternity had been changed into fear,” and so forth—does *eternity* mean anything other than divinity?

Who likewise would deny that divinity is denoted by the term *eternity* in these words from Fragment II, no. 32: “Therefore the immutable and unchangeable Son of God, in assuming humanity, brought glory to corruption rather than blemish to eternity”? For they mean scarcely anything else than the words in Book IX of *On the Trinity*, no. 4: “His willing acceptance of humiliation is our advancement, since he neither loses what he is as God nor fails to gain for the human being that he may be God”—that is, the Word lost nothing by assuming our flesh, while to us there accrued a very great increase of glory.

This is illustrated by the words of an ancient author in *On the Orthodox Faith*, included in Ambrose’s Appendix to tome II, chapter 8: “When he deigned to put on humanity, he did not bring blemish upon eternity, as though he changed the Spirit into flesh,” and so forth. Since, then, Hilary customarily signifies the divine nature by the word *eternity*, when he says in the cited passage of Book VIII, “He mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity,” the plain and genuine sense is this: he did not leave in the sacrament of the Eucharist the bare nature of his flesh, detached from the Word, but flesh mingled and united with his divinity, so that, by communicating his flesh, he might make us partakers of his divinity.

88. Understood in this way, Hilary’s demonstration is straightforward. [Col. 0048B] For if the nature of Christ’s flesh, substantially united with the Word—which is one in nature with the Father—is truly bestowed upon us, it follows that we are naturally one with Christ and, through him, naturally one with the Father. This was what he had undertaken to prove.

Thus, the two propositions quoted above—“If we truly receive the Word’s flesh as food from the Lord,” and “If he has mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity under the sacrament of flesh to be communicated”—differ only in this: the former signifies both the nature and the reception of the Eucharistic sacrament, while the latter signifies only its nature and institution. The same meaning is confirmed by what he adds by way of conclusion: “Therefore, if Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body, and that man who was born from Mary is truly Christ—that is, God—and we truly receive under the mystery the flesh of his body, and through this shall be one, because the Father is in him and he in us: how can a unity of will be asserted, when the natural property bestowed through the sacrament is the sacrament of perfect unity?”

What does this mean except that, since we receive the true flesh of him who is truly God, we possess that through which we are joined with the Father: because through the true flesh of Christ imparted to us we are in him who, by the nature of divinity, is in God the Father. Thus the natural property bestowed through the sacrament is the sacrament of perfect unity; that is, the proper nature of Christ’s flesh, bestowed upon us through the sacrament of the Eucharist, is the bond of perfect unity among us, Christ, and the Father.

89. Scultetus therefore evaded the issue in vain; in vain he maintained that the discourse in which Hilary declares in so many and such diverse ways that he is speaking of our communion with God through the Eucharist was spoken not of the symbol of the supper, but of some sharing in glory. Nor could he remain consistent in that forced interpretation. For when he reaches the passage just cited, “and we truly receive under the mystery the flesh of his body,” he finally concedes that the earlier statement, “we truly receive the Word’s flesh as food from the Lord,” was also said concerning the sacrament of the supper.

For in the latter phrase he thinks he has grounds for deception and smoke, because he finds added to it, “under the mystery.” As though the Church ever taught or believed that in this sacrament we receive Christ’s flesh bare and raw, rather than veiled under mystical species [Col. 0049A]. But if he accepts “under the mystery” in the one passage, let him accept “we truly receive flesh” in both; let him accept in the first, “we receive the Word’s flesh truly”—that is, the very flesh which the Word assumed from Mary and made now inseparable from himself. Certainly, anyone who weighs Hilary’s whole passage will not deny that he believed that, in receiving the Eucharist, we receive Christ’s flesh as truly as he truly assumed ours in his temporal birth, and as truly as he received the Father’s substance in his eternal birth.

90. Indeed, since Hilary seeks to persuade the Arians concerning the latter point—which was in dispute among them—by the manner in which we receive Christ’s flesh in this sacrament, it must have been admitted among them that in receiving the Eucharist we receive the true nature of Christ’s flesh. For, from these Gospel words—“As the living Father sent me, and I live through the Father; and he who eats my flesh shall also live through me”—he concludes: “Therefore he lives through the Father; and in the same way in which he lives through the Father, we live through his flesh.”

Then he presses the argument: “If therefore we live through him naturally according to the flesh—that is, having received the nature of his flesh—how can he not have the Father in himself naturally according to the Spirit,” that is, according to divinity, “since he himself lives through the Father?” He then continues: “But he lives through the Father because his birth did not bring to him an alien and different nature,” and so forth.

This could by no means be established from the comparison he has made if we received merely a figure of Christ’s flesh, or even a substance different and alien from it. But why should we add anything of our own here, when Hilary immediately explains what he means by “we live through him naturally according to the flesh”—“that is, having received the nature of his flesh”? Is there any place here for understanding a figure? What agreement can there be between a figure of flesh and the nature of flesh?

91. But if anyone has not yet found Hilary’s opinion sufficiently proved and clear, let him consider also this statement from the same passage: “This, therefore, is the cause of our life: that we who are fleshly have Christ abiding in us through flesh, we being to live through him on the same condition on which he lives through the Father.” What is that condition on which the Son lives through the Father? Surely no other than that he receives the Father’s true, not figurative, substance. Therefore, either Christ’s true flesh received in the sacrament of the Eucharist will be the cause of our living through him, or we shall not live on the same condition on which he lives through the Father.

Further, who could think here of a merely spiritual eating, where “we who are fleshly have Christ abiding in us through flesh”? What does “through flesh” mean except not only according to the spirit but also according to the very substance of flesh; not only spiritually, but also bodily? Nor did he omit this very word. Having rebuked the heretics who admitted no natural unity between us and the Father and Son, in these words—“as though no proper natural communion through the sacrament of flesh and blood were bestowed”—he immediately confirms that, in this sacrament, the Son, abiding in us bodily, bestows a true and natural unity.

92. [Col. 0050A] Hilary does not place this bodily, so to speak, presence of Christ merely in us, or merely in use. For absolutely, and before any use, he thus affirms the reality of flesh and blood: “No room has been left for doubting the reality of flesh and blood; for now, both by the Lord’s declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood.” He then explains the use and effect of this sacrament in these words: “And when these have been drunk and received, they bring it about that both we are in Christ and Christ is in us.”

Moreover, he says that there is no room for doubt about the reality of flesh and blood after Christ has attested this by his declaration. Yet Christ declared before their reception: “This is my body; this is my blood.” Again, when above he had stated that Christ mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of divinity “under the sacrament of flesh to be communicated” [Col. 0050B], does he not sufficiently indicate that both flesh and divinity are present even before the flesh is communicated, while it is still to be communicated? Scultetus indeed reads there, “under the sacrament of flesh communicated,” but in bad faith, as we have already noted.

Finally, this can be confirmed from the words in *Against Constantius*, no. 11. There Hilary, lamenting what had been done at Toulouse by the impious attendants of Constantius, says: “Deacons were beaten with lead, and hands were laid upon Christ himself—as the most holy persons with me understand it, upon Christ himself.” That by “upon Christ himself” we should understand the Eucharist is indicated by the intervening admonition, “as the most holy persons with me understand it.” This is equivalent to the customary formula used by other Fathers whenever, for caution’s sake, they speak somewhat obscurely about this sacrament: “the faithful understand.” Therefore the Eucharist is Christ himself; and Christ is such that impious hands could be laid upon him, and in fact were laid upon him. But they were not laid upon him in the use of the sacrament. It follows, then, that Christ was in it even before its use.

93. Hilary certainly saw that human feeling and wisdom resist this faith of ours concerning the reality of Christ’s flesh in the Eucharist. Yet, however loudly they protest, he wisely meets them and imposes complete silence upon them with these words: “In matters concerning God, one must not speak according to human or worldly understanding; nor must perversity be forced upon the soundness of heavenly utterances by violent and imprudent preaching. Let us read what has been written,” and so forth.

But we read that Christ gave us his body. Whatever the feeble reasoning of human beings may object, therefore, must not be heard. “For now, by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood.” But how can one and the same body be in so many and such widely separated places at once? Hilary answers: “What Christ affirmed—is this not truth?” Let it indeed happen that this be untrue for those who deny that Christ Jesus is truly God: that is, for those who deny that Christ is omnipotent or able to perform what he says he performs.

This is his safe refuge in matters difficult to believe. Although he does not grasp how the Son was begotten from the Father’s substance, how Christ entered to the disciples when the doors were shut, or by what means he offers us his true flesh under mystical species, he nevertheless never doubts in the least of the Lord’s words, knowing certainly that Christ can do more than human reason can comprehend. He gives another example of this faith when he explains a mode of our unity distinct from the two preceding ones, which must now be briefly considered.

Yet before that, it should not be passed over that Cyril of Alexandria also, *Dialogue* 1, p. 407, uses the example of the Eucharist to refute those who think that there is no unity among us except agreement of will. “For,” he says, “we have become one body with Christ, nourished with one flesh and sealed with one Spirit; and since Christ is indivisible—for he is by no means divided—we are all one in him. Therefore he said to the Father, ‘That they may be one, as we also are one.’ See how we are all one in Christ and in the Holy Spirit, both according to body and according to spirit.”

## III. The unity of Christ and human beings: how Christ makes us one with the Father

94. The third mode of unity, which Hilary treats first, concerns the life to come. The unity Christ prays for his own in these words, “That they may be one, as we are one,” he understands from the following words: “And the glory which thou hast given me I have given them”—so that they will then be one when they are made participants in the glory that he received from the Father.

“All,” he says in Book VIII, no. 12, “who will believe in him shall be one with the Father and the Son.” And how they shall be one, we are immediately taught: “And the glory which thou hast given me I have given them.” “And now I ask whether glory is the same thing as will, since will is a movement of the mind, while glory is a nature, form, or dignity.”

From this he later concludes: “Therefore all are now one—the Father, the Son, and the faithful—in glory; because no glory other than that received from the Father has been given by the Son to the faithful, and it was given for no other reason than that they might all be one.” Thus the glory of the Son raises all believers into unity with the Father’s glory.

Although he declares himself certain by faith of this unity promised him by Christ, he nevertheless admits in the same place that he does not yet properly know its rationale, adding: “I hold the faith and receive the cause of unity; but I do not yet grasp how the glory given accomplishes that all are one.”

95.
