In no. 16 he briefly embraces that threefold mode of unity, and explains why he has discussed it: “These things have been recalled by us for this reason: because those who feign that there is only a unity of will between the Father and the Son used the example of our unity with God”—here is the reason—“as though, when we are united to the Son, and through the Son to the Father, only by the obedience and will of religious devotion, no proper natural communion through the sacrament of flesh and blood were bestowed; whereas, both through the glory of the Son given to us”—this is the first stage of union with Christ, common glory—“and through the Son abiding bodily in us”—the second, his flesh given to us in the Eucharist—“and through us being united to him bodily and inseparably”—the third, our flesh assumed by him and never laid aside—“the mystery of true and natural unity must be proclaimed.”

Once this unity of our nature with Christ had been thus explained, Erasmus had no basis for any suspicion of error.

96. But neither is it more suspect that Hilary asserts that we too are one with the Father by nature. For he proves this only with Christ intervening and performing the office of mediator. Since Christ’s flesh and ours are of one substance, while the Word who possesses our flesh and the Father are of one nature, it follows that, being naturally joined with Christ, we are likewise joined with the Father, with whom Christ is naturally joined. “Thus,” he says in no. 13, “we are all one, because the Father is in Christ and Christ in us.”

More clearly, in no. 15 he explains his meaning thus: “If he had wished only a unity of will to be understood, why did he set forth a certain grade and order of the consummation of unity” (John XIV.19), “unless it were that, as he is in the Father by the nature of divinity, so we might be believed to be in him through his bodily birth, and he in turn to be in us through the mystery of the sacraments; and that thus perfect unity through the Mediator might be taught: namely, that while we abide in him, he abides in the Father, and while abiding in the Father, abides in us; and that thus we might advance to unity with the Father, since he who is naturally in the Father according to his birth, we too should naturally be in him, he himself naturally abiding in us.”

97. In commending this unity of human beings with God, other Fathers agree with Hilary. Gregory of Nyssa, on the words of 1 Corinthians XV.8, tome II, says: “From the whole human nature with which divinity was mingled, the human being who is in Christ stood forth as the first-fruits of the dough; through him the whole was joined and mingled with divinity.” He then teaches that Christ fulfills the office of mediator precisely because he has united all to himself.

These words of Paulinus of Nola, Letter formerly numbered 33, are excellent: “Through Christ we are joined and grafted to God, so that in our earthly nature we may hold the Holy Spirit, whom he gave us, as God’s earnest, and may have Christ’s flesh in God as the pledge of ourselves. For that immeasurable interval by which mortal things are separated from divine things he joins together by his mediating intervention, common to both, as by a kind of bridge, if I may so speak, so that by his path earthly things may be brought into union with heavenly things.”

Cyril of Alexandria asks in his *Dialogue on the Trinity*: “Is the Only-Begotten to be judged Mediator only because he banished afar the sin that kept us from God’s love and fellowship?” He answers that Christ has, besides, another hidden and mystical ground for the name and reality of mediation. He later explains this mystery thus: “Therefore he is also deemed Mediator in this manner: by showing in himself united and joined those things which are greatly separated in nature and divided by an immeasurable interval—namely, divinity and humanity—and by joining us through himself to God the Father. For he is of the same nature as God, because he is from him and in him; and he is also of the same nature as ourselves, for he too is from us and in us.”

## § III.—Whether Hilary denied that Christ was subject to hunger, fear, pain, and other human affections

98. The controversy over what Hilary thought concerning Christ’s passion has become so celebrated from day to day that we cannot possibly pass it by untouched. In this matter, moreover, there were formerly, and still are, both accusers and defenders. Some affirm that he thought Christ altogether free from sorrow, fear, pain, and other affections of this kind; others deny it.

## I. Hilary’s principal critics and defenders in this matter

99. Among the ancients, Claudianus Mamertus was the first who, in Book II of *On the State of the Soul*, chapter 9, observed two things in Hilary’s writings that he deemed contrary to the truth: one, that Hilary said that nothing created is incorporeal; the other, that Christ felt no pain in the Passion—supply, “he said.” He adds: “If his Passion was not real, neither could our redemption have been real.” The first part of this criticism will have its place below; for now, it is enough to examine the latter.

100. Many centuries later, Berengar, no doubt fearing that the weight of Hilary’s authority might crush his own notion concerning the Eucharist, sought to evade it by damaging the reputation of so great a man. As Lanfranc testifies, Letter 50, he wickedly spread abroad the claim that Hilary “held perverse opinions in his treatise on faith and advanced unsound opinions concerning the Lord Jesus Christ in his book on the divine Trinity.” Not much later, the same John who stubbornly insisted that Hilary had thought wrongly about Christ’s conception contended, in the same letters, no less obstinately that Hilary’s opinion concerning Christ’s Passion was at variance with right faith.

Baronius too, at the year 563, no. 4, speaks less circumspectly than usual concerning Hilary, when he writes that the error renewed by the Aphthartodocetae was one already condemned in Hilary; yet he adduces no authority for this condemnation beyond the judgment of Claudianus Mamertus. Erasmus and Scultetus likewise spare Hilary nothing in this matter. Many others, although they do not openly condemn the holy bishop, either defend him lukewarmly or incline toward the opinion of those who believe that he erred. Some adopt a middle position: while admitting that in the books *On the Trinity* he taught erroneous things contrary to the right faith, they suppose that he corrected and retracted this error in later writings.

101. No less distinguished were those who defended the faith of the venerable doctor against his critics. First, against Claudianus Mamertus alone one may set all the Fathers of the Church who praised Hilary. Lanfranc already did this elegantly in Letter 50, where he rejects Berengar’s censure chiefly on the ground that whoever brands Hilary with any heresy also implicates in the stain of the same error many leading orthodox authorities who extolled him with great praise.

For, as he later adds, “Pope Gelasius, in his decrees, counts his books among Catholic writings . . . his authority is most worthily mentioned, received, and praised in the sacred canons”—that is, in the Council of Chalcedon, Session II; Toledo IV, chapter 10; Seville II, chapter 12; and so forth—“Saint Augustine, in Book VI of *On the Trinity*, chapter 10, exalts him with extraordinary praise . . . Blessed Jerome” (see Letter 7 [Col. 0054A], to Laeta), “praises him and all his books so highly in certain encomia of his that it cannot be contained within the brevity of a letter; and all other teachers of the sacred religion who have said anything concerning him have not dissented from their judgment in this respect.”

He then proposes this excellent rule to those who may take offense at difficult opinions in their reading of the holy Fathers: “It is therefore safer for a reader, when confronted with the most difficult opinions of the holy Fathers, which the weakness of his intellect cannot grasp, to ask about what he does not know and say that he does not know, rather than, through stubborn arrogance and arrogant stubbornness, define things contrary to faith, not without harm to himself and others; especially where the person concerned is such as appears to carry the weight of authority by learning, integrity of life, or rather by both together.”

102. Above we heard a similar judgment from Abbot Philip. Following it himself, he steadfastly maintained in three letters that Hilary’s teaching was not what Provost John attributed to him. But when the provost resisted obstinately, Hunaldus was sought as arbiter of the dispute; he attempted to reconcile both sides in such a way that he by no means allowed Hilary’s faith to be regarded as suspect. Hunaldus’s opinion, together with John’s three letters, appears at the end of the letters of Abbot Philip.

103. Not long afterward, Saint Thomas, *Third Part*, question 15, articles 5 and 6, and Bonaventure, following the Master, in the *Third Book of Sentences*, distinction 16, likewise labored to ensure that the statements of the Catholic bishop should be understood in a Catholic sense. They answered the objections and restored to sound faith those statements which seemed to bear some appearance of error.

To avoid prolixity, we refrain from recounting what those learned men—Lanfranc, Philip Lombard, Thomas, Bonaventure, and many others—answered to the opponents in this controversy, so that we may investigate Hilary’s genuine meaning from his own statements. This indeed cannot be accomplished in few words, although the preconception of many may be overturned, or at least weakened, once it has been shown to them what we undertake to establish in the following proposition.

## II. How many things Hilary taught contrary to the error imputed to him
104. The principal charge brought against him is that he held that fear, sorrow, and other such affections—especially pain—did not at all befall Christ [Col. 0054D]. Yet what could be more opposed and contrary to this error than to proclaim that Christ assumed all our affections and weaknesses? And indeed, in *On Psalm* LIII, no. 4, he teaches that Christ so framed his prayer that, since he suffered all things according to man, he also speaks all things according to man; and that, having borne the weaknesses of those for whom he prays, he entreats God in their words. What does “he suffered all things according to man” mean but all that human beings commonly suffer? For with him the expression *according to* often has the force of “after the manner of”; nor can there be doubt that here “according to man” must be understood as “after the manner of other human beings.”

He himself explains his statement more fully in no. 7:

> That we might have a most complete example of human lowliness, he both prayed and suffered all things that belong to human beings. And from our common weakness he sought salvation for himself from the Father, so that it might be understood that our birth—that is, our nature—had entered upon the very offices of our weakness. Hence it is that he hungered, thirsted, slept, was wearied, fled the assembly of the impious, was sad, wept, suffered, and died.

Did he understand Christ to have experienced all these things, which no one undergoes without some sensation of pain or torment of soul, in some different way? If so, he falsely asserted that Christ suffered all that belongs to human beings. Further, if you say that hunger, thirst, weariness, and weeping are passions of the body alone and not of the soul, what then of sadness? Yet in no. 8 he declares that he understands this to reside not in Christ’s flesh but in his soul, in these words: “The mighty seek his soul,” which in the Gospels is often sorrowful and sad [Col. 0055A–B].

105. Nor will anyone deny that anxiety is an affection proper to the soul. Yet Hilary, in *On Psalm* CXXXIX, no. 2, proclaims Christ anxious because of bodily weakness; and this, as he explains in *On Psalm* CXLI, no. 1, not as though he had a natural fear of suffering—for the Word—but in order to display the affection of the man whom he bore, “so that he might be understood to be not a feigned but a true man.” From this it also follows that the fear of Christ which he assumed, in order that he might be understood to be a true and not a feigned man, was true and not feigned. Why it is denied to be natural will be discussed below at length.

He affirms this same affection of the human mind more plainly of Christ in *On Psalm* CXXXIX, no. 11. Having asked whence the prayer of one and the same Christ could be at once accompanied by trembling and by security, he replies:

> This can be said of him on the ground that, bearing the nature both of man and of God, he has from human weakness the affection of trembling, and from the consciousness of divinity the confidence of security.

To these words must be added *On Psalm* LIV, no. 6:

> And indeed all these things which belong to our necessity rushed upon him; yet they were assumed by him through the power of his nature, while, though able not to die our death, he nevertheless did not refuse to admit into himself even the fear of death as it came upon him.

This passage contains many points worthy of notice. First, Hilary said these things in explaining the words of the Psalm: “My heart was troubled within me, and the fear of death fell upon me; fear and trembling came upon me”—words which he does not hesitate to interpret of Christ. Next, as though it were not enough to ascribe disturbance of heart, fear, and trembling to Christ, he also states generally of him: “He determined to suffer all things in himself”; shortly afterward, “Having undergone all things that are weak”; and immediately thereafter, “He endured all that belongs to our death and fear” [Col. 0055C–D].

He then touches upon the reason why Christ suffered all things: namely, that he endured them not for himself, but in order to accomplish the mysteries of human salvation. After stating the reason for which he suffered, he explains as follows: first, since it is most difficult for human weakness to keep inward disturbances and agitations of mind from breaking forth, Christ restrained them within himself and was therefore their master; secondly, since the nature of his divinity was not abolished, he underwent all things that are weak while the dignity of his majesty remained safe. From this it follows, finally, that all which he endured in the assumed flesh befell rather the person of the God who assumed it than existed in his own proper nature [Col. 0056A]. In this summary is contained nearly the whole of Hilary’s doctrine concerning Christ’s passion, a doctrine differing in nothing from the Catholic faith.

106. Perhaps you still expect a clear statement concerning Christ’s pain, the point over which the controversy is greatest. You have one, both clear and explicit, in *On Psalm* LXVIII, no. 23:

> Therefore the Lord was struck, taking upon himself our sins and suffering pain for us.

And shortly afterward:

> They therefore persecuted him thus struck by God, adding to the pain of his wounds the pain of this persecution. For, according to the prophet, he suffers pain for us.

Again, another statement no less evident occurs in no. 25. Hilary first asserts that the nature of the assuming Word was not abolished by the assumption of the form of a servant; so that what was assumed was not an inward property, but an outward addition. He then confirms this statement from the words of the Psalm: “But I am poor and sorrowful; and the salvation of thy countenance, O God, hath received me.” He explains them thus:

> He is poor who, according to the Apostle, though rich in all things, made himself poor that we might be enriched; he is sorrowful who, according to the prophet, suffers pain for us. But the salvation which is the countenance of God received this poor and sorrowful one.

He then briefly explains how he who is the image, countenance, and form of God bestowed salvation in himself upon that poor and sorrowful man whom he assumed. Thus he recognizes that the cited words of the Psalm signify Christ’s twofold nature; and that the divine nature did not fail, but bestowed salvation and glory upon the human nature [Col. 0056B–C], and did so after it had experienced poverty and pain.

107. Nor should it be omitted that, in explaining Psalm LVII, no. 5, he says:

> We remember that the power and pain of sins are signified by the thorn, when it is said: “I fell into misery when the thorn is fixed”; because, humbled even unto death, Christ condemned sin in the flesh through sin, as it were when fixed by the thorn.

Since he asserts that pain is signified in the thorn, and considers a single testimony concerning Christ’s passion sufficient proof of this point, he plainly shows that he does not even doubt that Christ, in his passion, was not without the sensation of pain. Certainly, if he regarded Christ as incapable of pain, he ought either not to have referred to Christ the words “I fell into misery when the thorn is fixed,” or else he was needlessly moved by that passage to remind us that the power and pain of sins are signified by the thorn.

That he did not remove pain from Christ is again demonstrated by these words from *On Psalm* LXVIII, no. 1:

> Having undergone the lot of all human sufferings, he speaks according to the weaknesses which he assumed from us; and indeed he suffers pain while placed beyond the necessity both of fear and of pain, yet accommodates himself to those things which he assumed, so that, being born a man in our flesh, he might speak both in the complaints of our pains and in the prayer of weakness [Col. 0056D].

108. Since it is evident from so many passages that Hilary attributed to Christ in clear and explicit words hunger, thirst, grief and sorrow, the affection of trembling, fear of death, pain—in short, all affections and passions of human weakness [Col. 0057A]—why has he been thought by some to deny these things to him? Why is the judgment of so many still uncertain concerning his opinion?

St Bonaventure, *III Sentences*, distinction 16, question 1, article 1, bears witness that some said he had retracted his earlier opinion, and that he had himself heard the bishop of Paris, William, specifically report that he had seen and read through the book of that retraction. Dionysius Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, book X, chapter 5, suspects that this book of retraction is Hilary’s own Commentary on the Psalms. He admits that in it, and particularly in *On Psalm* LXVIII, there are many things opposed to that error, from which he thinks Hilary cannot otherwise be cleared, especially in the books *On the Trinity*.

Let it meanwhile stand that in the Commentary on the Psalms—which we acknowledge, and shall prove, to be later than the books *On the Trinity* [Col. 0057B]—Hilary not only did not hold Christ to be devoid of sorrow, fear, and pain, but also taught much contrary to this error. Let us now inquire whether in the books *On the Trinity* he set forth things equally contrary to the same opinion.

## III. In Hilary’s Books *On the Trinity* There Are Many Things Contrary to Christ’s Freedom from Pain

109. It must not be denied that, for those who maintain that Christ’s incapacity for pain was defended by Hilary, book X contains a great many things which seem to favor their opinion. For what else can no. 23 seem to mean than that, although a blow or wound befell Christ, these brought on the assault of suffering but did not inflict the pain of suffering? When this is further illustrated by the comparison of a missile cast into water, fire, or air—which, though its nature is to pierce, prick, and wound, nevertheless neither pierces nor pricks nor wounds, because it is not in the nature either of water to be pierced, air to be pricked, or fire to be wounded—the preconception derived from the former words is wonderfully strengthened [Col. 0057C].

For those who think otherwise, no. 15 creates no smaller difficulty, where it is denied that Christ experienced the pain of our body because he was conceived and born not in the human manner, but through the power of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin. Thus he truly existed in the form of a servant because of the flesh assumed from the Virgin, but, because of his spiritual conception (no. 25), was free from the sins and vices of the human body.

110. Indeed, after sampling the earlier pages of this book, we were almost deterred from the very purpose of vindicating the holy man, judging it better to yield than to contradict manifest truth. But when, warned by his own instruction, we withheld assent until the end of the book, light shone from the later statements by which the darkness of the earlier could be dispelled.

Nevertheless, there would have been no occasion to think ill even of the beginning of book X, if the following final words of book IX had been beyond doubt:

> Just as, when according to man he either weeps, sleeps, or is sad, God is not to be confessed as subject to tears, fear, or sleep; but, while the truth of the Only-begotten remains sound in himself, it is necessary to understand that, according to the weakness of the flesh, he suffered weeping, sleep, thirst, weariness, and fear; and in like manner, according to man, he must be understood to have professed ignorance of the day and hour [Col. 0058A].

For these words posit, as certain and beyond controversy, that Christ as man experienced fear, sorrow, and the rest, although as God he did not know them. From this the less clear point follows: in the same way, as man he professed ignorance of the day of judgment, although as God he was not ignorant of it. With this established, the Catholic faith is upheld and every occasion for judging adversely of the following book is shut off.

No one hitherto doubted that these words were Hilary’s. Therefore there was no sufficient reason for doubting the sincerity of his faith. But let us now demonstrate this from still more certain evidence.

111. First comes the statement in book III, no. 10:

> From the cradle and infancy he had come to full manhood; through sleep, hunger, thirst, weariness, and tears he had enacted the part of a man, etc. [Col. 0058B]

Then, in book VI, no. 25, while Hilary proves by many examples that Christ not only did not conceal but repeatedly declared his bodily lowliness, he also cites this saying of Christ: “Now is my soul troubled.” He therefore held that Christ’s soul could be troubled, and actually was troubled; consequently, that the movement of suffering could affect his soul as well as his flesh.

112. That in book X he remained exactly of the same opinion is manifest even from nos. 24 and 66. There he often teaches that sorrow was assumed by Christ. “He,” he says in no. 36, “who is sad not because of death, but unto death: we must inquire whence he is sad.” And shortly afterward: “So far is the sorrow from having been assumed because of death, that it is abandoned by death”; which he repeats in no. 39.

Thus in no. 63 he teaches that Christ does not weep for himself, but for us, so that the very affection assumed from ordinary human experience might testify to the reality of the assumed man. If you desire more, you have no. 42: “He does not fear because of death, who is anxious unto death”; no. 54: “The infant cries”; no. 55: “There is no doubt that Jesus Christ truly wept”; no. 56: “He who both wept and suffered pain.” This deserves all the more notice because in that place he defends the reality of Christ’s weeping and, consequently, the reality of his pain [Col. 0058C]. Finally, in no. 67 you hear in general terms: “The only-begotten God indeed suffered what human beings can suffer.”

113. Nor did he leave any doubt about the extent to which he excluded fear, sorrow, and pain from Christ. In no. 48, after setting out at length what belonged to Christ’s human nature and what to his divine nature, he concludes that according to man Christ suffers all weak things for us, but according to God triumphs in them all. Using the same distinction again in no. 62, he says:

> In him who complains that he has been abandoned unto death, you have him because he is man; in him who dies yet professes that he reigns in paradise, you have him because he is God [Col. 0058D].

114. Gradually and imperceptibly, the conjecture collapses and falls of those who think Hilary exempted both Christ’s divine and human nature from the affections of our weakness. They suppose they confirm this contention by arguing that, although he could easily have extricated himself from the objections by employing the distinction of the two natures, he nevertheless took another route and resorted to other defenses [Col. 0059A].

Certainly, how far he was from neglecting this distinction is again witnessed by *On Psalm* LV, no. 2, where he proposes to regulate his discourse thus: because Christ “bore the weaknesses of all and often used both the voices and tears of our sins, the affection and speech that belong to man are without reproach to God.” For there God and man are distinguished in Christ; and, since in the man the speech and also the affection of weak man are acknowledged, we are warned that this is to be understood without reproach to God.

Likewise, in the Commentaries on Matthew, which it is almost certain were written before the books *On the Trinity*, he distinguishes the weakness of the flesh in Christ from the power of the Word. He thus grants that Christ’s hunger was real according to the weakness of the flesh, yet that it did not steal upon him except insofar as the power of the Word willed and permitted it. Therefore, in chapter 3, no. 2, he says:

> When the Lord hungered, it was not the working of a middle nature that crept in; rather, that Power, unmoved by the fasting of forty days, abandoned to its own nature the man. For the devil was to be conquered not by God, but by the flesh; and he would certainly not have dared to tempt it unless, through the weakness of hunger, he had recognized in it the things that belong to man [Col. 0059B].

And in no. 3:

> Therefore in tempting he proposed the condition of a work through which he might recognize in God, from the changing of stones into bread, the power of authority; and in man might mock, by the delight of food, the endurance of hunger.

He knew so well how to distinguish in Christ what belongs to God and what belongs to man that, while asserting in him the power able to avert hunger, he freely also confesses the weakness that was permitted to undergo hunger—a hunger so real that because of it he attributes to Christ the merit of endurance [Col. 0059C].

115. Moreover, Hilary observes repeatedly, and expressly in book XI, no. 6, that the source of all the errors which he undertook to refute was this: his opponents seized upon the dispensation of the assumed body in order to dishonor the divinity, and took grounds of impiety from the mystery of our salvation. He says that one must deal with them in such a way that, by distinguishing what belongs to God from what belongs to the times and mysteries, divinity receives no dishonor and the dispensation introduces no error. He further reminds us that on this basis all their objections are dissolved, and that he had dissolved them in the preceding books.

We can scarcely wonder sufficiently how he has been said to have neglected this manner of answering. Is it because that method is not peculiar to him alone, or at least because he did not inculcate it frequently enough? But when the Arians denied Christ’s divinity on account of what he suffered, would he have done enough if he had merely answered that these things befell his human, not his divine, nature? Would he not have seemed, as they say, to beg the question?

It was necessary for him not only to say but also to demonstrate that besides the weak nature like our own there was in Christ another nature, vastly superior, wholly ignorant of weakness, incorruptible and immutable, to whose power nothing did not yield. This was the task; this was the labor. It is also the purpose of the whole of book X. The understanding of that book especially determines the understanding of those statements on account of which the Catholic bishop fell under suspicion of error. In order that this may become clearer [Col. 0060A], something must first necessarily be said concerning those heretics who maintained that Christ’s divinity suffered, and who are therefore called Theopaschites.

## IV. On the Heresy Which Asserted That Christ’s Divinity Suffered

116. After Philastrius of Brescia, Augustine, in *On Heresies* 75, addressed to Quodvultdeus, mentions a certain heresy without naming its authors. It asserted that in Christ the divinity suffered pain when his flesh was fastened to the cross. The Roman council under Damasus condemned it in its letter to Paulinus of Antioch, in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 11, in these words:

> If anyone says that in the passion of the cross the Son endured pain in his divinity itself, and not in the flesh and rational soul which he assumed in the form of a servant, as Sacred Scripture speaks, let him be anathema [Col. 0060B].

Perhaps from this arose the ancient custom that a bishop about to be ordained should be asked: “Do you believe that the Son of God is impassible and immortal in his divinity, but suffered for us and for our salvation in his humanity through a true suffering of the flesh?” Certainly Pelagius, in Augustine, Appendix, Sermon 236, no. 5, condemns the same error in express terms in the confession of faith sent to the Apostolic See.

117. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 46, relates that Apollinarius was an advocate of this heresy, and testifies that he had in his hands a treatise by him in which Apollinarius taught and tried to prove that the Only-begotten God, judge of all, author of life, destroyer of death, was mortal; that he suffered in his own divinity; and that in that three-day death of the body, the divinity also died together with the body, and was thus restored from death to life again by the work of the Father. Pope Leo plainly agrees with Gregory in letter formerly 73, now 97, chapter 2.

Yet Apollinarius, in Leontius, *Against the Frauds of the Apollinarians*, tries to prove himself alien from this view, where he anathematizes anyone who does not say that Christ’s flesh was from Mary, and anyone who says that this flesh is of an uncreated nature and *homoousios*—of the same substance—with God; indeed, also anyone who says that divinity is passible and that the passions of the soul arise from divinity itself. Likewise he approves, in these terms, Athanasius’s letter to Epictetus, written to suppress the same error:

> We have strongly approved the letter of my lord sent to Corinth; and we have condemned the great madness of those who say that the flesh is consubstantial with God.

Although these letters may appear either spurious, or rather to be letters of an inconsistent heretic [Col. 0060C–D]. For Gregory of Nazianzus observes that Apollinarius and his disciples did not remain consistent with themselves; and near the end of *Oration* 52 he shows that they sometimes distinguish Christ’s diverse natures and sometimes refuse to distinguish them. Theodoret notes a similar inconsistency in Apollinarius’s doctrine in *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 3, cited by Liberatus, chapter 3.

118. Although Apollinarius can with great difficulty be cleared of the perverse opinion of the Theopaschites, nevertheless the canons 11 and 12 of the Council of Sirmium in the year 351 demonstrate that he was not its first author:

> If anyone supposes that the Word was transformed into flesh, or that he underwent change by taking flesh, let him be anathema.  
>   
> If anyone, hearing that the only Son of God was crucified, says that his divinity endured corruption or passibility (*pathos*, πάθος), or change or death, let him be anathema [Col. 0061A].

For Apollinarius did not begin to be called a heretic before the year 360.

119. Indeed, those who wrote against him—Liberatus, chapter 3; Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 51; and Athanasius near the end of *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ*—represent him not as the originator of this invention, but as an imitator of the Arians. From the words of Phoebadius of Agen it appears that Potamius was a teacher of the same blasphemy.

Likewise, if credence is due to the letter of the Synod of Sardica, in the longer form of that portion found in Theodoret, Ursacius and Valens were deposed because they asserted that the Word and the Spirit were crucified, wounded, died, and rose again. Baronius also writes, under the year 324, nos. 109 and 110, that Eusebius Pamphili was infected with the madness of the Theopaschites. But what he adduces from Eusebius’s letter to Constantia in proof of this establishes nothing. Indeed, from book IV of Eusebius’s *Evangelical Demonstration*, chapter 13, you would more suitably infer that he thought otherwise. Nor was this error common to all who favored Arius, but peculiar to certain notable Arians, and especially to the Anomoeans [Col. 0061B].

120. In order more easily to defend that perverse doctrine, those faithless enemies of Christ invented the claim that the Word assumed a body alone, without a soul. Theodoret is witness, at the beginning of Dialogue II, that this fiction was not invented first by Apollinarius but received by him from the Arians. There he says that Arius and Eunomius held the divinity of the Only-begotten to be created, and said that he assumed a body alone.

Augustine too was aware of this Arian opinion, which he considered less well known. Thus he writes in *On Heresies*, chapter 19:

> In holding that Christ assumed flesh without a soul, the Arians are less well known; nor have I found that anyone has contended against them on this matter. Yet Epiphanius did not conceal that this was true—*Heresy* 69, nos. 49 and 50, and *Ancoratus*, no. 33—and I have learned it with complete certainty from certain of their writings and conversations [Col. 0061C].

Nevertheless, many others learned it as well. Athanasius plainly discloses this view of theirs at the beginning of *On the Saving Advent*:

> Arius confesses flesh alone for the concealment of the divinity; and for our inward man—that is, the soul—he says that the Word was in the flesh, daring to ascribe the sensation of suffering and resurrection from the dead to divinity.

The Arians were well known in this respect also to Eustathius of Antioch, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Phoebadius.

121. They differed from the Apollinarians only in this: among the Apollinarians it was the primary doctrine that the Word assumed a body without a soul; whereas the Arians taught this only secondarily, in order that their capital proposition concerning the weakness of the Word’s divinity might prevail. Athanasius touches upon this distinction between them near the end of *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ*. Refuting those who held that the Word supplied the place of a soul, he says:

> Thus it will follow that the wounding of the body is held to be a suffering of the Word himself. For this is the source of your assertion that God suffered. It is an apt saying, one that suits you very well and agrees most excellently with the Arians. For they too establish the same thing in their doctrines [Col. 0062A].

But Eustathius of Antioch, in Theodoret, Dialogue 3, more plainly uncovers the purpose of the Arians in asserting the assumption of an inanimate body. He asks, “Why do they make much of showing that Christ assumed an inanimate body?” and replies: in order that, if they can persuade anyone of this, then by attributing the changes of affections to his divine Spirit, they may more easily persuade them that what is mutable was not begotten from an immutable nature.

Thus Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 51, no. 13, testifies that they proclaimed Christ to be an inanimate man in order to ascribe suffering to his divinity, as though that which moves also itself suffers. And Leontius, *On Sects*, act III:

> For this reason the Arian doctrine taught that Christ’s body was inanimate: so that we might attribute such lowly utterances not to Christ as man, but to God the Son, and from his own statement find the Son to be less than the Father [Col. 0062B].

The words of Phoebadius of Agen, Hilary’s contemporary, concerning a letter sent from east and west—or, as conjectured, from the west to the east—serve the same purpose:

> One of you asserts that, when Christ’s flesh and Spirit were coagulated through Mary’s blood and made into one body, God became passible.

There is no need to remind us that here, following ancient usage, “Spirit” means the divine nature. That this was the opinion not of one but of many he immediately indicates in these words:

> You apply to God whatever has been said concerning his manhood, so that God himself is joined to human weakness and perhaps is wounded.

These men, holding that God was joined, after the manner and in the place of a soul, to the flesh taken from Mary, could conceive him to have become passible just as a soul, over which bodies in themselves have no power, becomes subject to suffering through its union with flesh. But let it stand that the Arians held that God the Word, as Hilary says in *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 50, “failed into a soul”; and that they held this in order to subject Christ, according to his divine nature, to hunger, fear, sorrow, and pain [Col. 0062C].

122. Although this is already established more than sufficiently, the lies of certain schismatics who violently inveighed against Cyril will help illuminate the truth of the matter. Their testimony is somewhat long, but highly relevant. They say of Cyril, in their Letter to Rufus, volume III of Labbe’s Councils, p. 739:

> He teaches that the divinity of the only-begotten Son of God suffered, but not the humanity; since the indwelling divinity attributed the sufferings of the body to itself as though they were its own, although in its own nature it suffered nothing. He further adds that one nature was made from divinity and humanity. … He curses those who distinguish the evangelical and apostolic utterances concerning Christ the Lord, referring the lowly ones to the humanity and the divine ones to Christ’s divinity.

They continue:

> The Arians and Eunomians, holding this view and referring the lowly utterances of the dispensation to divinity, did not hesitate to assert that God the Word was a creature and a thing made, of another substance and unequal to the Father.

Anyone can readily understand what blasphemy follows from these principles. For the natures are confused, and these words are attributed to God the Word: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” and, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me”; likewise hunger, thirst, angelic strengthening, and the rest [Col. 0062D–0063A]. Anyone can easily see that these accord plainly with the impiety of Arius and Eunomius.

With these things premised, it will be easier to see what Hilary proposes to do in book X of *On the Trinity*, and what his opinion is.

## V. Hilary Argues Concerning Christ’s Sorrow, Fear, Pain, and the Rest Against Heretics Who Attributed Them to the Word. How He Resists Them

123. Hilary seems chiefly in two places to remove fear, pain, sorrow, and other affections of human weakness from Christ: namely, in *On Matthew*, chapter 31, and in book X of *On the Trinity*. Yet in both places it is quite plain that he is contending against heretics who referred these things to Christ’s divinity itself.

For immediately at the beginning of chapter 31 of *On Matthew*, he declares that he is dealing with those whose opinion is that sadness could have fallen upon God on his own account, and that fear of the coming passion broke him because he said, “My soul is sorrowful,” etc.; and who maintain that, because of bodily weakness, suffering clings to the Spirit [Col. 0063B].

Nor does he propose to defeat any other opponents throughout book X of *On the Trinity*. For after he had attacked in the preceding books a doctrine common to the whole sect, he now addresses himself to what not all Arians, but most of them, defended with greater impiety concerning Christ. Before setting out their arguments against himself, he explains their views in no. 9:

> For most of them wish him not to have been in the nature of the impassible God; so that, because he feared and suffered pain, he was not in that security of power which does not fear, nor in that incorruptibility of Spirit which does not suffer pain, but, being of a nature inferior to God the Father, trembled from fear of human suffering and groaned at the severity of bodily punishment [Col. 0063C].

He then appends their objections, which furnish the subject matter of the whole book. But to attack heretics of this kind is to defend the proposition that Christ suffered according to his human nature. For, as Gregory of Nyssa says in *Oration* 5 against Eunomius, cited by Theodoret, Dialogue 3: “Since the question is twofold and ambiguous—whether divinity or humanity suffered—the rejection of one will be the confirmation of the other.”

124. That Hilary rejected our weaknesses from Christ’s divinity alone is evident from the fact that, after he said that the heretics wished suffering to adhere to divinity because of the assumption of the body, he rebukes them in these words:

> As though the assumption of flesh infected that power of incorruptible substance with the lot of its weakness, and eternity received the nature of frailty. If it is sad because of fear, weak because of pain, trembling because of death, then it will also be subject to corruption [*On Matthew*, chapter 31, no. 2; Col. 0063D].

He then shows that God is wholly free from corruption or change; he does not at all consider man. Indeed, he sufficiently indicates that he does not wish to ascribe the same prerogative to Christ’s human nature, since he admits that this Arian doctrine agrees with the opinion by which they believe the Son of God to be created and not eternal. “For,” he says in no. 3,

> their whole meaning is that they suppose fear of death fell upon the Son of God, since they assert that he was not brought forth from eternity nor existed from the infinity of the Father’s substance, but was made from nothing by him who created him; so that he was assumed from nothing, begun by a work, and confirmed in time. And therefore in him there is anxiety of pain, and therefore a suffering of Spirit with the suffering of body [Col. 0064A].

Thus, just as they imagined for themselves a created divinity of the Only-begotten and consequently constructed the claim that it suffered and was crucified, so Hilary, after showing it to be uncreated and eternal, concludes far more effectively: “Therefore nothing in God could die, nor is there any fear in God from himself.” Why, I ask, did he add “from himself,” unless because he did not doubt that, from the side of the man to whom God in Christ is joined, both fear and death could be in God?

125. So little did he doubt it, and so certain and evident from Scripture did he think the matter, that without lingering to prove it, he immediately hastened to investigate the causes of such affections. He continues:

> Since we read that the Lord was sorrowful, let us find the causes of his sorrow.

Having examined these, he adds in no. 4:

> Therefore he is sorrowful unto death. It is not death, then, but the time of death which is feared.

No sound person seeks the causes of a thing that does not exist. These few remarks on the Commentary on Matthew are sufficient [Col. 0064B].

126. Moreover, in addition to what we have said, Hilary himself sufficiently declares in the argument to book X set at the beginning of his work, book I, nos. 31 and 32, that book X is directed against those alone who assail the divinity of the Word. He says:

> Because certain persons, through the judgment of foolish understanding, seized upon the character and profession of Christ’s passion to dishonor the divine nature and power in the Lord Jesus Christ, it was necessary to show that these very things had been understood by them in a most impious manner.

Thus the sole purpose of book X is to convict those heretics, who seized upon Christ’s words and deeds in his passion to dishonor his divine nature, of having understood them most impiously. He soon makes clearer in what way they understood them impiously: namely, by forgetting the nature and profession of divinity, they employed the deeds and sayings of the dispensation as an argument for their impiety. If these words seem ambiguous to anyone, let him compare book IX, no. 5:

> Hence there is an opportunity for heretics to deceive the simple and ignorant, by falsely asserting that those things which were said by him according to man were said according to the weakness of the divine nature [Col. 0064C].

From this the following argument may be formed. Hilary professes that in book X he will dispute with heretics who wish the words and deeds of the dispensation to befall God; and the heretics with whom he disputes seize upon whatever is written concerning Christ’s fear, sorrow, and pain, in order to show him to be a weak God. Therefore he grants that all that is written concerning Christ’s fear, sorrow, and pain belongs to the words and deeds of the dispensation—that is, that it befalls the man assumed by the Word [Col. 0064D]. But let us proceed to the book itself.

127. As Hilary does not in that book turn the attention of his mind away from the opinions of the aforesaid heretics, so neither ought the reader to turn his attention away from their opinions. They are indeed varied, but may suitably be reduced to two. Some so confuse the Word with the flesh that, according to their opinion (no. 50), God the Word “failed from himself” while he gives life to the body in the office of a soul; others so divide him from the man that, as the spirit of prophecy was in the prophets, so the Word of God was in Jesus [Col. 0065A].

128. Whoever attends to these points will have no difficulty with the many passages in which Hilary often seems to deny what he merely wishes to show cannot possibly be explained from the opinions of his adversaries. Nor will it escape him why, for example, in no. 10, before he refutes the objections, he attacks his opponents in these words: “And I ask those who think thus whether it is consistent that He should have feared to die, who, banishing from the Apostles every terror of death, exhorted them to the glory of martyrdom . . .; and further, what pain of death should He fear, who was to die by the freedom of His own power?” By this kind of argument, frequent in that book [Col. 0065B], the advocates even of opposing opinions are, as it were, pierced by a two-edged sword: since neither party has anything by which to reconcile Christ’s power with infirmity. Certainly, while in nos. 55 and 56 he pursues those heretics with this reasoning, one might think that he had altogether rejected the reality of Christ’s weeping, unless he had added at the end of no. 55: “And yet there is no doubt that Jesus Christ truly wept”; and had concluded no. 56 thus: “It is not the part of one who is to give life to weep, nor of one who is to glorify to grieve; and yet He gives life, He who both wept and grieved.”

129. He used that manner of argument all the more willingly because it was especially suited to restraining the arrogance of those who, boasting that they comprehended all Christ’s mysteries, defined them at their pleasure. For what Athanasius says rather obscurely at the end of his book *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ* [Col. 0065C]—“Foolish are those who ascribe suffering to His divinity, or do not have faith in His humanity, or divide the one into two, or attempt to determine the measure of His flesh, defining how great it was and in what manner, apart from the holy Scriptures”—is illuminated by this tenth book of Hilary, whose entire latter part is occupied in restraining those who claim for themselves another knowledge of Christ than that revealed in Scripture.

130. Nor, content merely to shut the mouths of those speaking wickedly, after having somewhat tormented them by the question posed in no. 10, does he fail to turn to the utter overthrow of their opinions, laying the foundations on which the truth may be established. For immediately considering Christ’s unique birth and conception, he shows Him to be true God and perfect man [Col. 0065D], with the natures so distinct that the power and nature of the Word did not depart from itself, and so united that the Son of God is not one person and the Son of Man another. To what end, I ask, is the distinction and conjunction of the natures in Him asserted in order to remove from Christ the disgrace of our sufferings? Let us not forget that he is resisting those heretics to whom Phoebadius speaks thus: “Not distinguishing the twofold condition of the Lord’s power, each differing in its own property, you apply to God whatever is said of His manhood, so that God Himself may be joined to man in weakness. And therefore you wish this twofold condition to appear not united but confused”; and shortly afterwards: “Therefore let not Spirit be flesh, nor flesh Spirit, as these excellent teachers desire, so that our Lord and God may, that is, have become passible through this mixture of substances.” Their advocate, at the beginning of Theodoret’s third dialogue, first affirms that Christ assumed flesh so that what was impassible might endure suffering; and then, when asked by the Orthodox speaker, “To which nature should weariness be assigned—to the divinity or to the body?” he answers, “I do not dare divide what has been united.” The Orthodox: “Then, as appears, you attribute weariness to the divine nature.” Eranistes: “So it seems to me.” Whoever keeps these matters in mind will easily perceive that Hilary explains so laboriously the distinction and conjunction of the natures in the one Christ for this reason alone: that from it he may give the reason why sufferings which properly belong to the one human nature are attributed to the impassible God. Therefore, when he maintains against those heretics that Christ God received no sensation of pain from the sufferings of the body, it is as though he said: “You deprive Christ of that property of nature which cannot suffer, because you either confuse the Word with the flesh or separate it from the flesh. But your opinion is false. Although the Word is so joined to the body that the sufferings of man are attributed to Him, and He is therefore thought to suffer pain, nevertheless He remains so unconfused that, although the body receives those sufferings from which pain naturally follows, they lack that effect upon His own proper nature.” This explanation, which we now offer on probable grounds but shall be able to demonstrate conclusively from the final pages of the book, will contribute greatly to understanding the entire work.

[Col. 0066C] 131. Yet there is a difficulty, because in that passage he discusses Christ’s unique conception in such a way as to seem to exempt not only the divine nature of the only-begotten God, but also His body, from the common law of our sufferings. Indeed, we were initially so disturbed by this that we have already confessed ourselves almost deterred from defending him. But, rereading the opinions of the heretics against whom he contends, we discovered that they proclaim Christ to be a mere man who, because both Adam’s body and soul were in sin, received Adam’s flesh and soul also, and into whose soul a DOMINATING fear of impending sorrow entered, and so forth. Nor thereafter did it remain hidden from us how, with faith wholly safe and sound, he defends even the privilege belonging to Christ’s body.

132. For since fear, sorrow, and pain dominate us only because of original sin [Col. 0066D], he rightly maintains that Christ, even according to His manhood, was not subject to those dominating disturbances, showing from the manner of His conception that He was free from the defects of our origin. Hence, when he says in no. 27: “Was there weakness in His body, at whose encounter the terrified ranks of His pursuers fell?” we understand from the words immediately following—“What weakness, then, do you believe DOMINATED the body of Him whose nature possessed such great power?”—that he did not remove every weakness from Christ’s body (otherwise he would contradict himself), but only dominating weakness.

133. To the same purpose belongs the statement in no. 24: “The assumed flesh—that is, the whole man—was permitted to the natures of suffering; yet not so permitted that it should be overcome by the injuries of sufferings.” It is as though he said: The assumed man, both in body and in soul, was permitted to our sufferings insofar as they are natural, not insofar as they are injurious and disgraceful. Now it is natural to man that, when the body suffers, the soul should be moved by some motion; but that it cannot restrain that motion whenever it wishes is injurious and disgraceful to it, being a penalty of sin. In this way he could, in no. 15, deny that Christ experienced the pain of our body, and in no. 47 say: “He grieves for us, and yet does not grieve with the sensation of our pain.” For our pain necessarily stings us and dominates us even against our will and resistance; His, however, was entirely voluntary and freely assumed. For, being offered when He willed, just as He laid down His soul by His own power, so He assumed pain by His own power. Indeed, if Augustine’s definition is true, one who suffers voluntarily must be denied to suffer pain. For pain of the flesh, as he defines it in *The City of God*, book XIV, chapter 15, is simply an offence of the soul arising from the flesh, and a certain dissent from its suffering; just as pain of the soul, called sorrow, is dissent from things which happen to us against our will. When these things are understood, no suspicion, even a slight one, of error will remain in what Hilary expounds in commending Christ’s unique conception. From this he rightly proves that God assumed man and, in assuming him, did not depart from Himself; and therefore that there is something in Christ free from our infirmity. Nor does he less fittingly demonstrate in accordance with our faith that Christ, even according to His manhood, because He derives His origin from the power of the Word and not from our manner of conception [Col. 0067C], was not subject to our sufferings, although He voluntarily submitted Himself to them.

134. He is chiefly occupied with this argument concerning Christ’s unique conception down to no. 26. Then he returns to the reasoning which he first employed and which holds first place throughout the book: namely, by which he shows heretics who affirm Christ’s divinity either to be nonexistent or emptied, that in all His deeds and sayings—even those by which He signifies Himself to be man and weak—another nature may be discerned, one able to expel every weakness from itself and to exercise every power. For, as he observes, when He is born, He derives His birth from a Virgin and the Holy Spirit; when He hungers, by a word alone He withers a tree; while thirsting, He supplies from Himself rivers of living water [Col. 0067D]; He bears a body and walks upon the waves; He weeps and yet rejoices at Lazarus’ death; He dies, yet no one takes His soul from Him, but He Himself gives it up and has power to take it again. Similar instances are scattered throughout; of these we select here what he states more compactly in no. 67, in the manner of a conclusion:

“Christ was born of a Virgin; but according to the Scriptures He was conceived of the Holy Spirit. Christ wept; but according to the Scriptures, in that wherein He wept, He rejoiced. Christ hungered; but according to the Scriptures God acted without food upon the tree which had no fruit. Christ suffered; but according to the Scriptures He was then to sit at the right hand of Power. He complained that He was forsaken unto death; but according to the Scriptures He then received His confessor with Himself in the kingdom of paradise [Col. 0068A]. He died; but according to the Scriptures, rising again, the Lord sat at the right hand of the Lord.”

See similar statements in Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 35, p. 575.

135. In these passages, moreover, he so frames his words that, while denying in Christ those infirmities and affections which would dishonor a man substantially joined to God, he nevertheless often affirms their reality in Him. Thus no. 67 cited above begins: “The only-begotten God indeed suffered what men can suffer.” This is again evident from what he says in nos. 55 and 56 concerning Christ’s weeping. Often also, from the accompanying circumstances, it is understood that he removes every mark of weakness from the one nature whose power is wholly divine; for example, when he says in no. 34: “This bodily fear does not possess Him, who penetrates hell indeed, but is extended everywhere by the power of His nature”; and in no. 44: “Therefore the anxiety of human trembling is not in that nature which is above man.”

136. But from those passages in which he either seeks or explains the causes of Christ’s sorrow, fear, and pain, we are much more certainly persuaded that he removes from the human nature of our Mediator and Redeemer only the disgrace, not the reality, of these affections. That disgrace consisted in His either grieving for His own sake or being overwhelmed by dominating pain. Certainly, as has already been observed, one is far from denying sorrow or pain in a person concerning whom one asks whence he is sorrowful or whence he suffers pain. And lest Hilary’s opinion in explaining these causes should appear unique, one should refer here to the words of Ambrose, both in *On Luke*, book X, nos. 57 and 61, and in *On Faith*, book II, chapter 7, no. 54; of Augustine on Psalm XL, no. 6; and of Jerome on Matthew, chapter 26, copied by Bede on the same passage. But whoever wishes may compare what Augustine says in the cited passage with Hilary’s tenth book, no. 10; and the words of Ambrose, Jerome, and Bede with no. 37 of the same book, as also with chapter 31 on Matthew. Meanwhile, let us hasten to examine the conclusion of the said tenth book.

137. Finally, after setting Christ’s manifold power against the heretics who look only to His one infirmity, and convicting them of possessing nothing in their own faith by which they may escape from the difficulty of sayings and deeds so diverse, he opens for them an easy path in the faith of the Church. For, since it confesses distinct natures in the one person of Christ [Col. 0068D], it has no difficulty reconciling matters so opposed. “For,” he says in no. 62, “one and the same is the Lord Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, signifying Himself through all these things: when He signifies that He is forsaken unto death, He is man; but while He is man, He reigns as God in paradise,” etc. And at the end of the same number: “In the mystery of the Son of Man and the Son of God, we have Him who dies reigning, and Him who reigns dying.” Thereafter, all the way to the end, he is entirely engaged in commending and expounding this faith of the Church. Hence it is clear why in the opening pages of his book he attacked the heretics who either confused or divided Christ’s natures: namely, so that, having overthrown their defenses, he might lay the foundations of the Catholic faith, according to which God, by reason of His conjunction with man, is truly said to have suffered and been crucified [Col. 0069A], yet is believed to have suffered with the nature of His divinity safe and whole. Thus his doctrine is approved as entirely consonant with sound and orthodox faith. To make this clearer, the force of certain terms must be considered.

## VI. What “suffering” or “to suffer” means for Hilary; what Christ is; and what Christ’s nature or power is

138. He himself explains unambiguously in *On the Synods*, no. 49, what he means by the word “suffering,” when, on the twelfth canon of the Council of Sirmium, he adds:

“It is plainly shown why the Word, although made flesh, was not nevertheless transformed into flesh. For although these kinds of sufferings affect the weakness of the flesh, yet God the Word, made flesh, could not by suffering become changeable from Himself [Col. 0069B]. For to suffer and to be changed are not the same thing, because every kind of suffering changes all flesh by sensation, pain, and endurance. But the Word which was made flesh, although He submitted Himself to suffering, was not changed by the passibility of suffering. For He could suffer, yet could not be passible; because passibility is the signification of a weak nature, whereas suffering is the endurance of things inflicted. And since God is unchangeable, although the Word was made flesh, these things had in Him matter for suffering without the weakness of passibility. Therefore His nature remains unchangeable even in suffering, because the substance born, not different from its Author, is of an impassible essence.”

139. Whether, having confessed here that the Word could suffer, he consistently said that He was not passible, does not belong to the present inquiry. Perhaps he was compelled to this manner of speaking in order to close every entrance to the heretics, who held that the Word, by assuming flesh, had become capable of suffering in His own substance. But because definitions of terms depend upon choice, there is no difference where the several matters are distinctly explained. Nor is it obscure that he calls “suffering” that by which the Word is denominated to have suffered, while “passibility” is that which affects and changes the very nature of the Word. Once this is granted, he rightly denies that the Word was made passible by the suffering of the flesh. Yet he sufficiently indicates that he claims this privilege of impassibility for the Word alone, since he defends it for the Word on that one ground—that His nature is unchangeable. Indeed, when he grants that every kind of suffering changes all flesh by sensation, pain, and endurance, and confesses that the Word made flesh submitted Himself to suffering, he confesses that Christ, according to the assumed man [Col. 0069D], was changed by sensation, pain, and endurance. For, just as when he says that the Word was made flesh he understands that the whole man was assumed by the Word, so he understands that the whole man was subjected to suffering by the Word, when he says that the Word made flesh submitted Himself to suffering. “The assumed flesh,” he says in *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 24, “that is, the whole man, was permitted to the natures of suffering.”

140. If you next consider what “Christ” signifies in Hilary, you will observe that, when he uses this term without qualification, he is accustomed to understand and denote the nature of the Word alone. A clear example occurs in *On the Trinity*, book IX, no. 14:

“The emptying has this effect: that the form of a servant advances, not that Christ, who was in the form of God, should cease to remain CHRIST; since none but CHRIST received the form of a servant.”

It would be superfluous to adduce more examples, since anyone, now admonished, may do so for himself.

141. Perhaps he used this manner of speaking because Christ is the name of a person, and there is no person in Him other than that of the Word. Or, wholly intent upon defending Christ’s divinity, he was accustomed to contemplate most willingly in Him that which is divine. Thus the sweet name of Christ tasted to him of God and resounded God. We are confirmed in this opinion not a little by these words from no. 5 of the same book:

“Hence heretics have an opportunity to deceive the simple and ignorant, by falsely asserting that what He said according to the man assumed by Him was said according to the weakness of the divine nature; and because one and the same is speaking all that He speaks, they maintain that He spoke OF HIMSELF [Col. 0070B].”

Why, I ask, does he deny that those things which Christ said according to the man assumed by Him were said by Him concerning Himself? Surely not because he thinks that the Word and the assumed man are not one person, since he complains that the heretics seize upon this as an occasion for deception. Rather, because he regards as assumed—and consequently as, in a sense, adventitious and extraneous in Christ—whatever does not suit Him as Word and God. In this manner of speaking Ambrose agrees with him. For, considering Christ’s words in *On Luke*, book X, no. 61—“My soul is sorrowful,” and “My soul is troubled”—he says: “Therefore it is not He who assumes, but that which is assumed, which is troubled. For the soul is subject to passions; divinity is free. Finally, the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. He is sorrowful, however, not HE Himself, but His soul.” Augustine agrees with both of them in many passages, and especially on Psalm XXXVII, no. 11, where he says: “For Christ did not show HIMSELF on earth, but showed His flesh.” Likewise Justin, at the beginning of the First Apology, teaches that the names Christ and Jesus must be distinguished, the latter referred to the flesh and the former to divinity:

“The Son of God, who alone is properly called Son, is called CHRIST because through Him God fashioned and adorned all things . . .; but JESUS has both the name and designation of man and Savior.”

142. It follows from this observation that what Hilary affirms or denies concerning Christ simply stated should, for the most part, be referred to His divine nature [Col. 0070D]. If to this you add what has just been observed concerning the word “suffering,” you will without difficulty hear that Christ had a body capable of suffering and did suffer, but did not have a nature capable of pain. For in these words nothing else presents itself than that the Word in Christ was capable indeed of suffering, since He assumed passible flesh, but not capable of pain, since change cannot in any way belong to His nature.

143. It will sometimes also be helpful to remember that by “flesh” or “body” alone the entire human nature is signified, while the divine nature is often signified by the terms “spirit” or “eternity.”

144. The meaning of the word *nature* is of much greater importance. Hunaldus, in Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, observed that understanding it was necessary for grasping Hilary’s statements [Col. 0071A], but he himself did not understand it sufficiently perfectly. Now it is clear from many examples that Hilary constantly opposes Christ’s nature to His dispensation and assumed infirmity, just as he opposes His natural attributes to His assumed attributes. Hence in book IX, no. 33, he divides all Christ’s names and titles into natural and assumed ones. And in book X, defending that Christ is at once in the form of God and in the form of a servant, he explains in no. 22 the distinction by which He contains both forms in Himself:

“For He who is in the form of a servant is also in the form of God; and the latter belongs to NATURE, but the former to DISPENSATION,” etc.

Again, no. 65: “Having in Himself, one and the same, through DISPENSATION and NATURE, in the form of God and in the form of a servant,” etc.; and no. 66: “Though He was man BY DISPENSATION, He nevertheless remained God BY NATURE”; and shortly afterward: “Thus, though weakness came from the form of a servant, NATURE remained from the form of God.”

145. Had Erasmus observed these things, when on Psalm LXVIII he encountered no. 9—“Therefore in the only-begotten God there was not NATURAL weakness, but ASSUMED weakness”—and no. 18—“All our weaknesses that were in Him are not NATURAL, but ASSUMED”—he would never have objected: “How are they not natural to Him who assumed nature?” For he would have understood that they are denied to be natural not to the assumed man but to the Word who assumes; and that they are called assumed because, by assuming the nature of flesh, He assumed them into Himself, though previously He was alien to them by His own nature. For, as Augustine says on Psalm XCIII, no. 19: “The only-begotten God assumed sorrow as He assumed flesh.” But, as our Hilary says on Psalm LXVIII, no. 9 [Col. 0071C], “He assumed a body alien to His own nature.” Hence in the letter ascribed to Dionysius of Alexandria, tome I of the Councils, p. 854, Christ is asserted to be man not by nature but God by nature: **οὐ φύσει ἄνθρωπος, ἀλλὰ φύσει θεός**—“not man by nature, but God by nature.” And Cyril, in *On John*, book XI, chapter 12, teaches that human nature was united to God the Word **σχετικῶς**, “relatively” or “by relation,” not **φυσικῶς**, “naturally,” since of itself and by its own condition it does not possess the capacity to be one with God. Therefore sorrow and our other weaknesses were alien to Christ’s nature and, consequently, not natural to Him: not natural, I say, not to His mortal nature, but to the nature from which He had the power of rising again. Hilary explains this on Psalm LIII, no. 7, where, after saying, “He both prayed and suffered all things that belong to men . . . hence He hungered, thirsted, and so forth,” he adds: “And so that it might be understood that He was subject to all these things NOT BY NATURE [Col. 0071D], BUT BY ASSUMPTION, having undergone them all, He rose again.”

146. Nor is it obscure why he employed this manner of speaking. For what was observed above concerning the force of the term “Christ” has much greater application here. Since there is one person in Christ, that of the Word, whose proper nature is divine, and to whom the human nature was added, although through substantial conjunction, yet by voluntary assumption, why may He not regard the latter as extraneous? But if the assumed man is, as it were, something extraneous to Christ, then everything belonging to the assumed man will likewise be extraneous to Him. Therefore, when on Psalm CXXXIX, no. 2, he says: “For that He is God belongs to His own nature, but that He was man is an assumption of our nature”; and when on Psalm LXVIII, no. 25, he proves the assertion that the assumption of the servant-form is not nature in the sense of a condition and origin genuinely His own, on the ground that what is assumed is not an inward property but an outward addition—he speaks consistently with himself in *On the Trinity*, book IX, no. 7, when he calls the things of the assumed man the things of our nature, while calling divine things the things of His own nature, as follows:

“The man born spoke according to the custom of our nature. For although in birth, suffering, and death He performed the things of OUR NATURE, He nevertheless performed all those very things by the power of HIS OWN NATURE: while He Himself is the source of His birth; while He wills to suffer what He cannot be made to suffer; while He dies who lives.”

147. It is now therefore clear how, without injury to the faith, he could say on Psalm CXXXVIII, no. 3: “The assumption of weakness did not make Him weak, because it is one thing to be a nature and another to have assumed a nature; and an addition by will lies outside the necessity of kind.” Nor is this statement any more suspect, from the exposition of Psalm LIV, no. 6: “He endured all things belonging to our death and fear in such a way that they rather fell upon Him than existed in Him, since they are more our weakness than something natural in God.” For our weaknesses fall upon the divine person to whom they are attributed, but do not exist in His proper nature, because the nature assumed from us is subject to them. It will now also be easier for anyone to agree that, in those passages where Hilary seemed altogether to exempt Christ from our weaknesses, he vindicates from them only His proper nature, not that which He received from us [Col. 0072C]. That this may be established still more fully, we must now consider what force he assigns to the term *power* (*virtus*).

148. Nothing was more customary among the ancients than to denote Christ’s divinity by the word *virtus*, “power”; the testimonies alone which Theodoret collected from them at the end of Dialogue 3 against the Theopaschites furnish ample proof. To these we add one passage of Ambrose, *On Faith*, book II, chapter 7, no. 56: “Christ is troubled as man; His power is not troubled, His divinity is not troubled; but the soul is troubled, troubled according to the assumption of human frailty.” As concerns Hilary, although he frequently uses this term when speaking of Christ, it does not occur to me that he ever refers it to anything other than His divinity. He clearly signifies this by the term on Psalm II, no. 25, when he says:

“He is not therefore not the Son of God because He is also the son of man. For the addition of humility does not occur by a departure from divinity; nor did POWER receive the disgrace of sharing in weakness, since weakness was endowed with the honor of POWER.”

Nor less clearly, in chapter 9 on Matthew, no. 7, we read: “The assumption of the body did not enclose the nature of POWER; rather, POWER assumed the frailty of the body for its redemption.” A similar passage occurs in the exposition of Psalm 143, no. 7, where the emptying of the Word is explained thus: “Nor did POWER, though restraining itself into humility, depart from itself; and humility, sustained in itself by received Power, when it began to be what it was not, received its advancement from that Power which had not departed from itself.” So in *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 16: “The power of the Word, remaining in no bodily mode, was not absent from where it had descended.” But more closely relevant to our purpose is what he says in the same work, no. 66, explaining Paul’s words: “Although He was crucified from weakness, yet He lives from the power of God.” He interprets Christ’s power as His divine nature and His weakness as His human nature:

“Paul says that the same One was crucified from weakness who lived from the power of God; so that, although weakness came from the form of a servant and nature remained from the form of God, it might be unambiguous in what mystery—that is, in what nature—He both suffered and lived; so that, since in the same One were both WEAKNESS unto suffering and the POWER OF GOD unto life, He who suffered and lived might not be other than, or divided from, Himself.”

Since this is so, what prevents us from understanding, in these words from *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 48—“Does this POWER, then, seem to you to yield to the nail of the wound and, terrified by the stroke of piercing, to have changed itself into a nature capable of pain?”—that the nature of the Word alone is exempted from pain? Indeed, who could judge that these words should be understood otherwise?

149. Not only the term *power*, or “power of God,” but also “power of the body” in Hilary pertains to the nature of the Word. Thus, in the books *On the Trinity*, “power of the body” has the same meaning for him as, in chapter 9 on Matthew, no. 7, “power remaining within the body,” or, in chapter 8, no. 7, “He Himself placed in the body.” Certainly it was permissible for him to call the Word joined to man “the power of the body”: both because the assumed flesh borrowed from His presence and fellowship whatever power it possessed, and because he held in particular—as was shown at length in §1—that the body which He received from the Virgin was conceived by the power of the Word.

[Col. 0073C] 150. With this meaning accepted, the whole controversy arising chiefly from the words in *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 23, is resolved:

“The Lord Jesus Christ indeed suffered while He was struck, suspended, crucified, and died; but the suffering rushing upon the Lord’s body was neither not suffering, nor yet did it exercise the nature of suffering, while it raged with penal ministry, and the POWER OF THE BODY received, without sensation of punishment, the force of punishment raging almost fiercely against itself.”

For if “power of the body” there means the Word who assumed the body, the words mean that the suffering by which Christ was struck was both real and not real: real indeed in His body, or in the man assumed by Him, whom it consequently changed by pain, sensation, and endurance, as was observed above in no. 139; but not real in the Word joined to the flesh, in whom it lacked the aforesaid effect of change. There is therefore no cause for dispute on this account, since no Catholic doubts that the Son of God, after becoming the Son of Man, received without sensation of punishment the force of punishment raging against Himself—that is, was said to suffer what He underwent in the flesh without any change in Himself.

151. But that “power of the body” in the cited passage means the Word will not be doubted by anyone who compares it with this statement on Psalm LIV, no. 6:

“All these things which belong to our necessity indeed rushed upon Him; but they were received by Him through the POWER OF HIS OWN NATURE, while, being able not to die, He did not reject our death, nor even the FEAR of death impending upon Himself.”

Or compare it with *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 47:

“Therefore the only-begotten God suffered all the weaknesses of our sufferings rushing upon Him, but suffered them by the POWER OF HIS OWN NATURE, just as He was born by the power of His own nature; for though He was born, He did not fail to retain the nature of His omnipotence in birth.”

And shortly afterwards, instead of “by the power of His own nature,” he says “by the power of His body,” namely, insofar as He so suffered in the body from the weakness of our body that He received the sufferings of our body by the POWER OF HIS BODY. In the exposition of Psalm CLXI, no. 8, he expressed this more briefly and clearly: “Although He gave Himself to suffering, yet ETERNAL POWER did not receive the pain of suffering.” Hence it is clear that “power of the body,” “power of His own nature,” and “eternal Power” were synonymous expressions for Hilary, signifying the Word, by whom the man, with those things which belong to man, was assumed without any change in the Word Himself.

[Col. 0074B] 152. We read in Theodoret, at the end of the dialogue *The Impassible One*, that Hippolytus also called the Word made flesh “the power of the body” and “the power in the body”:

“The body, although dead in the human manner, has in itself great power of life. For from it flowed things that do not flow from dead bodies: blood and water, so that we might know how much the POWER dwelling in the body avails for life.”

Likewise he says: “The bone of the holy lamb is not broken, the figure showing that suffering does not touch POWER. For the bones are the power of the body; and therefore they prefigure the Word, which is the power of the assumed body.”

153. But no passage is better suited to illustrate the aforementioned place in book X of *On the Trinity* than that found on Psalm LIII, no. 12. From it will clearly appear that “power of the body” there was for Hilary equivalent to the nature of divinity [Col. 0074C].
