And it will not be unwelcome to hear from Hilary himself not what he newly thought concerning the Lord’s suffering, but what he always preached concerning it; so that those may be challenged who think that he erred in the books *On the Trinity*, but later retracted his error in the expositions on the Psalms. In that passage he thus gives a brief summary of his whole doctrine concerning Christ’s suffering:

“As regards the fact that the only-begotten Son of God was led to the cross and condemned to death, He who by the birth which is natural to Him from the eternal Father is eternal, we frequently—indeed ALWAYS—preach that He was subjected to suffering not from the necessity of nature but from the mystery of human salvation, and that He willed rather to submit Himself to suffering than was compelled to do so. And although that suffering was not of condition and kind, because no force of injurious disturbance could wound the unchangeable NATURE OF GOD, yet it was voluntarily assumed, being itself indeed to satisfy the penal office, but not to injure the sufferer with sensation of punishment: not because it lacked, by the very nature of the quality of suffering, the capacity to injure, but because the NATURE OF DIVINITY does not feel pain. Therefore God suffered, because He voluntarily subjected Himself to suffering; but, while receiving the natural powers of the sufferings rushing upon Him—sufferings which must necessarily inflict pain upon those who suffer them—He Himself nevertheless did not fall from the power of His own nature so as to suffer pain.”

Now compare this with the words in no. 23 of *On the Trinity*, book X, which until now have seemed difficult to many and suspect to still more; no discrepancy will occur except in the sound of the words. In one place Christ is said to have suffered; in the other, to have been subjected to suffering. In this place it is said that He satisfied a penal office; in that, that suffering raged with penal ministry. In both, it is without sensation of punishment; in both, the capacity to injure is not denied to the quality of suffering itself. In both, moreover, the reason why it lacked its natural effect is immediately added: more obscurely in *On the Trinity*, because the Power of the body received the force of punishment raging against itself; but more manifestly in the Psalms, because the nature of divinity does not feel pain, and because God, having suffered, did not fall from the power of His own nature so as to suffer pain. Thus the darkness caused by the former passage is dispelled by the latter.

154. Finally, that power of the Word by which He received the sufferings of the flesh without any change in Himself is most aptly illustrated by the comparison of a weapon cast into water, fire, or air. For just as a weapon, though by its own nature fitted to prick, pierce, and wound, lacks those effects when cast into these elements because they do not receive them into themselves, so likewise, because no place for pain is open in the divine nature, suffering—though by itself naturally apt to inflict pain—falls ineffectually upon Christ’s divinity.

155. Other writers, Hilary’s contemporaries or even his predecessors, explain and confirm the same truth of our faith by further comparisons. Eustathius of Antioch, in Theodoret, Dialogue III, uses the comparison of the sun: “But if the sun, whose body can be seen and perceived by the senses, suffers everywhere upon earth so many and such great insults, yet neither changes its course nor feels any blow, small or great: are we to suppose that incorporeal Wisdom is defiled and changes its nature if its temple is fastened to the cross, or undergoes destruction, or receives wounds, or admits corruption? The temple indeed suffers; but the substance, free from all defilement, retains on every side its unstained dignity.” Eusebius Pamphilus employs the same comparison for the same reason in Book IV, chapter 13, of the *Demonstration of the Gospel*. Eusebius of Emesa also shows that in this matter he did not associate himself with the Arians, when, in the cited work of Theodoret, he says: “If I say that a camel flies, you immediately call it absurd, because it does not suit its nature; and rightly so. If I say that men live in the sea, you do not tolerate it; and rightly so, for nature does not permit it. So, if I say that that Power which is before the ages, incorporeal by its nature, incapable of suffering by its dignity, and with the Father, at the right hand and in glory—if I say that that incorporeal nature suffers—do you not [Col. 0075D] stop your ears?” etc. These matters being considered, who will not now be persuaded that Hilary had the Theopaschites alone in view, and that, when in Book X he introduces the comparison of a weapon, he intended to demonstrate that the one nature of the Word is immune from pain? If in that passage or elsewhere he seems to attribute some other privilege to the assumed flesh, it comes to this alone: that he means only what he teaches in the aforementioned *Exposition of Psalm LIII*, no. 12—namely, that Christ, even according to the flesh, willed rather to submit himself to suffering than was compelled to do so. Therefore no one should now doubt that this judgment, transcribed by Theodoret from Gregory of Nyssa, is true also of Hilary: “Since the opinion is twofold and ambiguous—whether divinity or humanity suffered—the rejection of one will be the confirmation of the other.” But so that everyone may more easily recall the arguments by which [Col. 0076A] this has been demonstrated, the principal points must be briefly set out.

## VII. Summary of the Arguments by Which Hilary Is Shown to Have Held Rightly Concerning Christ’s Passion

156. First, before Claudianus Mamertus no one, and after him Berengar was the first, to reproach Hilary for denying the reality of Christ’s sufferings. On the contrary, the most eminent doctors and holy councils always spoke of him as a venerable and catholic teacher and a most vigorous defender of the faith. But had he held an opinion so singular that no trace of it could be found in the writers of that age—indeed, one contrary to the faith received by the common consent of all—they would by no means have celebrated him with so many praises. Still less would heretics have spared him. Although they made little of blackening other Catholic opponents with fabricated [Col. 0076B] heresies and slanders, they always greatly feared his integrity and authority.

Further, it never occurred to the Aphthartodocetae, who, during Justinian’s reign and with his support, defended the error attributed to Hilary by some, to strengthen their own opinion with the name of so great a man, whose writings had long been famous among the Greeks.

Thirdly, this error is in fact not at all supported by what he says in Book X, no. 24: “The assumed flesh—that is, the whole man—was surrendered to the natures of sufferings.”

Fourthly, he repeatedly opposes it, teaching not only consistently that Christ did, said, and suffered whatever belongs to human beings, but also acknowledging in various places that he assumed thirst, hunger, sorrow, and fear, and that he was anxious and troubled, wept, and suffered pain.

Fifthly, he was so convinced that Christ had truly assumed all those human affections that he devoted care and effort to explaining their causes, and proved that Christ endured them not for his own sake but for ours, and in order to convict of falsehood the heretics who denied the reality of the flesh assumed by him.

Sixthly, when in Book I of *On the Trinity*, no. 32, he declares that he composed the tenth book against heretics who, forgetful of the divine confession and nature, seized upon the deeds and sayings of the dispensation as an argument for their impiety—that is, as he speaks more plainly in Book IX, no. 5, those “who falsely claim that what was said by him [Christ] according to man was said according to the weakness of the divine nature”—we must consider [Col. 0076D] what those things are which, in Book X, heretics object against Christ’s divinity. Now they object what has been said concerning Christ’s sorrow, fear, and pain. Hilary therefore freely grants that these things were truly said of him according to man.

Seventhly, lest we should be ignorant of the purpose of his undertaking, at the beginning of Book XI (no. 6), as is his custom when recalling what he has accomplished in the preceding book, he confirms that in Book X he disputed against heretics “who drag the dispensation of the assumed body into an insult against divinity, and seize reasons for impiety from the sacrament of our salvation.” If they held fast to apostolic faith, they would understand that he who was in the form of God assumed the form of a servant, and would not turn the form of a servant to the dishonour of the form of God. [Col. 0077A] Thus this is his one complaint against the heretics: not that they attribute our infirmities to Christ, but that, not knowing how to distinguish the form of God and the form of a servant, they refer to the form of God what belongs to the assumed man. But in Book X they drag into an insult against divinity everything written of Christ’s sorrow, pain, and fear. Therefore, in Hilary’s judgment, these belonged to the assumed body.

Eighthly, if we weigh the opinions of the heretics whom he refutes in Book X—who, namely, either divided Christ or confused the Word with the flesh—and again consider to what end so many questions were raised and why the distinction of the natures in the one and same Christ is so laboriously insisted upon, it will not escape us that all the arguments of this most prudent teacher aim at convincing the heretics, by many considerations, that Christ’s diverse deeds and sayings cannot at all be explained according to their own opinion; and at gradually leading them, once convicted, to the faith of the Church, which, confessing one person of Christ and two natures, has the means to reconcile in one and the same person clear signs both of power and of weakness. In no. 60 and what follows, he plainly signifies that this was his aim in the preceding discussion.

157. Accordingly, he alone defends this faith of the Church—that Christ is believed to have undergone all that is weak, while the dignity of his majesty remains intact—when he vigorously pursues the heresy which inferred the weakness of God the assumer from the pains of the assumed flesh. More than once he observes that this had been foretold in Isaiah’s words: “He suffers for us, and we thought him to be in pains”; [Col. 0077C] as though he said: “He suffers for us according to the nature assumed from us in time, and we thought that he was in pains according to his higher nature, which he possesses before the ages.” The same meaning is expressed in *Exposition of Psalm LXVIII*, no. 23: “Thus they persecuted him as smitten by God, adding to the PAIN of his wounds the PAIN of this persecution. For according to the prophet he suffers for us, and for that reason was thought to be in pains.” From this we may suitably understand what is said in Book X of *On the Trinity*, no. 46: “Therefore the judgment of human estimation is deceived when it thinks that he suffers pain in what he undergoes.” This is illuminated by *Exposition of Psalm CXXXVIII*, no. 3, where, after first setting forth Isaiah’s words, “He bore our infirmities,” he immediately adds: “And lest anyone should suppose that weakness came upon the impassible and unchangeable divinity, [Col. 0077D] he [Isaiah] added: ‘And we thought him to be in pains.’ Therefore he assumed infirmities because he is born a man; and he is thought to suffer pain because he suffers: but he himself is free from pains because he is God.” To whom would Hilary not here seem to concede that Isaiah’s earlier words, “He suffers for us,” etc., are spoken of Christ’s flesh, and merely to contend that the words which follow show beforehand the perverse mode of argument of those who impute the infirmities of the assumed flesh to the divinity of the Word who assumed it? He again notes the sophistries of the same people in Psalm LXVIII, no. 12: “Christ sometimes weeps, groans, and is sorrowful”—according to human nature—“and this very thing is adduced as an example of weakness against the divine nature.”

158. But since these same people boasted that human disturbances had fallen upon Christ just as upon us, and had mastered him, Hilary had to show that Christ was not in the least subject to them of himself, and always remained master of the infirmities he had assumed. He establishes the first point by a full exposition of the holiness of that birth; the second by the power of Christ’s deeds, by which Christ clearly enough indicated that he could keep every infirmity away from himself.

159. Therefore, to gather so long a discussion into a few words: disputing against heretics who thought Christ’s condition in suffering identical with that of other human beings, Hilary shows that his infirmities differed from ours in four respects. Since ours are compelled, affect us because of our own desert, rule over us, and leave nothing in us that is not subject to them, he shows that Christ’s infirmities were voluntary; that he assumed them for us, not for himself; that they were regulated at his command and will; and that they touched not the nature which he possessed by eternal birth, but only that which he received by temporal assumption. Everything Hilary says concerning the passion of our Saviour is directed to vindicating these four privileges of Christ.

## § IV. On Christ’s Death: Whether Hilary Thought That the Word Departed from the Flesh When Christ Died

160. We have scarcely emerged from one difficult passage when we encounter another. For those following Christ’s mysteries, immediately after his passion comes his death. Many have been troubled because Hilary, commenting on Christ’s dying words, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” adds (*Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 33, no. 6): “The cry to God is the voice of the body, testifying to the discord of the divinity departing from it”; as though he meant that the Word departed from the body which he had assumed before Christ died.

161. At first we had no intention of opposing them, since, with truth whole and unimpaired—a truth from which it is never safe to depart—this interpretation seemed impossible. At that time we thought that we needed only to show that this opinion was neither unique to Hilary nor shared by him with heretics. But afterwards, when rereading his other works, we found that he did not persist in that earlier opinion, but asserted the opposite view in his later writings. Finally, when we came to prove this point, he seemed to contend so resolutely against those who divided Christ even in death that no slight suspicion remained that he had ever agreed with them. We therefore did not hesitate to revise the plan of our proposed discussion and adopt another: first, we do not deny that his quoted words differ little from the words of Fathers, some of whom can scarcely be thought not to have held that the Word was separated from Christ’s dead body; then we show, from Hilary’s other modes of expression, that his very words can suitably be understood without any separation of the Word; finally, by selected judgments in which he disputes so vehemently against Christ’s dividers that he should be considered their conqueror rather than their supporter, we establish that those words not only may, but must, be so understood.

## I. Which of the Ancients Seem to Have Held That the Word Was Separated from Christ’s Dead Flesh; and How They Differed from the Heretics

162. First comes what Epiphanius says, *Heresy* 69, no. 62, in reference to Christ’s aforesaid words, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”: “That same humanity was so united with divinity that the sanctity of both was one, and in that humanity it knew all things most perfectly, being joined to God and united into one divinity; seeing that divinity was already in a certain readiness to leave the holy body, he spoke from the person of the Lord’s man himself—that is, of the human nature assumed by the Word (for divinity had decreed to accomplish all things pertaining to the mystery of the passion and to descend to hell with the soul): … the cry addressed to the united divinity was, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’” Likewise Leporius, in his *Book of Correction*—to which Augustine and other bishops testify that they subscribed, in a letter included among Augustine’s letters, no. 219, §13—professes that Christ cried on the cross, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” in order to show himself truly and manifestly, according to the flesh, to be the Son of God about to die; and, as it were using the voice of the flesh itself and putting the past for the future, to testify to us before it occurred that, by the death of the cross, the earthly body necessarily had to be left by God for a time, not only by God but also by its own soul, which was united with God. And shortly afterward he says: “Divinity, together with the soul united to it, did not abandon the crucified man to punishment, but left the lifeless flesh for a time.”

163. Athanasius might be thought to agree with these writers in *On the Incarnation of Christ*, p. 75, where, defending the impropriety of Christ’s dying by the force of illness, he expresses Christ’s death by a word which suggests the Word’s departure from the body: “If his body had suffered from disease, and the Word had departed from it when it was dissolved,” etc. But in *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ*, p. 645, he leaves no room for doubt about his opinion, since he does not wish Christ’s death to be called a separation of divinity, but a mortification of the body; so that at that time divinity deserted neither the body in the tomb nor the soul in hell, as he repeatedly demonstrates. Perhaps with greater right one might refer to the former opinion the words of Eusebius of Caesarea at the end of chapter 13, Book IV of the *Demonstration of the Gospel*: “Thus indeed that dead body of the Word also, when a little of the Word’s power touched it, was immediately raised and returned to life”—as though the body had died when the Word departed and returned to life when he came back.

164. Ambrose most nearly of all imitates the words of our Hilary in Book X of his *Commentary on Luke*, no. 127, where he interprets Matthew’s words, “Crying with a loud voice, he gave up the spirit,” thus: “In this there is either the glorious profession that he descended, even unto death, for our sins … or the evident declaration testifying to the departure of divinity from the body; for thus you have it: ‘Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying: My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?’ The man cried out, about to die through the separation of divinity.” This latter judgment is included in the exposition of the Apostles’ Creed, or *Treatise on the Trinity*, printed under Ambrose’s name in the appendix to volume II, chapter 13.

165. Finally, since it follows that the Word would have been separated from the body when the soul was dissolved from it, if the Word had been joined to the body only through the mediation of the soul, all who favour this opinion should rightly be judged to support the former view. Hence this consequence also follows: if it was permissible, without any mark of heresy, to teach that the Word was united with the flesh only through the mediation of the soul, it was likewise permissible to say that the Word departed when the soul departed from the body.

166. Therefore, even if one grants that some Fathers, like the heretics, interpreted Christ’s words upon dying on the cross—“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—as a departure of the Word from the flesh, one must not immediately concede that the basis of one and the same interpretation was the same in both. The heretics imagined that the divinity of the Word, as though weak and fearful lest death and suffering had to be endured by it, departed from the Christ who was about to suffer. Against them Gregory Nazianzen says, *Oration* 36, no. 20: “For he was not, as some suppose, forsaken either by the Father or by his own divinity, as though it feared the passion and for that reason withdrew and contracted itself from the sufferer.” But the Fathers who seem to agree with them imply this rationale of their opinion: they judged divinity’s power so great that death, which Christ had resolved to undergo to fulfil the Father’s will, could by no means come upon a body united with it. “For since divinity,” says Ambrose in the passage just mentioned, “is free from death, death could not exist unless life departed; for life is divinity.” The author of the exposition of the Creed in Ambrose has the same statement. To this may be referred what Tertullian says in *Against Praxeas*, no. 30: after saying that Christ died in yielding up the spirit, he adds, “For while the Spirit remains in the flesh, the flesh cannot die at all”—if, however, as is his practice elsewhere, he understands divinity by “Spirit,” which is not entirely clear. Yet from this it is evident that Fathers and heretics differ most of all: the latter, thinking more meanly, the former in some manner more sublimely, of Christ’s divinity, teach its separation from the dead body.

167. Moreover, they differ in this: heretics proclaimed that the Word was separated from the body before Christ’s death, indeed even before his passion; Catholics, however, only in death itself. Thus Leporius’s booklet, cited above, warns that in the words “Why have you forsaken me?” the past is put for the future; and Epiphanius observes that this voice of the flesh was addressed not to divinity already separated, but to divinity still united, when it was already, as it were, ready to leave the holy body. From this arises the great difference between them: the former maintain that a mere man suffered and died for us, while the latter maintain that the true God did so; hence the price of our redemption is set as infinite by the latter and finite by the former.

168. Finally, Epiphanius, Leporius, and other Catholics maintain that the Word’s union with Christ’s soul remained unimpaired even through death. “With his divinity and soul,” says Epiphanius, *Heresy* 20, no. 2, “he descended to hell, led captivity captive, and on the third day rose to life with his most holy body. This body he united with his divinity, never again to be dissolved.” But the heretics maintained that the whole man Christ had been abandoned and separated from divinity. Yet the aforementioned author of the exposition of the Creed, while adding something to Ambrose’s words, approaches the heretics’ opinion. For in chapter 13 he says: “This is the blessed soul which on the cross cried to divinity, saying, ‘My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?’” etc. And shortly afterward he adds: “Therefore God, who is Word and Spirit, who breathes where he wills, did not unwillingly abandon the flesh or soul he had assumed,” etc. Nor are there lacking those who interpret the Fathers’ quoted judgments in such a way as to maintain that they did not believe the Word separated even from Christ’s dead body. Their interpretation may perhaps gain some support once Hilary’s words on the matter have been carefully examined.

## II. How Hilary’s Words Concerning Christ’s Forsaking Agree with the Faith

169. Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, Book III, distinction 21, §1, replies to the aforementioned passage of Ambrose that he meant only that divinity separated itself from the flesh by withdrawing protection, not by dissolving the union; or that it separated itself outwardly, so as not to be present for defence, but did not fail inwardly in respect of union. “For,” he says, “if it had not restrained its power there, but had exercised it, Christ would not have died.” Whether this interpretation fits Ambrose is not now our concern; but nothing prevents its being applied to Hilary’s words on Matthew. For immediately after the disputed words he declares in this manner that he understood Christ’s forsaking to be that which was necessary if he was to die: “Finally, why is he forsaken? He cries out, saying: ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ But he is forsaken because he still had to accomplish death.” That he said this without prejudice to the unimpaired substantial union of Word and flesh is illustrated from the same Commentary, chapter 3, no. 2, where he says: “When the Lord was hungry, the operation of hunger did not steal upon him; rather, that power of forty days, unmoved by fasting, left the man to his own nature.” Certainly no one would suppose that Hilary thought this forsaking—in which he taught that the man was left by the Word to his own nature so that he could be hungry—occurred through substantial separation. Why, then, should he not likewise be thought to declare that the same man was forsaken so that he might die, while the substantial union remained safe and intact? This is further supported by the fact that, although he understands “Spirit” almost everywhere as the divine nature, in Book X of *On the Trinity*, no. 61, he argues that the words “He gave up the spirit” can in no way be understood in that sense. “For,” he says, “that spirit frequently signifies the soul is clear even from this very fact: Jesus, when about to die, gave up the spirit.” Why is it clear from this very fact, unless because he judges it clear that only the soul, and not also the substance of the divine Word, departed from the body of the dying Christ?

170. If this is not yet sufficiently plain to anyone, another answer comes to the aid of the words objected: namely, that the flesh testified to the discord of divinity departing from it because, although divinity did not in reality depart, it nevertheless displayed no sign of its presence in it, just as if it were not there at all. We do not invent this answer ourselves from our own imagination; we derive it from similar modes of expression in Hilary, especially from what he says concerning the emptying of the Word. For to one who only lightly touches his first words in Psalm LXVIII, no. 4, would he not seem to assert that the divine nature was so exhausted by assuming flesh that it was utterly without its own substance? First he says: “The heavenly nature had to be drained, so that, emptying itself, it might fall from the form of God into the form of a servant and man; and therefore the waters penetrate even to the soul, because it has no substance fixed in the mire of the deep.” Then he immediately explains what heavenly nature had to be drained, and what substance he says does not remain after the assumption of flesh: “Certainly it was not that the substance which had been assumed was not there, but rather that substance which, emptying itself, had drained itself.” What then? Did the divine substance perish? “Not at all,” he says immediately afterwards: “He who emptied himself in emptying himself was not deprived of himself; yet that very thing did not seem to exist which, in emptying itself into another, had yielded itself.” Behold the mystery: the substance of the emptied Word is not nonexistent because it has failed, but because it existed in such a way as not to seem to exist.

171. But for what purpose, and in what manner, did the divine substance then seem not to exist? He explains this in Psalm CXLIII, no. 7: “For the emptying of the form of God does not know loss to its own detriment; rather, it again acquires the form of God for the assumed servant-form. Thus Power, though restraining itself in humility, did not fail from itself, since it is what it was; and humility, assumed with Power restrained within itself, when it began to be what it was not, received its advancement from that Power which had not failed from itself.” More plainly, in Book XI of *On the Trinity*, no. 48: “Remaining in the form of God, he assumed the form of a servant, not changed, but emptying himself, hiding within himself, and himself made empty within his own power; while he adapted himself even to the form of human appearance, lest the weakness of assumed humility should not bear the mighty and immeasurable nature; but that unbounded Power might regulate itself so far as it was fitting for it to obey unto suffering the body joined to it. But that he contained himself while emptying himself within himself,” etc.

172. Given these points, Hilary’s words in *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter XXXIII, are readily shown not to differ at all from our faith. For he who said that in Christ, after the assumption of flesh, the substance of divinity was not present because, although intact, it was hidden within itself so as not to seem to exist—why should he not be thought to have believed Christ’s divinity undivided also in death, and thus only to have said that it withdrew because then it restrained itself within itself? Certainly, just as divinity was hidden far more in death than in the assumption of servant-form, so it seemed far less to exist.

173. For illustrating Hilary’s opinion, the following words of Pope Leo (*Sermon* 66, *On the Lord’s Passion* 17, chapter 2) contribute greatly: “That the Lord was given up to suffering was as much the will of the Father as his own; so that not only did the Father forsake him, but he himself in some sense forsook himself—not by a fearful departure, but by a voluntary yielding. For the power of the Crucified restrained itself against the ungodly; and that it might employ a hidden dispensation, it chose not to employ manifest power.” If you add what Augustine writes concerning the very mystery of Christ’s incarnation (*Sermon*, now 77, no. 11): “He is God and becomes man; he sets aside divinity—that is, in a certain manner separates, that is, conceals what was his; what he had received appears”—there will be no reason why, in Hilary’s language, you should not understand the departing divinity as divinity concealing itself and restraining its power, so that the man may accomplish death.

174. Moreover, divinity is commonly said to depart from the place in which it was formerly conceived to be when, in a new way and a new order, it manifests itself in another place. Thus, when the Word assumed flesh, we customarily say that he left heaven and descended to earth. In that respect Augustine also teaches in Psalm XLIV, no. 12, that the Father was left by the Son: “For he left the Father in a certain manner; he did not leave him altogether, as by a separation, but for the assumption of human flesh.” Thus Hilary too could say that, when Christ died, divinity departed from the flesh—not because it left it altogether, as by a separation, but for the assumption of death. And indeed the Word in a certain manner withdrew from the flesh, which here he surrendered to human power, while descending with the soul into hell and there displaying new signs of his power and might. Finally, since *dissidium* means only difference, not separation, and since Hilary writes in Psalm LXVIII, no. 4, that Christ consists of two substances which differ by nature, the disputed words—“It is the voice of the flesh testifying to the discord of divinity departing from it”—may be understood thus: it is the voice of the man testifying that he is joined to another nature, which he calls departing in order to signify that it differs greatly from him and will no more be injured by his death than if it had departed.

175. Nor should anyone be troubled that in Psalm LV, no. 12, he says: “He himself granted to this body, dead and left within the tomb, fellowship with his divine nature,” as though he meant that the body lost fellowship with the Word in death and regained it in resurrection. For he is not here speaking of the fellowship by which the body is substantially joined to the divine nature, but of that by which it becomes a participant in its glory, which it lacked so long as it was mortal. For there he praises Christ because he expects glory neither from another source nor for another body than that which had died: “Those things which he hopes for are not outside himself; nor are the vows of praise which he will render to be obtained from without. For he himself is lord of his resurrection; he himself granted to this body, dead and left within the tomb, fellowship with his divine nature. For not even to all who are to rise is a body acquired from external matter,” etc.; how much less to Christ? Moreover, nothing occurs in Hilary from which he may be judged to have divided Christ in death. On the contrary, many things are available by which he shows himself to have remained far from this opinion. This is what remains for us to consider.

## III. Hilary Most Vigorously Defends That Christ Must Never Be Divided

176. We pass over, first, the words in Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, no. 8: “How is he not to be believed to remain naturally in us, who, having been born man, has already assumed our nature as inseparable from himself?” For perhaps there will be those who wish to refer the phrase “already inseparable” to the time after the resurrection. Yet the more natural sense of these words is that the only-begotten God, from the time when he was born man, assumed our nature inseparable from himself. That this is how they must be understood is confirmed by what he teaches in Book IX, no. 7: namely, that God was born man so that man might remain in God eternally; especially since he immediately adds: “Therefore God is born for our assumption, while our man remains in God”—that is, while man, from the very moment of assumption, remains in God for eternity, never to be separated from him. For he himself observes that this is the force of the word *remains*: it signifies that something will endure perpetually. Furthermore, in Psalm CXXXI, no. 9, he expresses Christ’s death in such a way that his words signify that God remained in the body at that time: “But he rested for whom death is sleep; and what is for us a penal change was rest for the Only-begotten God remaining even in the body.” But one ought not to insist too obstinately on a single expression when the same matter is established through whole pages.

177. But we should not pass so lightly over this passage in Book III of *On the Trinity*, no. 15: “The Son of God is crucified, but on the cross God conquers human death; Christ the Son of God dies, but all flesh is made alive in Christ; the Son of God is in hell, but man is brought back to heaven.” From this, I say, it follows that the Word did not depart from the flesh before Christ died—since the Son of God dies—and consequently that the price of our redemption was infinite. Moreover, Hilary was so constant in this teaching concerning the death of God that in one passage, no. 7 of Book IX, he first says that God willed to die; then shortly afterward, that the immortal God had placed himself within the law of death; and at the end, that God died through the flesh. He declares the same thing in more than one manner in Psalm LXVII, no. 23, and first says: “Through the security of eternity, death itself in God dying is confidence.” He even calls the dead Christ “God” in Book IX of *On the Trinity*, no. 54. Then, returning to the cited passage, if the Son of God is in hell, it follows that he did not believe even Christ’s soul to have been deserted and separated from the only-begotten God through death. From this one may also conclude that he did not think the flesh deserted either, when he said in Matthew, “It is the voice of the flesh,” etc. For just as, in Book III of *On the Trinity*, no. 16, commenting on Christ’s words, “Glorify me,” he says, “This is the prayer of the flesh,” and it is beyond doubt that by “flesh” he means the whole man, and especially the soul; so too, when explaining our Lord’s words, “My God, why have you forsaken me?” and adding, “It is the voice of the flesh testifying to the discord of divinity departing from it,” he cannot be denied to mean by the same term “flesh” the whole man, namely flesh and soul. Now he taught that Christ’s soul remained united to the Word even after death. Therefore he held the same concerning the flesh. But let us establish this more plainly.

178. We can more certainly test his faith from no passage than that in which he explains Christ’s words, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” He is occupied almost entirely with their explanation from no. 51 to no. 65 of Book X. We therefore have here a very broad field for setting forth his genuine opinion. First, it is worthy of note that he calls the heretics who object the aforesaid words of Christ against him “those who divide Christ into three”—Word, soul, and body. He would not escape the odium of this designation if he had ever divided Christ. On the contrary, in no. 52 he professes adherence to the faith of the Church, which, instructed by apostolic doctrines, knows a birth in Christ but does not know a beginning; knows a dispensation but does not know a division … nor does it by a threefold faith divide Christ into Word, soul, and body—he whose garment woven from above is uncut—so as to cut Jesus Christ into Word, soul, and body. Moreover, what does he mean when, about to say, “It knows a dispensation, but does not know a division,” he immediately precedes this with, “The faith of the Church knows a birth in Christ, but is ignorant of a beginning,” unless to signify that the Church knows no moment of division in Christ’s temporal dispensation any more than it knows any beginning of existence in his eternal generation? Then, pursuing the same dividers of Christ more sharply, he says in no. 62: “If the voice and speech are those of the same one—of him who complains that he is forsaken and of him who declares that he reigns—by what reasoning of unbelief do we divide our faith, so that he who died is not the same one who also reigns at the same time?” It is as though he said: Why, when you hear Christ say, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” do you divide him and assert that he has been deprived of divinity? Did not that same one say to the thief at the same time, “Today you will be with me in paradise”? But while he lay dead on earth, how could he reign in paradise if at that time he had been divided and abandoned by divinity?

179. He repeatedly insists that even then He was not divided. For after warning, in no. 60, that the natures must be distinguished—one being buried, the other raising; and accordingly that one must not suppose Him to have been buried whom one understands to have raised, nor doubt that He raised whom one does not dare deny was not buried—he immediately emphasizes that both are joined in one and the same Word. “For,” he says in no. 63, “He who dies and He who reigns are not different; nor is He who commends His spirit and expires different; nor is He who descends into hell and ascends into heaven not one.” And in no. 64: “Was Christ divided, so that one [Col. 0085D] is Jesus crucified, another Christ the power and wisdom of God?” Then at the beginning of no. 65: “The apostle knows nothing else, nor judges that he knows anything else; but we, with feeble intellect and still feebler faith, rend, divide, and duplicate Christ Jesus . . . For to us one Christ is crucified, another is the wisdom of God, another is buried.” [Col. 0086D] And shortly afterwards, from the apostle’s words, “He who descended is the same also who ascended,” he thus presses those same dividers of Christ: “Will the body which lay in the tomb be said to have descended into hell? Therefore, if He who descended is the same as He who ascended, and if the body is not believed to have descended into hell, while it is not doubted that the body rising from the dead ascended into heaven, what faith remains here except that of the hidden mystery, unknown to the world and to the rulers of this age? [Col. 0086A] So that, since He who descends and He who ascends is one and the same, for us also Jesus Christ may be one: both Son of God and Son of Man, both God the Word and man, flesh; both suffering, dead, buried, risen, received into heaven, and seated at the right hand of God; possessing in Himself, one and the same, through dispensation and nature, in the form of God and in the form of a servant, without any partition of Himself in that which He is as man, and without division in that which He is as God.”

If Christ is without division in all these things, then He is divided in none of them: neither in the Passion, nor in death, nor in the tomb. Therefore the Word remained joined to the flesh even in the tomb. The same book contains many more passages of this kind; but it is enough to have indicated the place and produced these few examples from it. We add one passage from Book IX [Col. 0086B], which may not be passed over in this discussion. For none of the Fathers develops more expressly than Hilary, in that place, the principal argument by which they maintain that the Word was not separated from Christ’s buried flesh. For this reason, as Paulinus of Aquileia states (Book I against Felix, in Alcuin, p. 1785), Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is declared according to the Scriptures to have suffered, died, been buried, and risen: because after the mystery of the assumption, the impassible and unchangeable divinity is never said to have been separated from the flesh. Gregory of Nyssa also, in his letter to Eustathia and Ambrosia, where he asserts that Christ’s divinity was at once in paradise with the soul and in the tomb with the body, confirms his statement thus: “For this reason the body itself is called the LORD [Col. 0086C], because of the divinity inhering in it”—or resting upon it.

For the same reason Ferrandus the deacon, in his letter to Severus, no. 8, first lays down: “The whole Christ was in hell according to His rational soul, but not wholly, because the flesh, with which He is whole, was not there. The whole Christ was in the tomb according to the flesh, but not wholly, because the soul, with which He is whole, was not there. Yet the Word of God was both with His soul in hell and with His flesh in the tomb.” And because the Word was with the soul in hell and with the flesh in the tomb, he then declares it follows that the whole Christ may rightly be said to have been in hell and the whole Christ in the tomb, namely because of the unity of the person of the Word, the rational soul, and the flesh. Augustine’s opinion is similar, *Tractate 69 on John*, no. 3. In a word, these writers chiefly maintain from the Creed of faith—by which we confess the flesh to have died, been buried, and raised, and Christ to have died, been buried, and passed from death to life—that the Word was not divided from the flesh in Christ’s death. But let us hear how consistently Hilary himself establishes this.

180. Turning first to the heretic, he says in no. 11: “I ask you who it is that strips Himself of flesh, and what is the flesh that is stripped?” He immediately presses the point: “For if Christ who died is not the same as the flesh that was stripped, show the name of the stripped flesh; and again, explain the nature of Him who stripped Himself of flesh. For I find that God Christ was raised from the dead—He who stripped Himself of flesh—and again that Christ, the stripped flesh, was raised from the dead.” Finally he himself answers the questions [Col. 0087A] in this manner: “For the stripped flesh is Christ who died; and again, Christ who raises Christ from the dead is the same Christ who strips Himself of flesh. Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; recognize the dispensation of man in death. And though each action belongs to its own nature, yet remember that He who is both is one Christ Jesus.”

If both are one, He is also undivided in death; nor is He undivided in death unless divinity rests upon the stripped flesh. Again, the stripped flesh and He who raises the flesh are not one and the same unless the stripped flesh is Christ whole in such a manner as He who raises the flesh is Christ whole. But He is not whole if the Word is absent from the stripped flesh. Yet why should we mix foreign words with Hilary’s? His words are themselves plain and clear. [Col. 0087B] Recognizing that Christ performed different things in different natures, he nevertheless professes with most steadfast faith that in those different actions Christ was everywhere one and the same; and he recognizes absolutely no division of Him before death, in death, or after death. Nor do we think anyone will suppose that, because Hilary above calls the dying Christ one who strips Himself of flesh, he says this because he believed the Word had put off the flesh and withdrawn from it. For, because of the unity of person, Christ is rightly said to strip Himself of flesh when He strips the flesh only of the soul; just as He is said to lay down the soul when the body alone is separated from it.

181. This being so, Hilary deserves no low place among those who taught that the Word was never separated from the flesh which He assumed. [Col. 0087C] The holy Fathers repeatedly handed this down to us with great agreement: in particular Athanasius, near the end of the book *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ*; Gregory of Nyssa, in the letter to Eustathia; Ambrose, likewise in Oration I against Eunomius; Pope Leo, Sermons 65, ch. 7, and 66, ch. 1; Theodoret, Book V of the *Heretical Fables*, ch. 15; Fulgentius, Book III to Trasimund, ch. 16; Ferrandus the deacon and Paulinus of Aquileia in the places mentioned; John of Damascus, Book III, ch. 27; Oecumenius on Colossians II; Alcuin, Book III *On the Trinity*, ch. 16; Bernard, Book V *On Consideration*, ch. 9.

## § V. Singular Expressions Concerning the Glory of Christ and of Other Human Beings after the Resurrection Explained

182. Christ’s Passion is followed by the glory which, when raised from the dead, He bestowed upon His humanity. Although we know of no one who has expressly criticized what Hilary wrote concerning Christ’s glory, we hope nevertheless to perform a service not unwelcome to the reader if, in these preliminaries and according to our ability, we explain Hilary’s opinion on this subject—an opinion which it is highly important for anyone approaching his writings to understand clearly. For most often he is contending against the Arians or seeking to fortify Catholics against their deceitful artifices. Since they were accustomed, in order to diminish Christ’s glory, to object His weak words and deeds, nothing was more customary for the zealous defender of Christ than to discuss His glory and power in order to exalt the name of his Lord. Therefore anyone to whom Hilary’s modes of speaking about Christ’s glory are obscure will stumble on almost every page. [Col. 0088A] He often employs unusual expressions. That these have not hitherto been understood is shown by the fact that those who revised Hilary’s works not only in recent centuries but even eight hundred years ago most seriously corrupted precisely those passages in which he speaks more abundantly and magnificently of Christ’s glory. Others, more scrupulous, noted in the margins of manuscripts passages which they did not dare alter. Read cautiously.

183. Certainly, if one attends only to the sound of the words, one will suppose that the statements encountered in Book IX *On the Trinity*, no. 38, signify that Christ’s human nature so passed into the divine that it changed its kind, and that hence the nature of God and of the assumed man became one. The same impression is produced by what he declares in chapter 27 on Matthew, no. 4: that God and man in Christ are now both one. Others will find obscure what he teaches in [Col. 0088B] Psalm 143, no. 7, and Fragment VI: that Christ’s servile form acquired through glory the condition of being the form of God and ceased to be a servile form; or what he writes in Book III *On the Trinity*, no. 16: “The Son, now made flesh, prayed that the flesh might begin to be to the Father what the Word is.” Nor are these discordant with the following in the *Treatise on Psalm 54*, no. 7: “He hastens to fly away as a dove,” that is, “to return into a spiritual nature”; and shortly afterward: “He had assumed that which is mortal in us, so that, having become flesh, He might fly away into Spirit.” Who would not also find unusual the statement in the *Treatise on Psalm 68*, no. 25: “The Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father,” that is, “the assumed man is received into the nature of divinity”? Or this in Book XI *On the Trinity*, no. 40: “God being all in all, the nature of the assumed body of ours is brought into the nature of the Father’s divinity . . . so that He may not be God in part, but wholly God . . . [Col. 0088C] with no nature of an earthly body remaining in Him in any part; so that, whereas formerly He contained two within Himself, now He is God alone”—while, as no. 41 explains, man and God are now wholly God. “For,” he says in no. 42, “God glorified Him in Himself,” that is, “in the nature in which God is what He is, so that God may be all in all, the entire dispensation whereby He is man now remaining in God.” Hence, when in Book IX, no. 6, and on Psalm 138, no. 19, he distinguishes three states of Christ—before man, in man, and after man—that is, before He assumed flesh, while He bore mortality, and after He put off mortality—he confesses Him to be God and man only in the middle state, while in the final state, as in the first, he declares Him to be God alone.

184. Apelles will readily claim these and similar statements of Hilary for himself. [Col. 0088D] According to Tertullian’s testimony, *On Prescription*, no. 51, Apelles held that in the resurrection Christ, as He ascended, restored to each element whatever He had borrowed in His descent; and that thus, with all the parts of His body dispersed, He restored only the spirit to heaven. Hence Hilary will seem to have confused Christ’s two natures, if not after the first assumption of the flesh, at least after the resurrection; and thus to have sown certain seeds of the Eutychian fiction, not being remote from the error against which Augustine warns in Letter 187, no. 10: namely, lest we establish the divinity of the man in such a way as to destroy the reality of the body. To guard against this, Augustine first says: “As He was seen to go into heaven, that is, in the same form and substance of flesh: to which indeed [Col. 0089A] He gave immortality, but did not take away its nature.” And since Jerome, in the preface to Book XVIII of his *Commentary on Isaiah*, professes, “I confess that bodies shall rise incorruptible and immortal,” and adds, “so that they may change glory, not substance,” there is no slight ground for conjecturing that at that time there were persons who taught that the truth of human nature is abolished by resurrection glory. A suspicion of this error will be easily fabricated against Hilary by anyone who cites, torn from its context, this definition of Christ’s subjection from Book XI *On the Trinity*, no. 35: “Subjection also is a concession from nature into nature, while that which ceases to be from itself what it is is subjected to that into whose form it yields.” Indeed, whoever hears this will scarcely doubt that Augustine marks it in chapter 37 *Against an Arian Sermon*, where he says: “Although there were not lacking those who thought that this subjection of the [Col. 0089B] Son should be understood as a change of His human form into divine substance, as though a thing is subjected to that into which it is converted and changed.”

185. But every suspicion will collapse at once when we show that Hilary proclaims the glory of the flesh without impairing its reality. To begin with subjection: in Book XI he explains that there are two kinds, the first of obedience and faith, the second either of concession or transformation. Then he defines the latter in no. 35 thus: “It is a concession from nature into nature, while that which ceases, according to what it is, to be from itself, is subjected to that into whose form it yields”—but immediately adds, as a safeguard: “It ceases, however, NOT SO AS NOT TO BE, but so as to advance; and through transformation it becomes subject, passing into the appearance of another kind which it has received.” Thus, when in the already cited [Col. 0089C] passage from no. 40 he asserts: “There is no other cause of subjection than that God may be all in all, with no nature of an earthly body remaining in Him in any part, so that whereas formerly He contained two within Himself, now He is God alone,” he extinguishes the wrong interpretation arising from those earlier words by these later ones: “Not by the casting away of the body, but by its translation through subjection; nor abolished by destruction, but changed by glorification . . . He is subjected, indeed, not so as not to be, but so that God may be all in all; possessing in the mystery of subjection that which is not, both to be and to remain, and not losing Himself through destruction so as not to be.” Certainly, in these words Hilary guarded no less carefully than Jerome and Augustine against seeming, in speaking of Christ’s fleshly glory, to destroy the reality of the body.

186. [Col. 0089D] He again removes this opinion far from himself when he affirms that Christ reassumed the very body which He had received from the Virgin, and that in it the resurrection of a portion of our flesh—indeed, of our body—is made visible. Thus, on Psalm 124, no. 4, he says that by glory Christ became a mountain in whom we behold ourselves through the assumption of our flesh and body. “For we are in Him, contemplating our resurrection in the resurrection of our body in Him.” And although it is plain that we are said now to be in Christ because He took from us, in the Virgin, flesh which He carried into heaven, he states this more openly on Psalm 65, no. 12: “The nature of the flesh assumed from the Virgin is translated into His eternal glory.” Nor does the statement in chapter 3 on Matthew, no. 2, mean otherwise: “He brought back to heaven the man whom He had assumed, the gift awaited by God the Father”; nor what he writes in chapter 4, no. 14: that Christ, returning from death to life, carried to heaven the material of His assumed body, joined to the eternity of His Spirit and substance. Nothing further seems required to establish, from Hilary, the reality of Christ’s glorious flesh, since we have just heard him say that Christ carried into heaven not only the man whom He assumed, but also the nature of the flesh assumed from the Virgin; not only its nature, but also the material of the assumed body, and the flesh of us all.

187. To these we add this statement from Book III *On the Trinity*, no. 20: “The Lord, intending to confirm Thomas’s faith by the conditions proposed, [Col. 0090B] stood present and offered the opportunity of touching the body and handling the wound; and surely He who is to be recognized as pierced must necessarily have brought the body in which He was pierced.” And shortly afterward: “For He stood bodily, not feigned or deceptive.” Yet in that body in which He was seen by Thomas, He sits gloriously at the right hand of God, as is not obscurely declared in these words from the same book: “This is the prayer of the flesh, in which all shall see Him pierced on the day of judgment and recognize Him from the cross; in which He was prefigured upon the mountain; in which He was lifted into heaven; in which He sat at God’s right hand; in which He was seen by Paul; in which He was honored by Stephen.” Indeed, here it is openly taught that Christ sits in the very flesh in which He was transfigured on the mountain and in which, before death, He cried to the Father, “Glorify me.” Hilary therefore understood Christ’s flesh after it had received glory [Col. 0090C] to be as real as it was before death.

188. He no less clearly disclosed his view concerning the reality of the bodies which are to be restored to other human beings by resurrection. For on Psalm 55, no. 12, having first said of Christ, “He Himself is Lord of His resurrection; He Himself granted fellowship with His divine nature to this body, dead and left within the tomb,” he continues his discussion of the resurrection of all humanity thus: “For no body is acquired for all who shall rise from some external matter, nor is a nature of foreign origin and external causes restored; but that very thing rises into the advancement of eternal brightness, and by transformation rather than creation becomes in it something new.” This is also clear in the *Treatise [Col. 0090D] on Psalm 2*, no. 41: “He will repair what has been broken, bestowing upon them the form of beauty pleasing to Himself, not from any other matter, but from the old matter itself of their origin; so that the resurrection of corruptible bodies into the glory of incorruption may not destroy nature through annihilation, but transform it by a condition of quality. For it shall not rise as another body, although it shall rise into another state . . . Transformation therefore takes place, but abolition is not brought about. And when that which was rises into that which it was not, it has not lost its origin but advanced unto honor.” Nor should we pass over what he says on Psalm 67, no. 35: “Can any utterance of power be greater than to gather the dust of dissolved bodies into form and the solidity of limbs, restore life again to human beings and souls, and transform the corruption of weak nature by the incorruption of heavenly [Col. 0091A] nature? This is the true and perfect assurance of human hope.” In these passages Hilary guards no less wisely against Origen’s suspect views of our resurrection than, in the preceding passages, against Apelles’s and like errors concerning Christ’s glory.

189. What then does he mean by such magnificent modes of speech concerning the glory of bodies? In our judgment, nothing other than what is commonly believed on this subject. For in express words he teaches that the same body, from the old matter itself of its origin—indeed, the very dust of the dissolved body—is to be restored into the form and solidity of its limbs, so as to become new by transformation rather than creation: new, I say, through a new condition of quality, not through the destruction or abolition of nature. It remains, then, to inquire in what he places [Col. 0091B] this transformation, from which that new and glorious condition follows. On Psalm 1, no. 13, he explains that it will occur when incorruption has swallowed up corruption, eternity weakness, and the form of God the form of earthly flesh; or, as he says on Psalm 55, no. 12, when the weakness of bodies is removed—that is, falls and tears—when incorruption devours corruption, when immortal power swallows death, when God is all in all, when the light of the living is in God, the light of the living, and man himself is to please Him. Whatever else he says concerning the glory of the bodies of the blessed is chiefly reducible to these gifts: immortality, incorruption, and a form of brightness and light. Endowed with these, in Tertullian’s words, *Apology*, no. 48, “we shall be the same persons that we are now, and not [Col. 0091C] others, although clothed over with the proper substance of eternity.” But since these gifts are foreign to the nature of the body and more suited to the nature of spirit, and since the nature of God alone possesses them by its own proper and supreme right, a body clothed with them may not improperly be said to have passed into the nature of spirit, indeed into the form and nature of God, with no nature of body any longer remaining in it—that is, with no faults or works at all remaining which follow the nature of an earthly body (see Tertullian, Book V against Marcion, no. 104).

190. This blessed transformation of bodies is obtained through participation in the divine nature. For if, where two natures are joined, the lesser must yield to the greater, the weaker to the more powerful, and the darker to the brighter, how much more must the associated nature of man yield to the nature of God? Can the form of a servant resist the form of the Lord, corruption incorruption, or mortality life? The stronger always conquers the weaker. Even before the resurrection, the Word joined human nature to Himself, yet did not impart this glory to it; [Col. 0091D] but this was the marvelous plan of His benevolence. Having decreed this, He had to restrain within Himself the power of His nature, as Hilary notes on Psalm 143, no. 7, so that to Him fixed in the mire of flesh the substance of divinity might not even appear to be present. But our Lord and Redeemer, when the mysteries of His dispensation had been completed, then for the first time granted fellowship with His divine nature, for advancement into eternal brightness, to the body which was dead and left in the tomb. [Col. 0092A] That is, no longer restraining His divine splendor within Himself, He made His assumed man also a participant in it; and thus carried into heaven the material of the assumed body joined to the eternity of His Spirit—or divinity—and substance. Immediately, as Hilary says in Fragment 6, man became God. For the greatness of the Lord overcame the smallness of the servile form, so that the servile form itself ceased to be servile through the Lord who assumed it.

In what sense is He understood to have become God? Precisely in the sense in which the Word is said to have become flesh. For as the Word became flesh when the glory of the Word lay hidden within the humility of the flesh, so man became God when the humility of human flesh lay hidden within the glory of the Word. Some, however, refer Hilary’s immediately preceding words [Col. 0092B] to the first assumption of mortal flesh and suppose that they explain why Christ’s human nature lacked a proper person. But who could grant them this? For he does not there declare that the servile form lacks personhood, but that the form itself ceases to be servile. Moreover, he who said that by the assumption of mortal flesh Christ was wholly in the form of a servant (on Psalm 143, no. 10), because the emptied form of God did not appear to exist except in the form of a servant, was far from asserting that His servile form had at that time ceased to be servile.

191. By the same reason by which Christ is said to be wholly in the form of a servant, while God lies hidden in the assumed man, He is also said to be wholly God when the assumed man was flooded and encompassed by the light and glory of the assuming God. Yet there is this difference [Col. 0092C] between the two states: God hidden in man remained unchanged in the power of His nature, and sometimes manifested Himself through the greatness of His works; but man hidden within God does not remain in the weakness of his nature, but happily passes into eternity, incorruption, and glory, which are proper to the divine nature. Thus it is understood how God, when through resurrection glory He shall be all in all, with no nature of earthly body remaining in Him in any part but with the nature of the Father’s divinity brought in its place, is nevertheless to be such not through rejection of the body or its abolition by destruction, but with the old matter itself of its origin retained. Nor is it more difficult to perceive how, in the book *On the Synods*, no. 48, assumed flesh is said even before the resurrection to have begun to be what the Word is, since, as is explained there, [Col. 0092D] it already had power to do what belongs to the Word. Nor would the statement on Psalm 143, no. 7, remain obscure: “To the very servile habit is granted the condition that it might be what He was”—God the Word—“namely, that it might be in the form of God”; even if we did not have it explained in more explicit words on Psalm 141, no. 8: “This is its recompense from God: that eternity of the Father’s glory is bestowed upon the body which He assumed.”

Who thereafter will find obscure the statement that before the resurrection Christ contained two within Himself, but is now God alone? For who will not immediately perceive that the two denote distinct natures affected by their natural properties? Nor will it be more difficult to understand that Christ returned through glory into the unity of the Father’s nature, whose harmony [Col. 0093A] the novelty of the dispensation had disturbed. For every discord disturbs unity. Christ, whose natural condition with the Father was one, whose blessedness was one—for with Him He was impassible, omnipotent, eternal, always in splendor, always in glory and brightness—began to differ from Him when, assuming the weaknesses of our flesh, He became weak, passible, mortal, and despised. Conversely, He is said to have returned to the former unity according to the assumed man when, having put off mortality and received the glory of God, He ceased to be weak, passible, and liable to the other conditions of human nature. From this it follows that He was God and man only when He possessed in Himself the natural properties of both God and man. This is said not because, after receiving [Col. 0093B] resurrection glory, He ceased to possess human substance, but because man is accounted God when, casting off the weakness and obscurity which follow his nature, he receives the glory proper to God. For whenever Hilary speaks of glory, by the name of the nature, as also of the form, of God, he understands the natural glory of God, which he sometimes calls, without any ambiguity, “the form of glory” and “the habit of the superior nature” (Book IX *On the Trinity*, no. 39; Book XI, no. 43).

192. With his words thus clarified, the more obscure sayings of the ancients may now more conveniently be explained, especially those of Gregory of Nyssa, vol. II, p. 17, and Oration 4 against Eunomius, p. 584, and elsewhere, in which he establishes the divinity of the assumed man in such a way as to seem somewhat to shake the reality of the body. Nor are these distinctive modes of speech peculiar to Hilary [Col. 0093C] alone. Ambrose also said, Book I *On Virgins*, ch. 3: “The Word became flesh, so that flesh might become God”; and in *On Faith in the Resurrection*, no. 91: “Then”—before the resurrection—“He was man according to the flesh; now He is in every respect God; for now we no longer know Christ according to the flesh.” What of Augustine’s words on Psalm 35, no. 14, even concerning our own soul: “When that ineffable joy has been received, the human mind perishes in a manner and becomes divine”? Bernard excellently illustrates the same point in *On Loving God*, ch. 10. Having first spoken there of perfect charity, which he later declares is perfect only in the blessed, he expounds its power and nature thus: “To be thus affected is to be DEIFIED. As a small drop of water poured into much wine seems wholly to lose itself, while assuming both the wine’s flavor [Col. 0093D] and its color; as heated and glowing iron becomes most like fire, stripped of its former and proper form; and as air flooded with sunlight is transformed into the same brightness of light, so that it appears not so much illuminated as to be light itself: so every human affection in the saints must then, in some ineffable manner, melt away from itself and be wholly poured into the delight of God. Otherwise, how will God be all in all, IF ANYTHING OF MAN REMAINS IN MAN? Substance will remain, but in another form, another glory, and another power.”

Maximus the Martyr expresses this same, so to speak, deification of man in divine words, chapter 26 of *Theological Chapters*, chapter 20: “The Word of God, having become man, again filled with knowledge human nature [Col. 0094A] emptied through knowledge; and, strengthening it unto immutability, made it divine not in nature but in quality, sealing it forever with His own Spirit and tempering it, like water with the quality of wine, into power and firmness. For He truly became man in order that by grace He might make us gods.” Nor did Hilary leave unknown the manner in which he said that the nature of divinity is to be brought into our body while the truth of its nature remains unharmed. On Psalm 118, letter 17, no. 12, he explains his thought in these words: “The Prophet prays for the face of the Lord for his illumination. For from the majesty and countenance of God who sees us we receive light, and the countenance of His mercy turned toward us shines upon us with the grace of spiritual power. Or certainly, when He shall be present on the day of judgment, when He shall stand visible in the glory of the Father’s majesty, then He will [Col. 0094B] illuminate us with the light of His face. For as certain metals and gems reflect the brightness OF THEIR OWN NATURE upon things near them and confer a likeness emulating them from their neighboring appearance; and as Moses received light from contemplating God’s glory, so that the people could not look upon the honor of his glory: so also the Prophet, confessing himself God’s servant, prays to be illuminated and made, according to the Apostle, conformed to the glory of God.”

193. Whoever considers these things will take no offense when reading in various places in Hilary that Christ, according to His assumed humanity, exists through glory in the form, nature, kind of nature, and unity of the nature of God, so that God and man in Him are now both one; or, what is the same thing, that through resurrection glory He is born into that which He was before times, [Col. 0094C] yet was not wholly in time; likewise, that He is begotten unto that which was His own, begotten into the perfect Son of God, takes His wings, flies away into Spirit, returns into spiritual nature, and becomes wholly God (*On Psalm 54*, no. 7; Book XI *On the Trinity*, no. 41). For all these statements mean only a full and perfect conformity with God, so far as this is permitted to man; they are spoken without any impairment of human nature’s reality. This conformity he chiefly places in the succession, in place of corruption, mortality, and weakness, of incorruption, immortality, power, and the splendor of eternal brightness—properties entirely of divine, not human, nature. As each obtains these through participation in the divine nature, so Christ the man would have obtained them as soon as He was assumed by the Word, unless the Word had restrained the power of His nature for the sake of the mystery of the [Col. 0094D] dispensation. But once that was completed, the power of the divine nature, having been released, so overcame human nature, vastly inferior as it is, that, wholly absorbed within it—that is, clothed with the aforesaid divine properties—it displayed nothing but what was divine. Then other human beings, because they are joined to Christ through fellowship of flesh, will receive into themselves from Him those divine qualities flowing round them; through these they will also be made conformed to Christ’s glory, and thus God will be all in all. This is the whole of Hilary’s doctrine concerning the glory of Christ and of human beings, contrary in nothing to the catholic faith, although expressed in distinctive modes of speech.

194. Yet Hilary indicates not obscurely that he was led to these modes of expression by the authority of Scripture, especially by John 13:32, “God glorified Him in Himself,” and Philippians 2:11, “The Lord Jesus [is] in the glory of God the Father.” From these, in Book IX *On the Trinity*, no. 42, he draws this argument: “For He whom the Father glorified in Himself must be confessed in His glory; and He who must be confessed in the Father’s glory, and whom the Father glorified in Himself, must beyond doubt be understood to be in those things which belong to the Father; since the Father both glorified Him in Himself, and He is to be confessed in His glory. For He is not merely in the glory of God, but in the glory of God the Father; nor did glory glorify Him externally, but glorified Him IN HIMSELF. Restoring Him to the glory which is His own, and to the glory which He had with Him, He glorifies Him both with Himself and in Himself.” And as though the force of the saying, “God glorified Him [Col. 0095B] in Himself,” had not yet been sufficiently expressed, he explains it again in no. 42 thus: “For God glorified Him in Himself, that is, in the nature in which God is what He is, so that God may be all in all.” Similar are the deductions which, from other words in John 17:3, he draws in the same book, no. 39, where he says: “But ‘Glorify me with Yourself’ is not the same as ‘Glorify me.’ For He does not ask merely that He Himself be glorified in such a way that something of glory might belong to Him personally; rather, He prays to be glorified by the Father with the Father Himself,” etc. From other words of Paul—for example, “A spiritual body shall rise,” “Death has been swallowed up,” “that God may be all in all”—and similar passages, Hilary’s expressions concerning the glory of Christ and of human beings are derived.

## § VI. The Kingdom of Christ Distinguished from the Kingdom of God the Father
195. Since Christ’s kingdom [Col. 0095C] pertains to his glory, and Hilary speaks of it in such a way that difficulties are not lacking, the preceding discussion would rightly seem incomplete unless we attempted, in these preliminaries, to remove those difficulties or at least to indicate them in advance. Now he considers Christ to reign in a twofold manner, corresponding to his twofold nature. Of his divine nature, indeed, when he has said, on Psalm LXV, no. 12, “As that [nature] is always ruling, so it will always rule,” he adds, no. 13, concerning the human nature: “The only-begotten Son of God, although he has always reigned, has not always reigned in the body.” Nor is there any reason for dispute regarding this everlasting reign of Christ. For wherever Hilary demonstrates that the glory, power, authority, and nature of the only-begotten God are one with the Father’s, he establishes beyond doubt that no distinction is to be made between their kingdoms. The question undertaken, therefore, concerns entirely [Col. 0095D] the kingdom which came to Christ as man in time. To discern when Scripture speaks of Christ’s temporal kingdom, he gives this rule in the same Treatise: “Where the dominion of the age is contained as designated and, as it were, pointed out, there is shown that time in which, when the body has been glorified into the glory of God, both the name of God and the kingdom are bestowed upon it.” Hence it is to be understood that Christ began to reign in the body when he received glory in the body. Concerning this kingdom of Christ three questions especially must be asked: first, how Hilary distinguishes it from the kingdom of God; next, how he does not support the error of the Millenarians and others akin to them; finally, in what he understands both God’s kingdom and Christ’s kingdom to consist. From this it will follow that he is not at variance with the received faith of the Church concerning the blessedness of the saints who depart hence [Col. 0096A].

## I. How Hilary distinguishes Christ’s kingdom from the kingdom of God

196. He appears to distinguish these two kingdoms by times, places, names, and degrees of blessedness. To Christ’s kingdom he assigns no other time than that which extends from each righteous person’s death to the day of judgment. From that point, however, he begins to grant God’s kingdom to the righteous. Thus Christ’s kingdom is in the souls of the righteous released from their bodies, whereas God’s kingdom is in those same righteous persons endowed with resurrection glory. For these, as he declares on Psalm CXLVIII, no. 7, the seat of that blessed kingdom is appointed not in this world, nor in the air, but in the higher places. But to Christ’s kingdom—perhaps because it consists only of souls [Col. 0096B], to which a bodily place is not suitable—he does not so expressly assign a bodily place. Unless perhaps we ought to understand a bodily place from the words in the Treatise on Psalm CXX, no. 16, where saints rejoicing in Christ’s kingdom are said meanwhile to be placed in Abraham’s bosom, to which the impious are prevented from coming by an intervening chasm.

Far more fitting for souls separated from bodies is that place in which he elsewhere teaches the Lord’s kingdom to be situated: namely, that the peace and unanimity of the saints should be the place in which they happily rest. For, he says on Psalm CXLVII, no. 2: “The kingdom of our Lord is in the peace and unanimity of the saints” (“and his place was made in peace”); that assembly of the blessed, which is the kingdom of God—or, more correctly, of the Lord—is called Jerusalem as the city of peace. Nor can anyone deny that these things must be referred to Christ’s kingdom, since they are said of that Jerusalem which [Col. 0096C] has not yet been consummated through the resurrection, concerning which he immediately adds: “But this city, built of living stones, as the Apostle says, the assembly of saints, conformed to God’s glory, is consummated by the resurrection.”

197. As regards names, he distinguishes the kingdom of God the Father from the Son’s kingdom chiefly by two epithets: he calls the former either the heavenly kingdom, when he considers its location, or eternal, when he considers its age. For what you hear called, in Psalm CXLIV, no. 16, and Psalm CXLVIII, no. 8, “the eternal kingdom”; in Psalm CXX, no. 16, “the heavenly kingdom,” “the kingdom of heaven,” “the eternal and blessed kingdom”; and in the Prologue to the Psalter, no. 11, “the times of the holy city and heavenly Jerusalem”—all this undoubtedly belongs to the one kingdom of God. But although he calls Christ’s kingdom by many splendid titles, nowhere does he call it heavenly or eternal [Col. 0096D]; why he does not do so will be explained below.

198. Yet, although he nowhere calls it an eternal kingdom, on Psalm LVII, no. 6, he calls it eternal rest. “Meanwhile,” he says, “the joy of every righteous person is displayed, as of Lazarus resting in Abraham’s bosom. … The joy of the righteous is when he sees vengeance; for, when sinners are to be punished, he rejoices that he is led by angels into ETERNAL REST.” And that he understands this rest to consist in God’s reception, he indicates on Psalm LIII, no. 10:

> Let innocent religion therefore have this confidence: that … if at any time the force of an unjust death is brought upon it, the soul departing from the dwelling of the body may know that it rests in God’s reception.

Here, however, we would prefer “in the Lord’s reception,” so that the Lord’s reception might mean what the Lord’s protection means in the same Treatise [Col. 0097A] on Psalm CXX, no. 16: “Those departing from the body shall be preserved by the Lord’s PROTECTION until their entrance into the heavenly kingdom,” being, that is, meanwhile placed in Abraham’s bosom.

199. From the two preceding passages one might define that kingdom of the Son as follows: it is the eternal rest of the righteous soul which, departing from the dwelling of the body, rests in the Lord’s reception; or, from the last passage, it is Abraham’s bosom, in which the faithful are preserved by the Lord’s protection until their entrance into the heavenly kingdom.
