We have already heard, from the Treatise on Psalm CXLVII, no. 2, that the same kingdom is called the assembly of the blessed, the congregation of saints, the city built of living stones, which, because it is a city of peace, is called Jerusalem. Again, on Psalm II, no. 48, it is called the dwelling-place of the blessed; on Psalm CXLVIII, no. 8, the blessed kingdom of holy Jerusalem; and on Psalm CXLI, no. 5—unless perhaps Hilary meant that a place was granted [Col. 0097B] to the thief different from that granted to the other righteous—the land of the living, the habitation of paradise, and the kingdom of Christ’s inheritance.

200. Hence it is clear that he attributes to this kingdom of Christ not rest only, but also blessedness, joy, glory, and honour. This he confirms on Psalm CXVIII, letter 18, no. 10, where he says of Lazarus’s blessed departure: “He is contained in Abraham’s bosom, and exchanges the misery of a toilsome life for the honour of blessed rest.” Yet he does not appear to make this kingdom’s happiness equal to the blessedness of God’s kingdom. For, in the Prologue to the Psalter, no. 11, when he distinguishes a threefold stage toward salvation, he assigns only the second to Christ’s kingdom and reserves the highest for God’s kingdom. For the first stage toward salvation is to be reborn into the new man after remission of sins [Col. 0097C]; then, after the confession of repentance, comes that kingdom of the Lord reserved for the times of that holy city Jerusalem; and afterward, when heavenly glory has been consummated in us, we advance through the kingdom of the Son into the kingdom of God the Father, and so forth.

Again, on Psalm LXII, no. 7, mentioning a threefold life—namely, in the world, in Abraham’s bosom, and in heaven—he asserts that the last, which he calls mercy because it is prepared through God’s mercy, is better than the other two:

> For there is a life after the life in which one must live in Abraham’s bosoms, in which the name of God is blessed in the rest of the poor, according to the prophet’s saying: “The dead shall not praise thee, O Lord, but we who live bless the Lord.” Above these lives, therefore, is that mercy which has prepared for those who love the Lord what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.

[Col. 0097D] 201. Thus Hilary may seem in some manner to have regarded Christ’s kingdom as an intermediate state, free from the miseries which we suffer here, but not yet sharing in that happiness promised to us in heaven. Accordingly, on Psalm CXIX, [Col. 0105B] no. 1, he proves that we ought not grieve over the death of our own people because their departure is an accelerated hastening toward the common hope; and, at no. 11, he teaches that, by Christ’s command, we should pray for the hastening of the heavenly kingdom, since we are commanded by him to say, “Thy kingdom come”—as though we shall not obtain our hope until the Father’s kingdom comes with all the saints perfected. Yet although he strongly confirms both passages by Paul’s words in which the Apostle desires the dissolution of his body and Christ’s [Col. 0098A] fellowship and fellowship with Christ, nothing follows from this that proves the blessedness of Christ’s kingdom and that of God’s kingdom to be different.

202. Perhaps this is more effectively established by what he says on Psalm CXLVIII, no. 8, concerning Christ’s kingdom: “That is the kingdom of the saints, through which, while the Lord reigns, they will ascend to the blessed kingdom of God the Father”; and shortly afterward: “This hymn properly belongs to those who, through this blessed kingdom of holy Jerusalem, near to the eternal kingdom, will pass after the kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ into the kingdom of God the Father, as the Lord gathers them”; and at the end: “This, therefore, is the people drawing near, near to the kingdom of God the Father through the kingdom of the Son of God. Thus the Lord reigns, about to deliver the kingdom to God the Father—not because he will lack the power of the kingdom, but because he will deliver us, who are his kingdom, to God the Father into the kingdom. The delivery of the kingdom is our advancement: so that we who shall be in the Son’s kingdom may also be in the Father’s [Col. 0098B] kingdom; worthy of the Father’s kingdom through this, because we shall be worthy also of the Son’s kingdom; near then to the Father’s kingdom when we shall be in the Son’s kingdom.”

For who would place in the same degree of blessedness those who draw near to God and those who have arrived at him; those near to the eternal kingdom and those who have obtained it; those for whom something yet remains to be ascended and those who have attained the supreme summit of blessedness? But before we investigate more deeply wherein that difference lies, certain suspicions arising from the preceding words must be removed.

## II. Hilary is cleared of the error of the Millenarians and others akin to them

203. First, care must be taken lest, when Hilary teaches [Col. 0098C] that one arrives at the Father’s kingdom through the Son’s kingdom, he be thought to have said this in the sense in which Irenaeus asserts, Book V, chapter 32, that Christ’s kingdom is the beginning of incorruptibility, through which kingdom those found worthy gradually become accustomed to receive God. For Irenaeus said this under the influence of the chiliastic error of Papias and his followers, from which Hilary’s opinion is certainly far removed. Hilary places the Lord’s kingdom in spiritual delights—namely, in the peace and unanimity of the saints, fellowship with Christ, and the blessing of God; they place it on earth and in earthly pleasures. Thus Augustine rightly calls those thousand years carnal, in Book XX of *The City of God*, chapter 21, no. 2, because they are located in an abundance of carnal things.

Moreover, according to them, the saints do not enter Christ’s kingdom until after the general resurrection; but according to Hilary every righteous person enjoys it [Col. 0098D] immediately after death. Further, of the opinion by which they say that saints are detained in Christ’s kingdom until they gradually become accustomed to receive God, there is not even the faintest trace in Hilary. Finally, the Chiliasts received their name because they confined the Lord’s kingdom on earth within a period of a thousand years; Hilary defines it by no fixed span of places or times, but extends it indefinitely as far as the judgment.

204. Nor should he be thought, in the Treatise on Psalm CXX, no. 16—“Those departing from the body shall be preserved by the Lord’s protection until their entrance into the heavenly kingdom”—to mean what Lactantius means in Book VII, chapter 21: “Yet let no one suppose that souls are judged immediately after death. All are held in one custody [Col. 0099A] until the time comes when the supreme Judge will examine their merits.” Although he agrees with Lactantius in the single word “custody,” he differs greatly in its meaning: for in Lactantius custody denotes a certain place resembling a locked prison, whereas in Hilary it means the Lord’s protection, by whose fellowship the saints are protected from every evil. Hence on Psalm CXIX, no. 1, he teaches that we need fear nothing from the violence of the world, since death acquires fellowship with Christ.

They differ also most of all in this: with Lactantius all souls, righteous and unrighteous, are detained in one custody, and indeed without any prior judgment; with Hilary only faithful and righteous souls are preserved in the Lord’s custody and, as he indicates on Psalm LVII, no. 7, after a prior judgment.

205. Closely related to Lactantius’s opinion is Tertullian’s view [Col. 0099B] (*On the Soul*, no. 55): although he grants paradise to martyrs, he nevertheless detains other souls until the day of the Lord in a most secret recess, covered within the earth and enclosed inside it. But Hilary knows nothing of this distinction: he makes not martyrs alone but all the righteous companions of Christ, not in the subterranean darkness of Hades, but in the honour of blessed rest.

206. Nor does he support Vigilantius, whom Jerome, after relating in *Against Vigilantius* that he believed the souls of apostles or martyrs to have taken their seats either in Abraham’s bosom, or in a place of refreshment, or beneath God’s altar, and to be unable to be present at their tombs or wherever they wished, then sharply attacks in these words:

> They are apparently of senatorial rank, so that they may be shut up not among murderers in a foul prison, but in free custody, in the islands of the blessed and the Elysian fields [Col. 0099C]. Will you impose laws on God? Will you put chains on the apostles so that they may be held in custody until the day of judgment and not be with their Lord, of whom it is written, “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes”? If the Lamb is everywhere, then those who are with the Lamb must likewise be believed to be everywhere. And while the devil and demons roam throughout the whole world and by exceeding swiftness are present everywhere, shall martyrs, after shedding their blood, be enclosed beneath an ark and unable to depart from it?

And indeed, who can deny that Hilary agrees with Jerome rather than with Vigilantius? For with Jerome he asserts that the saints are not only Christ’s companions, but on Psalm CXXIV, no. 5, he also proclaims that they are our guardians and protectors. Indeed, in Book XI of *On the Trinity*, no. 3, he does not pass over among the testimonies of Christ’s divinity the fact that “the tombs of apostles and martyrs resound with him through the working [Col. 0099D] of miracles.” What workings of power occurred at the tombs of saints he explains thus in *Against Constantius*, no. 8: “Everywhere the blood of blessed martyrs has been received as holy, and their venerable bones daily bear witness: demons howl in them, illnesses are driven away, works of wonder are seen,” and so forth. Thus there can be no doubt that he approved prayers poured out before saints’ tombs and believed that they could perceive them and, having perceived them, obtain from the Lord for us in their compassion those things of which we stand in need.

207. In what, then, does he distinguish the Son’s kingdom from the Father’s kingdom? Or how does he at least not favour the error for which Marcellus was once condemned and deposed, since [Col. 0100A], like Marcellus, he seems to prescribe an end to Christ’s reign? How is he consistent with himself when, on Psalm LXV, no. 13, he teaches that Christ will rule the age after he has abolished every rule and authority—which will occur only at the last judgment—whereas on Psalm LX, no. 5, he has taught that Christ will reign until he puts his enemies beneath his feet, so that the time during which he must reign until he puts his enemies beneath his feet is comprised “from generation to generation,” that is, as he explains there, from the time of our mortality until that in which, receiving immortal bodies, we are to be regenerated into eternal life? In one passage the final judgment is understood as the beginning of Christ’s kingdom, in the other as its end; how is this not a contradiction?

208. He does not contradict himself [Col. 0100B], nor does he favour Marcellus’s error. For, as in other places repeatedly, so also on Psalm LXV itself, no. 13, he expressly declares that Christ reigns even now. Nor does he teach that Christ will reign simply from the judgment onward, but that he will reign alone, so that his kingdom—now somewhat disturbed by the prince of this world—will then be whole and complete, distracted by no opposing power. “Then,” he says, “he ALONE will rule the age in his power. For now, although he reigns, nevertheless the prince of this world has asked to sift the apostles as wheat; and there are spiritual wickednesses against which blessed Paul equipped us with spiritual arms.” By this he sufficiently indicates that he does not restrict Christ’s kingdom to the time extending to the judgment.

And on Psalm LX, where he says, “He who sits in the eternal kingdom must reign until he puts his enemies beneath his feet [Col. 0100C],” wisely guarding against being thought to assert, with Marcellus, an end to the kingdom, he adds: “not so that he himself may then not be king; but when he has delivered the kingdom to God the Father, he will reign together with those who are kings.” Thus, while we consider what it is for the kingdom to be delivered to God, and how Christ does not yield the kingdom which he delivers to the Father, we gradually learn what the kingdom of God is; once this point is clearly grasped, what Hilary thinks about Christ’s kingdom will be less obscure.

## III. In what Hilary holds the kingdom of God and the kingdom of Christ to consist

209. The kingdom of God is, as he himself defines it on Psalm II, no. 42, where sin is conquered, where death is destroyed, where the enemy does not reign. But death is not destroyed except through [Col. 0100D] the glorious resurrection, according to Augustine’s saying in Sermon 233, no. 5: “Death too will die in us; but when? At the end of the age, in the resurrection of the dead.” Hence Hilary immediately adds after the words cited: “This will be God’s kingdom for us, when, with all the stings of our vices crushed, the stain of bodily weakness shall be swallowed up.” God’s kingdom, therefore, is the glory of the body, over which death will no longer have dominion, but in which there will be blessed and eternal life. Thus Christ’s delivering the kingdom to God the Father means nothing else than making us conformed to the glory of his body.

Nor is it hidden why he calls this God’s kingdom or why he says that Christ delivers it to him. Since eternity is proper to God, Christ subjects us to God’s property when he makes us eternal. Explaining [Col. 0101A] the delivery of the kingdom in this sense, Hilary rightly declares that nothing is taken from Christ but much is gained by us, in Book XI of *On the Trinity*, no. 39:

> He will therefore deliver the kingdom to God the Father: not as though, in delivering it, he yields up power, but because, made conformed to the glory of his body, we shall be God’s kingdom. For he does not say, “He will deliver his own kingdom,” but “He will deliver the kingdom,” being about to deliver us, made through the glorification of his body, as a kingdom to God.

Similar are those words from the Treatise on Psalm CXLVIII, no. 8, already quoted above: “Thus the Lord reigns, about to deliver the kingdom to God the Father—not because he will lack the power of the kingdom, but because he will deliver us, who are his kingdom, to God the Father into the kingdom. The delivery of the kingdom is our advancement.”

Indeed, if we shall then be delivered as a kingdom to God when we are made conformed to the glory of Christ’s body, that delivery will add much to us but detract nothing from Christ’s [Col. 0101B] kingdom. Rather, since we shall receive this glory from him, we shall then be subject to him far more completely. This can be proved more clearly thus: Christ delivers us as a kingdom when he makes us kings; he makes us kings when he makes us heirs of God, who is the greatest King; and he makes us heirs of God when he makes us his co-heirs. These are not our words but Hilary’s own, explaining his thought on Psalm II, no. 43:

> Those who will be heirs of God the Father and co-heirs of our Lord Jesus Christ must obtain this consequence from being co-heirs of the eternal King: that they are kings.

But nothing of Christ’s inheritance and glory will then perish; therefore nothing of his kingdom either. Rather, as he says on Psalm LX, no. 5, “he himself will reign together with those who are kings,” with the special glory that they have from him the fact that they are kings. And then, just as he himself [Col. 0101C], reigning in the glory of the body, will be subject to him who subjects all things to himself, so we shall be subject to the glory of his reigning body, so that we may be in that splendour in which he reigns in the body, because we shall be conformed to his body.

210. Therefore, since Hilary is far removed from the Millenarians’ opinion, and since he understands God’s kingdom, granted to the saints only after the resurrection, as the glory of the body, nothing prevents us from believing that he thought eternal blessedness and the very vision of God are granted to the saints immediately at death. Nor does anything else follow from his saying in Book XI of *On the Trinity*, no. 39: “He will deliver the kingdom to God the Father, and then those whom he has delivered as a kingdom to God will see God.” It no more follows from this that they had not seen God before than it follows, when on Psalm LXV, no. 13, he teaches that Christ will rule the age [Col. 0101D] after abolishing every rule, that he did not rule before.

The same must be said of these words in the Treatise on Psalm LXII, no. 3: “This is the soul’s desire, this is the thirst of its hope: that the vision of God may come to it, that as soon as possible, caught up in clouds and raised to meet God Christ, it may appear.” Indeed, in order to conclude from the words “that the vision of God may come to it” that the day of judgment is indicated as the time when the desired sight of God comes to the saints, it must first be proved that these words concern the same time as the following words, “that as soon as possible, caught up in clouds,” and so forth.

Even if this is granted, you will have established a day abundantly attested in Scripture on which the vision of God is to be granted to the whole assembly of the righteous; but you will not thereby have established that this blessedness is denied to individual saints departing daily from us [Col. 0102A]. Or else one who appeals to the last judgment while committing iniquity must, by equal reasoning, be thought to believe that punishment for crimes is postponed until that day. But if the order of the preceding words indicates an order of events, the vision of God comes to the saints before they go to meet Christ when he comes for judgment; and thus before the judgment, and in Christ’s kingdom, they behold God’s face. But let us investigate, if possible, more distinctly what may be discovered about that kingdom of Christ.

211. First, on Psalm II, no. 42, occurs: “Christ reigns in us when, through him, we ourselves rule by the right of masters over ourselves.” Although this is said more generally and may seem applicable to those still living in the flesh, so long as we have continual conflict not only against spiritual wickednesses but also against flesh and blood [Col. 0102B], who will grant that we rule over ourselves with a full and complete right of masters? To what extent the righteous obtain this through Christ is not yet clear.

212. The Treatise on Psalm CXIX, no. 1, gives somewhat clearer evidence. There Hilary, relying on the Apostle’s words, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ,” explicitly declares that death obtains fellowship with Christ for the righteous. We think no other reason need be sought why he calls the time following the righteous person’s death Christ’s kingdom, than that fellowship with Christ which the Apostle hopes for when his body is dissolved.

He also explains, on Psalm XCI, no. 9, by other words of the same Apostle, how he understands the righteous, stripped of flesh, to dwell with Christ:

> It must be understood how the pious and [Col. 0102C] those subject to God can enter into the rest which the impious will not enter; for it is necessary that the hope denied to the evil be left to the good. But if Christ is God’s rest, then those who are in Christ will be in God’s rest. The Apostle cries out that he wishes to be in Christ, saying: “But I pursue, if I may apprehend that for which I also was apprehended,” etc.

And shortly afterward he concludes: “Therefore, by union with the flesh assumed, we have been taken up into Christ: we indeed for the present by faith, but the saints, so to speak, in reality.” For, as he says also on Psalm XIII, no. 4, “we all run to apprehend that for which we have been apprehended by Christ,” that is, “to be found in his body, which he himself assumed from us; in which before the foundation of the world we were chosen by the Father; in which we were reconciled from enemies and acquired from the lost; in which the Apostle, with the loss of all things, desires to be found, saying: ‘And I count all things as dung, that I may gain [Col. 0102D] Christ, and be found in him.’”

213. What, I ask, do these words mean? Unless our judgment deceives us, Hilary, interpreting Paul’s words, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ,” by the same Apostle’s words, “But I pursue, if I may apprehend that for which I also was apprehended,” understood that the saints, when they lay aside the flesh, are joined to the flesh which Christ assumed from us and rest in it until they receive their own bodies. He called this rest of the saints in Christ’s body Christ’s kingdom.

This understanding is confirmed by his exposition, on Psalm XIV, no. 5, of the words, “Who shall rest on thy holy mountain?”:

> What is higher than Christ? Or what more exalted than our God? His mountain is that body which he assumed from man, in which he now dwells, high and exalted [Col. 0103A] above every rule and authority and every name.

And after a few words:

> If, therefore, all the hope of our rest is in Christ’s body, and if we are to rest on the mountain, we can understand the mountain to be nothing other than the body which he received from us. For after dwelling in the Church one ascends to it; in it one rests in the Lord’s exaltation; in it we shall be joined with the choirs of angels, since we too are God’s city.

That to which one ascends after dwelling in the Church can mean nothing else than that to which those who die in the Church’s bosom and charity pass immediately after death. The concluding words of the same Treatise pray for this grace for us: “Dwelling in the Church, may we finally rest in the glory of Christ’s body.”

214. To this may be referred what he says in chapter 4 on Matthew [Col. 0103B], no. 3: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.” “He promises the meek an inheritance of the earth, that is, a dwelling in that body which the Lord himself assumed.” Nor should it now be obscure why, on Psalm LXII, no. 4, after recalling several virtues of a holy man, he adds: “Only those proved by these will be either assumed by Christ or caught up in clouds to meet him.” For the reward of those whose life has been approved is expressed differently according to the different time at which they depart this life: if they die when judgment is imminent, they are caught up in clouds with their own bodies to meet Christ; if before then, they are assumed by Christ and rest in his body [Col. 0103C]. Or certainly—which comes to the same thing—a twofold state of the same saints is distinguished: first, after this life, they are assumed by Christ and rest in his body; finally, on the day of judgment, having received their own bodies, they are caught up in clouds to meet Christ.

In the same sense, in the same place, according to those different states, the saints are called either appearing to the Son or received by the Son: appearing to the Son when they are caught up in clouds to meet him, but received by the Son when they rest in his own body. This recalls what we heard above from the Treatise on Psalm LIII, no. 10: that the soul departing from the bodily dwelling rests in God’s—or the Lord’s—reception; that is, it has been received by the Son until, having received its body, it appears to meet him in the clouds.

215. Hilary indeed, on Psalm LXI, no. 5, Psalm LVIII, no. 6, and elsewhere, looking to the one right conferred by Christ upon all human beings through his assumption of our flesh—namely, that they might dwell in his glorious [Col. 0103D] body—speaks generally of human beings as raised together in Christ and seated at God’s right hand in the heavenly places. But he declares without ambiguity on Psalm LI, no. 17, that the glory of this dwelling comes only to those who, persevering until death in faith in and love for Christ, have not fallen away from the right granted to them:

> For whoever shall not remain in Christ will not be an inhabitant of Christ’s kingdom. Yet he will not be so because the dwelling was not open to him; for it is open to all that they may be companions of God’s body and kingdom, because the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, assuming in himself the nature of the whole human race, etc.

From that passage one may observe, first, that for Hilary becoming a companion of Christ’s kingdom and becoming a companion of Christ’s [Col. 0104A] body are one and the same; next, that he establishes this distinction between human beings living in the flesh and those who have put off the body: to the former there is an open entrance into Christ’s kingdom, while to the latter actual dwelling in it is granted. It also follows that dwelling in Christ’s kingdom belongs especially to those who have departed this life, though others too, because of the right granted them and the entrance opened to them, are sometimes said to be in Christ’s body and consequently in Christ’s kingdom.

Accordingly, on Psalm LI, no. 19, he calls the Jews, because they have fallen from that right and shut against themselves the entrance formerly open through their unbelief, torn away not only from Christ’s body but also from that kingdom of blessedness. Indeed, on Psalm CXVIII, letter 15, no. 12, having affirmed that the faithful who remain in sins fall from heaven and are therefore sinners of heaven [Col. 0104B], he says:

> Whoever, having become a partaker of heavenly teaching and spiritual grace, remains in sin, is not a sinner of earth but of heaven.

He gives the reason for his assertion: “For our Lord Jesus Christ raised together with himself and seated in the heavenly places all who believe in him; whoever falls from these is rebuked as a sinner of heaven.” Thus, just as we call sons heirs either when their father’s inheritance has actually fallen to them or when it has merely been appointed for them, so Hilary says that they dwell in Christ’s body and kingdom both when Christ has earned this grace for them and when he has granted it to them. But as great as the distance between an inheritance appointed and one acquired, so great did he believe the distance between human beings to whom the power of dwelling in Christ’s kingdom has been granted and the righteous for whom death obtains fellowship with Christ [Col. 0104C].

216. Whether, however, those saints for whom death obtains fellowship with Christ in some new manner dwell in Christ otherwise than by cleaving to him through love and resting in the blessed contemplation of that body until, having received their own bodies, they are made conformed to the glory of that body—Hilary does not explain this, and neither do we wish to determine it. We leave others also to determine whether he thought that, apart from the glory of their bodies, they lacked nothing for blessedness. Yet what could they desire if they enjoy God? Or who could think that he did not believe them to enjoy God when he believed them to be with Christ and in Christ?

For Gregory reasons thus in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 25: “Truth itself testifies: ‘Wherever the body shall be, there the eagles will be gathered’; because where our Redeemer himself is [Col. 0104D] in body, there without doubt the souls of the righteous are gathered. And Paul says: ‘I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.’ Therefore, whoever does not doubt that Christ is in heaven does not deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven.” Hilary certainly would not deny this: though he does not doubt that Christ is in heaven, he nonetheless affirms that after death the righteous are where Christ is. For, he says in Book IX of *On the Trinity*, no. 50, “Since the Father wills that those who believe in the Son should have eternal life, the Son wills that believers should be where he himself is. Unless, perhaps, dwelling with Christ is not eternity.” But if dwelling with Christ is eternal life, then those who are with Christ possess eternal life. Now, according to Hilary’s view, those who are in Christ’s kingdom are with Christ; therefore they [Col. 0105A] possess eternal life.

Another argument may be drawn from the same source. Those who dwell with Christ are where Christ is; Christ is in heaven; therefore those who dwell with Christ are in heaven. Further, those who are in Christ’s kingdom dwell with Christ; therefore they likewise are in heaven.

217. Moreover, on Psalm CXLII, no. 9, he indicates not obscurely that those who deserve to become Christ’s companions after this life behold God’s face, in these words: “Do not turn thy face from me, and I shall be like those descending into the pit.” “Scripture,” he says, “mentions the pit as the penal place of hell. … Therefore, unless the face of God—who is certainly Christ, the image of the invisible God—is present to every saint, he will be like those assigned to the punishment of hell, who have departed this life without hope of rest.” Hence, on Psalm CXIX, no. 4, he does not hesitate to say that Adam has already been endowed with glory: “Adam, having confessed, was reserved for pardon and glorified in Christ.”

218. It is also clear from elsewhere that Hilary’s opinion was never that heaven was open to no saint before the judgment. On Psalm II, no. 26, he declares that he believes those who rose at the Lord’s passion to be its inhabitants even today. Nor should I believe that he thought so poorly of his Lord’s kindness that, when on Psalm LXVII, no. 27, he relates that Christ ascended to heaven with the heavenly Powers and the souls of the saints going before his way, Christ would have allowed those blessed souls of the saints to accompany his journey but disdained to receive them with himself into their heavenly homeland.

Indeed, even after Christ’s ascent into heaven, he indicates on Psalm LVIII, no. 6, as will be observed there, that the protomartyr Stephen withdrew there [Col. 0105C] and, as he came, was met by the Father in the heights of heaven. He likewise testifies, on Psalm LXV, no. 23, that the hope of the other martyrs was that, when their bodies had been slain, they would fly to heaven:

> Therefore, through these kinds of punishments, the martyrs devoted their bodies as whole burnt offerings in testimony of faith, so that, when the sacrifices of their victims had been completed, they might enter God’s house, that is, the dwelling-place of the heavenly abode.

Certainly, if—as Ambrose says in Epistle 29 to Irenaeus, no. 8—the Lord Jesus himself is the highest good, it is exceedingly difficult to understand how those for whom death has acquired fellowship with Christ do not enjoy the highest good or are not supremely happy, especially in light of Hilary’s view explained in the preceding section, according to which he professes Christ, even according to his humanity [Col. 0105D], to be wholly God. And indeed, in Book X of *On the Trinity*, no. 34, he makes the thief a participant in Christ’s kingdom, which he had confessed, in such a way that he obtains in it not some ordinary happiness but the delights of consummate blessedness.

219. Having pursued this discussion concerning the condition of the righteous who depart from us rather too curiously, we inquired whether it could be demonstrated from the firm tradition of the Church that heaven is granted to them immediately. Hence a treatise of no small extent had been prepared, in which we set forth first what our forefathers thought concerning martyrs, and then what they thought concerning the other righteous. But lest a preface which has already exceeded its proper bounds should grow without measure, and lest we seem to range beyond the limits of our Hilary, we judged it should be suppressed. If, however, any still doubt the faith by which we believe that heaven, opened by Christ, always stands open to the saints, let them here consider for themselves the chief grounds by which we have established that this faith has always prevailed in the Church. The Greek and Latin Fathers, indeed, with the exception of a few imbued with the error of the millenarians, teach with great unanimity that martyrs enjoy heaven. Indeed, the effort of Irenaeus and Tertullian to root this belief out of the minds of the faithful proves that it had already been received in their age. Moreover, when they reread the authentic Acts of the Martyrs, they will scarcely find a single righteous man who did not suffer in this hope: that, dying, he would pass into heaven. God frequently made this faith, which most profess in explicit words, more certain by visions. So public, indeed, was it that we read of Christ's martyrs being questioned about it by their judges and mocked for it by pagan crowds. Nor is the devout custom of the Christian people a slight testimony to the same faith: they were accustomed to hasten to the martyrs and ask them, when they had reached God in heaven, to deign to remember them before him. Why mention those who composed the Acts of the Martyrs, when very many declare that the martyrs attain heaven and God, and not one denies it? Finally, no one who consults the ancient Roman Order, or the Gothic Missal published in book III of *De Liturgia Gallicana*, as well as the Gallican Sacramentary inserted in volume I of the *Museum Italicum* from a manuscript written a thousand years ago, and other monuments of sacred antiquity of this kind, will deny that this same faith was formerly recorded in the public prayers of the Church. Now, since it is not our blood but charity that opens heaven, once it is opened to martyrs it is easily proved to stand open also to the other righteous; and this, in truth, we have found established by the authority of the same Fathers and by almost the same arguments.

## § VII. ON THE LAST JUDGMENT: WHETHER HILARY EXCLUDED ANY PERSONS FROM IT

220. A highly celebrated man wrote not long ago that Hilary's error concerning the last judgment is intolerable. Although he does not there state wherein that error consists, he had previously made sufficiently clear that this censure of his falls upon Hilary's statement in *On Psalm I*, no. 16:

> For when he says, “He who believes in me shall not be judged,” he exempted believers from judgment; and when he added, “But he who does not believe has already been judged,” he did not admit unbelievers to judgment.

And in no. 17:

> But, judgment having been removed from believers and unbelievers, the Lord added the cause of judgment and those responsible for it, upon whom judgment had necessarily to be passed. For there are some among the ungodly and the godly who are intermediate, mixed from both groups, yet properly belonging to neither, because they consist of both together: they are not to be reckoned among believers, since some unbelief is implanted in them; nor assigned to unbelief, since they also possess something of faith.

And, shortly afterward:

> Therefore those will be judged who, neither as godly persons, will not be judged, nor, as ungodly persons, have already been judged.

He explains this again in *On Psalm LVII*, no. 7.

221. Origen had long before warned, in volume I of Huet's edition, p. 42, that some had been led by these words of Psalm I—“Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment”—to deny judgment to the ungodly. “Relying,” he says, “upon the authority of this passage, certain simpler believers deny that the wicked will share in the resurrection or be deemed worthy of God's judgment.” Lactantius seems to have struck upon this same rock in book VII of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 20, where he writes concerning the final judgment:

> Yet not all will then be judged by God, but only those who have been occupied with the religion of God. For those who have not acknowledged God, since a sentence of acquittal cannot be rendered concerning them, are already judged and condemned; as the sacred Scriptures testify that the ungodly shall not rise in judgment. Therefore those who have known God will be judged, and their deeds—that is, their evil works—will be weighed against their good works: so that, if their good works are more numerous and weightier, they may be justified unto the blessed life; but if evils prevail, they may be condemned to punishment.

Whether Hilary too fell into this error must now be considered.

222. First, it must be observed that Hilary distinguishes two judgments: one at the consummation of the world, and another after the death of each individual. He mentions the latter, or perhaps both, in *On Psalm LVII*, no. 7, where he explains these words of the same Psalm, “Indeed, there is a God judging them on earth,” as follows:

> Thus, when a man says whether there is fruit for the righteous, there is no doubt that he awaits judgment; yet the righteous man has already been judged on earth, because through angels he has been led into Abraham's bosom.

There he proves that the righteous man has already been judged on earth because he has been led by angels into Abraham's bosom; this could not have occurred without a preceding judgment. The other judgment, however, may be understood to be that which he declares is still awaited. Nor does he merely affirm that the righteous man, but also the unbeliever, is judged before the last judgment. In the same place he states repeatedly:

> Therefore, since the saint is not to be judged, because he is to pass from death into life, and the unbeliever has already been judged unto punishment, it is understood that judgment remains for those who are intermediate between sin and faith, according to the quality of their deeds.

When, however, the ungodly person is judged unto punishment, he explains in *On Psalm II*, no. 48, in these explicit words:

> This wrath, by which they perish from the righteous way, is not slow, lest anyone flatter himself meanwhile with a gain of delay in punishment during the postponements of judgment. For wrath is kindled quickly. Avenging hell receives us at once; and, when we depart from the body, if we have lived thus, we immediately perish from the right way. The Gospel rich man and poor man are witnesses for us: angels placed the one in the seats of the blessed and in Abraham's bosom; the region of punishment immediately received the other. Indeed, punishment received the dead man so immediately that his brothers still remained above. There is no delay or postponement there. For the day of judgment is the eternal recompense either of blessedness or of punishment; but the time of death holds each person meanwhile under its own laws, while either Abraham or punishment reserves each one for judgment.

We have not hesitated to quote this passage in full, in order to confirm what we said in the preceding section: nothing prevents us from believing that Hilary thought the saints were granted heaven before judgment, although in *On Psalm CXX*, no. 16, he writes that they are reserved for entrance into the heavenly kingdom under the Lord's guardianship. For he likewise teaches that the ungodly are reserved for judgment, even though he nevertheless declares that they are meanwhile received and punished by avenging hell.

223. Moreover, our question is considerably illuminated by the very passage just cited. For what does this mean: “Either Abraham or punishment reserves each person for judgment”? Does it not mean simply that both believers—who have been placed in Abraham's bosom—and ungodly persons—whom avenging hell has received—are to be presented anew before the supreme Judge on the last day? Indeed, Hilary himself plainly affirms this in *On Psalm LV*, no. 7:

> Although all flesh has been redeemed in Christ so as to rise again, and all must stand before his tribunal, yet glory and honor in rising are not promised alike to all.

Accordingly, in book III of *On the Trinity*, no. 16, he explains Christ's words, “Glorify me,” thus:

> This is the prayer of the flesh, in which all will see him pierced on the day of judgment and recognize him from the cross.

224. Therefore, just as Hilary is acquitted of the error by which certain simpler persons denied that the wicked would share in the resurrection, since he affirms that all flesh will rise, so also, since he indicates that all will stand before Christ's tribunal, he must not be associated with those same persons who again believed that the wicked would not be deemed worthy of God's judgment. For why should all flesh stand before Christ's tribunal, unless to receive his sentence? Hilary was so persuaded of this that, regarding the righteous and ungodly whom either Abraham or punishment meanwhile reserves for judgment, he asserts in the passage cited: “The day of judgment is the eternal recompense either of blessedness or of punishment.” But how is it a recompense of punishment or blessedness except through the sentence of one condemning or rewarding? Thus he believed that on that day the unrighteous, no less than the righteous, would be judged.

225. Furthermore, if anything is inferred from the exposition of the first Psalm, it must be said that Hilary removed not only the unrighteous but also the saints from the last judgment. Yet it is clear that he considered no saint exempt from the final judgment; for in *On Psalm CXVIII*, letter 3, no. 12, he does not even except the Mother of God, whom he nevertheless sufficiently indicates to excel all other human beings in merit of holiness when he says:

> If that Virgin of God, capable of entering into the severity of judgment, is to come there, who would dare desire to be judged by God?

Therefore it is wrongly concluded from the exposition of the first Psalm that Hilary did not believe the ungodly would be judged. And indeed what he writes in *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 5, no. 12, means something altogether different:

> If immortality is granted to the Gentiles for this reason, that they may soon be assigned to the fire of judgment, etc.

For we read that God will restore to unbelievers the eternal substance of their bodies, not that they may burn immediately, but that they may soon be assigned to the fire. We understand that the sentence of the supreme Judge has not yet been pronounced, but will soon be pronounced. This is further indicated by the following word, by which he declares not simply that they are to be delivered to fire, but to the fire of judgment. To this belongs what he says in *On Psalm II*, no. 44: unbelieving and impenitent Jews will be judged by the Ninevites and the Queen of the South; and, generally, all criminals by the saints.

226. What, then, does it mean when he elsewhere denies that they will be judged? To reconcile these statements, a twofold force of the word “judgment” must be distinguished. For although it denotes the action of a judge, the judge may be regarded either as pronouncing sentence or as examining the matters concerning which he is to pronounce sentence. If you take the word in the former sense, Hilary admits that the ungodly will be judged; if in the latter, he denies it. But if you reject this distinction, you will encounter the same conflict of words not merely in different passages, but in this very book VI of *On the Trinity*, no. 1:

> He himself will judge all, and, through the mercy befitting his majesty, will temper, in consideration of ignorance, the punishment deserved by error; those who deny him, however, he will certainly not judge, but deny.

For, according to this, the Lord will judge all, yet will not judge all, but will not judge those who deny him.

227. Why he said that the godly and ungodly would not be judged in the former sense, he himself explains in *On Psalm I*, no. 17:

> For what need is there to judge the believer? Judgment arises from uncertainty; and once uncertainty is removed, the examination of judgment is not required. Hence unbelievers too need not be judged, because no uncertainty remains as to whether they are unbelievers.

And Paulinus, in poem 7, says this in exact agreement with Hilary and directly relevant to our subject:

> Because they will bear the imminent mark of death,  
> not bearing the sign of salvation on their foreheads.

This is not said as though anything were obscure to God. The uncertainty applies not to God, but to those being judged, or even to those attending the judgment. Therefore the investigation will occur only so that, to speak with Origen, being conscious of the things done by us, we may clearly perceive why we are affected with punishment or honor (Origen, Huet edition, vol. I, p. 346). Nor will it be long. For God, as the same Origen teaches in the same place, willing to recall to everyone's memory whatsoever has been done throughout the course of all time, so that each may be conscious of the things he has done well or badly, will accomplish this by ineffable power. Then, when each person's well- or ill-done deeds are clear to him, the faith, charity, and repentance of the good will judge and condemn the unbelief, negligence, and impenitence of the wicked. Thus Hilary explains in *On Psalm II*, no. 44, how it will be granted to the good to be judges of the earth. In this he differs from Lactantius no less than in teaching that the wicked will rise, and will rise for judgment—that is, in order to be judged.

228. Paulinus of Nola's poem 7 greatly illustrates Hilary's teaching concerning the last judgment:

> Therefore the scattered flocks of human beings  
> dispersed throughout the world will be divided in this order:  
> the ungodly, who denied God the worship due to him,  
> will not rise to be judged, but to be punished;  
> for, seeing his own crime,  
> he will not need an inquiry to disclose it,  
> because they will bear the imminent mark of death,  
> not bearing the sign of salvation on their foreheads.  
> But the sinner who is nevertheless not ungodly—  
> and this is a great multitude—will not rise to glory,  
> but will rise to be assigned to examination;  
> for he cannot sit as a judge with the godly  
> while he must render account of his own acts  
> and, according to his varied deeds, be either approved or found guilty.

Thus, to summarize Hilary's view of the final judgment: three conditions of human beings must be distinguished—the righteous, who are granted blessedness immediately at their death; the ungodly, whom avenging hell receives when they leave this life; and those intermediate between the two, who remain uncertain of their lot until judgment. All will stand before Christ's tribunal: the righteous and the ungodly, so that their eternal recompense, whether of blessedness or punishment, may be confirmed; but properly speaking, judgment, with inquiry and examination, will concern those who occupy the intermediate condition. When this view is rightly understood, the statement of Caesarius in Augustine's Appendix, Sermon 77, no. 4, may more conveniently be explained:

> For neither pagans, nor heretics, nor Jews come to judgment, because it is written of them: “He who does not believe has already been judged.”

Nor does what Firmilian says expressly concerning heretics in Cyprian, Epistle 75, mean much else:

> It is evident that all these have condemned themselves and, before the day of judgment, have pronounced against themselves an inexcusable sentence.

229. The statement of Cyprian in Epistle 52 to Antonianus likewise seems referable to the same opinion:

> It is one thing to stand for pardon, another to attain glory; one thing to be sent to prison and not leave it until one has paid the last farthing, another immediately to receive the reward of faith and virtue; one thing to be cleansed and purified from sins by long torment and long purged by fire, another to have purged all sins by suffering; finally, one thing to hang in suspense until the day of judgment for the Lord's sentence, another to be crowned immediately by the Lord.

The printed editions indeed read “to hang in suspense on the day of judgment.” But when we conjectured that the reading should be “until the day,” our conjecture was confirmed upon consulting the Germanensis manuscript of excellent authority. Cyprian therefore distinguishes in that passage those who, since they are not good enough to deserve immediate crowning, remain uncertain until the day of judgment—not, as Pamelius thinks, a particular judgment, but the general judgment—until they are declared by the Lord's sentence worthy of eternal punishments or rewards. Cyprian's words, in the elucidation of which many learned men have labored, are thus neatly explained in accordance with Hilary's mind. Hence there is almost no doubt that those who wish Cyprian, throughout the passage cited by us, to speak only of penitents, whose condition he compares with that of martyrs, have not understood it sufficiently. He does indeed speak of penitents in the first words, “It is one thing to stand for pardon,” and thereby shows them that those who live in crimes or in holiness are held by the Church in a very different position, and thus that the reins are not to be loosened for sins through penance. Thereafter, however, he proves that the Church acts in this matter no otherwise than the Lord himself acts toward us after our life has ended: he immediately grants some the reward of faith and virtue; sends others into prison until they pay the last farthing; immediately crowns others who have purged all sins by suffering; and purifies and cleanses by prolonged fire others for whom much remains to be cleansed. Hence Pamelius, together with many others, rightly judged that the Church's belief in purgatorial fire is approved in this passage of Cyprian. The things handed down by other Fathers concerning the fire of judgment confirm it no less. Of that fire we must now speak.

## § VIII. ON THE FIRE OF JUDGMENT

230. Various questions arise concerning the fire of judgment: first, whether Hilary and other Fathers believed that absolutely everyone must undergo it; second, on what grounds they believed this; third, whether they believed that saints would suffer any punishment from it; fourth, whether they thought that fire would differ from that in which the devil and his own are to be tormented forever; and finally, whether, in their opinion, no one is afflicted by its punishment before judgment. Each point must be touched upon briefly.

231. Hilary sufficiently indicates that he believes the fire of judgment must be undergone by all in *On Psalm CXVIII*, letter 3, no. 12, where he says:

> Since we shall have to render account for every idle word, shall we desire the day of judgment, in which that unwearied fire must be undergone by us, in which those grave punishments for the soul's expiation from sins must be undergone? The soul of blessed Mary will be pierced by a sword [a flaming sword], so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed. If that Virgin of God, capable of entering into the severity of judgment, is to come there, who would dare desire to be judged by God?

It is as if he said: If not even the most holy Mother of God is to be exempt from this fire, who can confidently promise himself exemption from it? Hilary is agreed with Origen, Homily 6 on Exodus and Homily 3 on Psalm XXXVI; Lactantius, book VII, chapter 21; Ambrose, *On Psalm CXVIII*, sermon 3, no. 14; Paulinus of Nola, Epistle 28, no. 2, and Poem 7; Caesarius of Arles, in the Appendix to Augustine, Sermon 104, nos. 4 and 8; and Eligius of Noyon, Homily 8. This opinion was at last so accepted among the ancients that Ambrose writes concerning Saint John the Evangelist in *On Psalm CXVIII*, sermon 20, no. 12: “Some have doubted concerning his death; we cannot doubt concerning his passage through the fire.”

232. They adopted this opinion, prompted both by Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 3:13, “Fire will test what sort of work each person's is,” and especially by Genesis 3:24, where, after Adam and Eve had been cast out of Paradise, God is said to have placed the cherubim with a flaming sword at its entrance. They therefore believed that no one had a way to Paradise except through that flaming sword. Ambrose certainly suggests this quite clearly in these words from the aforementioned sermon 3:

> There is also a baptism at the threshold of Paradise, which was not there before; but after the sinner was excluded, the fiery *romphaea* [sword] which God placed there began to be.

And in sermon 20 on the same Psalm CXVIII, no. 14: “Therefore iniquity will be burned up by that fiery sword.” Accordingly, Tertullian, *Apology*, no. 47, defines Paradise as “a place of pleasantness appointed for receiving the spirits of saints, separated from knowledge of the common world by a certain enclosure of that fiery zone.” This is the point of his statement in *On the Soul*, no. 55: “The *romphaea*, guardian of Paradise, yields to none except those who have died in Christ.” Moreover, since Hilary interpreted Simeon's prophecy to Mary—“A sword will pierce your soul”—as concerning passage through that flaming sword, he reasonably concluded, on the basis of his pre-established opinion concerning the Virgin's merit and holiness above all human beings, that everyone must fear judgment and that no one, however great his holiness, would be exempt from the testing of the flaming sword.

233. But while they proclaim with great unanimity that all must be tested by the fire of judgment, they also proclaim that not all will feel its power equally. Lactantius, book VII, chapter 21: “Those whom full and perfect righteousness has ripened will not feel that fire.” Origen, Homily 3 on Psalm XXXVI: “All of us must come to that fire. Even if one be Paul or Peter, he nevertheless comes to that fire; but such persons hear: ‘Even if you pass through fire, the flame will not burn you.’” Ambrose, in the aforementioned sermon 20, no. 13: “He who has here the fire of charity will not be able there to fear the fire of the sword”; and shortly afterward, concerning Peter: “But he,” he says, “will be tested as silver; I shall be tested as lead.” For, as Paulinus says in Epistle 28, the fire will receive men like Peter as approved and touch them with a gentle lick; and, as Eligius states in Homily 8, they will prevail over that fire with as much strength as in life they have kept the commandments through the charity of faith and love of Christ. Aptly, therefore, Gregory Nazianzen, near the beginning of Oration 26, calls it the last fire, “by which all that is ours will be weighed or purified”: for while it cleanses stains, it only weighs and tests holiness. Caesarius touches upon this twofold property of the fire in the Appendix to Augustine's Sermons, Sermon 15, no. 4:

> Therefore, in order that our God might present holy Jacob in judgment as purified gold, he first wiped away from him all stains of sins, so that the fire as arbiter could find in him nothing to burn.

And in Sermon 104 of the same Appendix, no. 8, he says generally:

> Those who build upon the foundation gold, silver, and precious stones will pass through that fire—of which the Apostle says, “For it will be revealed in fire”—without any harm.

234. But if those in whom nothing remains to be purified will pass through this fire without any harm or delay, it follows that those who have more stains of sin to be wiped away will feel its force more sharply, or even be detained in it longer. This is taught above all by the homily of Eusebius Gallicanus, which we believe to be by Faustus of Riez. In it one reads:

> As great as the material of sin has been, so great is the delay in passing through; as much as guilt has required, so much will a certain rational discipline of flame claim from the person; and as much as foolish iniquity has committed, so much will wise punishment rage.

These words are again copied in the Appendix to Augustine, Sermon 252, no. 3.

235. Because of the discrimination by which that fire, while punishing sins, reveres holiness, Faustus calls it “a rational flame” and “wise punishment”; Paulinus, Epistle 28, no. 2, as also in the other appended letter to Marcella, “a wise fire”; Caesarius of Arles, in the cited Sermon 15, “the fire as arbiter”; and Paulinus of Nola, Poem 7, again bestows this same title on it.

236. This being so, nothing detrimental to the glory and holiness of the most pure Mother of God follows from Hilary's words, “If that Virgin of God, capable of entering into the severity of judgment, is to come there.” For he quite plainly signifies that he was compelled by the authority of Scripture to confess that she would pass through the flaming sword in judgment. When he concludes from this, “Who would dare desire to be judged by God?” he implies that no one is comparable to the blessed Virgin either in holiness or in privileges. But she who passes through the flame by the common law will pass through it all the more gloriously insofar as she passes through it more unharmed. For if, as Faustus says in the cited homily, the righteous will pass there as through pleasant streams, while the fires change their nature, and bodies untouched by the fires will be honored by the very punishments, because they are not burdened with sins, how much more must Hilary be thought to have believed this concerning the blessed Virgin? That he himself believed a human being could attain such innocence that he need fear nothing from that fire is clear from the same exposition, letter 3, no. 13. Noting that the Prophet does not merely desire judgment but desires it eagerly, he explains wherein the reason for this desire lies:

> Namely, that he may remain in such great innocence that he may now safely, and without fear of judgment, desire its terror.

It was important to observe these points in order to show that this most devout bishop intended the honor of the inviolate Virgin to remain unimpaired.

237. It is of less importance to know whether the same fire by which the reprobate are to be tortured is also that by which the remnants of sins are to be expiated. Faustus expressly teaches in the cited homily that it will be different. Nor are Ambrose's words in *On Psalm CXVIII*, sermon 3, any less clear:

> One is this fire by which sins that are not voluntary but accidental are burned up, which the Lord Jesus prepared for his servants, in order to cleanse them from this dwelling-place which is mingled with the dead; another is that fire which he appointed for the devil and his angels.

Therefore, when Hilary calls the fire of judgment “unwearied fire,” he must be understood to have regarded not so much its eternity as its nature: its force is not in the least weakened even by a long ministry of burning. Tertullian, indeed, in *Apology*, no. 48, speaking of judgment, mentions unceasing fire, eternal fire, and unceasing judgment; but there he has regard only to the reprobate.

238. There remains the no less important question of expiatory punishments before judgment, which already had its opponents in Augustine's age. He answers them in book XXI of *The City of God*, chapter 16:

> Therefore, whoever wishes to escape everlasting punishments should not only be baptized, but also be justified in Christ, and thus truly pass from the devil to Christ. But he should suppose that no purgatorial punishments will occur except immediately before that last and dreadful judgment.

Augustine, while in some measure allowing them this opinion as permissible, later does not conceal that he himself thinks otherwise. Much has already been established from which Hilary's view on this matter can be explained. For we have heard him say that each person is judged immediately upon death, and that, besides those who are entirely good or entirely evil, a class of human beings intermediate between the two must be distinguished. He assigns a different lot to each: in his view, avenging hell immediately receives the ungodly, death gains for the righteous fellowship with Christ, and judgment upon those who are intermediate is reserved until the Lord's day—not because God does not know what they deserve, but because, by a more profound counsel, he judges that it ought not to be revealed to them. Who, then, can deny that even from this view of Hilary's it follows that this intermediate condition suffers punishments that are not light? Is it a light punishment for a soul created to enjoy God to be delayed from fellowship with Christ, through whom we possess God? What shall I say of that anxiety by which the intermediate condition is meanwhile tormented, until at the last judgment it learns whether it is worthy of love or hatred, of the punishments of hell or the joys of the heavenly assembly?

239. Moreover, if one considers what he says in *On Psalm CXXXVIII*, no. 22—“It is a law of human necessity that, when bodies are buried, souls descend to the underworld”—it will first be inferred that he considered no one exempt from this law, especially when the words immediately following are added: “The Lord did not refuse this descent, for the consummation of true humanity.” It will then easily be understood that Hilary says that all other human beings are necessarily subject to this law, which Christ fulfilled in order to demonstrate himself in every respect to be a true human being, because all, after death, must be tested through fire as to whether they are worthy of Christ's kingdom; just as absolutely all, on the day of judgment, after receiving their bodies, must pass through fire before being conveyed into the kingdom of God the Father. Granted this, it must not be denied that those in whom the fire finds many things to burn away are kept and tormented in the underworld as long as some stain of sins must be purified from them.

240. Lest this interpretation of ours seem alien to Hilary, the words of Origen, whom—as is well known—he knew intimately, should be added. They openly affirm what is less fully explained in Hilary. In his *Commentaries on 1 Kings* XVIII, Huet edition, p. 36, Origen teaches that our condition is much happier than that of those who lived before Christ, because none of them—not Abraham, not the patriarchs, not the prophets—was granted permission to pass into the place where the tree of life was. “But we,” he says, “who have come at the consummation of the ages, possess something outstanding beyond others. What is it? If we depart from this life good and upright, not bringing along with us burdens of sins, we shall pass through the flaming sword, nor shall we come to that place in which those who had rested before his coming awaited Christ. We shall pass through without suffering any injury from that flaming sword. But fire itself will test what sort of work each person's is. If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire. Therefore we shall pass through,” etc. What could be clearer? Christians are permitted to reach Paradise before judgment; yet no one reaches it except through the flaming sword. But some pass through that fire unharmed, while others suffer loss.

241. Tertullian also proves expiatory flames at the end of his book *On the Soul*. For after showing that it is just that, since the soul has the chief part in good or evil deeds, it should also be the first, before receiving the body again, either to be punished or refreshed, he finally concludes:

> In short, since we understand that prison which the Gospel shows to be the underworld, and interpret the last farthing as every slight offense that must there be paid by delay of the resurrection, no one will doubt that the soul pays something in the underworld, while the fullness of the resurrection through the flesh remains preserved.

This confirms what was observed in the preceding section concerning Cyprian's words: “It is one thing to be sent to prison and not leave it until one has paid the last farthing, another immediately to receive the reward of faith and virtue; one thing to be cleansed and purified from sins by long torment and long purged by fire,” etc. Namely, these words are spoken not of living penitents but of departed believers, for whom either nothing or something remains to be purified. We deliberately pass over the opinions of other Fathers on this matter. Our purpose is not so much to prove the Church's belief in purgatorial punishments as to illuminate Hilary's opinion and show it to be consonant with that belief.

## § IX. WHETHER HILARY LACKED KNOWLEDGE OF SPIRITUAL REALITIES; WHAT HE THOUGHT OF GRACE

242. We have already noted that Claudianus Mamertus, book III of *On the State of the Soul*, chapter 9, criticized Hilary for saying that nothing created is incorporeal. The words in *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 5, no. 8, gave occasion for this criticism:

> There is nothing which is not corporeal in its substance and creation; and the elements of all things, whether in heaven or on earth, whether visible or invisible, have been formed. For even the kinds of souls, whether possessing bodies or exiled from bodies, nevertheless receive a corporeal substance of their nature, because everything created must necessarily exist in something.

And indeed, if only the *Commentaries on Matthew* survived, we would readily grant that he agreed with Methodius, at the end of Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 234; Cassian, *Conference* 7, chapter 13; Theophilus of Alexandria, *Against the Anthropomorphites*, in Gennadius; and finally Gennadius in Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 11—all of whom declare God alone incorporeal and all other natures corporeal. But since in other writings he expressly establishes, in several places, spiritual natures other than the divine nature, it is unfair to judge his true opinion from one obscure passage. Nevertheless, one can scarcely find anyone who corrects Claudianus's criticism without counting Hilary among those who taught that the human soul is corporeal. Indeed, it has recently been written that he did not have a sufficiently clear understanding of spiritual realities. Let us now see whether this is correct.

243. We recognize only three spiritual substances in the order of nature: God, angels, and the human being in respect of the soul. As for God, nearly every page of his works bears witness to the extent of Hilary's knowledge. Who thinks more highly of him? Who speaks of him more magnificently? But he also hands down so much concerning angels that scarcely anything is known of them even now which he did not teach clearly. Whether we consider their nature, their offices, or their glory, how lucid is his doctrine on every point! For he not only calls them superior to our nature, but openly proclaims them spiritual, incorporeal, and immortal by nature, since, by the lot of nature which they have received, they receive that they may always exist.

> **Note:** In *On Psalm CXXXVII*, no. 5, and *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 5, no. 11, he understood angels to be spiritual and incorporeal.

244. As regards their offices, since they perform some duties toward God and others toward human beings, he discusses both kinds [Col. 0116A] so admirably and at such length as openly to show that he regarded them as incorporeal. Certainly, although he testifies that some, as if by the law of their particular office, possess the privilege of standing by the throne of God, he nevertheless represents all of them, by the common lot of their condition, as standing before the brightness of God, attending upon God’s throne, and persevering with unceasing voice in the praises of God. And although he holds that they always stand by God’s throne in heaven and never fail to rejoice in his blessed vision, and for that reason are called gods in heaven (*On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 6, no. 8; *On Psalm* CXXIX, no. 7; *On Psalm* CXXXVI, no. 11; *On Psalm* 132, no. 17), yet, because of the things which God accomplishes on earth through them, he calls them here “eternal and blessed powers,” there “the aids of divine ministries,” and elsewhere the eyes, ears, hands, and feet of God. But lest this redound to God’s dishonor [Col. 0116B], he prudently adds: “Therefore God’s nature does not require the intercession of these beings; our weakness does.”

Nor does he omit the many ways in which they assist our weakness; and while recounting one kind of service—or, as he calls it, “justification in relation to the angels”—he implies that, because of the benefits bestowed, they ought to be honored by us with some measure of reverence. But we shall not linger over this. We may also note in passing that he declares their glory to have been granted apart from the reward of work. “The lilies,” he says, “which neither toil nor spin, are to be understood as signifying the brightnesses of the heavenly angels, to whom, apart from the instruction of human knowledge and the reward of their own work, the radiance of glory was granted by God, lest they should be thought to possess anything through their own labor or skill.” Who, then, would agree that Hilary’s knowledge of the angelic [Col. 0116C] nature was either carnal or insufficiently clear, when he places them both in heaven and on earth, aiding human beings and standing before God (*On Psalm* CXXXVII, no. 5; *On Psalm* CXX, no. 7; *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 1, no. 12; *On Matthew*, ch. 5, no. 11)?

245. Nothing need be observed concerning the various orders of angels, unless Cotelerius, in book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, p. 312, had remarked that in these words of Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book II, no. 9—“The archangels do not know; the angels have not heard; the ages do not comprehend”—the term *saecula* (“ages”) designates a new order of angels. But we are prevented from agreeing with his opinion: first, because, although Hilary very frequently enumerates various orders of angels, he nowhere calls any among them *saecula*. Further, in his commentaries on the Psalms he often has occasion to explain the word *saeculum*; yet in not even one place does he turn its interpretation toward angels [Col. 0116D]. Indeed, in *On Psalm* LXV, nos. 12 and 13, expressly examining the force of the Greek word αἰών (*aiōn*, “age”), he recognizes it as signifying nothing but a determinate period of time. This indicates that he either did not know of, or rejected, the aeons of certain Greeks; as indeed, in book VI of *On the Trinity*, no. 9, he rejects Valentinus’ aeons, which there he calls “eternities,” not *saecula* (“ages”). Finally, he uses *saecula* in other places too, but never even once understands angels by that name—unless perhaps, when in that same book II, no. 13, he says: “Times pass away, ages are carried onward, generations are removed”; and shortly afterward: “But my unlettered, untaught fisherman, free from time and released from ages, has overcome every beginning”; and in book VI, no. 37: “By revelation Peter learned the mystery hidden from the ages”—unless, I say, he called *saecula* angels [Col. 0117A] rather than times. Thus, what “has not been heard from the age” in the simpler language of the Prophets is, in the cited passage, elegantly expressed by Hilary as “the ages do not comprehend.”

246. If we pass from good to evil angels, there will be ample occasion to admire how extensive and varied was his knowledge of their malice, power, devices, and punishments. But who could suspect that he was uncertain whether their nature is spiritual, when he had not only heard them commonly called “spiritual wickednesses,” but had also read in *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 1, no. 8, that the devil traverses the whole vastness of this world in a moment of time, so as to have grounds upon which to accuse us? To what nature belongs such swiftness, if not a spiritual one? Divide any body whatever into the finest and most mobile parts that you can conceive: you will certainly never enable it [Col. 0117B] to traverse the whole extent of this world in a moment of time. Yet Hilary grants this power to the devil, although he confesses that the devil’s strength has been crushed and broken by the Lord’s coming. For he teaches that after judgment the devil will be consigned to heavier punishments, in such a way that even now, touched by God’s power, he smokes, though he is not yet wholly burned (*On Psalm* CXLIII, no. 11). The comparison is drawn from wood not yet fully kindled, in which the fire laid beneath begins to exert its force and already produces smoke.

247. Let these preliminary remarks on angelic natures suffice. From them it is no less clear that Hilary did not grope in darkness concerning all spiritual natures than that he affirmed something incorporeal besides God. If, moreover, one consults the discussions in *On Psalm* LII, [Col. 0117C] no. 7; Psalm CXVIII, letter 10, no. 6; and Psalm CXXIX, nos. 4, 5, and 6, where the human soul is repeatedly said to be not merely of a spiritual nature—which perhaps would not remove every doubt—but also of an incorporeal nature, all will be persuaded that he held nothing to be corporeal which we recognize as lacking body. Yet it is worth the effort to illustrate and confirm by several arguments his view concerning the nature of our soul.

248. First there presents itself the statement in Psalm CXVIII, letter 10, no. 6: that the human being contains within himself an inward and an outward nature, discordant one from the other, and that from two kinds he has been constituted one rational living being. If this human being, constituted from two kinds and containing within himself a nature discordant one from another, has received a corporeal soul just as he has received a body, then what follows? Must not the soul, however subtle it may be, if it is conceived as corporeal, be said to belong to one and the same kind as the body? Subtlety may perhaps alter its appearance; but corporeal parts will subject it to one kind, and consequently the human being will not contain within himself two kinds of things, nor a nature discordant one from another.

249. He perceived so great a difference between these two substances that in *On Psalm* LXI, no. 3, he implies that it is a greater miracle for body to be joined with soul in a human being than for the human being to be joined with God in Christ; and, since the former has occurred, there should be no doubt that the latter could occur. As if, he says against the philosophers who denied that God could be united with an assumed human being, it were more difficult for God to assume a human being [Col. 0118A] than to form that human being amid so great a distinction of nature and life. This is as if he said: Why do you reject as incompatible the union of human and divine nature? Surely God and the human being, with respect to the soul, differ less than soul and body. For soul and body are wholly different in kind; but although the soul is surpassed by God through infinite degrees of perfection, their kind is nevertheless not different. But body could be joined with soul; therefore God also can be joined with the human being.

250. This interpretation will commend itself to everyone, especially when, in the same place, one reads that it is as though implanted and impressed upon all that they should judge a divine origin of souls to be present within us, since the mind itself recognizes in itself no small kinship with the HEAVENLY KIND [Col. 0118B]. That Hilary commonly uses “heavenly” in place of “divine” will be shown there by several examples [Note: [Col. 0118D] In the notes on no. 12 of the exposition of Psalm CXIX.], and the preceding context sufficiently demonstrates that it is so used here. But unless our soul is spirit, as God is spirit, what kinship of divine kind, what affinity, is there in it? Thus, just as above he openly teaches it to be incorporeal, since its nature is discordant with the body, so now, in declaring it endowed with kinship to the divine kind, he no less plainly indicates that it is spiritual.

Nor did he say that souls have kinship with the heavenly kind and a divine origin because, with the Priscillianists mentioned by Augustine, *Heresies* 70, he thought every soul to be a part of God, of the same nature and substance as God. For although Origen was suspected of this error, Hilary shows that he did not follow him in this matter: he testifies that the soul has its origin and is God’s work, not from God’s substance, but from God’s breath (*On Matthew*, ch. 10, no. 24), and from the treasures of divine power (*On Psalm* LXVII, no. 22; *On the Trinity*, book X, no. 20)—that is, from the one omnipotence of God [Col. 0118C]. We pass over also those places in which he denies that division can in any way apply to God.

But if he does not believe that the soul comes from God’s substance, he was no less persuaded that it cannot arise from human substance. For, strongly rejecting those who maintained that Christ assumed from the Virgin both flesh and soul, he says: “As though, if he had assumed only a body from the Virgin, he had also assumed a soul from her; whereas every soul is God’s work, but the generation of flesh is always from flesh.” Soon afterward he firmly asserts that the Word assumed from himself [Col. 0118D] a soul “which certainly is never furnished from the originating sources of human procreation.” This scarcely permits doubt that he judged a soul unable in any way to be furnished by a human being. It follows plainly that he considered the soul not corporeal. For whoever regards it as corporeal must also grant that it may be divided and propagated after the manner of flesh, and consequently supplied by parents.

251. But why pursue consequences, when he himself, in *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 10, no. 6, plainly and clearly declares his judgment concerning the soul’s simplicity and its kinship with the divine nature? There, carefully considering the words of Genesis which narrate the creation of the human being [Col. 0119A], he distinguishes a threefold operation of God: the first, by which he created the soul by word alone, after in some manner taking counsel concerning its creation; the second, by which he formed the body from received dust; and the last, by which he joined the two. Concerning the soul he then adds: “The first work does not contain within itself the origin of an assumed other nature; whatever is then begun by the determination of counsel is INCORPOREAL, for it is made in the image of God.” He expressly indicates, first, that the soul is neither a part of the divine substance nor of any other substance; secondly, that it is incorporeal; and finally, that it must be believed incorporeal because it was undoubtedly made in God’s image. Hence it is clear that Hilary held the soul’s kinship with the divine nature to consist especially [Col. 0119B] in this: that it, like God, is incorporeal. This he confirms in no. 7 with these words: “In that first work the divine and INCORPOREAL was to be created, which was then made according to the image and likeness of God: namely, a certain pattern of the image and likeness of God was established in us. Therefore, in this rational and INCORPOREAL substance of our soul there is the first thing which was made in the image of God,” etc.

252. In *On Psalm* CXXIX he explains more fully in what respect the human being was made in God’s image.
