First, in no. 3, he says that God must be understood to be incorporeal, not consisting of certain parts and functions of limbs, from which a single body is formed. “For we read in the Gospel that God is spirit,” that is, an invisible, immense, eternal nature, remaining within itself. Here it should be observed that, for Hilary, that is not spirit which is not without parts. He continues: “But God, who is both everywhere and in all things, hears wholly, sees wholly, acts wholly, moves wholly . . . Therefore God’s power, which is equal and undivided, has the names of functions and limbs: so that the power by which he sees is eyes, the power by which he hears is ears,” etc.

Having thus defended God’s simple, incorporeal, and spiritual nature, in no. 4 he addresses the Anthropomorphites, who, because of Genesis’ words, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” hold God to be corporeal, as though the human being could not be in God’s image if God were incorporeal. He replies that the constitution of human beings contains two natures, soul and body: one spiritual, the other earthly. Yet they do not possess the privilege of being in God’s image in both these parts of themselves, lest God in turn be conceived as composed both of soul and body [Col. 0119D]. Then, in no. 5, having observed that the Apostle calls the soul the inward human being and the body the outward human being, he assigns to the soul alone the privilege of displaying in itself God’s image. Finally, in no. 6, he explains in what it imitates its Creator:

“Therefore the inward human being was made in God’s image: rational, mobile, moving, swift, INCORPOREAL, subtle, eternal. So far as lies within itself, it imitates the form of the supreme nature”—that is, the divine nature—“when it passes across, when it flies around, and more quickly than speech is now beyond the Ocean, now flies up into the heavens, now is in the depths, now surveys East and West, while it is never abolished so as not to exist”—though God’s nature is present in all these respects—“nor, in order to be present elsewhere, departs from another place.”

253. In this latter passage the words “mobile,” “moving,” “swift,” and “subtle” might perhaps be referred to a corporeal nature, if the intervening word “incorporeal” did not prevent it. Nor is it obscure that the mind is called swift and subtle because more quickly than speech it is now beyond the Ocean and now flies up into heaven; and it flies in such a way that, while it is present elsewhere, it does not depart from another place. Likewise, with respect to the will—which in book VIII of *On the Trinity*, no. 12, is defined as a movement of the mind—the mind is aptly understood to be both moving and mobile. Yet no one who has read immediately beforehand in the same place will be misled by the ambiguity of these terms: “The human soul was made in this mobility of its perception in the image of its Maker: while the enduring mobility of the soul imitates the nature of God, [Col. 0120B] it has NOTHING CORPOREAL in itself, nothing earthly, nothing heavy, nothing perishable.” Everyone knows that the mind may be called mobile because of the movement of the will; but here it is also called so because of the mobility of perception. Since this mobility signifies activity, not levity of mind, was it for this reason called enduring by Hilary—because he understood our soul’s thought to be perpetual, thereby imitating its Maker, who is never idle and never ceases to work?

254. In the cited passage he mentions as a second mark of God’s image impressed upon our mind that it is eternal. He testifies that the eternity and immortality of the soul are established for him both by faith and reason. Apart from the authority of sacred Scripture, he gives this one reason for his assertion: that God created it from his mere goodness, and that it would not accord with his goodness—because of malice—to destroy in us this gift by which we come into being. Moreover, as he says in book I of *On the Trinity*, no. 9, reason itself showed that it was unworthy of God to abolish what he had made. This is indeed a strong and effective argument for one who holds with certainty that the soul is incorporeal and composed of no parts, and who consequently concludes that it cannot be divided or destroyed by any created force, but can be established, and likewise destroyed, only by God. Otherwise the same argument would prove beasts also immortal.

255. Hilary was so firmly persuaded that the soul is simple, indivisible, and without parts that, in *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 19, nos. 8 and 9, when explaining how the incorporeal God is wholly wherever he is, is not anywhere merely in part, but is wholly in all things, he uses as a more familiar and better-known comparison that of the human soul, which is wholly present in all the limbs and wholly present in each of them, and does not know itself to be severed when they are severed. “God is everywhere after the manner of the corporeal soul, which, diffused through the limbs, is absent from none of their parts. Even if it has a certain private and royal seat in the whole body, nevertheless it is poured into the marrow, fingers, and limbs,” etc. In this place the text had hitherto read “after the manner of the incorporeal soul”; but from the manuscripts we judged “corporeal” preferable.

Nor is it obscure why the soul is called corporeal here. Angels may be regarded as souls freed from body, and certainly every human soul is either bound to a body or released from it. But neither a soul released from body nor angels [Col. 0121A] would suitably illustrate the majesty of the utterly simple God as present everywhere. For understanding this, the knowledge that the soul, although simple by nature, is nevertheless present in every limb of its body is uniquely useful. It is therefore plain that the soul is here called corporeal because of its relation to the body to which it is united and joined.

256. Thus, anyone who considers the several meanings accepted among the ancients, and by Hilary himself, for the word *corpus* (“body”) will not be troubled by his words on Matthew so as to suppose that he there regarded the nature of souls as corporeal—souls which in many places he so expressly affirms to be spiritual, incorporeal, and without parts. In what various senses “corporeal” may be understood will be explained in chapter 5 itself, on Matthew. But what Hilary says at the end of book VIII and the beginning of book IX of *On the Trinity* concerning the bodily indwelling of divinity in Christ will contribute no little toward understanding this difficult passage.

For when there he interprets “bodily divinity” as divinity which is one, true, full, and whole—“Divinity,” he says in book VIII, no. 56, “is bodily in Christ, not in part, but wholly; it is not a portion but fullness”—so it may suitably be understood that he opposes “corporeal” to what is not full, whole, and complete, when in his commentary on Matthew he says: “There is nothing which is not corporeal in its own substance and creation; and the elements of all things, whether in heaven or on earth, whether visible or invisible, are formed. For even the kinds of souls, whether possessing bodies or exiled from bodies, nevertheless receive the corporeal substance of their nature.” Indeed, he sufficiently explains his meaning when he repeats this earlier assertion, “There is nothing that is not corporeal,” in the words, “the elements of all things are formed”; so that there “corporeal” means what here is “formed,” and “formed” means what is not shapeless and imperfect [Col. 0121C].

It follows that Hilary means that all God’s works are good and perfect, and that none of them lacks anything necessary to the completeness of its substance. Thus he aptly rebukes the curiosity of those for whom God’s promises ought to have made it certain that souls would live eternally with bodies, but who, inquiring how they would live and failing to discover it, rendered God’s promises doubtful. This passage is therefore adduced in vain to prove that he maintained the corporeal nature of our soul, since it does not even speak of the soul’s nature.

257. Of less consequence is another point, which others have observed as though he had thought contrary to the common opinion. For although, as they wish and as his words in Psalm CXVIII, letter 10, and Psalm CXXIX imply, he may have believed that the first human being’s soul was created some interval before the body, he held this innocently concerning the first human being which he neither said, nor could be permitted to say, concerning that human being’s descendants, since the Church’s faith concerning original sin would thereby be seriously undermined. Yet he himself never wavered in this faith. Although he speaks very magnificently of the human being everywhere, especially in *On Psalm* CXXXIV, no. 14, he no less often insists that the human being fell from his original state through the first human being’s sin, and through that fall descended into every kind of weakness and misery [Col. 0122A].

258. From this there naturally arises a question, not inferior to those already settled: namely, what Hilary thought concerning grace. Mere sophistries, undeserving of refutation, are the arguments advanced by Scultetus, p. 410, to evade Bellarmine’s testimonies concerning Hilary’s doctrine of free will, justification, and the merits of good works. To prove that Hilary sometimes excludes the merits of good works, he opposes Hilary’s first words in *On Matthew*, ch. 7, no. 2: “The whole salvation of the Gentiles is from faith,” while suppressing what follows: “and in the Lord’s commandments is the life of all.” Again, he seems to exult because he reads in ch. 8, no. 6, that Christ remitted what the law could not relax: “for faith ALONE justifies.” As if Hilary had said this in any sense other than that in which Romans 3:28 says that a human being is justified by faith apart from works of the law. There Paul, as Augustine observes in *On Faith and Works*, ch. 14, no. 21, does not mean that works of righteousness should be despised after faith has been received and professed, but that each person should know that he can be justified by faith even if works of the law have not preceded it.

But what Hilary thinks concerning faith deprived of works he clearly reveals in *On Psalm* LI, no. 15: “If anyone has been unbelieving toward the God born in the body, or, though believing, remains without the fruits of his faith, he shall be rooted out either because of unbelief or because of the barrenness of the fruits denied.” Whoever has heard this and many other statements of the same kind will never agree with Scultetus’ claim that Hilary, in an inconsistent judgment, sometimes commended works and sometimes rejected them.

259. [Col. 0122C] Others do not fail to assert that he did not sufficiently understand the necessity and nature of grace. Nor must it be denied them that in several places he seems to attribute somewhat to the will which the Church later taught to be grace’s gift. Yet they themselves must confess: first, that the general disease of the human race was by no means unknown to him; secondly, that the need of a physician was not unknown to him; thirdly, that he was convinced both that the grace of justification is gratuitous (*On Matthew*, ch. 18, no. 10; ch. 20, no. 7), and that concupiscence remains in those justified (*On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 15, no. 6), so that in no one here is goodness perfect (*On Psalm* LII, no. 11), in no one is obedience to the commandments perfect (*On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 3, no. 6), and in no one is the human being upright and undeviating according to the nature of the first human being; fourthly, that he held grace necessary for attaining eternal life [Col. 0122D], for repelling temptations, for enduring evils, for fulfilling God’s commandments not only in deed but also for understanding them, for understanding the Scriptures, for praising God, for believing (*On the Trinity*, book VIII, no. 30; *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 1, no. 12), and for praying (*On Psalm* CXLII, no. 10).

Then, if they doubt whether the perversity and weakness of our will were known and evident to him, let them hear him say in *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 10, no. 18: “As we must learn faith from the prophet, so too humility and modesty, as he prays that a spotless heart may be made for him . . . He therefore prays that this may be made spotless, from which the beginnings of so many and such great vices are suggested, as though from a kind of tinder.” And in letter 17, no. 8: “If no hindrance occurred anywhere, if adversaries were not present against him on every side, he himself would be strengthened by his own powers for the things he wished to do. But where there are snares, where there is war, the help of one stronger is necessary, lest all injustice rule in him.” Let them read also similar passages in letter 3, no. 6, and elsewhere. From these it is plain that Hilary considered necessary not only the grace that enlightens the intellect, but also that which helps the will. Thus in *On Psalm* CXXVI, no. 13, he explains the addition of sorrow through knowledge to the weakness of the will left to itself: “For while the knowledge of truth urges our will toward the progress of attaining what is beneficial, the habit of nature restrains the will, though it knows that it ought to advance; the progress of knowledge is the progress of sorrow.”

260. Let these same persons afterward hear him teach in *On Matthew*, ch. 12, no. 8 [Col. 0123B], that finding Christ is gratuitous; and in *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 6, no. 4, set forth and praise, against human presumption, the example of the Prophet, who wills that everything be begun in him by God’s goodness. Of him Hilary also writes in no. 2: “He first asked for mercy, then for salvation. For our salvation is from God’s mercy, and this is the gift of his goodness in us; and prayer began where the petitioner’s salvation also begins.” Then let them return to *On Psalm* LI, no. 20: “It is the height of folly and impiety not to understand that one lives under God and from God, but in what one does and expects to prefer confidence in one’s own power; whereas whatever there is in oneself is from God. Therefore let all our hope be in God, and all confession [or possibly ‘trust’: *confisio*?] be in God.”

Next they will encounter in *On Psalm* CXXIII, no. 2: “For what place has been left to us for glorying, when we remember that all things are from God?” And shortly afterward: “If God’s mercy is not necessary in all things, let us glory that everything is ours as though from ourselves.” And in no. 3: “Let us refer our joys to him who dwells in us; let us owe to him whatever is in us, taught by blessed Paul, who says that nothing is to be considered ours: ‘For what have you that you did not receive?’” Proceeding from there to the exposition of Psalm CXXVI, you will learn whence comes the beginning of good works and whence perseverance, as follows in no. 5: “The Prophet rightly prophesied that the works of human labor are vain. He knows that the watchfulness of human guards is useless; he knows that the early cares of those who rise are in vain . . . Therefore the house which endures must be built by God, because unless it is built by the Lord it will not endure. The city must be guarded by God lest it perish, because unless the city is guarded by God [Col. 0123D], it will be destroyed.”

261. Very many examples of this kind repeatedly recur. At one time he considers human beings as dashed down and prone to falling, threatened always by a fresh fall and a new wound of sin (*On Psalm* CXLIV, no. 14; *On Psalm* CXLII, no. 4). At another time he compares even the soul of a saint to earth which, without water, is dry and unfruitful, and ever awaits irrigation by the rain of heavenly shower (*On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 6, no. 4). And because he knew with certainty that the human being continually needs God’s help, and considered this to be the doctrine of our hope—that God, when entreated, both has mercy and saves—he most aptly concludes in *On Psalm* LXIII, no. 6: “Therefore one must be watchful in prayer to God, and pray always, so that, when the soul begins to grow weary and be afflicted by the stings of creeping enticements, God, ever entreated, may hear.” And in *On Psalm* CXLIV, no. 14: “Therefore, wholly dashed down and falling, they look to God with their eyes, nor should anyone so trust in himself as not always to fear that he may fall and be dashed down.”

Finally, from the words in the exposition of Psalm CXVIII, letter 14, no. 20—“Lest what is often said by many should have any authority of reason, when they assert that it is God’s own gift for someone to be occupied in God’s concerns and works, excusing their unbelief because, God’s will toward them having ceased, they remain unbelievers,” etc.—it appears that the doctrine then common held all our good things to be gifts of God. Hence very many unbelievers had seized upon this as an occasion to excuse their obstinacy: that they had not yet obtained from God the gift of being faithful. While Hilary seeks to overcome their perversity [Col. 0124B], he makes certain statements which are not sufficiently exact according to the standard of a more polished and precise theology. But if, in this and similar passages, we attend not so much to the literal sound of his words as to his intention, it will not escape us that he is concerned only to avoid being thought, along with the Manichaeans, to destroy free will.

262. Indeed, not sufficiently distinguishing what in a good will comes from God and what from ourselves, he denied that it is given by God insofar as such a gift would remove freedom and introduce necessity, as he himself explains in *On the Trinity*, book VIII, no. 12: “Certainly not [did God give a will] which, if it had been given, faith would not have a reward, since the necessity of an imposed will would produce faith in us.” But if in those particular passages, in which he is wholly intent on defending free will, he attributes something to the will which it cannot do by itself without God’s grace, his doctrine, diffused throughout all his writings, establishes that he judged all glory for works to be ascribed to God’s grace, and denied it nothing except what would overthrow our freedom. Indeed, he speaks everywhere as though opponents of grace had already existed. For he scarcely praises any acts of virtue without immediately reminding us that we must remember our weakness; that if anything is to be done, we must hope for strength from God; and that if anything has been done well, we must refer it to that same help.

263. A subject of such importance would demand more, and we had prepared more as well; but we feared to detain the reader too long in matters so scrupulous. If anything has here been made clear which was previously insufficiently evident, let him give thanks [Col. 0124D] to Hilary, relying on whose help more than on the powers of our own ability we undertook this work. But if anyone is offended by its length, let him pardon the affection through which we have sought to restore to its integrity the authority of the most holy Confessor, somewhat diminished by insinuated suspicions, and thereby make the reading of his works more beneficial for all.

Yet it will not suffice to have explained his views unless we also set forth his deeds. We have indeed reported nearly all of these, both in the prefatory material to each work in order to elucidate its individual composition, and in the notes appended to them. But it is pleasing to gather all the pieces together and fashion from them, as it were, one body, so that an account of his life, arranged in continuous order, may be presented at a single glance in this threshold. Though the brush of the delineator be crude [Col. 0125A], the greatness of the subject, the variety of deeds performed, and finally the truth of the words—which we shall draw from the purest springs, namely Hilary himself and the most approved authorities—will stir and refresh the minds of readers.

Accordingly, while we give attention to relating his more notable deeds, which fall under the eye, we shall endeavor, according to our measure, to portray the mind of the holy Doctor: his blameless character from childhood; in his episcopal office, his holiness, learning, and erudition; his outstanding eloquence in speaking and writing; his fearless zeal for the faith; his almost divine strength against heretics, especially Arians; his unbroken patience in hard and adverse circumstances; and, finally, his invincible patience, gentleness, and mildness toward all—contrary to what has hitherto been believed by certain persons who do not know Hilary thoroughly.

This belief, to say so in passing, is sufficiently refuted [Col. 0125B] by Ruffinus’ testimony alone [Col. 0126A], in which Hilary is described as “a man gentle and peaceable by nature, learned as well, and eminently suited to persuasion,” one who instilled the truth of the faith in minds not only by eloquence and learning but also sought to insinuate it by gentleness, mildness, indulgence, and speech adapted to the obstinacy of others—which is the best means of winning acceptance for truth. Hence he sometimes relaxed somewhat the strictness of discipline, in order by a certain pious leniency to call back into the Church’s bosom those whom either error or ignorance had led astray. Hence at one time he preferred *homoiousion* to *homoousion*, and at another patiently endured the impious blasphemies of the Anomoeans, in order that through this gentleness he might gain all for Christ. Let these brief preliminary remarks suffice; with God’s favor, they must now be explained more fully.

[Col. 0125]

# LIFE OF SAINT HILARY, BISHOP OF POITIERS

COMPILED FOR THE FIRST TIME FROM HIS OWN WRITINGS AND ANCIENT RECORDS.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. Hilary’s birth: whether he was born of Christian parents.

No one has ever denied that Hilary, the most illustrious star of the Church, was born in Gaul. “For who,” says Augustine (*Against Julian*, book I, ch. 3), “does not know that Bishop Hilary was a Gaul?” Indeed, all agree that he was of Aquitanian origin, a region which Sulpicius Severus, supported by Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, ch. [Col. 0125C] 11, indicates to have surpassed the other provinces of Gaul in refinement at that time. Jerome also records that he was not only a Gaul but born at Poitiers (Jerome, Preface to book II of the *Commentary on Galatians*). Since Venantius Fortunatus agrees completely with this (*Poems*, book VIII, poem I, and book II, ch. 16), and another Fortunatus—if he was indeed another author of Hilary’s Life—does not disagree, that city cannot easily be deprived of the glory in which it believes itself adorned, not only by so great a man’s episcopate but also by his birth.

Saint Antoninus calls him a native of Bourges; Saussaye, however, states that he was born in the district of Clair. But who would not prefer the authority of Jerome and Venantius to that of more recent writers?

2. In a manuscript of Cardinal Ottoboni, not especially ancient, Hilary’s father is called Francarius. Bouchet also reports (*Annals of Aquitaine*, ch. 6) that, twenty years before publishing his work—that is, around the year 1500—the tomb of Hilary’s parents was discovered in the parish church dedicated to Hilary near Clisson, and that the same name was attributed there to his father. But whatever may be the case concerning his parents’ names, the distinction of his family certainly cannot be called into doubt. For, according to Fortunatus, he “was not obscure among Gallic families in the radiance of nobility, but rather was adorned above the rest by the distinction of high birth.”

[Col. 0126B] 3. Here arises the well-known question whether he was born of Christian parents. Most deny it, and confirm their view from the very opening of the books *On the Trinity*, in which Hilary seems to relate how he came to know the Christian faith. First, indeed, he states that, while considering what was the proper and religious duty of human life, by which life might become useful [Col. 0126C] and desirable, leisure and wealth at once presented themselves; but he judged these unworthy of human happiness, since they were not far removed from the habits of brutish pleasure. Then, as he considered the opinion of those who thought that to act and understand well was precisely to live well, he declares that this view, though less foolish, still did not seem sufficiently suited to a blessed life (no. 2). For they enclosed the blessed life within themselves, whereas his own mind raised itself toward God, to whom he owed his whole self; by serving whom he thought himself ennobled; to whom he referred all expectation of his hope; and in whose goodness, amid so many calamities of present affairs, he rested as in a most secure and familiar harbor (no. 3). Thereupon, he says, he weighed the various opinions of philosophers concerning God [Col. 0126D] and approved none of them; because, though most worshipped a plurality, he himself held it certain that in God nothing was venerable except what is eternal and powerful, and that omnipotence and eternity belong to one alone. Finally, he testifies that he acquired, as if by chance, the knowledge for which he had searched so anxiously (no. 4), in this manner: “Thus, while reflecting on these things and many others of the same kind, I came upon those books which the religion of the Hebrews declared to have been written by Moses and the prophets.” He then relates how greatly he profited from these books (no. 5): namely, that he marvelled [Col. 0127A] at how the words of Exodus 3, “I am who I am,” expressed the incomprehensible knowledge of the divine nature in language most fitting for human understanding; and that he afterwards learned from Isaiah 40:12 and 66:1 that God is immeasurable; from Psalm 138:7 that he is infinite beyond all understanding; and from Wisdom 13:5 that he is the most beautiful of all beauty.

4. After reading these things, his mind no longer wavered uncertainly over whom he ought to worship; yet it was troubled partly by its own fear and partly by fear for the body (nos. 6 and 7). For he possessed a natural conviction that some hope of incorruptible blessedness ought to sustain the profession of piety—a blessedness which a holy belief concerning God and good morals might merit. But from the beginning of John’s Gospel his trembling and anxious mind found more hope than it had expected. From it he was first instructed in the knowledge [Col. 0127B] of God the Father (nos. 9 and 10); then he learned that those attributes which he had formerly, by natural intuition, ascribed to the eternity, infinity, and form of his Creator also belonged properly to God the Only-begotten; and finally he heard that power was given to each person to become a child of God, and that therefore the Word became flesh, so that flesh, through God the Word made flesh, might advance into God the Word. Hence, when he finally concludes: “Accordingly, my joyful mind received this doctrine of the divine mystery, advancing into God through flesh, called through faith into a new birth, and granted power to obtain heavenly regeneration,” he seems to indicate that, already advanced in years, he was led by reading the Scriptures from pagan religion to Christianity (no. 11).

5. Nevertheless, what Fortunatus writes concerning him [Col. 0127C] (*Book I*, no. 3)—“From the cradle his earliest infancy was nourished by such great wisdom that even then it could have been understood that Christ had commanded a soldier to be raised up in his own cause, necessary to him for obtaining victory”—rather suggests that Hilary had put on Christ from childhood and had sucked in Christian teaching with his mother’s milk. Nor does the opening of the books *On the Trinity* conflict with this. For, since selected testimonies of Scripture there demonstrate how much greater the knowledge of God is among believers than among philosophers, it reflects less the mind of one recounting the first rudiments of his faith than that of a teacher deeply versed in sacred and secular literature, who either seeks, under the figure of himself, to lead a pagan philosopher by certain stages toward Christian religion, or to confirm himself ever more deeply, through a higher contemplation of realities, in the religion with which he was already imbued. Certainly, a man of such penetrating intelligence, capable by the accidental reading of sacred books of clearly and distinctly perceiving for himself the most hidden mysteries of Christian religion, would not only then have begun to think nobly of God when he reached Exodus. Genesis contains many things that wonderfully commend the majesty and glory of God. Even before he had reached Isaiah, he would have encountered in other books very many things confirming the conception of God that he had formed from Exodus. Nor does Hilary anywhere mention having abandoned the error of paganism. For when, in the words already cited above, he says that he gladly received the doctrine by which the mind is called to a new [Col. 0128A] birth and granted power to obtain heavenly regeneration, he should no more be thought to speak of his recent regeneration through baptism than to rejoice that he had been trained in that religion in which a new and imperishable birth of the soul, and a divine regeneration of bodies after this life, are hoped for; and that he was thus freed from the fear by which he had previously said he was troubled—lest soul or body should perish.

6. Nor do the ancients prove more effectively that Hilary was initiated into Christian mysteries only in adulthood. Jerome explains Isaiah’s words, “The glory of Lebanon shall come to you,” in such a way as to join and compare our Hilary with Cyprian, who, it cannot be denied, was long enslaved to the worship of idols:

> “The holy and most eloquent martyr Cyprian, and Hilary, confessor of our own time—do they not seem to you to have been trees once lofty in the world, which built the Church of God?”

But it is plain that Hilary and Cyprian are joined here in this single respect: both were lofty trees. Yet who would deny that Cyprian, insofar as he was a pagan, was not a lofty tree but rather one creeping upon the ground? Thus Jerome does not say that they were once lofty trees in paganism, but “in the world”: the world is set in contrast to the clergy, because, having been distinguished there by nobility of birth, brilliance of learning, and exceptional uprightness of character, they transferred all that glory, upon entering the clergy, to the usefulness, splendor, and ornament of the Church. Nor is it any more obscure what Augustine means by these words: “Do we not observe with how much gold, silver, and clothing Cyprian, that most delightful teacher and most blessed martyr, came out of Egypt; how much Lactantius, how much Victorinus, Optatus, Hilary; and, not to speak of the living, how much innumerable Greeks?” (Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, ch. 40). For it is evident that by “Egypt” he does not here signify superstitious worship, but secular learning. Since those distinguished men had been excellently trained and enriched by it, they afterwards turned to the uses of the Church all those treasures which they had gathered from reading pagan authors. But even if this were less clear, the addition of Optatus—whom we never read to have been anything but a Christian—would make it manifest that they are compared with one another not on account of superstition but for some other reason.

7. Whether, then, Hilary was ever devoted to the worship of idols is highly uncertain. To prevent this from being regarded as certain, we have judged it necessary to treat the question somewhat more carefully—not from a contentious spirit. For what Vincent of Beauvais and St. Antoninus write, namely that he was always an excellent Christian, is no less probable than the commonly held opinion that he was not subject to the law of Christ from his cradle (Vincent of Beauvais, Book XIV, ch. 25; St. Antoninus, title XI, ch. 3).

## Chapter II

8. Hilary’s learning, faith, and manner of life until his admission to the clergy.—That great Hilary, whom, by the testimony of Jerome and Augustine, we know should be compared with those who flourished in the world through learning and the renown of exceptional virtues, was, if certain later writers are to be believed, slow-witted in his early years. But after going to Rome and thence to Greece, he overcame his natural difficulty by ten years of continuous study and acquired the adornments of rare wisdom, learning, and eloquence. However this may be, the ancients unanimously proclaim—and his own writings confirm—that he excelled no less in greatness of intellect than in acuteness. The books *On the Trinity* alone are sufficient to establish this. If the first of them be granted to have been written before the others—and arguments for this are not lacking—the magnitude of his mind will appear astonishing, since from the very beginning he could so accurately comprehend and so exquisitely outline so vast a work.

9. Whether he cultivated his mind at Rome, or also in Greece, through the study of the liberal arts, I would not rashly affirm—especially since Jerome has recorded in writing [Col. 0129B] (*Epistle* 4 to Rusticus) that studies then flourished most vigorously in Gaul. He acquired such renown for eloquence that Jerome himself deservedly called him “the most eloquent man of his time” and “the Rhône of eloquence” (*Preface to Book II of the Commentary on Galatians*; *Epistle* 141). He also cultivated poetry and employed that art—which many twist toward corrupt and impure uses—to celebrate the praises of God and sing of the deeds of the apostles and the struggles of martyrs. Jerome asserts that Hilary had acquired merely a slight breath of Greek learning, and had used the assistance of the presbyter Heliodorus in understanding the more obscure words of Origen (*Epistle* 141 to Marcellus); but this is the one place in which he may justly be judged to have spoken with insufficient circumspection. For there, out of excessive reverence for Hilary, he did not dare criticize one whom he suspected of error; he thought first of excusing him and transferring the fault to another, rather than weighing Hilary’s true opinion. But I would not believe either that Heliodorus accompanied him when he was carried off to the East, or that Hilary abstained throughout the whole period of his exile from reading Greek writers. Jerome, indeed, if conjecture does not deceive, judged Hilary to be only slightly versed in Greek literature from no other source than the book *On the Synods*, in which his translations appear somewhat involved and insufficiently free and fluent. Yet, if there is any fault in them, it may suitably be attributed to the age in which he wrote. For then translators thought they exceeded the proper bounds whenever they did not preserve the same order of words. [Col. 0129D] Hence, although he knew that many translations of Eastern confessions of faith were in circulation, he nevertheless undertook to produce a new one himself (*On the Synods*, no. 9), because a translation rendered word for word from Greek into Latin generally produced obscurity. Indeed, one could hardly imagine that he might have adhered more closely to the Greek letter; yet from this one must grant that, in this kind of writing, he allowed himself some liberties which his predecessors did not think permissible. But if anyone would deny that he excelled in knowledge of Greek, no one would deny that he excelled in philosophy.

10. Because of the various riches that he transferred from this learning to the use of the Church, Augustine rightly said (*On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, ch. 40) that he came from Egypt to the Church laden [Col. 0130A] with much gold and silver. Yet he blended them into his writings so purified and cleansed of every dross that one finds in them nothing profane, nothing unworthy of a priest. Even before he was raised to this rank, not content with philosophical learning alone, he also formed his character according to the perfect laws of philosophy. Indeed, from infancy, if Fortunatus is to be believed (*Book I*, no. 3), he was nourished by a certain divine wisdom.

11. Yet his manifold learning would have proved vain and sterile unless faith had made it fruitful. That he received this faith abundantly in baptism will be clear from what follows. But when he was initiated into this saving sacrament is uncertain. This one thing is certain: his baptism preceded his episcopate by no small interval of years. For he himself says (*On the Synods*, no. 91): “Long ago regenerated, and having remained for some time in the episcopate, I never heard of the Nicene faith except when I was about to go into exile.” From this passage the opinion of those who deny that Hilary was born of Christian parents might perhaps receive support, unless it were universally acknowledged that it was customary in those times for baptism to be frequently deferred until advanced age.

12. But by this testimony he clearly proves that the Council of Nicaea, although it used the new term *consubstantial* (*consubstantialis*), nevertheless decreed nothing new. For before he heard the Nicene creed, he had always understood that the same doctrine was to be believed from both the Gospel words by which baptism is administered and the Apostles’ Creed which is learned before baptism, [Col. 0130C] and had firmly believed it. Accordingly, he urges Constantius (*Second Address to Constantius*, nos. 4 and 7) that, if he fears to subscribe to the Nicene decrees, he should retain the first and sole evangelical faith confessed and understood in baptism. At the beginning of Book II of *On the Trinity*, he complains that, although the mystery of the Trinity had been declared sufficiently clearly in the words of baptism, the Arians received the simplicity of heavenly words according to the meaning they wished them to have, rather than according to the plain sense of truth itself, interpreting them otherwise than the force of the sayings required. Elsewhere he reproaches them also for not adhering to the faith sealed in the Apostles’ Creed, without the profession of which no one receives baptism:

> “Faith,” he says, “must be written down, as though it were not in the heart. Those regenerated through faith are taught unto faith, as though that regeneration were without faith. We learn Christ after baptism, as though any baptism could exist without faith in Christ.” (*On the Synods*, no. 63; cf. *On the Trinity*, II, no. 6.)

By contrast, he congratulates the Gallican bishops because the bishops had not found it necessary to read what newly regenerated neophytes held and believed in their hearts. He himself declares in various ways how deeply he had absorbed that same faith in the sacrament of his regeneration. At one time he says (*On the Trinity*, VI, no. 21): “I have so believed in you; through you I have so been reborn; and from then on I am so yours.” At another: “I have been imbued with these things beyond remedy; and forgive me, almighty God, because in these things I can neither be corrected nor can I die.” And a little before (no. 20): “For I have learned these things thus, believed them thus, and hold them with the faith of a mind made firm, so that I can neither believe otherwise [Col. 0131A] nor wish to.” Finally, he gives at the end of the *Second Address to Constantius* this reason why he cannot believe or be taught otherwise: that this faith accords both with evangelical doctrine and with the creed of his regeneration. Since this reason applies equally to the remaining articles of our faith, no one may rightly doubt that he penetrated their truth with equal insight and was always furnished with equal constancy to defend every one of them.

13. He subjected philosophy to faith (*On the Trinity*, I, no. 13).—Illumined by so great a light of faith through baptism, he could never be led into error by any deceptions of vain philosophy. Rather, obeying the apostolic precept, “See that no one despoil you through philosophy,” he armed himself with this declaration as a shield against all the darts of human reason:

> “Constant faith rejects the captious and useless questions of philosophy; nor, yielding to the deceptions of human follies, does truth offer itself as spoil to falsehood.”

For in true philosophy he saw that acts accomplished by God beyond the understanding of human nature cannot, in turn, yield to the natural perceptions of minds, because the operation of infinite eternity requires an infinite conception for its measure. Since such infinity is lacking to the human mind, it possesses no means by which to grasp divine mysteries. He also saw that human reason, since it is created, cannot be perfect and therefore cannot comprehend the Creator: “For,” he says, “the imperfect do not conceive the perfect” (*On the Trinity*, III, no. 24).

14. He attributes to faith alone this glory: that by its heavenly power man attains what he cannot reach [Col. 0131C] by his own strength. For this reason he shows that Christians, who know how to subject understanding to faith, are much wiser than the wise of the world, by whom they are considered foolish, because they penetrate mysteries far more profound. He himself gladly glories in this wise foolishness of theirs at the beginning of Book V; and rightly, indeed, since it was by this path that he arrived at the highest wisdom. It is worth showing by a single example how he conquered natural philosophy by faith. He hears from the Gospel that Christ, after the resurrection, bodily—not in appearance or deception—entered the locked house in which the disciples were gathered. Philosophy immediately suggests to him: “Does he penetrate the structure of walls and the solidity of wood, passing through their impenetrable nature?” Hilary, as though assenting, replies: “Certainly, nothing gives way from what is solid; nor by their nature do wood and stones admit anything as by an imperceptible slipping through.” Then philosophy, as though already victorious, presses its point: “Let us say, then, that it did not happen, because we do not grasp the manner of what happened; and, once our perception has failed, let the effect of the event itself also fail.” But Hilary, equipped with the weapons of wise foolishness, tramples down that foolish wisdom; taking away the victory over which it had begun to congratulate itself, he confidently cries:

> “Do not require from me, an unlearned man who believes concerning God in all things just as they have been said by him, an explanation of this event. I hear the Lord; and because I believe what is written, I know that the Lord stood in the midst of the disciples when the house was shut.”

And afterwards he exhorts all to despise with him the vain and empty reasonings of worldly prudence:

> “Do not deny that he stood there, because through the weakness of your understanding you cannot comprehend the entrance of the one standing there—especially when you have the example of many works of God from which you ought to believe that God can accomplish things whose manner of accomplishment you cannot understand.”

He proceeds further still. “For if,” he says, “human understanding is restricted in regard to visible and bodily things, how much more in regard to invisible and divine things? If we do not attain by reason to the entrance of Christ in bodily form through closed doors, how much less to his eternal generation from the eternal Father?”

15. By the same reasoning, in Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, no. 14, he cuts off every occasion for doubting the reality of flesh and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist. But from the example cited—which we have illustrated by balancing Hilary’s own opinions and words against one another, though never twisting them into an alien meaning—it may be understood how cautiously he avoided the rocks threatening faith, and how, breaking beyond the boundaries of reason, he became foolish in order that, by obeying God’s words, he might become wise. Would that the heretics of our age followed in the footsteps of so wise a fool, and did not prefer certain empty reasonings—or rather, to speak more accurately, plausible delusions—to the firmness of faith which the Church preserves inviolate. They would soon return to the bosom of the Church, which they miserably tear apart. For the present, we wish to note only that Hilary rejects that human wisdom which does not know how to submit to faith, until in the following chapter we show how highly he valued learned faith, or knowledge that serves faith.

16. He avoids association with heretics.—Moved by that supreme zeal for preserving an uncorrupted faith, he recoiled so strongly from the enemies of Catholic religion that, although Fortunatus testifies that even in his own age it was extremely difficult to refrain from dining with Jews or heretics, Hilary shared with them neither table nor even a greeting when passing by (Fortunatus, Book I, no. 3). Yet the course of conduct that he commendably maintained as a layman he afterwards prudently relaxed. For, once made bishop, in order to win heretics to Christ, he did not regard it as blameworthy for anyone to pray or converse with them, nor did he himself refuse conversations with them (*Against Constantius*, no. 2).

17. Moreover, since he knew that faith is dead unless it works through charity (*On Psalm* 51, no. 16), [Col. 0132D] and that human beings are to be cut off from Christ’s body not only because of unbelief but also because of barrenness, he taught first that the mind must be formed by ecclesiastical rules and evangelical precepts. Then he disciplined himself by his own rule, remaining unshorn, so that even then he seemed to be preparing himself as an irreproachable priest in Christ’s temple. He exercised himself in various works of piety so that, while still in the lay state, he possessed by divine ordinance the grace of a bishop. Finally, he poured out upon others the God with whom he was filled. For, as Fortunatus testifies, now instructing some in the confession of the holy Trinity, now inviting others by the promise of the heavenly kingdom, in a word exhorting all concerning the devout practice of religion, he did not cease to sow among the people [Col. 0133A] words of truth overflowing with the fruit of faith.

18. God granted so great a man a wife worthy of him, by whom he had an only daughter named Abra. Although no records have transmitted to us her name, family, or course of life, Hilary himself sufficiently commended her piety, intelligence in divine matters, and zeal in following evangelical counsels. For, writing to his daughter and exhorting her through certain riddles and parables to modesty and virginity, he tells her, if she understands anything imperfectly because of her age, to ask her mother. To what else can this point than to a most devout mother, who, rejecting every worldly hope, was united with her husband in the single purpose of devoting herself to the worship and service of God, which was most dear to them? Hence he adds that she had no greater wish than somehow to beget her daughter anew through her excellent moral character, and to bear her for God.

## Chapter III

19. He receives the episcopate: what he thinks of its office; how he fulfills it.—Thus Hilary, though joined in marriage, lived as though not bound by it; most fully furnished with every kind of knowledge, most pure in moral uprightness, distinguished by integrity and constancy of faith, burning with zeal for souls, and finally adorned with all the gifts that Paul requires in a bishop. When the voice of the people agreed—or rather, when the Spirit of God proclaimed—this man, long devoted to mysteries, was at last chosen as priest for the sacred altars (Fortunatus, Book I, no. 4). Lupus of Ferrières writes in the Life of Maximinus that he succeeded Maxentius, brother of St. Maximinus, in the episcopate of Poitiers; but neither he nor anyone else records the year. Many indeed suppose that he received the episcopate only in 355; but this opinion does not accord well with what he did as bishop before his exile (see below, nos. 29 and 30). For the influence that he seemed to possess in the Church in 355, and the public reputation for sanctity that perhaps long before that year drew Martin from the borders of Gaul to him, require that he should have attained episcopal rank some years earlier. Nor does the passage from *On the Synods*, no. 91, which they cite, conflict with this reasoning: “Long ago regenerated, and having remained for some time in the episcopate, I never heard of the Nicene faith except when I was about to go into exile.” These words establish only that less time elapsed from Hilary’s ordination to his exile than from his baptism to that exile. Certainly, the phrase “for some time” (*aliquantisper*) may be extended to five or six years just as readily as it may be confined to one. Indeed, the wider the scope allowed this expression, the more forceful Hilary’s argument becomes in suggesting that the Gallican faith concerning the equality of Father and Son did not begin with the Nicene Synod; for that Synod was so unknown in Gaul that he had long ago been regenerated and had even sat among bishops for some time before hearing anything of it.

20. At least this is clear from the passage cited: when the people of Poitiers chose him bishop, he was not a neophyte, in accordance with the Apostle’s precept. His wife had not yet died; but at that period, because either virgins were not as numerous as needed, or did not perform—or were not regarded as performing—works appropriate to virginity, married men were often chosen for the priesthood. Yet that they were ordained on the condition that they thereafter abstain from marital relations was affirmed by Jerome (*Against Jovinian*, Book I), and Jovinian—though an opponent of continence—did not dare deny it. Indeed, willingly or unwillingly, he confessed that one who fathers children while in the episcopate cannot be a bishop; otherwise, if discovered, he is to be held not as a husband but condemned as an adulterer. The same custom of the Church is supported by Pope Siricius, *Letter to Himerius of Tarragona*, ch. 7; Innocent I, *Letter to Victricius*, ch. 10; Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book I, ch. 50, no. 257, and *Letter* 63, to the Church of Vercelli, no. 62.

21. Grynaeus’s falsehood regarding the canons of St. Hilary.—Hilary willingly submitted to this rule, and elsewhere clearly proved how highly he valued virginity and continence. He had one only daughter, most dear to him; having persuaded her to prefer virginity to honorable marriage, he preferred that she should be taken from him by an early death while holding the noble purpose of this virtue than live longer in its peril (see Hilary’s *Letter to Abra*, no. 7, and Fortunatus, no. 13). Nor did he find his wife opposed in this matter. Worthy of so chaste a husband, she joined with equal zeal, as already noted, in love for continence. More laughable than refutable is the rashness of Grynaeus, who, relying solely upon the authority of his utterly lying associate, asserted that St. Hilary had permitted marriage to the canons of Poitiers. As though Jerome, a curious investigator and admirer of Hilary’s affairs, [Col. 0134C] could have been ignorant of or concealed this, and nevertheless so confidently said against Vigilantius that “the Churches of the East, Egypt, and the Apostolic See either accept clerics who are virgins or continent.” Certainly, one who so earnestly dissuaded his daughter from a lawful marriage was not so disposed as to permit clerics to marry against divine right and the laws of the Church. But leaving such calumnies aside, let us investigate the truer views of the holy bishop.

22. The office of bishop.—He held an exceedingly exalted view of the episcopal rank. When he wished to commend himself to the emperor, this was the first thing the emperor heard from him, as being worthy of every reverence: “I am a bishop.” For he regarded a bishop as the perfect leader of the Church, who must be equipped and adorned with the complete goods of the greatest virtues (*Second Address to Constantius*, no. 2; *On the Trinity*, VIII, no. 1). He did not think innocence of life sufficient without learning, nor abundant learning sufficient without holiness. Since a bishop is appointed for the benefit of others, he does not profit those whom he cannot teach; just as teaching from which life dissents is sterile. He therefore wishes uprightness and learning in a priest mutually to support and adorn each other: that his life may be adorned by teaching and his teaching by life. For an innocent person benefits only himself unless learned; and a learned person lacks the authority of teaching unless innocent. Above all, he requires from bishops not a bare faith impoverished of reason, but a faith which, against heretics relying on human doctrines, retains a steady confidence to resist (*On the Trinity*, XII, no. 20; see also VIII, no. 2); a faith whose wisdom surpasses worldly wisdom by as much as divine things surpass human, so that the heavenly reason exceeds earthly pursuits as far as divine matters differ from human; and finally a faith able both to instruct the peoples entrusted to their care in every kind of Christian duty and to stop the mouth of those speaking wicked things.

23. Hilary fulfills this office rightly.—Hilary lacked nothing needed to make a useful priest, since he united uncommon learning with singular integrity of character. Therefore, as soon as he was raised to the summit of the episcopate, he did not cease to distribute to his people the food of truth upon which he had previously fed in the secret of his heart. Thus Paulinus said of him after he had been restored from exile to our Gaul:

> While the teacher of Poitiers flourished in their lands,  
> Giving to untamed peoples the precepts of salvation, etc.

(*Book I, Poem on the Life of St. Martin*.)

Hilary himself relates of himself in Book I of *On the Trinity*, no. 14: “What the mind believed for itself, it also preached to others through the ministry of the priesthood imposed upon it, extending its gift to the service of public salvation.” At this point, when you suddenly hear of a bishop whom immediately before you had followed as though still laboring in the search for true religion, you can scarcely believe that in the preceding passages he described the first beginnings of his Christian life. Having noted this in passing, let us consider how he extended his gift to the service of public salvation.

24. He expounds the Scriptures to the people.—Not without reason does he seem to have begun his teaching by expounding Matthew’s Gospel. For although all Scripture is divinely inspired and useful for teaching, yet because in the Old Testament the New is concealed and in the New the Old is revealed (Augustine, *Instruction of Beginners*, ch. 4), an explanation of the former is more profitably preceded by an explanation of the latter. Among the books of the New Testament, Matthew’s Gospel holds the first place. That Hilary interpreted it before the people of Poitiers and then published his sermons is thought all the more likely because he does not separately weigh every word, as commentators usually do; rather, as is more characteristic of a preacher, he omits some matters, touches others briefly, and treats still others at greater length (*On the Trinity*, VI, no. 1). Yet, just as he declares that he was moved to write the books *On the Trinity* by the necessity of his zeal and duty, because as bishop of the Church he felt that he owed the Church the ministry of evangelical preaching, so there is no doubt that he was induced by the same reason to make public the private sermons he had reduced into one body of commentaries: namely, that he might benefit not one congregation only but the whole Church. In these works he gives not so much attention to explaining literal senses as to drawing out mystical ones, either because this was especially agreeable to people in that age, or because it was more useful to them. Indeed, since the Scriptures, fruitful in various senses, were handled by all and their literal sense lay readily before everyone, it was the part of a prudent and diligent shepherd to disclose certain deeper meanings.

[Col. 0136A] 25. He expounded not only Matthew’s Gospel, but also a great part of John’s. Since John wrote his Gospel for the purpose of asserting Christ’s divinity, it supplied Hilary abundantly with material for defending that same truth. We have imperceptibly passed on to the books *On the Trinity*, in which he fully discharged the twofold duty of a Christian teacher: instructing the people in the truth of Catholic faith and blocking the devices of heretics. But the order of events calls us elsewhere.

## Chapter IV

26. Hilary’s actions from the Synod of Milan to that of Béziers.—The Arian plague, which had wrought such devastation in the East, was wholly unable to spread into the West so long as Constans held power. At that time Hilary could still be unaware of the Council of Nicaea. But after Constans had died and Magnentius had been destroyed (10 or 11 August 353), peace was soon taken also from this part of the world. For Constantius, returning to Arles on 10 October of the same year, immediately convened a council there, at which he ordered both subscription to the Arian heresy and condemnation of Athanasius. When Paulinus, bishop of Trier, refused to obey these commands (*Fragment* I, no. 6), the Arian bishops judged him “unworthy of the Church, worthy of exile by the king.” What else occurred at this synod is unknown. Its acts, which Hilary had prefixed to the acts of Rimini, have perished, to the great loss of history. Yet these were the first beginnings of the evils which the Arian heresy, supported by Constantius’s authority and promoted especially by Valens, Ursacius, and Saturninus, introduced into the West.

[Col. 0136C] 27. Two years later, when Constantius held a council at Milan, he left no means untried to procure the destruction of the Nicene faith and force Athanasius’s condemnation (Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*, p. 831). The legates of the Apostolic See resisted, saying that the canons did not permit an absent and unheard person to be condemned. To them he said: “Let my will stand in place of a canon.” But the legates, more horrified by the emperor’s words than by his threats and punishments, accepted exile rather than betray the cause of truth and innocence. The same sentence enveloped others also (Athanasius, *Apology*, p. 692). The remaining bishops suffered no ordinary violence and grievous insults. Whether Hilary attended this council or was absent from it, and why he did not come—or, if he did come, why he suffered no harm there—may be asked; it would be rash to decide. He may have refused to go there for the same reason Eusebius of Vercelli had initially refused to come. Perhaps Constantius also spared him when present, lest he provoke the feelings of the Gauls.

28. Hilary, setting private advantages aside, resolved to uphold the faith. — “While all things were thus in turmoil and the truth was being obscured by Arian devices, Hilary, like the rest, was given the opportunity to flourish in the world, enjoy domestic leisure, abound in every comfort, even boast of imperial favour, and become influential with individuals and with all alike, publicly and privately, under the Church’s dominion—provided only that, complying with the emperor’s will, he abandoned the defence of evangelical truth. [Col. 0137A] He also had at hand a means of clearing himself, in popular opinion, from every disgrace: he could easily excuse the corruption of the judgment by pleading another’s decision; and, under the difficulty of the public understanding, counterfeit uprightness—or rather, although he himself was held guilty by his faith of the sacrilege of heresy, console the guilt of conscience with the soothing pretence of ignorance. But charity, abiding through faith and hope in Christ in simplicity of heart, could not endure these empty consolations of a deluded mind; nor did it allow him not to prefer the endurance of every injury for Christ’s confession to an ambitious silence regarding a guilty conscience” (*Fragment* I, no. 3). Taken up into the hope of heaven and joined to God by charity in an inseverable affection, No desire for earthly things (*Fragment* I, nos. 2 and 3), nor any force of worldly disturbances, could detach him from God or divide him from Him. Never uncertain [Col. 0137B] what he should choose, he said boldly: “I cling to the name of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, although in confessing Him I must endure every evil; I reject the fellowship of the wicked and association with unbelievers, although with them I might hope for an abundance of every good.”

29. A prudent resolution for the Church’s safety. — Having thus satisfied his own conscience by this resolve of mind, he judged that he must provide for the safety of the West. For many, terrified by threats and deceived by fraud and stratagems, had embraced communion with the Arians at the Council of Milan; and there was reason to fear that before long the whole Christian world would be infected by their contagion. To meet this evil, immediately after the exiles of Eusebius, Lucifer, and Dionysius—that is, after the aforesaid council—he resolved that Saturninus, Valens, and [Col. 0137C] Ursacius, the authors of the entire evil, should be separated from the communion of the faithful, while the other members of their party were granted an opportunity to repent. He himself speaks thus of this resolution (*Book addressed to Constantius*, no. 2):

> Foreseeing long beforehand the gravest danger to the faith, after the exiles of the holy men Paulinus, Eusebius, Lucifer, and Dionysius, I separated myself with the Gallican bishops from the communion of Saturninus, Ursacius, and Valens, granting their other associates an opportunity for repentance; so that the will for peace might not be absent, while the foul and advancing members of the principal diseases, tending to the corruption of the whole body, might be cut away—if only it had then pleased us to maintain this decree issued by the most blessed confessors of Christ.

This decree, in which the serpent’s prudence is joined to the dove’s simplicity and gentleness, is altogether worthy of priestly wisdom; and it is the more pleasing because, with greater modesty, it leaves its approval to the holy confessors. How equitable it has always seemed, it is superfluous to demonstrate point by point. Certainly, after the Council of Rimini, it was received by various synods and confirmed by Pope Liberius; nor was it ever rejected except by schismatics. Hilary may deservedly be regarded as its author and chief director, although he does not claim this glory for himself alone. Nor does there appear to have been any other reason why Saturninus conceived such particular hatred for him that, not long afterward, he compelled him to come to Béziers and from there banished him to Phrygia on fabricated accusations. If this is so, who could believe that he had only begun to sit among the bishops a few days before? Though distinguished by no prerogative of his own see, he nevertheless possessed such authority among the Gallican bishops that he himself laid down rules which others readily followed. Again, if the preceding words—“Foreseeing long beforehand the gravest danger to the faith”—refer to the time when he separated himself from the communion of Saturninus, Valens, and Ursacius, then he must necessarily have been a bishop long before doing this. Yet they may also be understood to mean that he foresaw the gravest danger to the faith not long before separating himself from those men, but long before writing the book in which he relates these matters. At any rate, from the year 355 he shone among the bishops in such a way that the Catholic bishops of Gaul always regarded him henceforth as a head and father, while heretics regarded him as their foremost enemy.

[Col. 0138B] 30. Indeed, even earlier, if Sulpicius is not to be denied belief, Hilary’s fame was so great that it did not escape Martin, while serving in the army on the Rhine, and led him to choose Hilary as his guide in the spiritual life. Sulpicius’ words are these (*Life of St Martin*):

> Martin, having then left military service, sought out Saint Hilary, bishop of the city of Poitiers, whose faith in matters of God was then held in high and acknowledged esteem; and he remained with him for some time. This same Hilary tried to bind him more closely to himself by imposing the office of deacon upon him and to attach him to divine ministry. But as Martin repeatedly resisted, declaring aloud that he was unworthy, Hilary—a man of lofty intelligence—understood that the only way to bind him was to impose upon him an office in which there seemed to be some element of indignity. Accordingly, he ordered him to become an exorcist. Martin did not refuse this ordination, lest he should seem [Col. 0138C] to have despised it as too humble. Not long afterward, warned in a dream by the will of Saint Hilary, he departed for Pannonia. Bound by Hilary’s abundant tears and prayers to return, he went away sorrowfully, declaring to the brethren that he would suffer much on this journey. There he freed his mother from the error of paganism, though his father persisted in evil. Then he suffered much from the Arians and was at last compelled to leave the city. When, within Gaul also, he discovered that the Church had been thrown into confusion by the departure of Saint Hilary, whom the violence of heretics had forced into exile, he established a monastery for himself at Milan.

Certainly, since Hilary was banished in 356, so many acts of Martin which preceded that exile can scarcely be compressed more narrowly than within one or two years.

[Col. 0138D] 31. Fortunatus, the writer of Hilary’s life; Venantius Fortunatus, whom some maintain to be distinct from the former; and Gregory of Tours seem indeed to contradict Sulpicius. Fortunatus, in his *Life of Saint Hilary*, relates that Martin was made an exorcist after the holy confessor’s return from exile. Venantius, moreover, after recounting the peace with the barbarians obtained through Saint Martin’s prayers and merits, portrays him not as rushing to Hilary but as crossing the Alps and hastening through the Milanese territory into Pannonia. Finally, Gregory of Tours (*History of the Franks*, Book I, chapter 39) first mentions Martin, as a light newly rising in Gaul, when he recounts that Hilary was permitted to return home.

Sulpicius also conflicts with himself when, shortly before this, he writes that Martin served first under Constantius and then under Julian, and did not obtain his discharge before envoys of the barbarians, meeting Julian at Worms, had arranged peace. For it will be plainly demonstrated in the following chapter that Hilary’s exile occurred before Julian’s arrival in Germany.

32. But although one may wish Sulpicius had shown greater care in recording chronological details, there is nevertheless no reason to accuse him of insincerity in narrating events. Nor is there any room for doubt that his work has reached us genuine and wholly uninterpolated; for Paulinus—who, as Gregory of Tours testifies, having received from Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, summaries of this same Sulpicius (*On the Miracles of St Martin*, Book I, chapter 2), related in concise prose what Sulpicius had set forth more expansively—recounts Martin’s aforementioned deeds in the same order. These things, therefore, are either wholly false, or the single falsehood is that Martin served under Julian. Who would not judge the latter concession preferable to the former? For an error in the name of a single emperor is easier than an error throughout so extensive a sequence of events. Nor is it unusual for writers of this age to attribute deeds done under one emperor to another. And, indeed, when Sulpicius in the *Life of Saint Martin* was about to relate Martin’s singular and final deed in war against the barbarians, Julian’s name more readily slipped in because his achievements against the Alamanni were then more famous and more recent. Therefore, we do not reject what he says: that Martin seized the opportunity when the emperor was distributing the donative [Col. 0139C] to request his discharge. But Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVII, chapter 7, opposes assigning this to Julian’s time; Julian himself also opposes it in Marcellinus, Book XX, chapter 9. They testify that in 358 a serious mutiny arose because the soldier, exhausted by Gallic campaigns, had received neither donative nor pay; and that the disturbance was eventually calmed, not by distribution of a donative—which Constantius did not permit to be distributed according to custom—but by various kinds of blandishment.

33. Moreover, if Martin died in A.D. 397, aged eighty-one, as Gregory states; and if Sulpicius is likewise not mistaken in writing that he was seized, bound in chains, and enrolled under the military oath in the fifteenth year of his age, it follows that, born in A.D. 316 and enrolled in military service in 331, he completed his legal term of service before Julian obtained the rank of Caesar. He could therefore, according to Roman law, have sought discharge in 351. But if to the years of completed service you add the two years during which, overcome by his tribune’s entreaties, he is said to have remained in service, though in name alone, you must allow that he left military life at least in 353. And indeed it is far more probable that one who had been forcibly taken into military service and yearned for another manner of life sought discharge before completing his term than that, after completing it, he remained longer in the same way of life.

34. Finally, anyone who observes with what eagerness Martin sought Hilary after his journey into Pannonia will scarcely doubt that he met this same confessor of Christ [Col. 0140A] before Hilary went into exile; that he remained with him for some time; and that, by Hilary’s will, he departed for his homeland and performed the other things narrated by Sulpicius and Paulinus (Paulinus, *Life of St Martin*). For why, when expelled from Pannonia, did he seek the Gallic shore? Why, when he heard that Hilary had been driven from Gaul, did he give no further thought to Gaul but establish a monastery at Milan? Was it because he feared to go where the Arians had been able to expel the holy man? Yet in Italy those same persons had even greater power—the men through whose activity Eusebius had been expelled from Vercelli, Lucifer from Cagliari, Liberius from Rome, and indeed Dionysius from Milan. Is it not more credible that he, bound by Hilary’s prayers and tears to return to him after his journey, sought that one man alone in Gaul in order to fulfill his promise? [Col. 0140B] Nor does any other explanation occur for why, although he had fixed his dwelling on the island of Gallinaria, yet as soon as he learned that the holy bishop had been granted permission to return (Sulpicius, p. 296), he not only attempted to meet him at Rome, but, after Hilary had already left there, followed directly in his tracks until he reached him.

Whatever follows from this, one must grant that Martin stayed with Hilary for some time before his exile; and consequently that not everything Sulpicius writes concerning Martin’s early years is false, though the name of another emperor, under whom he served, must be substituted for Julian’s. Hence no one can deny that the name of the bishop of Poitiers was already great even before the year 355.

35. In that same year, 355, when the barbarians, having broken, as Ammianus says (*History*, Book XV, chapter 8), the peace of the frontiers, poured into Gaul and shamefully ravaged it; when Constantius, as Victor testifies (*On the Caesars*), feared lest the Gauls, naturally prone to rashness, should attempt some innovation; and when there were no lack of whisperers (Hilary, *First Book to Constantius*, no. 3) to increase the suspicions of the fearful emperor: Hilary sent the emperor a petition and sought to calm his fear in such a way as to advance the Church’s cause on that occasion. This petition still exists, though perhaps not entire. Although it informs Constantius that all is quiet and that there is no suspicion of sedition, its principal purpose is to repel the wrong done to ecclesiastical faith and discipline. Above all, he entreats the emperor with words and tears: first, that Catholics should not suffer the most severe persecutions from their brethren in the Church; second, that the cases of clerics should not be heard by provincial governors; third, that the people should freely follow Catholic bishops and not be compelled by force to submit to heretics; finally, that distinguished priests detained in deserts or exile should be restored to their sees. Since he makes all these requests in the name of many persons, it is a reasonable inference that this petition was sent by him with the agreement of the Gallican bishops, or perhaps, to carry greater weight, was subscribed by many. Baronius, under the year 355, no. 18, attributes to these petitions the law providing that cases of bishops be heard only by bishops.

## Chapter V

36. Hilary’s actions and exile at the Synod of Béziers. — Hence Hilary began to hope for more (*Fragment* XI, [Col. 0141A] no. 4; and Sulpicius, p. 262) and to cultivate the emperor’s goodwill; but the heretics feared more and more that their heresy, which depended entirely upon Constantius’ deceived religious conviction, would be utterly overthrown by the counsels of so great a man. Accordingly Saturninus, bishop of Arles—a thoroughly wicked man, of evil and perverse disposition, who most impiously opposed sound counsels and wholesome resolutions—and Ursacius and Valens, his equals in wickedness, stirred both by the decree recently issued expressly against them and afresh provoked by Hilary’s petition, resolved that he must be banished far away.

They undertook this most evil plan at the gathering of Béziers. Hilary sufficiently indicates that it was convened at the instigation of these three bishops, when, after naming them, he immediately declares that he had been forced by the faction of these false apostles to the Synod of Béziers (*Book to Constantius*, no. 2; *On the Synods*, no. 2; *Against Auxentius*, no. 7). That it was convened to plan his destruction was shown by its outcome. We suppose that Saturninus presided over it, and that for this reason Hilary repeatedly calls him the author of his exile. Several bishops of sound faith from Gaul were also present; Hilary calls them witnesses of the matters there transacted by him (*On the Synods*, no. 2). Of these actions he reports only this: forced to attend, he offered a formal inquiry for demonstrating the Arian heresy and publicly denounced its advocates; but, fearing the public judgment of their conscience, they refused to hear what he brought forward.

What else he proposed there, and in what manner, *Fragment* I, no. 5, seems to narrate in these words: “For at that time these matters were proposed by us in haste: the corruption of the Gospels, the perversion of the faith, and the simulated blasphemous confession of Christ’s name.” And in that discourse everything necessarily had to be too hurried, unarranged, and confused; for the more urgently we sought a hearing, the more stubbornly they resisted hearing us. Saturninus, on the other hand, together with his associates demanded Athanasius’ condemnation. What they had begun at the Synod of Arles they prosecuted at Béziers in such a way that Sulpicius judged both to be included under one heading. Hilary again opposed the acts of Sardica and strengthened the wavering bishops in almost the same words with which he later rebuked certain cowardly apostates: “Will you deny that you knew Athanasius, whose condemnation Valens, Ursacius, and Saturninus demand from you, had been restored to communion by Hosius, Maximinus, and Julius?” (*Fragment* II, no. 18.) But he whom no argument could defeat was forced to yield to calumnies: Julian Caesar was deceived, and through false reports of the synod Hilary was denounced to Constantius by impious men and received sentence of exile.

37. What charge was brought against him as the accused is unknown. But at that time the enemies of truth could easily make his faith and integrity suspect from Gaul’s wretched condition—as though he misused the authority which he possessed among the Gauls to incite rebellion (*Second Book to Constantius*, no. 2). He himself indicates in some way that he was accused of conduct unworthy not merely of the holiness of a bishop but even of the integrity of a layman (*ibid.*, no. 3). Certainly, all the matters brought forward to procure his exile were so openly false that he was always prepared, in the presence of the very official through whose agency he was exiled, to bring him to confess the falsehood of what he had done. For Constantius’ letters were readily available to prove that he had been entrapped. Julian Caesar, too, was present as a witness of the events; and because he had permitted himself to be shamefully deceived, he endured more insult in this sentence of exile than the exile himself endured injury.

38. From Hilary’s account it is plain that Julian, already proclaimed Caesar, was either at Béziers or not far away while these matters were taking place in that city. The date of this Synod of Béziers can therefore be discovered without much difficulty. For certain historical records establish that Julian was proclaimed Caesar at Milan on 6 November, in the consulship of Arbetio and Lollianus—that is, in 355—and that, leaving thence for Gaul on 1 December, he remained at Vienne until June 356. Then, setting out for Germany, he did not revisit those same regions of Gaul before 360. From this it follows certainly that the assembly at Béziers was held in 356, before June. Sulpicius’ calculation of the years of Hilary’s exile does not conflict with this. According to him, Hilary was already entering the fourth year of his exile when called to the Council of Seleucia. But the Council of Seleucia was held in September 359. Therefore Hilary was banished before September 356 (*On the Synods*, no. 2); how much earlier within that interval may be determined from other circumstances.

Moreover, Hilary indicates that he wrote the *Book on the Synods* after he had already spent a full three years in exile. He wrote it late in 358, or at least early in 359. Thus it is also plain that Hilary’s exile occurred at the beginning of 356, and therefore before Julian’s expedition against the Germans. Since this cannot be called into doubt, one must likewise admit that the cited passage of Sulpicius, in which he relates that Martin retired to Hilary after receiving discharge from Julian, requires some correction.

39.
