But although the leaders of the Arians had put forward a pretext for Hilary’s banishment both before Julian and before Constantius, they could not conceal from the Gallican bishops the one true reason which Hilary himself touches upon in these words in *On the Synods*: “They compelled us to choose exile by imposing upon us the necessity of impiety.” Accordingly, they never succeeded with the Gallic bishops in securing the appointment of another in the place of the man to whom they were united in faith and spirit (*On the Synods*, no. 2). Hence Hilary truthfully calls himself a bishop before Constantius: “Remaining in exile, yet in communion with all the Gallican churches and bishops, and still distributing the Church’s communion through his presbyters” (*Second Book to Constantius*, no. 2).

Indeed, the Gauls thereafter so abhorred Saturninus that they steadfastly denied him their communion until at last, after the Council of Rimini, in that same city of Béziers, he was convicted not only of the disgrace of heresy but also of many monstrous and unspeakable crimes, and expelled from the Church (Sulpicius, p. 263). Thus he paid the just penalty for the unjust sentence pronounced against Hilary.

40. The place to which Hilary was banished. — It is established by the testimony of Jerome, Sulpicius, and Fortunatus that the holy confessor of Christ was carried away to Phrygia; whether to any particular place is unknown. He writes at one time that he is residing within the ten provinces of Asia; at another, that he has informed the Gauls from many cities of Roman provinces what was happening in the East. The Gauls themselves, writing to him in 358, affirmed that the delay of their letters had resulted from the distance and concealment of his exile; and Hilary accepted their excuse. Hence it may be understood that no fixed place of exile had been assigned him.

Rodanius, bishop of Toulouse, was banished with him to Phrygia and learned in his own case how greatly the fellowship of the strong benefits the weak. For though by nature gentler (Sulpicius, p. 248), and though he did not withstand the Arians so much by his own strength as by Hilary’s companionship, he nevertheless shared the same glory of confession with him. Having gathered, so far as could be gleaned from Hilary’s words, these points about the proceedings of the Synod of Béziers, let us examine his pursuits in exile.

## Chapter VI

41. Hilary’s pursuits and actions in exile until the end of 358. — “Made the bravest confessor of Christ outside Gaul, he changed his place, not his mind. His adversaries found him neither more bitter nor more broken and wavering in spirit; nor did those who had fallen through error or fear find him more haughty. But once he had been driven into exile, he resolved never to depart from Christ’s confession, while also determining not to reject any honourable and credible means of attaining unity” (*Book to Constantius*, no. 2).

He further resolved that, though injured and subjected to the gravest wrongs, he would not complain at all about the times (*On the Trinity*, Book X, no. 4). He fulfilled this resolve so consistently that in the fourth year of exile he could say: “Since then I have written or spoken nothing abusive against the times, nothing defamatory or worthy of their impiety against that body which then falsely claimed to be Christ’s Church but is now the synagogue of Antichrist” (*Book to Constantius*, no. 2). The crimes committed everywhere by the Arians urged him to write and furnished abundant material for his eloquence; yet he saw it to be of greater importance not to give even the slightest appearance of an impatient spirit. For he knew that people are not ordinarily healed by harsher language and that such language should be used only when every remedy which gentleness suggests has first been tried and applied. The great forbearance he exercised is shown by what he then permitted. Unless charity, the ruler of all laws, excused it, this could scarcely be defended against the charge of excessive relaxation of ecclesiastical discipline: “He did not count it a crime for any Catholic to converse with Arians, even though sacramental communion was suspended” (*ibid.*), to pray in the same church with them, or to wish them peace in greeting; although Canon 3 of the Council of Laodicea, confirmed by many others, required otherwise: “One ought not to pray with heretics or schismatics” (see Apostolic Canon 10; Antioch, Canon 1; Carthage IV, Canons 70, 72, and 73).

Augustine aptly observes, on Psalm 100, no. 8, that these stricter laws exist for the sake of healing:

> For the sake of some correction, he says, we even refrain from our brethren and do not eat with them, that they may be corrected. We rather eat with strangers, with pagans, than with those who are joined to us, if we see that they live badly, so that they may be ashamed and be corrected.

Where correction of the Arians was more readily hoped for through granted rather than denied intercourse with Catholics, he ought not to deny them this, since he knew that the spirit of ecclesiastical laws must be preferred to their letter.

42. He rejoices that his exile makes the truth manifest. — We do not yet address those who refuse to believe that Hilary was gentle by nature and suspect that, through a certain impatience with exile, he burst into invectives against the Arians under the guise of piety. Exile was not burdensome to him, since he saw that it illuminated the truth which he uniquely cherished. Reflecting on the Apostle’s prophecy, “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine,” he rejoiced greatly: “For,” he says, “iniquity has revealed itself through this time of our exile; impatient of truth, it banishes the preachers of sound doctrine in order to heap up teachers for itself according to its own desires. Rejoicing at our exile and rejoicing in the Lord, we recognize that in us the fullness of apostolic prophecy has been fulfilled” (*On the Trinity*, Book X, no. 4). Again, perhaps content with and rejoicing in his own lot, he exclaims elsewhere (*On the Synods*, no. 78): “Let us always be exiled, provided true doctrine begins to be preached.”

The purpose for which they banish heralds of orthodox faith to remote regions is that sound doctrine, which they cannot endure, may go into exile with them. But they hope for this in vain. For the word of God, which could not be bound and detained, was not exiled with our bodies (*ibid.*, no. 8). Indeed, exile provided a greater opportunity to refute their errors and defend the faith. There is scarcely any doubt that he devoted the first leisure of his exile to composing the books *On the Trinity*. Charity pressed him not to allow Christ’s adversaries any longer to profit from the absence of pastors. Yet after completing the third book, he interrupted the work for some time—presumably, as one may suppose, while other affairs of greater importance occupied him. But after he completed the whole work, he no longer feared that the true faith might be exiled together with its heralds. Rather, rejoicing that it was neither hidden nor obscure to those who loved it, he said (*On the Trinity*, Book X, no. 4): “Although sound doctrine is now exiled by many who heap up teachers for themselves, it is nevertheless not exiled from the saints—that is, from lovers of the orthodox faith—nor shall the truth of preaching be exiled from them. For through these books we exiles shall speak, and the word of God, which cannot be bound, shall run free.”

Rufinus elegantly described the usefulness of those books in these words (*Book I*, chapter 31): “He produced nobly written books on the faith, in which he so carefully exposed both the subtleties of heretics and the deceptions and credulous simplicity of our own people that, by a most complete instruction, he corrected both those present and those far away to whom he could not himself speak in person with a living voice.”

43. Though abhorring heresy, he is gentle toward those who err. — Any harshness in these books falls only upon the comparatively few whom he recognized as leaders of the rest, seducers of the simple, and persons stubbornly fixed in heresy by a deliberate will toward impiety. “Sometimes,” he says, “to be indulgent and obliging is not perfect charity” (Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book IX, no. 25). Since he perfectly loved the integrity of faith, he could not speak without horror of those who defended heresy by every wicked art. But toward the rest, whom ignorance held in error (*Book VI*, nos. 2 and 15), he was moved by mercy rather than any indignation; he endeavoured by every means possible to assist them. The more readily he hoped that they might be corrected, the more earnestly he laboured to explain the mysteries of our faith more clearly to them. Indeed, he was so moderate toward all that throughout his entire work he omitted the odious name of the Arian sect.

[Col. 0145B] 44. He expounds the Book of Job. — Among the fruits of his exile may be counted his studies on Job, praised by the ancients. For although whatever is written in the sacred pages was written for our consolation, meditation upon this book is especially suited to enduring the hardships of exile and acquiring that steadfastness in which he shone pre-eminently among the bishops of his age.

45. How deeply he suffers from the Church’s distressing condition. — From the time he conceived the hope of the blessed life, he had learned to regard none of his own troubles as significant, knowing certainly that through the hardships of this present life one reaches the goods for whose love he burned. The endurance of present circumstances is, for those who seek the reward of immortality, what letters are for the education of childhood, medicine for the sick, swimming for the shipwrecked, discipline for youths, and military service for those who are to command. But with what pain was he tormented when he either saw himself or heard from others of the devastations which Arian heresy was producing everywhere? How often did he weep when he contemplated the condition of the regions in which he was exiled—so miserable that even among the bishops there was scarcely one who truly knew God and retained any traces of sincere faith? “For apart from Eleusius,” he says, “and a few with him, the ten provinces of Asia in which I dwell truly do not know God” (*On the Synods*, no. 63; *ibid.*, no. 1).

His anxieties were greatly increased by the profound silence of the Gauls, although he had frequently informed them, from many cities in Roman provinces, what the Eastern bishops were doing in matters of faith and zeal. He then feared that, amid so great a danger of calamitous impiety among so many bishops, their silence had been adopted out of despair concerning a polluted and impious conscience. This grieved him all the more because he loved Gaul so ardently—not merely as his dearest homeland, but as a chosen portion of Christ’s inheritance, which until then had remained almost wholly uncontaminated by the infection of Arian heresy. Yet he stood unmoved in his faith; though all others might abandon it, he did not even waver slightly. Nor did he boil over in headlong anger against his own countrymen, whom he suspected of having fallen and whom he knew, having often admonished them, could not have fallen through ignorance. “But mindful of the Lord’s judgment, by which He commanded that those who, after a first and repeated admonition, remained disobedient even under the Church’s testimony should be treated as heathen and tax collectors, Hilary resolved that he too should be silent among them, seeking henceforth no consolation except that supplied by the testimony of an unstained conscience.”

In addition, in 357, sorrow was heaped upon him (*ibid.*, no. 2), when he learned of the fall of Hosius of Córdoba and of the blasphemy issued at Sirmium. Thus heresy, breaking forth under public authority, now began openly, like a victor, to profess what it had formerly whispered secretly in corners.

46. How greatly he is refreshed by more favourable reports from Gaul. — But God, who sometimes tests His servants yet never leaves them deprived of all consolation for long, greatly refreshed Hilary when, at the beginning of 358, he received letters from the bishops of Gaul and Britain. He learned that, still refusing communion to Saturninus, they were united to him in faith and spirit; that they had not merely refused to yield to Saturninus’ threats, powers, and wars, but had condemned the impiety of the faithless creed sent from the town of Sirmium. The *Book on the Synods* bears witness to the joy with which these reports filled him. Throughout it the powerful emotions of a holy and rejoicing soul are disclosed, yet he often seems to lack words adequate to express his joy according to its full measure.

This joy was somewhat moderated by threats, powers, and wars through which he heard that Saturninus was still raging throughout Gaul. Yet he was less disturbed by these because he was assured that his brethren resisted them courageously. Calamities borne and overcome with courage are reasons not so much for mourning as for rejoicing. It is highly probable that these wars of Saturninus were undertaken first shortly after the Synod of Béziers and then renewed in the following year: first, so that those who, at Hilary’s instigation, had denied him communion might restore it once Hilary had been removed; and afterward, so that the creed sent from the town of Sirmium might be received by all.

He also had a particular occasion to rage against the Church of Toulouse: when its holy bishop Rodanius had ended his life as an exile in Phrygia, Saturninus left no stone unturned to intrude an Arian into his see. There is likewise reason to assign to this time the persecution in which, according to Hilary, clerics at Toulouse were beaten with rods, deacons crushed with lead, and hands laid upon Christ Himself (*Book to Constantius*, no. 11). On the occasion of the letters through which he was informed both of Saturninus’ violence and of the Gauls’ steadfastness in maintaining the faith (*On the Synods*, no. 5), several bishops indicated that they wished to learn from him what the Easterners were doing and had done in their professions of faith, and what he himself thought of all their statements. At no other time, it seems, was the letter of his beloved daughter Abra delivered to him, in which she told him that she was held by a remarkable longing for him.

47. Immediately the report of the Gauls’ untroubled and unshaken faith spread throughout the East, undoubtedly through Hilary’s advice and encouragement; and their zeal in condemning heretics at last stirred certain Eastern bishops to some shame over the heresy they had long fostered and enlarged. Encouraged by the authority of their example, shortly before the feast of Easter in the year 358 they gathered at Ancyra, where several had already assembled for the dedication of a church [Col. 0147A], and brought together as many as could come without delay. In hostility to the recent council of Sirmium and to the council of Antioch which had followed it closely, they issued decrees which no one could properly defend without professing the Nicene faith. In one of the later decrees they did indeed condemn the *homoousion*; but their envoys, immediately sent to Sirmium, either wishing to win the favour of the Catholics or realizing that this decree could not at all stand with their earlier ones, suppressed it along with a few others and offered the Emperor the profession of faith thus corrected. While the Emperor received this embassy honourably and, warned by the envoys, recognized the falsehood of those whose authority had made him odious—and thus saw that the error was not so much his own as that of his advisers—he cleared himself of blame before God [Col. 0147B] and before men. Then Valens, Ursacius, Germinius, and others who, agreeing with and confirming the opinion of Potamius and Hosius, had likewise consented to it (nos. 79 and 81; cf. no. 3), and who by chance had not yet left Sirmium, were compelled to explain why they had rejected the *homoousion* and the *homoiousion* in the Sirmian formula. They could offer no other excuse than that they did not know what was signified by these terms. When this excuse was accepted, they were compelled to condemn what they had formerly done at Sirmium and to subscribe to the faith proposed by the Ancyran envoys.

48. Hilary praises (no. 63) this patience of the Easterners, for whom, after their willingness toward blasphemy, a profession of faith made at least under compulsion was enough. For although the subscription of most of them was altogether suspect, he nevertheless thinks that they should be congratulated that, amid the heretical obstinacy of so many blaspheming [Col. 0147C] bishops, one of them was received as penitent. Nor did it escape him that they could easily have been convicted of falsehood: both because they had always deceived on other occasions, and because the excuse of ignorance which they advanced was devoid of all credibility. Yet the man, mild and peaceable by nature, does not complain greatly (no. 69) that pardon was too readily granted, because it is religious to reserve to God what belongs to God, and error from ignorance is human. And although he says that it is extremely difficult not to think Ursacius and Valens, in particular, were lying, he shows this so modestly that even here his innate gentleness reveals itself. “But let the two bishops Valens and Ursacius forgive me,” he says (ibid.), “for not believing that, given their age and experience, they were ignorant. And it is exceedingly difficult not to think those men lie who can clear themselves in another matter only by lying. But may the Lord rather grant that we think ill of them than that they were not ignorant.”

The outcome proved that his judgment of them was not rash; just as the remarkable constancy with which Germinius eventually defended what, compelled at Sirmium, he had ratified by his subscription (Fragments XIII and XV), confirmed Hilary’s sense that it can sometimes be useful for heretics, even unwillingly, to be compelled to profess the right faith.

49. Because of these actions of the Easterners at Ancyra and afterwards at Sirmium, Hilary conceived the highest hope that truth might be restored to that part of the world from which it had previously been almost wholly banished. The long-desired time now seemed at hand when he might be allowed to address the Emperor and drive the Arian heresy from the entire world. For, secure in the goodness of [Col. 0148A] his cause, he also held such a favourable opinion of Constantius’s piety that, if he were given an opportunity to set forth the faith before him, he did not doubt that the favour which the Emperor had hitherto shown to heretics would thereafter be turned to the benefit of Catholics. Therefore, in order to attain his desire (see *Apologetic Reply*, no. 3), judging the good will of the Easterners, who had great influence with the Emperor, necessary to himself, he henceforth strove more eagerly to win it. Although he hoped to obtain this all the more easily because the Easterners, having declared fierce war upon the Arians, now recoiled less from Catholics, standing, as it were, between the two parties, he nevertheless thought this had to be secured by skill. The following actions will explain what means he used.

## CHAPTER VII

50. What Hilary did from the end of 358 until [Col. 0148B] the Council of Seleucia.—The letters sent to Hilary by the Gallican bishops gave him occasion for the work commonly called, following Jerome, the *Book on the Synods*. Although it must be discussed in a special preface, it cannot be passed over here, lest this account of so illustrious a life lack its more important part. For in no other work will one see more clearly what gifts, both of nature and of grace, God bestowed upon Hilary. In it shine forth sincere devotion to God; singular prudence in the affairs of God and the Church (no. 78); reverence toward the Emperor (no. 8); love of country; zeal for peace; Christian humility; and a zeal moderated by the knowledge of devout discernment—in a word, every virtue becoming a Prince of the Church at once most devout and most courageous.

51. How he prepared Easterners and Westerners for mutual [Col. 0148C] peace.—Especially in order to satisfy the wishes of the Gauls, who had asked him to inform them more fully about Eastern affairs, he undertook this work late in 358 or early in 359. He began it with a humble preface, declaring that a heavy burden had been laid upon one more unskilled and unlearned than all others. From the outset he set himself this rule: knowing that Gauls and Easterners were held apart by mutual suspicions, he would not increase but diminish these suspicions, and would prepare both sides to establish concord in the councils soon to be held. This was indeed a difficult undertaking, demanding the greatest caution and prudence. Conscious of this difficulty, he did not trust in talent, personal acuteness, or industry (no. 65); rather, to obtain what he attempted from love of Christ alone, he sought and obtained divine aid through continual prayers. [Col. 0148D] For not without God’s providence did he so regulate his discourse as both to conciliate the Easterners and to leave the Gauls no just cause for offence.

He judged that the Easterners should be treated like persons recovering from sickness, in whom there was hope of complete health, though traces of their former disease still remained. They still needed to be cherished and helped; as they rose from the abyss of error, a helping hand had to be extended so that they might emerge entirely from it. Desiring to accommodate himself to their weakness, he at times excuses them, at times extols them with praise, and everywhere refrains from abuse. Then, after offering them proof of his own disposition in kindly speech, he introduces the truth so gently that they cannot wholly reject it. Thus he indulges them [Col. 0149A] without concealing that they themselves still lack something of the true faith (no. 63); thus he excuses their failure to stand by one faith, while proclaiming far more blessed and glorious those who, retaining the perfect and apostolic faith in the profession of their conscience, have hitherto known nothing of written creeds. Thus he praises them for resisting heretics without failing to say that they are still liable to just rebuke. Finally, he does not reject a soundly understood *homoiousion*—for he judges it unworthy to quarrel about words where there is agreement concerning the things themselves—yet he demonstrates that the *homoousion* is to be preferred and that the Nicene Council must be upheld. He grants them only this: “If anything is to be added for the interpretation of this term, let us deliberate together. The best condition of faith may be established between us, so that things rightly settled are not disturbed and things wrongly understood are cut away” (no. 90).

[Col. 0149B] 52. He offended the critics of his book.—By this method he most prudently guarded against incurring the offence of the Gauls or others to whom the Nicene faith was exceedingly dear and the authors of new formulas deeply suspect. Yet he could not avoid all offence. For he was soon reproached by some, and particularly by Lucifer, because, by approving the *homoiousion*, he had considered its Eastern defenders orthodox and had lavished such praise upon them that he could by no means escape the charge of shameful flattery. We think this happened not without a special providence of God, since many matters hitherto insufficiently clear are elucidated by Hilary’s replies, which we now for the first time bring forth from manuscripts.

53. He composed his defence in exceedingly modest language.—[Col. 0149C] First, this makes Hilary’s character more certainly known. “An insult received proves what sort of person each man is within,” says Pope Gregory (*Dialogues*, I.5). No graver insult could be suffered by one most devoted to right and faith than to be accused of approving false faith because of a fault of flattery. Yet Hilary not only does not return injury for injury (*On the Synods*, no. 6), but does not even complain that judgment was rashly passed on him, although at the beginning of his work he had earnestly implored that no one should think him to be judged until the reasoning of his words had been examined through to the end. Taking the whole fault, as it were, upon himself, as though his own obscurer language had given occasion for just criticism, he replies that he was insufficiently understood (*Apologetic Reply*, no. 4). He modestly demonstrates this from his own words, by which he praises the Easterners in such a way as to declare that they brought not the true faith, but only the hope of true faith.

[Col. 0149D] With no less modesty he explains the purpose of the praise which he gave them: first, that he might avoid the foulness of insolent abuse, which especially befits a bishop (*Reply*, no. 4); secondly, that he might not seem to make malicious accusations concerning matters that could be defended as excusable (*Reply*, no. 5), since it is religious to reserve to God what belongs to God, and where manifest malice is absent it is safer to judge well than ill of others; thirdly, that the gentle language of his address might prepare them to hear more usefully those things in which the hidden scandals of certain expositions would be exposed more bitterly and shamefully (*Reply*, no. 4); and finally, that by thus gaining their good will [Col. 0150A] he might be heard by the Emperor against Ursacius and Valens, the disturbers of East and West, just as they had already been heard against Eudoxius and other supporters of the Anomoeans.

But what sweetness of character breathes in his answer to the objection concerning his approval of likeness? “Brother Lucifer, it could sufficiently and plainly have been known that I mentioned the *homoiousion* unwillingly. But because you proclaimed the likeness of the Son to the Father, I had to expound its demonstration without fault” (*Reply*, no. 6). So great was Hilary’s zeal for peace, so great his reverence for Christ’s confessors, that rather than differ from any of them he adapted himself even to their not entirely precise ways of speaking. Would that Lucifer had been Hilary’s imitator rather than his critic. He would surely not have stained the glory of his confession by a persistent schism.

54. He always held the Eastern faith suspect.—[Col. 0150B] These replies also offer Catholic writers a rare example of the modesty with which they ought to give account to those who may perhaps take offence at something in their writings. From them likewise all doubt is removed whether Hilary regarded the Easterners as orthodox and wholly free from suspicion of heresy. For he plainly declares that he had by no means removed suspicion from them, nor had said that they brought the true faith. He further adds that he called the understanding of “similar substance” pious not only because he knew it could also be understood impiously, but because he had expressly warned that only the understanding which proclaims unity of substance is pious. Accordingly, he testifies of them only that some of them set forth certain things piously in words (*Against Constantius*, no. 12; *On the Synods*, [Col. 0150C] no. 8); he affirms nothing about anyone’s pious intention.

For the same reason he praises the Gauls summoned into the East because, keeping themselves within its communion, they abstained from the rest beyond Gaul—lest they be defiled by an incautious communion with those who preached the *homoiousion* impiously. He does not indicate that he is without fear and suspicion even concerning Basil of Ancyra, Eleusius, and Eustathius, whom he especially commends. “For I fear,” he says to them, testifying that their faith is not yet whole, “I fear the heresies of the East, which spring up in every successive age” (no. 90). He rejoiced that they were withdrawing from the Arians, yet groaned that they still retained something of the old leaven. Certainly, although they condemned Arian teaching, they did not accept Catholic teaching. [Col. 0150D] Indeed, when they issued a decree against the *homoousion*, they appeared Arian; when they later suppressed it, they were thought to wish to return to the Catholics.

In this situation Hilary conducted himself so that anyone who encounters heretics returning to a sounder judgment, though it is not yet certain that they have abandoned their former errors, may model himself upon his example. For it is the part of prudence kindly to receive those withdrawing from heresy and to draw them toward orthodox faith: to praise what they have done in such a way that they understand they still lack something; and, among Catholics, to bring it about that they are less averse to receiving them, yet neither rashly trust them nor, by hasty communion with them, expose the faith to danger. By this course Hilary, although he did not entirely achieve his aim, came very close [Col. 0151A] to attaining it. For thenceforth the Easterners, won by his goodwill, and the Gauls, inclined in their favour, acted accordingly. Hence, when the Easterners were unjustly treated by the Anomoeans at Constantinople, they fled to Hilary with the utmost confidence; nor did the Gauls assembled at Paris refuse them friendly letters.

55. He urges his daughter to virginity and modest dress.—Though occupied with such great cares for the Church, he did not neglect to devote attention to training his daughter in virtue, lest he should fail in any respect in his duties. He was not content merely to pay to the Church the service due from his ministry and to send to the Gallican bishops the voice of his episcopate in Christ; he was also concerned to transmit to his daughter Abra a memorial of paternal affection (*Book* I, no. 6). He had learned, either through God’s revelation, as Fortunatus says, or from his wife’s letter, that a young man highly distinguished by birth, beauty, and wealth sought her hand [Col. 0151B] in marriage. Believing that it would be a great reward for his exile and for the sufferings he had endured for confession of God (see *Letter to Abra*, no. 2), if his daughter might be found worthy to receive Christ as her bridegroom, he had obtained this favour for her from God through many prayers.

First, therefore, he seeks to instill in her love for so glorious a bridegroom; then he exhorts her to make herself worthy of him and his gifts. Above all, he persuades her that, having cast aside every garment of silk, dyed fabric, or gold ornament, she should henceforth say to anyone offering her such vain adornments: “The wool of my sheep is enough for me; the colour supplied by nature is enough for me; an inexpensive fabric is enough for me. Let not those useless and shabby pearls be an obstacle to me, who await another pearl, [Col. 0151C] most precious, most beautiful, and most useful” (no. 6). For it was an ancient custom in the Church, strongly attested by Cyprian’s book *On the Dress of Virgins* and by many letters of Jerome, that consecrated virgins, rejecting sumptuous dress, should use only ordinary clothing.

Yet this father, endowed with wisdom no less than piety, knew that virginity may be counselled but that no one ought to be compelled to it. Thus he commends its glory to his daughter without imposing any necessity on her. Indeed, he promises nothing to the heavenly bridegroom whom he had chosen for her until she herself has indicated that she prefers him to all others. Therefore he commands her to write back to him by whatever means she can (no. 7), after consulting no one, lest, if she consulted someone, her reply might be thought adapted to that person’s rather than to her own judgment. Nevertheless, [Col. 0151D] he advises her that, should she meet with any difficulty either in the letter or in the hymns which he sent with it, she should consult her mother, who with equal wishes desired her daughter’s holiness.

## CHAPTER VII

56. How Hilary conducted himself at Seleucia.—While these pledges of domestic and ecclesiastical love were being carried into Gaul, Hilary, now spending the fourth year of his exile in Phrygia, was compelled, along with the other bishops, to be present at Seleucia, having been given travel authorization through the vicar and the governor. Having said this, Sulpicius (p. 254) adds that the Emperor gave no special command concerning him, but that the judges, following a general order commanding all bishops to be compelled to attend the council, included him among the others who were to go. This happened, Sulpicius says, by God’s providence, so that a man [Col. 0152A] most learned in divine matters should be present when the faith was to be debated.

But if the order was general, why do we not read that Lucifer and Eusebius of Vercelli were summoned? Why, among so many exiles, was Hilary alone compelled to attend? Was this not perhaps done through the influence of Basil of Ancyra, by whose direction many things were then carried out, since he hoped to be considerably aided by one whom he had recently found to be his champion? Nor was Hilary the kind of man who would strongly resist when an opportunity, which he had eagerly sought, to illuminate and defend the truth seemed to offer itself. Meanwhile God manifested his holiness by a remarkable sign.

57. For on a Sunday, scarcely had he entered the church of a certain village (Fortunatus, Book I, no. 7) when a pagan girl named Florentia, breaking through the crowd of people, loudly declared that the [Col. 0152B] servant of God had arrived there. Immediately falling at his feet and begging him to initiate her into Christ by the sacred sign of the cross, she did not rise until her request had been granted. Soon baptized together with her father Florentius and her entire household, she followed the holy confessor of Christ as far as Poitiers. She was accustomed now to call him her father—not the one from whom she had been born, but the one through whom she had been reborn.

58. “When he came to Seleucia,” says Sulpicius (p. 255), “he was received with great favour and drew to himself the minds and interest of all. The first question put to him was what the faith of the Gauls was, because the Arians were then spreading false reports about them, and the Easterners suspected them of believing, in accordance with Sabellius, in a three-named unity of the solitary God. But after he had set out their faith [Col. 0152C] according to what had been written by the Fathers at Nicaea, he bore witness for the Westerners. Thus relieving the minds of all, he was received within the assurance of communion and into their fellowship, and was admitted to the council.”

59. At this council, not without immense sorrow, he found as many blasphemers as Constantius had wished (*Against Constantius*, no. 12). Yet, in order to benefit more people, he believed that he must conceal his grief and make himself approachable to all. Meanwhile he carefully investigated each person’s faith and intentions. At the first session, held on 27 September 359, when the council divided into three parties, he found that one hundred and five bishops stood for the *homoiousion*, nineteen for the *anomoiousion*, and that the *homoousion* was defended with complete constancy only [Col. 0152D] by the Egyptians, excepting George of Alexandria even among them. He admits that some of those who proclaimed the *homoiousion* uttered certain things piously in words, but he does not dare affirm this of all of them, nor anything concerning their inner conviction, since he testifies that the defenders of the *anomoiousion*, by contrast, asserted nothing but what was most profane.

How great was the horror that struck him when, in his presence and in a public assembly, the abominable blasphemies of Eudoxius were read aloud, arguing that generation could in no way apply to God? “O my wretched ears!” he cries (no. 13), “which heard the sound of such a deadly utterance—that such things should be spoken of God by a human being and preached of Christ in a church!” Nor could ears less insensitive in matters concerning Christ’s glory patiently endure this. [Col. 0153A] When these statements were read, a tumult arose and the council was divided in different directions.

60. On the following day, those supporting the *homoiousion* (Socrates, II.39), meeting in the church at Seleucia, shut the doors and, after reading the profession of faith issued at Antioch for the Dedication, confirmed it with their subscriptions. There is no doubt that Hilary, together with the Egyptians, was absent from this meeting, since he was a private individual and belonged to only one party. But many doubt whether he entered the council on the third day, or at least whether he left it before Count Leona compelled all to gather together again. For Socrates (II.40) relates that the Acacians initially refused to come to the council unless [Col. 0153B] both those previously deposed and those presently accused were first expelled; and that, once those charged had withdrawn, they entered. From the number of those compelled to withdraw, some suppose Hilary was one.

But who would call deposed a man in whose place no one had been substituted? Or who would think presently accused a man received by the council with great favour and attracting to himself the minds and interest of all? Nor can one easily prove that he was hateful to the Acacians themselves, since even after this session they are known to have sought a conference with him and to have candidly disclosed to him their more secret beliefs. He himself thus relates what happened that day.

61. “When those also who say that God is unlike understood that human ears would not accept words of so great an impiety—such as those which at the first session had been read under Eudoxius’s [Col. 0153C] name—they again, changing their words but not their intention, and therefore being deceivers rather than bishops of the Church, drew up a creed. At the third day of the council they presented it through Leona to the synod, and in it they condemned the *homoousion*, the *homoiousion*, and unlikeness. Since this contradicted their own meaning as understood by their hearers, I myself questioned one of them who had perhaps approached in order to test me, pretending not to know the proceedings: what did this mean, that men who had condemned the Son’s being of one substance with the Father, or had denied his being of similar substance, should condemn unlikeness?

“Then he told me that Christ was not like God but was like the Father. This still seemed obscure to me. When I questioned him again, he spoke as follows: ‘I say that he is unlike God, but can be understood as like the Father, because [Col. 0153D] the Father had willed to create such a creature as would will things like himself; and therefore he is like the Father because he is a son of will rather than of divinity. . . .’ Hearing this, I was stunned and did not believe it until, publicly and by the agreement of them all, the rationale of this utterly profane likeness was proclaimed” (*Against Constantius*, no. 14).

If Hilary’s words are considered more attentively, one of two conclusions follows: either he did not attend the third session of the council, or the man who came to probe his mind did not think that he had attended it. It further appears that, among the two parties into which the synod was principally divided, he openly favoured neither. Moreover, one must marvel at how kindly he receives a man whose impieties he detested, and how calmly, without any dispute, he listens while the man lays open his heretical [Col. 0154A] views. Finally, after shrewdly discovering the mysteries of the entire sect, he tries in a friendly manner to bring him back to truth by suggesting that these views do not cohere with one another. What shall we say of that fairness and restraint of spirit by which he did not immediately, as commonly happens, attribute to the entire sect what he heard from one man, but withheld all assent until the same thing was publicly proclaimed by the consensus of all (Socrates, II.40)? Since Acacius, with the agreement of his whole party, proclaimed this impious interpretation of the Son’s likeness to the Father at the fourth session of the council, one may reasonably suppose that Hilary sat with the others at it. For he speaks as an eyewitness of what was then done.

62. On the following day, after the Acacians had repeatedly been summoned to the council and refused to come, “those who proclaimed the *homoiousion* [Col. 0154B] condemned all who, without any shame for their impiety, spoke the words mentioned above” (Socrates, ibid.; Hilary, *Against Constantius*, no. 15). “Among their number,” says Sulpicius (p. 256), “were George of Alexandria, Acacius, Eudoxius, Uranius, Leontius, Theodosius, Evagrius, and Theodolus.” Socrates (II.40) adds Patrophilus and lists others whom they removed only from their own communion. The condemned men flew to their Emperor (*Against Constantius*, no. 15; Sozomen, IV.23); received honourably, they strengthened their impieties with every exertion they could make.

Meanwhile, as instructed, the other party chose ten envoys to inform the Emperor about their decisions (Theodoret, II.27; Sulpicius, p. 256). [Col. 0154C] Hilary followed these envoys to Constantinople. Among them the foremost were Basil of Ancyra, Eustathius of Sebaste, Silvanus of Tarsus, and Eleusius of Cyzicus. At that time they seemed so disposed that Catholics did not think association with them should be avoided. Thus Athanasius himself, in the work *On the Synods*, written at that time, argued that they should be treated as brothers rather than adversaries: if they said merely that the Son was similar to the Father in substance, they did not thereby necessarily assert that he was consubstantial—for tin is similar to silver, and brass to gold—but when they add that he is not from another substance, what else do they imply except that he is from the Father’s own substance? Hence the Council of Seleucia, being composed for the most part of those who agreed with Basil, Silvanus, and the [Col. 0154D] rest, was called Catholic by some; and even now Sulpicius honours it with the title of a Catholic council.

63. In so great a disturbance of affairs, Hilary’s anxieties were somewhat relieved by the overthrow of Anomoean treachery, though not for long. For when he reached Constantinople, oppressed once more by the deepest grief, he groaned that there a few had prevailed over many (*Against Constantius*, no. 15). That is, nineteen bishops openly professing impiety, having preoccupied the Emperor’s mind, so prevailed over the one hundred and five, some of whom at least gave expression to piety, that they compelled even these to yield in turn to those by whom, in the preceding year, they had been compelled to condemn their impieties. As the affairs of the Church thus went to ruin, [Col. 0155A] Hilary did not withhold his help. Receiving the afflicted bishops in his kindness, he thereafter disclosed to the West the dark schemes of the impious with such wisdom that they soon began almost to collapse into nothing. This must now be recounted.

## CHAPTER IX

64. What Hilary did at Constantinople.—[Col. 0155A] Hilary was then at Constantinople, having received no definite instructions concerning himself and awaiting the Emperor’s will, in case he should be ordered to return to exile (Sulpicius, p. 261). At that time Ursacius returned there as envoy of the Council of Rimini, together with Valens, Magdonius, Megasius, Gaius, Justinus, Optatus, Martialis, and two others whose names are not recorded (Fragment X, no. 1). These had already come to the Emperor as delegates sent by the Arians. After causing the orthodox envoys to fall at Nicaea in Thrace, they had returned to Rimini in order to draw the remaining [Col. 0155B] fathers, now softened by weariness from their journey, to their own view. Once they achieved this by fraud, they hurried again to Constantinople so that Constantius might learn as soon as possible of their successful actions.

65. They are unsuccessfully deterred from association with the Anomoeans by letters of the Easterners.—Meanwhile the Easterners did not know what was being done at Rimini among the Westerners. Since they did not doubt that their party would be strengthened by association with these men, they were astonished that, upon entering Constantinople, the envoys immediately joined themselves to their adversaries. Nevertheless Silvanus (Fragment XI, no. 1) and his associates judged it their duty to make the acts of the Council of Seleucia known to them, lest they sin through ignorance. They therefore informed them that they were delegates of the entire council, representing more than one hundred bishops; and that the impieties [Col. 0155C] of those whom they opposed under the council’s mandate were so great that, when the Emperor heard them, deeply moved, he immediately ordered them to be anathematized. They warned that this had been done fraudulently: since Aetius, the author of the heresy, was condemned, the sentence appeared to have been pronounced against a person rather than against the doctrine. Therefore they abstained from entering the church. They asked the delegates not to become associates of the impious and allow heresy to gain strength within the Church, but to report the entire situation promptly to the Westerners (ibid., no. 2). The envoys of the Council of Rimini, having received these letters of the Eastern envoys, to which the blasphemies of the Anomoeans were attached, did not at all withdraw from their association. Rather, such rage possessed these hypocrites when their deceit was exposed that they decreed the danger of deposition against the man who had received the letters.

66. Through Hilary’s action the Easterners bind the Gauls to themselves.—[Col. 0155D] Distressed that their warnings had been despised and especially grieved that the shameful heresy was being reinforced by the accession of the Riminian envoys, the Easterners decided that the entire matter should be communicated to Hilary. They had already experienced his kindness, his zeal for peace, and his energy, diligence, and greatness of spirit in administering ecclesiastical affairs. They therefore wrote to him, informing him of what they had done with the Western envoys, and at the same time sent copies of the documents by which they had attempted to deter them from association with the Anomoeans. They also seem to have attached other letters to the bishops of Gaul, asking them to exclude the said envoys from their communion (Fragment XI, no. 1).

Then Hilary, the faithful preacher of the Lord’s [Col. 0156A] name—as we speak with the Council of Paris, from which we borrow this entire narrative—not only fulfilled but in some sense exceeded all their expectation. For it was sweet to him, amid so vast a multitude of blasphemers, to find some defenders of Christ. Though he judged their faith not yet sufficiently purified, he nevertheless did not despair that it could be freed of every dreg, since it was then proved by persecution from heretics. He therefore sent to Gaul not only every item which they had communicated to him, but also praised among the Gauls their constancy in retaining the term *ousia* (“substance”). He testified that some among them were most undeservedly in exile and that other bishops had been substituted in their places. Finally, he announced that he held Auxentius, Ursacius, Valens, Gaius, Magasius, and Justinus excommunicated and would never have peace with those who followed their [Col. 0156B] errors.

67. Occasion and acts of the Synod of Paris.—From these reports of Hilary, sent early in 360, immediately after very many Easterners had been driven from their sees by the Synod of Constantinople, the Gauls received no less benefit than the Easterners. Meeting at Paris without delay, they discovered that they had been deceived at Rimini and at Nicaea in Thrace. For they had been induced to suppress the term *ousia* on this sole pretext: that the Easterners strongly recoiled from it, and that, if it were retained, there would be no hope of making peace with them. Then, in a reply to the Easterners—that is, to those in the East who defended the *homoiousion*—they freely acknowledge their [Col. 0156C] error and rejoice that they have been delivered from it by the letters both of the Easterners and of Hilary. Therefore, with joy, they restore what they had rejected unwillingly and under a false pretext.

Praising the Easterners for defending the *homoiousion*, they cautiously indicate that it concerns the Easterners to defend the *homoousion*, since that term had been devised against the heresy of the Ariomaniacs by the very Council of Nicaea—that is, the council held in the East and composed for the most part of Easterners. They declare, in words almost taken from Hilary, that they profess this term after excluding every heretical meaning. They then revoke the acts of the Council of Rimini and declare its envoys, the architects of the entire deceit, excluded from their communion—“and this,” they say, “in accordance with the profession of our brother Hilary.” They further condemn the blasphemies of the Anomoeans attached by the Easterners to their letters, and declare that they will not regard as bishops those substituted into the sees of persons undeservedly exiled. [Col. 0156D] Finally, they threaten deposition from the priestly rank against all who henceforth allow anything to be taught in Gaul either against God or against the majesty of Christ, the only-begotten God, or who profess the *homoousion* with a faith and meaning other than that which they have expounded; and they specifically pronounce Saturninus unworthy of the episcopal name.

68. Date of this synod. Hilary did not attend it, but was nevertheless its guiding influence. — This straightforward account makes clear the date of the Council of Paris, concerning which scholars have until now held differing opinions remote from the truth. For who now fails to see that this Parisian council was so closely connected with the Council of Constantinople, held in the first days of the year 360, that no more time need be supposed between the two than was required, once the news had reached Gaul from Constantinople, for the bishops to be summoned together? For the Gauls had but this one reason for assembling: to reply to the letters of the Easterners. The strongest indication that they received these letters shortly after the Council of Seleucia and the Council of Constantinople that followed it is that the Gauls profess there that they then first learned what the Easterners’ faith and zeal had been in those synods. Yet they ought to have been impatient to learn what had been done by them, since they eagerly desired concord between East and West and, for its sake, had somewhat relaxed their former practice. Therefore you will not rashly assign the Council of Paris to the very year in which the Council of Constantinople was held.

It is commonly believed that Hilary attended this council, but this is by no means probable. For the synod consistently speaks of him not as present, but as an intermediary. It was indeed his office to communicate to the Westerners as soon as possible what the Easterners had entrusted to him for announcement. Nor is there even the slightest reason to suspect that he failed in this duty in a matter of such importance, since, even when not asked, he was accustomed, out of his singular concern, carefully to make known to the Gauls the various positions of the Easterners. Once these reports had been received, the Gauls immediately assembled at Paris; they therefore did not wait for Hilary’s return, since at that time every hope of seeing him again so soon seemed removed.

Yet I would grant that Hilary not only attended the Parisian synod but even presided over it, in the sense that nothing was done there except at his prompting and by his counsel. For, with him as it were carrying the torch before them, the Gauls recognized their error; and thereafter they conceived flames of holy hatred against the heretics all the greater in proportion as they saw that they had been more wickedly deceived by them. They then conformed their faith to his faith, and removed from their communion those whom he had removed. Following his example, moreover, they embraced the Easterners with such brotherly charity that they themselves declared that they did not reject *homoiousion* (“of like substance”), but preferred *homoousion* (“of the same substance”) properly understood, and prudently invited the Easterners to accept this term.

69. A difficulty concerning the date of this synod resolved. — One difficulty still remains: how Hilary could have commended the Eastern delegates to the Gauls in honorable terms at the very time when elsewhere he writes that they yielded to the will and violence of Constantius. Philostorgius resolves this difficulty when he relates that, as they were being led into exile, they revoked their subscriptions by which they had confirmed the creed of the Council of Rimini; and the former again proclaimed the Son consubstantial, while the latter proclaimed him of like substance (*in Constant.*, nos. 25 and 26; *Hist.*, book V, ch. 1, in Valesius, *De Synodis*, no. 63). Nor is it surprising that Hilary then undertook their defense, since nothing was ever more welcome to him than to receive back one who had fallen through weakness and was repentant.

While we follow him as he sent the Easterners’ instructions into Gaul, the sequence of connected events has led us to Paris. Yet certain events intervened which bring us back to Constantinople, to be considered in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER X

70. Hilary’s remaining labors for the Church while he was at Constantinople. — Assisted by the alliance of the delegates from Rimini, the Anomoeans accomplished everything in their power to oppress the Easterners, through whom some hope still remained of restoring the true faith. It was not enough for them that, on the day before the Kalends of January [31 December], they had compelled those men to subscribe to the perfidy of Rimini; they soon also deposed them and drove them into exile. Hilary then, as we have said, received their letters and faithfully transmitted them to Gaul (Sulpicius Severus, p. 261).

But when the best bishops had either been frightened by fear or led away into exile, and all yielded to the perfidy of a few, Hilary perceived that the faith was in its last extremity. He therefore requested from the emperor permission to debate the faith with his opponents face to face. Fortunatus, following Sulpicius, writes that he made this request in three pamphlets; but both seem to have confused the three books which we still possess, either against Constantius or addressed to Constantius.

71. He clears himself of the charge of exile, not for his own sake (*Book II to Constantius*, no. 2). — There still survives the petition which he presented to Constantius at Constantinople, when an opportunity of appearing in person had been afforded him. From its very beginning he establishes that he had been punished by an unjust sentence of exile; and he asks that he may confront Saturninus, through whose agency he was in exile, until he brings him to confess the false acts he had committed. In this he was moved less by longing for his homeland than by fear that, being suspected by the emperor because of the name of exile, he might fail in his requests (*On the Synods*, no. 92). For he was not greatly troubled about exile: uncertain whether it would be as delightful for him to return from it in the Lord as it would be safe to die in it, he undertook the defense of truth with courage at the very time when its defenders were being driven into exile.

72. Certain of his own faith, he is concerned for others’ salvation. — Nor is it the mark of an arrogant mind when he says: “I ask a hearing not so much for myself as for you and for the Churches of God”; or when, explaining this statement, he adds: “For I fear the peril of the world, the guilt of silence, and the judgment of God; but my concern for hope, life, and immortality is now not so much for myself as for you and for all.” Since the faith which is the foundation of eternal life is one and cannot be altered, he deeply feared for the eternal salvation of the emperor and of others, for whom faith had become a matter of times rather than of the Gospels: it was being prescribed according to years, not retained according to the confession of baptism; and increasingly there came to be many faiths for the very purpose that there might be none at all. Hilary himself, however, was in no way uncertain about his faith, since he preserved inviolate and undefiled the faith which he had received at baptism from the Apostles and the Gospels.

73. He warns that a faith is not always true merely because it appears to rest on Scripture. — He wisely praises the emperor for seeking a faith only according to what is written; yet he also warns him that there is no heretic who does not now falsely claim to preach according to the Scriptures the things by which he blasphemes. By these words he silently teaches that the interpretation of Scripture depends not upon any individual’s private judgment but upon the judgment of the Church. Hence it comes about that heretics, though they employ and vaunt the words of Scripture, because they do not listen to the Church, speak Scripture without Scripture’s meaning and put forward faith without faith (*Book II to Constantius*, no. 9).

Then, lest he himself seem to evade the Scriptures and lest the heretics boast that they support them (no. 11), he promises to say nothing not drawn from them; meanwhile, he offers a specimen of what he will say.

74. He removes every apparent obstacle to his petition. — Nor, following the manner of heretics, does he demand to be heard secretly and with witnesses excluded. Rather, he asks to be heard under public scrutiny, before the divided synod, and—as he had said a little earlier—before “the synod now disputing concerning the faith”; that is, before a great multitude of people, upon which wickedness, deceitful artifice, and favor at the imperial court exercised great influence. So greatly did he trust his cause; so strongly did he feel himself moved and helped in its defense by a certain divine power of the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, while he removes everything that might obstruct his petition, he omits none of the things that seemed likely to favor it. He leaves it to the emperor’s discretion how far and in what manner he should command him to speak, and promises to say nothing except what may profit faith, unity, eternity, and the peace of East and West; nothing except with honor to the imperial office and the emperor’s faith; indeed, that he will say nothing even about Saturninus unless commanded to do so. This the Arians, by whose prompting and judgment the emperor was governed, most emphatically refused. These were precisely those of whom Hilary himself speaks in *On the Trinity*, book VI, no. 15: “Although an answer to folly is easy, the correction of fools is difficult; through it [that is, folly], first, the reasoning of understanding is not sought, and then what is communicated by one who understands is not received.”

75. He considers another means of aiding the West especially. — Thus he lost the hope of speaking to the emperor concerning the faith and of recalling him from error, even though the opportunity seemed to have been offered for which he had been most earnestly striving for more than a year. He was convinced that the readiest remedy for the greatest evils of the Church would be to draw Constantius back from heresy. When he had tried this in vain, and foresaw what devastation would be wrought by the heresy which was preparing, under the authority of the Councils of Rimini and Seleucia, to overthrow the Nicene faith, he considered how he might oppose its designs by whatever means he could.

He judged nothing more suitable to this purpose than to compose a simple history of those synods. He therefore undertook that work which Jerome entitled *Against Valens and Ursacius: a History of the Councils of Rimini and Seleucia*. He believed that this would bring it about that each person, henceforth relying upon his own judgment, would not follow another’s opinion (*Fragment I*, no. 7); and that, once everyone possessed an uncorrupted record of those councils’ proceedings, no one would readily believe those who boasted of their supposedly legitimate authority.

76. He begins the history of the Councils of Rimini and Seleucia at Constantinople. — He himself indicates the time and place where he began this work in the words: “I attempt to bring before the public conscience a work grave and manifold . . . made foreign by the hopelessness of the places in which the matter was transacted and in which we are active.”

> [Note: At [Col. 0160D] one could also read *disparatione* rather than *desperatione*; the work would then be “foreign” because it leads us to various places where different synods were held.]

What places could those be in which Hilary was active after the Council of Seleucia, other than the regions of the East and, above all, the imperial city? Certainly that most evil affair which he then strove to remedy was transacted in the city into which hastened the delegates sent by the Arian party, who there forged all the evils which subsequently poured forth into the Church.

At Constantinople the plan was devised by which the Catholic delegates of the Council of Rimini were first held for a long time at Nice in Thrace and afterwards overthrown, and the whole council was then brought over to the Arian view. There the delegates from Seleucia, conquered by the emperor’s violence, subscribed to the blasphemy of Rimini. That city was rightly deemed hopeless: it rejected the heralds of truth and permitted the followers of Aetius, Christ’s most hostile enemies, to rule within it. Most of the Eastern provinces were likewise hopeless, for the convention at Constantinople set Arian bishops over them after expelling those of better hope. Despairing, therefore, of being able to benefit these places, Hilary undertook a work foreign to them, one which would especially benefit the regions of the West, from which he was absent.

77. By this work he endeavors to meet Arian deceits in the West. — The Council of Rimini had indeed inflicted a grave wound even upon the Western Church; yet its recovery was far less hopeless. For heresy did not dare to show itself openly and plainly there; it was compelled to cover its foulness with the veil of peace and unity, and to falsify the true faith beneath plausible words. Thus one who exposed it naked, with its mask removed, seemed likely to restrain it.

For this reason Hilary took care to embrace in his history of the Councils of Rimini and Seleucia the deeds of the Arian party, especially in the West, and to set them forth before the eyes and view of all. For as a tree is known by its fruits, so, by the Lord’s own teaching, hidden heresy is recognized from its deeds. Indeed, from the letters and other documents alone from which this work is composed, Arian heresy readily appears to every discerning person deceitful and mendacious in its words, cruel and turbulent in its actions, fickle and unstable in its faith, and contrary both to the Fathers and to itself. By these marks it is most clearly distinguished from the true faith, which is simple, peaceable, consistent with itself, and consonant with the Fathers.

So that the difference between the two might shine out ever more clearly, he sets against the Council of Arles, in which Athanasius was accused, the Council of Sardica, in which he had been acquitted; against Arian formulas, the Nicene formula; and against the decrees made at Rimini before the Fathers were bent by the terrible threats of Constantius, those later extorted through fraud from those same Fathers after fear had conquered them. Moreover, since heresy is discerned from the character of its authors and followers, he not unwisely entitled this book *Against Ursacius and Valens*—the principal authors and agents of all that Arianism had accomplished in the West.

Their lies are so evident, and their depravity and instability of character so plain, that a doctrine resting on advocates and defenders of this sort is rightly judged either false or suspected of falsity. Hilary himself identifies another mark of falsity in Arian heresy: “because the ministers of Constantius everywhere act, tremble, and press on in such a manner that their anxious labor and concern to prevail plainly disclose the injustice of their claim” (*Fragment I*, no. 4). We cannot sufficiently lament the loss of a book so useful and necessary for elucidating Arian affairs; and the fragments at last published from the Library of Pithou increase our longing for it. From them it is clear that Hilary began it at Constantinople in such a way that thereafter, for as long as he lived, he added to it individual documents relating to Arian history.

78. He interrupted it in order to write against Constantius: the motive that moved him. — This work was not yet completed when he judged it necessary to interrupt it, in order to apply some more forceful and immediate remedy to the suffering Church. For while some were terrified by Constantius’ edicts and threats, and others held fast by his counterfeit and false religion, they did not possess the calmness of mind necessary to perceive the truth of the matter set forth in that book.

Meanwhile, to use Jerome’s words, “the little boat of the Apostles was in peril; the winds pressed upon it, the waves beat against its sides, and no hope remained” (Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians), unless the impiety of Constantius were made manifest to those whom his authority was leading into error. He was a wolf raging with edicts against Christ’s flock; but, concealed under the pretext of peace and unity, he displayed the skin and face of a sheep, and beneath a counterfeit appearance of piety inflicted destruction no less than he did by open violence. The Church’s most watchful shepherd therefore judged it his duty to remove the sheep’s covering and show the wolf to his Lord’s flock.

Yet he was held back for some time by his consideration that the royal authority of Constantius had been given by God and ought to receive the highest reverence. How far this consideration restrained him is shown not only by the petitions presented to Constantius and other writings in which he always speaks of him with the greatest reverence, but also by the history of the Council of Rimini which he had recently begun (*Fragment I*, no. 5). There he expressly recalls that, because every kingdom is from God, the highest reverence must be rendered to the king. He only warns that there is a power higher than the king’s authority, and that the emperor’s judgment is not to be admitted on equal terms with episcopal decisions, because what belongs to Caesar must be rendered to Caesar, and what belongs to God to God.

79. Judging that this evangelical rule must be obeyed, he at last resolved to disclose Constantius’ faith, character, and actions which it concerned the Church to know. Aware that he was undertaking a matter liable to cause offense, he provides many arguments from the very beginning to justify his decision. Although he may not yet have persuaded some that no fault of human agitation prompted him to write, we, after so many well-tested examples of his moderation, would scruple not to believe his own testimony:

> “Nor do I complain of an injury, which I passed over when it was recent. And, lest I should be thought to speak anything from my own cause, I have allowed so much time for silence. Now I have no other reason for speaking than Christ: to him I owed even this, that until now I was silent; and to him henceforth I understand that I owe it not to be silent.” (No. 3)

Thus, just as his long silence did not arise from timidity, so his forceful speech did not arise from pride. One and the same love of Christ taught him both to be silent prudently and to speak courageously. He was moderate in this also: everywhere he so restrains his language that, while recounting only what Constantius did against the Church, he wholly abstains from identifying his other faults. Even though he himself breathes martyrdom with all his heart and powerfully inspires others toward it by word and example, he does not wish anything to be taken from Caesar’s majesty in what is its due, even while he kindles courage to despise Constantius’ edicts, obedience to which would be sinful.

80. Finally, this book serves to remind Catholics—when there were those who commended Constantius’ piety in worshipping Christ and protecting his Church—that he was a heretic, defended heresy, commanded heresy, and enforced heresy. Thus they might be persuaded to beware of him as of a tyrant all the more dangerous because, while displaying greater zeal for faith in words, he planned to tear faith from their hearts.

That the book was directed to Catholics, and not, as is commonly supposed, to Constantius himself, is clear from its opening, in which Hilary addresses “Brothers,” not Constantius. You may rightly understand these brothers to be the Gallican bishops, to whom he did not hesitate to write whenever something new occurred, ignorance of which caused him some anxiety for them. Yet I would not deny that in that very work he also wished to consult for the emperor’s eternal salvation, and tried whether perhaps one whom he had been unable to awaken to sound faith by gentle speech—being, as it were, bewitched and lulled asleep by Arian arts and tricks—might be recalled to it by sharper speech.

81. Whether he published the book during Constantius’ lifetime. — There is room to conjecture that, either on his friends’ advice or under the guidance of his own prudence and moderation, he suppressed this work for a time, since he was not fully assured of its usefulness—especially because, shortly afterward, he was permitted to return to Gaul and could accomplish far more effectively in person what he had proposed through this book.

Thus Jerome’s words, by which he entitles it a book *Against Constantius, Now Dead*, are reconciled with the truth of events, although Hilary himself indicates that he wrote it in the fifth year after the Council of Milan of 355, and therefore while Constantius was still alive. Some, however, without attending to the place where it was written, suppose it to be the product of a more vehement disposition; others wonder that such great courage coexists in it with such natural mildness, and do not doubt that whatever appears forceful proceeds from ardent desire for martyrdom. The examples of his innate gentleness which he displayed after returning from exile make this still more convincing.

## CHAPTER XI

82. Hilary’s return from exile and his labors to purge Gaul of heresy. — Since the enemies of truth could no longer endure Hilary’s many efforts to suppress heresy in the imperial city itself, as in its own fountainhead, they persuaded the emperor to command him to return to Gaul as though he were a seedbed of discord and a disturber of the East. Glorious indeed was this charge against him: that he did not allow the wicked to enjoy their perverse peace, and that he was a kind of seedbed from which those who opposed the heretics were continually stirred up. Fortunatus testifies that Valens and Ursacius were the authors of this plan by which he was sent back to Gaul.

Sulpicius says that he was sent into Gaul “without a remission of exile,” and this has given occasion to various scholarly conjectures: that he was entrusted to the custody of some soldier; forbidden to leave Poitiers; or compelled everywhere to bear some mark of exile. Yet how free he was to travel wherever he wished is sufficiently proved by what he did immediately after his return to Gaul. Fortunatus may rightly be said to have intended to interpret Sulpicius’ words when he says that “Hilary, compelled to return to Gaul, thought that he would suffer exile still further, because, having obtained no final settlement of the dispute there, he would leave the Church’s disturbance behind” (Fortunatus, book I, no. 8).

Perhaps he was also said to have been dismissed without remission of exile because the emperor, wishing to remove a troublesome petitioner from himself, ordered him home, as though in indignation, until his case might be more carefully considered.

83. Then the Church of Gaul embraced Hilary returning from battle—not, indeed, after Constantius’ death, as Jerome’s words in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians* seem to imply, but, as he writes more accurately in the *Chronicle*, in that emperor’s final year. In the former work, while describing the common joy of the churches at the return of exiled bishops, he did not take much care to distinguish Hilary from those whom Julian, after being raised to the dignity of Augustus, permitted to return to their churches.

He did this much as Sulpicius and others relate the exiles of Paulinus, Eusebius, Lucifer, Dionysius, Hilary, and Rhodanus in such a fashion that, although they had been expelled by three different councils, one might suppose they were all expelled by one and the same council. Sulpicius and Fortunatus agree with Jerome’s *Chronicle*: for they relate that, after Hilary had presented his petition to the emperor at Constantinople, it was Constantius himself, not Julian, who dismissed him to his church. Gregory, bishop of Tours, supports each of these accounts (*On the Glory of the Confessors*, ch. 2). Since he records that Hilary returned to Poitiers in the fourth year of his exile, and since it has been established above by certain and manifest arguments that he was banished at the beginning of 356, he must necessarily have been granted leave to return from exile shortly before the year 361, Constantius’ last.

84. News of this permission soon spread throughout the West and reached Martin also (Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*). First driven from Illyricum by the Arians, and then expelled from the monastery which he had established for himself at Milan by Auxentius, Martin had then withdrawn to an island in the Ligurian Sea called Gallinaria [Albenga]. On hearing the news, he hastened to attempt to meet his most welcome master in Rome as he returned. But the ardent desire to see his flock again had already carried the pious shepherd away from the City. It was fitting also for the humble Confessor of Christ to flee as swiftly as possible from the applause and honors which the splendor of his genius, learning, and virtues, together with his many labors expended for the Church, had deservedly won for him there.

85. But when he came near the island—which in some manuscripts is called Gallinaria and in others Dives (Fortunatus, book I, no. 20)—the neighboring inhabitants warned him that it was uninhabitable because of the multitude of serpents. With the help of the cross going before him, he landed there and, setting up a piece of wood, prescribed a boundary for the serpents. This island appears to be different from the one which, as is clear from Martin’s residence there, was not uninhabitable.

86. It is easier to imagine than to describe the applause and favor with which he was received at Poitiers. Fortunatus testifies (no. 11) that the people’s joy was then as though their homeland itself had been restored to them with him, for they considered themselves exiles without him. At nearly the same time Hilary was refreshed by the sight not only of his most beloved people but also of his dear disciple Martin. For Martin had gone to Rome; when he heard that Hilary had already passed through, he followed his tracks so closely that not long afterward he himself arrived at Poitiers. There, after being most warmly received by Hilary, he established for himself, not far from the city of Poitiers, a monastery called Locogeiacum.

> [Note: At [Col. 0164D]: Commonly Ligugé, now occupied by the Jesuits.]

The greater attention we give to Hilary’s intense longing for Martin, the more firmly we are persuaded that there had long existed a close association between them; and that what Sulpicius relates about Martin’s staying with Hilary before Hilary’s exile is true, except that he made the single error of allowing Julian’s name to slip in place of another emperor’s.

87. He raises an infant from the dead. — On returning from exile, Hilary shone not only in holiness but also in miracles. For a few days later, a mother afflicted by the twofold death of her infant—who, having died without the regeneration of baptism, had lost the present light and was not exempt from the punishment of the age to come (Fortunatus, book I, no. 12)—asked Hilary with many prayers and tears to restore her son either to herself or to baptism. Moved by this, the devout father of his people had recourse, before the watching crowd, to the accustomed weapons of prayer. He did not rise from the ground on which he lay prostrate until the infant had risen from the dead.

Fortunatus’ words deserve notice here. For, while above he says that an infant dying without the grace of baptism is not free from the punishment of the age to come (no. 13), and further praises Hilary because by this miracle he despoiled the underworld, he sufficiently declares his own view concerning the punishments of such infants.

88. He obtains death from God for his daughter Abra and her mother. — The same writer no less marvels at the power by which Hilary obtained death for his daughter Abra than at that by which he restored life to the dead infant. Loving her for heaven rather than for the world, he had already betrothed her to a heavenly bridegroom, provided only that she also chose him for herself. When, therefore, he learned that she was held by ardent desire for him, he did not cease from prayer until she departed without pain and without defilement from the world’s mockery to Christ.

Hardly had he committed Abra with his own hands to honorable burial when her mother, longing for heaven, asked him that, if she were worthy, she too might be rescued from the world’s guilt and sent with her daughter to the glory of the heavenly kingdom. By his continual prayer she obtained this not long afterward. Thus, since Hilary’s manner of life was in heaven, he hastened to send there those whom he loved on earth only for heaven’s sake. Bouchet reports, from Hildebert of Le Mans (*Annals of Aquitaine*, book I, ch. 14), that he buried both in the church dedicated to Saints John and Paul.

89. He frees Gaul from the stain of heresy. — But if those miracles were great, this was no less astonishing: that God restored him to his see while he was resisting the heretics courageously, at the very time when men were being expelled from theirs for having yielded somewhat to them. Nor do I think this happened without God’s special providence toward Gaul.
