For when the wound received by the Gauls at the Council of Rimini had recently been exposed through the letters sent by the Easterners, the skilled hand of a physician was needed to bind it up as soon as possible and heal it with suitable remedies.

Hilary came at the right moment, to raise up the downcast and, according to his inborn moderation, calm troubled minds. There were those who considered that iron and cutting were necessary; but he employed oil and forgiveness, and in a short time restored everything to its former condition. Thus, while he had to resist hardened heretics with strength and invincibility, he was ready and merciful in pardoning the penitent. It is difficult to decide whether he contributed more to the Church by greatness of courage or by a kind of pious compassion.

Before his exile he had, by courage, barred heresy’s entrance into Gaul; but, having been introduced by stealth while he was in exile, he expelled it so quickly by gentleness after returning from exile that Jerome says in his *Chronicle*, under the very year 360 in which Hilary returned from exile: “Gaul, through Hilary, condemns the deceits of the perfidy of Rimini.” Sulpicius explains how this was done:

> “When [Hilary] had traversed almost the whole world infected with the evil of perfidy, uncertain in mind and agitated by a great burden of cares, since it seemed to many that he ought not to enter into communion with those who had accepted the Council of Rimini, he judged it best to call many back to amendment and repentance. In frequent councils throughout Gaul, after nearly all the bishops had acknowledged their error, he condemned what had been done at Rimini and restored the faith of the churches to its former state.”

For it should be read thus, not, as in the common edition, “they restore” and “they condemn.”

90. The deposition of Saturninus. — Because of these words of Jerome and Sulpicius, we have already said that the conjecture of those who conveniently understand “dismissed without remission of exile” to mean that Hilary was forbidden to leave Poitiers seems less likely. For if, in that very year 360, Gaul through him condemned in frequent councils the deceits of the perfidy of Rimini, then, just as it cannot be denied that Hilary attended those councils, so it must be granted that he left Poitiers while Constantius was still alive. In carrying out the king’s commands where this was permitted by a safe conscience, his religious integrity should not be suspect to us. He was therefore never forbidden to leave Poitiers.

Sulpicius supports the view that Hilary spent not only that part of 360 in which he was restored to Gaul, but also 361 and perhaps the following year, in repairing the ruins caused by the Council of Rimini. For, after testifying that this was done in many councils, Sulpicius next mentions one held at Béziers, in which Saturninus, convicted not only of the disgrace of heresy but also of many shameful and base crimes, “was expelled from the Church . . . Paternus likewise, from Périgueux, equally deranged and not refusing to profess perfidy, was driven from the priesthood; pardon was given to the rest.”

But would the Gauls have dared to assume such authority that, while Constantius was defending the Arian sect with all the strength of his empire, they could expel its chief supporter from his church? Since Sulpicius writes that Saturninus was expelled from the Church in such a way that the forces of the Arian party were broken by the loss of their leader, he must be understood to have been expelled not only from ecclesiastical communion but even from the see of Arles itself. The Council of Paris, indeed, testifies that he had already twice been excluded from ecclesiastical communion; and the party’s forces had then been no more weakened. It follows that this Council of Béziers was not held until Constantius had ceased to live. For while he was alive, no authority of synods could have expelled Saturninus from his own church.

91. Among the shameful crimes of which that wicked heretic was convicted, not the least was the one by which he had procured Hilary’s exile. The innocent confessor of Christ was then granted the opportunity which Constantius had formerly denied him: to bring that informer to confess the falsehoods he had committed against him. Thus, by God’s just judgment, Saturninus paid the deserved penalty of deposition in the very city where, by fraud and falsehood, he had contrived the unjust sentence of exile against Hilary. Thereafter his name was erased from the sacred diptychs (*Analecta*, vol. III, p. 431). At least he does not appear in the old list of bishops of Arles, believed to have been extracted from that church’s diptychs, any more than does Marcianus, who in the preceding century had adhered to Novatian. Saturninus’ successor is commonly thought to have been Saint Concordius, who attended the Council of Valence in 394 (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 33).

92. Hilary’s enduring protection of Gaul against the Arians. — At last, when Hilary’s wisdom and labor had dispersed the darkness of the Arian sect, and its leader had been expelled—the one through whom the spirit of falsehood had led very many Gauls into error—it became established among all that Gaul had been freed from the stain of this heresy by Hilary’s benefit alone. Nor did he protect his native people from this same heresy only while alive; he did so also after being taken from the living.

The first Christian king of the Franks, Clovis, experienced his aid through a manifest sign even two centuries later. As he advanced against Alaric, the Arian king of the Goths, he saw above him a fiery beacon emerging from the basilica of Saint Hilary at Poitiers. “That,” says Gregory of Tours, “aided by the light of the blessed confessor Hilary, he might more freely defeat the heretical battle-lines against which that same bishop had so often contended for the faith” (Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, ch. 37).

Indeed, immediately admonished by a voice to pray in that venerable place and then hasten to engage in battle, he proceeded to war with such success—another fighting on his behalf—that before the third hour of the day he obtained from the Lord a victory beyond human hopes (Fortunatus, book II, *Life of Saint Hilary*). Having celebrated this notable victory, Fortunatus declares that he holds this view by Hilary’s own inspiration: namely, that Hilary, now at rest, was no less concerned for the Catholic religion than when he lived in the body. May heaven grant that, through his merits and prayers, the revived Arian plague may be driven far from our borders, and that the undefiled faith and veneration of the most holy Trinity may ever flourish in the hearts of the Franks.

93. When and why he wrote against Dioscorus. — The book addressed to Sallustius, prefect of Gaul, against the physician Dioscorus, of which only the title has come down to us from Jerome’s literary notices, must be assigned to the period when Saint Hilary was applying himself so vigorously to drive the Arians from Gaul. For Sallustius is called in that title merely prefect, not consul (Ammianus, book XXI, ch. 8; the same, book XXIII); and since it is otherwise established that Julian made him prefect of Gaul in 361 and that, two years later, he was admitted to the *collegium of the trabea*, that is, chosen as a colleague in the consulship, it is clear that this book was written neither before 361 nor after 363. The same conclusion follows from the fact that this same Sallustius went with Julian in 363 on the expedition against the Persians and, subsequently appointed prefect of the praetorium of the East by Valentinian and Valens, did not return to Gaul (the same, book XXVI, ch. 5). Suidas testifies that this prefect possessed remarkable humanity. Rufinus and Theodoret likewise show that he expressly shrank from persecuting Christians (Rufinus, book I, ch. 36; Theodoret, book III, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 7). Hence it may be conjectured that he was appealed to in this book in order to restrain the violence of the physician Dioscorus, who perhaps, under Julian’s authority and in his name, was persecuting Christians excessively.

## Chapter XII. [Col. 0167D] 94. Hilary’s labours in Italy, and the schism of Lucifer. — Hilary’s zeal for the Catholic religion could not confine itself within the borders of Gaul. Having therefore restored peace there, he crossed the Alps in order to assist Italy and the neighbouring regions, which had been much more grievously corrupted by the fury and contagion of the Arian heresy. Eusebius, returning to Vercelli from the Alexandrian council and recalling each of the churches of the East and Italy from renounced unbelief to the health of right faith, found Hilary in Italy engaged in these same efforts to restore the churches and repair the faith of the Fathers (Rufinus, book I, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 30); and he gladly joined him in the same work.

You may reasonably believe that this particular association of the two confessors began about the beginning of 363, especially since the death of George, the pseudo-patriarch of Alexandria, which occurred after the middle of 362, preceded the Alexandrian council from which Eusebius was then returning. Although Rufinus testifies (ibid., ch. 31) that these two men, like splendid lights, so illuminated Illyricum and Italy with their radiance that they drove away even the darkness of the heretics from hidden corners and obscure recesses, he nevertheless assigns this particular praise to Hilary: because he was gentle and mild by nature, learned as well, and eminently suited to persuasion, he conducted the affair with greater diligence and fitness.

This is indeed a wholly unsuspect eulogy, in which an Italian presbyter prefers a Gallic bishop to an Italian bishop. But if plain truth and fresh memory of the events led him to say this, why does he attribute this glory above all to the gentleness of Hilary’s nature? Certainly, unless this virtue had shone forth in Hilary in a singular manner, it would have been enough for Rufinus to ascribe the cause of this greater facility in winning minds to his supreme eloquence. Whether Hilary and Eusebius did anything in Italy without consulting Liberius, I would not venture to affirm. Yet Fragment XII makes it clear that Liberius burned with the same zeal for restoring the faith. I would therefore readily concede that the councils of Italy and Illyricum mentioned in that Fragment—in which the bishops of both regions, acknowledging that they had been deceived at Rimini, renounced fellowship in unbelief—were convened at Liberius’ prompting, just as they were through the activity of Hilary and Eusebius.

[Col. 0168C] 95. Lucifer disapproves. — Lucifer of Cagliari opposed the sound counsels of those holy men. He had become somewhat alienated from Eusebius because he had disapproved of what Eusebius had recently done at Antioch. As was observed above, Hilary’s very great moderation toward the Easterners in the book *On the Synods* had long displeased him as well. Although I believe that prudent replies from Hilary had softened him, the offence readily flared up again when he understood that Hilary was siding with Eusebius rather than with himself.

Thus disposed, Lucifer—being by nature rather harsh and not greatly inclined to clemency—could not but condemn Hilary’s readiness to receive those who had lapsed at Rimini. For this reason Hilary was spoken of unfavourably throughout Lucifer’s whole sect, as one who had forfeited the reputation he had gained in the Church by favouring traitors—if we do not also call them heretics—against whom he had pleaded with all the powers of his eloquence (Marcellinus and Faustinus, in the *Petition-Book*). On the other hand, among those whom the darkness of schism had not blinded, he not only did not diminish or impair the glory he had earned through his earlier writings and deeds, but almost increased it: for, by setting forth the light of truth and offering ready pardon, he restored to the Church those whom the fraud and terror of heretics had taken away from her.

96. How unjust was Lucifer’s judgment. — It certainly seemed harsh and alien to Christian gentleness and simplicity either not to believe, or to deny pardon to, persons who were regarded as heretics without being conscious of it and who testified that they had suspected nothing evil in their faith concerning the body of the Lord and whatever is holy in the Church (Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*). For it was plain that they had accepted the creed proposed at Rimini solely with a view to peace, and that they had not agreed to it until, by adding many things prompted by Catholic conviction, they had supposed themselves to have sufficiently supplied the force of the suppressed term *consubstantial*.

Hence, as soon as the fraud hidden in the accepted formula was exposed, especially through Hilary’s efforts, the whole world groaned and wondered that it was Arian: that is, it was astonished to find itself publicly proclaimed and called Arian, though it not only detested Arius and his doctrine sincerely, but also believed that by its subscription it had more than sufficiently condemned him.

97. When disciplinary rigour should be relaxed for those who have lapsed. — Yet it must not be denied that those who, through weakness, abandoned the Nicene creed at Rimini in order to accept a new formula from men whose faith they had good reason to suspect can scarcely be excused from sin. But their offence was not of such a kind as to deserve expiation by public and mournful penance; and therefore the canons established at Nicaea—according to Innocent, Epistle 6—which exclude penitents even from the lowest clerical offices, did not apply to them.

But even if they had been liable to public penance, the rigour of those canons could nevertheless prudently have been relaxed in their case. For Augustine acknowledges (*Epistle* 185, no. 44) that clerics, even bishops, ought not to remain after penance; yet he advises that this law of the Church must be supplemented unless the compensation afforded by peace preserved the contrary course. “For,” he says a little later, “the rule established in the Church, that no one after penance for any crime should receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office, was made not because pardon was despaired of, but because of the rigour of discipline.”

He illustrates, by an image taken from grafting, how the Church sometimes beneficially relaxes disciplinary strictness (no. 44): “When a branch that has been cut off is grafted in, another wound is made in the tree, by which it can be received and live, though it was perishing without the life of the root. Thus also, when these persons come to the Catholic root, and the honour of clerical and episcopal office is not taken from them even after penance for their error, something is indeed done, as it were, in the bark of the mother tree contrary to the integrity of severity,” etc. He concludes: “Thus the Church is accustomed to succour multitudes perishing through schisms and heresies.” He then notes Lucifer’s fall: “This displeased Lucifer . . . and, because it displeased him, he fell into the darkness of schism, having lost the light of charity.”

98. As Hilary always cherished Lucifer’s friendship, so he grieved over his fall. — Hilary undoubtedly grieved deeply at the fall of so great a man, whom the whole Church deservedly admired for his exceptional constancy. How great was the reverence in which he held him is evident even from this: he used the term “likeness” (*similitudo*), from which he somewhat recoiled, when he understood that Lucifer habitually used it (*Apology in Reply*, 3 and 6). For he knew well that harmony of minds and judgments is very necessary for those defending the same cause amid enemies, and that this harmony is easily dissolved unless those who have greater command of themselves accommodate themselves to associates less masterful over their own minds.

With this same spirit, when later Lucifer reproached him on account of his book *On the Synods*, Hilary did not repay injuries with injuries, but overcame him by gentleness of speech and cogency of argument. [Note: [Col. 0170D] Book I of the poem on the life of Saint Martin.] Hence we judge that Hilary left nothing untried to recall Lucifer from schism, whose friendship had always been so dear to him. Is it believable that one who spared no labour to raise up the fallen would have failed to exert every effort to prevent the fall of one who had hitherto stood so courageously? But what Rufinus says, taking occasion from Lucifer’s own fall (book I, ch. 30)—“Things rashly begun are accustomed to be corrected only by time”—was truly said, if of anyone, of Lucifer, a man of a disposition not easily bent.

99. Hilary’s authority was capable of restraining Lucifer’s schism. — Yet Hilary’s labour was not fruitless. It seems that both his exertions and his authority should be credited with the fact that so few adhered to Lucifer’s schism that, according to Jerome, the entire sect died out with the deacon Hilary. Nor was it easy for Lucifer to persuade others that Hilary pardoned the lapsed out of laxity of spirit rather than pure charity, since they knew with certainty that in every danger Hilary had otherwise stood fearless and unconquered for the glory of the Lord. Indeed, when the cause required it, all Italy itself saw at that very time how far he was from being soft or lax.

## Chapter XIII. 100. Hilary’s encounter with Auxentius. — Hilary had spent part of 362 and all of 363 in Italy when Valentinian, having obtained imperial power, arrived at Milan on 26 February 364. Although Hilary could rightly have gloried in the success of his actions for the Church, he judged that he had as yet done nothing so long as anyone remained who opposed Christ’s divinity. Far from empty glory, he declares that he had taken care to seek the true peace that had been lost, to restore it when disturbed, and to maintain it when found; yet he immediately adds (*Against Auxentius*, no. 1): “But neither have the sins of our time deserved that we should become either participants in, or authors of, this very peace.” Thus he speaks as though his desire had by no means been fulfilled.

Others agree that through Hilary’s benefit alone Gaul was freed from the accursed defilement of heresy; that through his industry, gentleness, and eloquence peace was restored to Italy and nearly all Illyricum; and that Arius’ formerly vast inheritance in the West was thereby reduced to only Valens, Ursacius, Germinius, Gaius, and Auxentius. Hilary alone does not congratulate himself that this wretched inheritance had been reduced to so few; rather, because it had not been utterly extinguished, he considers that he has as yet accomplished nothing. He therefore exerts his strength, although, in order to evade his efforts, even those heirs of so impious a master deny that they are such. For the same spirit of Satan by whom Arius was formerly stirred up and animated does not dare openly show itself in them; it is compelled to transform itself into an angel of light, so that it may lie concealed more easily.

101. He attempts to expel Auxentius from Milan. — Auxentius above all played this game by such artifice, but he could not deceive Hilary. The more Auxentius strove to conceal his poison, the more vigorously Hilary applied himself to expose it and to free from him, as from a venomous serpent, the city of Milan, which had always been dear to him because of its exceptional devotion to the Catholic faith. Auxentius, conscious of his own guilt, immediately anticipated Hilary before Valentinian. Falsely claiming in words to be Catholic, he complained that Hilary was disturbing his people.

When he heard this, the king, a lover of peace and desirous of confirming peace by his arrival, was readily induced to order by a stern edict that no one should disturb the church of Milan. Hilary could not endure that a Catholic prince should, under the appearance and intention of unity, entrust the Church to a heretic. He therefore urgently petitioned Valentinian, declaring that Auxentius was a blasphemer and must altogether be regarded as an enemy of Christ, and that he believed differently from the emperor himself and all others.

Moved by this, the emperor ordered Auxentius and Hilary to be heard by the quaestor and the *magister*, in the presence of about ten bishops. Among them shone conspicuously Eusebius of Vercelli, Hilary’s helper and associate. Auxentius first attacked Hilary’s standing and refused to have him heard as a bishop, since Saturninus had formerly condemned him. Hilary had a ready reply: he had never been deposed from the episcopate; exile was vainly objected against him, since he had been expelled through Saturninus’ influence, and Saturninus had achieved this so unjustly that Hilary had requested Constantius’ permission publicly to convict him of the lies by which he had perpetrated this crime, and had finally convicted him at the Council of Béziers. What answer was made, however, Hilary, hastening to other matters, thought proper to pass over in silence. He only observes that those conducting the hearing then decided that the question of faith should be discussed instead, as the emperor desired.

Here Auxentius revealed his skill: fearing to deny that Christ is God, he professed Him to be of one divinity and substance with God the Father. It was decided that this profession should be put into writing; and it was done at once. Hilary offered the emperor through the quaestor a petition setting forth what had been agreed. Thereupon Auxentius was compelled by the judgment of all to profess openly and confirm in writing what he had already confessed. After long deliberating upon his plans, he composed his language so as to evade the emperor’s faith. At length, through Hilary’s exposition, those who were not deceived by his double-faced malice spread abroad that his belief differed.

102. He is exposed by Hilary. — Auxentius seemed defeated, since he could not escape that encounter except by pretending to agree with the man whom he had formerly been accustomed to call a heretic. Hence the glory of having subdued his adversary accrued to Hilary. But Hilary, preferring that his Lord should conquer rather than himself, did not know how to rejoice in a victory that conferred nothing upon Him. Fearing, therefore, that the enemy of Christ, whom he knew had not changed, might lay snares for the devout flock committed to him, he protested that everything was a pretence, that faith was being denied, and that God and human beings were being mocked. Yet, disregarding his warning, Valentinian ordered him to leave Milan and entered into communion with Auxentius.

103. He publishes the proceedings against Auxentius and gives an example of moderation. — Hilary obeyed the emperor’s command, but he did not abandon the Church of Milan or others. By publishing the proceedings of the whole encounter and revealing Auxentius’ fraud, he enabled lovers of the sincere faith to guard themselves against him. In this writing, what should one admire more: his penetrating ingenuity in uncovering the wiles of a most crafty heretic, and his constancy of faith in refuting them; or his prudence and moderation in excusing the emperor?

Valentinian had read the letter sent to him by Auxentius. In it that heretic represents Hilary and Eusebius as blasphemers (nos. 13 and 15); approves the councils of the impious, by which those illustrious confessors of Christ had been unjustly condemned; wishes their labours to restore the churches of Italy to be regarded as acts of schismatics; and finally praises the proceedings of the Council of Rimini, boasting that he adheres to its faith. Who could fail to see that he thereby openly betrayed an Arian mind? Yet Hilary nowhere accuses the emperor of an unjust judgment because he rejected Hilary and received lying Auxentius. The recent injury draws nothing from Hilary’s pen in which one might miss the reverence due to the emperor.

Always master of himself, he allowed no agitation to prevent him from recognizing the proven sincerity of the emperor’s faith. Being human and a lover of peace, he readily pardoned the prince, who had erred through excessive humanity and a single-minded desire for peace. And he who had formerly praised the Eastern bishops because, though they had believed heretics speaking however plausibly, it was religious to reserve judgment for God, did not change that view when it was in his own interest that a heretic should not so quickly be believed. Accordingly, more eager to excuse Valentinian than to accuse him, he describes the emperor as entering into communion with Auxentius, yet adds that he did so because of the sincerity of faith which he thought that heretic professed. And when he states that the emperor had been deceived, he places all blame upon Auxentius, because he played with words capable of deceiving even the elect—as though he feared that even a suspicion of negligence might fall upon the emperor.

104. From love of truth, he rebukes Auxentius’ wickedness more harshly. — He spares not only the emperor but also the counts and all others whose trust Auxentius had abused. He sharpens his pen against that single impostor. For the same love of truth and sincerity—which cannot be pure without vehement hatred of falsehood—stirred in Hilary both compassion for those deceived through simplicity and indignation against the one who had deceitfully deceived them. Indeed, when charity burns, it conceives flames: while these enlighten the ignorant and cherish the cold with kindly warmth, they punish and consume the hard and stubborn with just grief.

As Hilary had formerly displayed these distinct effects of ordered charity (*To Constantius*, no. 2), when he decreed that those who led others into error ought to be cut off while granting their associates opportunity to repent, so now he displays them by sparing the deceived and pursuing the sole author of falsehood and deceit. As intensely as he recoiled from this man’s wickedness, so he omitted nothing by which he might deter others equally from his fellowship. No other reason appears why he attacks so fiercely those whom an ill-conceived love of buildings had captivated—who, under such roofs, impose the name of peace and wrongly venerate the Church of God in walls and roofs—except to cut off every opportunity for entering into communion with Auxentius.

He knew that Valentinian had been all the more inclined to judge Auxentius’ faith free of Arianism because, though unwilling to seize churches from this heretic by force, he had wished to exercise his own religious worship harmlessly in those which Auxentius occupied. Hilary himself, therefore, inflamed with zeal for a purer religion, tries to remove the emperor’s scruple, and that of others who perhaps had fallen into the same pretence, by these fiery words: “Mountains, forests, lakes, prisons, and chasms are safer for me; for in these the prophets either dwelling or submerged prophesied” (*Against Auxentius*, no. 12); “since,” he says, “it is not doubtful that Antichrist will sit beneath the roofs of sacred buildings.”

Then, lest Auxentius’ hypocrisy remain any longer concealed, like an anxious shepherd who cries out that a wolf is present when he sees it lying in wait for the flock, Hilary too proclaims that Auxentius is an enemy of Christ, an angel of Satan, a destroyer of the faith; and that no hardships whatever will ever induce him to desire peace either with Auxentius or with anyone except those who, according to the deliberation of our Fathers at Nicaea, having anathematized the Arians, proclaim Christ to be true God. If anyone judges these words somewhat too vehement, let him recall what the most gentle Lord uttered against hypocritical Pharisees of this kind. Again, if anyone doubts whether, prompted by the good Spirit, Hilary could call Auxentius “devil,” let him remember that Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to Elymas: “O man full of all deceit and all fraud, son of the devil” (Acts 12:10 [OCR; Acts 13:10]).

The Lord himself shows that falsehood is proper to human beings insofar as they are from the devil their father (John 8:44), because he did not stand in the truth from the beginning and speaks falsehood from his own resources. What then prevents sons from being called by the name of their father? Certainly, just as Judas, Christ himself saying it, was truly a devil because “he was animated through him,” as our Hilary says (*On Psalm* 142, no. 2), so Auxentius too was truly a devil, because he acted with that being as author and instigator. For the devil had put it into the heart of each to betray the Lord.

105. Even in this he restrains himself. — Yet Hilary does not loose the reins of his just and holy indignation against Auxentius so far that he does not prudently keep silent about what should remain unspoken. “Shame,” he says, “prevents me from bringing forward many other matters to the Church; and I dread committing to a letter the shameful blasphemies of the Arians.” He thinks it enough to expose the poison of Auxentius’ confession; but he prefers himself to set out the entire secret of so deadly a mystery rather than commit it to writing, so that neither should those be unaware whom it concerns to know all the intrigues and impieties of heretics, nor should it reach those for whom it is beneficial to remain within the simplicity of faith. The Church, Christ’s bride, is chaste and modest and cannot but be offended by insults to her bridegroom. It was therefore prudent to spare her modest ears and reveal nothing to her except what would serve her salvation.

[Col. 0174A] 106. The fruit of this labour. — Having attempted through this writing to meet the danger which he feared for the Church from Auxentius’ fraud, Hilary returned to Gaul, filled as much with joy as with triumphs over the Arian heresy—if he could have convinced Valentinian of the deceit of this double-faced heretic. But where, in this world, is perfect and complete joy? We dwell in a cursed earth which, although cultivated in the sweat of the brow, yields fruit in such a way that it also produces thorns and thistles. Hilary’s anxiety was nevertheless somewhat relieved by the fact that Auxentius was compelled so to conceal the poison of his heresy that, under the priest of Antichrist, Christ’s people did not perish (no. 5); and that, if he ever began to reveal it, Eusebius, Hilary’s fellow-worker and helper, would be at hand, and, supported by the authority of the orthodox emperor, would by then restrain him.

107. Certain fables arising from this. — The outcome of Hilary’s entire affair gave occasion to certain fables. For by what other name should one call, or to what deeds of Hilary should one refer, the story reported by Rufinus (*On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, in Jerome, vol. IX, p. 131): that a book full of instruction, written by Hilary of Poitiers for the correction of those who had subscribed to the perfidy of Rimini, was so corrupted by his enemies that later, when they began at a council of bishops to call him a heretic, according to what they knew they had altered in his booklet, and when the booklet was produced and found to be of such a kind that he did not recognize it, they caused him to leave the gathering of the council excommunicated?

Jerome rightly cries out against this (*Second Apology against Rufinus*): “The synod from which he was excommunicated—where was it held? Name the bishops; produce the decisions and subscriptions, whether differing or agreeing. Tell us who were consuls in that year, which emperor ordered that synod to be assembled, whether the bishops were only from Gaul or also from Italy and Spain, and certainly for what cause the synod was convened. You name none of these things.” But if we understand the book mentioned by Rufinus to be that in which Hilary had included the history of the councils of Rimini and Seleucia, and if we grant that this book already existed at that time in a corrupted and mutilated form, it is not difficult to discover whence Rufinus constructed this whole narrative. Having merely heard that Hilary had been called a heretic by Auxentius and that, shortly after a hearing had taken place, he had been ordered to leave the city of Milan, Rufinus easily imagined that the alteration of the book, which he had heard was corrupted, consisted not simply in the mutilation of one among its many parts but in errors inserted through the work of heretics, and that the book’s author had been expelled not only from the city but also from the assembly because of those errors.

108. No less absurd is what is recounted in many manuscripts among Hilary’s miracles: namely, that he once attended a council over which Pope Leo presided, and, when a seat was denied him, lay down upon the ground, which at once rose so high that it quickly became level with Leo’s throne. Who cannot see that this monstrous story was fabricated both from the acts of our Hilary in his encounter with Auxentius and, especially, from the celebrated controversy that arose much later between Leo and Hilary of Arles in the case of Celidonius? But leaving these matters, let us continue to follow Hilary as he returns once more to Gaul.

## Chapter XIV. 109. Hilary’s remaining acts and death. — Since various affairs of the Church had repeatedly withdrawn Hilary from his people for many years, it was fitting that he should at last be restored to them: that they might be refreshed by the sweet sight of him, instructed by his teaching, and formed by his example unto true piety. He too had at last deserved peaceful and tranquil days, after having long endured troubled ones. It was fitting that in the last years of his life he should enjoy the peace in which the Church rejoiced especially through his efforts. Thus, about the end of 364, leaving Italy, he retired to Poitiers.

Although the record of his acts fails us here, there is no doubt that, devoting himself to continual prayer and forming the people entrusted to him in Christian discipline, he fulfilled the duties of a perfect shepherd. Indeed, it follows in a manner necessarily from his exposition of the Psalms that he then expounded them, since in that exposition he refers to his books *On the Trinity* as having already been published. For after the publication of those books he had scarcely any leisure, except in these final years, to complete so great a work. It is probable that he undertook to explain, from all Scripture, especially the more hidden meanings of the Psalms in order that they might be sung more sweetly and profitably.

That psalm-singing was then customary in the church over which he presided is suggested both by *Treatise on Psalm* 118, letter 5, no. 14, where he recalls Christians from vain spectacles to more pleasing objects: “Unless perhaps those divine utterances of human hope are not sung more pleasantly than the obscene plays of shameful spectacles”; and especially by *Treatise on Psalm* 64, no. 12: “The Church’s progress into the delights of morning and evening hymns is a great sign of God’s mercy. The day begins in prayers to God; the day closes in hymns to God.”

110. Perhaps it will seem incredible to some that, after Hilary’s second return to Gaul—that is, after many disputations and frequent battles with the Arians—he wrote the extant treatises on the Psalms, since in them he spares those sworn enemies of the faith as though he had never known them. Those who think that he merely interpreted Origen’s words readily escape this difficulty, since it is hardly surprising that the interpreter should keep silent about heresies which had not yet arisen in his author’s age. But many considerations oppose this opinion, to be more suitably set forth in a separate Preface; and it is especially contradicted by the fact that in these same treatises doctrine contrary to Arian error is repeatedly established in a manner that does not at all savour of Origen’s style. It is therefore more credible that Hilary passes over Arian impieties in silence both because his disposition was removed from all quarrelling and contention and because he considered that recalling them would not benefit his people.

111. He publishes books of hymns and mysteries. — The books of hymns and mysteries mentioned by Jerome may likewise be assigned to this period. After approving among the Easterners the established singing of hymns and other devout usages in the celebration of the mysteries, Hilary may subsequently, on his return, have directed his attention to enlarging or embellishing the rites of the Western Church by imitation of them. The Fourth Council of Toledo, of 633, relates that some of Hilary’s hymns were customarily sung in the Church.

It is clear from the final Fragments that at this time he laboured to make fuller and more complete the history of the Council of Rimini and the Synod of Seleucia which he had begun, and that he devoted effort to gathering the records relevant to these assemblies. But whether in old age he wrote on the Song of Songs, whose exposition many later writers made the crown of their works—indeed, whether he ever wrote such a work—who can affirm it? Jerome alone mentions this composition, merely upon uncertain report, to which he himself seems somewhat to withhold belief.

112. He devoted labour to copying books. — Another work of Hilary, not to be passed over, had almost slipped from memory. That he did not neglect manual labour, but spent the time remaining from ecclesiastical cares in copying sacred books, is indicated by the will of Saint Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, made in the year of Christ 474. In it he leaves to Euphronius, bishop of Autun, a book of the Gospels “which Hilary of Poitiers, formerly a priest, wrote” (*Spicilegium*, vol. V, p. 106). This work, which Jerome so strongly approved because “the hands labour for food and the mind is nourished by reading” (Jerome, Epistle 4, to Rusticus), was wholly worthy of Hilary: so that he might not only proclaim aloud before hearers the Gospel which he bore in his heart, but also transmit it afar by the devout craftsmanship of his hands.

There is still preserved in the Church of Saint Gatianus at Tours an old Latin codex of the Gospels, thought to have been written by Saint Hilary and left to that church by Saint Perpetuus. Since Perpetuus himself survived Euphronius, this may be inferred from the wording of the will. It may also be interpreted from the statement of the Christian Druthmar, an Aquitanian by nation and monk of Corbie, who flourished about the ninth century: “I saw a book of the Gospel written in Greek, which was said to have belonged to Saint Hilary, in which Matthew and John came first, and before [read: after] the others, namely Mark and Luke.” That book, then, was called Saint Hilary’s because it had been written in his own hand.

It is likewise probable that he expended the same diligence in copying other books, especially the acts of synods. From that labour he would have had materials readily at hand for composing the history of the Council of Rimini when the Church’s circumstances required it. Whatever acts of Hilary we have thus far taken pains to draw out and investigate from ancient monuments as accurately as we could, Fortunatus comprises in this brief summary: “While he lived in this world, he either wrote testimonies of ecclesiastical faith, or by fighting trampled down heretical crimes, or granted the aid of miracles to those who sought it. So holy a life could be consummated only by a precious death.”

We shall append at the end of Book II of the *Life* written by Fortunatus certain matters pertaining to that death, on the authority of the manuscripts of Saint-Germain and many others. According to the testimony of Jerome and Gregory of Tours, he died at Poitiers. Learned men dispute in what year and on what day.

### 113. On the day and year in which Hilary died

Most hold that his death fell on 13 January 367. On that day, indeed, the deposition of St. Hilary is recorded in the standard martyrology of Jerome, as also by Bede, Florus, and other later writers. Supporting this is the Calendar printed in volume X of the *Spicilegium*, copied from a Corbie manuscript of the year 900, in which appears: “The Ides of January: the Octave of Epiphany and the deposition of St. Clarius, bishop.” For *Clarius* must plainly be read in place of Hilary—or, corruptly, Elary. Without any error, a codex given by Charlemagne to the monastery of Gellone has: “The Ides of January: the deposition of St. Hilary, bishop.” We have moreover consulted very many exceedingly ancient books of Sacraments, Masses, and Collects, in which the same is read. Sulpicius favors the same opinion when he writes that Hilary died in his native country in the sixth year after his return.

Yet the words of Jerome and Gregory of Tours, to be considered presently, cannot readily be reconciled with it. Nor is Hilary’s commemoration so uniformly entered on the Ides of January in all ancient books consecrated to ecclesiastical offices that it is not also observed otherwise in them—for example, on another day in January, on 26 June, or on the Kalends of November. When defenders of the foregoing opinion hear this, they immediately object that it arose either from various translations of the saint’s body itself, or from more recent rites for celebrating feasts, by which the octave day of Epiphany and the feast of St. Hilary may not be celebrated together with equal solemnity.

It must indeed be granted that there was once a different custom. This is made persuasive even by a single Sacramentary codex written by order of Ratold, abbot of Corbie, before 986. There one first finds the heading: “The Ides of January: the Octave of Epiphany and the deposition of St. Hilary.” Then, before the Collect for St. Hilary, the Collect for Epiphany is placed; next, in an inverted order, the commemoration of St. Hilary is celebrated first over the offerings, and afterwards only his praises resound in the Preface. There follow three blessings concerning Epiphany alone; and finally, to complete the service, the first prayer is again for Epiphany, the latter for St. Hilary.

But this answer does not satisfy those who have consulted the manuscripts themselves. For although they are not so numerous, there are codices no less ancient, and not adjusted to our rites, in which the feast of St. Hilary is recorded on the Kalends of November. On that day an ancient exemplar of the church of St. Gatianus at Tours contains five Masses: the first for All Saints, the second for St. Caesarius, the third and fourth likewise for All Saints, and the fifth for St. Hilary, with this inscription: “On that same day also, the Solemnity of St. Hilary, bishop and confessor.” We would readily concede that some solemn translation is indicated here, unless in a royal codex written about the year 900, and in a very ancient pontifical of the church of Évreux, not merely a solemnity but the *Natale*—the feast of the heavenly birth—of St. Hilary were marked on those same Kalends.

### 114.

With this latter date, unless perhaps Sulpicius be excepted, everything transmitted in ancient records concerning Hilary’s death agrees far better than with the former. First, Gregory of Tours testifies that in the fourth year of Valentinian and Valens, St. Hilary, at Poitiers, “full of holiness and faith, after displaying many miracles on every side, passed to heaven.” But the fourth year of Valentinian and Valens began on 27 February 367. Therefore, as the Ides of January 367 do not fall within that year, neither do they coincide with Hilary’s death. The Kalends of November, however, fit both exactly.

The same conclusion follows altogether from Jerome’s *Chronicle*, in which Hilary’s death is recorded under the year 367 in such a way that Gratian’s elevation to imperial rank is mentioned first. For, according to Idatius, Gratian received the empire on 24 August 367. Thus, in Jerome, the order of events is properly arranged if Hilary departed this life on the Kalends of November 367, but not if he died on the Ides of January.

What shall we say of Hermann the Cripple? Although he commemorates Hilary’s death in 367, he places it in the second year after Gratian had become co-emperor, and thus speaks inconsistently. Nevertheless, he departs less widely from the words of Jerome and Gregory as explained above.

There are besides Fragments XIV and XV of the history of the Synod of Rimini, containing the letter issued by the conventicle at Singidunum on 18 December 366 and the reply of Germinius, sent somewhat later. Who could allow that these documents could have been carried from Pannonia to Hilary while he was staying at Poitiers, and incorporated by him into his work before the Ides of January?

### 115.

For these reasons, those who, persuaded by the authority of nearly all the manuscripts, hold that Hilary’s final day was marked by the Ides of January, believe that he lived until 368. Gregory of Tours’ words agree very well with this opinion, nor does Jerome’s *Chronicle* oppose it. “For,” they say, “since Hilary’s death occupies the final place under the year 367, it will fall at the beginning of 368 if the numeral date 368 is raised by only one line.”

Sulpicius’s statement that Hilary died in his native country in the sixth year after his return fits either opinion less easily. For it is nearly certain that he returned either about the end of 360 or about the beginning of 361. Blondel and others, however, deceived by a false reading in earlier editions, wrongly hold that Hilary’s conflict with Auxentius took place ten years after the Synod of Rimini, and therefore falsely place his death in 371. Since Jerome’s *Chronicle* places an earthquake—known to have occurred at Nicaea in 358—after this death, it is evident that this illustrious light was removed from our world before the end of 358, that it might shine more brightly in heaven.

## Chapter XV. St. Hilary’s miracles, relics, and disciples

### 116. St. Hilary’s miracles, relics, and disciples

Hilary did not ascend to heaven in such a way as wholly to abandon the earth. Very many experienced his help and power even afterwards. So many miracles were performed at his tomb that Fortunatus composed an entire book from those wrought in his own age. Fortunatus himself—or another author of the first book of Hilary’s Life—testifies (*Preface to Book II*, no. 2) that his tomb became daily more celebrated because of the miracles which, he says, “continue even to the present day.” Nicetius, bishop of Trier, confirms this in a letter to Chlodosuind:

> “What shall I say of the Lords Germanus, HILARY, and Lupus, bishops, where such great marvels appear today as I cannot express even in words?”

### 117.

Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book I, chapter 39, reports that Hilary raised the dead; and in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 2, content to recall those things contained in the second book of Fortunatus, he adds another miracle accomplished through Hilary’s relics in the territory of Gévaudan. There is, however, reason to suspect that Gregory, deceived by similarity of names, attributed to Hilary of Poitiers what belonged to Hilary, bishop of Gévaudan or Mende.

Nor did Hilary’s power in working wonders shine forth only within the borders of Poitiers or in places where his relics were preserved. Flodoard testifies (*History of the Church of Reims*, Book IV, chapter 48) that two churches were built at Reims in honor of the holy confessor, and that both were renowned for miracles.

### 118.

Other accounts occur in various manuscripts, apparently collected in the ninth century by uncertain authors. Though their reliability is doubtful in matters remote from their own times, it should not be scorned concerning events which they attest took place in their own age. Such a collection is contained in Colbert manuscript 59. It first relates the tale of earth suddenly rising in a synod before Leo. Then follows the miracle of a woman who offered a cloak at St. Hilary’s tomb against her husband’s will.

Thirdly, another woman is mentioned who, disabled throughout her body, was sent by Blessed Hilary to the basilica of St. Peter and healed. Next they present a certain Goda, blind and lame, who, having recovered health through Hilary’s aid, could not return to her own people and dedicated herself to sweeping his basilica. Fifthly, they tell how, when his sacred remains were brought into the basilica of St. Peter—now St. Geneviève’s—by Abbot Frothald, two serpents were driven from the apse; and at the same time they recall what he himself had accomplished while alive on the island of Dives. Sixthly, mention is made of a noblewoman, apparently delivered from a demon in the author’s own age. Of her he says: “She is reported even to be living to this day, and seems annually to render a votive offering for the salvation of her soul and body to the lights of the Saint.”

Eighthly appears a boy who, having swallowed a serpent alive through his open mouth, was led to the island of Dives, where a basilica had been built under the invocation of St. Hilary, and was healed. Finally, it is related how Hilary passed the last day of his life in the presence of Leon(i)us. Vincent of Beauvais copied these last two accounts in the *Historical Mirror*, Book XIV, chapter 51.

A manuscript codex of the Cistercian monastery of Longpont contains nearly the same accounts and others, which its author declares he collected because they had been neglected by others or passed over through indolence. The third among these tells of a Dane who received baptism deceitfully, in order that, having been received from the sacred font by the hands of Count Ramnulf, he might obtain generous baptismal garments.

We omit what is found in the Ottobonian manuscript, and what Bouchet, author of the *Annals of Aquitaine*, added to the foregoing and Bollandus transferred from him. Yet this should not have been passed over here, had we not already mentioned it: when Clovis the Great entered upon the contest against Alaric, king of the Goths, he received an omen of his future victory in the church of St. Hilary; and therefore commanded his soldiers to abstain from plundering that region and from violently taking anything from the property of its citizens.

### 119. Hilary’s name was formerly recited in the sacred canon of the Mass

The Church has always honored with singular veneration the outstanding holiness of this illustrious bishop, which God attested by so many wonders. Most ancient Sacramentaries commemorate him in the canon of the venerable sacrifice immediately after the martyrs. E. C. Bona mentions three from the Vatican Library that display the name of the holy Confessor in that place. In agreement with them are a Corbie codex about 700 years old; a Remigian codex written in the age of Charlemagne; a German manuscript formerly given by Charlemagne to the monastery of Gellone; and very many others, which it would be tedious and superfluous to enumerate. In the Mozarabic liturgy itself he occupies the first place among confessors.

### 120. Very many basilicas were built in his honor

Moreover, to show their reverence toward him, our forebears built very many basilicas in his honor everywhere. Especially notable was the devotion of St. Aredius, abbot of Attane in the territory of Limoges. Of the possessions that had fallen to him from his noble parents, he devoted a great part to erecting a sacred building under the invocation of St. Hilary; and he determined that his own body should be buried there.

This abbot had such confidence in Hilary’s merits that, when he wished to relieve the grief of Nectarius, a very wealthy citizen of Limoges, he ordered Nectarius’s only son, lifeless, to be brought to him and laid before the sacred relics of Blessed Hilary the bishop. There, after prayer, he immediately restored the child safe and sound to his parent.

### 121. The first translation of his body

The first and celebrated translation of those sacred relics is said to have occurred in the times of King Clovis and Abbot Fridolin.

> **Note [Col. 0180D]:** On this translation see C. Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 538, nos. 41, 42, and 43.

Peter Damian, preaching on its anniversary, testifies that the holy body was carried by the very hands of angels to the place prepared for it. The same miracle is found in a manuscript of the church of Beauvais; it further adds that from that time no one dared either touch the sacred body or transfer it elsewhere. For this reason, it says, his sacred relics are found nowhere else, except perhaps his priestly vestments, or dust gathered from his tomb, which is there said to have been covered with silver.

### 122.

If these things are true, that scrupulous reverence toward Hilary’s sacred bones seems at least not to have endured long. Gregory of Tours’ own account nearly persuades us that they were dispersed in his time. He relates that a priest of God, wishing to recall a people of the territory of Gévaudan from empty superstition concerning a lake, built a church in honor of Blessed Hilary of Poitiers, placed his relics in it, and exhorted the people in these words:

> “Do not defile your souls with these vain rites; rather, know—or perhaps worship—God, and bestow veneration upon his friends. But worship St. Hilary, bishop of God, whose relics are deposited here; for he can serve as an intercessor for you before the mercy of God.”

As we said, it is probable that Gregory, deceived by similarity of names, falsely supposed these to be relics of Hilary of Poitiers, when they belonged to Hilary of Mende. Yet there remains no room to doubt that he believed such relics could be possessed elsewhere than at Poitiers, and in fact were so possessed.

To this must be added what we related above from the Life of Blessed Aredius, written, if the title is to be trusted, by the same Gregory. From this it is clear that some relics from the limbs of Blessed Hilary had been taken to the people of Limoges. Yet this would be more certain if it were not known that in that age not only saints’ bones, but also whatever was taken from the places where they rested, was called by the name of relics.

Bollandus further testifies that within the borders of Belgium, not far from the monastery of Laetium, there is a village commonly called Wallers, in which a bone of Hilary’s arm is still preserved in a silver shrine; and crowds of people gather there to render him due reverence.

### 123. The second translation, to the basilica of St. Dionysius

Later, tradition says that St. Hilary’s body was transferred by King Dagobert to the celebrated basilica of St. Dionysius. Although this did not seem certain to Charles Cointius, under the year 638, no. 6, it is nevertheless refuted by no evident argument.

One may indeed oppose it with Alcuin’s statement: “More blessed Pictavia rejoices in the relics of Blessed Hilary the bishop than in the contention of sales and purchases” (*Homily on the Nativity of St. Willibrord*). For if, in Alcuin’s age, the city of Poitiers rejoiced in Hilary’s relics, the monastery of St. Dionysius falsely boasts that it possesses them by Dagobert’s benefaction.

But it may equally be answered that Alcuin spoke of the saintly bishop’s ashes and tomb, to which people then flocked, moved by the frequent miraculous signs daily wrought at Poitiers. Peter Damian’s words may likewise be understood in this way. Comparing Moses’ burial with Hilary’s translation, he asks why the former’s tomb is unknown, while the latter’s is visited daily with such glory of Christian devotion.

Indeed, many places famous for saints’ tombs are still visited by great crowds, though the saints’ bodies have been transferred elsewhere. To avoid a lengthy discussion: who, intending to implore the aid of St. Fiacre, would not hasten to the place made most famous by his tomb and frequent miracles, although the church of Meaux retains the body of that saint?

### 124.

Far less weight should be given to the assertion of some that the holy confessor’s body was burned at Poitiers in the preceding century by Calvinist sectarians. For in two charters issued in 1394 and reported by Bollandus, the people of Poitiers themselves declare that the sacred relics of their patron and shepherd were no longer preserved among them, but in the monastery of St. Dionysius.

### 125.

But what can Cointius oppose to an ancient document of the monastery of Reichenau, written around the beginning of the ninth century, in which its associations with various other monasteries are recorded? There one reads: “From the Cell of St. Dionysius, where Hilary, confessor of Christ, lies buried, Abbot Hilduin” (*Analecta*, vol. IV, p. 644). From this it follows that it was so widely known in the ninth century that Hilary’s sacred remains rested in the religious house of St. Dionysius in France that, even among the Germans, this single designation distinguished it from other monasteries of the same name.

Will he answer that this does not indicate the abbey of St. Dionysius in France, but a priory of the same monastery in Alsace? Yet the earlier words of this document, which place St. Dionysius immediately after the monasteries of St. Germanus and St. Michael, show that the monastery in France is meant. Nor does the name of Abbot Hilduin allow doubt: in 814 he was set over the monks of St. Dionysius in France.

But grant that “Cell” here means a dependency possessed by the famous monastery of St. Dionysius in Alsace, not the monastery of St. Dionysius itself. Do the words quoted above then mean that Hilary the confessor rests in this cell? Or rather that this cell belongs to that celebrated monastery of St. Dionysius in which Hilary, confessor of Christ, lies buried?

### 126.

Perhaps he would answer that Hilary of Gévaudan is indicated there, if Cointius had not himself admitted that this saint’s translation to the praised monastery was later, under the year 638, no. 12. But who, on hearing Hilary adorned with the title “Confessor of Christ,” would not immediately think of the bishop of Poitiers? Nor can I readily persuade myself that Hilary of Gévaudan once had such renown that the most celebrated monastery of St. Dionysius was named from his sacred remains, especially among Germans.

Would you suppose this came about because, once a report had spread that Hilary rested in the basilica of St. Dionysius, he was immediately supposed in distant regions to be the one who surpassed all others of that name both in age and achievements? But this cannot be thought, since the church of St. Dionysius congratulates itself upon possessing relics not of one Hilary but of both—of Hilary of Poitiers and Hilary of Gévaudan.

Now, indeed, by removal of a letter, it distinguishes the bishop of Gévaudan, named Hilari, from Hilary of Poitiers; but among ancient writers this distinction is almost absent. Even the bishop of Poitiers, especially in the genitive case, is constantly called *Hilari*. Hence an ancient writer cited by Photius, while praising our Hilary’s writings, calls him bishop of the Gabali because of the similarity of names.

Moreover, as we have said, the sacred bones of St. Hilary of Gévaudan had not yet been brought to the basilica of St. Dionysius when that ancient document of Reichenau was written. Therefore, in the ninth century it was beyond doubt that the great Hilary rested there.

### 127.

The monastery of St. Dionysius therefore rightly rejoices in so great a treasure. Nothing certain is reported concerning its loss—indeed, nothing but what is false—and no other place boasts of possessing it. I think Cointius would not have called this matter into doubt had he been able to see the ancient document of the monastery of Reichenau. So close to error is one who inclines, on any slight conjectures, to reject what has been received from one’s forefathers.

Giving greater credit to them, we believe that Hilary, confessor of Christ, rests in the monastery of St. Dionysius; and we venerate with due devotion his sacred bones, which deserve to be held in great honor and esteem by all Catholics. But enough on these matters. It remains to touch briefly upon Hilary’s holy disciples.

### 128.

Among the first they count St. Justus, whom Blessed Hilary endowed with the rank of priesthood and sent to Périgueux, and who was buried near Limoges. His commemoration is observed on 25 November. The Life of Hilary which they say was written by him and discovered in the treasury of the great Hilary is either false or at least interpolated. For who could persuade himself that a disciple of Hilary authored a work in which occurs Hilary’s dispute with Pope Leo in a Roman synod—a sheer fable already refuted by us?

### 129.

At Poitiers, on the first day of February, there is a celebrated feast of St. Leonius, said to have been Hilary’s inseparable companion in his labors. In certain manuscripts we read that he was summoned by Blessed Hilary as he was about to die and stood by as witness to his death. Nothing further concerning him occurs in ancient writers earlier than Vincent of Beauvais.

### 130.

Gregory of Tours mentions Lupianus, instructed and baptized by Hilary. As soon as he had been washed in the saving laver, he departed this life and, buried in the village of Ratiate near Nantes, became renowned for miracles. In several churches the first day of July is sacred to St. Lupianus; and at Clermont, the translation of St. Lupianus is commemorated on 17 February—whether the same man or another is uncertain. Certainly there is no Lupianus in the calendars of Auvergne.

### 131.

Above, mention has already been made of Florentia. Although the people of Poitiers honor her on 1 December, Ferrarius, on the authority of Canisius, commemorates Florentia, Hilary’s female disciple, on the first day of July and places her also in Denmark.

### 132.

Florentia’s example seems to have been imitated by the distinguished Triasia, who, having left her parents and despised riches, is said to have sought out Hilary in order to receive from him a model for ordering her life. At Poitiers there still stands a parish church bearing her name, on the very site where tradition says that she remained hidden in a cell for many years until death. Some suspect that she was the recluse whom Sulpicius mentions with no ordinary praise (*Dialogues*, II, p. 415), who so refused the sight of all men that she would not even admit St. Martin when he wished to visit her out of duty.

### 133.

But if Hilary’s glory was increased by his disciples, how much accrued to him through Martin’s formation! Through Martin he scattered seeds of holiness among innumerable bishops and monks whose devout way of life afterwards adorned Gaul. May those seeds, in our own age, through the merits, patronage, and examples of these two most holy pontiffs, sprout and flourish again, especially in the Gallican Church, so that in future it may neither admit the monsters of heresy nor suffer the dignity and holiness of the priesthood to be obscured or defiled.

[VITA SANCTI HILARII, AUCTORE HIERONYMO.]

## Life of St. Hilary, by Jerome

(*On Illustrious Men*)

Hilary, bishop of the Aquitanian city of Poitiers, was banished to Phrygia from the Synod of Béziers through the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles. He composed twelve books against the Arians; another book, *On the Synods*, which he wrote to the bishops of Gaul; commentaries on the Psalms, namely on the first and second, from the fifty-first through the sixty-second, and from the one hundred eighteenth to the end. In this work, imitating Origen, he also added some things of his own.

There is also his petition to Constantius, which he presented to him while he was living at Constantinople; another work against Constantius, written after that emperor’s death; a book against Valens and Ursacius, containing the history of the Synods of Rimini and Seleucia; a work addressed to the prefect Sallustius, or against Dioscorus; a book of hymns; another, *On Mysteries*; commentaries on Matthew; treatises on Job, translated in sense from Origen’s Greek; another elegant treatise against Auxentius; and several letters to various persons.

Some say that he also wrote on the *Song of Songs*, but this work is unknown to us. He died at Poitiers while Valentinian and Valens were reigning.

# Life of St. Hilary Written by Fortunatus

> **Note [Col. 0183D]:** In the Colbert manuscript: “The Life of St. Hilary by his servant Fortunatus, priest and afterwards bishop.”

## Notice concerning the two following books

Although the two books concerning Hilary’s life name Fortunatus as author, are both dedicated to Pascentius, and agree in the same manner of preface and opening, it is nevertheless not altogether clear whether one man authored both, or who he was. For just as many Fortunati are found after Hilary, so also the *Annals of Aquitaine* mention two Pascentii: one, namely, Hilary’s disciple and successor in the see of Poitiers; the other, who assumed the government of the same church in the age of St. Radegund.

The writer of the first book appears to make himself a contemporary of Hilary when he testifies that he undertook this work at the request of Pascentius, whom “the most holy Hilary had affectionately raised from his very cradle before his own feet, like a special household servant”; and shortly afterwards adds that it would have been more fitting to entrust this account to Blessed Ambrose for writing concerning his brother.

But, as Bollandus very well observed, the earlier words can conveniently be explained as saying that Pascentius was twice instructed from childhood in the church of Poitiers; and the latter as desiring someone eloquent like Ambrose, who might celebrate Hilary with fitting praises, just as Ambrose celebrated his brother Satyrus. Would an author contemporary with Ambrose have said of him, “whose words were blooming,” or called Hilary “a most ancient priest”? Would it have been possible for him to say not a word about the Council of Béziers, Saturninus of Arles, or the encounter with Auxentius? If one considers the style also, it certainly does not savor of the fourth century. In most manuscripts the first book alone is found; in the second there is no mention of the first, nor is the other promised in this one.

Concerning the other book, this is established: it was written after the time of Clovis, while Probianus was still alive. He is commonly believed to be the bishop of Bourges who attended the Council of Paris in 555 and, according to Cointius, died in 568; particularly since, at that very time, as Gregory of Tours recorded in *History*, Book IV, chapter 18, Pascentius presided over the church of Poitiers.

Hence Gregory’s statement in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 2—“Many miracles shown at St. Hilary’s tomb are reported, which the book of his Life contains”—can scarcely be referred to the other book. And because Venantius Fortunatus, later bishop of Poitiers, had then come from Italy into Gaul, Bollandus, with many others, judges that the Life of Hilary contained in the two following books was published by this Fortunatus after he had brought it forth from ancient records and polished it somewhat. From this he explains the difference in style from Fortunatus’s other works. He might also have added that certain expressions proper to Venantius are discerned in that work.

Yet Bollandus did not conceal that Gregory of Tours, though he never mentions the works of his friend Venantius without naming their author at the same time, nevertheless praised this work, as we have seen, without naming its author. Molanus, following the martyrology of the church of Paris on 18 June, mentions another Fortunatus, by whom the Life of St. Marcellus, bishop of Paris, was written at the request of St. Germanus, and whom St. Germanus himself survived. This Fortunatus was therefore somewhat earlier than Venantius Fortunatus, from whom the deeds of St. Germanus have come down to us.

But whether these writers were different persons or one author of both books, whether he should be considered Venantius Fortunatus or another somewhat earlier writer, matters little. This at least cannot be denied: the later book was composed no earlier than the middle of the sixth century.

## [Life of St. Hilary Written by Fortunatus]

### Author’s Preface to Book I

> **Note [Col. 0185D]:** In place of this preface, the Compiègne codex, written about the year 800, contains a shorter prologue. Though corrupt, it may be useful to append some of it here:
>
> “Prologue from the deeds of St. Hilary, bishop and confessor of Poitiers. The Ides of January. We have learned the life or works of the most blessed confessor Hilary, transmitted to memory for the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ by the report not of one but of many; and that the warrior of Christ was most clearly adorned in their little works against Arius’s perfidy with a brilliant flower, and they wove together in them manifold deeds toward the confession of the true faith. Blessed Jerome, the greatest sponsor, shines forth in such a matter. How and in what manner the soldier of Christ fought at the Synod of Rimini in the time of Emperor Constantius, under the prefect Taurus, endured exile in Phrygia, and lived in exile for five years, is known to all followers of right and devout faith.”
>
> This prologue is followed by Fortunatus’s Life in the same words, though repeatedly altered.

**To the holy lord and father most blessed in merits, Pope Pascentius, Fortunatus.**

### 1. Fortunatus is commissioned to write St. Hilary’s life

Most blessed Pope, prompted by the urging of a devout heart, you are continually occupied in divine works, with the holy course of life which you have undertaken, and you strive to be ever more so occupied. Thus it is easy to see that you were both born and advanced for the cultivation of ecclesiastical discipline. For, as guardian, you inviolably preserve the foundations of the Catholic doctrine established of old; and, like a good instructor, you hasten, not without divine fear, to continue the summit of the structure by adding something for the edification of the people whom you greatly love.

Anticipating me in love for this work, you deigned urgently to request that I make some return in words for the lavish favor bestowed by the deeds of the most sacred man Hilary the confessor, who affectionately reared you from your very cradle before his own footsteps, like a special household servant; and that, if not fully, I might at least set forth in a concise account some part of those deeds.

> **Note [Col. 0186D]:** Several manuscripts read *rependeres* or *rependeris*: “that you might repay”; then: “and, if not fully, might at least touch upon them in part.”

Thus, while in some manner the voice and life of that most ancient shepherd resounded in the ears of the flock, he might approve the ministry, and you might not conceal your own affection.

### 2. Fortunatus declares the work beyond his powers

But when I measure the narrowness of my own talent, I recognize the mighty vastness of Blessed Hilary so fully that it seems to me almost equally possible to say this as to touch heaven with a finger. Especially since, as I hear, that torrent-like eloquence of Blessed Jerome declined to undertake it; he judged himself so unequal to this subject that he remained silent.

As for me, no well-watered streams of learning come to my aid; scarcely does a thin drop of poor dripping moisture touch me; I draw no breath from a spring of my own. With what rashness should I wish to extend dry channels amid the great rivers—the Euphrates of Blessed Hilary and the Nile of Jerome—when even whatever the most learned men could say about him is less than he deserves? And since it would be more prudent for me to admire this most holy man than to speak of him, it would have been more fitting to entrust this account to Blessed Ambrose for writing concerning his brother, whose words flourished in union with virtues.

Yet although, with shame on my part, I render obedience to you and perhaps an injury to him of whom I speak unworthily, we believe that what is done wrongly from devotion is granted pardon. And lest a prolonged page produce weariness rather than draw on the listener, let us now set forth his life.

## Book I

### 3. St. Hilary’s native land, noble birth, and virtues

Blessed Hilary, bishop of the city of Poitiers, was born in the region of Aquitaine.

> **Note [Col. 0186D]:** In an old Colbert manuscript: “the region of Aquitaine.” In printed editions alone: “in the regions of Aquitaine.” Here the author seems to have wished to avoid repeating the city of Poitiers, already named.

Aquitaine is separated from the British Ocean by nearly ninety miles.

> **Note [Col. 0187D]:** The Gemeticensis manuscript, together with the Compiègne manuscript, reads “eighty.”

Among Gallic families he was not obscure in the brilliance of nobility; rather, adorned above others by the grace of noble birth, and with the splendor of his mind added, he came forth shining like the morning star among the stars.

From his cradle his early childhood was nourished with such wisdom that even then it could be understood that Christ, for gaining victory in his own causes, had judged it necessary to raise up a soldier for himself. Though he had a wife and daughter, he nevertheless gave his venerable soul to be formed by the ecclesiastical rule through the fullness of the Lord. While still maintaining a lay state of life, by divine appointment he possessed the grace of a bishop; and, though untonsured, he restrained himself by his own discipline as though indicating his future appearance, so that an irreproachable priest might be prepared in Christ’s temple.

> **Note [Col. 0187D]:** Thus the better manuscripts. The word indicates the period when Hilary had not yet been joined to the clergy through the tonsure. Other books read *intentus*, “intent.”

For among mortals it still seems exceedingly difficult for anyone to be so cautious as to abstain from food shared with Jews or heretics. Yet this most holy man so abhorred the enemies of the Catholic religion that he would not merely refuse to dine with them; he would not even exchange a greeting with one of them when passing by. He avoided these things, supported by David’s example, lest by sharing a table with heretics it become for him a snare (Psalm 68:23).

O most perfect layman, whom even priests desire to imitate! For him, to live was nothing other than to fear Christ with love and to love him with fear. His followers run toward glory; those who turn aside run toward punishment. Rewards come to the believer, torments to the refuser. Admonishing all concerning the devout work of religion, instructing some in the confession of the inestimable Holy Trinity, inviting others by the promise of the heavenly kingdom, he did not cease to sow among the people words of truth overflowing with the fruit of faith.

4. He is chosen bishop. — When this became known concerning St Hilary—since so great a light could not remain hidden even had he wished it, for he was needed (variant: “necessary”) to bring others’ darkness into light—by the unanimous favour of the people, or rather by the proclamation of God’s Spirit, the man long appointed for a mystery was at last chosen as a priest for the sacred altars. Daily there grew in him the reputation attendant upon his virtues; nor was his fame content merely to illuminate the surrounding Gauls, but, as the grace of his merits spread abroad, it filled foreign peoples and regions. Thus it came about that the glory of the blessed bishop swiftly made progress throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0187D] 5. Opposing the Arians, he is exiled to Phrygia. — Accordingly, in the time of Emperor Constantius, when the Arian heresy, poisonous in its root, was putting forth a toxic flower:

[Note: [Col. 0187D] Some manuscripts read “of a toxic flower.” One might prefer, with the Compiègne manuscript, “was putting forth dreadful contagions,” if another witness supported it.]

then that most holy man, stripped of fear and clothed with the fervour of faith, like a standard-bearer and warrior, fearlessly thrust himself into the midst of the battle-lines, amid hostile roarings and heretical swords. Secure in Christ’s love and fearing nothing for his own death, he feared only this—that, God forbid, he might live openly under prejudice against religion.

[Note: [Col. 0188D] In the printed editions: “He feared only lest the injury done to religion—God forbid—should prevail.” More elegant is the reading presented here from the better manuscripts. One of them has *illatae* (“inflicted”), not *in lato* (“openly”). Shortly afterwards we likewise restore from these manuscripts “through perverse belief,” where the received text had “through cruelty.”]

Therefore Valens and Ursacius, bishops who persistently strove to disturb the Church of God through their perverse belief, persuaded the Emperor to condemn to exile the very learned man of whom we speak, together with Dionysius of Milan and Eusebius of Vercelli.

[Note: [Col. 0188D] This did not happen in one and the same year.]

For no heretic could prevail before the invincible eloquence of St Hilary. The enemy of the faith hoped that he could spread some clouds before the Catholic brightness if such a man, shut away in exile, were absent from the contest. For if any perverse man wished to contend with him, he was like one mute and lame: he could neither utter words nor run in reply; rather, like one swimming in the sea, he was drowned before the wave of Hilary’s eloquence. And so he was sent into exile in Phrygia, a region of Asia:

[Note: [Col. 0188D] An old Colbert manuscript reads: “into Phrygia, the religion of Asia.”]

There, to increase his virtue, he gave thanks to God, because, in proportion as he went farther from his native soil for Christ’s name, he deserved to become nearer to heaven.

6. His letter to his daughter, persuading her to virginity. — When he had reached this desirable place, we must not be silent about what was divinely granted him. For at that time, through a revelation of the Holy Spirit, he learned that a certain most noble, very wealthy, and very handsome young man sought to bind his most blessed daughter Abra—whom he had left at Poitiers with her mother—to himself in marriage.

[Note: [Col. 0188D] In many manuscripts she is consistently written “Apra.”]

But Hilary, by the intervention of continual prayer, had provided for her, without defilement, a heavenly bridegroom. Soon, having found an opportunity, he sent his daughter a letter written and signed in his own hand:

[Note: [Col. 0188D] The words “written and signed in his own hand” were added here, below after the second book; they slipped from the margin into the text.]

It was seasoned with sufficient salt and, as it were, infused with aromatic ointments. It is kept at Poitiers as a preserved gift. In it he told her that her anxious father had provided such a bridegroom for her: one whose nobility ascended to heaven; whose beauty surpassed comparison with roses and lilies; whose eyes outshone the light of gems;
