[Note: [Col. 0188D] The Gillot edition reads “whose eyes shone with light.” The Compiègne manuscripts: “whose eyes illumined lights.”]

whose garment eclipsed the whiteness of snow; whose ornaments flourished with inestimable brilliance; whose riches enclosed kingdoms within themselves; whose wisdom flowed forth incomprehensibly; whose sweetness made honey from the comb seem inferior; whose chastity remained undefiled; whose fragrance breathed sweetness; and whose treasures endured without failing. He added, therefore, this admonition: that his daughter should join herself to no one before she was separated by death, but should await what her father had promised her,

[Note: [Col. 0188D] Thus the Compiègne manuscript. Others read: “that she should await what her father had promised her.” Earlier, four manuscripts wrongly read “before she was separated,” rather than “before she was separated from her mother.”]

and the bridegroom who would come together with the promise.

[Col. 0189A] Abra sweetly received this, and, as if embracing in her father’s letter her future bridegroom, followed the admonition, binding herself to no one in marriage. But how she came to that bridegroom is reserved for its place in what follows.

7. On his journey to Seleucia he baptizes Florentia. — Meanwhile, while the perversity of the Arian heresy was spreading throughout the entire world, a general edict of the Emperor was issued that all eastern bishops should assemble at Seleucia, a town of Isauria, to debate what they held concerning the truth of the faith. Then, in the fourth year already of his exile, St Hilary was compelled to come from Phrygia to the stated place for the synod, being granted travel authority.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Several manuscripts read “being granted conveyance,” or “travel authority.” Sulpicius Severus: “being granted the opportunity for travel authority.” Book XII of the Code *On the Public Post* has: “When the need arises to depart for us, Our Serenity has granted authority for travel.”]

When he came to a certain fortified village, he entered its church on the Lord’s Day. Immediately Florentia, a pagan girl,

[Col. 0189B] broke through the crowd and loudly declared that the servant of God had arrived there. Running to his feet, she did not cease asking until she had faithfully obtained from him the sign of the cross,

[Note: [Col. 0189D] By which she might become a catechumen.]

to be made upon her. Her father Florentius followed her, and he and all the household deserved to be baptized together in the Lord’s name. This Florentia left her parents and, cleaving to Hilary’s footsteps, was brought as far as Poitiers. She proclaimed that she had as father not the man from whom she was begotten, but the one through whom she was reborn.

8. His actions at Seleucia and then Constantinople. — When he reached Seleucia, he was received with great favour by all, because divine mercy had brought forth into the spectacle of the world such a most prudent man, proven in singular learning, where judgment upon the faith was to be made.

[Col. 0189C] There, after the enemies had been examined, recognized, and overcome, decrees were composed in writing, and a delegation carrying the synod’s successful outcome was sent to the Emperor. St Hilary went with it, although this had not been imposed upon him, because he feared that condemned perfidy might still breathe against the doctrines of religion.

But it would take long to explain how, at the Synod of Rimini, heretical fraud crept in with serpentine stealth, advancing one thing from another through a fabricated assertion:

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Without doubt one should read *mentitione*, “a lie.” This refers to the lie of the Arians, by which they shamelessly alleged that the Easterners wholly rejected the term “substance.” The Compiègne manuscript has “a fabricated lie.”]

and how afterwards, through the Emperor’s injustice, that very calumny was brought against the Seleucian delegates. Yet Christ’s blessed athlete Hilary, recognizing this, grieved deeply that the devil’s lie had prevailed at Rimini, so greatly as to infect even the Eastern party with a similarly fabricated colouring of perversity.

To the Emperor, however—so Sulpicius Severus says, book 2, p. 261—

[Col. 0190A] he presented three petitions and poured out prayers that, with his opponents assembled in the Emperor’s presence, he might be permitted to debate religion against the heretics: lest falsehood overshadow truth, injustice prevail over equity, the Emperor resist God, or perfidy rebel against faith.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] The printed editions read: “lest the perfidy of iniquity rebel against the faith of the Trinity”: the work of an interpolator.]

Therefore Valens and Ursacius, terrified by the guilt of their consciences, knew that, if an opportunity for contest were granted, they would immediately be overthrown in debate by Hilary. They therefore worked upon the Emperor’s mind, held captive by so malignant a party,

[Note: [Col. 0190D] Thus the better manuscripts. An older Colbert manuscript: “held captive by so malignant a thing through artifice.” Other books: “already for the greater part held captive.”]

so that he urgently ordered the man of God himself to return to Gaul, saying that while he was present heretical schemes could not prosper. On this pretext he was compelled to return to Gaul, thinking that he suffered a greater exile because he left behind there the disturbance of the Church, without the controversy having reached its conclusion.

O blessed bishop, who, at the height of danger and even before a judge hostile to himself, approached the tribunal of imperial power without fear of torture! Truly he loved Christ’s kingdom with all his heart,

[Col. 0190B] since he did not fear Constantius in his sovereignty. For, in exposing himself so to open danger for the Lord, he desired martyrdom, if only an executioner had not been lacking; yet his courage received glory, even if the time did not bring punishment. But I testify that he was preserved by divine ordinance for the correction of all.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] The editions read “many,” against most manuscripts, supported by Sulpicius, p. 262: “He judged it best to recall all to repentance through frequent councils in Gaul,” etc.]

For the testimony of many declares that, by councils frequently held in Gaul, nearly the whole world, confused by grave error, was led back to the path of truth through Hilary. And what difference does it make whether he alone was made a martyr for eternal life,

[Note: [Col. 0190D] The printed editions read “or if.” Many manuscripts: “or himself.” The reading “or for himself” is preferable with the better manuscripts—that is, what would have benefited him alone.]

or whether he lived longer so that the rest might not perish? Thus, although the persecutor’s sword did not take away his most holy soul, it did not take away his martyr’s palm.

9. St Martin accompanies him on his return. — Therefore,

[Col. 0190C] as he was returning home, Blessed Martin—likewise not hidden in the light of his merits—

[Note: [Col. 0190D] An older Colbert manuscript reads “not obscure.” Then the Compiègne manuscript reads: “whom Hilary, the holy protector, [made] exorcist,” omitting “afterwards,” which Bollandus judges to have entered here through a gloss. Otherwise Fortunatus would certainly conflict with Sulpicius, who writes that Martin was ordained exorcist by Hilary before Hilary went into exile.]

who was afterwards appointed exorcist by this same St Hilary, learned of his arrival and hurried to meet him at Rome. When he learned that Hilary had already passed by, he pursued him as far as Gaul. For Martin—as Sulpicius Severus says in the *Life of St Martin*, p. 298—who, while still a catechumen, deserved to see Christ clothed in his own cloak, would not have run to meet him with such devotion unless he had foreseen in him a Spirit full in every respect of mysteries. Nor is it surprising that he who first saw God in a poor man afterwards recognized Him as dwelling in a teacher.

10. From the island of Gallinaria he drives away serpents. — Nor is it fitting that we should pass over so notable a miracle.

[Col. 0191A] For when he was approaching the island of Gallinaria:

[Note: [Col. 0191C] Many manuscripts read “near the island of Dives in Gaul”; Bouchet reads thus and thinks this island lay by the Primaliensian rocks. Not far from La Rochelle, as Bollandus observed, maps of Aunis show the village of Yves and the bridge of d’Yves. Valesius, however, in *Notitia Galliarum*, p. 390, note 2, observes that the island of Diva lies near both the mouths of the Sèvre and another island, called in Latin Oja or Ogia, commonly *l’Isle-Dieu*. Though we retain “the island of Gallinaria” on the authority of the older manuscripts, we judge it to have been different from the island of the same name in the Tuscan Sea inhabited by Martin. Otherwise Martin would have waited for Hilary there,

[Col. 0191D] and would not have tried to meet him at Rome, if that had been Hilary’s route. It would also falsely have been called uninhabitable, if Martin had inhabited it.]

he learned from the report of the neighbouring people that enormous multitudes of serpents wandered there without number. Hence, although the island seemed near to them, because the place was inaccessible it appeared more distant to them than Africa.

When he heard this, the man of God, knowing that victory over a beastly battle was coming to him, descended to the island in the Lord’s name, aided beforehand by the cross. At the sight of him the serpents turned to flight, unable to endure his presence. Then, planting his staff in the ground as though it were a boundary-marker, he indicated by the power of his virtue how far they must run; nor were they thereafter free to occupy what he had forbidden, as though the remaining part of the island

[Note: [Col. 0191D] The printed editions read, “and as though this island.” Two manuscripts of good quality read: “as though a part of land were not land.” The other manuscripts read as in the text.]

were not land but sea. Because they always feared to touch that part,

[Col. 0191B] it was easier for them to cross the sea than to cross his word.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] The oldest Colbert manuscript reads: “than to be here.”]

O unchangeable boundary, planted by a spoken word! It is clear how much better the second Adam is than the first. The first obeyed the serpent; this one has servants who can command serpents. The first was cast from Paradise through a beast; this one excluded serpents from their lairs. The serpent put aside its ancient lie

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Thus the old Colbert manuscript. Others read “the ancient lie.” Next, some manuscripts read “O sweetness of Hilary”; and subsequently, with the Gillot edition, “medicine and merit.”]

when it learned to fulfil the command. O sweetness of Hilary, medicine and pure remedy, before whom poisons fled without delay! He added land for human beings, because an inhabitant moved into the place of beasts. But let us return to the order of the narrative.

11. How he was received at Poitiers. — When he returned from exile and entered Poitiers, everyone applauded together with the greatest favour, because the Church had received its bishop,

[Col. 0191C] the flock its shepherd. And just as though all had then returned home with him, so they lamented that without him they had been exiles.

12. He raises an infant who died without baptism. — Thus, when he had ordered Blessed Martin to settle in the village named Locogeiacum,

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Sulpicius relates that this monastery was situated not far from the town, but does not name it; nor do the manuscripts agree in writing it. In the old Colbert manuscript it is *Locojacum*; in another, not later manuscript of Casalis Benedicti, *Locotejacum*; in the Compiègne manuscript, *Locodiacum*; and in many others, *Legudiacum*. Thus also in Bollandus this village is elsewhere called Legudiacus, Tyacus, and Goteloicacus; in the Sarum Breviary, Lugduniacus. He himself prefers, with the Gillot edition, *Tegiacum*.

[Col. 0192D] From the first two manuscripts we derive *Locogejacum*: so much so that in the first the letter *g* has fallen out, which the ancients, not pronouncing it in speech, more readily omitted in writing also. From the other we supply the letter *e*, in agreement with the French name Ligugé. *Legugejacum* would not be displeasing.]

the blessed Martin deserved, by divine power, to raise a dead man there. Then, after a few days, a certain infant died without the regeneration of baptism. Condemned to a double death, he had lost the present light and was not free from the punishment of the age to come.

Then the mother of the dead child—who was no longer a mother when she no longer had her son—fell at St Hilary’s feet. Preceded by tears, she laid out the body of her child, crying: “Martin, while still a beginner, recalled a dead catechumen. You, bishop, restore, I pray, my son either to me or to baptism. Since you are acknowledged as father of the people, obtain, I beg you, that I may be called a mother.”

Thus, as she asked more with tears than words, the man of God was moved by compassion; and, while the people looked on, he resorted to his customary weapons:

[Note: [Col. 0192D] The Gillot edition reads “to familiar weapons,” which has some affinity with what Venantius later says in the *Life of St Germanus* about the dying woman healed: “that after the pallor of death her face might pass into redness.”]

he fell upon the ground. Soon,

[Col. 0192B] little by little, the dead child’s pallor changed into redness; his cold limbs grew warm as his spirit returned; his eyes, as the doors of the eyelids opened, recognized the unfamiliar light; his voice, formed as air was drawn from the dwelling-place of his chest, was uttered; restored to life, he stretched out his steps upon their former tracks; the whole structure was renewed to the condition of its earlier foundation.

What more need be said? The bishop lay in the dust until both rose together: the old man from prayer, the infant from death. Behold a praiseworthy life which, by prayers, drove death out of another’s body and despoiled Tartarus, having hope in Christ. There death held no rights where Hilary applied the force of prayer. But so great a matter cannot be adorned more by our words than by his own merits. Now it must be recalled what we passed over above:

[Col. 0192C] how he crowned his other miracles with the miracle that follows.

[Note: In one manuscript: “we set forth above.”]

13. By prayers he obtains death for his daughter Abra and his wife. — Finally, when he found his most blessed daughter Abra, to whom he had sent a letter from exile, safe and well, he addressed her with all the sweetness of a father and eloquence of an orator available to him. What shall I say? Hilary addressed her—he whose eloquence we scarcely dare compare with anyone after himself, unless that person too had, like him, been filled with the divine Spirit. He tested her mind, asking whether she wished to attain the bridegroom whom a father’s affection had provided for her.

[Variant readings: “had foreseen” or “might foresee.”]

Then she freely and eagerly desired to be joined to him swiftly. Recognizing her wish, her devout father did not cease in prayer until, without pain or defilement and in his presence, his daughter passed from the world’s mockery to Christ. He committed her with his own hands, as was fitting, to honourable burial.

O glory of death, held better than life, because what it took away from earth it sent to heaven! Truly, as I see it, to die thus was greater than to be raised again.

[Col. 0193A] For it is certain salvation not to be defiled by sins. How many would desire, after surrendering their possessions with their life, to procure such a passage, if perhaps they could find a merchant! What difference is there between the mystery of the revived infant and that of the daughter put to death? He raised the one for baptism; he predestined the other

[Note: [Col. 0193D] The Colbert manuscript reads “sent”; the Compiègne manuscript, “transferred.”]

for the kingdom—except that in the former the possibility of sinning still remained, while she had ended immaculate.

When the mother of blessed Abra saw this, she asked the bishop that she also, if worthy, might be snatched from the world’s guilt and presented with her daughter to the kingdom. Considering her prayer, by continual prayer he likewise sent her before him to glory. Who could judge how greatly such a man loved the Lord, when he despised attachment to wife and daughter? Yet it is recognized that he loved them more in this very thing, since through him they were transferred to everlasting light.

[Col. 0193B] 14. Hilary’s learning. — Who could undertake to unfold the abundance of his fertilizing genius, or match his words with words? How he composed books upon the undivided Trinity in a swelling style,

[Note: [Col. 0193D] The oldest Colbert manuscript reads: “How he composed books in division”—perhaps “in diverse [matters]”—“in a swelling style.” The Compiègne manuscript reads: “How he published books against Arius’s perfidy; how he unlocked the book of Psalms passage by passage in elevated speech; and how he was ready even in the exposition of hymns”—where the text had been wrongly printed “in discrimination.”]

or unlocked, passage by passage, the writings of David’s song in elevated discourse! How provident he was in exposition, profound in treatment, eloquent in letters, marvellous in virtue, manifold in syntheses, subtle in analysis; shrewd according to the prophet—or rather prudent, according to the Lord’s word, as a serpent, without losing the grace of the simple dove (Matt. 10:16). He himself was the seasoning of a polished intellect, the fountain of speech, the treasury of knowledge, the light of teaching, the defender of the Church, the assailant of enemies. Whoever reads his sayings will think that he does not speak,

[Col. 0193C] but thunder.

[Note: [Col. 0193D] In the Compiègne copy there follows: “The aforesaid bishop Hilary died on the day before the Ides of January. His relics are laid at Poitiers, where divine benefits continue to be worked to this day, through him who lives,” etc.]

This was wisdom beyond human measure: to judge concerning religion with such caution.

15. But whoever wishes to know him, let him recall his exiles,

[Note: [Col. 0193D] In Gillot: “let him recall his aids.”]

consider his merits, read again his volumes, weigh his sayings, and recount his daily signs. While he lived in this world, he either wrote proofs of the Church’s faith, or by fighting trampled down heretical crimes, or granted the aid of miracles to those who asked. By the Lord’s will these endure through his prayers to the present day. But my tongue is insufficient to recount individually, as is worthy, all that the Holy Spirit, who both worked and spoke through him, accomplished.

16. May the devout man forgive me for passing over much, though I have scarcely written a little.

[Note: [Col. 0193D] In the Ottobonian, German, Colbert, and some other manuscripts this book is fuller here as follows:

“Therefore, lest this page, extended at too great a length by the rusticity of its style and the excessiveness of its speech, become cheapened, we must now establish the limits of writing. Yet it is worthy and helpful to relate this one thing alone: how the soul of this holy man was received by the radiance of divine light when it departed.

“For when so great a light of the Church began to grow dim through illness, he ordered the venerable man Leonius, a presbyter of the same city, to be summoned secretly to him one day. This priest was held by him to be faithful and dearly beloved. As the shadows of night approached, he ordered him to go out and report to him whatever he heard outside. Returning, Leonius declared that he had heard the voices of the city’s people still in uproar. Leonius therefore kept watch and awaited the end of the righteous man,

[Col. 0194D] refreshing his spirit with Hilary’s last and dearest exhortations.

“Then, when night was fully advanced, the saint again asked him to go out and report to him as he lay in bed whatever he could hear. When Leonius reported that he had perceived no sound or murmur from anyone, immediately a radiance of inestimable brightness entered through the window on the altar-side of that basilica in which the most healthy man lay ill. For, though weak in flesh, according to the Apostle he was stronger in spirit. His soul—not merely any soul, but a most blessed one—freed from the bonds of the body, departed and, as we believe, was received by that very light of divine brightness; and, in its passage, entered the pleasantness of Paradise’s everlasting splendour. There, now and always crowned with the diadem of a precious stone, flooded with blessed light in heaven’s eternal citadel, he rejoices with the exulting saints. Thus the blessed bishop Hilary,” etc.]

Thus blessed Hilary passed with glory from the life of this present age to Christ, while Valens and Valentinian were reigning:

[Col. 0193D] earth mourning, heaven rejoicing, through the same Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages.

[Col. 0194A] Amen.

## Prologue of Fortunatus to the Second Book

[Note: [Col. 0194D] In one Colbert manuscript there is added here: “then a presbyter, but afterwards bishop of Poitiers.”]

Fortunatus, to his holy lord and father, Pope Pascentius, most blessed in merits, and to the inhabitants of the Church of Poitiers, ever flourishing in Christ through flower-bearing love.

1. Different reasons and rewards for writing among pagans and Christians. — The ancient pagan authors of books were stirred by inflated ambition to display the pomp of their eloquence to all. Amid prayers for kingdoms or funerals—that is, prosperous or adverse events—they seemed, in a confused ordering of speech, somehow both to sing and to weep together:

[Col. 0194B] so that those of whom they spoke, or who spoke, might at least live in books, even though they had perished vainly in empty deeds.

Why, then, should I, stirred by the impulse of a better hope, permit the living merits and victories of the highest confessor to be passed over in silence—not without, God forbid, incurring heavenly vengeance—when I would scarcely discharge my due obligation if I were to sing continually, with tireless voice, day joined with night, of the brightness of blessed Hilary’s unfailing lamp? What ignorance could entangle me, or what offence impel me, that I should persist under the burden of this body in such a resolve: that while those deceived men, in lengthy treatment, fashioned certain things concerning the dissolved image of shadows, and gave life, as it were, through false praises to corpses reduced to dust, I should say nothing of the saints who endure and,

[Col. 0194C] what is happier, daily flourish in Christ’s kingdom? Especially since the grounds of reward for the two differing parties are seen to differ: the pagans wished the fruit of their labour to consist solely in empty favour;

[Col. 0195A] but we ought to plant ours in the intercession of blessed men, to whom, if we render words here, we obtain joys there.

2. Many of Hilary’s miracles are unknown to the author. — Therefore let my moving tongue render praise to him from whom our hearts first conceived this affection. For it will plainly be thought that we envy his good works if the things we have learned about him seem to be hidden in silence. With good reason, then, he compels even me, among others, to speak of him—he who causes even the mute to speak.

But however many things he did while alive in the body, or however great the works he performed after he passed, as victor from the world’s contest, to Christ and eternal rest, while angels rejoiced over him—these I could not reach because the antiquity of years has taken them away.

[Col. 0195B] Yet I desire not to deprive a needy memory even of those miracles which, in the present time, he has mercifully bestowed. Thus whoever receives these things with faithful hearing, as is fitting, may rejoice that he knows the past and may trust that similar things will be done in the future by the confessor’s power.

## Second Book: On the Miracles of St Hilary

3. The dying Probianus is healed. — Thus Probianus,

[Note: [Col. 0195D] Bouchet, chapter 15, and Claudius Robertus say that this was Probianus, or Probatianus, the twenty-fourth bishop of Bourges. He subscribed to the Second Council of Paris in the second year of Pope Pelagius, the forty-fourth of Childebert, and A.D. 555; two years later he presided over the Third Council of Paris, and thus lived into the time of Venantius Fortunatus. Bollandus.]

was already hanging at the uncertain end of life, and envious death hurried to take from his parents all hope of the child’s recovery. It had regard neither for the bitter funeral of the little one nor for the longing of grieving old age; greedy, it enclosed everything it found outside its allotted possession. Yet for the dying child one occasion of salvation remained: the intercession of Blessed Hilary.

His father Franco and his mother Periculosa—whose name, in an ironic reversal, indicated that she was in peril over her son’s death—already anticipating, as it were, the funeral of one dead, brought him with great grief and tears to the confessor’s shrine.

[Col. 0195C] Then St Hilary, displaying the medicine of a secret art from his Creator, accustomed to make recovery of health out of the loss of death, suddenly raised by the working of his word the failing structure of the child’s limbs and restored it to its former condition, as though nothing in it had been loosened. Immediately he dried the parents’ tears by the weight of happiness that came upon them and stopped their groans as their desire was fulfilled; now they wept not through sorrow but from joy.

What pains and torments death itself then endured when it thus lost what it believed it was seizing!

[Col. 0195D] Certainly, when it could not strike down the other as conqueror, defeated it struck itself. Yet this Probianus afterwards deserved to attain the rank of bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0195D] The Ottobonian manuscript reads “the bishopric of Bourges”; and shortly after, “to the thresholds,” where the others have “to the lamps.” A similar passage occurs in Venantius Fortunatus’s *Life of St Germanus*, no. 11, where he says of a dying woman healed: “Each year she pays the tribute of life as its price.”]

And to this very day, as one owing his life, each year he pays tribute at the lamps of his physician.

[Col. 0196A] 4. Two lepers are cleansed by dust from the tomb. — This singular miracle too must be recalled to the people’s memory for the glory of its giver. For when two men came from Cahors, altered by leprous spots, they continued to place their hope of health in the intercession of St Hilary. They washed their heads with water mixed with dust that had been wiped from his tomb, and anointed their other limbs; and they faithfully continued this treatment until the ulcerous diversity of the disease migrated as a captive from the body which it had held captive. Deceived of its own comforts, it left unharmed the complexion it had invaded and did not retain

[Col. 0196B] the ugly appearance it had brought with it.

After innumerable wounds, a single restored skin covered all the limbs. The face, erased by long-continued filth,

[Variant: “filthiness.”]

began in both men to be repainted in its own image, and could no longer be recognized as it had been in sickness. For in that most faithful washing with dust, a cleansing Jordan was found for them at Poitiers; and it was not they who came to the river, but this river that came to them. In this the confessor’s highly praiseworthy mercy was made clear: he spared them the labour of a long journey and granted the fulfilment of their wishes for health.

O what proofs of inestimable powers shone forth, where the impurities of a tomb cleansed leprous spots! What craftsman could have the care to accomplish this—one who could bring the benefits of medicine from such dust? Of these men, Castorius was made deacon and Crispus

[Variant: “Crispio.”]

subdeacon; and through the one by whom they were healed they remained attached to his service until their end.

[Col. 0196C] Rightly did they choose to bear the Lord’s yoke under him by whom they had been made free from punishment.

5. A contracted hand is healed. — A certain girl, on entering this life, had brought with her a dead right hand. As nature formed her, contracted strands of sinews had gathered the weak hand into the shape of a ball.

[Note: [Col. 0196D] Thus the Ottobonian manuscript; in others, “a globe.”]

The slack web of her fingers withered in its own thread.

[Note: [Col. 0196D] In Gillot: “they withered.” Compare Venantius Fortunatus, *Life of St Germanus*, no. 14: “the web of sinews is rewoven.”]

Then, coming to the burial-place of most blessed Hilary, her hand was ordered into living functions through his intercession. Little by little, moving strength entered her numb joints and nails.

[Note: [Col. 0196D] Variant: “ointments”; perhaps “stiffened [nails]”?]

After a long time, a hand was then born for her when she experienced the confessor’s gifts. A lifeless hand came from the womb; a living hand returned from the saint’s tomb. Behold how generous is the compassion of the rewarder:

[Col. 0196D] where nature did not produce a limb, he supplied one.

6. Sight is restored to a blind man. — Nor should we pass over what happened with happy success to a blind man after his vows. Intent on hastening to the shrine of Blessed Martin to receive sight, he entered as he passed by the church of St Hilary. While the clergy there were observing the customary office of vigils, morning came; and, with his eyes opened, he began himself to announce the day to others—he who had always needed to hear it announced. For him there had always been one night:

[Col. 0197A] St Hilary cleared his darkness away in that night. For one who had never seen the ornaments of day, a new sun of wondrous brightness began to rise. Then all things were made for him when he deserved to see their making; and, if I may so put it, the world was in a sense born after him when, having been made, it became known to him.

The blind man was hurrying to reach the church of Blessed Martin;

[Note: [Col. 0197D] Our manuscripts read: “He was hurrying to his brother, Blessed Martin.”]

but this man deigned to give him light in his own church. How great is the grace of the giver, which anticipates the petitioner’s wishes!

7. Victory is granted to Chlodoveus, promised by light and voice. — What worthy thing, too, shall I relate concerning so royal a mystery, conferred by him upon a king? For when King Chlodoveus had set his armed battle-lines in motion to fight against a heretical people,

[Note: [Col. 0197D] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “had armed battle-lines.” On this miracle see Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 43, who relates that Chlodoveus, in the fifth year before his death, thus A.D. 507, fought King Alaric of the Goths in the field of Vouillé, ten Roman miles from Poitiers, and, after routing his army, killed the king himself with his own hand.]

in the middle of the night he deserved to see a light coming upon him from the basilica of Blessed Hilary.

[Col. 0197B] He was also warned that he should hasten, but not without prayer at the venerable place, to descend and fight against the enemy. He carefully observed this and, having gone to prayer, advanced to war with such success—while another fought on his behalf—that before the third hour of the day he received from the Lord a victory beyond human hopes. There the multitude of slain bodies was seen to have raised hills from itself.

[Note: [Col. 0197D] The Gillot edition: “So great a multitude lay there that the hill itself seemed on this account to have raised itself on high”: it has the look of an interpolation. Bollandus and the Colbert manuscript: “It seemed to have raised hills of mountains from itself.” The reading of the Gemeticensis manuscript seemed clearer.]

Behold prodigies terribly to be feared and miracles delightfully to be embraced. It was too little for the king’s consolation merely to show a sign of light, unless he had also added open counsels of a voice. Something similar occurred in the time of the people of Israel by the power of this event. There a pillar of fire went before the people; here the form of a lamp gave warning.

[Col. 0197C] **8. Even dead, he wages war against the Arians.**—I should like to know what hidden mystery lay behind so great a zeal, so plainly displayed. Yet, insofar as I seem to recognize it through his own inspiration, I shall not keep silent. For against the ranks of heretics, just as formerly in the body, he did not cease to fight in spirit. [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Bollandists, as also the Ottobonian and Colbert manuscripts, add here: “Thus he believed that the courage to fight once more against the Arian Alaric was returning to him.” The Gemeticensis manuscript: “He believed that Constantius, an Arian, had then returned again against Hilary.”] Since such was always his eagerness for the worship of the Catholic religion, is it surprising that, though laid to rest, he still possesses an abundance of concern? For he who then, in the synod, brought forth faithful words to confound the enemy, here took up the weapons of victory upon the field.

**9. A woman’s withered hand is restored to health.**—A woman in the village of Tonacium, while carrying water for her work on the Lord’s Day—though it is not for me to know by what sin she had been overtaken—had her hand contracted, as the course of its veins dried up. Then she was warned by revelation that, if she wished to be healed, she should hasten to the shrine of the saint.

[Col. 0198A] Trusting this message, she joyfully hastened there as though accompanied by the very guide of her healing. And while psalms were being sung in the church, on the Lord’s Day, just as the punishment had come on that day, so joy followed in her release. Behold the lovable custom of this singular patron: in order to find something to grant, he even seeks out occasions. O blessed Hilary, to be sung by every heart, mouth, and voice! His kindness is so abundant that he not only does not hide himself from anyone, but even offers himself unasked. Let us come to other venerable fruits of miracle.

**10. Several miracles are manifested in one girl.**—A certain paralytic girl, grown in years but not in merit, lived without the functions of life. Within the tomb of her lifeless body only the surviving soul faintly stirred; throughout the whole corpse,

[Col. 0198B] her eyes alone seemed to retain vigor, and her watchful eyes guarded limbs as though dead within her. Her tongue, torpid within the vault of her palate, did not run freely into speech [the Ottobonian manuscript: “into words”]; nor could a voice drawn from the depths of her breast and formed there arrange words. Her hand, since nature had become slack and feeble, did not perform its due services; nor did her unsteady foot support the structure of her limbs. [Note: [Col. 0198D] Printed editions: “supported the ruins of the limbs”; corrected from the Ottobonian and Colbert manuscripts.] Moreover, the unformed mass of her entire body lay inert.

Placed within the basilica on the feast of Blessed Hilary, she rose up, to the great acclaim of all who watched. Thus in the body of one infirm girl the saint accomplished several miracles. He strengthened the wasted traces of her knees; made her stiff tongue fit for flexibility and ease of speech; equipped palms formerly weak for the work of spinning; and by the grace of his merciful gift restored life to the features of her inward parts.

[Col. 0198C] At last the aged infant burst into words; and, remarkably, with her first utterance she asked for milk. Therefore, what else is meant by her asking for such food before all else, except that when she was healed she then believed herself to have been born for the first time?

**11. Wax offered at Hilary’s tomb.**—Nor should that most trustworthy mystery be withdrawn into harmful oblivion. When two merchants came to the basilica of the blessed man, carrying a wax image held jointly, one of them urged the other to offer it willingly to so great a confessor, however small the thing might be. But he spent his words in vain upon the unwilling mind of his companion.

Yet he himself prostrated himself in prayer together with his colleague and secretly placed the wax before the rails of the awe-inspiring tomb.

[Col. 0198D] Immediately the mass of wax divided itself into equal portions: the part belonging to the faithful offerer was accepted, while the other part, before the eyes of many, rolled away as far as the other rails and, by divine direction, was repelled with every mark of disgrace. It was as though the saint would not take what the other, who was not devoted to him, had not offered; and because he had always abhorred whatever does not come from faith, he was as certain in judgment as he was merciful toward a vow.

O how incorruptible is this judge! He is more chaste—or, according to another reading, more cautious—in the examination of judgment than that creature which produces pure wax is in choosing flowers. Then the man who had refused to offer, put to shame by his own testimony to the sin he had committed and struck by the guilt of immense embarrassment,

[Col. 0199A] saw such reproaches of shame springing from the root of his own conscience and beheld the crimes of his secret knowledge revealed before his face. He considered, groaned, and wept, so that he might at least wash away with the flowing fountain of tears what he had defiled through the sinfulness of his heart. Afterwards, compelled by the chastening judgment of the wax, he offered more.

**12. A candle customarily lit at night.**—Likewise, when on a certain night, according to custom, a candle had been lit there, it happened that it fell burning upon his tomb—the tomb of him who by his intercession gives life to the dead [Note: [Col. 0199B] The words “gives life to the dead” are absent from the manuscripts]—and it burned completely upon the cloth upon which it fell, without causing any damage. For along the entire length of the candle, the wax was found lying there, while the paper had been consumed; as though the wax itself had made a boundary between fire and cloth,

[Col. 0199B] so that the cloth was found protected by that through which it might have been burned.

Consider the benefit. In order that the confessor’s command might be obeyed—he who always knows how to subdue [Note: [Col. 0199B] The Bollandists add here: “and consume.” But in Gilbert: “that it might obey the command. He who always knows how repeatedly to consume, here the wax,” etc.]—the fire feared the wax; and that which it had employed to assist its burning

[Col. 0200A] seemed itself to resist it. But amid these matters it is more fitting to say that, by the confessor’s power, the wax extinguished the flames which it had drawn along, and, in a reversal of order, choked that by which it might have been devoured. Different things seemed to have changed their own natures: so that fires should injure nothing, the cloth became marble and the wax became a river. But how slight a thing is it for him to extinguish a candle’s light who kindles light for the blind? Or, when at another’s burial he restores the fire of the eyes to a corpse, how readily should we believe that from his own tomb he can drive away flames?

**13.**—I should still like, insatiably, to sing in particular of the miracles of this most sacred man; but I fear that, where I desire to display my devotion, I may seem to block the hearer’s mind by producing weariness. Grant me, holy one, pardon

[Col. 0200B] for the smallness of this composition; blame circumstance for it, lest, while I seek to avoid human weariness, I appear to incur the confessor’s displeasure. For I would say little of him even if I filled books. Yet I venture to say less of you in order that brevity may invite the people more eagerly to read of you; with the help of our Lord God, now and always. Amen.

[Col. 0199]

# ON THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT HILARY: A SERMON OF PETER DAMIAN

**1.** Let us rejoice and exult, most dearly beloved, as we gather solemnly to commemorate the sublime merits of Blessed Hilary. For the very dignity of his illustrious name summons us, so that our minds, moved by spiritual gladness, may rejoice with fitting applause. It is equally fitting,

[Col. 0199C] while we celebrate the translation of the blessed man, that we too transfer our minds from earthly desires to heavenly things. Thus, while we see the clod of his body and its slight dust honored among men so greatly, our minds may consider what weight of glory he possesses in heaven, where true and incomparable honor is found.

But now I wish briefly to survey the history of this translation, so that henceforth no one may have any reason whatever to doubt the illustrious origin of this solemnity.

**2.** While Fridolin, confessor of Christ, was praiseworthily governing the monastery of Blessed Hilary situated in the suburb of Poitiers, and was there distinguished by the notable disciplines of holy conduct and by splendid uprightness of character, Blessed Hilary appeared openly to him in a vision.

[Col. 0199D] Among several other matters, he commanded him with the authority of a living command that he and the bishop of Poitiers should without delay approach the king of the Franks, who then held the reins of government, and confidently request an outlay of funds by which the monastery might be enlarged and made more magnificent. He further added that, once the monastery had been newly restored, the holy abbot should provide a suitable place in which his body might be deposited after its translation.

[Col. 0200B] The king received those who had discharged the embassy of this blessed oracle with clemency and kindness and bestowed upon them magnificent gifts of royal generosity. Thus the servants of God, rebuilding the monastery from its foundations through stonecutters and masons and restoring it splendidly,

[Col. 0200C] labored unweariedly at the undertaking until they had not only carried the great structure of the rising building through to completion, but had also clothed its walls on both sides—that is, within and without—with the radiant beauty of mosaic work. In this work, when the resources of the royal gift failed, the bishop did not cease to supply from ecclesiastical revenues what was lacking.

At length, when the monastery’s structure had been completed and it had also been dedicated by the blessings of priestly office, they immediately demolished the tomb in which the holy body had been buried.

**3.** The day appointed for transferring the sacred limbs having arrived, the bishop and the abbot spent the preceding night together in vigils and prayers. Suddenly they saw blessed angels draw the holy body from the tomb,

[Col. 0200D] which had already been opened, and carry it with their own hands into the place prepared for it.

After this had been done, Blessed Hilary warned Saint Fridolin in a vision to substitute in the government of the monastery a certain relative of his, a man of Scottish origin; Fridolin himself was to hasten to the island of Gallinaria in order to build a church in honor of the same Blessed Hilary. The saint obediently and humbly complied at once with the priest’s command, and built not only what he had been ordered to build but also four other monasteries

[Col. 0201A] in Hilary’s honor.

Although the Life of Blessed Fridolin, in which this history is said to be reported, has by no means come into our hands, what has here been written became known through the testimony of a brother’s account. This, therefore, is the cause of this sacred solemnity; this is the venerable subject of today’s celebration: that the devoted multitude of the faithful may rightly rejoice in the translation of the sacred body, whose obsequies were performed by an army of angels.

**4.** Moreover, on the occasion of this venerable translation, the other deeds of the blessed man likewise return to our memory, so that things performed long ago may now, when brought again before our eyes, seem in a manner fresh and new. For as soon as we begin to speak of the deeds of this venerable man, we immediately recall what an impenetrable wall of the Church

[Col. 0201B] he stood against the darts of heretics, and what an unconquerable warrior he was in crushing the perverse teaching of the Arians by the grace of Catholic truth.

Nor is it without significance that, as he was traveling to the Isaurian town of Seleucia to fight against the unbelief of heretics, a pagan girl, divinely instructed, announced the coming of the holy priest; and accordingly she, with her father Florentius and her entire household, was granted to receive the sacrament of divine baptism.

Nor has that notable miracle been forgotten: on the island of Gallinaria, the venomous fury of enormous serpents could not endure the power of so illustrious a bishop. Terrified as though by a thunderbolt’s crash, they did not dare even to cross the boundary marked out by the worthless staff which he had set before them.

And there likewise comes to mind that the same outstanding bishop not only restored alive and unharmed to his mother a boy who had died without the grace of regeneration,

[Col. 0201C] but also instructed him in the first principles of true faith and added him to the children of holy Church.

These, then, and many other notable signs of his powers come before us on the occasion of this venerable translation, stirring us to the love of God and devotion to this illustrious priest. Certainly, while holy Church venerates the translations of many righteous persons, which were arranged through human care, with how much more devoted zeal should this one be solemnly commemorated, since it was carried out by the hands of angels!

**5.** But why did the Lord himself bury Moses’ body, and yet refuse to let his tomb become known to men; whereas he not only transferred Blessed Hilary’s body in the sight of men by angels, but also exalted it to the glory of such honor and the reverence of the whole Church?

For it is written of Moses: “Moses, the servant of the Lord, died there in the land of Moab at the Lord’s command; and he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Phogor, and no man has known his tomb unto this present day” (Deut. 34:5–6).

[Col. 0201D] Why, then, is the one unknown, while the other is daily visited with such glory of Christian devotion? Why, I ask, is Moses removed from human knowledge, except that any occasion might be taken away whereby the faithlessness of the Israelite people might render divine honor to one known to have been so dear and familiar to God?

But the bodies of the other saints are not hidden, so that, while they are frequented by the approach of Christian devotion and radiant signs of powers are performed through them,

[Col. 0202A] an accumulation of blessed merits may increase for those who visit them. Furthermore, some of the faithful are placed after death in distinguished tombs so that they may impress their memory upon the living, lest the living fail to render them offices of piety. Hence burial is customarily called *memoria*, “memorial”: namely, so that the living may remember through it and the dead may receive refreshment.

**6.** But why did some saints take such great care to provide tombs for their bodies? Abraham, indeed, purchases from the sons of Heth the double cave for four hundred shekels of silver. Jacob and Joseph direct the whole desire of their souls to that same cave (Gen. 23:16), and request that their bodies be carried there after death.

What, then, is the reason why the holy patriarchs,

[Col. 0202B] who plainly profess themselves dust and ashes, who surely despise bodies and all bodily things in their contemplation of heavenly realities, desire with such longing that their bodies rest in the land of the Canaanites? Why do they select that place for their rest above all other regions of the world, except because they knew that the author of human salvation would be born there from their seed?

Hence Jacob entreats his son Joseph, saying: “If I have found favor in your sight, put your hand under my thigh, and you shall show me mercy and truth: do not bury me in Egypt, but let me sleep with my fathers; carry me out of this land and place me in the tomb of my ancestors” (Gen. 47:29–30).

Why did Jacob require that his son’s hand be placed under his thigh as a pledge confirming the promise,

[Col. 0202C] except because he knew that he who is supreme Truth would spring from his own seed? Thus the blessed men already clung with their whole hearts to the boundaries of that land which in the spirit they already saw to be trodden by the Savior’s footsteps, which with their inward eyes they already saw made purple by the precious blood of the Lord’s body. They wished their bodies to await their resurrection there, where they knew that the author of blessed resurrection himself would rise again.

**7.** To him, most beloved, let us direct the clear gaze of our mind. Though we cannot go to him by the progress of our feet, let us hasten toward him with ardent desire. And while we show the reverence of worthy devotion to the relics of any saints whatever, let us direct the gaze of our mind to that one unique body,

[Col. 0202D] which we believe has been raised ineffably in the glory of the Father’s majesty.

That is indeed the land for which the blessed patriarchs and prophets then sighed: the land flowing with milk and honey. Milk flows from the breasts of flesh, while honey comes from above. And because the substance of the Lord’s body came forth from the Virgin’s womb, while his divinity descended from the Father’s majesty, the Savior’s body is rightly called the land of promise. That land is said to flow with both milk and honey because in the body of our Redeemer are truly both substance and the ineffable sweetness of divinity. For in him, as the Apostle says, “all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily”; and elsewhere: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19).

[Col. 0203A] May he deign to bring us into this land of the living, he who did not disdain to endure the mortal things of our earth, so that there we may feed upon milk and honey and be satisfied by the presence of our Savior and the honey-sweet sweetness of his divinity—he who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0203]

# SELECT TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING SAINT HILARY

Jerome, from Letter VI to Florentius.

I ask you also to copy for me the exposition of the Davidic Psalms and the very lengthy book on the Synods by Saint Hilary, which I myself copied out for him at Trier in my own hand.

The same, from Letter VII to Laeta.

Let her run with unhindered step through the letters of Athanasius and the books of Hilary; let her delight in their treatises and their intellects, in whose books the piety of faith does not waver.

[Col. 0203B] Let her read others in such a way as to judge them rather than follow them.

The same, from Letter XIII to Paulinus.

Saint Hilary rises in the Gallic buskin; and, though adorned with the flowers of Greece, he is sometimes entangled in long periods and lies beyond the reading of simpler brethren.

The same, from the *Apology against Rufinus*.

If he was furnishing his work with authority, wishing to show whom he followed, he had readily at hand Hilary the confessor, who translated nearly forty thousand lines of Origen on Job and the Psalms.

The same, from Letter LXXXIII to Magnus.

Hilary, the confessor of my own times and a bishop, both imitated the twelve books of Quintilian in style

[Col. 0203C] and matched them in number; and in the short book he wrote against Dioscorus the physician, he showed what he could do in literature.

The same, from Letter LXXXIX to Augustine.

Among the Latins, however, Hilary of Poitiers and Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, translated Origen and Eusebius.

The same, from Letter CXLI to Marcella.

I am surprised that you have not read in Hilary’s commentaries that he interprets “the children of the shaken” as the peoples who believe . . . What, then, shall I do? I do not dare to criticize so great a man, the most eloquent of his age, who is celebrated wherever the Roman name exists for the merit of his confession, the earnestness of his life, and the brilliance of his eloquence, etc.

The same, from Letter CXLVII to Amandus.

[Col. 0203D]

I am surprised that you should have wished to ask this of me, when Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, completed his eleventh book against the Arians with this very question and answer.

The same, Preface to Book VIII of the Commentary on Isaiah.

If they desire a river of eloquence and polished declamations, let them read Tully, Gallio, Gabinianus, and, to come to our own writers, Tertullian, Cyprian, Minucius, Arnobius, Lactantius, and Hilary.

The same, Preface to Book II of the Commentary on Galatians.

Hilary, the Rhône of Latin eloquence, himself a Gaul

[Col. 0204A] and born at Poitiers, calls the Gauls unteachable in the poem of the Hymns.

Rufinus, *On the Falsification of Origen’s Books*.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, was a confessor of the Catholic faith. When he had written a book full of instruction for the correction of those who had subscribed to the perfidy of Rimini, etc.

Another testimony by the same author may be seen above, col. 167, D.

Augustine, Book VI of *On the Trinity*, chapter 10.

[Col. 0204B]

Someone, wishing very briefly to indicate the distinctive properties of the individual persons in the Trinity, said: “Eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift.” And because he proved to be a man of no slight authority in the treatment of Scripture and the defense of the faith—for Hilary put this in his books—having investigated the hidden meaning of these words, namely “Father,” “Image,” “Gift,” “eternity,” “form,” and “use,” etc.

The same, Book I *Against Julian*, chapter 3.

Hear also what may move and disturb you still more—and would that it might change you for the better. Who does not know the venerable bishop Hilary, a most vigorous defender of the Catholic Church against heretics,

[Col. 0204C] a Gaul? When he was treating of Christ’s flesh, attend to what he said.

And Book II, chapter 8, §§26, 27, and 28.

Hear also from most blessed Hilary where he places the perfection of man . . . In a certain homily on the book of holy Job, observe what he says . . . In his exposition of the first Psalm, the same teacher does not hesitate to say . . . A Catholic speaks; an outstanding teacher of the Churches speaks; Hilary speaks.

Cassian, Book VII *On the Incarnation*, chapter 24; whose words were copied by Alcuin in Book IV *Against Felix* and by Ratramnus, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 335.

Hilary was a man eminent in every virtue and adornment, and distinguished in eloquence no less than in life. He grew both as a teacher of the Churches and as a priest, not merely through his own merits but also through the advancement of others; and amid the storms of persecutions he stood so immovable that, by the strength of his unconquered faith, he began even to possess the rank of Confessor, as he testifies in the first book on the faith, etc.

Vincent of Lérins, in the *Commonitorium*.

Tertullian, only slightly faithful to Catholic doctrine—that is, to universal and ancient faith—and much more eloquent than fortunate, afterwards changed his opinion and in the end did what Blessed Hilary the confessor writes somewhere concerning him: “By his subsequent error, he robbed his sound writings of authority” (*On Matthew*, chapter 5, §1).

Facundus of Hermiane, Book I, chapter 4.

[Col. 0205A]

If, therefore, Hilary also, a most learned bishop and a most courageous confessor, etc.

The same, Book X, chapter 7.

Blessed Hilary, the most powerful and vehement conqueror of the Arians and the most steadfast confessor of the Christian faith, in the letter that he wrote from exile to the bishops of First Germany, Second Germany, and First Belgica, etc.

The same, *Against Mocianus*.

Let him dare to criticize Hilary, the wise and moderate governor of the Church.

Cassiodorus, *On the Institutes of Divine Literature*, chapters 17 and 18.

Then, in that most holy choir of Fathers, you will be able to choose for yourself one with whom you may converse most pleasantly. It is difficult to say how, when they find a frequent opportunity, they powerfully unfold the Holy Scriptures in most appropriate places, so that in passing you suddenly learn what you recognize that you had carelessly passed over.

[Col. 0205B] Witnesses are the most learned men, outstanding in diverse forms of praise, through whom the Church shines as the sky does with glittering stars. Among them walks Saint Hilary, bishop of the city of Poitiers, subtle in his extraordinary depth and a most cautious disputant; reverently bringing forth into view the deep abysses of the divine Scriptures.

Venantius Fortunatus, Book I, *On the Life of Saint Martin*.

And because Hilary, the supreme summit of faith, virtue, and honor,  
was casting the rays of his fame throughout the world,  
rightly governing the inner laws of the priesthood, [Note: [Col. 0205D] Printed editions: “of the priest.”]  
a fearful trumpet-blast, a trumpet of the Law, herald of the Thunderer,

[Col. 0205C] more beautiful than electrum, more fiery than gold refined three times,  
more generous than the Eridanus, more torrential than the broad Rhône,  
more abundant than the Nile, more lavish than the noble Danube,  
skilled in pouring forth the streams of an overflowing heart,  
sprinkling thirsty breasts with the springs of his genius, [Note: [Col. 0205D] Edition: “thirsting.”]  
his mind full of the twice-two books of the Gospel, [Note: [Col. 0205D] Edition: “Gospel.”]  
pouring forth through his own mouth four new rivers for the world,  
an ornament of the Church, a mighty shining diadem,  
like a radiant fillet gleaming among the members of Christ the Head,  
warring in his breast, an adamantine topaz by skill,  
a mind unshaken in the arenas of virtue,  
gem-bearing in his speech, more radiant in utterance than precious stones,  
an apostolic teacher, by reason making sophists empty,  
forming his followers by doctrine, light, faith, and virtue.

Since he was grievous and unconquerable to his enemies,

[Col. 0205D] he was led into exile, to far-off Seleucia. [Note: [Col. 0205D] Edition: “because of the long silences.”]  
There the soldier seeks his rewards with the king’s aid; [Note: [Col. 0205D] Edition: “here.”]  
in whose absence wandering Gaul yields to error,  
and the region totters when so great a tower is moved.

When Martin learned this with haste,  
he established a cell beneath the height of Milan, etc.

From an ancient inscription.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, lies in this tomb,  
a terrible defender of our faith.  
Serpents could not bear the sight of him:

[Col. 0206A] I know not what darts the saint has in his face.

Alcuin, Poem 63.

Father Hilary, the bishop, adorns this altar,  
renowned far and wide throughout the world, a holy teacher everywhere.  
On this altar he is remembered the more as victor through his merits,  
a renowned soldier, mighty in the arms placed upon him.

Hincmar, *On Predestination*, chapter 3.

Saint Leo, in confirming the Council of Chalcedon, counts testimonies of this same Blessed Hilary even among the foremost examples of Catholic doctors; and Blessed Gelasius reckons him, together with Saints Augustine, Cyprian, Leo, and Jerome, among the most fully accepted writers in the catalogue of ecclesiastical and illustrious authors. And concerning him, as is well known, one famous man says of another:

[Col. 0206B] “Hilary, bishop, the morning star of the Romans, lamp of the Churches and precious light, speaks all things with a beautiful and golden mouth.”

And chapter 25.

Blessed Hilary, a Catholic teacher, who because of his outstanding teaching is called the morning star of the Romans.

See Lanfranc’s testimony above, col. 53, D. Fulbert of Chartres, Letter XXI to Abbo.

You too have forsaken us, holy father Hilary, who once defended the Church’s unity with the sword of the Holy Spirit.

From Royal Library Sacramentary 3865, in which the Nicene Creed occurs without the addition *filioque*, on the Kalends of November, the feast of Saint Hilary.

[Col. 0206C] Let us earnestly entreat the Lord with more abundant prayers as the people solemnly renew the venerable feast of the most blessed bishop Hilary, whose tongue thundered in the world for the equality of the Holy Trinity in such a way that, as a soldier of Christ, he overthrew the prince of this world and entered victorious into the court of the heavenly King. May he who made Hilary so vigilant amid diverse battles that he rendered him secure amid warfare deign to grant us, through his intercession, to attain what we ask in his honor. [Note: [Col. 0206D] F.: “adorable … with the feast … recurring.” The same encomium occurs on the same Kalends in the manuscript of Saint Gatianus, in the form of a prayer offered to God.]

From the same royal codex, and also from the manuscript Missal of Ratold and Colbert 1927, in the preface of the Mass.

It is truly worthy and just to give thanks, fulfill vows, and consecrate offerings to you, Lord, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, who chose for yourself Blessed Hilary, your confessor,

[Col. 0206D] as bishop of your sacred confession: radiant with great light, mighty in gentleness of character, burning with zeal for faith, and flowing as a torrent from a fountain of speech. The crowds at his tomb, the cleansing of those assailed, the healing of the sick, and the signs of wondrous powers show what his glory is [Royal manuscript: “glorification”]. Although here nature ended through death, there the merits of the bishop live after the tomb, where the presence of the Savior, Jesus Christ our Lord, is; through whom, etc.

From the manuscript Missal of Saint Gatianus of Tours.

[Col. 0207A]

It is truly worthy and just, eternal God, who filled Blessed Hilary, your confessor, with the teachings of knowledge and enriched him with the adornments of virtues; whom you imbued with such manifold piety that through Christ he himself was for you altar, sacrifice, priest, and temple, etc.

From the Benignian manuscript Missal, and likewise the manuscripts of Noyon, Corbie, Colbert, Royal, etc.

God, by whose mercy sinners are changed unto pardon and the righteous are transferred unto the palm of victory: you who, poured into the heart of Blessed Hilary the bishop, gave responses of faith as though from your own temple, graciously grant that, as you then made your illustrious confessor unafraid of Caesar, so through his intercession you may protect from the spiritual enemy

[Col. 0207B] the people who entreat you, so that the people who rejoice in his solemnity may be defended by his faithful prayer.

From the same manuscripts, over the offerings.

Creator of the universe and restorer of humankind, almighty God, we beseech you, heed our prayers, that we who admire in the teacher whom we honor may be worthy in the gift which pleases you. And as you gave to Blessed Hilary, your confessor and bishop, grant to your Church harmony and glorious remembrance; through his intercession,

[Col. 0208A] may our sacrifice by his merits be made acceptable to you. Or, as in the manuscript of the Church of Reims: “As by the merits of Blessed Hilary, your confessor and bishop, you gave your Church harmony and glorious remembrance, grant that the sacrifice,” etc.

From the manuscript Missal of Saint Gatianus of Tours, Collect.

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we may both rightly understand and truly confess the excellence of your Word which Blessed Hilary, your glorious confessor, defended.

From the Pontifical of the Church of Évreux, Benediction.

God, founder of faith, giver of priesthood, gathering of the people, sanctification of the confessor: you who armed Blessed

[Col. 0208B] Hilary—perhaps, “for this purpose”—with the power to serve you in faith, grant to this household that he whom it honors in faith as bishop through its prayers may be its intercessor. Amen. May he be an advocate before you for us, who then stood forth as your defender against heretics; so that, by your recompense, the people may grow innumerable, for whom the priest labored in faith. May he bless you. Amen. Which he himself [grant]. Amen.

[Col. 0207]

# LITERARY NOTICE ON SAINT HILARY, BY SCHOENEMANN

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. 1, pp. 273–294.)

§ 1. Life.

[Col. 0207B]

Hilary was born at Poitiers in Gaul at the beginning of the fourth century, of pagan parents of no humble rank. This enabled him to receive an excellent education in letters and the liberal disciplines, whatever their condition in Gaul at that time; and through his pursuit of learning he encountered the sacred books. Captivated by their excellence and especially by the gravity of their teaching, he devoted himself, his wife, and his daughter Abra to the Christian faith. Both his early years spent among Christians and the period during which he still remained a pagan lie in obscurity. There can be no doubt that he earned the highest summit of ecclesiastical rank through learning, integrity of character, and a mind wholly devoted to religion. But whether he rose gradually through the lower ranks of the clergy or was suddenly elevated to the episcopal seat is difficult to determine. The year in which he took possession of the episcopal see seems more certainly to be placed at 350.

Hilary considered that this office had been assigned to him chiefly in order to defend against the attacks of the Arians the orthodox faith which he had received through instruction. This he performed alike by his writings and by his spoken word, with an intrepid spirit, though with excessive ardour and vehemence, and not everywhere with the prudence demanded by the affairs of the Empire and of the Church. [Col. 0207D] Thus, in this cause, in 355—after the councils held at Arles and Milan in 353 and 355—he sent one book to Constantius, exhorting the emperor to cease persecuting the adherents of the orthodox faith. At the same time he barred Saturninus, bishop of Arles, and Ursacius and Valens—bishops who upheld the Arian party throughout Gaul, Pannonia, and Moesia [Col. 0208B]—from all communion with himself.

Not with impunity. For Saturninus, who possessed great influence with the emperor, secured the calling of a council at Béziers [Col. 0208D: Béziers in Languedoc], [Col. 0208C] from which Hilary was not permitted by Constantius to absent himself, although he could easily foresee the dangers there threatening both Athanasius and himself. Accordingly, whatever he advanced at that council on behalf of Athanasius and the formulations of the Council of Nicaea against the Arians—matters which they could handle only intermittently—served merely to overwhelm him personally with odium before the emperor; and by Constantius’ command he was sent into exile in Phrygia, with Rhodanus, bishop of Toulouse, as his companion. There his enemies undoubtedly thought that the penalty of exile would be made especially severe, since he would find not merely Phrygia but all Asia Minor full of Arians.

And so it happened; but the grief was mitigated by letters from the Gallican bishops, in which they declared that the bond and communion between him and the Gallican Church would remain safe and whole, whereas Saturninus would not be admitted to communion with the Church. From there he wrote to them the book *On the Synods*, or *On the Faith of the Easterners*, and completed the books *On the Trinity*. In 359, when the councils of Rimini and Seleucia were held, Hilary also was summoned—by whose authority and instigation is uncertain, but certainly not at the emperor’s command. When the Anomoeans had prevailed, he went with the delegates of the synod to Constantinople, awaiting instructions whether he should return to Phrygia or to Gaul. [Col. 0209A] From this one may infer that Hilary believed himself to have been sent to Rimini by the emperor’s order.

There he reconciled certain Eastern bishops, who had embraced almost the whole Nicene formula, with the Gallicans, so that, united, they might more readily defend themselves. In order that he might be granted an opportunity to dispute with the Arians, he demanded it; and, after the council held at Constantinople in 360, which had gone in favour of the Anomoeans, he presented to Constantius a second petition, written in no gentler spirit. But he was immediately ordered to leave Constantinople and return to Gaul. He nevertheless travelled slowly on this journey, during which he also issued his book *Against Constantius*, the offspring of black bile.

When he thereafter returned to Gaul—perhaps after Julian had already become emperor—his first concern was to recover for the Church those Gallican bishops who had subscribed to the formula of the Council of Rimini and were considered fallen by the defenders of the orthodox faith. [Col. 0209B] He achieved this chiefly through councils held here and there. Some years later, under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, he was seized with concern to purge Italy of heretics; and he attacked above all Auxentius, bishop of Milan, a great pillar of the Arian faction in the western regions and one enjoying great favour at the imperial court. Yet, after various intrigues and after publishing against him the book which still survives, he himself was ordered to withdraw from the city. He spent the remainder of his life quietly; and, having composed as his final work the *Expositions on the Psalms*, he is thought to have died in 368, on 13 January.

## § 2. Writings

Hilary’s surviving writings, in chronological order, are: the First Book *To Constantius* [Col. 0209C], 355; the *Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew*, about 356; *On the Synods*, or *On the Faith of the Easterners*—in old editions, *On the Synods of Greece*—358; the twelve books *On the Trinity*, completed in 359 or 360; the Second Book *To Constantius*, 360; *Against Constantius*, 361; *Against Auxentius, Bishop of Milan*, 365; the *Expositions on the Psalms*, composed in extreme old age and enlarged after the Verona edition by Edmund Martène; and Hilary’s fragments from the book embracing the history of the Councils of Rimini and Seleucia and entitled *Against Valens and Ursacius*.

The following are falsely attributed to Hilary: the *Letter to his Daughter Abra* and the Morning Hymn to the same, although accepted as genuine by the Benedictines; the poem *On Genesis*; the book *On the Unity of the Father and the Son*; the book *On the Essence of the Father and the Son* [Col. 0209D], both pieced together from the books *On the Trinity*; the Confession *On the Trinity*, belonging rather to Alcuin, whose books *On the Trinity* it follows; finally, the Letter or Treatise and the Sermon *On the Dedication of a Church*, published by Trombelli.

The number of lost works is not small, and among them are several titles of considerable promise: namely, a Book to Sallustius; *Against Dioscorus the Physician*; a Book of Hymns; a Book of Mysteries; Letters collected into one volume; Treatises on Job translated from the Greek of Origen; and, though this is doubtful, works on the Epistles of Paul. “Some say,” Jerome writes [Col. 0209D: *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 100], “that he also wrote on the Song of Songs; but this work is unknown to us.” [Col. 0210A] Oudinus, following Coustant, treated each work at length and learnedly, vol. I, ch. 5, p. 452 ff., Weidmann edition.

## § 3. Editions

A few of Hilary’s shorter works, including his chief work *On the Trinity*, together with Augustine’s book on the same subject, were first brought out of obscurity at Milan by Georgius Cribellus, a Milanese priest, with Leonard Pachel as printer, in 1489. He writes that he corrected throughout the only copy he was able to find. But how much this achieved is difficult to say. In any event, he seems to have bestowed more care on Augustine than on Hilary, as we shall note below. These works were printed again at Venice; and Jodocus Badius Ascensius reissued them in 1510, [Col. 0210B] in three volumes of no great size, adding, not without honourable self-congratulation, the more important remaining works supplied to him by several learned men. Yet so great a cloud of errors had spread its darkness over the whole that very many readers were unable to discern his judgments and dicta, and the use of the printed Hilary nearly ceased.

Erasmus aptly came to the aid of this misfortune. Investigating the character and causes of the corruption, he accomplished more—both by correcting the more serious errors and by distinguishing spurious writings from genuine—than could have been expected in 1523, when Froben’s presses brought the work to light, from anyone other than such a man. Yet it was neither one man’s task nor the task of that age to wash away every stain and restore Hilary to his former brilliance—a brilliance concerning which, because of the character of his diction and the subjects not previously treated by Latin Fathers, judgment itself was bound to be confused and uncertain.

Still less was it in harmony with Erasmus’ [Col. 0210C] genius to hunt diligently through the uncertain traces of manuscripts for plausible readings, and, when these failed him, to stand still in the shallows. Rather, as soon as he gave himself to understand an author, he immediately measured the whole in his mind: the force of the argument, treatment, and style; what was derived from elsewhere and what from the author himself; in a word, whatever virtues or defects presented themselves. He observed and weighed them in his mind, and shaped for himself from all these elements a kind of image of the author, which he followed in polishing the text. By this means he achieved the result that no one judged the causes and various kinds of errors more correctly, and no one detected them more successfully. But he was by no means born to remove them all; he left the completion of his labours to the diligence of posterity—would that they had possessed his genius as well.

Accordingly, during the course of the sixteenth century, [Col. 0210D] two learned men took up Erasmus’ work, unequal not so much in ability as in the diligence each applied: Ludovicus Miraeus, who had Hilary printed in 1544 by Charles Guillard; and Martinus Lypsius, through whom a revised edition appeared at Basel from Froben’s press in 1550. Both employed manuscripts; but the Benedictines complain that Miraeus alone displayed diligence, though he himself had neither a great abundance of manuscripts nor manuscripts for all the treatises, and placed rather too much trust in the genius and conjectures of his predecessor; whereas Lypsius indulged his own conjectures beyond due measure and, in many places, corrupted Hilary rather than corrected him.

Meanwhile, some light also began to be brought to the understanding of our author by careful observation of the life and age he illustrated. This kind of work was first attempted, though rather unsuccessfully, by Johann Jacob Grynaeus, who published Hilary at Basel in 1570 through Eusebius Episcopius. [Col. 0211A] Greater success attended the Paris edition published by the Frenchman Jean Gillot of Campania through Nivelle in 1572, prefaced by a learned and elegant dissertation on matters relating to Hilary, as well as on his style and writings.

Up to this point, though Hilary had been repeatedly published in various forms, the number of his books had received no increase. For Gillot again removed the spurious treatise *On the Essence and Unity of the Father and the Son*, which had been added to Erasmus’ reprint by Froben in 1535. But in 1598 a new work, surviving from the lost history of the Council of Rimini under the name *Fragments*, was published from the library of Pierre Pithou by Nicolas Faber. It illuminated both Hilary’s affairs with a new brilliance and the ecclesiastical events of that period with a clearer light. To ensure that the confused order and complicated connection of events should not impede the work, the editor’s discernment and learning supplied a remedy.

At the beginning of the seventeenth century, in 1605, the Paris Typographical Society undertook the preparation of an edition of Hilary which included the good work of earlier editors and was enriched with new additions from manuscripts. It prevailed for almost a whole century and was reprinted several times by the same publishers, and also at Cologne. But the Benedictines thought little of it; to them Hilary owes at last his highest honour and a worthy condition. By their industrious diligence, under the leadership of Pierre Coustant, it was brought about that almost nothing could be added to the edition magnificently produced at Paris toward the end of the century, in 1693, by the Verona edition prepared in 1730 by the most learned Marquis Scipio Maffei. [Col. 0211C] It is deservedly reckoned among the most outstanding monuments of the industry of the brethren of that congregation.

## Fifteenth Century. 1489

Milan, through Leonard Pachel, folio. Hilary and Augustine, *On the Trinity*. At the end: “Printed at Milan by Master Leonard Pachel, in the year from the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ 1489, on the seventh day before the Ides of July.” At the end of Augustine: “in the year as above, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.” In Gothic type, rounded and clear. Titles and book numbers are printed on every page. Saxius, *History of Milanese Printing*, p. 585; Pin. I, p. 90.

There precedes [Col. 0211D] a letter [Col. 0211D: in Saxius, p. 494] from Georgius Cribellus to Guido Antonio Archimboldus, Archbishop of Milan, in which he writes that from the sole copy of these books which he had been able to obtain in the city of Milan, he had copied them with his own hand, corrected them as much as possible, and caused them to be printed at his own expense. Besides the books *On the Trinity*, there are included: the book *Against the Emperor Constantius*; the two books *To Constantius*; the book *Against Auxentius*; Auxentius’ own exculpatory letter; and the book *On the Synods of Greece*, which, he says, “that eloquent nation so admired that it arranged for its translation into its own language.”

No place stated, together with Augustine’s *On the Trinity*. Venice, through Pagano [Col. 0212A] de’ Paganini, quarto. The twelve books of St Hilary *On the Trinity against the Arians*.

## Sixteenth Century, 1510–1600

### 1510

Paris, at Ascensius, folio.
