Several works of St Hilary, bishop, gathered in this order: twelve books *On the Trinity against the Arians*; one book *Against Constantius the Heretic*; two books *To the Emperor Constantius*; one book *Against Auxentius the Arian*; one letter of Auxentius, full of blasphemies; one book *On the Synods Held against the Arians*; one letter of the divine Hilary *To his Daughter Abra*; two books or commentaries *On the Psalms of David*; one book *On the Gospel of Matthew*. Sold where printed, at the Ascensian press in Paris, on the royal road near St James, under the sign of the Three Pikes (*tribus luciis*) (1510).

Robert Fortunatus of Saint-Malo prefaced the volume with a dedicatory letter to [Col. 0212B] John, bishop of Rennes and confessor to the Queen of France, dated from the Collège de Plessis in Paris, 7 January 1510. It concerns Hilary’s life, his extant and lost writings, and their style. After mentioning the books published by Cribellus, he adds:

> “John Solidus of Cracow, a man approved in learning and morals, especially at the urging of Jacques Lefèvre of Étaples, a philosopher praised on many grounds, rescued the two commentaries explaining the Psalms from neglect and squalor by keen watchfulness and no small labour. Moreover, William Parvus, confessor to the royal household, transmitted from the monastery of St Benignus at Dijon to the workshop of Badius the treatise on Matthew and the letter of the divine Hilary to his daughter Abra, so that a man so scrupulously Latin might be printed in Latin type.”

Appended to this letter is an Ascensian epigram to William Parvus. At the end of the letter to Abra, folio 92 verso, where the first part of the edition concludes, these words are read [Col. 0212C]:

> “The work of Saint Hilary, bishop, *On the Synods*, has been completed: useful as well as necessary for all defenders of orthodox religion, against the Arians and against prevaricators who support the Arians. Printed with diligent labour at the Ascensian press on the fourth day before the Ides of September, in the year 1510.”

The *Explanation of the Psalms* forms, as it were, the second part; the third begins with the Table of Canons of the Gospel of Matthew. Its conclusion bears these words, folio 35 recto: “End of the treatise of Saint Hilary, bishop, on Matthew, concerning which this ancient epigram survives”:

> This work of Hilary was set forth by a bishop’s voice:  
> He joined things expressed literally with things expressed typologically;  
> He placed fulfilled words beneath the sacred figure,  
> And expounded as mysteries what he wrote in a gentle vein.

A more recent couplet on Saint Hilary [Col. 0212D]:

> The glory of the Gauls—a Gaul, not a cock, but a hero—  
> Learned Hilary flies abroad through learned utterance.

“This work has been printed with the greatest diligence possible, given the scarcity of exemplars, at the Ascensian press and at its expense, in the year of our salvation 1510, on the Kalends of January.” On the same folio, verso, there is a brief account of the life and works of Blessed Hilary by the Spanheim writer, Abbot Trithemius.

### 1523

[Col. 0213A]

Basel, at Froben, folio. With this title:

> “Johann Froben sends greetings to the pious reader. The writings of the divine Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, corrected by Erasmus of Rotterdam with no slight labours, we have, so far as we could, adorned with our type and our own work. We do not condemn the earlier edition; but, excellent reader, you will yourself learn the difference by comparison—and fare well. You will find the catalogue on the next page. At the Froben workshop in illustrious Basel, February 1523.”

The books are presented in the same order as in the preceding edition, except that the *Commentaries on the Psalms* make up the second volume, which also includes an index by some learned person to all the books. Newly added was the hymn to his daughter Abra, but it was declared spurious together with the letter to her. This edition is further prefaced by Erasmus’ famous dedicatory letter, detested by Roman Catholics, to John Carondelet, Archbishop of Pavor. [The abbreviated place-name in the supplied text is uncertain.] [Col. 0213B] In it he bitterly complains of interpolations committed in Hilary over many centuries and of the reckless ventures of many people; he explains with equal freedom and skill the arguments, causes, and origins of the individual writings; and finally he discusses Hilary’s genius and character in such a manner that we should rightly be surprised if this edition of Hilary had not been placed among prohibited books. The Benedictines’ complaints concerning Erasmus’ hasty judgments are moderate.

### 1526

Basel, at the same press, folio. A reprint of Erasmus’ edition. Cave, who was unaware of the first Erasmian edition, gives 1516 through an evident error of the eye in place of 1526. It was reprinted there for the third time from Froben’s workshop in 1535. [Col. 0213C]

### 1528

Basel, folio. “St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, *On the Unity of the Father and the Son and the Interpretation of Certain Passages of Holy Scripture*,” in the *Antidote against Diverse Heresies*, pp. 83–91.

### 1544

Paris, at the widow Charlotte Guillard, folio. The works of St Hilary, edited by Ludovicus Miraeus.

This edition of Miraeus, though in our judgment more correct than all those published before and after, is nevertheless so rare that, having searched several Parisian libraries, we had begun to despair of being able to discover it, when we found it in the great convent of the Carmelites. [Col. 0213D] Ludovicus Miraeus greatly praised Erasmus’ work, but himself surpassed him in diligence. For, having carefully compared manuscript copies, he recorded with no less care every reading he found in them differing from the Froben edition. He testifies that he collated many manuscripts of remarkable antiquity; he names only the Victorine manuscripts, which certainly are far surpassed by many others in their claim to antiquity. From the same library of St Victor he obtained the book *On the Essence of the Father and the Son*, two letters to Augustine, and the poem on Genesis. — Benedictines.

### 1550

Basel, at Hieronymus Froben and Nicolaus Episcopius. The extant writings of St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, formerly corrected by [Col. 0214A] Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam with no slight labours, now anew most diligently collated with and revised against several copies by Dr Martin Lipsius.

On the reverse of the title page, after the catalogue of contents, the following is read:

> “While we were occupied with this work, a certain writing was added to us bearing this title, ‘Hilary, *On the Unity of the Father and the Son*.’ We soon discovered that it was not a new work of Hilary, but a rhapsody of some compiler, partly stitched together from the second book *On the Trinity*, but for the greater part from the ninth, with arbitrary omissions and additions; so that it sufficiently appears that whoever dared this intended to deceive the reader. He appended an addition on the various names of Christ, from I know not what author, for the phraseology differs greatly from Hilary’s. We judged that this too should be left in, so that it might be clear what faith should be placed in titles; and Erasmus did not without cause rage in his preface against those who permit themselves every liberty with the monuments of celebrated men. There were therefore added the book *On the Essence of the Father and the Son*, a letter to St Aurelius Augustine on the remnants of the Pelagian heresy, another letter to the same person in which several questions are proposed, and a poem on Genesis to Pope Leo.”

Of his own labours Lypsius says not a word beyond what the title declares. The Benedictines, however, judge that Lypsius’ vigilance in removing typographical errors cannot be denied; but that he devoted far less care to seeking out and examining manuscripts than to devising conjectures, in which he was not always—indeed, rarely—successful. He may also be considered blameworthy [Col. 0214C] in wholly neglecting Miraeus, whom the words just cited do not permit us to believe that he did not know.

### 1570

Basel, through Eusebius Episcopius and the heirs of his brother Nicolaus. The same edition reprinted. Added was the *Life of St Hilary* by Johann Jacob Grynaeus, written on the Kalends of April, 1570, which underwent sharp criticism from Gillot and the Benedictines.

### 1572

Paris, at Sébastien Nivelle, folio. The works of St Hilary, collated with several copies and now most carefully restored, from the edition of Jean Gillot of Campania.

A dissertation is prefixed, in which are first presented [Col. 0214D] matters relating to Hilary’s history, collected from his own writings and those of other ancient authors; then it discusses his style and writings; and finally it notes suspect passages and, so far as possible, interprets them favourably. It is a work refined and worthy of praise for that age, although very much can be found in it which somewhat offends those accustomed to history now more polished and exact. To this dissertation Gillot added several encomia of Hilary; a life by Jerome from the book *On Holy Churchmen*, by Fortunatus and Gregory of Tours; and also Peter Damian’s sermon on the translation of St Hilary. He suppressed the books *On the Essence* and *On the Unity of the Father and the Son*, noting only the centos from which they are composed. Finally, [Col. 0215A] he demonstrated his diligence in identifying most passages of Holy Scripture; but he left the text entirely untouched, and even several errors entered it through Nivelle’s carelessness. — Benedictines.

### 1578

Basel, octavo. A fragment of St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, *On the Holy Trinity*, in the embassy of Emperor Manuel Comnenus to the Armenians, pp. 601–605.

### 1598

Paris, at Robert Nivelle, octavo. Fragments of Blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, from a historical work, never before published, from the library of Pierre Pithou; and the life of the same Pierre Pithou, edited by Nicolas Faber. Catalogue of the Royal Library, pp. 364 and 370.

## Seventeenth Century. 1605

[Col. 0215B]

Paris, at the expense of the Typographical Society, under the sign of the Great Ship, folio. The works of St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers: corrected through collation of ancient manuscripts, illustrated with variant readings, and enriched with the addition of certain treatises, through the study and care of Jean Gillot of Campania.

The printers explain what they accomplished in this undertaking in these words:

> “First, they say, we took care that the works of Hilary should be collated, by one accustomed to prepare books for the press, with the best manuscripts supplied to us: Nicolas Faber for the books *On the Trinity*; Jacques Bongars for the treatises on the Psalms; and Paul Petau, elder of Paris, for revising the commentary on Matthew. Then, since a most learned man did not refuse us his assistance in entering variant readings in the margin, we decided to have him select those which seemed preferable to the received readings and remove the rest. We also thought it necessary to obtain from another person that he should collect at the end of the book the readings tolerated in earlier editions, lest you perhaps desire those too, whether because some testimonies cited elsewhere might occur in their wording, or because you might wish to judge for yourself whether they ought to be set aside in favour of these new readings. We have further added the fragments from the historical work, which Pierre Pithou made public in 1598 through the agency of Nicolas Faber, at Ambrose Drouart’s press [Col. 0215D: thus inserted by the Benedictines], and, copied from the same manuscript books, the treatises on Psalms 13, 14, 149, and 150.”

Yet the Benedictines judge that Hilary’s writings emerged little purer from these labours, whether because the man who offered his assistance in selecting variant readings possessed judgment not especially refined, [Col. 0215D] or because he discharged the task perfunctorily. They observe that he very often altered what should have been retained and, conversely, retained what should have been altered. “And the Paris printers,” they say, “who borrowed from elsewhere what did not belong to their craft, neglected so much what belonged to their own diligence that, because of the multitude of errors, the Basel editions seem readily preferable to theirs.”

### 1617

Cologne, folio. Reprint of the latest Paris edition.

### 1625

Frankfurt, at Daniel and David Aubry and Caspar [Col. 0216A] Schleich, octavo. Hilary’s poems, with notes by Master Johann Weitz.

### 1631

Paris, at the same printers, folio. Reprint of the first edition, though with the variant readings formerly relegated to the end placed in their proper locations and entered in the margin. But, what is more praiseworthy, readings which had prevailed in earlier editions but had been incorrectly moved by the editor of the first edition were more than once restored.

### 1652

Paris, at the expense of the Typographical Society of Liturgical Books established by royal order, folio. Reprint of the preceding edition.

### 1693

[Col. 0216B]

Paris, printed by François Muguet, printer to the King, the Gallican clergy, and the most illustrious Archbishop of Paris, folio. The works of St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, corrected from Gallican, Roman, and Belgian manuscripts and from old editions; enlarged by several treatises; furnished and illustrated with preliminary discussions of difficult passages, prefaces, notices, notes, a new life of the holy Confessor, and very copious indexes of Scripture, subjects, and glosses; through the study and labour of monks of the Order of St Benedict, of the Congregation of St Maur.

The Benedictines’ excellent work brought it about that Hilary at last appeared not merely purer and more correct, but also easier to understand and more convenient to read. With the utmost consideration, they established the text according to the authority of manuscripts agreeing together, [Col. 0216C] and placed in the margin variant readings—of which they had gathered a vast number from all Gaul, Britain, and Italy—where correction seemed less secure. They explained the reason for changed earlier readings in fairly frequent appended notes, at which, though they themselves feared it, I think no reader will be angry.

The same notes illustrate and explain unusual expressions, involved phrases, and distinctive statements; they adduce from the works of other learned men whatever might contribute to an easier knowledge of the events Hilary touches upon; and they reconcile passages that seem contradictory or suspect, defending them from error chiefly by Hilary’s own words. Certain more celebrated or difficult points are examined more carefully in the prolegomena, so that his writings might not be offered [Col. 0216D] before the principal clouds of suspicion had been wholly dispersed.

For more convenient use of the work, each writing is preceded by notices or prefaces in which the editors themselves explain whatever concerns its occasion, date, purpose, authenticity, and similar matters, sometimes also appending a synopsis of the entire work. In addition, arguments are indicated by short summaries in the margins of the books, and the treatises themselves are divided into various numbered sections. The arrangement of the whole volume is as follows. After a dedicatory letter to Cardinal César d’Estrées, the learned monks discuss in a general preface the editions of Hilary’s works, lost works, the causes of the obscurity of Hilary’s language, and finally the purpose of this edition; they then attempt to explain at length Hilary’s more difficult opinions, such as those [Col. 0217A] concerning Christ’s conception, and so forth.

To all these are appended three Lives of Hilary: first, one collected from his own writings; second, one by Jerome; and third, one by Fortunatus, in two books; as well as Peter Damian’s sermon on the translation of St Hilary. Hilary’s works follow in this order: Commentary on the Psalms; Commentary on Matthew; twelve books *On the Trinity*; the book *On the Synods*; apologetic replies to the critics of the preceding book—here first published; letter to Abra; hymn to the same; first book *To Constantius*; second book *To Constantius*; book *Against Constantius*; book *Against Auxentius*; fragment of a book containing the history of the Synods of Rimini and Seleucia; fragments from other works. Finally, by way of appendix: poem on Genesis; book *On the Unity of the Father and the Son*; [Col. 0217B] book *On the Essence of the Father and the Son*; Alcuin’s Faith under Hilary’s name, translated into Greek; Nicolas Faber’s preface to Hilary’s *Fragments*, with marginal notes added by the Benedictines; a list of the manuscripts against which Hilary’s works were revised; and a threefold index of passages from Holy Scripture, subjects and opinions, and glosses.

## Eighteenth Century. 1730

Verona, at Pietro Antonio Bernam and Giacomo Vallarsi, folio, 2 volumes. Hilary’s works, corrected, enlarged, and illustrated through the study and labour of monks of the Order of St Benedict of the Congregation of St Maur; now further enriched by careful examination of the books *On the Trinity* and the commentaries on the Psalms against two manuscripts of the Chapter of Verona, easily surpassing in antiquity and excellence all those known to this day, and by the addition of eight especially variant [Col. 0217C] treatises.

This edition was prepared by the most celebrated Marquis Scipio Maffei. His preface provides a description and specimens of the two most ancient and excellent Verona manuscripts; at the end it presents eight Hilarian treatises on the Psalms, very different from the published text. The method of this edition was to reprint entire the Benedictines’ work, restoring the books *On the Trinity* and the commentaries on the Psalms through the assistance of these manuscripts where this could safely be done, while placing the remaining variations of reading separately beneath the text, apart from the Benedictines’ notes, and distinguishing them by numbers. Joseph Blanchini of Verona, then canon and librarian of the church, collated the said manuscripts against the Benedictine edition.

### 1733

[Col. 0217D]

Paris, folio. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers: Interpretation of Certain Psalms—15, 31, and 41—previously unpublished, from the manuscript of Anchin. From the same manuscript is added a sermon for Easter Day, in which Psalm 149 is explained; if it is not Hilary’s, it is at least the work of a very ancient writer. In Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand, *Very Full Collection of Ancient Writers*, vol. IX, cols. 55–84.

### 1749

Venice, at Giacomo Capellati, folio, two volumes. Hilary’s works, reproduced according to the Verona edition. The celebrated Oberthür mentions this reprint of the Verona edition, but adds that it was handled so negligently and corrupted by errors that the bookseller evidently looked only to base profit. He aptly observes that Venetian printers displayed such negligence [Col. 0218A] and disgrace also in the works of other Fathers. I recall reproving it in Tertullian.

### 1751

Bologna, 4 May. St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers: A Paraenetic Letter and a Sermon on the Dedication of a Church attributed to Hilary, now first published by the Canons Regular of St Saviour in *Ancient Latin Treatises Never Previously Published*, vol. II, pp. 38–185. The editor is Giovanni Aloysius Mingarelli; but Feltri states that the commentaries and the three dissertations, in which the letter is claimed for Hilary and its more difficult passages illustrated, are by Giovanni Chrysostom Trombelli. To Feltri we owe the learned dissertation in which he sought to take it away from Hilary, [Col. 0218B] published at Rome in 1762 under this title:

> *Dissertation on the Letter or Treatise Published in 1751 under the Name of St Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, by the Canons Regular of the Most Holy Saviour, Showing That That Letter or Treatise Is Not to Be Attributed to Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers*, by Angelo Maria Feltri of St Anthony, Professor of Sacred Theology in the new Calasanz College.

### 1769

Venice, from the press of Giovanni Battista Albrizzi, folio. St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers: Interpretation of Psalms 15, 31, and 41, lacking from the new editions. Added is a sermon for Easter Day by an anonymous most ancient writer, explaining Psalm 149, in Andrea Gallandi’s *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. V, pp. 85–95. These are accurately transcribed from Martène. A notice of Hilary is prefixed [Col. 0218C] in the Prolegomena, ch. IX, p. 15 ff.

### 1785–1788

Würzburg, from the Stahel press, octavo, four volumes. The complete works of St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. Reprinted by Dr Franciscus Oberthür (*Complete Works of the Latin Holy Fathers*, vols. VIII, XI).

The celebrated editor chose to provide a Hilary more fully equipped and more elegantly presented than the other Fathers issued from this press, both because of the particular power and gravity of his writings and in honour of a friend whom he greatly esteemed, the Most Illustrious and Holy Roman Baron von Fechenbach, to whom this edition was to be dedicated. Therefore, from everything written by the Benedictines to elucidate Hilary’s life, doctrine, and the present form of the text of his books, and from the material added to their labours by Maffei, he distributed the more important portions throughout the several volumes of this edition as follows: the first, with part of the works, [Col. 0218D] contains (I) the Life of Hilary and (II) a List of His Writings; the second and third, with the remaining books, contain a brief compendium of Hilary’s dogmatic theology, or a summary critical discussion of Hilary’s writings under Coustant’s guidance; the fourth, finally, contains (I) a short critical review of the summary criticism—in which he excuses himself for having neglected Semler’s arguments against Hilary’s orthodoxy advanced in Baumgarten’s *Polemics*, vol. III, concerning which the editors of the *Helmstedt Literary Annals* and Roesler had warned him—[Col. 0219A] (II) a literary history of Hilary’s works, (III) certain doubtful and spurious works attributed to him, (IV) variant readings and observations on certain passages of Hilary, and (V) an index of scriptural texts expounded outside their proper places.

### 1789

Paris, at the expense of Pierre Didot, eldest, folio. Hilary’s book *On the Synods*, illuminated by notes and the context of the whole history, in the *Collection of the Councils of Gaul, Both Published and Unpublished*, by the monks of the Congregation of St Maur, vol. I, pp. 145–185.

### Manuscripts

The old manuscript of Cribellus.

The manuscript of the monastery of St Benignus at Dijon, containing the Commentary on Matthew and the Letter to his Daughter Abra, which William Parvus brought to Badius.

The manuscripts of Ludovicus Miraeus. He did not indicate what they were like. He names specifically one from the library of the monastery of St Victor at Paris. [Col. 0219B]

Codices of Nicolas Faber, Jacques Bongars, and Paul Petau, which were available to the Paris printers for the edition of 1605. But what they were like, and which shorter works each contained, cannot be determined clearly from the accounts of them.

The Benedictines employed quite a number of very ancient codices, which they identify according to the assistance each gave in correcting particular books. Taken collectively, these were available: the Albinese; the Bec; the Boherian; two Chartres codices; the Cistercian; five Colbert codices; the Corbie, then the Saint-Germain; the Elnonese, commonly called Saint-Amand; then one in the library of the Archbishop of Reims; the Germanensis; the Martinian; the Michaelinian; the Micy codex; the Ottobonian; the Pratellensis; two Royal codices; the Reims codex in the archbishop’s library; two Remigian codices; the codex of the monastery of St Mary of La Sauve-Majeure; two Sorbonne codices; the Tellerian; the Theoderician; and the Tours codex.

[Col. 0220A] Three Vatican codices, one of which belonged to Christina, Queen of Sweden. One belonged to the Vatican basilica; its variant readings, first noted from the recension of Latino Latini, then of Pietro Ciacconio, and finally of Giovanni Battista Bandini, had been transmitted to the editors; the Victorine; the Vendôme codex. [Note: [Col. 0220B] The codices whose names are printed in round type [Col. 0220C] were used only for the shorter works, such as the Letter to Abra, the Two Books to Constantius, the Book to Constantius, and the Book against Auxentius.] Moreover, they had at hand Nicolas Faber’s transcript, used by him in publishing Hilary’s Fragments, from the Colbert Library, together with the Pithoean exemplar.

There remain the two codices of the Chapter of Verona examined by the celebrated Maffei in the Verona edition. In its preface he provided a description of them together with engraved specimens. The first, containing the books *On the Trinity*, was written in the fifth or sixth century, as he observed in opposition to Mabillon, who in *De re diplomatica*, book V, p. 356, had assigned it to the end of the fourth or beginning of the fifth century; it is most accurate and marred by very few errors. The other, rivaling any other codex both in antiquity and in its very appearance of age, contains the commentaries on the Psalms, manuscript copies of which occur exceedingly rarely. It likewise establishes and edits here the commentaries on Psalms IX, XIII, and XCI, until then found only in the Vatican manuscript.

Add to these the Aquicinctine codex, about six hundred years old, which Edmund Martene examined while travelling in Germany. Having discovered the previously unpublished Psalms XV, XXXI, and XI, he described it in *Collectio veterum scriptorum*, I, above, p. 1. It contained most of Hilary’s works under the heading: “The Twelve Books of St Hilary *On the Trinity*, and other works of the same author”; elegantly written.

[Col. 0219]

## LIST OF MANUSCRIPT AND PRINTED CODICES BY WHICH THE WORKS OF SAINT HILARY HAVE BEEN ESTABLISHED AND CORRECTED

### THE TREATISES ON THE PSALMS HAVE BEEN COLLATED WITH MANUSCRIPTS

Three Vatican codices, one belonging to Christina, Queen of Sweden, formerly of the monastery of St Maximinus at Micy near Orléans, containing all the Treatises that we possess, about eight hundred years old.

One Royal codex of the best quality, containing most of the Treatises—namely, from Psalm LI to Psalm LXIX, and from Psalm CXIX to Psalm CXXXVIII—which was written eight hundred years ago.

One Tours codex, namely that of Marmoutier, copied by a learned hand about seven hundred years ago.

The other Royal codex, in which there survive only the Treatises on Psalms CXVIII and CXLII, about six hundred years old.

The Albinese codex, or that of the Abbey of St Albinus at Angers, containing the same material and somewhat more recent in date.

The Tellerian codex, once belonging to St Martin’s at Tournai, now preserved in the library of the most illustrious Archbishop of Reims. In it survives only the preface, written about five hundred years ago.

Likewise with the editions: that of Badius Ascensius, published at Paris in 1510; Erasmus’s, printed by Froben at Basle in 1523; Martin Lipsius’s, printed there in 1550; and the Paris editions of 1605 and 1652.

### THE COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW HAS BEEN CORRECTED BY MANUSCRIPTS

The Vendôme codex, six hundred years old; the Chartres codex, namely from the monastery of St Peter in the Valley, of no lesser age;

the Michaelinian, at least five hundred years old; the Colbert codex, [Col. 0220D] somewhat more recent; the Bec codex; one from the monastery of St Mary of La Sauve-Majeure; the Micy codex, supplied to us from the library of the Queen of Sweden; and a Vatican codex.

### THE BOOKS ON THE TRINITY

Have been revised from the manuscript of the Vatican basilica, namely that preserved in the archive of St Peter’s Basilica in Rome, copied at the beginning of the sixth century. The variant readings of this exemplar, first recorded in the recension of Latino Latini, then of Pietro Ciacconio, and finally of Giovanni Battista Bandini, were sent to us.

The Colbert codex, formerly of the Abbey of St Denis in France, [Col. 0221A] the most uncorrupt of all; it should therefore be considered equal to, or even preferred to, the preceding one; it appears to be about one thousand years old.

The Martinian, that is, of the distinguished Church of St Martin at Tours, equal to the preceding, if not older. This codex contains only the latter six books, and those not always complete.

The codex of Chartres Cathedral, not much less ancient.

The Corbie codex, now the Germanensis codex, apparently the one which Hincmar complained had been corrupted by Felix of Urgel, the unfaithful keeper of the library at Aachen; about nine hundred years old.

The second Colbert codex, formerly of the monastery of Fleury. We observed that, as far as Book VIII, it was copied from the aforesaid codex of Chartres Cathedral, with the readings of the first hand left intact, whenever they occurred, and corrections entered by a second hand; at least seven hundred years old.

A Remigian codex of the same age; the Germanensis, about seven hundred years old; another Colbert codex, six hundred years old; the Faurian, now belonging to the most illustrious Archbishop of Reims, of not much later date; the Vendôme codex, more than five hundred years old; the Pratellensis, not of a later age; the Victorine, more than four hundred years old; a Colbert codex of the same age, from which, or from a similar exemplar, these books were first published; the other Remigian codex, written about the same time; the Theoderician; that of the monastery of La Sauve-Majeure; the Elnonese, commonly St-Amand, now belonging to the most illustrious Archbishop of Reims; the Cistercian; three Vatican codices; one Sorbonne codex, like the preceding ones about four hundred years old; and the other Sorbonne codex, three hundred years old.

### THE BOOK ON THE SYNODS

[Col. 0221C]

Has been corrected with the aid of the manuscripts of the Vatican basilica; Chartres; Corbie; Germanensis; Pratellensis; [Col. 0222A] La Sauve-Majeure; Faurian; Elnonese; Sorbonne; Remigian; and Theoderician—of which we have already spoken above in relation to the books *On the Trinity*.

Likewise, with the two Colbert codices there listed first; and also with a third, less ancient one; a second Chartres codex of more recent date; the Michaelinian, more than four hundred years old; and, finally, one from the library of Queen Christina.

### THE LETTER TO ABRA

Together with the following hymn, we have revised it from three Colbert manuscripts; one Saint-Germain manuscript; the Boherian; the Vatican; and the Ottobonian.

### THE TWO BOOKS TO CONSTANTIUS HAVE BEEN COLLATED WITH MANUSCRIPTS

Of the Vatican basilica; Theoderician; Remigian; Michaelinian; Sorbonne; Chartres; La Sauve-Majeure; and Elnonese.

### THE BOOK TO CONSTANTIUS

[Col. 0222B]

Has been established from the eight manuscripts just mentioned, and also from one Colbert manuscript of good quality, about six hundred years old, and another from the distinguished Church of St Martin at Tours, about eight hundred years old.

### THE BOOK AGAINST AUXENTIUS

Has been revised and collated with the same manuscripts with which the books to Constantius were collated, and additionally with a manuscript of Chartres Cathedral, about nine hundred years old, and a Colbert codex seven hundred years old.

### FRAGMENTS

We collated these with the transcript used by Nicolas Faber, preserved in the Colbert Library, and with the Pithoean exemplar, which the distinguished Francis Desmares most kindly lent us.

### APPENDIX

[Col. 0222C]

We corrected the poem on Genesis from manuscripts of Laon Cathedral, the Victorine codex, and the Colbert codex.

## [TREATISES ON THE PSALMS]

[Col. 0221]

## NOTICE CONCERNING HILARY’S TREATISE ON THE PSALMS

I. Holy Scripture is owed such reverence by us that we judge works concerning it to deserve precedence over others. Accordingly, preserving the order of subjects rather than chronology, we place the expositions of the Psalms first; and we do so all the more gladly because, arranged in this way, they will be of no small assistance to those who read Hilary in his entirety. For, since his difficult meanings are either expressed more plainly in these works or intermingled with clearer ones, we hope that, read without weariness, they will gradually be grasped more easily, and that the reader’s mind will proceed from them more ready and better equipped to understand the more obscure books *On the Trinity*.

II. That these expositions are later than those books is evident from the Treatise on Psalm LXVII, §15. There, after recounting the inventions of Photinus, Sabellius, and Arius, Hilary adds: “To these, I hope, a fuller and more copious answer has been given elsewhere.” Who can deny that the books *On the Trinity* are indicated here? So too, on Psalm LIII, §8, he guards so cautiously against Apollinaris’s error—that Christ assumed flesh without a soul—that it is plain that he was already aware of that heresy. Yet Apollinaris was never accused of heresy before the year 360. Nevertheless, it must not be denied that the same invention had been devised earlier by the Arians before Apollinaris defended it.

But we infer as follows that these Commentaries were written after 360. First, they are later than the books *On the Trinity*, and consequently were not published before Hilary’s exile. Secondly, the name “Arian” is strikingly absent from them: there is no argument against that sect, no controversy. From this one may conclude that he wrote them for Catholics, not Arians, and therefore after he had been restored to his entirely Catholic flock, not while, as an exile, he lived among Asians who were almost all Arian. Finally, since from his return to Gaul until his conflict with Auxentius—that is, from 360 to 364—he had scarcely any leisure, it remains that he pursued this distinguished work in the final years of his life, which he spent more peacefully in his church. Indeed, in treating and explaining matters concerning belief in Christ’s embodiment, he breathes the spirit not of a novice teacher but of a most learned old man thoroughly practiced in the subject.

III. Cassiodorus not only mentions this work in the preface to his *Commentary on the Psalter*, chapter 12, but also expressly praises its prologue in his exposition of Psalm VI. The author of the commentary on the Psalms circulated under Jerome’s name also praises the Treatise on Psalm LVII. Jerome himself, in Letter CXLII to Marcella, mentions the expositions of Psalms CXXVI and CXXVII as unquestionably Hilary’s offspring. Augustine too, wishing to defend the Church’s case against the Pelagians by Hilary’s authority, adduces various testimonies from various Treatises—namely on Psalms I, LI, and CXVIII, letters 3, 15, and 22—which we have not thought it burdensome to note in their places. Following him, Hincmar gathered into a single chapter—chapter 25 of his book *On Predestination*—very many passages extracted from fourteen different Treatises.

IV. It may be asked whether Hilary expounded all the Psalms. Cassiodorus, in book *On the Institutions of Divine Letters*, indicates that he treated only some of them. When Jerome published his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, he had seen only the Treatises on Psalms I and II, from LI to LXII, and from CXVIII to the end. To these are added in the Royal codex and several ancient manuscripts seven others—namely, from Psalm LXII to Psalm LXIX—whose authenticity no one could ever doubt. Their agreement with the others is so complete, their connection so close, that they openly show themselves to be children of one parent. Certainly, in Psalm LXV, §1, there is recalled what had been treated in the Prologue, §20; in Psalm LXVII, §15, what had been argued more fully and copiously in the books *On the Trinity*; and in Psalm LXVIII, §1, what had been expounded in explaining Psalm LIX, §2. Moreover, at the beginning of our own century, the Treatises on Psalms XIII and XIV were published from an ancient codex of St Maximinus at Micy. Nor, as Sixtus of Siena attests, are there lacking persons who assert that Hilary wrote Treatises on the entire body of the Psalter, and that this complete work survives in Spain. Whether it survives there or not, let the authors themselves be responsible for the assertion; but many arguments are available to establish that he expounded every Psalm.

V. First, in Psalm CXLII, §2, he clearly indicates that he had treated Psalm III. In Psalm LXIX, §1, he signifies the same thing, although somewhat less clearly, concerning Psalm XXXVII. His words in Psalm LIX, §2, concerning Psalm XLIV are plain. Likewise, from his own words in Psalm CXLIX, §2, it can scarcely be doubted that he expounded Psalms XCV and XCVII. Finally, in Psalm CL, §1, he declares that he had explained both Psalm L and Psalm C. From this it follows that Hilary expounded Psalms III, XXXVII, XLIV, L, XCV, XCVII, and C, although we now possess nothing on them. Indeed, scarcely any reason can be imagined why he should not be thought to have commented on the entire Psalter, having expounded so many Psalms so widely separated from one another, without ever prefacing an explanation of why he treated one rather than another.

VI. No much weaker argument is supplied by passages in which he recalls that he had frequently discussed certain matters of which no mention occurs in the earlier Treatises that now survive. Thus, on Psalm LII, §18, he recollects that he had often said that Jesus is “Saviour”; yet this is otherwise unheard of, except in that part of the Treatise on Psalm XIII now published for the first time. Again, in Psalm LIV, §2, he declares that he had frequently admonished readers that, in understanding the Psalms, we should so govern our minds as to remember that Christ is both God and man—though this admonition has nowhere been heard previously.

To bring more examples together: in Psalm LVII, §4, he says that he had frequently spoken of sinners’ teeth and lions’ jaws; shortly afterwards, that he had frequently shown the severity of God’s judgment to be signified in the ark of God; likewise, in Psalm LX, §4, that the preceding Psalms had dealt with the protection of mercy signified under the covering of wings; and finally, in Psalm LXII, §7, he recalls that he had frequently taught that the lifting up of hands signifies not a posture of prayer but the token of an exalted work. Yet in the preceding material sinners’ teeth have been treated only once, and the meaning of wings is not explained more often—if indeed one may call it explained when he merely touches on the matter in Psalm LVI, §4—while concerning the rest there is total silence. But this silence cries aloud that many of Hilary’s Treatises on the Psalms either still lie hidden or have even perished.

VII. Thomas of Sarzana [Note: [Col. 0224D] He flourished in the fifteenth century.] was once possessed by the desire for these works. Therefore, writing in an unpublished letter to Niccolò Niccoli, he says: “In the monastery of Pomposa, which lies between the borders of the territories of Ravenna and Ferrara, I found Hilary of Poitiers on certain Psalms. The work is indeed most excellent both in the weight of its thoughts and in its elegance of expression. I believe that you possess it. Yet I would have wished to compare that volume with yours and see whether one contains more than the other.”

Burning with the same desire, we surveyed libraries beyond the sea and beyond the Alps, not without some, though little, result. For although manuscript copies of this work are exceedingly rare, it was granted us to recover from the Vatican Library works hitherto hidden on Psalms IX, XIII, and CXI. Thus our conjecture—that Hilary expounded all the Psalms—is increasingly confirmed. Fortunatus also favours it when he says of Hilary (*Book I*, §11): “He unfolded, one by one, the writings of David’s song” (more explicitly, the manuscript of Compiègne reads, “the book of Psalms”) “in elevated speech.”

VIII. In expounding these Psalms, he avoided two extremes equally. He did not approve those who find in the Psalms nothing beyond the letter, nor those who wish to refer everything to Christ. He indeed praises the piety of their purpose; but he recognizes that, if one persists in it, violence must often be done to the truth. For sometimes the faith and calling of the Gentiles are announced in the Psalms; sometimes the sins of the Jewish people are rebuked or vengeance proclaimed; at times we are instructed toward fear, at times toward the praise and confession of God.

While he teaches that these matters which represent something other than Christ must be carefully distinguished, he also warns that, in matters which concern Christ himself, one must observe what has been prophesied about the birth of Christ’s divinity, which he has from the Father; when the person of the man whom he assumed is under discussion; and where his activity, passion, and resurrection are proclaimed. Nevertheless, he does not deny that all the words of the Psalms are directed to one end: that we may be formed, advanced, and gained for Christ; and, to that extent, that each is referred to Christ.

In this sense he also grants that whatever is written in the Psalms belongs to Christ (on Psalm CXLVII, §1). Although many things must be referred to the persons of the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, the first generation and the subsequent generation—that is, the synagogue and the Church—nevertheless all are about Christ; because all the teaching of the Psalms accomplishes this: that he may be known, in whom and through whom all things exist. Yet to those who love the letter, he does not at all deny—even when he seems to deny—the truth of the events proclaimed in the Psalms; he merely insists everywhere that one must not remain fixed in this simple understanding.

IX. Having deeply absorbed the apostolic teaching that all things happened to the ancients as figures, Hilary did not doubt at all that the events written and enacted in the Law were shadows of evangelical times. He declares that this is especially his view of the Psalms in Psalm CXLII, §1: “We recognize nothing in the Psalms except what is prophetic.” Accordingly, he commonly calls their author “the Prophet,” by a kind of antonomasia, both because of the certainty of his prophecy and because he observes that future events are frequently described as though already accomplished.

He elsewhere calls him an “evangelical man,” not only because he diligently observed evangelical precepts, but also because his words and deeds were prophecy of what would occur in evangelical times. Thus he teaches in the Prologue that the book of Psalms was not written by one author, yet in Psalm CL, §1—overcome, I suppose, by the custom by which it was ascribed to David alone—he regards it as though it were the work of a single prophet: “Since, therefore, the volume has been arranged beyond the opinion of the letter by the meaning of a loftier understanding, it was fitting that it should itself be brought to an appropriate conclusion, so that, in accordance with the glorious fulfillment of our hope, the book too of so great a prophet might be completed.”

Indeed, even in Psalms which, according to the rules he himself lays down, bear another author’s name, he sometimes regards David himself [Note: [Col. 0225D] See the Treatise on Psalm CXXVI, §15; on Psalm CXLI, §3.] as speaking in them. Convinced that the great king had prefigured all the Lord’s words and deeds both by the faithfulness of a servant and by the example of a prophet, he often frames the relation between David and Christ in such a manner that what he grants and explains as truly enacted in David—so that through the prophet’s action the meaning and language of prophecy might become known—he wishes to be referred to the understanding of Christ’s mysteries, since, he says, “the prophet prophesied not so much by the Spirit as by sufferings.”

X. Nor was he unaware that this twofold manner of understanding one and the same utterance would not please everyone, and that there would be those who might judge him to do violence to truth through the manifold ingenuity of the human mind: namely, by transferring through the subtleties of many figurative interpretations to the Lord and our Saviour what had been spoken in David’s person. But, in answer to them, he shows that it was not without God’s will that, while Christ is prophesied in the Psalms and in those Psalms that concern him speaks many things as man which could be applied to other human beings, he nevertheless inserted certain words which could suit no one except one enjoying a divine nature.

“For,” he says in Psalm CXLI, §3, “whenever the prophecy of the Psalms is uttered in the person of the Lord, it has never failed to add something peculiar to him which cannot be common to another together with him.” Nor does he find such indications only when Christ is prophesied. When other matters are foretold in the Psalms, he observes that they contain certain signs warning us to seek a meaning other than that which first presents itself.

Accordingly, he begins the Treatise on Psalm CXXV with these striking words:

> “Unless there were in the Psalms certain prophecies such that they could not apply to the events and people of the times in which they were written, many would certainly dare to think that nothing is spoken spiritually in the Psalms. They would suppose that we seek fabricated assertions and fictitious interpretations by which we might seem to have understood something loftier and deeper than the sense of others—as though we adjusted what is written to our own understanding, rather than deriving from what is written the meaning attained by careful and diligent interpretation.”

To this belongs Augustine’s statement in his exposition of Psalm CIII, Sermon 1, §18: “Why does the Holy Spirit mingle certain apparently absurd things among visible realities, except in order that, from what we cannot receive literally, he may compel us to seek these matters spiritually?”

XI. Imbued with this view, Hilary cannot tolerate those who, through excessive love of the letter, fail to understand the force of words or perceive the prophet’s spirit, and think the Psalms must be understood by an earthly intelligence. He complains that they create obscurity for us and injure the prophets, in these words:

> “Many create obscurity for us by wishing to judge the Scriptures solely by the ear, and by judging that they contain nothing other than what is heard under each individual name for whatever things. In willing this, they make the prophets say not merely heavenly things, but not even earthly things, rationally.”

But if those who pursue spiritual meanings differ from him, he leaves them to their own judgment with such moderation that, when he declaims against excessive reverers of the letter, we cannot doubt that he does so from love not of his private opinion but of the one faith and truth. And indeed, since prophecy is the greatest argument for our faith, and no source confirms more of its truths than the Psalms, he could not calmly hear it said that they contain nothing prophetic—he whose chief concern was always the defense and propagation of faith.

XII. In order to unfold the meaning hidden beneath the bark of the letter, Hilary applied himself not so much relying on the powers of his own mind as on prayer. For although he knew that human intelligence was insufficient to understand matters hidden through so many and such great periods of time, obscure through so many ages of the human race—matters in understanding which kings had laboured in vain and teachers and masters themselves had erred—he nevertheless did not doubt that they could be disclosed and opened to Christians through prayer.

Accordingly, he concludes: “Therefore what we understand does not come from ourselves, but from him who has made understandable what was unknowable. Understanding, then, must be hoped for from him who will open to those who knock, show to those who seek, and not deny to those who ask.” He testifies with this modest confession that such understanding was not denied him: “We do not constrain the understanding of any individual. But what we have understood according to the gift of spiritual grace, we shall discuss without injury to anyone.”

Similar are these words: “We take nothing away from the judgment of those”—namely, those whom he does not approve—“for we do not attack the sense of this understanding, leaving to each person’s choice what they may prefer to follow from what they have read or understood. Yet we could not adapt our discourse except to those things which we understood.”

XIII. Although aided in this labour by Origen’s writings, he was not their copyist or translator. To imitate is one thing; to translate or copy is another. Nor does one perform the office of a translator who adds some things, removes others, and recasts the rest in his own style. But Hilary, as Jerome attests in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, imitated Origen in this work and added some things of his own. And, as Jerome says in Letter LXII to Theophilus, “cutting away whatever was harmful, he translated what was useful.”

The manner of that translation is established by the testimony of the same Doctor. For whenever Jerome is criticized for expounding Origen’s books in such a way that, delighting in his own style, he becomes the father of the expression rather than a translator, he has no more habitual defense than to reply that he had imitated Hilary in this respect. “We are no more unfaithful than Hilary,” he says to Pammachius and Oceanus, in Letter LXV, “nor more faithful than Victorinus, who translated his [Origen’s] Treatises not as translators but as authors of their own work.” And in Letter CI to Pammachius: “For the present, it is enough to mention Hilary the Confessor, who rendered into Latin homilies on Job and many Treatises on the Psalms from Greek; he did not sit by the slumbering letter and torture himself with the stale translation of rustics, but, as one who had captured their meanings, transferred them into his own language by the right of a conqueror.” Jerome makes the same reply in Letter LXII to Theophilus.

XIV. Many other arguments confirm that Hilary does not owe everything he discusses in these Treatises to Origen. First, it cannot be denied that he undertook to expound a Latin text; therefore he had to explain some things that Origen had not addressed. Secondly, since Origen, according to Ambrose’s testimony (*Sermon 4 on Psalm CXVIII*), preferred *distillavit* (“has distilled”), whereas our Hilary preferred *dormitavit* (“has slumbered”), it is clear that Hilary departed from Origen in translating ambiguous scriptural words. Hence it is necessary that he did not agree with him in expounding them either.

Thirdly, Origen’s understanding of the word *diapsalma*, as found in Jerome’s Letter CXXXVIII to Marcella, differs from Hilary’s view in the Prologue to the Psalms. Fourthly, who could persuade himself that what Hilary discusses throughout concerning Christ’s dignity, power, eternity, and dispensation was borrowed from Origen? Fifthly, on the resurrection, eternal punishments, and other subjects, he has much that is utterly foreign to Origen’s teaching. Sixthly, Jerome approves the inference (*Letter CXLII to Marcella*) that Origen’s expositions on the letter *Phe* of Psalm CXVIII and on Psalm CXXVI had already disappeared in Pamphilus’s time, because that martyr did not list them in his catalogue. Yet we do not find Hilary’s Treatises on those Psalms inferior to the others, or even slightly divergent from them in style.

Seventhly, fragments of Origen on Psalm I still survive, and these have no affinity whatever with Hilary’s exposition of the same Psalm. Hilary did imitate three of them more closely; so that anyone might compare them, we published them below: the first at col. 235, note b; the second at col. 240, note h; and the last at col. 246, note g. But this especially shows that he so adapted the ideas borrowed from Origen that he could rightly claim them as, in a sense, his own.

Finally, when, in the preface to Psalm I, he testifies that he had found many people, either in conversation or from their letters and writings, to hold such opinions—“but they did not teach this either in method or in reason,” and so forth—he sufficiently indicates that in obscure passages of the sacred text he had read not only Origen’s writings but those of many others; indeed, that he had also consulted his associates, and accepted nothing from anyone unless he had first weighed and approved it.

XV. Among those with whom Hilary was familiar and whom he consulted in conversation, Jerome, a competent witness in this matter, specifically mentions the presbyter Heliodorus. Yet Erasmus refuses credence to Jerome’s related assertion that Hilary had acquired only a slight smattering of Greek literature, and therefore was accustomed to ask this Heliodorus about matters in Origen’s sayings which he could not understand by himself, and was twice deceived. “Especially,” Erasmus says, “since what he offers is nothing but conjecture.”

“For,” he continues, “to speak briefly in Hilary’s defense, it does not seem plausible to me that so great a man was so credulous as to depend wholly on another’s judgment in explaining divine writings; nor so untrained in Greek literature that he could not himself grasp the meaning, especially in Origen, whose expression is wonderfully clear.” And indeed, although someone recently has refused to agree concerning the clarity of Origen’s style, one can scarcely bring oneself to believe that Hilary, especially after his return from exile, remained such a novice in Greek that he required another’s aid to understand Origen’s words and to imitate them in the manner observed.

It can scarcely be denied that Jerome spoke here from mere conjecture—and that, under pressure from the necessity of quickly copying out a stolen work, severe stomach pain prevented him from giving the truth of the matter more careful consideration. Thus it is not surprising that he said certain things which do not sufficiently cohere. But if he did err, he is excused by the piety and reverence alone which led him into error concerning the holy man.

XVI. Moreover, Latin and Greek manuscripts of the sacred text—which Hilary testifies more than once [Note: [Col. 0228D] Prologue, §2, and on Psalm CXVIII, letter 8, §1.] that he consulted in order to attain a readier understanding of the Psalms—prove that he did not depend on Origenian interpretations. From the Greek texts he cites, in Psalm LXV, §25, two readings, one of which occurs nowhere else known to us. He usually follows the Latin text, probably the one then accepted in ordinary use. He often observes that it adheres somewhat too closely to the letter, and that its translators, not daring to alter or regulate the arrangement and order of words in comparison with the original, have explained the exact force of the expressions less clearly.

It is not at all surprising that the Psalter of this codex differs from what is called the Gallican Psalter, since this is precisely the text Jerome later corrected. Yet Hilary does not adhere to it so scrupulously as to be always consistent when repeating the same reading. He often employs the words of our Vulgate when repeating a verse to be explained, although he first proposed a reading differing from it. Indeed, he sometimes sets out the text otherwise than we now have it, but subsequently explains it as if he had read only what now prevails among us. Thus, on Psalm CXXIII he gives: “Perhaps our soul would have passed through the immense water”; but then explains it as though he had read “unbearable,” not “immense.”

XVII. From this it might seem that our Vulgate was familiar to Hilary. Yet several readings now found in it were unknown to him. For in Psalm LXV, §18, he declares plainly enough that he knew of no Latin version which, at verse 8 of the same Psalm, read: “Make heard the voice of his praise.” Again, in Psalm CXVIII, letter 10, §3, while observing that in some codices, after the words “Your hands made me,” there is written “and prepared me,” and in others “and formed me,” but does not add that in others “and fashioned me” circulated, he signifies quite plainly by this silence that he knew no copy in which the latter reading occurred.

Moreover, it is clear from his treatment of the verses themselves that he was unacquainted with Latin codices in which Psalm CXVIII:89 had been translated “For ever, O Lord,” rather than “Unto the age, O Lord,” and Psalm CXX:5, “upon your right hand,” rather than “upon the hand of your right hand.” Finally, when he read in Psalm CXLV, §5, “The Lord makes the blind wise,” would he rightly have added, “If the prophet spoke of bodily gifts, he would rather have mentioned that light was granted to the blind,” if he had found in any codex: “The Lord enlightens the blind”? These and other points may be viewed as examples of passages which Jerome subsequently corrected in the Old Latin version.

XVIII. He sometimes adapts his discussion to the various renderings of different codices, as is shown by the Treatise on Psalm CXIX, where one may read interchangeably “with the tents of Kedar,” “with the dwellings of Kedar,” and “with the inhabitants of Kedar.” But whenever one reading must be selected from divergent versions, he prefers the translation of the Seventy Elders. It has such authority for him that he considers it unsafe to depart from it.

He assigns it such weight, first because it is lawful—that is, issued under the Law and long before Christ by Jews bound to the Law, and therefore wholly unsuspected. Secondly, although produced under the Law, it is nevertheless spiritual: that is, it does not slavishly adhere to the Hebrew letter, which is highly ambiguous, but reveals and expresses in unambiguous words the spirit hidden in it. It is especially for this reason, in Psalm LIX, §4, that he places below it Aquila’s translation, which understands nothing beyond the letter. Finally, because that spiritual meaning was not devised by human ingenuity, but received by Moses from tradition.

For Hilary thinks that Moses, lest anyone be deceived by the ambiguity of the Hebrew language, selected seventy elders who might be both guardians and witnesses of the genuine meanings of Scripture; their successors, he thinks, were the Seventy who first rendered the Scriptures into Greek. In commendation of the same edition Augustine adds (*On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, II.66): “The Seventy translated by the same Spirit by which the things they translated had been spoken.”

XIX. How highly he also valued the book of Psalms as corrected among the Greeks according to the Hebrew is attested by what he left at the beginning of letter 8, Psalm CXVIII: there, abandoning a previously held opinion, which the Latin codices and some Greek ones supported, he departs from it on the authority of that version alone. In commending the same book, as throughout his exposition of Psalm CXVIII, Ambrose agrees with him at the same passage. The words of both might aptly be referred to the work of the martyr Lucian, concerning whom Euthymius testifies (Preface to the Psalms): “Having examined all editions and compared them most carefully with the Hebrew truth, he gave Christians his own edition, containing nothing defective and nothing superfluous.” [Col. 0230B] Yet the authority of Jerome opposes this (Preface to the Four Gospels), where he writes: “I pass over those codices which a perverse contention of a few men asserts to be called after Lucian and Hesychius.” But who are these “few men,” if they are asserted to be such not only among Greeks, but also among Gauls and Italians? Moreover, Jerome was held by Hilary in too great reverence for him to brand, as “perverse contention,” an opinion which Hilary himself maintained. Besides, Lucian revised the whole Scripture, whereas Hilary and Ambrose mention only the book of Psalms.

XX. Both from this passage, in which he values so highly a book corrected according to the Hebrew, and from another (on Psalm LXV, §3), in which he indicates that Greek codices have somewhat more authority than Latin ones because they are closer to the Hebrew source, he makes his view of the Hebrew text clear. He does not, indeed, impugn the integrity of this text, but merely warns that one must guard against its ambiguity. Rather, if we understand his words on Psalm II, §3, the Hebrew books were compared after the Lord’s resurrection with those published by the seventy translators; and, when found to agree faithfully, an indissoluble authority was established for both, by the privilege of doctrine and antiquity. Certainly, when in the same place he admits that the translations of the seventy Elders were not necessary for the Hebrews, and when in §4 he shows that Paul, a Hebrew, was permitted among Hebrews to use the Hebrew text, he plainly indicates that he does not suspect it of corruption.

XXI. What shall we say of those Psalms which are prefixed in their entirety to the individual treatises? They were first published in the Paris edition of 1605 from an ancient codex formerly belonging to St. Maximinus of Micy, later to Queen Christina of Sweden, and finally to the Vatican Library. At its end this date and imprecation are noted:

> This is the book of the monastery of St. Maximinus of Micy, which Abbot Peter ordered to be written; and Pilio (that is, Nestorius) provided it through his labor and arranged it. On the day of the Lord’s Supper he offered it, to be kept upon the sacred altar of St. Stephen, to God and St. Maximinus, under a vow of this kind: that whoever at any time removes it from there by deceit, without intending to return it, may receive condemnation together with Judas the betrayer, Annas, Caiaphas, and Pilate. Amen.

The Vatican codices of lesser antiquity present the same Psalms. But they occur neither in the remaining manuscripts nor in the printed editions. That they are an alien work is shown by the text of Psalm CXIX before the preface to the Songs of Ascents, and likewise by the first octave of Psalm CXVIII before the preface to the whole Psalm, both placed in a wholly unsuitable location. Moreover, the individual Psalms differ in so many places from the text followed by Hilary in his expositions that no one could be persuaded they are his. We therefore at first judged that this text, as adopted from elsewhere, should be rejected, or at least corrected according to the version used by Hilary. But since it differs no less from the Vulgate than from Hilary’s Psalter, we decided to preserve the version which derives authority from the antiquity of the manuscripts, while adding in the margin the readings in which Hilary differs from it, so that no one may employ it as Hilary’s.

XXII. In the Royal and Tours manuscripts, in which an entire Psalm nowhere occurs before its exposition, each exposition is entitled either simply “Psalm” or “Treatise on the Psalm.” That individual pieces were designated by Hilary himself by this title “Treatise” is clear from his own words on Psalm CXXX, §1, and Psalm CXXXV, §§12 and 14. But whether these treatises were delivered to the people may rightly be asked. It is scarcely credible that a bishop so learned and eloquent, who even as a layman did not cease to sow words of truth overflowing with fruit, neglected the chief duty of pastors. Nor is it less incredible that, although he vigorously fulfilled it, none whatever of his sermons should have reached not only our knowledge but even Jerome’s. Certainly, the exhortatory ending of many treatises, the doxology appended at the close of all or almost all of them, the very words of the Treatise on Psalm CXXXVIII, §15—“From this point it is no longer a question of time (not place), nor of the issue”—and, finally, the entire manner of speech have something of the sermon about them. Yet we do not venture to assert or call them sermons, since Jerome calls them commentaries and Augustine expositions. For although Augustine, in Book II Against Julian, chapter 7, after quoting certain passages from letter 13 of Psalm CXVIII, subsequently recalls others from letter 15 with the words, “again in the same sermon,” it is manifest that he there designates by the term “sermon” not the same treatise on the same letter, but the whole exposition of Psalm CXVIII. And indeed the prefaces—not only at the beginning, but also before Psalm CXVIII and before the Songs of Ascents—belong more to one publishing commentaries than to one delivering sermons. Further, while the other Fathers in their sermons customarily address their hearers by the affectionate name “brethren” or some other designation, Hilary nowhere calls them “Brethren” in these treatises, nor does he anywhere expressly turn his discourse to the hearers.

XXIII. Nevertheless, for the reasons given above, we are readily led to suppose that these treatises were first delivered before the people, then, after certain alterations, collected and published in one volume of commentaries. This opinion is supported by the fact that in Zeno of Verona there occur, among the treatises falsely attributed to him—as we shall demonstrate on Psalm CXXVI—two on the same Psalm CXXX: one, namely, in the form of a commentary, as it stands in Hilary; the other, with very few changes, delivered to the Brethren in the manner of a Sermon. From this it may be judged what kind of treatises he spoke to his congregation, and into what form he afterward reduced them as commentaries. There is nothing that would require us either to refer these two different forms of treating one and the same subject to different authors, or to explain one from the other in some different way. In the same Zeno, the sermon on judgment, entitled “On Psalm One Hundred,” is composed so wholly in Hilary’s manner [Note: Compare with this sermon what he says on Psalm I, §15, etc.] that we suspect it too to have been appropriated from him along with the others. And in Hilary himself, the opening of the Treatise on Psalm XIV, “The Psalm which has been read is entitled a Psalm of David,” and likewise the words in §2 on Psalm XIII, “The Psalm which has been read is entitled ‘For the end,’” mean what else but that the Psalms mentioned were expounded immediately after their reading in church before the people? Concerning the usefulness of this work, we offer this single general observation: in it the holy doctor has, as it were, embraced whatever he thinks concerning the chief doctrines of our faith.

[Col. 0231]

# TREATISES OF SAINT HILARY, BISHOP OF POITIERS, ON THE PSALMS. (C)

[Note: Although our most ancient book, deprived of its earlier leaves, now begins with the words of §9 and is later than Psalm Fifty, it does not deprive us of the title prefixed to this prologue; for on every page is written “Instruction on the Psalms.” Although this is a fitting and highly appropriate title, we did not wish to suppress the title prefixed by the most learned Benedictine editor, especially since we find that it has prevailed from the age of Cassiodorus onward. For, in expounding Psalm VI, he cites “Hilary in the Prologue to the Psalms.”]

# PROLOGUE TO THE BOOK OF PSALMS

[Note: The Micy manuscript bears this title alone, which, with the support of the Royal exemplar, we prefix as suitable to the whole work: “Treatises of Saint Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, on the Psalms.” The title “Prologue to the exposition of the Psalms,” found in the printed editions, is not inaptly given from the Tellerian manuscript as “Prologue to the Book of Psalms”; for it concerns not so much the exposition of the Psalms as the Psalter itself, which Hilary presently chooses to call the Book of Psalms.]

## The Book of Psalms Is One, Not Five; Nor Is It David’s Alone

1. From the books which many have left written, we have learned that there are various opinions concerning the Book of Psalms. [Note: The Tellerian codex reads, in a different sense: “We have learned, from the books which different commentators have left written, that there are various opinions in the Book of Psalms.” One might rightly suspect this codex to be interpolated here and in several other places.] For some Hebrews maintain that they are divided into five books: the first book extends to Psalm XL; the second from Psalm XL to Psalm LXXI; the third from there to Psalm LXXXVIII; and the fourth to Psalm CV—because all these Psalms have, at their conclusion, “Amen, amen” [literally, “May it be, may it be”]; then the fifth book is concluded in Psalm CL. Others have thought that the Psalms should be entitled, “Psalms of David,” intending by this title that all were composed by David. [Note: The Paris edition of 1605 has, “that they should be so entitled.” Augustine permits the entire Psalter to be attributed to David as author in his exposition of Psalm IX, §35. Indeed, in *The City of God*, VII.14, he regards it as far more credible that all the Psalms proceeded from David. They are unhesitatingly ascribed to him in Rufinus’s Preface to the Psalms. Cassiodorus likewise affirms in his Preface to the same work that certain indications demonstrate that they belong to the prophet David alone. Euthymius, in his Preface to the Psalms, prefers this opinion to that maintained by our Hilary.] But we, according to apostolic authority, call and write it the “Book of Psalms.” [Note: The Tellerian manuscript reads, “and now call and write”; this is not approved. Moved by Hilary’s authority and arguments, Cassiodorus defines in chapter 12 of his Preface to the Psalter that there is one Book of Psalms. But it is remarkable that there he attributes to Jerome the division of the Psalms into five books, which Jerome wholly rejects in his Preface to the Psalter translated from Hebrew. Augustine, in Psalm CL, II.2, admits that he does not know the basis for this division and prefers to submit to the authority of canonical Scripture. The author of the Preface to the Psalms in Rufinus follows the same authority.] For we remember that it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “For it is written in the Book of Psalms: ‘Let his dwelling be desolate, and let another take his episcopate’” [Acts 1:20]. Therefore it should be called neither “Five Books,” according to certain Hebrews, nor “Psalms of David,” according to the simplicity of many; but, according to apostolic authority, it must be recognized as the “Book of Psalms.”

## They Belong to Those Whose Names They Bear

2. There are, however, several authors of these Psalms. For David is designated as author in some, Solomon in some, Asaph in some, Idithun in some, the sons of Korah in some, and Moses in one. [Note: Another Vatican manuscript reads: “in some, the sons of Korah; in one, Moses.” Moses’s name is prefixed to Psalm LXXXIX. Augustine, however, does not agree that Moses is its author in his exposition of that Psalm, §2; he prefers that the whole Psalter be attributed to David. Jerome, by contrast, in his letter to Cyprian writes that Moses is author not only of this Psalm but also of those following it: “He left us not only five books—Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy—but also eleven Psalms, from LXXXIX through XCIX.”] Consequently it is absurd to call the Psalms “David’s,” since so many authors are disclosed by the very titles of their inscriptions. [Note: The Micy manuscript has: “indeed, it is absurd.” It then adds with the Paris edition: “to call or name them Psalms of David, when there their authors are commended by the very titles of their inscriptions.” Other books have the text as printed, except that the Tellerian reads “are believed” for “are disclosed.”] And it will more correctly be called the Book of Psalms, since prophecies of different authors and different times have been gathered into one volume. [Note: The printed editions read “Prophets”; corrected from the manuscripts.] Some have thought that the names of Jeremiah, Haggai, and Zechariah should be prefixed to the superscriptions of certain Psalms; yet nothing of the kind is found so published in the authentic books of the seventy translators, so much so that in very many Latin and Greek codices the simple titles of the Psalms alone occur, without their names.

## Psalms Without a Named Author Belong to the Author Named in the Previous Psalm

3. Concerning those which occur under different superscriptions without the names of their various authors, this is the tradition of ancient men: [Note: In the Micy manuscript: “this is the ancient tradition of the Latins.” The author of this tradition is declared to be Ezra at the end of §4.] from the Psalm whose author is placed in its superscription, the following Psalms which succeed without superscriptions naming their authors are to be considered his, until a Psalm appears whose superscription bears the name of another author. Thus, if a Psalm bears the superscription “A Psalm of David,” those which follow without a title are to be considered David’s until another prophet’s name is placed in a superscription; and from that point until another prophet, those intermediate Psalms which lack an inscription belong to the one whose name began to be placed as author in the superscription of the preceding Psalm. [Note: Two manuscripts read “are published.”]

## Why Samuel May Be Named in a Psalm of Moses

4. But if anyone perhaps withdraws credence from this understanding because it is written in those Psalms which follow the Psalm in which Moses is set forth as author—namely, in Psalm XCVIII—“Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name,” and considers that it cannot have been prophesied by Moses because Samuel’s name, though he was born so long after Moses, occurs in the Psalm: let him remember that no one ought to consider it strange or difficult that so great a prophet should have uttered the name of so great a prophet, though he was yet to come. For in the books of Kings the name of King Josiah was prophesied before his birth, when the prophet said: “Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to David; Josiah shall be his name” [3 Kings 13:2]. Thus it ought not to be regarded as incredible that Samuel was foretold by Moses, [Note: Thus in the manuscripts, more correctly than in the printed editions: “was foretold.”] especially since, according to Jeremiah’s saying, “Not even if Moses and Samuel should stand” [Jer. 15:1], Samuel is named alongside Moses and equated with him because of the merit of his holiness. If this tradition, believed to have come from Ezra when he collected the Psalms into one book after the captivity, is considered false or implausible, those who dispute it must identify the authors of these Psalms. For it is certain that they could not have been prophesied except by prophets while prophesying.

## The Psalms Sing the Gospel History; Prophecies Are Closed and Sealed to Those Who Do Not Know Christ

5. There should be no doubt that what is said in the Psalms must be understood according to Gospel preaching: so that, from whatever person the Spirit of prophecy may have spoken, [Note: The Tellerian manuscript alone reads “may nevertheless have spoken.” In the editions of Badius Ascensius, Erasmus, and Lipsius, the verb “may have” is lacking here, as is the particle “to” before “the glory of our resurrection,” which the Paris edition also omits.] all of it nevertheless refers to the knowledge of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, his embodiment in flesh, his passion, his kingdom, and the glory and power of our resurrection. All prophecies, however, are closed and sealed against worldly understanding and the wisdom of the age, according to that saying of Isaiah: [Note: The Tellerian codex, following the Vulgate, reads: “And the vision of all shall be for you like the words of a sealed book,” etc. (The Vulgate thereafter agrees, as do the LXX.) See Treatise on letter 17 of Psalm CXVIII, §4. What is contained in this and the following section is related to a fragment of Origen, from volume I on Psalm I, printed in volume I of the Greek works of Origen edited by Daniel Huet, p. 37. We have therefore judged it right to set it down here, so that by comparing Hilary’s words with Origen’s, anyone may more readily perceive what has been transferred from the latter into the former:

> “The divine oracles testify that the sacred Scriptures are closed and sealed, and this by David’s key, perhaps also by the seal of which it is written: ‘Holiness to the Lord, the figure of a seal.’ This ought to be understood of the power of God who granted it, a power represented by the seal. For John in the Apocalypse declares the Scriptures to be closed and sealed in these words: ‘Write to the angel of the church at Philadelphia: Thus says the holy and true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shall shut, and shuts and no one shall open: I know your works; behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut.’ Then shortly afterward: ‘And I saw at the right hand of him seated on the throne a book written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw an angel proclaiming in a loud voice: Who is worthy to open the book and loosen its seals? And no one in heaven or on earth or beneath the earth could open the book or look upon it. And I wept, because no one was found worthy to open the book or look upon it. And one of the elders said to me: Do not weep; behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and its seven seals.’ Isaiah speaks concerning sealing alone: ‘All these words shall be for you like the words of this sealed book. If they give it to a man who knows letters, saying, Read these things, he will answer, I cannot read it, for it is sealed. And this book shall be given into the hands of a man who does not know letters, and he will say, I do not know letters.’ These words must not be thought to concern only John’s Apocalypse or Isaiah’s prophecies, but must be understood entirely of the whole sacred Scripture. This is indeed acknowledged by those who have attained even a moderate knowledge of the divine writings, which are filled with coverings of riddles, parables, obscure expressions, and various other kinds of obscurity difficult for human intelligence to grasp. The Savior, wishing to show this, said that the key was with the scribes and Pharisees, who made no effort to find the way of opening; and he said: ‘Woe to you lawyers, for you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves have not entered, and you do not permit those entering to enter.’” Thus far Origen.]

“And all these words shall be for you like the utterances of this sealed book” [Isa. 29:11–12].
