If it is given to a man who knows letters and he is told, “Read these things,” he will say, “I cannot read them, for it is sealed.” And if this book is given into the hands of a man who does not know letters, and he is told, “Read this,” he will answer, “I do not know letters.” The inability to read and understand the book of prophecy is shown in the person of both men: the learned man’s capacity for reading, unable to approach the seal of the closed mystery, is compared to the ignorance of the unlearned through the common deficiency of both in understanding. For all things are woven together with allegorical and typological powers, through which are disclosed the mysteries of God’s only-begotten Son: his begetting in flesh, suffering, death, resurrection, eternal reign with those who believe in him and are glorified together with him, and judgment of the rest. And because the scribes and Pharisees, refusing to receive the Son of God born in flesh, denied every entrance into prophetic understanding, the Lord rebukes them under a denunciation of punishment: “Woe to you, teachers of the law, who have taken away the key of knowledge: you yourselves do not enter, and you do not permit those entering to enter” [Luke 11:52]. For by denying Christ—whose coming is the subject of the prophets—they took away the key of knowledge; because the denial of faith in the bodily coming shuts up the knowledge of the Law which proclaimed the Lord’s coming in flesh.

## The Key of the Psalms Is Faith in Christ

6. This must indeed be understood as said concerning every kind of prophetic Scripture: unless their meanings are understood and recognized as referring to the coming of the Lord, born from a Virgin as a human being, the force of those meanings remains sealed and shut. [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “the force of the interpretations.” Another: “their interpretation, without force.” The Tellerian agrees with this, where it shortly afterward reads “nevertheless,” not “indeed.”] Yet we are taught by the Apocalypse of blessed John that the Book of Psalms cannot be understood except through faith in his coming: “Write to the angel of the church in Philadelphia: Thus says the holy and true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shall shut; who shuts and no one shall open” [Rev. 3:7]. [Note: The printed editions read “keys,” contrary to the manuscripts and the sacred text.] Therefore he has David’s key because he himself, through these seven seals concerning his embodiment, passion, death, resurrection, glory, kingdom, and judgment, which David prophesies of him in the Psalms, unlocks them. [Note: The manuscripts more correctly read “through these,” rather than the printed “by a certain force.” The Tellerian manuscript, omitting “which,” soon reads “prophecy” in place of “prophesies.”] He opens what no one shall shut, and shuts what no one shall open; for by this prophecy fulfilled in him he opens what no one will close; and conversely, when faith in the prophecy fulfilled in him is denied, he shuts what no one can open. For no one except he in whom these things were prophesied and fulfilled will grant the key to this understanding.

Finally, he taught this same point in what follows, saying: “And I saw at the right hand of him seated on the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals. And I saw another mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice: Who is worthy to open the book and loosen its seals? And no one could, either in heaven or on earth or beneath the earth, open the book or see it. And I wept because no one had been found worthy to open the book or see it. And one of the elders said to me: Do not weep; behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered to open the book and its seven seals” [Rev. 5 and following]. This book, containing past and future things in what was written within and without, is worthy to be opened by no one; and the Apostle’s tears arise from longing for understanding and grief at the difficulty. But the lion of the tribe of Judah and root of David conquered to open the book and its seals, because he alone unlocks, through the mystery of his embodiment and divinity, those seven seals by which, as we have taught above, the book is closed. The Lord himself testified to this after his resurrection, saying: “It is necessary that all things written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” [Luke 24:44]. By these things, therefore, the whole book of prophecy is both sealed and closed, because when what has been fulfilled through him is believed, all those things that are sealed and closed will be opened and unlocked.

## The Psaltery Represents Christ’s Body

7. Although we know from the Lord’s own declaration that all things were spoken by the divine Spirit through David, the form of this prophecy itself teaches that it contains teaching of heavenly and celestial knowledge. For prophecy was delivered by that instrument called in Greek the *psalterion*, in Hebrew the *nabla*, which alone of all musical instruments is completely straight, containing nothing crooked or oblique, nor anything set in motion from lower places to produce the sound of musical harmony. Rather, it is an instrument fashioned in the form of the Lord’s body: straight, without any bend or deflection; moved and struck from above, given life for song by a heavenly and celestial ordering, and not, like the other instruments of earth, sounding forth with a lowly and earthly spirit. For he did not proclaim lowly and earthly things in the instrument of his body, as he himself testified: “He who is from the earth is earthly and speaks from the earth; but he who comes from heaven bears witness to what he has seen and heard” [John 3:31]. Through this heavenly Spirit, therefore, God is sung in the Psalms, in the form of the Lord’s body in which the heavenly Spirit spoke; the figure of this earthly musical instrument, sounding in harmony from above, being correspondingly compared with it.

## The Psalms Were Undifferentiated Among the Hebrews, Collected by Ezra, and Ordered by the Seventy

8. It must not be ignored that among the Hebrews the Psalms have an undifferentiated numbering and are written without any indication of order. There, no first, second, third, fiftieth, or hundredth Psalm is marked; rather, they are intermingled without distinction of order or number. [Note: The printed editions read “without any superscription”; corrected on the authority of the manuscripts. Euthymius notes two opinions concerning the collection of the Psalms: “Some,” he says in the Preface to the Psalms, “say that Ezra, others that Hezekiah, collected the Psalms into one.”] Ezra, according to ancient traditions, collected and brought them together into one volume, since they were unarranged and dispersed according to the diversity of authors and times. But the seventy Elders, abiding in the synagogue according to Moses’ tradition for the preservation of the teaching of the Law, [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “for the preservation of the Law and doctrine”; another, “for the preservation of the Law and for doctrine.” Nothing can certainly be altered in view of Psalm II, §11, where these matters are more fully narrated.] after King Ptolemy had entrusted to them the task of translating the whole Law from Hebrew into Greek, [Note: One or another Vatican manuscript reads “after King Antiochus,” contrary to the other books. Thus, too, on Psalm CXVIII, letter 16, §16, the history of the seventy translators is related under Ptolemy, not Antiochus.] understanding with spiritual and heavenly knowledge the powers of the Psalms, arranged them in number and order, assigning to each number, according to its efficacy and completion, [Note: The Paris edition reads “in its completion,” which Lipsius wrongly added.] the appropriate order of Psalms that are perfect and efficacious.

## The Seventy Did Not Preserve Chronological Order but the Order of Events

9. Although this may be understood from the powers of the individual Psalms, we are taught it most completely in the historical record of deeds and times: namely, that the arrangement of the Psalms was ordered according to the efficacy of perfect numbers. [Note: The printed editions read “comparisons”; corrected from the manuscripts. The word *collatio* occurs in the same sense in Book *On Synods*, §9.] For Psalm III, according to history, comes after Psalm L. The inscription of each differs by a great interval of time and age. The latter embraces the events concerning Uriah and David; [Note: In the Tellerian manuscript: “concerning Uriah and David.”] the former signifies David’s flight while his son Absalom pursued him. [Note: We have substituted “him” for the earlier “formerly” from the Tellerian codex, restoring “yet” shortly afterward and “thus” a little later. We write *Abessalon*, not *Absalon*, as the Greek and manuscripts agree.] Yet the power and mystery of number bring it about that this Psalm and that are thus placed under fitting and mutually congruous numbers.

## The Mystery of the Number Fifty

10. The inscription of Psalm L, in historical order, is later than the inscription of Psalm LI. But the power and perfection of the number fifty [Note: These words are cited on Psalm LI, §2.] required that the earlier be placed after, and the later before, because Doeg the Idumean’s impenitent hatred toward David demanded it: so that remission of sins might be placed at number fifty, and the punishment of unbelief, exceeding the number of established remission, might lack pardon because it had lost both the time and number of repentance. For since, in the fiftieth—which is the Sabbath of Sabbaths—remission of sins is established according to the prefiguration of the Jubilee year, this Psalm, in which remission of sins is sought through repentance set beforehand, is fittingly placed in the order of this number.

## What the Three Sets of Fifty Psalms Signify

11. The Book of Psalms consists of three fifties; and this arises from the pattern and number of that blessed hope of ours. Let one carefully consider the completion of the Psalm at the end of the first fifty, the second fifty, [Note: “Psalm one hundred,” as in the Vatican manuscript.] and again the third fifty, in which is the end of the book: [Note: The word “Psalm” is absent from the Tellerian manuscript. In the Vatican manuscript, however, “hundredth” occurs before “Psalm”; we would prefer it afterward. Hilary’s three fifties prefigure a threefold life of the righteous: first, in a mortal body; second, in Christ’s kingdom, with the body laid aside; and finally, in the kingdom of God the Father, when the body is resumed. He again mentions this threefold life on Psalm LXII, §7. As he teaches on Psalm CXVIII, letter 12, §14, that those who are in Christ’s kingdom are transferred from that kingdom into the Father’s kingdom, so here too he appears to imply that they are reserved for the times of the heavenly Jerusalem and therefore are not yet in it. See Preface, §6.] he will understand that the providence which arranged the Psalms in this order agrees with the dispensation of our salvation. For since the first step toward salvation is rebirth into a new human being after remission of sins; and since, after confession of repentance, that kingdom of the Lord is reserved for the times of the holy city and heavenly Jerusalem; and since afterward, when heavenly glory has been fulfilled in us, we advance through the kingdom of the Son into the kingdom of God the Father, in which the whole company of spirits shall proclaim the praises owed to God: we readily understand that, in the powers of the individual Psalms placed in each sequence of fifty, the mystery of this threefold arrangement of fifties is contained. [Note: Earlier editions read “under the number of a fifty,” neither good Latin nor elegant, though “of a fifty” occurs immediately again. We correct it on the authority of the Verona codex.] [Note: The Tellerian manuscript reads “fiftyfold.”] [Note: With the aid of the same codex, we print “arrangement” for “dispensation”: the subject is the order and arrangement of the Psalms.]

## Fifty as the Sabbath of Sabbaths; the Lord’s Day as the Perfect Sabbath

12. That this is the Sabbath of Sabbaths is shown by the number seven counted seven times over into sevenfoldness; yet the octave completes it, because the same day is both first and eighth, being added in the last Sabbath according to Gospel fullness. [Note: “Added.”] This Sabbath of Sabbaths was indeed observed by the apostles with such religious devotion that during those fifty days no one worshiped with the body prostrate on the ground, nor hindered the festivity of this spiritual blessedness by fasting. [Note: The Tellerian codex reads “in contrast,” erroneously. Hilary’s words teaching that the festival is impeded by the aforesaid observances should be noted. Tertullian also calls this unlawful, *On the Crown*, §3: “On the Lord’s Day,” he says, “we consider fasting or worshiping on one’s knees unlawful; and with the same exemption we rejoice from Easter Day until Pentecost,” where he also reports that this practice was received from tradition. Jerome, in Letter LIV to Marcella against Montanus, denying that three Lents in the year must be observed, nevertheless grants that one may fast throughout the year, except during Pentecost—that is, the fifty days after Easter.] The same rule has externally been established also for the Lord’s Days, which are added beyond the number of the Sabbath through the fullness of Gospel preaching. For although the name and observance of Sabbath are established on the seventh day, we rejoice on the eighth day—which is itself also the first day—in the festival of the perfect Sabbath.

### 13. The Perfection of the Octave

It is fitting to contemplate the perfect power of this octave, endowed with heavenly mysteries, in the Psalm arranged eighth in number [Note: [Col. 0240C] “Contained” in two manuscripts.], to which the title *For the winepresses* is appended: vessels prepared for new fruits and renewed for containing the heat of fermenting [Note: [Col. 0240C] Thus the Vatican manuscript, with the Tellerian. Other books read: “the liquid of new wine.”] new wine. This number has been appointed for receiving evangelical fruits, when these perishable vessels of our bodies have been refashioned according to the evangelical octave. The wording and discourse of this Psalm itself [Col. 0240B] attest it.

The power of this octave is also contained, as it were, in the power and number of the sixth Psalm, in which there is prayer “for the eighth” [Note: [Col. 0240C] “As it were, in”; shortly afterward, “these” instead of “this.”]. The rationale of the number accomplishes this: that in the sixth there should be prayer for the eighth, and that in the eighth the title *For the winepresses* should be added. This superscription concerning the winepresses is found in three numbers. For the eighth, eightieth, and eighty-third Psalms bear this title, so that the order of this perfect blessedness might stand in perfect numbers; yet in such a way that the simple octave and the decade of the octave should enclose the mystery of the Triad—which among us is called the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0240C] The Tellerian manuscript reads here, “should contain it in itself”; opposite, in the margin: “Eighteen multiplied by three, with eighty added, make eighty-three and signify the perfect blessedness to be given to the faithful by the holy Trinity, who is one God.”].

### 14. Psalm CXVIII

We may recognize this perfection of the octave also in the one hundred and eighteenth Psalm. For, among the Hebrews, its beginnings are arranged according to the number eight [Col. 0240C], with eight verses for each individual letter; and the very force of the Psalm teaches the mystery of the octave. There are twenty-two octaves in it: eight verses are assigned to the beginnings of the individual letters. This is arranged for the reason that, since this Psalm brings the perfect man to completion according to evangelical teaching, we may be instructed through all twenty-two letters of the Hebrew language under the mystery of the octave [Col. 0241A].

> **Note [Col. 0240D–0241C]:** A fragment of Origen on the Psalms, inserted in the edition mentioned above, p. 41, provides an example of what our Hilary borrowed from Origen. There he says:
>
> “Nor should it be ignored that the books of the Old Testament, as the Hebrews hand them down, are twenty-two, equal in number to the Hebrew letters. For just as the twenty-two letters appear to be an introduction for human beings to wisdom and to divine teaching impressed in those forms, so the twenty-two books of Scripture are a foundation and introduction to the wisdom of God and the knowledge of things.”
>
> There follows the series of Old-Testament books in the order in which they are listed here, with the Hebrew name assigned to each book and an interpretation of that name. “The twenty-two books among the Hebrews are these: the first, which we call *Genesis*, is called by the Hebrews *Bresith*, a name taken from the beginning of the book itself, meaning ‘In the beginning.’ Then *Exodus*, called by the Hebrews *Vellesmoth*, that is, ‘These are the names’; third, *Leviticus*,” and so forth.

### 15. Twenty-Two, or Twenty-Four, Books of the Old Testament. The Three Principal Languages

This is the reason why the Law of the Old Testament is reckoned as twenty-two books [Note: [Col. 0241C] The Tellerian manuscript reads, “the Law and the Old Testament.” Many are mistaken from this passage in supposing that Hilary regarded no books other than those listed here as canonical. First, he mentions Judith as a book of the Law in *On Psalm* CXXV, §5. He also cites Tobit in *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 2, §6, and *On Psalm* CXXIX, §7. Moreover, he attributes Wisdom to Solomon in *On Psalm* CXXVII, §6. Indeed, in *On the Trinity* I.7, and in *On Psalm* CXVIII, letter 2, §8, as well as *On Psalm* CXXXV, §11, he adduces testimonies from it as from a Prophet. Thus he recognized it as a prophetic book.
>
> The same must be said of Ecclesiasticus, which he himself attributes to Solomon in *On Psalm* LXVI, §9 and says is commonly attributed to Solomon by the Latins in *On Psalm* CXL, §4. Finally, he cites the prophecy of Baruch under Jeremiah’s name in *On Psalm* LXVIII, §19 and near the end of Book IV of *On the Trinity*. Nor does he reject the passage from the history of Susanna, Daniel 13:4, cited by Arians as Scripture in Book IV of *On the Trinity*, §8. Indeed, in §7 he recognizes that passage and the other testimonies there cited as drawn from divine books.
>
> Hilary therefore enumerates here the canon of these books according to the Hebrews, not according to the usage received in the Church in his own time. Origen indicates this still more clearly in the passage already cited, where he begins their catalogue: “The twenty-two books among the Hebrews are these,” etc. Nor can one reply that Hilary approved books other than those received into the Hebrew canon merely as hagiographical, and not as canonical [Col. 0242C]. For if he had viewed them so, he would not have given Judith the name and authority of the Law, nor assigned to Solomon’s Wisdom the title of prophecy.
>
> To say something also concerning New-Testament Scriptures: we observe that Hilary frequently cites the Epistle to the Hebrews, calling it the Apostle’s in *On Psalm* XIV, §5; LIII, §12; CXVIII, letter 8, §16; and *On the Trinity* IV.11; and that even the Arians themselves cite it. Likewise above, §6, and elsewhere, he attributes the Apocalypse to blessed John—indeed, to John who wrote the Gospel, as may reasonably be inferred from the encomium with which he commends him in *On the Trinity* VI.16 and 39. Finally, he expressly cites the Second Epistle of Peter under that Apostle’s name in *On the Trinity* I.18.], so that it may correspond with the number of letters.

According to the traditions of the ancients, they are counted thus: the five books of Moses; Joshua son of Nun as the sixth; Judges and Ruth as the seventh; First and Second Kingdoms as the eighth; Third and Fourth Kingdoms as the ninth; the two books of Chronicles as the tenth [Note: [Col. 0242C] In Origen: “First and Second Chronicles in one book, *Dibrē ai amīm*, that is, *Logoi hēmerōn* (‘Words of Days’); First and Second Ezra,” etc. Did our Hilary perhaps, following this, wrongly attach the words *logoi hēmerōn*, which Origen uses to explain *Dibrē ai amīm*, to Ezra?]; Ezra, “the words of days,” as the eleventh; the Book of Psalms as the twelfth; Solomon’s Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs [Col. 0241B] as the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth; the twelve [Note: [Col. 0241B] “All” is inserted, as in the Tellerian manuscript.] Prophets as the sixteenth [Note: [Col. 0242D] The Tellerian manuscript adds “all”: perhaps for “minor”? There is no mention of this in the cited Origenian exemplars; plainly it is a scribal error. For there twenty-two books according to the Hebrews are first asserted, and then only twenty-one are listed.]; then Isaiah, Jeremiah with Lamentations and the Epistle, Daniel, Ezekiel, Job, and Esther complete the number of twenty-two books.

Some, however, have thought that, by adding Tobit and Judith [Note: [Col. 0242D] Origen says nothing concerning Tobit and Judith; but in their place he adds: “Outside this enumeration are the books of the Maccabees.” Hilary likewise cites certain passages from those books in *On Psalm* CXXIII, §3 and CXXXIV, §24, and several more in *Against Constantius*, §6.], the books should be numbered as twenty-four, according to the number of Greek letters, with the Roman language also included between Hebrew and Greek. For it is chiefly in these three languages that the mystery of God’s will and the expectation of the blessed kingdom are proclaimed [Col. 0242A]. Hence Pilate’s inscription, declaring the Lord Jesus Christ to be King of the Jews, was written in these three languages (John 19:20). For although many barbarian nations have acquired the knowledge of God through the preaching of the Apostles and the faith of churches remaining there to this day, nevertheless evangelical doctrine has its special seat in the Roman Empire, under which Hebrews and Greeks are contained [Note: [Col. 0241B] “In the Roman Empire, under which Hebrews and Greeks are contained.”].

### 16. The Fifteen Songs of Ascents

It follows that, after this number of twenty-two octaves according to the octave, the number which follows is contained in the fifteen Psalms of the Songs of Ascents [Note: [Col. 0242B] “To be contemplated in what precedes.”] [Note: [Col. 0242D] One Vatican manuscript reads “contained.”]. For after the perfect teaching of the preceding octaves, it was fitting that this Song of Ascents should consist in fifteen [Note: [Col. 0242D] Printed editions read “in fifteen Psalms and two”; corrected with the aid of the manuscripts.] Psalms [Col. 0242B], composed from two perfect numbers, namely the hebdomad and the octave—that is, the seventh and eighth numbers.

For through observance of the Law, which is established in the hebdomad, and through evangelical progress, which is completed in the octave both by present religious practice and by hoped-for expectation [Note: [Col. 0242D] The Tellerian manuscript reads awkwardly, “and consecrated.”], one ascends by this Song of Ascents to heavenly and eternal things. By this number of steps the chief priests also ascended into the Holy of Holies in the Temple [Note: [Col. 0242B] The printed editions read “in the Temple.” For “they ascended,” our manuscript reads “they climbed.”]. Thus, because neither the hebdomad of the Law without the evangelical octave [Col. 0243A], nor the evangelical octave without the hebdomad of the Law, could produce a perfect man [Note: [Col. 0242D] Thus the Tellerian manuscript. The printed editions read: “hebdomads”; “the hebdomad” would not be objectionable.], whoever had perfectly believed these things might be placed in the perfect and blessed Holy of Holies, made perfect in both the hebdomadic and octaval number contained in the fifteenfold Song of Ascents [Note: [Col. 0243C] In the same manuscript: “whoever that man”; then, “this perfect and true man, who is in the fifteen … number.” The sense appears to be that whoever had perfectly believed the perfect and true number of hebdomad and octave contained in the Song of Fifteen Ascents should be placed among the perfect and blessed Holy of Holies.] [Note: [Col. 0243C] Thus the Vatican manuscripts support the reading; the Tellerian manuscript has “until that man,” not “until those things.” Printed editions read: “Whoever had perfectly believed those things should place this perfect man, who is in the Song of Fifteen Ascents, among these perfect and blessed Holy of Holies.”].

### 17. The Various Titles of the Psalms

Although these matters have been spoken by us according to the numbers fulfilled in observance of the Law [Note: [Col. 0243C] “And pleasing by observance of the Law”; afterward, “yet absolutely the force of each …”] [Note: [Col. 0243D] Three Vatican manuscripts read “pleasing.”], and distributed in the evangelical mystery, nevertheless we shall attain a full understanding of the force of each number from the superscriptions of the Psalms and from the meaning of their actual words.

The titles of all superscriptions are various. Besides those marked beforehand by the names of their authors, or by indications of events or times, there are others bearing the title *For the end*; others simply *Psalm of a Song* or *Song of a Psalm*. Different superscriptions must necessarily have had different causes. It is not without purpose that, amid so great a diversity of matters, this order of titles changes: now *For the end*, now *Psalm*, now *Song*, now *Song of a Psalm*, now *Psalm of a Song*, so that it may be prefixed as a distinction of the Psalm which follows [Note: [Col. 0244D] Printed editions read “which is subject”; incorrectly.] [Note: [Col. 0244C] “Which follows” in the preceding text.].

And although we shall endeavor, in each individual Psalm, to give the reasons for its particular inscription, nevertheless, for the concise benefit of eager understanding, we compress into a brief account [Note: [Col. 0244C] “Into a brief little discourse.”] the force of all the superscriptions.

> **Note [Col. 0243D–0244D]:** What remains from this point to the end of this Prologue forms the first part of the Preface to the Commentary on the Psalms published under the name of Rufinus of Aquileia. There is no longer room for doubt whether this entire Prologue, or at least this latter portion, is a genuine work of Hilary: both because of the close connection of this section with what precedes and, indeed, with the subsequent exposition of the Psalms, and because this latter part is expressly cited by Hilary himself in *On Psalm* LXV, §1, just as the first part is cited by Cassiodorus.
>
> By contrast, Rufinus’s whole Commentary bears considerable marks of spuriousness. First, it silently excerpts so extensive a passage without Hilary’s name. Second, to the excerpt from which the exposition of the Psalms was to begin, it awkwardly attaches much else concerning the names, division, authors, and subject matter of the Book of Psalms. Third, the Commentary consists in large part of selected opinions of Augustine [Col. 0244C], although Origen was far more familiar to Rufinus than Augustine.
>
> Finally, the words near the end of the Preface—“Some ask to what branch of philosophy the Book of Psalms is to be assigned. The answer should be: insofar as it treats morals, it may be assigned to ethics; insofar as it treats nature, to physics”—and similar matters savor of an author much later than Rufinus. For the present, it is enough to have noted these points, for others to investigate more deeply [Col. 0244D]. We add, however, that these Commentaries are very worthy of reading and rich in an excellent selection of concise observations. An anonymous copy of the same Commentaries, written four hundred years ago, exists in our Germanensis Library.

### 18. What “For the End” Means

The end is that for the sake of which all other things exist, while it itself furnishes its reason to no other thing [Col. 0243C]. Everything is for the sake of the end; but there is nothing further after the end. One moves toward the end [Note: [Col. 0244C] “And one comes to an end.” Subsequently, as in the Paris edition preceding the Benedictine edition: “and extending itself toward nothing else.”], but comes to rest in the end [Col. 0244A]. Thus the end is both the completion of what preceded [Note: [Col. 0244D] The manuscripts restore this passage, corrupted in the printed editions.] and, extending itself toward nothing else, is its own possession in itself.

The Psalms entitled *For the end* [Note: [Col. 0244D] Printed editions read “the titles”; manuscripts more suitably supply “thus.”] are therefore to be understood thus: they arise from perfect and complete teachings and forms [Note: [Col. 0244C] “Hopes.”] of eternal goods, because the course of our faith should stretch toward the things spoken in them and, advancing no farther [Note: [Col. 0244D] The word “advancing,” absent in printed editions, is restored on manuscript authority.] [Note: [Col. 0244C] Does not contain “advancing.”], should rest in that very end of desired and attained blessedness.

### 19. The Four Kinds of Musical Art

In the musical arts there are these varieties of functions and kinds [Note: [Col. 0244D] In Rufinus and the Tellerian manuscript: “These are the kinds and varieties of functions.”]. A *Psalm* is when, the voice being silent, only the sound of the resonant instrument is heard. A *Song* is when the choir of singers, using its own freedom and not bound to conform to the instrument, rejoices in a hymn solely of melodious voice [Col. 0244B].

A *Song of a Psalm* is when, with the instrument leading, the answering and emulous voice of the singing choir is heard [Note: [Col. 0244D] Rufinus perversely assigns to this description the heading “Psalm of a Song,” and to the following one “Song of a Psalm.”], imitating with vocal melodies [Note: [Col. 0244C] “Modes.”] the measure of the psaltery. But a *Psalm of a Song* is when, with the choir singing first, the art of the accompanying instrument is fitted to the hymn of human singing, and the psaltery is modulated with equal sweetness to the vocal melodies that lead.

Accordingly, fitting superscriptions are adapted to the individual Psalms according to these four kinds of musical art. The character of each superscription is shown from the force of the Psalms and from these distinctions of musical teaching.

### 20. What the Individual Psalm Titles Indicate

In the Psalm whose heading is simply *Psalm*, there is contained either teaching or confession concerning faithful works and religious deeds. When the prophet recounts [Col. 0244C] what he has done, he instructs us in the practice of similar deeds, our bodily instrument being tuned to the devout uses of its functions [Col. 0245A].

But when simply *Song* is placed first in the title, there is in it spiritual knowledge and understanding of the heavenly mystery [Note: [Col. 0245C] The Tellerian manuscript and Rufinus read: “the heavenly understanding is understood,” omitting thereafter “there is.”], which a person gains through the knowledge of wisdom. For, without recounting works of faith, it displays perfect teaching concerning the knowledge of God alone. Not every kind of knowledge is immediately expressed in a good work; nor, conversely, does every good work attain true knowledge.

Hence there is also the third kind of superscription, *Song of a Psalm*, when teaching of knowledge is joined to the effectiveness of good works. For one must first live in good works, so that the perfect knowledge of the divine mystery which follows may be possible, according to the saying: “Do you desire wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you” (Ecclus. 1:35) [Col. 0245B]. Therefore the Lord grants wisdom to those who, through the merit of good works, attain the grace of understanding. From these pursuits of works and teaching, then, the import of the Psalm entitled *Song of a Psalm* is to be understood.

But where there is *Psalm of a Song*, the practice of good work is treated through the knowledge of understanding: whenever [Note: [Col. 0245C] Printed editions read “when desired,” against the manuscripts. Editors have often cut the particle *cum* (“when”) from its places; it has been restored according to the manuscripts.] a prior knowledge of God grants us the desirable effectiveness of faithful deeds.

### 21. Recapitulation; What the Absence of a Superscription Signifies

This fourfold distinction of musical art is thus fitted to the variety of Psalms: *Psalm* is through the motion of the bodily instrument in the recounting of deeds; *Song* contains within itself the knowledge of teaching through the understanding of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0245C] “Thus we read in our manuscript. Previously it has.”]; *Song of a Psalm* occurs when knowledge is granted through the preceding merit of deeds; and *Psalm of a Song* occurs when, through the understanding of knowledge attained, the work of faithful deeds is undertaken and performed [Col. 0245C].

Through these properties of the superscriptions, therefore, we must seek the understanding of the Psalms, because to each kind of prophecy a corresponding kind of musical comparison has been fitted in the particularity of its titles [Col. 0246A].

But those which are found without any inscription of special significance [Note: [Col. 0245C] “Are found.”]—such as the first and second, and many others—must be understood as having been sung from the teaching of the Holy Spirit for the spiritual knowledge of general instruction, so that each person might seek from them, according to the sincerity of his faith, the rationale of spiritual understanding.

### 22. Other Superscriptions

Other superscriptions, which signify events according to history, or times, or days, or embrace some other matter, show from the interpretation of names, the comparison of deeds, or the likeness of comparable things, the matters of which the Psalm consists. Thus, where there is *For the sabbath day*, *For the hidden things of the son*, or *For the eighth day* [Col. 0246B], the spiritual utterance of the Psalm is to be understood through the bodily sense of the superscription.

Or when *Of David*, *For David*, *Absalom*, *Saul*, or *Doeg* is prefixed [Note: [Col. 0246C] “Are prefixed.”] in the title under the history of events, we are to discern the prophecy contained in the Psalm either from the force of pronouns—such as *for David* or *of David*—or from the meanings of names, as in Absalom, Saul, and Doeg.

### 23. What “Diapsalma” Means

As for *diapsalma*, which is inserted in many Psalms, it should be understood to mark a change either of person or of meaning, together with a change in the mode of music [Note: [Col. 0245C] The Vatican manuscript reads “in the diapsalm.”] [Note: [Col. 0246D] The Tellerian manuscript, as in Rufinus, reads “of the musical metre.”]. Thus, whenever a *diapsalma* occurs, we should understand either that something else is said, that it is said by another person, or that it is sung in another mode of musical art.

Wherever we find a *diapsalma* intervening, we shall endeavor to explain its rationale with regard to persons and meanings [Col. 0246C]. The Greek and Latin translation, however, could not preserve the discipline of the musical mode [Note: [Col. 0246D] The Paris edition after Lipsius reads, incorrectly and contrary to the manuscripts, “the mode of musical discipline.”]. These matters our discourse has gathered into concise brevity, hastening toward the exposition of the Psalms themselves [Note: [Col. 0246D] Rufinus and the Tellerian manuscript read: “These statements suffice; now let us hasten to turn our discourse to the exposition of the Psalms themselves. But there is …” The compiler of this Rufinian commentary here failed to take sufficient care: while pretending to speak with Hilary and to hasten to the exposition of the Psalms, he nevertheless lingers over many other matters before approaching it. Thus we have above detected a second mark of spuriousness.].

> **Note [Col. 0245C–0246C]:** The Vatican manuscript reads “in the diapsalm.” The ancients disagree about the meaning of this word. Cassiodorus, in his Preface to the Psalter, ch. 2, follows Hilary’s view after Augustine, *On Psalm* IV, §4, though he knew that Jerome held an opposing opinion. Asked by Marcella about the word in Epistle CXXXVIII, Jerome says:
>
> “Some have said that *diapsalma* is a change of metre; others, a pause of the Holy Spirit; some, the beginning of another meaning; others, a division of rhythm and . . . a certain variety of music.”
>
> Euthymius explains it in much the same manner in his Preface to the Psalter: “*Diapsalma* signifies a change either of meaning or of song, or a pause, or a kind of interruption of instrumental performance, or the shining forth and illumination of the divine Spirit which then appeared to the singers; for all these things were diligently written down by them.”
>
> Jerome approves none of these opinions, chiefly because the word sometimes occurs even at the end of Psalms and, conversely, is wholly absent from several Psalms of many verses. Following Origen, whose expertise in this matter he praises, he observes that where Theodotion, Symmachus, and the Seventy translated *diapsalma*, Aquila always rendered another term. He therefore prefers to understand the word as connecting what precedes and follows, or at least as teaching that what has been said is everlasting. This single example proves what we have already observed: Hilary was by no means a mere follower of Origen.

### 24. The Key to the Psalms

Careful and well-weighed judgment [Col. 0247A] must be applied to the exposition of every individual Psalm, in order that it may be known by what key of understanding each must be opened. For the whole book is like a beautiful and great city, containing many diverse houses whose doors are shut with their own distinct keys. When the keys have been gathered and mixed together in one place, they create the greatest difficulty for one wishing to open each house, if he does not know how to find the key for each house.

It belongs either to familiar knowledge quickly to choose, from that gathered abundance of diversity, the known key; or else it requires immense labor to discover the proper and suitable key for opening each entrance. For reason and propriety do not allow keys that are not their own to be fitted to unlike locks. Therefore, by God’s mercy [Col. 0247B], as we are about to discover the key for opening each Psalm, let us open the entrance to this first Psalm with its own proper and suitable key.

> **Note [Col. 0246D–0247D]:** In the Origen on the Psalms published by Huet, vol. I, p. 39, there appears here a third example of matters which Hilary seems to have imitated from Origen:
>
> “As we are about to begin the interpretation of the Psalms, we shall set forth an excellent instruction handed down to us by a Hebrew concerning Scripture. He said that the whole divinely inspired Scripture, because of the obscurity in it, was like many dwellings enclosed within one building; that a key not suited to the particular dwelling was set at each dwelling; and that the keys had thus been scattered among the dwellings, none corresponding to the dwellings at which they were placed. It was an exceedingly difficult task to find the keys and fit them to the chambers which they could open. Thus the obscure Scriptures are understood not from arguments brought in from elsewhere, but from the mutual principles of interpretation found within them, since they contain in themselves the scattered means of their own exposition.”

## PSALM ONE

Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence. But his will was in the Law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0247D] In two manuscripts, *was* is here omitted in conformity with the Vulgate; thereafter, however, they consistently retain the word in conformity with the Greek. The readings Hilary customarily follows in explaining the Psalm will henceforth be noted in the margin.], and in his Law he shall meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters, which shall yield its fruit in its season. And its leaf [Note: [Col. 0247D] Hilary below reads, “but the leaf of this tree shall not …”] shall not fall; and all things whatsoever he does shall be rightly directed [Note: [Col. 0248D] Vatican manuscripts: “shall prosper.”]. Not so the ungodly, not so; but like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth. Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous [Col. 0247C]. For the Lord knows [Note: [Col. 0248D] Hilary: “because the Lord recognizes.”] the way of the righteous, and the path [Note: [Col. 0248D] Hilary: “way.”] of the ungodly shall perish.

## KEY, OR ENTRANCE, TO THE FIRST PSALM

### 1. One Must Consider Who Speaks to Whom in the Psalms

This is the primary principle of interpretation in the Psalms: that we must be able to discern from whose person, or concerning whom, the things said are to be understood [Note: [Col. 0248D] For *oporteat*, “must,” manuscript authority restores here *oporteant*, “must be”; similarly in *On the Trinity* II.2, *oportuissent*.]. Their composition is not uniform and undifferentiated, as though they did not possess both authors and diverse kinds [Note: [Col. 0247C] “Distinct.”].

For we find that the person of God the Father is frequently presented in them [Col. 0248A], as in the eighty-eighth Psalm, where it is said: “I have exalted one chosen from my people. I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him. He shall call upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation. And I will make him firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0247C] “My” is absent; it occurs neither in the Septuagint nor in Jerome’s commentary on Isaiah 55.]

The person of the Son is likewise introduced in very many places: as in the seventeenth Psalm, “A people whom I did not know served me”; and in the twenty-first, “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots over my clothing.”

But the matter itself plainly teaches that this first Psalm cannot be understood either in the person of the Father or in that of the Son. For it says: “But his will was in the Law of the Lord, and in his Law he shall meditate day and night.” In the Psalm in which we have noted that the Father’s person is represented, things proper and fitting to him are stated [Col. 0248B], when it says: “He shall call upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.” And in the Psalm in which the Son is shown to speak, he declares himself, from the matters which he recounts, to be the author of his own sayings: “A people whom I did not know served me.”

For while the Father says, “He shall call upon me,” and the Son says, “A people served me,” they show themselves to be those who speak concerning themselves. But now, when it is said, “But his will was in the Law of the Lord,” no person of the Lord speaking about himself is shown. Rather, another person proclaims the blessedness of the man whose will is in the Law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0248D] Bad., Er., and Lips. read: “Rather, the blessedness of another, his …,” thereafter omitting “proclaiming.” Paris reads: “Rather, by the blessedness of another … it is proclaimed.” The true reading is supplied by a Vatican manuscript, in which after “rather, another” the word “person” is easily understood.].

Therefore we must recognize here the person of the Prophet, through whose mouth the Holy Spirit speaks, instructing us through the service of his speech in the knowledge of the spiritual mystery [Note: [Col. 0248D] One Vatican manuscript reads “spiritual”; another, “instructing us in spiritual mysteries.”].

### 2. Of Whom He Speaks. Many Understand This Psalm to Concern Christ

Since he speaks these words [Note: [Col. 0247C–0248C] “And since the Holy Spirit poured into this Prophet speaks these words.”], we must inquire concerning what man we should understand him to speak. For he says:

> Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence. But his will was in the Law of the Lord, and in his Law he shall meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters, which shall yield its fruit in its season. And its leaf [Note: [Col. 0248C–0248D] “Shall not fall,” according to the Roman Psalter and more closely to the Hebrew. The same author has this reading below, §8, and elsewhere.] shall not fall; and all things whatsoever he does shall be rightly directed.

I have found many, either from their present discourse or from their letters and writings [Col. 0249A], to have thought concerning this Psalm that our Lord Jesus Christ is signified and must be understood in it, and that his blessedness is proclaimed in what follows [Note: [Col. 0249C] Origen has this view in Corderius’s *Catena of the Greek Fathers*. Commentaries attributed to Jerome, and those bearing Rufinus’s name, explain it of Christ as man, with Augustine.]. But they have taught this neither in proper manner nor by sound reasoning. Their impulse indeed proceeds from a good opinion, because all prophecy of the Psalms must be referred to him; but it is the task of rational knowledge to discern by truth where and when the discourse of prophecy itself refers to him.

### 3. It Does Not Suit the Son of God as God

The matters placed at the beginning of the Psalm do not at all suit his person and dignity; and the contents of the Psalm itself rebuke this incautious ease in so interpreting it. For when it says [Note: [Col. 0249C] The words “for when it says” are absent from the manuscript; likewise “on this account” shortly afterward.], “And his will was in the Law of the Lord,” since the Law was given through the Son of God, how can blessedness be attributed to him on the ground that his will was in the Law of the Lord, when he himself is Lord of the Law?

That the Law is his, he himself testified in the seventy-seventh Psalm, saying: “Attend, my people [Note: [Col. 0249C] “My people. Then, ‘your ears.’ The Septuagint has *to ous hymōn*, in agreement with the Hebrew.”], to my Law; incline your ears to the words of my mouth. I will open [Note: [Col. 0249C] “In a parable,” according to the Hebrew and Jerome’s translation.] my mouth in parables.” The Evangelist Matthew confirms that these words were spoken by Christ himself: “Therefore he spoke in parables, that what had been said might be fulfilled: ‘I will open my mouth in parables’” (Matt. 13:34–35) [Col. 0249B]. The Lord therefore fulfilled his own prophecy [Note: [Col. 0249C] “His own” is absent from one manuscript.] by the events themselves: for he spoke in parables, as he had promised that he would.

Further, the statement “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters”—in which the progress of blessedness is shown comparatively—how can it be adapted to his person, so that a planted tree should be more blessed than the Son of God [Col. 0249C], and he should be blessed because at some future time he attains, by progress in blessedness, its likeness [Note: [Col. 0249C] Manuscripts read “progress.”] (Prov. 8:22; Titus 1:2; Col. 1:15–16)?

Then, since according to Wisdom and the Apostle he is before the ages and before eternal times, is the firstborn of all creation, and all things were created in him and through him, how can he be blessed when he becomes like things which were established by him? The power of the Creator needs no comparison with a creature for the perfection of its blessedness; nor does the antiquity of the Firstborn permit a later temporal comparison in the phrase, “He shall be like a tree” [Col. 0250A].

For that which shall be through a time still awaited [Note: [Col. 0249C] In one manuscript *per* is absent; another has *post*, “after,” in its place. Then three manuscripts, instead of “in the nature of things,” read “to possess nature.”] cannot be regarded as either having been or already being in the nature of things. Whatever already is does not require a delay of time in order to begin becoming what it shall be [Note: [Col. 0249C] One Vatican manuscript reads thus. Bad., Er., and Lips. read, “in order that it may begin toward something.” Paris agrees, except that it omits “toward.”], since by the antiquity of its beginning it already endures.

### 4. To Whom It Does Apply

Therefore, since these things are understood to be foreign to the divinity of the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, we must suppose that this man is proclaimed blessed by the Prophet who has rendered himself, through devotion to equity and perfection in every righteousness, conformed to that body which the Lord assumed—that is, the body in which he was born as man.

And indeed a fuller exposition of the Psalm will show that this is how it must be understood.

5. How many lessons are contained in this psalm. — The Holy Spirit chose this most splendid and most worthy opening for the psalms [Col. 0250B], in order to exhort human weakness, through the hope of blessedness, to an innocent pursuit of religion; to teach the mystery of God made flesh; to promise a share in heavenly glory; to announce the punishment of judgment; to show the distinction of resurrection; and to display God’s providence in recompense. Thus, with a complete and consummate rationale, he began the sequence of so great a prophecy.

> [Note: The printed editions, except Paris, and two manuscripts read “the order of providence” [Col. 0250C]: wrongly; for here the book of psalms, distinguished from its beginning by the title of prophecy, is commended.]

So that the hope of the blessed man might draw human frailty toward zeal for faith; the blessedness of the tree, set forth in comparison with the blessedness hoped for, might promise hope’s blessedness; severity announced to the ungodly might restrain insolent impiety within fear; the ordered distinction of condition might distinguish differences of merit among the counsels of the saints; and established justice might display God’s magnificence in knowing the ways of the righteous [Col. 0250C].

> [Note: “That human frailty.” Immediately before, “the blessedness of the tree,” as P. Coustant restored it.]

> [Note: The printed editions read “the likeness of the tree.” “The blessedness of the tree” is preferable, with a Vatican manuscript.]

Now let us discuss both the matters themselves and their words.

# TREATISE ON PSALM I

## 1. The blessed man’s fivefold observance. The distinction between the ungodly and the sinner.

**VERS. 1–2.** “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence. But his will was in the law of the Lord, and on his law he shall meditate day and night.”

The Prophet declares that five kinds of observance belong to the blessed man: first, not going in the counsel of the ungodly; second, not standing in the way of sinners; third, not sitting in the seat of pestilence [Col. 0251A]; then placing one’s will in the law of the Lord; and finally meditating upon it day and night.

> [Note: Our manuscript consistently reads “in the counsel.” Then: “not going,” “not standing,” afterward “not sitting,” and “meditating.”]

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “not going,” and thereafter “not standing,” “not sitting,” “not meditating.” But here and in what follows the printed editions consistently prefer “into the counsel of the ungodly,” although both the Greek and Latin sacred text disagree, and the manuscripts scarcely agree with them even in one place. Moreover, Hilary’s interpretation requires “in the counsel”: he maintains that the ungodly never stand still, but, once they have seized upon counsels, quickly proceed farther; “a place for standing in those counsels is never found,” he says at the end of section 2.]

Therefore it is necessary to distinguish the ungodly person from the sinner, and the sinner from the pestilent person; especially since the ungodly have a counsel, the sinner a way, and the pestilent person a seat; and since one goes, rather than stands, in the counsel of the ungodly, whereas one stands, rather than goes, in the sinner’s way. To understand the reasons for these things, we must discern how greatly the sinner differs from the ungodly, so that we may thereby understand why a way is assigned to the sinner and counsel to the ungodly; then why one must stand in the way and go in the counsel, although ordinary human usage decides that one should stand in counsel and walk in a way.

> [Note: This confirms the reading “in the counsel,” which we prefer to the common “into the counsel.” What Hilary adds concerning the difference between sinner and ungodly person is expressed in nearly the same manner in Jerome, *Against the Pelagians*, book I, where the ungodly person is defined as one who either never had faith or lost it through heresy: “For ungodliness properly belongs to those who do not know God, or who have changed the knowledge once acquired through transgression.”]

Not everyone who is a sinner is also ungodly; but the ungodly person cannot fail to be a sinner. Let us take an example from common moral awareness. Children may love their parents, even though they are drunken, lustful, and prodigal; amid these vices they lack not guilt, but they do lack ungodliness. Yet the ungodly, even if they excel in the chief virtues of self-restraint and frugality, surpass every other crime besides ungodliness in insulting their parent.

## 2. The ungodly are atheists.

Accordingly, on the basis of this illustrative example, there is no doubt that the ungodly are distinguishable from sinners. Common human judgment, by nature itself, shows that those are ungodly who disdain to seek knowledge of God; who irreligiously suppose that there is no Creator of the world; who assert that the world came into its present condition and adornment through chance movements; and who, so that no judgment may await them from their Creator for a life lived either rightly or wickedly [Col. 0251C], wish to be born by natural necessity and to be dissolved again by the same necessity.

All their counsel, therefore, is shifting, uncertain, and wandering; it is carried along in and through the same things, without any station in which to stand.

> [Note: It proceeds with no basis for standing.]

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “it proceeds with no basis for standing”; and a little earlier, with the Baden and other editions, “and empty,” rather than “and wandering.”]

For it does not maintain the limit of any definition. Their discourse has not dared to teach that the world has a Creator. For when you ask why the world exists, when it exists, and to what extent; whether the world exists for humanity or humanity for the world; and why death exists, or how long it lasts, or what it is like: their counsels of ungodliness are forever occupied with these questions, and move onward, since no place for standing can be found in such counsels.

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts and older editions. But the Paris edition reads “and escapes”; this reading may be tolerated, so that it signifies what follows below: “they evade the very conclusion of the argument under discussion” [Col. 0252D]. Yet Hilary consistently used above the verb “to go,” to which this “goes” corresponds, not “to depart”; although below he has “has not gone” once.]

## 3. Nor do heretics stand.

There are also other counsels of the ungodly: namely, of those who have fallen into heresy and are held by the laws neither of the New nor of the Old Testament. Their discourse, bent always into the circuit and circle [Col. 0252A] of error, holding nothing and standing upon nothing, is tossed back and forth in the course and recurrence of an indefinite opinion.

> [Note: This applies especially to the Arians, concerning whom, in *To Constantius*, book II, section 4, it is said: “They have brought upon the world the circle of everlasting error and of controversy returning upon itself.” See the remainder of that work, and *To Constantius*, section 23.]

Their ungodliness consists in measuring God, not by God’s own self-disclosure, but by the will of their own judgment. They do not know that it is no less ungodly to invent God than to deny him. When you ask them to what end of hope and faith they hold such opinions, they are confused, disturbed, evasive, wandering about; and they avoid the very conclusion of the argument under discussion.

> [Note: “Their ungodliness consists in …”]

Blessed, therefore, is the man who has not gone in this counsel of the ungodly; that is, who has not admitted even the will to go in that counsel. For to have even thought what is ungodly is already a crime.

## 4. The way of sinners, in which one must not stand.

It follows that one who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly [Col. 0252B] must also not stand in the way of sinners.

> [Note: This passage is cited by Augustine, *Against Julian*, book II, chapter 7.]

For many people, though separated from ungodliness by their confession of God, are nevertheless not thereby free from sin. They remain indeed in the Church, but do not keep the discipline of the Church: such as the greedy, drunkards, quarrelsome persons, shameless people, the proud, hypocrites, liars, and robbers. Our natural impulse drives us toward these vices; but just as it is beneficial to leave the way to which we are carried, so also we must not stand there, but turn back from it without delaying our departure.

> [Note: The printed editions read “by which we are carried.” One Vatican manuscript reads “when we turn back”; another, “by which we are borne along.” With a third, older manuscript we restore “to which we are carried,” namely by the impulse of our nature.]

And therefore blessed is the man who has not stood in the way of sinners: nature indeed carrying him into this way, but religious faith bringing him back from it.

## 5. The seat of pestilence.

The third stage in attaining blessedness [Col. 0252C] is not to sit in the seat of pestilence. The Pharisees sat in Moses’ seat while teaching; Pilate also sat on the judgment seat. Which seat, then, shall we judge pestilent? Certainly not Moses’ seat: the Lord condemns those who sit there rather than the seat itself, when he says: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat in Moses’ seat; therefore do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:2). The sitting of this seat is not pestilent, since obedience to it is commanded by the Lord’s authority.

That seat, therefore, will be pestilent whose contagion Pilate avoids by washing his hands. For ambition for secular honors corrupts many who are even established in the fear of God; and, though subject to the laws of the Church, they wish to judge according to the laws of the forum.

> [Note: Those subject to the laws of the Church are here understood to be those described above in section 4 as “remaining indeed in the Church, but not keeping the discipline of the Church”: namely, all Christians. Below, “in the holiness of ecclesiastical law” likewise means “in the holiness of evangelical law.” Hence, in section 6, a “secular man” is one not yet numbered among the Church’s members through baptism. This should be noted lest anyone suppose these remarks concern only ecclesiastics and not secular judges also. Erasmus’s marginal note is therefore unsatisfactory: “Secular business is dangerous for clergy and good people,” as though clergy had been expressly named.]

Although, in the very offices which they discharge, they bring with them a religious intention, showing themselves benevolent and self-restrained, nevertheless they must be defiled by a certain pestilent contagion of the business in which they engage. For the course of public cases does not permit them, even when willing, to remain in the holiness of ecclesiastical law.

> [Note: “Them” is absent.]

And although they hold firmly to their religious purpose, nevertheless, by the necessity of the office they have obtained, they are compelled—albeit with reluctance of will—to inflict insult, injury, and punishment.

> [Note: “Although with a reluctant will they undertake these things, and necessity makes them …”]

> [Note: One manuscript reads “although with so great a will”; another, “although with a reluctant will they undertake these things.” The word “necessity,” lacking in the printed editions, has been restored from the manuscripts.]

Necessity makes them participants in necessity itself, as they are imbued with it as with a diseased contagion. Therefore the Prophet calls their seat the seat of pestilence, because by its contagion it infects even the will of a religious mind.

> [Note: We add “even” from the manuscripts; shortly before, they read “in which,” not “because.”]

## 6. God’s law must be obeyed by will, not fear.

Yet the blessedness of the man is not completed merely by his not having gone in the counsel of the ungodly, not having stood in the way of sinners, or not having sat in the seat of pestilence [Col. 0253B].

> [Note: “Not having gone.”]

For these things can also be found in a secular man: he may believe that one God is Creator of the world; he may restrain himself from sins through the pursuit of modest innocence; he may prefer the leisure of a private and quiet life to the dignities of office.

> [Note: “Leisure.”]

But now the Prophet, fashioning the perfect man for God and setting him as an example in the great matters of eternal blessedness, teaches that he is not to employ common virtues for this purpose, but must be made perfect—if he is to be blessed—by what follows: “But his will was in the law of the Lord.”

> [Note: “Supports.”]

> [Note: One manuscript reads “supports.”]

Abstaining from the foregoing things is useless unless earnest intention is added in what follows: namely, that one’s will be in the law of the Lord [Col. 0253C]. The Prophet does not require fear. Fear holds many within the law, but will establishes few in the law; for it belongs to fear not to dare neglect what is fearful, whereas it belongs to perfect religion willingly to obey what is prescribed. Therefore blessed is the man whose relation to God’s law is not fear but will.

> [Note: Here our manuscript inserts “for.”]

## 7. God’s law must be meditated upon night and day; how this can be done.

Yet something is sometimes lacking even to will, and merely willing does not attain perfect blessedness unless action follows will. It follows: “And [Col. 0254A] on his law he shall meditate day and night.” Continuous and unwearied meditation on the law makes this man blessed. But perhaps the nature of human weakness does not permit this: by that nature we must rest, sleep, and attend to food. Must we therefore fall from the hope of attaining blessedness even because of the necessity of natural functions, since we must sometimes cease from day-and-night meditation through bodily business?

The Apostle uttered a similar saying: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17).

> [Note: Here the following words are inserted.]

> [Note: Thus according to our manuscript and one Vatican manuscript; the earlier edition reads “praying.”]

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript, in accordance with our copies of the sacred text, reads “pray.” Then the Baden, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions read, “as though our nature could not recover its strength.” The earlier edition reads “praying.”]

As though the necessity of our nature, which must attend to its own concerns, could always pray without any interruption of time. Meditation on the law, therefore, is not only in reading words, but also in the religious character of one’s conduct. It does not mean merely reviewing books and Scriptures, but meditating through deeds and actions upon what is contained in the Scriptures and books, so that the works of day and night may always put the law into practice [Col. 0254B].

> [Note: The Baden and Erasmus editions, with the Micy manuscript, read “is of reading.” The Leipzig and Paris editions, with other manuscripts, read “of the reader.” From both readings we establish “is in things read,” as the sense requires.]

> [Note: The first Paris edition reads “that we may always be exercised through the law.” The last retained “that we may be exercised,” deleting “through.” The earlier Leipzig edition substituted “that we may exercise” for “they exercise,” against the Baden and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts.]

Thus the Apostle says: “Whatever you do, do all to the glory of God, whether you eat or drink or do anything else” (1 Cor. 10:31).

> [Note: “You do.”]

This enables us to pray without ceasing: through works pleasing to God and always performed to his glory, the whole life of every holy man becomes prayer; and thus, by living according to the law night and day, life itself will be the law’s nocturnal and diurnal meditation.

> [Note: The previous edition reads “becomes.”]

## 8.

But once the perfect blessedness of this man has been shown—who, abstaining from the counsels of the ungodly, the ways of sinners, and the seat of pestilence, willingly meditates upon God’s law day and night—it must be explained how great will be the fruit of this blessedness which he has gained. For to wish to be blessed proceeds from the expectation of blessedness itself. It follows, therefore:

**VERS. 3.** “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall give its fruit in its season; and its leaf shall not fall.”

> [Note: Elsewhere the reading differs.]

Perhaps this example of comparative blessedness will be considered ridiculous and absurd: the planting of a tree, watercourses, the giving of fruits, its own season, and a leaf that does not fall are proclaimed. According to worldly people, perhaps these things will be considered of no importance. But let us see, according to prophetic teaching [Col. 0255A], how great a glory of the blessedness being compared is placed in these very things and words.

## 9. The tree is Christ.

In Genesis 2:9–10, where the lawgiver shows that paradise was planted by God, he also declares that every tree beautiful in appearance and good for food was produced; that in the middle of paradise there was the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; and that paradise was watered by a river later divided into four heads.

> [Note: The common editions read “for use.” Better is the reading of one Vatican manuscript, “for food,” supported by Genesis, where it is called good “for eating,” not “for use.”]

What this tree of life was, the prophet Solomon taught, saying of the honoring of Wisdom: “She is a tree of life to all who embrace her, and to those who lean upon her as upon the Lord” (Prov. 3:18).

> [Note: The Verona manuscript, with a Vatican manuscript, reads “of Wisdom” and omits the following words, “as upon the Lord.”]

> [Note: Of the Vatican manuscripts, one reads “of Wisdom”; another, “of the honoring of Wisdom.” Perhaps “of the honoring” should be read, especially since just above Wisdom is mentioned in Greek: *παν δὲ τίμιον οὐκ ἄξιον αὐτῆς ἐστι*—“nothing precious is worthy of her.” In one manuscript the words “as upon the Lord,” which belong to the Septuagint, are lacking. Incidentally, we observe that here and elsewhere Hilary calls Solomon a prophet. Thus Eusebius of Caesarea’s futile and empty reproach in *Against Marcellus*, book I, chapter 2, is invalid: he criticizes Hilary for calling Solomon himself a prophet and Proverbs prophecies, since, Eusebius says, Solomon received the gift of wisdom, not prophecy, and did not lead a prophetic life such as we read of prophets going about clothed in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, oppressed, and afflicted. If that argument were valid, the title of prophet would have to be taken even from the Psalmist. The Verona manuscript, with the Vatican manuscript, reads “of Wisdom” and omits the following words, “as upon the Lord.”]

This tree, then, is living; and not merely living, but also rational. It is rational to such a degree that it gives fruit; and it gives not indiscriminately or inappropriately, but in its own season [Col. 0255B]. This tree is planted beside streams of water—that is, in possession of God’s kingdom, in paradise, where the river flowing forth is divided into four heads. For it does not say, “after the streams of water,” but “beside the streams of water,” from which the divisions first receive their flow.

There this tree is planted, where the Lord, who is Wisdom, introduced that thief who confessed him as Lord, saying: “Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). And since we have shown from prophetic authority that Wisdom, who is Christ, is called the tree of life on account of the mystery of his future embodiment and passion, the appropriateness of this interpretation must also be established from the Gospels. The Lord himself compared himself to a tree when the Jews said that he cast out demons by Beelzebub: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for a tree is known by its fruit” (Matt. 12:24). Since casting out demons was the very best fruit, they said that he was Beelzebub, whose fruits are most evil.

Nor did he disdain to teach, in reference to himself, the power of comparison with this blessed tree, when, going [Col. 0256A] to the cross, he said: “For if they do these things in the green tree, what will happen in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). By the illustration of the green tree he indicated that there was in himself nothing subject to the dryness of death.

> [Note: “He did not disdain the comparison,” followed continuously by “when going,” etc., as in one Vatican manuscript.]

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “he did not disdain the comparison when going,” etc.]

## 10. The blessed man is like Christ.

The blessed man, therefore, will become like this tree when, in the manner of the thief translated into paradise, he too is planted beside streams of water. Then there shall be that blessed and unuprootable new planting which the Lord signifies in the Gospels, when he complains of an alien planting, saying: “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13).

> [Note: The word “heavenly” is lacking. But perhaps this is not due to a copyist’s carelessness: in one excellent Bodleian Library manuscript at Oxford [Col. 0256C], the name *ὁ οὐράνιος* (“the heavenly”) is absent.]

This tree, then, will give its fruits. Whenever divine discourse indicates anything about the fruits of trees, it speaks of their making rather than giving fruit, as when it says: “A good tree cannot make bad fruit” (Matt. 7:18); and when, according to Isaiah, there is complaint concerning the vineyard: “I expected it to make grapes, but it made thorns” (Isa. 5:2). This tree, therefore, will give its fruits, governed by the choice and reason of giving.

> [Note: This is what he said in section 9: the tree is living, and not only living but rational; rational indeed to such a degree that it gives fruit. In this freedom of giving he especially locates rational nature.]

For it will give them in its own season. And at what season? Surely the season of which the blessed Apostle speaks, so that he might make known to you “the mystery of his will, according to the good pleasure which he purposed in him, for the dispensation of the fullness of times” (Eph. 1:9).

> [Note: The Baden and Erasmus editions read “to make known to you”; the other printed editions, “I make known to you.” Another Vatican manuscript reads, “he wished to make known to you.” We follow a better Vatican manuscript, which agrees more closely with the sacred text.]

This, then, is the time of the dispensation, in which the opportunity both to receive and to give is regulated: when it will be the proper time for those to receive to whom it gives.

> [Note: “For” is added. Then “will be given” is read instead of “will give.”]

But the delay of time depends upon the fullness of times. For the dispensation of giving fruit is reserved for the fullness of times. What, then, is this fruit to be dispensed? Surely that of which the same Apostle speaks: “And he will transform the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21).

> [Note: “Conformed to the body of his glory,” according to the Greek text: *σύμμορφον τῷ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ*—“conformed to the body of his glory.”]

> [Note: Here the Vatican manuscripts disagree: one has “transformed,” etc.; another, “conformed to the body of his glory”; a third, “made conformable to the body of his glory.” See *On the Trinity*, book XI, section 35, from which and many other places it is clear that Hilary does not always cite the same scriptural passages in the same form.]

He will give us, therefore, those fruits which he has already perfected in the humanity he assumed, and which is signified in the tree, transferring it into the nature of his immortality after mortality had been absorbed. Thus the blessed man will be as this tree [Col. 0257A], when he himself stands conformed to his Lord in the glory of God.

## 11. The leaves are God’s words.

But the leaf of this tree shall not fall. Nor is it surprising that its leaves do not fall, since its fruits are to be given rather than fall: not knocked down by ripeness, not shaken off by external force, but gathered by the dispensation of a rational office.

> [Note: The common editions read “measured.” Two Vatican manuscripts read “gathered,” from which we judged that “gathered” should be restored.]

What is signified by the leaves is made clear by comparison with bodily things. We see that the nature of leaves is to spring forth around fruits in order to protect them, surrounding the tender beginnings of apples with a kind of enclosure. The teaching of God’s words, therefore, which clothes the fruits promised to us, is signified in the leaves. By these words the hopes set before us are shaded; amid the storms of this age they are covered by the protection of these words [Col. 0257B].

These leaves, therefore—that is, God’s words—will not fall; because the Lord said: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). Nothing of what God has said will slip away or fall.

> [Note: Here and shortly afterward, “shall pass away” is read instead of “shall pass.”]

## 12. The usefulness of these leaves.

That these leaves of this tree are not useless but salutary for the nations is attested by Saint John in the Apocalypse:

“And he showed me a river [of the water of life], bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb, in the middle of its street; and on either side of the river, the tree of life, which produces fruit twelve times, yielding its fruit each month; and the leaves of that tree are for the healing of the nations” (Rev. 22:1).

> [Note: The printed editions read “living water,” contrary to the manuscripts and the sacred text.]

The heavenly—that is, spiritual—mystery is explained through bodily forms in such a way that those bodily forms, although unable to fulfill the spiritual meaning [Col. 0257C], nevertheless do not mutilate it when applied to bodies.

> [Note: Erasmus conjecturally wrote in the margin, “are not useless for comparison,” which Leipzig thereafter adopted; but this is contrary to Hilary’s meaning. He intends that, insofar as we can grasp them, spiritual things are so shadowed forth in Scripture by bodily things that these cannot be referred to bodies except inappropriately, because something necessary is lacking for their genuinely fitting bodily application. This can be confirmed from *On Matthew*, chapter 21, section 13, where the holy Doctor teaches that sometimes something is lacking, on that condition, from the rationale of sensible and present things, so that they may lead us without any loss to the understanding of spiritual and future things. Therefore, although defective, we prefer the reading of the Micy manuscript, supported by three Vatican manuscripts, in which it reads, “they do not mutilate when applied to bodily things,” as also in the Baden edition and Erasmus’s text. If we were permitted to add something of our own, we would restore it thus: “Yet, in relation to bodies, they are not defective”; or, “yet in relation to bodies they are so defective that in relation to spiritual things they are not defective.” Moreover, for Donatus, *mutilare* means to remove something without which a thing cannot exist. In Cicero’s *Orator*, “mutilated” and “gaping” are synonymous.]

It would have been appropriate to say that there are trees on either side of the river shown, rather than “the tree.” But because the tree of life is everywhere one in the mystery of baptism, furnishing the fruits of apostolic preaching to those who come to it from every direction, one tree of life stands on either side of the river.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “living from itself.”]

For one Lamb is seen upon God’s throne, one river, and one tree of life. All these contain within themselves the mysteries of embodiment, baptism, and passion. Its leaves—that is, the words of preaching—confer salvation upon the nations through the teaching of a word that does not fall away.

## 13. The endowments of eternal glory.

“And whatever he does,” he says, “shall prosper” [Col. 0258A].

> [Note: Here and below, “shall prosper.”]

> [Note: The manuscripts read “shall prosper”; the Micy manuscript also has this below in place of “shall be prosperously directed.”]

Now, unlike in Adam, his gift and established condition will not be disturbed. Adam lost the blessedness of the immortality established for him through the sin of transgressing the law. But through the redemption of the tree of life—that is, the Lord’s passion—when we become like the tree of life itself, whatever comes about in us will henceforth be eternal; and eternal with the consciousness of blessedness.

All that is done will prosperously be directed: not through uncertain change, nor in a weak nature, when incorruption has absorbed corruption, eternity weakness, and the form of God the form of earthly flesh.

> [Note: “Has absorbed.”]

The blessed man, therefore, will be like this planted tree, which in its own season gives these fruits of its own; he too will be planted in paradise, so that God’s planting may remain unuprootable [Col. 0258B], and in him everything done by God may prosperously be directed, never again to be uprooted by any change—whether of our weakness or of time.

## 14. What body the ungodly will have after judgment.

Once the perfect blessedness of this man had been demonstrated, it followed that the punishment awaiting the ungodly should be shown. For it continues:

**VERS. 4.** “Not so the ungodly, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth.”

No hope of this comparative blessedness remains for the ungodly.
