Rather, there remains for them a wandering, crushed, winnowed, scattered, and restless bone—or body—so that, shaken from the firmness of bodily solidity, they may be assigned to punishment as the sport of dust. They are not dissolved into nothing, so that there may be matter for punishment in them; but they are ground into an empty, light, and dry condition, so that they may be tossed about in the mocking mobility of punishment.

> [Note: The Baden, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions, with the Micy manuscript, read “a wandering bone”: wrongly. Here the bones or bodies of the blessed are compared with the bones of the ungodly.]

The same Prophet mentions this punishment elsewhere: “I shall crush them like dust before the wind; I shall destroy them like the mud of the streets” (Ps. 17:43). Thus a comparison is established both of blessedness and of punishment. For just as the wind has no difficulty scattering dust, and just as those walking in streets scarcely feel that they have trodden on mud, so the punishment of hell easily destroys and scatters the ungodly. The logic of sins has both dissolved them into mud and ground them into dust, leaving no substance of firmness, since they are dust and mud; and precisely as dust and mud they are preserved only in the nature of a substance for punishment.

> [Note: “Almost” is absent.]

## 15. The ungodly will rise, but not for judgment.

And because, through this transformation of firmness crushed into dust, they will not share in the good which in its season will be given to the blessed man from the fruit of the tree, he accordingly adds:

**VERS. 5.** “Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment.”

By their not rising, annihilation is not announced for those who will nevertheless be dust; rather, resurrection for judgment is denied them.

> [Note: “They shall not rise.”]

> [Note: Here and in what follows, the Verona manuscript joins “in judgment” to the verb “to rise.”]

For they will not lack awareness of punishment by not existing, because what will escape punishment is that which will not endure for punishment. Yet they will endure because they will be dust.

> [Note: The printed editions read “who will be.” Two manuscripts read more explicitly, “because they will be.” Shortly above, “will make punishment a gain” means “will gain escape from punishment”; Pliny uses *lucrifacere iniuriam* in the same sense.]

To become dust through dryness or crushing is not to have lost the nature of subsistence, but to have entered another nature. But by their not rising in judgment it is made clear that they have not lacked the nature of rising, but have lost the order of rising for judgment.

What this order of resurrection and judgment is, the Lord shows in the Gospel when he says: “Whoever believes in me is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged. And this is judgment: that light came into this world, and people loved darkness more than light” (John 3:18–19).

## 16. If neither believers nor unbelievers are judged, who then are to be judged?

The Lord’s saying perplexes the negligent hearing of listeners and the careless indifference of readers.

> [Note: “Negligent hearing, and the uninquiring carelessness of the negligent” [Col. 0260D].]

For when he says, “Whoever believes in me shall not be judged,” he exempts believers from judgment; and when he adds, “Whoever does not believe has already been judged,” he does not admit unbelievers to judgment. Therefore, if he has exempted believers and rejected unbelievers, allowing neither group the lot of judgment, how can he be thought consistent with himself when he says this third thing: “And this is judgment: that light came into the world, and people loved darkness more than light”?

> [Note: “In” is omitted.]

For no place can be left for judgment if neither unbelievers nor believers are to be judged.

> [Note: The Paris edition reads “a place appears to be left for judgment.” The other printed editions read “a place appears to be left remaining for judgment.” Hilary’s view concerning judgment has been discussed in the Preface.]

To negligent hearers and careless readers, these things will indeed seem to be so. Yet the force of the words themselves contains within it the precise sense and understanding of the statement.

### 17. Those who are, as it were, midway between the godly and the ungodly

“He who believes,” he says, “shall not be judged.” For what need is there to judge the believer? Judgment arises from matters that are uncertain; when uncertainty has been removed, the examination of judgment is not required. Hence even unbelievers need not be judged, since there remains no uncertainty that they are unbelievers. But, judgment having been removed from believers and unbelievers, the Lord added both the cause of judgment and those authors upon whom judgment must necessarily be passed.

For there are some who stand midway between the ungodly and the godly, mixed from both, yet properly belonging to neither, because they have taken their position from both: they are not to be counted among the faithful, because some unbelief has been inserted into them [Note: Lipsius and Paris read “weakness,” against the other books.]; nor are they to be reckoned among the unbelieving, because they possess something of faith also. For the fear of God keeps many within the Church; yet the allurements of the world draw these same persons toward worldly vices. They pray, because they fear; they sin, because they wish to. They call themselves Christians, because the hope of eternity is good; they act as Gentiles, because present things are alluring. They do not remain ungodly, because God’s name is held in honor by them; they are not godly, because they pursue what is foreign to godliness. And they must necessarily love more those things through which they cannot be what they call themselves, according to the stronger inclination of their works rather than the inclination implied in their name.

Therefore, after the Lord had said that believers are not to be judged and that unbelievers have already been judged, he added: “And this is the judgment: because the light came into the world, and men loved darkness more than light.” Judgment, then, falls upon those persons for whom it has already been effected in the unbelieving, and is unnecessary in believers: because they loved darkness more than light. Not that they did not also love the light, but because their love of darkness was more strongly inclined. For love is commonly preferred to love by comparison. And herein lies judgment: although they loved Christ, they nevertheless loved darkness more. These, therefore, will be judged: those who neither, as godly persons, will not be judged, nor, as ungodly persons, have already been judged; upon whom judgment falls because of their more strongly preferred love. [Note: Judgment lies upon them. And this indeed.]

### 18. The ungodly will not be judged, but sinners will

The prophet also grasped the logic of this evangelical arrangement, saying: “Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous.” He leaves no judgment for the ungodly, because they have already been judged; but he denies to sinners—the persons whom in the preceding discussion we taught to be distinguished from the ungodly—the counsel of the righteous, because they are to be judged. Ungodliness makes the former already condemned beforehand; sin holds the latter for judgment. Thus neither ungodliness, which has already been judged, is consigned to the judgment of sinners; nor are sinners, who are to be judged, worthy by merit to belong to the counsel of the righteous, who will not be judged.

### 19. How God knows or does not know

And the order of this distinction proceeds from this point.

**Verse 6.** “For the Lord,” he says, “knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly shall perish.” Sinners therefore do not enter the counsel of the righteous because the Lord knows the way of the righteous. But he knows, not by a knowledge that presupposes ignorance [Note: Or, a knowledge which supposes ignorance to have preceded it; see *On the Trinity*, book IX, §62.], but by the condescension of recognition. For this is not in God a change of human affections, so that he either knows something or does not know it.

The blessed Apostle Paul explained on what principle we are known by God, saying: “If anyone among you is a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I write to you are the Lord’s; but if anyone does not acknowledge them, he shall not be acknowledged” (1 Cor. 14:38–39). Thus he shows that those are known by God who have known the things that are God’s: receiving recognition when they have come to know them, that is, obtaining the favor of divine recognition through the merit of the religion they have recognized. Thus what is known is to be understood as the advancement, not of one who had been ignorant, but of the person known.

The Lord plainly shows in Adam and Abraham that he does not know sinners, but knows the faithful. For after Adam’s sin it was said: “Where are you, Adam?” (Gen. 3:9). This was not because God did not know that he was in paradise, when he still had him in paradise; but because, in being asked where he was, Adam was shown to be unworthy of God’s recognition because of his sin.

But Abraham, long unrecognized—though God’s word had already come to him when he was seventy years old—after proving himself faithful to the Lord by offering Isaac, is received into the intimacy of God by this declaration of favor: “Now I know that you fear the Lord your God, and have not spared your beloved son for my sake” (Gen. 22:12). Certainly God did not fail to know Abraham’s faith, which he had credited to him as righteousness when Abraham believed him concerning Isaac’s birth. But because Abraham had given a great proof of his fear by offering his son, he is now known, now approved, now worthy not to be unrecognized.

Thus God both recognizes and does not know: Adam the sinner is not known, and Abraham the faithful is recognized—being worthy, that is, to be known by God, who surely is ignorant of nothing. Therefore the way of the righteous, who are not to be judged, is known by God; and for this reason sinners, who are to be judged, are excluded from their counsel. But the ungodly shall not rise for judgment, since their way has perished and they have already been judged by him who says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Psalm II. Without a title among the Hebrews

“Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things? The kings of the earth stood ready, and the rulers assembled together, against the Lord and against his Christ. Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us. He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them. Then he shall speak to them in his wrath, and [Note: Hilary: “in his indignation.”] trouble them in his fury. But I have been established king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, [Note: Hilary: “proclaiming.”] declaring his commandment. The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ Ask [Note: Hilary: “Request.”] of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall rule them with a rod of iron and break them like a potter’s vessel. And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Embrace instruction, lest perhaps the Lord be angry and you perish from the righteous way. When his wrath has blazed forth in a short time, blessed are all who trust in him.”

## Treatise on Psalm II

The apostolic authority leaves many of us uncertain whether this psalm is to be thought continuous with the first and, as it were, the conclusion of the first [Note: Thus the better manuscripts. The printed editions have “the end.” Georgius, who is sometimes also called Gennadius, says in Corderius’s *Catena of the Greek Fathers*: “Having obtained two Hebrew copies, we found in one that this was the beginning of the second psalm, but in the other that it was joined to the first.” Yet it should be understood that no Hebrew copy has a number appended to the Psalms. The paraphrast in the same Corderius says: “It should be known that among the Hebrews the first and second psalms are not separate, but joined.” Jerome likewise agrees in the Vulgate on Psalm 1. Justin Martyr, in his *Second Apology*, copies both in one continuous sequence, as though they were one psalm. The psalm now called second is called first by Petilianus in Augustine, *Against the Letter of Petilian*, book II, ch. 92, §202.]; or whether it should instead be counted as the following, and second, psalm.

For in the Acts of the Apostles we are taught, in the prayer of blessed Paul, that it is regarded as the first: “And we preach to you the promise made to the fathers: this God has fulfilled to your children [Note: “Our children.”], raising our Lord Jesus, as it is written in the first psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you,’ when he raised him from the dead, no longer to return to corruption.” [Note: In some Greek copies one reads τῷ πρώτῳ, “in the first”; in others, τῷ δευτέρῳ, “in the second.” The Vulgate Jerome on Psalm 2, Oecumenius on Acts, Bede, and others, read τῷ πρώτῳ after Hilary.] Because of this apostolic authority, it is believed that through an error of copyists this psalm is numbered second in the sequence, though it is known to be first on the testimony of the teacher of the Gentiles himself. We must therefore discover why it should be understood by us as second, while the Apostle has shown it to be first.

### 2. The seventy elders and the Hebrew Scriptures

In the middle period of the Law [Note: About 300 years before Christ.], before the only-begotten Son of God, God the Word who existed before the ages, was born as man, seventy elders, at King Ptolemy’s request, translated the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew letters into Greek. Now Moses had earlier established that there should be seventy teachers in every synagogue. For Moses himself, although he had committed the words of the Old Testament [Note: Manuscript of Marmoutier: “had committed the words of the Testament to writing.”] to writing, nevertheless privately disclosed to the seventy elders, who were thereafter to remain teachers, certain more secret mysteries drawn from the hidden recesses of the Law.

The Lord also refers to this teaching in the Gospels, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore observe and do whatever they tell you; but do not act according to their deeds.” Thus their teaching [Note: Lipsius deleted the word “remained”; we restore it from the editions of Baduel, Erasmus, and the manuscripts.] remained for posterity, having been received from the author of the Law himself and preserved in the number and office of the elders.

Accordingly, when these elders translated the books, and had attained, according to Moses’ tradition, a spiritual knowledge of hidden meanings, they rendered the ambiguous utterances of the Hebrew language, and certain expressions carrying various meanings in themselves, according to the force of the matters concerned, in fixed and proper significations of words—moderating that manifold understanding of expressions by their learned knowledge. [Note: In one manuscript: “tempering that manifold understanding of expressions with knowledge of the teaching,” less elegantly. Compare Psalm 142, §1: “But for them the knowledge of the Law and prophets extended beyond the prescribed limits and ambiguity of the letter.” Hilary attributes this knowledge to tradition; others, to the prophetic Spirit. Thus Augustine does not hesitate to say, *Harmony of the Gospels*, II.66, that the Seventy translated in the same Spirit in which the sayings they translated had been spoken; and, in *Questions on Genesis* 169, not under the servitude of translation but with the authority of prophecy. For, he says, *City of God*, XV.23.3, the Seventy interpreters are rightly believed to have received the prophetic Spirit, so that if by its authority they altered anything and expressed otherwise what they were translating, this too would not be doubted to have been divinely spoken. Jerome also supports this view, asserting in his preface to *Chronicles* that they were filled with the Holy Spirit.]

From this it happened that those who translated later, interpreting in different ways, brought great error to the nations: ignorant of that hidden tradition proceeding from Moses, they themselves published, according to their own uncertain judgments, matters ambiguously expressed in the Hebrew language.

We shall give one example of the ambiguity of Hebrew speech, from which it may be understood that other instances of this sort are of the same character and are to be understood accordingly. *Bresith* is a Hebrew word. It has three meanings in itself: “in the beginning,” “in the head,” and [Note: Jerome seems to refer to this passage of Hilary when he says in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: “Many suppose, as is written in the dispute of Jason and Papiscus, as Tertullian argues in his book *Against Praxeas*, and as Hilary affirms in his exposition of a certain psalm, that the Hebrew reads: ‘In the Son God made heaven and earth.’ The truth of the matter proves this false. For the Seventy interpreters, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated ‘in the beginning’; and in Hebrew it is written *Beresith*, which Aquila translates ‘in the head,’ not *Beben*, which means ‘in the Son.’ It is therefore about Christ according to the sense rather than according to the translation of the word.” Yet Hilary asserts that “in the Son” is found in Hebrew in such a way that he neither adheres to this interpretation himself nor thinks it ought to be adhered to. We note incidentally that this statement is nowhere found in Tertullian’s *Against Praxeas*, though in §5 he says of Praxeas’s followers: “They do indeed say that Genesis begins thus in Hebrew: ‘In the beginning God made for himself a Son’; but other arguments persuade me that this is not established.” Although we readily concede that Tertullian’s passage should be corrected from Jerome. Tertullian himself commonly reads “in the first beginning”; and in *Against Hermogenes*, §20, according to the force of the Greek word, allows it to be read “in rule and power.”] “in the Son.” Yet the seventy translators rendered it “in the beginning,” while the others translated it differently; and from this ambiguity arose, in all their translation, this confusion.

### 3. The authority of the Seventy interpreters

But the authority of these seventy interpreters remains complete. [Note: Opposite this word Erasmus wrote: “Jerome thinks otherwise.” Yet Jerome himself acknowledges, in Letter 101 to Pammachius, that the Septuagint version prevailed in the churches, whether because it was first and preceded Christ’s coming, or because it was used by the Apostles. Irenaeus likewise highly commends its authority, *Against Heresies*, III.24, because it was produced by Jews themselves long before the coming of our Lord, leaving no suspicion that the Jews, in order to accommodate us, had translated it thus. Chrysostom also values it highly, *Homilies on Matthew*, V, because so many translators, arriving together to translate before the Lord’s coming, are freed from every suspicion. To conclude this note with Jerome’s words: he doubtless had this in view when, in the preface to the four Gospels, he says that after the Seventy nothing in the sacred Scriptures can be altered or corrupted without all fraud and deceit being exposed by their translation.]

First, because they translated before the Lord’s bodily advent, their translation cannot be accused of flattery adapted to its time, since it belongs to an age so much earlier. Secondly, because these very men were leaders and teachers of the synagogue, and, beyond their knowledge of the Law, had also been perfected by Moses’ more secret teaching, they could not fail to be credible judges of translation: they who were the most certain and weighty authorities for teaching.

Thus, in translating the Psalms among the other books, they reduced them to number, arranged them in order, and divided them with *diapsalmata*, though among the Hebrews they all were and remain undivided and confused. Their translations, therefore, were not necessary for the Hebrews at that time, who used only their own language. Yet after all these things had been preserved with diligent and reverent care [Note: Erasmus again rather unwisely says here, “The fable of the seventy cells,” although no mention of cells is made. But even if something is lacking here—which we could not restore because of the scarcity of manuscripts—the following words clearly show that this must be understood of the sacred Scriptures: written before Christ’s dispensation, afterwards preserved with diligent and reverent care, and after his resurrection compared with the edition of the Seventy and found concordant with it. What text, moreover, can be understood as compared with the Septuagint edition except the Hebrew, especially since Hilary seeks to show that Paul, among his fellow Jews, was free to cite Scripture according to the Hebrew text, although he himself and the other Apostles commonly set it forth according to the Septuagint. This passage thus strongly supports the Hebrew text, to which Hilary grants, together with the Septuagint, an indissoluble authority because of the preeminence of teaching and antiquity.], after the Lord had fulfilled the entire Law by the mystery of his incarnation, passion, and resurrection, they were compared with those books which the same translators had produced for the king, and found faithfully [Note: Lipsius and Paris read “to agree,” against Baduel, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. If, as the preceding note showed, the passage concerns the Hebrew text and the Septuagint, this agreement should be understood in the chief mysteries of our faith. For in other matters of lesser importance Augustine observes, on the testimony of those skilled in Hebrew, that the two texts differ from each other: *Questions on Genesis* 169; *Harmony of the Gospels*, II.66.] to agree. An indissoluble authority was thereby established through the privilege of teaching and antiquity.

### 4. Why Paul called this the first psalm

Blessed Paul, then, a Hebrew of Hebrews according to his profession, also according to Hebrew [Note: “Constitution.”] knowledge and faith called this psalm the first. He did not employ the translators’ division, because he was especially concerned, in preaching to the leaders of the synagogue, to show from the teaching of the Law that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, having been born, suffered, risen again, reigns forever. Thus he adopted this method: being himself a Hebrew and preaching to Hebrews, he used Hebrew custom. But we must use the authority of the translators, interpreting the Law not through the ambiguity of the letter but through learned knowledge.

### 5. Whom, when, and to what extent this psalm concerns

The apostolic authority now provides the most complete interpretation of person, time, and cause. For what the Apostles themselves thought concerning this same psalm in the book of Acts, we shall state in their own words. It is written (Acts 4:24 ff.):

“And as they spoke, ‘Lord, you are he who made heaven and earth and sea and all things in them, who through the mouth of our father David, your holy servant, said: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things? The kings of the earth stood ready, and the rulers assembled together [Note: “in one and the same place,” nearly according to the Septuagint, ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό.] against the Lord and against his Christ.” For truly in this city Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the people of Israel, assembled against your holy servant [Note: παῖδα, “servant” or “child.”] Jesus, whom you anointed, to do whatever your hand and counsel had determined beforehand to be done. And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant your servants to speak your word with all confidence.’”

It is therefore not uncertain what the psalm, in prophecy so long beforehand, revealed. The nations raging and the peoples meditating vain things were then joined together in Herod and Pilate and stood together with their rulers and kings. For the passion of condemnation against the Lord was confirmed by the joint judgment of the governor [Note: Lipsius and Paris read “the provincial governor” here and below. We restore the older reading, “praetor,” from Baduel and the manuscripts.] and tetrarch.

### 6. The raging nations

And indeed, according to prophetic knowledge, the proper sense of every single class and name is carefully fitted to the individual words: the nations raged, that is, being moved by an ignorant and disorderly impulse, while seeing and hearing the Son of God in the body [Note: The preceding edition reads “hating.”]. They raged so greatly that they pierced him with a crown of thorns, mocked him when clothed in royal dress by greeting and honoring him as king, struck his head with a reed, gave him vinegar and gall to drink, and pierced his side with a spear. For the troop of soldiers subject to Pilate committed these deeds in the raging of unrestrained wrath.

### 7. The peoples meditated vain things

But the peoples meditated vain things: that is, though occupied in vain meditation upon God’s teachings, they did not understand through meditation upon the Law him who was proclaimed in the Law. For already at that time the people of the synagogue was not composed only of Abraham’s physical descendants; rather, people from many nations, under the one name of the people Israel, contained a diversity of many peoples. This is written thus in the book of Acts (2:5): “There were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven.” These peoples, gathered from many peoples into one people, therefore meditated vain things.

### 8. The kings stood ready

The kings also stood ready—Pilate and Herod, namely—in whom the kings of the earth are understood; and each, as required by the laws over which he presided, fulfilled the duty of his office. But those who, in their ungodly and irreligious counsel, plotted against the Lord in many assemblies—these rulers assembled together: namely, often in Caiaphas’s house, with all the chief priests gathered. Finally, Herod the tetrarch and Pilate the praetor were called kings of the earth because they stood ready by the right of earthly rule. But the others who assembled together were neither kings of the earth nor chief priests: they did not possess, as subjects, the authority of their own kingdom over the Roman praetor and tetrarch; and they no longer deserved to be called chief priests, since they had become ungodly toward God and the Lord of that very priesthood.

### 9. The Father speaks what precedes; the Apostles utter what follows

And since, according to apostolic authority, it is not uncertain that the psalm begins in the person of God the Father—for they said, “You who spoke through the mouth of our father David, your holy servant”—therefore, to make the change of speaker understood, the translators inserted a *diapsalma*, although it was not contained in the Hebrew books.

The speaker who changes, then, must be understood to be the Apostles, who say, **Verse 3:** “Let us break their bonds and cast [Note: “Throw.”] their yoke away from us.” They must detest those whom they condemn. Therefore they break the bonds and cast off the yoke of those who both raged and meditated vain things.

And it is not uncertain that casting off a yoke differs from breaking bonds. Each action corresponds to each of the two classes and names mentioned above: that the nations break the bonds, while the peoples cast off the yoke. For the nations are bound in the chains of their sins, from which they cannot free themselves through unbelief, according to what was said: “The sinner is bound with the cords of his own sins” (Prov. 5:22). But the Jews are burdened with the yoke of the Law, which the Apostles cast from themselves, as blessed Peter says: “Now therefore why do you test the Lord by putting upon the neck of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

They cast off from themselves this yoke of the peoples, because they had been subject to it; but they break the bonds, not for themselves, but for the nations. Thus the rationale of both expressions is preserved. Where they break bonds, they add no indication of their own persons; but where they cast off the yoke, there, in saying, “Let us cast away from ourselves,” they are understood to speak not of others but of themselves. Thus, casting off that heavy and intolerable yoke, they submitted themselves to that sweet and light yoke of evangelical sanctification to which they had been invited; while through the liberty of preaching they broke the bonds of the nations, according to what they said in their recollection of this psalm: “And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant your servants to speak your word with all confidence” (Acts 4:29). For these teachings of the Apostles break all the snares of unbelief and sin. [Note: “Sins.” Prudentius, *Apotheosis*: “stained by the evil sin of the first man, Adam.”]

### 10. Contempt for the Son is contempt for the Father

And because above a twofold person was maintained when it said, “against the Lord and against his Christ,” there now follows a twofold sense of laughing and mocking. For the dishonor of one is not distinguished from that of the other, nor is the honor of worship divided between them. Those who, according to the genuine, lawful nature of Father and Son, are one in the glory of divinity are likewise one both in the injury of contempt and in the reverence of honor; and each is either honored or despised in the other.

The Lord himself testified to this, saying: “As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father. He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John 5:21 ff.). Honor is not divided; dishonor is not distinguished. Equal worship is required for both, and the affront of contempt shown to one is contempt for both. Thus, since both are despised in the one, and both are one in divinity through glory, so too both are one in worship through honor.

Accordingly, those who assembled against the Lord also assembled against his Christ; and those whom he who dwells in heaven laughs at, the Lord also mocks.

### 11. The Son descended without leaving heaven

This does not mean that the Lord was not always in heaven, for he himself testified of himself: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13; see *On the Trinity*, book X, §16). He is not absent from heaven, therefore, because although the Son of Man descended from heaven and remained and spoke, he was nevertheless in heaven when he spoke these words. [Note: Lipsius and Paris: “had descended from heaven.” More correctly Baduel, Erasmus, and the manuscripts: “in heaven”; for there is an allusion to “the Son of Man who is in heaven.” The punctuation of this passage in earlier editions was wholly disturbed and confused.]

The Son of Man had indeed descended, but by the power of his nature the Son of God was not absent from the place whence he had descended. Nor, when he was born as man, had he exhausted what he had been before; [Note: Paris reads “had assumed,” erroneously. Shortly below, Lipsius alone reads “had ceased” instead of “had failed.”] nor, having become Son of Man, had he ceased to be Son of God. Indeed, the Son of Man is so truly Son of God that, descending from heaven, he was Son of God, and through the power of his substance [Note: “Son of God through the power of his substance”; this inversion of noun order is customary in Hilary. This passage confirms what we asserted in the Preface: in Hilary, when Christ is under discussion, the terms “power” and “nature” refer to his divinity; and we do not know whether *power of nature* is ever referred elsewhere.] the same Son of Man was in heaven.

### 12. The distinction of Father and Son

But the prophet wished, by distinguishing the persons, to signify the Father: he who, even while his Son stood upon earth as Son of Man, remained in that eternal and blessed seat of his, at rest without any dispensation of descent [Note: “Departure.”] [Note: Manuscript of Marmoutier: “distinction,” incorrectly. The sense is that the Father rests in heaven because he did not descend to earth, and did not descend because he exercised no earthly dispensation.]. Therefore he says, **Verse 4:** “He who dwells in heaven shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them,” so that by him who laughs while dwelling in heaven, the Lord who mocks from heaven might also be understood.

Mocking and laughing do not differ; both are effected by the action of the mouth in accordance with the disposition of the will. For, according to our understanding, the meanings of divine things are expressed through bodily forms, so that mockery and laughter are named in deriding those who had assembled against the Lord and against his Christ. This is not because any relaxing or drawing of the mouth could occur in the incorporeal God, but so that from the practice familiar to our nature we might know how the ungodly were mocked by the judgment of the divine will. [Note: The printed editions read, “what the judgment of the divine will against the ungodly would be,” omitting, in Baduel, Erasmus, and Lipsius, the word *illusum*, “mocked,” or, as the manuscripts have it, *inlusum*; from which Paris erroneously produced *inclusum*. The manuscripts correct the text; nor should the Vatican manuscript’s reading be despised: “how the ungodly man was mocked by the judgment of the divine will.”]

They were therefore mocked and laughed at. For those who had contrived false witnesses, purchased betrayal, accepted his blood upon themselves and their children, cried, “Crucify him,” said, “Come down from the cross, if you are the Son of God,” sealed the tomb, and purchased from the soldiers both silence about the resurrection and the story that the body had been stolen, lost all the labor of their great ungodliness. He whom they fastened to the cross is God; he whose tomb they sealed is eternal. Ungodliness is mocked when it strives for what is unlawful, seeks what is not permitted, loses what it hopes it has gained, and recognizes as God him whom it condemns as a man.

### 13. Disturbances do not occur in God

Therefore this appropriately follows:

**Verse 5.** “Then he shall speak to them in his wrath, and in his indignation shall trouble them.”

For after the Son of God had risen from the dead—he whom death had touched through the appearance of the body he assumed—the rashness of fruitless ungodliness was mocked. God speaks to those whom he had mocked and troubles them in indignation.

But before we show what this speech of wrath is and what this disturbance of indignation is, readers and hearers must be warned not to believe that any changes of affections or disturbances of emotions can occur in God. For nothing new can happen to that eternal and perfect nature. He who is such that he is what he is and always remains what he is, lest he should at some time not be the same, cannot be made something other than what he always is.

It belongs to earthly and imperfect natures to become changeable through alteration of nature: sorrow disturbs joy, anger gentleness, offense goodwill, envy evenness of temper, and anxiety security. Through these we are sometimes other than we were, when the affection presently occupying the mind is unsettled by the intrusion, through our inconstancy and weakness, of the impulse of another desire; and a sudden change transforms us from what we were into what we are.

But blessed and perfect God does not need advancement, since he lacks nothing; he is not made new by change, since he lacks an origin. He is “HE WHO IS”: what he is, he is not from another. He is in himself, with himself, from himself [Note: Earlier edition: “toward himself.”]; he belongs to himself, he is all things to himself, and, because he is wholly and entirely all to himself, he leaves no room for anything else to come upon him—a being devoid of every change that novelty entails. [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “does not leave”; the negative particle seems superfluous. Yet perhaps Hilary wrote thus, in a Hellenism not unfamiliar to him.]

### 14. Why God, who needs nothing, created creatures

From this excellent and benevolent blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, proceeded [Note: Printed editions: “perfected.” The manuscripts more correctly read “proceeded.”] all creations of heavenly and invisible things, all constitutions of spiritual and bodily things—not so that God might gain some advancement from those to whom he imparted existence. For no one needs what he gives from himself, nor gains through that for whose existence he is the author. Things that bring advancement are external, because the things that remedy want are alien to the one who lacks them.

God, therefore, from whom all things are, needs none of those to whom he has granted existence; rather, he created all things for the advancement of the things brought into being. And because the discussion would be long if we began also with heavenly and invisible things, let us reason from ourselves, to whom the prophecy of the psalm is addressed.

15. Whatever God asks of man benefits not Himself, but man. — He established man, not because He needed his service in any respect, but because He is good: He created him as a participant in His own blessedness, and made the rational creature perfect in life and understanding for the purpose of bestowing His eternity. This is plainly understood from His own words. For He says: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all His ways, love Him, serve the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and keep the commandments of the Lord God and His ordinances, which I command you, that it may be well with you?” (Deut. 10:12–13).

God asks of us nothing but the obedience of innocence, religion, and faith. [Col. 0270A] He requires that we love Him, not because He Himself receives for His own sake some benefit from our love, but because that very love benefits us who love Him. For He desires to be loved by us and to receive our obedience, in order that it may be well with us [Note: [Col. 0269D] “He waits, that we may be worthy of blessedness and,” etc.], so that, through the merit of our love and obedience, we may be judged worthy of the gift of His blessedness and goodness.

The use of goodness, like the brightness of the sun, the light of fire, or the fragrance of a juice, benefits not that which supplies it, but that which uses it. Therefore, what we are is our own advancement rather than that of Him who established us in what we are. For God, not grudging the eternal goods that are within Himself (or, “not envious”), admits us to the understanding and enjoyment of His blessed goodness.

16. He created man to attain blessedness, and therefore free. — But He who is perfect and good exercised His goodness [Col. 0270B] and blessedness toward us not without reason and measure. For He granted each of us freedom of life and perception, not fastening necessity upon either alternative, so that a law should compel each person by nature to be either good or evil. Rather, He who had created us through benevolence for the enjoyment of His blessedness established our advancement toward it through the merit of an innocent and honorable life.

What honor of reward would this necessity of goodness deserve, if some implanted force did not permit us to be evil? Goodness, therefore, was entrusted to the will, so that the will might gain for itself the reward of goodness, and so that our advancement into, and enjoyment of, this eternal blessedness might come by merit, not by an indiscriminate legal necessity. And although He attracted us to the willing of goodness—that is, to living well and honorably—by the hope of attaining and enjoying His goodness, He nevertheless added the punishment of goodness avoided and despised. Thus, while He left us the freedom of will by which to attain goodness, since necessity of nature could not possess merit, the very freedom was daily reproved by the terror of the penalty set before it on the contrary side.

Thus freedom is granted, by the principle of equity and justice, for the merit of reward; and, through God’s goodness, the force of freedom is constrained by fear of the established [Note: [Col. 0270D] “The right of freedom has been constrained by fear of the ordinance, so that the hope of one meriting by willing well …”] ordinance [Note: [Col. 0269D] We had thought that “of appointed vengeance” should be read; but after *ordinance* one need only understand the word *penalty*. Otherwise MS Mic.: “The right of freedom has been constrained by fear of the ordinance, so that the hope of one meriting by willing well …”], so that the hope of merit might exhort one to will what is good, and the penalty of threatened vengeance might persuade one not to will evil.

17. God’s wrath is the punishment of sin. — Accordingly, for those to whom malice has been more pleasing through freedom of will, the appointed retribution is believed to be God’s wrath. This is not because that immutable and tranquil nature of God grows heated with the agitation of turbulent impulse [Col. 0270D], but because the one who, by the ordinance of punishment, remains in punishment, perceives the author of that ordinance as angry with him [Note: [Col. 0270D] In the Paris edition, *who* is absent. Shortly after, the Basel and Erasmus editions read “remains in punishment.” Lipsius corrupts the whole passage thus: “whom, through the ordinance, punishment awaits, he perceives punishment,” etc. In agreement with Hilary, Augustine, Epistle 190, §10, defines God’s wrath as fixed and just vengeance; and the commentary ascribed to Rufinus defines it as the force by which He judges most justly.]. For the punishment endured is believed to be the wrath of the one decreeing it.

And thus God is angry when those who are punished feel themselves, through the pain of punishment, to be punished by the wrath of the decree [Col. 0271A] [Note: [Col. 0271D] That is, those who are punished.]. This wrath has not been stirred from placability into anger through a change [Note: [Col. 0271D] “A denotation of nature.”] of nature [Note: [Col. 0271D] For *has been stirred*, one manuscript reads *of the stirred nature*, evidently.], but is wrath for those to be punished by virtue of the ordinance of punishment.

John shows in the Gospel that this ordinance of punishment is called, and is, wrath, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” (Matt. 3:7). Although they deserved to be punished, because of their impiety, under the ordinance of punishment, they nevertheless escaped this coming wrath by the confession of repentance. The Apostle also speaks of this wrath: “For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more now, having been justified by His blood, shall we be delivered from wrath through Him”—clearly indicating by “wrath” the punishment of the ordinance that awaits them (Rom. 5:10).

[Col. 0271B] 18. God’s wrath does not arise from a sudden impulse. — God, therefore, is not subject to change, nor is He to be transferred from one state into another, since He is Himself of a fixed and constant nature and remains what He is; for He has said, “I am who I am, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6). That blessed, perfect, and eternal goodness of power admits no conversion and is not altered from one thing into another by the impulse of an incidental movement [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Approaching.”].

The Prophet, speaking here by the Holy Spirit, testifies to the same thing: “God is a righteous judge, strong and long-suffering; will He be angry every day? Unless you turn back [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Turn back,” approximately in accordance with the Roman Psalter and the excellent Verona manuscript of the Chapter-headings of the Psalms; for both contain *turn back*.], He has brandished His sword [Note: [Col. 0271D] It is clear from what follows that this, rather than “He will brandish,” as in the printed editions, must be read.], bent His bow, and made it ready; in it He has prepared instruments of death; He has fashioned His arrows for those who burn” (Ps. 7:12 ff.).

Therefore, the long-suffering One is not changed into wrath; rather, as a mighty judge, He has decreed punishment for guilt. For against those who do not turn back He has brandished the sword, bent the bow, prepared instruments of death in it, and fashioned His arrows for those who burn. Yet He fashioned them not in a sudden movement of wrath, as though suddenly inflamed by a desire for vengeance; rather, He fashioned them for those who burn, who through an unrepentant will appoint themselves to be burned.

For those who would not turn back, the sword has been brandished—not to be drawn against individuals from a change into wrath (for He who is long-suffering is not angry every day), but because He has decreed judgment: His sword is now ready by virtue of the ordinance of punishment. The spiritual ministries of punitive judgment are themselves denoted by sword, bow, and arrows [Note: [Col. 0272D] “Since these are held prepared for those who burn, not from an impulse,” etc.], because they are prepared for those who burn. They are not prepared through a passing impulse of wrath; rather, God has ordered them through the ordinance of His decree, governed by the most even balance of His goodness. He has not, that is, left the severity of this ordinance hidden [Col. 0272A] and unknown, but has forewarned of its terror by denunciations, while delaying even that punishment—though decreed—for a long time [Note: [Col. 0271D] In one manuscript, corruptly: “long-suffering toward,” etc. Moreover, through this delay of punishment God is shown in Psalm 144, §9 to be both merciful and just in punishing: retaining justice in punishment after patience has not succeeded; displaying mercy in punishment by exercising justice after patience.], for repentance from sin.

19. How God speaks in wrath. — Therefore, after the nations raged and the kings stood forth; after the peoples, devising vain things, assembled together against the Lord and His Christ; and after they were mocked and derided, it is added: “Then He will speak to them in His wrath, and trouble them in His indignation.”

We shall offer one most weighty and outstanding example from prophetic teaching of the manner in which the Lord has always spoken in His wrath. Isaiah says:

> “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; [Col. 0272B] give heed to the word of the Lord, people of Gomorrah. What is the multitude of your sacrifices to Me? says the Lord. I am full. I do not desire burnt offerings of rams, fat of lambs, or blood of bulls and goats; nor, when you come to appear before Me—for who required these things at your hands?—shall you continue to tread My court. If you bring fine flour, it is vain; incense is an abomination to Me. Your new moons, sabbaths, and great day I cannot endure. Your fasts, holidays, new moons, and festivals My soul hates. For you have become an excess to Me; I can no longer endure your sins. When you stretch out [Note: [Col. 0272D] Thus the manuscripts. But the Basel, Erasmus, and Lipsius editions read “and if you stretch out.” Greek: ὅταν ἐκτείνητε, “when you stretch out.”] [Note: [Col. 0272D] “When you stretch out your hands,” according to the Hebrew.] your hands, I shall turn My eyes from you; and if you multiply prayer, I shall not hear you; for your hands are full of blood.” (Isa. 1:10 ff.)

These words are indeed harsh and full of wrath: the noble family of Abraham is called rulers of Sodom; Israel, chosen as an inheritance, is called the people of Gomorrah; sacrifices are unacceptable, solemn observances abominable, fasts wearisome [Note: [Col. 0272D] In one manuscript: “despised fasts.”]. The eyes of God are to be turned away from those who approach Him; His ears are to be closed to the prayers of those who plead, because their hands are full of blood. What threat is more grave? What menaces more severe? But let us see how God speaks in His wrath.

42. 20. How God’s harsh words are nevertheless full of kindness. — For it follows, after the words, “Your hands are full of blood”:

> “Wash yourselves; be clean; put away wickedness from your souls, from before My eyes. Learn to do good; seek judgment; [Col. 0272D] deliver the oppressed; judge for the orphan [Note: [Col. 0272D] “The fatherless.” Shortly after, *let us reason together*, Greek διελεγχθῶμεν.], and justify the widow. Come, and let us reason together, [Col. 0273A] says the Lord. Though your sins are as scarlet, I shall make them white as snow; and though they are as crimson, I shall make them like white wool. If you are willing and hear Me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not hear Me, the sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Has spoken these things”; likewise with the Septuagint.].

Kindness follows terror. For those to whom retribution for sin is already due still have before them the blessed confession of a repentant conscience. God does not immediately destroy in His wrath, but speaks; and, while punishment is still withheld, troubles them only in indignation. Those who were crimson and scarlet, discolored by blood overflowing upon their hands, will become white as snow and be clothed in the whiteness of blessed fleece.

Let these points have been drawn from the authority of the Old Testament. Let us see whether God’s wrath is understood in the New Testament also to be such as saves.

21. For John exhorts to salvation those whom he reproaches as a brood of vipers because of the malice of their inherited impiety: “Produce fruit worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3:9). Again, the Lord Himself says: “Come to Me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

And to those raging against Him—not only in His Passion, but even after His Passion, not merely gathering together, but breathing persecution against the Church, flight of the apostles, and slaughter of martyrs—God speaks thus in wrath: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” He said, “Who are You, Lord?” And the Lord replied: “I am Jesus the Nazarene [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Nazaraean.”], whom you persecute.” Then he, trembling and terrified by what had happened to him, said: “Lord, [Col. 0273C] what do You want me to do?”

Thus He speaks in wrath; thus He troubles in indignation: to those upon whom punishment has been decreed because of the merit of their impiety, He brings fear and terror through an admonition to cease.

22. How He troubles for healing. — Yet the Prophet has not passed over even the chief and greatest proclamation of speaking in wrath and troubling in indignation. For after saying, “Then He will speak to them in His wrath, and trouble them in His fury,” he added, in order to show what that utterance of wrath was and what trouble would arise from it:

> Vv. 6–9: “But I have been appointed king by Him over Zion, His holy mountain, proclaiming His command. The Lord said to Me: You are My Son; today I have begotten You. Ask of Me, and I shall give You the nations as Your inheritance, [Col. 0273D] and the ends of the earth as Your possession. You shall rule them with a rod of iron, and break them like a potter’s vessel.”

Speaking in wrath and troubling in indignation, He moderates both the manner of His anger and of His speech. He neither conceals His wrath by displaying power, nor departs from His goodness by setting terror before them, so that the fear of Him whose power He displays may call us back from impiety [Note: [Col. 0273D] Printed editions: “so that it may bring us to piety.” Then the Basel, Erasmus, and Lipsius editions: “may the fear of Him whose power was displayed.” The manuscripts read more aptly: “so that … from impiety,” etc.; moreover, according to Hilary above, on Psalm 1, §6, fear is suited not so much to bring the mind to piety as to bring it back from impiety.] [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Whose power had been displayed, might call us back.”].

Thus those who rage and devise vain things are troubled when they know Him as king, hear Him called the Son of God, learn that He possesses the ends of the earth and inherits the nations, recognize that the right of ruling is His in the rod of iron, and understand that peoples are to be shattered with the ease and manner of a potter’s vessel. Thus He speaks in wrath; thus He troubles in indignation: not punishing the impiety already committed, but troubling the unrepentant, through terror at the power declared, toward a confession of repentance.

23. The foregoing words were spoken concerning Christ. — Although it may plainly be understood that all these things were spoken in the person of the Only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ—since, through the spirit of prophecy, God is accustomed, in His unambiguous foreknowledge of events to be accomplished, to signify the future as though it were past—and although it is the greatest unbelief to bring to these matters a hesitant mind of uncertain opinion, nevertheless it must also be shown from evangelical and apostolic teaching that the Prophet foretold beforehand everything that was to be done and proclaimed. This is especially necessary because no small error arises among the ignorant and simple from the statement: “Today I have begotten You.”

For since the Only-begotten Son of God abides before times, it is understood to be neither fitting nor consistent that He should have been begotten in a day, since every day belongs to time. According to the knowledge set before us by Moses, times have been measured out into their movement [Col. 0274C] and course from the beginning and constitution of the world, being distinguished by moments, hours, months, and years in a recurring succession within themselves. Time has been instituted from time, because the mutual succession of all times both generates and terminates them.

For this reason, a day is in time: through it all time, having begun, comes to an end, and, ending, begins. But the Only-begotten Son of God, as He is the Word of God, so also “the Word was God”; He is not with times, but before times; not in some things, but before all things. For He existed when times were made, since He made them. Therefore He always existed. He is not bounded by time or subject to number; rather, He is He through whom exists the origin of all things which are and can be said to be. From the birth of His own infinite eternity, as begotten from eternity, He continues to be.

Therefore, in order that the meaning of the prophetic utterance, “Today I have begotten You,” may be understood, evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic authority must be brought to bear, so that we may understand either the Prophet through the Apostle or the Apostle through the Prophet [Col. 0275A]. The same order of evangelical sayings, moreover, must be retained as that of the Psalm.

24. That Christ is king. — For this comes first: “But I have been appointed king by Him over Zion, His holy mountain.” And I do not know how it can safely be doubted that Christ is king, when the thief himself confessed this in the Passion of the cross [Note: [Col. 0275C] Either read *himself*, or understand the rest thus: “the thief himself confessing this in the Passion of the cross.”]: “Remember me, Lord, when You come into Your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

But the confession of the thief, declaring Him to be king, is not enough. The Magi, who came to worship, also testify when they ask, “Where is He who has been born king of the Jews?” (Matt. 2:2). Pilate also testifies when he asks, “Are You king of the Jews?” (Matt. 27:11). The Lord confesses it too when He replies, “You have said it” (ibid.). When questioned, He does not deny it, nor does He boast when about to be humbled unto death. Since confession comes only through His reply, He neither put Himself forward as the originator of the declaration, nor withheld from the questioner the truth of knowledge [Col. 0275B] [Note: [Col. 0275C] *Thus* is omitted. It continues: “He neither put Himself forward as the originator of the declaration, nor withheld from the questioner the knowledge of truth.”] [Note: [Col. 0275C] Basel, Erasmus, and Lipsius: “from the questioned.” Then one manuscript: “the knowledge of truth.”].

25. That the Son of God is God and man. — Yet it is not enough that He answered that He is king. Let us also hear who this king is. For the chief priest even questions Him under oath, saying: “I adjure You by the living God: tell us whether You are the Christ, the Son of God” (Matt. 26:63). Jesus says to them: “You have said it.”

Once again, the question is not rejected, but the display and boasting of a spontaneous declaration is avoided; still, the truth sought is not denied. Thus the modesty of humility and the confession of truth are balanced, so that duty belongs to the answer and knowledge to the question. But we must await the result of this answer—that Christ is the Son of God—namely, what follows upon the words “You have said it”: “Truly I say to you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming on the clouds of heaven” (ibid., v. 64).

He who is the Son of Man is also the Son of God. In the assumption of the Son of Man, the nature of His noble birth is not lost. He is not therefore not the Son of God because He is also the son of man. For the assumption of humility does not occur through a loss of divinity [Note: [Col. 0275C] In the earlier editions: “There is no diminution of divinity with the addition of humility.” Observe here that the term *power* is referred to divinity.]; nor did power incur disgrace through partnership in weakness, since weakness has been honored with the dignity of power. For the Son of Man sits at God’s right hand, to be seen coming with the clouds of heaven. In this saying is fulfilled the prophecy: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at My right hand, until I make Your enemies the footstool of Your feet” (Ps. [Col. 0276B] 111).

26. What is proclaimed by His being king of the heavenly Zion. — This king, therefore, has been appointed over Zion, God’s holy mountain, proclaiming the Lord’s command. This is surely not the mountain of that ruined—according to another reading, earthly—city, Jerusalem, mourned over as murderous and parricidal. It is rather the Jerusalem that is in heaven, which is our mother, the city of the great King. Its inhabitants, as I think, are those who rose at the Lord’s Passion and are there even today [Note: [Col. 0275C] These remarks concern the resurrection of bodies seen at Jerusalem shortly after Christ’s Passion; the ancients did not agree on this matter. Athanasius (*Oration III against the Arians*, p. 386) agrees that Christ not only rose, but also raised ancient dead persons from their tombs; whether in an eternal or a temporary resurrection, he does not say. Epiphanius, however, though in *Heresy* 64, §65, considering only those restored to life to live again among human beings, admits that Christ is called the firstfruits of those asleep because those who rose before Him died again, nevertheless in *Heresy* 75, §7 teaches those who heed his words that those raised from the dead at Christ’s Passion entered the bridal chamber with Him and have no bodily remains on earth; that they first entered earthly Jerusalem, and afterwards, as the Savior ascended into heaven, were taken up with Him. Hilary here inclines to this view. It is supported both by Rufinus in his exposition of the Creed and by those who, in Tertullian—who by no means agrees with them—hold that patriarchs and prophets migrated to Paradise as appendages, as it were, of the Lord’s resurrection.

Jerome, *Epistle* 3, seems to support the same view: “After Christ, the thief is in Paradise. And therefore, at His resurrection, many bodies of those asleep rose and were seen in the heavenly Jerusalem.” Yet the letter inscribed in the names of Paula and Eustochium, *Epistle* 17, takes a different view: “Nor, as it says there, is heavenly Jerusalem to be understood in this place, as many absurdly suppose; for there could have been no sign among human beings of the risen Lord if the bodies of the saints were seen in heavenly Jerusalem.”

Augustine, noting advocates of this opinion, says in *Epistle* 164, §9: “I know that some think that at the death of the Lord Christ such a resurrection was already granted to the righteous as is promised us at the end.” Departing from them, he adds: “If, indeed, they did not sleep again after their bodies had been laid aside anew, it must be considered how Christ can be understood as the firstborn from the dead if they preceded Him in that resurrection.” Further, it seems difficult that David should not have been in that resurrection of the righteous if eternal life had already been given to them, etc., when Peter nevertheless testifies that he had not yet risen (Acts 2:20). Finally, it would also imperil the statement concerning the ancient righteous in Hebrews: “Because better things were provided for us, lest they should be made perfect without us.”

The author of the *Questions* attributed to Justin, *Response to Question* 85, adopts a middle position. First, he grants that the resurrection of those discussed here was real. He also acknowledges that they did not die again, but remain immortal. Yet he denies that they are conformed to Christ’s body of glory or are in the heavenly kingdom; instead, like Enoch and Elijah, they await a future transformation. “For,” he says, “no resurrection has yet occurred into immortal and incorruptible life except that of Jesus Christ. Therefore He has been proclaimed both the firstborn of the dead and the firstfruits of those asleep.”] (Matt. 27:52).

Accordingly, this appointed king proclaims God’s command, so that they may remember that He will come with the clouds of heaven—He against whom they rage and assemble—and, troubled by the knowledge of His divine coming, may repent of the insult offered to His bodily humiliation.

46. 27. Christ’s temporal birth through the glory of the flesh. — [Col. 0277A] Evangelical teaching preserves the order of the prophecy. For the meaning of both sayings is contained in that very utterance: “I have been appointed king by Him over Zion, His holy mountain, proclaiming His command. The Lord said to Me: You are My Son; today I have begotten You” (v. 6).

For when He says, “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Matt. 26:64), He indicates the time at which the Son of Man—who is both Christ and the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0277C] We emend thus, where previously the reading was “son and sitting”; for in manuscripts the word *is* is often changed into the conjunction *and*. Shortly after, Basel has, as does MS Mic., *worthy*, not *to be made worthy*.]—would be deemed worthy to share God’s seat. Thus, He who had previously been the Son of God would then also be the Son of Man; and that which was then the Son of Man would, through the power of resurrection, be begotten into the perfect Son of God—that is, into the resumption and bestowal upon the body of the glory of His own eternity [Note: [Col. 0277C] Here also we restore *because* for *who*, since the letter *a* could easily have dropped out before the similar following letter.] [Note: [Col. 0277C–D] Here, to convey Hilary’s meaning, *and* (which here has the force of *also*) had to be substituted for *so that*. Those experienced in working through old books know that no alteration is more frequent. Thus passages in which Hilary discusses Christ’s glory after the resurrection have for the most part been corrupted, evidence that his distinctively expressed view was never adequately understood. This led us to explain it at length in the Preface, §5. Here it is enough to warn the reader what it means for Christ to be begotten into the perfect Son of God: namely, as he says in *On the Trinity* XI, §41, to become wholly God—not that Christ through glory ceases to be man or Son of Man, but that He ceases to be weak, mortal, and so forth, passing into the immortality, incorruption, and power of the Word and of God. See *On Psalm* 143, §7, or the Preface just mentioned.].

That glory He sought from the Father as one embodied. For He who was in the form of God had received the form of a servant. For this assumed form of a servant He asks for the glory of God in which He had remained, saying: “Father, glorify [Note: [Col. 0277C] “Make glorious.”] Me with Yourself with the glory which I had with You before the world was” (John 17:5). He seeks no new thing and desires nothing foreign; He asks to be such as He had been. Yet He prays that He may become what He previously was: that is, that He may be begotten into what had been His own.

He was not then wholly that which He prayed to become; and to become whole was nothing other than what He had been asking [Note: [Col. 0277D] Because according to the flesh He was weak, lowly, and without glory. Thus the word *whole* here refers to the natures: He is wholly the Son of God, Word and man—or, more explicitly, Word, soul, and flesh. These are Augustine’s words, *Sermon* 214, §7. Ferrandus, however, in his letter to Severus, §8, refers *whole* to the person and *the whole* to the natures. Thus he says: “The whole Christ was in the lower regions according to His rational soul, but not wholly,” etc. But that Hilary applies *whole* and *the whole* interchangeably to the same thing is suggested by the present passage. Again, *whole* concerns the natures in *On the Trinity* IX, §38, where he says: “The Son is now whole, that is, man and God”; whereas in Book X, §28, it concerns the person, where he teaches that the Son of God and the Son of Man are one and the same because the whole Son of Man is the whole Son of God.].

But since He is what He was [Note: [Col. 0278C] That is, glorious according to the flesh, as He was before the ages as the Word. Because of the unity of person, Christ is proclaimed both always to have possessed glory and, during the time of the dispensation, to have lacked it; and in receiving it, both to have become what He was not and to have become what He was.], and will become what He was not, that which was not wholly what it had been was being born by the beginning of a certain new birth [Note: [Col. 0278D] Printed editions: “was being born by a certain new birth.” Therefore they are corrected from the manuscripts.], into what it had been. This day, therefore, is the day of His resurrection for assuming glory, through which He is born into what He was before times. Yet, although He is born into what He was before times, He is born in time into that which He was not.

Therefore the Son of Man is from that point onward to be seen seated at the right hand of power, because the nature of the flesh, glorified after the resurrection, was advanced into the fullness of the splendor which it had previously possessed. The Son of Man was to sit with the Father and, with the corruption of the flesh absorbed into immortality, was then to be born into the living Son of God, who dies no more.

28. He who by eternal birth is the firstborn of every creature becomes by temporal birth the firstborn from the dead. — The blessed Apostle has distinguished and separately explained this new, temporal birth in Him from the generation that is before times. For, after speaking of that blessed birth bounded by no times, he says: “The firstborn of every creature, because in Him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” (Col. 1:15–16). He also calls Him firstborn from the dead in the resurrection, saying later: “The firstborn from the dead, that He might Himself have primacy in all things” (ibid., v. 18).

For He is born into what He was not, while becoming what He had been. He is the firstborn from the dead who was the firstborn of creation; therefore He is firstborn from the dead so that He may remain firstborn of creation. For He who is firstborn from the dead is the same one who was firstborn of creation.

29. How He is reborn both into another state and into the same. — He is not now something different from what He was before [Note: [Col. 0278D] He is not now something different from what He was before, because the same Word continues in the glory which He always had and never abandoned. Yet He is another thing from another: namely, from the form of a servant, formerly cast down and in dishonor, now at last exalted and in glory—in the glory which the Word had always possessed and during the time of the dispensation had in some way concealed beneath the coverings of flesh. Thus He has been reborn into the same thing: that is, into the same glory in which the person of the Word already existed.], although He Himself was also something different from another. Yet that which, though from another, was also something different, has nevertheless been reborn into the same thing from which it had formerly come forth.

For He who was born man from the Virgin was even then the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0278D] Namely, before He was born; who subsequently, by a new birth, gave to the Son of Man that, because of the unity of person, He might be the Son of God.]. But He who is the Son of Man was also the Son of God. And He who was then the Son of God was born again from baptism [Note: [Col. 0278D] That is: He who then existed as the Son of God was also born again from baptism, so that He might be born both into the same thing—because by nature He was the Son—and into another thing, because in baptism He was declared to be what He had not yet been declared to be. After this arises a question not easily resolved: whether Hilary read in some manuscript of Matthew that after Christ’s baptism it was said to Him, “You are My Son; today I have begotten You.” For he reads this not only here, but also in *On the Trinity* VIII, §25, and indeed in the Commentary on Matthew itself, chapter 2, §6; whereas in *On the Trinity* VI, §23, and on Psalm 138, §6, agreeing with our manuscripts, he reads: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Nor can the earlier reading be attributed to a lapse of memory, since Justin Martyr gives the same reading in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 331: “For after Christ came up from the river Jordan, there was uttered a voice concerning Him: ‘You are My Son; today I have begotten You,’” etc.] and thus was the Son of God, so that He might be born both into the same thing and into another thing. For it is written, when He had come up [Col. 0279A] from the water: “You are My Son; today I have begotten You.”

But according to the generation of a man being reborn, He Himself was then also reborn to God into a perfect Son [Note: [Col. 0279C] Printed editions: “into a son, indeed.” The manuscripts more correctly read: “into a perfect Son,” according to the manner of speaking in §27, where the Son of Man is said through glory to be begotten into the perfect Son of God. Thus, just as He who existed before the ages acquired anew for Himself through birth from the Virgin that He might be the Son of Man, so, having become man, through the generation of baptism He acquired for Himself—or rather was declared to be—the Son of God. If anyone should hence suspect that Hilary thought Christ needed regeneration, let him read what he says in the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 3, §5, and *On the Trinity* X, §25.], so that the Son of Man might thus have the Son of God joined to Him in baptism.

30. “Today I have begotten You” concerns the resurrection. — But the words now found in the Psalm, “You are My Son; today I have begotten You,” concern neither the Virgin’s childbirth nor the generation of the washing, but the firstborn from the dead: such is apostolic authority. For in the book of the Acts of the Apostles it is thus said: “We also proclaim to you the promise made to the fathers. God has fulfilled this promise to our children by raising our Lord Jesus, as it is also written in the first Psalm: ‘You are My Son; today I have begotten [Col. 0279B] You,’ when He raised Him from the dead, no longer to return to corruption” (Acts 13 ff.).

According to the Apostle, therefore, this utterance of God the Father occurred on the day of the resurrection. Let us see whether the Evangelists teach the same. For the Lord, having risen, addressed the apostles in these words: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Go now, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:18). For, having risen, He received every right in heaven and on earth. In saying, “has been given to Me,” He shows that He asked for what He received.

31. The Nations, Christ’s Inheritance.—For it follows, VERSE 8: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” Therefore he received the inheritance of the nations for which he asked. For he asked when he said, “Father, the hour has come: glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you. As you have given him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (John 17:1–2). And again: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (ibid., 20). This, then, is his inheritance: that he may give eternal life to all flesh, that all nations, baptized and taught, may be regenerated unto life; no longer allotted to the dominion of angels according to that divine song of Moses, nor divided according to their number, but received into the household of the Lord and counted among God’s household; and transferred from the unjust, sinful, and perverse rule of their former masters into the eternal and divine kingdom.

> [Note: Lips. and Par. have *dedicatae*, “dedicated,” corruptly. This opinion concerning the division of the nations according to the number of the angels rests on these words in the Septuagint: “He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” [Deut. 32:8]. Nor was Hilary alone in holding it. Thus Origen reads in Homily 11 on Numbers: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and each nation was placed under that angel, but the one chosen nation, Israel, was the Lord’s portion.” Hence Eusebius, *Demonstratio evangelica*, book IV, chapter 7, teaches that the nations were entrusted to the governance and protection of angels, but Jacob—or the race of those who worshipped God—to Christ, the Word of God. Augustine refers to this in Sermon 1 on Psalm 88, §3, saying: “God did not shut the fountain of his goodness even to the foreign nations, whom he had placed under angels, making the people Israel his own portion.” Jerome’s statement on Micah 6:2 bears on this: “In judgment the charge will be brought either against the angels, if they did not do all that belonged to their office, or against the people, if, although the angels did everything, the people themselves despised to listen.” Hence also Chrysostom, Homily 3 on Colossians: “At first the angels were according to the number of the nations; now, however, they are not according to the number of the nations, but according to the number of believers.” We have thought these matters worth adducing here, because Hilary often alludes to this same passage of Deuteronomy.]

> [Note: In Par., “from unjust sinner,” etc. In the other editions, “from unjust and perverse rule.” Light for understanding this passage is supplied by the Fathers cited shortly below, and further by Rufinus in his *Exposition of the Creed*: “From the beginning,” he says, “when God had made the world, he set over it and appointed certain powers of the heavenly virtues, through whom the race of mortals might be governed and administered. Moses indicates that this was done in the passage of Deuteronomy just mentioned concerning the number of angels. But some of these … did not regulate the authority given them by God according to the laws under which they received it; nor did they teach humankind to obey the divine commandments, but to comply with their own transgressions. Thus written bonds were drawn up against us … By this bond, therefore, each person was held by those evil rulers; Christ, coming, removed it and stripped them of this power,” etc. See *Tractate on Psalm* 61, §2.]

For Israel alone is no longer the Lord’s portion, nor Jacob the cord of his inheritance; but all the nations—formerly divided according to the number of angels—are now the one people of the one God, and this whole multitude of nations is the one people of God. This is the eternal inheritance of all who rise from the dead, belonging to this firstborn from the dead, the eternal heir.

32. Not Earth Alone Was Given to His Dominion.—In the added words, “and the ends of the earth as your possession,” one must not suppose that a repeated expression signifies the same thing, as though possession had been given to him only of the lands inhabited by the nations. For he does not say, “and your possession unto the ends of the earth,” but “the ends of the earth.” What is bounded differs from what bounds it. To be limited is not the same as to limit; nor is receiving a measure the same as regulating. Of these, one receives its measure inwardly, while the other regulates from without by a certain encircling boundary and surrounding presence.

For the earth is not so sunk into depth, extended in breadth, or raised in height that it is not on every side held in check by the presence of a nature either surrounding it or lying beneath it. The submerged and immeasurable abyss of the lower vastness supports it; the breath of the surrounding and upper air overshadows and encompasses it.

> [Note: Ms. Mic. has *immersa*, “immersed.”]

That it hangs suspended above the abyss beneath it, the prophet testifies when he says: “He founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (Ps. 23:2). And again: “Who established the earth upon the waters” (Ps. 135:6). Scripture is accustomed to call this immeasurable and infinite expanse “abyss,” as when Jonah, praying within the whale, says: “The deep abyss surrounded me” (Jonah 2:6).

> [Note: Par. reads: “Jonah praying within the whale.” We restore the ancient reading, which is also that of the manuscripts.]

> [Note: “Jonah prays within the whale and says.”]
