This infinite immensity, therefore, which is understood to be signified in the abyss according to the proper force of the word, is encompassed by the power of the spiritual and divine substance, according to the Apostle: “For all things are from him and through him; to him be glory for ages of ages” (Rom. 11:36). That this lower region and vast abyss has many inhabitants, we are taught by the Apocalypse of blessed John (Rev. 5:3–4): “And no one was found worthy to open the sealed book, neither in heaven, nor upon the earth, nor beneath the earth.” Certainly this is not to be understood of the dead buried in the earth; for, in order to indicate a third dwelling-place, it says not those who are within the earth but those who are beneath the earth; nor those who are dead, but those who live, had any author among themselves capable of unsealing the book.

> [Note: Bad. and Er., with two Vatican manuscripts, read *illum*, “that [one].” Lips. and Par. read *nullum*, “none.” We restore *ullum*, “any,” from another Vatican manuscript of better quality.]

Therefore, when possession of the ends of the earth is given to the Lord, not so much the earth itself as those things by which the earth is bounded are given. For he received the boundaries of the earth by which the earth itself is delimited.

33. What Was Given to Christ Is Explained from the Apostle.—Blessed Paul—for Christ spoke concerning himself through his mouth—expounded the entire mystery of this matter, saying: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:6 ff.).

Remaining, therefore, in the form of God, he received the form of a servant—namely, being born as man from God. And after the death of the cross he is exalted to the name above every name: that is, he is advanced into God, because there is no name above God; and this is granted to him when he asks for it, namely, that he should be what he had been before. For, while remaining in the form of God, he had taken the form of a servant. He then received possession of the ends of the earth: namely, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. Not earthly things alone, but heavenly and infernal things also are given, and those things by which the earth is enclosed.

> [Note: “Not earth alone.”]

And in the glory of God the Father he is born “today,” that is, the taking of the form of a servant is ennobled, through the reward of death, in the form of God in which he had previously remained. Thus, within time, there occurs a new yet not unprecedented birth: when he who, though in the form of God, had been found in the form of a servant, was born as firstborn from the dead in order to resume the glory of God the Father.

> [Note: In Par. the particle *in* was absent. Then the other editions read, “with the form of God remaining before,” whereas the Mic. manuscript, which we follow, expresses Hilary’s thought more clearly. Shortly afterward Bad., Er., and two manuscripts read *adhonestatur*, “is ennobled,” not *honestatur*. Erasmus, marking this passage of Hilary with a censor’s stroke, says: “It has a smell of something Origenist.” But since this commentary occupies the last place in his edition, while the holy Doctor expounds the same teaching in his other books, why did Erasmus postpone his censure so long? This surely shows that he uttered his judgments from the bias of a prejudiced mind, not from consideration of the facts. Here, moreover, Christ’s glorification is expounded: it is called a new birth with reference to the man, but with reference to the Word it is neither new nor unfamiliar.]

34. Whether Ruling with an Iron Rod Conflicts with God’s Goodness.—It then follows: “You shall rule them with a rod of iron, and break them like a potter’s vessel.” To many who either think wrongly or do not know the force and proper meaning of the divine utterances, these words appear contrary to God’s goodness: that the nations which the Son of God asked for as his possession and received as his inheritance should be ruled with the terror of an iron rod and broken in the manner of a potter’s vessel. For it is not the part of anyone good to give and receive things in order to destroy them. And he who prefers the repentance of sinners to their death (Ezek. 18:32) is not thought likely to act contrary to the declaration—or, according to another reading, promise—of his own nature, if he breaks with an iron rod those whom he asked might be given to him as an inheritance.

> [Note: *Mavult*, “prefers.”]

35. “You Shall Rule” Here Says Nothing Harsh.—First, then, lest room be given to this rash and impious presumption, we must ascertain the proper meanings of the words as translated into Latin. For our text has, “You shall rule them with a rod of iron.” Although the very phrase “you shall rule” is neither tyrannical nor unjust, but denotes a rational governance according to the judgment of equity and moderation, nevertheless the Greek expression indicates an even gentler disposition in the ruler. For where our text has “you shall rule them,” the Greek has ποιμανεῖς αὐτούς, that is, “you shall shepherd them”: you will rule them with the care and affection of a shepherd. For he himself is the good shepherd, whose sheep we are, and for whom he laid down his life (John 10:11).

But lest we suppose that the rod signifies tyrannical authority, we must learn from the New and Old Testaments what is the proper meaning of the term “rod.”

36. In the New Testament the Rod Is God’s Teaching.—Writing to the Corinthians, whom at that time he was recalling from many sins to repentance by a moderate and beneficial exhortation, blessed Paul says: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4:21). Did Paul have magisterial authority, so that he threatened them with a rod and came to Christ’s Church with the office of a lictor? Certainly this must not be supposed. Rather, because every word of God by which we are recalled from error to God’s truth, by which through the threat and terror of judgment we are guided into the way of innocent and holy life, is called a rod—by which, restrained within the discipline of divine fear, we are corrected by the admonition of a moderate and provident ruler—therefore the blessed Apostle set before those whom he admonished the choice concerning his coming: whether they preferred him to be present in severity of teaching and rebuke, or in a spirit of gentleness.

> [Note: “God’s” is absent from two manuscripts.]

> [Note: Par., following Lips., has “and prudent.” More correctly, the other books have “and provident,” that is, foreseeing and giving counsel.]

Both courses were necessary according to the rule of moderation, so that he might come more gently to the obedient but more severely to the insolent. This, indeed, has been established from the authority of the New Testament.

37. Likewise in the Old: Christ Is Both Rod and Flower.—That this teaching of the Word is called a rod is known from the Old Testament, where it is said: “A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 44:7). For this is the direction of the rod by which we are directed through teaching into an even and beneficial way; and the rod of the kingdom must itself be the teaching of the kingdom.

> [Note: Lips. preferred, “for this indeed is”; nor would it displease us if the manuscripts supported it. The same editor then restored “the rod of uprightness,” which Par. also adopted, against the ancient books. Further on, in the words “and what rod,” the particle *and*, as often elsewhere, is taken in the sense of “also.”]

We have further received that our Lord himself is called a rod because of the beneficial and measured preaching of his teaching, Isaiah saying: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 11:1). And lest anyone dare to suppose tyrannical severity in him because he is called a rod, the prophetic speech immediately added: “And a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (ibid.), so that the sweetness of the flower might temper the severity of the rod, while the fearful governance of teaching should bring to each of us the rule of perfect blessedness.

> [Note: “It shall rise from the root; then, ‘the Spirit of God,’ with the Greek.”]

Therefore, with this rod he will rule the nations given to him—not a corruptible, transitory, or fragile rod, but an iron one: that is, the strongest and, in accordance with its own nature, the firmest in solidity.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript has *non facili*, “not easily [bent].” Rufinus, as commonly printed, agrees with Hilary’s thought: “The iron rod is understood as inflexible justice: a rod because it is straight, iron because it is hard—straight for the good, hard for the evil; gentle for the righteous, harsh for the perverse.”]

38. He Breaks Those Given Him So That He May Reform Them.—With this iron rod, therefore, as he rules, so also he will break and crush them.

> [Note: “Thus also, ‘he will break’ or ‘he will crush.’”]

For this is more exactly expressed by the Greek wording according to the Septuagint translators. Thus it is written: Ὡς σκεῦος κεραμέως συντρίψεις αὐτούς, “Like a potter’s vessel you shall crush them.”

> [Note: Other editions have ὡς σκεύη, “like vessels,” as is also read in Theodoret and others; but our Hilary reads *vessel*, not *vessels*, below as well, in accordance with the better Septuagint copies. For this reason we have adopted σκεῦος from our book.]

But whether he crushes or breaks, he is not for that reason to be thought to ask for an inheritance in order to break and crush it into destruction and annihilation; for a contrite heart is his best sacrifice. That crushing or breaking, therefore, is what pulverizes in us bodily pleasures and the incentives of worldly vices, and makes us worthy of the Lord’s gracious favor, according to the prophet’s saying: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

> [Note: “A contrite heart,” in agreement with the Septuagint and both Psalters, the Roman and the Gallican.]

But how great an explanation does the comparison with a potter’s vessel supply for this understanding? It is not without reason that he will, while ruling with an iron rod, break like a potter’s vessel those whom he asked for as an inheritance—unless the example of the comparison shows that the loss caused by this kind of breaking serves toward the restoration of the same vessel.

39. The Same Thing God Taught through Jeremiah the Prophet, Explaining What Our Breaking Like a Potter’s Vessel Is: “Arise, and go down into the potter’s house; and there you will hear my words. And I went down into the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work upon the stones. And the vessel which he was making in his hands fell; and he himself again made another vessel, according as it pleased him in his sight to make it. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Can I not do to you, house of Israel, as this potter? Behold, as clay in the potter’s hands, so are you in my hands. In a word, I shall speak concerning a nation or concerning a kingdom, that I may strike and destroy them; and if that nation turns from its evils, I shall repent of the evils which I thought to do to them. And in a word I shall speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, that I may rebuild and plant; and they shall do evil before me, so as not to hear my voice; and I shall repent of the good things which I said I would do to them’” (Jer. 18:1 ff.).

> [Note: Ms. Mic. has *cogitabo*, “I shall think.” The Vulgate has *cogitavi*, “I thought,” following the Greek ἐλογισάμην.]

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “that I may build with a rod,” a reading not permitted by the sacred text.]

Thus God will break and crush the nations sought and obtained as his inheritance in order to reform them. For God breaks in all persons every insatiable desire, seductive wantonness, burning anger, empty superstition, swelling pride, and impious opinion. But he reforms us toward the rational use of life by contempt for money, shame at luxury, restraint of anger, knowledge of truth, fellowship of life, and the duties of religion; when through the rule of teaching and the terror of judgment we revive into these virtues after those vices.

For he does not say, “You shall break them like a potter’s hardened vessel,” lest an irreparable vessel be understood through the fragment of a potsherd; but he says, “a potter’s vessel,” one being formed in the very working of the craftsman, so that, according to the example set forth, the restoration of that same broken vessel might be ready at the craftsman’s will.

> [Note: Bad. and Er. have *figulus*, “potter,” a word subsequently deleted in other editions. We restore *figulum* from a Vatican manuscript, although we would prefer *figlinum*, “earthenware.” By a *potter’s vessel* he means a vessel already hardened into a potsherd; but “a vessel of the potter” means a vessel still soft and in the hands of its maker. Hence Jerome here says: “A potter’s vessel, before it has hardened into a potsherd, if it is broken up, can be re-formed … But if a potsherd has once been broken, it can by no means be joined again into wholeness.”]

40. As a Potter Can Easily Restore a Vessel, So God Can Restore the Penitent.—But this vessel of irrational matter is also adapted, under another interpretation, to the rationality of human will: people indeed fall through these vices; but if they repent in them—that is, if they cease from them—God too is said to repent regarding those things which he had determined as punishment for this fall. This does not mean that a change of mind according to human nature could occur in God, but that repentance for deeds is the measure of what is to be done or recompensed to a human being.

> [Note: Earlier editions have “of man.” With the Mic. manuscript, “to man” is preferable, and refers to things to be done: repentance is thus the measure of those things which are to be done or repaid to a human being. God also mentions his repentance with respect to punishment: those who ceased to be ungodly would cease to be punished.]

God also speaks of his repentance concerning punishment, because those who had ceased to be ungodly would cease to be punished. Therefore, as it is easy for a potter to reform a lost vessel into its former shape, or into whatever shape he wishes, so it is easy for God, after falls into vice, to restore to piety from ungodliness those who are willing to return to their origin, through the instruction of his teaching.

41. These Predictions Apply to Both Spiritual and Bodily Resurrection.—Nor should we overlook that breaking “like a potter’s vessel” which will occur when these bodies have been dissolved and broken by the fall of death, and restoration will be given according to the will of the maker. The prophetic speech appears to have indicated both senses in the same statement. For when it shows the usefulness of repentance in those matters previously done, it teaches that in this present life a new kind of restoration from vices to virtues ought to take place in the body, God’s anger toward them ceasing as the will to commit sins ceases.

Although it has expressed this by the comparison of the potter, nevertheless, when it says of that same potter, “And he himself made another vessel according as it pleased him in his sight” (Jer. 18:4), it is also understood to signify the future restoration of the bodies of those who rise, according to God’s will. For as it pleases him and is worthy in his sight, he will restore what has been broken, bestowing upon them a form of beauty pleasing to himself, not from some other matter, but from the old matter itself, that of their own origin; so that the resurrection of corruptible bodies into the glory of incorruption may not destroy their nature by annihilation, but transform it by a change of quality.

> [Note: Par. has “transform the condition of quality.” Other editions, with two Vatican manuscripts, have “transform quality by condition.” The reading of another Vatican manuscript of better quality seems truer: “transform nature by a change of quality,” with *nature* understood. Here it should be observed how carefully Hilary avoids the error concerning the resurrection attributed by many holy Fathers to Origen. Among them Epiphanius, in the letter to John of Jerusalem preserved as Jerome, Letter 60, says: “Who could patiently endure Origen’s denial of the resurrection of this flesh by slippery arguments, as he declares most plainly in the volumes of his exposition of the first Psalm and in many other places?”]

For it is not another body, although it rises into another state, as the Apostle says: “It is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it shall rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it shall rise in power. It is sown a natural body; it shall rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:42 ff.). Thus a transformation occurs, but annihilation is not brought about. And when that which was rises into that which it was not, it has not lost its origin but has advanced to honor.

> [Note: “It shall rise a spiritual body,” in accordance with the Greek text.]

Let us therefore rejoice that we are broken like a potter’s vessel, whether now or then: so that now, in the manner of a potter’s vessel, having died and been buried with the Lord in baptism, we may walk in newness of life (Rom. 6:4); and, putting off the old person, may be reborn into the new person of Christ (Col. 3:9–10); and then, through the progress of this new birth, may be re-formed into that blessed form of our renewed restoration which is pleasing to God.

> [Note: Lips. deleted the words “of life” and “of Christ,” which we restore from Bad., Er., and the manuscripts.]

42. Kings Are Called to Understanding.—The Prophet, not ignorant of this good, afterward exhorts and says, VERSES 10–15: “And now, understand, O kings; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling. Lay hold of discipline, lest perhaps the Lord be angry and you perish from the righteous way. When his anger is kindled swiftly, blessed are all who trust in him.”

> [Note: Our manuscript lacks “before him”; the consistent omission below indicates that the version used by Hilary did not have it. It is also absent from the Hebrew, and Jerome marks it with an obelus in the Gallican Psalter.]

The order of this teaching is most beneficial, because it makes known the blessedness of the things to which it exhorts us; for it is difficult to stretch mind and hope toward what is unknown. Therefore, wishing to exhort us to understand the matters he had mentioned above, the Prophet first set forth the honor of understanding itself, saying, “And now, understand, O kings,” thus showing that those who would understand are kings.

But we must ask which kings this prophetic exhortation admonishes to understand, lest anyone perhaps suppose that it means those whose kingship now extends over human bodies, the affairs of war, and the fear of nations. These are not the eternal and blessed kings before God; for they have already fallen away from God’s commands and are allotted to the kingdom of the devil. The same one says, when the devil was tempting the Lord: “And the devil led him up onto a very high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. And the devil said to him: ‘I will give you this power and their glory, because they have been delivered to me’” (Luke 4:5–6).

> [Note: “By the commands themselves.”]

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “since if they themselves fall away from God’s commands”; this reading is less harsh, but it more fully indicates what the scriptural testimony adduced to prove the point implies. Yet Hilary should not be thought to have held this opinion of every king without exception. Rather, since he held it of most, he spoke as though of all; for, as he himself says on Psalm 58, §9: “The whole is reckoned in the greater number.” And shortly afterward: “Since few among all the nations are believers, the few do not prevent all from being unbelievers.” Thus, since few kings have been removed from the devil’s kingdom—among whom it would be wrong not to count David—the few do not prevent all the rest from being delivered to him. In this way he is cleared, from his own statements, of the blemish for which Scultetus reproaches him here.]

But the Gospels show us other kings: namely, those in whom the kingdom of God has drawn near, and those who, reigning within themselves, have conquered sin—who are kings of their own bodies, subjecting every incentive of vice to their own dominion. For this is the kingdom of God within us. Thus Christ also reigns in us when, through him, we ourselves reign by the authority of the Lord over those things which are within us, according to the saying: “The kingdom of God does not come with observation; nor will they say, ‘Look, here!’ or, ‘Look, there!’ For behold, the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:20–21).

> [Note: Lips. has corruptly: “when we ourselves reign by their dominion, of lords,” etc. For *him* refers to Christ. Aptly Augustine, and after him the commonly printed Rufinus, say: “Understand now, O kings—that is, you who are able to rule whatever is servile and beastly in yourselves, chastising your bodies and bringing them into subjection. Those who serve the heavenly King are without doubt kings.”]

The blessed Apostle mentions this kingdom when writing to the Corinthians: “Already you reign without us; and would that you did reign, so that we also might reign with you” (1 Cor. 4:8).

> [Note: Thus Par., with the manuscripts, following the Greek ὑμῖν συμβασιλεύσωμεθα. Other editions have “that we may reign with you.” But on Psalm 60, §5, both printed and manuscript copies have: “and would that you did reign, so that we also might reign together with you.” We have already noted that Hilary does not always cite the same passages of Scripture in one form.]

This, therefore, is the kingdom of God: where sin is conquered, death is destroyed, and the enemy does not reign. For “death reigned from Adam until Moses” (Rom. 5:14); and the Apostle says: “Let not sin therefore reign in you” (Rom. 6:12). Through this kingdom of God, when the kingdom of sin has been dissolved and we ourselves have already become kings by overthrowing the opposing kingdom, this will be the kingdom of God for us: when all the stings of our vices have been crushed and the stain of bodily weakness has been swallowed up.

43. What They Are to Understand.—The Prophet therefore exhorts these kings to understand: that they may know that kings raged against the Lord and his Christ, and that peoples devised vain things; that they may also understand him who laughs from heaven, speaks in wrath, and has appointed a king upon the holy mountain of Zion, proclaiming the commands of God the Father. Let them recognize who it is that was begotten as Son, and also that time when he who made times was begotten in time. Let them understand in what respect he asked for the inheritance of the nations and possession of the ends of the earth; nor let them be ignorant what this iron rod is, by which, ruling them, he breaks them in the manner of a potter’s vessel.

For understanding these things, they will recognize the whole mystery of the divine will; and when through obedience to the commandments they become heirs of God the Father and co-heirs of our Lord Jesus Christ, then through that by which they are co-heirs with the eternal King they must consequently attain this: that they themselves are kings.

44. The Judges of the Earth Are Saints Whose Lives Condemn the Ungodly.—Since the Gospels and the Apostle testify concerning kings, it follows that we must learn who the judges of the earth are, and that they too, like kings, ought to be instructed. This is especially so because he calls kings merely by the bare name, without any designation of a kingdom, in order to show that they are his kings and kings within him; but he calls them judges “of the earth.”

We know by the very practice of earthly custom that judge and king differ: reigning is not the same as judging; for kingship is dominion, while judgment is the measure of equity.

> [Note: “Indeed, kingship.”]

Therefore all the saints are to be understood as judges of the earth, whose life and faith are judgment upon unbelievers and the wicked.

> [Note: The printed editions have, “serve in place of judgment,” against the manuscripts.]

The Lord showed this in the Gospels when he said: “The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment and will judge this generation, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, one greater than Jonah is here. The queen of the South will rise in judgment and will judge this generation, because she came from the farthest parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, one greater than Solomon is here” (Matt. 12:41–42).

Such will be the judges of the earth: those whose faith and fear, by comparison, condemn the impenitent and ungodly.

> [Note: Par. has “by comparison.” Then two manuscripts have “faith and fear,” and one has “and death.” The sense is sufficiently clear in itself: the comparison of their faith and fear, etc.]

For if the repentance undertaken by the Ninevites at Jonah’s preaching attained the fruit of repentance, their obedient repentance must judge the insolent impenitence of these people. Or does not the queen of the South, hearing the wisdom of Solomon which she had desired from the farthest parts of the earth, condemn by her foreign hearing the unbelief and negligence of those present?

> [Note: “Hear.”]

> [Note: That is, of those who heard Christ, the true Wisdom, while he was present. The foreign hearing is then contrasted with hearing in his presence; unless it is called foreign because it involved undertaking a journey abroad.]

Yet Christ, their author, adds a judgment of disobedience and refusal to hear that differs from that of Solomon and Jonah. The Apostle plainly shows that these are judges of the earth, saying: “Do you not know that the saints shall judge the world, and the world is judged among you?” (1 Cor. 6:2).

> [Note: Our book has, “the world is judged here,” in agreement with the Greek.]

For through the merit of their attained blessedness, their holiness, set in comparison, condemns the lives of the guilty.

45. Let Fear, Joy, and Trembling Temper the Mind of God’s Servant.—The Prophet immediately adds the work of this understanding and instruction, saying: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling.” He does not permit service to be secure or negligent.

> [Note: “That service should be.”]

He wills fear to be mingled with every duty of service. For just as servants who fear serve their earthly masters more diligently, because fear joined to obedience elicits the purpose of more watchful service, so also those serving God, if they fear through the fear set before them, will not be negligent in the service they have undertaken.

But lest this fear be thought to be the terror of tyranny among believers, he added to the words, “Serve the Lord in fear,” the further words, “and rejoice before him,” so that the exultation of joy might temper the fear of service, when fear itself brings the cause of joy through the consciousness of faithful service. Yet, lest the freedom of joy exceed the limits of fitting moderation, he added: “Rejoice in trembling,” because joy free from trembling would dangerously lead to forgetfulness of fear. Thus the ordering of the prophetic utterance is preserved: fear holds service in check, exultation moderates fear, and the consequent trembling restrains exultation.

46. Let There Be Zeal in God’s Service.—The Prophet taught that this service, fearful yet exultant and exultant yet trembling, consists in what follows: “Lay hold of discipline.” The force of the expression indicates a will impatient and, as it were, hurrying prematurely toward its object: it teaches that discipline is not so much to be sought as seized.

> [Note: “The force of the expression [indicates] an impatient meaning,” etc.]

He is not satisfied with lukewarm faith in keeping this obedience, but desires the ardor of the Spirit in eagerness to seize it.

> [Note: The printed editions have “not in the time of faith”; they are corrected from a Vatican manuscript.]

Thus the Lord delighted in the forceful seeker who seizes the kingdom of heaven, saying: “From the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matt. 11:12), because, though possession of the kingdom of heaven was proclaimed to Israel, the faith of the nations seized this possession for itself while Israel was unbelieving.

> [Note: Thus Ms. Mic. In the other books: “for itself, while Israel is unbelieving”; there *for itself* refers to the Lord, in whom Israel disbelieves or refuses to believe, and from whose hand the nations snatch the kingdom.]

47. Paul’s example. — Thus blessed Paul also runs in order to lay hold, saying: “But I pursue, that I may lay hold of that for which I too have been laid hold of” (Phil. 3:12). He hastens not with a slow step, nor does he pursue in an idle course; for he pursues in order to lay hold. Indeed, it might seem sufficient for him to have said that he pursued in order to overtake; but he too wishes to bring force to bear, hastens to lay hold, and, by the manner—perhaps *amplexus*, “embracing”—of a bodily example, to seize upon it. Yet he knows that, precisely in hastening to lay hold, he has already been laid hold of.

For if God, born as man, has laid hold of us—who through our bodily nature differ from his own nature—by himself becoming what we are, it is now ours to strive to lay hold of what he is, so that our eager haste may enter into that glory into which he removes the nature of this bodily corruption. Thus we shall lay hold of that for which we were laid hold of, if we attain the nature of God, God having first attained our human nature. Discipline, therefore, must be laid hold of and seized, as it were, in an embrace and bodily bond, lest it slip away or fall from us.

[Note: [Col. 0289D] The printed editions, except Paris, read *diffidentes*, corruptly; nor is Paris’s *discidentes* any better. Yet *dissidentes* would not be objectionable. From the manuscripts we restore *dissidentis*, in this sense: “If God, born as man, has laid hold of us who, by bodily nature, differ in nature from the divine” (*suae* being in the third case). Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 35, §88, following Hilary, says that he laid hold of us so that “I too might become God to the same extent that he became man.”]

59. 48. Those alien to it perish from the righteous way. — The prophet then supplied the reason for this diligent embrace and bond, saying: “Lay hold of discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry, and you perish from the righteous way. When his wrath has burned out quickly.” For the day of punishment is at hand, signified by the Lord’s wrath burning fiercely; and on that day, unless we hold fast the discipline which we have laid hold of, we shall perish from the righteous way.

Whatever is taken away from anything perishes in relation to it; and what is lacking already appears lost to that from which it is lacking. For though it may remain in its own nature, it does not remain for the one from whom it is absent. Thus the wicked perish from the righteous way because they shall not be in it. But they perish from the righteous way when his wrath is kindled in a short time.

The wicked suffer the penalties of hell immediately after death. — This wrath, by which they perish from the righteous way, is not slow, lest anyone flatter himself during the intervening delay of judgment with the prospect of some gain from punishment. For his wrath is kindled in a short time. Avenging hell receives us at once; and, when we depart from the body, if we have lived in such a way, we immediately perish from the straight way.

The Gospel’s rich man and poor man bear witness: angels placed the one in the dwellings of the blessed and in Abraham’s bosom, while the region of punishment immediately received the other (Luke 16). Indeed, punishment received the dead man so immediately that even his brothers still remained above, on earth. There is no delay or postponement there. For the day of judgment brings either the eternal recompense of blessedness or that of punishment. Meanwhile, the time of death holds each person under its own laws, while it reserves each either for Abraham or for punishment until judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0289D] The Paris edition reads *Non mora*, incorrectly. Here the opinion of certain ancients is refuted, including Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, VII.21: “Yet let no one suppose that souls are judged immediately after death: all are kept in one common custody until the time comes when the greatest Judge examines their merits.” See the Preface.]

[Note: [Col. 0290D] Here the term “hell” should be understood, or even expressed; in relation to it, the brothers who remain on earth are then said to remain “above.” Tertullian says of the region below, *On the Soul*, §55: “For us, the lower regions are a vast expanse in the hollow and depth of the earth, a hidden abyss in its very bowels.” Shortly afterward he places them again “in its innermost and interior recess, covered within the earth itself, shut up within it, and built over by yet lower abysses.”]

49. Trust in God is necessary. — Therefore the prophet concludes this psalm, so rich in heavenly mysteries, thus: “Blessed are all who trust in him.” The perfection of blessedness requires neither trembling nor uncertain hope. Trust is needed for this work: that is, a firm conviction and an unchangeable will; for to trust is more than merely to hope. We must therefore trust, lest the wrath of God, swiftly kindled, destroy us from the straight way. For faithful is he who says: “Whoever believes in me shall not be judged, but shall pass from death to life” (Job 5:24). Our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM IX

### TREATISE ON THE TITLE OF PSALM IX

[Note: [Col. 0291D] This treatise, published by Fr. Coustant from a Vatican manuscript, is confirmed—indeed, corrected and somewhat supplemented—by the excellent book of the Chapter of Verona. At the end of the preceding exposition it has, as in the Vatican manuscript: “Psalm II ends. The treatise on the title of Psalm IX begins, happily.”]

“To the end, for the hidden things of the son. A psalm of David.”

[Note: [Col. 0291D] From our manuscript we have supplied the word *filii*, “of the son,” which appears below in the exposition.]

[Note: [Col. 0291D] The word *filii* is missing, though it is expressed below; there one reads once and again *pro occulta*, “for the hidden things.” Greek: Ὑπὲρ κρυφίων τοῦ υἱοῦ, “for the hidden things of the son.”]

60. This now first appears from Vatican manuscript 231, written about five hundred years ago. After the exposition of the second psalm it adds: “Psalm II ends. The treatise on the title of Psalm IX begins, happily.” It bears no marks of forgery, but very many of authenticity.

1. It employs expressions familiar and congenial to Hilary: *absolutio*, “exposition,” *absoluta intelligentia*, “complete understanding,” and the like.

2. Its explanation of the word *finis*, “end,” agrees with what is said on the same matter both in the Prologue, §18, and in *On the Trinity*, II.28.

3. It has a particular manner of expressing Christ’s birth from a virgin.

4. It teaches entry into the kingdom of God the Father through Christ’s kingdom.

Finally, in the Prologue, §17, Hilary promises to give the reasons for the individual inscriptions in each psalm; and in §22 he says that this is because they show of what matters a psalm consists. Here especially he performs what he promised, teaching in §2 that the title was added so that one might know of what the psalm itself consists. It would be desirable that this little work had reached us in a more corrected form, together with the exposition of the whole psalm, which Hilary must be thought to have appended to it.

1. Some psalms are easy, others difficult to understand. — Some psalms possess a complete intelligibility; others have a more obscure meaning. The diversity of prophecy naturally produces this diversity.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] “Both kinds.”]

For through many varied modes of discourse the Holy Spirit instructs human beings in the knowledge of God: now comprehending hidden mysteries through natures and comparisons drawn from human beings; now commending the simplicity of faith through a clear exposition of words; now confirming the order of life by the truth of commandments; now showing, through the person of the prophet who writes the psalm, what must be foreseen and avoided. Thus, through this manifold and rich abundance of teaching, by certain stages and advances in learning, the structure of complete understanding is attained.

A psalm will be offered us as an example whose superscription is this: “To the end, for the hidden things of the son: a psalm of David.” Therefore, the understanding of the psalm must be sought from the nature of those things which are both hidden and at the end.

2. The title indicates the matters treated. — The psalm is not inscribed “To the end, for the hidden things of the son” except for this purpose: that one may know of what matters the psalm itself consists. For all additions to the title of a discourse testify to the matters from which the discourse begins. It is not fitting that one thing should occur in a discourse and another in its title, because the title is like an index of the matters written about.

Accordingly, the meaning of the expression “at the end” must be understood. At the end is that beyond which there is nothing; at the end is that which surpasses the present time. For the end comes from all things; not all things from the end. Everything ceases in it, and it is a kind of final point of a thing done or said. Unless it is the finality of the whole universe, it will not be an end; for what has something final beyond itself cannot be ultimate.

From this we must understand that whenever a title has “at the end,” it contains not present matters but ultimate ones.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] The preceding edition read: “whenever titles have ‘at the end.’” Certainly one should read not *quotiescumque* here but *quotiensque*; nevertheless this manuscript regularly uses *quotiensque* for *quotiescumque*.]

Hidden things are things created and concealed, hidden away in secret, inaccessible, and impenetrable places—known only to him who created them, unless they are brought forth for certain persons to know.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] Either something is missing here, or one should read *quod ei*, “which is known to him,” instead of *in quo ei*.]

Therefore the psalm is inscribed “To the end, for the hidden things.” And since it is fitting first to explain, from the nature of things, what understanding lies in the names “end” and “hidden things,” then the things themselves which are at the end and among the hidden things must be explained.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] After *et deinde*, “and then,” words are lacking to complete the sentence.]

[Note: [Col. 0292B] We would prefer *edidimus* to *et deinde*.]

3. Blessed Paul is our witness concerning these matters, saying: “As you read, you are able to understand my insight into the mystery of Christ, which in other ages was not made known to the children of men as it has now been revealed” (Eph. 3:4–5). And again: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: among the Gentiles to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of his mystery, hidden from the ages in God” (Eph. 3:8–9).

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “Paul” is added.]

This, then, is the hidden thing of which the Lord also says: “Nothing is concealed which shall not be known, nor covered which shall not be revealed” (Matt. 10:26). But the psalm contains hidden things, not merely one hidden thing. This is rightly so, for what follows teaches that they were many, not one.

It is a hidden thing that God, for the sake of human salvation, appeared not in the heavenly glory and radiance of his name, but put on the form of a human body. It is also a hidden thing that he assumed the nature of human flesh not according to the common manner of origin, but came forth from a virgin and was born of a virgin, brought forth without the beginning of our ordinary birth. It is a hidden thing that he who died should live through death, resuming from the body the glory of immortality. Yet this is not, indeed, the end.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] The words *virgine* are absent from the Verona manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0292D] Perhaps: “that he came from a Virgin and was born without our beginning of birth,” etc. Thus in *On the Trinity*, X.13: Christ is said not to have lived in the body through the beginnings of our body and soul, because other human beings have their origin from man and woman, whereas he had his origin from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin. See the fuller discussion in the cited place of *On the Trinity*.]

4. What end it signifies. — The end signifies not some cessation of things, but the measure and consummation of things that run their course; it does not mean that they cease in annihilation, but that the matters under discussion are gathered into a certain abiding consummation. What, then, is this end, what is the complete perfection of all things, and how hidden it is, the blessed Apostle declares to the Corinthians:

“For as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; then those who are Christ’s, who believed at his coming; then the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every principality and authority. For he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet; for God has subjected all things under his feet. The last enemy conquered in him is death. But when he says, ‘All things are subjected,’ it is excepted that he who subjected all things to him is not included. Then he himself shall be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all.”

[Note: [Col. 0293D] At *On the Trinity*, XI.22, we shall note that the word *crediderunt*, “believed,” is absent from the older manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek.]

[Note: [Col. 0293D] We reject the pronoun *ei*, which the preceding edition inserted here, on the authority of our manuscript. Thus Hilary will agree with himself, for he reads this way elsewhere, namely in *On the Trinity*, XI.8 and again §36. The Greek text also supports this.]

[Note: [Col. 0294D] As in Books I and II of *On the Trinity*, so here it is absent in all or nearly all manuscripts: “But when all things shall have been subjected to him.”]

This, therefore, is the end for the hidden things—or perhaps “for the hidden things” or “hidden”: the resurrection of the dead, the glorification of the saints, the abolition of ruling wickedness, and the destruction of death; and through this, Christ’s kingdom, and also the kingdom of God the Father.

For when these things have been accomplished, after all things have been subjected by the Father to the Son, this does not take eternity away from the kingdom through subjection. Rather, he introduces us—made glorious, clothed with immortality, and conformed to the glory of his body—into the Father’s kingdom: now worthy of his co-inheritance, now received into the Father’s household, now sharing in his goods and glory. Thus he may reign with the Father in us, and God may be all in all, when, through the subjection of obedience, the weakness of human assumption is absorbed into the divine nature.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] See *On the Trinity*, XI.35–36.]

[Note: [Col. 0294D] “Conformed,” likewise from our manuscript, in place of “confirmed,” as the editor had suspected.]

[Note: [Col. 0294D] Perhaps: “through subjection, which is rightly that of obedience, because then, with every desire removed, spirit and flesh will be wholly obedient to God.”]

Therefore this eternal praise is owed through the Son to God the Father: when all who have lived by faith from Adam until the time of the kingdom have been raised; when, transformed with heavenly form from—and perhaps “with”—the body; when all wickedness has been removed; when the devil has been consigned to the punishment of eternal fire; and when his name has been removed from human memory. These hidden things are sung in the psalm; these are celebrated when the end has been consummated. And because the Son knows all future things, these are praised as though already completed, because all things are in him, with him, and through him. To him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] The earlier edition read “when all have been raised in all,” which obscures the sense.]

[Note: [Col. 0294D] The earlier edition had *vixerunt*, “lived.”]

## PSALM XIII

“The fool has said in his heart: There is no God. They have become corrupt and abominable in their desires; there is none who does good, not even one. The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one. Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they dealt deceitfully; the venom of asps is beneath their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their paths, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes. Shall not all who work iniquity know, those who devour my people as bread is eaten? They have not called upon the Lord. There they trembled with fear, where there was no fear. For God is in the righteous generation; you have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope. Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion? When the Lord has turned away the captivity of his people, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall rejoice.”

[Note: [Col. 0294D] Hilary: “Let Jacob rejoice and let Israel exult.”]

### TREATISE ON THE PSALM

In the Paris edition of 1605, the first portion of this treatise was published for the first time from the manuscript of Saint-Maximin of Micy, though truncated from §1 through §3. It is now presented complete from the aforementioned Vatican manuscript, where it follows at the end of the preceding little work: “The treatise on the title of Psalm IX ends. Psalm XIII begins. Read happily. ‘The fool has said in his heart: There is no God,’ and the rest. ‘The Apostle instructing us in many things,’” etc.

Its language, doctrine, and manner of interpretation breathe Hilary’s vein and genius. For example: its long periods; its manner of surveying the themes of the whole psalm through repeated use of the particle *ubi*, “where”; the same method by which the definitions of the Synod of Ancyra are surveyed in *On the Synods*, §27; the statement in §3 that “the particular virtues in each individual word must be explained”; and other points indicated in the notes—all suit him exceedingly well. Yet this and the following treatise have more the character of a sermon delivered immediately after the psalm’s reading than do the others.

1. With what reverence God’s word must be handled or heard. — “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God,” and the rest. The Apostle, instructing us in many things, teaches us also that the word of God must be handled with all reverence, saying: “Whoever speaks, let him speak as the utterances of God” (1 Pet. 4:11).

[Note: [Col. 0295D] Thus we read in our manuscript. Earlier: “thereby instructs.”]

For it is not right that, in these matters, there should be the indiscriminate freedom customary in our own speech. Rather, when we speak what we have learned and read, honor must be rendered to the author by careful speech. Human custom in the duties of life offers us an example of heavenly teaching. If someone interprets a king’s words and conveys his commands into the ears of the people, he carefully and cautiously takes pains, in reverence for his office, to satisfy the king’s dignity, so that everything may both be read and heard with honor and reverence. How much more fitting is it that, when we reconsider the utterances of God for human knowledge, we should prove ourselves worthy of this duty?

For we are, as it were, an instrument of the Holy Spirit, through which the variety of voice and diversity of doctrine are to be heard. We must therefore watch and take care that we say nothing lowly, fearing the rule of this pronouncement: “Cursed is everyone who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48:10). Set before us, conversely, is the reward for the care and diligence of those who, with reverence and fear, commend the Holy Scriptures to themselves as God’s words and convey them with fitting dignity to the minds of their hearers, as the Lord says: “Upon whom shall I look, if not upon the humble and gentle person, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Preachers, therefore, must consider that they are not speaking to human beings; and hearers must know that words of men are not being offered to them, but the voices of God, God’s ordinances, and God’s laws. The greatest reverence is fitting for each office.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] The reading was *utriusque*, “of both.”]

For it is a matter of the greatest danger either to utter anything superfluous from God’s treasures, from the hidden mysteries, from the eternal testament, or to hear them negligently. All must be sealed into our souls and entrusted to our understanding, because there is nothing in God’s words that is not to be fulfilled; and everything that has been spoken already bears a certain necessity of coming to pass, because God’s words are decrees.

2. The psalm that has been read is inscribed “To the end.”

[Note: [Col. 0295D] This has the sound of a sermon.]

If all were inscribed in this way, there would be no difficulty, for their uniformity would exclude every question. But since one bears one inscription and another another, the diversities of inscription must necessarily have arisen from differing causes.

There is a twofold meaning in those inscribed “to the end”: either they contain the matters that shall be at the consummation, or the ending of the psalm supplies the exposition of what is said throughout the whole psalm. Now all things in this psalm are harsh, dreadful, grievous, full of blasphemies, filled with crimes, and heavy with complaints. There is no confession of God, no joy in gladness, no song in choirs; but accusation against the profane, complaint against the stubborn, and grief for the afflicted.

For it says, verse 1: “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God. They have become corrupt and abominable in their desires; there is none who does good, not even one,” and the rest. At the end follows, verse 7: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion? When the Lord has turned away the captivity of his people, let Jacob rejoice and Israel exult.”

3. When the world is ruined, a physician is sought. — As when someone—perhaps “if anyone”—enters a plague-ridden city, sees all its inhabitants without exception wasted by disease, burning with fevers, and exhausted by various kinds of sickness; and, finding no physician there, groans and laments that no help, no remedy is present for such great evils; and perceives the pestilence of the limbs growing more savage each day; and knows that a physician situated far away could cure them if he were present: then, as the sole thing left, he cries out in the pain of despair, saying, “Who can make him present and bring his healing?” He turns every anxiety into prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] Paris, from Micy: “which alone can, in despair over sufferings,” etc. The Vatican manuscript’s reading seemed more elegant.]

In the same way, the Holy Spirit, seeing the error of humankind, seeing the increasing evils of this world and the disease spreading with incurable death: where God is denied by the fool; where all have been corrupted by the abominable deceits of pleasures; where no one is willing to do good; where their throats are graves for the innocent; where their tongues serve fraud; where the venom of asps is poured upon their lips and words; where the mouth is full of bitterness and cursing; where their feet run swiftly to shed blood; and where, because through these things they do not know the way of peace, misery increases along all the paths of their life; where there is no reverence for God; where the devastation of God’s people is, for persecutors, as bread to be eaten; where the deaths, losses, and torments of the innocent become the satiety of the wicked; where God is not invoked and they tremble at nothing, reverencing the creature in idols and abandoning the Creator; where God is despaired of as dwelling in the righteous generation; where the counsel of the poor is confounded, and hope, patience, and justice are mocked—when these evils thus rage and rule throughout the world, the Holy Spirit, knowing who alone can bring help, cries: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?”

[Note: [Col. 0296D] “Beholding.”]

[Note: [Col. 0295D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “where they are talkative.” From this manuscript we restore below the word “asps.”]

[Note: [Col. 0296D] The preceding edition reads “will become.”]

For neither Moses, nor Elijah, nor Isaiah, nor the prophets gave it; all the works of the Law were powerless against so great a plague of diseases.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] See below, Treatise on Psalm LII, §20.]

A physician was needed, who by one and the same aid could cure all alike, and heal the countless and various illnesses throughout the whole world—not by art, not by work (for when could art and work applied separately to each have sufficed?), but by the power of his word.

[Note: [Col. 0296D] Here Hilary does not, with Pelagius, require merely the external grace of the teaching and preaching of God’s word for the healing of human sicknesses and ailments. Otherwise he would wrongly have denied that this had been given through Moses, Elijah, Isaiah, and the prophets. Rather, he intends an inward grace—one which, while preserving human freedom, heals the illnesses of the soul as effectively as Christ healed the various ailments of bodies.]

The Spirit seeks this physician and awaits him: the one at whose coming fever would cease, blindness end, paralysis no longer exist, and death not prevail. He awaits him, proclaims him, and prays for him: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?” But in the individual words, the individual virtues must be explained.

4. Zion is Christ’s body. — The Apostle teaches what Zion is when he says: “Let us approach Mount Zion, the city of the holy Jerusalem” (Heb. 12:22). For we all run to lay hold of that for which we have been laid hold of by Christ (Phil. 3:12): that is, to be found in his body, which he himself assumed from us; in which we were chosen by the Father before the foundation of the world; in which we have been reconciled from enemies and acquired from among the lost; in which the Apostle, counting all things loss, desires to be found, saying: “I count all things as dung, that I may gain Christ and be found in him” (Phil. 3:8).

Therefore, because these diseases of our body could be taken away only through the assumption of our flesh, and because all our salvation is in God through the assumption of flesh, it says: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?”

[Note: [Col. 0297C] Our manuscript has supplied a splendid correction. The earlier text read: “the salvation of all is in the Lord,” which produced either scarcely any sound sense or none.]

[Note: [Col. 0297D] “Flesh” or “human being” is understood. Hence, in *On the Trinity*, II.23, Christ is preached as inhabiting inwardly the whole of universal flesh through the assumption of one flesh; and in Psalm LI, §15, as having assumed in himself the nature of all flesh—that is, the nature of the whole human race; and in Psalm LIV, §9, as having become the flesh of our universality. Moreover, as here, so in Psalm CXLVII, §1, Hilary interprets Zion as Christ’s body.]

5. “Salvation”: the name of Christ promised to the Gentiles. — But in the word *salutare*, “salvation,” lies the power of the name. We do not devise or invent it; rather, in the books of the Old Testament we are taught that the Lord our God is called “Salvation,” and that this name was properly always granted to the Gentiles by promise.

For Isaiah says: “The Lord has revealed his holy arm in the sight of all nations, and all the ends of the earth shall know the salvation of our God” (Isa. 52:10). Therefore it has been revealed to all nations and known by all. Again, in the psalms the Holy Spirit cries: “Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wondrous things. The Lord has made known his salvation; in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. 97:1–2). Again: “Declare his glory among the nations, and his salvation among all peoples” (Ps. 95:3). Again: “Show us your mercy, O Lord, and give us your salvation” (Ps. 84:8).

[Note: [Col. 0297D] From the Vatican manuscript we restore the previously omitted word *ostendit*, “has made known.”]

The Lord showed the desire of this hope in the Gospel, saying: “Many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see and hear what you hear” (Matt. 13:17).

[Note: [Col. 0297C] “In the Gospels.”]

Simeon waited long for this salvation; and when he received it in his hands, he recognized it, and amid the cries of infancy and the uncleanness of the cradle saw God through faith. Recognizing and worshipping him in such things, he said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles.”

[Note: [Col. 0297D] The earlier edition reads “in the revelation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Thus from the Verona manuscript, in accordance with the Greek: εἰς ἀποκάλυψιν, “for revelation.”]

This salvation, therefore, is proclaimed to the Gentiles, not to fleshly Israel, which on the mountain beheld, saw, and heard the Lord of majesty; which stoned, struck down, sawed apart, and killed in the prophets. But this whole discourse concerns the Gentiles, and is the salvation of the Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Paris reads “in death”; but the Vatican manuscript, “on the mountain.” The time is meant when the Israelite people received the Law, not when they crucified the Lord. Shortly after, *expectavit* seems, according to ancient usage, to be written for *spectavit*, “beheld.”]

[Note: [Col. 0298D] The latest Paris edition restored *salutare*, against the manuscripts. In Psalm LXVI, §4, we have: “That Jesus is called ‘Salvation’ is the very language of propriety.” Elsewhere this word is used in the same way.]

6. Thus it says: “When the Lord turns away the captivity of his people.” Captivity properly belongs to the Gentiles: those who had said in their heart, “There is no God”; who trembled where there was no fear; who had confounded and mocked the hope of the poor, because the Lord is his hope; who had denied that the Lord would dwell in the righteous generation; who were captive to the religions of demons, superstitions about times, and services rendered to the creature.

[Note: [Col. 0298D] Thus Vatican manuscript; Paris has “had introduced.”]

[Note: [Col. 0298D] Paris reads: “because his hope is from the Lord,” and then omits “righteous.”]

This captivity is called forth; this slavery is removed.

[Note: [Col. 0298D] Formerly Paris, and Micy in the first hand, read *appellatur*, “is called”; then *pellitur*, “is driven away.” But *apellitur*, “is called forth,” is more correctly restored in the same manuscript—a word customary with Hilary.]

But Israel will be the one who believes; Israel will be the one who sees God with the eyes of the heart. For Israel is “one who sees God,” and, after captivity has been turned away, such a person recognizes this salvation of God. Jacob rejoices, and Israel rejoices: captivity turned away, freedom granted, God contemplated, and Abraham and Jacob called fathers through adoption into the family.

[Note: [Col. 0298C] The words “Israel will be the one who believes” do not appear in our manuscript and do not at all suit the etymology of the name.]

[Note: [Col. 0298C] “With the city destroyed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0298C] “Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.” At the end: “Psalm XIII ends. Psalm XIV begins. ‘Lord, who…,’” etc.]

Therefore, in these things let us rejoice and exult, knowing that through our redemption there is joy among the angels in heaven over the salvation of one repentant person (Luke 15:7). And since heavenly joy is for us, our joys ought to be perpetual in Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XIV

“Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain? One who walks without stain and works righteousness; who speaks truth in his heart; who has not practised deceit with his tongue, nor done evil to his neighbor, nor accepted reproach against his neighbors. The wicked person is reduced to nothing in his sight; but he glorifies those who fear the Lord. One who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive; who has not lent his money at interest nor accepted gifts against the innocent. One who does these things shall not be moved for ever.”

[Hilary: “magnifies.”]

### TREATISE ON THE PSALM

At first, as we reviewed this treatise, it was not sufficiently evident why we should confidently attribute it to Hilary. Indeed, our inclination strongly tended to reject that attribution. Its style is somewhat plainer than usual for him. Moreover, it seemed unfitting that an invincible defender of faith and truth should have been a teacher of the permissibility of an officious lie—especially since Augustine, *Letter* 180, §3, had defended Hilary’s ninth book *On the Trinity* from such a suspicion.

Yet, on examining §§3 and 4, we found no lack of indications by which to recognize its author as Hilary. First, there occur expressions familiar to him: for instance, *sacramentum*, “mystery,” and “the force of words must be considered,” in §2; and “the power of eternity” in §5. Then, what is said in §5 about Christ’s body closely resembles innumerable passages in Hilary; and what is discussed in §11 concerning self-confidence and arrogance is again touched upon in Psalm LII, §15. Many other such features are easier for attentive readers to perceive than to demonstrate to others.

Therefore, since it is attributed to him not only by the Micy manuscript but also by the Vatican manuscript, there is no sufficiently strong reason to deny it to him. Nor is it surprising that the exposition should be less intricate and obscure in a psalm which, as is said at the beginning, contains neither prophecy nor obscurity. Nor is it more remarkable that Hilary, reading and sometimes excerpting Origen—who, together with several others, did not consider an officious lie unlawful—might, without examining the issue very closely, have adopted a view greatly congenial to his own disposition, which was highly inclined toward kindness.

But even if an officious lie, under the appearance of charity, imposed upon our Hilary—whereas a lie is evil in itself and cannot be approved under any pretext, as Augustine has well and fully demonstrated in *Against Lying*—this treatise includes many excellent precepts conducive to the best morals: against arrogance, usury, the use of gifts, and other matters most worthy of Hilary. Nor should it be left unsaid that Christian humility ought to be free, steadfast, and, so to speak, proud in resisting powerful persons and rulers who command unjust things. Hilary showed this by his actions, and here too, in §12, commended it in writing.

1. Scope of the psalm. — The psalm that has been read is inscribed “A psalm of David,” because the Holy Spirit spoke these things through him. And this fittingly suits the psalm, for nothing is directed to another time, nothing is brought forth from hidden things, but its entire work concerns the present. Thus it begins, verse 1: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?”

It is the simple prayer of one beseeching and desiring the Lord to know what character, what pursuit, and what disposition belongs to one who is to dwell with God and rest in his heights and heavenly places.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] “Of one beseeching God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0299D] Paris reads “and praying,” and shortly afterward, “those who are to dwell.” We follow the Vatican manuscript.]

For it is no mark of a lowly spirit or mediocre work to be joined to God and deserve fellowship in the same dwelling.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] We restore *Deo*, “to God,” from the Vatican manuscript, which then reads: “to be joined in the fellowship of the same dwelling”; and shortly above, “of a certain name,” in place of “of a certain spirit.”]

Therefore, the answer is immediately given concerning those of whom the question is asked, so that, because these things are arduous and difficult to obtain, it may be understood by what means they are to be attained.

### 2. It contains many excellent precepts in few words.

For, in answer to what was asked, it says, v. 2: “He who walks without blemish and works righteousness,” and what follows in the psalm.

[Editorial notes: Vatican manuscript: “of the following psalm,” where the earlier reading was “of the psalm”; “what follows in the psalm.” Vatican manuscript: “lofty things,” for “His height.” The first Paris edition reads “we pursue”; restored from the Vatican manuscript is “we shall pursue,” from which the word “very” was supplied above.] By such precepts, by such admonitions, is formed and instructed the person whose way leads to God, whose ascent is to His height, whose rest is in His eternal realm. Every command is compressed into brevity, so that it may be committed to memory, adhere to the mind, and be retained—outside and at home, publicly and privately, by day and by night—obeyed, and diligently pursued. For this brevity is rich and inexhaustible, gathered from all the commands and ordinances of the Old and New Testaments, and most suitable for children, women, men, and old people alike. And so that the richness of this very brevity may be more commendable, we shall pursue what mystery is contained in each word.

This is neither prophecy, nor obscurity, nor an example. It is the voice of one who asks, the goodness of One who answers, the confirmation of one who hears. But in these words the power of the words is to be discerned.

[Editorial note: The Vatican manuscript reads “confirmation” instead of “the confirmation of one who hears”; on its authority “to be discerned” is substituted below for the earlier conjectural reading “to be inferred.”] For He has distinguished thus: dwelling in the tabernacle, resting upon the mountain; and dwelling in the tabernacle comes first, resting upon the mountain afterward. Therefore, if the difference between dwelling and resting is to be understood, the proper character of the mountain and the tabernacle must be explained.

### 3. Tabernacles established by Moses.

The tabernacles which we read were first in existence were slight, perishable, withering shelters, temporarily roofed with woven branches—such as we ourselves sometimes make in order to escape the heat, so that beneath their shade we may avoid the burning and heat of the sun.

[Editorial note: “Woven.”] Tabernacles of this kind were established for the people through Moses. But they dried up and were dissolved. For they were figurative, made after a pattern.

[Editorial notes: Vatican manuscript: “and made after a pattern.” “And made after a pattern.”] For God said to Moses: “See that you make all things according to the pattern which I showed you on the mountain” (Exod. 25:40).

David also, desiring to build the Temple, called it a tabernacle, as he says:

[Editorial note: Paris reads “called it the covenant.” The text “I will not give …” is corrected with the aid of the Vatican manuscript.] “I will not give sleep to my eyes until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob” (Ps. 131:4–5). But the tabernacle of Moses and Solomon also fell; and afterward the Apostles established very many tabernacles, and in every region of the inhabited world—even on islands of the Ocean—they prepared many dwellings for God.

[Editorial notes: Vatican manuscript: “But the tabernacle of Moses and Solomon also fell; but afterwards the Apostles,” etc.; it then omits “of the Apostle.” Once that word is deleted, “very many,” not “very much,” is to be read. Nevertheless, nothing is to be altered. Comparable is Tertullian, *On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 20: “Immediately, therefore,” he says, “the Apostles … having first borne witness through Judaea to faith in Jesus Christ and established churches, thereafter went forth into the world and proclaimed to the nations the same doctrine of the same faith; and consequently founded churches in every city, from which the other churches thereafter borrowed, and daily borrow, the offshoot of faith and seeds of doctrine, so that they may become churches. For this reason they too are reckoned apostolic, as offspring of apostolic churches. Every kind must necessarily be reckoned according to its origin. Thus the many and great churches are that one first Church from the Apostles, from which all … Thus all are first and apostolic, while all prove their unity by being one.” So Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*: “The Church is one, which spreads more widely into a multitude through the increase of fruitfulness, as the sun has many rays, but one light”; and Epistle 52: “One Church, one throughout the whole world, divided into many members.” Another note: “But the tabernacles of Moses and Solomon also fell; and afterwards the Apostles,” etc.; shortly before, speaking of Moses’ tabernacles: “But these dried up and were dissolved.”

The Vatican manuscript more neatly reads “in every place that can be reached,” rather than the Paris reading “can be reached, even from the islands of Ocean.” If anyone doubts whether there were churches on islands of Ocean in Hilary’s age, let him consult Hilary’s *On the Synods*, addressed, along with others, to the bishops of Britain.] Of their glory the Holy Spirit testifies: “How lovely are Your tabernacles, O God of hosts! My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:2–3).

[Editorial note: The reading is “Lord of hosts”; in Greek, Κύριε τῶν δυνάμεων, “Lord of powers.” Then: “in the courts of the Lord.” The earlier edition read “ordered” instead of “adorned.”]

Therefore the Prophet does not desire one tabernacle—whether the leafy one made through Moses, that desired by David, or that adorned by Solomon with every work of human craftsmanship—but many and innumerable tabernacles. For although the Church throughout the world is one, yet each city possesses its own church; and it is one in all, although there are many, because the one Church exists in the many.

### 4. How blessed is unceasing dwelling in the temples.

The first and greatest step, then, for those ascending to heavenly things is to dwell in this tabernacle, and there to spend, night and day, the life of the whole age: removed from worldly cares and leaving behind the business of this world. Thus many of the saints never withdrew from the tabernacle. Of Joshua the son of Nun it is written: “And Joshua, a young man, did not depart from the tabernacle.” And Anna the prophetess “did not depart from the Temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day” (Luke 2:37).

After this one must rest upon the mountain of the Lord.

[Editorial note: As Cyprian says in *On the Unity of the Church*: “If one who was outside Noah’s ark could escape, then one who is outside the Church will escape,” etc.] For those departing hence, the way leads there; nor is there any way except through this dwelling. Therefore inquiry had first to be made concerning dwelling in the tabernacle, because from it there would be an ascent to the mountain. Moreover, dwelling belongs to time and labor. Rest, however, is not interrupted from without, but is unbroken, perpetual leisure, free from trouble, remaining in its own condition; for if disturbance mingles with it, it loses both the nature and the name of repose.

### 5. The mountain on which one rests is Christ’s body.

But there is no mountain of the Lord upon earth; for all the earth has long been subject to the curse through human sins.

[Editorial note: Thus our manuscript corrects the text, as Coustant suspected should be corrected in the margin. Earlier: “harmful through curses.”] It deserved offence in Adam’s deeds and Abel’s blood; under Noah it was full of the sins of its inhabitants; and even now every lofty and elevated mountain is defiled by shrines, temples, and sacred rites. Therefore this mountain is not to be sought among such things.

[Editorial note: Thus the Vatican manuscript. Paris has: “this mountain is not to be looked for in those things,” where *expectandus* means “to be looked upon.” The immediately preceding remarks make clear that this work was written while idolatrous worship was flourishing.]

But just as the highest parts of the ground are called mountains, so among heavenly things we must understand the greatest and loftiest realities under the name of a mountain. And what is more sublime than Christ? Or what is higher than our God?

[Editorial notes: See *Treatise on Psalm 13*, §4. The words “Or what is higher than our God?”—formerly absent—are restored here from the Vatican manuscript.] His mountain is that body which He assumed from humankind, in which He now dwells, lofty and exalted above every principality and power and every name.

Upon this mountain the city has been built which cannot be hidden; for, as the Apostle says, “No other foundation is there except Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11). Therefore, since those who belong to Christ were chosen in Christ’s body before the foundation of the world; since the Church is Christ’s body;

[Editorial note: Paris reads “Christ is the body of the Church,” contrary to the manuscripts. Again below, *Treatise on Psalm 51*, §4, reads: “the Church, which is Christ’s body.”] since Christ is the foundation of our building; and since the city is built upon the mountain—this is that mountain in which the question is asked who can rest.

In another psalm we read of this same mountain: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in His holy place?” (Ps. 23:3). Isaiah also shall be our witness: “And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be manifest; and they shall say, ‘Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob’” (Isa. 2:2–3).

[Editorial note: “Mountain of the Lord”; so in Greek, τὸ ὄρος Κυρίου. Likewise, “to the house,” as in the Septuagint.] And Paul again: “You have come to Mount Sion, and to the city of the living God, Jerusalem” (Heb. 12:22).

If, then, all hope of our rest is in Christ’s body; and, since we are to rest upon the mountain, we can understand the mountain as nothing other than the body which He received from us—before which He was God, and in which God is, and through which He will transform the body of our lowliness, making it conformable to the body of His glory—

[Editorial notes: The words “and in which God is,” omitted in Paris, are supplied from the Vatican manuscript. The manuscript reads *transfigurabit*, “will transform,” rather than *transfiguravit*, “transformed.”]provided that we too have fastened the vices of our body to His cross, so that we may rise in His body: then after dwelling in the Church one ascends to that body; in it one rests in the Lord’s sublimity; in it we shall be joined with the choirs of angels, since we too are God’s city. And there is rest, because no pain arises from weakness, no fear from want;

[Editorial note: The Vatican manuscript reads more correctly “no pain from weakness,” whereas Paris has “pain from impiety,” and then omits “no.”] but, as all enjoy their own firmness through the power of eternity, they rest in realities that lack nothing external.

### 6. Avoid vices; pursue virtues.

Therefore, to the question, “Lord, who shall dwell in Your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon Your holy mountain?” the Holy Spirit answered through the Prophet: “He who walks without blemish and works righteousness.” Thus the person who enters undefiled and lives free from every stain of sin is declared to be the one who, after the washing of baptism, has no filth adhering to him, but is spotless and clean: whose body is not polluted by sexual debauchery, whose eyes are not made foul by theatrical spectacles, whose mind is not drunken with wine, whose life is not enslaved to money.

It is a great thing to abstain from these; but in such abstinence the rest of the journey is not immediately accomplished.

[Editorial note: “Tempted” in the note tradition; the text is corrected to read “but not in these” (*non in his*), rather than “but in these.”] For the way is begun in these things, not completed. For it follows: “And works righteousness.” Good is not so much to be conceived as to be carried out; goodwill is not to be undertaken but fulfilled. The fruit of willing righteousness is that it should be done. And certainly in these things the course toward the Lord is profitable; yet much remains.

For there remains, v. 3: “He who walks without blemish and works righteousness, who speaks truth in his heart.” Those earlier things, great and excellent though they are, are nevertheless commonly shared with the Gentiles, who avoid vice in order to acquire a reputation for goodness. But this is the virtue of natural persons, not spiritual persons.

For the Apostle has set forth the carnal person, the natural person, and the spiritual person. The carnal person neglects divine and human things after the manner of beasts;

[Editorial notes: “Acquires a reputation for goodness.” “Neglecting all divine and human things.”] his life is a servant of the body, busied with food, sleep, and lust. The natural person, however, by the judgment of human feeling perceives what is fitting and honorable, withdraws himself from all vices under the direction of his own mind, and distinguishes useful and honorable things by his own natural judgment: he despises money, is moderate in fasting, lacks ambition, resists pleasures, and is revered for goodness. But the benefit of these qualities is confined to the present life and to human beings among human beings.
