Of such things the Teacher of the Gentiles says: “According to the teachings and commandments of men, which indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility of mind, in unsparing treatment of the body, not in any honor toward the satisfying of the flesh” (Col. 2:22–23).

But the spiritual person is one whose earlier pursuits are directed toward the Lord, and who acts through knowledge of God, understanding and knowing what His will is; understanding, through the revelation and gift of the Holy Spirit, the secret counsel hidden from the ages of the world; and knowing the purpose for which flesh was assumed by God, the triumph of the cross, the power of death, and the operation that lies in the power of the resurrection. As the same Apostle teaches, “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, nor can he understand them, because they are spiritually examined. But the spiritual man judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:14–15).

### 8. Works without faith are barren.

The Holy Spirit therefore knew that the higher things—innocence of life and works of righteousness—are common both to Gentiles and to heretics.

[Editorial note: The Vatican manuscript reads “they deify” (*deificant*) where the text has “wear down” (*defatigant*).] For many of them wear down their bodies with fastings, demonstrate continence by the distribution of their estates, and bring chastity to completion in virginity. But because these things and many others of this sort would abound among them, the Lord spoke thus to His disciples: “Amen, I say to you, when the Son of Man comes, do you think He will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

He knew that virginity, continence, and fasts must be cultivated; and that these do not advance toward holiness unless they are fulfilled in Christ—that is, unless they agree with Christ’s truth.

[Editorial note: “Toward salvation.”] Therefore the Prophet added to what he had said above: “And speaks truth in his heart,” showing that the preceding things are useless unless they are undertaken in the truth of confession. In these things, indeed, there is a lofty step for those ascending to the rest of the mountain of the Lord—namely, in innocence, works, and confession. Yet although we have advanced through many things, other and higher matters still remain.

[Editorial notes: “Higher” is restored from our manuscript and from the context; earlier editions read “other.” Paris first mistakenly read “you will add,” then “other things.” From the Vatican manuscript “higher things” is restored, although “other things” can also be read.]

### 9. Profess the truth of faith in speech and deed.

Many habitually display a glorious appearance of understanding words,

[Editorial note: The earlier edition reads “of words” rather than “of understanding words.”] and falsely represent the dignity of their will and judgment even by the respectability of their speech. Although they think and speak well concerning God, they deny by their conduct and works what they affirm in words and thought. These are those who hate the things they say and are enemies, in their very deeds, of what they preach.

Therefore, to truth in the heart he added: “Who has not practised deceit with his tongue,” so that he may not belie in words the truth which he thinks; so that the profession of Catholic doctrine, and the resolve to think and preach in this way, may also be followed by action. For, according to the Apostle’s testimony, as one believes in the heart, so confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:16). Therefore, in order that ascent into God’s rest may be worthy, one must live in truth of speech and tongue, so that by faithfulness in our actions the words of our thought may not be false.

### 10. A serviceable lie.

But this is a narrow path, difficult through the wickedness and vices of the world.

[Editorial note: “Path” is added from the Vatican manuscript.] For a lie is often necessary, and falsehood is sometimes useful: when we lie to one who would strike concerning someone in hiding; when we frustrate testimony against one in danger; or when we deceive a sick person concerning the difficulty of the cure. And, according to the Apostle’s teaching, our speech ought to be seasoned with salt (Col. 4:6).

Therefore the Holy Spirit has qualified the inclination toward falsehood by the circumstances of lying,

[Editorial note: In the first Paris edition the word “Origenian,” having crept in from the margin, appeared here; the manuscripts do not contain it.] saying: “Who has not practised deceit with his tongue, nor done evil to his neighbor,” so that the guilt of lying may consist in another’s harm.

### 11. One must not be insolent toward others or self-confident.

But even if the things said above are fulfilled—if one enters innocent, works righteousness, embraces truth in the heart, does not deceive oneself in the things one has spoken, and inflicts no evil upon one’s neighbor—one will nevertheless not be perfect in these things. There is still something within us to be subdued, cast out, and destroyed. What it is, the Prophet who confirms the foregoing statements has added, saying:

[Editorial note: Thus from the manuscript of the Church of Verona, exactly as Coustant had reached by his marginal conjecture, and certainly more correctly than the earlier edition: “the Prophet who confirms [this] through what precedes,” although there is concern that the reading may not be genuine.] “And has not accepted reproach against his neighbors.”

He thus drives away the vices of insolence and self-confidence and removes the common evil of pride. For what is so empty, so wretched, as one human being being proud toward another, or placing confidence in oneself? Do we not see many who, through the arrogance of wealth, reproached the poverty of the needy and, after losing everything, became needy themselves;

[Editorial note: “They reproach the needy.”] who despised the misery of others, only to need the pity of those who had pity? Do we not see many who, through presumption based on a life long innocent, fell into crimes;

[Editorial note: The text is corrected thus; it previously read “innocent [persons] brought down into all things.”] and while reproaching others for sins, scarcely attained the pardon of repentance themselves?

Therefore reproach against one’s neighbors must not be undertaken. But if anything careless, wanton, negligent, or uncontrolled is found in them, it must be corrected without the bitterness of reproach, by the gentleness of correction.

[Editorial notes: The first Paris edition reads “by the blandishment of speech,” against the manuscripts. The words “if anything negligent” were supplied above from the Vatican manuscript. Paris has “this above fear,” incorrectly.] This is what humility and distrust of oneself through fear—fear which is the strongest guardian of confidence—provide:

[Editorial note: The Vatican manuscript reads “of the erring [Pharisee]”; Paris has “of the praying [Pharisee].”] that admonition may not be an insult, correction not a reproach, and instruction not abuse.

Thus the Lord condemned in the Gospels the confidence of the praying Pharisee, when, standing in the midst, he spoke thus: “I give You thanks, Lord, that I am not like other men—adulterers, greedy men—or like this publican.” But the publican was praying in secret: “Lord, have mercy on me, a sinner” (Luke 18:11, 13). Scripture added concerning his prayer: “The publican went out more justified than the Pharisee” (Luke 18:14). The publican obtained God’s mercy by confession of sin; the Pharisee, through the insolence of reproach, lost the honor of the things he alleged concerning himself.

### 12. Humility must not lack steadfastness.

But perhaps someone who has attained all these things already believes himself worthy of God’s promises, since after innocence, goodness, and prudent restraint he has also moderated himself by humility.

[Editorial notes: “After prudence.” Vatican manuscript: “after prudence”; Paris then reads “he knows moderation.”] Yet much still remains.

For just as the Prophet indicated that there is sin in a lie if the liar’s falsehood brings harm to another, so now, when he decrees that reproaches against neighbors are not to be taken up, he adds the proper rule of humility itself. What this rule is follows in the verse: “And has not accepted reproach against his neighbors. The malignant person has been reduced to nothing in his sight.”

Humility ought not to lack steadfastness, and the liberty of God must be retained by us amid the service we owe to all, lest we be frightened by the assaults of the powerful or yield to the wishes of malicious people. For at times we slavishly flatter even kings when they demand unjust things, and through weakness of conscience we indulge other people’s vices.

Therefore, if someone has already plunged into the profession of wickedness, as the verse explains—“The malignant person has been reduced to nothing in his sight”—such a person ought with us to be regarded as of no account at all: to be nothing to us, erased and destroyed.

[Editorial notes: “Of no account.” The word “nothing” was formerly missing and is supplied from the Vatican manuscript. Paris reads: “to regard such malevolence as of no account”; the passage is repaired from the Vatican manuscript.] For one who contemplates spiritual and heavenly things ought to despise the passing consequences of human wickedness, and with a lofty and exalted mind to regard such a malicious person as though he did not exist.

### 13. Honor must be denied to none who fears God.

But perhaps the Prophet will be judged to have elevated the greatness of our faith too highly against the wicked. Yet we must consider what follows: “The malignant person has been reduced to nothing in his sight; but he magnifies those who fear the Lord.” Therefore, just as, without distinction of persons, no wicked person ought to count for anything with us, so also, without distinction of persons, everyone who fears the Lord must be honored.

Let not the innocent poor person move us; nor the fasting old woman;

[Editorial note: Thus the Vatican manuscript; Paris incorrectly reads “the fasting healthy person.”] nor the faithful servant; nor the foreigner confident in his dwelling within the Church. Rather, let us revere all by an equal judgment, so that our humility in magnifying those who fear the Lord may be equal to the freedom which ought to govern our counting malicious people as nothing.

### 14. What is sworn in baptism must be steadfastly kept.

And because, at the birth of our regeneration, we swear to these sacraments—renouncing the devil, the world, and sins when we answer those who question us—

[Editorial note: “In this sacrament.”]the Prophet establishes that the faith of this confession must be retained to the end, saying: “He who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive.”

For although someone may have remained long in God’s commandments, yet if at some point he has proved false, he no longer remains when he has proved false; and prior righteousness is lost through later unrighteousness. In the Gospel: “Blessed are those who shall have remained unto the end” (Matt. 24:13).

[Editorial note: From our manuscript the preposition “in” has here been deleted. Thereafter the text reads: “And therefore in the Gospel.”] Therefore Solomon proclaims all praise at the end, because in the things promised to God one must never prove false (Ecclus. 11:30).

### 15. The injustice of usury.

But the heavenly admonition extends to perfect completion. Having wiped away every vice from a person, does it also turn away the desire for money which holds us so firmly? It says: “He has not given his money at interest.” This is taught to be a deceptive kindness, fraudulent humanity, and ruinous benevolence.

For what is more intolerable than to grant a favor to a needy person in such a way that he becomes more needy, and, while intending to bring aid to the poor person’s misery, to increase it? If you are a Christian, what reward do you expect from God, when you yourself look to human beings not for benefits but for losses?

[Editorial note: Paris reads, “what reward of reward do you expect from him,” etc. On the authority of the Vatican manuscript, “from God” is restored and “reward” deleted.] If you are a Christian, why do you place your unproductive money so as to yield a return, and make the need of your brother—for whom Christ died—your treasure?

[Editorial note: “Unproductive” is added from the Vatican manuscript, that is, sterile. The same manuscript reads “as a return”; shortly afterward, as is also preferred here, “your treasure,” not “your treasure-house.”]

If you are a Christian, I do not ask that you give generously; at least demand back what is owed in such a way that you do not despoil. Remember that the person from whom you exact interest is needy and poor, for whose sake Christ willed to be needy and poor. Thus, whether you inflict injury or grant a benefit upon a poor person, know that you do it to Christ; for, though He was God, He deigned for that person’s sake to take on want and its name.

### 16. The lawful and unlawful use of gifts.

But lest this admonition be judged harsh, as though under the name of usury it had altogether forbidden concern for possession, it did not abolish the care of acquiring. Indeed, it also set a measure upon receiving gifts, adding to what it had said, “He has not given his money at interest”: “And has not accepted gifts against the innocent.”

There is a certain customary giving of gifts which brings honor to the giver, so that it is a very great grief to have gifts offered despised, and a greater loss to have what was given received.

[Editorial note: Paris reads “greater”; this would be acceptable if supported by the manuscripts. The first edition reads “which to have given”; the later, “which gifts to have given.” The Vatican manuscript corruptly has *quaedam indonasse*; it is corrected as “than to have given loss,” especially since the Mic. manuscript reads “than to have given losses.”] Therefore he forbade those gifts which would work injury to another. For if he had prohibited the use of gifts altogether, it would have been enough to say: “And has not accepted gifts.” But because the simple use of gifts arises either from respect for a human being or even from reverence for God, he prohibited those gifts which corrupt the integrity of judgment, purchase injury to the innocent, and contain no duty of mutual charity.

For just as God does not need the things we offer Him, but through us the duty of due reverence is fulfilled,

[Editorial note: Thus from our manuscript, more correctly than the earlier edition’s “we are fulfilled in the duty.” Then: “to be observed.”] so he teaches that this principle must be observed in gifts: that we receive those things which are pleasing and useful to those who offer them, not those which make us venal, lay snares for the innocent, or burden the givers with expense; received from duty rather than greed, presented in honor rather than fear, accepted from charity rather than gain.

### 17. “He who does these things shall not be moved for ever.”

By these things, then, there is dwelling in the tabernacle; by these things, rest upon the mountain. What remains is the keeping of the precepts and the performance of the commandments. The psalm must be stored within our inmost being, written upon the heart, marked in the memory; and this treasury of rich brevity must be acquired for ourselves by night and day, so that, having gained this abundance as provision for eternity, we may dwell in the Church and at last rest in the glory of Christ’s body.

## Psalm 51

For the end: understanding for David, when Doeg the Idumaean came to him and informed Saul, saying: “David has come to the house of Achimelech.”

[Editorial note: The Verona copy gives the title thus: “For the end, understanding for David, when Doeg the Idumaean came and reported to Saul and said to him: David has come to the house of Abimelech.”]

Why do you glory in malice,  
you who are mighty in iniquity?  
All day your tongue devises injustice;  
like a sharp razor, you have wrought deceit.

[Textual notes: Hilary reads “glories” for “do you glory”; “mighty in iniquity all day”; “has devised”; and “a sharp razor.”]  
You have loved malice rather than kindness,  
iniquity rather than speaking righteousness.

[Textual note: Hilary reads “rather than speaking justice.”]  
*Diapsalma.*

You have loved every word of destruction,  
a deceitful tongue.  
Therefore God shall destroy you utterly;  
He shall pluck you out and remove you from your tabernacle,

[Textual note: Hilary reads “shall pluck out and transplant you.”]  
and your root from the land of the living.  
*Diapsalma.*

The righteous shall see and fear,  
and shall laugh at him and say:  
“Behold the man who did not make God his helper,  
but trusted in the multitude of his riches  
and prevailed in his vanity.”

But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God;  
I have hoped in the mercy of God  
for ever and ever.  
I will confess to You for ever, because You have acted;

[Textual note: Hilary reads “age” (*saeculum*) for “for ever.”]  
and I will await Your name,  
for it is good in the sight of Your saints.

## Treatise on the Psalm

### 1. Verses 1–2. The superscription itself of the psalm requires careful diligence in seeking its meaning.

For at its very beginning there is written: “For the end: understanding.”

[Editorial note: The alternative reading is “in the end” for “for the end.”] The psalm is thereby shown to contain matters not belonging to its own time, since its title bears the superscription “for the end.” And since understanding is in—or for—the end, the understanding contained in it cannot concern anything else more than the end itself.

Now the end is, as we have frequently shown, that in which all things are concluded, for whose sake the other things exist, and toward which all the works of hope, affairs, and undertakings hasten.

### 2. What this psalm concerns.

The understanding of the psalm, therefore, consists in Him for whom all things exist and apart from whom nothing exists. And who He is, the superscription itself—which seems to contain history—shows. For it is as follows: “For the end: understanding for David, when Doeg the Idumaean came and informed Saul and said to him: ‘David has come to the house of Abimelech.’”

[Editorial notes: The manuscripts consistently read *Doec*, following the Greek, rather than *Doech* in printed editions or *Doeg* in the Vulgate. An anonymous author of the *Breviary on the Psalter* misled P. Coustant here: when he writes that an error entered the Hebrew Psalter more easily because of the likeness of two letters, he shows himself wholly ignorant of Hebrew letters. In the Hebrew text the word *Achimelech* is written; it is by no means written with the letter alleged. Lipsius and Paris here and subsequently consistently have *Achimelech* in accordance with the Vulgate. So too the Hebrew Psalter, in which, says the author of the Commentary on the Psalms cited by Jerome, the error entered more easily because among the Hebrews the letters *beth* and *caph* are distinguished by a small stroke. But the editions of Badius and Erasmus and the manuscripts, together with that author and Augustine, following the Septuagint, have *Abimelech*. Augustine discusses the mystery of this name at length in his exposition of this Psalm, §5.]

That we may grasp the rationale of the superscription more fully, the course of the events themselves must be set forth. Doeg was Saul’s chief over the mules. He said to Saul: “I saw the son of Jesse coming to Noba, to Abimelech son of Achitob. And he inquired of the Lord for him, gave him food, and gave him the sword of Goliath the foreigner.”

[Editorial notes: Augustine and the common edition of Jerome observe that *Achimelech* is written at this point in the book of Kings. Yet our manuscripts are consistent here too, with the newest edition of the Septuagint translators, corrected against many manuscripts, in which Αβιμέλεχ, not Αχιμέλεχ, is likewise read. Badius, Erasmus, and all the manuscripts read, with support from the Septuagint, ἠρώτα αὐτῷ διὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, “he inquired of God for him”; Lipsius and Paris read “he inquired of him in the house.”] When he heard this, the king gave Doeg authority over the priests and the city (1 Sam. 22:9).

Then Scripture adds: “And Doeg the Idumaean went around and struck the priests, and on that day killed eighty-five, all wearing the ephod; and he overthrew Noba, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword” (ibid., vv. 18–19).

[Editorial note: The royal manuscript reads “and the cities,” which is not approved. Scripture records not cities, but the city of Noba, inhabited by Abimelech, as handed over by Saul to Doeg’s power along with the priests.]

This, then, is the whole trustworthy account of the events. From it only so much has been taken for the psalm’s title as would satisfy both the mystery of the psalm and prophetic teaching. For the superscription contains only this: “When Doeg came and informed Saul and said: ‘David has come to the house of Abimelech.’”

And necessarily this psalm, earlier in time but later in order, is placed after the fiftieth psalm—in which, as we taught in the introduction to the Psalms (Prologue, §10), remission of sins is contained according to the power of that sanctified number—so that what is inscribed “understanding for the end” may be understood only after every kind of mystery has been perfected and brought to completion.

### 3. What Abimelech signifies

Abimelech, by interpretation of the word, signifies “the rule of my brother.” For what we call “the rule of my brother” in our language, the Hebrews call Abimelech. Therefore, when it is said to Saul, “David has come into the house of Abimelech,” it is announced to that enemy of David that he has entered the house of brotherly rule. But the Apostle Peter teaches what the house of brotherly rule is, saying: “You yourselves also, as living stones, are built up into a spiritual house for a holy priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:5).

[Note: Col. 0310D. Printed editions read “spiritual houses.” But the manuscripts read “spiritual house,” agreeing with the Greek and Latin sacred text. We should then prefer “and a holy priesthood.” Below, in section 20, occurs: “You are built up, a spiritual house, a royal priesthood.” But “a royal priesthood” is cited not from the same context, but from verse 9 of that chapter.]

And below: “But you are an elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (ibid. 2:9). We are built into this spiritual house, into a royal race, if, through the spiritual edification of our bodies, having been made conformed to God, we deserve to be perfected as a royal race. Therefore that true, holy David—the king, the righteous one, the Rising One—entered this house of Abimelech, that is, the house of brotherly rule, by being made man for our body. This house is his brotherly kingdom, because in the glory of that same body we are co-heirs of his kingdom, as he himself says: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

[Note: Col. 0310C. The reading “of my brother” was formerly printed, less correctly.]

That those whose royal house he entered are his brothers, he testifies through the prophet in the Psalm, saying: “I shall proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I shall praise you” (Ps. 21:23). Therefore, once the remission of sins has been granted according to the preceding Psalm, the Word made flesh dwells in us: we who are both brothers, a spiritual house, and a royal race.

### 4. Who betrays the entrance

But the impious, parricidal, and treacherous people, signified in the person of Doeg, betrays to its king—namely David—its enemy, that he is in the house of Abimelech.

[Note: Col. 0310D. We have added *persona* (“person”) from the Royal manuscript. Shortly afterward, with the same manuscript, “enemy” is preferable to the printed reading “to his enemy.”]

[Note: Col. 0310C. *Persona* is absent from our copy.]

This occurs when he is handed over to Pilate; when the man to be crucified is offered up; when, having rejected its king, it confesses Caesar as its king. It thus betrays that he is in the house of Abimelech, but does not understand that, when he is in the house of Abimelech, he is in the house of brotherly rule: that is, in the body in which the Church of saints, which is Christ’s body, conformed to him, shall reign with him.

[Note: Col. 0310D. Manuscripts read “confess.”]

[Note: Col. 0311D. We restore from the manuscripts the words omitted in earlier printed editions: “when he is in the house of Abimelech.”]

[Note: Col. 0311D. In Bad. and Er. *ei* is lacking. In its place Lips. and Par. preferred *et*; but the Royal manuscript has *est*. We follow the Vatican manuscripts.]

This is also the body in which he received the food he had desired: “For I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover” (Luke 22:15); and from which he took the weapons of Goliath, that is, of the devil—for he himself plundered the strong man (Luke 11:22). After this, through this same Doeg—that is, through the treacherous people—the Apostles were killed and the churches overthrown.

[Note: Col. 0311C. “After this same Doeg.”]

Thus the title of the Psalm is: “Unto the end; for understanding,” because in Christ—who is David, the Rising One, the righteous one, king, eternal one, and shepherd—the consummation of all our hope and the end of the Law are understood to be. According both to the title and to the order of the Psalm, he was betrayed in that house of his body which is signified as the house of his brotherly rule.

### 5. Verse 3. One glory is good, another evil

“Why does he glory in malice, mighty one, in iniquity all the day?” The Prophet’s complaint is that one mighty in malice glories continually in iniquity. Such glory is, indeed, censured as glory in iniquity. Yet there is also a glory that ought to be sought, confessed, and uttered with a certain affection of exultant joy. Another prophet shows both things in the same words:

“Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories glory in the Lord” (Jer. 9:23–24).

[Note: Col. 0311D. Paris, following Lipsius, reads “Why do you glory?” The older editions, more correctly, together with the manuscripts, read “Why does he glory?” Augustine also reads thus; with Hilary he had the active Greek ἐγκαυχᾶ from ἐγκαυχάω, not from ἐγκαυχάομαι. Shortly afterward Bad., Er., and Lips. read: “The Prophet makes a complaint that he glories,” etc.]

[Note: Col. 0311C. “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty,” etc., in accordance with the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin Psalters.]

[Note: Col. 0311D. The phrase “continually in” is absent from the Royal manuscript. Symmachus, cited by Theodoret, translates “all the day” as “on each day,” καθ᾽ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν. Hilary’s interpretation agrees with this version; with him Jerome explains “all the day” as “throughout the whole time of life.” Augustine explains it as “without interruption,” and Rufinus as “continually.”]

For, after first forbidding the causes of blameworthy glory, he in turn shows the fitting cause of glory. Following this example, the blessed Apostle knows that he should glory in nothing except in one thing only, when he says: “But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Therefore it is not glory of this sort but glory in iniquity that offends; and glory in that iniquity which lasts “all the day.”

We recall that “day” is commonly used for a person’s lifetime or time, as when it is said, “I have not desired the day of man” (Jer. 17:16); or when Abraham desired the day of the Lord (John 8:56); or when the Apostle hands a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, “that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5:5). It indicates not this day bounded by sunrise and sunset, but the day of an appointed time or lifetime. Therefore, mighty in malice, he glories in iniquity all the day.

[Note: Col. 0312D. Thus the Royal manuscript, in accordance with the Greek and Latin sacred text. Printed editions read “unto the day.”]

### 6. Doeg—that is, the Jews—always in iniquity

Yet, taken literally, the reason for this complaint does not fit the person of Doeg. What power did a keeper of mules possess, one allotted authority over the animals used for royal transport, or merely reporting that David had entered Abimelech’s house? Did he glory in iniquity all the day? Rather, under his person we must understand the people whose entire lifetime was in iniquity, and whose glory in iniquity itself abounded from the power of malice.

[Note: Col. 0312D. Printed editions read “or merely.” With the Royal manuscript, “or even merely” is preferable.]

For that people was mighty when, while it served, it was visited by the Lord; when Egypt was struck with so many plagues on its account; when, amid three days’ darkness, it did not experience the darkness itself because light remained with it; when it left Egypt stripped of silver and every ornament, abandoned to its destruction; when, according to the times of day and night, the column was now cloudy, now fiery; when it crossed the Red Sea on foot; when it lived upon the food of angels; when it saw the majesty of God descending upon the mountain; when it heard the voice speaking from the fire; when it overthrew many kingdoms by severe wars; when it saw the Jordan flow back so that it might be dry for it; when it had prophets; when it made use of priests for cleansing from sins and redemption of its soul; and when it deserved to obtain its kingdom.

[Note: Col. 0312D. Older editions read “when the servant was visited.” The Royal manuscript reads “when, while serving, it was visited.”]

[Note: Col. 0312D. Lips. and Par. read “feet,” against the other books.]

[Note: Col. 0312C. Earlier there was “on foot.” On Psalm 119, letter 5, section 2, it reads “crossed on foot.”]

[Note: Col. 0312D. Bad. and Er. read “speaking from the cloud.” The Royal manuscript reads “God speaking.”]

But although it was mighty in all these things, it was always mighty in its malice: when it desired onions and the other things of Egypt, together with meat; when, because of the habit of vices, it preferred impious slavery to pious freedom; when it worshiped the calf, cursed Moses, abhorred God, vowed its children as sacrifices to demons, killed the prophets, and even raised up on the cross its own God and Lord—made man for its sake—betrayed to the governor. Thus, glorying in iniquity throughout the whole day of its life, although it was mighty, it nevertheless continued to be mighty in malice.

[Note: Col. 0312D. Royal manuscript: “Moses.”]

[Note: Col. 0312D. Royal manuscript, together with Bad., Er., and Hincmar, *On Predestination*, ch. 25: “as sacrifices.”]

[Note: Col. 0312D. At Lips. and Par., as above on Psalm 2, “governor” had been substituted for “praetor,” against the older books.]

### 7. The function of the tongue

After this complaint of prophetic grief concerning him, the discourse is now turned upon him himself:

“Your tongue has devised injustice” (v. 4).

The office of the human tongue is, impelled by natural reason, to distinguish voice into words by a varied yet measured movement, so that through it, from the confused sound of breath bursting forth, articulate speech may arise for the understanding of things. Though this rational movement is indeed its means of accomplishing this, the tongue itself is understood to be subject to reason rather than to possess rational understanding. But that which lacks the faculty of understanding also lacks the impulse of reason; and whatever lacks the impulse of reason also lacks deliberation of counsel. How, then, can it rightly be understood that the Prophet says the tongue devises injustice, when thought begins from the rational faculty of the living soul, while the tongue has been established not for undertaking reasoning by nature, but for serving rational nature?

[Note: Col. 0313D. In the Royal codex: “through it,” which may refer to the varied motion.]

[Note: Col. 0313D. Only the Paris edition reads “the sense of reason”; then, with the others, “is understanding.”]

Yet another prophet demonstrates the authority of this complete and prophetic saying: “The heart of fools is in their mouth” (Ecclus. 21:29). Since they treat nothing by the counsel of reason or weigh it by meditation of the heart, they utter only random, unconsidered, chance, and disorderly things by the reckless movement of an unadvised tongue. Therefore the heart of fools is in their mouth: they do not speak what they have thought, but think what they have spoken.

This is said of the fool’s tongue. But of the wise tongue we read: “The tongue of the intelligent shall meditate wisdom”; and again: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. 44:2). The tongue of the intelligent proceeds from meditation upon wisdom; and, again, like a scribe’s pen, it does nothing unordered or uncertain, but promptly obeys, by the reason of counsel, the things that have been thought or read.

[Note: Col. 0313D. The Micy manuscript reads “tongue of the wise.” Another Vatican manuscript reads, “In the tongue of the intelligent wisdom meditates.” From what scriptural place Hilary draws these words is unclear. Only Ps. 36:30 occurs: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom”; and Prov. 10:31: “The mouth of the righteous shall bring forth wisdom.”]

[Note: Col. 0313D. “Shall meditate.”]

### 8. A tongue devising evil aptly compared to a razor

Since the tongue serves thoughts conceived by rational nature rather than itself thinking, this tongue which devised injustice is shown not to have employed the offices of its own nature. For it follows: “Like a sharp razor you have wrought deceit.” A razor is sharpened for the adornment of the face, so that by shaving the rough and bristling beard it may make the face smooth. If it wounds instead, it has wrought deceit: prepared for adornment, it has offered its service for a wound.

[Note: Col. 0313D. The Royal manuscript reads “make smooth”; supported by the Micy manuscript, which reads “make alive.”]

Therefore this tongue, devising the iniquity of one mighty in malice, has wrought deceit. That is: though nature had prepared it to utter the rational thoughts of a deliberating heart, it instead devises irrational iniquities. For that people, which must be understood to be signified in Doeg, was chosen to magnify God’s name and prepared to celebrate his praises; yet it dishonours him, hands him over, and, so far as lies in it, puts him to death by crucifixion. It accomplishes this by the sharp razor of its tongue, through which it cried, “Crucify, crucify!” Thus this tongue, devising iniquity, wrought deceit like a sharp razor; and the following words teach what kind of deceit it was.

[Note: Col. 0313D. “Is signified, must be understood.”]

### 9. Malice loved with goodness neglected

For it follows:

“You have loved malice more than goodness, iniquity rather than to speak righteousness” (v. 5).

The charge of this deceit becomes graver by comparison when malice is loved and goodness neglected; when iniquity is done, and the speech of righteousness passed over. The Lord condemns this affection of malice inclined toward evil in the Gospels, saying: “And this is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light” (John 3:19).

[Note: Col. 0314D. “The affection of love inclined toward malice.”]

[Note: Col. 0314D. Thus the Royal codex; Hincmar likewise reads it in *On Predestination*, ch. 25. Printed editions read, “the affection of love inclined toward malice.” “Inclined malice” is said of that which outweighs and is preferred to the love of God. See Psalm 1, section 17: “Not that they did not also love the light, but that their love of darkness was more inclined.”]

Therefore the people for whose redemption the Word was made flesh, and God was born man, so that it might be freed from the curse of the Law through justification by faith—when it preferred to serve the curse in transgression of the Law—handed over its own God to the penalty of his blood, taking it upon itself so that the governor might be innocent. In doing this, it changes the habit of its own nature. For it loves malice more than goodness and turns its love from good things toward the worst. It also chose to love injustice rather than to speak righteousness.

[Note: Col. 0314D. Bad. reads “the penalty: his blood.” Er., Lips., and Par. read “the penalty of blood,” against the manuscripts and Hincmar’s edition in the cited place.]

### 10. The Jews’ hatred toward Christ

In accordance with Jewish idiom, the prophetic utterance maintains a rationale in the very force of its words when it says: “You have loved malice more than goodness, injustice rather than to speak righteousness.” For where it says, “You have loved malice more than goodness,” it condemns nothing beyond the love itself by comparison. But where it says, “Injustice rather than to speak righteousness,” it reproves not merely the affection of a preferred love, but that very hatred expressed in speech, saying, “rather than to speak righteousness.”

For Jews can and often do, even though they do not love goodness, nevertheless feign it in speech. But they cannot in any manner speak of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, according to the blessed Apostle Paul, “became for us righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30). They cannot endure even a little patience in discourse whenever the only-begotten God—born before the ages, and in man suffering, crucified, and dead—is shown to them from prophetic authorities. Then they avoid and flee every discourse concerning him; and if there is nowhere for them to withdraw, oppressed by a kind of silent violence of grief, they stop their ears with their hands and exclude the hearing lest it penetrate into them. They do not love so great a goodness, although at times they speak of it; but they neither love nor speak of righteousness, which is Christ.

[Note: Col. 0315D. “Lest it penetrate.”]

[Note: Col. 0315D. The Tours manuscript reads “so much” for “so great.”]

[Note: Col. 0315D. “So much.” Shortly afterward, “nevertheless” is omitted.]

[Note: Col. 0315D. “Because Christ is righteousness.”]

### 11. The diapsalma changes the sense

The intervention of the *diapsalma*, although it has not brought a change of person, is nevertheless understood to have made a change of meaning. For although the discourse remains both that of the one who spoke before and addressed to the one addressed before, the same discourse now signifies something other than it did previously.

The foregoing words were weighty with complaint—so much so that, from the Prophet’s grief, they were censured before they were stated: when the tongue devises injustice; when it works deceit like a sharp razor; when malice is loved more than goodness; and when injustice is preferred to the utterance of righteousness. For these reasons a kind of accusation by the Prophet before God was introduced, rebuking when it says: “Why does he glory in malice, mighty in iniquity all the day?” And lest the grief of the complaint should be found empty, the very cause of the complaint was supplied.

[Note: Col. 0315D. The Royal manuscript reads “loves malice more than goodness”; shortly afterward, with Bad. and Er., “more than righteousness.” We should prefer “rather than the speech of righteousness.”]

### 12. After the sin has been set out, punishment is added

But now, with the diapsalma intervening, no complaint precedes; rather, after the exceedingly grave cause of sin has been demonstrated, this sentence of condemnation is added:

“You have loved every word of drowning, a deceitful tongue; therefore God shall destroy you unto the end, pluck you out and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living” (v. 6).

[Note: Col. 0315D. The Royal manuscript here and shortly afterward reads “a deceitful tongue.” This is not wholly wrong; for there is reason to suspect that the discourse is turned to the deceitful tongue itself, or to fools who do not moderate the motions of the tongue.]

[Note: Col. 0315D. Our book omits the pronoun “your,” which is absent also from the Septuagint; it has only ἀπὸ σκηνώματος, “from [your] tent.”]

As in Genesis we read: “Because you have done this, you are cursed from the earth” (Gen. 3:14); and again: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife” (ibid. 3:17); and likewise in the Apostle, who, after listing the gravest crimes of human impiety, says: “For this reason God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1:28). So here: “You have loved words of drowning, a deceitful tongue; therefore God shall destroy you unto the end.”

[Note: Col. 0316D. The words “and again, Because you have listened to the voice of your wife,” do not occur in our manuscript.]

[Note: Col. 0315D. Lipsius had substituted “your spouse,” on no authority.]

[Note: Col. 0316D. From the Verona codex we restore “God,” which the Greek text also has: παρέδωκεν αὐτοὺς ὁ θεός, “God gave them over,” etc.]

The Latin wording has not retained the force of the word. What for us are “words of precipitating” are called by the Greeks ῥήματα καταποντισμοῦ, “words of submersion.” This expression means that what is for us a falling headlong is for them a sinking into the depth of the sea. Yet in our general usage *praecipitatio* may mean not only a fall into the sea, but the fall of persons descending from lofty houses, cliffs, or places of any kind. Therefore, according to the explanation given of “precipitation,” because Doeg loved words of destruction by plunging down, he was subjected to the most severe condemnation.

### 13. The unbeliever like a shipwrecked man

Every unbelieving soul, shipwrecked in the deep as though in the sea of this world, is carried about by uncertain and wandering motion. It fluctuates, tossed by the surge of diverse desires, mocked by the power of the devil who inhabits the world; and it stands firm with no strength of solidity placed beneath it to resist and oppose him. Thus it is easy for it to be tossed, hanging and wandering, by the inducements of surrounding desires.

[Note: Col. 0315D. In the first Paris edition, from the Micy manuscript, “if by power”; the particle *if* is superfluous and absent from the other books. Shortly afterward Bad., Er., and Lips. read “dashed against,” not “mocked,” against the manuscripts and the words of Psalm 103:26, to which this refers.]

That the movement and surge of this world is compared to the waves of the swelling sea, and that the devil has his habitation there, Psalm 103 shows according to a prophetic and allegorical understanding, though under the bodily signification of creatures:

“This sea is great and broad; there are creeping things without number there, small and great animals. There ships shall pass through; this dragon, whom you formed to sport with him.”

And again, in Psalm 68: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has sunk me.”

Therefore the only-begotten Son of God, the Word of God, and God the Word descended to draw us out of the shipwreck in the depth of this world, intending to draw out all these kinds of fish by the net of his teaching, to which the kingdom of heaven is like (Matt. 13:47). He is betrayed and dishonoured by the impious people; and that people, made like the dragon’s companion for sport, sinks itself and plunges itself into this deep to share in his habitation.

[Note: Col. 0316D. Two Vatican manuscripts read “to instruct us.” Then Bad. and Er.: “from on high he descended into the deep shipwreck of the world.” Later editions omit “the Word descended.” The manuscripts, with Bad. and Er., read “net,” not “nets.”]

[Note: Col. 0316D. Thus the Royal codex. But printed editions read “the people conformed.” At first we conjectured that the reading should be “conformed to peoples,” namely Christ, who descended into the world as a participant in our nature; especially since the old editions and manuscripts then added “to sport with the dragon.” But the following words plainly show that this conformity is asserted of the Jewish people.]

Thus also the Egyptian people, unbelieving toward Moses, deserved to be plunged down and submerged; and the returning waves of the sea swallowed up that impious nation, which loved words of drowning when it resisted God.

### 14. The Jews uprooted from their homeland

Therefore, because the Jewish people, unbelieving and betraying its king, loved words of plunging down, saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), it neglected God as king and confessed a man as king. It plunged itself into this deep of the world. Therefore it is destroyed unto the end: for it has lost the kingdom of its ruined city until the consummation of the age. It has been plucked out and removed from its tent; it now wanders throughout the whole world, everywhere a stranger, all its sins having reached their completion in the Lord’s Passion.

[Note: Col. 0316D. “Of precipitating.”]

### 15. On the rites of the Law

Because it loved words of plunging down, it lacks that tent in which the Prophet was always filled with God’s Spirit; in which were awesome contemplations of holy powers and saving visions; in which were useful offerings of sacrifices for redemption of the soul; in which was the paschal lamb, guardian of the faithful amid Egypt’s devastation and a powerful sign in the blood upon the doorposts; in which were temporal festivals emulating the eternal ages. Plucked out from that tent, they lack these honours of spiritual gifts.

[Note: Col. 0317D. Paris, following Lipsius, reads: “The Prophet … was filled,” against the manuscripts, though with a sense not alien to the passage. For here “Prophet” is understood indefinitely.]

### 16. On the body of Christ, God and man

But they have been plucked out not only from this earthly tent, but from that of which it is said: “I shall raise up the tent of David that has fallen” (Amos 9:11): namely, that holy and venerable body and temple of God, born of the Virgin. Whoever believes in it shall dwell in it as a sharer in the Lord’s flesh.

Every unbeliever, however, shall be plucked out and removed from the kinship of this body in which he has not believed—that is, from God’s tent—being unworthy to dwell in this spiritual tent. The Lord is understood to signify this when he says: “I am the true vine; you are the branches; my Father is the husbandman. Every branch not remaining in me and not bearing fruit shall be uprooted. And every branch remaining in me my Father will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1 ff.).

[Note: Col. 0317D. “Every branch of the world.”]

Therefore those who, through faith in the embodied God, deserve to remain in the nature of the body assumed by God are cleansed so as to bring forth eternal fruits from themselves. For it is necessary that a branch remaining in the vine retain the nature of the true vine. But one who is unbelieving in the body of God born from the Virgin—or who, though believing, remains there yet lacks the fruits of faith—shall be uprooted, either for unbelief or for the barrenness of fruits withheld.

[Note: Col. 0317D. Corruptly in Hincmar, *On Predestination*, ch. 25: “born.” Therefore, Hilary says in *On the Trinity*, book 9, section 54, looking to the same Gospel passage, that he warns us to remain in him through faith in the assumed body.]

For the Son of God, born from the Virgin, was not then first the Son of God when he became the Son of Man; but the Son of Man was also in the Son of God, so that the Son of Man might be the Son of God. He assumed in himself the nature of all flesh, and by this became the true vine, holding in himself the whole stock of every branch. Therefore, if any branch is unbelieving or fruitless, it makes itself fit to be uprooted: it remains indeed by nature, but is plucked out through unbelief or uselessness.

[Note: Col. 0317D. See *On the Trinity*, book 2, section 25.]

Thus this impious Doeg is both plucked out and removed from this tent, as from the true vine: remaining by nature both in the tent and in the vine, but through unbelief worthy to be plucked out.

### 17. On Christ’s kingdom

But when plucked out from the tent, he shall also be uprooted from the land of the living. For whoever does not remain in Christ shall not be an inhabitant of Christ’s kingdom. He shall not be so, not because habitation in it was not open to him—for it stands open to all, so that they may be sharers in God’s body and kingdom, because the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, assuming in himself the nature of the whole human race—but because each person, according to his deserts, makes himself fit both to be plucked out of the tent and uprooted from the land of the living. He was never prohibited from being within it, because through the assumption of nature he was received as an inhabitant; but he is uprooted because of the offense of unbelief, having proved unworthy of fellowship in that nature.

[Note: Col. 0317D. Lips. and Par. read “who through the assumption of nature.” More correctly Bad., Er., and the manuscripts read “because,” etc. For the same point is repeated here as shortly before: “it stands open to all,” etc., “because the Word was made flesh.”]

Therefore he is uprooted from the land of the living, which is prepared in the blessed region for the saints who reign with the Lord. The Lord himself mentions it in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matt. 5:5); and this same prophet says, “I shall be pleasing to the Lord in the region of the living” (Ps. 114:9). The treacherous people deserved to be uprooted from it after it had been destroyed unto the end and had both been removed and plucked out from the tent.

[Note: Col. 0318D. Hincmar, *On Predestination*, reads “gathering together,” erroneously.]

### 18. The land of the living; and how the dead live to God

It is called the land of the living because every believer in the Lord, though dead, nevertheless lives to God, as it is said: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; he is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22:32). And again, through Jacob: “Let Reuben live and not die” (Deut. 33:6); and: “Let Ishmael live before you” (Gen. 17:18).

There is also the saying of the Apostle—if indeed it seems so to the reader, since it has a twofold meaning: “And we who live, who remain, shall be caught up with clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:17).

[Note: Col. 0317D. “To meet Christ.”]

The interruption of bodily life brings a temporary occasion of death; but the established law of dying does not take away the law of rising again, because a law does not impose necessity upon the one who decrees it. Nor does God, in decreeing for us a law of dying, take away from himself the right to give life. Death is lawful only for those upon whom it has been decreed. But all live to God, by whose law they have died.

[Note: Col. 0318D. Printed editions except Paris read “upon whom it has been lawfully decreed.” The Royal manuscript reads “upon whom the decree is lawful.” This means that death has no force except through the law and decree of God.]

Nor can death, which prevailed only by the law of the one decreeing it, itself prevail so as to prevent its being changed by the one who decrees the law of renewed life.

[Note: Col. 0318D. Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions read “prevail in them.”]

[Note: Col. 0318D. Printed editions add here “by the law of living,” which we have removed on the authority of the Royal codex, since this change is sufficiently expressed by “the law of renewed life.” Shortly before, “by the one decreeing” means “by him who decrees.”]

[Note: Col. 0318D. Our book adds “by the law of living.”]

For the power of the one who decrees has changed, by the law of dying, the law of life established from the beginning in Adam under the condition of the decree.

[Note: Col. 0319D. “The life of the law.”]

[Note: Col. 0319D. The manuscripts read “the life of the law,” perhaps more correctly, so that it is a figure familiar to Hilary. Bad. and Er. read: “the life of the law has changed the law of dying.”]

Therefore all saints and faithful persons live to God. For when he says that he is the God of those who had died, namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and immediately declares that he is God not of the dead but of the living, he teaches thereby that those who are thought dead by the judgment of human opinion are not dead but living to him who decrees the law.

[Note: Col. 0319D. Royal manuscript: “faithful to God.”]

### 19. The diapsalma, though it did not change the person, nevertheless renewed the sense

For after Doeg’s condemnation had been foretold—he to whom the discourse had been addressed as though present—the Prophet now turns to the significance of a different exposition:

“The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh over him, and shall say: Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (vv. 8–9).

Once Doeg has been destroyed unto the end, plucked out and removed from the tent, and uprooted from the land of the living, all saints must necessarily fear, when they see that a people adopted, aided, and benefited by so many and such great helps of divine mercy, after the immense dignity of a glorious kingdom beyond human resources, has furnished in itself the greatest and final example of human misery.

[Note: Col. 0319D. “Assumed.”]

For who could recount from memory its ancient glories and innumerable blessings, some of which we have mentioned above? After Egypt’s destruction, the sea divided for its journey; a pillar of cloud shaded it from the heat of day; a pillar of fire dispelled the darkness of night; heaven provided it the food of angels; a spring flowed from the rock; the Jordan flowed back; a great city fell level with the ground by the circuit of the ark of the covenant; the sun, restrained in its course, prolonged the day; and the ordinance of the divine Law, from that tireless and undisturbed movement of the heavenly elements, interrupted their course to delay the battle.

[Note: Col. 0319D. Thus the manuscripts. But Bad. and Er. read “when the food of heaven,” etc.; Lips. and Par. read “when heaven provided the food of angels.”]

[Note: Col. 0320D. We restore “greatest” in place of “great” from the Royal codex, which afterward reads “by the circuit,” not “the circuit,” so that the sense is that the city of Jericho fell by the circuit of the ark and was levelled to the ground.]

After that familiarity with the sight and hearing of divine majesty, they were consumed in wars, died by famine, fed upon the corpses of those who had earlier died to prolong their famine, and then the survivors were reduced to slavery. Everywhere they are exiles; everywhere they have degenerated; recognized nowhere; always newcomers; always obscure through change of dwelling; always strangers.

[Note: Col. 0320D. In the siege of Jerusalem by Vespasian.]

[Note: Col. 0319D. “To the death of famine.”]

[Note: Col. 0320D. From the Tours manuscript we preferred to read “to prolong famine” rather than “to the death of famine,” as in the earlier printed editions.]

And if anyone raises spiritual eyes, of which the Lord says, “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are white for harvest” (John 4:35), then he will know that they have been plucked out from fellowship in God’s body, from that kingdom of blessedness, and from that honour of resurrection; that they are without God’s Spirit and without understanding of prophecy; and that they are appointed as fuel for Gehenna, to be devoured by the immortal worm and burned by unquenchable fire (Isa. 66:24). He will know whose is the legislation, whose are the covenants, whose are the fathers, from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all (Rom. 9:4–5).

How greatly, then, will all saints behold these condemnations of their present and eternal misery with fear, since the contemplation of those punished is an example so terrible! Therefore the righteous shall see and fear, understanding from so great a calamity of these people that nothing is not to be feared for themselves.

[Note: Col. 0320D. “In so great [a calamity].”]

But because they are righteous, although they fear because of the example, they will nevertheless rejoice in the fruit of their own righteousness. For they shall laugh over him—laughing, therefore, and fearing, because they are subject to God, whose severity toward those punished is terrible. Laughter therefore tempers fear: fear comes from the example, and laughter from merit. Again fear moderates laughter, so that in rejoicing in good things they may not lack the terror of the example. For it belongs to an impious conscience, distrustful of itself, to fear without joy; and to an arrogant nature, to rejoice without fear.

20. All our hope is in God.—But those who will laugh while fearing will add this also to their laughter tempered by fear, saying: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper.” It is the height of folly and impiety not to understand that one lives under God and from God, but, in what one does and expects, to wish rather to rely on one’s own power—although whatever one has in oneself is from God. Therefore let all our hope be in God, and all confession be in God, following the example of the Prophet, who says: “O Lord, my helper and my redeemer” (Ps. XVIII [19]:15); and again: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXX [121]:1) . . . . . Let us therefore always fear, lest that eternal fire at some time burn us up and the immortal worm consume us, since we hear what the righteous, fearing and laughing, say: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches.”

21. Against the arrogance of the rich.—Wealth makes certain rich persons insolent, and above all an empty confidence in riches turns them away from the fear of God. They are foolish, not understanding that they ought to be more devout precisely because they are rich, since it is fitting that they render thanks to the giver of the good things they desire; and that the charge of avarice is thereby all the more inexcusable, because wealth does not excuse the necessity of avarice. How unhappy, indeed, is confidence in an empty thing: to despise God because one possesses gold, as though gold were not among God’s creatures; or to suppose, by the judgment of a sound mind, that one acquires any advantage toward a blessed life because one has gold lying buried away; or that from this a person may become other than he was born—a human being sharing the common nature of soul and body—or that, when he departs this life, he will use his gold in death!

[Note: [Col. 0323C] The printed editions read: “and hence they become of a more noble soul and body, and another person,” etc. They are corrected by the authority of the manuscripts. There is no reason for anyone to suppose that Hilary adopted the opinion of the Pythagoreans, whom Cato, in Cicero, says “never doubted that our souls were derived from the universal divine mind.” For Hilary repeatedly insists that the substance of God is simple, uncompounded, and free from every division. Elsewhere he certainly affirms the divine origin of souls, not because they are from God’s substance, but because every soul is God’s work, not man’s, as he states in *On the Trinity*, X.20. Thus he calls human beings of a common soul and body because all receive a body of the same kind—the body from Adam, but the soul from God. See *Tractate on Psalm LXII*, no. 3, and what we discussed concerning the soul in the Preface.]

He will indeed use it, if he uses it rightly in life: if he feeds the hungry with his bread, clothes the naked with his garment, relieves the sick at his own expense, or restores the captive to freedom.

[Note: [Col. 0321C] “Uses.”]

These are indeed the solicitous embassies of human treasures before God; this is the power of obtaining pardon for sins and true advocacy. Thus we shall be transformed through gold, so that from earthly persons we become heavenly, and from mortal persons eternal. This unbelieving people, however, not considering these things and despising God’s commandments, imagining itself rich through the Law—which is a shadow of future good things—and misusing the riches it had obtained, was rooted out and driven away from the land of the living and from its tabernacle. Thinking itself mighty in vanities—in the glory, that is, of its kingdom, in the gold of the Temple, and in human commandments—it acted according to the Prophet’s saying: “They worship me in vain, teaching doctrines and commandments of men” (Isa. XXIX:13, according to the Septuagint), God’s Law having been dishonoured and altered by observance of human custom.

[Note: [Col. 0321D] Bad. and Er., with the royal manuscript, read *diligentes*, “loving.” Other books more correctly read “God’s Law”; for the reference is to Matthew XV:6.]

22. David, evangelical while under the Law.—But the Prophet, whom we must understand to be righteous, speaks differently of himself in the confidence of his hope:

> VERSE 10. “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God for ever and unto age upon age.”

The ages of men indeed differ in time, but the Spirit of prophecy is the same. The Prophet says that he remains in God’s house like a fruitful olive tree, a tree always green and bearing the best fruit. The Apostle teaches that, when the branches of this olive tree had been broken off because of unbelief, believing Gentiles from a wild olive were grafted in (Rom. XI:17), so that, contrary to the nature of their stock, they might receive the nature of the root.

But though the Prophet speaks while remaining under the Law, he is nevertheless at once evangelical and prophetic; both in the Law and in the Gospels he continues in God’s house with his fruit. He is not to be broken off in his branches, not to be left as a trunk,

[Note: [Col. 0322D] One Vatican manuscript, with the royal manuscript, reads “in the trunk.”]

nor himself, now useless, to be offered to a wild olive for grafting; nor is he to transfer the vigour of his root to an alien tree. Rather, whole and uninjured as he is, he is a preacher of apostolic faith—not one who must be grafted, from the Gentiles, into the root of the Law so as to receive evangelical faith, but one who, even amid the evangelical faith of the Gentiles, is himself wholly fruitful from the rich awareness of the Law, through the power of the root and branches that are his own.

[Note: [Col. 0322D] The royal manuscript reads “his own,” which is the same thing.]

[Note: [Col. 0321C] “Of his own root.”]

Now the house of God, according to the Apostle Peter, is the Church and all followers of evangelical faith, as he says: “Be built up into a spiritual house, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II:5, 9). And Paul says: “That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth” (I Tim. III:15).

[Note: [Col. 0322D] The royal manuscript reads *diversari*, “to dwell/conduct oneself,” as is read with the strong agreement of manuscripts. In the Tours manuscript, however, these words of the Apostle are given in the better order: “That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth.” This reading is confirmed by *Tractate on Psalm LXIV*, no. 6, and Psalm CXXXII, no. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0321D] “To dwell/conduct oneself.”]

Therefore in this house of God the righteous and holy Prophet stands as a fruitful olive tree, using his own fruitful and rich root.

[Note: [Col. 0322D] The printed editions read “properly.” More suitably, one Vatican manuscript reads “by his own root,” which is opposed to grafted branches living from an alien root.]

He hoped in the mercy of God—not for a time, not merely for the brief age of this bodily life, but unto age upon age. For he extends his hopes to the endless duration of eternity, nor are they terminated by the event of death. He knows that he is to live in Abraham’s bosom after the example of poor Lazarus; he knows also that, by the transformation of the glorious resurrection, he will remain coeternal and conformed to God. And he will remain because of what follows:

> VERSE 11. “I will confess to you, O Lord, in the age, because you have done [it]; and I will await your name, because it is good in the sight of your saints.”

[Note: [Col. 0322D] The printed editions here and below read “unto age”; but in the third occurrence they read “in the age,” which the royal manuscript consistently has, supported by the following exposition.]

[Note: [Col. 0322C] The Verona manuscript reads “unto age,” in accordance with the Hebrew, the Septuagint, and the Gallican Psalter.]

23. God’s mercy is necessary for attaining blessedness.—Hope in God’s mercy is for ever and unto age upon age.

[Note: [Col. 0322D] Augustine cites this in *Against Julian*, II.7.]

For the works of righteousness themselves will not suffice for the merit of perfect blessedness unless God’s mercy also does not impute the faults of human changes and impulses even in this will toward righteousness. Hence the Prophet’s saying: “Your mercy is better than life” (Ps. LXII [63]:4). For although the life of the righteous is commendable through the practice of righteousness, yet through God’s mercy it will attain a greater merit. From this life it advances into eternal life;

[Note: [Col. 0322D] “Advances.”]

and God’s mercy rewards the work of righteousness so greatly that, having mercy on the will toward righteousness, it grants each righteous person also a share in God’s own eternity. Therefore hope in mercy is for ever and unto age upon age; but confession is only in the age, not also unto age upon age.

For confession of sins exists only during the time of this age, while each person is left to his own will and possesses, through life’s freedom, the choice of confession. For in departing from life we depart at the same time from the right of free will. Then the law, already established according to the merit of one’s past will, receives the will of those leaving the body either into rest or into punishment. The Prophet shows this will, no longer free but necessary, when he says: “In those days I have no will.”

[Note: [Col. 0323C] We have not found from where Hilary drew this passage, unless perhaps he read ἐν ἡμέραις, “in days,” instead of ἐν ὑμῖν, “among you,” at Malachi I:10. Moreover, in Hincmar, who copied this passage of Hilary together with many others in *On Predestination*, ch. 25, “For when freedom of will ceases” is corruptly given as “For free wills cease.”]

For when freedom of will has ceased, the effect of the will—if any remains—will also cease. The rich man, wishing to pass to Abraham, is not allowed, because of the chasm lying between them (Luke XVI:26), although through freedom of will he could have been in Abraham’s bosom. Freedom of will is therefore shut off, because there is no confession for the dead, according to what is said: “For who shall confess to you in hell?” (Ps. VI [7]:6).

Therefore the Prophet, hoping for mercy for ever and unto age upon age, confesses only in the age: he performs the temporal duties of confession during the time of this age, but stretches forth eternal hope through the eternity of ages. He adds the cause of confession, saying: “Because you have done [it],” confessing, that is, that the Lord is the author of this whole creation and teaching that none other is to be confessed than he who made the fruitful olive tree by the mercy of hope unto age upon age.

[Note: [Col. 0323C] In *On Confession*, IV.33, Dallaeus misuses this passage of Hilary to reject confession to priests. Replying to him, the distinguished Dean of the Church of Sens, in his *History of Confession*, ch. 8, maintains that this passage concerns not confession of sins but confession of praise. The Micy manuscript excellently confirms this judgment: it reads not *nulli alii* (“to no other”), but *nulli alium* (“no other”), that is, teaching that no other is to be confessed and praised by anyone than God, who made the fruitful olive tree. This is further supported by the immediately preceding phrase, “confessing that the Lord [or, in the royal manuscript, God] is the author of this whole creation.” No less does what follows support it, since God’s having made the fruitful olive tree supplies matter for praise rather than lamentation and confession of sins.

Yet even if it be granted that confession of sins is here under discussion—as it closely coheres with the immediately preceding statements about that confession for which, after this life, no place remains—Dallaeus would still gain nothing for his position. It is plain that here, as in many other places, Hilary understands by “confession” not only that part of penitence which acknowledges or declares sins, but the whole penitence itself, which can both change the will and erase sins themselves. Such confession must certainly have regard to him alone against whom alone sin is committed and from whom alone pardon is to be hoped. And just as every sin is against God, so every pardon is from him.

Hilary himself says this in his eighteenth chapter on Matthew, no. 10: “Therefore all pardon is from him, since after the return of confession he forgives even those things that are sins against himself.” Yet, although he maintains that every pardon is from God, he explicitly teaches in the same place that it is obtained through the ministry of the Apostles: “Those,” he says in no. 8, “whom they have loosed, having received salvation through the confession of pardon, are loosed also in heaven by the ordinance of the apostolic sentence.” Why, by the same reasoning, should he not affirm that penitential confession, although directed to God alone, is to be made to the Apostles and their priestly successors, so that they may pronounce a worthy and fitting judgment? An occasion will again arise to discuss this matter in connection with the aforementioned passage from the commentary on Matthew.]

[Note: [Col. 0324C] The royal manuscript reads *spei misericordiam*, “the mercy of hope.” We would prefer *spe misericordiae*, “by hope of mercy,” or *spe in misericordia*, “by hope in mercy,” especially since no. 21 begins with the words, “Hope in the mercy of God,” etc., unless we knew that Hilary is fond of such figures of expression. Thus above, at no. 17, we noted that all manuscripts have “the life of the Law,” not “the law of life.”]

24. The Psalmist awaits the sight of Christ.—And he shows who it is that has done these things, saying: “And I will await your name, because it is good in the sight of your saints.” He will therefore await the name of God to whom he confesses, through whom all things were made, as Paul says: “For there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (I Cor. VIII:6).

He therefore awaits his name: that is, he awaits the sight of Jesus, to know his Saviour, as the Angel says: “And you shall call his name Jesus, for he himself shall save his people from sins” (Matt. I:21).

[Note: [Col. 0324D] The printed editions read “from their sins.” The word *their* is consistently absent from the more carefully corrected manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0323C] “From their sins,” as in the Septuagint.]

He awaits the sight of Christ so that, by professing a noble family, he may be a Christian. This name is good: Angels and Archangels worship it; demons tremble at it and cannot endure it; men take it up for salvation. For it is written: “And everyone who calls upon his name shall be saved” (Rom. X:13).

He does not await it secretly, timidly, or alone, but in the sight of his saints: with free faith, not refusing either to give testimony of his expectation under the awareness of the heavenly saints, or, following the Prophet’s example, to provide in himself to all saints on earth an example of expectation.

[Note: [Col. 0324D] The printed editions read *testimonio*, “by testimony.” More correctly the royal and Micy manuscripts read *testimonium*, “testimony,” namely, not refusing to offer it in the sight of the saints who are in heaven; or, if “saints” are understood to mean those on earth, offering them, as a prophet, an example of hope in himself. Hence the reading in Bad. and Er., and in the royal manuscript, “by the example of prophecy,” is less satisfactory.]

## PSALM LII

David, for the end, for Abimelech, an understanding of David.

[Note: [Col. 0324D] Hilary lacks “David.”]

[Note: [Col. 0324C] In the Verona manuscript: “For the end; David’s understanding concerning Meleth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0324D] Hilary: “Maeleth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0324D] Hilary: “to David.”]

“The fool said in his heart: There is no God. They were corrupted and became abominable in their iniquities; there is none who does good, not even one. God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside; together they became useless; there is none who does good, not even one. Shall not all who work iniquity know, who devour my people as the eating of bread? They did not call upon God; there they feared where there was no fear. For God scattered the bones of those pleasing men; they were put to shame, because God despised them. Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion? When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad.”

[Note: [Col. 0324D] Hilary: “The senseless one.”]

[Note: [Col. 0324D] Hilary: “goodness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0325D] Hilary: “was.”]

[Note: [Col. 0325D] Hilary: “while he turns back.”]

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. The distinction between the present Psalm and Psalm XIII.—VERSE 1. The present Psalm is almost identical with Psalm XIII; yet within this very similarity of words it contains no small difference of meaning. First, by the force of its title itself. For Psalm XIII bears this title: “For the end, of David.”

[Note: [Col. 0325D] “Son of David.”]

[Note: [Col. 0325D] In the Vatican manuscript, “son of David,” erroneously. In the Septuagint, however, Psalm XIII is not titled τοῦ Δαβίδ, “of David,” but τῷ Δαβίδ, “to David.”]

By this title it is indicated that that Psalm was prophesied by David. But this one reads: “For the end, for Maeleth, an understanding addressed to David.”

[Note: [Col. 0325D] The printed editions, with the royal manuscript, read “Abimelech.” The Vatican manuscript has “Amalech,” which is also read twice in Jerome’s exposition of the title, although the Psalm itself is titled *Mahalath* by Jerome; the same reading appears in Ruffinus’s edition, whereas the manuscript has *Melech*. We restore *Maeleth* with Augustine, Theodoret, and the Septuagint edition, on the authority of the Micy manuscript, in which *Meleth* occurs—perhaps through an error of dictation and writing, e having been changed to ae because the speaker pronounced ae as e and the copyist received it as e. But this word, though variously written in Augustine, Ruffinus, and Jerome, is always interpreted in one way: “sorrowing” or “in labour.”]

Where “for the end, an understanding” occurs, it signifies exhortation and admonition, by which we are commanded to bring the judgment of our understanding to bear according to the knowledge of the end, so that we may understand that the things announced in the Psalm will be fulfilled at the end, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Then comes the end, when he has delivered the kingdom to God the Father. When he has abolished every rule and authority and power, then he himself also shall be subjected to him who subjected all things to him. And the last enemy to be abolished is death” (I Cor. XV:24 ff.). This, then, is the end understood in the Psalm.

But the fact that the Psalm is inscribed “to David” shows that all is prophesied concerning Christ, who is the true David. For where it is inscribed “of David,” it signifies him who speaks; but where it is “to David,” it indicates him to whom it is spoken.

2. Everyone is persuaded that God exists; this is what the impious would not have.—“The fool said in his heart: There is no God.” It is a human fault not to dare to commit shameful utterances to spoken words, but, under the compelling impulse of inward wickedness, to speak them within the heart. Thus, while the wickedness of the will struggles against the obligation of public shame,

[Note: [Col. 0326D] Only the Paris edition reads “pleasure,” contrary to Hilary’s meaning, which indicates that the intellect is indeed convinced that God exists, but the wicked will resists, because it would not have God as the avenger of its vices.]

what one is ashamed to say one is not ashamed to think. And therefore the fool says in his heart, “There is no God,” because if he wished to utter this in spoken words, he would be reproved by the judgment of public agreement as being, what he is, a fool. For who, beholding the world, does not perceive that God exists?

[Note: [Col. 0326D] Vin. below, on Psalm 65, no. 10.]

Yet it often happens that, although the necessity of truth compels us to confess God, the delight of vices persuades us that God does not exist for us; and what we believe contrary to faith, we nevertheless utter from the counsel of an impious heart. Hence God’s saying through the Prophet: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX:13), because they do not wish to believe what they cannot deny.

3. Iniquity, the cause of denying God.—He then gives the cause of this most foolish utterance in the heart, saying:

> VERSE 2. “They were corrupted and became abominable in their iniquities.”

Whatever is outside the Law is iniquity. Those who overstep God’s Law are first subject to corruption and then to abomination, because iniquity brings corruption, and corruption deserves abomination. When anyone transgresses God’s Law, he will then deny God; and to deny God is corruption. For our Lord, to drive away corruption, became the Word made flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0326D] The printed editions, except Paris, read “to overcome.”]

For, according to the Apostle, corruption must put on incorruption. But the one who is wicked, who does not believe that the Word, God, became flesh,

[Note: [Col. 0326D] The Tours manuscript reads: “who [does not believe] that he is God”; with the addition of *who*, the reading becomes clearer.]
