and who says in his heart that God does not exist, will remain corrupt and abominable. Psalm XIII, instead of “they became abominable in their iniquity,” says: “They became abominable in their devices.” The meaning and the offence do not differ,

[Note: [Col. 0326D] That is, the sense of the words of the two Psalms, and the offence expressed in each by different wording.]

because men, following what pleases themselves, have transgressed the ordinances of the divine Law.

4. Good things sometimes on the tongue, scarcely in deeds.—Then follows this complaint: “There is none who does goodness.” Since this verse is repeated below with an addition, we shall discuss it in its proper place. Yet it is fittingly and appropriately added here: when all have been corrupted and made abominable, no one is found good in works, because although we are accustomed sometimes to speak what is good, we nevertheless perform with difficulty the good things themselves.

5. God’s various look upon humanity.—And lest God’s will toward human beings be thought negligent, he added, saying:

> VERSE 3. “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God.”

[Note: [Col. 0326D] The words “to see” were absent from the earlier printed editions. They occur in the Vatican manuscript, in the sacred Greek and Latin text; and the final words of this section show that Hilary did not omit them.]

The Lord’s looking down from heaven is known to have occurred frequently: whenever, moved by the sins of humankind, he either chose Noah before the flood for the sake of our salvation, justified Abraham through faith, promised Isaac the heir of his promise, foreshadowed in Jacob the birthright of the later people,

[Note: [Col. 0327D] Vatican manuscript: “of the better people.”]

[Note: [Col. 0327D] “Of the better people.”]

appointed Moses as prophet and leader and established him as giver of the Law, or inspired prophets throughout every time of the Law. By these workings of his power he thus looked down upon the children of men, to see whether anyone might be understanding and seeking God.

6. The fewness of those seeking God, and the manner of seeking.—What God deigns to look down in order to see is not easily found; and it is a great thing that he examines so diligently whether it can be found in anyone. For God looks down from heaven to see whether any human being seeks him intelligently. For which person among men will you find who wishes to seek God with perfect understanding? One who first investigates the causes of created things, and then the constitution of the human race, and through rational understanding seeks the author and father of so great a universe? Then, further: why the world exists; why human beings; why the times of the age; why a patriarch was chosen; why the Law was established; why a prophet was sent beforehand; and toward what purpose the origin of all causes has been directed? Further, what benefit the powers of heaven, the ministries of angels, the authorities of archangels, the kingdom of the devil, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and God’s only-begotten Son, God from God, confer upon us through such diverse kinds of offices?

[Note: [Col. 0327D] Er., Lips., and Par. read “what powers.” More correctly, Bad. with the manuscripts reads “what purpose,” namely, what benefit.]

God looks down in order to see the person who seeks him through understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0327D] The Tours manuscript reads “through understanding of truth,” a reading that has the appearance, but not the reality, of truth.]

7. Understanding is proper to man.—For understanding possesses no small merit, Solomon saying: “Good understanding is for all who find it”; and again through another prophet: “O Israel, what does God require of you, except to do judgment and understand righteousness?” (Deut. X:12). For understanding is the proper function of human reason; and therefore the nature of a spiritual soul has been implanted in us, so that through it we might strive toward the perception of understanding, which alone shares in reason. But, overwhelmed by vices and oppressed by bodily heaviness of nature through the pleasures of the body, we turn aside from the pursuit of intelligent seeking.

8. Sin produces the disposition of turning aside from God.—But we turn aside after we have begun to be useless; this is what the prophetic utterance signifies:

> VERSE 4. “All have turned aside; together they have become useless.”

They do not become useless when they turn aside; rather, once they have begun to be useless, they turn aside. The force of this statement is easy to understand from the customary course of human change. For when we begin to be evil instead of good, and by vices and disgrace separate ourselves from the company of prudent people and from the respectability of public reputation, then, rendered useless thereby, we avoid all encounters with reputable men, follow byways, and shun the presence of good people out of shame before our own conscience.

Finally, Adam, rendered useless through sin, then avoided God’s coming (Gen. III:10). But while he lived innocent for a time, and was useful through keeping the commandments,

[Note: [Col. 0327D] The Paris edition reads “useful to himself.” *To himself* is absent from the other printed editions and from the royal manuscript, from which *but* is also absent shortly before.]

he did not flee God’s familiar approach; he fled it as soon as he began to be useless.

9. Is no one good—not Abel, Seth, and so on?—Since none were found seeking God intelligently, and all, as soon as they became useless, turned aside, the complaint is repeated in the pain of grief:

> “There is none who does good, not even one.”

It is a weighty declaration of God and an unalterable judgment upon human vices when no one does goodness, not even one. After this it will be asked how Abel pleased God, Seth was approved, Isaac was heir, Enoch was translated, Noah was preserved, Melchizedek was sanctified, Abraham was chosen, Jacob became Israel, Job was blameless, Moses was a friend, Aaron was an anointed one, David was after God’s heart, the Prophets were spiritual, and the Apostles received the keys of heaven, if, with only One excepted, no one is good.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] The royal manuscript omits what follows as far as “was chosen.” The Vatican manuscript places the preceding words, “Isaac was heir,” after “Abraham was chosen,” in a better order.]

Moreover, how will this saying be understood: “A good man brings forth good things from a good treasure” (Matt. XII:35)? And this: “Good servant, enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV:21)? For how shall anyone be called good if no one does goodness?

10. To whom “There is none who does good” applies.—First, lest we suppose that the declaration of this general judgment applies even to those most approved men whom we mentioned above, the meaning of the preceding statements opposes this. The entire discourse began with the foolish, corrupt, and abominable. God looked down from heaven to see whether anyone was seeking intelligently; and, after they began to be useless, all turned aside. No one was found doing goodness, not even one—that is, among those who were foolish, corrupt, and abominable, and who began to turn aside after they had become useless. The sentence of divine judgment rightly applies to those with whom the discourse began.

But in saying “not even one,” he does not except one person from all; rather, when none of all the useless and turning-aside persons does goodness, not even one is separated from all. He does not say “except one,” but “as far as one.” In “except one” an exception of one is signified; but in “as far as one,” the general totality, through the knowing diligence of him who looks down from heaven,

[Note: [Col. 0328D] The printed editions, except Paris, and the royal manuscript read “knowing diligence.”]

is contained under a certain particular and personal number.

11. What perfect goodness is, and how it is in no one.—Yet we must remember that such is the weakness of human nature that, in comparison with divine goodness, no one is good. But that incomparable exception of divinity has not excluded the work of goodness, so that, by human comparison, no one among human beings should be good. For perfect goodness is, first, that which rests in the power of an unchangeable nature: it never knows how to be other than it has been, and cannot fail to be what it always is.

Human impulses, however, are often diverse through change itself; and the imperfect nature of earthly law becomes other than it was, changing as another impulse disturbs it. The movement of varied affections drives us to this: when insult makes us angry, when loss moves us, when wrath inflames us, when fear disturbs us, when love bends us, when hatred drives us, when joy exalts us, when sorrow goads us, when judgment makes us disagree, when age changes us. Subject, therefore, to these weak impulses of nature, we cannot remain the same, since we are changeable both in affection and in time. Thus perfect goodness is in no one, because the incitements of natural disturbances alter it.

Yet,

[Note: [Col. 0329C] The printed editions read “when we are good,” and otherwise gave the remaining words somewhat confusedly. They are corrected with the help of the manuscripts.]

when we are in goodness either by will or by deeds, we cannot even then fail to be what we are. And although we are imperfect in this, that we are not always what we are, nevertheless what we are at a given time—though, through the weakness of nature, subject to a change of goodness—does not take away from us our being good at least when we are so.

12. God indulges the lapses of a good will through weakness. — But God alone is good by his own unchangeable nature, always God; he was not a harsh judge of this changeability of ours, [Col. 0330A] but, in view of the merit of the will by which we delight to be good, granted pardon to our weakness, through which we do not always remain good. He has been more gracious toward what we wish than angry at what we cannot do.

For when he had said to Moses—certainly his faithful friend, whom he had made a god to Pharaoh—“Because you did not glorify me [at] the waters of contradiction, ascend the mountain and die,” he afterward preserved him for himself, his burial-place being known to no one, to be seen by the Apostles on the mountain together with Elijah, as a participant and martyr—that is, witness—of his blessed and eternal kingdom.

[Note: “At the waters of contradiction.” Thus the Septuagint: *apo tou hydatos antilogias*, “from the water of contradiction.”]

[Note: The manuscript of Micium has “into the waters of contradiction”; Tours, “at the waters of contradiction”; the Royal manuscript, “in the water of contradiction.”]

[Note: That is, a witness. Then the Royal manuscript reads, “will preserve.” Here Hilary confirms what he teaches in chapter 20 on Matthew: that Moses, together with Elijah, will precede Christ’s final coming.]

And not to run through the examples of God’s goodness in Aaron, David, Solomon, and many others of this kind—though their offences of changeableness were rebuked, pardon was nevertheless readily at hand because of the merit of faith. The Lord knew human weakness when he said to the Apostles, “All of you will suffer scandal in this night” (Matt. 26:31); and to blessed Peter, three times, not so much as a pronouncement of condemned denial, but because the changeable human being, through fear of the flesh, was about to deny him when forewarned; and yet he did not take away from the denier the keys of the kingdom of heaven. For although denial had crept in through alarm, the firm faith of his will to confess—even unto martyrdom—did not fail.

[Note: At the margin of this passage an ancient hand in the Royal manuscript wrote: “You may know, whoever seeks the reason of truth, that Solomon obtained pardon by the merit of faith.” Yet Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, Hilary’s defender, published a treatise on Solomon’s condemnation. But whatever he adduces from the Fathers to confirm his opinion proves, for the most part, only that Solomon fell from his former goodness; it does not sufficiently establish that he persisted in sin without repentance.]

[Note: See *Tractates on Psalm* LXVII, §10.]

[Note: The Micium manuscript has “of condemned change”; the sense is the same. Hilary means that Peter’s fall—by which, through denying the Lord, he fell away from his former goodness through changeability—was not liable to eternal condemnation, because he quickly repented of his fall. Thus anyone attentive to his purpose will not judge that Hilary wishes to clear Peter of guilt, but only that he had not fallen from goodness insofar as he quickly corrected his fault and persevered in good will. Likewise, Hilary had not exempted Aaron, David, and Solomon from fault. This bears on his statement in chapter 32 on Matthew: “He wept most bitterly, recalling that he had not been able, even though warned, to avoid the fault of that fear.” In accordance with this, Augustine calls Peter’s fault, *Epistle* 185, §46, “a lying fear.” Yet, lest anyone suspect that Peter’s restoration is here attributed to will alone apart from grace, let him recall what occurs in Book X of *On the Trinity*, §41: “The Father is prayed to, that he may now save in his own name those whom he had saved through him.” And he saves so completely that Peter’s faith, though terrified, does not fail after repentance follows. Therefore Peter’s faith does not fail because the Father saves: behold the power of grace. But the Father saves after Christ has prayed: behold merit.]

And it is one thing not to will, another not to be able. Peter, frightened though he was, could not, through the inclination of the flesh, maintain constancy in his reply; yet through the faith of his mind he immediately wept. When he recognized that he had been struck down from what he willed, he poured out in the pain of tears the affection of faith. The very same moment was that of denial and of weeping: [Col. 0330C] namely, according to the changeability of alarm, but with the stronger firmness of his will. For steadfast faith immediately wept over the inconstancy of alarm, thereafter confirming, by the confession of martyrdom, the firmness of apostolic constancy, tested beyond all doubt.

[Note: Our manuscript adds “was.”]

[Note: The Royal and Micium manuscripts read “through denial”; the printed editions read “through will.” Both readings give one sense.]

[Note: Badius has “of bargaining,” through a copyist’s error; Paris has “of change.” We restore “of denial” from Erasmus, Lipsius, the Royal manuscript, and three Vatican manuscripts: that is, Peter did not long delay repentance, but the same time was both that of denial and of weeping.]

[Note: Paris has “pleasure,” which entirely misses Hilary’s purpose: he contends that Peter did not lack the will to confess Christ even unto martyrdom; that will, yielding briefly to alarm, finally proved stronger.]

[Note: Erasmus and Badius lack “constancy.” In other printed editions the word “faith” was substituted in its place, followed by “firmness.” We repair this passage with the aid of the manuscripts.]

We have recalled these matters here so that we might not suppose the statement to be universal: “There is none who does goodness, not even one.” For these many and great men pleasing to God, although through nature’s changeability they had fallen somewhat from the purpose of faith, nevertheless obtained for themselves, through the greatest and most beautiful works of goodness, the glory of heavenly judgment.

[Note: “Might be supposed.”]

[Note: Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “and pleasing”; the Vatican manuscript, “and so acceptable”; the Royal manuscript, “and so pleasing.”]

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “obtained for themselves the judgment of heavenly glory.”]

13. And the verses that follow establish this line of interpretation: verses 5 and 6: “Will not all who work iniquity know, who devour my people as food of bread? They have not called upon God; there they feared where there was no fear. For God scattered the bones of those who please men; they were put to shame, because God despised them.”

[Note: “Will they not know?”]

[Note: “There they feared fear,” in accordance with the Greek: *ekei ephobēthēsan phobon*; and also with the Hebrew. Yet below it is repeated: “they trembled.”]

[Note: In the Vatican manuscript, as in the Vulgate, “there they trembled with fear.” In Greek, *ekei ephobēthēsan phobon*. Yet the reading of the other books seems truer.]

[Note: Greek: *anthrōpareskōn*, “those pleasing men.” The Royal manuscript reads “of men who please,” which does not suit the following exposition.]

For if no one does goodness, not even one, how is there a people of God, devoured as food of bread by those who work iniquity? The universality of the statement is therefore removed when workers of iniquity are separated from the people of God, who, it is beyond doubt, remain engaged in works of goodness.

Thus the workers of iniquity devour the people of God as food of bread: those who live by injuries done to the saints, who delight in the harassment of prophets, the devastation of the Church, and every activity of iniquity. So too do those devour the people of God as food of bread who tear them apart with the bite of detraction and the rending of envy, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5:15).

[Note: The word “also” has been supplied from the Tours manuscript; it was lacking in the earlier printed editions.]

And there are also those who devour the people of God as food of bread, whose god, as the same blessed Apostle says, is their belly (Phil. 3:19). They turn ministry into trade, enriching themselves from the contributions and gifts of the people; they seek costly banquets under the pretext of religion; they fill their storehouses with the needless attendance of the devout—although the custom, instituted by the Apostles, of this necessary contribution was intended only for the daily sustenance of those who had renounced the world or were needy through poverty. Of these it is written: “Devouring the houses of widows, and praying at length” (Matt. 23:14).

[Note: That is, from the nonessential contributions of pious people.]

These, then, devour God’s people as food of bread, and have not called upon the Lord. For fools have said in their heart, “There is no God.” Therefore they do not call upon him whom they deny. Or certainly, if any who are within the Church devour God’s people as food of bread through detraction, persecution, and expense, even though they believe that they call upon the Lord, they will hear what was said in the Gospel: “For we know that God does not hear sinners” (John 9:31).

[Note: “They devoured God’s people at the cost of persecution.”]

These therefore have not called upon the Lord, because prayer is not a profession of words, but of faith.

[Note: The printed editions read “activity.” The Vatican manuscript more correctly has “prayer.” Then the Royal manuscript reads: “is not a profession of words, but of faith.”]

14. They fear what ought not to be feared. — But those who do not call upon God add this further to their impiety: they fear what ought not to be feared—for “there they trembled, where there was no [Col. 0332B] fear”—worshipping stones, metals, oak trees, fire, water, the ether, kings dead and yet to die, or the other superstitious inventions of religions. By this very impious fear of empty things, and by contempt for necessary fear, they are to be condemned by comparison. For it is not so impious to forget the fear of God as it surpasses all impiety to prefer the fear of empty things to fear of him.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “and trees.” We nevertheless judge that nothing should be altered. Hilary perhaps has Druidic religion in view. The same manuscript has the word “worshipping” before “stones.”]

[Note: “And contempt” is lacking in the Royal manuscript. Contempt for the fear of God consists in preferring to it, by comparison, the fear of empty things. Love is likewise customarily said to be preferred to love by comparison, as we saw in Psalm I, §17. Moreover, the phrase “by comparison” here may be referred to “to be condemned”: those who have preferred the fear of empty things to the fear of God are to be condemned by comparison with those who have preferred the fear of God to the fear of empty things; just as in Psalm II, §44, we have that the ungodly and impenitent are to be condemned by comparison with the faith and fear of the righteous. Hilary commonly places words in the middle so that they may refer equally to what precedes and what follows.]

But the Lord taught that there ought to be in us only fear of those things that are truly to be feared, when he says: “Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). Impious fear, therefore, arises when things that ought not to be feared are feared, and things that ought to be feared are not feared.

And often we suppose that we piously flatter kings as a duty of religious observance, because they have some power over our body; yet they have no more power over us than a robber, fever, fire, shipwreck, or collapse.

[Note: “Over us they are permitted.”]

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads: “By these kinds,” omitting “of bodies.” It then adds: “for the brief pain of the body.”]

[Note: One Vatican manuscript has “by these occurrences only”; another, “by these kinds,” and afterward, “for the brief pain of the body.”]

For by such accidents they rage against bodies with what amounts to their utmost power; and for brief pain we surrender the liberty of the Church, the confidence of our hope, and the confession of God, not fearing God, the punisher and destroyer of both our body and soul in the fire of judgment. We prefer momentary and vanishing punishments to the eternal penalties of divine vengeance, while we glory in impious servitude because we please these rulers and remain in their favour.

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads: “we cast down the liberty and desires of our hope by the confession of confidence.”]

15. When the pursuit of human favour is sinful. — Divine judgment itself condemns this in a most severe decree. For after saying, “Will not those who work iniquity know, who devour my people as food of bread? They have not called upon God; there they trembled where there was no fear,” he adds, as the conclusion of the argument begun: “For God scattered the bones of those who please men; they were put to shame, because God despised them.”

These, then, who work iniquity, devour the people as food of bread, have not called upon God, and trembled at things not to be feared—will they not know that God scattered the bones of those who wish to please men?

[Note: “Will they not all know?”]

[Note: The printed editions here and below read “will scatter”; the manuscripts read “scattered,” more truly. For, as Hilary says below in §17, the language is spoken as though of the past because of the definitiveness of the decree.]

That holy teacher of the Gentiles feared the judgment of this prophetic saying when he declared: “If I were still pleasing men, I should not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10). The pursuit of human favour is useless and irreligious. We must please men more in obedience to God than in contempt of God: we please through divine ordinances and through the uprightness of a faithful and innocent life. But to wish merely to please men is to displease God.

[Note: “For from God.”]

[Note: We correct this from the Tours manuscript. Formerly the text read: “For, from God, more.”]

Yet God does not call the minds of the righteous, or the reasonable holiness of the faithful, away from human favour. Let us hear him speaking through Paul: “Be without offence to Jews and Greeks and to the Church of God, just as I please all men in all things, [Col. 0333C] not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:32–33).

[Note: The printed editions read “in all things to all.” The particles “in” and “to” are absent in the Royal manuscript and in Greek.]

[Note: “What is useful to me,” from the Greek, *to emautou sympheron*.]

This is to please not men but God: by pleasing God, one also pleases men. For from the reason for pleasing God arises a reason, acceptable to men, for pleasing them too. But the effort expended merely to please men is not directed toward what ought to please God, because it is employed solely for the sake of those whom one pleases.

Nor is there a stronger bond for pleasing men than that no one should wish to please those whom he pleases for his own sake. For what is done to advance one’s own advantage cannot fail sometimes to cause offence from circumstances that arise, since what benefits one person often harms another. But one who wills nothing for his own sake and does all things for the advancement of another’s advantage must acquire for himself a reason for inoffensive acceptability: he pleases from others’ advantages and does not offend from his own. The Apostle teaches that this was his acceptable reason for pleasing all: disregarding his own advantage, he had devoted himself to the advantage of others.

[Note: The printed editions read, “wish anything,” omitting “to please those whom he pleases,” which we restore from the manuscripts. Here is shown the bond by which each person binds all to himself.]

[Note: The manuscripts read “advantage” rather than the printed editions’ “will.”]

16. By bones is signified the hope of eternity. — Therefore God scattered the bones of those who please men. These are not to be understood as bodily bones scattered; rather, the hope of eternity is customarily signified in bones, as in the saying: “This now is bone of my bones” (Gen. 2:23). Because this is a great mystery, the blessed Apostle refers it to Christ and the Church (Eph. 5:31), which borrows the substance of eternity from the eternity of its Adam.

This bone was not broken though the Lord’s body was wounded and nailed: “His bone shall not be broken” (Num. 9:12). For although the wicked had a right of suffering against his flesh, suffering had no power over the eternal and impassible nature of divinity.

[Note: “The force of the passion.”]

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads “internal,” which first pleased us, though it is less to the point. It then, with other manuscripts, has “of divinity,” not the printed editions’ “divinity.” Here Hilary plainly explains which nature of Christ he holds to have been exempt from suffering.]

We also remember that an entire and incorrupt hope of eternity is signified in bones where it says: “The Lord keeps all the bones of the righteous; not one of them shall be broken” (Ps. 33:21). For according to the resurrection shown to Ezekiel, its mystery is revealed under the signification of bones (Ezek. 37). Therefore, as God keeps the bones of the righteous, so he scattered those of people-pleasers; and he scattered them not so that they would lack the existence they had, but so that, through contempt of God, they might become worthless, as though lost and cast away.

[Note: See *Tractates on Psalm* I, §§14–15.]

17. The ungodly suffer a twofold shame after judgment. — For this follows: “They were put to shame, because God despised them.” Every person is put to shame both by the disgrace of his own dishonour and by comparison with another’s honour. This is what the Apostle signifies when he says: “We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51). The prophet too distinguishes the shame of resurrection from honour, saying: “Some shall rise to life, but others to eternal shame” (Dan. 12:2).

Thus those whose bones were scattered, whom God despised, whom he cast away as unworthy to be conformed to his glory and resurrection, will be put to shame. They will rise indeed, so that they may be ashamed; but they will not be changed, and for this reason they will be ashamed. This is the fixed condition of resurrection; and therefore the language is spoken as though of the past, because of the definitiveness of the decree, since it has been ordained that it remain so.

18. Hope, the one consolation of this life. — Having recalled the human impieties of arrogance and iniquity, the Prophet, so that the “understanding unto the end” set forth in the title may be understood, confirms the hope of the blessed end with this exhortation: “Who will give out of Zion salvation to Israel? When the Lord turns away the captivity of his people, Jacob shall exult and Israel shall rejoice.”

For this one hope remained to human weakness and faith, through which, amid so many calamities of the present life, they might rest in expectation of eternal goods. And therefore the Prophet, certain of this blessedness, cries out as though from the vast depth of human miseries: “Who will give out of Zion salvation to Israel?” For according to another prophet: “Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3). This Word of the Lord became flesh. This flesh is Zion and Jerusalem, the city of new peace and our watchtower. From here comes the Saviour; from here comes Jesus. For Jesus, as we have often said, is by the very meaning of his name “Saviour.”

[Note: This has hitherto been said only once, in Psalm XIII, §5. Yet it may have been said in Psalms IX and others where the word “Saviour” occurs; this is evidence that Hilary treated psalms other than those expounded thus far.]

But the law from Zion was not saving: it gave life through works, but did not justify by faith.

[Note: The printed editions read “weakness”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

19. Jesus is the Saviour. He was given to Israel, but not to carnal Israel. — This Saviour was expected and was given to Israel, but not to that carnal Israel. “For it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are reckoned as seed” (Rom. 9:8). John also testifies that Abraham’s children are not so according to the flesh, since they can even be children of vipers; and God is able to raise up children to Abraham from stones.

The Lord himself taught that the rightful claim of succession arises from works of faith, and that the origin of children is not reckoned according to physical generation, when he said: “If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39). Daniel too, condemning the elders, says not, “Seed of Abraham,” but, “Seed of Canaan, and not of Judah” (Dan. 13:56). Ezekiel likewise, rebuking the iniquities of the people, says: “Your father was a Canaanite, your mother a Hittite; your root and your generation are from the land of Canaan” (Ezek. 16:3).

Thus this is not the Israel of bodily succession, to which, because of unbelief, descent from a most profane race is imputed. Nor was salvation given to him who did not receive the salvation offered, but to him who, when captivity had been turned away, became the people of God.

[Note: “Who does not receive what is offered”; below, “when captivity has been turned away.”]

20. The captive people: the Gentiles. — He set free into the liberty of faith and the name of the heavenly household the minds of ignorant nations, held captive and subjected to most impious vices and religions. Those who were the slaves of demons became God’s people. And he himself testified who it is that turns away captivity.

For neither law, nor patriarch, nor prophet, nor angel, nor any other power among the heavenly beings—whether dominions, powers, thrones, or virtues—turned it away. Rather, it was he who, after receiving the book in the synagogue and reading these words, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me to preach release to captives and sight to the blind, to send the broken forth in release, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord” (Luke 4:18 ff.), indicated the faith and authority of prophecy brought to fulfilment and said: “Today this prophecy has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21).

[Note: See *Tractates on Psalm* XIII, §3.]

[Note: “Or thrones.”]

[Note: The Royal manuscript has “or throne.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “authority”; the printed editions, “author.”]

[Note: “This, therefore.”]

This, then, is the captivity of God’s people turned away: when the eyes of understanding are opened; when hearts broken by sins are released into rest; when the acceptable year of the Lord is proclaimed, in which the confession of our repentance is acceptable to God; when nothing past is counted as a crime; when all things are new—new liberty, new children, and eternal joy.

[Note: The printed editions read “understanding.”]

[Note: “In which the confession of all our repentance”; then, “in which nothing of the past.”]

21. Jacob the supplanter. — “Jacob shall exult, and Israel shall rejoice.” For the same patriarch received both names in accordance with his merit. Because at birth he held his brother’s heel with his hand, he was called Jacob; he was afterward to supplant his brother both by buying the birthright and by obtaining the blessings (Gen. 27:27).

[Note: “And of the name’s interpretation.”]

Genesis itself explained the force of the interpretation: he was called Jacob because he was the supplanter of his brother (ibid. 36). But through the knowledge of the God whom he confessed, when he asked to be blessed by the man over whom he prevailed in the wrestling match—because with the eyes of faith he had seen in a body the God against whom the people of his race, in accordance with the mystery of the future Passion, prevailed in the wrestling of flesh—he deserved to be named Israel, because Israel means “one who sees God.”

And according to the prophecy of Genesis itself, it has been established that the younger people, who would believe from among the Gentiles, are signified in Jacob. Therefore Jacob shall exult, and Israel shall rejoice. In the order of the Church, this is one people, possessing a double profession and honour; for the heavenly utterance does not signify the same thing by doubled statements.

[Note: “Here, therefore.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “here therefore”; the Royal manuscript has “this therefore.” The reading of the Tours manuscript is clearer: “This, therefore, is: Jacob shall exult.”]

But because faith is first when someone prays that God’s name be invoked upon him, the Gentile by faith supplants the earlier people, when he desires to be faithful while the Jew is unbelieving. This, then, is Jacob, exulting in the hope of a blessing taken beforehand. But when, reborn by baptism and perfected in faith, he has looked upon God with the eyes and mind of understanding, then Israel shall rejoice, because, having now supplanted the elder, he sees God by faith and will see him with a truer sight, according to that promise of blessedness: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads “is proclaimed, by the earlier faith,” which is unsatisfactory. The whole phrase appears to mean: faith is first when someone prays that God’s name be invoked over him; the Gentile by faith supplants the earlier people when, etc.]

[Note: The printed editions read “insulting”; corrected from the Royal manuscript.]

[Note: “Of mind.”]

Of our Lord and God Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LIII

Unto the end, in hymns, an understanding of David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: “Is not David hidden among us?”

[Note: Thus the Micy manuscript. The printed editions read, “in songs . . . had come . . . had said.” That some read “in songs,” while he himself, though allowing this translation, customarily prefers “in hymns,” Hilary sufficiently declares at the beginning of his tractate on Psalm LIV.]

“God, save me in your name, and judge me in your power. God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth. For strangers have risen against me, and the mighty have sought my soul; and they have not set God before their sight.” DIAPSALM. “For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the defender of my soul. Turn evils upon my enemies; in your truth destroy them. Willingly shall I sacrifice to you, and I shall confess to [Col. 0337B] your name, O Lord, for it is good; for you have delivered me from every tribulation, and my eye has looked upon my enemies.”

[Note: Hilary reads “turn” rather than “turn away.”]

[Note: “Give ear,” alternatively “incline your ear.”]

[Note: Paris reads “has looked down upon.”]

## TRACTATE ON THE PSALM

1. David, a follower of evangelical teaching. — Holy and blessed David was not ignorant of evangelical teaching. Though living in the age of the Law and conducting this bodily life, he nevertheless fulfilled, insofar as lay within him, the precepts of the apostolic command. He offered proof of his faith toward God by God’s testimony concerning him, when it was said: “I have found David, son of Jesse, a man according to my heart” (Acts 13:22).

[Note: “Testimony concerning him.” Then: “who is of Jesse.”]

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads “who is of Jesse,” rendering the Greek *ton tou Iessai* literally.]

For he did not pursue his enemies in war, nor resist armed combat against those who plotted against him. Rather, following the example of the Lord, whose name and gentleness he foreshadowed, he prayed when betrayed, sang psalms in danger, and rejoiced while enduring hatred. Therefore he was found to be according to the Lord’s heart. For though twelve thousand legions of angels could have stood by the Lord in the time of his Passion (Matt. 26:53), he nevertheless allowed himself to be subjected to suffering and weakness in order to fulfil every office of humility, praying only and saying: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46).

[Note: See Book X of *On the Trinity*, §41; and *Tractates on Psalm* LIV, §6.]

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads “he permitted himself to be subject to weakness.”]

Following this example, David, a prophet of the Lord’s future Passion through the likeness of his own sufferings, does not contradict or resist his enemies, nor return evil for evil, as the Gospel commands. Rather, emulating the Lord’s gentleness, when harassed, betrayed, and pursued, he entreats the Lord, who alone uses arms against the ungodly.

2. In this psalm David bears Christ’s person. — The title of this psalm is prefixed from its history; but before the history it is shown how, when, and concerning whom we are to understand what is said under the historical narrative. For first comes verse 1: “Unto the end, an understanding of David.” Then follows verse 2: “When the Ziphites came and said to Saul: ‘Is not David hidden with us?’” Therefore this betrayal of David by the Ziphites must be understood “unto the end.” It shows that the things then being done to David in the present contained within themselves a foreshadowing of the future time: when innocence is harassed by persecution; when a prophet is mocked with insults; when one pleasing to God is sought for death; when a king is betrayed by his own enemy—as the Lord was by Herod and Pilate—by those [Col. 0338B] with whom he ought to have been safe.

[Note: “The historical title.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “assembled,” incorrectly.]

[Note: “Among us,” Greek: *par’ hēmin*.]

Therefore this psalm of understanding is “unto the end,” and its understanding is in that David in whom is the end of the Law, who possesses the key of David, opening the entrance to understanding when he fulfils the prophecies made of himself through David.

[Note: The printed editions read “then opens,” but the manuscripts read “opening.”]

3. “Ziphites” in Hebrew: sprinkling of the mouth. — The very interpretation of the name according to its Hebrew sense contributes no little to our understanding. For the Ziphites signify “sprinklings of the mouth which are with us”; these are called *Ziphaei* by the Hebrews.

[Note: Yet in Augustine, Jerome, and Rufinus, “Ziphites” is rendered differently, namely “flourishing ones.”]

Now sprinkling under the Law was a cleansing of sins, purifying the people by faith through sprinkling of blood. The same blessed David recalls this sprinkling when he says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50:9). This was a sacrament of the future sprinkling from the Lord’s blood, while faith supplied in advance, through the blood of legal burnt-offerings, what the future sprinkling would accomplish.

[Note: The Royal manuscript has “sprinkle me.”]

[Note: The printed editions, except Paris, read “represents,” as also does the Royal manuscript; it subsequently reads, “and here is the people.” From this we at first thought that “representing, but this people” should be restored. But the reading of Paris was finally judged better; it is supported by the Vatican and Micium manuscripts, one of which has “supplying in advance,” the other “supplied in advance.” The point is that the Jews were purified through the sprinkling of bulls’ blood, faith supplying the efficacy which the sprinkling of the Lord’s blood would possess in itself. If, however, anyone prefers “representing,” because of the preceding words, “a sacrament of the future,” let him choose as he pleases. Indeed, let no one separate either reading from the meaning.]

But this people, as a people of Ziphites, sprinkled rather with the mouth than with faith, receiving the cleansing of sprinkling more with lips than with heart, proved faithless and a betrayer of its David. This had been said beforehand by the Prophet: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). They were inclined to betray David because, faith of heart having ceased, they had performed all the sacraments of the Law through deceitfulness of mouth.

4. Christ is in every respect consistent with human beings. — Verses 3 and 4: “God, save me in your name, and judge me in your power. God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.” According to the explanation of the title already given, the Passion of David the prophet is an image of the Passion of God and our Lord Jesus Christ. And therefore David’s prayer too is adapted to the understanding of the prayer of him who became the Word made flesh, so that he who suffered all things as man may also speak all things as man, and may entreat God in the service of those whose weaknesses he bore and whose sins he took upon himself.

[Note: Our manuscript has “save me” twice. Hilary himself indicates that he wrote this by explaining the verse: “He asks that he be saved in God’s name”; and later in §14: “For at the beginning he had said, ‘Save me in your name.’”]

[Note: “He who was made Word flesh.”]

The distinctive qualities and force of the words require, even if we are reluctant and hesitant, this understanding: that we should not doubt that all things in the psalm are said in his person. For he says: “God, save me in your name.” In the humility of the body, the only-begotten Son of God makes this prayer beneath the words of his prophet; he who was also seeking again the glory which he had possessed before the ages. He asks to be saved in the name of God, in whose name he was both called and born, so that, in the body in which he was born, the name of God might preserve him safe in that very state which was proper to his prior nature and birth.

### 5. That is, God’s name and power.

And since this entire prayer is spoken from the person of the form of a servant, that servant-form which was assumed even unto the death of the cross, he prays for salvation in that Name which is God’s; and, having said that he is to be saved by God’s Name, he immediately adds: “And judge me in thy power.” For, by the merit of humility—because he had emptied himself, taking the form of a servant—he now again claimed, in the humility which he had assumed, the form shared with God; the man himself, in whom God had consented to be born, being saved in God’s Name. And in order to teach that the honour of this Name, in which he prayed to be saved, is not merely that of an empty designation, he prays that he may be judged in God’s power.

For first, what he deserves follows from judgment: “He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also exalted him, and gave him the Name which is above every name” (Phil. 2:8–9), so that the Name which is above every name might be given to him. Then, further, this very judgment is to be exercised in the power of judgment: because by God’s power he who, being from God, had died as man, likewise rose again into God from dead manhood; according to the Apostle: “He was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4); and again: “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Rom. 1:16).

Through the power of judgment, therefore, bodily weakness is saved into God’s Name and nature; and thus, by the merit of obedience, it is advanced through the power of judgment into the salvation of God’s Name, so that in him are both God’s Name and God’s power. Otherwise, had this expression begun from ordinary human usage, the Prophet would have asked to be judged rather in mercy or equity than in power. But there was need for the work of power in judgment where, after the Son of God had been born as Son of Man through the Virgin’s childbirth, the Name and power of the Son of God had to be restored by the power of judgment to that same Son of Man.

> [Note: Col. 0339D] In the Tours manuscript, “unto the death of the cross,” not “unto the cross of death.” Yet inversions of such nouns are not unusual in Hilary.

> [Note: Col. 0339D] The particle *nunc* (“now”), omitted in the Lipsius and Paris editions, is restored from the royal manuscript. In its place the Badius and Erasmus editions wrongly read *non* (“not”).

> [Note: Col. 0339C] “In the form.”

> [Note: Col. 0339C] “So that by that Name.”

> [Note: Col. 0339D] Supply: “He prays that.”

> [Note: Col. 0339D] The printed editions, “in God’s Name and nature,” do not adequately express Hilary’s meaning: that Christ, through participation in divine glory, even according to the form of a servant, passed into God’s Name and nature—not by abolition of nature, but by participation in divine immortality and incorruption, as has often already been said. It should incidentally be observed here that by the term “power” God’s nature is understood. Hence what he now says, “he is saved into God’s Name and nature,” he immediately explains thus: that in him are both God’s Name and power.

> [Note: Col. 0339C] “To be restored.”

### 6. The confidence of the one praying here belongs to Christ alone.

It follows: “God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.” It would have been easy for the Prophet to say, “God, hear me.” But because he speaks in the person of him who alone knew how to pray, a confident petition for a prayer to be heard is displayed. Blessed Paul teaches that no human being knows how he ought to pray, saying: “For we know not what we should pray for as we ought” (Rom. 8:26). It is not, therefore, characteristic of human weakness to ask that one’s prayer be heard, since the Doctor of the Gentiles, even after the Lord had already established the pattern of prayer, did not know what, or to what extent, he should pray.

But this confidence belongs to him alone who sees the Father, who alone knows the Father, who alone can pray through the night—for according to the Gospel the Lord spent the night in prayer (Luke 6:12)—and who, through the mirror of words, while we pray, disclosed beneath ordinary expressions the very form of the most hidden mystery. And he who asked that his prayer be heard, in order to teach that this was a distinctive feature of his confidence, added: “Give ear to the words of my mouth.”

Could anyone suppose that it belongs to human confidence to wish the words of one’s mouth to be heard? Are these not the words by which we utter the movements and impulses of our minds: when we blaze with anger, rail in hatred, complain in grief, flatter through adulation, lie either through hope of gain or shame at the truth, or curse because we are offended by an insult? And who has ever lived so blamelessly and patiently in all things as not to be subject to these faults of human changeability? He alone could confidently desire this, who “did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth”; who offered his back to scourges, did not turn his cheeks away from blows, did not reproach the indignity of spitting, and in no respect offended the will of him to whose will he willingly obeyed in all things.

> [Note: Col. 0339C] Thus our text, with the better manuscripts, where the printed editions read *inaurire* (“give ear”).

> [Note: Col. 0340D] Thus the Micy manuscript, with the Vatican and Royal manuscripts agreeing below, which here read “give ear.” But in the printed editions, in both places, appears *inauri*.

> [Note: Col. 0340D] The Paris edition after Lipsius reads “to be granted.” Erasmus has in the margin, “to be obtained”; but in the text, with Badius and the Royal and Micy manuscripts, “to be requested”—as we suppose, through a scribal error for “to be heard.” We restore “to be heard,” on the authority of the Vatican manuscript.

> [Note: Col. 0340C] “Ought.”

> [Note: Col. 0340C] “Although also.”

> [Note: Col. 0340C] “The Gospels.” In fact, three mention this.

> [Note: Col. 0340D] Vatican manuscript: “and who anywhere?”

> [Note: Col. 0341D] Royal manuscript: “turns away.”

### 7. Every complaint of Christ arises from the affections of human nature.

He next adds the reason why he prays that his words may be heard:

> **Verse 5.** “For strangers have risen up against me, and the mighty have sought my soul; and they have not set God before their eyes.”

The only-begotten Son of God, the Word of God, and God the Word—since assuredly he himself could do everything that the Father could do, as he says: “Whatsoever things the Father doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise” (John 5:19), so that, where the divine Name and nature were undivided, the power also was undivided—became, for us, the most perfect example of human humility: he both prayed and suffered all that belongs to human beings. From our common weakness he prayed to the Father for salvation for himself, so that it might be understood that he had entered into our birth together with the very functions of our weakness.

Hence it is that he hungered, thirsted, slept, was weary, fled gatherings of the ungodly, was sorrowful, wept, suffered, and died. And in order that it might be understood that he was subject to all these things, not by nature—insofar as he is God—but by assumption—insofar as he is also man—he rose again after undergoing all of them. Every complaint of his in the Psalms, therefore, springs from the affections of our nature. Nor is it surprising if we thus understand the words of the Psalms, since the Lord himself testified, according to the Gospel, that the mysteries of his Passion were written in the Psalms (Luke 24:44).

> [Note: Col. 0341D] The Micy codex reads, “and in the undivided [Name],” perhaps not wrongly, if “and” is understood after *ut* (“so that”).

> [Note: Col. 0341D] Printed editions with the Royal manuscript read “to be present”; they are corrected from the Micy and Vatican manuscripts.

> [Note: Col. 0341D] Vatican manuscript: “he was among the assembly of the ungodly.”

### 8. Who are the strangers? Who are the mighty? They did not know Christ, who is God and man, to be God.

“Strangers,” therefore, rose against him. For they are no longer children of Abraham, nor children of God; but a brood of vipers, slaves of sin, the seed of Canaan, with an Amorite father and a Hittite mother (Ezek. 16:3), and, having the devil as father, children of the devil’s will. The mighty also seek his soul: when Herod asks the chief priests where Christ was to be born (Matt. 2:4), and when the whole Synagogue conspires against him with false witnesses.

But, regarding this soul as belonging to human nature and weakness, “they have not set God before their eyes,” because God, remaining what he was as God, had humbled himself even to the origin of human birth—that is, so that he who had previously been Son of God might become Son of Man. For the Son of God is none other than the Son of Man; and the Son of Man was not so only in part, but was born. For the form of God emptied itself from what it was into what it was not, in order that it might be born into a soul and body; and therefore he is both Son of God and Son of Man, therefore both God and man—that is, the Son of God was born in the condition of human origin.

God’s substance humbled itself even to the nature of the man to be born, who can be formed wholly from soul and flesh. Therefore, when strangers rise against him, when the mighty seek his soul—which is frequently sorrowful and troubled in the Gospels—they have not set God before their eyes. For God the Son of God, who existed before the ages, had been born as man, consisting of our body and soul, in the condition of human nature through the Virgin’s childbirth. They did not understand from the magnificence of his works that the Son of Man, whose soul they sought, had become, with respect to that which he had begun to be as man, what he had always remained as Son of God.

> [Note: Col. 0341C] “Where he ought to be born.”

> [Note: Col. 0341D] He does not deny that Christ’s soul was like ours either in nature or weakness; otherwise he would conflict with what was said immediately above in §7, and his later statement that Christ was man of our body and soul would not stand. But he denies that it belonged to human nature and weakness because it belonged to a divine person—that is, to the Son of God, who is God by nature and omnipotent. This passage sheds some light by which the truth of certain highly obscure statements in Book X *On the Trinity* may appear.

> [Note: Col. 0342C] “Not from a father.”

> [Note: Col. 0341D] In the Royal manuscript, after “but born,” the words “the Son of God, united to man—that is, he who was became Son of Man” were added on a second revision. Without this interpolation, the mind of the holy Doctor is sufficiently clear: in this one place he explicitly condemns in advance three heretics at once—Eutyches, Nestorius, and Apollinarius—whom the Arians had preceded.

> [Note: Col. 0342D] “From the Son of God,” that is: having first existed as Son of God, which he always remained, even when he thereafter began to be Son of Man. By this manner of speaking, very familiar to him, Hilary means that the Son of God both existed before becoming man and remained after becoming man.

### 9. By the intervention of the *diapsalma*, the person changes: not the speaker’s, but that of the one addressed.

For now the discourse is a general prophetic utterance. For after that prayer addressed to God—so that the confidence of the one praying might be understood—he immediately added, at the very time of the prayer in which he had obtained what he asked:

> **Verse 6.** “For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the protector of my soul. He will turn evils upon my enemies.”

He assigned corresponding effects to the several petitions, teaching that God is not heedless of our prayer, nor that the bestowal of his mercy ought to be regarded as irrational, since he hears us according to what we pray for. Thus, corresponding to “For strangers have risen against me,” is “God helps me”; corresponding to “And the mighty have sought my soul,” the distinctive effect of the heard prayer is: “And the Lord is the protector of my soul”; and corresponding to “And they have not set God before their eyes,” he fittingly adds:

> **Verse 7.** “He will turn evils upon my enemies.”

God, therefore, both helps against those who rise up and receives the soul of his saint which the mighty seek; and, though not set before their eyes or thought upon by the wicked, he turns evils themselves upon his enemies. Thus, while they do not think of God when seeking the soul of the righteous man and rising against him, after he has been helped and received, they may feel him—whom amid their works of wickedness they did not think of—as the avenger through the recompense of their own evil.

> [Note: Col. 0342D] In the Royal manuscript here: “of the diapsalm”; elsewhere one finds “of the diapsalma.”

> [Note: Col. 0342D] Badius and Erasmus, with the Royal manuscript, read “having obtained,” whence Lipsius produced “obtained.” We prefer, with the Micy manuscript, “of the one obtaining,” since the word refers to the one praying.

> [Note: Col. 0342D] The printed editions read “Turn evils,” against the manuscripts and the preceding statements, which indicate that the person formerly addressed has now been changed. In Greek: ἀποστρέψει, “he will turn away.”

> [Note: Col. 0343C] The printed editions read “him.” More fitting is the manuscripts’ “him,” namely, the avenger. Then the Micy manuscript reads, “the recompense of his evil from his own evil”; a reading not to be despised.

### 10. The confidence of the righteous amid calamities.

Let innocent religion, therefore, possess this confidence: amid human persecutions and dangers to the soul, it should not doubt that God is its helper; and, if the violence of an unjust death is ever inflicted, it should know that the soul, leaving the dwelling-place of the body, rests in God’s protection. Let it also possess the most certain assurance of vengeance, since all evils return upon those who inflict them.

God cannot be accused of injustice, nor is any impulse or movement of malicious will mixed with perfect goodness. For he does not maliciously stir up evils, but turns them back as avenger; nor does he bring them from his own malice, but turns them into what our merits deserve. For these evils are established for all as instruments of vengeance, together with the law of life, the righteous moderating this by the stern equity of judgment.

But by the law of justice these evils are both kept away from the righteous and turned upon the wicked by the equity of judgment. Both are just: that they are ready for the righteous as a warning, yet are not mingled with them because they are righteous; and that they are turned upon the unrighteous as punishment because they have deserved them. They are neither mingled with the righteous, though ready, nor absent from the unrighteous, because they are ready.

> [Note: Col. 0343C] Since the Psalmic statement “the Lord is the protector,” etc., is in view here, “of the Lord,” not “of God,” seems to be required. This would better suit Hilary’s customary teaching: that the righteous after death are received by the Lord, in order to be handed over to God after the resurrection of all. Yet, in Psalm I, §9, he teaches that Paradise, into which he admits the thief and other righteous persons, is situated in the possession of God’s kingdom.

> [Note: Col. 0343D] The printed editions read “ministries of flatteries”; they are corrected from the Royal manuscript. What then is meant by “with the law of life”? Perhaps that, just as God appoints death and evils for the wicked, so he appoints life and rewards for the good? This is discussed more fully in Psalm II, §16. But the law of dying and the law of living are discussed more explicitly in Psalm LI, §18.

> [Note: Col. 0343C] “The righteous moderating this by the stern equity of judgment.”

> [Note: Col. 0343D] We restore the word *id* (“this”) from Badius and the Royal manuscript. The printed editions, except Paris, read “they moderate by secure equity”: corruptly. But one Vatican manuscript has: “the righteous, moderating by stern equity in judgments.”

> [Note: Col. 0344C] Royal manuscript: “these mingled”: erroneously. Subsequently the printed editions read “and upon the unrighteous,” not “and upon the unrighteous [as a destination].” On how usefully punishments are set before the eyes of the righteous, see Psalm II, §§36–37.

### 11. The Jews are destroyed in truth.

Then there is again a turning to the person of God, to whom the prayer had first been addressed: “Destroy them in thy truth.” Truth refutes falsehood, and falsehood is destroyed by truth. We have shown that the entire preceding prayer is that of the man in whom the Son of God was born; and now he also prays to God the Father that he may destroy his enemies in truth.

And there is no doubt what the truth is: namely, he himself who said, “I am the life, the way, and the truth” (John 14:6). Thus enemies are destroyed in truth when, having procured Christ’s condemnation by false witnesses, they hear that he has risen from the dead and recognize that in God’s truth he has resumed his glory. For afterwards, as punishment, they were put to the cross, consumed and destroyed by famine and war: they who condemned the author of life to death, and did not contemplate in him the truth of God through the magnificence of his works. God’s truth, therefore, destroys them when, rising in order to resume the majesty of paternal glory, he has proved the truth of complete divinity in himself.

> [Note: Col. 0343C] In the preceding passage: “nor God in truth.”

> [Note: Col. 0344C] Vatican and Micy manuscripts: “God’s truth in him.”

> [Note: Col. 0344C] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “the complete [truth].”

### 12. Hilary’s view of Christ’s Passion.

As for the fact that the only-begotten Son of God was led to the cross and condemned to death—he who is eternal by that birth which he has naturally from the eternal Father—we frequently, indeed always, proclaim that he was subjected to the Passion not from necessity of nature but from the mystery of human salvation, and that he chose rather to submit himself to the Passion than was compelled to do so.

Although that Passion did not belong to his condition and kind, because no force of injurious disturbance could affect the unchangeable nature of God, nevertheless it was voluntarily undertaken. It would indeed satisfy the penal obligation, yet would not wound the sufferer by the sensation of penalty—not because the Passion itself, given its character as Passion, lacked a nature capable of causing injury, but because the nature of divinity does not feel pain. God, therefore, suffered, because he voluntarily submitted himself to the Passion; but though he assumed the natural forces of sufferings coming upon him—which must inflict pain upon sufferers—he nevertheless did not fall away from the power of his nature so as to feel pain.

> [Note: Col. 0344D] The printed editions read, “is natural and eternal”: confusedly. The manuscript reading is clearer.

> [Note: Col. 0344D] Thus the Royal codex. In other copies, “is to be understood as having been subjected, and as having willed,” is a gloss. More conveniently, after “as for the fact,” supply “it concerns”: namely, “As for the fact that the only-begotten Son of God was led to the cross,” etc., “we frequently, indeed always, proclaim that he, who is eternal by the birth which…” was subjected not from necessity of nature, etc.

> [Note: Col. 0344C] What is voluntarily undertaken is undertaken voluntarily.

> [Note: Col. 0344D] The Royal codex has “nature.” Then the printed editions, except Paris, read “of incongruous [sufferings].” Subsequently even Paris reads “it is necessary that these powers be inflicted.” We delete *these*, on the authority of the Royal manuscript. This is the original order of the words by which Hilary signals that his doctrine of Christ’s Passion must be drawn from the foregoing as well as the following: “assuming the natural forces of sufferings coming upon him, by which pain must be inflicted upon sufferers when a nature capable of pain is joined to that which receives the Passion; he himself, however, according to divinity, though joined to flesh upon which Passion falls, did not fall away from the power of his nature so as to feel pain.” The reason is given immediately above: not because that Passion lacked, in accordance with its character, a capacity for harming, but because divinity’s nature does not feel pain. Here might be cited the comparisons in Book X *On the Trinity*, §23, concerning a dart thrown into water, fire, or air: though it is naturally adapted to prick, pierce, and wound when driven into a nature susceptible of such effects, it accomplishes none of these in water, fire, or air—natures into which an impact may indeed fall, but not a wound, and so forth.

### 13. The superiority of Christ’s offering over the offerings of the Law.

For it follows:

> **Verse 8.** “I will sacrifice unto thee willingly.”

The sacrifices of the Law, consisting in holocausts and offerings of goats and bulls, do not contain a profession of willingness, because a sentence of curse was decreed against those who violate the Law. For whoever neglected sacrifice made himself liable to the curse (Deut. 27:26). Thus what was done had to be done, because the addition of the curse did not permit neglect of sacrifice.

Our Lord Jesus Christ freed us from this curse, as the Apostle says: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Gal. 3:13), because it is written: “Cursed is every one that hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23). Therefore he offered himself to the death of those under the curse, in order to dissolve the curse of the Law, voluntarily offering himself as a victim to God the Father; so that through a voluntary victim the curse added on account of the guilt of a compulsory and omitted sacrifice might be dissolved.

Elsewhere in the Psalms he mentions this sacrifice: “Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but thou hast prepared a body for me” (Ps. 39:7), offering to God the Father, who rejected the sacrifices of the Law, the pleasing victim of his assumed body. Of this offering the blessed Apostle speaks thus: “For this he did once, when he offered up himself” as a sacrifice to God (Heb. 7:27), intending to redeem the whole salvation of humankind by the offering of this holy and perfect victim.

> [Note: Col. 0345C] “Freed.”

> [Note: Col. 0345D] The printed editions read “hung.” From the Royal codex, which reads “hangs,” we restore “hangs,” in accordance with the sacred text.

### 14. Christ gives thanks for the petitions he has obtained.

Because all these things were thus accomplished, he gives praise to God the Father: “I will confess thy Name, O Lord, for it is good,”

> **Verse 9.** “For thou hast delivered me out of all trouble.”

He gives to each proposition its proper resolution. For at the beginning he had said, “Save me in thy Name.” After the fulfilment of his prayers, an appropriate declaration of thanksgiving was required: that he should confess the Name in which he had prayed that he might be saved. And because he had sought help against strangers rising against him, he declares that he has obtained that very thing; and thereby he commemorates his exultation of joy: “For thou hast delivered me out of all trouble.”

Further, because, while the mighty sought his soul, they did not set God before their eyes, he splendidly teaches the eternity of his unchangeable divinity in the words: “And mine eye has looked upon my enemies.” For the only-begotten Son of God was not cut off by death. To complete human nature, he submitted himself even to death—that is, to the separation, as it were, of soul and body—and entered the infernal regions—something that seems due to man. Yet he remains, rising again, and looks down upon his enemies with immortal eye, glorified into God and, from Son of Man, into Son of God, inasmuch as he had even begun to be Son of Man, now reborn through the glory of the Resurrection.

He looks down upon his enemies, to whom he had said: “Destroy this temple, and after three days I will rebuild it” (John 2:19). Therefore, after this temple of his body had been built, from on high he sees those who had sought his soul; and, himself exalted above the law of human death, he looks down upon the authors of his death: suffering death, yet unable to die—God, man, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed unto ages of ages. Amen.

I of the *Museo Italico*. With great agreement the holy Fathers maintain it from the Scriptures, so that Augustine, *Epistle* 164, §9, and 187, §5, rightly counts it among the truths of faith established by the strongest authority. These are Augustine’s own words in *Epistle* 164, §9: “Scripture openly declares that according to his soul he was among the lower regions, both foretold through prophecy and sufficiently expounded by apostolic interpretation.” These incidental remarks are directed against those who, contrary to the great consensus of the ancients, confuse Christ’s descent into the lower regions with his burial and maintain that they are the same thing.

## Psalm LIV

[Col. 0346C]

**For the end; in hymns, an understanding of David.**

Give ear, O God, to my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me, and hear me. I am troubled in my exercise, and disturbed by the voice of the enemy and by the oppression of the sinner; for they have turned iniquities against me, and in anger they were troublesome to me. My heart has been disturbed within me, and fear of death has fallen upon me. Fear and trembling have come upon me, and darkness has covered me. And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove’s? I will fly away and rest. Behold, I have fled far away, and remained in solitude. **DIAPSALMA.**

I awaited him who saved me from faintness of spirit and tempest. Overwhelm them, O Lord, and divide their tongues, for I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city. Day and night iniquity will surround it upon its walls, and toil and injustice are in its midst; usury and deceit have not departed from its streets. For if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would surely have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me enjoyed sweet foods: in the house of God we walked in concord.

Let death come upon them; let them descend alive into hell, for wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst. But I cried out to God, and the Lord heard me. Evening, morning, and noon I will recount and declare, and he will hear my voice. He will deliver my soul in peace from those who draw near me, for they were with me among many. God will hear me and humble them—he who is before the ages. **DIAPSALMA.**

For there is no change in them, and they have not feared God. He stretched out his hand in repaying. They have defiled his covenant; they were divided by the anger of his countenance, and his heart drew near. They made his words softer than oil, yet they are darts. Cast your thought upon God, and he will nourish you; he will never allow the righteous to be shaken. But you, O God, will bring them down into the pit of destruction. Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days; but I will hope in you.

## Treatise on the Psalm

### 1. This Psalm concerns Christ.

The superscription of this Psalm contains no history, only this:

> **Verse 1.** “For the end; in hymns, an understanding.”

Some of our translators called hymns *carmina* (“songs”); most, however, used “hymns” from the Greek term itself. There is no difference in the name, provided that the one thing signified either by “hymns” or “songs” is understood. Therefore this must be understood concerning the Psalm: what is contained in its hymn or song must be understood with reference to the End—namely, with all our understanding referred to our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the Apostle teaches to be the end of the Law (Rom. 10:4).

### 2. Christ is at once God and man.

We have often warned that in understanding the Psalms our thought must be guided by this principle: we must remember that he of whom and through whom all prophecy exists was born, from the Son of God, as Son of Man; and that the divine nature, remaining before all ages, was born into human nature through the Virgin’s childbirth. Thus the addition of the later nature brought no defect to the earlier nature; nor did he who had also begun to be man cease to be what he had remained before becoming man—namely, God.

Therefore, while assuming the frailty of our flesh and remaining both his own and ours, he acts, prays, professes, and awaits all those things which are ours in such a way that among them he also mingles those things which are his own. At times he speaks in the person of man, because he was man, was born, suffered, and died; but at other times all his speech belongs to him according to God, because, being man from God, he had become Son of Man from the Son of God. In his words he did not forget the confidence of that nature which, even in assuming manhood, he did not lack. Thus, speaking from us and from our weakness according to the customary usage and practice of human speech, he nevertheless speaks from himself and from his own power things proper and worthy of God—as may be recognized in the present Psalm, which begins thus.

> [Note: Col. 0348D] The Royal codex, here omitting the particle “and,” shortly afterwards has “begotten,” not “begotten [feminine]”: wrongly.

> [Note: Col. 0347D] “Who had also already become man.”

> [Note: Col. 0348D] The printed editions read “who had already become man.” More fittingly, the Royal manuscript reads “who had also become man.”

> [Note: Col. 0348D] Royal manuscript: “which.”

### 3. Verses 2–8

> “Give ear, O God, to my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me, and hear me. I am troubled in my exercise, and disturbed by the voice of the enemy and by the oppression of the sinner; for they have turned iniquity against me, and in anger they were troublesome to me. My heart has been troubled within me, and fear of death has fallen upon me. Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me. And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove’s? I will fly away and rest. Behold, I have fled far away and remained in solitude.”

Although at the beginning of the Psalm he employs a voice of humility when he says, “Give ear, O God, to my prayer,” he is nevertheless understood to have said this not without a certain consciousness of higher confidence. For it belongs to no ordinary innocence to ask that God give ear to one’s prayer. God’s ears are always open to human prayer that is readily offered; for he who grants to humankind the capacity of hearing cannot himself be outside the nature of hearing (Ps. 93:9), and he who everywhere works in us this sense of hearing cannot fail everywhere to possess in himself what he bestows.

God, therefore, always and everywhere hears; but it is not the merit of all persons that what he hears he also gives ear to: the voice of the one praying reaches his hearing, but only the innocence of prayer earns the condescension by which what is heard is received attentively.

> [Note: Col. 0348D] “A consciousness of higher confidence.”

> [Note: Col. 0349D] Royal manuscript: “by merits”; one might not object if the preposition “in” were supplied.

### 4. Three kinds of prayer.

At the beginning, moreover, a threefold petition of prayer is presented. First, that the prayer may be received attentively; next, that the supplication may not be despised; third, that he may attend to him and hear him. The nature of each kind must be distinct: giving ear is not the same as not despising; and, again, attending and hearing differ from both.

Since we have shown what may be understood by a prayer being received attentively, we must consider what this means: “Do not despise my supplication.” Prayers are despised when they are frivolous, lacking trust, useless, anxious with worldly cares, entangled in the desires of bodily things, and barren of the fruits of good works. Such prayers are therefore contemptible and unworthy of God’s condescension. Of them he says through the prophet Isaiah: “And when ye spread forth your hands unto me, I will turn away mine eyes from you” (Isa. 1:15). He immediately adds the reason why prayer is to be despised: “Your hands are full of blood” (ibid.). Therefore, wherever the working of iniquity is found, there the petitioner’s prayer is despised.

But God attends to the one who hopes when the faith of silent hope is held fast in the devotion of a godly conscience. We have a most perfect example of each property. The Lord gave ear to the words of the Canaanite woman who often cried out (Matt. 15:28); he despised the prayer of that young man who sought a division of an inheritance from the giver of eternity (Luke 12:13–14); but he attended to the woman who, in the silence of faith, sought healing for herself even from the fringe of his garment (Luke 8:44).

> [Note: Col. 0349D] The same manuscript reads: “In the prayer at the beginning, a threefold prayer is set forth.”

5. Christ’s ordeal in this world.—Having thus distinguished the kinds of his whole prayer, he now set forth the very reason for his supplication: because in his ordeal he was troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner. An ordeal is never undertaken except for useful and salutary ends; and since the impious cannot endure these even in a holy man, they strive to afflict him with every injury and to wear him down even to the fear of death. But this ordeal in the Lord Jesus Christ is the working of our salvation, advanced through the exercise of diverse healings and then of his Passion itself. Exercising himself also in this world through fellowship with our weakness—an exercise prefigured by Isaac’s going out into the field when Rebecca was brought riding on a camel (Gen. 24:63): Christ, as bridegroom of the Gentiles, exercising himself in this world, meets her—he is troubled also by the enemy’s voice, when he is called a Samaritan and said to have a demon (John 8:48), and when, because he does not rescue himself from the cross, he is denied to be salvation for others. Those who direct against him the iniquity of false witness and the sentence of death are also troublesome to him in their wrath, raging with scourges, blows of the fist, and slaps.

[Col. 0350B] 6. Patience; weakness without loss of divinity.—Yet amid these things, though he had the power [Note: [Col. 0349D] Erasmus here charges a lapse of memory, because, he says, Matthew chapter 22 has only twelve legions. Yet the reading here is one and consistent in the sounder manuscripts: in the preceding Psalm, no. 1; in Book X of *On the Trinity*, no. 41; indeed also in Matthew, as Erasmus himself admits he found in an ancient codex. Wherever, therefore, another reading occurs, this variation must be attributed not to Hilary but to copyists or pedants.] to summon twelve hundred thousand legions of heaven, he is not moved to anger nor provoked to vengeance. For it follows: “My heart is troubled within me.” He resolved to suffer all things in himself, provided only that he might accomplish the mysteries of human salvation.
