Yet it is exceedingly difficult for human weakness to restrain within itself the disturbances and agitations of the mind, so that, even by a silent motion, some indication of anxiety or indignation does not break forth as far as an alteration of the countenance itself.

But although our weakness was assumed by the only-begotten God, the nature of his divinity was not [Note: [Col. 0349C] “Forgotten.”] [Note: [Col. 0349D] The printed texts read “the forgotten nature”; they are corrected from the manuscripts. Then Erasmus, the Leiden and Paris editions read, “so that he did not perform these things”; this is better, except that *not* is absent in the Badian edition and the manuscripts, from which Regius has the particle erased, after a dot had been placed beneath it in the ancient manner. The sense is the same.] abolished, so that, while the dignity of his majesty remained unharmed, he underwent all these weak things: he endured all that belongs to our death and fear in such a way that these things rather befell him than inhered in him, [Note: [Col. 0349D] In the Royal codex, after these words, “while it is more our weakness than it is natural in God,” the following has been erased for the reason just stated and substituted above it: “while it belongs more to our weakness, which he suffers in the assumed man, than to the divine nature, which is impassible.” There you have Hilary’s thought more fully expressed than his words. It must be carefully retained that, for Hilary, only that is natural to Christ which belongs to his divine nature; what belongs to the human nature is regarded as foreign to him, as ours and not his own. Thus what we would say, “remaining God and man,” he says above, no. 2, “remaining his own and ours.” Accordingly, here he confesses that Christ, insofar as he is ours and man, endured fear, pain, death, and other human weaknesses; but he denies that he experienced them insofar as he is his own and God.] while it is more our weakness than natural in God. Finally, the following words establish this same point when he says: “And the fear of death fell upon me. Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness [Note: [Col. 0350C] “Wrapped me about with darkness.”] wrapped me about.” All these things that belong to our necessity indeed rushed upon him; yet they were assumed by him through the power of his own nature, since, though able not to die, he did not refuse even [Note: [Col. 0350D] Thus the Vatican codex. Others read: “when fear of death was impending upon him.”] the fear of death impending upon him.

7. He does not take wings from elsewhere.—Although these same things had fallen upon him as upon a man, to rule over his weakness, he nevertheless added, to teach that he was not subject to the things that threatened him: “And I said, Who will give me wings like a dove’s? And I shall fly and rest.” [Note: [Col. 0351C] The printed texts read “for he is weak”: an error. Shortly afterward Erasmus, the Leiden and Paris editions read, “wings must be taken from elsewhere,” with *not* erased: an error arising from an error. The manuscripts correct both.] He is not weak, for he does not need to obtain wings from elsewhere in order to fly away from the darkness covering him and from the fear of death. For when he says, “Who will give me?” this is not the language of one asking another, but of one not hoping from elsewhere. He hastens to fly like a dove—that is, to return to his spiritual nature. For the Spirit, in the form of a dove, rested on him in flight (Matt. 3:16), having at last found a dwelling in that man who then rose from the waters of Jordan.

And this is indeed the reason for the prayer: burdened by bodily weakness, he had assumed that mortality which is ours, so that, having become flesh, he might fly into spirit. [Note: [Col. 0351D] The Royal codex reads “in spirit.” The others more correctly read “into spirit,” as Hilary said shortly before, “to return to spiritual nature.” Elsewhere he calls this becoming God even according to the man, being begotten into the perfect Son of God, at times returning to the natural unity of the Father which he had lost according to the man, and more often reassuming with God that glory which he had with him before the world was.] In another Psalm he speaks thus of these his wings: “If I take up my wings before dawn and dwell in the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me” (Ps. 138:9). Therefore, he will take his own wings, [Note: [Col. 0351D] Erasmus and the Leiden edition read “so that it may not be understood”; the first Paris edition properly corrected this, but it was wrongly restored in the last edition despite the manuscripts. Next, the Royal manuscript reads *eas et his*. And then only the Paris edition reads *evacuatis*. From these texts retain *evacuatus*: namely, emptied of that glory by which Christ was raised above men and angels; emptying himself of it and being made a little lower than angels, he descended even to men.] so that it may be understood that, having emptied himself of them, he assumes them again.

8. The wilderness to which he withdraws for rest.—But, having taken wings so as to rest in flight, he shows where he is to rest, saying: “Behold, I fled far away and remained [Note: [Col. 0352C] The Royal manuscript reads “in solitude”; Hilary approves this reading as well as the other immediately afterward.] in the wilderness.” Darkness fell upon the light, but the darkness did not overcome it. For he fled far away, since he could not be overcome even [Note: [Col. 0351C] “By those containing.”] [Note: [Col. 0352D] The printed texts read “by the Gentiles.” One Vatican manuscript reads “by those containing”; another, together with the Royal manuscript, “by those touching.” More correctly, a third Vatican manuscript and the Micy codex read “by the covering [darknesses]”; that is, by the darknesses of which no. 7 had already spoken: “He is not weak, who does not need wings taken from elsewhere in order to fly from the darkness covering him,” etc.] by the darknesses that covered him. Therefore he also flees those who persecuted him; made far from them, he dwells in the wilderness.

What this wilderness is, or what this solitude is—for Greek expresses both by the same word—another prophet likewise declares: “Let the thirsty wilderness rejoice; let the wilderness exult and flower like a lily; let the wildernesses of Jordan flower and exult. Strengthen feeble hands and weakened knees; comfort the faint-hearted; take courage in understanding and do not fear. Behold, our God [Note: [Col. 0352D] *Our* is absent from the Royal manuscript here and below in Psalm 65, no. 11.] will render judgment; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; the tongue of the dumb shall be instructed. Then the lame shall leap like a stag” (Isa. 35:1 ff.). He had indeed come to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; but, driven away by them, he makes these wildernesses glad. For in these he remains, [Note: [Col. 0352D] The printed texts read “and remained.” The manuscripts more correctly read “and remains.” Hilary likes this sort of repetition whenever he wishes an adjunct of the matter to be considered more attentively.] and remains after he has rested in flight. For this is God’s rest, which is denied to the impious when it is said: “If they shall enter into my rest” (Ps. 94:11). Having resumed his spiritual glory, the only-begotten God rests among these bodies which were formerly wildernesses, as in a temple worthy of himself, because “the children of the desolate are more numerous than of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1).

9. Those who desire the letter alone in the Psalms.—I am not unaware that many, considering only the sound and letter of the words, judge that scarcely anything in almost all the Psalms is [Note: [Col. 0352C] “Anything fitting to the person.”] [Note: [Col. 0352D] In the Micy and Vatican manuscripts, after *fitting*, “anything” is added.] fitting to the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, and suppose that the whole is occupied with the Prophet’s complaints. But we do not raise a dispute. We do not destroy but build up, adding understanding of obscure matters rather than subtracting from simple ones. For whatever David either suffered or lamented was also fulfilled in the sufferings of him who became the flesh of us all. And, I think, what follows will confirm the course of our interpretation.

10. Christ awaits salvation.—Yet the inserted *diapsalma* changes the sense. For all the speech is again directed against those concerning whom the complaint is made, though the honor of him to whom he is accustomed to refer everything is set first. It follows: “I awaited him who would save me from faintheartedness and storm.” This expectation of his is not new; for in that Psalm which is undoubtedly spoken in his person, he prayed thus: [Note: [Col. 0352D] Thus in the Royal manuscript, as also below in its place. In the printed texts: “Save me.”] “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even to my soul. I am sunk in deep mire, and there is no standing-place. I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68:2–3). Therefore from this storm and this faintheartedness—for he had been humbled [Note: [Col. 0352D] The Royal codex reads “humbled and exposed to death.”] unto the death of the cross—he awaits salvation from him to whom he prayed, saying: “Father, glorify me with yourself by the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5).

11. How the Jews are now sunk and divided in tongues.—But while awaiting his own salvation, he now awaits more than the hope of salvation. It follows: “Cast them down, O Lord, and divide their tongues.” Latin, as often happens, has not expressed the precise force of either the Hebrew or the Greek word. For what is rendered “cast down” is expressed among them as καταπόντισον (*katapontison*, “sink in the depths”); by this expression the prayer is not that they be cast down, but that they be submerged in the deep. He therefore prays that they be submerged and that their tongues be divided. We know that one of these occurred under Noah (Gen. 7:4), the other after the building of the tower (Gen. 11:8): the deep consumed the former when they were submerged by the flood, while the division of tongues separated the latter for the cause of perpetual mutual conflict, so that, as they neither understood nor trusted one another, they might not maintain the conspiracy undertaken against God. Thus no dissimilar punishment is now demanded against these: namely, that, according to the law of the nations, [Note: [Col. 0353D] The printed texts read “after the manner of the nations,” against the manuscripts. One manuscript reads “by the savagery of nations”; the others, “by the law of nations.”] which we have recalled are signified in the waters, they should be consumed and, divided among all the languages with which they now dwell and which they speak, lose the dignity of their life and kingdom.

[Col. 0353B] 12. But so that we might know that these things would follow because of the vices of the city and its contradiction of his commandments, he added: “For I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city. Day and night iniquity shall surround her [Note: [Col. 0353D] The Royal manuscript reads, “upon her walls are iniquity and sorrow, and they shall not fail.”] upon her walls, and toil in her midst; and usury and deceit have not failed from her streets.” Therefore, because of these vices and crimes, the punishment of future captivity and dispersion is demanded; but chief among the crimes are iniquity and contradiction. For rejecting him whom the Law and Prophets had announced, they spurned him with impious contradiction. This contradiction, surrounding the walls of that city by night and day, passed over them even on the night of his Passion, when, as he confessed that he would be seen in the assembly and at the right hand of Power, they contradicted him with the charge of blasphemy, even tearing their garments (Matt. 26:64–65).

By “walls,” we recall, the protection of salvation is signified. Thus, when the building and fortification of the new Jerusalem—that is, the construction and guardianship of the heavenly Church—is desired, it is written: “Do good, O Lord, in your good pleasure to Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Ps. 50:20). At that time, then, spiritual guardianship was present in that people, and the administration of the Law, ordained through angels, provided protection. But when, after the Mediator of the Law himself had been rejected, surrounding iniquity passed over these walls and this guardianship, sin began to be greater than the fortification itself, so that iniquity overcame the will of the guardianship, [Note: [Col. 0353D] The printed texts read “of the guardian.” We prefer “of the guardianship” with the manuscripts. For above, not a guardian but a guardianship is mentioned; and since this is spiritual, it is not without will, indeed without good will—whose goodness, however, the malice of the Jews is here proclaimed to overcome.] with usury and deceit and the abundance of the other things forbidden in the Law.

[Col. 0353D] 13. Christ complains not of the Passion but of the betrayer; why not of the Passion.—Displaying the enormity of this great iniquity, he added: “For if my enemy had reproached me, I would certainly have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would certainly have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food, we entered the house of God in concord.” The complaint is not about the Passion, but about the apostle who betrayed him. For, when by the death of the cross which he undertook he bestowed salvation on the human race, he cannot seem to find fault with this mystery of great mercy. Certainly, if the persecutor had been an enemy, there would have been no cause of complaint, since in him was accomplished what he himself had willed to suffer for our salvation.

And if one hating him had spoken great things against him, he would have been hidden from him, because God would not have been known by that man; and therefore the crime of one who did not know would have been less. For the Gentiles had not learned from a Law that foretold to them that the Word would be made flesh—though this was adapted, even in the events themselves, to foreshadow future truth for those under the Law: [Note: [Col. 0354D] The Micy manuscript reads “foreannounced.”] Abraham worshipped a man (Gen. 18:2), and Jacob saw God in a man (Gen. 32:30). The Gentiles would assuredly have borne these reproaches: that, being a man, he made himself God; that, having a demon, he deceived the people. For they would not have known that all these things were contained in the Law delivered to Israel.

Nevertheless, when one who is of one mind with him, his guide, and his acquaintance does these things: “of one mind,” because he was chosen [Note: [Col. 0354D] The Royal codex reads “to the apostleship.”] as an apostle; “guide,” because, while the Lord delayed, he himself was sent ahead to the towns to preach his coming, and was appointed by him a guide and prince of the coming kingdom; and “acquaintance,” because he had learned all his comings and goings, recognized in the Son of Man also the Son of God, shared in changing water into wine and in making barley sweet—or, perhaps, multiplying it—for food for the people, and had shared the same meal and continually entered God’s house with him: having been admitted to this fellowship of divine ministry, he furnished a greater cause of complaint against himself.

14. Punishment of the wicked.—But although these things were spoken particularly about that man’s impiety, the decree of punishment is extended to many: “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell, for wickedness is in their dwellings [Note: [Col. 0354D] The printed texts present what follows in a very disordered and confused manner. We supply the sounder reading from the manuscripts.] and in their midst”—death thus coming upon them, so that they descend alive into hell to experience punishment, since works of wickedness surround them wholly, both within and without, in their dwellings and in their midst.

[Col. 0354D] 15. But he showed that, while they did and meditated these things, the one in whom his hope and prayer were placed was he of whom he said: “I cried to God, and the Lord heard me.” Verses 17–20: “At evening and morning and noon I shall declare [Col. 0355A] and proclaim, and he will hear my voice. He will deliver my soul in peace from those who draw near to me, because they were among many with me. God will hear me and humble them—he who is before the ages.” The Lord immediately hears a faithful cry; and he will declare, at evening, morning, and noon, this rejoicing at his cry having been heard, indicating the whole day by the divisions through which the day is contained.

This order of times has been arranged only by prophetic knowledge, so that he declares at evening, morning, and noon, [Note: [Col. 0355D] In the printed texts *and* is added here; then the reason Hilary gives for the Prophet’s beginning the day from evening cannot be perceived.] because according to the Law and the observance of the Law, the day begins from evening (Lev. 23:32), and is counted as such even to noon, since not the return of light in the morning but the onset of night in the evening completes the beginning of the day. He therefore declares and proclaims what the Psalm contains: that God hears his voice and delivers his soul in peace—for “he made peace in heaven and on earth” (Col. 1:20)—and delivers him from those drawing near to him. For the preceding complaint concerned those close to him, when the man of one mind with him, his guide and acquaintance, did these things, although he too had been chosen as an apostle with the other apostles.

God, therefore, who is before the ages—that is, through whom all things exist, [Note: [Col. 0355D] The Royal manuscript reads “who,” not “because.”] because he is before all things—will hear him and humble them, when they are made unworthy of the glory of eternal resurrection.

16. The Jews’ punishment for impenitence.—For, after the *diapsalma*, he cuts off every hope from them because of their impenitent profession of impiety, saying: “For there is no change in them, and they did not fear God.” All will rise again according to the Apostle, but not all will be changed (1 Cor. 15:51), because they did not fear God. For it would have been right, [Note: [Col. 0355D] The printed texts read: “They might have been ignorant of God in the man, if nevertheless they had believed that God rose from the dead.” The Royal manuscript does not differ, except that it lacks *if*. The text is corrected from the Vatican and Micy manuscripts.] though ignorant of God in the man, nevertheless to believe that God rose from the dead; repentance and forgiveness still lay open to them even after the expiation of the Passion. [Note: [Col. 0355D] One Vatican manuscript reads “the forgiveness of repentance.”] For not only did they fail to fear God; but when he stretched forth his hand to repay them—that is, offered aid—they defiled his covenant, rejecting him who was foretold for salvation in the covenant of the Law.

It follows, verses 21–22: “He stretched out his hand in repaying. They defiled his covenant; they were divided from the anger of his countenance.” And for this reason change was not left to them: because he died once for sin and, rising again, bestowed change only on those who both died with him and will rise with him through faith. But those others he divided from the anger of his countenance when their city was destroyed, assigning their portion with the unbelievers; he either scattered them among all peoples or separated them from the saints.

17. Judas’ flattering speech.—Then, from the general complaint, the discourse returned to the signification of the man who had been his guide, companion, and acquaintance: “And his heart drew near. His words were softened beyond oil, and they are darts.” Mingled with the apostles and administering the care of the poor—undertaking, that is, the great work [Note: [Col. 0355D] The Royal codex reads “of ministry.” One Vatican manuscript reads *sancti* (“holy”) for *scilicet* (“that is”). Both were written alike in ancient books.] of ministry—he drew near with his heart, for he had rejoiced that his soul was delivered from those drawing near to him; but he drew near not in the ministry of faith, but toward the wrath of God and the defilement of his covenant.

Moreover, this flatterer, deceiving others with speech softened beyond oil by professing concern for the poor, complained even when the alabaster vessel of precious ointment had been poured out, as though it ought rather [Note: [Col. 0355D] “To be sold.”] [Note: [Col. 0356D] The Royal manuscript reads “to be sold.”] to have been sold for the expense of the poor (Matt. 26:9). But he sought an occasion for theft from the collection of money. Perhaps the Prophet avoids this kind of flattering [Note: [Col. 0356D] The Micy codex reads “the flattering oil of theft”: wrongly.] oil in another Psalm when he says: “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5), because under the appearance of a good work it sets the weapons of malice in motion. There are also darts in words, just as teeth are a shield and arrows, and the tongue is a sharp sword (Ps. 56:5). He therefore detests these darts of speech, which are more harmful beneath flattery and adulation.

18. What we ought to care for.—But he remains undaunted amid the enemy’s darts and shows us a secure and trustworthy harbor. [Note: [Col. 0355D] We have added “trustworthy” on the authority of our codex; the word is missing in the printed texts.] [Note: [Col. 0356D] The Tours manuscript reads “safe and trustworthy.”] It follows, verse 23: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he will nourish you; he will not allow the righteous to be shaken forever.” The Lord also removed from us in the Gospels the necessity of anxiety, saying: “Do not be anxious [Col. 0356C] about tomorrow, for sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34). “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, [Note: [Col. 0356D] *His* is absent from the Royal manuscript. Below also we have “and righteousness is to be placed,” without *his*; the Micy manuscript has “and his righteousness is to be placed.”] and all things will be given to you” (ibid. 33): that is, all care is to be placed in attaining God’s kingdom and righteousness.

Therefore care must be cast upon him; for he himself will nourish us, according to the words: “He nourished me beside the water of refreshment” (Ps. 22:2). And in nourishing us, he will not leave us amid the waves of this world, just as Jacob, nourished by him, escaped every storm of hatred and harsh servitude, saying: “God who nourished me from my youth” (Gen. 48:15). For he is the author of life; he is the giver of food—not only earthly food, but spiritual food also.

19. The well of life and the well of death.—But after the one nourished beside the water of refreshment and delivered from the waves of the storm, fitting punishment follows the impious, when he says: “But you, O God, shall bring them down into the pit of destruction. Men of blood and deceit [Note: [Col. 0356D] The Royal codex reads “shall not halve.”] shall not halve their days; [Col. 0357A] but I will hope in you, O Lord.” There is indeed a well of living water; but there is also a pit of destruction, according to the words: “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor let the deep [Note: [Col. 0357D] “Swallow.”] swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16). Therefore, while the righteous is not left [Note: [Col. 0357D] The reading was “in shaking.”] to be shaken, they will be brought down into the pit of destruction, whose mouth could not remain closed over the only-begotten God rising from hell. [Note: [Col. 0357D] Thus from the manuscripts. The printed texts read “rising.” Then the Royal manuscript reads “and from hell.”]

Moreover, after the Lord’s Passion, the victory of war immediately consumed them with the destruction of their city: every age indiscriminately was slain to satisfy the conquerors, their youth cut down without reaching half their days. But full days are reserved for saints and believers, according to the words: “And full days shall be found [Note: [Col. 0357D] We have added the preposition *in* from the Verona codex, as it stands in Greek and the Vulgate.] in those whose hope is always in the Lord,” who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

127 [Note: [Col. 0358D] Our book does not contain the treatise on this and the following Psalm.]

## PSALM 55

[Col. 0357B]

For the end; for the people that has been made far from the holy ones; an inscription of the title by David, when the foreigners seized him in Gath.

Have mercy on me, O Lord, for man has trampled me down; fighting all day, he has afflicted me; my enemies have trampled me down all day. From the height of the day [Note: [Col. 0357D] Hilary: “of days.”] I shall not fear, for many who fought against me feared [Note: [Col. 0357D] Hilary: “because many who fight against me will fear.”]; but I will hope in you. In the Lord I shall praise my words all day; in God I shall hope; I shall not fear what flesh may do to me. All day they cursed my words; all their counsels against me are for evil. They will dwell and hide themselves; they will watch my heel. As they awaited my soul, you will save them for nothing; in anger you will crush the peoples [Note: [Col. 0357D] Hilary: “you will bring down.”]. O God, I have declared my life to you; you have set my tears in your sight, according to your promise. Let my enemies turn back on whatever day I call upon you. Behold, I have known that you are my God. In the Lord I shall praise the word [Note: [Col. 0357D] Hilary adds: “and in God I shall praise the word.”]; in the Lord I shall hope; I shall not fear what man may do to me. In me, O God, are your vows, which I shall render to you as praises [Note: [Col. 0357D] Hilary: “vows which I shall render as praise.”]; for you have delivered my soul from death and my feet from slipping, that I may please God in the light of the living.

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. David’s suffering: a prophecy of Christ’s sufferings.—The superscription of this Psalm contains many things which, beyond the account of events, intimate the meaning of another interpretation: verse 1 calls it “for the people made far [Col. 0357D] from the holy ones”; it bears an inscription of the title; and finally the beginning itself is marked “for the end.” If the present discourse sang only the complaint that David, while fleeing the foreigners, was seized at Gath, it would direct its whole movement merely to the rebuke of that iniquity. But since these things have been set before the statement of the event in order to instruct and direct the understanding of readers, we undoubtedly understand that, through the effects of the events enacted in David, there is impressed upon us, according to the spirit of prophecy, knowledge of those realities signified under these headings. Thus, what David suffered was a prefiguration of the sufferings of our Lord Jesus Christ; and the title-inscription signifies the eternity of him who conquered by dying, because an inscription of the title—called by Greek usage *stelographia* [Note: [Col. 0357D] The printed texts read *stelographia*; the Micy manuscript, *stylographia*; the others, *stelographiam*. From the following treatise, no. 2, this was inscribed on tombs.]—is granted for the glory of immortality especially to those who, living commendably, did not fear to die in war even for their country’s safety.

[Note: [Col. 0358D] The Leiden and Paris editions read “people,” against the Badian and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts. Yet we would prefer “for the people,” as above, following the Greek ὑπὲρ τοῦ λαοῦ, *hyper tou laou*.] By the people made far from the holy ones, Israel must be understood: made unworthy of the sanctification of the Gentiles and departing far from it. And “for the end” must be understood as proper to him who is the end of the Law; this will be recognized from the end of the Psalm itself, when the very words with which the Psalm concludes most clearly declare the completion of this interpretation.

2. This Psalm must be interpreted both of David and of Christ.—Therefore, from those things joined to the superscription beyond the narrative of events, we shall interpret the Psalm also in the person of the Lord, yet without departing from the complaints of the Prophet himself. Nor should he be thought not also to have groaned in the things which he suffered; for the events are joined precisely to those matters which intimate a spiritual sense, so that through the Prophet’s action the sense and language of prophecy might become known, since the Prophet prophesied not so much by the Spirit as by his sufferings. The discourse, therefore, will be tempered between David himself and the man Jesus Christ, so that—because he bore the weaknesses of all and frequently used both the voice and tears of our sins—the feeling and speech that belong to man may be without dishonor to God.

3. The ungodly against the godly: the assistance of demons.—Verses 2–3: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for man has trampled me down; fighting all day, he has afflicted me; my enemies have trampled me down all day.” We have learned that “day” frequently signifies an age; [Note: [Col. 0358D] See *Treatise on Psalm 51*, no. 5.] thus, where it is “the whole day,” the entire time of life is indicated. For neither David nor the Lord was vexed by persecution for a single day only. Yet he who asks God’s mercy and complains that he has been trampled down possesses the weapons of his security and strength by which he sustains not only earthly hatreds but also the wars of spiritual wickednesses—against which, rather than against flesh and blood, the Apostle teaches that our struggle is directed (Eph. 6:12). For they employ the services of the ungodly [Note: [Col. 0359D] The manuscripts read “against vexations.”] for the vexing and afflicting of the saints, penetrating their hearts and inciting them to every onset of a turbulent mind.

4. The terror of the wicked.—Therefore, not fearing the towering and self-exalting height of this world, the Prophet says, verse 4: “From the height of the days [Note: [Col. 0359D] Jerome, in his letter to Sunia and Fretela, maintains that this negative particle was added and should be erased.] I shall not fear, because many who fight against me will fear.” He knows the day of eternal judgment and knows the eternal fire prepared for eternal punishments. Therefore those who attempt to defeat him will fear more, because, while the saint does not fear, the terror of judgment presses more heavily upon them. In confidence of his security he adds, verse 5: “But I will hope in you. In the Lord I shall praise my words all day.” He places all his hopes in God and praises his words throughout his lifetime. Nor is it obscure what he praises in himself as speaker.

5. He who hopes in God does not fear flesh; or God assuming flesh.—The words which follow are worthy of a saint: “In God I shall hope; I shall not fear what flesh may do to me.” The terror of the world does not break this man, nor do the hatreds of those conspiring against him disturb him. For hope which is in God does not fear the terrors of human hatreds. We frequently understand “flesh” to signify human beings, who are contained in a body: [Note: [Col. 0359D] The Tours manuscript reads: “or when this is said concerning the ungodly.”] as where Scripture says of the ungodly, “My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3); or, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6); or the Apostle’s words, “Are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man?” (1 Cor. 3:3). He therefore remains undaunted beneath God’s mercy; and thus, hoping in him, he fears none of flesh’s attacks or persecutions.

But these words are plainly worthy also of the only-begotten God: though, emptying himself from the form of God, he assumed the form of a servant, that form did not take away God’s power and nature. For God, made flesh, remained God even in the assumption of flesh, exercising the power of his strength in fellowship with our body (see Book X of *On the Trinity*, no. 23). He was not weighed down by flesh so that he could not walk upon the waves; nor so that the power of divine authority could not go out even to the hem of his garment; nor so that he could not forgive sins, kindle in eyes blind from the womb the capacity for sight by his spittle, heal the wound of an ear cut off from its injury by restoring the ear, or penetrate solid walls as his body passed through them. Therefore the Prophet does not fear flesh while hoping in God; nor does God, under the assumption of flesh, fear it while accomplishing divine works.

6. In what follows likewise, the significance of the event itself is contained. For he says, VERS. 6–7: “All day long they execrated my words; all their counsels against me are for evil. They will dwell and hide themselves; they themselves will watch my heel.” For nowhere except by secret counsels were false testimonies and deceitful questions prepared against him: dwelling together and concealing their malicious schemes. Nor did they endure the rebuke of his words, by which he did not cease to reproach their impiety [Col. 0360B]; and they watched all his goings at his heel, while they agreed in a fraudulent conspiracy to supplant him. [Note: The printed editions read “of judgment” (*judicii*). With the Royal manuscript we prefer “of the Judge” (*judicis*), of whom it is immediately said: “Thou shalt save [them] unto nothingness.” Those who charge Hilary with the intolerable error concerning judgment, as though he had thought that the wicked were by no means to be judged, should consider this passage. For why does he immediately assert that every human being must stand before Christ’s tribunal, except that each may receive the Judge’s sentence?]

On this account this fitting sentence of the Judge encompassed them.

7. Salvation unto nothingness: Christ has merited this for them—the resurrection of the wicked.---For it follows, VERS. 8: “As they waited for my life, thou shalt save them unto nothingness; in wrath thou shalt bring down peoples.” This is a new manner of speech in the prophet: that God should save unto nothingness those who wait for his life. And since to be brought to nothing and to be saved are different things, the salvation now to be wrought upon them is unto nothingness. Is there then something that can be saved unto nothingness? Certainly: whatever, though granted resurrection, is not deemed worthy of transformation. For although all flesh has been redeemed in Christ so as to rise again [Col. 0360C], and it is necessary that all stand before his tribunal, yet glory and honor in rising are not promised indiscriminately to all. Therefore those to whom resurrection alone, and not transformation also, has been granted are saved unto nothingness. For in wrath those peoples will be brought down for whom the salvation of resurrection has been appointed so that they may feel punishment. The Apostle promises that we shall be delivered from this wrath, saying: “For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, having been justified in his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath” (Rom. V, 8–9).

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads “righteous,” not “justified.”]

Therefore he died for sinners unto the salvation of resurrection, but those sanctified in his blood he will save from wrath.

8. The hope of the righteous, and whence their merit comes.---Finally, after the peoples have been saved unto nothingness and brought down in wrath, this holy man declares the hope of his life, saying, VERS. 9: “O God, [Col. 0360D] I have declared my life to thee; thou hast set my tears in thy sight, as in thy promise.” He is worthy of God’s promise because of his steadfastness in preaching and the merit of not keeping silence. For his tears—those which either the prophet shed for himself, or the Lord for us—are in the sight of God [Col. 0361A], and their advocacy will be employed to obtain what God has promised.

[Note: The printed editions read “for himself” (*per se*); the manuscripts more rightly read “for himself” (*pro se*). Here the distinction is made between Christ and the prophet: the latter had reason to weep for himself, whereas the former had none. Relevant is the statement of the Roman clergy in Cyprian, Epistle 31: “Let the lapsed send tears as envoys for their sorrows; let groans drawn from the depths of the breast perform the office of advocacy, proving sorrow for the crime committed and shame.”]

131 9. The punishment of the wicked.---But when he is about to enter into the grace of the eternal promise, his enemies will be turned backward, in order to show where they will be brought down in wrath. For this follows, VERS. 10: “My enemies will be turned backward, on whatever day I call upon thee.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “into grace”; and shortly afterward, with the Royal manuscript, “about to go,” not “about to enter.” The Tours manuscript reads: “about to go into the grace of the eternal promise.” From the same manuscript we have next corrected a corrupt reading: “that in wrath,” etc.]

When he calls upon God, they will be turned back to the place from which they came, God’s wrath bringing them down, their bodies restored so that they may be punished.

[Note: Bad., Er., Lips., and the Royal manuscript read “Let my enemies be turned backward.”]

10. The Word is God.---But when they have returned after the resurrection to hell for eternal punishment, he performs the office of his rejoicing, saying, VERS. 11: “Behold, I have known that thou art my God, and in God I will praise the Word.” Therefore he praises this Word of his in God, because he has known that he is his God [Col. 0361B].

11. A voice worthy of the saints amid human persecutions.---Nor does he praise this alone, but also the fact that he hoped in him and did not fear what man might do to him. This indeed is a voice worthy of all saints: to maintain steadfast faith amid human persecutions, not to be moved by fear of earthly disturbance, and, with the most certain hope, not to fear that man can effect anything against the eternity of the soul. For after the intervention of this death, both our corruption and our weakness will be changed into immortal glory.

[Note: The Muron manuscript reads, “that nothing [can be done] against ….” If one reads it thus, something must be retained: “not to fear that something,” etc. But if the particle *quod* is joined with the preceding words, “with most certain hope,” *nihil* must be restored.]

Accordingly, he praises his words, by which he declares that, hoping in the Lord, he does not fear human violence: “In the Lord I will praise the word; in the Lord I will hope; I will not fear what man may do to me.” Thus he praises his word in the Lord because, hoping in him, he will not fear man [Col. 0361C].

12. Christ, master of his own resurrection. The same body will rise. He who is God in those raised.---But to teach that for this reason he fears nothing from man—because, if he had displayed any of his power in the body, the glory of resurrection would restore it again without injury to the body—he added, VERS. 12–13: “In me are, O God, the vows of praise which I shall render thee, because thou hast delivered my soul from death and my feet from falling, that I may be pleasing before God in the light of the living.”

[Note: Thus the Royal manuscript, agreeing with the Greek; the explanation that follows confirms it. The printed text reads: “Thy vows, which I shall render to thee as praises.”]

Those things for which he hopes are not outside himself; nor are the vows of praise which he will render to be acquired from without.

[Note: Printed editions: “which are to be rendered from without.”]

For he himself is master of his resurrection; he himself grants to this body, dead and left within the tomb [Col. 0361D], participation in his divine nature.

[Note: This seems to favor those who think that Hilary believed the divinity of the Word to have been separated from Christ’s dead flesh. But his words point elsewhere: he means only that the glory of resurrection was granted to that very body which had been left dead in the tomb—not to another body newly created—and that this body obtains anew the glory through participation and communion with the divine nature. His meaning, then, is simply this: to that same body which was dead, that same one who was dead grants glory.]

For the body is not acquired for all who are to rise from some external material, nor is a nature of foreign origin and external causes restored [Col. 0362A].

[Note: The Paris edition, from the Mic. manuscript, reads “is employed”; the other editions, with the Vatican manuscript, “is received.” From the corrupt reading of the Royal manuscript, *redibitur*, it is evident that *redhibetur* must be restored. The aforesaid Vatican manuscript supports this, since shortly before it reads *reciperet* (“would receive”) for *redhiberet* (“would restore”).]

Rather, that same body emerges into the advance of eternal brightness, and becomes new by transformation rather than creation. Therefore the vows which he will render are within himself: when the weakness of bodies is removed—that is, their falling and their tears; when incorruption devours corruption; when immortal power swallows up death; when God is all in all; when, in the light of the living, he himself will be pleasing to God in that same light of the living. For if, at the creation of the world, according to Wisdom’s declaration (Prov. VIII, 31), the Father rejoiced over the children of men, much more must he be understood to be pleasing to the Father in the reconciliation of the world [Col. 0362B]. For our Lord Jesus Christ is the true light of the world, enlightening every person coming into this world; he is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LVI

For the end; “Do not destroy”; of David, for the inscription of the title, when David fled from Saul’s presence into the cave.

“Have mercy upon me, O God, have mercy upon me, for my soul trusts in thee. And in the shadow of thy wings I will hope, until iniquity passes away. I will cry to God Most High, to God who has dealt kindly with me. He sent from heaven and delivered me; he gave to reproach those who trample me. God sent his mercy and his truth, and delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs; [Col. 0362C] I slept troubled. The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword. Be thou exalted above the heavens, O God, and thy glory above all the earth. They prepared snares for my feet, and bowed down my soul. They dug a pit before my face and fell into it. My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready: I will sing and make psalmody to thee. Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and cithara: I will arise at dawn. And I will confess thee among the peoples, O Lord; I will sing psalms to thee among the nations, because thy mercy has been magnified even unto the heavens, and thy truth even unto the clouds. Be thou exalted above the heavens, O God, and thy glory above all the earth.”

[Note: Hilary omits *me* (“me”), and here *diapsalma* is prefixed.]

[Note: “And” is omitted.]

[Note: Hilary: “psaltery and cithara.”]

133 [Note: Hilary: “I will make psalmody.”]

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. Connection of this psalm with the preceding one.---In the superscription of the following psalm, only this has been changed from the preceding one: where it was “concerning the people far removed from the holy ones, of enigmas,” it now has “Do not corrupt” or “Do not destroy.” The Greek expression τὸ μὴ διαφθείρης embraces both meanings in one phrase. For it was fitting that, since corruption was to abide upon those who departed far from the holy ones, the holy man should pray that he not be subjected to it. For in another psalm he expresses his joy that this corruption has been turned away from him, saying: “Nor wilt thou give thy Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10). Nor is it doubtful that, according to the confession of the Apostles, this psalm must be understood to speak in the person of the Lord.

[Note: That is, Psalm XCV, mentioned just before and understood by Peter, Acts II, 27, as spoken in the person of Christ. From this passage in Acts Augustine also demonstrates, *Epistle* 187, §5, that Christ’s descent of the soul into hell was both foretold in the Psalms and proclaimed by apostolic teaching.]

[Note: Lipsius divided this word into two as *aenigma tum*. The Paris editor then substituted *enotatum* in its place, against the testimony of the other books. It is rendered from the Greek αἰνίσσομαι or αἰνίττομαι, which, according to Budæus, sometimes means “I cause to be understood” or “I allude to something.” From it, *aenigma* is defined in Isidore’s glosses as “figure, type, or appearance.” Thus Prudentius, teaching that the form and features of the face will be restored at the resurrection, says in Hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, v. 133:

> Cover the body committed to thee;  
> Its Maker and Author will not forget  
> To reclaim his own gifts  
> And the enigmas of its proper countenance.

Therefore, just as in Psalm IX, §2, the title of psalms is called an index of the matters about which they are written, so it can also be called a face and likeness, and hence an enigma—from which comes *aenigmari*—by which the subject of the psalm may be recognized.]

2. Explanation of the title.---Accordingly David, awaiting the time of the Lord’s resurrection unto the glory of human flesh, now prays that he may not be corrupted and, by the prophet’s foreknowledge, rejoices that corruption has been turned away from him in the one in whom are the firstfruits of resurrection [Col. 0363B].

[Note: Lipsius here substituted “of prophecy” for “of the prophet,” and conversely below “of the prophet” for “of prophecy.”]

For this reason, VERS. 1 bears the inscription “For the end,” because both a life undertaken gloriously for the honor of eternity and a death beneficial to many brave men are inscribed upon tombs; and all these things must be referred to him who is either the end of the Law, or whom the end of the psalm itself indicates.

[Note: The Paris edition alone reads “tombs.”]

That he speaks these things while shut up in a cave refers to the time of prophecy, when he is understood to have written the psalm, prophesying by that very dwelling in the cave the humility of the Lord, who was to remain in the body.

[Note: The Paris edition, following Lipsius, reads “which was to remain”; the other editions, “for one who was to remain.” From the Tours manuscript the correct reading could be restored.]

Otherwise, it cannot seem plausible that someone who, through fear, was concealed within a cave should make a clamor, as the psalm testifies, with psaltery and cithara—that is, with the entire apparatus of musical art.

3. For whom God’s mercy is to be hoped; its benefit and duration.---He began thus, VERS. 2: “Have mercy upon me, O God, have mercy upon me, because my soul trusts in thee.” He asks for mercy because he trusts in God, teaching that God’s mercy is to be hoped for by those who believe. He then shows its force and effect: “And in the shadow of thy wings I will hope until iniquity passes away.” It belongs to the nature of birds to cover the weakness of their young with their wings, and to defend them from the violence and mischief of creatures flying over them. We especially observe this in hens, when they either shade or protect their brood gathered beneath their feathers [Col. 0364A].

[Note: Thus the Royal and Mic. manuscripts, except that the latter has “they are shaded.” The printed texts read either “they cover” or “they protect.”]

The Lord recalls this custom as an example of his own care when he says to Jerusalem, murderer of the prophets: “How often I desired to gather thy children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and thou wouldst not” (Matt. XXIII, 37). Therefore the holy man hopes in the shadow of God’s wings until iniquity passes away: that is, until he escapes either the scandals of the world, the iniquities of the wicked, or the weakness of earthly lowliness; until (perhaps, “in the manner in which”) David, now shut up in this kind of cave of his dwelling and body, escapes it.

[Note: The Tours manuscript: “namely the dwelling of his body, in which David is now enclosed.” And: “hoping.”]

4. Prophetic knowledge. *Diapsalma*. Death is sleep. The disturbance of one sleeping: Christ’s Passion. Who are the lion cubs?---Hoping under the shadow of God’s wings, he is always intent upon the office of his hope, saying, VERS. 3: “I will cry [Col. 0364B] to God Most High, to God who has dealt kindly with me.” He who cries while fleeing and hiding cries by faith rather than voice. Moreover, in the speech of one who hopes there is not rejoicing over things already obtained; rather, it belongs to prophetic knowledge and faith to rejoice in things to be done no otherwise than in things already done. Thus he cries to him who, under the unchangeable decree of goodness, has already dealt kindly with him. And he teaches in what respect the Lord has dealt kindly with him by what follows, VERS. 4–5: “He sent from heaven and delivered me; he gave to reproach those who trample me. God sent his mercy and truth; he delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs; I slept troubled.” Even if there were no change of person or sense, it was appropriate for a *diapsalma* to intervene, because the understanding of believers needed to be raised to comprehend these sayings. God dealt kindly with his holy one by sending from heaven, so that, when he was delivered, those who trampled him might be given over to reproach. And he sent his mercy and truth to deliver his soul from the midst of lion cubs, when he had slept troubled.

[Note: The Paris edition reads “Thus death”; other editions, “Just as death.” Shortly afterward Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris read “thus the disturbance of one sleeping.” In both places we restore *si* (“if”), in place of *sic* or *sicut* (“thus” or “just as”), on the authority of the Royal manuscript. For this is a long period, in which, after many accumulated arguments, the conclusion is finally drawn: “there is no doubt that they are given over to reproach,” etc.]

If death is signified by sleep—whether when David is about to sleep with his fathers, when Lazarus sleeps and is to be awakened, when the centurion’s daughter is not dead but sleeping, or when we shall not precede those who have fallen asleep at the resurrection—if the disturbance of one sleeping signifies the Passion, when it is said, “Now my soul is exceedingly troubled” (John XII, 27), he nevertheless prayed beforehand that it might be delivered from the hand of the dog: “Deliver [Col. 0365A] my only one from the mouth of the lion and from the hand of the dog” (Ps. XXI, 22). And no others can be understood as the cubs of dogs or lions than those who are also a “brood of vipers,” from whose midst the soul is delivered; and it is delivered through the mercy and truth sent from heaven, according to that saying, “Mercy and truth have met” (Ps. LXXXIV, 11). And if mercy and truth are the Lord Jesus Christ, there is no doubt that those who trample the Lord in his Passion, and do not believe these things, will be given over to reproach. For their reproach is that they have lost the coming of the only-begotten God and the forgiveness of sins.

[Note: The Paris edition has “the mercy and truth promised from heaven”; the ancient reading, which is also that of the manuscripts, ought not to have been changed.]

[Note: Thus the Mic. manuscript, supported by Bad., Er., and the Royal manuscript, which have “will be given.” Lipsius preferred “may be given”; the Paris editor, “may be brought down.”]

5. Vices of the mind are designated by the functions of the body.---And because both the hatreds of persecutors and the opposition of deniers would always stand against this hope of the saints, after recalling the mysteries of human salvation he added: “The teeth of the sons of men [Col. 0365B] are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.”

[Note: The Tours manuscript reads “shield.”]

Divine discourse signifies the vices and movements of souls through bodily functions. Thus in the song of Deuteronomy (Deut. XXXII, 15), “The beloved grew fat and kicked,” where luxuriant impiety is reproved under the signification of a bodily habit; or, “They devour my people as the food of bread” (Ps. LII, 5); likewise, “Thou hast crushed the teeth of sinners” (Ps. III, 8); and also the Apostle’s saying: “If you bite one another, take care lest you be consumed by one another” (Gal. V, 15). Thus what is assigned to each individual member for its function and action is referred to the workings of minds and souls. So now, intending to recall the effects either of persecutors or detractors, he says: “The teeth of the sons of men are a shield and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword,” since they both consumed by the cruelty of power and wounded by the darts of detraction [Col. 0365C].

[Note: In the Paris edition “weapons” had here been restored, whereas the other books, as also in Psalm LIV, §17, read “shield,” although the earlier term “weapons” is preferred.]

6. God cannot be exalted unless he first descends. By the gift of the Holy Spirit, all the earth is full of the Lord’s glory.---Yet amid these things which the Prophet knows and awaits, he did not keep silence.

[Note: Lipsius and Paris read “which he thirsts for and awaits,” a reading first introduced by Erasmus himself. These words in §7 refute it: the prophet does not fail to know that he is to be placed in heavenly places; he knows through faith and awaits through hope.]

Having prayed that he might not be corrupted, he longs for the time when this corruption is to be swallowed up, saying, VERS. 6: “Be thou exalted above the heavens, O God, and thy glory above all the earth.” Things raised on high from a low condition seem to be exalted because, through a certain advance, they attain what is higher. But what is to be exalted above the heavens must first descend from heaven to the lower regions, so that it may in turn be exalted above the heavens [Col. 0365D]. The Apostle states this most conclusively: “When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men. But what is ‘he ascended’ except that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same who ascended above all heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. IV, 8 ff.).

[Note: The Paris edition, from the Mic. manuscript, reads “gifts in man.”]

Thus he indicates that the reason for being exalted above the heavens lay in having assumed the humility of descending even to the lower parts of the earth. Therefore the prophet, as a prayerful desire, foretells that God will be exalted above the heavens. And because, exalted above the heavens, he was to fill all things on earth with the glory of his Holy Spirit, he added: “And thy glory above all the earth,” since the gift of the Spirit poured out upon all flesh would declare the glory of the Lord exalted above the heavens.

7. In what sense David calls Christ’s glory or Passion his own.---But all this advancement is desired not for the divine nature, but for human weakness. For the prophet knows that through the assumption of flesh he is to be placed in heavenly places, since we have become embodied with and fellow-partakers in Christ Jesus.

[Note: The printed books and manuscripts read “bodily,” not “concorporate”; but they seemed to require correction from similar passages in Psalms LX, LXVIII, CXXVIII, etc., since a manifest scribal error occurred: after the preceding particle *cum*, the following *con* was easily dropped. Athanasius similarly says, *Oration 2 against the Arians*, p. 349: “Nor are the heavenly powers struck with astonishment when they see us, made one body with Christ, brought into their seats and regions.” Leo, *Sermon 1 on the Ascension of the Lord*: “Those whom the poisonous enemy cast down from the blessedness of their first dwelling, the Son of God, making them one body with himself, placed at the Father’s right hand.”]

Therefore he joined these things to the weakness of his flesh, which was both to be afflicted in the Lord’s Passion and exalted above the heavens, VERS. 7: “They prepared snares for my feet and bowed down my soul. They dug a pit before my face and fell into it.” Through the faith of fellow-suffering, the prophet, himself suffering in the suffering Lord, speaks as though he too had suffered. But when they have fallen into the pit they prepared, the experience and penalty of that very death are assigned to those who persecuted the Lord of majesty.

[Note: That is, since the prophet himself was suffering in the suffering Lord.]

8. *Diapsalma*. By the psaltery and cithara David signifies himself.---And because the faith of suffering and dying with Christ glorifies us in him, the prophet stands, as it were, ready for the battle-line of this hope and faith, saying, VERS. 8–10: “O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make psalmody to thee. Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and cithara. I will arise at dawn; and I will confess thee among the peoples, O Lord; I will make psalmody to thee among the nations.” After a *diapsalma* had intervened, the prophet addressed this speech to God, meanwhile singing, in the faith of the psalm, these same things for which his heart is ready. He exhorted the joys of both his soul and body under the signification of psaltery and cithara, and showed himself in the one who sings and makes psalmody. For he says: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and cithara; I will arise at dawn,” clearly declaring that he himself is signified in the psaltery and cithara. For when, upon the summons to rise, the cithara and psaltery are awakened, it is rather he himself, who is signified in them, who rises [Col. 0366D].

[Note: Printed editions read “he shows”; corrected from the Royal manuscript.]

Rising at dawn, he sings with his glory the glory of evangelical hope, at the fitting time of dawn, prayer, and salvation. For what follows is: “And I will confess thee among the peoples, O Lord; I will make psalmody to thee among the nations.” Since he is to praise God among peoples and nations, he must praise in him the salvation of the nations: because the cord of inheritance is no longer confined to Israel alone, nor is Jacob the sole portion, but the fullness of the earth now belongs to God; nor are we now the image of the earthly man, but the image of the heavenly.

9. What “truth unto the clouds” means. Mercy unto the heavens; flesh free from corruption.---He shows what should be confessed among the peoples and sung among the nations: VERS. 11: “Because thy mercy has been magnified unto the heavens [Col. 0367B], and thy truth unto the clouds.” Therefore this is the confession among peoples and nations: that mercy has been magnified unto the heavens and truth unto the clouds. For when the saints are caught up in clouds to meet the Lord (I Thess. IV, 16), raised in him who is that cloud by reason of his body in resurrection; when, according to the Apostle, all creation is to be freed from corruption (Rom. VIII, 22); and when all things in heaven and on earth have been reconciled through him (Col. I, 20), rightly is our truth—or perhaps, “the truth of our resurrection”—raised unto the clouds in him, and his mercy is magnified unto the heavens, once the corruption of creation that groans together has been expelled.

[Note: The Paris edition reads “raised”; the others: “raised by that cloud into the glory of the resurrection of the body,” except that Bad. lacks “glory.” We follow the Royal manuscript. Here the saints are said to be raised in the Lord, who is a cloud by reason of his risen body. The risen body is a cloud because, as is suggested in Psalm LXVII, §3, like clouds it lives beyond earthly and mortal origin, is sustained and moves through the air, etc.]

[Note: Thus the Royal manuscript, not “and about to be reconciled,” as in the printed editions. The Vulgate Jerome here seems, as it were, to imitate Hilary: “Thy mercy has been magnified unto the heavens; for by my resurrection all things in heaven and on earth have been reconciled to thee.”]

This elevation unto the clouds and unto the heavens, however, is signified in their case; but it belongs uniquely to him to pass beyond the heavens and transcend every conception of imagined sublimity.

10. The glory of God exceeds every understanding; how he remains on earth.---The prophet therefore concluded by repeating the prayer of his hope, VERS. 12: “Be thou exalted above the heavens, O God, and thy glory above all the earth.” There is no limit to God’s exaltation, for his elevation is above the heavens. The Lord of creatures must be understood as beyond creatures. And since for us there is nothing else in knowledge beyond heaven, he who is exalted above the heavens is beyond every understanding and exceeds the capacity of knowledge.

[Note: The editions, except Paris, and also the Royal and Vatican manuscripts read “excludes.” We retain “exceeds” from Paris and the Mic. manuscript. The same word is found in Jerome at v. 6, in language clearly imitative of Hilary: “There is no limit to the divine exaltation. We know nothing else concerning the heavens beyond what we have seen. For when he says ‘above the heavens,’ he exceeds human knowledge.” Concerning the glory that is above the earth, the intended meaning is what the Lord himself says elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you,” etc.]

His mercy has indeed overflowed even to us, but it will shortly be magnified unto the heavens in the heavenly things to come. And although his truth has been raised unto the clouds, when we are to be caught up to meet him in a cloud, he himself, who will grant all the heavens from the right hand of God, nevertheless transcends them all [Col. 0368A]. His glory too will remain upon earth—that is, with us—when he says: “Behold, I am with you all the days of life, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20): our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LVII

For the end; “Do not destroy”; of David, for the inscription of the title.

“If indeed you speak righteousness, judge uprightly, sons of men. For you work iniquities in your heart; on earth your hands join together in iniquity. Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; [Col. 0368B] they have spoken falsehood. Their indignation is according to the likeness of the serpent, like that of a deaf asp stopping its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor the sorcery that is healed by the wise man. God has crushed their teeth in their own mouth; the Lord has broken the molars of lions. They will come to nothing like water running away; he will bend his bow until they are weakened. Like melted wax they will be taken away; fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun. Before the bramble brings forth your thorns, he will thus swallow them up in wrath while they are living.” The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner. And he will say: ‘If indeed there is fruit for the righteous, surely there is a God judging them upon the earth.’”

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “righteousnesses,” as also below in §2.]

[Note: Hilary: “uprightly.”]

[Note: Hilary: “wrath.”]

[Note: Hilary: “the medicine of one medicated.”]

[Note: Hilary: “They will be despised.”]

[Note: Hilary: “he will swallow you up.”]

[Note: Hilary: “judging.”]

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

[Col. 0368C]

1. Subject of the psalm.---VERS. 1. From the superscription of the preceding psalm, only any indication of events is absent. For it has “For the end,” “Do not destroy,” and “for the inscription of the title.” The psalm contains no prophecy through deeds, such as in the others, where holy David prophesies both in his sayings and in his actions. Rather, it contains rebuke directed against the ungodly, God’s declaration of judgment upon sinners, the recompense of joy to the saints, and the fruit of righteousness for the righteous person. This, therefore, is the “end” in the psalm; this is the confidence of removing corruption; this is the inscription of the title belonging to him who redeemed us through death.

[Note: We restore the particle *ut*, deleted by Erasmus and subsequently omitted, from Bad. and the manuscripts. Shortly afterward we restore *prophetet* (“may prophesy”), where the Royal manuscript and the Bad. edition read *prophetae*; the other editions read *prophetat*.]

[Note: The printed editions and the Royal manuscript read “of every man”; the Vatican manuscript, “of man.” The Mic. manuscript’s “for man” seems truer: namely, for the righteous person there is fruit of his righteousness, in accordance with v. 12.]

[Note: Printed editions read “to be removed”; corrected from the Mic. manuscript.]

2. The language of righteousness is common, not its pursuit. Sin of the heart. The heart lies open to God.---The whole psalm itself indeed presents this very theme. VERS. 2–3: “If indeed you speak righteousness, judge uprightly, sons of men. For you work iniquities in your heart; on earth your hands join together in iniquity.” The language of righteousness is common, but the pursuit and practice of equitable judgment belong to few. Yet a person should rightly be judged truly to speak righteousness when he maintains the judgment of truth, since God judges not human utterances but the works of the heart—that is, the enterprises of thought. Now iniquity is usually not committed under the shame imposed by public awareness; and therefore, though hands have not joined together in iniquity, the heart works iniquity before God on earth. Hence adultery conceived in the heart alone is already a crime; hence, according to Paul’s Gospel, God judges the secrets of human beings, beholding human wills in the very beginnings of human birth. For since the power of a mighty nature enters not so much into the fibers of the inward parts as into the desires of the mind, it must take its beginning not from the motions of senses perceived, but through the knowledge of its nature apprehend beforehand even the future motions of the senses.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “examines,” which diminishes the force of Hilary’s words.]

3. Foreknowledge of sin does not impose necessity. — And therefore, concerning those who accomplish in their hearts the iniquities which their hands have clasped together [Note: Par.: “with clasped hands”], he immediately added, Verse 4: “Sinners have been alienated from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood.” Thus Esau was alienated from the womb, when it was foretold, even before he existed [Note: Col. 0369C: In one Vatican manuscript, “before he came forth.” Then in the Miciac manuscript, “is named,” not “is foretold.” Paul’s statement in Romans 9:11 is meant: “For when they had not yet been born,” etc.], that the elder would serve the younger; God was not ignorant of his future will, since both the falsity of his speech and the error of his life were from the womb. This was so because God knew it beforehand, rather than because someone had been born into a necessity and nature of sin. And lest the fault might be attributed to origin [Note: Col. 0369D: As the Manicheans wish], he reproaches them with the guilt of a will hardened against obedience, saying, Verses 5 and 6: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp which stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor the charm prepared by a wise man.” [Note: Col. 0369D: Bad., Erasmus, and the later royal manuscript read *medicamentis medicati* (“of remedies prepared”); Lipsius and Paris, *medicamentis medicatis* (“of remedies made ready”); Hincmar’s edition, where this passage is cited in *On Predestination*, ch. 25, *medicamentis medicata*; and the Vatican manuscript, *medicamenti meditati*. We restore from the Miciac manuscript *medicamenti medicati* (“of a prepared remedy”), as Augustine also reads it, in accordance with the more accurate Septuagint edition, φαρμάκου τε φαρμακευομένου (“of a drug being prepared”). In place of this Theodoret has φαρμακοῦται φαρμακευομένη (“it is drugged, being drugged” [grammatically uncertain]); Theodore, in Corderius’s catena, censures that reading as ignorant. “For,” he says, “the sense is this: They are like the asp, which pays attention neither to the voice of charmers nor to the remedy prepared by them. He calls the incantation itself the remedy.” Symmachus makes this clearer, saying, “the song of the charmers.”]

[Col. 0370A] No natural necessity is excused in guilt. For a serpent could be innocent if its ears were by nature stopped as though deaf: it does not hear the charmer’s voice, since it does not perceive remedies prepared by the wise man. Nor does he here speak of the songs of the Marsi [Note: Col. 0369D: Bad.: “biters,” wrongly. Nor is “saints,” in one Vatican manuscript, any better. A Marsus, in Augustine, Jerome, and Rufinus on this passage, is one who charms asps and brings them from dark caverns into the light. On the Marsian people and this art, see Leandro Alberti, *Description of Italy*, p. 225.] and the silenced hissing of vipers, because these very things grow numb with even greater inertness through faith in the name and power of God [Note: Col. 0370C: Bad.: *enertia*, from which Erasmus derived *energia*; this later prevailed even in Hincmar, contrary to the manuscripts and Hilary’s meaning. He holds that this deafness may elsewhere be understood positively: through the power of faith, the art of sorcerers exerts itself more vainly upon believers’ hearts than the Marsian songs upon the stopped ears of asps. But that sense has no place here.]. Rather, he teaches the stubborn and insolent disobedience of the ancient serpent, deafening itself against the songs of the saints and the remedies prepared by the wise man. Though it is daily commanded, under the proclamation of the divine name, neither to deceive, nor steal in secretly, nor bite, it nevertheless rages on with stopped hearing [Note: Col. 0370D: Par., from the Miciac manuscript: “to whom also daily”]; from it comes the brood of vipers obedient to the Gospel [Note: Col. 0370D: Bad., Erasmus, Hincmar, and Vatican and royal manuscripts: “the offspring of vipers.” This would be especially attractive, were “brood” not consistently preferred in Psalm 56, no. 4, and Psalm 59, no. 4, etc.; the Miciac manuscript also has it here.].

4. The breaking and futility of the ungodly. — But because his power and that of his followers are crushed, and every weapon of cruelty in them is broken, these words follow. Verses 7–9: “God has crushed their teeth in their mouth; the Lord has broken the molars of lions. They shall be despised like flowing water; he shall bend his bow until they are weakened. They shall be taken away like melted wax; fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun.” We have often spoken of the teeth of sinners [Note: Col. 0370D: In the Miciac manuscript, “of sinners’ teeth.” Something on this occurs in the preceding treatise, no. 5. Nothing has yet occurred concerning lions’ molars, or the severity of judgment signified by the bow, though this, often demonstrated already, will shortly be mentioned.] and the molars of lions, because they signify the impulse of raging malice. When these are broken and crushed, they will be despised like flowing water.

For the course of all overflowing waters is useless: each person diverts from them only what he judges useful for himself; the rest runs onward in its channel to perish, being carried all the way to the seas only for its own disappearance. And in another psalm he mentions this nature and contemptibility of water, when it is said: “I am poured out like water, and all my bones are scattered. My heart became like wax melting in the midst of my belly” (Ps. 21 [22]:15). Indeed, many things which dissolve from solid into liquid change their appearance without losing their nature, as rigid things flow [Note: Col. 0371D: Bad.: “acting,” which Erasmus retained and perhaps emended in the margin to “being cold.” Lipsius more boldly substituted “furnaces.” The manuscripts more correctly read “from rigid things,” that is, when they were previously rigid and not liquid. The reference is to wax which disappears when exposed to fire, not wax merely melted in vessels.]; but wax, once it has received fire, melts so as to perish.

In the same way he has now set forth both kinds of created thing as examples for the destruction of sinners: “They shall be despised like flowing water; he shall bend his bow until they are weakened; they shall be taken away like melted wax.” First, therefore, they shall be despised, flowing away uselessly without hope of standing or remaining. Then the Lord’s bow will remain bent until they are weakened. Once weakened, they shall be taken away like melted wax [perhaps *liquefactae*, “melted,” feminine]. We have often shown that the bow signifies the severity of God’s judgment, continually aimed at sinners for the punishments which are to be inflicted. And the following words make clear that, with the bow bent, they are to be taken away by the fire of judgment like melted wax: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun.” The fire cast upon them will therefore take them away so that they may not behold the sun of righteousness; for they are unworthy to be fellow-heirs of eternal light.

5. The ungodly suffer the punishments of fire immediately after death. — And lest the statement, “They shall be taken away like melted wax” [Note: Col. 0371D: Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and the final Paris edition, with the royal manuscript, read: “but like wax, when melted, they shall be taken away.” Then Bad. and the royal manuscripts read “descending, and as to their annihilation”; other editions have “falling down” for “departing.” From these readings a sense wholly contrary to the holy doctor’s mind was constructed. We give the genuine reading from the Roman Miciac and Vatican manuscripts. Those who collated them did not note whether the particles “and as to” occur before “annihilation.” Yet it is evident that they must either be absent or altered into something else, for example “like.” See Treatise on Psalm 1, no. 15.]—with fire falling upon them lest they see the sun—might signify their annihilation rather than punishment, he added, Verse 10: “Before your thorn-bush produces its thorns, as living persons, so in wrath he swallows you up.”

The rhamnus is a kind of thorn-bush which, like a bramble, produces numerous thickly clustered thorns; it flowers in spring, warmed along with the other plants. Therefore, before the thorn-bush produces the thorns of sinners, fire in wrath swallows them up while living [Note: Col. 0372D: We restore the particle *ut* here from the royal manuscript. Then the Vatican manuscript has “meanwhile” for “in wrath”: “he swallows up.”]. For it was not fitting that sinners should rest without punishment while the time of judgment was still deferred [Note: See Treatise on Psalm 2, no. 48.]. Thus fire swallows them up while living—that is, while they retain the capacity to feel punishment—even before they rise again.

The resurrection of bodies is signified in the thorn-bush; those bodies will themselves present within themselves thorns by which they are to be pierced [Note: Col. 0372D: Vatican manuscript: “when they themselves.” The phrase “which itself” refers to bodies.]. For some they will bear the fruit of the eternal flower; but for others they will be awakened only to put forth in themselves the sharp prickles of thorn-bush thorns. We have recalled that a thorn signifies the force and pain of sinners, when it is said: “I fell into misery while the thorn was fastened” (Ps. 31 [32]:4) [Note: Col. 0371C: “He fell.”] [Note: Col. 0372D: Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and the royal manuscript read “will fall.” Then the same witnesses, except Lipsius, read “while the thorn is broken.” Hilary would vainly cite this one passage, which he applies to Christ’s passion, to prove that the thorn signifies sinners’ force and pain, if he believed that pain had not fallen upon Christ.]. For, humbled even unto death, he condemned sin in the flesh on account of sin, as though a thorn is fastened when it fastens another. And each person, according to the Apostle, will receive in the flesh either good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10), since the sinner will possess the very material and sense in which he may be pierced.

Before the resurrection of the flesh—that is, before the thorn-bush puts forth its thorns—his soul is swallowed up alive for punishment, like the soul of the rich man in the Gospel, which is punished while living (Luke 16:23).

6. Hands washed in the sinner’s blood: innocence. — But amid these things [Note: Col. 0371C: The words immediately enclosed in brackets are omitted by the Verona manuscript], the joy of every righteous person [“resting, like Lazarus, in Abraham’s bosom”] is shown. For it follows, Verses 11 and 12: “The righteous man shall rejoice when he sees vengeance; he shall wash his hands in the sinner’s blood. And man shall say: ‘Is there indeed fruit for the righteous? There is indeed a God judging them on earth’” [Note: Col. 0372C: “And man says: ‘There will indeed be fruit for the righteous. There is indeed a God judging them on earth.’ The Hebrew agrees.”].

The righteous person’s joy is his joy at seeing vengeance: for, when sinners are punished, he rejoices that he has been led by angels into eternal rest. He does not wash his hands in sinners’ blood; rather, since sinners are in blood, because they are guilty of bloodshed, he keeps his hands washed clean of every guilt of blood [Note: Col. 0372D: The author of the exposition of the Psalms attributed to Jerome borrows the following from Hilary, introducing it with this praise: “Because this little verse is difficult to understand, I shall bring forward the very words expounded by earlier writers. Blessed Hilary, bishop and, if I may so put it, a great supporter of the Church amid the storms of the world, speaks of it thus,” etc.].

He attested the same thing in another psalm, saying: “I hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly; I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. 25 [26]:5–6) [Note: Col. 0372C: “I have hated.”]. And after recounting the duties of innocence [Note: Col. 0372D: The printed editions here add “God,” which is absent from the royal manuscript, as from the Greek.], he added: “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood” (ibid., 9). Thus he will wash his hands among the innocent in the blood of sinners.
