Indeed, these are men of blood to such an extent that the blood of all those slain from Abel to Zachariah will be required of them (Matt. 23:35); and when Pilate washed his hands, they declared that the righteous man’s blood was upon themselves and their children (Matt. 27:24–25).

7. But when the righteous washes his hands and rejoices, man will say: “Will there be fruit for the righteous?” And he says that there certainly will be, because God is judging them on earth. Therefore, when man asks whether there is fruit for the righteous, he is undoubtedly awaiting judgment. Yet the righteous man has already been judged on earth [Note: Col. 0373D: Hilary expressly says here that the righteous are judged before the final judgment, and proves it from the blessed lot already granted them. He sufficiently suggests the same concerning the wicked from the cited Johannine passage. Jerome, a frequent imitator of Hilary, explains the same passage: “Those are judged before the end, in this earth, of whom we said above: ‘He who does not believe has already been judged.’”], since he has been led by angels into Abraham’s bosom, according to the saying: “He who believes in me is not judged, but passes from death into life; but he who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18–19).

Since, therefore, the saint is not to be judged, because he is to pass from death into life, and the unbeliever has already been judged for punishment [Note: See Treatise on Psalm 1, no. 17.], it is understood that judgment remains for those who, according to the quality of their deeds, are to be judged between sin and faith, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Psalm LVIII

For the end: “Do not destroy”; of David, for an inscription on the title, [Col. 0373B] when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him.

“Deliver me from my enemies [Note: Col. 0373D: Hilary adds “O God”], and free me from those who rise against me. Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and free me from men of blood. For behold [Note: Col. 0373D: “Behold” is absent in Hilary, and also the following “and.”], they have hunted for my soul, and the strong have rushed upon me. Neither my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord; without iniquity I have run and made straight. Rise up to meet me and see; and [Note: Col. 0373D: “And” is absent.] you, O Lord, God of powers, God of Israel, attend to visit all nations: do not [or, “lest you”] have mercy upon all who work iniquity. Diapsalma.

“They shall return at evening and suffer hunger like dogs, [and] go around the city. Behold, they shall speak with their mouth, and a sword is in their mouth: for who has heard? But you, O Lord, will deride them; you will count all nations as nothing. I will keep my strength for you, because God is my protector” [Note: Col. 0373D: Hilary adds “you are.”]. “My God, his mercy will go before me. God [Note: Col. 0373D: Adds “my.”] will show me among my enemies. Do not kill them, lest they ever forget your law. Scatter them in your power and destroy them, O Lord, my protector. The sin of their mouth, the word of their lips—and let them be caught” [Note: Col. 0373D: Hilary: “they shall be caught.”] “in their pride. And because of cursing and falsehood they shall be overthrown in consummation” [Note: Col. 0373D: Hilary: “They shall be overthrown in consummation: consummation in the wrath of consummation.”]: “in the wrath of consummation, and they shall be no more. And they shall know that God rules Jacob” [Note: Col. 0374D: Hilary: “God rules Jacob and the ends.”] “and the ends of the earth. Diapsalma.

“And they shall return at evening; they shall suffer hunger like dogs and go around the city. They shall scatter themselves to eat; if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur. But I will sing of your power; in the morning I will exalt” [Note: Col. 0374D: Hilary: “I will exult.”] “your mercy, because you have become my protector and my refuge in the day of my affliction. My helper, I will sing psalms to you, because God is my protector, my God, my mercy.”

## Treatise on the Psalm

1. Christ’s passion foretold in this psalm. — Verse 1. The superscription of this psalm does not differ from that of the preceding one; but the psalm differs in that certain events which occurred to David himself are placed before us: when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him. Yet if prayer were to be directed to God on that account, the preceding words—namely, “for the end,” “do not destroy” or “corrupt,” and “for an inscription on the title”—need not have been added.

Although these words are above all arranged according to a spiritual rationale, since Christ is the end of the law, his eternity was not subject to corruption, and the inscription of his glorious death lies in the salvation of the nations, nevertheless the very matters written beforehand concerning his deeds show themselves to be prophetic. For the prophet, not ignorant of the Lord’s passion, has shown himself a prophet both by suffering and by speaking, under the occasion and time of the hatred he endured.

We shall treat the psalm so as not to burden the understanding of those who think according to the letter, but also so that we may see that David’s being guarded by Saul for slaughter is a prophecy of the time when Christ was shut up, as in his own house, by the people and in Jerusalem, and guarded for death [Note: Col. 0374D: Thus Paris from the Miciac manuscript. Other books read “a prophet than an apostle.” Neither reading is complete. Ours may easily be repaired by substituting “in which” or “when” for “than,” and then adding or supplying “Christ.”].

2. The progress of iniquity. — Verses 2 and 3. “Deliver me from my enemies, O God, and free me from those who rise against me. Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and free me from men of blood.” He has embraced the causes and progressions of human vices, so that we might know from what source impiety arose and to what it would issue. Therefore the Gospel has restrained anger, quarrels, and enmities: for one who is angry with his brother without cause is liable to Gehenna; an offering of a gift is not permitted unless the quarrel has first been reconciled; and it decrees not only that enemies must be loved (Matt. 5:22–23), but also that prayer must be offered for them (ibid., 44), because from these things one proceeds to become a man of blood.

For first they are enemies; next, they rise up against him whose enemies they are; those who rise up are workers of iniquity; finally, workers of iniquity advance as far as becoming men of blood. Men of blood are brought to completion not only by murder committed, [Col. 0374D] but also by murder contemplated [Note: Col. 0374D: One Vatican manuscript has “known”; another, “to things contemplated”; a third, “stirred up”; the royal manuscript, “agitated.” At first “contemplated” did not seem sufficiently expressive, because, when the highest degree of quarrelling is made to be that of a man of blood, such a man seemed to require completion by some greater crime than a worker of iniquity, being thus named because of murder committed. But for Hilary a man of blood is guilty of blood because of murder perpetrated either in act or intention. He is placed at the highest degree of anger, not as another stage of wickedness but as its final result; just as being a worker of iniquity is merely a designation following upon a man’s rising against another. See the preceding Treatise, no. 6. Therefore we do not alter “contemplated,” although “agitated” or “stirred up” is not displeasing. We note in passing that the royal manuscript, supported by one Vatican manuscript, reads “of murder,” not “murders.”].

3. David’s complaint is more fittingly applied to Christ. — For it follows, Verses 4 and 5: “For they have hunted for my soul; the strong have rushed upon me. Neither my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord; without iniquity I have run and made straight.” David’s soul was hunted when he was shut up in his house to be killed. And although he was delivered from Saul’s hands, yet those who desired his blood were men of blood. But according to the psalm’s superscription, the prayer ought to have been against one man—namely, the king who wished these things [Note: Col. 0375C: Bad. and Erasmus: “wishing.” The manuscripts: “with the king certainly wishing these things.” Their sense is: only Saul is mentioned in the title as desiring to kill David; why, then, do “men of blood,” rather than “a man,” occur here?] [Note: Col. 0375C: Our text, with the remaining manuscripts: “with the king certainly wishing these things.”].

But prophetic prayer had to be governed in its language, so that the complaint might refer to the people when the strong hunt for his soul and rush upon him—those, indeed, whom the strong one armed [Note: Col. 0375C: The manuscripts read “the strong,” a reading not to be rejected.], he who also entered Judas’s heart for the service of betrayal. These strong men, therefore, hunt for the soul—his soul in whom there is neither iniquity nor sin, who ran and made straight without iniquity.

4. David was not without sin. — And I do not know whether the preceding psalm permits this to be referred to David in such a way [Note: Col. 0375D: Thus the royal manuscript. Others: “permits these things.” Then we restore from the Vatican manuscripts “in which,” where other editions read “which is said.” The natural order and sense of all this is: “I do not know whether the preceding psalm, in which it is said, ‘Behold, I acknowledge my iniquity,’ etc., permits that statement, ‘Without iniquity I ran,’ etc., to be referred to David as to Christ.”] when it says [Note: Col. 0375C: “It permits these things, which is said.”]: “Behold, I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50 [51]:5). Such a great difference does not suit the order of the psalms, so that both statements should be understood as spoken by the same person.

But if, because the psalm confessing sin, though earlier, comes later in time, David is thought to have spoken these words before his sin, as one ignorant of sin, let us remember that, while still under the same sin [Note: Col. 0375D: That is, still subject to sin; unless one prefers, “under the same psalm.”], he said in confession of human necessity: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (ibid., 7), according to the saying: “For who will boast that he has a pure heart before God, not even though he be an infant of one day?” Even according to the Apostle, both the origin and law of sin remain in us (Rom. 7:23). This utterance, therefore, cannot suit human consciousness.

5. Christ, ignorant of guilt. — But let us see whether perhaps these words, denying iniquity in himself, belong to the complaint of him “who committed no sin, and in whom no guile was found,” and who said: “Behold, the prince of this world will come, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30)—that is, he will find no ground for accusing him of sin, through which he was to condemn sin in the flesh on account of sin.

Therefore he must be understood to complain that his soul has been hunted and that the strong have rushed upon him. He also had this confidence in his complaint: that he could profess neither iniquity nor sin to be in himself, and say that he had run without iniquity, according to the words: “He will rejoice as a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the height of heaven, and his meeting is even to its height” (Ps. 18 [19]:6–7) [Note: Col. 0375D: Thus the royal manuscript, following the Greek *agalliásetai*, “he will rejoice.” The printed editions have “he rejoiced.”].

6. He prays that, on his return, he may be met from heaven. — Therefore he alone, who ran and made straight [Note: Col. 0375D: Paris reads “he will have said,” wrongly. The words of the psalm, “I ran” and “I made straight,” are in view.], went out from heaven by taking on the lowliness of our weakness and returned to heaven. Bringing us back with himself and about to offer a gift to God, he prayed, Verse 6: “Rise up to meet me, and see, O Lord, God of powers, God of Israel. Attend to visit all nations; do not have mercy upon all who work iniquity.”

For he prays that the God of powers may rise to meet him in order to visit all nations. In him the nations have risen with him and been seated at God’s right hand in the heavenly places [Note: Col. 0375D: Printed editions: “in which, having been raised”; previously Lipsius and Paris had “indeed” for “for.” They are corrected from the manuscripts. Hilary teaches that all nations were raised with Christ and seated with him at God’s right hand because, as he explains in Psalm 51, no. 15, Christ, by assuming flesh, assumed in himself the nature of the whole human race.]. And it was fitting that his return should be adorned by the honor of a heavenly meeting, lest paternal condescension from heaven [Note: Col. 0376C: “From heaven” is absent in the royal manuscript and three Vatican manuscripts.] should be lacking to him as he entered heaven.

Nor is this surprising, since, at the meeting of the first martyr of his name, Stephen (Acts 7), the Father descended, as it were, in the foremost ranks [Note: Col. 0376C: “In” is absent.] of heaven [Note: Col. 0376C: Miciac: “in the earlier ranks”; one Vatican manuscript: “one of the foremost.” We retain, with the other books, “in the foremost ranks,” meaning that the Father did not himself descend, but descended through the principal inhabitants of heaven. What Hilary means here may be understood from the Gallican liturgy, vol. I of *Museum Italicum*, published from a manuscript written a thousand years ago. No one is ignorant that he devoted effort to arranging liturgical matters. Thus the collect of the Mass of St Stephen, p. 292, reads: “Lord, who opened the heavens to your martyr St Stephen, walking from strength to strength, for glory, as you had opened them to him for the merit of holiness, that he might receive the fruit of his confession.” More relevant is the attestation of that same Mass: “While he nevertheless lays his earthly limbs to rest with the earth, he raised his heavenly spirit to heaven in angelic hands.” What else, then, shall we understand by the Father’s descending in the foremost ranks of heaven, except that he received St Stephen’s spirit, lifted to heaven in angelic hands? Hilary therefore did not believe that heaven was closed to all until the final judgment. But perhaps elsewhere we shall examine more carefully both his opinion and that of the ancients in this matter. There are indeed many facts by which we may demonstrate that the faith now received in the Church is not as new as many persuade themselves.].

He therefore prays that all nations may be visited at his meeting, according to the saying: “For God did not send his Son into this world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17). For angels rejoicing and heavens opened honored his descent into flesh and birth from Mary. Thus this prayer for his meeting is not presumptuous: for, as another psalm and apostolic testimony state, at his encounter as firstborn from the dead this voice was addressed to him: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7; Acts 13:33).

Thus he prays for this signification of his meeting in the nations to be visited in himself [Note: Col. 0377C: Printed editions read “by himself,” against the manuscripts; and shortly after they read “in him . . . visited,” not “by him.”], yet without the severity of judgment being omitted, since mercy is withheld from all who work iniquity. All nations are visited in him, because he became flesh; but all who work iniquity are equally judged [Note: Col. 0377C: Lipsius wrongly added the particle “in” here, and later editions retained it; we remove it on the authority of the old books.].

7. The misery of the Jews. They are forbidden to enter Jerusalem. — For, after the Diapsalma [Note: Col. 0377C: Printed editions read “the Diapsalma,” against the manuscripts.], he declares what punishments would remain upon [Note: Col. 0377C: “In” is omitted. Codex Tours reads “which impiety,” without “in”; this reading is supported by no. 12 below: “Meanwhile punishment awaits them,” but conflicts with *On the Trinity*, book 10, no. 13: “that pain remained in suspended flesh.”] the impiety of the people. Immediately thereafter followed the desolation of the temple, the overthrow of the city, and captivity for those same persons. Even now they are forbidden by an edict of the Roman emperor to enter that city [Note: Col. 0377D: Printed editions have “entry”; the manuscripts more correctly have “at entry.” This is the edict issued by Emperor Hadrian in A.D. 137, under the consulship of Pompeianus and Acilius, after the end of the Jewish war in Palestine. Eusebius says in the *Chronicle*: “From that time permission to enter Jerusalem was taken away from them, first by God’s will, as the prophets had foretold, then by Roman prohibitions.” And in *Ecclesiastical History* 4.6: “Aristo of Pella relates that from that time the entire nation was absolutely forbidden ever to set foot in the territory of Jerusalem, and was prevented by legal decree and Hadrian’s ordinances—for he had expressly commanded this—from even seeing their ancestral soil from an elevated place.” Tertullian testifies in *Apology* 21 that this edict remained in force in his day, saying of the Jews: “Scattered, wandering, exiles from both their sky and soil”—words copied by Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*—“they roam over the world without a man, without God as king, and are not permitted even by the right of strangers to greet their native land with the sole of their foot.” Again, *Against the Jews* 13: “It is forbidden that any Jew should remain in the confines of that region.” After citing certain prophecies, including Isaiah 33:17, “Your eyes shall see the land from afar,” he continues: “Because, after the conquest of Jerusalem, you are deservedly forbidden to enter your land, you are permitted only to see it from afar with your eyes.” The strictness of this edict was gradually relaxed. First, according to Eusebius, they could not even look upon their ancestral soil from an elevated place; in Tertullian’s time they might look upon it but not approach it; finally, in Hilary’s own age, though entrance into Jerusalem was denied, they were permitted to travel only around the surrounding regions. Jerome also mentions this dispersion in his commentary on Daniel 9 and Jeremiah 31.].

When they remember that the Holy of Holies has been deserted, that prophecies are silent, that sacrifices of propitiation are lacking, and that every dignity of Levitical ministry has been disfigured, they now turn back, afflicted with hunger for God’s word and saving food, and habitually go around the city as a consolation amid their present miseries. This is what follows, Verse 7: “They shall return at evening, suffer hunger like dogs, and go around the city.”

God, announcing through another prophet the famine of this time [Note: Col. 0378D: Miciac manuscript: “the time of this famine.” Only the Paris edition reads “another prophet.” Supply “God” after “announcing,” who then speaks in his own name: “Behold, I bring,” etc.] [Note: Col. 0378C: “The time of this famine, and through a prophet.”], says: “Behold, I bring a famine upon the land: not a famine of bread nor thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11). By calling them dogs he reproves their shamelessness and rage, according to the words: “Deliver my only one from the lion’s mouth and from the dog’s paw” (Ps. 21 [22]:22). They do indeed have this inward pain of conscience when they groan over their scattering, captivity, and tributary condition—without temple, priest, or kingdom—and this after they laid impious hands upon the Lord of majesty and Savior of the world.

8. Their envy. Why all nations—that is, most nations—are to be derided. — Verses 8–9: But when they are reproved for the sin of crucifying the only-begotten God, they do not cease to be ungodly; inflamed by grief at the transfer of divine knowledge to the nations, they continue to rage in mouth and words. For it follows: “Behold, they shall speak with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips.”

9. But the divine word condemns this ungodliness of slandering and attacking not only in them, but also in the nations which refuse to hear, in this way: “For who has heard? And you, O Lord, will deride them; you will count all nations as nothing.” Because no one hears, they are derided by God. For where “who?” is said, either few or none are indicated: none, according to the words, “Who is like you among the gods, O Lord?” (Ps. 88 [89]:7); but few in the words, “Who will give Israel salvation from Zion?” (Ps. 52 [53]:7).

Therefore those who do not hear, and in whose mouth and lips is a sword, are derided; because God dwelling in heaven will mock the kings and rulers gathered together against God and his Christ (Ps. 2:4). He will also despise all the nations that have been visited and yet have not obeyed. For although some portion of believers, however small, comes from them, the whole is reckoned according to the greater number, according to the Lord’s saying: “When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8).

This does not mean that faith will not be found in some, to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). But since faithful persons are few among all nations, it is not brought about by the few that all nations should not be unbelieving [Note: Col. 0378D: The negative particle, wrongly rejected in the Paris edition, is restored from the other books.]. The chief reason why the nations are to be derided [Col. 0379A] is that, while they reproach as folly to worldly wisdom one who was crucified, dead, and buried, they do not understand the mystery of great mercy and do not believe that the Son of God, raised from the dead, is Lord of majesty.

### 10. God Receives Christ in His Death

But he, having power to lay down his life and to take it up again, because he had received this command from the Father (John 10:18), after the nations had been mocked and despised, added, Verses 10–12: “I will keep my strength for thee, because thou, O God, art my receiver. My God, his mercy shall go before me; my God shall show me among my enemies.” He will keep his strength for God—that is, by taking it up again, his life which he laid down; for no one takes it away from him (Luke 23:45) [Note: “Will take away.”]—and because God is his strength and his refuge, into whose hands he commended his spirit.

His mercy will go before him, so that even before the resurrection he may be understood to be the Son of God: when, as he died, the light failed as the sun was darkened; when, as he hung upon the cross, the earth quaked (Matthew 27:52); when, as he descended into the underworld, it did not hold his saints; when, as he gave up the spirit, the veil of the temple was torn apart, as though a spiritual guard were breaking out from there; and finally when the centurion cried out: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Mark 15:39).

[Note: Augustine prefers that sinners, rather than saints, were brought out of the underworld. “I confess,” he says, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XII, chapter 33, §63, “that I have not yet found the name ‘underworld’ applied to the place where the souls of the righteous rest. Yet it is not without reason believed that Christ’s soul came even to those places in which sinners are tormented, in order to release from punishments those whom his justice—hidden from us—judged should be released, by that power whereby he is Lord.” He adopted this view because of Acts 2:24, where Christ is proclaimed to have been raised by God “when the pains of hell had been loosed.” But if the righteous are said to have suffered because they ardently longed for Christ, the Savior whom they needed, why should their pains not be said to have been loosed by his presence?

Origen aptly explains the reason for Christ’s descent into hell, in 1 Samuel 28, cited by Huet, vol. I, p. 33: “The inward longing which cannot be healed by others, he himself heals; what could not be cured by any physicians is healed by Christ Jesus.” Shortly afterward he adds: “Nor, indeed, are those who need Christ without need of the prophets and of those who prepare Christ’s presence and coming.” Then, after some intervening remarks, he adds that the righteous descended into hell “not simply, but as saints”; and this because “although they descend to where the souls are that are in hell, they are lower in place, yet not lower in will. And I am certainly persuaded that they prophesied things above the heavens.” Thus Origen illustrates Hilary, whom he undoubtedly anticipated. Yet from this it is not sufficiently clear how a great chasm lay between the righteous and the unrighteous if one place contained both. But one may answer this also: they were not so far apart that they could not see one another.]

Therefore he keeps his strength for God, because “the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:4); and because his mercy went before him, God showed him among his enemies, since he was his receiver—even as this became manifest through the confession of his enemies. For the centurion truly proclaimed him to be the Son of God. These things, then, were known at that time.

### 11. The Jews Will Receive Christ’s Faith at the End of the Age

But because, according to the saying, “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10), God will also in the future show among Christ’s enemies that he is his receiver: for, according to the Apostle, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, what remains of Israel shall be saved, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “There shall come out of Zion one who shall deliver and turn away ungodliness from Jacob” (Isaiah 59:20). “And this is my covenant with them, when I shall take away their ungodlinesses” (Romans 11:25).

[Note: Printed editions read “of Israel.” But the manuscripts have *Israel* in the second case, as below; the printed editions likewise support this.]

Therefore, to signify this mercy and hope that are being reserved, he added, Verses 13–14: “Do not kill them, lest they ever forget thy law. Scatter them in thy power, and destroy them, O Lord, my protector. The sin of their mouth, the word of their lips, and they shall be caught in their pride; and for cursing and falsehood they shall be overthrown in the consummation. A consummation in wrath, a consummation, and they shall be no more; and they shall know that the God of Jacob rules the ends of the earth.”

[Note: Thus the manuscripts, as also the Greek; printed editions read: “will rule.”]

[Note: The old edition, with the Royal manuscript, reads, in agreement with the Greek, “they shall be caught.”]

They are enemies indeed on our account, but beloved on account of the fathers (Romans 11:28); what remains of them is reserved for mercy. Meanwhile scattered among nearly all nations, they shall nevertheless be delivered through the equally holy root, despite their scattering.

[Note: The Tours manuscript reads: “but their scatterings.”]

[Note: Printed editions read, “the holy root also.” We prefer, with the Royal manuscript, “through the equally holy root”: that is, although scattered because of their crimes, they shall nevertheless be delivered for the sake of the root, which always remains equally holy.]

They shall therefore be destroyed according to the prophecy—not killed, but scattered; and they shall be destroyed in the sins of their mouth and in the speech of their lips, when the deliverer comes from Zion, of whom they cried: “Crucify, crucify” (John 19:6); and to whom they said: “We have Abraham as our father” (John 8:33); and again: “Who gave thee this authority?” (Luke 20:2); and: “By what authority doest thou these things?” (Matthew 21:23).

They shall therefore be caught in this pride when they do not recognize that these things were inflicted by themselves upon their Savior. When ungodliness has been turned away, they shall be torn away from cursing and falsehood; and this shall occur in the consummation, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then what remains of Israel shall be saved. Yet in the wrath of consummation they shall not be no more, because he who comes from Zion will turn away their ungodlinesses. They shall not be no more, because they too will come to know; and they shall know that the God of Jacob rules the ends of the earth—not now to be known merely in the allotment of inheritance and in Jacob’s portion, but as the God of Jacob: that is, as he who in a man was understood and seen as Jacob’s God, and is ruler of the ends of the earth, whose Creator he must also be confessed to be.

[Note: The Royal manuscript, with two Vatican manuscripts, reads, “because in a man.” The integrity of the sense requires: “that is, to be known because he who in a man ….” Here it is acutely observed that he whom the Jews are foretold to recognize as ruler of the earth is not simply called God, but “the God of Jacob,” that is, God embodied, or God made man, such as Jacob saw.]

[Marginal reading: “Because in a man.”]

### 12. The Jews’ Dispersion, Spiritual Famine, Empty Food, and Impenitence

But in the meantime the punishment of their desolation and dispersion awaits them. For although, at the consummation of the ages, this dispensation of mercy is reserved on account of the fathers and the elect, yet after an intervening *diapsalma* it is shown, by a repeated statement, what has meanwhile been appointed concerning them. For it follows, Verses 15–16: “And they shall return at evening, and shall suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go about the city. They themselves shall be scattered for food; but if they are not filled, they shall murmur.”

[Note: Here again the printed editions read “diapsalma,” against the manuscripts.]

Having lost their city and deserted their temple, and going about the city only in accordance with the edicts of the Roman emperor—not entering it—their hunger will be not for this bread and food, but for offerings, sacrifices, and visions, by which they shall be filled; barking with the insolence of dogs against their guardian.

[Note: The Tours manuscript has, as in the edition of Badius, “by which they were filled.” “By which they were formerly filled” would not be displeasing. Or perhaps read: “by which they were not filled.”]

And they shall be scattered for food because in various places they imitate the outward form of that lawful priesthood, and of the burnt offering, and of circumcision, though these things have been established as lawful only within Jerusalem.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “otherwise lawful.”]

But, scattered for food, they are not filled. For they shall be fulfilled only by holy observances pleasing to God and religiously performed in that very place, according to the ordinance of the temple.

[Note: We restore from the Royal manuscript the particle *nisi* (“except”), omitted in printed editions.]

But they will still murmur. Not even subdued by this hunger for their festivals, they will not, after the manner of the murmuring whereby they provoked God in the desert, come to their senses in the quietness of repentance.

### 13. The Prophet’s Rejoicing in God. Aptly Applied to Christ’s Resurrection

But amid these matters he concludes all his hopes and rejoicings at the end of the psalm, saying, Verses 17–18: “But I will sing of thy strength; I will exult in thy mercy in the morning, because thou hast become my receiver and my refuge in the day of my tribulation. My helper, I will sing psalms to thee, because God is my receiver, my God is my mercy.”

[Note: Thus the Royal manuscript, in accordance with the Greek; printed editions read, “I will exult.”]

[Marginal reading: Printed editions: “I will exult.”]

These words may all be referred to the prophet’s rejoicing, but they are not different from the Lord’s own confession. For this dispersion of theirs followed upon the ungodliness of the Passion. But the rejoicing in the morning because, in God’s mercy, he has become his receiver and refuge appears to be referred to the time of the resurrection. For although praise of God must be sung by the prophet at all times, yet for the Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead at dawn and returning to heaven, the exultation of morning rejoicing is especially fitting. He is blessed unto all ages of ages. Amen.

152

## Psalm LIX

[Note: Psalm LVIII ends. Psalm LIX begins. “Unto the end, for those things which are changed, for the inscription of the title, of David, for instruction … and he struck the valley of Salt,” etc., according to the Greek, *pharanka* (φάραγκα, “ravine” or “valley”).]

Unto the end, for those who shall be changed [Note: Hilary: “were changed”], for the inscription of the title [Note: Hilary: “inscription of the title”], of David for instruction, when he burned Mesopotamia and Syria of Sobal, and Joab returned and struck twelve thousand in the valley of salt.

“O God, thou hast cast us off and destroyed us; thou hast been angry, and hast had mercy on us. Thou hast shaken the earth and troubled it; heal its breaches, for it has been moved. Thou hast shown thy people hard things; thou hast given us wine of compunction to drink. Thou hast given a sign to those who fear thee, that they may flee from the face of the bow.” *Diapsalma.* “That thy beloved may be delivered, save with thy right hand and hear me. God has spoken in his holy one: I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of the tabernacles. Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the strength of my head; Judah is my king. Moab is the vessel of my hope. Upon Idumea I will stretch out my sandal; the foreigners are subject to me. Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me even into Idumea? Is it not thou, O God, who hast cast us off? And wilt thou not go forth, O God, with our forces? Give us help out of tribulation, for human salvation is vain. In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself shall bring to nothing those who afflict us.”

[Note: “Thou hast cast us off”: variant, “Thou hast repelled us.”]

[Note: Hilary: “unto us.”]

[Note: Hilary: “shaken.”]

[Note: Hilary: “save with thy right hand.”]

[Note: Hilary omits “God.”]

[Note: Below, *dimetiar*, “I shall measure out.”]

## Treatise on the Psalm

### 1. The Psalm Does Not Agree with the History. Aquila’s Translation. The Seventy

Verses 1–2. Many things are set forth in the psalm before the narrative of events, and these must, for the indication of some understanding, be given precedence over what was accomplished: namely, “Unto the end,” “for those who shall be changed,” “the inscription of the title,” and the superscription, “of David for instruction.” After these is added the time of the events: “He burned Mesopotamia and Syria of Sobal, and Joab returned and struck twelve thousand in the valley of salt” (2 Samuel 8). In all this the psalm differs from the history.

[Note: Printed editions: “in the inscription of the title,” against the manuscripts.]

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “Jobal”; Royal manuscript: “Subab.” Then the Paris editions: “and Jacob returned.” The Royal codex subsequently has, “and he struck the valley of Salt,” according to the most recent edition of the Septuagint: *kai epataxe tēn pharanka tōn halōn* (καὶ ἐπάταξε τὴν φάραγκα τῶν ἁλῶν, “and he struck the valley/ravine of salts”); yet 2 Samuel 8 has *en gebelem* (ἐν γεβελεμ). Here also Augustine, Jerome, Theodoret, and Rufinus read “in the valley,” a reading which our Hilary soon follows.]

For when Sobal had been struck, together with Mesopotamia and Syria, which had been stirred up and inflamed for war by him and captured, immense joy of rejoicing followed that victory in a great war. But the entire psalm is sad and mournful: there is grief over a people cast off and destroyed; there is lamentation over an earth shaken and troubled; there is prayer for the healing of its breach.

[Note: “Which psalm.”]

[Note: We restore *omnis* (“entire”) here from the Royal manuscript.]

[Note: “Mesopotamia was struck.”]

Moreover, what is mentioned concerning the valley of salt appears neither in the history nor in the understanding of any translators.

[Note: Jerome, in the received text, observes that it is commonly asked where this history is written. He himself answers that it is most plainly read in the books of Kings, but that there, instead of “the valley of salt,” the Septuagint translators put the Hebrew words *gemelach*—now found as *gebelem* (γεβελεμ)—whose meaning is unknown to those unacquainted with Hebrew. This history is read in the Vulgate at 2 Samuel 8:13, except that there not twelve but eighteen thousand are said to have been struck; nor do the Septuagint disagree.]

For according to Aquila—who, after the Lord’s Passion, was the translator of the Law for the Jews—it is written thus: “When he struck the valleys.” But he, writing according to the letter and remaining outside spiritual understanding, gave the site of the battle.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “of the Jewish [Law]”; another, “a Jew.” This reading greatly pleases us, since Aquila, having defected from the Christian to the Jewish religion, was, according to Jerome on Isaiah chapter 8, a disciple of Akiba, the bitterest enemy of Christians. Yet we do not alter the received reading, which is that of the Royal and Micy manuscripts. We learn that the Jews valued his labor so greatly that, as Jerome attests in Ezekiel chapter 3, they called his second version *kat’ akribeian* (κατ’ ἀκρίβειαν, “with precision”). He undertook it after Christ’s Passion to such an extent that, according to the calculations of Epiphanius and Euthymius, he published it in the twelfth year of Emperor Hadrian.]

[Note: Royal codex: “having”; “departing” would not be unwelcome. The Micy manuscript subsequently has “gave the place of battle.”]

[Note: For, as Jerome says in *On the Best Kind of Translation*: “Aquila, a proselyte and contentious translator, who attempted to translate not only words but also the etymologies of words, is rightly rejected by us.”]

But the translation of the seventy elders, both authoritative and spiritual, undertaken before the Lord’s Passion and the events suffered by him, even now, as in all the psalms, makes known the subject and meaning through the character of names and natures. In its recollection of the events it indicates not the argument of the psalm, but its time: not in order that the psalm may be recognized as written about what is contained in the events, but in order that it may be recognized as written when those events occurred.

[Note: Badius and Erasmus, with the manuscripts, read “and of the events”; but the Tours manuscript reads “and the sequence of the events undertaken.”]

[Note: “The Passion of God, and of the events undertaken.”]

### 2. To Whom and for What the Psalm Was Written; When It Was Written

But before speaking about the time of the prophecy, because it greatly assists the understanding of the psalm to know when it was written, let us discuss the superscription. Its meaning is referred to the end and to those who shall be changed: those, namely, who cease from ungodliness and vices and are transferred to religion and innocence, and who are changed from the sins of the Synagogue to the grace of the Church.

This is as we showed in the psalm which was first written “for those who shall be changed,” when it says: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline thine ear; and forget thy people and thy father’s house, because the king has desired thy beauty” (Psalm 44:11). And again in the same psalm: “Instead of thy fathers, sons have been born to thee; thou shalt appoint them princes over all the earth” (ibid., verse 17).

[Note: This Treatise is not extant here.]

[Note: “They were made.”]

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads “they were made,” and Symmachus translates thus; Eusebius approves this reading.]

Therefore, when sons have been changed in place of fathers, she forgets her paternal house, being more pleasing to God the King as queen—a queen renewed unto life through his death. And therefore the inscription of the title, “for those who shall be changed,” is appended to the glory of his death, who died for all, as the inscription of the title bears witness; and it also bears witness, “for David’s instruction,” so that we may all know him as David, who is both rising, righteous, kingly, and eternal. He slew the hostile powers that opposed and assailed us, together with their leader, destroying all those who were accustomed to kindle against us the wars of vices: not in a valley of weeping nor in a valley of tabernacles, but in the valley of salts.

[Note: The Tours codex reads “glory.” If the reading is genuine, the punctuation should be changed thus: “The inscription of the title for those who shall be changed is appended, bearing witness to the glory of his death ….”]

[Note: Royal manuscript: *sallium*, and later *sallem*; Greek: *tōn halōn* (τῶν ἁλῶν, “of salts”).]

For the Greek expression makes “salts” clearer than “salt-works”: now this valley of the present world offers from itself no longer mournful dwellings or lamentable tents, but rather salt—namely, those and such as they to whom it was said: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13). In them especially the ancient enemy who was inflaming us has been destroyed.

[Note: Lipsius and Paris have “mounting,” corruptly. The reference is to the heading: “when he burned.”]

Therefore this psalm is written for those who are to be changed at the end, and who are to be instructed under the testimony and inscription of the title concerning David—not at any time other than when the prophet Nathan announced that the king of the eternal throne would come from David’s seed (2 Samuel 7:12–13).

[Note: We restore here the particle *ad* (“for” or “to”) from the Micy and Royal manuscripts. Then Badius, Erasmus, and the Micy manuscript read “instructing,” supported by the Royal manuscript, which has “instructing [plural].” “Instructing” may be referred to “title,” but the other reading is soon confirmed.]

[Note: “Instruction.”]

[Note: The Royal manuscript omits “to be.”]

For at that time the things which are set forth in the narrative were accomplished, the time in which the prophecy of the eternal king was revealed. The psalm, therefore, must be understood as written for those who shall be changed, to instruct them concerning David the eternal king, and concerning those who, by the change, will now be sons in place of their lost fathers. Thus indeed he began.

### 3. The Merciful Wrath of Fathers toward Sons; God’s Wrath toward Human Beings

Verses 3–6. “O God, thou hast cast us off and destroyed us; thou hast been angry with us and hast had mercy on us. Thou hast shaken the earth and troubled it; heal its breaches, because it has been shaken. Thou hast shown thy people hard things; thou hast given us wine of compunction to drink. Thou hast given a sign to those who fear thee, that they may flee from the face of the bow.”

According to the common understanding of the world, anger and mercy do not agree; nor does each of these two dispositions agree in the same person toward the same people, so that a desire for mercy may be mingled with a desire for vengeance.

[Note: That is, the same person. For Hilary commonly uses the pronoun *ipse* in this sense. The received editions then read, “each of these two is the same,” a phrase we have struck out on the authority of the Royal manuscript. Certainly the two dispositions are not the same, but different.]

[Note: The Paris edition reads “as a fault”; the others, “as vengeance.” Then all alike have “will,” “the will of mercy,” etc., with the sentence disordered. The manuscripts restore a lucid reading.]

But this is fitting only for fathers who are piously angry: their anger in their children’s sins is merciful. So too the blessed Paul says (1 Corinthians 5:5), when he delivers a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord, showing that the severity of present punishment serves the salvation of the spirit.

Therefore that eternal heavenly Father of all, who also said, “I will kill and I will heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39), so casts off and destroys his own that, even when angry, he has mercy. He destroyed the temple of Jerusalem, but restored to the saints the heavenly city; he cast them off from the works of the Law, but granted justification by faith, justifying the ungodly by faith; he dissolved the earthly kingdom, but appointed kings in heaven. Thus mercy followed anger, since the loss of present earthly things is compensated by a great recompense of eternal goods.

[Note: Since he here mentions the blessings which followed closely upon the destruction of Jerusalem’s temple and the obsolescence of the ceremonies of the Law, he seems to mean nothing else than that heaven was already opened to the saints at that time. One might refer this to those whose bodies were seen in Jerusalem after Christ’s Passion; but the statement appears more general, as similar sayings soon confirm.]

[Note: A Vatican manuscript has “gifts,” not “goods”; the word “goods” is absent from the Royal manuscript, which shortly afterwards has “fitting” for “fitted.”]

### 4. The Opening Words of the Psalm Concern the Whole Human Race. The Bow as Preparation for Punishment. The Signs of Christians. The Cup of Wrath and the Cup of Life

And these things apply no more to Israel than to the whole human race, because from one man the sentence of death and the burden of life went forth to all (Romans 5:18), when it was said: “Cursed is the earth in thy works” (Genesis 3:17). But now, through one, the gift of life and the grace of justification have abounded to all (Romans 5:18), so that those whose earth was cursed may now have bodies made conformable to God; and so that the earth which was shaken by fear, troubled by ignorance, worn down by toil, and pierced by the very drink of wine that gives joy, may now, in the secure strength of the sign it has received, escape the power of future wrath.

[Note: The Paris edition contains *exiit* (“went forth”). The word more expressly signifies the punishment of sin flowing from one person.]

[Note: The conjunction “and” is supplied from Vatican manuscripts. In other books, and also in the Royal manuscript, the preceding words “through one, to all” were omitted.]

[Note: The Tours manuscript reads “of sanctification received,” a fairly plausible conjecture, unless it is manifest that there is an allusion to the words, “Thou hast given a sign to those who fear thee.”]

For in the bow, as we have often explained, is shown the terror of wrath prepared to punish the ungodly (see *Treatise on Psalm* 57, §4; Psalm 7:12, etc.), according to the words: “Will he be angry every day? He has bent his bow and prepared in it instruments of death; he has made his arrows for those who are to burn.”

[Note: We remove from here “unless you are converted,” which Badius, Erasmus, Lipsius, and the Royal manuscript do not have.]

[Note: “And he shall prepare it; and in it he prepared.”]

Therefore he gave to those who fear him a sign—whether the sign upon their foreheads, faith in their hearts, testimony in their works, glory in their confessions, or victory in their martyrdoms—so that they might flee from the face of the bow and of wrath, as it was said: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” (Matthew 3:7).

[Note: The manuscripts read “in martyrs.”]

This, then, is the voice of the human race rejoicing after the reign of death, the terrors of the devil, the burdens of labors and sins, and the sorrow of unhappy pleasure; for when the pleasures of vices are recognized, they sting. For, according to the Apostle (Ephesians 5:18), dissipation is in wine. And as there is wine that gladdens the heart of man, so also there is wine that pierces the heart of man. For there is a cup of wrath, just as there is a cup of life.

### 5

After these things, therefore, and after this wine of compunction, when the sign has been granted for fleeing from the bow and wrath, the whole body of believers rejoices in eternal hopes. For the *diapsalma* immediately following declares this, Verse 7: “That thy beloved may be delivered, save with thy right hand and hear me.” “The right hand of the Lord has done mightily” (Psalm 117:16), and the Power of God, raised together with itself in the flesh of our lowliness, has sat down with God at his right hand.

[Marginal reading: “At God’s right hand.”]

[Note: Thus the Micy and Royal manuscripts, except that the Royal manuscript has *secus* for *secum*. But the received editions read: “and the Power of God, raised together with the humility of our flesh, at the right hand of God,” and do not convey Hilary’s meaning. For Hilary holds that the Power of God is the divinity of the Word, to which being raised together cannot apply. Rather, that being raised together concerns us. The original arrangement of the whole is: “And the Power of God sat with God, raised together with him at the right hand, or through the power of the right hand, in the flesh of our lowliness.” The Tours manuscript reads “and at the right hand of God,” but this is not preferable to our reading now explained.]

Thus, when the sign for fleeing from the face of the bow has been given, the beloved are delivered and saved through God’s right hand. The Apostle teaches from what face of the bow they are delivered and saved, saying: “Who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians 1:13). Therefore the beloved are to be delivered and saved through the right hand of God.

### 6. Holy Christ. Samaria Divided by Faith and to Be Divided in Judgment

But the prophecy of this salvation must be known for the firmness of faith. For it follows, Verses 8–10: “God has spoken in his holy one: I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of the tabernacles. Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the strength of my head; Judah is my king. Moab is the vessel of my hope. Upon Idumea I will stretch out my sandal; the foreigners are subject to me.”

[Note: “I shall measure out” for “I shall measure.”]

God spoke in the Holy One—namely, in him to whom even the demons cry: “We know that thou art the Holy One of God” (Luke 4:34), and of whom the angel announces: “That holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). In this Holy One, therefore, he spoke when he says: “The Father who speaks in me, he does his works” (John 14:10).

God, therefore, having spoken in the Holy One, rejoices at the beginning of his discourse. For “he shall rejoice as a giant to run his course” (Psalm 18:6), and he shall rejoice in dividing Shechem. Shechem is Samaria, which is also Shechem, and which Jacob assigned to his son Joseph under the blessing of the Spirit (John 4:5).

[Note: The Royal manuscript reads, “Shechem is in Samaria.” Jerome says here: “Some suppose Shechem to be Samaria.”]

Although it had remained in ungodliness during all the preceding times of the Law, it received the Gospel of the Lord in part. For even today part of it persists in its old pursuit, with most irreligious zeal. There cows were worshiped; there a mountain was chosen after the sanctuary was abandoned; there a kingdom was raised up against Judah.

[Note: Printed editions read “against Judea.” The manuscripts more correctly read “against Judah,” since the division of Judea began from that schism.]

But when the Lord first came there (John 4), and the Samaritan woman believed and asked for a drink of living water, he brought faith; then, when the apostles preached, they were made partakers of the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:5). Shechem was therefore divided when believers are separated from unbelievers. And this is a certain division of the future judgment, as it is written: “The lord of that servant shall come in a day when he does not expect, and at an hour which he does not know, and shall divide him and appoint his portion with the hypocrites” (Luke 12:46).

[Note: The received editions read “that division.” We prefer with the Royal manuscript “a certain division.” Augustine says concerning both divisions in this verse: “They are divided now by faith; afterwards they will be divided in judgment, the sheep to the right and the goats to the left.”]

Samaria, therefore, has been divided either by judgment or by faith, according to the saying: “I came not to send peace upon the earth, but division” (Matthew 10:34).

### 7. The Measuring of Mortals

Nor did God, speaking in the Holy One, divide Shechem only; he also measured out the valley of the tabernacles. This is the lowly and sunken abode of human habitation, which elsewhere, because of the sicknesses of life and the laments of calamity, he calls the valley of weeping, saying: “They laid down in the valley of weeping” (Psalm 83:7).

[Note: There is no doubt that this passage is taken from Psalm 83. Three points should be observed there: first, that Hilary read *diethento* (διέθεντο) in the plural, whereas others read *dietheto* (διέθετο); second, that he translated this verb “they laid down,” not “they arranged”; third, that although the following words—namely, “in the valley,” etc.—are separated from the same verb by a full stop in most other writers, they are here joined to it. Yet Theodoret and some others agree with Hilary in this punctuation.]

Therefore he has measured it, because the fullness of the Gentiles is awaited. And where there will be a limit to the number of believers, there is the test of measurement: one part is to be gathered within the Church, while another part remains in the same valley.

[Note: Received editions read “partly,” and Lipsius and Paris alone then read “partly in the same valley,” contrary to the manuscripts. The Tours manuscript alone has “by a part.”]

[Marginal reading: “Partly within.”]

### 8. Gilead and Manasseh

Whoever measures anything must necessarily measure what is his own. For Gilead is his, and Manasseh is his. This mountain belongs to the Phoenicians and borders Arabia and Mesopotamia; it was assigned in possession to the tribe of Manasseh. Thus Manasseh is his, showing under the name of Manasseh that the fullness of the land is his, just as under Gilead he shows that the whole world is his. But in claiming these things, nothing is shown beyond a right of ownership.

### 9. Ephraim as a Type of the Church

But Ephraim is the taking up of his head, and Judah is his king. These words are spoken by the Holy One in whom God speaks—the one who blessed Ephraim through Jacob by the sanctification of his hands crossed over, and who showed that the king would come from Judah and would be the expectation of the Gentiles (Genesis 48:13).

[Note: The Tours manuscript has “Ephraim, a taking up,” as is read more than once in Numbers chapter 9.]

Ephraim, then, is the taking up of his head, and not Manasseh—although both are Joseph’s sons. But since in the head is contained also the signification of the body, according to the saying, “He shall drink from the torrent in the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Psalm 109:7), and every saint is a head of the body of Christ, Ephraim is the taking up of his head because, contrary to the order of generations, in Ephraim’s preference and Manasseh’s postponement, the younger was placed before the elder in order to prefigure the Church’s sanctification.

Therefore Ephraim is the taking up of his head—that is, of the people whom he prefigured in Ephraim; or rather, the Church is taken up into the body.

[Note: Printed editions omit the verb *est* and then add: “Ephraim, that is, the people.” We restore “is” and add “of the people” from the manuscripts.]

[Note: Tours manuscript: “the people whom.”]

### 10. Christ to Be Born from Judah

Judah also is my king—that is, he is appointed and chosen by himself. Certainly neither is David himself king of Judah—for he himself is the first king from Judah—nor is he king to God speaking in his Holy One. Rather, this Holy One in whom God speaks must be understood to say these things to him who filled Jacob with the Spirit for the prophecy of this eternal king, when he said: “A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up; and he is the expectation of the Gentiles” (Genesis 49:10).

[Note: Printed editions have “David himself”; contradictory readings stood together here.]

[Note: “Until the seed comes for whom …”; then, “and he himself is.”]

### 11. Christ to be born of sinners. The spiritual cauldron.

And because the assumption of flesh by this Holy One of God was to be undertaken not only from this line of saints, but also from a sinful origin—because God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3)—therefore Moab too is the cauldron of his hope. This generation of Moab, indeed, according to the judgment recorded in Genesis, received the reproach of a divine curse. [Col. 0389A]

> [Note: [Col. 0389D] In the Royal manuscript, “divine”; and shortly afterward, “through the stages of succession,” where the printed editions wrongly read “of assumption.” Yet we do not find where Moab is cursed in Genesis. Moreover, in Deut. 23:3 and 2 Esdras 13:2, we read that Moabites are not to be admitted into the Church of God even after the tenth generation. Nevertheless, the received text of Jerome agrees with Hilary on this same passage: “Moab received in Genesis the reproach of a curse, who after ten generations is received into the Church.” Indeed Ambrose, on Psalm 48, no. 24, recalls that Moabites were forbidden entrance into the Church of the Lord only as far as the third and fourth generation.]

But after ten generations, through the stages of succession, it becomes worthy of a holy lineage (Deut. 23:3). And this Holy One, deriving his origin from Judah and Moab—

> [Note: [Col. 0389D] That is, from Ruth the Moabitess. Paulinus seems plainly to have imitated this passage in Epistle 3, now 23, in these words: “Therefore he says, ‘Moab is the cauldron of my hope,’ because he assumed a body not only from Judah but also from Moab—that is, not only from the origin of saints but also of sinners; and, having as it were boiled away through the cauldron of our flesh its rawness, he sanctified his flesh as food for us forever. For, as he himself says, his flesh is truly the food of life.” Thus clearly does Hilary affirm here that Christ’s flesh was received not only from Mary but also from Mary’s ancestors, so that Erasmus’s suspicion, by which he represented him as holding contrary views, can scarcely be excused. [Col. 0390D]]

—having boiled away, as through a cauldron, the rawness of flesh, is signified under the figure of eternal food, since his flesh is truly the food of life (John 6:56). There is also the cauldron in Jeremiah, burning and removing sins (Jer. 1:13); just as the Lord himself came to cast fire upon the earth (Luke 12:49), and, according to the Apostle, many shall be saved as through fire (1 Cor. 3:15), when their vices have been purged and burned away, so that, like refined silver, they may be judged approved. [Col. 0389B] Therefore Moab is the cauldron of his hope: from Moab also—that is, from flesh, certainly raw and defective—the heavenly sanctification of that flesh for the food of life is now held in hope.

### 12. The whole human race must be instructed by the Gospel.

Indeed, he says that he will extend his sandal even into Idumaea, namely as far as the defection of Esau, because Idumaea is Esau’s dwelling-place, and that he will direct there the steps of apostolic preaching. For “beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Gospel” (Rom. 10:15); and in the sandal the feet are shown, while in the feet the steps are shown. Nor does he extend the course of preaching into Idumaea alone: the foreigners also are made subject, in accordance with the saying, “Hear, O God, prayer; to thee shall all flesh come” (Ps. 64:3). [Col. 0389C]

> [Note: [Col. 0390D] The Royal codex reads, “Hear, O God.” Then the printed editions have “my prayer.” In the manuscripts *my* is absent; and Hilary himself observes, in his exposition of Psalm 64, no. 3, that it is absent from the authentic texts. In the same exposition, no. 5, he explains “all flesh” as the whole human race.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0389C] “Hear, O God.”]

For it is worthy of God that all nations should be subject to him and that the whole body of flesh should be instructed unto confession of this eternal mercy. [Col. 0389C]

### 13. The Jews first rejected, then to be received. With God’s withdrawal there is no strength.

But after learning, according to the title’s inscription, what persons shall be changed, and after receiving the doctrine of him who is the eternal David, the prophet hastens to enter the eternal Jerusalem, the city in heaven of the firstborn and of the saints who surround God (Heb. 12:23), awaiting the guide who will lead him there. For it follows:

> **Verses 11–12.** “Who will lead me into the city of encirclement? Who will lead me even into Idumaea? Is it not thou, O God, who hast cast us off, and wilt not go forth with our forces?” [Col. 0390A]

> [Note: [Col. 0390D] The printed editions read “in the heavenly places,” against the sacred Greek and Latin text together with the manuscripts.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0389C] “Wilt not go forth, O God,” as in the Vulgate.]

Esau is “defection,” and Edom, according to Genesis, is “failing” (Gen. 25:30); and according to the Apostle, the remnant of Israel is to be saved (Rom. 11:25). Therefore, while desiring to be led into the city of encirclement, the prophet knows that he must first come as far as Idumaea—that is, to that defection of the former people, in which the elder shall serve the younger (Gen. 25:23).

> [Note: [Col. 0390C] “Because the elder”; shortly afterward, “will turn.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0390D] In the Royal manuscript, “because the elder”; and shortly afterward, “will turn,” not “will not turn.”]

And the final preaching will turn the hearts of fathers toward their children (Luke 1:17), when he who comes from Zion removes sins and impieties from Jacob. Yet the same one will lead them who earlier destroyed and cast them off because of their impiety. For when Jerusalem was captured and the kingdom abandoned, he left them unworthy and rejected, though formerly he had been accustomed to support them with spiritual aids and to protect them against the wars of their enemies by a heavenly army. [Col. 0390B] But now, with the guardianship of the Holy Spirit having left them, there is no help of divine defense in their forces—that is, in their armies.

> [Note: [Col. 0390D] The words “that is, in their armies” are absent from the Royal manuscript. The same Hebrew word signifies both “armies” and “powers.”]

Therefore, because he destroyed them, he will not go forth with their forces.

### 14. Our salvation depends upon God.

But, with hope restored because he will save the remnant that is Israel, the prophet did not keep silence concerning mercy, saying:

> **Verses 13–14.** “Give us help out of tribulation, for human salvation is vain. In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself shall bring to nothing those who trouble us.”

He knows that salvation hoped for from human beings is vain, because without God’s mercy there is no use even in this life, according to the saying: “Thy mercy is better than life” (Ps. 62:4). Unless life is undertaken for the advancement of eternity, it will be in us the source of miseries rather than of life. [Col. 0390C] Therefore help from God prevails in tribulations, because human salvation is vain.

He asks for help out of tribulation, intending, through help given, to perform mighty deeds in God: so that, all of us having been freed from the law of sin (Rom. 6:22), we may remain rather in God’s justification; so that we may wage battle not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual wickednesses (Eph. 6:12) and the rulers of the world.

> [Note: [Col. 0390D] Thus the manuscripts, following the Greek, *τοὺς κοσμοκράτορας* (*tous kosmokratoras*), “the world-rulers.” The printed editions read “powers of the world.”]

God himself slays Satan by the spirit of his mouth; the sin which previously troubled us no longer reigns in our immortal body (Rom. 6:12); and death is swallowed up by life in the conflict of victory—

> [Note: [Col. 0391D] The Royal codex reads “in the conflict of victory.” Paul’s passage is intended here, where the Greek has *εἰς νῖκος* (*eis nikos*), “into victory”; or, according to others and to Hilary himself, *εἰς νεῖκος* (*eis neikos*), “into conflict.” Here he combines both readings.]

—through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages (1 Cor. 15:53). Amen. [Col. 0391A]

## Psalm LX

> For the end.  
> A hymn of David.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0391D] In the Hymns, in agreement with the Greek.]
>
> Hear, O Lord, my supplication; attend to my prayer.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0391D] Hilary: “O God, [hear] my prayer.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0391D] “To my prayer.”]
>
> From the ends of the earth I cried to thee, while my heart was distressed. Thou hast exalted me upon a rock. Thou hast led me—
>
> [Note: [Col. 0391D] Hilary: “thou hast brought me forth.”]
>
> —because thou hast become my hope, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy. I shall dwell in thy tabernacle for ages. **Diapsalma.** I shall be protected under the covering of thy wings, because thou, O God, hast heard my prayer; thou hast given an inheritance to those who fear thy name. Thou wilt add days upon days to the king; his years unto the days of generation and generation.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0391D] Hilary: “of generation.”]
>
> He remains forever in the sight of God. Who shall seek his mercy and truth for them? Thus will I sing praise to thy name, O God, for age upon age, that I may render my vows day by day.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0391D] Below, “O God” is absent.]

## Exposition of the Psalm

### 1. The psalm is of one longing in eternal hope.

**Verse 1.** This is a simple psalm, containing the prophecy of eternal rejoicing. For its superscription includes neither events accomplished nor titles indicating some meaning.

> [Note: [Col. 0391D] Royal manuscript: “a title.” The editions of Bad., Er., and Lips. read “titles of some meaning.”]

It is only “a hymn for the end,” so that it may be understood that what the Prophet sang is to be unfolded at the end, whether of the psalm or of the times.

> [Note: [Col. 0391D] We restore “at the end” from the manuscript of St. Michael, where other editions preferred “for the end.” The Royal codex, omitting the preceding particle *ut* (“so that”), does not then contain “is to be understood.”]

It is the prayer of a righteous person hoping for eternity and rejoicing that he has been raised together in Christ into the heavenly places. For he begins thus. [Col. 0391B]

### 2. The confidence of the righteous. Hence, though in the flesh, he is a stranger to the flesh.  
*(See Exposition of Psalm 64, no. 10.)*

**Verses 2–3.** “Hear, O God, my prayer; attend to my supplication. From the ends of the earth I cried to thee, while my heart was distressed.”

> [Note: [Col. 0391D] “To my supplication.”]

This saint asks that his supplication be heard; and such is his confidence that he desires attention to be given to his prayer—whether it is innocent, chaste, and faithful, and whether it proceeds from the inmost fear of conscience and heart. For according to Paul (Rom. 10:10), one must believe with the heart and confess with the mouth unto salvation.

> [Note: [Col. 0392D] “According to the Apostle.”]

The reason why his prayer deserves attention is that, while distressed in heart, he cried from the ends of the earth. He did not dwell in the furthest wildernesses or beside the ocean’s shore, and thus cry with a distressed heart from earth’s ends. [Col. 0392A] Rather, knowing that while he dwells in flesh—which is earth—he already lives at the end of the flesh, since, according to the Apostle, while dwelling in the body he is absent from the body (2 Cor. 5:8)—

> [Note: [Col. 0391D, 0392D] The Paris editions wrongly read “is absent from the Lord.” Paul’s statement intended is: “We prefer rather to be absent from the body.”]

—and since, while living, he no longer lives for himself, nor does he himself live, but Christ lives in him (Gal. 2:20), yet groaning in this dwelling-place (2 Cor. 5:4), hastening to be clothed over: therefore he cries with a distressed heart from the ends of the earth, because he has both the necessity of living in the flesh and the hope of ceasing from the flesh’s vices, saying: [Col. 0392A]

### 3. Christ is his hope and strength.

**Verses 4–5.** “Thou hast exalted me upon a rock. Thou hast brought me forth, because thou hast become my hope, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy. I shall dwell in thy tabernacle for ages.”

> [Note: [Col. 0392D] The words “thou hast brought me forth,” omitted in the printed editions, are restored from the manuscripts. In Greek we read *ὡδήγησάς με* (*hōdēgēsas me*), “thou hast guided me”; the Vulgate has *deduxisti me*, “thou hast led me.” Accordingly, shortly afterward we have “led into the hope of eternity,” not “brought forth.”]

Thus the saint now cries from earth’s ends because he has been exalted upon the rock. Now the rock, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 10:4), is Christ, whom God exalted and to whom he gave the name above every name (Phil. 2:9). In him he also chose us before the foundation of the world in the heavenly places (Eph. 1:4). [Col. 0392B] Through him we have been led into the hope of eternity, and in this hope we are not put to shame.

> [Note: [Col. 0392D] “We shall be put to shame.”]

For this same hope has become for us a tower of strength against the enemy. Although there is a strong and firm defense in walls, the entire strength of the walls themselves lies in towers. Therefore God, who exalts us upon the rock, has become a tower of strength, because through this hope we withstand the devil’s force and his snares, enclosed in the most secure defense of faith against him and his spiritual wickednesses, since we shall dwell in God’s tabernacle for ages—remaining through ages and times flowing endlessly into eternity, without any limit of duration. [Col. 0392C]

### 4. His protection is God’s mercy; prayer obtains it.

But because these things, though laid up in hope for the saints, are still deferred under the dispensation of time—

> [Note: [Col. 0392D] Thus the manuscript of St. Michael, supported by the Vatican manuscript, which reads less well, “hope laid up already for the saints.” The printed editions read, “though by hope they already belong to the saints.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0392D] The editions inserted the particle “and” here, against the manuscripts.]

—he shows, by the interposed *diapsalma*, what defense keeps one safe in the meantime, saying:

> **Verse 6.** “I shall be protected under the covering of thy wings, because thou, O God, hast heard my prayer.”

The divine utterance signifies the protection of God’s mercy under the covering of wings. Since this has been treated in the preceding psalms—

> [Note: [Col. 0392D] Nothing has so far been discussed concerning this meaning, unless perhaps in Psalm 56, no. 3, and even there so briefly that it is scarcely perceptible.]

—it would now be superfluous and idle to speak of it. But the merit of protection is granted through the faith of prayer, according to the saying: “Ask, and it shall be given you” (Matt. 7:7). [Col. 0393A]

### 5. The inheritance of the saints. Christ to be King of kings after the general resurrection.

He also indicates the hope for which he is to be sheltered under the protection of God’s wings, saying: “Thou hast given an inheritance to those who fear thy name.”

> [Note: [Col. 0393D] The Royal and St. Michael manuscripts read “to those who fear thee.” We retain “to those who fear thy name,” because the exposition that follows agrees with this reading.]

**Verses 7–8.** “Thou wilt add days upon days to the king; his years unto the days of generation and generation. He remains forever in the sight of God.”

This inheritance of the saint is life, incorruption, kingship, and dwelling coeternally with God.

> [Note: [Col. 0393D] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read “with God.”]

This inheritance is not written for Israel alone, but for those who fear God’s name. For the king’s days are eternal: either because the saints, who will not be slaves of sin, are kings (see Exposition of Psalm 2, no. 42), according to the Apostle’s saying, “Already you reign without us; and would that you did reign, that we also might reign with you” (1 Cor. 4:8); [Col. 0393B]

> [Note: [Col. 0393D] “You have reigned.”]

or because this Prophet too is king; or because, in the eternal kingdom, he who sits at the right hand must reign until he places his enemies beneath his feet. This does not mean that he himself will then cease to be king; rather, when he has delivered the kingdom to God the Father, he himself will reign together with those who are kings.

> [Note: [Col. 0393D] The printed editions read “with them.” The Royal manuscript’s “he himself” is more elegant. Hilary prudently avoids here the error concerning the end of Christ’s kingdom which Eusebius attributes to Marcellus.]

This, I think, explains why days of generation and generation are now added to the days upon days of his years, while he remains forever in the sight of God.

> [Note: [Col. 0393D–0394D] The editions read “to remain forever,” with wholly faulty punctuation before and after. Hilary interprets “unto the days of generation and generation” concerning Christ’s kingdom, which is followed by the universal resurrection; but he refers the following words, “He remains forever in the sight of God,” to God’s kingdom, which begins from the foretold resurrection of all but has no end.]

Thus the period in which he must reign until he places his enemies under his feet is comprehended from generation to generation, because this generation is followed by the generation of spiritual birth from the dead; while the reservation concerning his eternity is proclaimed by the statement that he is forever in the sight of God. [Col. 0393C] He himself is the firstborn from the dead (Col. 1:18).

The Lord mentioned this regeneration to the apostles in these words: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). He therefore reveals the time of this generation, and the years of the king are increased, even unto this generation, beyond days upon days. But he himself will remain eternal in the sight of God—

> [Note: [Col. 0394D] In the printed editions *ipse* (“he himself”) is repeated here, but not in the manuscripts. Then the Royal manuscript reads, “will remain eternal, now in all things.”]

—when all whom he has redeemed have been assumed as kings of heaven and coheirs of eternity, as he delivers them as a kingdom to God the Father.

### 6. The blessed lack nothing to desire.

And because, having become sharers, members of one body, and conformed to him, corruption and death will no longer rule in them, when they are filled unto all the fullness of God, the spirit of prophecy added: “Who shall seek his mercy and truth for them?” [Col. 0393D–0394A]

> [Note: [Col. 0394D] Royal manuscript: “him,” contrary both to the Greek and to the exposition that follows.]

Those generations whom he will regenerate in himself from the dead unto life, and who have remained in the hope of God’s glory, will no longer lack his mercy and truth. Then, when they have been handed over as a kingdom to God the Father, they will be received as kings, his mercy and truth having been fulfilled in them all, through whom they rejoice that they have been redeemed unto life and all have access to the Father. After this, nothing of mercy and truth is sought from the Lord, since they are filled unto God’s fullness.

The saying of this prophet resembles what the Lord spoke to the apostles: “Now indeed you have sorrow; but I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you. In that day you shall ask me nothing” (John 16:22). [Col. 0394B]

> [Note: [Col. 0394D] “Shall take away.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0394D] At first we conjectured that “from you shall be” ought to be read; but the ancient reading must be retained, because these are no longer Christ’s words but the interpreter’s words, confirming the prophet’s words by Christ’s saying.]

For then no one will take their joy from them.

### 7. The work of the blessed.

Therefore the Prophet confirms himself in this hope of eternity, saying:

> **Verse 9.** “Thus will I sing praise to thy name for age upon age, that I may render my vows day by day.”

He will sing praise for age upon age and render vows day by day, enclosed by no end of times, rendering in eternal hymns the joys of eternal vows. When every weakness of earthly bodies has been removed, he will live the heavenly and angelic life, rendering vows day by day, according to the saying: “I will render my vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the sight of all his people, in the midst of thee, O Jerusalem” (Ps. 115:18–19)—that is, of the heavenly mother and the free city—through God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0394C]

## Psalm LXI

> For the end, for Jeduthun. A psalm of David.
>
> Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation. For he himself is my God and my savior,
>
> [Note: [Col. 0394D] Hilary: “my protector.”]
>
> my helper: I shall no longer be moved. How long do you rush upon a man? You all kill, as against a leaning wall and a battered fence. Yet they have devised to cast away my honor; I ran in thirst. With their mouth they blessed, and with their heart they cursed.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0394D] Below, “they devised.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0394D] Hilary has *diapsalma* here.]
>
> Yet my soul shall be subject to God, because from him is my patience. For he himself is my God and my savior,
>
> [Note: [Col. 0394D] Hilary: “He is God and Savior.”]
>
> my helper; I shall not depart. In God is my salvation and my glory; God is my help.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395D] Hilary: “God of my help.”]
>
> My hope is in God. Hope in him, every assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him, because God is our helper. **Diapsalma.** Yet the sons of men are vain, the sons of men deceitful in the balances, so that they may together deceive by vanity itself. Do not hope in iniquity, nor desire plunder. If riches abound,
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395D] Hilary: “flow.”]
>
> do not set your heart upon them. God has spoken once; these two things have I heard: that power belongs to God, and mercy to thee, O Lord; because thou wilt render to each one according to his works.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395D] Hilary: “to each individual.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395D] Hilary: “his.”]

## Exposition of the Psalm

### 1. The aim of prophecy; what this psalm teaches.
