The utterance of prophecy is written only for some profit to its hearers: either to teach knowledge or to strengthen innocence of will, as does this psalm.

> [Note: [Col. 0395C] We have removed “ad” on the authority of our manuscript.]

**Verse 1.** It is sung by David “for Jeduthun,” in which one is instructed in the fear of God, in steadfast endurance of human and spiritual wickednesses, and is strengthened in contempt for wealth, because avarice is the root of all evils.

> [Note: [Col. 0395D] Thus the Royal manuscript. The editions read “to Jeduthun … from the fear of God.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395D] The Tours manuscript reads “we are instructed … we are strengthened,” instead of “one is instructed … is strengthened.”]

For in these lies the certain condition of blessed and eternal life: if there is both piety toward God, patience amid adversities, and contempt for riches. Therefore the psalm begins with confession of God. [Col. 0395B]

### 2. The theology of the pagans is dark and erring. How great a light shines from the sacred books. By faith the mind has a resting-place.

**Verses 2–3.** “Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation. And he himself is my God, and my savior, my protector; I shall no longer be moved.”

> [Note: [Col. 0395C] “My Savior.”]

The prophet begins the confession of God in accordance with the common feeling of humankind: after the long night of ignorance; after the doubtful and uncertain doctrine of human opinions; after the varied judgment of diverse religions—

> [Note: [Col. 0395C] “Vain.”]

—when for a long time people had erred and inquired concerning God, whether he is one or many; whether of one sex or of two; whether equal or unequal in power; uniform or varied in age; whether unbegotten in nature altogether, or whether some were at some time begotten—

> [Note: [Col. 0395D] In the Royal and St. Michael manuscripts, “or,” and so consistently thereafter, in place of “whether.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0396C, 0395D] One Vatican manuscript reads “begetter”; another, “begotten”; the Royal and St. Michael manuscripts, “begotten [plural].” Shortly afterward the editions read “with some,” omitting “from.”]

—and then, after some had struggled with great age and long labor to establish either that no gods exist at all or that they are remote from the care of human life; after most had argued either that the sun and the other stars are gods, or that the world itself, enduring in the appearance of eternity and in its changes, is God together with all that it brings forth from itself; and after many had bestowed the divine name and honor upon fire, water, or spirit; while others worshiped wood, stones, and metals in the forms of human beings, birds, and beasts: finally, when most of them, exhausted and frustrated in all their inquiries—and especially the wise among them (Socrates, in Cicero, *Academicae Quaestiones*, book 4)—had taught that they knew this one thing, namely, that a human being knew none of these things, then, after this ignorance which was, as it were, a necessary confession—

> [Note: [Col. 0396C] “Ignorance.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0395D–0396D] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “ignorance.” We would prefer “the necessary confession of ignorance,” but we have already observed more than once examples of inversions of this sort. Not only did Socrates, according to Cicero, confess generally that he knew only this, that he knew nothing; Cicero himself, in book 4 of the *Academicae Quaestiones*, specifically makes this confession concerning knowledge of God: “We are compelled, by the disagreement of the wise, to be ignorant of the Lord.”]

—every wise person who turns to the prophets and apostles receives the whole law of God under the mystery of the eternal dispensation. In it he considers the reason for the soul’s being brought into and joined to this body—

> [Note: [Col. 0396D] The Royal manuscript has “joined,” without the particle *-que*. This appears to mean that from Scripture we receive how the soul has been brought into the body and in what its bond with the body consists. But in fact Hilary means only this: Scripture testifies to us to the eternity of the soul joined to the body. For, according to the Gospel (Matt. 10:28), a human being does not kill the soul together with the body, as he says more expressly in his exposition of Psalm 62, no. 11.]

—in it he receives the division of nations according to the number of angels (Deut. 32:8; see Exposition of Psalm 2, no. 31); in it he hears both that there is a ruler of this world (John 14:30) and of the election of one people (Deut. 32:9); in it he is not ignorant of the author of human death; and he feels and groans that the law of sin dwells in his flesh, resisting the law of his mind (Rom. 7:23). [Col. 0396B]

Afterward he comes to know that the Spirit of God, the Power of God, the Wisdom of God, the Son of God, and the only-begotten God became man for the remission of sin and the condemnation of sin’s law.

> [Note: [Col. 0396D] The Paris editions read “the only-begotten of God,” less well. It is noteworthy that among the titles of the Word assuming flesh Hilary first lists “the Spirit of God,” then “the Power of God,” because in the angelic words, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High,” etc., he understood the person of the Word.]

Having undergone the lot of human sufferings, he died in order to condemn in himself the impious temptations of heavenly wickednesses, and to bring eternity to all who were dying through the law of sin dwelling in our flesh. Then, having received this mystery of piety and having been set, after the night of ignorance, in the light of knowledge, he says: “Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation. For he himself is my God, my Savior, and my protector; I shall no longer be moved.” [Col. 0396C]

Having found the settled ground of faith after wandering errors and the judgment of impiety—

> [Note: [Col. 0396D] Royal manuscript: “who [is] protector.”]

—because he has recognized his protector and Savior, he is no longer moved. For what remains beyond this for humanity’s ignorance and anxiety, when the eternity of soul and body—that is, of the whole human being—is proclaimed; when God’s assumption and taking up of our earthly flesh is shown under the mystery of this great piety; when remission of sins is granted through the condemnation of sin’s law; and when our humanity has a seat at God’s right hand in heaven? [Col. 0397A]

### 3. Those who deny God’s embodiment. How ruinous their arguments are.

But pagan impiety undermines this hope of human blessedness, denying that a human being may advance to God because of the emptiness of worldly wisdom, and taking away from God his fellowship in an assumed body, as though they were judges and regulators of divine power. They act as though it were more difficult for God to assume humanity than to form it amid so great an order of its nature and life.

> [Note: [Col. 0397D–0398D] For the conjunction of soul with body—or of the incorporeal with the corporeal—appears more difficult than the conjunction of the incorporeal God with a human being who is incorporeal in respect of the soul. Augustine, in *The City of God*, book 10, chapter 29, explains Hilary’s thought, speaking against Porphyry and the Platonists: “What is said to you to be incredible when God is said to have assumed a human soul and body? … It ought more readily to be received in faith that spirit should be joined to spirit, or, to use words current among you, incorporeal to incorporeal, even if the human is joined to the divine and the mutable to the immutable, than that body should cleave to the incorporeal.” The latter, however, occurs daily in a human being. For, as he says in Epistle 137, no. 11: “If the soul is not deceived concerning its nature, it perceives itself to be incorporeal; much more is the Word of God incorporeal. Therefore the union of God’s Word and soul ought to be more credible than that of soul and body.” The same point is expounded no less clearly by Augustine himself, or another writer, in Sermon 371, chapter 3.]

The prophet immediately rebukes their impious detraction, saying:

> **Verse 4.** “How long do you rush upon a man? You all kill, as against a leaning wall and a battered fence.”

> [Note: [Col. 0397C] “To form their detraction.”]

For these ignorant and impious arguments impel toward vices a person inclined to them, and plunge one already shaken and falling, destroying him by the counsels of deceptive and harmful exhortations—as though the will itself, the pander of vices, were too little for him, while despair of eternal judgment and recompense further urges that will toward the use of present and bodily things alone.

> [Note: [Col. 0398D] The Paris editions read “pleasure,” wrongly, as is clear from the following relative pronoun *quam*, “which.”]

### 4. David thirsts for righteousness. He gives no place to detraction.

But he knows that this wall of his body, which lust, drunkenness, greed, and anger had formerly pierced, has now been built up in himself into God’s house with living stones; and he remembers that he was created in God’s image. Certain that he is being prepared in conformity with God’s glory, he added:

> **Verse 5.** “Yet they have devised to cast away my honor; I ran in thirst.”

> [Note: [Col. 0398D] The editions here and below read “into thirst,” against the manuscripts and the Greek.]

While they plan to take away his honor, he runs in thirst. For there is in the saints a thirst for eternal goods and a spiritual hunger, concerning which it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5:6).

> [Note: [Col. 0398D] Royal manuscript: “For thirst for eternal goods and spiritual hunger are …,” omitting “there is.”]

Therefore, thirsting, he held to the course of righteousness throughout his whole life, preserving that life unimpaired even against the detraction of those who opposed him.

> [Note: [Col. 0398D] The printed editions read “knowing”; corrected from the Vatican manuscript.]

For he also learned from his Lord that all his works should be praised even by the judgment of Gentile testimony, when it is said: “So let your works shine before men, that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). Thus Paul too, pleasing all in all (1 Cor. 10:33), gives offense neither to Jews nor Greeks nor the Church, lest an adversary have anything evil to say of him. [Col. 0398A]

> [Note: [Col. 0398D] The editions here inserted the particle “through,” which is absent from the Royal manuscript and the Greek, as also above in Psalm 52, no. 16, where the manuscripts and Greek agree in reading “all” without “in.”]

The adversary indeed retains the purpose and desire of detraction, although Paul rendered himself free from every occasion for detraction. This too we recognize in this saint running in thirst. For it follows: “With their mouth they blessed, and with their heart they cursed.” Outwardly, they blessed his honor by acknowledging his virtuous life, while inwardly they cursed through the malice of hatred.

> [Note: [Col. 0398C] “They preserve.”]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0398D] The St. Michael manuscript reads “they preserve.” Nothing should be changed. Those are meant here who outwardly praise persons of approved life while tearing them apart with inward hatred.]

### 5. Meanwhile he cultivates patience.

But this saint repeats, with the intervention of a *diapsalma*, what is especially salutary to him, showing that there must be in us perseverance of unwearied confession. For it follows:

> **Verses 6–10.** “Yet my soul is subject to God, because from him is my patience. For he is my God and Savior, my helper; I shall not depart. In God is my salvation and my glory; the God of my help, and my hope is in my God.”

> [Note: [Col. 0398D] The Paris editions read “my help.” Shortly afterward we restore from the Royal manuscript “in my God,” where the printed editions preferred “in God is.”]

Let these persons indeed strike the leaning wall and the already shaken fence, and, though blessing with their mouth, curse with their heart. Yet he knows that his soul must be subject to God, because his patience comes from him. For from him he learned neither to turn away his face from spitting nor to withdraw his cheeks from blows, neither to refuse vinegar mingled with gall to drink nor to curse after buffetings and scourges. He himself is his God and Savior, and also his helper, lest he should be moved and depart from the perseverance of this patience and the confidence of his hope. [Col. 0398C] For in him are his salvation, glory, and hope: he will raise him together with himself and render him conformed to his heavenly glory.

### 6. He exhorts others to pour out their hearts. What this means.

And because he himself, as a prophet, is also the preacher of this hope to others, he added: “Hope in him, every assembly of the people, and pour out your hearts before him, because God is our helper.”

Nothing hidden, nothing closed, nothing bound is to be retained in the heart under confession of God. Every affection must be poured out before him, so that we have no confidence in ourselves, but may be helped through him, before whom we pour ourselves out as though on account of sin. [Col. 0399A]

But our hearts must be poured out before him in tears and weeping, according to the saying: “My tears were my bread day and night, while it was said to me daily, ‘Where is thy God?’ I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me” (Ps. 41:4).

> [Note: [Col. 0399D] Thus according to the Greek and the Royal manuscript. The printed editions read “loaves.”]

This shows that the pouring out of the soul consists in the shedding of tears, because he who alone is the faithful helper must be entreated through them.

### 7. Among the vain it achieves nothing. The vain are liars.

But the prophet, having discharged his duty, knows that his admonition carries little weight with the ungodly. For immediately, after the intervention of a diapsalm, he adds, V. 10: “Nevertheless the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, that they may themselves deceive from vanity into the same.” Men are vain [Note: [Col. 0399D] “Who either …”] because either they themselves hope in vain things, or it is vain to hope in them [Note: [Col. 0399D] In the printed editions: “vain men themselves hope in vain things, or it is vain to hope in him”: a mutilated reading, restored with the help of the manuscripts.]; and they are liars also because, in their awareness of their ungodliness, they either are deceived or deceive others. And they are liars in this respect: that they deceive in the balances, that is, while acting unjustly under the name of justice. For where they promise an examination governed by measured prudence, there they pursue the aims of unrestrained ungodliness, entangling themselves in the very error which they professed to drive away from others. And therefore they themselves are deceived from vanity into the same thing—that is, into that from which they boast of having escaped.

### 8. Desire for riches must be cut off.

But the chief root of iniquity lies in the desire for money; whoever pursues it is submerged in the shipwreck of a most grievous storm. It follows, V. 11: “Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire plunder. If riches flow, do not set your heart upon them.” [Note: [Col. 0399D] In Greek, ἐὰν ῥεῇ, “if it flows,” which the Royal manuscript renders more expressly as *si fluant*, “if they flow,” rather than the common editions’ *si affluant*, “if they abound.”] For in these there are great enticements of desire and affection: they carry off minds and seize wavering thoughts. Therefore not only must their plunder not be desired; rather, our will must be withdrawn from them, even if they are offered [Note: [Col. 0399D] Thus the Royal and Mic. manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “and even if they abound, [our will] must be restrained.”] and flow in abundance, lest, once desired and coveted, they rule us. For these goods are not coeternal with our hopes; nor do they descend with us into hell, nor rise with us from hell. Faith, piety, self-control, and kindness must be sought; above all, the knowledge of God must be pursued. But these things are vain and, by their own nature, snares leading to every necessity of wrongdoing; they must be avoided.

### 9. Father and Son are one God. The power of both is one.

And the prophet added what ought rather to be sought in hope of eternity, saying, VV. 12–13: “God has spoken once; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and mercy to thee, O Lord, because thou wilt render to each according to his works.” Though God spoke once, he heard two things; and what is known under the meaning of one utterance must necessarily be connected.

For at the beginning of the psalm he had directed a prophetic confession to God [Note: [Col. 0399D] “By prophetic confession.”], saying: “Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation.” Thus the frenzy of Jewish impiety had absolutely to be driven away, so that the Son might be taught to be signified in God the Father, just as now one is also shown in the other. For he testified that this was the faith by which his soul was to be made subject to God: because his salvation was from him [Note: [Col. 0400D] “His Saviour.”]. And it has often been discussed that Jesus is the Saviour.

When God spoke once, therefore, two things were understood and heard: just as in the words, “Father, I have manifested thy name to men” (John 17:6), he signified the Son in the Father; [Note: [Col. 0400D] Paris edition: “as now, in one [utterance], once,” etc. This reading would not be objectionable.] so now, when the Lord God spoke once, he heard these two things: “That power belongs to God, and mercy to thee, O Lord, because thou wilt render to each according to his works.”

Paul knows both in the one—that is, he confesses neither apart from the other—when he says: “There is one God, and one Lord” (1 Cor. 8:6), because the Lord is signified in God, and God in the Lord. Thus, when God speaks once, these two things are heard: “That power belongs to God, and mercy to thee, O Lord.” For from him is his Salvation; and the Son has received all things from the Father, and therefore in him the power of God is either received or begotten. “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). Therefore he who is judge is the requiter of each person. But the power belongs to him from whom the only-begotten God has been born as judge; and his power is from God, since he received judgment from the Father. Thus neither does he who is judge lack power, nor does he who is God lack mercy.

Certainly, one who does not confess both in the one must remain guilty before eternal judgment, although he who is both is not to be understood as a single one, since our Lord Jesus Christ says, “The Father is in me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38). He is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LXII

A psalm of David, when he had gone into the desert of Idumaea.

“O God, my God, I watch for thee at dawn [Note: [Col. 0400D] Hilary: “I watch from the light.”]; my soul has thirsted for thee, and likewise my flesh. [Note: [Col. 0400D] Another reading: “In a deserted, trackless, and waterless land.”] In a desert, trackless, and waterless land, so have I appeared before thee in the sanctuary, that I might see thy power and thy glory. For thy mercy is better than life; my lips shall praise thee.” [Note: [Col. 0400D] Hilary adds, “O Lord.”] “Thus shall I bless thee in my life; in thy name I shall lift up my hands. As with marrow and fatness let my soul be filled, and lips of exultation shall praise thy name. [Col. 0400D] If [Note: [Col. 0400D] Hilary: “I remembered thee.”] I have remembered thee upon my bed, in the mornings [Note: [Col. 0400D] Hilary: “I meditated.”] I shall meditate on thee, because thou hast been my helper. And in the covering of thy wings [Note: [Col. 0400D] Below: “I shall hope.”] I shall exult; my soul has clung [Col. 0401A] after thee; thy right hand has upheld me. But they have sought my life in vain; they shall enter into the depths of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes. But the king shall rejoice in [Note: [Col. 0401C] Hilary: “God.”] the Lord; [Note: [Col. 0401C] Hilary adds, “and.”] everyone who swears by him shall be praised, because the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.”

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

### 1. David, a type of Christ, intent upon divine matters in the desert.

V. 1. The book of Kings records that David lived in the desert (1 Sam. 22:5), so that he who prefigured the sufferings of the Lord might, even while dwelling in the desert, prophesy of them—of the only-begotten God likewise to dwell in the desert. But, as was fitting for a holy man and worthy of so great a prophet, when he had withdrawn from the hatred of the ungodly into solitude, he occupied himself with the greatest mysteries of heavenly things. Far removed from every gathering of human impiety or ignorance, he directed his mind toward those things by which knowledge of eternity and merit were acquired.

Not occupied or hindered by the common concerns of life and of the world, but in the peaceful and unoccupied seclusion of his solitude—where nothing offensive came before his eyes or mind—he was busily engaged solely in divine pursuits. [Note: [Col. 0401C] Mic. manuscript: “enjoying leisure.”] Let us see, then, with what the speech of the psalm begins.

### 2.

V. 2. “O God, my God, I watch for thee from the light.” [Note: [Col. 0401C] Paris edition and Mic. manuscript: “at dawn.”] The day has truly begun unto the joy and knowledge of God for one whose very beginning of prayer to God is the beginning of light. He prays to the God of the universe, yet to God as his own through the knowledge of recognition.

### 3. Hope of eternity is implanted in us. Souls are implanted by God. As the soul, so also the flesh will have eternity. They must be distinguished. David’s thirst is spiritual. He thirsts to see God.

Prayer consists not so much in words as in feeling; and therefore he adds, V. 3: “My soul has thirsted for thee—how simply likewise my flesh—in a deserted, trackless, and waterless land.” [Note: [Col. 0401C] Royal manuscript, here and below: “how manifoldly”; but the following exposition conflicts with this version. Hilary’s translator must necessarily have read πῶς ἁπλῶς, “how simply,” in place of the Greek ποσαπλῶς, “how manifoldly.” Then the printed editions, except the Paris edition, read: “in a deserted and trackless and waterless land.” Hilary reads below: “in a desert and in a trackless,” etc.] Thus his soul thirsts for God, with whom is the fountain of life, earnestly desiring to drink.

Indeed, every person’s mind is borne by a kind of natural impulse toward the knowledge and hope of eternity, because it is as though implanted and impressed upon all that we should judge the origin of our souls to be divine, when the mind itself recognizes no small kinship with a heavenly race within itself. [Note: [Col. 0401D] In the Royal manuscript and one Vatican manuscript: “knowledge.” The question of wherein this affinity of the soul with the divine race consists is discussed in Psalm 129. Hilary proclaims the soul akin to God, yet teaches that it was made, since, as he says in *On the Trinity*, book X, §20, “every soul is a work of God.” Thus he has nothing in common with the error attributed to Origen, and by Augustine, *Heresies* 70, to the Priscillianists, who hold that the soul is a part of God, of the same nature and substance as God. Rather, he anticipated Augustine’s rule concerning the origin of souls, *Letter* 190, §4: “that we should believe it not to be a part of God but a creature; not born from God, but made by him, and by a wondrous condescension adopted into his kind, not by equality of natural dignity.” Hilary’s view is also illustrated by Prudentius, *Apotheosis* V.829:

> Let it be a thing of God—I do not deny it; yet that thing  
> Which began in time must by no means be called a part of God.

[Col. 0402D] And V.833:

> It is indeed the breath of the Lord; but it is not the full Spirit and power of God,  
> Sent forth under so great a restraint as the Breather chose  
> To preserve in breathing the measure of his breath.

Quintilian, *Institutes of Oratory* I.1, says, “The origin of the mind is believed to be heavenly”; and Cicero, at the end of *On Ends* II, says, “The most learned ancients thought that there is in souls something heavenly and divine.” This confirms what Hilary here asserts: that this is, as it were, implanted in human beings.]

But these earthly bodies, which are compacted into material for vices, while infected by those things in which they take pleasure as though naturally, despair [Note: [Col. 0401C] “If not themselves.” Then the words “to be able to attain” are omitted.] of attaining [Note: [Col. 0402D] Royal manuscript: “if not themselves.” We would prefer *hi*, “these.” The same manuscript also lacks “to be able to attain.”] fellowship in and the gift of heaven—as though the soul’s nature were not also infected by the vices in which the body delights [Note: [Col. 0402D] Printed editions: “delights.” The Royal manuscript more correctly has the singular, “delights,” namely the soul.]; or as though, when bodily delight flows over into the mind, the body did not draw the mind with it into the affection of pleasure. But whatever shares the same pleasure must share the same condemnation. [Note: [Col. 0402C] “By will.”]

Yet we, instructed by spiritual teaching, know that salvation has been given by God to both soul and body, provided that, after the grace of regeneration, bodily sense is imbued with the joys of the mind—that is, provided that we live not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit (Rom. 8:4). For, according to the Apostle (Gal. 5:19 ff.), the works of spirit and flesh are distinguished [Note: [Col. 0401C] “Is distinguished.”] by the pursuits of vice and self-control. [Note: [Col. 0402D] We emend thus from the Tours manuscript. The printed editions have the singular, “is distinguished.”]

It is difficult, but most true, to hope for eternity for the body as well as for the soul. Therefore the prophet adds to his soul’s thirst: “My soul has thirsted for thee, and likewise my flesh,” retaining within himself nothing uncertain in the ambiguity of unbelief; but he professes that his flesh thirsts just as simply as his soul thirsts for God. For, thirsting, it thirsts not for the body but for God.

Although the necessity of nature itself held him, while he remained in a desert, trackless, and waterless place, in bodily thirst, he nevertheless knew that faith must be tested even through these sufferings of hunger and thirst in believers: so that, thirsting even for the body, the soul may thirst more for God than for the body. For neither hunger, nor distress, nor any kinds of suffering shall separate the Apostle from the love of God which is in Christ (Rom. 8:35). Therefore the holy man thirsts for God. And what he thirsts for, he testified in another psalm when he says: “My soul has thirsted for the living God: when shall I come and appear before thy face?” [Note: [Col. 0403C] “Before the face of God,” according to the Greek text.] (Ps. 41:3). This desire of the soul, this is the thirst of its hope: that the vision of God may come to it, that as soon as possible, caught up in clouds and raised to meet Christ God, it may appear before him.

### 4. Prophecy recounts as accomplished things that are yet to be done. One who appears to the Son also appears to the Father.

The prophet now also declares the feeling of this desire. For after the profession of thirst, after the privation of the desert, the trackless, and the waterless place—because in these, as it were, lie faith’s warfare and victory—he adds, V. 4: “Thus have I appeared before thee in the sanctuary, that I might see thy power and thy glory; because thy mercy is better than life.” [Note: [Col. 0403D] Printed editions, except the Paris edition: “of prophetic knowledge.”]

It is the characteristic of prophetic knowledge to recount as done things which are yet to be done. Hence there are frequent instances: “They gave me vinegar to drink,” though it was still to be drunk in the Passion (Ps. 68:22); and “They divided my garment,” though it was yet to be divided (Ps. 21:19). So now, thirsting for God in bodily thirst, he appears to him in his Holy One—through simplicity of flesh, thirst of soul, and prayer at dawn—because only those who have been tested through these things will be received by Christ or caught up in clouds to meet him.

But in the Holy One of God they will appear before God only according to the words, “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), and, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). For in the Son’s nature and name is contained the signification of the Father’s nature and name. One who appears to the Son [Note: [Col. 0403D] The common editions wrongly repeat here: “But one who appears to the Son.” It is worthy of notice how Hilary here distinguishes those who will be received by Christ from those who will be caught up in clouds to meet him. This resolves the puzzle of the distinction between Christ’s kingdom and God’s kingdom: first are reckoned the blessed before the resurrection, who reign only in Christ’s glorious body and are therefore frequently proclaimed co-raised with Christ and seated at God’s right hand; secondly, after the resurrection, those who reign in their own right.] or is received by the Son will appear to the Father in the Son.

### 5. Thirsting for the Holy One, he desires to see the Son.

And in order, by the meaning of this thirst, to show his desire for the Holy One in whom he was to appear before God, [Note: [Col. 0403C] “(2) By desire.”] he added: “That I might see thy power and thy glory”—that is, that he might see him who, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 1:24; Phil. 2:11), is both the Power of God and is in the glory of God. He will see him for no other purpose than to gain fellowship in eternity and obtain the eternity of the heavenly kingdom, because these things are prepared through God’s mercy beyond the blessedness of this life.

### 6. Hope of the future excels the present life. Resurrection is God’s mercy.

For this follows, V. 4: “Because thy mercy is better than life.” It is indeed a great gift of God that we have come into life; nature herself guides us to rejoice in being born. But because our whole lifetime is full of anxieties and pains, there is more hope in God’s mercy than in life: for death follows this life under the law of sin, while mercy restores eternity from death.

Just as the sowing and dissolution of wheat are more excellent than the preservation of wheat itself (1 Cor. 15:37–38)—for God clothes it as he wills in the ear—so it is a great gift of God’s mercy if, having died with Christ, we live in Christ. For Adam’s death itself was appointed under the signification of mercy, lest he should remain in eternal punishment; and the Apostle judges that for himself to be dissolved is better (Phil. 1:23). The prophet also declares his joy in abiding death, saying: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). [Note: [Col. 0403D] Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and the Royal manuscript: “of the death that will abide for him.” One Vatican manuscript: “abiding from death.”] For through it, once the law of sin has been dissolved, eternity of soul and body will now be rendered back, without the body of sin, with the advancement of glorious transformation. [Note: [Col. 0403C] “Because through him, once they have been released from the law of sin, of transformation …”] [Note: [Col. 0403D] Thus the Tours manuscript. The Royal manuscript has “because through him.” Then the printed editions read: “once released from the law of sin, of transformation,” etc. [Col. 0404D] But the reading of the Tours manuscript, which we have reproduced, is more polished.]

### 7. The lifting of hands is a lofty work. Life in Abraham’s bosom. Another, happier life.

Therefore, confident in God’s mercy, which is better than life, the prophet performs the duty of thanksgiving, saying, V. 5: “My lips shall praise thee, O Lord. Thus shall I bless thee in my life, and in thy name I shall lift up my hands.” He praises and blesses God both in speech and in deed; for while blessing him in his life, he will lift up his hands in his name.

By the lifting of hands we have often taught that there is signified not the posture of prayer but an indication of lofty work. [Note: [Col. 0404D] Paris edition: “a command”; the others: “a judgment.” Psalm 140 has “a duty.” But in the Treatises presently available, nothing has yet been said concerning this kind of meaning.] Therefore in this present life he has praised God because his mercy is better than lives. [Note: [Col. 0404D] In the Royal manuscript, here also, “life.” Although above Hilary preferred the singular “life,” here he must be thought to have read, with the Greek, “lives.” For he plainly distinguishes three lives: the first, in the world, full of pains and anxieties (§6); the second, peaceful in Abraham’s bosom and occupied with God’s praises; and the last, happier than both, which receives what eye has not seen, etc. This is called mercy, not because it is not given according to merits, but because the merits by which it is given were themselves given. We add that in Augustine, *Against Julian* II.8.29, where Hilary’s words from *Treatise on Psalm 51*, §23, are praised, the reading “better than lives” has been restored from manuscripts.]

For there is life after life, because one must live in Abraham’s bosom, where God’s name is blessed in the repose of the poor, [Note: [Col. 0404D] “In the repose of the poor.”] according to the prophet’s words: “The dead shall not praise thee, O Lord, nor all who descend into hell; but we who live bless the Lord” (Ps. 113:17–18). Above these lives, then, is that mercy which has prepared for those who love the Lord what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and has not entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2:9).

### 8. God is to be worshipped with a living and intelligent sacrifice.

Therefore he praises and blesses this mercy, no longer expecting sacrifices from the holocausts of cattle and the fatness of fat, but offering himself to God as a sacrifice in the confession of his soul alone and in the praise of blessing. This accords with: “The sacrifice of praise shall glorify me” (Ps. 49:23); “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (ibid. 14); and “For if thou hadst desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; thou wilt not delight in holocausts” (Ps. 50:18). For, when the prescription of the letter and of the allegories of the law has ceased, God is to be honoured by the praises of a living and intelligent sacrifice. [Note: [Col. 0405D] Paris edition: “of the allegorical law.”]

For he adds, V. 6: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness, and lips of exultation shall praise thy name.” He does not condemn those former things as though they were abominable, but confirms these as more desired, when he asks that his soul be filled with praise of exultation as with marrow and fatness, which were held to be the firstfruits of sacrifices.

### 9. Meditation on God at night and in the morning.

But these are duties not so much of words as of the mind, so that the sacrifice of praise may proceed from the holiness of works. Therefore he immediately adds, V. 7: “If I have remembered thee upon my bed, in the mornings I meditated upon thee.” [Note: [Col. 0405D] Thus the Royal manuscript, according to the Greek, ἐμελέτων, “I meditated.” So also what follows concerns meditation as a past act, not a future one; accordingly, the common editions’ “I shall meditate” was wrongly printed.]

Nocturnal remembrance completes morning meditation; and therefore he watches for God from the light, because from the purity of the couch—that is, of the bed—come both confidence and the conscience for morning prayer. Therefore he restrained thoughts creeping in beneath the secrecy of night by remembrance of God; and, struggling against incentives of the flesh, he aided himself by the fear of his God’s name.

For it follows, V. 8: “Because thou hast been my helper, and in the covering of thy wings I shall hope”; he is protected by meditation on God, through which God is his helper. For he has no concern other than pleasing God, when he remembers him alone upon his bed. He also meditates upon him in the mornings from his nocturnal remembrance because God is his helper; and he exults beneath the covering of God’s wings—that is, he is safe under the protection of the One who shelters him.

### 10. Those separated are also united by love.

But from this comes the advance and the cause of all these things, since it follows, V. 9: “My soul has clung after thee; thy right hand has upheld me.” Such is love’s power: that we cling to those whom we love even if they are absent, since neither place nor time can tear apart the affection implanted within us. Therefore the prophet has clung to God, with neither worldly allurements nor bodily vices drawing away from him his love and charity. For, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 6:17), “he who clings to God is one spirit”; [Note: [Col. 0405D] The common editions insert here “with him,” which is more correctly absent from the Royal manuscript, as also from the Greek text of the Apostle.] and the Lord prayed for his disciples: “Father, as we are one, that they too may be one in us” (John 17:22).

Therefore, clinging to God, he has been upheld by God’s right hand: that is, by God’s power, signified in the right hand, he has been taken up by him who is the Power, Wisdom, and Word of God made flesh, and he will now become conformed to the body of glory.

### 11. The security of the righteous; the lot of the wicked. Foxes are demons.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] “And because.”] And he who has been upheld by God’s right hand has cast from himself every fear that can arise from his enemies. He has not kept silent about the security of his confidence, nor is he ignorant of the severity of God’s righteous judgment, saying, VV. 10–11: “But they have sought my life in vain; they shall enter into the depths of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes.”

Thus they have sought his life in vain. For according to the Gospel (Matt. 10:28), a human being does not kill the soul together with the body; and God’s mercy is better than lives; [Note: [Col. 0405D] “It is better than life, and from this point …”] and he has already here been upheld by God’s right hand. But they shall enter the lower depths of the earth because they are separated from the saints by a trackless chasm (Luke 16:26); [Note: [Col. 0406D] Royal manuscript: “which [separates them] from the chasm.”] and they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword because, according to the rich man, the power of punishment, signified in the edge of the sword, will be exercised against the ungodly.

They shall also be portions for foxes, destined to receive the lot of deceitful little beasts; for Herod is a fox (Luke 13:32), [Note: [Col. 0406D] Royal manuscript, here and elsewhere: “fox.”] and foxes destroy the bridegroom’s vineyard (Song 2:15), and they have made their dens in the hearts of the ungodly—while the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58). There can be no doubt that the wickedness of demons is signified in these, for whom, together with their prince, the fire of Gehenna has been prepared.

### 12. Christ must be acknowledged as God; it is no longer lawful to deny him.

But amid these matters he shows the joy of him who often rejoiced before the Father because of the joy of human salvation, [Note: [Col. 0406D] In the Paris edition, the word “rejoiced”; in the other printed editions, “shows,” is lacking. But Erasmus, to complete the sense, added “hear” after “but amid these,” against the manuscripts.] V. 12: “But the king shall rejoice in God, and everyone who swears by him shall be praised, because the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.”

He indicates the reason why the king rejoices: because whoever swears by him will be praised in God through the religious solemnity of this oath—one, that is, who knows the king to be Christ Jesus, who is also God over all (Rom. 9:5); who, according to Paul, confesses the coming of the Saviour, the great God (Titus 2:13); and who, according to Isaiah (Isa. 65:16), “he who swears [Note: [Col. 0406D] “He who swears by God shall swear.”] shall swear [Note: [Col. 0406D] Royal manuscript: “he who swears by God.” “He who swears by him” or “in him” would be preferable. Here, as in *On the Trinity* V.29, Hilary proves Christ’s divinity from these words of Isaiah.] by the true God.”

For the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped because Christ is proclaimed from the law and the prophets; and the Apostle teaches that in him the Father both chose us before the foundation of the world and blessed us (Eph. 1:3–4), and that he himself has raised us together and seated us at God’s right hand in the heavenly places (ibid. 20). [Note: [Col. 0407D] Bad. and Erasmus: “has exercised us”; Lipsius and Paris: “has raised us.” These are corrected from the manuscripts.] And they shall see him, in his majesty, judging the living and the dead. By these things the mouth of those speaking iniquity shall be stopped.

For he himself is king forever, and at the name of the Lord Jesus Christ every knee shall bend—of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings—and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father, who is blessed unto all ages of ages (Phil. 2:9). Amen.

## PSALM LXIII

[Note: [Col. 0407D] For this Treatise and the following two, we do not report here the variant readings of the Verona codex, because, differing widely from the printed editions, we copied them out in full and presented them in the prefatory Dissertation.]

For the end: a psalm of David.

“Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication to thee; [Note: [Col. 0407D] Hilary below: “when I am troubled,” omitting “to thee.”] deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy. Thou hast protected me from the assembly of the malicious, from the multitude of those who work iniquity; [Note: [Col. 0407D] Hilary: “who … their tongues.”] for they have sharpened their tongue like a sword; they have bent their bow—a bitter thing—that they may shoot the blameless in secret places. [Note: [Col. 0407D] Below: “in darkness.”] Suddenly they shall shoot at him and shall not fear. They have strengthened for themselves an evil word. They have discussed how to hide snares; they have said: ‘Who shall see them?’ They have searched out iniquities; they have failed while searching in a search. Man shall approach the deep heart, [Note: [Col. 0407D] Hilary: “and heart.”] and God shall be exalted. The arrows of little children have become their wounds, and their tongues had nothing against them. All who saw them were troubled, and every person was afraid. And they declared the works of God and understood his deeds. The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright in heart shall be praised.”

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

### 1. This psalm must be understood spiritually.

V. 1. The superscription of this psalm contains no history. It is simple, issued by the prophetic Spirit; yet merely by being inscribed “for the end,” it declares that it contains matters not belonging to the time when it was written. We must ask from whose person it was spoken and what it declares as to its own meaning; for without doubt it must be regarded as spiritual.

For even those psalms which, according to the inscriptions of their titles, are believed to contain historical events, differ in many respects from the particular character of their title, events, and persons; and through the mention of names and deeds they signify rather the effects of spiritual operations. What then shall be understood of this psalm, in which there is only the simple inscription, “a psalm for the end to be understood,” unless it establishes a pattern of spiritual teaching?

### 2. Those who refer all utterances of the Psalms to Christ are to be praised, not censured.

I remember that there are many who consider everything written in the books of the Psalms to be referred to the person of our Lord, the only-begotten Son of God, [Note: [Col. 0407D] Thus from the Tours manuscript. The printed editions: “and nothing else in it …”] and to contain nothing other than what belongs properly to him. Their opinion cannot be censured. For this whole understanding arises from the disposition of a devout mind; and there is no fault in the inclination of zeal that fits all things to him through whom all things themselves exist.

Although this may sometimes be done unskilfully, nevertheless, because all things are referred to him, what belongs to him properly must be proclaimed truly and faithfully. But care must be taken lest, while we suppose that all things apply equally to him, the eager pursuit of this assertion detract greatly from the dignity of his divinity, the mystery of his embodiment, the power of his works, the efficacy of his Passion, and the glory of his resurrection.

### 3. How they may rightly be referred to Christ.

A proper measure must therefore be maintained, and it must be carefully and cautiously determined [Note: [Col. 0408D] The Tours codex: “must be cautiously considered”; not wrongly.] what has been prophesied concerning his divine birth from the Father; when the person of the human being whom he assumed is treated; [Note: [Col. 0408D] That is, substance and nature. The same use of the term occurs in these *Treatises on the Psalms*, Psalm 138, §5: “The person of divinity and of body must not be confused.” That Hilary recognized one person in Christ is established in innumerable passages, so that proving it would be altogether superfluous.] where his work, Passion, and resurrection are proclaimed; what belongs to each particular time; when the faith of the Gentiles is announced; when the sins of the former people are rebuked; and when instruction in the fear of God and training in confession are provided through the prophet’s prayer.

For in these things consists the order of spiritual prophecy. And if the Lord is proclaimed, the progress of this knowledge is useful for faith. If we are taught his fear and confession, we are formed by the Lord, we advance, and we are gained, so that, redeemed through his Passion, we may likewise please him through the ordinances of his teaching.

### 4. Certain things in the present psalm can be applied to Christ.

I understand that in the present psalm there are certain things which may seem capable of application to the human being whom the Lord assumed, where it says: “They searched out iniquities; they failed while searching in a search.” [Note: [Col. 0408D] Royal codex, here and below in §9: “into iniquities”; the Paris edition also agrees with the Mic. manuscript in the latter occurrence.]

For perhaps the Jewish conspiracy may be thought to be signified here: when testimonies by which he could be accused are sought but not found, and all the abilities of those investigating fail. Then, too, they may be wounded by the arrows of little children—that is, by the teachings of the Apostles—against whom they have found no ground for just persecution, and therefore their tongues have failed against them.

We do not set these things aside as implausible; [Note: [Col. 0409D] The common editions read “we set forth.” The manuscript more correctly has “we set aside.” By this word Hilary modestly declares that he is entering upon an interpretive approach different from the preceding one.] but there are certain other matters in the psalm that obstruct this line of interpretation. Yet the discourse of our exposition will not differ far from these things.

### 5. It is the psalm of every righteous person amid the storms of the world. Diverse temptations.

For we judge that this psalm contains the confession not only of the Apostles, who were first, but of every holy person who hopes in the Lord. For we are placed amid the greatest storms of the age and the gravest impieties of the human race against God. Now philosophy mocks the faithful and true confession of God made by us; now the frenzy of heretics attacks it; now the pursuits of avarice condemn it; now the favour of ambition disturbs it.

For overlooking, enduring, avoiding, and rebuking all these things, our mind is not sufficient unless it is instructed by God. With how many and how grievous stings of arguments does philosophy assail God’s providence and his primary and incomprehensible sovereignty in the world created by him—now conceding the name of God to waters, now to earth, now to atoms, now to heaven! With what ingenious use of cunning does the heretic falsify the teaching of faith! With what danger to hearers does the miser commend the glory of wealth! With what ruin to self-control does the advocate of pleasures set forth the delights of bodily enjoyment! And how pestilential is the eloquence of ambitious persons in their exhortation toward honours!

Against all these things vigilant care, night-long prayer, and perpetual confession to God will contend. Because of these perils to our faith and eternal salvation, therefore, the prophet is understood to pray in this psalm, showing in his own person how we ought to hope in God.

6. Evils must be averted by watchfulness and continual prayer—even before they come upon us.—For he says, “VERSE 2: Hear, O God, my prayer when I am in distress; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.” When the things mentioned above press upon us, through which our faith and hope are endangered, prayer is directed to him who alone can heal these things. For there is fear lest the soul, weak by nature and by its partnership with the flesh, be engulfed by the heat of enticements creeping in from every side. They are indeed present daily and wage war by deceptive blandishments, bringing forward certain engines of ruin. Thus, by the teaching of heavenly instruction, we are admonished to devote a sleepless care to faith, to fear [perhaps, “and to fear”] [Col. 0409D] the ever-plotting enemy, lest he, stationed on the watch, assail our unguarded security.

We must therefore keep watch in prayer to God and pray always, so that, when the soul begins to grow weary and be afflicted by the stings of creeping enticements, God, ever invoked, may hear us and deliver us from the things we fear. For he says: “Deliver my soul from fear [Col. 0410A] of the enemy.” God is not to be prayed to only when the things feared have come upon us; rather, those things must be feared which, when they begin to be present, gain mastery. He must be prayed to always and with unwearied petitions, that he may deliver us from fear of those whose dominion we dread.

For it is written in Proverbs: “When I called, you did not listen; and when I stretched out my words, you gave no heed; but you made my counsels void and did not attend to my counsels. I too will mock at your destruction. Therefore, when you call upon me, I shall not hear” (Prov. 1:24 ff.). The prophet, therefore, though earlier in time—let us say, than Solomon, whose words have just been cited—was nevertheless not ignorant of what would later be said. Always anxious amid impending tribulations, and watchful against every fear of the enemy, [Col. 0410B] he prays to God because of the things he fears [Note: In the Tours manuscript: “and that, when he is in tribulation, He may hear him”: less sound.]; and he entreats him both to be with him in tribulation and to hear him. For it is not our fear but faith that earns God’s mercy; and a long course of preparation [Note: Royal manuscript: “instruction.”] is needed if we are to deserve to be heard. The prophet therefore remembers that he is delivered from all these things by prayer [Note: The printed editions, except the Paris edition, read “to be delivered by praying.” The Royal manuscript reads “to be delivered from sins.”]; and teaches that his prayer is heard not because what he feared had gained dominion, [Note: Royal codex: “but because dominion is merited.” In the editions of Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius: “but heard because faith is merited”: a gloss.] but because he feared its dominion.

7. The murderous tongue, aimed against those newly reborn.—For he says, “VERSES 3–5: You have protected me from the assembly of evildoers, from the multitude of those who work iniquity, who have sharpened their tongues like a sword; they have bent the bow, a bitter thing, that they may shoot the spotless one in the dark.” The prophet does not here fear weapons of war, swords, javelins, or the bow’s engines. [Col. 0410C] For all his fear is in the tongue [Note: The word “his,” omitted in the printed editions, is restored with the help of the Royal manuscript.]: he fears its swords and its darts. By his faith he is indeed safe from them; for he says, “You have protected me from the assembly of evildoers.” Yet the bow of the murderous tongue is always drawn, and the sword’s edge is ready in its tongue.

Its deadly arrows fly, and there is no doubt what they accomplish: namely, “that they may shoot the spotless one in the dark.” The precision of the word must be understood. They shoot not the holy man, nor the believer, nor the righteous man, but the *immaculatus*, the one whose stains and blemishes of former crimes have recently been washed away through the sacrament of Baptism. He is not yet established in faith, not yet trained in spiritual doctrines, not yet contending against these weapons of the hostile tongue; he is simple and tender in the infancy of his new birth. Him, then, set in darkness through ignorance of realities, they will wound without fear of any contradiction, [Col. 0410D] with the bow already long drawn.

For he says, “VERSE 6: They will suddenly shoot at him, and will not fear”: that is, the simple nature, inexperienced through the newness of the spotless condition. [Note: The printed editions read “spotless.” But the manuscripts read *immaculati*: this is a Hellenism in which the neuter is used substantively; or after *immaculati* one should understand “state,” or something similar.] For they deceive this nature, stretch hidden snares before it, and glory in the concealed secrets of their plots.

[Col. 0411A]

8. Snares are always ready against faith.—For it continues: “They have strengthened for themselves an evil word; they have plotted to hide snares; they said, ‘Who will see them?’” There is a distinction of time, both for inflicting the wound and for the plan already made firm. When it says, “They will suddenly shoot,” an act of the future is taught; but when it says, “They have strengthened an evil word,” a plan of a will long since fixed is shown by the past tense.

For ruins are always ready against faith, and the deceits of deadly exhortation lie in wait through hidden and deceptive snares, which they suppose can be perceived only by a few. Hence it was said: “They hid snares and said, ‘Who will see them?’” For if the heretic attempts to corrupt faith, it is incredible with how many deceits he strives to overthrow it. If the philosopher attacks our hope of eternity, he will place every good of this present life in the body [Col. 0411B]; each of them, with all the ardour of his intelligence, searching out the means by which the institution of heavenly doctrine may be undermined.

9. They have no power against God. The world is not from chance. The soul is immortal. The flesh will rise again. God cares for humanity.—But what is human perversity to God? What is the ingenuity of a work against its maker? Let them seek, by all the petty questions of their argumentation, the destruction of truth: the assertion of falsehood will nevertheless fail in its destruction of truth. Therefore it follows, “VERSE 7: They have searched out iniquities; they failed while searching in their search.”

The failure of those who search shows the failure of their futile exhortation against God. What intellects, indeed, will not be shaken when bent upon contradicting truth? Let them search out [Col. 0411C] every secret of natural causes, and with the stubborn vigour of their studies investigate even the inward workings of the heavenly motions: yet in the very pursuit of their undertaking they will fail, refuted by spiritual teachings.

Those who teach that all things are driven by chance movements will hear from us that the God of eternal power does not exist amid chance occurrences, [Note: The Royal manuscript lacks the particle *in*.] but is the creator of the world—unlimited alike in essence and in power—himself from no one, but all things from him; governing and containing all things themselves. Whoever proclaims that the soul perishes with the body will hear that the soul is not earthly, but, born from God’s breath, is joined to the elements of the body; that death is not its destruction but its departure from the body. Whoever denies the resurrection of the flesh will know that its restoration will not be difficult [Col. 0411D] for him to whom its first beginning was easy. Moreover, whoever removes from God the care of human conduct will learn that the God of the eternal kingdom is judge; and that humanity was not created merely in order to exist—for what use to God was it that man should exist?—but that, brought forth into the knowledge of God, it might hope for its own advancement through knowledge of its Maker.

10. The nature and works of the Son of God.—Further, if the heretic destroys faith, [Col. 0412A] he will learn that the Son of God has always existed, separated from the Father by no interval of time; that he is the Word, the Power, and the Wisdom of God; that he was the maker of the world and also the creator of humanity; that he washed away the first crimes of the world by the flood; that he gave the Law to Moses; that he was in the prophets and through them proclaimed those great mysteries of his incarnation and passion; and that, rising in the body, he bestowed upon perishable flesh the splendour of spiritual glory and absorbed into the nature of his divinity the first beginnings of earthly corruption.

11. Profane knowledge yields to divine knowledge.—Those who investigate these matters against such truths will therefore fail. Through a man trained in the teaching of God and raising the humility of his heart on high, these proclamations of divine activity will be set forth [Col. 0412B], so that this exalted greatness of God may be praised by the confession of those who hear these things. Therefore it follows thus: “They have searched out iniquities; they failed while searching in their search. A man and a lofty heart shall draw near, and God shall be exalted.”

For, once the failure of those who search is known and the person of lofty heart draws near, the greatness of divine goodness is recognized. How great, moreover, will be the advance of spiritual teaching? For who will not magnify God when he has recognized him as the maker of this world? Who will not fear him when he knows him as judge? Who will not wish to be reborn into innocence, when the sacrament of new birth grants remission of sin? [Note: The Munich manuscript reads “the remission of sin”; then the Royal manuscript, “by the sacrament.” Perhaps one should read “is granted.”] Who, once reborn, will not cease from sin and wish to remain in the innocence of a little child, when he knows that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these (Matt. 19:14)?

This confession of ours weakens the intellects of those who investigate. These missiles of our teaching—which are the arrows of little children by reason of the beginning of those who have been regenerated—wound foolish disputations and ridiculous doctrines concerning God. The contradiction of a profane tongue cannot oppose these things: all these [Note: Royal manuscript: “our disputations, and the trembling [Col. 0412D] of those who reject them, is. For, once they have been proclaimed, etc.” We would prefer: “Against all these disputations and exhortations of ours stand the faith and trembling of rejecting heretics and the fear of the Gentiles who hear them”; see *Tractatus on Psalm 143*, §12.] disputations and exhortations of ours evoke faith, trembling in those who reject them, and fear in those who hear them.

12. Our faith terrifies the wicked and refreshes the righteous.—For once the works of God have been proclaimed, his deeds will then begin to be understood; then the righteous person will rejoice in them; then all the upright in heart will praise him. The psalm itself teaches this very thing [manuscript: *ipsud*] as follows, “VERSES 9–11: A man and a lofty heart shall draw near, and God shall be exalted. The arrows of little children became their wounds, and their tongues had nothing [Col. 0412D] against them. All who saw them were troubled, and every person feared. And they proclaimed the works of God and understood his deeds. The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright in heart shall be praised.”

The tongue of opponents had nothing to say against the wounding arrows of little children. Those who saw the little children shooting are troubled [Col. 0413A] and afraid, when they recognize themselves to be in error [Note: The printed editions read “in these errors”; corrected from the Royal manuscript. They recognize that the brightness of God’s teaching disperses, with the light of its radiance, that dense and concerted power of demons, as explained in Psalm 143, §11.]; when they acknowledge the day of judgment and the recompense for the life lived in the body; when they hear the works of God and understand his deeds.

In these things lies the joy of the saints; in these, their most steadfast hope. For these reasons those upright in heart praise God, knowing him to be the forgiver [Note: The printed editions read “remission”; the Royal manuscript more fittingly reads “forgiver.”] of sinners, the destroyer of death, and the conqueror of the devil; the judge of the age, the giver of eternity, our God and Lord, who is blessed unto ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LXIV

**For the end. A Psalm of David.**

“O God, praise is due to you in Zion, and to you a vow shall be paid in Jerusalem. Hear my prayer: to you all flesh shall come. The words of the wicked [Note: Hilary below: “have prevailed.”] have prevailed over us, [Col. 0413B] and you shall be propitious to our impieties [Note: Hilary: “you shall be propitious to our impieties.”]. Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up: he shall dwell [Note: Below: “that he may dwell.”] in your courts. We shall be filled with the good things of your house; holy is your temple, wonderful in righteousness. Hear us, O God our Saviour, the hope of all the ends of the earth and those far out at sea. You prepare the mountains in your strength, girded with power; you trouble [Note: Hilary: “the bottom.”] the depths of the sea, the sound of its waves. The nations shall be troubled, and all who inhabit the ends shall fear [Note: Hilary: “all who inhabit.”] at your signs; the outgoings of morning and evening are delightsome [Note: Hilary: “delights.”]. You have visited the earth and made it drink deeply; you have multiplied it, to enrich it. The river of God is filled with [Note: Hilary: “water.”] waters; you have prepared their food, for such is its preparation [Note: Hilary: “your preparation.”]: make its streams drink deeply, multiply its generations; in its falling drops that which springs up shall rejoice [Note: Hilary: “when it springs up.”]. You shall bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields [Col. 0413C] shall be filled with abundance. The ends of the wilderness shall grow rich, and the hills shall gird themselves with exultation. The rams are clothed with sheep, and the valleys shall abound with grain; indeed, they shall cry aloud and sing a hymn.”

**TREATISE ON THE PSALM**

1. What the psalm foretells.—VERSE 1. The present psalm fittingly follows the preceding one. It too is “for the end,” and announces the gathering of the nations that are to praise the Lord. The psalm itself will establish the reliability of this interpretation.

2. Nothing should be begun without praise of God. Zion is the Church.—At its beginning, in accordance with his customary practice, the prophet directs the whole prayer to God. Every undertaking and utterance of ours must be begun with confession of God. Yet the prophet knows that many, according to the diversity [Note: Royal codex: “according to the diversity of pursuits,” etc.] of their activities and pursuits, linger over vain matters; he therefore demands from us the particular and proper honour due to God [Col. 0414A], saying, “VERSE 2: O God, a hymn is due to you in Zion.”

Zion is indeed a mountain adjoining Jerusalem; but we have always understood this mountain, its name, and even that of the city itself, to signify the Church, which is Christ’s body. The Lord says in the Psalms: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2:6). And lest we suppose that he was established in the kingdom of this hill, it is said in the Prophets (Zech. 9:9), and also in the Gospels (Matt. 21): “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your king comes to you.” And the Apostle says: “But the Jerusalem above is free [Royal manuscript: ‘made free’], and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:26).

This hymn, therefore, is fitting for God when it is innocent in the spiritual and ecclesial song of Zion, and sweet [Col. 0414B] in God’s praises [Note: In the Royal manuscript, the first hand reads “God,” the second “to God”: incorrectly.].

3. The austere life of philosophers and heretics. Vows outside the Church are vain, since the Spirit does not intercede.—He condemns every kind of superstition outside the religion of God. For many are situated in the deepest abyss of error who commend the perversity of their teaching by a certain display of pointless labour. We see philosophers shivering with naked bodies; even teachers abstain from the use of marriage [Note: Royal manuscript: “magicians abstain.” Perhaps in the first place the nakedness of the Gymnosophists among the Indians is noted; in the second, the continence of the renowned Magi among the Persians; in the third, the xerophagies of the Montanists, which the faithful, in Tertullian, *On Fasting*, ch. 2, call by a new name of an affected observance, closely akin to pagan superstition.]; heretics live on dry bread as food. But what, after all, is the benefit of this idle purpose? The whole thing is empty and ridiculous and, along with the very grounds of the superstition, pitiable.

Contempt for the body, the preservation of chastity, and endurance of fasting must therefore be vowed to God. Accordingly he says: “And to you [Col. 0414C] a vow shall be paid in Jerusalem.” For only vows of ecclesiastical religion are profitable. When they are approved both by songs worthy of God and by the zeal of observance undertaken in the Church, then we shall be worthy persons for whom the Holy Spirit may intercede with God. For he both speaks and teaches through the Prophet. He himself, according to the Apostle (Rom. 8:26), intercedes for us with unutterable groanings. Thus it is said here: “VERSE 3: Hear prayer”; for “my” does not follow [Note: This word is also absent from the Psalter translated by Jerome from the Hebrew. It is, however, found in Greek copies and in Augustine, Theodoret, etc.], so that the person of the speaker can be understood.

Although many have added it as though something were missing, it is not found in the authentic texts. For the prophet does not speak from his own understanding, but under inspiration: “Hear prayer.”

4. “All flesh” means every human being. Humanity must be freed from error and sins through Christ’s blood.—It follows that he shows whose prayer is to be heard. Nor does he long delay our expectation; for he adds: “All flesh shall come to you.” Scripture designates the entire human race by the name of flesh, as in the Law: “And God said, ‘My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh’” (Gen. 6:3); and again: “For all flesh had corrupted its way” (ibid. 6:12); and in the prophet the Lord says: “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28); and in the Gospel: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

God will hear the prayer of this human race, which was held fast by the empty teachings of unhappy superstitions, when pagan precepts had trained them all in zeal for impiety by proclaiming God to be in wood, stones, and metals, and by placing the maker of the world and father of our soul within inanimate matter [Note: The printed editions read “within empty matter.” Hence the Royal manuscript’s “within inanimate matter” is more correct, establishing a contrast between his being the father of our soul and his being confined within inanimate matter.]. The nations therefore confess this error: that the eloquence of philosophy had held them in error [Col. 0415B]. At last they recognize that their old offences and the crimes of ancient impiety must be propitiated to God through Christ.

For according to the Apostle, he himself is our propitiation. He says: “Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Rom. 3:25), and again: “He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2). Therefore all flesh shall come to him, saying, “VERSE 4: The words of the wicked have prevailed over us, and you shall be propitious to our impieties.”

5. Every human being must be delivered.—But what, after all, is the result of propitiation? Or what benefit is there in abandoning pagan error and rejecting impious teaching? He has not concealed this either, saying, “VERSE 5: Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up, that he may dwell in your courts.”

All flesh indeed shall come—that is, we are gathered from every [Col. 0415C] class of human beings [Note: Royal manuscript: “they are gathered.”]—but blessed is whoever has been chosen. For, according to the Gospel, many are called, but few chosen (Matt. 22:14). The chosen are those distinguished by the wedding garment, radiant in the pure and unblemished body of new birth. Thus election is not an act of indiscriminate judgment, but a distinction made from selection according to merit [Note: The Royal codex’s first hand has “from choice,” its second “of love,” incorrectly. This entire passage concerns not eternal election and predestination, but the temporal recompense of eternal glory. Hence those just called chosen are not those who will be so, but those already distinguished by the wedding garment, etc. Hence, in §6, we are invited to hasten thither where those already chosen dwell. No one but a heretic can deny that this election is made from a selection according to merit. [Col. 0416D] Scultetus therefore cites this passage in vain among Hilary’s blemishes.].

Blessed, therefore, is the person whom God has chosen; blessed for this reason, that he is worthy of election. We must understand, however, to what this blessed person has been chosen: namely, to what follows—“He shall dwell in your courts.” Every perfection of good things consists in the rest of heavenly dwelling [Note: The Paris edition reads “of rest”; other printed editions, “in the rest of heavenly dwelling.” We follow the manuscripts. For clarity, the whole phrase should be reversed thus: “The rest of heavenly dwelling is the perfection of every—or of all—good things.”].

The Lord testifies that there are many dwelling places in heaven (John 14:2); but he prays to the Father that the apostles may remain where he himself is, saying: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, there they also may be with me” (John 17:22). From the many dwelling places, then, he shares with his apostles that one which is his own [Col. 0416A]. The prophet knows how great is the blessedness of being in God’s courts, saying elsewhere: “My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3).

Yet hope of heavenly goods is not removed if not all are chosen for cohabitation with God. For many dwelling places are prepared for the differing rank of their inhabitants. But although rank differs—for “star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41)—nevertheless all who are found worthy of dwellings, though various ones, will receive the fruit of faith and the honour of heavenly glory.

6. What God’s house is; what its goods are; and by what merit they are obtained.—After the blessedness of the person chosen to dwell in God’s courts, this follows: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house; holy is your temple, VERSE 6, wonderful in righteousness.” We shall therefore be filled with these good things of God’s house, because the blessed person will dwell in the courts of God.

For the present, we may understand the good things of the house to be the gifts of the Church, which Christ granted it according to its manifold fruit; for it too, according to the Apostle, is God’s house: “That you may know,” he says, “how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth” (1 Tim. 3:15). This house, then, has thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit [Note: Royal manuscript: “thirtyfold, sixtyfold, hundredfold.”].

With these good things of God’s house the faith of believers will be filled, which is presently adorned by divisions of gifts, as it is written: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” [Note: In the Royal manuscript: “For to one is given the word of wisdom, to others the word of knowledge.”], “to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of tongues” (1 Cor. 12:8 ff.) [Note: The printed editions read “interpretation of sayings,” contrary to the manuscripts, which, in accordance with the Greek, here have—as in *On the Trinity*, II.33 and VIII.29—“interpretation of tongues.”].

Yet there are other full and perfect gifts of God’s house, not at all to be estimated by the natures [Note: The Paris edition reads “by the natures.”] of fleshly senses. The Apostle, caught up to the third heaven, knew these things, and proclaims: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). We shall therefore be filled with these good things of God’s house.

He teaches the merit by which these fruits are received, saying: “Your temple is holy, [Col. 0416C] wonderful in righteousness.” For the Apostle teaches that all believers’ bodies are God’s temple, saying: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy” (1 Cor. 3:16–17). This temple of God must therefore be adorned with holiness and justice, so that it may be filled [Col. 0416D] with the good things of God’s house and may be wonderful through works of righteousness and faith.

But it is also easy to understand God’s house as the humanity assumed by the Son of God [Col. 0417A], because in it all the fullness of divinity dwells and the Father dwells in it through the property of nature; thus filling each person with its good things [Note: The word “thus,” omitted in the printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts.]—that is, with power, glory, and eternity—who has kept himself a temple holy to God and wonderful in righteousness.

This, then, is the hope of us all: that we may be filled with the good things of God’s house, that we may be his holy and wonderful temple. Blessed indeed are those already chosen by God to dwell in his courts; but it is fitting that we hasten into the fellowship of this blessedness, seeking it by works and prayers [Note: Paris edition: “attaining it.”].

7. No nation is excluded from the hope of blessedness.—For this reason it follows: “Hear us, O God our Saviour, the hope of all the ends of the earth and those far out at sea.” This prayer does not suit the Jew. Though this book belongs to the Law, [Col. 0417B] the prophecy is not that of one nation. For this hope belongs to all the ends of the earth; and wherever the temperate region of this inhabited world extends, Christ is the hope of all.

Indeed, even the islands of the inner and outer sea [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “of the inner sea,” without “and outer.” If the latter words were absent elsewhere, we might suppose that the islands far out within the sea were called islands of the inner sea, in imitation of prophetic language; concerning these see the *Treatise on Psalm 14*, §3: “Moreover, even in the islands of Ocean the apostles prepared many dwellings for God.” Florus also mentions the outer and inner sea, IV.2. Ptolemy called Ocean the outer sea; Pliny, *Natural History*, III.3 and V.2, etc., called the Mediterranean the inner sea.] rest in the power of this name. For he is “the hope of all the ends of the earth and those far out at sea.” Yet hope must not arise from empty presumption, lest it be the presumption of uncertain things rather than the expectation of things known.

8. Mountains here do not signify earthly mountains.—Accordingly, he teaches in what respect he is the hope of all in what follows, saying, “VERSES 7 and 8: You prepare the mountains in your strength, girded with power; you trouble the bottom of the sea, the sound of its waves.” This passage does not concern the nature of earthly mountains. They were established, not prepared; preparation is the beginning of a future operation. Further, the preparation of the mountains mentioned consists in being girded with power and strength. But the whole earth was commanded to stand forth from nothing; and a thing whose existence depended on the ease of a command did not require the girding of power.

It is useful, moreover, to know whenever mountains are mentioned in Scripture. The prophet says: “Hear, all peoples, and let the earth attend, and all who dwell in it. And the Lord God shall be a witness against you, the Lord from his holy house. Therefore behold, the Lord shall come down from his place; he shall come down upon the heights of the earth, and he shall crush the mountains beneath him, and the valleys shall melt like wax before fire, because of Jacob’s impiety. All these things are because of the sins of the house of Israel” (Mic. 1:2 ff.).

And again: “The earth was shaken and trembled, and [Col. 0417D] the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because he was angry with them. Smoke rose from his wrath, and fire [Col. 0418A] from before his face shall blaze [Note: The printed editions read “blazes,” a reading found in Augustine and in the old German, Milanese, and Roman Psalters; but the following context does not permit it. In the kindling of the fire is contained a future sense, necessarily requiring “shall blaze,” as found in the Royal manuscript, Theodoret, and the old Chartres Psalter.]; coals were kindled by him.
