He bowed the heaven and came down, and darkness was beneath his feet.” And later: “He sent his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightning flashes and troubled them” (Ps. 17:8 ff.).

In these words, as the reading shows, the Holy Spirit through the prophet sets forth the Lord’s descent from heaven, [Note: The printed editions read “the movement of the earth,” less suited to Hilary’s meaning, who insists that the preceding passage does not signify something earthly; corrected from the manuscripts.] the earth’s fear, and the mountains’ trembling, because the Lord was angry with them, smoke having risen from his wrath and fire thereafter to be kindled from before his face. In the smoke that rises, the matter belongs to past time; but in the fire’s being kindled, a future sense is contained. Then, lest it be thought that anything is said of a dull and immovable nature, these mountains are scattered by arrows shot and troubled by multiplied lightning.

9. The mountains are the devil and his followers. They are crushed by Christ.—[Col. 0418B] By the name of mountains, therefore, we must understand every power set on high, which, exalting and lifting itself against God, has subjected itself to God’s wrath. God the Word, therefore, coming down and girding with power the humanity assumed by him, first brought down these mountain-peaks: that is, he crushed the stubborn exaltation of the devil and his followers and, by the power of this first crushing, prepared them for the punishment of eternal judgment.

The prophet has preserved the same sequence, saying: “Smoke rose from his wrath, and fire from before his face shall burn.” For smoke presently envelops those who will burn in fire; and therefore the present psalm says: “Preparing the mountains in your strength, girded with power.” The girding of power is fitted to the body which needed power [Note: Understand: “power.”]. For Power itself is not girded; rather, the man whom the Lord assumed is girded with power in [Col. 0418C] the Power of God.

10. The sea is the world.—We must consider what follows the preparation of the mountains: “Who troubles the bottom of the sea, the sound of its waves.” He troubles not the sea, but the sea’s bottom; nor its waves, but the sound of the waves. The sea, as prophetic language teaches, denotes the world, as it says: “The Lord shall bring a terrible and great sword upon the crooked serpent-dragon, and shall kill the dragon that is in the sea” (Isa. 27:1). And again: “This sea, great and broad; there the dragon shall rest, which you formed to sport in it” (Ps. 103:25). Or, more plainly: “I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68:3).

The mountains, that is, all opposing and exalted powers, [Col. 0418D] are prepared for the punishment of judgment; and the foundations of the sea are troubled. For the world stood in confidence in these hostile powers, and they lay hidden in the invisible depths of this world. The sound of the waves is also disturbed together with the sea’s bottom. For when the devil is disturbed, every instrument of his terror is disturbed; and the sound of hostile powers, by which the nations were terrified, trembles.

Let us recall the mutterings of soothsayers, the disorderly roars of Bacchants, and how sometimes, when the hearers’ perception was confused, some indistinct sound of images seemed to ring in the air; in short, how the whole world echoed with the profane chant of ceremonies. But now that the Lord Christ has been proclaimed, all things, refuted and trembling, fall silent: the gods of temples and nations are subjected by the power of believers to punishment; they are tortured, torn, and burned by believers’ words; and natures invisible and incomprehensible to us [Col. 0419B] are restrained, punished, and driven away by a word, while the soothsayers are silent and the temples mute. By these means, then, they are now prepared for judgment.

And what does this preparation accomplish? It has accomplished [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But Badius and Erasmus read “it accomplishes”; Lipsius and Paris, “they accomplish.” Juvenal also spoke of the silence of oracles:

> “The oracles at Delphi cease,  
> and the darkness of the future condemns the human race,”

he says in *Satire* 6. Indeed, Plutarch wrote a book entitled *Why Oracles Have Ceased to Give Answers*. But concerning demons’ subjection to believers, there is Tertullian’s splendid statement, *Apology*, §23: “Fearing Christ in God and God in Christ, they are subjected to the servants of God and Christ; thus, struck by contact with us, by our breath, by contemplation and representation of that fire, they even depart from bodies at our command, unwilling and suffering, and ashamed in your presence,” etc. Hilary’s words are no less clearly confirmed and illuminated by Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*: “Be ashamed to hope for protection from those whom you yourself protect. Oh, if only you would hear and see them when they are adjured by us, tortured with spiritual whips, and driven from possessed bodies under the torments of lashes and blows; when, wailing and groaning, feeling lashes and blows through human voice and divine power, they confess the coming judgment . . . You will see us entreated by those whom you entreat, feared by those whom you worship; you will see them stand bound beneath our hand and tremble as captives,” etc. See *Against Constantius*, §8.]: namely, “The nations shall be troubled,” VERSE 9, “and shall fear,” seeing, that is, their gods mute and merely groaning out the sounds of their punishment at the laying on of our hands. But after the nations’ disturbance, others will fear; for the disturbance will bring fear. Will all, then, both be troubled and fear? Certainly not all who are troubled will also fear.

### 11. They Will Fear Who Neither Wholly Follow Nor Abandon the Things of the Flesh

Who, then, will fear? Those who dwell at the extremities. Scripture did not add, as it usually does, “the extremities of the earth”; for here it was not speaking of the earth’s extremities. Therefore the course of the argument does not permit us to suppose that this was added. [Note: In the printed editions: “that it was thus said.” More suitably in the royal manuscript: “that this was added,” namely, the word “earth.”] For it says: “Those who dwell at the extremities.” Will the nations also that are within the boundaries not fear? Will only the outermost parts of the lands fear God, while the rest situated in the middle are exempt from fear of him?

An extremity, however, is not the thing itself, but the outermost part of a thing. The outermost part is that at which the thing itself comes to an end. Who, then, dwell at the extremities? Clearly, those who, though placed in the flesh, neither yet act wholly according to the flesh nor have altogether attained the end of sin through the habit of ceasing from sins. They wish to cease, yet do not cease utterly; and, while still dwelling in the extremity—that is, in a certain near-ending—of sin and flesh, they are neither apart from the flesh nor wholly engaged in its inner workings.

But while the Apostle is in the body, he is absent from the body (II Cor. 5:8). While he is alive, nevertheless he dies daily (I Cor. 15:31); and now it is no longer he who lives, but Christ lives in him (Gal. 2:20). He has passed beyond all these boundaries of an ambiguous will; he dwells even beyond the limits of body and sin, absent from the body while in the body, and dying daily while living, [Note: The printed editions read, “dying, he lives to God”; corrected from the royal manuscript. The same point is here repeated in other words as shortly before: “While he is alive, nevertheless he dies daily.”] and living no longer himself in himself, but Christ.

The trembling of those who fear, on the other hand, comes from the uncertainty of their ambiguous dwelling: while they fear the extremities in which they still dwell, they have not yet wholly passed beyond that in which they dwell; yet, by their will to cease, they already inhabit the end of ceasing. [Note: The royal codex reads, “the boundaries of dwelling”; this is not approved. For their fear arises because, though at the extremities of the flesh, they still dwell in it, or have not yet ceased to think the things of the flesh.]

### 12. Signs of God’s Mercy: Morning and Evening Praises of God

But let us see why these who dwell at the extremities will fear, and whence fear comes upon them. Nor is this hidden; for it follows: “And those who dwell at the extremities will fear at your signs.” Therefore all fear arises from the signs. But what will these signs be? “The outgoings of morning and evening are delights. Verse 10: You have visited the earth and made it drunk; you have multiplied it to enrich it. The river of God is filled with water; you have prepared their food, because such is your preparation.”

From these signs, therefore, fear has arisen. For in each one of them there is a great sign. After the preparation of the mountains in the girding of power, and the disturbance of the sea’s deep and the sound of its waves, [Note: The Paris edition, with the manuscripts: “the disturbance of the sea’s deep and the sound.”] the progress of the Church into the delights of morning and evening hymns is a very great sign of God’s mercy. [Note: Royal manuscript: “the procession of the Church.” Then, in place of “into the morning,” we restore conjecturally “into the [delights] of morning [hymns],” supported by Jerome on the same passage: “God is delighted by the Church’s morning and evening hymns through the faithful soul which, abandoning the rite of vain superstitions, has devoutly praised him.”] The day is begun in prayers to God; the day is closed in hymns to God, as it is said: “May my praise be pleasing to him” (Ps. 103:34); and again: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2).

### 13. Drunkenness and Spiritual Wealth

This following sign also comes next: “Verse 10: You have visited the earth and made it drunk; you have multiplied it to enrich it.” This earth which we use is not enriched, but enriches from the abundance of its fruits. Therefore the statement cannot refer to it, since it lacks awareness of being enriched, and since it is its function to enrich.

But God visited the earth, that is, the birth of the human race; and, visited by God, it grows rich through multiplied gifts of grace. As the Apostle says: “In everything you were enriched in him, in all speech and knowledge” (I Cor. 1:5). We are filled with these goods, and, drinking without ceasing, daily draw upon the gift of heavenly goods, full of divine abundance and drunken. For this enrichment is shown to be what was above called drunkenness.

### 14. The Gift of the Holy Spirit

The fruit of this enrichment and drunkenness must be considered. Nor is its nature left unspoken: “The river of God is filled with water; you have prepared their food, because such is your preparation.” [Note: The printed editions read “his,” which Lipsius also restored below while retaining “your” above. The manuscripts consistently have “your.”] There is no room for uncertainty about the river. For the Prophet says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5). And the Lord himself says in the Gospels: “Whoever drinks from the water which I shall give, rivers of living water springing up into eternal life shall flow from his belly” (John 4:13–14). And again: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers shall come forth from his belly” (John 7:38–39). But he said this concerning the Holy Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive (John 7:38–39).

Therefore the river of God is filled with water. For we are inundated with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the river of God, filled with water, is poured into us from that fountain of life. We also have food prepared. And what is this food? Clearly, that by which we are prepared for fellowship with God: through communion in the holy body, to be thereafter established in communion in the holy body. [Note: The printed editions read “from whom.” More rightly the manuscripts read “in whom.” A twofold effect of holy communion is here indicated: the soul’s present salvation through reception of the Savior, and its future glory and fellowship with God, for which this fellowship in the holy body prepares it.] For the present psalm means this when it says: “You have prepared their food, because such is your preparation”: because, although by that food we are saved at present, yet we are prepared for the future.

### 15. The Foregoing Concerns the Future

The Prophet, however, maintains his custom of distinguishing the times of which he speaks. The earlier discourse was as though about the past; but things still to be done he mentioned, through faith and knowledge of what was to be done, as though already accomplished. But in order to teach that all these things belong to future time, he says: “Verse 11: Make its streams drunk; multiply its generations; in its drops it will rejoice when it springs up.”

This whole passage is the speech of one praying and asking God to fulfill the things which have been recounted. The earth, however, has been visited and made drunk; how, then, are its streams now made drunk? But we must remember that, if anyone drinks of the Lord’s water, rivers will flow from his belly. Thus drinking the water is necessary in order that rivers may flow. We ourselves are made drunk when we receive the Holy Spirit, who has been called a river.

Then, because various streams of graces flow out from us, the Prophet prays that the Lord may make these streams drunk, so that, when they have been made drunk and drenched with the gift of divine bounty, our generations may be multiplied. Thus the good earth, receiving the seed of the word according to the Gospel comparison, may become rich with thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit (Matt. 13:8).

For us who have been reborn through the sacrament of baptism there is great joy when we perceive certain beginnings of the Holy Spirit within us: when understanding of the sacraments enters us, knowledge of prophecy, speech of wisdom, steadfastness of hope, gifts of healings, and dominion over demons made subject to us. These penetrate us as drops, and, gradually begun, overflow in abundant fruit. Therefore, amid these drops, the earth will rejoice when it springs up. But the drops are multiplied in order that they may become streams; and the streams are made drunk in order that they may become rivers.

### 16. The Prophet Confirms the Whole of Our Hope

It follows that the Prophet confirms our whole expectation and teaches what consummation the preparation of the mountains, the disturbance of the sea’s deep, the visitation and drunkenness of the earth, and the fullness of the river will have. He accordingly teaches in what follows, saying, “Verses 12, 13, and 14: You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields will be filled with abundance. The extremities of the wilderness will grow fat, and the hills will be girded with exultation. [Note: The printed editions read “will rise”; the manuscripts and the Greek oppose this.] The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys will abound with grain; indeed, they will cry out and sing a hymn.”

We have learned from prophetic and apostolic teaching about the year of God’s goodness. For it is said in the person of the Lord: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he anointed me, sent me to proclaim good news to the poor, to preach release to captives and sight to the blind, to call the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense” (Isa. 61:1–2). This plainly declares the year of that eternal and blessed age. For this is the year of the Lord’s goodness, in which those indestructible times of gracious recompense will begin.

The most delightful and sweet fruit of the visited and drunken earth will bless the crown of this year of God. [Note: The manuscripts read “the crown will be blessed.” Jerome says of it: “He called the circular and ever-returning times of the year a crown.”] For this is Christ’s victory: the corruption of our bodies having been driven away and the power of death destroyed. This crown is the Lord, blessed with the flower of our sanctified earth, glorious in the choir and encircling assembly of his saints.

Then the fields will be filled with abundance; then the extremities of the wilderness will grow fat; then the hills will be girded with exultation; then the rams of the sheep will be clothed. [Note: Royal manuscript: “will be girded exultantly.”] For that is the time of recompense.

### 17. Distinctions of Glory among Saints, Martyrs, and Leaders of the Church

But the distinction within that recompense must be considered. [Note: The printed editions previously read “before that recompense,” in place of “within that recompense.”] In the fields, whose cultivation is useful, works performed under the law and cultivation of God will obtain abundance. [Note: One manuscript reads “from the cultivation of God.” Jerome’s common text makes Hilary’s obscure thought clearer: “The fields of the law, which produced no fruit of delight in the letter, now, spiritually understood, are filled with the abundance of the fruit of evangelical doctrine.”]

Where the extremities of the wilderness grow fat, the people of the Church, long deserted, are enriched with the goods of promise. In the hills girded with exultation, the glorious joys of the martyrs are announced; for these are higher than the rest of the earth. When the rams of the sheep are clothed, the eternal and blessed garment of patriarchs, prophets, and apostles—who are leaders of the holy flock—is shown. Of it the blessed Apostle Paul says: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption” (I Cor. 15:53); and again: “In this we do not wish to be unclothed, but to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Cor. 5:4). With this garment, therefore, the rams of the sheep are clothed, and with this attire of glorious immortality they are vested.

### 18. The Valleys

Yet, although diverse gifts of recompense have been shown, God grants a considerable hope of his mercy beyond these, saying through the Prophet: “And the valleys will abound with grain.” That is, persons humbler than the rest, yet not of impious faith and conduct, will obtain the fruit of life. They will not be filled with abundance like the fields, nor grow fat out of the wilderness, nor be girded with exultation like the mountains, nor be clothed like the rams of the sheep—in all of which a determinate gift of glory is displayed. [Note: The printed editions read “indeterminate.” The reading of the royal manuscript, “determinate,” is preferable: that is, proportioned to their merits and specifically signified through the exultation of the hills, the garment of the rams, and so forth. What Hilary here says about believers whose righteousness is humbler and more ordinary, as also what he says above in §5—that not all saints are chosen for fellowship with God—might raise doubt whether he grants heavenly glory and blessedness to all saints, unless in that same §5 he added: “But although their dignity is diverse … nevertheless, all who are deemed worthy of dwellings, though diverse, will receive the fruit of faith and the honor of heavenly glory.” From this it is clear that “fellowship with God” there denotes a particular degree of glory, to be granted especially to the apostles by a singular prerogative.]

But they will abound with grain; that is, they will not lack the sustenance of life, because they are humble through weakness of faith and, like valleys, depressed by the hills rising around them.

### 19. The Foregoing Must Be Understood Spiritually

And lest the prophetic discourse be thought to signify these fields, wildernesses, hills, rams, and valleys that lie before our eyes, things without voice or sense, it adds: “Indeed, they will cry out and sing a hymn”—that is, they will sing God’s praises with tireless and very great voices for these diverse rewards of recompense.

## PSALM LXV

For the end, a song of a psalm.

Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise. Say to God: “How terrible are your works, O Lord! In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you. Let all the earth worship you and sing psalms to you; let it sing a psalm to your name.” DIAPSALMA. Come and see the works of God, terrible in his counsels over the children of men. He who turned the sea into dry land: they will pass through the river on foot; there we shall rejoice in him who rules in his power forever. His eyes look upon the nations; let not those who provoke him to anger exalt themselves. DIAPSALMA. Bless our God, O nations, and make heard the voice of his praise. He who has set my soul unto life and has not allowed my feet to be moved. For you have tested us, O God; you have tried us by fire as silver is tried. You brought us into a snare; you placed afflictions upon our back; you set men over our heads. We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment. I will enter your house with burnt offerings; I will pay you my vows, which my lips pronounced and my mouth spoke in my affliction. I will offer you fat burnt offerings with the incense of rams; [Note: Hilary: “with incense and rams.”] I will offer you bulls with goats. DIAPSALMA. Come and hear, and I will tell you, all who fear God, how great things he has done for my soul. I cried to him with my mouth, and rejoiced beneath my tongue. If I regarded iniquity in my heart, God will not hear. Therefore God heard me and attended to the voice of my prayer. Blessed be God, who has not removed my petition or his mercy from me.

[Note: Variant readings: Hilary reads, “Let all the earth worship you, and let them sing psalms to you; let it sing a psalm”; “they will cross over”; “will rule”; “you led us out”; “all who fear”; “I exalted”; “may [God] hear”; and adds “me” after “God heard.”]

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

### 1. The Title of the Psalm

Verse 1. The superscription of this psalm differs from that of the preceding one in that it contains “A Song of a Psalm,” whereas the former was published as “A Psalm of a Song.” Yet both are equally inscribed “For the end.” Accordingly, following the explanation of title-inscriptions which we gave in the beginning, [Note: In the Prologue, §20.] it is clear that this psalm is sung because the precepts of spiritual teaching have been attained through the merit of good works. For when the superscription is “A Psalm of a Song,” the deeds of good work are contained in the psalm through the proclamation of heavenly knowledge; but when it is “A Song of a Psalm,” a hymn of spiritual knowledge attained through obedience in action is shown.

For song is an office of the voice; whereas a psalm is produced by the arrangement of an instrument, which they call *harmonia* [harmony]. By the skill of the artist, an apt, harmonious, and pleasing melody is made from unequal and dissimilar modes. By this example, through the various ministries of our duty and knowledge, we produce a work pleasing to God and harmonious in itself. The authors of the psalms themselves will establish this understanding for us: when it is “A Psalm of a Song,” the proclamation of good work occurs through the teaching of knowledge and understanding; but in “A Song of a Psalm,” thanksgiving for knowledge attained is understood through the merit of deeds.

For this reason, therefore, in the present psalm the spirit of prophecy began with teaching concerning rejoicing. That the psalm proceeds in the person of the prophets is shown by the subject itself and by the argument.

### 2. The Order of Praise

Verses 2 and 3. “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise. Say to God: How terrible are your works! In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you.”

First, therefore, he commands that God be acclaimed with joy; second, that a psalm be sung to his name; then that glory be given to his praise; then that God be told, “How terrible are your works!”; and finally that this be confessed: “In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you.” But in order that we may understand the reason and order of this arrangement of the discourse, it is necessary briefly to resolve what presents difficulty.

### 3. What “Jubilus” Commonly Means: According to the Force of the Greek Word, It Is a Military Cry

In the Latin codices we read: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.” So far as the usage of our language is concerned, we call *jubilus* the sound of a pastoral and rustic voice, when, in lonely places, answering or seeking another, a sound of the voice is heard, drawn out and forcibly uttered through the signifying effort. [Note: In the Badius edition, “unto a measured extent”; in other editions, “unto an immeasurable extent.” The reading of the royal manuscript, “with effort,” seems truer, expressing a new accompaniment of the *jubilus*. For Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 32, exposition 2, §8, *jubilus* is a certain sound signifying that the heart is bringing forth what it cannot express in words. This applies not only to one fighting, but also to those singing at harvest, in a vineyard, or in some fervent work; filled with such joy that they cannot explain it in words, they turn away from verbal syllables and pass into the sound of jubilation. Jerome on Psalm 32 and Rufinus on this Psalm 65 explain *jubilus* similarly. Theodoret, however, on Psalm 32, says that *alalagmos* is a cry of victory raised by conquerors against those fleeing.]

But in the Greek books, which are closer to the Hebrew, the same sense is not written. For they read: **ἀλαλάξατε τῷ Θεῷ πᾶσα ἡ γῆ**, “Raise the battle-cry to God, all the earth”; and with them **ἀλαλαγμός** (*alalagmos*), which they render in Latin as *jubilum*, means the cry of an army fighting, either when it tramples the enemy in battle or when it bears witness by a cry of exultation to the success of victory.

Since the principle of translation has thus adapted the expression, we understand it more fully in another psalm, where it says: “All nations, clap your hands; shout joyfully to God with a voice of exultation” (Ps. 46:2). A voice of exultation differs from *jubilus*; but owing to the conditions of translation, because no proper designation for the voice of exultation was found, the voice of one exulting is expressed by the word *jubilus*.

### 4. We Are Commanded to Use It in Fighting the Devil

Therefore, placed amid the battles of this life and fighting, with spiritual weapons, in this conflict of our flesh and blood against the devil and his army, we are commanded to shout joyfully to God with a voice of exultation. And lest the statement be referred to this inanimate mass of earth, the totality of us who are born from the earth in our first parent Adam is indicated by the plural number when it says: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.” [Note: The word “born” refers to “our,” having the same force as “of us.”] Thus both the duty of all and their origin are taught.

Accordingly, every profane hearer must be terrified by the speech of our confession; we must fight the devil and his weapons with the sound of our prayers; and the victory of our warfare must be displayed by the voice of exultation. Let one standing outside the Church hear the voice of the praying people, behold the celebrated sounds of hymns, and, amid the offices of the divine sacraments also, receive the response of devout confession.

Every opponent must necessarily be terrified; the devil must be fought; and death must be conquered by faith in the resurrection, through this *jubilus*—that is, this cry of our exultation. Let him know that this is pleasing to God, that these public and victorious cries of our exultation are the testimony of our hope. The Prophet is not neglectful of them, recalling elsewhere: “I went round about and offered in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation” (Ps. 26:6). And lest we should consider this teaching and practice of jubilation empty, he declares elsewhere: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88:16). It is therefore necessary to our faith, since blessedness lies in knowing it.

### 5. God Must Also Be Pleased through the Body

For first in the order of his exhortations the Prophet arranged that all the earth should shout joyfully to God; second, that it should sing a psalm to his name. Therefore we must shout joyfully to God, because the duty of an exultant voice is owed to him by us. But we must sing psalms to his name because, just as the psalm is made through an instrument, so also we must please God by skillful works of our body, which is the instrument of the soul, affections, and all actions.

Therefore we must act worthily of God’s name, so that, as far as may be possible, we obey the Lord’s words: “So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). For the uprightness of our life must be referred to the praise of him for whom we live.

Finally, this same thing is taught by what follows. For it says: “Sing psalms to his name; give glory to his praise,” because from the psaltery of our instrument—that is, from the actions of the body serving the soul—glorious praise is offered to God through us, when the nations behold our works and glorify our Father who is in heaven. Glory will be given to his praise if we worthily sing psalms to his name by the activity of our instrument, that is, of our body.

### 6. How Fearful God Is

We are also taught by the succeeding exhortations the order of obedience, as the Prophet, or the Spirit through the Prophet, thus commands: “Say to God: How terrible are your works!” [Note: The manuscripts read: “We are also taught … the Prophet, or the Spirit through the Prophet”; the printed editions: “We are therefore taught … by the order of prophetic obedience,” etc.]

For who would not tremble at his majesty, he who established the ages, created the world, measured out time by its recurring alternation and course, adorned heaven with stars, filled earth with fruits, enclosed the sea with barriers, and chose humanity either to use these things or rule them? Through all these things the eternity of his power and might is known, as the Apostle says: “For his invisible things, understood through the things made from the creation of the world, are clearly seen—his eternal power also and divinity” (Rom. 1:20). [Note: The printed editions, except Paris, read “his things made”; Paris, “his thing made.” The manuscripts more rightly read “through his things made,” unless one prefers “his things made” from the Greek **τοῖς ποιήμασι**.]

These things make the Creator’s name terrible, and the dignity of the works displays the majesty of him who performed them. Therefore God must be proclaimed by us and confessed by others as the Creator of these works; we must not falsely declare that all these things are gods.

### 7. The Diverse Errors of the Pagans concerning God, and the Source of Their Many Invented Gods

Some assert that these things came into being by chance; others affirm that they have existed eternally. Therefore they contend that the world itself is God: either because it arose of its own power whenever it chose, or because, since it lacks a beginning, it lacks the will of a ruler.

Others call heaven alone God because it is fiery; others call the air God because it is carried around by motion and an indivisible nature; others call the waters God because they flow without weariness. Many have worshiped the earth’s metals, trees, rocks, and plants as gods. Some have falsely claimed as gods either the bones of decayed bodies or the tombs of funeral pyres still burning, not knowing God as the Creator of all these things.

Therefore the Prophet taught that the order of our confession ought to be this: “Say to God: How terrible are your works! In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you”—namely, inventing the worship of false names as gods because of the multitude of God’s powers.

### 8. From These the Human Being Is Recalled to the One God

But because enemies lie, what all ought to do is taught thus, in verse 4: “Let all the earth worship you and sing psalms to you; let it sing a psalm to your name, Most High.” Once the lie of enemies in their naming of gods has been displayed, the principles of our salvation are supplied: that all our earthly origin, abandoning the lies of impiety, may worship and sing psalms to the Most High, recognizing him as the true God and Creator of all things.

### 9. Those Far from God Are Called to Behold God’s Works

The *diapsalma* marks a change of thought. For the discourse, directed to God in prayer, is now addressed to human beings, whom the Prophet, as standing far from the knowledge of God, calls to draw near, saying: “Come and see the works of God.”

The Apostle also taught that many are placed far from God, whom an exhortation of teaching has brought, as it were, into the neighborhood, when he says: “And when he came, he preached peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near” (Eph. 2:17). For many who were, as it were, nearby through the law believed, while the nations were summoned from afar.

### 10. Namely, the Works by Which He Provided for Human Salvation in the Time of the Law

Therefore the prophetic proclamation called all to behold God’s works—but not those works which lie before the sight of all, heaven, air, earth, and sea, for all behold these. Rather, it calls them to those works known only by the zeal of believers, by which provision was made for human salvation amid the great terror of marvelous powers: Pharaoh, restrained by punishments for his impiety, being made an example for human fear, so that dread of the condemnation of irreligious people might initiate religion through fear.

Thus, when the sea dried up into a road across the land and the waters were turned to dry ground; when the people crossed the Jordan on foot, and, as Israel entered the promised land, the waters were commanded to stand while the remaining riverbed ran down to provide secure passage—to behold these works of God in the law and prophets the Prophet calls the nations, saying in verses 5 and 6: “Come and see the works of God, terrible in his counsels over the children of men. He who turned the sea into dry land: they will pass through the river on foot.”

For he must be understood to be God through whose terrible counsels provision was made for human salvation by these works, so that our knowledge may confirm the conviction about God—since no one who beholds heaven fails to perceive that God exists [Note: Cicero acknowledges this in *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “What can be so plain and evident, when we have looked up to heaven and contemplated heavenly things, as that there is some divine being of outstanding intelligence by whom these are governed? … Whoever doubts this, I truly cannot understand how he could fail equally to doubt whether the sun exists or not.” So Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* I.2: “For no one is so uncultivated, so savage in habits, that, lifting his eyes to heaven, even if he does not know by whose God’s providence all that is seen is governed, does not nevertheless perceive from the very magnitude, motion, arrangement, constancy, usefulness, beauty, and order of things that some being exists.” Hence Orosius at the beginning of Book VI of his *Histories*: “Any human being can disregard God for a time, but cannot wholly fail to know him.” This is what Hilary himself said on Psalm 52, §2: God can be denied by the deliberation of an impious heart, but contrary to the faith and judgment of a sound mind.]—and may establish us in the knowledge of the author of such works.

### 11. How Those Works Concern Everyone

Yet although these are works of God’s power, they do not by themselves satisfy the hope and salvation of all. For the sea was changed into land only for the people of the law, and the Jordan dried up for their journey. But what benefit does this give to the salvation of the whole earth? For the command “Come” belongs to all, because it had been written concerning all: “Let all the earth worship you.”

What, then, does the Jordan, dried up so long before I was born, give to my salvation? It does indeed give something. For first, in its waters the washing away of sins was granted when John preached repentance; and through the river by which a way had been made for the people into the promised land, the way into the heavenly kingdom was opened for us, and possession of eternal bodies begins in the washing of new birth, the waters themselves having been consecrated by the Lord’s baptism.

Therefore, after the words, “Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his counsels over the children of men, he who turned the sea into dry land; they will pass through the river on foot,” it is added, lest the assurance of our hope be cut off by the things done long ago: after saying of the future, “they will pass through,” it therefore adds, “There we shall rejoice in him.” For through these waters of the Jordan there is passage, and has been passage, by the steps of bodies to be washed, into those good things of the land promised by the prophets; and there we rejoice in the beginnings of the heavenly sacrament.

Another prophet bears witness both to the time and cause of this rejoicing, saying: “Let the thirsty wilderness rejoice, and let the wilderness exult and blossom like a lily; let the wildernesses of the Jordan blossom and exult. Strengthen weak hands and feeble knees; comfort those of faint heart; strengthen yourselves in understanding; do not fear. Behold, our God will render judgment; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear, and the tongue of the mute will be heard. Then the lame will leap like a deer” (Isa. 35:1 ff.). [Note: The Tours manuscript reads “strengthen,” which might seem more suitable than “comfort,” if the Greek did not read **παρακαλέσατε**. “Our” is absent from the royal manuscript, as above also in Psalm 54, §8.]

This, then, is what is signified by “There we shall rejoice in him,” things fulfilled at the coming of the Lord, in the baptisms of the Jordan, and in the healing of every infirmity. And “there we shall rejoice” refers to the Jordan. For it says: “They will pass through the river on foot; there we shall rejoice.”

### 12. Christ Will Rule Over Us: As Man, Though as God He Always Reigns

But as to the phrase “in him”—who is this one in whom we shall rejoice? The Prophet adds, saying in verse 7: “He who will rule in his power forever.” We do not doubt who this will be if we remember the Gospel saying: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth; therefore go and teach all nations” (Matt. 28:18). [Note: “All” is omitted in the Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius editions and in the royal manuscript.]

And the Apostle says: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9 ff.). This is not said concerning the power of his divinity. For as it always rules, so it will always rule; rather, the nature of the flesh assumed from the Virgin is transferred into his eternal glory.

For Jesus is the name of the man who was born of Mary, and the name of Jesus, which is above every name, is given to him. Here it is not, as elsewhere, “Jesus Christ,” but “Jesus” alone. For to him, worshiped by heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings and confessed by every tongue to be in the glory of God the Father, is granted authority over the eternal kingdom.

But, as often, our Latin translation here too has not expressed quite precisely the meaning of the Greek phrase. What is written in our text, “He who will rule in his power forever,” is read in Greek thus: **τῷ δεσπόζοντι ἐν δυναστείᾳ αὐτοῦ τοῦ αἰῶνος**, “to him who exercises lordship in his power over the age.” What among us is “forever” is general, simple, and applicable to every time without the particular force of a definition; but their **τοῦ αἰῶνος** signifies an age that is definite and designated. [Note: Since Hilary consistently reads “he who will rule” and does not say that the Greek term differs from the Latin, he must have read **τῷ δεσπόζοντι**. Shortly afterward, in the Tours manuscript, the article **τῇ** is inserted before **δυναστείᾳ**; above it, in Latin letters, the same hand has written “ti,” as is done wherever a Greek word occurs, a detail noted so that the pronunciation then current may not be unknown.]

13. When He Will Obtain That Kingdom of His. — For although the only-begotten Son of God has always reigned, He has not always reigned in the body. Therefore, where the dominion of a designated and, as it were, pointed-out age is contained by the force of the expression *tou aiōnos* (“of the age”), [Col. 0429D] that time is shown in which, when the body has been glorified unto the glory of God, both the name of God and the kingdom are bestowed upon it. The Apostle expressly teaches the time of this reign, saying: “When He has abolished every principality and power and might, the last enemy, death, shall be conquered” (1 Cor. 15:24). Then He alone [Col. 0430A] shall reign in His power over the age.

For now, although He reigns, nevertheless the prince of this age asked that he might sift the Apostles as wheat (Luke 22:31); and there are spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, against which blessed Paul equipped us with spiritual weapons. Against them, while we fight, the Angels of our faith—who, according to the Gospels, daily behold God the Father in heaven—attend us, and God’s mercy protects us (Matt. 18:10).

14. The God Who Either Turns His Eyes Away or Turns Them Toward Us. — And for this reason there follows: “His eyes look upon the nations.” For the face of the Lord is turned away from everyone who remains in sins. This is the meaning of God’s unchangeable turning: not that He, as though by a bodily nature, turns Himself away in one direction or [Col. 0430B] turns Himself back in another; but that, remaining always equal and the same, He either withholds or gives His help to each person according to the diversity of merits.

Thus it is written in the person of sinners: “Turn Your face away from their sins” (Ps. 50:11); and again: “Why do You turn away Your face and Your right hand?” (Ps. 73:11); and again: “You turned away Your face, and I was troubled” (Ps. 29:8). But where the person of the righteous is concerned, these things are said: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears unto their prayers” (Ps. 33:16); and again: “Let Your eyes behold righteousness” (Ps. 16:2); and then: “The light of Your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7). Therefore the incorporeal God, by the eyes of His mercy and, as it were, by the ministry of serving Angels, protects the nations and pours out upon all believers [Col. 0430C] the gift of His divine compassion.

> Note: We add “Himself” (*se*) from the Royal manuscript. Hilary shortly indicates what he more plainly explains in Psalm 129, §7: Angels may be called members of God, through whom He provides for us.

15. The Jews Who Provoke God to Wrath. — The Jews deny this; the unbelieving people oppose these works of God, arrogating to themselves the glory of the chosen race in Abraham. In the words that follow, the Prophet shows this, joining to what he had said, “His eyes look upon the nations,” the clause: “Let not those who provoke Him to wrath exalt themselves.” The Lord condemns this self-exaltation in the Gospels, saying: “Do not say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father’; for God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones” (Matt. 3:9).

> Note: The Royal manuscript has *praeferre* (“set forth, advance”) rather than *proferre* (“bring forth”): a word quite suited to Hilary’s point, though differing from the Greek *legein* (“say”).

As for their provoking Him to wrath, the prophets speak of it everywhere. Isaiah: “You have provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger” (Isa. 1:4).

> Note: Thus the Royal manuscript, following the Greek *parōrgisate*. But the printed editions have “you have provoked to anger.” Our Vulgate has “they blasphemed.”

The Spirit also speaks to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I send you to the house of Israel, who have embittered Me” (Ezek. 2:3); and in the Psalms: “They embittered His spirit” (Ps. 105:33); and again: “Often I delivered them, but they embittered Me” (ibid., 43). Therefore all who deny God’s work and mercy for the salvation of the nations provoke to wrath the author of mercy and salvation, [Col. 0431A] because, glorious and exalted in themselves, they embitter Him who alone can make persons glorious.

16. Up to This Point the Speech Was Prophetic; It Is Now Apostolic. — The insertion again of the *diapsalma* teaches a change both of sense and of persons. For under this sign a distinction is frequently made of one party, and sometimes of both. The preceding discourse was wholly in the person of the Prophet, saying: “Come and see the works of God, how terrible He is in His counsels over the children of men.” The following discourse, however, had to be apostolic, so that, with the former inviting and the latter preaching, the one doctrine might contain the proclamation of both the Old and New Testaments.

17. An Exhortation to Praise the True God. — Their exhortation, then, is directed to the nations when it says, verse 8: “Bless, O nations, our God.” The Prophet did not add “our” [Col. 0431B] without purpose. It is not those whom you thought gods—the names of heroes, the created elements, or the material of metals—but ours: Him whose works are recounted, who is terrible in His counsels over the children of men, who turned the sea into dry land, who rules in His power for the age. For this is proper to apostolic doctrine: to preach in the Gospels the God of the Law and the Prophets.

> Note: Paris, from the manuscript of Mic., reads *perturbatis* (“you were troubled”).

18. God Must Be Praised Openly. — But what follows—“And make heard the voice of His praise”—confuses the understanding. For the voice of praise is heard not from Him who is praised but from the one who offers praise. How, then, are the nations exhorted to hear the voice of His praise? But here too our Latin has not preserved in translation the exact force of the expression. For what is written among us, “and make heard the voice [Col. 0431C] of His praise,” is expressed by the Greeks thus: *kai akoutisate tēn phōnēn tēs aineseōs autou*—“and cause the voice of His praise to be heard.”

> Note: Erasmus and Lipsius read *akoustisate*; Paris, *akousēsate*. We restore from the Royal manuscript, in accordance with more accurate Greek copies of the Psalms, *akoutisate*, from *akoutizō*. Symmachus rendered the word by the two words *akoustēn poiēsate* (“make audible”); our Vulgate then rendered it by the same number of words, “make heard.” This was unknown to Hilary, but is certainly already approved insofar as this passage is concerned.

By this word it is signified that they are to make the voice of His praise able to be heard. This will be more fully understood by one who remembers that the Lord said in the Gospels: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops” (Matt. 10:27). For God must be praised by steady and public proclamation; nor should our faith shrink from recounting His mighty deeds.

19. On the Constancy of the Apostles and Martyrs. — But what voice of His praise is to be made heard? Surely this: that He has placed the soul of the believer in life; that He has granted steadfastness and perseverance in confession to apostolic preaching and the martyrs’ confession. By their journeys the proclamation of the heavenly kingdom ran through the world as though on certain [Col. 0431D] feet. “For their sound went out into all the earth” (Ps. 18:5). Elsewhere the Holy Spirit proclaims the glory of this spiritual journey: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good things, who proclaim peace!” (Rom. 10:16).

This, then, is the voice of God’s praise which is to be heard through the heralding of preachers, as the Prophet testifies, [Col. 0432A] verse 9: “Who has placed my soul in life and has not allowed my feet to be moved.” The Apostles were not turned aside from their course of preaching by the terrors of human threats; nor was the firmness of their standing feet shaken from the path of faith, so as to prevent their always preaching the Lord of judgment and the eternal kingdom.

> Note: In the Royal manuscript, “and perseverance” is absent.

20. What Belongs to Many Is Spoken of One Because of Their Unity of Mind. — Although the Spirit of prophecy spoke in the person of one, He indicates that the thing itself does not belong to one name alone. For when He had said, “And He has not allowed my feet to be moved,” He added, verse 10: “For You have tested us, O God; You have examined us by fire, as silver is examined.” Thus a discourse begun from one person is referred to many. For there is one Spirit and one faith of believers, according to what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “The soul [Col. 0432B] and heart of the believers were one” (Acts 4:32). Thus, when what begins from one is shown to extend to many, unanimity among the many is taught.

> Note: Thus the manuscripts consistently follow the Greek; the common editions have “one soul and one heart.”

But what likeness of comparison is this, that they were tested by fire as silver is tested? As I suppose, the sole reason for testing silver is that the impurities adhering from its original earthly material may be boiled away, and that what has been fraudulently mixed in from the nature of another metal may be cleansed. Thus God tests believers in Himself not as one ignorant of their faith; but because, even according to the Apostle, temptation produces proof, believers are tested not for God’s knowledge but for their own proving: so that, purified by fire and cleansed from the admixture of carnal vices, they may shine with the brightness of tested innocence.

> Note: The printed editions wrongly have *materiae* (“of matter”).

21. The Punishments and Victories of the Martyrs. — As we consider the kinds of temptations and the various victories of the martyrs, we know in what ways the soul is placed in life: by despising the ingenious devices of raging punishments, they are not moved from the path and testimony of faith. Some glory in the chains of prisons; others rejoice when struck in beatings; others submit the necks of their blessed heads to the authority of irreligious men to be cut off. Many run to the pyres that have been built, and, while the ministers of punishment tremble, leap into the fire with the spring of devoted eagerness. Others, to be plunged into the depths, fall not into waters that kill but into the refreshment of eternal blessedness, offering their entire bodies to God as a victim, like whole burnt offerings.

> Note: That is, punishments ingeniously devised. So again in Psalm 118, letter 18, §9: “I do not say that deaths are inflicted, but that they are renewed with devices of punishments.” In much the same way Pliny the Younger, in the *Panegyric*, calls an ingeniously elaborate banquet the *ingenium caenae*.

22. David Foresaw These Things. — The prophetic discourse therefore runs through these kinds of sufferings in the person of Apostles, Evangelists, and martyrs, saying: “You examined us by fire, as silver is examined by fire. Verse 11. You brought us into a snare,” that is, into the chains of custody. “You placed tribulations upon our back”: namely, the punishments of beatings, in which Peter rejoices with the Apostles [Col. 0433A] and Paul exults. “Verse 12. You set men over our heads. We passed through fire and water.” He plainly commemorates the glorious deaths of martyrs: by sword, fire, and the deep.

But whoever passes through fire and water is not destroyed in them, but through them is carried to something else. The Prophet knows to what place he is carried, saying: “And You brought us out into refreshment.” He recalls this refreshment elsewhere too, saying: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt kindly with me. He has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling. I shall be pleasing to the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 144:7 ff.). He exhorts his soul, that is, to the rest of that blessed resurrection in which, after the time of this death and after every stain of human calamity has been washed away, there is no grief, no weeping, [Col. 0433B] no sin, but life. They were therefore led through fire and water into the refreshment of this blessedness.

23. Why Water, Fire, and Refreshment Must Be Understood Spiritually. — And lest swimming through waters, leaping over fire, or entrance into the rest of some ordinary earthly place should be thought to be meant, he added, verse 13: “I shall enter Your house with whole burnt offerings.” Whole burnt offerings are entire bodies of victims; because they were wholly brought to the fire of sacrifice, they were called *holocausta*. Through these kinds of punishments, therefore, the martyrs vowed their bodies as whole burnt offerings for the testimony of faith, so that they might enter God’s house—that is, the dwelling-place of the heavenly [Col. 0433C] abode—when the sacrifices of their victims had been completed.

> Note: We have already observed at Psalm 58, §6 that Stephen’s entrance into heaven is indicated to have been open after death. The same thing is here preached more explicitly concerning the other martyrs. For what is dwelling in the heavenly home except possession of heaven? And if this is granted to martyrs when the sacrifices of their victims are completed, it must not be long delayed after the death by which they complete the sacrifices of their life and body.

24. Martyrs Vow to God Both Themselves and Those Who Will Imitate Them. — But what, then, did they vow in this offering of their bodies? Clearly, that by these examples of their martyrdom they might instruct the nations in the hope of the eternal kingdom. For those who then preached Christ preached not for themselves, to whom He was then known, but for us, who were still to come, or for those to whom He was then unknown. All their preaching kindles the faith of every later generation toward the desire for martyrdom. For they preached for no other purpose than that, by the example of their faith and martyrdom, they might train more martyrs. Paul taught this, saying: “I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for you Gentiles” (Eph. 3:1).

Accordingly, in the fruit of this preaching they confess that they render their vows to God, saying: “I will render to You my vows, verses 14 and 15, which my lips have uttered; and my mouth spoke in my tribulation. I will offer to You whole burnt offerings full of marrow, with incense and rams; I will offer to You oxen with he-goats.” Does the Prophet not know that he spoke in the Spirit in the person of God: “I will not take calves from your house, nor he-goats from your flocks” (Ps. 49:9); and, “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of he-goats?” (ibid., 13); and again, “For if You had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; You will not delight in whole burnt offerings” (Ps. 50:18)?

Let the error of our opinion therefore cease, that we may suppose the martyrs vowed these things. Rather, in the martyrdoms of those who come after them they render to God the vows which they uttered: first indeed, by vowing themselves to God and offering themselves as whole burnt offerings, because by these they will enter God’s house. In the tribulations of their sufferings they cry out in Paul’s words: “Who shall separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril?” (Rom. 8:35); and: “I am confident that neither [Col. 0434B] death nor life, nor things present nor things to come, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (ibid., 38).

These, then, are first the vows of the blessed martyrs in tribulation, which they declare and pledge amid their sufferings; then, secondly, that from among us whole burnt offerings full of marrow may be completed.

> Note: Thus the Badian edition with the Royal manuscript; Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris have *prima* (“first”).

They are full of marrow because faith is an office of soul and heart, a matter of inward will. Rams too are offered with incense. What incense is, we are taught in this same book of Psalms, when it says: “Let my prayer be set before You as incense” (Ps. 140:2), indicating that prayers are to be understood by incense. The preceding Psalm shows who are represented under the name of rams, when it says: “The rams of the sheep are clothed” (Ps. 64:14). For by them, as by the leaders of the flocks, it signifies priests, whom the instruction of apostolic teaching, together with the fragrance of prayers—“For,” according to the Apostle, “we are a good fragrance in Christ” (2 Cor. 2:15)—urges on toward the pursuit of martyrdom. Nor are only rams offered with incense; oxen are offered as well: that is, beasts of an obstinate nature are tamed for God’s cultivation, subdued by apostolic teaching unto martyrdom for the name of Christ.

25. But in the words, “I will offer You oxen with he-goats,” the Latin wording has not retained the force of the expression changed from Hebrew into Greek. For what we have is “I will offer You oxen with he-goats”; but among them it stands thus: *anoisō soi boas meta cheimarrōn*.

> Note: The Greek words were omitted in Badius’s edition. Erasmus, lacking manuscript copies of these treatises, supplied them as best he could from common Greek Bibles; here he wrote *meta chimarōn*, omitting the following word *cheimarroi*. From the very deformed letters of the Royal codex, written by a man wholly unskilled in reading and writing Greek, we restore this entire passage as far as possible. First, instead of *chimarōn*, we place *cheimarrōn*, from *cheimōn* or *cheimas*, “winter,” especially because Hilary immediately says that torrents increased by winter rains are signified by the same word; these are surely called *cheimarroi*, not *chimaroi*. Next, from the same manuscript we add *cheimarroi*, before which several characters occur, from which we conjecture—indeed, it is nearly certain—that the reading is: “from *cheimas*, *cheimarroi* among the Greeks,” etc.

*Cheimarroi* among the Greeks is not a proper name but a common designation for he-goats, especially those born in the very season of winter. Scripture calls them *cheimarrhous* only in this place; elsewhere it uses *tragous* [Col. 0435A], which we call *hirci*, “he-goats.”

> Note: In the Royal codex the word *tragos* is repeated here in Latin letters, just as shortly above *cheimarrhous* is expressed both in Latin and Greek characters.

The meaning of the spiritual interpretation is confirmed by the consistent and harmonious translation of others, who rendered *cheimarrois* as *tragous kairious*.

> Note: Editions after Erasmus, who translated *chimarous* as *tragous*, are restored from the Royal manuscript: “*tragoi* are signified . . . but *chimaroi*, etc.” Yet the manuscript gives *kairimous* or *kairialous*, and then more likely *kairimoi* than *kairious* and *kairioi*. It is certain, however, that this word derives from *kairos*, “season.” We have not been able to discover traces among the ancients of the translation which Hilary here mentions. The Tours manuscript has: “those who rendered *cheimarrois* as *kairikous*; but *kairikoi* . . .”

Now *tragoi kairioi* means he-goats born from the season itself; but *cheimarroi*, those brought forth by winter. For this reason Greek also calls torrents by the same word: winter causes them to increase from nothing into rivers.

26. Those Ignorant of the Faith Underwent Martyrdom by the Martyrs’ Example. — Therefore, when he says *boas meta chimarōn*,

> Note: The words *meta chimarōn*, omitted in earlier printed editions, are restored from the Royal codex, whose spelling, though inconsistent with the preceding forms, we retain. The Tours manuscript indeed has *meta cheimarōn*.

the prophetic discourse shows that it is not speaking of cattle, but that by the oxen it indicates people in the Church, and by the *cheimarroi* those whom the very storm of persecution has brought forth in the glory of martyrdom.

> Note: Paris, from the manuscript of Mic., reads “through the glory of martyrdom”; the other editions, “unto the glory of martyrdom.” We restore from the Royal manuscript, “in the glory of martyrdom,” although none of the other readings is displeasing. Hilary means that “oxen” signify persons born in the bosom of the Church, while *cheimarroi* signify those first born outside the Church who, embracing and publicly professing the faith through the example of martyrs, immediately attain the glory of martyrdom.

For we know that many persons ignorant of the divine sacraments have run to martyrdom through the example [Col. 0435B] of martyrs; having previously lived outside knowledge of the faith, but taught by the deed of present faith, they attained that very glory of faith completed in martyrdom. Such was the man who confessed the Lord in the very moment of his condemnation, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when You come into Your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). At once he received from the Lord such a reward of this martyrdom: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with Me in paradise” (ibid., 43).

> Note: Supply “the thief.”

The instruction of apostolic doctrine therefore offers to God those like him, together with persons born from long and fruitful cultivation, under the very storm of a raging winter.

> Note: Paris has *potestate* (“power”) instead of *tempestate* (“storm”).

But when God says, “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to Me? I am full. I do not desire the whole burnt offerings of rams, the fat of lambs, or the blood of bulls and he-goats. For who has required these things [Col. 0435C] from your hands?” it is superfluous to suppose that complete vows of ceremonial observance were pleasing in oxen and he-goats.

27. *Diapsalma.* David Relates to the Devout What God Has Granted Him. — As elsewhere, the insertion of the *diapsalma* changes person and sense, though without departing from the order of the teaching. For after he had shown, in the persons of Apostles, Evangelists, martyrs, and prophets, the ways in which his soul had been placed in life—that is, through the punishments and deaths of sufferings, through which it passed into the place of blessedness, rendering vows to God in whole burnt offerings—after this discourse, which he had addressed wholly to God, he now speaks to those whom he had trained for the solemn offerings of whole burnt offerings, saying, verse 16: “Come and hear, and I will recount to you, all who fear [Col. 0436A] God.”

> Note: The Tours codex reads, “the Prophet had shown.” This reading is confirmed by the beginning of §22.

He summons neither the uncertain nor persons toward uncertainty. For he teaches who those are whom he summons: “All who fear God.” The irreligious have neither the will to approach nor the will to hear. Then he indicates what he will recount: “How great things He has done for my soul.” For He placed it in life, led it into refreshment, and it will enter God’s house in whole burnt offerings.

28. What It Merited by the Cry of Mouth and Heart. — But for these things to happen to the soul, it merited that they should happen by their causes. He states by what causes it merited them, verse 17: “I cried to Him with my mouth.” Therefore the soul merited good things because it cried to Him with its mouth. But the cry of the mouth is often deceitful, and the sound of words does not always declare the disposition of the mind. Therefore the heart’s meaning must accompany the cry of the mouth; and it did accompany it. For the Prophet joined: [Col. 0436B] “And I exalted Him beneath my tongue,” not “on my tongue” but “beneath my tongue”: that is, in the hidden places of the tongue and by a kind of inward speech of silent will. This too pleased the Lord when He said in the Gospels: “Enter into your chamber, shut your door, and pray; and your Father, who sees in secret, shall reward you” (Matt. 6:6). Therefore God, who is now cried to with the mouth, is exalted beneath the tongue.

29. What It Merited by Purity of Heart. — But He who is exalted beneath the tongue must be worshipped with every purity of heart. Nor is it enough not to have committed anything impious if impiety is conceived in the mind. The Prophet teaches that the thought of such impiety must be absent from one who exalts God beneath the tongue, saying, verses 18 and 19: “If I have looked upon iniquity in my heart, may God not hear [Col. 0436C] me. Therefore God heard me and attended to the voice of my prayer.”

> Note: Thus the Royal manuscript, with Theodoret and the Septuagint; the common editions have “will not hear.”

He not only did not carry out iniquity in deed, but did not even look upon it in his heart. Or certainly, he did not behold iniquity in his heart: that is, he saw no vice of his own unrighteous will in his heart; and for that reason he was worthy to be heard. For his soul was placed in life, his feet were not moved, he was led into refreshment, and he will enter God’s house; and he has paid to God the vows which his lips uttered.

> Note: The printed editions here have “he entered”; above, at the end of §27, “he will enter God’s house.” At both places the manuscripts have “he will enter.” Should “he entered” perhaps be read in both?

Supported by confession of honour and glory, he says, verse 20: “Blessed be God, who has not removed my prayer and His mercy from me,” confessing at the end the praise of God begun at the opening of the Psalm—to whom be glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LXVI

For the end: a hymn (or, “in hymns”), a psalm of David’s song.

[Col. 0437A]

May God have mercy on us and bless us; may He make His face shine upon us and have mercy on us. *Diapsalma.* That we may know Your way upon earth, Your salvation among all nations. Let the peoples confess to You, O God; let all the peoples confess to You. Let the nations rejoice and exult, because You judge peoples in equity and guide the nations upon earth.

> Note: Hilary: “You will direct.”

*Diapsalma.* Let the peoples confess to You, O God; let all the peoples confess to You: the earth has yielded its fruit. May our God bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear Him.

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. Who Speak in This Psalm. — Verse 1. The Psalm [Col. 0437B] is brief and complete in evangelical preaching. For it is both “for the end” and “a psalm of song”: through this, confession is sung with knowledge of what must be done, and deeds are sung as advancing through teaching. Its beginning has been taken from the source from which it ought to have been taken. Every utterance in it belongs either to prophets or to Apostles: some taught that the only-begotten God would come in the body; others that He had come, enlightened by the Holy Spirit and filled with the honour of heavenly glory. Their prayer, therefore, must be recognized in the opening of the Psalm.

2. Forgiveness of Sins Is Gratuitous. — Verse 2. “May God have mercy on us and bless us; may He make His face shine upon us and have mercy on us.” In the order of doctrine, God’s mercy is sought first. For from the abundance of His goodness He grants mercy in the forgiveness [Col. 0437C] of sins; and forgiveness of sins is not the merit of uprightness, but the willing purpose of gratuitous pardon, the gift of compassion overflowing from the riches of goodness. Therefore He who is merciful is asked to bless.

We have already learned the fruit of blessing at the beginning of humanity’s formation, when Adam, still ignorant of sin, received this message: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and have dominion over it” (Gen. 1:28). Although many think these words were spoken only in a bodily sense, they have nevertheless offered a deeper power to those instructed in spiritual doctrine. For this blessing was not granted merely to Adam’s bodily descendants in succession. For although his offspring would be fruitful, they could not fill the earth; which, though inhabited in proportion to the multitude of people, is not filled to capacity. Rather, He willed that the earth of our body should be filled with spiritual teachings, and that knowledge [Col. 0438A] of God should be multiplied and increased.

For through Adam and in Adam himself, who was the first work of God, knowledge of God ought to have begun; but when he was stained by sins, the Prophets and Apostles pray for themselves for the fruit of this blessing.

> Note: The manuscript has *Profeta*. It is understood to mean David alone.

Having obtained it, the blessed Apostle thus boasts concerning himself: “Blessed be God, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in heavenly places in Christ” (Eph. 1:3). Therefore those who are heavenly in Christ increase, multiply, and are filled; and those blessed with a spiritual blessing in heavenly places are blessed. Let us see whether the prayer of this present Psalm asks for the fruit of this blessing.

> Note: “The present fruit”; “the present prayer.”

3. Our Light Is God’s Gift. — For after mercy and blessing there follows: “May He make His face shine upon us and have mercy on us.” We need God’s blessing, that His face may illumine us, that it may shed the light of His knowledge upon our darkened hearts, and that the Spirit of His majesty may grant light to the faculties of our understanding darkened by obscurity; so that thereafter we may be permitted to glory, saying: “The light of Your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7).

> Note: The printed editions read “the light of darkness”; corrected from the Royal manuscript.

The mercy by which He began in us through forgiveness of sin grants this illumination of His face upon us. The following discourse teaches the purpose for which they pray that God’s face may shine upon them.

4. Knowledge of God’s Way Is Sought for the Nations. — *Diapsalma.* Verse 3. “That we may know Your way upon earth, Your salvation among all nations.” The insertion of the *diapsalma*, although it did not [Col. 0438C] bring a change of person, did change the sense.

> Note: “It brought a change of person, but did not change the sense.” Thus the codex and Erasmus’s edition. There appears to be no change of sense here, and Hilary seems immediately to indicate a change of person: “For now the discourse is addressed to Him,” etc.

> Note: In the common editions the negative particle is missing here. Erasmus inserted it before *demutavit* (“changed”), and that reading subsequently prevailed. That reading would make this a change of person, not of sense, although Hilary teaches that it is a change of sense, not person. For the discourse continues to God, to whom it was addressed from the beginning; and, as he says in §1, all the discourse in this Psalm belongs either to prophets or Apostles. The sense changes because those who formerly began to pray for themselves now begin to pray for others, especially according to the force of the Greek wording, from which Hilary would have preferred the translation “that it may become known” rather than “that we may know.” The Royal manuscript provides the correct reading.

For what is written in Latin books as “that we may know Your way upon earth” is in Greek: *tou gnōnai en tē gē tēn hodon sou*.

> Note: We restore from the Royal manuscript *inter gnōnai* (“between *gnōnai*”), which was missing in the earlier printed editions.

Between *gnōnai* and “that we may know” lies this difference: *gnōnai* has no definition of person, whereas “that we may know” identifies the very persons who speak these words. Therefore, according to that true rendering of the Greek, they pray that they may be enlightened by God’s face in order that God’s way may become known [Col. 0439A] upon earth—the teaching of religious life. For by it one proceeds to God.

Christ is the teaching of the religious way, and in the Gospels He showed that He is this way, saying: “I am the truth, the way, and the life” (John 14:6); and again: “No one comes to the Father except through Me” (ibid.). The connected discourse of the Psalm itself testifies that He is the way. This way must be made knowable and known upon earth: that is, either to those born from the earth or to those who inhabit the earth. “That we may know Your way upon earth, Your salvation among all nations.”

The language of this expression itself says that Jesus is called “the Salvation” (*salutare*). For what is “salvation” among us is Jesus in Hebrew. The Angel confirms this, speaking to Joseph concerning Mary: “She shall bear a Son, and you shall call His name Jesus, because He will save [Col. 0439B] His people from sins” (Matt. 1:21).

> Note: Here again the common editions add “their,” a word already observed to be absent from the more reliable manuscripts in Psalm 51, §24.

The Angel therefore shows that He is to be called Jesus because He will be salvation to the people. Thus they show themselves unequal to so great a proclamation unless they are enlightened, unless they shine with some splendour from the Lord’s countenance. For according to the Gospel they too are “the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14)—the Lord Himself, however, is “the true light” (John 1:9)—enlightened by the Light so that the Apostles and Prophets might be light. Otherwise it would be superfluous for them to wish to be enlightened in order to know things which they preached as if already known.

5. The Source of Joy for the Nations. — This whole prophetic and apostolic teaching must be followed by the confession of the peoples and the joy of sins forgiven. Nor is it only the forgiveness of sins, [Col. 0439C] but also their knowledge that He who has forgiven sins will be the judge of righteousness, and that through Him all nations inhabiting the earth are directed into the way of life, being instructed in the knowledge of God after abandoning the error of idols. Therefore there follows, verses 4 and 5: “Let all the peoples confess to You. Let the nations rejoice and exult, because [Col. 0439D] You will judge peoples in equity and will direct the nations upon earth.”

> Note: The Royal manuscript has “You judge.” Then, following the Greek, “upon earth,” not “into the earth.” But the common reading better agrees with the explanation which follows.

When “the peoples confess,” those who believe or will believe from the twelve tribes seem to be indicated. When “all peoples confess,” no exception is made for the nations. When the nations rejoice and exult because He will judge peoples in equity and direct nations into the earth, the cause of their joy is proclaimed to arise from hope in eternal judgment and from the nations’ being directed into the way of life.

[Col. 0439D] **6. The twofold confession.**—The insertion of the *diapsalma* seems here to have introduced no novelty, especially since the sense is repeated in the same words, VERSE 6: “Let the peoples confess thee, O God; let all the peoples confess thee.” But when there is added, VERSE 7: “The earth has yielded her fruit,” it is understood that the repetition of the same words was not made without purpose—provided, indeed, that we are to understand the same thing as signified under the same words. For we find that confession must be considered in two ways: one confession of sins [Note: Bad., Er., Lips., and the Royal manuscript: “of confessed sins.”], when in the wilderness of Jordan they confessed their sins; the other, praise of God, when the Lord says to the Father: “I confess [Note: Paris edition from the Micacian manuscript: “I shall confess,” which the Royal manuscript also seems to have had.] to thee, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. II, 25). Therefore that first and earlier confession must chiefly be understood as confession of sins, because it is joined to prophetic and apostolic preaching. This following confession is to be understood as the praise of the peoples, and then of all peoples—that is, of all the nations—and this because the earth has yielded her fruit.

**7. The earth’s proper fruit, lost through the first Adam, restored through the second.**—But we must ask what fruit the earth yielded, on account of which all peoples praise God. Certainly, there is an everlasting reason for the praise due to God: that the earth supplies these bodily fruits necessary to us. Yet they are not the earth’s fruits. For they are either ours, to whom they are supplied, or God’s, through whom they are dispensed. Let us therefore inquire what fruits the earth both possessed and lost. By what it lost, we shall show that it had possessed them.

We remember that Adam’s earth, after his sin, was stripped of the honor of the blessings granted to him. For it was said to him: “For thou art earth, and into earth shalt thou go” (Gen. III, 19). Therefore, because he is earth, he is condemned by this curse after sin: “Cursed is the earth in thy works; in sorrows thou shalt eat it all the days of thy life; it shall generate thorns and thistles for thee” (ibid., 17). The element earth was free from guilt; therefore what was free from guilt was also free from the curse. But here Adam’s earth, made guilty through the enticement of food, is cursed. Thus it is consumed by every sorrow of this present life; it is eaten amid all the pains of sickness, pierced by the thorns and thistles, the stings of vices and desires. Every person, therefore, who resembles the earthly Adam yields these cursed fruits of his own earth.

But the one who is now conformed to the heavenly Adam possesses the innocent fruit of his earth: first, rich in the knowledge of God; then glorious in works of chastity, justice, and mercy, having put off the old man with his vices and desires. Therefore confession must be rendered to God because the earth has yielded its own fruit. Its own: because Adam, though he had possessed it, had lost it. Therefore it gave what was its own—that is, it displayed in that very first one, our Lord, who assumed an earthly body while committing no sin, the fruit that belongs to it in the knowledge of God.

**8. The God of the patriarchs is now, as though by inheritance, ours.**—For the purpose of showing and teaching these things, the gift of God’s blessing is again sought when it is said: “May God bless us.” And lest the blessing be thought hoped for from an uncertain and unknown God, there is added: “our God”—namely, the God of the patriarchs and prophets, now belonging to the apostles themselves as though by inheritance of succession [Note: Paris edition: “now nearest,” wrongly.].
