In them the earth yielded its fruit: continence, faith, justice, and mercy; indeed, even amid the tortures and deaths of most savage persecutions, martyrdom already devoted to the divine Name.

**9. What the fear of God ought to be.**—The prayer for blessing is then repeated: “May God bless us.” These petitions are not repeated without purpose, but so that, through God’s blessing, doctrine may increase and all the ends of the earth may fear God. For he says: “And let all the ends of the earth fear him.” Let all the ends of the earth, therefore, fear God—but our God, the God who blesses. Fear is no small office of faith. For it is numbered among the foremost gifts of spiritual graces, when Isaiah says: “And he filled him with the spirit of the fear of God” (Isa. XI, 3) [Note: Bad., Er., and Lips.: “and shall fill him,” in agreement with the Septuagint but against the manuscripts. The Paris edition then has “the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” The saying afterwards cited under Solomon’s name is shown by its very wording to have been taken, not from Prov. I, 7, but from Ecclesiasticus. In Psalm CXL, no. 4, and in the commentary on Matthew, ch. 7, the book of Ecclesiasticus is called Solomon’s.]. And through Solomon: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. I, 16).

Blessed is one who comes to fear [Note: “Fear.”] not from the trembling of human nature, but from rational knowledge. For one who fears anxious things through weakness becomes insolent again in favorable circumstances through the same defect of nature. But one who fears from knowledge always fears, and fears prosperity no less than adversity. Wisdom, therefore, takes its beginning from fear, by carrying out useful and approved things, which are proper and distinctive to wisdom.

The Prophet therefore desires this fear of God for all the ends of the earth, so that no nation dwelling upon earth may be outside his fear. The Apostle explains the substance of this desire when he says: “And every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 11), who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM LXVII

For the end: a psalm of David himself, a song. [Note: “For the end: a psalm, a song of David.”]

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered [Note: “dispersed.”]; and let those who hate him flee from before his face. As smoke fails away, let them fail away; as wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God. But let the righteous rejoice in gladness; let them exult in the sight of God, let them feast in gladness. Sing to God; make melody to his name; prepare a way for him who ascends above the setting; the Lord is his name, and exult [Col. 0441D] before him. They shall be troubled before his face—he who is father of orphans and judge of widows. God in his holy place: God makes those of one manner dwell in a house. He brings forth [Col. 0442A] prisoners in strength, likewise those who provoke him [variant: “were provoking him”], who dwell in tombs.

“O God, when thou wentest forth before thy people, when thou didst pass through the wilderness, the earth was moved. For the heavens dropped before the face of God; Mount Sinai, before the face of the God of Israel. Thou wilt set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for thine inheritance; and it was weakened, but thou hast made it perfect. Thy animals shall dwell therein; in thy sweetness thou hast prepared for the poor, O God.” [Note: Hilary: “In thy sweetness, O God, prepare for the poor.”]

“The Lord God will give the word to those who proclaim the good news with great powers: the king of the beloved’s powers; to divide spoils for the beauty of the house. Though you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of a dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the green brightness of gold. When the heavenly One separates kings over her, they shall be whitened with snow in Selmon. A mountain of God, a fertile mountain; a holy mountain, a rich mountain: why do you look with envy [Note: Hilary: “why have you looked with envy”] upon curdled mountains? The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell; indeed, the Lord shall dwell there unto the end.

“The chariots of God are ten thousandfold manifold, thousands of those rejoicing; the Lord is among them in Sinai, in the Holy Place. He ascended on high; he took captivity captive; he gave gifts among men. Indeed, that even those who do not believe might dwell with the Lord God.” [Note: Hilary omits “the Lord God.”]

“Blessed be the Lord God from day to day; the God of our salvations will make our journey prosperous. Our God is a God of saving; and of the Lord, the Lord [Note: Hilary does not repeat “Lord.”] are the issues from death. Yet God shall crush the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of those walking in their sins. The Lord said: ‘I shall return from Bashan; I shall return [Note: Below again: “I shall return.”] from the depths of the sea, that thy foot may be dipped in blood, and the tongue of thy dogs may be dipped from the enemies, by him.’

“Thy goings have been seen, O God—the goings of my God, my king who is in the sanctuary. The princes went before, joined with those making melody; in the midst were young maidens playing timbrels. In the churches bless the Lord God from the fountains of Israel. There Benjamin, the younger, is in trembling; the princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun; the princes of Naphtali. Command, O God, thy strength [Note: Below: “to thy strength.”]; strengthen, O God, what thou hast wrought in us. From thy temple in Jerusalem kings shall offer [Note: Hilary: “bring.”] gifts to thee. Rebuke the beasts of the forest, the assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples, that those tested by silver may be excluded [Note: Hilary here adds “not.”]. Scatter the nations that desire wars [Note: Hilary: “war.”]. Envoys shall come from Egypt; Ethiopia shall hasten her hands unto God.

“Kingdoms of the earth, sing to the Lord [Note: Below: “to God.”] and make melody to the Lord. Make melody to our God [Note: Below, “our” is absent.], who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east. Behold, he shall give his voice, the voice of power: give glory to God. His magnificence is over Israel, and his power is in the clouds. Wonderful is God in his saints; the God of Israel himself shall give power and strength to his people. Blessed is God.”

# TREATISE ON THE PSALM

[Col. 0443A] **1. This psalm is wholly woven from the mysteries of the Old and New Law.**—VERSE 1. The psalm is inscribed for the end, not *by* David but *for* David. Then it is not “a song of a psalm,” but “a psalm of a song,” so that the declaration of prophetic understanding and knowledge might be taught through it. It is wholly woven from the mysteries of the Law and the Gospels, and is filled with a great allegorical interpretation of sayings from both the past and the future. It contains in itself the teaching of the Law that was given; it supplies knowledge of the flesh assumed by the Lord; it reproves the impiety of the former people; it announces the faith of our future knowledge; it embraces the Lord’s ascension above the heavens; and it comprehends the glory of his kingdom to come.

The Prophet, however, took his beginning from that in which the result of our salvation consists [Note: Royal manuscript: “has consisted.”]. For he began thus:

**2. Christ’s resurrection is desired, and through it the flight of demons.**—VERSE 2. “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered [Note: Here again, “dispersed.”]; and let those who hate him flee from before his face.” This is the language of petitions [Note: Lipsius and Paris: “The sum of the petitions is,” against Bad., Erasmus, and all manuscripts.], not of one asking in uncertainty, but of one hoping from understanding and knowledge. For the time of resurrection in God is now desired: when, on account of sin, condemning sin in the flesh, he publicly exposed the powers of this world, triumphing over them with confidence in himself [Note: Thus the manuscripts here, as also in *On the Trinity*, I.13, and the Greek does not disagree: θριαμβεύσας αὐτοὺς ἐν αὐτῷ, “having triumphed over them in himself.” The printed editions instead read, “triumphing in himself.” Lipsius and Paris then read, “For he came into the world,” adding “into.”] (Col. II, 15).

For he came to conquer the world, to crucify the prince of the world together with the law of sin, and to abolish the decree of death through remission of sins. The Prophet therefore awaits this flight of his enemies. For the multitude of demons hating him could not endure [Note: “Endure.”] the encounter with him rising from the dead [Note: Royal manuscript: “hating him”; from the same manuscript we subsequently adopt “endure,” where the printed editions have “fully endure.” Thus in Psalm LI, no. 24, the name of Jesus is commended because demons tremble and cannot endure it.], when Satan is said to have fallen from heaven like lightning at the first proclamation of apostolic faith, after spiritual wickednesses had been subjected to them [Note: The editions read: “at the first utterance of apostolic faith, after the powers of spiritual wickedness had been subjected here, etc.” The Tours manuscript: “at the first teaching of apostolic faith, after the powers of spiritual wickedness had been subjected to these, Satan fell from heaven,” which has some appearance of truth rather than truth. The other manuscripts agree differently with the Gospel sayings. The allusion is plainly to the authority over demons which Christ gave the seventy disciples when he sent them. See Luke X, 18.] (Luke X, 18), and when the prince of the world was judged in the Passion (John XII, 31).

But those fleeing from the face of God show their terror precisely by fleeing; nevertheless, though they flee, they cannot escape the face of God. For the preceding psalm also declares the terror of these same spiritual wickednesses, saying: “He sent forth his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and troubled them” (Ps. XVII, 15). They are therefore troubled and flee in dispersal. Yet they do not escape the power of God’s countenance, according to the words: “Smoke went up in his wrath, and fire shall blaze from before his face [Note: “blazes.”]; coals were kindled by it” (ibid., 9) [Note: Royal manuscript: “blazes.” Nothing should be changed, as was observed in Psalm LXIV, no. 7.]. This flight of those enemies is therefore followed by the punishment both of destruction and of judgment [Note: Paris edition: “is followed by punishment”; others, “punishment will follow.” Corrected from the manuscripts.].

**5.** And indeed, the same order of prophecy that was distinguished in the preceding psalm is now followed. For there follows, VERSE 3: “As smoke fails away, let them fail away; as wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God.” When smoke rises, although it be in a thick and dense mass, it gradually fails and vanishes so as not to remain. Likewise wax melts before fire so as not to exist: smoke, through its lightness and thinness, being dissipated into nothing [Note: “In fire” is meaningless. Perhaps “into nothing,” rather than “in fire.”]; wax, however, being consumed by the force and heat of fire because, being weak in itself, it is seized by the burning of the stronger nature [Note: Printed editions: “weak”; but the manuscripts have “being weak” in the nominative, with “wax” understood.]. In this way all power of the wicked [Note: The Micacian manuscript: “of enemies,” which could be referred to the earlier words, “let his enemies be scattered,” were not the nearer words “so let sinners perish” present.] melts away before the face of God—that is, through God’s judgment.

**4. What the joy of the righteous is.**—And the joy of the righteous must follow this destruction of sinners before the face of God. For immediately there is added, VERSE 4: “And let the righteous rejoice in gladness” [Note: “In gladness.”]. For the equitable and just ordering of heavenly judgment is that, while it destroys sinners by death, it likewise rewards the righteous with gladness [Note: Bad.: “And because indeed.” The other editions, after deleting “because,” read “For indeed.” Restored from the manuscripts.]. To show this, the testing of judgment is further stated: “Let them exult in the sight of God; let them feast in gladness.” For those who are pure in heart, according to the merits of the Gospel blessing, are worthy of the sight of God (Matt. V, 8).

But to rejoice *in gladness* has a deeper [Note: Royal manuscript: “inner,” not badly. Perhaps one should read “further.”] significance, showing the cause of perfect joy. Many rejoice in things that will harm them: the wanton person delights in prostitutes; the thief rejoices in thefts; each person finds pleasure, according to his own vices, in what he practises. But one who rejoices in gladness receives the cause of joy from the honorable and beneficial truth of gladness itself [Note: Bad.: “from the propriety and such truth of gladness itself, etc.” Erasmus retained this in the text and wrote in the margin: “Perhaps: from the honorable and mortal things themselves.” Lipsius then substituted, “from its honorable and mental [truth].” The manuscripts provide the true reading.]. Therefore he says, “Let them rejoice in gladness,” because “they shall exult in the sight of God,” teaching that this is the joy of true exultation: joy made perfect by the delight of beholding God.

Holy Moses also recalls the joys of this exultation and feasting, from which comes the joy of the righteous, in that divine song of Deuteronomy: “Rejoice, ye heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him. Rejoice, ye nations, with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen them” (Deut. XXXII, 43) [Note: Printed editions: “and let all be strengthened,” contrary to the manuscript readings followed here. Yet Hilary, *On the Trinity*, IV.31, cites the passage otherwise: “and let all the angels of God honor him.” In the Greek Septuagint, with which the rest of this passage agrees, we have ἐνισχυσάτωσαν αὐτοῦ, “let them strengthen him/them,” as Epiphanius also read it, *Heresies* LX.60.]. In this gladness, therefore, the righteous too shall rejoice, of one mind in heavenly joy, rejoicing in fellowship with divine exultation [Note: Printed editions: “fellowship”; corrected from the manuscripts.].

**5. Exhortation is more effective if the reason for action is not kept silent.**—The Prophet now calls us to rejoice at that time under the confession of Gospel faith, saying, VERSE 5: “Sing to God; make melody to his name; prepare a way for him who ascends above the setting. The Lord is his name; and exult before him.” Although every exhortation greatly advances a certain movement of our will and mind, when we are led to desire and do something by a persuasive occasion or inducement [Note: Paris: “a persuasive occasion.” From the other editions and the Royal manuscript, “by a persuasive occasion” is restored: occasion is thus contrasted with reason, which, in moving the will, has of itself greater force than a mere occasion. Yet the earlier reading is not to be wholly despised.], nevertheless, if the reason for the exhortation itself is set forth, the mind already relies upon reason and a path as upon a most certain guide.

Thus the Prophet, having exhorted us to sing to God and make melody to his name, lest perhaps he leave any ambiguity, showed both to which God and to whose name melody was to be made; so that no mere exhortation, but knowledge received [Note: The printed editions: “command received.” The true reading is owed to the Royal manuscript.] might place us in God’s exultation and song.

**6. Why the Lord should be praised: his victory over death.**—Therefore melody must be made to him, and his way must be prepared, who ascends above the setting. By “setting” is understood the annihilation of all things that come into life. According to common human opinion, the annihilation of all things that set is thought to consist in death. Therefore melody must be made to him, and his way prepared by us, who ascended above the setting of death—that is, who, not held by the setting itself, passed beyond every setting through that very setting [Note: Erasmus here wrongly added “every,” which was retained thereafter, although the word occurs neither in Bad. nor in the manuscripts nor in the sacred text. Yet from the indefinite expression “he ascends above the setting,” the holy interpreter draws the general sense, namely every setting.].

His name is “Lord” [Note: “The Lord.”]—he who, emptying himself from the form of God and taking the form of a servant, made himself obedient even to the death of the cross. Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that at his name things heavenly, earthly, and infernal might bend the knee, and every tongue might confess [Note: “might confess.”] the Lord Jesus in the glory of God the Father. Therefore he ascended above the setting, he whose name is Lord; and, passing beyond that in which all things set, he came forth eternal from the dead, beyond the law of death [Note: “By the law of death.”].

Therefore his way must be prepared, according to the words: “Prepare the ways of the Lord; make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every hill shall be brought low” (Luke III, 3). When our way has been prepared [Note: Vatican manuscript: “our”; Royal and Micacian: “us”; Tours: “among us”; printed editions: “in us.”]—that is, when the swellings of our vices and unbelief have been lowered, and the lowliness of earthly ruin has been raised [Note: “Of a dreadful objection.” A little later, “may descend,” not “will descend.”] [Note: One Vatican manuscript has “objection” in place of “ruin”; “abasement” would be less displeasing. Then Bad., Er., and Lips. have “about to enter”; the Royal manuscript, “about to enter [plural].” Tours: “after the paths of life have been corrected and made level, he may descend into our hearts.”]—he will enter our hearts along the straight paths of justice and life. We shall therefore exult in the sight of him for whom the way must be prepared by leveling the swellings of arrogance and the gulfs of desires [Note: Printed editions: “from justice,” wholly wrongly; the Micacian manuscript, less wrongly, “from injustice.” The Vatican manuscripts more truly read, “having been leveled.”], and in whom, when we rise from the dead, we shall behold ourselves. For he ascended above the setting of our death: by rising in himself from the dead, he sought life for us from the dead [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “with life.” Because Christ became a sharer of our nature, Hilary here teaches in his accustomed manner that what Christ granted to his assumed humanity was granted to us also. To this pertains what was just said: “in whom,” namely, in the one rising, “we who rise from the dead shall behold ourselves.”]. This was the joy of the apostles when, after the resurrection, they saw and touched him.

**7. The twofold meaning of orphans and widows: whose father and judge God is.**—But the terror of those whom he conquered with the world follows the joy of the saints. For he says, VERSE 6: “They shall be troubled before his face—he who is father of orphans and judge of widows.” He also taught this as the cause of their disturbance: that he is father of orphans and judge of widows—for they shall flee before the face of the father of orphans and judge of widows—not leaving as orphans those who, knowing the Father in heaven, have renounced the devil as father; and judging those widows who, dead to the Law, have followed their spouse [Note: In one Vatican manuscript: “the Law.” More rightly in the others: “to the Law,” that is, those free from the Law, or for whom the Law no longer lives. Then truly Bad., Er., and the manuscripts: “have followed their spouse,” namely Christ. Lipsius should not have inserted “have subsequently followed their spouse.”].

For blessed Paul teaches that a widow free from the Law may pass to the marriage of another without the crime of adultery (Rom. VII, 3). He applied the whole illustration to the Church, which, dead to the Law, was to unite herself afterwards with Christ [Note: “dead to the Law”] [Note: Tours: “which is dead to the Law, so that she might afterwards join herself to Christ.” Our reading is preferred, and may thus be rendered: “he applied the whole illustration to the Church, which, dead to the Law, was to unite herself afterwards with Christ.”] [Note: Micacian manuscript: thus; one Vatican manuscript: “which had made herself dead to the Law”; another: “which [made] herself dead to the Law”; Royal manuscript with printed editions: “which is dead to the Law.” Then Bad. and Erasmus: “to join herself afterwards with Christ”; Lipsius and Paris: “joining herself afterwards with Christ.” Again the Micacian manuscript is followed, with the others agreeing except that they place “herself” before “might unite.” The sense is clear: the Church, dead to the Law, fitted herself to unite herself with Christ. The allusion is to Paul, Rom. VII, 4, where, after speaking of the widow freed from the law of her husband, he adds: “Therefore, my brethren, you also have been made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you may belong to another, who rose from the dead,” etc.].

There is also a highly suitable meaning according to the literal circumstances of this world: God, who gave us another Advocate from the Father lest we be orphans, is father of orphans in this world of the bereaved and judge of widows (John XIV, 18). For he has mercy on childhood bereft of parents, and is judge of widows who rest in him. He is judge because many under the title of widows are not truly widows: either because they desire, in sensuality, to marry in Christ (I Tim. V, 11), or because they deceive human judgments. Since the dignity of the name lies in a will faithful to its resolve, God, who searches hearts and reins, is judge because he alone judges their mind and disposition. These things, as I have said, are spoken concerning orphans and widows according to the desolation of the human condition.

[Col. 0447B] **8. The time of grace, in which God brings forth prisoners, those who provoke him, and dwellers in tombs.**—But that these words may be understood as signifying the whole Church, he immediately added: “God in his holy place; VERSE 7: God makes those of one manner dwell in a house, bringing forth prisoners in strength, likewise those who provoked him, who dwell in tombs.” [Note: Paris, from the Micacian manuscript, thus, in accordance with the Greek μονοτρόπους, “of one manner.” In the Royal manuscript the first hand has incorrectly *unimoris*, and subsequently a second hand wrote *unius moris*, “of one manner,” which Bad., Er., and Lipsius adopted. Later in the Royal manuscript: “those who provoke”; this is supported by the following phrase, “those who dwell,” since both are expressed in the same form in Greek: τοὺς παραπικραίνοντας and τοὺς κατοικοῦντας.]

Therefore this is a holy place for God: where there is a widow freed from the Law; where there is an orphan freed from the world; where there is a peaceful and harmonious assembly, of one manner and will—for, according to Acts of the Apostles, “the soul and heart of the believers were one” (Acts IV, 32); where those who are bound are brought forth in strength. For after the strong man had first been bound within his own house, he loosed those who were bound by their sins (Luke XIII, 16), just as by a word of power he led into freedom the daughter of Abraham, bound for seventeen years [Note: Paris: “eighteen years,” supported by the sacred text but opposed by the manuscripts.].

He also brought forth those who had formerly provoked him—that is, those who by transgression of the Law stirred up against themselves the wrath of God the Judge, or who spoke against his name in Gentile language—and trained them in the doctrine of divine knowledge. Thus from a persecutor he appointed Paul as apostle and teacher of the nations [Note: “Accomplished.”]. These provokers, formerly buried in tombs—that is, entombed within the dead dwellings of their own bodies—he brought into heavenly and spiritual life. For many are dead among the living. In the Gospels, too, those not reckoned dead [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “reckoned”; Paris: “called.” With Bad., Er., Lipsius, the other Vatican manuscript, and the Royal manuscript, “not reckoned” is preferred—that is, those commonly not thought to be dead.] are taught not to differ from the dead, when the Lord says: “Let [Note: “Allow,” in agreement with the Greek text, ἄφες.] the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII, 22). The Apostle knows some who are dead while living (I Tim. V, 6), that is, who are already dead while they live. But the Lord brought all these persons [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts: “all these”; others: “these persons.”] out of the tombs when they were regenerated as children of God.

**9. God is the same in the Law and the Gospel.**—But this God who, ascending above the setting, worked these things in us through the power of the resurrection, performed in the Law the same things in shadow for the preparation of this hope of ours, so that God of the prophets and God of the Gospels cannot be understood as different. Therefore he also fulfilled these things for us by acts corresponding to those through which he brought the people out of Egypt. For our fathers were under the cloud and were baptized into Moses [Note: Royal manuscript, second correction: “by Moses”; the original reading seems to have been “into Moses,” which agrees with the Greek εἰς Μωσῆν and is preferred to the common reading “in Moses.”] in the sea [Note: “Into Moses and in the sea.”]; they were fed by manna falling from heaven in the likeness of heavenly bread; and they drank with Christ, the rock, supplying water [Note: Thus the ancient editions and one Vatican manuscript. Paris: “water leading the rock onward”; Micacian manuscripts: “the rock going before, supplying water”; Royal: “water, the rock going before.” This reading had some appeal, so that not only the rock but also the water might be called Christ, of whom, according to the Apostle’s testimony, all drank the same spiritual drink.].

These things, though salutarily done in them, also had in themselves a figure of our salvation [Note: “Also the pledge of our salvation,” perhaps “of our [salvation].”], as the following prophetic utterance declares, saying, VERSES 8–9: “O God, when thou wentest forth [Note: The Verona manuscript also: “when thou goest forth ... when thou passest through.”] [Note: Bad., Er., and the Royal manuscript: “when thou goest forth”; and shortly after, “when thou passest through.”] before thy people, when thou didst pass through the wilderness [Note: “In the wilderness.”] [Note: Nobilius observes in his notes on the Septuagint that most Greek copies have ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, “in the wilderness.” The Royal manuscript agrees, as does Augustine. But since Hilary here, as usual, interprets the wilderness as the nations formerly abandoned by God, and further teaches that a transition from the Jews to the Gentiles is signified here, we have judged “into the wilderness” should be retained.], the earth was moved. For the heavens dropped before the face of God; Mount Sinai, before the face of the God of Israel” [Note: Micacian manuscript: “before the face of God of Sinai, before the face of the God of Israel,” a reading which Nobilius complains crept into the Septuagint edition through printers’ carelessness. A similar verse occurs in Judges V.].

We know that God went before the way of his people, when it crossed the wilderness, in a pillar of cloud and fire; and that manna fell from heaven until the people’s error [Note: Thus, with the Micacian manuscript and one Vatican manuscript. Other books: “terror.”] (Exod. XVI). But though he had recalled all the preceding matters which properly and fittingly belong to the Church—namely, when the Lord ascends above the setting; when he is father of orphans and judge of widows; when in his holy place, that is, in the house, he gathers those of one manner [Note: Bad., Er., and Lipsius: “he gathers those gathered of one manner.” Paris: “he gathers those gathered,” omitting “of one manner.” Corrected from the Royal and Vatican manuscripts. In these, however, “of one manner” occurs in the word *unimores*.]; and when he brings out from tombs the prisoners in strength and those who provoke him—yet he mentioned that he accomplished these things in going forth before the people and passing into the wilderness. Thus he now relates from the past that the earth was moved, the heavens dropped, and this was effected before the face of the God of Israel at Sinai.

This is so that, when he performed those things belonging to the Law, it might be known that in these too he prefigured the things belonging to the Gospels. For he went forth before his people and passed into the wilderness: namely, into that wilderness of Jordan in which lilies blossomed, in which the spring of living water watered those who were desolate and dry [Note: All manuscripts: “into that very wilderness.” The Royal manuscript alone shortly after: “watered the desolate and dry.”] (Deut. XXXII, 9). For Jacob had formerly been the portion of his inheritance [Note: “The hope of Jacob.” Subsequently: “while he looks” for “while he inspects”; “will grow fertile” for “grow fertile.”], and the abandoned nations had been subject to the power of the elements. But now, while he who had been God’s people looked on, God passed over to those things which had formerly been desolate; and the wildernesses of the ends of the earth, now watered by him, grow fertile [Note: Thus the Vatican manuscripts, supported by the Royal manuscript, which reads: “and now they grow fertile.” The printed editions instead: “so that they might now grow fertile.”].

And he is the same one who gave manna from heaven to the people. For if the Law was ordained through angels, if man ate the bread of angels, and if the heavens are written to have dropped at Sinai, there is no doubt that this ministry was performed by the heavens—that is, by angels [Note: “It was performed; there is no doubt, who is the same;” perhaps read, “indeed, from this, he is the bread who …”]. And the giver of it—the bread from heaven—is the same one who had granted manna at Sinai [Note: First Paris edition: “and indeed”; Royal manuscript: “who is the same”; one Vatican manuscript: “because he is the same.” This latter is not without plausibility, especially if before “who at Sinai” the verb “is” is supplied or understood, as the Micacian manuscript has it; shortly before, it reads: “and indeed the giver.” Another Vatican manuscript, sometimes corrupted by glosses, has: “that is, it was performed by angels;” then, “there is no doubt that he is the same giver.” Amid this diversity of manuscripts, the older editions are followed. Nor is Hilary’s meaning obscure; the author of the Commentary on the Psalms expresses it more clearly in Jerome: “He through whom manna flowed down at Sinai for that generation, the same one supplies in the Church to the Christian people the manna of his body and blood.”].

10. God’s Foreknowledge and Predestination.—But God, passing over into the wilderness—that is, transcending the once dry and desolate hearts of the Gentiles—set apart that blessed rain of good will (Gal. I, 13; Rom. VIII, 29). For he himself set Paul apart from his mother’s womb to be an apostle (Rom. VIII, 29), because “those whom he foreknew, he also predestined.” [Note: [Col. 0450C] “He marked out beforehand.”] He also announced this rain of discourse and preaching, in the Psalm of Solomon, as security for the earth’s hope, saying: “He shall come down like rain upon a fleece, and like dripping drops falling upon the earth” (Ps. LXXI, 6). And we remember that certain clouds were commanded not to rain upon the vineyard (Isa. V, 6). Holy Moses too, who concealed immense mysteries of heavenly hope beneath the veil of ordinary words, sang that his words should be received as rain and shower (Deut. XXIII, 2): rain watering the wilderness and the dry land, and God’s prepared inheritance. [Note: [Col. 0450C] “The Gentiles.”] [Note: [Col. 0449C] “To Solomon, for hope.”] [Note: [Col. 0450D] Thus the royal manuscript, whereas the printed editions have *que*, not *qui*.] [Note: [Col. 0450C] “A wilderness and dry land, and preparing God’s…”] [Note: [Col. 0450D] In one Vatican manuscript: “preparing an inheritance for God,” contrary to the thought of the holy Doctor, who understands “prepared” as the Gentile people foreknown and predestined. The Micy manuscript is not so bad: “watering the wilderness and dry land and the prepared inheritance of God.” The Tours manuscript: “prepared for God’s inheritance”; nor is this reading to be preferred to ours.]

Therefore it follows, Vv. 10–11: “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance; and it was weakened, but you have perfected it. Your living creatures shall dwell in it; in your sweetness you have prepared for the poor.” [Note: [Col. 0450D] The Paris edition, with the royal manuscript corrected by a second hand, reads “your sweetness for the poor.” It then adds “God,” a word absent from the manuscripts and the Septuagint, but joined to the following verse.]

For God, who foresees wills, set apart the voluntary rain by foreknowledge. [Note: [Col. 0450D] From the editions of Badius and Erasmus and from the manuscripts we restore *praesciendo*, “by foreknowing,” in place of *perficiendo*, “by perfecting,” wrongly substituted by Lipsius.] It was weakened when Paul “had the sentence of death in himself” (II Cor. I, 9); when Peter was moved by the scandal of the cross; when, though warned not to deny, he denied three times; when the Apostles feared, fled, and lost confidence. Yet because in them there was the disposition of good will, they were so perfected that they became both foundations and pillars of the churches. Thus this rain is set apart for God’s inheritance.

11. What God’s Inheritance Is.—What this inheritance is is not obscure: namely, that which is given to him who asks, when it is said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance” (Ps. II, 8). Therefore the nations, not understanding, like living creatures and cattle—and hence, since God has no concern for cattle (I Cor. IX, 9)—are shown to dwell in that inheritance, set apart in this voluntary rain. [Note: [Col. 0450C] “It is set apart in this.”] [Note: [Col. 0450D] The Paris edition, after deleting these three words, “is in it,” then adds, “they are shown to dwell.”]

For it follows: “Your living creatures shall dwell in it; in your sweetness you have prepared for the poor.” Thus the living creatures will dwell either in God’s inheritance or in the voluntary rain; and this inheritance or rain is prepared in sweetness for the poor. For the sayings of God are sweet in the mouths of the saints (Ps. CXVIII, 103), and “blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3). Though they were living creatures, they became spiritual. All these things, therefore, are set apart for the service of the inheritance, or for the ministry of the voluntary rain.

12. The Apostles: Many Powers of the One Christ.—[Col. 0451A] And so that, in accordance with the sweetness prepared for the poor, either the gathering of the Church, which is an inheritance for God (or: of God), or the word of apostolic preaching might be understood to have been signified, he added, Vv. 12–13: “God the Lord will give a word to the many powers that proclaim the Gospel: the king of the powers of the Beloved, and for the beauty of the house to divide spoils.” [Note: [Col. 0451D] The royal and Vatican manuscripts read “for beauty.” We prefer *pulchritudini*, “for beauty,” that is, “unto beauty,” as appears below.] [Note: [Col. 0451C] “By beauty.”]

Therefore, for watering the rain set apart unto the Gospel, the Lord will give the word, pouring it into our understanding and mouths, according to: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20). But the many powers which proclaim the Gospel are those to whom he will give the word: so that there is a power in Paul, a power in Peter, a power in John, and a power in the rest. Thus he signifies that there are many powers for preaching the Gospel. [Note: [Col. 0451D] In the printed editions, after a point, the word *sunt* (“are”) is repeated here, wrongly and against the manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0451D] In the Paris edition: “But these powers, to whom,” etc.]

Although God, Lord, and King gives the word to them, these powers are nevertheless the powers of the Beloved—that is, of him who is beloved by the King and Lord and God. [Note: [Col. 0451D] The royal and Micy manuscripts read “that is, of him.” Hilary here seems to say that the powers belong to the man beloved by Christ, and thus to refer “the Beloved” to the Apostles. But since below he asserts that it refers to Christ—of whom, as the common text of Jerome observes on this passage, the Father more than once testified, “This is my beloved Son”—“King” and “Lord” above must be understood as the Father, whose Beloved is the Son.]

The Latin translation expresses this with more labor and obscurity because it does not alter the arrangement of the words. But the whole statement, expressed from the Greek, speaks more clearly: namely, that this God and Lord is King of those powers which belong to the Beloved; so that the powers refer to the Apostles, but the Beloved to Christ, whose powers they are understood to be, whether in these persons or all together.

Yet, because of what follows, it was necessary to mention numerous powers, although in all there was one and the same Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0451D] In the royal manuscript the word “Spirit” was added by a second hand. In two Vatican manuscripts “Christ” occurs in its place; not improperly.] because he himself would divide the spoils of power for the beauty of the house. [Note: [Col. 0451D] It seems that one should read, “the powers themselves would divide the spoils,” as the following words suggest: “For, for the adornment of the Church, the spoils taken from them”—that is, from the powers, by which the Apostles were said above to be meant. Earlier printed editions read “from the devil,” omitting “them,” which we restore from the royal manuscript.]

For spoils of the Gentiles, taken from the devil, are divided for the adornment of the Church; and the beauty of the house is made complete even from these spoils, when men are drawn away from the altars and temples of demons to become priests of God for the sanctification of ministry. [Note: [Col. 0452D] Badius and Erasmus: “for the sanctification of mystery”; Lipsius and Paris: “for the signification of mystery.” Corrected from the manuscripts.] Watered by the Holy Spirit, they have become powers of the Beloved, proclaiming the Gospel. [Note: [Col. 0452D] The word “to be” is missing in the printed editions, which, except Paris, previously have “they were made,” not “they were made [feminine].”]

13. Adorned Here with the Gifts of the Holy Spirit, They Are Afterwards to Be Decorated with Immortal Glory.—The divine word refers back to these same powers, which either divide the spoils for the beauty of the house or are themselves the spoils, saying, V. 14: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of a dove are silvered, and the hind parts of her back are in the greenness of gold.”

These are the Prophet’s wishes, by which he desires that the spoils thus divided for the beauty of the house should remain among the midst of the lots: that they may persevere in the beauty of the house until the day of their consummation—for death is customarily signified by sleep. They are for the service of preaching, like the silvered wings of the dove; that is, precious through the gift and adornment of the Holy Spirit. But in what comes after them they shall stand in the greenness of gold: so that, after the preaching of the Gospel, royal honor and unfailing eternity may be rendered to them, from the fruit of their conscience, in the greenness of gold. Gold denotes honor, and greenness shows eternal vigor.

Thus “the hind parts of the back”—what the Greek expression *τὰ μετάφρενα* more particularly denotes, namely the space between the shoulders—are those things which, in time, come after good conscience and honor. They are to be honored beyond the honor of this preaching. Meanwhile the silvered wings remain under the abiding gift of the Holy Spirit; [Note: [Col. 0451C] “Abiding.”] [Note: [Col. 0452D] One Vatican manuscript reads “of the abiding [Spirit].” More correctly, the other books read “abiding,” namely, the powers proclaiming the Gospel.] and afterward, in the fruit of their conscience, they will obtain the greenness of gold, that is, the flower of perpetual honor.

14. They Are Kings with Christ; Peace and Whiteness Befit Them.—That these spoils, divided for the beauty of the house, for whom it was desired that they might sleep among the midst of the lots—that is, that they might be consummated in death as such persons—may be understood to refer to the rulers of the churches, through whom the beauty of the house stands, he immediately added, Vv. 15–16: “While the heavenly one distinguishes kings over her, they shall be made white as snow in Selmon; a mountain of God, a fertile mountain, a consecrated mountain, a rich mountain.” [Note: [Col. 0452D] The royal manuscript, with another Vatican manuscript, reads “that mortals might be consummated.”] [Note: [Col. 0452D] The Tours manuscript: “stands, may be understood to have been referred”; and shortly afterward, “distinguishes” for “will distinguish.”]

Therefore, while the Heavenly One distinguishes these kings over her—that is, while the Lord, descending from heaven, establishes as kings those who have been spoils, and appoints each one over that house which is made most beautiful through them—they shall be made white as snow in Selmon: that is, in peace, for Selmon is interpreted as “peace”; they will receive the glory of eternity. For this is God’s mountain, in which the peace of God is indicated by the force of its very name, and it is fertile, consecrated, and rich.

That they are kings is not obscure, for it was said of them: “Already you reign without us; and I wish that you did reign, so that we also might reign with you” (I Cor. IV, 8). [Note: [Col. 0452C] Our manuscript consistently has “you have reigned,” wherever it gives this Pauline passage.] Therefore the heavenly Lord—for “as is the heavenly one, such also are the heavenly”—will establish as kings in Selmon, over his own house, these kings, whitened as snow, through whom the house will be adorned by the division of spoils.

“For his place has been made in peace” (Ps. LXXV, 3), and, according to Isaiah, “your sins shall be made white as snow” (Isa. I, 18). But the kings in whose keeping is the beauty of the house must be granted to be beyond the whiteness of snow. [Note: [Col. 0453C] The printed editions read “to excel,” omitting the preceding “to be,” which we alter on the authority of the royal and Micy manuscripts. Thus it should be translated: “It is necessary that kings be granted to be beyond the whiteness of snow.”] For they are the light of the world; and whoever is worthy to ascend with the Lord the mountain of the heavenly kingdom shall be whitened beyond snow, because, when he showed himself to the Apostles in the appearance in which he was to reign with the saints, his garments were seen white beyond snow (Matt. XVII, 2). This mountain, therefore, and this kingdom belong to the God of peace.

15. Heretics Falsely Claim Peace.—But many people falsely assert the Church’s peace in the assembly of heretics, dissolving the connected and mutually joined order of the New and Old Testaments. For many fashion one God of the Gospels and another God of the Law. Some, opposing the nature and name of the only-begotten God, confess that he is merely a man born in time; they imagine not that he was brought down from the form of God into the form of a servant, but that he began only from the form of a servant. Others deny that God subsists in true divinity or by the property of his Father’s majesty and nature; instead, they declare that he consists of an external substance, different from God, chosen for adoption as Son—after the manner of creatures which have come to be out of nothing and possess no prior origin.

Others speak of the Father as extended into a body and flowing forth from himself; [Note: [Col. 0453C] The Verona manuscript reads “begotten,” but less correctly. Hilary customarily uses the verb “to extend,” as particularly characteristic of the Sabellian heresy, in order to identify it: *On the Synods*, 45: “Some have dared to extend the unbegotten God as far as the holy Virgin by an expansion of substance.” *On the Trinity*, I: “So that there is rather an extension into a man”; then, after a few intervening words: “The Father extended as far as the Virgin.”] [Note: [Col. 0453C] Printed texts have “remaining,” but the royal manuscript correctly has “flowing through.” For Sabellians are indicated here, who explained their heresy by the example of the sun streaming to us through its rays. This will be treated more suitably in *On the Trinity*, I, 16.] so that that assumption of flesh from the Virgin received the name of Son, rather than that he who previously was God’s Son was himself born in a body as the Son of Man.

And indeed all these notions are adapted to the appearance of human wisdom, once they have failed to comprehend the reasoning of heavenly wisdom. To them, as I hope, [Note: [Col. 0453D] That is, “as I trust”; Innocent I uses *spero* in this sense in Epistle 183, in Augustine, §2. Hilary answered these heretics at length and abundantly elsewhere, in the books *On the Trinity*, which throughout oppose the followers of Sabellius, Arius, Ebion, and Photinus, and of other heretics. Of them he complains immediately in Book I, §15, throughout Book III, and subsequently—as here—that, confining God’s mighty nature within the limits of their own nature, they enclose the infinite within the bounds of their own understanding.] fuller and more abundant reply has been given elsewhere.

16. Heresy Resembles Cheese.—Therefore, since the one true faith is this one seat pleasing to God, and since this one mountain of the eternal kingdom is in peace, the Prophet reproves us for having embraced very many such mountains, saying, V. 17: “Why have you embraced mountains of cheese?” (*Ἔρη τετωρωμένα*, “cheesed mountains.”) [Note: [Col. 0453D] Printed editions, except Paris: “This one is the faith.”] [Note: [Col. 0453D] In Paris *susceptis* is absent, and Lipsius wrongly substituted *suspectis*, “suspected,” against the other books. Hilary teaches that, since one faith exists in one Church, the Prophet rebukes the many faiths embraced by heretics in many congregations—or rather, as Augustine calls them, “scatterings” (*Sermon* 71, §37). Lipsius’ cause for error was that, with earlier editions, he read “why do you suspect?”, whereas Paris from the Micy manuscript reads “why do you embrace?” But the royal and Vatican manuscripts read “why have you embraced?”, with which the Micy manuscript agrees in its exposition of Psalm CXLIII, §9.]

When milk spoils, it thickens, and through corruption congeals into the appearance of curd and cheese. For one Greek expression includes both terms. Thus, just as milk itself, naturally such as it is, degenerates when corruption enters it, and through a kind of self-corruption coheres, so these kinds of doctrines, which derive the beginnings of knowledge from harmless and pure milk, are corrupted into vices; by their own corruption they become curdled or cheesed, so that they are no longer milk. [Note: [Col. 0454C] “*Coacescit*” (“coalesces”).] [Note: [Col. 0454D] Printed texts read *coacescit* (“coalesces”), and shortly afterward, “they derive from pure milk,” as in the Tours manuscript. They are corrected by the authority of the remaining manuscripts. Moreover, it is clear elsewhere that Hilary read *sincerus* and *sinceribus*, “pure,” as he did *infirmus* and *infirmis*. Augustine likewise reads *sinceres* in his exposition of Psalm XCI, §3.]

He recalls this same point elsewhere: “Their heart has curdled like milk; but I have meditated on your law” (Ps. CXVIII, 70). For the heart infected by impious counsels and acts, though through the simplicity of infancy it had possessed the nature of milk, afterward degenerating through the corruption of vices, had been thickened and hardened into curd. Therefore both mind and zeal must be turned away from all such things; and no mountain ought more to be inhabited than this mountain of peace. For after reproving the cheesed and curdled mountains, he immediately added: “The mountain in which God was pleased to dwell; for in it the Lord will dwell unto the end.” [Note: [Col. 0454D] *Etenim*, “for,” was absent from Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius; Paris had substituted “and him.”] Thus he shows that God is pleased to have the seat of his eternal dwelling in the mountain chosen as the seat of peace.

17. One Giver of the Old and New Law; One Faith.—But because, after the times of the Law, the prescription of circumcision, and the commandments concerning sacrifices, through the faith of evangelical confession, there seems to have been made by us—at least in the eyes of those who boast in the Law, that is, carnal Israel—a certain change in the peace of God and the introduction of another knowledge than that prescribed in the Law; while we teach that, through the Lord Jesus Christ, all things commanded by the Law are foreshadowed in evangelical hope, [Note: [Col. 0454D] The royal manuscript reads “through evangelical.” “Through the confession of evangelical faith” would be more pleasing, if one had not learned that Hilary frequently uses such inversions of words.] [Note: [Col. 0454D] The particle “which,” expressed here in one Vatican manuscript, is understood in the others.] [Note: [Col. 0454D] Two manuscripts read “into appearance.” The holy Doctor likes the word *spes*, “hope,” to signify faith joined to the promise of eternity. Here he anticipates Augustine, *On Instructing Beginners in Faith*, ch. 4: “In the Old Testament the New is concealed, and in the New Testament the Old is revealed.” Augustine likewise, ch. 6, in the letter to the Galatians, agrees that the old and new Law are Christ’s: “It is evident,” he says in §58, “that even that law of the Scriptures which was given to the former people is Christ’s law, which he came to fulfill by love, whereas it was not fulfilled by fear. Therefore the same law and commandment, when it constrains slaves who long for earthly goods, is called the Old Testament; when it raises free persons who burn with desire for eternal goods, it is called the New Testament.” These words of Augustine remarkably illuminate Hilary’s thought. Yet Augustine differs from him in this: Augustine holds that God the Father, or rather God the Trinity, gave the Law to the Hebrews through Moses, and through the Son gave the Gospel to Christians; Hilary holds that the Son gave both laws, the old through angels, the new through himself.]

They, on the other hand, boast that God the Father spoke with them and gave the Law. The answer is that this very prophecy of the Psalm shows rather that the Law was arranged through angels by the hand of the Mediator; that nothing has been changed by us, but that we remain in those things which alone are to be believed and confessed—that is, we inhabit one and the same seat of the God of peace—since we have the same Lord Jesus Christ as both preacher of the Gospel and giver of the Law. [Note: [Col. 0455D] It is not clear on what grounds Erasmus’ conjecture rests, proposing *salem*, “salt,” instead of *sola*, “alone.” It is more probable that “to be believed and confessed” is understood after this word. Hilary means that the faith preached in the Old Testament has not been changed by us; and at the same time he indicates that there is one sole faith, one house of peace, one seat of God, one Church, begun among the ancients before Christ and afterward continuing in us. Certainly he alludes rather to Mount Selmon than to the city Salem.]

For after speaking of the seat of the one mountain pleasing to God, in which the Heavenly One will dwell unto the end, so that this seat of evangelical peace might be understood to have been prefigured in the Law through the Mediator of the Law, he immediately added, Vv. 18–19: “The chariot of God is ten-thousandfold, many thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is among them in Sinai, in the holy place. He ascended on high, took captivity captive, gave gifts in men; indeed, unbelievers also to dwell [with the Lord God].” [Note: [Col. 0455C] In our manuscript too the particle “in” is omitted.] [Note: [Col. 0456C] “In” is absent from the royal manuscript and ancient editions. Yet in the exposition it is consistently read not “gave,” but “received gifts in men.” Augustine approves both readings here: the same Christ both gave as God and received in his body, which is the Church.] [Note: [Col. 0456D] The Paris edition adds “the Lord God,” words which in the Septuagint, as in our manuscripts, belong to the following verse.]

18. The Sum of the Entire Faith, the Splendor of God’s Seat, Christ the Giver of the Law.—These few words signify the whole faith, though they contain great and infinite realities by their own powers. The prophet Daniel described this dignity of God’s chariot or seat in no dissimilar way: “His throne was a burning flame; its wheels were a vast stream of fire flowing before him; thousands of thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII, 9–10). [Note: [Col. 0456C] “Wheel”; in Greek, *οἱ τροχοὶ αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον*, “his wheels [were] burning fire.”] [Note: [Col. 0456D] Thus the Micy and royal manuscripts and the Latin version of the Septuagint. The Greek, however, has *μύριαι μυριάδες*, “myriads of myriads.” Printed editions have “ten times one hundred thousand.” In Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, §3: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and thousands of hundreds of thousands appeared before him.”]

In these things, whether under the form of such adornment or as an example of symbolic meaning, the idea and understanding of the heavenly retinue is conveyed to us in the chariot: so that under a harmonious yoke we may understand the heavenly service of thousands of rejoicing ones. This too was shown by the blazing torches on Sinai, the shining fires, the overwhelming thunders, and the terror of the Lord’s entire coming: namely, that the ministries of angels stood by, arranging the Law in the hand of the Mediator. Thus God’s chariot is ten-thousandfold, and there are thousands of rejoicing ones.

And because the Lord is the Mediator of God and men, in whose hand the Law was given through angels, as has been said, the following statement adds: “The Lord is among them in Sinai”—namely, among those thousands of rejoicing ones; and the chariot is ten-thousandfold in number, that is, its infinity is represented under the multiplication of ten thousand. Therefore God is in Sinai among them.

19. The Gospels Are Supplements to the Law.—But lest the Gospels might perhaps seem in any respect not to be supplements to the Law, he who is the Lord among them in Sinai has here again ascended on high in the holy one and “taken captivity captive”: namely, in that holy one whose form he received when emptied from the form of God. That he is holy is testified both by many prophecies and by the angel Gabriel to Mary: “That holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35); and the demons cry: “We know who you are, the Holy One of God” (Luke IV, 34). [Note: [Col. 0456D] Paris: “because you are.”]

Thus he ascended on high in the holy one. And Paul explains, under the meaning of this very phrase, what it is to ascend on high: “Now, what is ‘he ascended,’ except that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens” (Eph. IV, 9). [Note: [Col. 0456D] Printed editions here add “on high,” against the manuscripts.] Therefore, ascending on high and bringing himself, as man, back from the dead into heavenly places, he received those who had been held captive by the devil; and he divided them as spoils for the beauty of the house.

Then he received gifts in men, when the firstborn from the dead himself testifies concerning himself: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession’” (Ps. II, 7–8). [Note: [Col. 0456D] The royal manuscript reads “request of me.”] Thus he received gifts in men, namely, the nations as an inheritance. In them, the firstborn from the dead ascended on high in the holy one, having taken captivity captive.

And because it surpasses the faith of human hope that he transformed the corruption of earthly flesh into heavenly glory, and that impious nations, formerly overtaken by the frenzy of vices and superstitions, should be brought to the knowledge and fellowship of God, he received gifts in those men who did not believe that they would dwell with God. [Note: [Col. 0456D] One Vatican manuscript here adds the word “all”; shortly afterward it reads “overtaken in all things,” not, as in the printed editions, “perverted.”] Thus the consummate knowledge of this Mediator from the Law is this: that he who had been among the thousands of rejoicing ones in Sinai, this same one, ascending again on high in the holy one, having taken captivity captive, should receive us as gifts, we who despaired of dwelling with him. [Note: [Col. 0457C] The Tours manuscript reads “having taken captivity captive,” which is supported by the expression in §20, “taking captivity captive.”]

20. God Is to Be Blessed Eternally.—After this inheritance of gifts received in men, against the despair of our hope, this worthy confession of the Prophet concerning God follows, V. 20: “Blessed is the Lord God from day to day; God will make prosperous for us the way of our salvations.” Therefore blessed is the Lord and God who ascends on high, takes captivity captive, and receives gifts in men—namely, those who did not believe that they would dwell with him.

Moreover, through the daily increase of the believing people, the confession of blessing is multiplied and enlarged, when Gentile superstitions and impious tales concerning gods, the altars of demons, and the vanities of idols are abandoned, and a way and progress toward salvation are directed for all. Therefore he is the Lord and God of our salvations, whose eternity is signified by blessings from day to day. For in what is daily there is both continuity and perpetuity, since the infinity of time extends as far as the succession of days after days proceeds.

21. The Wisdom and Power of the Cross.—The prophetic word, always most cautiously, warned us lest anyone, through Gentile myths and the teaching of philosophy, should disturb our understanding of the knowledge of divine truth. [Note: [Col. 0457C] Printed editions: “lest anything.” The royal codex more suitably reads “lest anyone,” that is, “lest any person.”] For their varied and most impious opinions have embraced many foolish and profane notions concerning God.

But we, instructed in the knowledge of God the Father and God the Son, have received the mystery of true and heavenly wisdom in the fact that “the Word became flesh.” For that very thing which is a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles (I Cor. I, 23)—that is, God’s passion, cross, death, and burial—is either heavenly wisdom, completed through the purpose of the divine will, or eternal power through the power of resurrection.

Therefore the Prophet instructs us in the knowledge of that God who suffered, died, rose again, and is Lord for us, saying, V. 21: “Our God is a God of saving, and of the Lord are the departures of death.” [Note: [Col. 0457C] The Paris edition repeats “of the Lord” here, against the other books and the Greek.] He makes known to us the God who, although he was God, underwent all things for the increase of our salvation. Therefore he is our God because he is the God of those who will be saved.

Our God saved us because he went forth through the departures of death; for this is contained in these words, which have been translated into Latin less distinctly and fully. I have already noted that interpreters commonly made the proper meaning of the statements less clear, because they did not dare to alter and adjust the arrangement and order of the words. Nevertheless, in the words, “Our God is a God of saving, and of the Lord are the departures of death,” both the God of our salvation and his going forth beyond the going forth of death are shown.

For what are the Lord’s departures of death? For all who come into life, there is an entrance into death; [Note: [Col. 0457D] The Micy and royal manuscripts read “into death.”] [Note: [Col. 0457C] “Into death.”] but the firstborn from the dead alone had a more proper going forth from death. [Note: [Col. 0457D] Thus Paris with the Micy and Vatican manuscripts. But Badius and Erasmus, with the royal codex, read the more fitting “so much the more proper.” Lipsius most wrongly substituted “so much nearer.”] [Note: [Col. 0458C] “Nearer.”] Therefore the Lord’s departure from death is proper to him, because this is the power of the flesh assumed by him: that after the departures of death he might raise the corruption of our nature into heavenly glory.

But neither the cause nor the reason of his assumed death was to be concealed; and it was necessary to reveal, for both the security and knowledge of our faith, what help the only-begotten God, emptying himself from the form of God and taking the form of a servant, brought us. [Note: [Col. 0457D] This particle, referring to the immediately preceding words, “that he might raise the corruption of our nature,” etc., omitted in earlier printed editions, is restored from one Vatican manuscript and the royal manuscript. Another Vatican manuscript and the Micy manuscript read, “truly of the assumed [death].”]

22. It Was Right That God Should Restore Life to Us in Himself.—First, indeed, it may not seem foreign to God’s mercy and goodness that he should restore life to all in himself from the dead. [Note: [Col. 0458C] “From the dead,” without “to the dead.”] [Note: [Col. 0457D] Thus Badius, Erasmus, and the royal manuscript. Lipsius and Paris read “indeed,” in the same sense. See the following tract, §6, where, in place of the printed “and breath of respiration,” we restore “for breath” on the authority of the royal manuscript—especially because the Vatican manuscripts have “for the breathing”; and shortly below the royal and Micy manuscripts read “the beginnings of life for the origins of spirit,” not, as the printed editions, “and the origins.” Light for understanding this passage may be borrowed from the exposition of Psalm CXVIII, letter 10, §8, where in the creation of man a kind of threefold divine action is distinguished: the soul is made in God’s image, the body formed from earth, and, by an inspiration of spirit through which both substances are united, man is moved into a living soul.]

For he had first poured forth to us the soul for the breath and respiration of life from the treasures of his power and divinity, when he established man according to his own image and likeness. [Note: [Col. 0458D] Hilary has nothing in common here with those who, in Augustine, *Epistle* CLXVI, §12, maintain that souls are not continually created, but are sent into bodies from some source or treasury which God made at the beginning of creation. First, he says not “he sent,” but “he poured forth”; second, he speaks not of some created treasury but of the uncreated treasures of his power, etc.—which means nothing else than that he created by his omnipotence; third, if he thought that souls were sent from a created treasury, he would vainly insist that they are first within God and bestowed upon us from God, since that treasury would be external to God. Hence it is also evident in what sense he understands souls to be God’s race.]

For, according to the Apostle, “we are his offspring” (Acts XVII, 28); and according to the same Apostle: “All things are from him and through him and in him” (Rom. XI, 36). That is, our dwelling and habitation are shown to have their seat in him, since he embraces all things by the power of his immeasurable might; the work and effect of an origin begun are shown through him, since he has effected in us that very thing which we are; and the beginnings of life given for the origins of spirit are made known as from him.

Therefore it was not foreign to the beneficence of divine goodness that he who had given us—the beings who are his offspring—the elements of life and spirit from himself should also inaugurate in himself, through the only-begotten God, the beginnings of our eternity. Thus we should now truly remain both from him, through him, and in him, when he who is all in all, being placed in this very dwelling and seat of this world, should again, through a fuller and more perfect fellowship of our flesh, begun in himself, through himself, and from himself, establish us after the departures of death as eternal. [Note: [Col. 0459D] Erasmus customarily deleted the particle “when” here. Paris also prefixed “in” before “us.” The natural order of these somewhat perplexing words is: “when he who is all in all, placed in this very dwelling, etc., should again establish us as eternal.” Yet “in us,” in the sense “in our nature,” is not displeasing: Christ, while living here, was situated in us, that is, in our nature; after death he situated us in himself.] [Note: [Col. 0459D] In the Tours manuscript, with the words “who is all in all” moved below, it reads “placed,” in place of “being placed”; less well.] [Note: [Col. 0459D] The words “and from himself,” omitted in Badius, Erasmus, Lipsius, and several manuscripts, are restored from one Vatican codex. Hilary customarily uses them to signify that Christ’s flesh was not born from man and woman, but was assumed by the Word himself from the Virgin. In place of these words Paris, from the Micy manuscript, wrongly repeated “and in himself.” Then, for “begun,” the printed editions except Paris had “in that” or “in this.”]

These things, indeed, have been said thus with reference to the meaning of divine goodness.

23. Christ, rising from the dead, restored this [life].—But the reason for the flesh’s being assumed by the only-begotten God, for His undergoing death, is treated more fully and profoundly both by the Apostle and now by the Prophet. First let us understand through the Apostle what was accomplished by the only-begotten God and the Lord of Majesty in the mystery of the cross and death, so that, instructed under his guidance, we may attain knowledge of prophecy. [Note: [Col. 0460D] Royal manuscript: “the Prophet’s knowledge.”] For he says:

“And you, when you were dead in sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, He made alive together with Him, forgiving us all our sins, blotting out the handwriting which was against us in ordinances, which was contrary to us; taking it out of the way and fastening it to the cross; stripping Himself of the flesh, and making a public display of the principalities and powers, triumphing over them boldly in Himself” (Col. 2:13 ff.).

Therefore, by first rising Himself from the dead and cancelling the decree of our death by which we had previously been held, He fulfilled the mystery of our salvation in Himself—the One who, risen from the dead, was now to remain eternal. But in this very fact—that He, the author of life for us, is in Himself life, while through the assumption of a body He was born and died as man, and is now again eternal from the dead—He also made a public spectacle of all hostile powers, the powers of the world, and the rulers of this air. [Note: [Col. 0459C] “He made a public display.”] That is, He made them spectacles either for our hope or for their own condemnation; and He made them, as it were, monstrous deities of this age. In triumphing boldly over them in Himself, He triumphed over them because, by the security of eternity, death itself in God who dies is an object of confidence; and because the authors of human death, being authors of death even in Him—through Judas’ heart, seized by Satan—were vanquished as He rose from the dead. Thus they were not exempt from the penalty of death, since the Eternal One had subjected Himself even to death’s weakness; and, since they had become authors of death against the Lord of eternity through the fact that the Word was made flesh, they should undergo every penalty of human death. [Note: [Col. 0459C] “Should undergo.”] [Note: [Col. 0460D] Printed editions: *exciperet*, “should undergo,” which necessarily had to be referred to Christ. More correctly, the Royal and Micy manuscripts have *exciperent*, “they should undergo”: namely, those of whom it was said above, “that they might not be exempt from the penalty of death.” This is because, as the first authors of human death, they became authors of death even against the Lord of eternity, insofar as the Word was made flesh.] Thus speaks the Apostle.

24. What Paul now teaches, David had already taught.—But the Prophet, though briefly, embraces the same meaning in words that signify the same things. [Note: [Col. 0460C] “But” is prefixed.] [Note: [Col. 0460D] In the Tours manuscript, “but” is added.] For when he had shown the Lord [Note: [Col. 0460C] “In the departure [into death]”; immediately afterward, “He crushed,” not “He will crush.”] going forth into death, he added:

VERSE 22. “Yet He will crush the heads of His enemies, the hairy crown of those who walk about in their transgressions.”

[Note: [Col. 0460D] Royal manuscript: “He crushed,” a reading supported by what follows.] For He made a public display of the principalities and powers, in which the heads of His enemies are denoted. Accordingly, He crushes these in His departure into death; and He teaches their spiritual wickedness and nature by saying that they walk upon the hairy crown. For they both stand over human heads as rulers, and, as spiritual wickednesses, trample upon that very hairy crown without the awareness of those on whom they stand. That is, they insinuate and penetrate even the bodies themselves as far as the seat of soul and mind, without being perceived. For they are powers of this air; and therefore they walk upon the hairy crown, whether by the lightness with which they tread, [Col. 0460C] or by their power of domination, [Note: [Col. 0460D] In the Tours codex, “and” is omitted. The words following—“according to that saying of the Apostle, God sent His Son,” etc., through “condemned sin”—are transposed after “they sin through the instigation of betrayal.”] moving through the whole world at every moment. But they do these things in their transgressions, since they cause each person to sin; according to the Apostle’s saying: “God sent His Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and concerning sin condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8:3). Thus He condemns sin in the flesh, deriving their cause and the beginning of sin from this very fact: that they sin in His flesh through the prompting of betrayal—that is, from the sin of the flesh.

25. Gospel events are prefigured by the Law.—The prophetic discourse therefore maintains the order of the divine dispensation, and declares through the very works of the Law that the deeds of the Gospels were prefigured by the Law. For many things have often been expressed and completed with such precision through the proper meaning of names that they seem intended not so much for events then to be done as for things to be signified in the future. Thus now, after so many and such clear proclamations of Gospel hope, the following order of sayings brings us something deeper, beyond the hearing of the ears. [Note: [Col. 0461D] Printed editions read “or deeds.” In the Paris edition, *convertar*, “I will turn,” is not repeated; the manuscripts oppose this.] 

VERSE 23. “The Lord said: From Bashan I will turn; I will turn into the depths of the sea.”

This indeed seems to have been the Lord’s speech when He turned to divide the sea for the journey and to unleash His wrath upon Pharaoh. But does the Law teach that He turned from Bashan? Certainly not. Bashan was a city of a hostile kingdom, formerly the dwelling-place of King Og; but the interpretation of its name signifies shame and confusion. It may indeed appear that God turned from the shame of the people enslaved in Egypt, when, oppressed [Note: [Col. 0461D] In printed editions, “by Pharaoh.” This word, following Greek usage, is almost nowhere declined in the manuscripts.] by Pharaoh, they had lost that very freedom by which their race might be preserved and brought forth, toward the depths of the sea—that is, toward the glorious deliverance of His people. But He who in the immediately following Psalm says:

“Save me, O God, for waters have entered even unto my soul. I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground. I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68:2–3),

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions read, “Save me, O God,” and then “in the mire of the deep.”] must undoubtedly be understood to have turned, after the shame of the human body—[Note: [Col. 0461D] These statements seem to conflict with those in *On the Trinity*, III.19: “Certainly Mary did not receive what she brought forth; but flesh produced flesh without the shame of our elements.” They must, however, be reconciled in the same way as the statement in *On the Trinity*, I.13, “He received sinful flesh,” with that in X.25, “Nor was that flesh sinful flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh.” The first statement shows the reality of our flesh in Christ; the latter removes concupiscence from Him.] for those very origins of our bodies and elements are shameful—into this sea, that is, into this storm of the world. He turned so that, subjected even to the shame of the final humiliation, namely the death of the cross, He might through it crush in Himself the heads of His enemies—making public spectacles of the spiritual wickednesses, all powers, and rulers of this air—and might triumph when, after He Himself had suffered and died, He assigned them to eternal punishment. [Col. 0461C] Therefore He is to be understood as having turned into the depths of the sea: that is, as having descended to the utmost sufferings of the world, so that, trampling upon the heads of His enemies, He might exercise the vengeance of divine power. [Note: [Col. 0462D] Printed editions read “might exercise”; the manuscripts oppose this.]

26. Divine vengeance is expressed by a human analogy.—The following saying seems to embrace this same point when it says:

VERSE 24. “That your foot may be dipped in blood; the tongue of your dogs may have its portion from the enemies, from him.”

The wrath of divine vengeance is signified by the example of human retribution. For He turned from Bashan into the depths of the sea in order that the foot might be dipped in blood, and that the tongue of the dogs also might be dipped in that blood which comes from the enemies. These things ordinarily occur when all are consumed by war, destroyed by captivity, and punished according to the decision and vengeance of conquerors. Therefore, by the customary manner of human affairs, as I said, when sword, bow, arrow, spear, and the other weapons of punishments and deaths are mentioned, the works of divine severity are signified.

All these things indeed happened to the Jews after the cross and death of the Lord, when they were captured by the Romans and endured every kind of punishment and misery, so that the feet of those walking were stained with the blood of the slain, and the tongues of dogs were sated. But this must no less be referred to the penalty and condemnation of those who, having been made public spectacles, are triumphantly conquered with confidence.

27. The salvation of the Gentiles began in the times of the Law.—Since beneath those things fulfilled among the Jewish people in the times of the Law, the future salvation of almost all nations under the form of mercy was begun, so that what was then done might teach also what was afterward to be done; and since those very persons in whom these things were then done were enclosed within Gospel hope and faith by the cloud’s shadowing, the journey through the sea, spiritual food of manna, and spiritual drink from the rock: now also, as always, the Prophet connects the New and Old Testaments in these same events when he says:

VERSE 25–28. “Your ways have been seen, O God—the ways of my God, of the King who is in the sanctuary. The princes went before, joined with those singing psalms, in the midst of young women playing timbrels. In the churches bless the Lord God from the fountains of Israel. There Benjamin the younger is in trembling; the princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.”

[Note: [Col. 0462D] Royal manuscript, here and below: “Diabulon.”]

The ways of God were indeed seen when the waters were congealed into ice, when He went before in the pillar of fire and cloud, and a dry way was made for the people; when young men singing psalms amidst timbrel-players sang of the Lord’s glorious glorification. [Note: [Col. 0462D] Bade’s edition reads “but of the name.” Other subsequent editions read “but no less”; corrected from the manuscripts.] But we know also other ways of the King in the sanctuary, when His way is preceded by heavenly powers and the souls of saints, in that Psalm which is sung on the first day of the week: “Lift up the gates of your prince, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory” (Ps. 23:9–10). [Note: [Col. 0462D] The Micy codex: “your princes.”] [Note: [Col. 0461D] “Which Psalm is sung on the first Sabbath.”] These therefore also are the seen ways of our God and King in the sanctuary, when such joys of heavenly assemblies go before His entrance. [Note: [Col. 0462D] The Paris edition omits “heavenly.” From the words immediately following, no other meaning comes to mind than the souls of saints who had fallen asleep before Christ and entered heaven together with Christ. Thus what the holy doctor in his exposition of Psalm 2, §26, thinks was granted to some after they had already received their bodies, he does not deny also to the souls of saints, though he is now silent concerning their bodies.]

28. Prophecy of the election of the Apostles: Paul from Benjamin; others from Zebulun and Naphtali.—But because the things formerly prefigured in Pharaoh and Israel were fulfilled in the overthrow of the devil and his own followers and in the salvation of all peoples, the Prophet exhorts us not to the confession of the synagogue but to the blessing of the Church.
