[Note: [Col. 0463D] The words “but to the blessing of the Church” are absent from the Royal manuscript. In their place the Micy manuscript reads, “but to the heavenly blessing.” We suspect that this phrase, like the preceding words, should be connected with “were fulfilled” above, not referred to the following exhortation.] He addresses those for whom he had affirmed that the ways of God and of the King in the sanctuary had been seen, saying: [Note: [Col. 0463C] “So that to those . . . they had been seen.”] “In the churches bless the Lord God from the fountains of Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0463D] Royal manuscript: “Bless the Lord from the holy ones of Israel.” But the following context makes clear that Hilary, alluding to fountains, teaches that the Church’s doctrine has flowed from the beginnings of the Law.] He thus recalls that the Church’s doctrine has flowed from the beginnings of the Law and from the prefiguration of events. [Note: [Col. 0463D] Bade and Erasmus: “prefiguration”; Lipsius and Paris: “prefigurations”; manuscripts correct these.]

And so that no ambiguity might arise in the churches that bless God, he shows who would be the greatest herald of Gospel hope, saying: “There Benjamin the younger is in trembling”—that is, Benjamin the younger was to remain in trembling at the fountains of the Church. [Col. 0463B] For after the consternation of terror, Paul was chosen from the tribe of Benjamin for Christ’s Gospel, devouring prey in the morning and dividing flesh in the evening for salvation (Gen. 49:27).

He also shows, lest the other leaders of Judah be unknown, those who were to be chosen by Him who was to come from Judah’s branch as the expectation of the nations (Gen. 49:10), revealing: “The princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.” [Note: [Col. 0463C] “Does he reveal?”] [Note: [Col. 0463D] Here too the Royal manuscript has “Diabulon”; below, however, “Ziabulon.”] For, as the Gospels declare, the selection of the Apostles began from these tribes, showing them as leaders of those who would assemble in the churches. Although leaders were established according to the Law from all tribes for each of the peoples, nevertheless, now that the leaders of the Gospel dispensation were being declared, the names are mentioned only of those tribes from which they were to be called. [Note: [Col. 0464D] Royal manuscript: “their,” and a little earlier “tribes,” not “of the tribes.” Many manuscripts similarly give this plural accusative form in Matthew.] [Note: [Col. 0463C] “Before.”] For after the great light rose in the regions of Zebulun and Naphtali, after the shadow of death, fishermen from these tribes were made fishers of men. Therefore, from that whole body of leaders, only that is mentioned under the meaning of prophecy which was to be fulfilled for the confirmation of the Gospel by the actual events and the election of the Apostles.

29. Christ’s coming is desired.—And because they were held fast by the hope of so great an expectation—[Note: [Col. 0464C] “They are held.”] for it is not doubtful that all saints and prophets desired with heavenly longing the time of Gospel blessedness, as the Lord says: “Amen, I say to you, many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear” (Matt. 13:17)—[Note: [Col. 0464C] “And saints,” not “and righteous.”] [Note: [Col. 0464D] Printed editions add here, “and did not hear”; we have deleted these words on the authority of the Royal manuscript, since “and did not see” does not occur before them. The passage is cited in the same manner in the exposition of Psalm 68, §8, and without them Hilary’s meaning is more neatly established here.] he prays that what he so greatly longs for may be accomplished, saying:

VERSE 29–30. “Command, O God, Your strength; confirm, O God, what You have wrought in us. From Your temple in Jerusalem kings shall bring You gifts.”

[Note: [Col. 0464D] Paris, here and below: “shall offer,” from whose meaning Hilary does not depart.]

He distinguishes the meaning, lest anything confused or ambiguous intrude in what he says: “Command, O God, Your strength.” Certainly this is spoken contrary to human understanding and the usage of natural custom. For no one appears to command anything to his own strength, because the effect of inward power is inherent through it; and since all things are done by strength, strength itself is not thought ordinarily to receive a command to act. But the Lord Jesus Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, [Col. 0464B] and He received from the Father a command both to lay down His life and to take it again (John 10:18). Therefore the saying does not seem contrary to the common understanding, though it is stated with the special precision of prophetic knowledge: God was to command His own strength, namely the only-begotten God, who is also God’s power.

Then, because no sudden and novel undertaking [Note: [Col. 0464D] Printed editions: “recent and sudden.” But the manuscripts have “new and sudden,” that is, “sudden.” Then one Vatican manuscript reads “motion,” not “undertaking.”] can occur in God, from whose knowledge the things to be done cannot escape, because His nature encompasses by the power of His strength all things that will be, the Prophet now asks that He confirm what God Himself has already wrought in us. This accords with the Apostle’s saying: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in heavenly places, in whom He also chose us before the foundation of the world, that we might be holy and blameless in Him” (Eph. 1:3 ff.). Thus God, who according to the Prophet has done things to come, has confirmed in the Lord what He wrought in us before the foundation of the world by determining the things to be done (Isa. 45:11, LXX). [Note: [Col. 0464D] In the Royal manuscript, “by determining the things to be done” is omitted; in the Tours manuscript the word “to be done” is absent.]

30. What temple, and what kings bring gifts from it to God.—The sequence of the words immediately continues what this means: “From Your temple in Jerusalem kings shall bring You gifts.” The temple in Jerusalem is that in which lawful sacrifices were offered; but now gifts are to be brought to God by kings from the temple in Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 0464C] “To be offered.”] This is surely contrary to the significance of places and the logic of the events: gifts are to be offered from the place to which they should rather be brought—that is, from the temple.

But since that heavenly Jerusalem is our mother, the assembly of those enrolled among the firstborn and of those gathered together (Heb. 12:22), and everyone reborn in Christ is the temple of God—especially the one in whom not death but rather life will reign, and who himself is king over that of which he had formerly been the slave, namely sin, offering himself as a living, rational sacrifice pleasing to God—then from this temple, that is, from this holy dwelling of his body, in that assembly of gathered angels, [Note: [Col. 0465C] “Of those gathered.”] namely in that heavenly Jerusalem, if there are any kings—that is, persons who no longer serve sin—they will offer themselves to God as a gift.

31. The assembly of bulls; beasts of the forest; those tested by silver.—Because carnal Israel, while arrogating God’s mercy as its own exclusive possession, seems to maintain that it belongs to it alone, the Prophet immediately adds:

VERSE 31. “Rebuke the beasts of the forest, the assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples, lest those tested by silver be excluded. Scatter the nations that desire war.”

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Paris, here and below: “who desire wars.” In the exposition, however, we have “wars” at the end of §32 and “war” at the beginning of §33.]

It is known from the books that cows were worshipped in Samaria. But the prophetic discourse declares that the rulers of that people are now leaders not of a people but of herds, when it says in the Lord’s person: “Fat bulls surrounded me” (Ps. 21:13). The beasts of the forest, however, must be understood as signifying the spiritual wickednesses that walk above the hairy crown in their sins, according to the saying: “The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it” (Ps. 79:14). [Col. 0465C] In that passage both the savagery and the power of the prince of this world, that is, Satan, are signified.

The Prophet therefore now asks that God rebuke either these beasts of the forest or this assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples, [Note: [Col. 0465D] Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions read, “so that, plainly, He rebukes these,” etc. One Vatican manuscript then has “the rebuke is,” for “He may rebuke.”] lest those tested by silver be excluded. Those tested by silver are those who, refined according to silver [Note: [Col. 0465D] Printed editions: “of sin.” More correctly the manuscripts: “refined.” Thus in the exposition of Psalm 65, §20: “Believers are tested . . . so that, purified by fire and refined from the mixture of carnal vices, they may shine with the brightness of tested innocence.”] and purified by the fire of every suffering, now shine spotless and without any admixture of earthly defilement.

32. Knowledge and peace are desired for God’s elect.—For though prophetic discourse proclaims the faith of the Gentiles and very often rebukes the perverse will of this hostile people, and though salvation from God has now been made known in and through all people, and this is known from the knowledge of God’s ordering: once the impiety of the people has been reproved, all saints are called to the hope of the heavenly kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0465D] Bade, with the Royal manuscript: “after the people’s reproach had been made.”] For “He is not the God of the Jews only, and not of the Gentiles also? Yes, of the Gentiles also; for there is one God, who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith” (Rom. 3:29–30). [Note: [Col. 0465D] “Yes, of the Gentiles also” is omitted in the Royal manuscript.]

Therefore, after those who deserved to be called rulers of Sodom and rulers of Gomorrah have been rebuked, [Note: [Col. 0465D] Printed editions, except Paris, read “the people of Gomorrah,” agreeing with Isaiah 1:10, to which reference is made here, but contrary to the manuscripts.] knowledge and understanding of God flowed out to the nations; and they are no longer kept within the error or contradiction of ignorance. [Note: [Col. 0465D] The negative particle is lacking in Paris. Then, in place of *inscientiae*, “of ignorance,” it has *inscitia*, “ignorance,” while other editions have *in scientia*, “in knowledge.” The Royal manuscript’s *scientiae*, “of knowledge,” is more probable, as though contradicted; yet one Vatican manuscript more truly has *inscientiae*, signifying that the contradiction arose from blindness of mind. In this sense the subsequent exposition, §20, calls the same Jews’ blindness “the ignorance of a blinded heart.”]

Having rebuked the beasts of the forest, the assemblies of bulls, and the cows of the peoples, he condemns those who still persist in contending through the ceaseless hatred of unbelief against the Gentiles’ hope and salvation, saying: “Scatter the nations that desire war.” For the Lord has made peace in heaven and on earth; and, according to the Apostle, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself” (Col. 1:20; 2 Cor. 5:19). Therefore he pronounces the scattering of those nations that reject the covenant of heavenly peace and prefer the wars of dissension, though under the collective designation of diverse nations.

33. Nearly all Egypt faithful; baptism; apostolic ministry.—For, to preserve and connect the entire meaning, after rebuking the assemblies of bulls and the beasts of the forest, and scattering the nations that desire war, lest arrogant and impious Israel should presume anything further for itself, he adds:

VERSE 32–33. “Envoys shall come from Egypt; Ethiopia shall quickly stretch out her hand to Him. Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord.”

These same things were fulfilled either when the Magi came from the East, or when the Holy Spirit came upon the Apostles, divided like fire. For there, people are recorded as having gathered even from Egypt to learn the Gospel proclamation, and, as envoys, to report the greatness of the divine gift; through them nearly all Egypt has now become faithful. Ethiopia, moreover, in the eunuch of Candace, anticipated by confession of faith; [Note: [Col. 0466D] Royal manuscript: “in Candace,” omitting “the eunuch.” A Vatican manuscript supports this: “in Candace Ethiopia has been anticipated by the confession of faith.”] [Note: [Col. 0466D] Bade and Erasmus: “confession”; then, with Vatican, Royal, and Micy manuscripts: “anticipates.” Lipsius substituted from himself, “her hands anticipate.” Perhaps the reading above should rather be restored: “Ethiopia shall anticipate with her hand,” somewhat supported by the Greek, *Αἰθιοπία προφθάσει χεῖρα αὐτῆς*—“Ethiopia shall hasten her hand.”] [Note: [Col. 0465C] “Profession.”] and with his own hand, [Note: [Col. 0465C] “With his own hand”; this reading is confirmed by what follows: “with his own hand, while he himself asks for the grace of baptism,” etc.] while he himself asks for the grace of baptism, saying: “See, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36). He anticipated the very sacrament of baptism with the eager desire of impatient longing, so that, desirous of salvation, [Col. 0467A] he demanded from the deacon the ministry of the apostolic office.

And because from that point onward the proclamation of divine knowledge shone forth through almost all nations; [Note: [Col. 0467D] “With *quia*”; shortly afterward, “Jesus Christ.”] and because all kingdoms, though late, shall understand the Lord Christ to be God, and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father, [Note: [Col. 0467D] “With the confirmation,” in a second hand.] he desires the consummation of this age, saying: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord.” He exhorts all, namely, to sing and make psalmody to God, either because in prophetic concern he rejoices in the salvation [variant: “by the salvation”] of all, or because, when all kingdoms know God, the eternity of the heavenly kingdom succeeds.

34. Christ’s divinity.—VERSE 34. And, as is his custom elsewhere, he now also shows to what God and Lord singing and psalmody are to be offered, saying: [Note: [Col. 0467D] Printed editions: “with God.” More correctly, the Royal manuscript: “to which God,” that is, to which divine Person.] “Sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the East; behold, He will give His voice, the voice of power.”

The honor of God ascending above the heaven of heaven toward the East is suitably sought now, so that, since His humiliation had been signified above, when He either ascends above the west or goes forth into death, now that He is known to have passed beyond not merely heaven but the heaven of heaven, the eternity of His divinity and majesty may not be unknown. “Toward the East” is used because He Himself, according to the Prophet, is the Dayspring from on high (Luke 1:78), so that He may be recognized as having returned to the place from which He descended, and as Himself the source for humankind of their rebirth into this ascent to the heavenly dwelling. [Note: [Col. 0467D] The word “Dayspring” is needlessly repeated here in printed editions; we have deleted it on the authority of the Royal manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0467D] Two Vatican manuscripts, with the Royal manuscript, read “of all,” not “for humankind.”]

35. The voice of power; the raising of bodies.—For the following saying signifies this very thing: “Behold, He will give His voice, the voice of power.” Indeed, in all that He did while remaining in the body, He gave a voice of power: when He says to the paralytic, “Rise and walk” (Matt. 9:6); when He calls Lazarus from the tomb (John 11:43); when He says to Peter and the other Apostles, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 18:16, 18). This plainly is a voice of power: to grant so much capacity to human weakness.

But we know that another voice of power still remains, concerning which He Himself testified: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who hear shall live” (John 5:25). Can any voice of power be greater than to gather the dust of dissolved bodies into form [Col. 0467D] and the solidity of limbs, to restore life again to human beings and souls, [Note: [Col. 0468D] “And to restore ways again into the souls of human beings.”] and to transform the corruption of frail nature by the incorruption of heavenly nature? This is the true and perfect assurance of human hope; this is the consummate goodness of divine majesty. Therefore He exhorts all to honor this so great power, saying: “Give honor to God,” so that we may refer the praise of immortality received to the honor of Him who is the giver of so great a gift.

36. Whose resurrection will be glorious.—VERSE 35. Then, lest either carnal Israel or the entire company of impious Gentiles should presume anything for themselves from these benefits of God’s mercy and knowledge, he shows by whom this honor is to be rendered to God, saying: “His magnificence is over Israel, and His power is in the clouds.” He thereby shows that magnificence shall be over that Israel which has already become spiritual in comparison with the clouds, or which, according to the Apostle, deserves to be caught up to meet Christ in the clouds (1 Thess. 4:10, 16). [Col. 0468B]

And for this reason His power is in the clouds: because it belongs to those who, living beyond earthly origin and mortality, have raised themselves into heavenly understanding and, so to speak, aerial life, and have stood lifted up in the clouds to meet Him, to rejoice in God’s power and magnificence. (I have often recalled that these same clouds, as perfected in reason and knowledge, were commanded not to rain upon the impious vineyard of Israel [Isa. 5:6], because those whom thorns and briars—that is, earthly vices—had already occupied were unworthy of holy speech.) [Note: [Col. 0467D] Manuscripts: “I have recalled,” not “he has recalled.”]

For although all must make use of the voice of power for the new beginning of resurrection, nevertheless the glorious honor of resurrection is not prepared for all. The Lord says: “Do not marvel at these things, for the hour is coming in which [Col. 0468C] all who are in the tombs shall hear His voice; and they who have done good shall come forth to the resurrection of life, but they who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29). Therefore God’s magnificence and power are over that Israel which is in the clouds, because, according to the distinction between innocent and impious life, the resurrection has a differentiated outcome: either into life or into judgment.

37. The unity and immortality of the blessed with God.—Then the following statement indicates the same thing, saying: “God is wonderful in His saints.” [Note: [Col. 0467D] Royal manuscript: “in Him”; then “which,” not “whom.” It subsequently reads “goodwill” instead of “beneficence,” and “will confer” instead of “confers.”] He is wonderful in those whom He will raise eternal unto the resurrection of life. He is wonderful when He will confer upon them every purpose of His beneficence, when He will place them within the perfection of heavenly glory; just as He prayed to the Father for them, saying: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with Me” (John 17:24); or again, “That they all may be one” (John 17:21), “I in them, and You in Me” (John 17:24). [Note: [Col. 0468D] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions read, “and they in Me.” Here part of verse 21 is joined to part of verse 24. This is an important passage for understanding the unity of Christ with the Father and our unity with God, repeatedly celebrated by Hilary, especially after the gift of the glorified body has been received. The Father is in Christ the man through the nature of divinity, which, before glorification, was as though hidden and emptied, but through the glorification of the flesh manifested itself more clearly. Christ in turn is in us through participation in His flesh; when by the glory of resurrection we are conformed to it, we shall also, to use Hilary’s word, be made one body with Him. Thus, through Christ as mediator, we shall be one with the Father. Such an affirmation of unity is wholly free from any suspicion of detracting from the reality of resurrected bodies, especially since §35 has already stated that the dust of dissolved bodies must be gathered into form and the solidity of limbs.]

Therefore God is wonderful in His saints: when He has made them conformed to the glory of His body, He will through Himself, who is the mediator, take them also into the unity of the Father’s majesty. For the Father is in Him by nature, and He in turn is in us by the fellowship of flesh. [Col. 0469A] He will place them in possession of the kingdom prepared for them before the foundation of the world, and, death having been swallowed up, He will give them immortal and eternal life.

For no longer will human life’s change and labor be borne through the growth of bodies, the nourishment of food, or the accidents of weakness. Rather, eternity will be granted to all—an eternity which, sustained by the power of its own nature, contains itself, that is, feeds and preserves itself. [Note: [Col. 0469D] “May be granted.”] [Note: [Col. 0470D] Manuscripts read “may be granted”; then, omitting “which,” they add “are contained,” not “may be contained.”] And all will be certain that they shall be everlasting, because they are no longer sustained in life from some other source—that is, externally—[Note: [Col. 0469D] “May be preserved.”] but from God, through whom they have risen and remain immortal and eternal. [Col. 0469B]

Therefore the Prophet concludes these mysteries of human hope with this faith of confession:

VERSE 36. “God is wonderful in His saints; the God of Israel Himself will give power and strength to His people. Blessed is God.” [Note: [Col. 0470D] Royal manuscript: “to His people; blessed are You, O God.”]

God therefore gives power and strength to His people, who, made immortal, are contained within life and power, and who, having put off the body, are clothed over with heavenly honor. Thus, with all corruption and weakness driven away, they bless God with the praise of their eternity, through His only-begotten and firstborn Son, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0469D] Manuscript heading: “Psalm LXVIII happily begins. To the end, for those things which shall be changed; for David himself”—more closely following the Greek.]

To the end, for those who shall be changed, a Psalm for David himself.

[Col. 0469C]

Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul. I am fixed in the mire (Hilary: *into the mire*) of the deep, and there is no firm ground. I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me. I have laboured crying out; my throat has become hoarse; my eyes have failed while I hope in my God. Those who hate me without cause are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head. My enemies, who persecute me unjustly, have grown strong: I was required to repay what I had not seized. God, you know my foolishness, and my offences are not hidden from you. Let not those who wait for you be put to shame in me, Lord of hosts; let not those who seek you be confounded because of me, God of Israel. For your sake I have endured reproach; shame has covered my face. I have become an alien to my brothers [Col. 0469D], and a stranger to the sons of my mother: for zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen upon me. I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me. And [Col. 0470A] I made sackcloth my garment, and became a proverb to them. Those sitting in the gate spoke against me, and those drinking wine sang of me. But I directed my prayer to you, O Lord: O God, it is a time of favour. In the multitude of your mercy hear me, in the truth of your salvation. Deliver me from the mud, that I may not stick fast, and from the deep

> [Note: Col. 0470D: The Vatican manuscript adds here: “deliver me from those who hate me.” Hilary’s discussion at section 15 makes clear that he read these words, although, contrary to his custom, they are nowhere expressly prefixed to the explanation of the individual verses.]

of waters. Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor the pit shut its mouth over me. Hear me, O Lord, because your mercy is sweet to me; according to the multitude of your mercies look upon me. Do not turn your face away from your servant, for I am troubled; hear me speedily. Attend to my soul and deliver it; rescue me from my enemies. For you know my reproach and my confusion and my shame; before [Col. 0470B] you are all who afflict me. My heart awaited reproach and misery. I waited for one to grieve with me, and there was none; and for one to console me, and I found none. They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. Let their table before them become a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block. Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their back for ever. Pour out your anger upon them, and let the fury of your wrath seize them. Let their dwelling become desolate, and let none dwell in their tents; for they persecuted him whom you struck, and added to the pain of my wounds. Add iniquity to their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness. Let them be erased from the book of the living, and not be enrolled with the just. But I am poor and sorrowful, and the salvation of your countenance, O God, [Col. 0470C] has upheld me. I shall praise the name of God in song, and magnify him in praise; and this shall please God more than a young calf bringing forth horns and hoofs. Let the poor see and rejoice; seek God, and your soul shall live. For the Lord has heard the poor, and has not despised (variant: “disdained”) his prisoners. Let heaven and earth praise him, the sea and everything that creeps in them (variant: “in it”); for the Lord will save Zion, and the cities of Judah shall be built; they shall dwell there and inherit the land. And the offspring of his servants shall possess it (variant: “shall possess [it]”), and those who love his name shall dwell in it.

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

### 1. The psalm concerns Christ and his Passion

**Verse 1.** This is the third psalm “for those who shall be changed.” Although it contains nothing under the heading of a historical commemoration—as we discussed in Psalm 59—and does not, as Psalm 44 does, offer something distinctive in its superscription, where “A song for the Beloved” [Col. 0471A] is prefixed (Ps. 44:1), yet, because it is inscribed not as a psalm *of* that David but as a psalm *for* that David,

> [Note: Col. 0471C: “For David,” then “unto the end.”]

the prophecy must be understood as referring rather to that David who is both the Rising One, the Just One, and the end of the Law. For by this it is taught that the psalm was sung not by him but

> [Note: Col. 0471C: “The psalm is shown to be concerning him.”]

concerning him.

> [Note: Col. 0471D: The manuscripts read “concerning him”; above, likewise, “unto the end,” which they almost always exhibit, not “in the end.”]

We have taught, moreover, in treating those who were changed (on Ps. 59, §2), that they signify believers in evangelical hope, who, changed either from observance of the Law or from Gentile impiety to the knowledge of God, flourished as though reborn in the brightness of incorruptible eternity.

> [Note: Col. 0471D: In the Royal manuscript: “flourished.”]

This very point will be discussed at the end of the psalm.

There is no doubt that the psalm itself contains the mystery of the Lord’s Passion. For John the Apostle (19:28), besides testifying that the giving of vinegar to drink accomplished [Col. 0471B] the Scriptures, also cites under the remembrance of the apostles this saying: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (John 2:17). This removes all ambiguity and confirms that everything spoken and done must be referred to him. Having therefore undergone the lot of all human sufferings, he speaks in accordance with the infirmities he assumed. He himself, indeed, is beyond the necessity of fear and pain; yet he accommodates himself to those things which he assumed, so that, being born a man in our flesh,

> [Note: Col. 0471D: Printed editions read “from pains.” The manuscripts read more coherently “and,” in place of “also.”]

he might speak both with the complaints of our pains and with the prayer of infirmity. Thus he began.

### 2. The law of death extends to all; Christ, as man, prays for salvation

**Verses 2–3.** “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul. I am fixed

> [Note: Col. 0471D: Thus the Royal manuscript, following the Greek εἰς ἰλύν, “into mire”; nevertheless, together with the printed editions, it sometimes gives “in mire,” which we have not altered in those places.]

in the mire [Col. 0471C] of the deep, and there is no firm ground.”

Death, appointed as the end of life, lays down its decree upon everyone. What then is the purpose of this prayer, which begs to be saved, when the law of death has been appointed for all? Further, the reason now given for praying for salvation is that the waters have entered even to the soul; and waters can enter to the soul because he is fixed in the mire of the deep; while for one fixed in the mire of the deep there is no firm ground. Therefore, since no one prays except for what he hopes for—and no one hopes not to die—this prayer properly belongs to one who, though about to die, was not to be held fast by death.

> [Note: Col. 0471D: Printed editions: “who was about to die.” The manuscripts more correctly read “who,” namely, one who was not to be mastered or detained by death, since he was to emerge victorious through receiving life.]

Thus the assumed infirmity performed the office of praying for salvation; but the consciousness of divinity held the hope of salvation to be hoped for in death. Therefore he who said, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46), prays to be saved.

### 3. What the waters signify

For when the waters entered even to the soul, he became subject to the death of the cross, since the onrush of all sufferings broke through even to the death of the soul. That waters customarily signify the persecutions of peoples and the commotions of nations is beyond doubt, as when it is said: “Our soul passed through the torrent” (Ps. 123:5), or: “Our soul passed through immense water” (ibid.). There are also waters that undermine a house built upon sand and drive it into collapse and ruin (Matt. 7:27). These waters, then, now entering even to the soul, compelled him to make the prayer for salvation.

### 4. Whence Christ had death and suffering: God’s self-emptying; the union of God and man in Christ

[Col. 0472B] But the source of these inexpressible sufferings, and of their power and force, was nothing other than the assumption of flesh. For the terror of our infirmities could not

> [Note: Col. 0472C: “Enter.”]

fall upon God, nor could sufferings display themselves except in the flesh of our body,

> [Note: Col. 0471D: In the Vatican manuscripts: “as though in subject matter lying beneath.” This would not be objectionable if “into flesh,” rather than “in flesh,” were read first. In this passage, badly corrupted in the old editions, Hilary explains briefly what he thinks concerning Christ’s Passion: namely, that as God he had no source from which he could suffer; he had it only from his assumption of humanity.]

as though in underlying matter. Yet the heavenly nature (the divine nature) had to be drawn down, so that, emptying itself from the form of God, it might descend into the form of a servant and of a human being. Therefore the waters penetrate even to the soul, because there is no firm ground for one fixed in the mire of the deep.

> [Note: Col. 0472D: The Royal manuscript, after correction, reads “fixed,” which also prevailed in the printed editions; although the first hand, with the manuscript of Mic., reads much better “for one fixed,” that is, for him who is fixed. Our Interpreter then subtly explains of which nature of Christ it is said, “There is no firm ground”: not, he says, of the human nature, but of the divine—not because Christ, having become man, ever lacked the substance of divinity, but because it was so hidden that it did not appear to be manifest. His words shed no little light on the explanation of other more difficult passages.]

It was certainly not that substance which he had assumed that was absent, but that which, emptying itself, had drawn itself down. He who emptied himself by making himself void did not in any way lose himself; yet what had already yielded itself by emptying itself into another was not seen [Col. 0472C] to be manifest. There is therefore no firm ground because he is fixed in the mire of the deep.

For the first man was from the mire of earth; and the second Adam, descending from heaven into the depth of this mire, fixed himself as one coming down from on high.

> [Note: Col. 0472D: “Coming, failing, he fixed himself.”]

Therefore, emptying himself—since there was no firm ground for him—he descended not merely into the depths of flesh but even into the depths of death, and every terror of the storm raging against us fell upon him. For when, contrary to the diversity of heavenly and earthly nature, he fixed himself by the power of his might in this mire,

> [Note: Col. 0472D: Printed editions: “into this ground.” It is clear that “heavenly and earthly nature” here designate the divine and human natures.]

then those things which differ by nature are joined to a certain solidity of union, not through affinity of kind [Col. 0473A] itself, but

> [Note: Col. 0473D: Printed editions: “by a stronger life, by which—or whom—they were fixed together.” We owe the correction of these words to one Vatican manuscript, supported also by others.]

as though fastened together by a stronger power. Then he began both to suffer and to be capable of dying, descending by the setting of death into the lower regions.

### 5. Prophecy of Christ’s death; the Scriptural expressions for death’s abode

For it follows: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me.” Jonah, an imitator both of the Lord’s death and of its timing, submerged in the sea and received by the whale, testifies that he was situated not so much in the sea as in hell: “I cried in my distress to my God, and he heard my cries from the belly of hell” (Jonah 2:3). And although the whale swallowed him as an image of infernal death, he says: “My head entered into the clefts of the rocks; I descended into the earth whose bars are

> [Note: Col. 0473D: In the old books it is consistently written *serrae*, with a double r.]

firm and everlasting.”

Even to holy Job, after that most glorious contest of all his sufferings, when he was now worthy of divine speech and knowledge of nature—after the gates of the sea had been broken within itself and its roaring terrors had been described as in its mother’s womb—the Lord further revealed what was signified in the sea, saying: “Have you come upon the springs of the abyss, or walked in the tracks of the sea? Have the gates of death been opened to you through fear?” (Job 38:16–17). By “the tracks of the sea,” that is, as in the deep or depth of the sea, he indicates that the gates of death are there. For since the depths of the sea lie beneath the earth, death’s abode must be shown in the deep—that is, in the lower regions.

Coming, therefore, into this depth of the sea, he was overwhelmed by the storm, which he recalls in the preceding psalm, saying: “All your heights and your waves [Col. 0473C] passed over me” (Ps. 41:8). And that other imitator of the Lord’s death, as I have said—whom that monstrous whale of this sea vomited forth from the firm and everlasting bars of the earth—complained in similar words: “All your billows and waves passed over me”

> [Note: Col. 0473D: Royal manuscript: “were passing over”; and shortly afterward, “by the storm of that sea,” not “of that death.”]

(Jonah 2:4). Thus, coming as far as the depth of death, he was overwhelmed by the storm of death itself and cast down by the tempests of hostile powers.

### 6. Christ’s cry and its cause

Yet he was not silent concerning those who were to offer themselves to the devil as weapons of service to sin—for he sometimes reproved the counsels

> [Note: Col. 0474D: One Vatican manuscript: “formed.”]

of their planned death, often cried out while standing in the temple, and frequently raised his eyes toward God—

> [Note: Col. 0473D: “For each thing,” then, “to look,” is understood as referring also to the Father.]

to look toward the Father in every great work of his divinity.

> [Note: Col. 0474D: Printed editions: “might be understood to look.” We follow the Royal manuscript, though it has *aspectaret*, not *aspectarent*.]

Accordingly it follows, **Verse 4**: “I have laboured crying out; my throat has become hoarse; my eyes have failed,

> [Note: Col. 0474D: “While I hoped.”]

while I hope in my God.” Assuming our infirmities and bearing sins, he spoke according to the use and habit of human weariness [Col. 0474A]; for he who often submitted himself to sleep and weariness also submitted himself to the necessities of thirst and hunger.

> [Note: Col. 0474D: Printed editions: “namely, he who”; they differ from the manuscripts in letters, not in sense. See the preceding treatise, §22.]

Thus his throat became hoarse and his eyes failed. He taught that the cause of his great cry and the intentness of his gaze was his hope in God: either when he cried, saying, “He who believes in me believes not in me, but in him who sent me” (John 12:44); or when, about to call Lazarus with a loud voice, he lifted his eyes on high and said, “Father, I thank you because you have heard me” (John 11:41).

### 7. Why those who hate him are more numerous than the hairs of his head; how they hate without cause

But while he bears witness to the majesty of the paternal name or undertakes the work of human salvation, hatred of him is multiplied in vain. For it follows, **Verse 5**: “Those who hate me without cause are multiplied beyond the hairs [Col. 0474B] of my head. My enemies, who persecute me unjustly, have grown strong; I was required to repay what I had not seized.”

The number of those who hate him is manifold beyond the hairs of his head: whether because of the abundant multitude of the ungodly; or because they are unworthy of God’s care—for we know that the hairs of the Apostles are numbered because God’s care for them is so great (Matt. 10:30); or because the number of the unbelieving exceeds the number of the believing. For just as the glory of the head lies in its hair, so all adornment of the Church, which is Christ’s body, lies in the glory of the Apostles. Beyond this glory of his head is the multitude of those who hate him.

They hate him freely, that is, without having a cause for hatred. And his enemies, having grown strong, persecuted him unjustly. For he had committed no sin and had practised no deceit; [Col. 0474C] and therefore he was required to repay what he had not seized. Since he was not debtor to death and sin, he was held as though he were a debtor to sin and death by those, namely, who exercised in him the law of sin which is in our members. For “he condemned sin in the flesh concerning sin” (Rom. 8:3).

### 8. Christ’s cross as foolishness; the fruit of this: the expectation of the righteous

Since in this he fulfilled the great counsel of divine wisdom, and death on the cross appeared to the Gentiles as foolishness in God, while it contained a great expectation of heavenly and earthly hope, he added, **Verses 6–7**: “God, you know my foolishness, and my offences are not hidden from you. Let not those who wait for you be put to shame in me, Lord of hosts; let not those who seek you be confounded because of me, God of Israel.”

God is aware of his foolishness, and his offences are not hidden from him: namely, the penalties of foolishness and offences, which he had not seized, but was required to repay. He is afflicted even to the foolishness of the cross—that is, because to the Gentiles it seems foolish that he should assume our sins in this way—as a sinner and fool, freely and unjustly.

But because he had assumed foolishness and offences for our wisdom and life, in order both to judge the ruler of this world and to condemn sin in the flesh concerning sin—when the ruler of this world came to him, that is, into the flesh of his body, in which no sin could be found, according to his saying: “Behold, the ruler of this world will come, and will find nothing in me” (John 14:30). This ruler of the world came and found nothing; nevertheless he exercised the penalty of sin, that is, the right of death.

> [Note: Col. 0475D: In the printed editions here, as often elsewhere, *exercuit* was substituted for *exseruit*. For the punishment which the ruler of this world and his followers suffered for this undertaking, see the preceding psalm, §23.]

By this, the author of human death, because he attempted death against the author of life who knew no sin, is judged. And this was the expectation of the saints: that all flesh might be redeemed in Christ, and that in him the first-fruits of eternal resurrection might come to be. He prays that those who await [Col. 0475B] the Lord may not be put to shame in him, and that those who seek the God of Israel may neither fear nor be ashamed because of him; because the time when he would assume flesh was longed for, according to: “Many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear” (Matt. 13:17). He therefore prays that nothing weak or infirm may remain in him, lest the weakness of his body and flesh should disappoint the hope of those who await him. For through him and in him all our expectation is toward God. Therefore, coming into a body, he prays that the hope of the saints may not be disappointed in him.

### 9. Christ’s infirmity was assumed, not natural; no one has a necessity of sin

That he assumed our infirmities for the salvation of humankind, by the Father’s will—because he came not to do his own will but the will of the Father who sent him (John 6:38)—he now also declares in what follows, **Verses 8–10**: “For your sake I have endured reproach; shame has covered my face. I have become an alien to my brothers and a stranger to the sons of my mother, because zeal for your house has consumed me.”

There was, therefore, no natural infirmity in the only-begotten God, but an assumed infirmity, because

> [Note: Col. 0475D: Printed editions: “for God’s sake.” But the manuscripts read “for his sake,” and this refers to the Father, whose will the Son was said just above to have come to fulfil. It has already been noted on Psalm 54, p. 119, note, that Hilary denies Christ what is natural to him insofar as it does not belong to him as God. Hence what he immediately says: “He assumes a body alien to his nature.” Just as the body is alien to his nature, so also is the body’s infirmity. For as the body, so the infirmity also was assumed. “The assumption of infirmity,” he says on Psalm 137, §3, “did not make him infirm”; for it is one thing to be a nature, another to have assumed a nature. Furthermore, he denies that it is natural here insofar as “natural” conveys necessity; he maintains that Christ’s infirmity was assumed through voluntary assumption, not through the necessity of nature.]

he assumed these reproaches of sufferings for the Father’s sake. Yet even in human natures there exists [Col. 0475C] no necessity of sin; rather, the practice of sin is taken up from the desire of the will and the delight of vices. Thus the Lord shows that he had not seized what he was required to repay, because desires contrary to nature

> [Note: Col. 0476D: Here are meant sins, which had just been said to arise contrary to nature from the disordered desire of the will.]

are seized; and all who owe such debts shall pay the last farthing (Matt. 5:26). Hence, in the prescription of the Lord’s Prayer, we pray that our debts may be forgiven us.

He endured reproach for God’s sake while he assumed a body alien to his nature, while, according to the Apostle (2 Cor. 5:20), the Father made him who knew no sin to be sin, while he became obedient even to the death of the cross, while he was reproached because, though saving others, he did not save himself, and while he endured the insults of spitting and blows (see *On the Trinity*, Book 10, §46).

### 10. How he differs from us; his zeal

Covered, therefore, with this shame for God’s sake, he becomes alien to his brothers and a stranger to the sons of his mother: alien, namely, from the vices of those who were regarded as his kinsmen according to the flesh.

> [Note: Col. 0476D: Manuscripts: “making himself alien.”]

He enters the temple and overturns the tables of the money-changers (John 2:15); he prohibits the trading in sheep and oxen; he reproaches those selling [Col. 0476B] doves because they have made his Father’s house a house of trade. For, seized by zeal for God’s house, he did these things.

This zeal is the indignation of devout love: when, as though heated by surging zeal, we are moved by insults offered to those whom we love. Thus, in zeal for the defiled house, as the Gospel testifies—as I explained above—he entered the temple and cast out the whole crowd of buyers and sellers. Zeal for God, even to the severity and end of death, is praiseworthy.

### 11. He brought reproaches upon himself

By this indignation at the desires rebuked in them, the reproaches of every curse were heaped upon him. All the insults customarily directed against the impious were turned into reproaches against him: he is called a blasphemer, a Samaritan, [Col. 0476C] Beelzebub, and one who has a demon (John 8:48). Accordingly he added: “The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen upon me.”

The reproach of blasphemy belongs rather to the one who charges God with insult; likewise, the disgrace of a demon belongs more properly to one who is alien from God. Since all these things were reproached against him because of his zeal for God’s house, the reproaches of those

> [Note: Col. 0475D: “Who reproach the Lord.”]

who reproach God are heaped upon him. Writing to the Romans (15:3), the Apostle recalls this saying with this sense of its meaning.

### 12. Christ’s deeds are slandered by every class of people; why he wept before raising Lazarus

Even the restraint of fasting became a reproach to him,

> [Note: Col. 0475D: “By whom he is tempted: Zabulo.” Thus it is written in the manuscript, and this form of the name occurs frequently in manuscripts. The same book prefers *Zabuli debellatorem* (“the conqueror of Zabul”) near the end of the discourse on Psalm 63. In Hilary’s commentary on Matthew, published by Erasmus, we read: “the offspring of Zabul,” “the power of Zabul,” and “that he might be tempted by Zabul.” Nor is this found in Hilary alone, but also in other Christian writers. Jerome, in *On Hebrew Names*, interprets the word in several ways, as though from Hebrew. Du Cange in his Glossary derives it from the Doric dialect; Macrius from the Aeolic. But such an inflection was introduced by the same softening of pronunciation by which ζιά is pronounced for διά. Thus Commodian has *Zacones* for *diacones* (“deacons”). This manner of pronunciation still persists among modern Greeks.]

when he is tempted by the devil, placed on the pinnacle of the temple, taken upon a mountain, and finally tempted, by all the world’s realm, to worship Satan. At times he weeps, groans, and is sorrowful (Matt. 4:1 and following), and this too is attributed to an example of infirmity. In short, he is made both a subject of slander and a song for every class of people. For those who sit in the gates in order to beg their food speak against and slander him, and drunkards sing about him.

He complains that all these things happened to him either according to the truth of the events or in accordance with ordinary human custom. **Verses 11–13:** “I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me. I made sackcloth my garment, and became a proverb to them. Those sitting in the gate slandered me, and those drinking wine sang of me.”

Fasting, therefore, became a reproach to him because, through the humiliation of hunger, he was tempted even to the insult of worshipping Satan (Matt. 4:9). A garment of sackcloth is the attire of mourning. Every feeling of mourning is expressed

> [Note: Col. 0477D: “Effect.”]

in weeping. When he weeps as he is about to raise Lazarus, he mourns the unbelief of the human race; for in the attire of mourning the disposition to weep is signified.

> [Note: Col. 0477D: Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions: “effect.”]

That he did not weep for Lazarus—whose death he even rejoices over (John 11:15), and whom he was about to raise from the dead—is made clear by the entire account of the Gospel. But since he wept that faith in the resurrection would not exist even in the work of resurrection itself, his weeping became a proverb,

> [Note: Col. 0477D: “It proceeds, and then a proof.” Thus they wrote *monimentum* (“memorial”).]

so that even then he was said by weeping to have provided proof of his love for Lazarus; and, because he wept, many even today charge him with weakness.

> [Note: Col. 0477D: Royal manuscript: *docimentum* (“proof”); it consistently presents the word in this spelling.]

[Col. 0477C] In the drunkards who sing and those sitting in the gate who slander, the insults of all the weak against him are indicated through this popular custom. Indeed, that no class of people was silent about him is clear from the fact that Cleophas is recorded as replying to him—who, as though ignorant of events, asked the cause of their conversation—thus: “Are you alone a stranger in Jerusalem and do not know the things that have happened there in these days?” (Luke 24:18). For astonishment at one person’s ignorance arises from everyone else’s knowledge.

### 13. Christ’s prayer

But amid all their slanders and insults against him, he was accomplishing the mysteries of human salvation; and he prays to God for salvation for the man whom he had assumed. For this follows, [Col. 0477D] **Verses 14–16**: “But I

> [Note: Col. 0477D: Earlier: “my prayer.” The Septuagint translators and Augustine agree with us; indeed Hilary himself, from what follows in §15, is wholly directed to God in his prayer.]

direct my prayer to you, O Lord: O God, it is a time of favour. In the multitude of [Col. 0478A] your mercy hear me, in the truth

> [Note: Col. 0478D: “Of my salvation.”]

of your salvation. Deliver me from the mud, that I may not stick fast,

> [Note: Col. 0478D: “And deliver me from those who hate me”: we have supplied this from our manuscript, since the words are also present in the Greek and Hilary’s explanation shows that he read them. He also prays to be delivered from those who hate him, and from the depth of waters.]

and deliver me from those who hate me, and from the depth of waters. Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor the pit close its mouth over me.”

While the rest are intent upon his insults and reproaches, he is wholly directed toward God in his prayer. Although he has assumed our infirmities in himself, yet in the things he suffers he performs the work of heavenly mercy toward us. Nor does he take these things unwillingly: in the multitude of mercy he shows that this is a time acceptable to God. Therefore he prays in this acceptable time, because he does not fail to know this prophecy of the Father concerning himself, also recognized by the Apostle Paul: “In an acceptable time I heard you” (2 Cor. 6:2; Isa. 49:8).

### 14. Nothing is evil in itself, but through human vice; what the acceptable time accomplished for the world through Christ

[Col. 0478B] All things that have been done must indeed be understood to please God because of the magnificence of his works; and when it is written in Genesis, “And God saw that they were good” (Gen. 1:31), no fault remains in the creatures of things.

> [Note: Col. 0478D: Printed editions: “although certain things”; corrected from the Royal manuscript.]

For although certain things have been corrupted by the wickedness of human ingenuity—poisons from remedies, a sword from iron, conflagration from fire, indigestion from food, drunkenness from wine, and finally even the parts and members of bodies themselves, formed for natural and useful functions, have offered themselves as instruments of vices and crimes—yet, although all things please God, this is nevertheless the acceptable time: when the only-begotten God, in the blood of our body, would reconcile to God all things in heaven and on earth which were, as it were, hostile and at odds; [Col. 0478C] when that manifold Wisdom of God, hidden in former times and unknown to any of the rulers and authorities of this world, was to be revealed for the praise of God’s glory (Col. 1:20; Eph. 3:5, 9–10); when the Gentiles would become co-heirs, members of the same body, and co-partakers with Christ; when in him all powers opposed to God would be dishonoured; when death, after having raged against God, would cease; when the law of sin in our flesh would be abolished; when all creation, groaning together, would hope for the revelation of the sons of God; when, in the Passion of the only-begotten God, the result of all causes and origins before the foundation of the world would be brought to completion,

> [Note: Col. 0478D: “Would be completed”; shortly afterward, “the ruler.”]

by judging the ruler of this world, redeeming humankind from the law of sin, freeing creatures from the vanity of corruption to which they had been enslaved, condemning spiritual wickedness by the Lord’s death, and praising God in all things and through all [Col. 0479A] by the gift of eternity and the splendour of our immortality.

All these things the power of the resurrection fulfilled:

> [Note: Col. 0479D: Thus the Royal and Mic. manuscripts. Printed editions have “and” in place of “because.” On this punishment of death turned back upon the authors of our death, see above, §8, and Psalm 67, §23.]

because, with death driven from the human race through the first-fruits from the dead, the penalty of eternal death was decreed against the authors of death. For in himself he stripped the principalities and powers and triumphed over them with confidence.

### 15. Christ’s incorruption and the two natures; the pit is hell

Therefore, after indicating the acceptable time, the whole prayer is for the granting of true salvation, so that the very truth of salvation which is hoped for from the resurrection might be understood. Next, he who was fixed in the mire of the deep prays that he may not stick fast in the mud, according to: “For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor give your Holy One to see corruption” [Col. 0479B] (Ps. 15:10).

For the one who is from earth and will return to the earth from which he was taken (Gen. 3:19) will cling to the mud and mire in which he is fixed,

> [Note: Col. 0479D: Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius, with the Royal manuscript: “dissolved into his own nature,” that is, into the origin of his body.]

being dissolved into the origin of his nature—that is, of his body. He also prays to be delivered from those who hate him and from the depth of waters, because the hatred of his persecutors broke forth even to his soul—that is, even to suffering.

Likewise, having come into the depth of the sea and been overwhelmed by the storm, he now prays that he may not be overwhelmed. Above, his confession that he had been overwhelmed expressed our assumed infirmity; now, however, when he prays that the storm of waters may not overwhelm him, this is the confidence in salvation of which he is conscious within himself.

> [Note: Col. 0479D: The Paris edition alone reads “conscious.” Bade reads “conscious of himself”; Erasmus and Lipsius, “conscious of his salvation.” It is familiar to Hilary to make the thing of which someone is conscious itself “conscious.” Such is the statement in *On the Trinity*, Book 7, §1: “Although we are recalled by the trembling of infirmity conscious of itself.” See also Book 7, §21.]

For it does not belong to the same nature both already to have been overwhelmed and to pray not to be overwhelmed; rather, it belongs to one which, though submerged through the body, is nevertheless not [Col. 0479C] to be held through the Spirit.

> [Note: Col. 0479D: It is clear from the final words of this section that, in the manner of the ancients, “man” is here understood through “body,” and “God” through “Spirit.”]

He therefore now prays that he may not be swallowed by the deep, nor the pit close its mouth over him. For the pit signifies the abode of infernal death; another psalm also bears witness when it says: “But you, O Lord, will bring them down into the pit of destruction” (Ps. 54:24), thereby showing that the abyss and depth of pits signify the underworld beneath the earth. He therefore asks that the pit may not close its mouth over him. For it is impossible for the God of life to be held by the gates of hell.

16. Christ, besides being man, manifests something more. — Verses 17–19.

And lest, in assuming the death of our weakness, he should, by human necessity, grieve over any bitterness of death that might cling to him, he therefore added: “Hear me, O Lord, for your mercy is sweet to me; according to the multitude of your mercies look upon me” [cols. 479D–480A]. For this is the acceptable time in the multitude of mercy: when God, having compassion in himself upon the life of all human beings, was about to bestow life from the dead, as the merciful God.

[Note: The reading is *haereret et subjecit* (“might cling, and he added”). Printed editions read *ei ex mortis acerbitate haereret*. We prefer *maereret* (“might grieve”) with the Mic. manuscript, especially since *ei* is absent in the other witnesses and *moereret* properly contrasts with *suavis est* (“is sweet”), to which the text passes.]

But because he testified that this mercy of God was sweet to him, he nevertheless does not relax the concern arising from our assumed weakness, saying: “Do not turn your face away from your servant, for I am afflicted; swiftly hear me. Attend to my soul and deliver it; rescue me because of my enemies.” He both suffers and speaks all things as a man. For through the assumption of flesh he is also a servant, according to: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul has been well pleased” (Isa. 42:1). He prays for prompt help in his affliction and asks that God attend to his soul, so that, through God’s attending to it, it may be worthy of deliverance [col. 480B].

[Note: The Reg. manuscript reads simply *Sed* (“But”); the printed editions read *sed qui suavem* (“but because [he testified] it sweet”). Only the Paris edition has *et mortis* (“and of death”); shortly afterward the common editions have *alia magis* in place of *aliqua*.]

These things, indeed, he prays as our man, obedient even unto death on the cross. But when he asks to be rescued because of his enemies, he exceeds ordinary human hope and custom. No one wishes to be safe for any cause more than for the sake of his own salvation; and anyone desires deliverance from evils in order that he may not be afflicted by them. But now he asks to be rescued from the things by which he is afflicted, not for his own sake but because of his enemies: for these enemies would shortly be disgraced in him as he suffered, and triumphed over with confidence when he rose from the dead.

17. He does or suffers nothing for his own sake. He longs for the Passion. The mystery of divine communion. — Finally, he teaches in what follows that he does and suffers nothing for his own sake, saying, verses 20–21: “For you know my reproach and confusion and shame; before you are all who afflict me. My heart awaited reproach and misery” [cols. 480C–D].

[Note: “My reproach” agrees with the Greek and the other Latin Psalters.]

The earlier profession is not unlike this, when he says: “O God, you know my foolishness, and my offences are not hidden from you.” Contrary to the error of human opinion, it was known to God alone that this weakness assumed by him was assumed rather than natural.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *terrorem* (“terror”), wrongly. “Was known” refers to God alone, not to the things assumed.]

And because he was to endure these things for his enemies, through which he provided for human salvation and eternity, he testifies to the disposition of this acceptable time, saying: “My heart awaited reproach and misery,” signifying that the sufferings of this time were desired by him, according to that mystery of divine communion: “With desire I desired to eat” [col. 480D] (Luke 22:15)—namely, the Passover, or the sacrament of divine communion; for in these desires for his Passion lay the accomplishment of the acceptable time.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “to eat the Passover,” as also in Psalm 51, no. 4. Here “the sacrament of divine communion” may be understood in place of “Passover.”]

18. Our faith is the consolation of the mourner. Christ is the fullness of the Law. — But while awaiting suffering for the advancement of our salvation, he was also held by the desire of another expectation. For it follows: “And I waited for one who would mourn with me, and there was none; and for one who would console me, and I did not find one.”

He seeks from the mourner and comforter not consolation but faith: that someone coming from the Law, and understanding the prophecy of all these sufferings, might stand with him as though at the completion of that very Law; just as afterward Paul (Col. 1:24), fulfilling the sufferings of Jesus Christ and buried with him in baptism, knows that Christ is the end of the Law. For he who was to be the end of human sufferings and prophetic utterances—the end of deeds—was also the end of complaints [col. 481B].

[Note: *Gestorum*, “of deeds,” is absent from the Reg. manuscript and is suspected to have been inserted by an interpolator.]

For this follows, verse 22: “And they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” These things were fulfilled exactly as they are written. The Gospels testify both that gall was administered to him and that he drank vinegar. According to Matthew (Matt. 27:34), he refused the gall that was offered; but according to John, he thirsted in order to drink the vinegar (John 19:28 ff.). The passage itself is spoken in these words:

> “After this Jesus, knowing that all things were completed, in order that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said: ‘I thirst.’ And there was a vessel set there full of vinegar. Therefore, putting a sponge full of vinegar upon hyssop, they offered it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is completed.’”

He had come to the lost sheep of the house of Israel and, awaiting one who would comfort and mourn with him, found none. This was not because he needed consolation, since he willingly suffered and died, but because he sought one who would grieve with him over the impiety of the whole people and would comfort himself by the very salvation of the one grieving with him. Thus, though all had committed so great a crime, he might receive consolation at least in those who would be saved, according to: “And he will be comforted in his servants” (Deut. 32:36), because Israel did not believe but the nations would believe in him [col. 481C].

[Note: The Reg. manuscript reads “and they would believe in him.” The true prophecy is not, etc.]

Yet he is written prophetically not to have thirsted naturally, but to have said that he thirsted in order that all things might be fulfilled: because all our weaknesses which were in him were not natural but assumed.

[Note: Erasmus asks: “How are they not natural, when he assumed nature?” The easy answer is that, because nature was assumed, the other things consequent upon nature were assumed too. As Augustine says in his exposition of Psalm 93, no. 19, he assumed sorrow as he assumed flesh: he did not possess it by nature, but by dispensation.]

Then, so that it might be known that he had satisfied prophetic Scripture, after drinking the vinegar he testified that all things had been completed, so that he might be the fullness of the Law and the Prophets, he who fulfilled the Law and the Prophets [col. 481D].

19. The table of sacrifices. The table of knowledge. The Jews struck with blindness and bent beneath the burden of the Law. — Since, within the completion of the offering of gall and the drinking of vinegar, the prophecy of the whole Passion also had to be completed, the discourse turns to the consequences that afterward followed the impiety of so great a crime, saying, verses 23–24: “Let their table before them become a snare, and a trap and a recompense and a stumbling-block. Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their back continually.”

The Apostle testified that there is a table of sacrifices when he said: “You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10:21).

[Note: The Reg. manuscript reads “partake.”]

But that there is also a table of knowledge must be understood not only from several passages but also from these very words. The same blessed Apostle, interpreting this passage when writing to the Romans, testifies that they were blinded so as to understand nothing (Rom. 11:7–8).

This table, then, from which the food of spiritual life is received, became before them a snare, a trap, a recompense, and a stumbling-block, when the precepts of the Law or the words of the prophets are expounded by men of the Church for the revelation of the divine counsel: when the only-begotten God, for faith in the assumption of flesh, is shown to have been worshipped by Abraham in human form and to have wrestled with Jacob; when a ruler coming from Judah is proclaimed as the expectation of the nations; when all the kindreds of the nations are to be blessed in Abraham’s seed; when the Lord of an eternal kingdom is preached as coming from David’s womb; when, according to Isaiah (Isa. 53:7), the Lord is led as a sheep to slaughter and turns neither his cheeks from blows nor his face from spitting; when, according to Jeremiah, “This is our God,” who, after giving every discipline to Israel his beloved, was afterward seen upon earth and conversed among human beings (Bar. 3:36 ff.); and, finally, when the utterances of all the prophets agree concerning his coming.

[Note: The printed editions read “is worshipped,” wrongly.]

This table of doctrine, or discourse of life-giving food, is therefore a snare, a trap, a recompense, and a stumbling-block, when we show that the God of Jacob is he whom they crucified. For this is the recompense for so great an impiety: that what is God’s power to us is a stumbling-block to them. Though ensnared and captured by the writings, they nevertheless lack understanding; and therefore their eyes were darkened so that they might not see, that is, so that they might not behold the light of understanding. For according to the Gospel: “To everyone who has, more shall be given; but from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away” (Matt. 25:29). They were unworthy, clearly, to receive the perception and light of understanding; and therefore, not having obtained knowledge of evangelical freedom, they are still continually crushed beneath the burden of the Law, so that they bear what they cannot sustain. This is signified, under the figure of bodily works, by the bending of the back.

20. The wrath of God. — But another punishment of due vengeance follows upon this ignorance of their blinded heart [col. 483A], verses 25–26: “Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your wrath seize them. Let their dwelling become desolate, and let there be none to dwell in their tents.”

[Note: *Inscientiam*, “ignorance,” is preferred from the Mic. manuscript as a word more familiar to Hilary than *inscitiam*; compare Psalm 67, no. 32, “the contradiction of ignorance.”]

We have often explained that by the wrath of God is signified the establishment of punishment, not an emotional agitation inflamed toward the desire for vengeance (see Commentary on Psalm 2, no. 16). It means not a punishment which he was suddenly intent upon inflicting, but one into which a person worthy of punishment would fall.

[Note: The manuscripts read *poena*, “punishment,” alternatively *poenam*.]

This condemnation, announced against this impious people by all the prophets, endured. For when the city was soon overthrown and destroyed, they were wiped out, its most glorious worship of the Temple abolished and its adornment stripped away. Therefore, with their dwelling desolate, none dwelt in their tents.

[Note: The printed editions read *habitabit*, “will dwell”; the manuscripts more fittingly read *habitavit*, “dwelt.”]

21. The crime of the Jews and the cause of their punishment. — Verses 27–29. But prophecy of punishment and vengeance is extended still further in proportion to the increase of their impiety: “For they persecuted him whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds. Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous.”

He shows that the reason for adding iniquity upon their iniquity, excluding them from entry into righteousness, blotting them out of the book of the living, and not writing them with the righteous, is this: they persecuted him whom God had struck and added further pain to the pain of his wounds.

[Note: The Turonensis manuscript reads “and of blotting out … and not writing.” Another reading has *sint*, “they are,” and then *addiderint*, “they added.”]

22. Whether one struck by God is struck unjustly. God’s merciful striking. — Perhaps they may seem not to have persecuted unjustly one whom God had struck. We must first discuss what ought to be thought of those struck by God, so that it may be understood how this striking is salutary and the persecution of the one struck is impious.

[Note: The printed editions read “and that striking is impious.” The reading adopted is supported by the Mic. manuscript.]

The Lord struck Sodom and Gomorrah, defiled and abominable through their final crimes (Gen. 19:24); and I find that their being struck profited them toward reconciliation with mercy, since it will be more tolerable for them on the day of judgment than for those cities in which the dust was shaken from the Apostles’ feet (Matt. 10:15). It is likewise known that the assembly of Dathan and Abiram was struck by a most deserved plague (Num. 16:32); yet, in their souls, the works by which they had most grievously sinned were sanctified [col. 484A].

[Note: The Paris edition has “were signified,” against the unanimous testimony of the other books. The passage alludes to Num. 16:37, where God says of Korah’s censers: “They have been sanctified in the deaths of sinners.” The Greek is: ὅτι ἡγίασε τὰ πυρεῖα τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν ἐν ταῖς ψυχαῖς αὐτῶν, “because he sanctified the censers of sinners in their souls.” Similarly, when Nadab and Abihu had been consumed by fire for the same offence, the Lord says: “I shall be sanctified in those who draw near to me” (Lev. 10:3). Referring to this passage, Sidonius, Book VIII, Letter 14, says more explicitly concerning Nadab and Abihu what our Hilary indicates concerning Dathan and Abiram: “Although we may believe that the souls of those who were killed are to be absolved, we nevertheless know that their persons were punished.”]

And, not to run through many individual instances: the Apostle delivers someone to the destruction of the flesh for the salvation of the spirit (1 Cor. 5:5), while the Lord himself shows what benefit comes from his striking when he says: “See, see, that I am he, and there is no God besides me. I shall kill, and I shall make alive; I shall strike, and I shall heal” (Deut. 32:39), showing that the reason for striking proceeds from the reason for healing.

23. Christ struck by God; struck also by the Jews. — Therefore the Lord was struck, taking our sins upon himself and suffering for us, so that, struck in himself even to the weakness of cross and death, health might be restored to us through resurrection from the dead. He himself testified that he had been struck, reminding the disciples of this saying: “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Matt. 26:31; Zech. 13:7).

[Note: Here he inserts his own words.]

The Apostle also confirms the meaning of this saying in no dissimilar way: “He did not spare his beloved Son” (Rom. 8:32). He did not spare, then, his beloved Son, whom he sent to the tenants of the vineyard, not ignorant that they would kill him (Matt. 21:37). Nor had he spared that first Adam, fashioned from the clay of the earth, whom he expelled from Paradise after his sin, lest, by touching the tree of life, he should remain in the eternity of punishment.

[Note: The Turonensis manuscript reads *in aeternitate poene*, “in the eternity of punishment.”]

Thus the second Adam from heaven, assuming the nature of Adam’s body and struck by an equal death, might call it back again into eternal life, now without eternity of punishment. They therefore persecuted him who had thus been struck by God, adding the pain of this persecution to the pain of his wounds. For according to the prophet he suffers for us (Isa. 53:4), and therefore they considered him to be in pains.

[Note: The earlier edition read *idcirco est esse in doloribus aestimatus*; it was corrected with the aid of a capitular manuscript. The reading *aestimatus*, “considered,” supported by Parisian, Vatican, and Mic. manuscripts and by *On the Trinity* X.46, is preferred to *aestimandus*, “to be considered,” in the Baden, Erasmus, Leipzig, and Reg. editions. Isaiah’s words “he suffers for us” are referred by Hilary to Christ’s human nature, but “we considered him to be in pains” to his divine nature, as is clearer from Commentary on Psalm 138, no. 3: “He assumed weaknesses because he is born human; he is thought to suffer because he suffers; but he is free from pains because he is God.” Compare the present commentary, no. 12: “He sometimes weeps, groans, and is sorrowful; and this itself is assigned as an example of weakness.” This cannot be reconciled unless weakness is excluded from the divine nature alone and true sorrow is attributed to human nature. Thus also in Commentary on Psalm 53, no. 4, Christ is proclaimed as undergoing death, yet as one who does not know how to die.]

It is known what hatred of his name they afterward incurred, how they purchased silence about the resurrection with money, and with what terrors and injuries they harassed the Apostles. Because they added these things to the pain of his wounds, iniquity shall be added upon iniquity.

24. Therefore the Jews are excluded from God’s righteousness, blotted out of the book of the living, and not written with the righteous. — The punishment for this added iniquity is that they may not enter God’s righteousness: that is, that they may not become one body and co-partakers with Christ, who, according to the Apostle, “was made for us by God righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30). Excluded from entrance into righteousness, they must necessarily be blotted out of the book of the living.

For they had been written in Abraham’s blessings, whose seed was to abound as the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea-shore. When Moses feared that the whole people would be blotted out from that book, he prayed that he himself might first be blotted out (Exod. 32:32), wishing, I suppose, according to the Apostle, to be anathema for his brothers (Rom. 9:3). And because, by adding the pain of persecution to the pain of his wounds, they lost the return of repentance, blotted out of the book of the living, they did not afterward deserve to be written with the righteous.

[Note: The Reg. manuscript reads *cursum*, “course,” for *recursum*, “return.”]

Thus it may be understood that the book of the living is one thing and the book of the righteous another. It is not doubtful that those are in the book of the living who, before any knowledge of Christ, lived devoutly under the Law and fulfilled all the Law’s commandments (Lev. 18:5). Concerning them the Apostle Paul teaches according to the Law: “Whoever does these things shall live in them” (Rom. 10:5). But those are written in the book of the righteous for whom Christ has become righteousness. “The righteous shall live by faith” (Gal. 3:11; Hab. 2:4). Concerning this book the Lord speaks thus to the Apostles: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

[Note: The Greek reads ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, *en tois ouranois*, “in the heavens.”]

There was therefore a twofold meaning in being blotted out of the book of the living and not written in the book of the righteous, because after the book of the living there remained the book of the righteous. To the Apostles, however, this is offered as cause for great rejoicing: to be written in the book of the righteous is greater than not to be blotted out of the book of the living (see Commentary on Psalm 138, no. 34).

25. The one Christ has a twofold nature; the human nature has through glory been received into the divine. — He maintains in himself the manner of confession which faith requires to be in us: that in him both the nature of man and the nature of God may be known. For, coming in the form of a servant, he emptied himself of the form of God. For how could he, remaining in the form of God, be able to exist in the form of man? Yet the form of God could not be abolished so that there should be only the form of a servant.

[Note: The printed texts read “in the form of God he was able”; on the authority of the Reg. manuscript, *qui* is placed before *potuit*: “he who remained in the form of God was able?” Though initially awkward, this is supported by other passages: in *On the Trinity* IX.50, “it was a property of nature, but the form of God was no longer there, because through his emptying the form of a servant had been assumed”; and earlier, no. 14, “since he who remained in the form of God could not receive the form of a servant except through emptying himself.” Thus, where the form of God is said to be emptied, it denotes not the nature itself but the glorious state fitting the divine nature; where it is later said that it could not be abolished, it denotes the nature itself.]
