For he himself both empties himself from the form of God and assumes the form of man, because that emptying from the form of God is not the destruction of the heavenly—that is, divine—nature; nor is the assumption of the servant’s form, as though it were a nature, of genuine origin and condition. What is assumed is not an inner property but an external addition [col. 486A].

[Note: The printed editions read *geminae originis*, “of double origin”; the manuscripts correct this reading. Christ’s weaknesses are denied to be natural because they belong to the assumed servant-form. That form is proved not genuine or natural to him as Son of God because it is assumed, according to Paul’s phrase, “taking the form of a servant.” It is therefore an outward addition to the one assuming it, not an inward property; Paris wrongly has *proprietatis*. What “nature of genuine origin and condition” means is illustrated in Commentary on Psalm 53: “Although that Passion was not of condition and kind …”]

He teaches this in what follows, saying, verse 30: “I am poor and sorrowful; and the salvation of your countenance, O God, has received me.” He is poor who, according to the Apostle, though rich in all things, made himself poor so that we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). He is sorrowful who, according to the prophet, suffers for us (Isa. 53:4).

[Note: The Paris edition, after Lipsius, reads *pauperavit*; the other witnesses oppose it. The note reads: “But now, shortly afterward, in both.”]

But the salvation which is the countenance of God has received this poor and sorrowful one. Form, countenance, face, and image do not differ. The common sense is that the same thing is signified by either of them.

[Note: The printed editions read “in both”; the manuscripts more fittingly read *in utro*, “in either.”]

Therefore the salvation of God’s countenance—which is the form of God—received this poor man into itself: that is, the only-begotten God, who is the image of the invisible God, placed within the life of his eternity the man assumed by himself. This life in God is understood to be salvation. For every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father: that is, the assumed man has been received into the nature of divinity.

[Note: From the Reg. manuscript, *ab se*, “by himself,” is referred here. The following words, “he placed [him] in the life of his eternity,” mean that the assumed man was received into the nature of divinity.]

26. The sacrifice of praise in Christ is preferred to the sacrificial victims of the Law. — The Gospel confession is that in him are the end of the Law and the sacrifice of praise, so that, with the blood and offering of victims brought to an end, the sacrifice of grace and praise is set above them. This follows upon that poor and sorrowful one received into the salvation of God’s countenance and form, verses 31–32: “I shall praise your name with a song; I shall magnify him with praise. And it shall please God more than a young bullock that produces horns and hoofs.”

[Note: The manuscripts read “with the blood and offering [of victims],” while printed editions read “from the offering.” The manuscripts have “with praise,” not “in praise.”]

This praise of God’s name and magnification of praise shall please him more than the young bullock (Lev. 4). Such a bullock was formerly offered in the Law for sin; its tender growth of hoofs and horns indicates its age. The honour of praise shall therefore please God more than the bullock for sin, according to: “The sacrifice of praise shall glorify me, and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:23). The way of showing God’s salvation, therefore, lies in the sacrifice of praise.

[Note: The Greek omits “in” in “there is the way.”]

27. The cause of our salvation. — The Psalm itself shows this in what follows. After saying that the magnificence of praise will please God more than the young bullock, it adds, verses 33–34: “Let the poor see and rejoice. Seek God, and your soul shall live, because the Lord has heard the poor and has not despised his prisoners.”

Let them rejoice when they see this time whose sacrifice is praise, because there God’s salvation shall be shown. Therefore God shall be sought by them for the life of the soul. He forbade fear of the judge of flesh and body, because God alone has power to cast the soul into Gehenna (Matt. 10:28). The reason for seeking God for the life of the soul is that God heard the poor man—namely, him who made himself poor so that we might become rich—whom he received into the salvation of his countenance, in whom he forgave us sins. He did not despise his prisoners: whether those bound to Christ, as Paul glories in chains (Eph. 3:1), or those whom Satan, armed and powerful, held bound by sins (Luke 11:21), according to: “You have broken my bonds; to you I shall sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:16–17).

[Note: The Paris edition has *quia est*, “because is”; *est* is superfluous and absent from the manuscripts.]

Let the poor therefore rejoice in the things that they see, because it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3).

28. All created things praise God for our salvation. — Since, when those poor in spirit are established in the kingdom of heaven, the whole creation, groaning and suffering together, is to be liberated into the glory of the children of God, having been subjected to vanity not of its own will (Rom. 8:19 ff.), now also, because of the poor who rejoice and seek life, because the poor man has been heard, and because prisoners have not been despised, that very creation which awaits the revelation of the glory of the poor is summoned to God’s praise, verse 35: “Let heaven and earth praise him, the sea and all things that creep in him.”

[Note: Paris follows the Vulgate in reading “in it”; the other books, following the Greek, read “in him.”]

By mention of these elements he signifies the perception and understanding of all creatures to be liberated, so that when heaven, earth, and sea are named, it may be understood that things heavenly, earthly, and infernal bend the knee to the Lord Jesus Christ. For by the things that creep in the sea—although swimming rather than creeping naturally belongs to aquatic creatures—are taught the beings that dwell in the lower regions, since we understand the depth of the sea as the seat of hell.

[Note: A prior reading is *natatura*; then, “in the lower regions.”]

29. Heaven’s praise and the cause of praise. The fruitfulness of the earth. — He shows why heaven, earth, and sea still praise God, saying, verses 36–37: “For the Lord shall save Zion, and the cities of Judea shall be built. And they shall dwell there and inherit the land. And the seed of his servants shall possess it, and those who love his name shall dwell in it.”

[Note: The Reg. manuscript, following the Greek κατέξουσιν, reads “shall possess,” not the printed “shall inherit.” “In it” is supplied. Earlier one should read *civitates Judaeae*, “cities of Judea,” not *Judae*; the loss of *ae* before the following *et* is inferred from what follows.]

Universal praise proceeds from admiration for things. Something appears worthy of praise when the work itself is so magnificent and illustrious that it contains both the prudence and power of its maker and the beauty and usefulness of what is done. Whatever surpasses the ordinary capacity and judgment of the mind deserves admiration and praise.

[Note: Paris reads *providentiam*, “providence”; a second apparatus note likewise records *providentiam*.]

Heaven therefore deserves praise, being distinguished and filled with so great an adornment, and preserving such movements and courses with incredible constancy and variety that it regulates and completes the year between winter and summer heat through the tempered seasons of autumn and spring. So too the earth, overshadowed by the natures above, whether it embraces within itself or receives seeds in its bosom, contains, nourishes, and makes them fruitful, and brings each kind to firmness and completion in usefulness and maturity according to its own nature.

[Note: The variant is “whether it embraces within itself or receives [the seeds].” “Use and maturity” is the reading. The Reg. manuscript’s omission of *ac* suggests *usui*, “for use,” rather than *usu*, “by use.” *Consolidet* means “bring to firmness or completion,” as in Psalm 91, no. 2.]

The sea too deserves praise: it is sustained and remains alive in a manner like our own life, now drawing breath and now giving it back; it regulates its motion in such variety by the laws of lunar increase and decrease; and by the barrier of its own boundless depth it surpasses human comprehension, so that we cannot apprehend by searching thought either what is outside it or what is within it.

Yet amid such great and admirable powers of things and natures, shall heaven, earth, and sea praise God because Zion has been saved and the cities of Judea are to be built? These are surely human and transient works, destined to be dissolved by time itself and old age. If their having been built is worthy of praise because they exist, would their being preserved so as not to be destroyed not contribute still more to praise?

30. All things are not summoned to praise God for earthly Zion or cities. — Therefore these greatest and most excellent natures of all things—or rather, the natures by which all things are contained and nourished—the sea, earth, and heaven, are not summoned to praise works that are nearly empty and trivial because Zion has been saved and Judea’s cities built: cities which, after the victory of the Babylonians and Antiochus, the war of the Roman ruler would also consume.

Further, ordinary knowledge and reason condemn this poor and impious interpretation. For the prophetic discourse declares that the cities of Judea are built in order that they may dwell in the Zion which has been saved. What intelligible meaning can this have according to human constructions and city-buildings? There is no praise in building things that will afterward be destroyed; nor does reason and nature permit cities to be built in order that they—the cities themselves—may inhabit a city.

31. Zion as contemplation. Zion as the glorious body of Christ. — But there is indeed praise worthy of God, to be offered by the confession of heaven, earth, and sea: that the daughter Zion, who was brought into Jerusalem with so great a company going before and following her, has been saved through God. The angels desire to look into her; the whole creation, groaning and suffering, looks toward her; in her we contemplate the glory and praise of our eternity; in her the built cities of the churches shall remain.

For Zion, though it is a little hill joined to the Temple which was in Jerusalem, is nevertheless called, by interpretation from Hebrew into Latin and Greek speech, “contemplation” (*speculatio*). In this body of the Lord, therefore, which rose from the dead, which sat down at the right hand of Power, which is in the glory of God the Father, we contemplate our hope and life.

[Note: The Reg. manuscript reads “which rose from the dead, which ….” One manuscript reads *aedificaturum*, “about to build”; another, *aedificatarum*, “of those built.”]

And because all creation itself, to be liberated into the same state, awaits the revelation of our glory in him, it praises the salvation of this Zion under the signification of heaven, earth, and sea: because all things in heaven and on earth have been pacified and reconciled to God through her (Col. 1:20), and because sin, death, and corruption have been swallowed up and consumed by life and immortality into the glory of resurrection, whose hope we contemplate in him risen from the dead. For if there is great joy among the angels in heaven over the repentance of one sinner, how much greater is the joy in the reconciliation of the whole world? (Luke 15:7).

32. The cities of Judea are the Church, not the Synagogue. — Since the Psalm is “for the end, for those who shall be changed,” the cities of Judea also are praised as to be built so that they may dwell in Zion. Who can doubt that cities themselves are gatherings of human beings? It is known that the Church is formed from an assembly of peoples.

[Note: The note supplies “of the people.”]

Therefore our dwelling is fulfilled in this Zion, which contains within itself even that city of the firstborn enrolled in heaven; we remain both the seed of Abraham and the seed of Judah. For it is not he who is a Jew in the flesh, but he who is such in the spirit (Rom. 2:28).

[Note: The Reg. and Mic. manuscripts and one Vatican manuscript read *qui in occulto Judaeus*, “who is a Jew inwardly.” Perhaps: *an qui in oculo Judaeus?*, “or who is a Jew in the eye”? The other Vatican manuscript reads *qui in manifesto Judaeus: sed qui in occulto*, “who is a Jew outwardly; but he who is inwardly.”]

Therefore, in these assemblies of ours, we too are cities of Judea.

33. — And lest impious Israel should claim for itself the glory of the city of Judea because it is seed of God’s servants according to the flesh, he shows that its inheritance and its dwelling in Zion belong to those who love the Lord’s name. Thus election is by devotion rather than descent, because the love of God which is in Christ surpasses all things. Our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, asks Peter nothing else than whether he loves him (John 21:15). He is blessed unto all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: The omitted words are: “which is in Christ, and is in Peter, and [Christ] asks Peter.” Although the editors do not venture to put these words into the text, they judge them genuine: Hilary commends Peter’s love, upon whom the Church was founded, in more than one place; see chapter 30 on Matthew and *On the Trinity* X.27, etc.]

## Psalm LXIX

[Note: “For the end, for remembrance”: εἰς ἀνάμνησιν, “for remembrance.”]

For the end. A Psalm of David for remembrance, because the Lord has saved me.

> O Lord God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to help me.  
> Let those who seek my life be confounded and ashamed.  
> Let those who wish—or, according to Hilary, devise—evils against me be turned back and blush.  
> Let those who say to me, “Well done! Well done!” be turned back at once, blushing.  
> Let all who seek you, O Lord—“O Lord” is absent below—exult and rejoice in you; and let those who love your salvation always say, “May the Lord be magnified.”  
> But I am needy and poor: O God, help me—or, according to Hilary, “helps me.”  
> Be my helper and deliverer, O Lord; do not delay. (Hilary’s reading: “You, O Lord, are my helper and deliverer; do not delay.”)

## Commentary on the Psalm
[Col. 0490B] 1. For whom the prayer of remembrance is made. What is sought in this psalm. — V. 1. This is another psalm “for remembrance”; for Psalm thirty-seven bears the same superscription. From the very meaning of this word and its ordinary use we are taught what is to be understood as prescribed by “for remembrance.” For a prayer of remembrance befits one who fears that he may fall into the forgetfulness of him from whom he seeks either aid or pardon [Note: [Col. 0489D] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have: “expects.”]; and who desires either that remembrance of himself may be made unto salvation, or remembrance of those unto punishment who are always hostile to him. And indeed, in the earlier psalm bearing this superscription, pardon and salvation were discussed; that psalm consists throughout in the person of the Lord suffering for us and bearing our sins [Note: [Col. 0489D] Namely, Psalm thirty-seven, which, as was said shortly before [Col. 0490D], has the same superscription, “for remembrance”; and to which what follows also applies, so that it is wholly in the person of the Lord suffering for us and bearing our sins.]. But in this psalm the necessity of seeking pardon has not been retained, because the psalm immediately preceding and adjoining this one has already concluded in praise of Zion saved and of the cities of Judah rebuilt. Yet here there is remembrance: vengeance upon the ungodly and recompense for the saints. And because the psalm “unto the end” concerns not David himself, but David as prefiguring another, it will, in accordance with the explanation previously given from the propriety of the name, be interpreted in the person of the Lord, as the psalm’s conclusion itself will show.

2. That Christ prays in it. — V. 2. “O Lord God, attend to my help.” This is the utterance of a devout confession, hoping for help from the Lord and God; but the wording here signifies more than is customary in petitions that hope for aid. For one who has been set as help over the mighty may seem now to pray that attention be directed to the help in which he has been placed [Note: [Col. 0490D] We have deleted the particle *ut* (“that”), which is superfluous here in the common printed texts, on the authority of the manuscripts.]. And who this is is not doubtful from the psalm in which it is written: “I have set help upon one that is mighty, and have exalted one chosen from my people. I have found David my servant” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 20). And lest anything might be referred to that David, son of Jesse, he added: “And I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth” (ibid., 28). And lest his being firstborn might be taken to mean the first beginnings of the kingdom granted him by God, he showed that this belongs properly to the Lord Jesus Christ alone, saying: “And his throne shall be as the sun before me, and as the moon shall remain perfect for ever, and as a faithful witness in heaven” (ibid., 38).

3. The punishment of Christ’s adversaries. — Therefore, he who has been set as help over the mighty [Note: [Col. 0491D] Thus, with the royal manuscript, the old editions. But the Paris edition has: “over the mighty.”], and who prays that attention be directed to his help, demands punishment upon those who oppose him, saying, VV. 3–4: “Let them be confounded and ashamed that seek my soul; let them be turned backward and blush that devise evil against me. Let them be turned back immediately, blushing, that say to me, ‘Aha, aha!’” Divine speech must be weighed according to the words of our own language and speech. Shame and confusion arise from disgrace; turning away arises from rejection; but return is to no places more truly than to those from which departure has occurred. Those therefore who seek the soul of this Holy One, who prays that attention be directed to his help, shall first be confounded; afterward they shall be turned away; and then they shall be turned away not to other places [Note: [Col. 0491D] The printed editions, except the Paris edition, read “but to the same places.” The meaning of “not to other places” is explained below: their flesh will not be changed, nor will they themselves pass into heaven, but they will return to the earth—indeed, to the lowest parts of the earth.], but backward. And the order of the words is also the order of events. For, in seeking his soul, they will be confounded when, having killed him, they learn that he lives; because he is Lord of life and resurrection. Thereafter they will be turned away, lest they meet Christ together with the saints who are caught up in the clouds to meet him [Note: [Col. 0491D] Paris edition: “caught up”—incorrectly.] (I Cor. XV, 5). Finally, they will be turned back, not elsewhere but backward. For, rising from the dead, they will again return to the lowest parts of the earth, from which they emerged, for the judgment of punishment and vengeance [Note: [Col. 0491D] Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius: “they will not go to other places. For the ungodly, rising from the dead, will again be cast down to the lowest parts of the earth, whence they had emerged,” with the word “they will return” afterward omitted. Paris: “rising not to any place other than backward, and, by the judgment of vengeance, to the lowest parts of the earth,” etc. We restore this passage with the aid of the Vatican and royal manuscripts.]. For every flesh will rise, but not every flesh will be changed (I Cor. XV, 51); and it is appointed that each shall receive in the body, whether good or evil, according to what he has done. Therefore those who seek the soul of the righteous [Note: [Col. 0491C] “Of the righteous” is absent.] and devise evil [Note: [Col. 0492D] “Of the righteous” is absent from the royal manuscript. Then Paris has: “and devising evil”; these words are lacking in the other editions.], and say “Aha, aha!”, shall be confounded, turned away, and returned: confounded in their resurrection, rejected from the encounter, recalled to the lower world. “Aha, aha!” is the cry of mockers [Note: [Col. 0492D] In Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius the reading is: “it is certain that they said ‘Aha!’ to the righteous one, who said, ‘He saved others,’ etc.”—a reading at once mutilated and interpolated.], namely of those who said: “He saved others; himself he cannot save” (Mark XV, 31).

4. The reward of those who seek God. God lacks nothing. How he is magnified by us. — But after this prayer concerning the ungodly, since this was a psalm for remembrance, prayer had also to be made for the hopes of the saints. For it follows, V. 5: “Let all who seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee, and let those who love thy salvation always say, ‘Let the Lord be magnified.’” As confusion and shame belong to those who seek the soul of the righteous, so exultation and gladness belong to those who seek God; because, according to the prophet, some shall rise unto confusion and others unto gladness (Dan. XII, 2). And as those who devise evil and say “Aha, aha!” shall be turned back, blushing [Note: [Col. 0491C] “Let them be turned away.”], so those who love God’s salvation advance to the confession of God’s magnificence: so that, from the grace of exultation granted them by God [Note: [Col. 0491C] “By God indulgent toward them.”], their confession of praise may increase.

For God, who is unchanging and eternal, has no need of anything [Note: [Col. 0491C] Our very ancient book confirms the common text, as does the very context of the discourse. In the preceding passage: “For God who is eternal has no need of anything.”], nor is there anything among the natures of things or the opinions of minds which he awaits [Note: [Col. 0492D] In the common texts: “God, who is the same and eternal, has need of something.”]. For whatever is changeable through increase is often changed through loss. But God, who is himself the origin and cause of beings that come to be, and is self-sufficient for the nature of eternal blessedness, leaves nothing outside himself which he lacks, so that he need seek it from elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0492D] In the Tours manuscript: “nor does he leave anything which he seeks from elsewhere.”]. Yet he is magnified with us through the increase of his benefits, when his magnificence is augmented by our awareness and joyful enjoyment of his gifts, and by the praise of gratitude that must be rendered. Therefore, whenever we say, “Let the Lord be magnified,” we either express prayers that a gift may be desired from God for us, or make confession of a gift received and obtained; and his magnificence comes to be praised with us through the increase of our blessings.

5. That the psalm applies to Christ, not David. — But a psalm which is “for remembrance unto the end” ought to be concluded with an end worthy of that remembrance itself. For it follows, V. 6: “But I am needy and poor: O God, help me [Note: [Col. 0492C] “God helps me.”] [Note: [Col. 0492D] The royal manuscript and the older Paris editions read, “God helps me,” in disagreement with the Vulgate and Greek text.]. Thou art my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; do not delay.” A profession of poverty and want suits neither royal dignity nor the wealth of a kingdom; but it is the voice [Note: [Col. 0492C] “It is his voice” is absent from the manuscript.] of him [Note: [Col. 0492D] “It is his voice” is absent from the royal manuscript.] who made himself poor that we might become rich (II Cor. VIII, 9), and who had not even a house for the paschal supper except one sought out and belonging to another. He therefore asks to be helped [Note: [Col. 0493D] Paris: “he therefore opposes himself”—an error. In the other editions: “therefore help for us”—a gloss.]. For in the form of a servant he became obedient even to the death of the cross. He also prays for swift aid so that he may be delivered, lest there be any delay in remembrance [Note: [Col. 0493D] Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius: “in which there may be no slowness of delay”; the manuscripts correct this.]: he who, unable to endure even those delays of the Passion, said to the traitor, “What thou doest, do quickly” (John XIII, 26), while the Lord Jesus Christ hastens, by the power of the ripened resurrection, to deliver in himself the weakness of the flesh which he had assumed [Note: [Col. 0493D] The printed editions, except Paris, have “to remember” in place of “while being delivered,” and “of the Father’s divinity” in place of “of the ripened resurrection.” In these and the preceding passages the editor seems to have supplied missing letters and words as best he could. We have substituted the true readings from the manuscripts, now adding for the first time from the Vatican manuscript the conclusion: “our Lord,” etc.], he who is blessed for ever. Amen.

[PSALM XCI.]

TRACTATE ON THE TITLE OF PSALM XCI

*A Psalm of a Song for the Sabbath Day.*

Brought forth from the Vatican Library, where it had lain hidden until now, from the very manuscript which supplied the preceding tractate on the title of Psalm IX and provided material for restoring the exposition of the psalm. The author may be recognized even from the language of this work. For whom other than Hilary do such expressions bring to mind: “when,” “thereafter,” “concorporate,” “co-heirs,” and “co-participants,” “kind,” “mystery,” “increase,” “subsists and remains,” “author,” “granted eternity,” and so forth? Add to this that, as in Psalm LXVII, no. 2, souls are said to have been poured forth from the treasures of God’s power, so here, no. 4, God is asserted to have brought forth each individual thing from the treasures stored up in himself, according to the decision of his eternal power. We shall indicate in notes other such passages agreeing with the other tractates. Moreover, in no. 2, by precisely the method he regularly employs elsewhere, he observes that the letter of the psalm does not cohere with itself, so that we may be warned to seek its spiritual meaning. Nor does he here omit what is especially characteristic of him: whenever the subject of the Sabbath occurs, he expands at length in order to maintain the single and identical work of Father and Son. Moved by these and other considerations, we judge it wrong to deny this tractate a place among the genuine works, although we suspect that the copyist—who elsewhere also allowed himself to omit or alter certain things—did not refrain from doing so here either. Why should we not grieve that, through his negligence, the explanation of the whole psalm, promised at the end, has been taken from us? Therefore, if this tractate seems to anyone less polished than the others, that may be attributed either to the copyist’s carelessness, or it may be supposed to have reached us as Hilary delivered it extemporaneously from the chair, rather than as he issued it, polished in a more secluded study.

[Col. 0493D] 1. The Law was beneficial through faith rather than through its effect. — “It is good to confess to the Lord, and to sing to thy name, O Most High,” and the rest. After the times of the Law and the knowledge of truth, it is fitting to behold the body itself rather than the shadow of the body. For the Law contains an image of those things which were to be fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ. It was not truth itself, but meditation upon truth in it, useful through faith [Note: [Col. 0493D] “And to them by faith.”] rather than through effect, by imitation rather than by kind [Note: [Col. 0493D] We think this should be read thus, since the manuscript has “and to them by faith”; that faith supplied to the Law what it lacked is taught in Psalm LIII, no. 3.]. For the things commanded to be observed were useful not by the power of their own accomplishment, but salutary through the faith of those who observed them: such as the various sacrifices, the rites of whole burnt-offerings, the observance of circumcision, and Sabbath rest. For all these things involved guilt if omitted [Note: [Col. 0494D] “For whoever withdrew from sacrifice thereby made himself liable to the curse,” he says in Psalm LIII, no. 13, where he proves that observance of the Law was not voluntary—that is, not so free that it could be omitted without guilt.], and were beneficial when performed in faith in things to come, as the blessed Apostle says: “But before faith came, we were kept shut up under the Law unto the faith which was beginning to be revealed. Therefore the Law became our tutor unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But when faith came, we are no longer under a tutor; for ye are all sons of faith” (Gal. III, 23 ff.).

Therefore, whenever anything from the Law is reread, the pattern of future things is to be seen in the performance of the present commandments. It would indeed have been fitting to give an explanation of each of the matters previously gathered together, so that, in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching, all might be understood to have been beneficial through faith in future things rather than through the power of their own accomplishment. Yet, lest everything assembled into one heap bring to its hearers not so much knowledge as burden, let us reconsider one part of the foregoing—namely, the part required by the present subject, the Sabbath day—because the psalm is so entitled, “A Psalm of a Song for the Sabbath Day.” Thus, when by the authority of the heavenly Scriptures we have learned what meaning is contained in Sabbath rest, we may perceive a corresponding efficacy in the other things contained in the Law.

2. The Jewish Sabbath. Another Sabbath is sung in the psalms. — Many commands, indeed, have been given concerning rest on this day. For on it the Lord rested after the completed perfection of this world [Note: [Col. 0494D] Here “solidity” signifies completeness, indicating a world perfected in all its measures; in this sense we have in Psalm LXVIII, no. 29, that the earth receives seeds into its bosom and brings them to maturity.]: for it is written, “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works which he had begun to make” (Gen. II, 2). And again, this same day is sanctified in the Law, so that every work is forbidden, as is written in Exodus: “Keep in mind the day of the Sabbaths, to sanctify it. Six days shalt thou labour and do all thy works; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord thy God: thou shalt not do any work on that day” (Exod. XX, 8 ff.) [Note: [Col. 0493D] “Keep in mind.” Then “Sabbaths,” a reading recommended by the Greek text and by the context itself.].

Thus on the Sabbath there are both God’s rest and human leisure. But how will this benefit the psalm, in which God’s handiwork is joy, his thoughts are deep, the sinner is to spring up like grass, and the righteous is to flourish like a palm tree and multiply like a cedar? No rest of the seventh day, no leisure from human works, is sung here. Therefore, since the psalm contains nothing about the rest of this Sabbath, the character of the rest and Sabbath prescribed in the Law must be sought in the psalms. We read, accordingly, that it is said of the ungodly: “As I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest” (Ps. XCIV, 11). God confirms by the sanctity of an oath that they shall not enter his rest. This does not, I think, signify the rest of this Sabbath, on which he is written to have rested after the building of the world. For all Jews enter into the solemnity and joy of this day, glorying in it; and necessarily many among them conduct their lives in sins. They honor this day as a certain testimony of God’s favor toward them. If, therefore, this is the day of God’s rest—said with due pardon—then God is already false, since those rebellious against him and parricidal toward the Son obtain the rest of this day.

3. God does not cease to work. — Further, since all persons without any exception are commanded to do no work at all but to rest in leisure, how again does the Lord set aside the Sabbath, saying: “Do ye not know that the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt?” Therefore this is not Sabbath rest, nor is this its leisure, since those who do not rest on the Sabbath are cursed (Exod. XXXI, 14) [Note: [Col. 0495D] It has been impossible to supply the gap, for in our manuscript too an empty space of four lines intervenes. Opposite it an ancient hand wrote: “Here something is missing which should be added.”] . . . [Col. 0495C] . . . receiving it under the law of permanence. If the sun and the other heavenly signs perform their courses and receive from him the capacity to remain in that in which they are, having been arranged by him for these courses and these offices; if the earth brings forth its fruits, daily receiving the material of fruitfulness through which a certain productive nature is subject to it according to the succession of seasons; if daily the beginnings of souls and the formation of bodies proceed through the hidden and unknown working of divine power—and it is a great gift to perceive the benefits of so great a bestowal, though their establishment remains unknown—yet, although these are God’s works, there is no labor in them. And though they have from their author and giver [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Ruler.”] the fact that they are such as they are, they nevertheless do not weary him from whom they originated and through whom they are daily such as they are.

4. That Christ works daily, and the Father in Christ. — These are indeed great works of God: to hold the heaven together, to give light through the sun with the other stars, to provide the growth of the earth’s sowings, to strengthen the human being, and to restore the soul [Note: [Col. 0496D] We have added the words, “to strengthen the human being, to restore the soul,” which were absent from the earlier edition, from our manuscript. They refer to what he said above: “if daily the beginnings of souls,” etc.]. Yet works far greater than these have been accomplished. Moses recounted only the creations of divisible things to the untaught minds of men, setting forth for the knowledge of God those things which could be understood and seen, so that through the greatness of visible works the power of him who worked might be known, and the Creator’s power might be understood through wonder at creation. But Paul, interpreter of the Testament [Note: [Col. 0496D] “Of the New Testament.”] [Note: [Col. 0495D] In the manuscript a recent hand added “New.” Would it not more correctly have added “Old”? It should not be overlooked that immediately before occurs “through wonder at creation.” Thus in *On the Trinity*, VII.5, Sabellius is said to have acknowledged Christ as God through wonder at his deeds; in VIII.30 the gift of the Spirit is said not to be hidden through wonder at the usefulness granted to each; and finally, in *Against Constantius*, 8, works of wonder are said to be seen before the venerable bones of martyrs.], no longer offering milk but the food of bread, delivered this concerning the Lord: “Who is the image of God, the firstborn of every creature; because in him were established all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers: all things were made in him and through him, and he is before all, and all things subsist in him” (Col. I, 15 ff.).

Thus the teacher of the nations draws us from material which can be known to the understanding of invisible things, and raises us from earthly and lowly matters to the knowledge of principalities, powers, thrones, and dominions. Yet these remain and exist, in heaven and on earth, by the will of God the Father; and although all things are through the Son, all things are from God. For he himself is head and beginning of all things, and all things were created in him, although afterward he brought forth each individual thing from the treasures stored up in himself, according to the decision of his eternal power. But while Christ works in all things, it is nevertheless the work of him who works in Christ; and therefore he says, “My Father works daily, and I work” (John V, 17). For whatever Christ the Son of God does while God the Father remains in him is the work of the Father; and thus all things are daily done through the Son, because the Father works all things in the Son [Note: [Col. 0496C] Perhaps *fiunt* (“are done”) should be added.]. Therefore Christ works daily; and, as I think, the beginnings of souls, the formations of bodies, and the progress and growth of living things show his work.

5. The healing of the paralytic on the Sabbath. — But if we are to understand more fully what God’s working is, and how the Father working works and the Son also works [Note: [Col. 0496C] Perhaps: “with the Father working.”], we must know the occasion of this saying. For among the other healings through which the Lord, in the flesh of a man, taught that he was God, displaying under visible material the power of invisible might, he found a paralytic of thirty-eight years in the pool beside Solomon’s portico, waiting for someone’s help, by whom he might be carried down when the water had been stirred by an angel. This possessed efficacy both in its time and in its human subject: when the spring of the pool had been stirred, whoever first entered the waters escaped every infirmity by which he was afflicted. These events were both useful by their present effects and pictured as a mirror of things to come, since, when the angel called persons to the waters, the removal of every sickness was ready at hand.

When the Lord saw this paralytic on the Sabbath day, he healed him by a word, effecting the sick man’s health by a command. He said therefore to the paralytic: “Rise, take up thy bed, and walk” (John V, 8). Now the paralytic was not only sound but had also become useful for bearing a burden. The Jews accuse the paralytic of violating the Sabbath, saying: “It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for thee to take up thy bed.” He answered them: “He who made me whole, he said to me, ‘Take up thy bed and walk’” (ibid., 10), presenting the same person as the author of his action as of his healing, so that blame for violating the Sabbath might not be thought able to arise from him at whose word the restoration of the human body had taken place. Therefore, because the Lord had healed the paralytic on the Sabbath, where reverence for the deed ought to have followed, there the hatred of all the Jews was stirred. The Lord answered them: “My Father works until now, and I work” (ibid., 17).

6. The equality of Father and Son. — But here a more serious indignation arises regarding the charge, as they thought, of violating the Sabbath [addition: “the accusation”], because he called God his own Father, making himself equal with God. But why do the Jews suffer pain at this? For he did not say in so many words, “God is my Father.” Yet truth exerted force, and reason wrested confession from unwilling men; for his works declared him equal with God. They are angry at what they hear, and are unwilling to endure what they cannot remain ignorant of; and in Christ they hate what they are compelled to understand.

What then is the Father’s work? It is plainly that which the Son does; for he says: “The Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (ibid., 19). He certainly did not deprive himself of power; rather, through obedience he bound himself to the Father’s will. For he does not merely say, “The Son cannot do,” but adds, “anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” Therefore, whatever he does is service [Note: [Col. 0497D] “Everything which he does.”] [Note: [Col. 0497D] The service and ministry of the Son are here taught in the sense in which *On the Trinity*, IV.16 teaches that he accomplishes what the Father commands, namely by reason of the authority by which the Father begets him. Thus Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, 12, represents the Father speaking with the Son and Holy Spirit as though with ministers and assessors, saying, “Let us make man,” etc.; and shortly afterward: “Moreover, although everywhere I maintain one substance in three who cohere together, nevertheless by necessity of meaning I must call him who commands one person and him who performs another.”], because he does nothing of himself but does what he sees; his ministry proceeds from an example, not of work, but of will [Note: [Col. 0497D] That is, he derived the power of accomplishing things not by gradual additions of powers granted for each work, but by knowledge; yet he derived this not from some bodily example of a work, as though the Father did something first and what you see afterward—see *On the Trinity*, VII.16; compare IX.44.], because the Father’s work is in his will. For the Lord says: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI, 38), teaching that he wills nothing other than what he who sent him wills. Therefore the Son beholds the Father’s will as the model of his activity, because all things are formed within the providence of the Father’s thoughts by a certain predestination of future things [Note: [Col. 0497D] Since the word “all” was absent in the earlier edition, the sense was incomplete.]. He beholds it through mutual love and nature; for he says: “The Father loves the Son, and shows him all things which he himself does” (John V, 20). Thus it is accessible to this God, who was himself born from God, to know the Father’s will; and it is gracious in the Father that he has begotten in the Son knowledge of his own will.

7. God works on the Sabbath. — Therefore, in answer to the issue of the Sabbath day, from which hatred had arisen, it was said: “My Father works until now, and I work.” Is there then a work of God on the Sabbath? Certainly there is. For unless there were, heaven would collapse, the sunlight would fail, the earth would not stand, the growth of every fruit would cease, and human life would perish, if through the law of the Sabbath the established activity of all powers [Note: [Col. 0497D] We have added “all” on the authority of our manuscript.] were idle. But there is no rest: the course remains the same, and the functions of all the elements are maintained on the Sabbath just as on the six days (*On the Trinity*, IX.44). Therefore, through these things the Father works at every time; and he works in the Son, because the Son is from him. And he through whom all these things are his work works these things in himself, as one at work [Note: [Col. 0498D] We emend thus, where the manuscript has: “because he works those things in himself, working.”] [Note: [Col. 0497D] “Working.”]; and the work of ministry is referred back to the work of the author. Thus the Son worked in the paralytic, as in the other cases, on the Sabbath; and through the Son the Father’s work is on the Sabbath. Therefore there is no rest in God, since no day is without work for God.

8. God’s rest. — Since, therefore, God’s works exist, we must inquire what his rest is [Note: [Col. 0498D] Either one should read, “his rest must be sought,” or “it must be sought what his rest is.”] [Note: [Col. 0498D] To show how admirably this chapter-manuscript completes the context of Saint Hilary, we give the defective and gaping sentence of the earlier edition: “what his rest is must be sought. Therefore the work of God is the work of Christ, because thus all things,” etc.]. God’s work is the work of Christ; but God’s rest is also Christ God, because all things which are God’s are truly in him, so that the Father rests in these things. For he is perfect from the perfect, because, as the Apostle says, “all things subsist in him” (Col. I, 17). And, as he testified of himself: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave to the Son also to have life in himself” (John V, 26); and again the Apostle says: “For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily” (Col. II, 9). Thus what is in him, or what is in himself, is perfect [Note: [Col. 0498D] Perhaps: “as in himself,” that is, in the Father himself, so that it refers to the preceding words, “As the Father has life in himself,” etc.]; and what subsists and remains no longer needs or expects anything from elsewhere, but [is] through the love and power of the Father [Note: [Col. 0498D] The verb “is” or “subsists” seems to be required here.]. Thus life is in the Son: although he is born from the Father, he nevertheless exists in that life in which the Father also lives.

For in him the principles of all things that were subsequently to be created stood firm; and, beholding all things in him, the Father delighted when all things had been completed through him: he rested in the Son who creates, and rejoiced in those things created which were worthy of the Son’s love. Hence the saying in Proverbs: “When he prepared the heaven, I was there” (Prov. VIII, 27); and: “I was with him, arranging all things” (ibid., 30): “he rejoiced with me when he delighted in the completed work.” This is the rest in which the Father delights, and into which, confirmed by the mystery of the oath, the ungodly shall not enter.

The Lord Jesus Christ is also to be understood as the rest of invisible things—thrones, dominions, principalities, powers. For all these remain incorruptible, unfailing, and perpetual. And therefore rest is to be thought present in them, because, through the eternity granted them, rest is now found in their completed creation.

[Col. 0499B] 9. The rest of the righteous: to whom it is open. — It must indeed be understood how the godly and those subject to God can enter the rest into which the ungodly shall not enter; for the hope denied to the evil must necessarily be reserved for the good. But if Christ is God’s rest, then those who are in Christ shall be in God’s rest. The Apostle declares that he wishes to be in Christ, saying: “But I pursue, if I may apprehend that for which I also have been apprehended” (Phil. III, 12); and again: “I have counted all things loss, and I consider them dung, that I may gain Christ” (ibid., 8); and again: “Blessed be the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ; in whom he chose us before the foundation of the world, that we might be holy and without blemish before him in love; who predestined us beforehand unto adoption through Christ in himself” (Eph. I, 3–5) [Note: [Col. 0499D] “Through Jesus in himself.”].

For the Word became flesh; and whereas we had formerly been alienated and enemies in disposition through evil works, now we have been reconciled in the body of his flesh. Therefore through union with the flesh he assumed, we are in Christ; and this is the mystery of God hidden from ages and generations in God, but now revealed to his saints: that we are co-heirs, concorporate, and co-participants in his promise in Christ. Thus entrance in Christ through union with the flesh lies open to all [Note: [Col. 0499D] Similar statements occur in the tractate on Psalm LI, no. 17: “It lies open to all to become partakers of the body and kingdom of God, because the Word became flesh,” etc.], if they put off the old human being, fasten it to his cross, and, from the things they previously did, are buried with him in his baptism unto life; and if, in order to enter into fellowship with Christ’s flesh, they crucify the flesh with its vices and desires. For he will conform bodies of this kind in the transformation of his own body, and will transfer their lowliness into the glory of his flesh: those who, crushing every sting of desire and washing away the stains of pleasures through the mystery of the new birth, remember that they do not possess their own flesh, but Christ’s.

[Col. 500A] 10. What must be prepared beforehand. — This is the perfect Sabbath, this the true rest, for which, after the manner of the worldly Sabbath, we are commanded to prepare on the preceding day all the necessities of life. For the Jews, according to the commandment of the Law, prepare on the day before the Sabbath everything needed for the Sabbath (Exod. 16:23); [Note: [Col. 0500D] It would be more natural here to place beforehand: “not understanding that in this a shadow of the truth to come is shown”; and then: “so food and drink too must be provided beforehand,” etc.] and all food and drink must be procured, prepared, and stored in advance, though they do not understand that in this a shadow of the truth to come is shown. For just as, to secure the Sabbath’s leisure, the duties of the preceding day must be doubled—for care must be taken of what is necessary both for that day itself and for the Sabbath—so, too, for us who await eternal Sabbaths, the things by which we may there live must be prepared amid the occupations of this present life: things necessary now indeed, but destined to purchase Sabbath rest.

Therefore, lest we be excluded from the rest of this Sabbath—that is, [Col. 0500B] as we have shown above, from fellowship with Christ and the angels—nor from the sacrament of God, we must work and earn; and by diligent works beforehand we must prepare the rest of eternity: by vigils of prayer, frequent reading, voluntary fasting, the tranquillity of humility, works of goodness, the brightness of chastity, and the strength of patience. These must be prepared beforehand for the leisure of the eternal Sabbath, so that, when the weakness of our corruptibility has been transformed into heavenly glory, neither the will may desire vice, nor ambition glory, nor pride honour, nor labour leisure, nor the body food, nor the weariness of the day the sleep of the night; but there may be for us eternal wakeful light, [Note: [Col. 0499D] Our manuscript supplied *life*, then “praises,” which is less displeasing than *of praises*, as was formerly read. The preceding words, “the heavenly, satiated word of God,” proceed rather unsuccessfully. Perhaps one should read: “the heavenly satiety of God’s word,” so that it may correspond somewhat better with the other clauses.] life, the common enjoyment of good things, the heavenly, satiated word of God, praises to God, and an eternal hymn with the choirs of angels. [Col. 0500C] This is faith’s reward; this is the glory of bodily resurrection, in which nothing is to be desired because nothing is lacking; nothing is to be coveted through envy, because life is lived in communion; there is neither grief from any weakness nor advancement in age, because endurance is in immortality. Rather, the devil must be burned, every evil destroyed, and the flower of our eternity attained.

For the rest of this Sabbath, therefore, the Son gives praise to God the Father. This is sung at the end in his person; this, as we shall learn from the interpretation of the individual verses, is celebrated when human immortality has been won.

[Note: [Col. 0500D] In the manuscript there is no mention of a treatise on the Psalm or of a Prologue, but only: “The one hundred and eighteenth Psalm begins. Aleph. Alleluia.”]

272. TREATISE ON PSALM 118.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0500D] 1. This Psalm teaches the rudiments of godly life. — Those being prepared for the teaching of rational and perfect wisdom must be taught from the very elements of letters, so that they may attain perfect and true reason as from the beginning of their first instruction. The holy Apostle Paul knew this: that the only true and [Col. 0501A] useful wisdom of teaching is that which begins from the earliest years and from infancy’s very first beginnings. Accordingly, among his great and illustrious praises of faith and zeal, he writes this to Timothy in the second Epistle: “But continue in those things which thou hast learned and believed, knowing [Note: [Col. 0501D] “From whom thou hast learned.” The Alexandrian codex supports this: *pará tínōn émathes* (παρὰ τίνων ἔμαθες).] from whom [Note: [Col. 0501D] The printed editions: “from whom thou hast learned,” contrary to the sacred text and the manuscripts.] thou hast learned them; and because from infancy thou hast known the sacred writings, which can instruct thee unto salvation” (2 Tim. 3:14–15).

This has been said with reference to the present Psalm, in which, since the knowledge of truth was to be set forth for the instruction of human ignorance, the order of teaching has been distributed through the very beginnings of letters and their elements. For according to the Hebrew letters, a separate letter stands at the head of each set of eight verses. The total number of verses is one hundred and seventy-six. For since all Hebrew speech is composed from twenty [Col. 0501B] two letters, and each letter expounds eight verses, this number of verses is completed by multiplication in groups of eight. I therefore think that this was the reason why the order of the whole Psalm runs through letters: so that, just as little children, the unlearned, and those being initiated into reading first learn the elements of letters by which connected words are formed for them, so also human ignorance might be trained in morals, discipline, and knowledge of God through this eightfold number assigned to each letter, as though from the very beginnings of childish instruction.

2. God’s grace is necessary for receiving instruction. — It is arduous and exceedingly difficult for a human being, either by himself or through the teachers of the world, to attain the meaning of the heavenly commandments. Nor does the weakness of our nature admit of being instructed in divine ordinances except through the grace [Col. 0501C] of him [Note: [Col. 0501D] Thus in three manuscripts, more neatly than in the received text: “who has given these things to them.”] who himself has given them. For those who simply read whatever comes into their hands think that there is no difference in words, names, or things. But if even ordinary conversation does not permit us to suppose that different things are not signified under different names, do we believe God’s utterances to be so unskilled and confused that they either lacked words to use [Note: [Col. 0501D] Repeated only in the printed editions.] or did not know the kinds of distinction?

3. Law, commandments, judgments, and the rest are different things. — Many, when they hear “law,” “justification,” “commandments,” “testimonies,” and “judgments”—all of which Moses arranged under the distinct force of each respective kind—suppose them to be one and the same. They do not know that law is one thing, [Col. 0502A] justification another, commandment another, testimony another, judgment another. That they differ and are distinct in many respects is testified to us by the eighteenth Psalm, which contains the proper character both of each designation and of each kind:

“The law of the Lord is undefiled” (Ps. 18:8, etc.), converting souls.  
“The testimony of the Lord is faithful,” instructing little children.  
“The justices of the Lord are right,” making hearts glad.  
“The commandment of the Lord is clear,” enlightening the eyes.  
“The fear of the Lord is holy,” enduring for ever and ever.  
“The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.” [Note: [Col. 0501D] Thus the Vatican and Micy manuscripts, following the Greek *eis to auto* (εἰς τὸ αὐτό). Others, following the Vulgate: “in themselves.”]

There are, therefore, differences in every one of these things; and it belongs to the prudent and intelligent person to discern in what is written where law, commandment, testimony, justifications, and judgments are appointed, lest the weakness of our ignorance, untaught through inexperience, confuse under a notion of sameness those things which prophetic speech has distinguished by the wonderful propriety [Col. 0502B] of each. Accordingly, this Psalm, the greatest and more abundant than all others, distinguishes all these through the individual letters, so that through these elements of words the method and distinction of teaching how to believe, live, and be instructed in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0501D] Two Vatican manuscripts read “in God”; then, with the others, “the method of teaching,” etc. The printed editions: “that the method might be distinctly taught in the doctrine of the Lord.”] might be taught.

4. Bare faith does not suffice, nor natural uprightness. How complete the number eight is. — Many suppose that simplicity of faith can suffice for the perfect hope of eternity, as though innocence according to the judgment of the world had no need of the ordinances [Note: [Col. 0502D] The printed editions: “the pursuit of heavenly teaching,” contrary to the manuscripts.] of heavenly teaching. But because the matter is otherwise, the knowledge of living innocently in God and of remaining religiously in innocence is now expounded with the abundant richness of prophetic speech. For it is difficult for anyone through himself—that is, through the institutions of the world—to attain this knowledge of religious innocence [Col. 0502C] and the true [Note: [Col. 0502D] “Toward the truth.”] practice [Note: [Col. 0502D] In the printed editions, “toward the truth.” Shortly after, *through himself* is absent from the Royal and Saint-Albin of Angers manuscripts.] of a godly and innocent life.

The Apostle also knew that human nature is weak in itself for acquiring this knowledge of how to live. For when he taught concerning the gifts of God’s charisms and endowments, after first placing the word of wisdom, he immediately added the word of knowledge. This is the gift of knowledge which follows wisdom from God, because the use of wisdom is perfected in the use of knowledge.

5. In the present Psalm we also encounter this difficulty: we have received only two Psalms written according to the Hebrew letters, namely the one hundred and tenth and the one hundred and eleventh [Note: [Col. 0502D] The printed editions and two manuscripts read “the one hundred and eleventh and the one hundred and twelfth.” The Micy and Vatican manuscripts more correctly give 110 and 111, two Psalms which among the Hebrews are marked by separate letters of the alphabet for each hemistich, as the common edition of Jerome also observes in his comments on Psalms 110 and 111. His words on Psalm 110 are: “This Psalm is written first according to the order of the letters, although many also think that the twenty-fourth and thirty-sixth are written in Hebrew according to the order of the letters; but in them some letters are either missing or superfluous.” See Ambrose, Prologue on Psalm 118, §3.], such that from the [Col. 0503A] first through the twenty-second Hebrew letter the number of verses corresponded, and each verse began with the initial of its respective letter. In this Psalm, however, each letter occupies eight verses.

But since the Psalm contains every commandment for living, believing, and pleasing God, all the beginnings of the letters are contained in that number which, according to the full and sacred significance of this number, is especially perfect, first [Note: [Col. 0503D] In the Paris edition the word *first* has been deleted, though the other editions and manuscripts oppose this.] of all numbers, by the equality of the parts agreeing within it from every side. For first it is equal in parts through two parts within itself, and then it agrees in four equal parts. Thus [Note: [Col. 0503C] “And equal in parts.”] the virtues of the Psalms which are placed in this number, either singly or multiplied, demonstrate [Note: [Col. 0503D] Thus the Royal and Albinus manuscripts. But in the printed editions *and* occurs in place of *thus*, and shortly after “demonstrate” occurs in place of “may demonstrate.”] that this number has a holy and sacred completeness.

[Col. 0503B] This number is holy even in the Law. For it was commanded that one born should receive the sign of circumcision on the eighth day (Gen. 16:12). This rule was also observed in the circumcision of the Lord; and on this number of days, though he had no need of circumcision, he was presented in the Temple, so that in his body the weakness of human flesh might be cut away (Luke 2:21). This number also purifies every kind of cattle so that they may be accounted worthy of sacrifices, for they are commanded to be offered on the eighth day (Exod. 22:30). And in this number, on the days of the flood, the origin of the human race is chosen anew (1 Pet. 3:20).

Thus the completion of our teaching and instruction is now concluded under the perfection of this complete number through the individual letters. Before it, no offering was clean for God; no one was admitted into the family of the race [Col. 0503C] while circumcision was lacking; and from it the beginning of the generation to be renewed again commenced. [Note: [Col. 0503D] The Micy manuscript, with the first Paris edition, reads “regeneration.”] Therefore these are the verses of the first letter. [Note: [Col. 0503D] In earlier printed editions these words were immediately followed by the first verse only, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way”; and after “seek him” was added “The order of the sayings,” etc., as below, without any heading. We supply the heading from the Royal and Albinus manuscripts, in which neither here nor subsequently is the whole octonary introduced. There is no need to repeat what we said on this in the Preface. We merely inform the reader that we have transferred this first octonary in the Paris edition, which was placed before the preceding Prologue from the Micy manuscript, here as a more suitable location.]

275. FIRST LETTER: ALEPH.

Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are they who search out his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart. For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways. Thou hast commanded that thy commandments be kept exceedingly. Would that my ways might be directed to keep thy justifications. Then they shall not be confounded (Hilary: *I shall not be confounded*) when I shall have looked (or: *I look*) upon all [Col. 0504A] thy commandments. I will praise thee in uprightness of heart, because I have learned thy justice (or: *the judgments of thy justice*). I will keep thy justifications: do not utterly forsake me.

1. What preparation is needed for obtaining light. — Verses 1 and 2: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are they who [Note: [Col. 0503C] “Search”; so also consistently below in §4.] search out his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart.” The order of these statements must not be neglected; unless we understand it carefully, we do not even attain the sequence of the beatitude set forth. For the first saying is not, “Blessed are those who search God’s testimonies,” but, first, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way.” For before entering upon the way of truth, one must first establish one’s character and order it, through the common honourableness of upright conduct, toward the pursuit of innocence; then [Col. 0504B] comes the searching of God’s testimonies, and the approach to investigation with a purged and cleansed mind.

Another prophet too, not forgetful of this order, says: “Sow yourselves in righteousness [Note: [Col. 0504C] “Into righteousness,” then shortly after, “into the fruit”; in Greek, *eis dikaiosynēn* and *eis karpon* (εἰς δικαιοσύνην and εἰς καρπόν).], reap yourselves into the fruit of life, and enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge” (Hos. 10:12). Illumination is not commanded first, but our sowing: so that, when first we have sown ourselves—that is, the practice of our life—in hope of fruits, [Note: [Col. 0504D] Two manuscripts read “we shall have sown.” Shortly afterward, with the same manuscripts, “let us enlighten ourselves” is preferable to the printed editions’ “let us be enlightened.” For the prophet’s words are, “Enlighten yourselves,” not “Be enlightened.”] and then reaped what was sown, we may at last enlighten ourselves with the light of knowledge. Therefore this order must be maintained: sowing, harvest, and illumination. Many of us hurry to be enlightened before sowing and harvesting, whereas sowing and harvest are a certain preparation for receiving light.

2. It is not enough to enter upon the Lord’s way. Christ is the way. — [Col. 0504C] The first beatitude, therefore, is that those who are undefiled in the way are blessed; but not in a chance, uncertain, or wandering way, but in the way in which one walks in the law of the Lord. For many think that they have entered a useful and necessary way, but they will not be undefiled in the way because they do not walk in the law of the Lord.

Yet this way must not only be entered, but also travelled. [Note: [Col. 0504D] Thus the manuscripts, where the printed editions read “completed.” The word “to be entered” denotes the entrance upon the way; “to be travelled” denotes progress and unfailing perseverance upon it.] For no one, while he is on the way, has attained that toward which he tends by the way. Accordingly blessed Paul says: “Not that I have already received anything, or am already made perfect; but I follow after, if I may apprehend that for which I have also been apprehended by Christ” (Phil. 3:12). Therefore he was still travelling; yet travelling [Note: [Col. 0504D] “Yet travelling” is here repeated for the first time on the authority of the Micy and Vatican manuscripts.] while forgetting the things behind [Col. 0505A] and stretching himself toward the things before him.

Thus, blessed is the one who goes along this way, extending himself toward the hope of things to come in forgetfulness of the past. And the Lord teaches what is the way in which every person walking is blessed, saying: “I am the way” (John 14:6). Therefore whoever persists in his commandments is blessed: while he restrains the vices of the flesh, subdues the wantonness of the mind, conquers the hunger of greed, and avoids the glory of earthly honours. Whoever remains in these things is undefiled in the way and walks in the law of the Lord.

3. There is a law of God and a law of sin. — The addition in the phrase “in the law of the Lord” (Rom. 7:23) is not idle. For there is also a law of sin, concerning which the blessed Apostle says: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive [Col. 0505B] [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Royal manuscript reads “leading me captive.” Earlier, the Micy manuscript reads “opposing,” not “warring against.”] into the law of sin.” Therefore, because there was also a law of sin, it is called the law of the Lord. For unless there were an external law as well, prophetic speech would not have spoken of “the law of the Lord” with this qualifying addition.

4. Law in the general sense. — The next verse of the first letter is: “Blessed are they who search out his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart.” In the first verse stands, “Who walk in the law of the Lord”; in the second, “Who search out his testimonies”; in the fourth—for the third gives a supplement to the second—he speaks of commandments: “Thou hast commanded that thy commandments be kept exceedingly”; in the fifth, of justification: “Would that my ways might be directed to keep thy justifications”; in the sixth, again of the effects of the commandments: “I shall not be confounded when I look upon [Note: [Col. 0505D] “All” is absent in one manuscript.] all [Note: [Col. 0505D] The word “all,” lacking in the printed editions, is present in the manuscripts in agreement with Scripture.] thy commandments”; in the seventh, of judgments: [Col. 0505C] “I will praise thee, Lord, in uprightness of heart, because I have learned thy judgments”; and in the eighth [Note: [Col. 0505D] “Of justifications.”] of justification: “I will keep thy justifications [Note: [Col. 0505D] We have deleted “Lord” here on the authority of the manuscripts and Scripture.]; do not utterly forsake me.”

If law is one thing, commandment another, judgment another, justification another, and testimony another, we must ask from him who established and created all these things the grace and gift of understanding. Yet all this is called “law” in a general sense. But among these there is something particular which possesses the proper designation of “law” in itself.

5. The Law is a shadow of things to come. What a commandment is. — What, then, is the Law? Clearly, as the Apostle says, the shadow of things to come. Nowhere is this written of the others: that justification, testimonies, or [Col. 0505D] commandments are a shadow of things to come. It is the Law alone that possesses this distinctive quality. For in many places the Apostle teaches that the Law is not to be treated according to the understanding of the letter, but according to spiritual teaching; its shadow of things to come is to be recognized.

For he says: “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out [Col. 0506A] the grain” (1 Cor. 9:9); and adds, “Is God concerned for oxen? Or was it not spoken and written on our account?” (v. 10). And again: “Have you not heard, you who read the Law, that Abraham had two sons, one by a bondwoman and one by a free woman? But he who was of the bondwoman was born according to the flesh; whereas he who was of the free woman was born according to promise” (Gal. 4:21 ff.). And because the Law was a shadow of things to come, he added: “Which things are allegorized” [Note: [Col. 0505D] The word *allegoroumena* was omitted by Bad., Er., and Lips. In its place the Paris edition had substituted *allegorical*, contrary to the manuscripts.]—for “these are the two Testaments” (v. 24).

Therefore, whatever things contain [Note: [Col. 0506D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “are encompassed by a shadow.”] the shadow of spiritual doctrines [Note: [Col. 0505D] “They encompassed.”] should be called law, because the Law is spiritual and is a shadow of things to come (Rom. 7:14).

6. But the commandment of the Lord is that in which the observance and keeping of precepts is contained; as, “Thou shalt not kill; thou shalt not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:13), and other [Col. 0506B] like commands. Since these are simple and bright, directing us into the true light by their observance, it is said: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18:9). It would not have been suitable to say this of the Law, which is holy through the shadow [Note: [Col. 0506D] “Because through the shadow.”] of things to come [Note: [Col. 0506D] The printed editions have added “is”; corrected from the manuscripts. The reference is evidently to Psalm 18: “The law of the Lord is undefiled,” or holy.] and converts souls through knowledge of the future; whereas the commandment enlightens through its observance.

7. What and how numerous God’s testimonies are. The whole world is full of angels. — Since those who search God’s testimonies are blessed, and since, as we have said, law is one thing, commandment another, testimony another, and the rest likewise, we must learn what these testimonies of God are. The entire book of the Law was given under testimonies. For Moses, when about to hand over the book of the Testament, called heaven and earth as witnesses. [Col. 0506C] Many things have been established as testimonies: Jacob says, “This heap shall be a testimony to you, and this stone shall be a testimony” (Gen. 31:52). And it is written in Joshua: “Take out twelve stones, that these may be a testimony to your children” (Josh. 4:5–6). To the leper who had been healed the Lord also says, “Offer thy gift [Note: [Col. 0506D] “For a testimony.”] as a testimony, which Moses appointed for them.”

The Apostle, saying many things by letter to Timothy, gives charge under witnesses: “In the presence of many witnesses I charge thee, and in the presence of God who quickeneth all things, and of Jesus Christ, and of the elect angels, that thou keep these things” (1 Tim. 5:21). God’s testimonies, therefore, are many and innumerable. Whoever wished to search them out through knowledge of the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, and the Apostles would remain in blessedness; [Col. 0506D] and, rather than living as though in an empty and solitary world, would know that he cannot sin except beneath a witness. For all things are full of divine testimonies; all this apparent emptiness is filled with God’s angels; and there is nothing which this multitude of divine ministries does not inhabit.

[Col. 0507A] 8. Their presence ought to deter us from sins. Angels are witnesses of our will. The devil’s power and malice. — Whoever has gained knowledge of these through instruction knows that he lives among witnesses. Human nature, in the weakness proper to it, is inclined to vices; yet it recoils even from sinning beneath a witness. Common experience itself teaches us this. Who does not fear to steal beneath a witness? Who chooses anything but secrecy for a crime? Who does not seek either solitude or night for adultery? [Note: [Col. 0507D] “And if at times, when minds are already inflamed for crime, it is ready,” then shortly after, “of pleasure.”] And if, when vices have become inflamed, the mind is already ready for crime, [Note: [Col. 0507D] The Paris edition reads: “And if anything is ready to minds already inflamed for crime.” Shortly afterward all manuscripts have *of pleasure*, not *of will*.] nevertheless the encounter with a witness restrains the frenzy of an insane desire; and sudden intervention has sometimes recalled human nature, when it had rushed headlong into wantonness.

If, therefore, fear of intervention delays a crime already purposed in the mind, [Col. 0507B] what ought a Christian do, knowing himself beset on every side by the testimonies of so many spiritual powers—not merely with respect to his deeds, I say, but even with respect to his will alone? When we are stirred by the goads of our weakness toward some intention of turbulent desire, should we not fear the choirs of angels standing around us on every side and the world filled with heavenly ministries? For if the angels of little children daily see our Father who is in heaven (Matt. 18:10), we can fear the testimony of those whom we know both remain with us and daily stand before God.

Indeed, we ought also to fear that devil himself through whom the incentives of our vices are offered, and all his own witnesses. In a moment of time he traverses the whole expanse of this world; [Note: [Col. 0507D] Thus Tertullian, *Apology*, §22: “Every spirit is winged—both angels and demons. Therefore they are everywhere in a moment; the whole world is one place to them. What happens where is as easy for them to know as to report. Swiftness is believed to be divinity.” See *Treatise on Psalm 67*, §24.] he delights that [Col. 0507C] we sin, so that he may glory in the testimony of our sins. For this is his own peculiar cunning: to incite to sin and to accuse those who sin. For it is said: “Dost thou not know [Note: [Col. 0507D] “What the devil is”; shortly after, “were these things.”] that the devil is present [Note: [Col. 0507D] Two manuscripts read “what is the devil”; with them, shortly after, “and because these things were” is preferable to the printed editions’ “and because these are.”], the accuser of your brethren?” (Rev. 12:10).

9. God’s testimonies must be sought with the whole heart. — Since hostile powers were also present among the other witnesses against us, it was fitting for the prophet to speak only of the holy ones when he said, “Blessed are they who search his testimonies”: not, that is, alien testimonies, but those which are God’s. The searching of God’s testimonies must not be negligent; hence it is said: “With their whole heart [Note: [Col. 0508D] “They seek,” with the Greek, *ekzētēsousin* (ἐκζητήσουσιν).] they seek him.” One must not devote oneself to heavenly teaching in part only; God’s testimonies must be sought with the whole heart, so that, because there are other testimonies [Col. 0507D] which are not God’s, we may search those we learn to be God’s without allowing the heart to be diverted to other concerns.

10. Many good ways, and what the one best way is. — Verse 3. The following verse then occurs: “For those who work [Col. 0508A] iniquity have not walked in his ways.” In the first verse “way” is mentioned in the singular; in this third verse, “ways” in the plural. From this we must understand that through many ways one arrives at the one way in which whoever is undefiled is blessed.

Jeremiah likewise speaks of many ways and one way, saying: “Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal ways of the Lord; and seek which is the good way” (Jer. 6:16). Therefore one must stand in many ways and inquire into many; these indeed are many, and are both the Lord’s and eternal; and in them one must discern which is the best way. There are many ways, many commandments of God, and many prophets, through all of whom one proceeds toward the one way; but workers of iniquity have not walked in them. For if they had remained in the Law, they would have reached that best way of the New Testament.

There is a way through Moses, through Joshua, through David, through Isaiah, through Jeremiah, and through the Apostles; and through all these one must arrive [Note: [Col. 0508D] “Arrive.”] at him who said, “I am the way,” and, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

We must understand that something similar is said under the name of the pearl. One must be a merchant of many pearls in order to obtain the one pearl of great price (Matt. 13:45). When pearls are spoken of, it suffices for their honour that they are called pearls; but that one pearl which is found is said to be of great price. So too, when many ways are spoken of prophetically, it is said that they are the Lord’s and eternal; but when among these ways one seeks which is the useful way, the one found is proclaimed best. Therefore, though [Col. 0508C] those ways too are eternal and pearls are honourable in their very name, one must stand in many ways in order to find the good way; and all the pearls must be sold so that, once found, the pearl of great price may be purchased.

11. Verse 4. Then follows this verse: “Thou hast commanded that thy commandments be kept exceedingly.” We have mentioned above that commandments signify one thing and the Law another. And concerning the Law, as I think, the Apostle has borne witness to us that it is a shadow of things to come, in which the form of truth is delineated as a body in a shadow (Col. 2:17). But a commandment is that which must be fulfilled through observance: for example, “Thou shalt not commit adultery; thou shalt not kill” (Exod. 20:13). For it does not contain the form of an image yet to come, but has the present effect of action: “Thou hast commanded that thy commandments be kept exceedingly.”
