[Col. 0508D] Therefore nothing is to be done with a lax mind or carelessly; rather, we ought with concern and anxious attentiveness to carry out the care of God’s commandments, so that we may perform what we do for the progress of our faith, with reverence toward him [Note: [Col. 0507D] Bad. reads “whose.” Then Erasmus added the word “business,” retained in other printed editions, without any manuscript authority.] for whom we do it. Otherwise, if we do anything with slack will and with thought occupied by other matters, the functions of the body will indeed be engaged in doing it, but through negligence we shall not obtain the merit of devotion.

12. God’s justifications are many; their coherence; they are not acquired without grace. — Verse 5. “Would that my ways might be directed to keep thy justifications.” After the keeping of the commandments, we now have also the observance of justifications. And above we have shown what we think commandments are. But justifications are many and diverse, to be observed in the individual kinds of duties. Unless we are directed by God for their keeping, we shall be weak [Note: [Col. 0509D] The Royal codex with Albinus: “we shall be so by nature.” Therefore we must be aided by his grace.] by our nature. Therefore we must be aided by his grace [Col. 0509B] and directed, that we may attain the ordered observance of the justifications commanded.

There is a justification established concerning [Note: [Col. 0509C] “A Hebrew servant.”] a servant; [Note: [Col. 0509D] In the Paris edition “a Hebrew servant”; the word “Hebrew” is superfluous.] one concerning a son, one concerning a father, one concerning brothers, one concerning faithful men, one concerning the rulers of the Church, one concerning angels, and one concerning God and our Lord, the only-begotten Word of God. In each kind and designation, therefore, the appropriate principle of justification must be observed. For unless all these are maintained through the corresponding offices of devout will, [Note: [Col. 0509D] Two manuscripts read: “we shall not hold fast the justification of God.”] we shall not hold fast God’s justification.

A person reverent toward his father, if he hates his son, has lost the measure of justification. One reverent toward a brother, if he hates a servant, [Note: [Col. 0509D] Paris: “has lost the justifications.” Other editions: “has abandoned the order of the aforesaid justification,” which is also found in one Vatican manuscript. We follow the reading which agrees with the Royal and Albinus manuscripts.] has lost the order of God’s justification. One reverent toward the Lord, [Col. 0509C] if he hates a priest, has by no means [Note: [Col. 0509D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “which” in place of “by no means.” Shortly afterward: “will fulfil.”] fulfilled the observance of justification in the worship of God, exercising hatreds within the very ministries of divine justification.

And indeed in the very truth of faith—that is, in the understanding of God the Father and the Lord—through which justification will be most especially proved in us, how great a need we have of God’s grace: that we may think rightly, that from prophetic and evangelical authorities we may hold one and the same understanding, lest our opinion and speech differ in one point or another, [Note: [Col. 0509D] “But toward all”; then, “may we be directed.”] but may be directed toward all [Note: [Col. 0509D] The printed editions read “but all”; and then “may we direct” in place of “may we be directed”: corrected with the aid of the manuscripts.] God’s justifications by an equal and uniform observance in works and teaching.

13. All the commandments must be kept, not merely some. — Verse 6. When we have attained this, then we may say what is contained in the following [Col. 0510A] verse: “Then I shall not be confounded, when I look upon all thy commandments.” For unless we attend to all his commandments and turn aside in various directions, so that some are passed over [Note: [Col. 0509D] Bad., Er., and Lips. read: “and some shall have been passed over.” Paris: “and we shall turn aside, and there shall be,” etc. We restore from the manuscripts *we shall turn aside*, a verb having here the same force as the frequentative of *to turn aside*. Before it the particle *if* is understood: “unless we are attentive, and if we turn aside here and there, there will be,” etc.] while others are observed according to our preference, we shall not retain the order of justification. But if our ways are straight, [Note: [Col. 0510D] Three manuscripts read “unbent by vices.” Perhaps this stands in place of “unbent ways.”] and our keeping is equal and alike in all things, then, confounded by no shame of forgetfulness or negligence, we shall confidently rejoice in the observance of all the commandments.

14. God, the author of an upright heart and of righteousness understood. — VERS. 7 and 8. The verse which follows is: “I will confess to thee in uprightness of heart, because I have learned the judgments of thy righteousness. I will keep thy ordinances.” Every perversity of the soul must therefore be cast off; and confession must be made with a heart made straight and turned aside toward no other direction [Note: [Col. 0510D] The Regius and Albinus manuscripts: “toward no evil direction,” which is quite pleasing.], lest the mind decline into worldly care, lest it wander from those paths of God’s teaching into byways. But the ground of this upright confession is that which is contained in the following verse: “Because I have learned the judgments of thy righteousness.” First, then, he prayed that his own paths might be made straight for keeping the ordinances. Second, he added that he would in no respect be put to shame when he looked to all God’s commandments. Third, too, he promised that he would confess God with an upright heart because he had learned the judgments of His righteousness—rendering praise to God, that is, through the teaching of a heart made straight and of righteousness understood. But this is the fruit of righteousness understood: that God’s ordinances be retained. And therefore he added: “I will keep thy ordinances.” For what fruit is there in having learned God’s judgments unless observance of the ordinances follows our knowledge?

15. God must always be prayed to, lest He abandon us in temptation. — But we must remember that, although knowledge is to be bestowed by God, we must nevertheless always pray that He may favour us in those things which we wish to keep while keeping His ordinances [Note: [Col. 0510D] “That in these things He may then cherish [us].”]: knowing indeed that we are often abandoned by Him for the sake of temptations, so that our faith may be proved by them. Yet, according to the Prophet, we must pray that He not abandon us utterly. For he says: “Do not utterly abandon me.” This is also contained in the order of the Lord’s Prayer, when it is said: “Do not abandon us in a temptation which we cannot bear” (Matt. VI, 13) [Note: [Col. 0510D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead have “into temptation, which we cannot bear.” We are led to believe that these latter words belong to the Lord’s Prayer by Sermon 84 of the Appendix to Augustine, no. 4, and by the work attributed to Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, V.4, from which the said sermon was copied. In both places the same words are cited as from the Lord’s Prayer.] [Note: [Col. 0510D] “Which we cannot bear.”].

The Apostle knows that we are abandoned in order to be tempted; but he also knows that God knows the measure of our weakness, saying: “God is faithful, who will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able” (I Cor. X, 14). When God allowed Job to be tempted, He wrested from the devil’s right the power over his soul, and left him the right to tempt only in accordance with the measure of human weakness [Note: [Col. 0511D] Two manuscripts: “and from the devil’s right,” which may fittingly be referred to “allowing.”]. Therefore, conscious of his weakness, the Prophet prays not to be abandoned greatly: that the Lord may take up his weakness, like Peter’s when he was sinking in the waves [Note: [Col. 0511D] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read “of one sinking.” The reference is to Matt. XIV, 30: “And when he began to sink,” etc.]; so that, although He will leave him to be tempted, He will not leave him utterly and greatly [Note: [Col. 0511D] We add “and greatly” from the manuscripts.], that is, not so as to abandon him to the peril of soul and faith.

## LETTER II. Beth

[Col. 0511B] “Wherewith shall a young man correct (Hilary: *adolescens*, “an adolescent”) his way? By keeping thy words. With my whole heart I have sought thee: do not drive me away from thy commandments. I have hidden thy sayings in my heart, that I may not sin (Hilary: “might sin”) against thee. Blessed art thou, O Lord: teach me thy ordinances. With my lips I shall declare (Hilary: “I have declared”) all the judgments of thy mouth. I have delighted in the way of thy testimonies, as in all riches. I shall exercise myself in thy commandments (Hilary: “I shall be exercised”), and shall consider thy ways. I shall meditate on thy ordinances.”

1. It is best to be imbued with good morals from childhood. The force of habit. — In the second letter of the following eight verses, the Prophet himself set forth the question to which he would respond, saying, VERS. 9: “Wherewith shall a young man correct his way?” [Note: [Col. 0511D] The Regius and Albinus manuscripts, in place of what precedes, contain only: “Letter I ends. Letter II, Beth, begins”; then they proceed: “Wherewith shall a younger man correct his way?” These words, etc.] These words are spoken in the person of one proposing a question. Then there is added, as though the confession of one answering: “By keeping thy words.”

It must be observed, according to the discourse with which we began, that the true and perfect precepts of the fear of God are contained under these elementary letters, by which we are formed, as it were, for the practice of confessing God from the very rudiments of childhood. Therefore the Prophet must be understood not to have spoken idly when he said: “Wherewith shall a young man correct his way?” It is indeed desirable for every age to be transferred from the vices of its body to the pursuit of innocence; for even late amendment is useful, since it brings forgetfulness of vices. But the Prophet, portraying a man pleasing to God, does not wait until, after a long and enduring habit of crimes, he is instructed by God’s teaching and the precepts of fear. Rather, he wishes years unseasoned by sins, and an age still ignorant of crimes, to be imbued not merely at some time with pursuits of innocence, but also with the very habit of adolescence [Note: [Col. 0511D] In the printed editions: “for every age”; then in Bad. and Erasmus, “late indeed”; and in Paris, “cleansing”—against the manuscripts.]. For it is difficult to cease from what is customary; difficult to be withdrawn from what is familiar. Habit has a great bond within itself; and therefore that man will be the best worshipper [Note: [Col. 0511D] “Will be.”] whom not only remission of sins has established as guiltless, but whom that very ignorance of vices has rendered innocent.

2. The privilege of a youth devoted to God. — The prophet Jeremiah knew the blessedness of this age, saying: “It is good,” he says, “for a young man, when he takes away the heavy yoke in his youth; he shall sit alone and keep silence” (Lam. III, 27) [Note: [Col. 0512D] “What is good.”]. He does not wait for the years chilled by old age, nor for the habit of vices, already dead through age. He desires a soldier for a long battle; he desires that servant of Christ whom not even the recollection of former crimes may defile. For in those who have believed already at a more advanced age, there is indeed, through the gift of grace, forgiveness of what is past; but through the nature of conscience there does not cease to be a recollection of deeds performed.

“It is good,” he says, “for a young man to take up the heavy yoke.” This burden years still untrained in obedience bear with difficulty; but tender age does not feel the hardship of a heavy burden, because virtue is growing. But what shall he do once he has taken up the burden in youth? “He shall sit,” he says, “alone and keep silence.” Rare is the person in whom perfection in the fear of God grows together with the increase of years; and therefore he shall sit alone, abandoning the wanton gatherings of adolescence and withdrawing even from the assembly of old men newly become believers, because it does not befit him to say: “Remember not, O Lord, the sins of my youth” (Ps. XXIV, 7) [Note: [Col. 0512D] The printed editions read “because it befits him not to say”; Lipsius and Paris, “because he has discovered that it does not befit him to say.” The manuscripts correct these readings.].

He will also keep silence, deeming silence fitting for faith and youth: not mingled with the tumults of worldly affairs, but silent through modesty, occupied only with knowledge of the divine mysteries [Note: [Col. 0512D] One Vatican manuscript: “divine [mysteries].”], and keeping God’s words by the silent observance of things and deeds.

3. Whether God drives anyone away from His commandments. — The Prophet then returns to his own person, that we may know that he had spoken above concerning himself, saying, VERS. 10: “With my whole heart I have sought thee: do not drive me away from thy commandments.” It does not seem compatible with God’s goodness that He should drive anyone away from His commandments. Yet the addition and force of the words, ordered according to the perfect reasoning of heavenly teaching, contain nothing doubtful or contradictory. Is He, then, who according to the prophet says that He prefers the repentance of sinners to their death (Ezek. XVIII, 23), to be thought to drive anyone away from His commandments? Far be it to think so. Nor is this what the Prophet now means, above all since he has sought God with his whole heart.

4. How David did not mean this. — But the resolution of difficulties must be sought in the very matters from which they seem to arise. For it is easy to know what the Prophet meant. We read in Jeremiah (Jer. XLVIII, 10): “Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently.” We also read written in the Gospels: “For to everyone who has, there shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away” (Matt. XXV, 29). Therefore he who has shall abound; but he who does not have shall lack even that which he has [Note: [Col. 0513D] These words, “but he who does not have shall lack even that which he has,” are absent from the manuscripts, as also from Hincmar, who introduced this passage of Hilary, with praise, in *On Predestination*, ch. 25.].

The Prophet is not liable to the condition of the curse, because he has not done God’s works negligently, seeking Him with his whole heart. Then he confidently asks not to be driven away from God’s commandments, because he seeks Him with his whole heart. For according to the Gospels, to him who has shall be given, and from him who has not even what he has shall be taken away. Therefore God does not take away except from one who does not have [Note: [Col. 0513D] “He takes away”; then, “He drives away.”], just as He does not drive away except the negligent. So full indeed is He of goodness that He rewards the one who has with abundance [Note: [Col. 0513D] Two manuscripts: “may reward.”]; and yet He so does not wish anyone to lack that He takes away from the one who does not have even that which he has.

5. Whom He will drive away. — Therefore He drives away no one except one who resists; He rejects no one except one who is negligent. For the Prophet gave this reason why he prayed that he might not be driven away from God’s commandments: because he had sought God not in part nor carelessly, but with his whole heart. From this we understand that he is driven away from the commandments who, through great neglect, has become unworthy to be admitted; and it is outside the ill-will of the one who excludes when the result proceeds from the fault of one who does not deserve admission.

6. It is sinful to disclose certain secrets of God. — VERS. 11. This is the third verse of the second letter: “I have hidden thy sayings in my heart, that I might not sin against thee.” We recall that a saying similar to this is commonly read where it is said: “It is good to hide the secret of a king.” We also recall that Paul, writing to the Corinthians, still infants in faith, concealed certain sayings of God when he said: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, nor indeed are you yet able” (I Cor. III, 2) [Note: [Col. 0513D] We restore the word “writing” here from the manuscripts.].

We read also in the Gospel (Matt. XIII, 44) that a treasure found in a rich and fruitful field is hidden after the field is bought. We know that pearls are not to be cast before swine (Matt. VII, 6), nor ought what is holy to be given to dogs [Note: [Col. 0513D] “To be given.”]. Therefore we understand that certain things must be held in the secrecy of our heart, which, if disclosed, will incur the guilt of an inexpiable sin. For he says: “I have hidden thy sayings in my heart, that I might not sin against thee”; because, although other sins are committed, according to the difference of their objects, either against ourselves or against others [Note: [Col. 0514D] “Are committed.”] [Note: [Col. 0513D] Thus the manuscripts; but the printed editions read “are practised.”], they then become sins directly against God when things which ought to be concealed in the secrecy of hidden hearts are betrayed to profane knowledge.

7. Knowledge of the ordinances is God’s gift. — But in this fourth verse which follows, the order of teaching must be considered. The first verse dealt with God’s commandments to be kept by the young man [Note: [Col. 0514D] “Was established.”]; the next, because he had sought God with his whole heart, asks not to be driven away from God’s commandments; then, because he had retained within the secrecy of his mind the hidden mysteries of wisdom and God’s secret mysteries. Now, fourthly, he prays that God may show him His ordinances; and he prays after first offering the honour of confession, saying, VERS. 12: “Blessed art thou, O Lord: teach me thy ordinances.”

We have treated some matters concerning the ordinances in an earlier discourse (*On Letter I*, no. 12), and it is superfluous to repeat the same things often. The greatest and chief labour, therefore, is to attain this knowledge of God’s ordinances; and the weakness of human nature attains with difficulty the knowledge of things so many and so great. Therefore he prays to be taught, because it is a gift of divine goodness to regulate the inexperience of the human mind toward an observance of duties appropriate and fitting to each kind.

8. God’s judgments are inexpressible; not the judgments of God’s mouth. — Then follows discourse also concerning God’s judgments, in which he says, VERS. 13: “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of thy mouth.” Great is the difference between things and their names [Note: [Col. 0513D] The printed editions: “and of things named.” One manuscript: “of things declared.” The others: “and of declarations”; before which “so great” is understood.]. First, from youth God’s commandments are kept; then God is sought with the whole heart; next God’s sayings are concealed, and instruction in the ordinances is desired; now judgments are proclaimed.

But perhaps the Prophet will be thought to have contradicted himself and to have forgotten either his own words or those of others. For we read in this book of Psalms: “Thy judgments are like a great deep” (Ps. XXXV, 7). The Apostle Paul says: “The judgments of God are unsearchable” (Rom. XI, 33); and again the prophet: “For thy judgments are great and inexpressible” (Wis. XVII, 1) [Note: [Col. 0514D] Wisdom is seen to be regarded as the work of a prophet. So too it is regarded in Psalm CXXXV, no. 11. It is attributed to Solomon in Psalm CXXVII, no. 8. But before Hilary, Cyprian, at the end of his book *On Mortality*, cited the same book both under Solomon’s name and as an utterance of the Holy Spirit.]. How, then, will the Prophet dare to say: “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of thy mouth”?

But he has now said nothing contrary either to himself or to another prophet of the same Spirit. For he does not say: “With my lips I have declared all thy judgments”; but: “All the judgments of thy mouth.” He knows that there is some difference between the judgments of God and the judgments of God’s mouth. When he says, “Thy judgments are like a great deep,” does he say, “The judgments of thy mouth are like a great deep”? But now he says: “I have announced the judgments of thy mouth.” Therefore those judgments which could be known through the prophets or from God’s words, he did not keep silent about [Note: [Col. 0515D] The printed editions read “those [judgments] [which] the prophet.” The manuscripts’ reading, “and, as it were, also,” is preferable. Ambrose, who elsewhere frequently agrees with Hilary, explains this distinction between the judgments of God and the judgments of His mouth more clearly: “We may regard as God’s judgments those which He has kept hidden from us; but as the judgments of His mouth, those which He has announced and spoken through the mouth of the prophets. For a prophet is understood as the mouth of God,” etc.]. They were proclaimed for this reason: that they might be taught.

9. The security of a good conscience. The Prophet rejoices in spiritual riches. — After the public and steadfast proclamation of the judgments of God’s mouth, there follows, VERS. 14: “I have delighted in the way of thy testimonies, as in all riches.” The Prophet does not fear witnesses to his life, but delights in them; and the awareness of those looking upon and observing him is pleasant to him [Note: [Col. 0515C] “Steadfastness.”]. For the fear of a defiled conscience trembles at every intervention; but where there is the firm confidence of an innocent life, the presence of many witnesses is welcome.

Yet the Prophet is not glad in accordance with the common manner of joy. For he delights “as in all riches” [Note: [Col. 0515D] Here the Regius and Albinus manuscripts add: “There are riches in gold,” omitting the rest.], not merely in riches but in all riches. There are riches in gold, in silver, in money, in garments, in houses, in fields, and in their vines, olive trees, or crops. But the Lord’s Prophet is made perfect by the rich harvest of teachings, and is rich in the resources of legal and prophetic instruction [Note: [Col. 0515D] Two manuscripts: “legal”; then “in all [the riches] of cognition, knowledge, wisdom, and every action of good works,” and “prophetic,” not “of the prophets,” as in the printed editions. Ambrose says the same words: “David therefore delighted in all the riches of cognition, knowledge, wisdom, and every action of good works.”]. Though he lived in an earlier age, he is nevertheless not ignorant of evangelical and apostolic precepts.

For Paul too, speaking to the Corinthians, knows these riches: “I give thanks to my God always for you for the grace of God which was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in all things you have been enriched in him, in all speech and in all knowledge” (I Cor. I, 4) [Note: [Col. 0515D] Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and the final Paris edition: “through the grace of God,” against the manuscripts, two of which add, “which was given to me among you.”]. In these riches, therefore, the Prophet is rich and delights. But he must not be thought to have delighted in comparison with worldly wealth, since he could not be rich in the Lord except through contempt for and poverty in this world.

10. He preserves these exercises. — Having delighted in the ways of God’s testimonies, he ought to perform the work of his delight; and there is no doubt that he does so. For he says, VERS. 15: “I shall exercise myself in thy commandments, and shall consider thy ways.” Exercise and constancy are therefore necessary, so that the practice of necessary things may be retained; for the indolence of human minds is dangerous and burdensome. And lest the habit of idleness creep in, assiduity in exercise must be applied.

But the order of reasoning is here also preserved. For one must first exercise oneself in God’s commandments; then His ways must be considered. Unless the practice of faithful works comes first, knowledge of doctrine will not be attained; we must act faithfully beforehand, that we may attain knowledge. Therefore, according to the earlier exposition (no. 10), we understand the ways to be the Law, the Prophets, all the Gospels, and the Apostles. Exercising himself in God’s commandments, the Prophet considered them in order to know them.

11. Commandments; ordinances; the practice of meditation and exercise. — He concluded the eighth number with this, VERS. 16: “I shall meditate on thy ordinances; I shall not forget thy words.” The Prophet does not depart from the order of perfect teaching [Note: [Col. 0515C] “He departs.”]. He exercises himself in God’s ordinances, concerning which he prayed to be taught, just as he meditates on the commandments. For this is the nature of commandments: they train us toward observance and the work of innocence, as in: “Thou shalt not kill; thou shalt not commit adultery,” and the other like commands. [Note: [Col. 0516D] In the printed editions: “Therefore these are exercised”; what follows does not fit.]

Therefore he exercises himself in these, because in them is the practice of action, strengthening himself through the exercise of present things for things to come. But ordinances are such provisions as this: that a Hebrew boy, a slave for six years, shall thereafter become free in the seventh year; that after six years of produce, a field must be left untilled; and the other things appointed for the observance of ordinances. These contain within themselves a great meditation on future hope through the effect of the present transaction [Note: [Col. 0516D] Thus the manuscripts, more correctly than the printed “affection,” as is clear from the following treatise, no. 21.].

Therefore he meditates on these in order that he may exercise himself in the commandments [Note: [Col. 0516D] The printed editions here read, “in order that he may exercise himself in the commandments,” and at the beginning of this number, “so that he may meditate on the commandments.” In both places we prefer the manuscripts’ reading.], because exercise retains the practice of an established habit, whereas meditation extends itself toward that which it has not yet obtained, so that through meditation it may attain what it seeks. This meditation on the ordinance accomplishes this: that forgetfulness of the words and promises may not creep in [Note: [Col. 0515C] On the authority of our manuscript, supported by another Vatican manuscript, we have added words omitted in the other manuscripts through the customary and almost perpetual scribal error in which, when the same word is repeated, the eyes move to the second occurrence when they ought to return to the first.] [Note: [Col. 0516D] In one Vatican manuscript this is inserted here: “This meditation on the ordinance accomplishes this.”] [Note: [Col. 0516D] In the Regius and Albinus manuscripts this is the conclusion of the present treatise and the beginning of the next: “Beth, Letter II, ends. Gimel, Letter III, begins. ‘Reward thy servant, that I may live’—without ‘and,’ and in agreement with the Greek—‘and keep thy words.’ Those whose conscience of a cleansed heart is not firm,” etc.].

[Note: [Col. 0516C] Letter II ends. Letter III begins, happily.]

## LETTER III. Gimel

“Reward thy servant, and I shall live: and keep thy words” [Note: [Col. 0516C] Both “and” and “that” are absent from the Greek and the Roman Psalter.]. “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of thy law. I am a sojourner upon the earth: do not hide thy commandments from me. My soul has longed to desire thy ordinances (Hilary: ‘that I may desire thy judgments’) at all times. Thou hast rebuked the proud: cursed are they who turn aside from thy commandments. Remove from me reproach and contempt, for I have sought thy testimonies. For princes sat and spoke against me; but thy servant exercised himself in thy ordinances. For thy testimonies are my meditation, and thy ordinances are my consolation (Hilary: ‘my counsels’).”

1. “Reward” is the voice of one who is innocent. — Those whose conscience of a cleansed heart is not firm cannot pray in the Prophet’s words, VERS. 17: “Reward thy servant” [Note: [Col. 0517D] The editions add here, “that I may live,” which is more correctly absent from the manuscripts.]. For if recompense is rendered according to our works as they deserve, we shall remain in the punishments for our sins and offences [Note: [Col. 0517D] The printed editions: “we shall deserve punishments,” omitting above “in,” against the manuscripts.].

Yet it is enough if anyone has even this confidence for rejoicing before the Lord: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities; for as high as heaven is above earth, He has removed our iniquities far from us, because He Himself has known our frame” (Ps. CII, 10) [Note: [Col. 0517C] “He has removed”; then “our frame.”] [Note: [Col. 0517D] Two manuscripts: “He has prolonged,” and then “our frame,” not “our formation.”]. It is a great thing to acknowledge in oneself so great a mercy of God, to know that the habit of crimes is far from oneself, and to have begun to be worthy of God’s mercy [Note: [Col. 0517D] The words “and to be worthy of God’s mercy” are absent from the Regius and Albinus manuscripts.]. But the Prophet here, in whose body God’s dwelling is worthy because, full of the Holy Spirit, he neither thinks nor speaks common or earthly things [Note: [Col. 0517C] “Thinking, he speaks these things.”], has the freedom to pray: “Reward thy servant.”

2. It is not uttered arrogantly by David. — But perhaps it is the audacity of an arrogant man to have desired the merit of recompense without any modest confession, and not to have remembered that he is situated in a body—that is, in a lowly and humble condition. But the Prophet excluded every notion of vanity and self-boasting concerning himself. For when he had said, “Reward,” out of confidence in innocence, he added, “thy servant,” from the duty of servitude and in confession of his condition. Therefore he asks this confidently, remembering that he is God’s servant, not sin’s servant [Note: [Col. 0517C] “Had remembered.”]; for everyone who sins is a slave of sin (John VIII, 34).

3. True life does not belong to this present time. — “That I may live,” he says, “and keep thy words.” “I shall live and keep” does not concern the present time; the meaning of this expression extends into the future [Note: [Col. 0517C] “A future time.”] [Note: [Col. 0517D] The Regius, Micyacensis, and Albinus manuscripts: “of the future.”]. For the Prophet knows when that blessed and true life of the living shall be. For now we remain in the dust of death and in the body of death, from which the Apostle prays to be freed, saying: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII, 24).

Even now we have mingled with us a substance subject to the law of death and sin; and in the dwelling of this frail and infirm flesh we contract the stain of corruption from association with it. Unless the body is glorified into the nature of spirit, true life cannot have its nature within us [Note: [Col. 0517D] That is, after the glorious resurrection, which will come to bodies in such a way that resurrection into the glory of incorruption does not destroy the nature of corruptible bodies by annihilation, but changes it in its condition of quality, as we read in Psalm II, no. 41. From this it is clear that Hilary by no means asserts that through resurrection bodies possess another nature, but only another condition. Nor indeed does he here say, “the body changed,” but “the body glorified into the nature of spirit”; that is, as we have at the end of the following number, after the transformation of resurrection our earthly body has been made of a more glorious nature. Augustine, *Epistle* 148, no. 16, thinks that the body will then be spiritual because of a certain ineffable ease of the spirit. And in *Against Adimantus*, 12.4, he interprets a spiritual body as a body wholly subject to the spirit, without any corruption or death. But Hilary calls the body spiritual rather by comparison with the spiritual and divine nature, because it is to be adorned with incorruption, eternity, and other endowments that belong of themselves to spiritual and divine nature alone.].

Let us hear him who remembers that he dwells in a body of death, saying: “For our life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, our life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with him in glory” (Col. III, 3–4) [Note: [Col. 0518D] The Micyacensis manuscript: “with Christ God.” Then the Regius and Albinus manuscripts, as well as ancient editions: “and we shall also appear with him.”] [Note: [Col. 0518C] “With him”; our manuscript does not contain it.]. Therefore the Prophet prays for this recompense, that he may live; and elsewhere he teaches the time of this future life, where he says: “I shall be pleasing to the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV, 9). He knows that this dwelling of the present world is not the land of the living. He knows that we must still be cleansed according to the prefiguration of the Law. For now we are mingled with what is dead; and in the Law, whoever touches a dead person is unclean (Num. XIX, 11).

4. The Law concerning not touching the dead: how it must be understood. — But far be it that any of these matters in the Law should be understood bodily, as though someone became unclean by touching a dead person. Moses himself, the giver of the Law, carried Joseph’s bones out of Egypt (Exod. XIII, 19) [Note: [Col. 0518C] “He carried”; shortly afterward, “a dead person grasped by the hand.”]; Elisha lay upon a dead man in order to restore him to life (IV Kings IV, 34); the Lord Himself drew dead persons back to life after taking them by the hand (Matt. IX, 25). If contact with a dead person had made one unclean, the Law would never have been violated by such great men, nor by the Lord, who Himself said: “I did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it” (Matt. V, 17).

But because the Law is a shadow of good things to come, it taught us through this prefigured signification that, in this dwelling of an earthly and mortal body, we cannot be clean unless we attain cleansing through the washing of heavenly mercy, after the transformation of resurrection has made our earthly body of a more glorious nature [Note: [Col. 0518D] What follows is so connected with what precedes that it allows no place whatever for suspecting that anything is missing here. Nevertheless, Augustine, citing this passage in *Against Julian*, II.8.26, seems to suggest that it was spoken on the occasion of the Lord’s words, “I give you my peace.” “Hear,” he says, “also the most blessed Hilary, where he places the hope of human perfection. For when he spoke of evangelical peace, where the Lord says, ‘I give you my peace’: ‘Because the Law,’ etc.” In fact, Augustine himself added these words of the Lord in order to set before the eyes the time at which Hilary asserts that human perfection is to be expected. To emphasize this, after quoting Hilary’s words, he added: “You see how the venerable Catholic disputant does not deny our cleansing in this life, and nevertheless hopes for human perfection—that is, the nature of a more perfect cleansing in the final resurrection.”] [Note: [Col. 0519C] Two manuscripts: “through transformation.” We retain “after,” with the other books and the very ancient copies of Augustine.].

5. There are different baptisms. — And perhaps, if anyone supposes that in the sacrament of baptism he has been given that perfect purity of innocence, worthy of heavenly life [Note: [Col. 0519C] The printed editions read “innocence.” We prefer, with the manuscripts, “purity of innocence.” Hilary does not here deny that baptized persons have the innocence which attains heaven, but [denies that they have] that purity which befits heavenly and incorruptible life and requires no further baptisms for its completion, since even after baptism concupiscence remains in us, called the law and source of sin in Psalm LVIII, no. 4.], let him remember that John the Baptist said: “I indeed baptize you in water unto repentance; but he who comes after me is mightier than I; he shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III, 11) [Note: [Col. 0519C] “After me” is absent in the Verona manuscript. Then *baptezat* stands for *baptizabit*, “he shall baptize.”] [Note: [Col. 0519D] “After me” is absent from two manuscripts.]; and let him remember that the Lord Himself, although baptized by John (Luke III, 21), while still in the body said: “I have yet to be baptized with another baptism” (Luke XII, 50) [Note: [Col. 0519C] “To be baptized with another baptism.”].

There is, therefore, so far as one may judge, a cleansing of that perfect purity reserved even after the waters of baptism: one which sanctifies us by the coming of the Holy Spirit; one which refines us in the fire of judgment; one which, through the injury of death, cleanses us from the stain and association of mortality; and one which washes us in the devoted and faithful blood of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0519D] Here one must understand “that cleansing.” Then, in the words “which sanctifies us by the coming of the Holy Spirit,” nothing prevents our understanding the sacrament of Confirmation, which seems again to be indicated in *On Matthew*, ch. XIX, no. 3: “The prompting to forbid children intrudes upon the typical completion to be bestowed by this sacrament upon those initiated by baptism. The Lord says that they ought not to be forbidden, because of such is the kingdom of heaven; for the gift and bestowal of the Holy Spirit, by laying on of hands and prayer, after the work of the Law had ceased, was to be granted to the Gentiles.” Similar are Tertullian’s words in *On Baptism*, ch. 8, where, after discussing the effect of baptism, he immediately adds: “Then the hand is laid on, through blessing invoking and inviting the Holy Spirit.”] [Note: [Col. 0520C] The relative “which,” absent from Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius and replaced by “who” in Paris, is, against our manuscripts, again referred to cleansing. Ambrose, in his third sermon on this Psalm, no. 14, says: “There is also a baptism at the threshold of paradise . . . the flaming sword which God placed [there] teaches that those who desire to return to paradise while retaining some stains are purified by it.” Origen treats the same form of baptism in *Homilies on Luke* 14: “I think that even after resurrection from the dead we need a sacrament which washes and purifies us; for no one can rise without stains.” Hilary’s discourse here on four baptisms besides water-baptism rests upon the two scriptural passages cited above, in which the term “baptism” occurs. The first is: “He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire”; the other: “I have yet to be baptized with another baptism.” He interprets the former both of the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the baptized through laying on of hands and prayer, and of the fire of judgment which burns away the remnants of stains; the latter either of death simply or of martyrdom’s suffering. Hence the reason why he mentions the baptism of the fire of judgment before the baptism of death or suffering is clear. The chronological order would indeed have required otherwise; but what was contained in the cited scriptural passages could not be placed later. There is also an easy reason why he adduces no more examples of things by which sins are washed away: namely, because he found in Scripture no additional instances to which the name “baptism” was applied.]

### 6. The commandments are not perfectly kept here.

And therefore the holy Prophet says that he will live when he lives—that is, that through this shadow of life he will be transferred to that true land of the living. In accordance with this pattern, just as he said, “I shall live,” so also he says implicitly, “I shall keep thy words.” For the present they are kept, according to the Apostle Paul, “in part” and “through a mirror” [Col. 0519C] (1 Cor. 13:9, 12). For there are many scandals of the world [Col. 0520A] which prevent the commandments from being perfectly kept in us. I say nothing of the conditions of our bodies, which for the present compel us to be imperfect, whether through weakness or through the incentives of vices. But when death has been conquered and its sting blunted, and when we shall hear and see face to face, then we shall truly both live and keep the commandments of God.

### 7. The law is shadowed forth: David desires to behold these things.

The order of understanding contained in the first verse is the same in what follows. For he says, verse 18: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of thy law.” He knows that a cloud of obscurity stands in the way of mortal, bodily eyes. He knows that those things which are commanded bodily in the law are a shadow and mirror of things to come. He does indeed read the law; but he desires to behold the wonders of the law [Col. 0520B]. He remembers that the sabbaths are holy; but he longs to be in the rest of the eternal sabbaths. He uses unleavened bread; but he hastens to cast out the leaven of the old nature. He sacrifices the paschal lamb; but he longs to stand beside the Lamb revealed through John (John 1:29). He fulfils the law of the seventh year; but, when seven thousand years have elapsed, he seeks to be free from the world.

> [Note: [Col. 0520C] The law commands that the fiftieth year be observed; he fulfils the law, but seeks the pentecost.]

He fulfils the law of the fiftieth year of Jubilee; but he hastens to obtain the remission and renewal of Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0520D] In the printed editions: “of the pentecost.”], 292. He knows that, by God’s command, altars were established by Moses according to the heavenly pattern, and that Aaron was clothed and adorned with priestly attire; but he hastens to participate in the ministries of the Prince of priests—Christ—in whose pattern these things were done. He prays also to be brought into the holy land, the land flowing [Col. 0521A] with milk and honey, as a pilgrim in relation to this whole world [Note: [Col. 0521D] MS Mic.: “already of the whole.” Two others: “as though of the whole.”]. The Jews indeed perform all these things bodily; but Paul understands them otherwise, saying: “For we know that the law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14). These, therefore, are the wonders of the law which are sketched in shadow before veiled eyes; and the Prophet prays that he may behold them—that, released from his frail and infirm body, he may see those things which are prefigured in heaven as great and wonderful through the bodily observance of the law.

### 8. One must be a pilgrim away from the flesh.

The disposition of the one praying does not change. For after this he says, verse 19: “I am a sojourner in the earth; do not hide thy commandments from me.” A sojourner inhabits land not his own [Note: [Col. 0521C] “But a stranger, not a pilgrim.”], but another’s; nor does a pilgrim expect the fruit of a temporary activity from it [Note: [Col. 0521D] The printed editions: “but a stranger and pilgrim expects the fruit of temporary …,” etc.; corrected with the aid of the manuscripts.]. The Apostle knew the order of this sojourning [Col. 0521B], saying that one must be away as a pilgrim from the body and dwell with Christ (2 Cor. 5:8). The Prophet, therefore, seeing by faith certain images of heavenly modes of life, though he inhabits a body, nevertheless inhabits something not his own, with the eyes of his mind raised toward heaven. He knows that treasures must be laid up in heaven, because where the treasure is, there the heart also will be (Matt. 6:21). He was not a sojourner in his own land in that sense [Note: [Col. 0521D] Printed: “he by his understanding,” etc. Two manuscripts more suitably: “in that sense,” namely the sense just stated. Nor is the reading in two others displeasing: “he, in his own understanding—that is, in his mind—a sojourner in the earth,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0521C] “He in his own understanding.”], who in the Gospel parable builds storehouses large enough for immense crops and exhorts his soul to pleasures because of present abundance—though the soul itself was to be taken away that very night as a fool (Luke 12:18 ff.).

### 9. One commandment is clear; others are hidden.

Therefore, confessing himself to be a sojourner, the Prophet prays that God’s commandments may not be hidden from him. For no one except one who is a pilgrim from his own body [Col. 0521C] is worthy of the knowledge of God’s commandments. Since God’s commandment is “clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18:9), it may now seem absurd that he says, “Do not hide thy commandments from me,” when they have in themselves this nature: that they are clear and enlighten. But carelessness of hearing creates a difficulty of understanding.

> [Note: [Col. 0521D] Thus the manuscripts, more suitably than the printed editions: “a difficulty of the senses.” Then understand there Psalm 18. Ambrose resolves the same question on the same grounds in his Sermon 3 on Psalm 118, no. 39: “If the commandment is clear, how is it hidden, when no one puts a lamp under a bushel? Unless perhaps one commandment is clear, while many commandments are hidden.” Therefore Hilary below, no. 17, testifies that here he has treated of one commandment and of many commandments.]

There the commandment is clear and enlightening; here the commandments are hidden. The clear commandment is that through which we are enlightened to behold the light of the commandments. Through the commandment which is first in the law, by which we are commanded [Col. 0522A] to love God with our whole soul and with all our strength (Deut. 6:5), we are made worthy [Note: [Col. 0521C] “And worthy.”] [Note: [Col. 0521D] In three manuscripts: “and worthy.”] of the illumination of knowledge. And just as we shall pass from glory to glory [Note: [Col. 0521D] Two manuscripts: “we pass”; moreover, the earlier printed editions lack “thus.”], so we shall see light in light, and so through a mirror we shall at some time see the very face itself. For by this commandment of bodily life we are now enlightened through the sacrament of baptism and God’s command; we use light and remain in glory. Again, by this commandment we shall see the commandments [Note: [Col. 0521C] “And the commandments.”] [Note: [Col. 0522D] First Paris edition with MS Mic.: “and the commandments.” Another Vatican manuscript: “and into the commandments.”]; by this, from light we shall see light; by this, from glory we shall be transferred into glory.

### 10. The ministries of angels are diverse.

Moreover, the Prophet knows that there are many commandments of God in heaven; he knows that, through the diversity of ministries, there are diverse observances of commands among angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, powers, and principalities [Col. 0522B]. It is certainly necessary that they differ in offices as they do in names, while nevertheless retaining an unceasing keeping of the commandments through the firmness of their nature. Therefore he prays that the mysteries of the heavenly commandments may be revealed to him, because he knows himself to be a pilgrim in the body of this earth.

### 11. Verse 20. This is the fourth verse of the third letter: “My soul has longed that I might desire thy judgments at all times.”

The speech of this Prophet is not common either with others or with the age; under the signification of familiar words he has raised the meaning of his understanding higher, saying: “My soul has longed [Note: [Col. 0521C] In the preceding passage it was read, “to desire thy justifications” [Col. 0522C]; but, as our book shows that Hilary read, both what precedes demonstrates this and what immediately follows.] that I might desire thy judgments 294 at all times.” For many will think it would have been stated more correctly: “My soul desires thy judgments [Col. 0522C] at all times.” And perhaps some may suppose that this very meaning is contained in these words.

### 12. How dreadful God’s judgments are to humanity.

But the Prophet remembers that to desire God’s judgments is arduous and most perilous for human nature. For since no living person is clean in his sight, how can his judgment be desirable? Or, since we shall render an account of every idle word, shall we long for the day of judgment—

> [Note: [Col. 0522C] “On the day”; then “to be undergone,” not “to be met.”]

—in which that unwearied fire must be undergone by us [Note: [Col. 0552D] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions: “to be met.” This sentence rests on Genesis 3:24. Hence Ambrose, Sermon 20 on this psalm, no. 12: “All who desire to return to paradise must be tested through fire; for it was not written idly that, after Adam and Eve were expelled from the seat of paradise, God placed at the exit of paradise a revolving fiery sword.” Paul’s statement, “The fire shall test what sort each person’s work is” (1 Cor. 3:13), confirms the same point. Yet, although Lactantius, book 7, ch. 21, and Origen, Homily 3 on Psalm 36, believe that all must undergo that fire, they do not think all experience it. In the passage cited, no. 14, Ambrose seems to exempt Christ alone from experiencing the fire. But in no. 12 he in fact exempts John the Evangelist, as also Peter in no. 13; there he declares generally: “Whoever has here the fire of charity cannot there fear the fire of the sword.” Hilary too, in no. 13, sufficiently indicates that there may be an innocence for which judgment may already be desired without fear.]

—and in which those grievous punishments for cleansing the soul from sins must be endured? A sword shall pass through the soul of blessed Mary, in order that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed (Luke 2:35).

> [Note: [Col. 0523C] Printed editions: “has passed through”; manuscripts: “shall pass through.” Hilary refers to Simeon’s saying to Mary, “A sword shall pass through thy soul,” which he understood not of the sword of unbelief, as Origen did in Homily 17 on Luke, but of the flaming sword placed at the entrance of paradise. Nor does this detract in any respect from the Church’s reverent estimation of Mary. For he sufficiently indicates that he considered her the purest and holiest of all, when, from her passage through fire—which he judged to be expressed in Scripture—he declares judgment to be fearful for everyone. Nor does Erasmus’s marginal annotation necessarily follow: “Others think differently, who free her from original sin.” For, as has just been observed, it is one thing to pass through fire, another to suffer something from fire. Hilary says indeed that Mary will pass through it, but does not say that she will suffer. Suffering alone indicates sin, not passage, especially according to the view of Hilary and other Fathers, who believe that heaven is open to no one except through the gate guarded by the flaming sword.]

If that Virgin of God, capable of facing the severity of judgment, is to come to it [Note: [Col. 0524C] Royal manuscript with Albinus: “where,” instead of “if.”], who would dare to desire to be judged by God? Job, who had completed the warfare and victory of all human calamities, who when he was tested said, “The Lord gave, the Lord took away; blessed be his name for ever” (Job 1:21), confessed himself to be ashes and, after hearing God’s voice from the cloud, decreed that he should speak no more (Job 40:1). And who will dare to desire God’s judgments, when so great a prophet could not endure his voice from heaven (Job 42:3, 6), nor could the apostles [Note: [Col. 0524C] The word “standing,” previously omitted, is restored from the manuscripts.] standing on the mountain with the Lord bear it (Matt. 17:6)?

### 13. David desires for himself that innocence by which the judgments become not dreadful.

The Prophet therefore observed the measure of human nature and conscience when he said, “My soul has longed that I might desire thy judgments at all times.” For he does not desire judgment; rather, he longs that he may desire it. The desire to desire, not the desire for judgment, possessed him. He longs to desire, that is, to remain in such great innocence that he may safely, and without the terror of fearing judgment [Note: [Col. 0523C] Restored from our manuscript, as it was read in earlier editions. The latest edition: “without the terror of fearing judgment, he may desire.”], desire it—

> [Note: [Col. 0524D] More simply, the royal and Albinus manuscripts: “not yet desiring the thing itself, but its desire,” etc.]

—not yet desiring the thing itself because of the consciousness of the human condition, 295 but longing for its desire, and longing for it to arise from the consciousness of perfect innocence [Note: [Col. 0523C] “If it should arise from perfect conscience.”] [Note: [Col. 0524D] Printed editions: “if it should arise from the consciousness of the perfect,” etc. We restore “and” for “from,” and “that” for “if,” on the authority of the manuscripts.]. He knows, moreover, that the longing for this desire must be continuous and tireless; and therefore he added, “at all times,” teaching plainly that no leisure [Col. 0523C] ought to be left to us [Note: [Col. 0523C] “Left” for “ought to be.”], in which we are not always held by the eagerness of this desire.

### 14. Pride provokes God’s wrath against us.

Then he says, verse 21: “Thou hast rebuked the proud: cursed are those who turn aside from thy commandments.” O unhappy pride, which disdains to live under heavenly commands, which in the swelling of an unbelieving mind despises divine commandments! There are many crimes of human vices and diverse and innumerable works of sins; yet nothing is more a cause of provoking God’s wrath against us than pride. For he rebuked not the greedy, nor the licentious—though rebuke is surely due to them—but the proud, because many, through pride by which they despise human beings, also scorn obedience to God.

### 15. It renders good works vain.

Let other works of faith be however splendid, and let devotion abide in every keeping of the divine commandments: nevertheless, if pride creeps in, remembrance of what we do rightly will be abolished.

> [Note: [Col. 0524D] Printed editions here and below read “when”; corrected with the aid of the manuscripts.]

With how much labor did that evangelical Pharisee set himself in the way of life, so that he might not be greedy for another’s property [Note: [Col. 0523C] “That he might not be greedy for another’s property.”], might not behave unjustly toward anyone [Col. 0524B], and might not be corrupted by adulteries (Luke 18:11 ff.)! He labored by fasting twice on the sabbath,

> [Note: [Col. 0524C] “And this unhappy, vicious body”; then later, “bestowed,” not “brought in.”]

and through abstinence from food disciplined his own body by the mighty power of great endurance [Note: [Col. 0524D] Thus the three more corrected manuscripts. Printed editions, however: “and this unhappy body of vices” or “vicious body”: wrongly and out of place.]. Then with how much labor, to conquer greed, did he devote the tithe of his possessions to the use of the needy? What is more splendid than these things [Note: [Col. 0524C] “What is more difficult than this matter?”]? What is more difficult than accomplishing them [Note: [Col. 0524D] Printed editions: “than the performance of these works,” contrary to the manuscripts.]? Yet he fell into the snare of pride, saying: “Because I am not like this sinner and publican” (ibid.); and, unhappy through this fault, he fell from great works into guilt [Note: [Col. 0524C] The words “and unhappy through this fault,” as absent from earlier printed editions, are likewise absent from our book.] [Note: [Col. 0524D] The words “and unhappy through this fault” were lacking in earlier printed editions. We restore them from the manuscripts.]. Thus, made insolent through this glorying in his virtues, he departed less justified than the publican.

### 16. Paul, who was delivered from it.

But why speak of the Pharisee? The Apostle, “not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ” [Col. 0524C] (Gal. 1:1), against whom the devil struggled with every art of his power, received an angel of Satan to buffet him (2 Cor. 12:7–8), so that through the unceasing troubles of all his sufferings no occasion for pride might creep in through idleness of time. He himself also, when laying down a certain rule for selecting and appointing a priest, after he had already placed him among the virtues by which he is worthy of a bishop, forbade the selection of a novice lest he become proud, saying: “Not a novice, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. 3:6). That is, lest through the newly acquired grace of regeneration he become insolent, he wishes him first to be tried by much warfare of sufferings; he wishes him to advance through many campaigns of humility and faith. For God does not despise a humbled heart, and a contrite heart is the best sacrifice (Ps. 50:29), because whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted (Luke 14:11).

### 17. Pride despises human things and neglects divine things.

And therefore those who turn aside from thy commandments are cursed, because the proud are rebuked: for through the pride of an insolent mind we both despise human things and neglect divine things [Col. 0525B]. But the force of the word placed here must not be heard carelessly. For it would have been easy to say, “Cursed are those who do not obey thy commandments.” (We have suitably spoken of one commandment and many commandments in the preceding verse, nos. 9 and 10.) But cursed are those who, instructed by this teaching of prophecy, turn aside from God’s commandments; that is, through desire for present vices, they fall away from the hope of eternal commandments. For one who turns aside avoids that in which he is, is led from one direction to another, and departs from the path by a kind of deviation [Note: [Col. 0525D] In the manuscripts: “falls away.”]. Thus even one who turns aside only slightly from God’s commandments is encompassed by the sentence of a curse. We may thereby understand how dangerous a thing it is altogether to be ignorant of those things [Note: [Col. 0525D] Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions: “to be ignorant of all things.”] from which it is cursed to turn aside.

### 18. Sins deserve reproach.

Verse 22. [Col. 0525C] “Take away from me reproach and contempt, because I have sought out thy testimonies.” Sins are worthy of reproach; and therefore sinners shall rise “unto eternal reproach” (Dan. 12:2). That all sins are worthy of reproach we learn in the Gospels, when the Lord began to reproach those cities in which his very many miracles had occurred and which had not repented: Chorazin [Note: [Col. 0525D] “Chorazin and Bethsaida.”] and Bethsaida (Luke 10:15). What began with them must happen to all who are equally guilty of the same crime [Note: [Col. 0525D] Paris edition: “of the crime alike.” Other books better: “equals,” that is, equally guilty.]; and then he will reproach humankind, because it has not repented and has not gone on the evangelical way, with the words contained in the psalm: “What profit is there in my blood, when I go down into corruption?” (Ps. 29:10). For he reproaches the proud and cursed because they judged that there was no benefit to them in the mystery of his blood and death [Note: [Col. 0525D] “Thou wilt cast away thy own,” if the authority of our manuscript is to be trusted.] [Col. 0525D] [Note: [Col. 0525D] “His own” is absent from two manuscripts.], though for our sake he was born, suffered, and died.

### 19. Confession turns it away, provided that God’s testimonies are also sought.

The Prophet also observed the condition of human weakness. He knows that certain things are in us which must be taken away through God’s mercy. He knows that God must be prayed to with such confession of our sins that, although we have things worthy of accusation [Note: [Col. 0525D] Basel, Erasmus, Leipzig, and Vatican manuscripts: “though we have things worthy of accusation.”], we are nevertheless not accused; for the crime must be confessed in order that pardon may be obtained. He knows, moreover, that after accusation the nations are reckoned as contempt—that is, as nothing [Note: [Col. 0525D] Two manuscripts: “to reckon.” The following words, “and all things which are of evil,” are now found neither in Latin nor Greek manuscripts of Isaiah. Yet Ambrose also read them, Sermon 3 on Psalm 118, no. 41, as is clear from note h, which observes that all manuscripts contain: “All things which belong to evil are reckoned as nothing.”]—because it is written: “All nations are nothing, and all things which are of evil are reckoned as nothing” (Isa. 40:17). But following the Prophet’s example, we ought to pray for reproach and contempt to be taken away from us with this hope and confidence: that we add to the words, “Take away from me reproach and contempt,” also the following words: “Because I have sought out thy testimonies.” He seeks God’s testimonies so that he need not be accused; and he prays that reproach and contempt be taken away from him so that he may not abandon shame. He confesses that there is in his nature a cause for accusation and reproach, which he prays may be removed from him; but through devotion to the testimonies he has sought out, he hopes that it will be removed.

### 20. Faith is hated by the rulers of the world.

The Prophet seeks out God’s testimonies not in leisure nor in the arrogance of prosperity, but while many sit against him and many speak against him, saying, verse 23: “For princes sat and slandered me.” He knows that every faith of prophecy is hated by the rulers of this world [Note: [Col. 0526D] Thus the manuscripts, except that one Vatican manuscript has “dangerous” for “hated,” and Mic. has “hidden.” Printed editions: “For he knows that every faith of prophecy is lacking to the rulers of this world.”]; he knows that the Apostles will become hateful to all because of the Christian name. The rulers sit against the Prophet and slander him when they hear him also saying: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; attend to the law of God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:10) [Note: [Col. 0526D] Printed editions read “Isaiah” for “also,” contrary to the manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0526D] “And attend”; then “people,” in accordance with the Greek.]. For by the counsel of such men Isaiah was sawn apart, Jeremiah was shut up in prison, Daniel was cast to lions stirred to savagery by hunger, Zechariah was slain between the temple and altar, and the apostles were beaten, cut to pieces, and crucified: so that the preaching of God might be taken away, the teaching of prophecy restrained, and the way of eternal life blocked. But steadfast faith despised these assemblies of rulers and these utterances of detraction. For it follows: “But thy servant was exercised in thy justifications.” While they make their outcry and prohibit him with every weapon of punishment, the spirit of God perseveres in the exercises of justifications [Note: [Col. 0526D] “Of God” is absent from two manuscripts. Either “servant of God” seems to be the reading, or, with a Vatican manuscript, “the spirit of God.”].

### 21. Meditation and practice of the law are preparation for eternal things.

But, as we have already discussed above (Letter 2, no. 11), the exercise of justifications and meditation upon testimonies [Col. 0527A] are that by which [Note: [Col. 0527D] “Because.”] [Note: [Col. 0527D] In the royal manuscript, “because,” not “by which”: a reading not to be despised, especially if a little earlier “meditation” is understood likewise as “also meditation.” For, as appears literally in the preceding Letter, no. 11, justifications contain in themselves a great meditation upon future hope through the effect of the present activity.]—although the works of the law are performed through bodily acts—by the exercise of justifications and meditation upon testimonies, a certain preparation for eternal goods is acquired through meditation on present things. But he shows whence meditation upon the testimonies arises. For he adds, verse 24: “And thy justifications are my counsels,” confessing that all concern for life and all the varied and diverse movements of his counsels [Note: [Col. 0527D] “Intent dispositions.”] are directed toward the justifications of God in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and honor for ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER IV. Daleth

> [Note: [Col. 0527D] Delth.]

“My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to thy word. I have declared my ways” (Hilary: “I have proclaimed”), [Col. 0527B] “and thou hast heard me; teach me thy justifications. Make me understand the way of thy justifications” (Hilary: “make me understand”), “and I shall be exercised in thy wonders. My soul has slumbered from weariness; strengthen me in thy words. Remove from me the way of iniquity; and have mercy on me in thy law” (Hilary: “and in thy law”). “I have chosen” (Hilary: “loved”) “the way of truth; I have not forgotten thy righteousness” (Hilary: “thy judgments”). “I have clung to thy testimonies, O Lord; do not put me to shame. I have run in the way” (Hilary: “in the way”) “of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart.”

### 1. The fellowship of earthly flesh is burdensome to the Prophet.

A manifold interpretation cannot contain difficulty of expression when, with all obscurity removed, there is a fuller choice of understanding; as we see in the first verse of the fourth letter. For he says, verse 25: “My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to [Col. 0527C] thy word.” This may be understood of persistence in prayer, as though the Prophet, from confession of sins, had prostrated himself upon the ground and clung to the pavement.

> [Note: [Col. 0527D] In two manuscripts: “and be understood also of the manner of his life”; a reading not to be despised.]

But in order to understand something deeper beneath these words, we judge it necessary to examine more carefully the force of the expressions. For he does not say, “I have clung to the pavement,” but, “My soul has clung to the pavement”; and we are instructed to understand that he is here lamenting the fellowship of soul and body. Many things admonish us to regard this interpretation as more probable. For the Apostle called it “the body of our humiliation” (Phil. 3:21); and the Prophet said, “My soul has been humbled into the dust” [Note: [Col. 0527D] “My” is absent from the royal and Albinus manuscripts. Immediately afterward, those manuscripts have “he led me down,” not “thou hast led me down.”] (Ps. 43:25); again he said, “Thou hast led me down into the dust of death” (Ps. 21:16). Therefore, whether because we dwell upon the ground of this earth or because we have been formed and fashioned from earth, the soul, which is of another [Col. 0527D] origin, is thought to have clung to the earthly body. It undertakes a very great struggle: that, although remaining in it, it may tear itself away from its fellowship and use its dwelling as a stranger would [Note: [Col. 0527D] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions: “that it, dwelling monstrously in itself.” The phrase “that it, although remaining,” etc., is expressed in other words in the commentary on Psalm 60, no. 2: while dwelling in flesh, which is earth, it already dwells at the end of flesh, since according to the Apostle, while dwelling in the body it is away as a pilgrim from the body, and while living it no longer lives for itself.].

### 2. He desires a better life.

The Prophet is not ignorant, though earlier in time, of the apostolic saying that those who cling to the Lord are one spirit with him. He also knows that he has proclaimed of himself, “My soul has clung after thee” (Ps. 62:9). Indeed, he reads in the law: “Thou shalt walk after the Lord thy God, and shalt cling to him” (Deut. 13:4). He therefore desires rather to cling to this than to that. But because he remembers that from fellowship with it he has contracted some stain of sin, he prays that through God’s word—even though his soul is mingled with earthly and mortal nature—he himself may be quickened into the life of heavenly life [Note: [Col. 0528D] Erasmus, Leipzig, and Paris: “into the way of life,” corruptly and contrary to the manuscripts. “The life of heavenly life” is the life of those who live in heaven; that their life alone is true life is shown in Letter 3, nos. 3 and 6.]. For he knows that he now clings to the pavement, not that he lives; but according to the word of God, to whom the dead live, he prays to be made alive unto life [Col. 0528B].

### 3. What it is to walk in one’s own ways and in God’s way.

Then follows, verse 26: “I have proclaimed my ways, and thou hast heard me; teach me thy justifications.” Those who live their lives according to bodily pleasures walk in their own ways. But those who, having abandoned every habit of fleshly vices, live in God’s commandments [Note: [Col. 0528D] “Dwell,” for “live.”], no longer journey in their own way but in God’s way. Let us hear this also in the command of Deuteronomy: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord thy God require of thee, except that thou fear the Lord thy God, walk in all his ways, love him, serve the Lord thy God with thy whole heart and with thy whole soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord thy God and his justifications, which I command thee today, that it may be well with thee?” (Deut. 10:12–13) [Col. 0528C]. Therefore, one who clings to God is in God’s way.

### 4. Confession of sins is the way to God’s instruction.

And in what sense should we think the Prophet speaks here when he says, “I have proclaimed my ways, and thou hast heard me; teach me thy justifications”? For if he proclaims his own ways, he must proclaim ways of sin, because whoever is not in God’s way is in the way of sin. But that saying appears to agree with this present statement: “I shall confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord” (Ps. 31:5); and again, “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17). Therefore the proclamation spoken of here is not praise, but confession of his ways—that is, a penitential profession of his sins. And in order that the Prophet might be worthy of the spirit of prophecy, he first confessed his ways, that is, his sins, so that after this proclamation [Col. 0528D] of them he might be capable of the teaching of God’s justifications. Both points are plainly taught. For when he says, “I have proclaimed,” he shows that this confession belongs to past time; when he says, “Teach me,” it is a prayer concerning the future, because one must first confess sins and, when the confession has been completed, learn [Col. 0529A].

### 5. He asks to be taught not the works of the law, but their aim.

But while remaining in the law, the Prophet does not ask to be taught from those things which were then carried out by bodily ministry, but from those things which, through the appearance of present matters, contained the mysteries that were to come. Verse 27: “Make me understand the way of thy justifications, and I shall be exercised in thy wonders.” The present language is seen to distinguish the justifications from their way [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Of them”; afterward, “everything to which,” then “by which one proceeds.”] [Note: [Col. 0529D] We substitute “of them” for “of those,” as the sense requires. Then the printed editions: “everything to which one tends by a way … by which one proceeds.” We prefer the manuscripts.]. And, as is understood from the matter itself, whatever is the object toward which one travels by a way is not the same thing as the way on which one travels. Therefore we must seek the reason why the Prophet [Col. 0529B] prayed that he might be granted understanding of the way of the justifications rather than knowledge of the justifications themselves. For he remembers that all the justifications of the law contain within themselves a shadow of holy justifications: when the Hebrew slave becomes free after six years of service (Exod. 21:2); when the produce of the seventh year is left to the needy and the beasts of the earth (Lev. 25:4); and when, after the fiftieth year, everything returns to the right of the family from which it had departed (ibid., 25:13). And because these things established in the law are the way of those whose pattern is prefigured in them, he prays that, understanding the way of these justifications, he may be exercised in God’s wonders—that is, may be occupied in the works of the law—because the law has been established as a mirror of future goods.

### 6. The Septuagint translation is preferred to divergent translations.

Regarding the following verse, I have learned that many have held diverse opinions because it had not been changed from the Hebrew by the other translators with the same precise sense in which it was written by the Seventy translators. For some, in place of what was said by them—

> [Note: [Col. 0529D] In the Basel edition, after “what was said by them,” there followed immediately, leaving a blank space of one verse, “But for us it is neither safe,” etc., with much omitted. Erasmus afterward inserted into that empty space, on his own initiative, that they rendered ἐνύσταξεν as “has distilled,” and nothing further was subsequently restored. We repair this passage from the royal, Albinus, and Mic. manuscripts, which give the complete reading, although the Greek words are considerably corrupted. Moreover, Ambrose preferred ἔσταξε, “has dripped,” in Sermon 4, no. 15, on Origen’s authority; for, as he adds in no. 16, after diligently examining many translations, Origen adopted “has dripped.” Jerome, however, translated from the Hebrew, “has distilled.”]

—have set down ἐνύσταξεν ἡ ψυχή μου (“my soul has slumbered”) as ἔσταξεν ἡ ψυχή μου (“my soul has dripped”). Some, moreover, translated not ἐνύσταξεν but κατέσταξεν (“my soul has dripped down”). Now ἐνύσταξεν, ἔσταξεν, and κατέσταξεν are understood to have different meanings. But it is neither safe for us to depart from the translation of the Seventy interpreters, nor does the reason and sense of the words fail to show [Note: [Col. 0530D] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions: “and sound reason is, and the sense.”] that the verse has been rightly and plausibly translated. For with them and with us it stands thus, verse 28: “My soul has slumbered from weariness.” The entire preceding [Col. 0529D] and following discourse contains a confession of humility and weakness: the soul has clung to the pavement; the ways of sins are confessed; it prays for understanding of the way of justifications. It consequently follows [Col. 0530A] that he now laments that his soul has slumbered through weariness of its mortal dwelling, since it does not yet understand the way of justifications and still clings to the pavement. Therefore he prays that he may be strengthened in God’s ways, because he slumbers through weariness.

### 7. The meaning of slumbering.

But here the distinction has been preserved: he says that he slumbers, not that he sleeps. For one who sleeps is engaged in the very act of sleep; but one who slumbers slumbers before he sleeps.

> [Note: [Col. 0530D] Paris: “before he languishes in sleep.” Other books: “he slumbers,” etc.; that is, slumber is a kind of prelude to sleep.]

The same distinction is maintained elsewhere when he says: “Behold, he who guards Israel neither sleeps nor slumbers” (Ps. 120:4). And where he says, “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids” (Ps. 131:4), he calls slumber the condition of the eyelids, but sleep that of the eyes, because it is the office of the eyelids to bring about sleep [Col. 0530B] from slumber. Therefore, although the Prophet slumbers, he does not sleep; and so that he may not fall asleep while slumbering, he added: “Strengthen me in thy words.” That is, strengthened by understanding of all the justifications which he mentioned above, he may not only fail to sleep, but may also keep watch without any slumber whatsoever.

8. David is free not from sin, but from the way of sin. He asks for the blessedness promised by the Law.—After this he says, V. 29: “Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me according to Your Law.” It would have been easy to say, “Remove iniquity from me.” Yet, although conscious of his weakness, and remembering that in his body there is a way leading to sin, he is nevertheless, through the fear of God, wholly removed from the commission of sin. He therefore prays that the way of sin—the way by which one is readily led on to sin—may be removed from him: that is, that every desire for bodily pleasures may be taken away, and that no temptation of desire or ignorance may come upon him, by which, as though along a road, one goes toward sin. Nor does he ask God for this alone, but also that He may have mercy on him through His Law.

He receives mercy through the Law in this manner: for, as was shown above, it is written in the Law: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, 302 except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all His ways, love Him, serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord your God and His ordinances, which I command you today, that it may be well with you?” (Deut. 10:12–13). Therefore, since the Law teaches that one must walk in God’s ways, in order that it may hereafter be well with the one who walks in them; and since the Prophet now prays that the ways of injustice may be removed from him and that God may have mercy on him according to the Law, he asks for that which the Law has prescribed: that, walking in God’s ways, he may be placed in blessedness.

[Note: Col. 0530D. The printed editions read “now perhaps the Prophet”; *perhaps* is superfluous and absent from our manuscripts.]

[Col. 0531A] 9. The way of truth: judgment.—Then follows, V. 30: “I have loved the way of truth, and I have not forgotten Your judgments.” Many love a way, but not all love the way of truth. Whoever enters upon the way of pleasures, riches, or honors, and those likewise who are carried hither and thither, uncertain and ungodly, by the teachings of heretics—these are indeed on a way, but they are not on the way of truth. But the Prophet speaks from the Spirit of Him who, after assuming a body, would later say, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).
