And because this is the judgment contained in the Gospels—“For this is the judgment: that whoever believes in Me may have eternal life” (John 3:15, 19)—the Prophet rightly says, “I have loved the way of truth, and I have not forgotten Your judgments.” These things were spoken later for our knowledge; but the Prophet both lives and speaks in them.

[Col. 0531B] 10. By cleaving to God’s testimonies, we are freed from shame.—The discourse coheres with the Prophet’s doctrine and confession. For he says, V. 31: “I have clung to Your testimonies, O Lord; do not put me to shame,” because by clinging to the Lord’s testimonies he has deserved pardon for his old and former sins. For he knows that God has said: “Behold, I will blot out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist” (Isa. 44:22). The Lord is able to remove all those things which are a cause of shame and confusion to us, if we too can say freely, “I have clung to Your testimonies.” For by clinging to them we are freed from the shame of disgraceful matters and former crimes.

[Note: Col. 0531D. “Which in us are matters of shame and confusion.”]

[Note: Col. 0531D. The printed editions read: “which are in us causes of shame and confusion.” The manuscript reading is more elegant.]

11. The steps toward running in God’s way. The narrow way of life.—But everything is brought to its conclusion in its proper order, by its appropriate stages. Above, [Col. 0531C] he said, “Remove from me the way of injustice”; then he added, “I have loved the way of truth”; thirdly comes, “I have clung to Your testimonies”; and now he concludes thus, V. 32: “I ran in the way of Your commandments when You enlarged my heart.” By stages one arrives at this: the way of iniquity is removed, the way of truth is loved, and there is an inseparable fellowship with the testimonies, so that one may run in the way of God’s commandments. But the way which leads to life is both narrow and afflicted: narrow, because one must enter it carefully and cautiously; afflicted, because it is approached through many 303 tribulations and sufferings. Shall the Prophet then be considered presumptuous because he boasts that he runs in this way?

[Note: Col. 0531D. On the authority of the manuscripts we have deleted here “and have mercy on me according to Your Law,” which, as the following context shows, is superfluous.]

12. One cannot run unless God enlarges the heart; who enlarges it.—Yet amid his pursuit of innocence the Prophet remembers that the force of his words must be moderated by a confession of humility. Therefore, after saying, “I ran in the way [Col. 0531D] of Your commandments,” he adds, “when You enlarged my heart.” The heart is enlarged when, through faith, it is opened so as to receive God’s teaching. This too was said of believers: “I will dwell and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:16).

[Col. 0532A] Therefore the heart is enlarged when the mystery of Father and Son abides within it, and when the Holy Spirit delights in it as a capacious dwelling. Solomon too recalls this when he says: “Wisdom is proclaimed at the outlets; in the broad places she speaks freely” (Prov. 1:20). The Latin form of both expressions either brings obscurity upon us or suggests a different interpretation. For what we call “outlets,” Greek, following the Hebrew, has rendered ἐν ἐξόδοις, “at the exits.” Properly, an *exodus* is the place where many narrow paths converge into one open road. What we call “streets,” Greek likewise calls πλατεῖαι (*plateiai*). But Greek speech indicates that *plateiai* are “broad spaces,” whereas we suppose them to be city streets. Therefore Wisdom, who is Christ, is proclaimed in that way in which, from many paths, there is for us an exit; and in the broad places [Col. 0532B] she speaks freely—those places in which He promised not only to dwell but also to walk about. Therefore the Prophet freely runs in the Lord’s way after his heart has begun to be enlarged. For he could not previously run in God’s way before he himself had become a worthy and spacious dwelling for God.

[Note: Col. 0531D. We reject “Amen,” because it appears neither in our manuscript nor in the others. Here, after the customary formula, “Letter IV ends. Letter V happily begins,” the name of the copyist is recorded: “The copyist Euthalius writes.” Thereafter, under the heading of the letter He, in the first verse only, he reads *pone* (“set”) for *statue* (“establish”), and *viae* (“of the way”) for *viam* (“the way”).]

[Note: Col. 0532D. “Amen” is absent from the manuscripts.]

304 LETTER V. He.

“Establish for me, O Lord, the law of the way [Hilary: of the ways] of Your ordinances; and I shall seek it always. Give me understanding, and I shall search Your Law, and I shall keep [Hilary: observe] it with all my heart. Lead me in the path [Hilary: on the path] of Your commandments, for I have desired it. Incline my heart to Your testimonies, and not to gain. Turn away my eyes lest they see vanity; [Col. 0532C] give me life in Your way. Establish for Your servant Your word in Your fear. Cut off my reproach, which I have feared; for Your judgments are pleasant. Behold, I have longed for Your commandments; give me life in Your righteousness.”

1. The Latin translation has not adequately expressed the Greek. The law of the way of God’s ordinances is sought.—In the first verse of the fifth letter we find an unusual and novel petition of the Prophet. For he begins thus, V. 33: “Establish for me, O Lord, the law of the way of Your ordinances.” But it is difficult to grasp the meaning of this verse from the Latin translation. The force of both the Hebrew and Greek expression could not be fully explained within the limits of our ordinary language. For the Greeks, translating from the Hebrew, rendered it: νομοθέτησόν με, Κύριε, τὴν ὁδὸν τῶν δικαιωμάτων σου, “Legislate for me, O Lord, the way of Your ordinances.”

[Note: Col. 0532D. The printed texts read “the way of Your ordinances.” This occurs once also at the end in the manuscripts, perhaps through copyists’ error; for elsewhere they consistently read “of the way,” and that is plainly the proper reading.]

In this verse he asks that a law of the ordinances may be established for him; and the Latin language could not render νομοθέτησον (*nomothetēson*, “legislate/establish a law”) so as to convey the same sense. The Prophet therefore asks that the Lord establish for him the law of the way of His ordinances: that is, that he may understand and know by what law he is to approach the way of God’s ordinances. For he does not merely speak of a way, but seeks the law of the way of the ordinances.

2. The law of ordinary roads. The law of the way of the people leaving Egypt.—And what, then, will be the law of the way of the ordinances? For on ordinary earthly roads we remember that there is a law consisting [Note: Col. 0533C. “By measures of distance.” The manuscript of St. Michael reads “in measures of distance.” This law of the road especially concerns soldiers. Ambrose, on this very passage: “A soldier setting out on a journey does not arrange his own order of travel . . . nor does he seek luxurious shortcuts, lest he depart from the standards; rather, he receives an itinerary from the commander.”] in measured distances: at intervals of a thousand paces certain markers, as prescribed by road-law, are set up; resting places at stations are arranged; and, up to the city [Note: Col. 0533C. Two manuscripts omit “when the repose of stations is arranged.” The term *mansio* is frequent in the Jerusalem pilgrimage itinerary, where various travelers’ stopping-places are identified as *mansiones*, *mutationes*, and cities. Pope Julius uses the same word in Athanasius, p. 748, where he says that the canons were violated by those who hailed Gregory, a foreigner, as bishop of Alexandria at Antioch, a place thirty-six *mansiones* distant from Alexandria. The itinerary of Antoninus agrees with Julius’s letter, assigning thirty-six places to travelers going from Antioch to Alexandria. If Godefrid Hermann’s opinion is true—that in his notes on ch. 9, book V, of the Life of St Athanasius a *mansio*, as Julius uses the word, denotes half a day’s journey—then *mansiones* must be called lodgings designated either for meals or overnight rest. But since that itinerary concerns not so much a lightly equipped traveler hastening to his goal as a burdened soldier, whose strength must be preserved against the enemy, it is not certain that each station denotes only half a day’s journey. When Tobit 6:1 says, “He lodged at the first station beside the river Tigris,” it appears to denote the place which Tobias reached on the first day of his journey and where he passed the night. Stations are generally not very far apart; nor are they equal, as Ambrose expressly teaches in his fifth discourse on this Psalm, §§5. Although in §2 he calls them *stativae*, places where an army, after marching three days, rested on the fourth, in §§3 and 5 he indiscriminately calls the stations of the children of Israel in the desert both *stativae* and *mansiones*. Thus here *mansio* may be understood as any travelers’ stopping-place, whether they remained there for an hour, for one day, or for several days. The latter point is already sufficiently clear from what has been said, and is further confirmed by Num. 23:1, where the forty-two places in which the children of Israel camped while crossing the desert are called *mansiones*. Tobit 6:10 is likewise relevant: “When he had reached the city of Rages, he said to the angel, ‘Where do you wish us to stay?’” But the former point—that a stop for an hour at noon might be called a *mansio*—is less certainly established.] suitable for the refreshment of travelers, the intervals of stations are again measured out.

[Note: Col. 0534C. The manuscripts read this more neatly than the printed “for refreshment.” Again, Ambrose’s words help to illuminate the passage: “Cities are selected in which three, four, or more days may intervene, if they abound in water and are well supplied with commerce.” Thus, for Hilary, the intervals are suited to the refreshment of travelers. The following words of Ambrose explain what “up to the city” means: “And so the journey is completed without hardship until one reaches that city which is selected as though royal, where rest is provided for weary armies.” Yet we read here that even the intervals in which travelers rested for some days are designated by Hilary as *mansiones*, so that *mansio* may be understood as any stopping-place of travelers, [Col. 0534D] whether they stayed there for an hour or for one or more days. This second conclusion is already clear, and is further confirmed by Num. 23:1, where the forty-two places at which the children of Israel camped while traversing the desert are called *mansiones*. Tobit 6:10 also bears on this: “When he had arrived at the city of Rages, he said to the angel, ‘Where do you wish us to stay?’” But the first point—that a stopping-place for the midday meal should be called a *mansio*—is not so fully established.]

But also, when the people crossed the Red Sea on foot after leaving Egypt, we remember that a certain law of the way was established for them [Note: Col. 0533C. “And” for “for them.”] [Note: Col. 0534D. The printed editions read “and” for “for them”: incorrectly.] not by human judgment but by divine direction, in the pillar of fire and cloud. For when the people had to journey, a pillar of fire went before them [Col. 0533B] at night, and a pillar of cloud by day (Exod. 13:21). But when it pleased God that the people should remain for a long time in the same camp, neither did the pillar of fire move at night nor did the pillar of cloud go before them by day. Thus He established this law of the way. And if we carefully review those stages, encampments, and conditions of places set forth in Exodus 15 and following, we shall see in them great wonders of the heavenly journey. Therefore the Prophet often prayed, saying, “I will consider the wonders of Your Law” (Ps. 118:18). But the Prophet does not now ask to be contained under those laws of travel; for he asks not for the law of the way, but for the law of the way of ordinances.

3. The many kinds of way. Which way’s law David desires.—He knows that there is a way of testimonies, when he says, “In [Col. 0533C] the way of Your testimonies I have delighted.” He knows that there is [Col. 0534A] a way of commandments, when he says, “I ran in the way of Your commandments.” He knows that there is a way of the Law, when he says, “Blessed are those who walk in the Law of the Lord.” He knows that there is this way of ordinances, concerning which he now prays. He knows also that there is a way in the Prophets, a way in the Gospels, and a way in the Apostles, of which he has often borne witness. Therefore, by the law of this way, he wishes to press on to that perfect way of life.

For there are many heretics who approve [Note: Col. 0534C. “Disapprove.”] the way of the Law [Note: Col. 0534D. Paris reads “disapprove.” But the other printed editions and manuscripts read “approve,” perhaps in the sense in which, in the preceding discussion, §9, those who fall into heretical parties were said to be on a way indeed, but not on the way of truth. Immediately thereafter two manuscripts read “For we know,” not “We also know.”]; many who approve the way of the Prophets; many the way of the Gospels; and many the way of the Apostles. We also know that some are not content with all these ways. But the learned scribe knows, following the example of the rich householder, how to bring forth old things and new from his treasures (Matt. 13:52). The Prophet therefore desires this law of the way of ordinances.

[Col. 0534B] For the law of ordinances is contained in certain disciplines of the devout heart, and has confined us within the boundaries of its own constitution, defining how we should use them [Note: Col. 0534D. The printed texts read “might turn themselves”; corrected from the manuscripts.], lest, by going beyond those limits, we wander into the notions of heretical interpretation. He therefore does not wish to depart from the law which he asks to be established for him.

4. To what end.—But for what purpose does he ask that this law be instituted? Clearly, that he may search it out. The Law of ordinances had been written through Moses, and the Prophet practiced it by works. He does not therefore ask that the Law already established and piously practiced by him should be established for him; rather, he asks for that which he desires to search out. What, then, does he desire to search out? The end of the Law. And what will be the end of the Law? Let us hear the Apostle: “For Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. 10:4). But through these ways of ordinances, for which the law is established, he desires to seek the end of the Law; [Col. 0535A] and not merely to seek it, but to seek it always. For thus he says: “And I shall seek it always.” The duty of seeking would not have been sufficient through mere willingness, unless it were also carried out by him in an unwearied continuance through time.

5. David’s prerogatives; what law, and by what law, he seeks understanding.—V. 34: “Give me understanding, and I shall search Your Law, and I shall keep it with all my heart.” We remember that it is written in Solomon’s Proverbs: “Wisdom shall be accounted to one who asks for wisdom without understanding” (Prov. 17:28, according to the Septuagint). The apparent sense is that one who does not understand, yet asks wisely, is considered wise.

[Note: Col. 0535D. Some manuscripts read “by understanding”: a copyists’ error. The St Michael manuscript more correctly reads *inintelligendo* (“in not understanding”). Thus in *On the Trinity*, book X, §30, and book XI, §47, *inintelligentia* means a lack of understanding. The printed texts read: “by ignorantly asking wisdom from those who ask wisely,” etc. Although the adverb “wisely” occurs in the Regius and Albinus manuscripts, it is more correctly absent from the St Michael manuscript. Otherwise Hilary, when introducing the interpretation of this passage, ought to have said “it is shown,” not “it seems to be shown.” The Greek agrees with the St Michael manuscript: ἀνοήτῳ ἐπερωτήσαντι σοφίαν σοφία λογισθήσεται, “Wisdom shall be reckoned to one without understanding who asks for wisdom.”]

This advances his case because the Prophet, remaining under the Law, and, according to the Apostle, “a Hebrew of Hebrews,” circumcised on the eighth day, and by descent of the tribe of Judah (Phil. 3:5), [Col. 0535B] and by the grace of bodily anointing both chosen as king and anointed one (*christus*), and worthy by the mystery of the Lord’s birth that Jesus Christ should be his son, nevertheless prays as a stranger to the Law: “Give me understanding, and I shall search Your Law, and I shall keep it with all my heart.”

[Note: Col. 0535D. Bad., Erasmus, Leipzig, and two manuscripts read “by the mystery of the Lord’s birth.” Only the Paris edition reads “according to the mystery, by the mystery of the Lord’s birth,” etc. The St Michael manuscript gives the uncorrupted reading.]

Therefore he does not yet keep it, has not yet searched it, does not yet understand it. He is not, then, speaking of the Law into which the Prophet was born, in which he was instructed, and which he practiced. Knowing, therefore, that the first part of prudence is for a person to ask wise people about what he does not understand and to understand what he does not know, he asks to receive understanding. But knowing that, once the spirit of understanding has been received, the effort of searching is needed, he says: “And I shall search Your Law.” And recognizing that the fruit of searching is the preservation of the thing found, he said: “And I shall keep [Col. 0535C] it.” Finally, understanding that perfect diligence in keeping lies in the whole service of the heart, he completed the entire sequence of his statement: “Give me understanding, and I shall search Your Law, and I shall keep it with all my heart.”

[Note: Col. 0535D. Paris reads “in the keeping of the thing found”; the other editions read “the keeping of this thing”: corrected from the manuscripts.]

6. Various rites of the Law.—But what, then, is this which he desires to understand, which he promises to search out and to keep with all his heart? He recalls that six days are not idly set forth in Moses’ book in the creation of this world (Gen. 1). He knows that the rest of the seventh day is not superfluous (Gen. 2:2). He remembers that in the religious observance of the new month the mystery of the heavenly festival is figuratively represented, as in a mirror [Col. 0536A] (Exod. 21:2).

[Note: Col. 0535D. The St Michael manuscript’s reading, “in the religious observance of the seventh month,” was wrongly preferred by the Paris editor to the other readings. For the feast of trumpets celebrated by the Jews in the seventh month is not mentioned here; it will shortly be mentioned in its proper order. Rather, this refers to the harvest of firstfruits, commanded in Exod. 23:16. Since in Exod. 23:15 this feast is also called the month of new things, and Paul in Heb. 12:23 calls the assembly of the blessed “the Church of the firstborn,” Hilary rightly declares that the mystery of the heavenly festival is prefigured in the observance of the new month: namely, that blessed time when the saints, renewed in life and body after passing from this age, shall receive the fruits of their works.]

He knows that year in which the Hebrew becomes free after six years of servitude (Lev. 25:4), in which the land rests after much cultivation (ibid. 13), its fruits being left for the resident alien, the poor, and the beasts of the earth, and in which all debts are remitted to all Hebrews. He desires also to search out the laws of the fiftieth year. He wishes to search what religious observance belongs to the tenth day of the first month through the fourteenth, and then through the twenty-first. He considers also the solemnity of the seventh month, whose memorial is in trumpets (Lev. 23:24); the propitiation on its tenth day (ibid. 27); and, after the fifteenth, the eight-day joy in tabernacles (ibid. 34), and how from these both the first holy day and the eighth are holy [Col. 0536B] (ibid. 35–36). He knows that circumcision was first instituted (Gen. 17:10), and that it was performed anew through Jesus (Josh. 5:2). He desires the holy unleavened bread, wishes to offer the Passover sacrifice, concerning which it is written in the very sacrifice of the lamb: “This is the Passover of the Lord” (Exod. 12:11). He knows that the land of promise, the land flowing with milk and honey, has not yet truly been obtained by the people circumcised a second time. For these things, therefore, he asks understanding; understanding them, he promises to search them out; having searched them, he professes that he will keep them; and, keeping them, he will guard them with all his heart.

[Note: Col. 0536C. “Rejoice.”]  
[Note: Col. 0536D. The St Michael manuscript reads “rejoice”; two others, “to rejoice.”]

7. After these words follows, V. 35: “Lead me [Note: Col. 0536C. “In the path”; later, “for I have desired it.”] in [Note: Col. 0536D. Paris here and below reads “in the path,” against the other books and the Greek.] the path of Your commandments, for I have desired it.” In this verse also the force of the expression has not been properly rendered within the limits of the translation. For [Col. 0536C] what our translators rendered, “Lead me in the path,” Greek has expressed thus: ὁδήγησόν με ἐν τῇ τρίβῳ, “Guide me in the beaten track.” Among the Greeks, τρίβος (*tribos*) means a path worn and frequented by repeated passage; but among us a *semita* may be a path and yet not be worn. Therefore, because Greek comprehends both notions under the same designation, let us understand that the *semita* too is the path which has been worn [Note: Col. 0536D. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “indeed let us know.”].

8. The way of the commandments has been trodden from the beginning of the world.—And one should observe that he here speaks not of the path of the Law but of the path of the commandments. For the way of the Law had those who walked in it only from Moses onward, [Col. 0537A] after it had been established. But it is a path of the commandments because, in God’s commandments, men have proceeded from the world’s beginning onward [Note: Col. 0537C. “May it have been traversed.”]. In this path Abel ran; Seth stood fast; Enoch pleased God; Noah deserved to be preserved; Melchizedek was able both to bless and to receive tithes; Abraham is God’s friend; Isaac is heir; Jacob is Israel; from Judah comes the expectation of the nations; and [Note: Col. 0537C. The Regius manuscript reads “Joshua”: wrongly, since this alludes to Ps. 80:6, “He appointed it as a testimony in Joseph.” Nor does Hilary usually read “Joshua,” but “Jesus.” See similar passages in Letter 19, §12, and on Psalm 52, §9.] Joseph was set as a testimony. Job, free from the Law, triumphs over the Law’s enemy; Moses vindicates the Hebrew; Jesus circumcises Israel a second time; and Samuel is chosen worthy to anoint a king.

9. We need a guide to it. Christ is the guide.—And now this man, anointed, king, and prophet, prays that he may be led in this path. For he knows that his nature is weak and that he cannot enter upon this path without a guide. God is the guide [Note: Col. 0537C. The words, “For God is the guide of all who travel this path,” are now restored for the first time from the Vatican and St Michael manuscripts.] of all who travel this path. For He is guide when it is said: [Note: Col. 0537D. Thus Paris, from the St Michael manuscript. Other books read, “Walk back after Him, because He will lead you. But He leads . . .,” except that the Vatican manuscript prefaces these words with “when it is said to Peter.” If it were permissible to correct from our own judgment, we would restore: “Walk after the Lord your God, and cling to Him, for He will lead you”; especially since Ambrose, on this same verse, adds: “No one can say this except one who follows what is written: ‘You shall walk after the Lord your God, and cling to Him, because He will lead you.’” Nor is it sufficiently clear where those two doctors found the words “because He will lead you.”] “Walk after the Lord your God, and cling to Him”; and again, “Walk after Him, because He will lead you” (Deut. 13:4).

He leads when He says: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me” (Matt. 10:38). He also leads because He was the first to tread the entire path of Gospel sufferings. If the Apostles teach, He taught first; for Wisdom established the friends of God and the prophets (Wis. 7:27). If anything is now done justly by us, He is the prince of our righteousness; for He Himself is righteousness (1 Cor. 1:30). If because of faith we are scourged unto terror [Note: Col. 0537D. The printed editions read “because of terror.”], He gave His back to scourges. If we are struck with blows on the face for insult, [Col. 0537C] He received them. If we are spat upon in contempt, He did not turn His face away from spittle.

10. That is, to those who love the Law.—He is guide in all things, but He is guide to those who love the Law, which the Prophet above declared that he would keep with all his heart. For here, according to Greek idiom, when he says, “For I have desired it,” this cannot be referred [Col. 0538A] to the path of the commandments. For in Greek, where “path” is written in the feminine gender, that which he desired is stated in the masculine gender [Note: Col. 0537C. “That which he says he desired.”], saying: ὁδήγησόν με ἐν τῇ τρίβῳ τῶν ἐντολῶν σου, ὅτι αὐτὸν ἠθέλησα: “Guide me in the path of Your commandments, for I desired it [masculine].”

[Note: Col. 0537D. The printed editions omit the word “saying” together with all the following Greek; in its place two manuscripts set a marginal sign indicating that the Greek is missing. We supply it from two other manuscripts. Yet in the Septuagint edition αὐτὴν, not αὐτόν, is now found. Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the fifth and sixth editions likewise refer the pronoun to the path.]

For “law” is called by us in the feminine gender, whereas in Greek it is νόμος (*nomos*), [Note: Col. 0538C. “For that reason it is expressed by them in the masculine gender.”] which they express in the masculine gender. And although “path” is there called feminine, what he desired is referred to that which was mentioned in the masculine gender by the propriety of Greek usage.

11. Everything is from God’s gift.—There now follows, V. 36: “Incline my heart to Your testimonies, and not to gain.” The Prophet attributes everything to God’s gift: whether that the law [Note: Col. 0538C. From the Vatican and St Michael manuscripts the word “way,” formerly lacking, is restored.] of the way of ordinances may be established for him by the Lord; that understanding may be bestowed upon him; that he may be guided in the path; or that his heart may be inclined to the testimonies—that is, to those things which were written in the presence of witnesses. For the Law was given with heaven and earth as witnesses (Deut. 30:19).

12. Objection and answer.—But perhaps someone, by occasion of the Prophet’s devout modesty, may dare to speak impiously in this way: “If,” he says, “everything is from God, then human ignorance is free from blame, since a person can obtain nothing unless he receives it as a gift from God.” First, it is a will of impiety [Note: Col. 0538D. The printed editions read “a will that is impious.” But the manuscripts read “a will of impiety,” a form of expression by which Hilary commonly denotes a will that is obstinate and, as it were, deliberately devoted to impiety.] to suppose that one fails to attain the things proper to believers because they have not been granted him by God. But the Prophet removes every occasion for this impious excuse.

For first, when he prays, he performs a duty suited to his weakness; then he joins the pursuits of human devotion to God’s gifts. For when he says, “Establish for me, O Lord, [Note: Col. 0538C. “The way of Your commandments.”] the way [Note: Col. 0538D. The Regius manuscript with the Albinus manuscript, as well as Bad., Erasmus, reads “the way of Your commandments.” Only here in the manuscripts does “way,” rather than “of the way,” occur.] of Your ordinances,” [Col. 0538C] he shows, according to the humility of our prayer, what belongs to God. But when he adds, “And I shall seek it always,” he sets forth the office of his own devotion. In the remaining clauses also he binds both elements together in a kind of mutual embrace: when he asks to be led in the path and when he himself desires that very thing. For he first honorably places before all else the things which are from God; and then he adds the things which are from man with a confession [Note: Col. 0538D. Thus one Vatican manuscript, supported by the St Michael manuscript and also by the Paris edition, except that the latter, omitting “and,” reads “then … with a confession” for “with a confession of humility and duty.” Other books read more briefly: “and then he added the things which are from himself with confession.” Here, but especially in Letter 14, §20, Hilary appears to teach that a certain beginning of good will and faith is from us, by which we can pray that God Himself may perfect what our weakness cannot accomplish. This teaching conflicts with the Second Council of Orange, canon 25: “We also profess and believe for our salvation that in every good work we do not begin and are afterwards helped by the mercy of God; rather, He Himself, with no preceding merits on our part, inspires in us both faith and love of Himself.” And canon 3, lest grace be believed to be conferred because of human prayer: “If anyone says that God’s grace can be conferred in response to human invocation, and not that grace itself causes us to invoke God, he contradicts Isaiah,” etc. Hence Augustine, Letter 194 to Sixtus, §10: “Let him not exalt even the merit of his own prayer . . . Faith prays which was given to one not praying; and unless it had been given, that person would not pray.” Hilary is excused on the ground that he wrote before the rise of the Pelagian heresy. At that time Optatus of Milevis also said, in book II: “To will is ours; to run is ours; to bring it to completion is God’s.” So too Basil, *On Repentance*: μόνον θέλησον, καὶ Θεὸς προαπαντᾷ, “Only will it, and God comes beforehand.” Augustine acknowledges in *Retractations*, book I, ch. 23, that he himself had elsewhere asserted that the beginning of faith came from us. Indeed Jerome, writing against the Pelagians, book III, says: “But where mercy and grace are present, free choice ceases in part; it remains only in our willing and desiring and in giving assent to what pleases us. It is now in the Lord’s power that, by His help and aid, we may accomplish what we desire and labor for.” Moreover, Hilary’s consistent doctrine makes it clear that the Church then believed that everything must be attributed to God’s grace, so that nothing remained to man in which he might boast. But since it was equally believed that man is free, cooperates with grace, and receives eternal glory or punishment according to the merits of works, it came about that, wishing to preserve unimpaired the doctrine of free choice, he seemed to attribute more than was right to human will. This matter has been treated at length in the general preface.] of his humility and duty. He therefore prays that God may grant. Thus the beginning is from us when we pray, while the gift is from Him; then, because His gift proceeds from our beginning, it is again from us that it is sought [Note: Col. 0539D. One Vatican manuscript reads “His gift is that it may be obtained”: a gloss.] and obtained and retained.

13. Avarice and gain are the same thing.—But in the phrase, “Incline my heart to Your ordinances, and not to gain,” some have translated: “Incline my heart [Note: Col. 0539B. “To Your ordinances.”] to [Note: Col. 0539D. Two manuscripts: “to Your ordinances.”] Your testimonies, and not to avarice.” The expression found in the Hebrew codices is appropriately suited to both interpretations in its ambiguity [Note: Col. 0540C. One Vatican manuscript reads “ambiguous.” The printed editions, with two manuscripts, read “is placed in the definition of both senses,” except Paris, which reads “is appropriate.” We retain the reading of the St Michael manuscript. In fact, the Hebrew word underlies each of these interpretations. Yet in the Septuagint, which Hilary here professes to follow, we now read πλεονεξίαν (*pleonexian*, “avarice/covetousness”), a word which Erasmus notes cannot here mean “gain.” Ambrose himself, reading “into avarice,” indicates by these words that the version reading “into gain” was earlier: “Others have ‘gain’; and I think it was changed [to ‘avarice’], because gain in a good thing seems something to be sought rather than avoided.” He then indicates that he prefers “into gain,” although, in imitation of Hilary, he adapts his explanation to both readings.] [Note: Col. 0539B. “Ambiguously.”].

But we, as is fitting, follow the devout and ancient authority of the Seventy translators, while drawing from the judgment of the other translators the distinctive sense of each interpretation, adapting it to [Col. 0539B] the intended meaning. For whereas these have said “to gain” and those “to avarice,” by this very fact it will be known how “gain” is used here. For worldly people call money, silver, gold, and the other instruments of wealth “gain.” Therefore, when the Prophet prays that his heart may be inclined to God’s testimonies and not to gain, he undoubtedly turns his heart, inclined to God’s testimonies, away from the things which are considered useful by human judgment. And indeed the verse which follows confirms the meaning of our interpretation.

### 14. Which eyes ought to be turned away, and from what vanity

For he says, V. 37: “Turn away my eyes, lest they behold vanity, and give me life in your way”; thus teaching that those things are vanity which human beings consider useful. We must ask which eyes, and from what vanity, he prays may be turned away.

He prays that both the eyes of the soul and those of the body may be turned away: those, namely, which are held captive and dwell upon theatrical games; those which are enslaved to the contests of the Circus; those which admire the prices of garments; those which are occupied by the brilliance of gold and the variety of gems. Unless, perhaps, the course of horses is more pleasing than the courses of the stars; and those obscene tales of shameful spectacles are sung more delightfully than those divine utterances concerning human hope. [Note: [Col. 0540A] *Cantarent*: “they were sung.”] [Note: [Col. 0540D] In Par. *cantarent* (“were sung”). This suggests that even then Scripture was customarily sung with a certain sweetness. From this same passage Ambrose takes occasion to call the people back from spectacles. In order to achieve this more easily, Augustine, in the manner of our Hilary, both in many places and especially in Psalm XXXIX, no. 9, invites them to Christian spectacles.]

Unless, perhaps, the stored-up riches, honor, and glory of eternity are not to be preferred to this use of earthly metals; and the appearance of gold will be more pleasing to me than that of humankind, earth, light, and heaven.

Therefore he prays that his eyes—both the bodily ones and those of the soul—may be turned away from their vanities. Of those who are blinded in this respect the blessed Apostle teaches when he says: “Darkened in the vanity of their understanding, alienated from the life of God” (Eph. IV. 18). [Note: [Col. 0540D] Par., with the manuscript of Micy, reads “from the way of God”; this conflicts with the other books and with the sacred Greek and Latin text. So too in Ambrose, no. 30, although “from the way of God” has been retained, the reader is warned that ten manuscripts have “from the life of God.”]

### 15. The reward of eyes turned away from vanity

And what reward belongs to eyes turned away from vanity need not be sought far off. [Note: [Col. 0540B] “What the first reward is.”] For it follows: “And in your way I shall live.” [Note: [Col. 0540D] Thus the Micy manuscript, whereas other copies have “give me life,” a reading with which neither the preceding nor the following words agree sufficiently.]

For the eyes must turn away from vanity so that we may have life in the way of God: not the life which now exists, but that which is laid up in heaven and hidden with Christ. For throughout this entire psalm he has spoken as though he were going to live, not merely as though he now lives. [Note: [Col. 0540B] “In this passage the prophet has spoken.”]

Therefore the eyes must be raised, so that they may behold Christ’s glory rather than the empty and vain things of this world. [Note: [Col. 0541C] Par., from the Micy manuscript, reads “may be seen. For we shall come into the life of God”; and shortly afterwards the Micy manuscript alone has “we shall come” for “we shall live.” This reading is not to be despised: just as above those who do not turn their eyes from vanity were said to be alienated from the life of God, so now, conversely, those who do turn away may be said to come into the life of God.] For, turning our eyes back from vanity, we shall live in the way of God.

### 16. God’s words must be received with fear

Then follows, V. 38: “Establish for your servant your word in your fear.” The prophet knows that very many receive God’s words without fear. Many treat the Scriptures of the heavenly utterance which they have heard as though they were a fiction about empty things; and with the grave danger of irreligious presumption they mock God’s words, which cannot pass away even when heaven and earth pass away.

He knows that the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom (Ps. CX, 10). He knows that, in that sevenfold grace of the Spirit, fear is reckoned last, as though the foundation of those things which are spoken above it (Isa. XI, 2). Therefore he prays that God’s utterances may be established in him in the fear of God, because he knows that those utterances will be profitable to us which are feared as God’s utterances.

He then adds, V. 39: “Cut off my reproach which I have suspected; for your judgments are pleasant.” The prophet speaks while placed in a body, and knows [Note: [Col. 0541B] “No one.”] that no one living can be without sin. [Note: [Col. 0541C] Erasmus, marking this passage with a censorial stroke, had written in the margin, “On the contrary, many now are.” Against Pelagius, who maintained that a human being could abstain from every sin even without God’s grace, Hilary was pressed into Pelagius’s service in Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, book 62, no. 72, because he had said, as we suppose, concerning Job: “What writings of Job had he read, that he abstained from every evil thing because he worshipped God with his mind alone, unmingled with vices? To worship God is the proper duty of righteousness.”

Augustine’s replies to Pelagius readily reconcile both the statements criticized by Erasmus and those distorted by Pelagius into a bad sense. For this purpose Augustine’s definition is sufficient, by which he explains what it is to be without sin: “He,” he says in the passage cited, “is most truly said to be without sin in whom no sin dwells, not one who says through abstinence from an evil deed, ‘Now it is no longer I who do it.’” And shortly before: “For he abstains from every evil thing even who has sin but does not permit it to reign in himself, and to whom perhaps an objectionable thought stealthily comes, but whom he does not allow to reach the completion of the act. Yet it is one thing not to have sin, another not to obey its desires.”

That Augustine was an interpreter of Hilary need not be demonstrated at length, since Hilary himself immediately declares at this place what he understands by being without sin, in these words: “But when he prays that reproach be cut off from him, he does not confess it as something admitted and perpetrated; but because,” etc. More clearly, book 4, no. 8: “He remembers that in his body there is a way of sinning; yet through the fear of God he remains wholly removed from the commission of sin.” He therefore means only that no one is without the law and root of sin; nor does he deny that some are without the act and guilt of sin.

For where he considers not that vicious root but deeds, he does not hesitate to affirm of David himself, Letter 19, no. 6: “In works of every kind of goodness he is himself perfect.” And above, in the passage abused by Pelagius, he expressly declares that Job “abstained from every evil thing.” Erasmus’s criticism therefore collapses of itself. Pelagius’s heresy is likewise overthrown by the very words which it adduces in its own defense. For when Hilary gives the reason why Job abstained from every evil thing, he indicates that Job did not lack the innate root of vices—by which, as Hilary teaches in Letter 13, no. 8, we are inclined toward every kind of crime—but only that, when these vices were ready, he did not mingle his mind with them by consenting.

The force of the phrase “unmingled” (*non admixta*) may be considered from the exposition of Psalm LIII, no. 10, where evils and punishments are said to be ready for the righteous, yet not mingled with them, because they are righteous, etc. For just as the righteous, by living righteously, separate themselves from the punishments set before them, so too, by resisting the desires of the flesh, they do not mingle their mind with them, but separate it from their contagion.

Moreover, the reader should be warned that this and similar passages of Hilary do no more conflict with the Church’s pious belief in the spotless purity of Mary than do Augustine’s assertions in Letter 167, no. 13, and elsewhere, that no one lives here without sin. In those places he does not except even that most holy Virgin, because his mind was not then directed to her; but finally, in one place, *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 36, he expressly declares that, where sins are in question, he wishes to raise absolutely no question concerning that holy Virgin.]

He remembers One who “did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” Therefore, when he prays that reproach may be cut off from him, he asks that sins may be cut off, because reproach follows sin. Yet when he prays that it may be cut off from him, he does not confess it as something admitted and perpetrated; rather, he suspects that it dwells in him through the weakness of his flesh.

For he does not say, “Cut off the reproach which is in me”; but he says, “Cut off my reproach which I have suspected,” showing his suspicion of reproach from awareness of his own weakness. [Note: [Col. 0542D] The editions, except Par. and the royal manuscript, have “my reproach which I have perpetrated”; but he says, etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0541B] “In judgment.”] For in the judgments many shall rise to reproach. [Note: [Col. 0542D] The Vatican manuscript has “for in judgment”: a copyist’s bold corruption, although the discourse here truly concerns the final judgment.] Since those judgments are pleasant to those in whom the reproach of sin shall not remain, he prays that even that suspicion of reproach which is within him may be cut off from him, so that God’s judgments may be pleasant to him.

### 17. Whom God gives life

And lest he should be thought to have prayed from consciousness of committed sin, he concludes with this confidence the whole prayer which he offers under each set of eight verses, V. 40: “Behold, I have desired your commandments; in your righteousness give me life.”

Above, he prayed that God’s utterances might be established in him in the fear of God; then, that the suspicion of reproach might be cut off from him. Now he shows his longing and desire for God’s commandments, and prays that he may be given life in God’s righteousness. He knows that it is the proper gift of divine righteousness to give life to one who has desired God’s commandments; for whom God’s judgments are pleasant when suspicion of reproach has been cut off; and in whom the utterances are established in the fear of God. [Note: [Col. 0542B] We have removed “Amen,” which is absent both from our manuscript and from the other manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0542D] “Amen” is absent from our manuscripts.]

## LETTER VI: Vau

“May [Hilary: “And may”] your mercy come upon me, O Lord, your salvation according to your word. And I shall answer a word to those [Hilary: “reproaching”] me, because I have hoped in your sayings. And do not take the word of truth wholly [Hilary adds: “exceedingly”] away from my mouth, because I [Hilary: “have hoped”] in your judgments. And I shall keep your law always, for age [Hilary adds: “and for age”] upon age. And I walked [Hilary: “I entered”] in spaciousness, because I sought out your commandments. And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and was not ashamed. And I meditated upon your commandments, which I loved exceedingly. And I raised my hands to your commandments which I loved [Hilary adds: “greatly”], and I exercised myself in your ordinances.”

### 1. Those who despise Scripture as devoid of wisdom; nothing in it is less than perfect

According to the Apostle, there are many who, following the wisdom of the world, have rejected the wisdom of God (I Cor. I, 19–20); for which reason God has made foolish the wisdom of the world. For what is more foolish than unbelievers, who, besides that common error of irreligious persons, add this further impiety: they think that the divine utterances of Scripture lack the rational character of perfect teaching.

Because, through the impiety of their own intellect, they cannot be capable of divine sayings, they burst forth into insult against heavenly words in excuse for their own dullness, saying that there is nothing rational and nothing perfect in them; wishing what they themselves say to be alone learned and polished by the teachings of true wisdom. [Note: [Col. 0543D] The editions, except Par. and two manuscripts, read “and polished by the prudence of their teaching.” Another Vatican manuscript corruptly reads “and stripped of teaching and true prudence.”] Foolish people deny to God what they themselves dare to claim.

Nor is it surprising that they hold irreligious opinions concerning things whose understanding they do not attain, through a dullness like that of cattle. [Note: [Col. 0543D] Thus the Micy manuscript. Two others have “of cattle”; the Vatican manuscript, “of beasts”; the printed editions, “of money.”]

Yet although, in the discussion which we held above, I judge that those who follow God’s wisdom know the perfection of heavenly sayings, and that there is nothing among them which is not complete and perfect in every respect, nevertheless this too may be understood more fully in the verses of this sixth letter. [Note: [Col. 0543D] In the printed texts the reading is “they,” and shortly after, “they think.” Par. then has “and that there is nothing in it.” The manuscript reading is more complete, by which Hilary contrasts those wise in the world with those wise according to God. Of the former he declares the perfection of heavenly sayings to be unknown; of the latter, known. The former wish there to be nothing perfect in them; the latter are persuaded that none of those heavenly sayings fails to be perfect in every respect. Augustine testifies to this in *On Christian Teaching*, book IV, no. 9. He asks whether the sacred books should be called only wise or also eloquent, and answers: “Where I understand them, not only does nothing seem wiser to me than they are, but nothing more eloquent,” etc.]

### 2. Our salvation is God’s gift

After the preceding meaning he speaks thus, V. 41: “And may your mercy come upon me, O Lord, your salvation according to your word.” He therefore first prayed for mercy, then for salvation. For our salvation is from God’s mercy, and this is the gift of his goodness in us; and the prayer began where the salvation of the one praying also begins.

Then, lest the Prophet should be thought to pray from uncertain and unexpected hope, he mentions mercy first and salvation second, and then third adds, “according to your word,” so as to show that this confidence in prayer proceeds according to God’s word, that is, according to the teaching of the law. [Note: [Col. 0543D] “From teaching.”]

### 3.

After this order of perfect prayer follows, V. 42: “And I shall answer those reproaching me with a word, because I have hoped in your words.” Perfect reasoning maintains its order. “If,” he says, “your mercy and your salvation according to your word come upon me; and if I have obtained mercy from you and have been preserved by you as you promised: it will follow that I shall answer those who reproach me with foolishness, with the error of hope, and with this word by which I hope in you.”

What, then, can an irreligious mind reproach against this reply of the prophet? Mercy is first prayed for from God; salvation too is expected from God; and then God is shown to have promised it through his word. Thus the impiety of those who reproach is refuted by those who hope in God’s words: when God is prayed to, [Note: [Col. 0544D] Three manuscripts read “is preached.”] and the faith of believers expects mercy and salvation from him, and this is the teaching of our hope—that, when prayed to, he will both have mercy and save.

### 4. David’s prayer rests on God’s mercy, not on his own merits

Then follows, V. 43: “And do not take the word of truth wholly away from my mouth, because I have hoped in your judgments.” Let human arrogance receive a lesson in humility and moderation. The prophet first prays that something may be granted to him, before showing himself worthy to obtain it. He wishes all things to begin in him from God’s goodness; yet he does not withhold the ground of his confidence.

For he says: “And do not take the word of truth wholly away from my mouth.” In this he first confesses the majesty of him who must always be prayed to; then he adds that he does not hope in vain, saying, “Because I have hoped in your judgments.”

But this is the way of human presumption: before it asks to receive anything, it asserts the merit by which it deserves it, and approaches the one from whom it asks something as though demanding a duty owed.

### 5. A preacher of God’s word must be free from guilt

But it is not enough for us that the Prophet has merely observed the principle of modesty. The arrangement and force of the words must also be understood: why he said, “Do not take the word of truth wholly away from my mouth.”

Every function of the mouth serves the understanding and movements of the heart. And the following words of this verse teach why the Prophet prays that the word of truth may not be taken from his mouth. For we must not suppose that the Prophet feared lest the word of truth should be taken from his heart; for he says, “Because I have hoped in your judgments.” [Note: [Col. 0544D] The printed editions read “from heart and mouth.” We have deleted “and mouth” on the authority of the manuscripts.]

Therefore, hoping in God’s judgments, he does not fear that the word of truth will be taken from his heart. But he knows that there are certain sins which take the word of truth away from the mouth. For God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous acts?” (Ps. XLIX, 16). [Note: [Col. 0545D] “My righteous acts.”]

He did not say, “Why are you forgetful of my ordinances?” [Note: [Col. 0545D] Erasmus, Lipsius, and Par. read “mindful.” Bad. and the manuscripts more correctly have “forgetful.”] Rather, he warned the person who remained in sin, as a sinner, to abstain from the office of preaching. For he wishes the preacher of heavenly teaching to be free from guilt; he wishes his utterances to be handled by the chaste mouth of a chaste body.

We must therefore take care lest at any time the utterance of the word of truth be taken from our mouth. Hence the Apostle’s admonition: “Do not neglect the gift that is in you” (I Tim. IV, 14), lest through negligence and idleness we become unworthy of preaching God’s word.

### 6. One alone is without sin

But the Prophet does not dare to wish to become so free from sin that he forgets that there is only One who did not commit sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found. He therefore adds, “wholly.” Through the modesty of confession, he prays that the word of truth may not be taken from him; and, in honor of him who alone is without sin, he asks that it may not be taken from him wholly, because he remembers himself to be a human being who, through the weakness of nature, cannot be without sin.

### 7. David promises to keep the law, and what is prefigured by the law

V. 44: “And I shall keep your law always, for age and age upon age.” The Prophet fears no end of his life. For his faith is not bounded by the ages; rather, he extends himself to the duty of keeping the law into the infinity of times.

He knows that the altar was built by Moses as an image of the higher altar. He knows also that Aaron the priest was clothed as a representation of the priest shown on the mountain. For God said to Moses: “Go; make all things according to the pattern which I showed you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV, 40).

Therefore he hastens toward those laws of eternal ages. For since the law is a shadow of things to come, that body of the true law must necessarily be eternal. He distinguishes his present duty from that unwearied continuity of perpetual duty, saying: “And I shall keep your law always, for age and age upon age.”

When he says, “always, for an age,” he allows no time in this temporal life for forgetfulness to creep in. But when he adds, “and for age upon age,” he knows that through this shadow of the law one ascends to the ministry of the true and eternal law. [Note: [Col. 0545D] In the final Paris edition, following Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius, “mystery” was substituted, although in the first edition the manuscripts had restored “ministry.” Here the word denotes the execution of the law, and therefore aptly answers the word “I shall keep.”] For he says, “age upon age,” as though a time of time, which will be the age to come after a certain succession of this age. [Note: [Col. 0545D] The word “which” was missing in the earlier printed texts and is restored from the manuscripts.]

### 8. God’s laws after this life

According to the rich man of the Gospel and poor Lazarus, he knows that there is a law for souls released from the body, by which one is separated from another by an impenetrable abyss (Luke XVI, 20). According to the Apostle Paul, he knows that there is also a law of resurrection, in which star differs from star in glory (I Cor. XV, 41).

He knows that there are laws of angels: some, standing before God, praise him with unwearied voice; others stand before the sight of the God invisible to us as though by a law of their own proper duty. [Note: [Col. 0545D] “Legions”; then, “the Cherubim standing by.” [Col. 0546D] The Micy manuscript has “Cherubim standing by,” which was transferred into the first Paris edition. Another Vatican manuscript has “standing by as Cherubim, who [praise] God,” etc.][Note: [Col. 0546D] Par., from the Micy manuscript, reads “more proper.” One Vatican manuscript has “nearer”; Bad. and Lipsius, “of nearer.” With Erasmus and the royal and Alb. manuscripts we prefer “of his own proper duty.”]

He knows also that the angels of little ones behold God’s face daily by a certain law (Matt. XVIII, 10). He therefore knows that there are eternal laws, and is confident that he will keep them all in that age of ages, because he now always observes in this age those things which have been established through a shadow.

### 9. The benefit and cause of an enlarged heart

V. 45: “And I walked in spaciousness, because I sought out your commandments.” The prophet is not constricted; and above he had already said: “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart.” [Note: [Col. 0546D] “The way.” Two manuscripts read “in the way.”]

He knows that amid the sufferings of human tribulations he must always have his heart open toward God. The Apostle himself teaches this, saying: “We are troubled in every way, but not constrained” (II Cor. IV, 8). [Note: [Col. 0546D] “Straitened.”] He knows that the same Apostle glories in this very breadth of heart when he says to the Corinthians: “You are not constrained in us, but you are constrained in yourselves” (II Cor. VI, 12).

Here too the prophet is open, whose heart is open to God, when God says: “And I shall dwell in them and walk among them” (ibid. 16). [Note: [Col. 0546D] Par. has “prophecy.” Other books more correctly have “prophet,” whose heart is open to God.] Therefore the hearts of sinners are narrow, and a defiled mind does not receive God as its guest.

For the incomprehensible God requires a spacious dwelling; and therefore the prophet walks in breadth, because the dwelling of God speaking in him is within him. [Note: [Col. 0546D] “God” is absent from two manuscripts and from the old editions. Shortly before, “incomprehensible” means one whom no place is sufficient to contain.] He teaches the cause of his breadth, saying: “Because I sought out your commandments.”

Let us recall the practice of our nature: whenever we devote ourselves to reading and examine God’s commandments and precepts, into how great a breadth of understanding the narrowness of our minds is expanded, and how open the understanding of our humility becomes for divine desires. But through consciousness of our sins every breadth of the soul is constricted; all things become difficult and narrow when we are unworthy of the indwelling of God’s word.

### 10. “Kings” may mean earthly rulers or saints

But the prophet, walking in breadth, must be occupied in a duty worthy of the breadth he has received; and indeed he is so occupied. For it follows, V. 46: “And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and was not ashamed.” [Note: [Col. 0547D] “Of the testimonies.” From the opening words of the following section Hilary seems to have read “in your testimonies,” as the Septuagint, Ambrose, and Augustine read it.]

This is the duty of an enlarged heart: that, from the abundance of divine teaching dwelling within it, words may proceed. [Note: [Col. 0547D] “Indwelling.” Three manuscripts, with Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius, read “from the divine indwelling,” etc.]

For the prophet speaks steadfastly, proclaiming God against the rulers of the earth. This sense has a double meaning. First, according to the Lord’s commands, Christ must be preached by us before kings and authorities (Matt. X, 18); nor ought earthly powers to frighten us (ibid. 26), so that, casting aside all shame, we should not deny with steadfast and public faith the God who will deny those who deny him (ibid. 33).

The passage may also be referred to those of whom the Apostle says: “Already you reign without us—and would that you did reign!” (I Cor. IV, 8). [Note: [Col. 0547D] “You reign, and would that you reigned.”] That is, the prophet may have spoken God’s testimonies as though in the sight of saints, who are often called kings of the earth; and he may not have been ashamed to set forth, by his preaching, the teachings of heavenly doctrine.

The reading itself offers a twofold interpretation: because both meanings are readily understood from the testimonies of Scripture, either both may be thought intended, or whichever seems more probable may be chosen.

### 11. The law must be in the mouth, mind, and heart

V. 47: “And I meditated upon your commandments, which I loved exceedingly.” Therefore it is not enough that we speak in God’s testimonies; we must also review all the commandments of the law in prolonged meditation. [Note: [Col. 0547D] Our manuscript too has “to retain by daily meditation.” All our manuscripts have “daily”; then the Micy and Vatican manuscripts read “to retain by meditation.”]

Nor is meditation alone useful unless the law itself which is meditated upon is loved. Nor is it enough to love with ordinary love unless what is loved is loved exceedingly. Therefore the prophetic utterance sets forth this whole sequence of perfect reasoning: “And I meditated upon your commandments, which I loved exceedingly.”

### 12. It must also be in the hands

But neither meditation on the law nor love lavished upon it is sufficient unless the fruit of works and the effectiveness of the will follow. Nor did the prophet stop at this. For he says, V. 48: “And I raised my hands to your commandments which I loved greatly.” [Note: [Col. 0548D] “And I lifted.”]

He raised his hands to the commandments that he loved: certainly not hands that are insulting or arrogant, but hands serving the commandments of humility, devoted to works of mercy, and carrying out the precepts of faith. [Note: [Col. 0548D] “Directed.”]

The service of work must always be intent and must never cease through the feigned idleness of negligence. The prophet testifies that he remains in this also, saying: “And I exercised myself in your ordinances.” Exercise shows constancy in action. He therefore teaches that his observance of the commandments is frequent and always intent, as he now exercises himself in the ordinances of the present law—the law shadowed forth from future realities—in preparation for the effects of those heavenly ordinances mentioned above. [Note: [Col. 0548D] Only the Paris edition, with the Micy manuscript, reads “service.”]

## LETTER VII: Zain

“Remember your word [below: ‘remember your word’] to your servant, in which you gave me hope. This comforted me in my humiliation, because your utterance will give me life [Hilary: ‘gave me life’]. The proud acted unjustly exceedingly; but I did not turn aside from your law. I remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and was comforted [Hilary: ‘exhorted’]. Faintness of spirit seized me because of [Hilary: ‘not because of’] sinners abandoning your law. Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my sojourn. I remembered your name in death [Hilary: ‘at night’], O Lord, and kept your law. This came to me because I sought out your ordinances.”

### 1. All Scripture calls us to eternal hope

Every word of God contained in the divine Scriptures calls us to hope in heavenly goods. Therefore the prophet, confident that he has remained in all God’s commandments, firmly says, V. 49: “Remember your word to your servant.” [Note: [Col. 0548D] Par., from the Micy manuscript, has “your words,” supported by the Greek *tōn logōn sou* (“your words”); but this is opposed by what follows and by the other editions and manuscripts. Moreover, below in no. 3, *memoror* (“I remember”) governs not the accusative but the genitive.]

Is God forgetful of his promise? Far be it that any kinds of human weakness should be believed able to creep into the eternal and unwearied Power. But the prophet, who has believed God’s promises, who is held by desire for heavenly things, and who has hoped for future things through contempt for present things, does not remind God to remember his word. Rather, he prays that God may remember his word in him, his servant: that is, that he may be judged worthy for God to deign to remember his word in him—the word in which he gave hope. [Note: [Col. 0548D] The word “God,” omitted in the earlier printed texts, is restored from the manuscripts.]

And hope ought not to be empty or preached merely in words, but demonstrated in the facts themselves: so that, if weaknesses, persecutions, losses, bereavements, or insults should occur, we may be comforted against these threats and powers of the present age by hope in eternal promises.

### 2. Hope comforts the afflicted; God’s word gives life

We are indeed taught all these things, but the prophet has now undergone them all, saying, V. 50: “This comforted me in my humiliation, because your utterance gave me life.” This refers to the hope which God caused him to hope. [Note: [Col. 0549D] Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and three manuscripts read “which made him hope in God.” Yet we retain with Par. and the Micy manuscript “which God made him hope,” since shortly afterwards hope is said to be granted by the Lord.]

It comforted him in humiliation: that is, when he is despised, mocked, harassed with injuries, or dishonored with insults, knowing that this is the warfare of present trials for him. [Note: [Col. 0549D] The Micy manuscript has “trial.” It is wrongly said on the same basis, Letter 3, no. 12: “Job had undergone the warfare and victory of all human calamities.” Ambrose says concerning this: “I consider the time of trials to be the time of our soul’s humiliation.”]

But amid these battles of his weakness he is comforted by the hope granted by the Lord; and he is given life by God’s utterances. He knows that amid these things there is an exalted glory in heaven for his humiliation. He knows that a soul renewed by God’s utterances contains within itself, as it were, nourishment for eternal life. [Note: [Col. 0549D] The printed editions read “filled.” The manuscripts more suitably have “refreshed.” For this, Ambrose says on the same verse, is “the living substance of our soul, by which it is nourished, fed, and governed; nor is there anything else that causes the rational soul to live.”]

Living in God’s utterances, he is not moved by the empty glory of the proud. For he knows that his own poverty is richer than their abundance. He knows that his fasts are satisfied with heavenly and evangelical blessing; he knows that his humility will be rewarded with the glorious prize of honor.

And therefore he adds, V. 51: “The proud acted unjustly exceedingly; but I did not turn aside from your law.” Amid the excessive and consummate injustices of the proud—for they acted very unjustly—the prophet does not turn aside from God’s law by any deviation.

### 3. God’s judgments must be remembered continually

But one who does not turn aside from God’s law ought to remember God’s judgments. In every kind of our life, the remembrance of divine judgment must be implanted and retained in us, so that whenever we act, with the remembrance of judgment dwelling in us—or rather, never departing from us—our works may serve God’s commandments. [Note: [Col. 0550D] The words “must be implanted and retained in us” are restored from the manuscripts, having been wrongly rejected in the Paris edition.]

Blessed will be whoever does all things not without remembrance of divine judgment. The prophet professes this concerning himself, saying, V. 52: “I remembered your judgments from of old, and was exhorted.”

This is now only “from of old,” not also “from age to age,” because all God’s judgments concerning us were established from the times of this age and world. [Note: [Col. 0550D] Par. reads, “But in these he was constrained,” and shortly afterward “pressing” instead of “attacking.”] In these judgments he exhorted himself: amid these whirlwinds of the world and these battles of bodily sufferings, the remembrance of God’s judgments encouraged his humility toward endurance and victory over the evils that assailed him.

### 4. David’s holiness: when struck, the saint grieves not his own condition but that of the striker

Then follows, V. 53: “Faintness of spirit seized me because of sinners abandoning your law.” [Note: [Col. 0549D] “Of spirit.”]

The prophet’s own virtues are not sufficient for his hope of eternal life: neither that he placed hope in God’s word; nor that he comforted himself in this same hope; nor that he is given life by God’s utterance; nor that he does not turn aside from the law; nor that he is always exhorted by the remembrance of God’s judgments. [Note: [Col. 0550D] The printed editions and the royal manuscript read “that he by remembrance.” The reading of the Vatican and Micy manuscripts seems truer: “that he always,” etc.]

Indeed, he is even wearied by sorrow at human impiety, and is faint because of the irreligious impieties of men. [Note: [Col. 0549D] “He exhorts remembrance of the judgments.” Shortly afterwards, “injustices” for “impieties.”] For every saint, when struck, pities not the humiliation of the one struck—himself—but the insolence of the one striking; just as a father insulted by a frenzied son, or a physician by a deranged patient, feels grief not because of what he has endured, but because the person whom he wished to be well has, in madness, inflicted an injury upon him.

And when one member suffers, according to the Apostle, the other members suffer with it (I Cor. XII, 26). Accordingly, faintness takes hold of the prophet because of sinners abandoning God’s law: he is wearied by the danger of wicked and irreligious people through the feeling of one who pities and grieves, as though members of his own body were in part sick.

### 5. How Psalms ought to be read, heard, and sung

He himself, so far as concerns him, remains always intent upon the ordinances of God; and in every place wherever he dwells, the hymn of religious confession never departs from his lips. For he says, verse 54: “Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my sojourning.” By his own example he teaches that the melodies of the Psalms, once received into the ears, must be retained in the heart, and that these offices of the mouth must continually be repeated. He does not read and hear carelessly, as he himself teaches; nor, after the manner of our irreligion, does he read the divine utterances with eyes occupied elsewhere or inattentive, or receive them only to forget them at once. Rather, they are songs to him—that is, sung without interruption.

Moreover, by saying, “in the place of my sojourning,” he teaches that the practice of psalmody must never be absent from any place of whatever kind. For he does not say, “in my sojourning,” but “in the place of my sojourning”: that is, in whatever dwelling he happened to remain. He understands himself to be a stranger in this world, yet God’s ordinances are always songs to him.

### 6. The benefit of nocturnal prayers

But he shows how much the ordinances of God are songs to him, since he omits no time in which he is not engaged in that work of the heavenly mysteries. For he says, verse 55: “In the night I remembered your name, O Lord, and kept your law.” He knows that the divine name must especially be remembered by us in the nighttime. He knows that then above all we must retain the keeping of God’s law, when impure desires steal into the mind. When the impulses of vices agitate the body after food recently taken, then God’s name must be remembered; then his law must be kept, establishing chastity, self-control, and the fear of God.

He knows that at this time especially God must be prayed to, entreated, and propitiated, saying elsewhere: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6:7). The mind must not be relaxed in the dangerous idleness of nocturnal vigils; rather, it must be occupied in prayers, entreaties, and confessions of sins, so that, when the opportunity for bodily vices is greatest, those very vices may especially be broken by remembrance of the divine law.

### 7.

There follows, verse 56: “This has happened to me, because I have sought out your ordinances.” This refers to remembrance, by which he remembered God’s name in the nights. And when he says, “This has happened to me,” he means that it is not something suddenly returning or assumed temporarily, but something always remaining within him, established within him by a kind of work of faith. It has happened to him because he has sought out the ordinances. Therefore it is useful to search out God’s ordinances without any interruption of time, because through seeking them we keep his remembrance perpetual within us, in Christ Jesus, to whom is glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER VIII. Heth

“The Lord is my portion. I said that I would keep your law. I entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your word. Because I considered my ways, and turned my feet toward your testimonies; I am ready, and have not been troubled, to keep your commandments. The cords of sinners have entangled me; yet I have not forgotten your law. At midnight I rose to confess to you concerning the judgments of your righteousness. I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments. The earth is full of the Lord’s mercy; teach me your ordinances.”

### 1. The Book of Psalms among the Greeks corrected from the Hebrew

When we read several manuscripts of the Psalms, we too had supposed that the verse which is first under the eighth letter—namely, “The Lord is my portion”—belonged among the eight verses of the preceding, seventh letter. For this is how it was written in the Latin manuscripts and also in some Greek ones; indeed, the sense seemed more complete that way. But when we read the Book of Psalms among the Greeks corrected according to the Hebrews, we found that this verse was not the last of the seventh letter, but the first of the eighth. Therefore, in accordance with this knowledge, we too have undertaken to treat of it.

### 2. Whose portion God is

For he begins thus, verse 57: “The Lord is my portion. I said that I would keep your law.” Rare indeed is anyone who has such confidence as to dare say that God is his portion. One must renounce the world and all its things if God is to be our portion. But if ambition holds us fast, if concern for money occupies us, if the attractions of lust seize us, if the affairs of household property delay us, God will not be our portion, while we are held by possession of worldly cares and vices.

### 3. God’s ministers have no earthly portion in the Law

When Moses was commanded to distribute portions of the land of settlement among the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, this command was given him concerning the Levitical tribe: “The sons of Levi shall have neither portion nor lot in the midst of their brethren” (Deut. 10:9), because the Lord God is their portion. And again we remember it written: “I, the Lord, am their portion” (Num. 18:20). Therefore the Law intended that those serving God should have no earthly portion, because God is their portion.

### 4. Peter has no possession

That preacher of the Gospel, Peter, also remembers that he possesses no share in human property when, asked for alms, he replies: “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you” (Acts 3:6). What is this, Peter, that you possess? You had renounced all things for your Lord, saying: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall we have?” (Matt. 19:27). And he had answered you: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (ibid., 28). And by your example he promised to all others who left everything that they would receive a hundredfold and afterwards possess eternal life.

What, then, is this, Peter, that you have? Certainly you have it; and I do not dare say that you possess more than a hundredfold. Yet I say that you possess without any multiplication of calculation. For you say: “What I have, this I give you: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, rise and walk.” O blessed possession! O perfect portion of God! You do not bestow earthly things, but dispense the riches of nature, and restore the losses caused by a defective birth. You command one born lame to walk, and urge a man of many years to move with an unaccustomed step. Such riches are granted by the one whose portion is God.

Paul too knows the glory of his riches, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Such is the Apostle’s glory; such is his portion.

### 5. The better portion belongs to those who renounce the world. What the hundredfold is in this life

Therefore, after the manner of human inheritances, let us choose the portion which is better and more useful. If, in dividing an inheritance among co-heirs, someone strives to obtain the more advantageous share, with how much more eager concern should we choose the portion of the heavenly inheritance? The Lord promises a hundredfold; and the hundredfold is not eternal, but present. The recompense of eternal goods, however, is immeasurable and infinite; whereas under the definition of a hundredfold, the measure of present things is enclosed.

But I wonder whether Peter’s portion exceeded this hundredfold. Certainly, according to the Lord’s command, the hundredfold gift is to be hoped for now, in this world, when all worldly things have been left behind. For God is our portion, who says: “And I will dwell in them.” Therefore the reward of the hundredfold is now that God should dwell in this little earthly body of ours. But why do I say, “dwell”? He himself also says: “And I will walk in them” (2 Cor. 6:16). The faithful heart is an open and spacious possession for God, that he may dwell and walk there.

But he who dwells, he who walks—what third thing did he add? “And I will be their God” (ibid.). Behold the portion promised to us by him: that we may be a dwelling-place for God, and, while he walks in us, that he himself may be our possession—if we renounce a perishable earthly possession, if we reject the inheritance of transitory things, if, while living, we depart from the world. For what reward is it to have left the world after the body has died and been dissolved as the soul departs? We must be without it by despising it. We must know it not by ignorance of its pleasures. We must die to it while we do not live for it. Paul knows that he no longer lives for himself, saying: “For what I live, now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

### 6.

Therefore the Prophet, living not for the world in accordance with the Apostle, says steadfastly and freely: “The Lord is my portion. I said that I would keep your law.” He has retained the manner which he employed above when he promised that he would keep God’s law. For he is not understood to speak of the law which he was keeping outwardly, since he confesses rather that he will keep it than that he does keep it.

### 7. David desires to see God, not with the eyes of flesh

There follows, verse 58: “I entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your word.” We remember that Moses entreated God that he might see him (Exod. 33:18). Perhaps the prayer of this Prophet will be thought related to that petition. But he remembers God’s saying: “No human being shall see my face and live.” Does he then ask that what he remembers was denied to Moses should be granted to himself?

Yet, although he is earlier than the evangelical saying, he nevertheless remembers that this blessedness of faith is reserved, as it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Therefore, although he knows that it was said in the Law that no one sees God’s face and lives, and although he does not doubt from the evangelical beatitude that all the pure in heart shall see God, he has expressed the longing of his desire with the restraint of perfect modesty, saying: “I entreated your face with my whole heart.”
