He knows that it is now impossible for him to see what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and what has not entered into the human heart. He knows that the glory of God is invisible to fleshly eyes. He remembers—not merely that the light of human sight is dim beside the splendors of angels—but that human bodily eyes could not bear even the glory of Moses’ face (Exod. 34:30).

### 8. How ardent is his desire

But let us measure the Prophet’s desires by human desires. With what anxious expectation do people run to the public appearances of kings? And what joy there is for those who see them when they present themselves to be looked upon! What, then, must we think this man, capable of the heavenly Spirit, wishes? With what burning longing does he desire to behold God, who measures that invisible majesty by the splendors of angels and by Moses’ glory, and knows that even those worthy of God’s presence will receive glory from beholding glory: that vision alone, and the condescension of contemplated majesty, will illumine them?

The holy Apostle, understanding this, speaks thus: “We all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, are transformed into that same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). And because he knows that this is impossible now for these bodily eyes, he desires it with his whole heart. And he whose portion is God confidently entreats his face, because, although no human being sees God’s face and lives, all the pure in heart shall see God. Therefore he asks this mercy from God: that the blessedness of seeing his face may come to him. And he asks it not without reason or without indicating the manner in which it may be bestowed.

### 9. God’s goodness and severity must both be considered

For he says: “Have mercy on me according to your word.” It is the voice of modest faith to entreat God’s mercy not according to consciousness of one’s sins, but according to God’s own words. He knows that God is also “a consuming fire” to sinners. For Moses says: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). He knows that the same God is light to the faithful, of whom the Prophet himself says elsewhere: “You shine wonderfully from the holy mountains” (Ps. 75:5).

The Apostle likewise distinguishes this pattern of God’s goodness and severity when he says: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward those who have fallen, but goodness toward you” (Rom. 11:22); and again: “Unless you remain in goodness, you too will be cut off; but they, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in” (ibid., 22–23). The Prophet awaits God’s goodness when he says: “Have mercy on me.” For he knows that no one who lives is without sin, and that all who are placed in the flesh need God’s mercy. Yet he is not forgetful of his duty and devotion when he says, “according to your word”: namely, that word by which God both announces punishment to sinners and promises the blessedness of eternal life to those who believe in him.

### 10. Each person should deliberate beforehand about what he is to do

Then follows, verse 59: “Because I considered my ways, and turned my feet toward your testimonies.” From the things which the Prophet recalls that he does or has done, he teaches what we too ought to do. For he considers his ways, and after considering them directs his foot toward God’s testimonies. He did nothing which he had not first examined in thought. He did not move his tongue to its task, put forth his foot toward any work he was going to perform, or stretch out his hand to do anything, unless he had first considered all these matters and thought had brought action and effect to the matters considered.

Thus he first surveyed all the paths of his life; and when he found one pleasing and commendable to himself, he then set his foot upon it. That is, having examined all the paths of human action, after considering what was useful to him, he turned the foot of his faith toward the divine testimonies. For thought cannot fear anything sudden, new, or unforeseen, when, by the judgment of counsel, all things that usually occur are anticipated, determined beforehand, and encountered. This is taught in the following verse.

### 11. Nothing disturbs one so prepared

For after the Prophet had considered his ways and turned his foot toward God’s testimonies, he says freely, verse 60: “I am ready, and have not been troubled, to keep your commandments.” Whoever prepares himself for something is prepared for that upon which his meditation is fixed by long practice, lest some force of sudden disturbance cast him off, unwatchful and unwary, from the resolution of his purpose.

The Prophet therefore knows that the world has very many stumbling-blocks. He knows that powers hostile and opposed to human nature lie in ambush. He knows that the reputation and ambition of worldly glory are dangerously sweet. He knows that encounters with wanton women are snares for chaste eyes. He knows that shameful bodily desires creep in through the attraction of agreeable pleasure. He knows that the other kinds of vices press in through seductive approaches. He also knows that he is subject to many hatreds of the irreligious and, because of the preaching of God and the teaching of piety, will be afflicted by various insults from persecutors.

Therefore, lest he might be troubled when so many and such great snares pressed upon him, he prepared himself against all these disasters of faith, saying: “I am ready, and have not been troubled, to keep your commandments.”

### 12. Paul’s example

The blessed Apostle has a corresponding confidence in this preparation of his, saying: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we have been counted as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we overcome and prevail through him who loved us” (Rom. 8:35 ff.).

And because he had prepared himself to endure these things, lest through them he might be separated from love, he added: “For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor powers, neither things present nor things to come, neither virtues, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (ibid., 38–39). No kinds of things that can happen disturb the Apostle, prepared and strengthened by such hope.

### 13. Exhortation to steadfastness

Therefore let this confidence and this utterance be in us as well, so that when desires creep in, passions press upon us, dangers weary us, and punishments torment us, we may dare to say: “I am ready, and have not been troubled, to keep your commandments.” Our Lord, the only-begotten Son of God, among his other commands says to his disciples: “Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid” (John 14:1).

Against whatever disturbance may arise from events, there is need of the firmness resulting from long preparation, so that faith, robust and strengthened, may keep God’s commandments.

### 14. Why sins are cords

The Prophet immediately adds the purpose for which he prepared himself and was not troubled so as to fail in keeping God’s commandments. He says, verse 61: “The cords of sinners have entangled me; yet I have not forgotten your law.” We are taught that sins are cords by Isaiah, who says: “Woe to those who bind sins as with a long cord” (Isa. 5:18): that is, ever drawing out sins like a long rope, which grows large from many small strands.

These are also the bonds of offenses by which human minds are tied, concerning which it is written in Proverbs: “Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins” (Prov. 5:22). For the devil binds and fastens us, and entangles us in these cords of vices, spreading snares throughout the whole course of our life. That he binds, we have learned in the Gospels, where it is said: “This daughter of Abraham Satan bound for eighteen years” (Luke 13:16). Therefore he binds by every kind of vice: by the habit of drunkenness, by desires for pleasures, and by the guilt of unbelief.

But amid these snares of cords, forgetfulness of the Law must not be allowed. For we ought to be prepared so that, if at any time these snares bind us about, we may cast them off, and may remember God’s Law at all times.

### 15. Why the Prophet rises at midnight

And indeed the Prophet remembers it, saying, verse 62: “At midnight I rose to confess to you concerning the judgments of your righteousness.” He does not spend whole nights sleeping, nor is he kept idle in bed. He rises to confess to God not only by night, but at midnight. He remembers this to be the time when the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck by the most deserved disaster for their impious obstinacy (Exod. 12:29); therefore during these hours he does not yield himself to sleep, lest he be joined to Egypt’s destruction.

At this time of night, when the bridegroom enters, the wise virgins will enter the wedding-feast with lamps (Matt. 25:6); therefore he watches, lest he deserve to be shut out with the foolish. At this time, as Paul and Silas the Apostles sing psalms, chains and bonds are loosed (Acts 16:25); therefore he does not sleep, lest he be bound.

The entire time of night is not possessed by sleep, nor does forgetfulness of his duty creep upon him in the repose of midnight; for he rises to confess to God. Confession, however, must not always be referred to sins; it must also be understood as praise of God. Now, therefore, he confesses to God concerning the judgments of his ordinances. He praises God because he has decreed nothing except in the righteousness of his judgments.

### 16. There are many sharers in Christ. David’s modesty. Who is a companion of those who fear God

We then read, verse 63: “I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments.” We remember the Apostle’s saying: “We have become partakers of Christ” (Heb. 3:14). We also remember that certain persons are indicated as companions of God in the forty-fourth Psalm, where it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.” Therefore, according to the Apostle and the Prophet, there are many partakers of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Whoever remains in righteousness will be his partaker, because he himself is righteousness. Whoever persists in truth will be his partaker, because he himself is truth. Whoever walks in newness of life will be his partaker, because he himself is resurrection. Therefore, though the Prophet knows that there are many partakers of God, he now, in a modest and restrained declaration concerning himself, remembers that he is a partaker of Christ because he himself has both been made and called a christ (an anointed one); yet he confesses himself rather to be the companion of all who fear God.

A person is also then a companion of those who fear God when he suffers with those who suffer, weeps with those who weep, and, as a member of the same body, feels pain at another member’s pain. Therefore let him be a companion of those who fear God through this sharing in sufferings. But whoever, through his arrogance, despises, provokes, or dishonors one who believes in Christ and has been redeemed by Christ is not a companion of those who fear God, since he is not their fellow-sharer in enduring sufferings.

### 17. Two kinds of those who fear God

The Prophet did not state this nakedly or in isolation when he says: “I am a companion of all who fear you.” Many fear God and yet are disobedient; many fear God and yet are unbelieving. Their created condition subjects them indeed to the fear of God, but the perversity of their own will calls them away from obedience to God.

Therefore it would not have been sufficient for the Prophet to say, “I am a companion of all who fear you,” unless he had added, “and keep your commandments.” For the fear of faith consists in obedience alone, and religious awe consists in following. Thus he is their companion who proves his own fear by keeping God’s commandments.

### 18. God bestows his gifts on the righteous and the unrighteous

Then follows, verse 64: “Your mercy, O Lord, fills the earth; teach me your ordinances.” The earth is full of God’s mercy—though it is defiled, corrupt, irreligious, unfaithful, and lost. And if anyone should perhaps dare with impious mouth to accuse the Prophet of falsehood, as though he believed that God’s mercy had not been poured out over all the earth, let him recall that the Lord said in the Gospels: “Be good as your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous” (Matt. 5:45, 48).

For God is patient and merciful. Since he prefers the repentance of sinners to their death (Ezek. 17:23), he bestows his gifts upon righteous and unrighteous alike, granting each person, through great long-suffering, a time for repentance.

### 19. David desires the Lord as his teacher

And because the Prophet remembers that he must always hope for this goodness of God’s patience and for the perfection which is bodily shadowed forth beneath those ordinances of the Law, he says: “Teach me your ordinances.” He had read all the ordinances in the Law; but because he hoped for heavenly realities, prefigured in earthly ones, he does not need an earthly teacher.

For he prays that he may be taught by the one who says: “Ask, and it shall be given to you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). The Prophet disdains to have a key opened or given to him by a teacher of the Law, while awaiting the Lord Jesus Christ as teacher of heavenly knowledge, to whom is glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER IX. Teth

“You have dealt kindly with your servant, O Lord, according to your word. Teach me your goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed your commandments. Before I was humbled, I myself sinned; therefore I have kept your word. You are good, O Lord; and in your goodness teach me your ordinances. The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me; but I will search out your commandments with my whole heart. Their heart has been curdled like milk; but I have meditated on your law. It is good for me that you humbled me, that I might learn your ordinances. The law of your mouth is good for me, above thousands of gold and silver.”

### 1. The purpose of Psalm 118. Thanks must be given to God in adversities

Already at the beginning of the Psalm we mentioned that it contains nothing other than teaching for human life, by which we might be instructed toward the knowledge of God as though by the elementary letters of children. For through his own person the Prophet establishes us in how we ought to conduct ourselves in every kind of divine service, so that through the discipline of the instruction we have received we may keep the order of faith. This is taught by the very first verse of the ninth letter. Thus it is said, verse 65: “You have dealt kindly with your servant, O Lord, according to your word.”

Perhaps some will suppose that the Prophet speaks of prosperity and returns thanks to God for things that have happened favorably to him. But he knows that thanks must also be given to God amid adverse circumstances. He knows that in every suffering and tribulation, the one by whose judgment these things come upon us must be honored with thanksgiving. He knows that a physician who loves does not spare the decayed recesses of wounds. He remembers that fathers’ severity toward their children is loving. He desires to be reproved by trials and approved by patience before God; and in what are considered adversities he gives thanks.

### 2. In all things God provides well for us

The verse which follows teaches that this is the meaning in which we should believe the Prophet prayed, saying: “You have dealt kindly with your servant, O Lord, according to your word. Teach me your goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed your commandments” (v. 66).

Whatever, therefore, God does to his servant is good, for he does it according to his word. And whatever is according to his word cannot be considered evil, because the will of him who alone is good is full of goodness.

### Editorial and textual notes

The following notes occur in the supplied text, in order.

- [Col. 0550D] “In whatever dwelling-place he lives.”
- [Col. 0550D] “To be retained.”
- [Col. 0550D] “He heard”; and below, “he received.”
- [Col. 0551D] In the Vatican manuscript, the words *at midnight* are inserted after “to be prayed to”; this is a gloss.
- [Col. 0551D] Augustine labors greatly to explain this expression and refers it to the night, since the Greek does not allow it to be referred to the law. Nobilius points out that it is a Hebraism, and that Jerome therefore translated it, “This has happened to me,” that is, “This good has befallen me.” Our Hilary and Ambrose interpret this good as the remembrance of God’s judgments. For the word “remembrance” did not precede, to which the pronoun “this” might be referred.
- [Col. 0551C] “Remaining.”
- [Col. 0551D] Manuscript Mic.: “but remaining with him.”
- [Col. 0551D] The Leipzig and Paris editions read: “through a more diligent remembrance of them we continually retain ourselves,” etc., without any authority.
- [Col. 0551D] It is absent from the royal manuscript. Hence it is clear how great authority, for Hilary, belonged to that book corrected according to the Hebrews: because of it he departed from the interpretation which he approved and which most manuscripts confirmed. He indicates that this edition was either recent or had only recently become known to him, when he declares that he changed the opinion he had formed from other manuscripts on the basis of its latest reading. Did he have this book in view in Letter 3, no. 12, Letter 4, no. 1, and elsewhere, when he praises the Greek translation from the Hebrew? Ambrose also mentions the same codex in his eighth sermon on this Psalm, no. 21: “Most codices,” he says, “place this little verse, which is first of the eighth letter, last in the seventh letter; but the Book of Psalms corrected according to the Hebrews among the Greeks taught us that this verse must be joined to the eighth letter.” [Cols. 0551D, 0552D]
- [Col. 0551C] “That I might keep” is absent.
- [Col. 0552D] Thus the manuscripts; but the printed editions read “to keep,” although Hilary expressly observes below, no. 6, that the Prophet does not profess to keep the law, but rather that he will keep it. The Greek is τοῦ φιλάξασθαι, “to keep.”
- [Col. 0552D] The word “children” is restored from the manuscripts.
- [Col. 0552C] “The law given.”
- [Col. 0552D] In the royal and Albinus manuscripts: “the law given.”
- [Col. 0553C] Formerly, “a hundredfold.”
- [Col. 0553D] The printed editions read “a hundredfold,” against the manuscripts.
- [Col. 0553C] “Work”; a little below, “the glory of his riches.”
- [Col. 0553D] The printed text reads “you repay a work”; it is corrected from the manuscripts.
- [Col. 0553D] We correct to “the glory of his riches” from the royal and Albinus manuscripts; previously the text read otherwise.
- [Col. 0553C] “We would choose the portion of the heavenly inheritance.”
- [Col. 0553D] The printed editions read “we choose.” Manuscript Mic. has “we choose”; the royal and Albinus manuscripts, “we select”; the Vatican manuscript, “we ought to select.”
- [Col. 0553D] In the royal and Albinus manuscripts, “of present things” is omitted, not wrongly. Hilary’s reasoning seems to be this: the recompense of eternal goods is immeasurable; but a hundredfold is a finite measure; therefore it does not belong to eternal recompense.
- [Col. 0553C] We supply the word “God,” absent from the printed editions.
- [Col. 0553D] “Not therefore.”
- [Col. 0553D] The printed texts have “not therefore,” as though “is it not therefore?” The particle “now,” substituted from the manuscripts, more suitably signifies that the promise of a hundredfold pertains to the present life.
- [Col. 0553D] Thus our manuscripts; the printed editions read: “the dwelling of God. And while he walks in us, he becomes for us,” etc. Ambrose interprets that reward of a hundredfold in the same way on this same verse. [Col. 0554D]
- [Col. 0553D] “If you slip into earthly possession.”
- [Col. 0554D] The printed texts read “if [you renounce] perishable earthly possession.” Just as above, Letter 3, nos. 3–5, it is stressed that we contract defilement from association with an earthly body, so now also from earthly possession.
- [Col. 0554C] The word *live* was absent in the preceding text; we restored it from our manuscript, which agrees with the other editions.
- [Col. 0554D] The printed editions read “it is no longer I who live.” The word *live* is absent from our manuscripts, as from the Greek.
- [Col. 0554C] The words “I said that I would keep your law,” omitted in the printed editions, are also passed over by our very ancient book.
- [Col. 0554D] The words “I said that I would keep your law,” omitted in the printed editions, are restored from the manuscripts.
- [Col. 0554D] The printed editions wrongly read “I remember.”
- [Col. 0554D] This passage weakens and entirely removes the suspicion arising from certain statements in the exposition of Psalm 64, nos. 5 and 18, already addressed at p. 193, note. For here all the pure in heart, without exception, are openly proclaimed as those who will see God and therefore dwell with God in heaven.
- [Col. 0555D] The Verona manuscript does not contain “image.”
- [Col. 0555D] “Image” is absent from the royal and Albinus manuscripts.
- [Col. 0555D] “Your God.”
- [Col. 0555D] Our manuscripts read “your God”; the sacred exemplars, “your God.”
- [Col. 0556D] The Paris edition adds “wrongly.” In these passages Hilary interprets *to consider* as to foresee and provide for what must be done or will happen.
- [Col. 0556D] “And then.” A little later, “after matters had been considered.” Then, “before all things.” The Erfurt, Leipzig, and Paris editions read “and then”; the manuscripts more fittingly read “when,” as does the Badius edition, with “unless” understood. The printed editions then read “thought had brought [something] to the matters considered.” We prefer the manuscripts.
- [Col. 0556D] Two manuscripts read “the ambition of glory,” omitting “reputation.”
- [Col. 0556D] Thus the manuscripts, where the printed editions have “destructions.”
- [Col. 0557D] Badius and Erfurt read “father”; Leipzig, “prepared”: corruptly.
- [Col. 0557D] (a) The royal and Albinus manuscripts omit the words enclosed in brackets.
- [Col. 0557D] “Faith.”
- [Col. 0557D] (b) Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “by faith.” Related is the statement in the exposition of Psalm 63, no. 6: “For it is not our fear but faith that merits God’s mercy; and the proof of long preparation is necessary if we are to deserve to be heard.”
- [Col. 0557D] (c) The printed texts read “they stretch out,” or “are stretched out, as with a long cord”; they are corrected with the aid of the manuscripts, where the word *stretching* must be referred to the particle “woe.”
- [Col. 0557D] “Bonds” instead of “bands,” supported by the Greek σειραῖς, “cords.”
- [Col. 0557D] “Of impiety.”
- [Col. 0558D] (d) The word “whole” was lacking in the earlier printed editions and is restored from the manuscripts, although we would prefer “of the whole [night].”
- [Col. 0558D] “With the oil of exultation above your companions,” in accordance with the Greek ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως, “oil of exultation.”
- [Col. 0558D] (e) The manuscript reads “above your companions.” We do not doubt that Hilary read it thus, since the same preposition in all manuscripts consistently governs the accusative case.
- [Col. 0559D] Two manuscripts read “redeemed in Christ.”
- [Col. 0559D] The printed editions read “who is not.” The reading of the manuscripts is preferable: namely, “those who fear God.”
- [Col. 0559D] The royal codex with the Albinus manuscript reads: “it is fitting that we be companions, who,” etc.
- [Col. 0559D] “Who is in heaven,” supplied from our manuscript.
- [Col. 0559D] “Amen” is absent.
- [Col. 0559D] Two manuscripts read “long ago already.”
- [Col. 0559D] The printed editions read “it is necessary, and through discipline”; later Paris after Leipzig reads “keep the order,” against the manuscripts.
- [Col. 0559D] “He knows one who does not spare”; later, “one who spares,” without *not*. The Paris edition reads “he knows one who indulges”; all omit the particle *not* before “sparing.” The manuscripts more correctly retain it and here put first: “He knows a loving physician,” that is, one who loves. [Col. 0560D]
- [Col. 0560D] The printed editions read “from God”; the manuscripts, “before God,” where *to be approved* means to become approved and acceptable.
- [Col. 0560D] Our codex does not repeat this little verse [65], but only the following one, where it reads “I have obeyed” for “I have believed.”
- [Col. 0560D] This entire verse 65 is not repeated in the printed editions. It is repeated in our manuscripts, and the following words appear to require this.

3. Believing this, David asks also to know it. Discipline, benefit, knowledge.—The second verse, then, as we have said, expounds the Prophet’s disposition when he prays, saying: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.” He had above confessed that goodness had been shown toward him: why does he pray to be taught it as though ignorant of it? Unless it is because then he rejoiced in a confession of faith, when he believed that whatever was happening to him was good; whereas now, because of human ignorance, he prays to be taught. Yet he wishes to learn that goodness to which discipline is joined. [Note: In the printed editions: “For discipline must be the office of severity”; the manuscripts have “they are corrected.”] For discipline is the necessary work of severity, which rebukes sins and corrects faults. But the correction of faults brings great progress in goodness. Therefore the discipline of severity is good; but the Prophet does not yet know it. For he wishes to be taught not merely goodness and discipline, but also knowledge, showing in this the disposition of his faith: although he does not yet know goodness and discipline, he nevertheless confesses that they are good for him from God. Concerning knowledge we have often observed that both the Apostle (1 Cor. 12:8) and the prophet count it among the chief gifts of spiritual graces (Isa. 11:2). Therefore, as he prays to be taught goodness and discipline, so also knowledge—and to be taught it because he believes God’s commandments—showing that only the faithful and believing can attain instruction in knowledge.

4. Humiliation, correction of sin.—The sense of the same interpretation remains also in the third verse. For he says, VERSE 67: “Before I was humbled, I sinned; therefore I kept thy word.” Tribulation in sufferings does not come upon us before sins have preceded it; nor are we first humbled through suffering before, by the iniquity of our sins, we have become worthy of sufferings. Thus the Prophet teaches that his humiliation is the correction of his sin; and therefore he knows that whatever comes from God is good for him, because he deserved to suffer what he began to suffer. And he knows that discipline is the correction of faults. He sinned first, and was humbled second; and through the discipline of humiliation he must be taught not to sin, and to remain in the words of God, because, having sinned, he has now been humbled and is to remain in God’s commandments so that he may sin no further.

5. Justification, the work of a just thing.—VERSE 68. “Thou art good, O Lord; and in thy goodness teach me thy justifications.” The Prophet knows that God’s justifications are good, because he who established them is good. He knows that nothing happens to him except by God’s justification, because he had first confessed that he sinned and afterwards was humbled. And because above he had prayed to be taught goodness, discipline, and knowledge, he now prays that he may be taught God’s justifications in goodness, because justification is the work of a just thing, which is unknown to him; because the justifications established in the Law [Col. 0562A] contained in themselves the shadow of heavenly justifications.

6. Reproaches of the wicked against the just; how they must be resisted.—Then he added, VERSE 69: “The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me; but with my whole heart I will search thy commandments.” Patiently and with equanimity enduring all things, the Prophet was brought under the reproach of the proud and wicked. For if anyone recalls the reproaches of the three kings against Job, he will understand how deeply the reproach of mockers wounds. For when irreligious persons see God’s servants being corrected through certain sufferings, they commonly reproach them thus: “Where is faith? Where is hope in God? Where is the power of him who helps? Where is the mercy of the good God?” Against these things one needs a steadfast and faithful spirit, intent upon and occupied with God’s commandments, [Col. 0562B] lest he yield when so many iniquities of the proud are multiplied against him, but may always say: “Thou hast done goodness to thy servant, O Lord”; as that glorious and blessed victor over human sufferings said: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

7. Like milk, pleasant in prosperity; like curd, bitter in adversity.—Then follows, VERSE 70: [Note: “It curdled like milk.”] “Their heart has curdled like milk; but I have meditated on thy law.” He says that the heart of the proud [Note: In two manuscripts: “as if milk.”] is like milk curdled. Milk is exceedingly pleasant in appearance and taste; yet through some corruption it commonly curdles, and, departing from the sweetness of its own nature, is spoiled by a useless and bitter taste. Therefore, formerly, when the wicked saw the Prophet in prosperity, they were friends of his happy circumstances, flattering him with an appearance of simplicity, and were like milk. But when, because of this humiliation of the holy man, pride and disdain took hold of them, they curdled from milk; and from pleasant and sweet flatteries they were reduced to the bitterness of a corrupting and coagulating taste. Yet while they had curdled like milk, the Prophet meditated upon God’s law—meditated upon it so as to say what is contained in the following verse.

8. What tribulations accomplish.—VERSE 71. “It is good for me that thou hast humbled me.” Although the iniquity of the proud is multiplied and their heart curdles like milk, the Prophet nevertheless knows that his humiliation is good for him. He knows, according to the Apostle, that power is perfected in weaknesses (2 Cor. 12:9). Every suffering is good; all tribulations are good, through which God’s justifications [Col. 0562D] are known: so that he may correct sinners by humiliation, restrain offenders by severity, and teach the ignorant by instruction. Therefore he says that it is good for him that he was humbled, [Note: “He says”: supplied on the authority of the manuscript.] because through humiliation he would learn God’s justifications. For he sinned before he was humbled; and humiliation is good for him because through it God’s justification is learned.

9. The law of God’s mouth, the law of Christ.—He concluded in this manner, VERSE 72: “The law of thy mouth is good for me beyond [Note: In our book, consistently: “thousands.”] thousands [Col. 0563A] of gold and silver.” The language of this conclusion is not simple. It would have sufficed for the Prophet’s rejoicing to say: “Thy law is good for me.” But when he says “the law of thy mouth,” he intends more to be understood. God spoke the Law through Moses; he spoke through the prophets. But this is God’s law, not also the law of God’s mouth. Now the mouth of God is he who is also the power of God, [Note: The Royal manuscript and Albinus: “who is also the wisdom of God,” namely the Lord; the rest is omitted.] who is also the wisdom of God, who is also the arm of God, who is also the image of God—namely God and our Lord Jesus Christ—saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3); saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (ibid., 4); saying: “Bless those who persecute you, and pray for those who slander and persecute you” (ibid., 44). The Prophet confessed that this law of God’s mouth was good for him—and good [Col. 0563B] not merely by a measured comparison, definition, or degree, but beyond thousands of gold and silver. The expression “thousands” is indefinite; for the law of God’s mouth is good without limit. By comparison with the things most precious on earth, he indicates the usefulness of the good things established by God [Note: “Signifying.” The words “in Christ. Amen” are absent below.] in Christ. Amen. [Note: These final words have been added on the authority of the manuscripts.]

## LETTER X. Jod

“Thy hands made me and [Note: “Prepared.”] formed me” (Hilary: “prepared,” or “fashioned,” me). “Give me understanding, that I may learn thy commandments. Those who fear thee shall see me and rejoice, because I hope” (Hilary: “have hoped”) “in thy words. I have known, O Lord, that thy judgments are equity, and in thy truth [Col. 0563C] thou hast humbled me. Let thy mercy come to be my encouragement, according to thy word to thy servant. Let thy compassions come upon me, and I shall live; because thy law is my meditation. Let the proud be put to shame, because unjustly they have wrought iniquity against me” (below: “upon me”); “but I will exercise myself in thy commandments. Let those who fear thee turn to me, and those who know thy testimonies. Let my heart be undefiled in thy justifications, that I may not be put to shame.”

1. Man surpasses God’s earthly works; for what end he ought to use created things.—It is a common judgment that among all God’s earthly works nothing is more useful than man, nothing more beautiful. For although some things are beautiful and adorned, they indeed testify to the greatness of him who produced them so beautiful; yet they themselves do not perceive the benefit of their appearance, adornment, and constitution. We speak [Col. 0564A] of those things subject to human sight: namely, things created in earth, sea, and air, and things mingled in their several kinds and natures. They are beautiful; but what good will the things created in Ocean, earth, heaven, [Note: Two manuscripts: “in the ether.” The entire phrase may more plainly be rendered thus: “What good will the things created in Ocean, earth, etc., obtain because they have been so created?” Why should animals not attain some good if they have perception?] or air obtain by having been so created? But whatever is in man benefits himself. And this one animal upon earth has been established as rational, understanding, discerning, and perceiving. Of all these kinds of things which are in him, nothing [Note: “To” is lacking in the manuscripts.] benefits [Note: The particle *ad* (“to”) is absent in the printed editions. Later, Lipsius and Paris substituted “in other things” for “and other things,” contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and Hilary’s meaning: he intends that all things, both a man’s own and others’, are destined for human use, while man himself was created for no other end.] anything else except that he may use both himself and other things, and those things among which he was born; and he is to use them to know and venerate him who is the author and parent of such great goods within him.

2. When man is something great; when he loses his name.—From this one may understand that great and remarkable saying of Solomon: “A man is great, and a merciful man precious; but a faithful man must be found.” [Note: “Found.”] For what is so difficult, or what requires such arduous effort, as finding one who remembers that he was made according to God’s image and likeness; who, intent upon the study of divine utterances, has come to know the nature of his soul and body, the origin and nature of both kinds, and finally the end toward which this constitution and origin of his tends? For this reason man is something great. But when, having neglected the knowledge of the matters mentioned above, he falls into vices, he loses this name, being judged unworthy henceforth to be called man. [Note: Manuscript Mic.: “and who is not according to”; and below, “but according to.” The word “but” was inserted at Paris. Hilary’s argument is this: a human being is one made according to God’s image and likeness; but one who falls away from innocence does not retain God’s image and therefore not the name of human being. Scripture, says Ambrose, following Hilary’s traces in commenting on the same verse, calls one a human being who is according to God’s image and likeness; but it calls a sinner not a human being, but either a serpent, horse, etc. And shortly afterward he says to the sinner: “After you sinned, you began to be something else; you ceased to be what you were . . . so that from a human being you might become a serpent, mule, horse, or little fox.”] And one made according to God’s image and likeness [Col. 0564C] bears, according to prophetic and evangelical reproaches, the names either of serpent, brood of vipers, horse, mule, or fox; and when he falls away from innocence, the proper character of his name is [Note: “Will be taken away.”] taken away.

3. The twofold origin of man.—But one who, with earnest faith, has searched out God’s teaching and commandments, and who by striving for innocence wishes to render himself worthy as one made according to God’s image and likeness, may himself use the Prophet’s words, saying, VERSE 73: “Thy hands made me and prepared me.” And in some manuscripts we find it written thus: “Thy hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, that I may learn thy commandments.” And it must undoubtedly be judged not without significance that it was not enough [Col. 0565A] for the Prophet to say, “Thy hands made me,” unless he added, “fashioned,” or “prepared.” But understanding the honor of his own creation, the Prophet intended by this to indicate the special dignity of his origin, saying first: “Thy hands made me.”

4. All things created by the word; man’s creation first deliberated.—In the creation of the world we have learned that all things were made by the word, when it is said, “Let there be light” (Gen. 1:3); “Let there be a firmament” (ibid., 6); “Let the dry land appear” (ibid., 9); “Let the earth bring forth grass, fodder bearing seed according to its kind” (ibid., 11); “Let there be lights in the firmament” (ibid., 14); “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls” (ibid., 20). Therefore everything from which or in which the whole fabric of the world [Col. 0565B] was created takes its origin from a word, and began to subsist in what it is from God’s word. But concerning man God spoke thus: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (ibid., 26). Therefore human nature and origin differ from the formation of all creation; and, uniquely, man’s coming into being is first discussed and affirmed, whereas the rest were commanded to exist without any deliberative decision. Thus the origin of man has this [Note: “First.”] first dignity: it was peculiar to him to be deliberated concerning beforehand.

5. Another privilege: that he is made by God’s hands; what is investigated here.—But this present prophetic saying also contains a great privilege of human origin. For the hands of the Lord did not make cattle, aquatic animals, or birds; nowhere have the Scriptures handed this down. Therefore this is excellent and distinguished in man: he is set apart from the rest by the dignity of the operation. But concerning the establishing of heaven, we read in one place: “I established heaven by my hand” (Isa. 45:12, according to the LXX). Is this element, then, made equal to the creation of man because it too is said to have been established by God’s hand? [Note: The Paris edition alone has “to him.” The argument which Ambrose draws from the LXX wording of Isaiah together with Hilary is not equally supported by the Vulgate, which reads, “My hands stretched out heaven.”] Yet although heaven was made by a hand, man was made by hands. The operation of two hands therefore surpasses the function of one; and what is sufficient for establishing heaven is insufficient in the creation of man. We must, however, understand why the Prophet says that he was made by hands: not only made, but also fashioned or prepared.

6. All things completed by one command of God, but not man.—The creation of all the other elements was both instituted and completed at the very time when they were commanded to subsist; no interval of time separates their beginning from their perfection, for their beginning attained completion in that which had begun. But man, since he contains within himself an inward and outward nature, differing one from the other, and since from two kinds he is constituted as one rational living creature, [Note: “Constituted.” Then, “is constituted” for “is instituted.”] [Note: The manuscripts read “constituted.” Scultetus failed to notice this passage when, among Hilary’s distinctive opinions, he listed the view that Hilary regarded the soul as corporeal. For if the soul is corporeal, man does not consist of two kinds, nor does he contain one nature differing from the other. For we know only two kinds of substances: one corporeal, the other without body.] was instituted with a twofold beginning. For first it was said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26); then secondly: “And God took dust from the earth and fashioned man” (Gen. 2:7).

7. The soul made according to God’s image; then the body formed from earth.—The first work has no origin from another nature assumed from elsewhere. Whatever is then begun by a deliberative decision is incorporeal; [Note: The particle *tum* (“then”), omitted in the printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts. Here and below the incorporeal substance of the soul is again affirmed in such explicit terms that it is difficult to see how later writers failed to correct Scultetus’s error. If Hilary speaks obscurely anywhere in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 5, §8, this should have been understood from these clear statements.] [Col. 0566B] for it is made according to God’s image. It is not God’s image, because the image of God is the firstborn of every creature; but it is according to God’s image, that is, according to the form of the image and likeness. What was then to be created was divine and incorporeal, according to God’s image and likeness: namely, there is in us a certain exemplar of God’s image and an instituted likeness. Therefore in the rational and incorporeal substance of our soul is the first thing which was made according to God’s image. But how greatly the making of the second work differs from the first institution! [Possibly: “from the first.”] God takes dust of the earth. For dust is taken, and earthly matter is formed into a human being, or prepared; and by the work and care of the craftsman it is fashioned from one thing into another. Therefore the first did not take, but made; the second he did not make as the first, but took, and [Note: Here again the printed editions lacked “then,” and the rest was placed somewhat confusedly. Hilary demonstrates that the soul was created from no pre-existent substance, but the body was not.] then fashioned or prepared.

8. “Prepared” may also rightly be said; why God’s hands, rather than hand.—Either reading [Note: Namely both “fashioned” and “prepared”: the body, considered in itself, may be called “fashioned”; but “prepared” if it is considered in relation to the soul, for receiving which it was fitted.] may rightly be understood, because we find both written: that he fashioned it into what it is, namely the bodily form; or prepared it for what is said: “And he breathed into him the spirit of life, and man became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7). Therefore it was prepared or formed for this breathing-in, through which the nature of soul and body was held together in the perfection of life by a kind of covenant of breathed spirit. [Note: Three manuscripts: “might contain the perfection of life . . .” Here Hilary interprets the breathing-in as a third action of God, as it were, in creating man, by which he joined the soul to the body.] Blessed Paul knows that he has a twofold nature within himself, when he delights in the law according to the inward man, and when he sees another law in his members [Col. 0567A] that makes him captive in the law of sin (Rom. 7:22–23). Therefore what is made according to God’s image belongs to the dignity of the soul; but what is formed from earth is the beginning of the bodily form and nature. [Note: “Bodily.”] And because God is understood either to speak to another when he says, “Let us make man,” or because a threefold perfection is recognized in man, made [Note: “And fashioned.”] and prepared beforehand [Note: So the manuscripts, corresponding to “prepared.” The printed editions have “and fashioned.”]—since he is made according to God’s image, formed from earth, and moved into a living soul through the breathing-in of spirit—the Prophet accordingly testifies that he was made and formed by hands, not by hand alone; because in his constitution there is shown an operation not merely of one person, [Note: The printed editions read “solitary.” There is not one explanation alone why God’s hands are said in the plural to have created man. Two are given: first, because it was not the operation of one person; second, because it was not one operation but three.] and likewise a threefold operation.

9. Human ignorance concerning itself; understanding must be sought from God.—And because the Prophet knows that this is deeply hidden and obscure—namely, in what sense he was formed by God’s hands—yet, that he may attain the full and complete account of this understanding, [Note: Manuscripts: “attain.”] he says: “Give me understanding, that I may learn thy commandments.” He speaks as one ignorant of these things, and as one who has not yet attained understanding prays that understanding may be given him. Yet—not men of the Church, I mean, but sophists of the Gentiles—dare to wish to discuss certain matters concerning the constitution of human nature; we too dare to boast that we have attained knowledge of a right and perfect life. But we ought to be taught by this Prophet’s example either to confess our ignorance of divine things or to pray for understanding of what is unknown. It is best to ask God in prayer for knowledge of heavenly commandments, acknowledging the weakness and poverty [Col. 0567C] of our own intellect. For according to the Apostle the first gift of graces is the gift of wisdom, and the next is that of knowledge (1 Cor. 12:8); and therefore the Prophet here too observed this order, saying: “Give me understanding, that I may learn thy commandments.” First he prayed for understanding, then also for knowledge.

10. The sight of the godly is grievous to the ungodly, joyful to the just.—Then follows, VERSE 74: “Those who fear thee shall see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in thy words.” It is the custom of the ungodly to be sorrowful at the sight of religious men. For the drunkard must hate the sober, the unchaste the self-controlled, the unjust the just; and, as though burdened by his conscience, he cannot endure the presence of any holy person. On the other hand, at the sight of a faithful man all religious persons who fear God rejoice; and they are gladdened even by the sight [Col. 0568A] of bodily contemplation alone, just as certain birds and herbs, which merely when seen [Note: Royal manuscript with Albinus: “are useful when looked upon. Therefore useful, etc.” Ambrose likewise, in the same letter, §23: “If there is such great power in natural things, that an animal when seen benefits jaundiced persons,” etc. Pliny, *Natural History*, book 30, chapter 11, identifies the animal: “The bird *icterus* is so called from its color; they relate that, if it is looked upon, that disease is cured and the bird dies.” I think it is called in Latin *galgulus*. Others call it *galbulus*; commonly, *Loriot*.] cure certain illnesses and infirmities. Therefore the presence of a holy person is beneficial to those who fear God, because they must receive some benefit from contemplating him. But the Prophet does not think that in himself only what is subject to [Note: “Public.”] fleeting [Note: So our manuscripts; the printed editions read “public.”] and common eyes ought to be seen. He wishes the uprightness of his life to be perceived; he wishes his justice, religion, and self-control to be seen. For those who fear God will rejoice not merely because they see him, but because they see him hoping in God’s words—and hoping not moderately, nor amid the confused error of human opinion, but declaring freely what follows.

11. The Prophet knows God’s present, not eternal, judgments.—VERSE 75. “I have known, O Lord, that thy judgments are equity, and [Note: At Paris here: “in thy truth”; below, however, “in thy truth.” In both places we have restored “truly” from other editions and two manuscripts, as Jerome translates from the Hebrew, also supported by the Greek, which reads *alētheia*, without *sou* (“thy”).] truly thou hast humbled me.” Elsewhere we recall that the Prophet is accustomed to say: “Give me understanding, and teach me, and I will keep thy commandments.” But now he professes as though he has attained it, saying: “I have known, O Lord, that thy judgments are equity.” Yet here the discourse is not about those eternal judgments, but about present ones. For those eternal judgments are, according to the same Prophet, “like a great deep” (Ps. 35:7); and according to the Apostle, God’s judgments are “unsearchable and inscrutable” (Rom. 11:33). But in these present judgments he knows that whatever happens to him happens by God’s judgment: all tribulations, all afflictions, all hatred in the form of attacks, all assaults of persecutions come upon him by God’s judgment, so that through these [Col. 0568C] he may be approved, corrected, and, as through fire, tested and purified.

12. The distinction between knowledge and faith.—There is, however, something more demanding in knowledge than in faith; and therefore here he did not believe but knew. For faith has the merit of obedience, but does not have the assurance of truth known. The Apostle made a great distinction between knowledge and faith, numbering knowledge later among the gifts of grace. For he proclaimed wisdom first, knowledge next, and faith third; because one who believes may be ignorant of what he believes, but one who has already known cannot, once knowledge has been attained, fail to believe what he has known. See *On the Trinity*, book 8, §10.

13. God’s judgments are just.—Therefore the Prophet admits no uncertainty here about his knowledge that God’s judgments are just: that is, the judgments concerning [Col. 0569A] his humiliation, tribulation, contempt, injury, and pain. For thus he says: “I have known, O Lord, that thy judgments are equity, and truly thou hast humbled me.” It is not without cause, that is, that he is subjected to tribulations; not without cause that he is given over to sufferings; not without cause that he is humbled [Note: “Through injuries.”] by injuries. Rather, in order to expiate the sins of human faults, he is subjected to humiliation by God’s just and true judgments.

14. David does not ask to escape these things, but to bear them courageously by God’s help.—But because he is involved in these sufferings by the equity of divine judgment, [Note: We have removed the following verse of the Psalm, verse 76, wrongly inserted here in the printed editions, and shortly restore it complete on the authority of the manuscripts.] he seeks from God’s mercy encouragement amid his present humiliations, since human weakness is unequal to bearing sufferings, saying, VERSE 76: “Let thy mercy come to be my encouragement [Col. 0569B] according to thy word to thy servant.” Yet he remembers that it is good for him to be humbled, good for him to be subjected to sufferings, and that all the things by which he is troubled are for him the purging of earthly faults. For he does not pray that humiliation and tribulation may be removed from him, but that encouragement in tribulation may be granted him through God’s mercy. Thus he desires [Note: The printed editions: “divine.” The reading “long-lasting,” with the Royal, Vatican, and Albinus manuscripts, is preferable.] to serve in a long-lasting battle amid these weaknesses of his body; he desires to stand in a prolonged conflict against the wickednesses of this world. But he hopes for encouragement from God’s mercy, so that, though troubled and afflicted, he may be strengthened by the help of divine encouragement. Blessed Paul too, having experienced every kind of trial, knows how to use the encouragement of divine mercy, saying: “Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassions and God of all encouragement, [Col. 0569C] who encourages us in every tribulation” (2 Cor. 1:3–4). The Prophet also knows that this encouragement has been promised him [Note: “Having the Father and Lord of compassions.”] by God the Father [Note: Royal manuscript with Albinus: “by that Father.” Micy manuscript with Vatican: “having the Father and Lord of compassions.” Then the printed editions read “who believes himself,” omitting “in.”] and the Lord of compassions, who tests through temptations the one who believes in him. Therefore he added, “according to thy word to thy servant”: that is, according to the promise by which he pledged that he would not abandon those afflicted by sufferings. For he said in the Gospels: “When they deliver you up, do not be anxious how or what you are to speak; for in that hour [Note: “On that day.”] what you are to speak will be given you. For you are not the ones speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matt. 10:19–20). And this concerns the present time.

15. Eternal life comes through God’s mercy; we do not yet truly live; the hope of true life and what nourishes it.—But the Prophet is not forgetful of future hope, saying, VERSE 77: “Let thy compassions come upon me, and I shall live; because thy law is my meditation.” The weakness of bodily nature needs God’s compassions. For it cannot attain the eternity of that blessed life by its own merit unless it is advanced by the compassions [Col. 0570A] of him who is the Father of compassions. The Prophet knows that he does not yet live the life which is life indeed; for no one of us would dare to regard what he now lives as life. For now we are in a body of death, as Paul says: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). And the same Prophet testifies to this thus: “Thou hast brought [Note: “Brought down.”] me into the dust of death” (Ps. 21:16). For our true life is hidden with Christ in God. Nor is this, in which we now live, the region of the living; rather, that is the region of which this same Prophet says here: “I shall be pleasing to God in the region of the living” (Ps. 114:9). And therefore he said, “I shall live,” because he does not live by the use of this present life, but will live through God’s compassion. Yet he hopes for this because God’s law is his meditation. Let us then devote ourselves to divine reading, to God’s commandments, and fulfill the works of the Law in the duties of our life; because, as God’s compassion comes upon him on account of meditation on the Law, the Prophet hopes that he will live.

16. David asks not for vengeance upon his enemies, but for their conversion.—Yet it is not enough for this Prophet to be concerned only for himself or to remember himself alone. He must undertake care for the human race, accept the disposition of public concern, and pray for those engaged in sins and irreligion. Accordingly, in the following verse he shows the concern of this disposition, saying, VERSE 78: “Let the proud be put to shame, because they have unjustly committed iniquity against me.” This is not a prayer of cursing, nor does he seek repayment for the injury done to him. Far be it from the Prophet, a preacher of the Gospel, to have exceeded the rule of evangelical love. For when the Lord says, “Love your enemies, and pray for those who slander [Note: “You.”] and persecute you” (Matt. 5:44), reason does not permit that he should now pray for vengeance upon the proud and injurious. But because one who ceases from sins is ashamed of them, and one who abandons vices must abandon them precisely because he hates them, the Prophet prays that those who have been unjustly proud against him may, through awareness of their faults, be ashamed of what they have done. For as long as anyone sins, he is not ashamed of the things in which he sins, through the habit and will of sinning. But once he ceases to sin, he has the end of sinning through shame for sin. He himself, however, exercises himself in God’s commandments: living justly, preaching religion, not repaying injuries, and enduring patiently. For this reason he bore the contradictions and iniquities [Col. 0570D] of many proud persons against himself.

17. Moreover, the following verse makes it clear without qualification that this is what we are discussing concerning the shame of the proud. For it follows, VERSE 79: “Let those who fear thee turn to me, and those who [Note: “Know.”] know thy testimonies.” Therefore the Prophet wishes those who have begun to fear God to turn to him, so that through his teaching they may be ashamed of their faults and crimes; knowing, of course, God’s testimonies, concerning which we have already said much, and, ashamed of their former sins, may submit themselves to the Prophet’s instruction and teaching. Their turning from pride and sins to piety and moderation is what is intended.

18. David’s humility rebukes our pride.—He concluded, according to his custom of modesty, saying, VERSE 80: “Let my heart be undefiled in thy justifications, that I may not be put to shame.” He exercises himself in the commandments, meditates upon the Law, has known the justice of God’s judgments, those who fear the Lord rejoice at the sight of him, and he was made and fashioned by God’s hands; yet he does not dare to say that his heart is undefiled. And do we sometimes dare to parade [Col. 0571B] our innocence, boast of abstinence from vices, and glory that we are pure from sins and iniquities? Rather, as we must learn faith from the Prophet, so too must we learn humility and modesty, while he prays that his heart may be made undefiled. For he knows that from it proceed, according to the saying: “For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, lusts, fornications, thefts, falsehoods, blasphemies, and things like these” (Matt. 15:9). Therefore he prays that this be made undefiled, from which, as from a kind of tinder, the beginnings of so many and such great vices are supplied. And he knows that it is made undefiled in this way: if it remains in God’s justifications. He understands this to be the fruit of the justifications: that while remaining in them he may not be put to shame. For shame arises from consciousness of sins and from the reproach of offenses. [Col. 0571C] Therefore where there is no shame, neither is there sin; and where there is no sin, one remains in God’s justifications. And God’s justifications will render the heart undefiled.

[Note: “The eleventh letter begins happily. Life to the writer; instruction to the reader. Kat.”]

## LETTER XI. Caph
My soul has failed in longing for your salvation, and I hope in your word. My eyes have failed in longing for your utterance, saying: “When will you console me?” For I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your ordinances. How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment upon those who persecute me? The wicked have recounted practices to me, but not according to your law. All your commandments are truth; wickedly they have persecuted me: help me. They have almost brought me to an end upon the earth; but I have not forsaken your commandments. According to your mercy give me life, and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth.

[Col. 0572A] 1. An immense longing produces faintness of soul. Jesus is salvation. — It belongs to human nature that, when it cannot obtain what it desires, it is held in a faintness of soul through the unceasing craving of desire. It is easy to recognize this from the very movements of our affections: into what a faintness of soul we are brought by awaiting those whom we desire. Therefore the Prophet, [Note: [Col. 0571D] Whose entire expectation is directed toward God.] whose whole expectation is toward God, whose entire desire is in His commandments, speaks and says, VERSE 81: *My soul has failed in longing for your salvation, and I hope in your word.* He has no other things to occupy his desire; and holy longing is not idle among worldly matters. Therefore he fails in longing for [Note: [Col. 0571D] salvation. Then, in the words of God.] salvation; and he fails for this reason, because [Note: [Col. 0571D] In Par. he hopes in the words of God. In the manuscripts Mic. and one Vatican manuscript: “he believes in the words of God.”] he hopes in the word of God. For Christ Jesus is the end of the Law, and He is the one of whom Moses and the prophets wrote.

Moreover, He is salvation by the very name by which He is called Jesus. For *Jesus*, according to the Hebrew language, means “salvation”; and the Angel, speaking to Joseph, teaches the same thing when he says: “You shall call his name Jesus” (Matt. 1:21), “for he shall save his people from [Note: [Col. 0571D] The printed editions here also add “their,” which is absent from the manuscripts, as above in Psalm 51, no. 24, and Psalm 66, no. 4.] sins.” Thus the cause of faintness is desire for salvation. The origin of that desire, however, is that [Note: [Col. 0572D] In the words of God.] he hopes in the word of God. For our salvation is Jesus, who was both desired and born. But we must understand what follows the faintness of the longing soul.

2. Faintness of the eyes. — He says, VERSE 82: *My eyes have failed in longing for your utterance, saying: “When will you exhort me?”* Therefore the faintness of the eyes follows the faintness of the soul. But, as we have discussed the nature of faintness of soul, let us see what the customary faintness of the eyes may be. Imagine, then, a wife awaiting her husband who is travelling, or a father awaiting a son long absent, whom he believes will return at any moment. Will he not continually fix his gaze upon [Note: [Col. 0572D] Along that route.] the route [Note: [Col. 0571D] Two manuscripts: “along that route.”] by which he supposes the other will come? Will not the intensity and sight of his eyes fail through expectation of that very gaze? The Lord bears witness that the prophets had such desires when He says: “Amen, I say to you, many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear” (Matt. 13:17). Thus the Prophet fails both in soul and in eyes.

3. The eyes here signify those of the mind. Exhortation to the saints resting in the underworld. — These eyes of the Prophet, however, although they desired to see the Lord, are not bodily eyes; for they speak and await. [Col. 0572D] This beholding and speech belong rather to the mind than to the body. For they say: “When will you exhort me?” He knows that the saints resting in the underworld desire this exhortation.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] Bede, in 1 Peter 3, undoubtedly refers to these words of Hilary, though without naming him, when he says: “Someone has interpreted this passage to mean that the saints resting in the underworld desired that consolation of which the Lord says to the Apostles, ‘Many prophets,’ etc., and of which the Psalmist says, ‘My eyes have failed,’ etc.; namely, that, when the Lord descended into the underworld, consolation or exhortation was also preached to those who were in prison and had once been unbelieving in the days of Noah” [Col. 0573D]. Rejecting this interpretation, he adds: “And he may have said these things; but the catholic faith holds that, descending into the underworld, the Lord led out from there not unbelievers but only His own faithful, and brought them with Himself to the heavenly kingdom.” We do not consider whether Bede judged Hilary’s interpretation to agree insufficiently with the catholic faith; but this at least is certain: he who, being content to recall Peter’s words alone, affirmed nothing further than what they contained, said nothing against the faith. For he did not assert that unbelievers were brought out from the underworld; this seems rather to have been Augustine’s view in *On Genesis according to the Letter*, book XII, ch. 33, no. 63. On this preaching performed in the underworld, see the same Augustine, Letter 164, and Cottelerius’s notes on book III of the *Shepherd*.]

He knows, as the Apostle Peter testifies, that when the Lord descended into the underworld, exhortation was preached even to those who were in prison and had once been unbelieving in the days of Noah (1 Pet. 3:19–20). Therefore his speaking eyes fail in longing for these utterances of God: he awaits not so much with bodily sight the Lord announced from the utterances of God, as through contemplation of soul and mind.

4. A wineskin in frost: the body chastened by self-control. Burning desire does not remember God’s ordinances. — Then follows, VERSE 83: *For I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your ordinances.* This is a cause of a new kind: that he has not forgotten God’s ordinances because he has become like a wineskin in frost. If we measure the matter merely by the ears, the Prophet’s statement will be thought empty and ridiculous. But he remembers that wineskins are used to signify human bodies, when the Lord says in the Gospels (Mark 2:22): “No one puts new wine into old wineskins.” Nor is there any doubt that by old wineskins He meant bodies grown old [Note: [Col. 0573D] One Vatican manuscript: “In old wineskins, bodies [Col. 0574D] in their sins”; then the printed editions read *veterna*, “worn-out,” not *vetera*, “old.”] in their sins [Note: [Col. 0573C] *Veterna*, “worn-out,” in the earlier printed editions.].

Through devotion to continence, however, the bodies of believers grow cold; and, once the heat of the inner nature has been extinguished, they are cold wineskins. Although inwardly they grow warm by nature through the boiling of vices, outwardly they stiffen through the endurance of continence, as though by the cold of frost. Therefore, in this coldness of the body, we cannot be forgetful of God’s ordinances. But whoever has grown hot through the burning of vices, like a full wineskin, and does not grow cold through the fear and worship of God, must necessarily forget God’s ordinances. The saint cannot forget them when, like a wineskin in frost, [Col. 0573C] growing stiff [Note: [Col. 0573C] “Growing stiff.”] outwardly, he is cold to every prompting of inner desires.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] In Par.: “growing stiff.” More correctly, this word in the other books refers to the saint. Then one of the Vatican manuscripts reads: “by the chastisement of all inward desires.” “Resistance to their prompting” would be preferable. Inner desires are not destroyed; rather, through continence one does not yield to their prompting, as was said immediately above.]

5. The judgment requested here is not the final judgment (Ps. 1:5), but the power by which the devil and his ministers are crushed. — Then follows, VERSE 84: *How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment [Note: [Col. 0573C] We have supplied “for me” from our manuscript, the Greek text, and Hilary’s exposition.] for me against those who persecute me?* The Prophet is not ignorant that judgment comes after the consummation of the age, when he says: “Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.” Why, then, does he now pray that judgment be executed upon those who persecute him? Certainly not that judgment which he remembers will occur in the age of resurrection, since he knows that, according to bodily life, he is a man of few days. Thus he says: “How many are the days of your servant?” When he says “how many,” he knows that they are not many. And above he had said that he was like a wineskin in frost.

Therefore, because he knows that he is of few days, he desires judgment to be executed against those who persecute him: namely, against the devil and his ministers. For there are spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places. Yet he also knows that the devil will be judged in the age of resurrection. Thus, though he himself is of few days, he desires this judgment to be carried out: namely, that, wholly perfected as a saint and perfectly pleasing to God, he may crush [Note: [Col. 0573D] Within himself.] the devil within himself, crush the hostile and opposing powers, and subject spiritual wickednesses to his soul’s faith. Therefore he does not yet trust in the firmness of his own nature, though he has already become cold like a wineskin; but he prays that by God’s mercy judgment may be executed upon his enemies [Col. 0574B].

The Lord gave His Apostles this power of judgment when He said: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). The Prophet had not yet heard this utterance of the Lord remaining in the body; yet he prays that this power may be given him, so that such judgment may be set against those who persecute him. For he is assailed on every side: the innate material of vices is present to him through the nature of the body [Note: [Col. 574D] The printed editions read “kindred material,” against the manuscripts. Here it is plainly taught that concupiscence is born with us, just as in the preceding section it is taught that it remains even in saints and the perfect—though for combat.]; the devil attempts to kindle it through the heat of a twofold desire; he is injured by the impious speech of irreligious persons; and he endures the profane arguments of the nations against God and their mad utterances.

6. The wicked falsely claim, but do not possess, the truth of doctrine. — Therefore he says next, VERSE 85: *The wicked have recounted practices to me, but not according to your law.* For how many are there who claim to teach certain rules of human life, while they kindle our soul, which ought to serve God more rightly, toward pursuit of worldly virtues [Note: [Col. 0574C] They kindle our soul’s pursuits, which should serve God more rightly.]? How many also falsely claim knowledge of the divine Scriptures and preach heretical and perverse doctrines? But the Prophet, knowing that perfect instruction in human doctrine is contained in God’s law, says: “The wicked have recounted practices to me, but not according to your law.” For those who preach these things are wicked.

And therefore [Note: [Col. 0574C] “Law” in place of “word of God.”] the word of God forbade a sinner to recite holy utterances, because iniquity does not receive the truth of heavenly teaching. For God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take my covenant upon your mouth?” (Ps. 49:17). “But you [Note: [Col. 0575D] Our book adds the words “you hate discipline,” as they stand in the Hebrew and Greek text and were absent from the printed editions.] hate discipline; you have cast my words behind you.” Therefore the Prophet does not tolerate these practices, knowing that nothing can equal the recitation of the Law.

7. The persecution of a righteous person is wicked. — Finally he adds, VERSE 86: *All your commandments are truth; wickedly they have persecuted me: help me.* Whoever persecutes a righteous person necessarily persecutes wickedly, because wickedness is the effect of unjust action. The Apostle too knows this wickedness of persecutions when he says: “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). “Many are the afflictions of the righteous” [Col. 0575B] (Ps. 33:20). Now Satan attacks; now his agencies assault; now the pretence of false brothers stealthily enters in order to harm through the craft of fraudulent persecution.

But the Prophet, remembering that God’s commandments are truth, endures the persecution of injustice with a faithful spirit. And because he knows persecution to be a proof of faith, he does not pray that it be removed from him; rather, he asks for help in it and prays for the aid and assistance of God’s mercy. He is not ignorant of this evangelical precept: “He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:38).

8. Truth. The necessity and usefulness of persecution. — Therefore truth is in God’s precepts. Truth has nothing false, nothing uncertain, nothing imperfect. But persecution directed against a righteous person is [Note: [Col. 0575D] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read: “is wickedness.”] wicked. For wickedness must hate the preacher of truth; but help from God belongs to the preacher of truth. He remembers that these troubles caused by persecutors are grave; and because they are beneficial to the righteous, he does not think they should be removed. For the peace of an idle faith is dangerous, and snares are easy where sentries are secure. But a man trained by wars will not quickly be caught by deceits; and a glorious contest is necessary if the crown of victory is to be bestowed. Therefore he does not pray that the occasion for struggle be taken from him, but that help to conquer be granted him.

9. David nearly yielded to temptations. — He remembers, however, that he is not in a slight battle with temptations. For he continues, VERSE 87: *They have almost brought me to an end upon the earth; but I have not forsaken your commandments.* Unjust persecutions had brought the Prophet almost to the end of faith—those, namely, of which we spoke above: the spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places, which incite us to bodily vices through the enticements of desires introduced into us. Thus the Prophet was almost brought to an end upon the earth; that is, he was almost cast down into bodily vices and sins. For there is a consummation of evils just as there is of goods.

Yet, though these most destructive enemies pressed upon and persecuted him, he does not forsake God’s commandments. [Col. 0576A] Although weakened by the frailty of his nature, he remains in God’s precepts; and his remaining in those commandments is all the more glorious because the frailty of his nature has almost been overcome.

10. He seeks the life to come, while promising meanwhile to keep the Gospel. — Then, in his customary manner of humility and hope, he concludes: VERSE 88: *According to your mercy give me life, and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth.* He prays to be given life as though he were not yet living; and he promises to keep the testimonies of God’s mouth as though he did not now keep them. But although he lives in the body, he does not desire the life of this age. And although he keeps the testimonies of God in the Law, he nevertheless promises to keep the testimonies of God’s mouth: testimonies renewed by evangelical precepts, which bring perfection through holiness of faith by abstaining not merely from adultery but even from [Col. 0576B] the desire for adultery [Note: [Col. 0575D] In Par.: “abstaining.” More correctly, the other books read *abstinentes*, “abstaining,” in the accusative.], according to Matthew 5:28; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the mouth, the right hand, the power, and the wisdom of God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

LETTER XII. Lamed.

For ever [Hilary: “age”], O Lord, your word remains in heaven. From generation to generation [Hilary: “generation”] is your truth; you founded the earth, and it remains [Hilary: “will remain”]. By your ordinance the day endures, because all things serve you. Unless your law were my meditation, then I would have perished in my humiliation [Hilary: “it is mine; then perhaps I would have perished in humiliation”]. For ever I shall not forget your ordinances, because in them you gave me life, O Lord [below, “O Lord” is absent]. I am yours: save me, because I have sought your ordinances. Sinners waited for me in order to destroy me; I have understood your testimonies [Hilary: “O Lord”]. I have seen an end to every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad [Hilary: “vehemently broad”].

1. Heavenly knowledge, a gift of God. — The Prophet’s discourse ought not to dwell on lowly or commonplace matters, but always to treat lofty things worthy of God; and in such a way that, while it instructs us in the observance of an innocent life, it also raises the humility of our understanding to comprehend the divine and invisible mysteries. Nor indeed could human weakness raise itself to heavenly knowledge unless God, by granting the gift of knowledge through the teaching of the Spirit, trained it for knowledge of the divine and unfathomable nature.

Therefore the Prophet, wishing to make us excellent and perfect, worthy of God, and knowing that this is laid up for human hope—that, [Note: [Col. 0576D] Absent in a manuscript of Regius and in Albinus; with these, “would ascend” was then preferred to “would approach,” found in the printed editions.] if it pursued the discipline of heavenly obedience, it would ascend to heavenly glory—begins thus, VERSE 89: *For the age, O Lord, your word remains in heaven.*

[Col. 0577A] 2. Heaven’s obedience to God’s word. — He says “in heaven,” because he knows that it does not remain on earth on account of human falsehood. The manner in which it remains in heaven is itself perceived with the assurance, as it were, of bodily observation. There is no transgression there, no change, no weakness, no idleness. Let us observe the yearly course of the sun, the monthly return of the moon, and the stations, revolutions, and changes of the stars. Are they not contained within their boundaries, fixed limits, and ordained alternations? Nothing there is changed, [Note: [Col. 0577C] In two manuscripts: “nothing is abandoned”; this can be understood as meaning that nothing there abandons the limits assigned to it.] nothing is deferred, nothing neglected; but each thing remains under the law of its own constitution and perseveres in the tireless services of obedience.

3. After this age God’s word will remain also in other creatures. — But the Prophet observed this distinction concerning offices [Note: [Col. 0577D] The printed editions read “and of offices already past”; corrected from the Regius and Albinus manuscripts.] that are to cease and [Col. 0577B] pass away, saying, VERSE 89: *For the age, O Lord, your word remains in heaven.* The Latin translators rendered this with an ambiguous and less exact meaning. For what the Greek has, **εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, Κύριε**—“unto the age, O Lord”—has been translated among us as *in aeternum, Domine*, “for ever, O Lord.”
