Now “eternal” can be understood to mean that what is eternal does not cease with any end. [Note: [Col. 0577D] In two manuscripts: “but according to”; this is not approved. Just as Hilary does, Ambrose also testifies that some manuscripts here prefer “for ever,” others “for the age.”] But “age,” which is *aiōn* (**αἰών**) in Greek, is contained within the span of a determinate time. For he does not say, “unto the age of the age,” nor “unto ages of ages”; but, “For the age your word remains.” He knows that after this age heaven and earth will pass away, as the Lord says: “Amen, I say to you, heaven and earth [Note: [Col. 0577C] “Will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”] will pass away [Note: [Col. 0577D] The Regius manuscript and Albinus: “will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” He also remembers.], but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). He also remembers that this age will pass away, so that there may be a new heaven and a new earth (Isa. 65:17).

For this reason he says: *For the age, O Lord, your word remains in heaven*: because, after this age has passed and heaven has passed away, the word of this established obedience must remain in the creatures that await the revelation of the children of God.

[Note: [Col. 0577D] The printed editions read: “after this age has passed, this word will be in heaven.” The manuscripts are truer, as in the text: they show that, after the new heaven and new earth have been established, creatures will constantly obey the word of God. Hence the phrase “in creatures” refers both to “established” and to “remain.”]

4. Whom it already inhabits, whom it leaves, and whom it shuns. — Yet God’s word is not therefore never on earth, although the Prophet proclaims that it remains only in heaven. For none of us fails at times to experience the gift of spiritual grace; none fails at some time to have God’s word within himself when sober, calm, self-controlled, kindly [MSS: *benevolens*, “well-disposed”], and merciful. For when we are such, God’s word remains in us, as we serve His precepts through obedience in good works.

But when the movements of turbulent affections creep in—when concern for money enters, when the heat of shameful and lustful desire is kindled, when the impulse of anger is stirred, when drunkenness is desired—then God’s word no longer remains in us. But it is in those who, according to the Apostle, have put off the old person with his sins and put on the new (Col. 3:9); who, having died and been buried with Christ, have now risen into newness of life and have been placed in heavenly places (Rom. 6:4); who, abandoning the image of the earthly, bear the image of the heavenly [Col. 0578B] (1 Cor. 15:49).

For God’s word remains in these as in heaven: in those in whom this word is not offended by anger, drunkenness, hatred, unbelief, or lust. For even though it sometimes remains in us, [Note: [Col. 0577D] In two manuscripts: “yet it does not remain, since these insults to its habitation,” etc. In the others, which we follow: “yet it does not bear these insults to its habitation.” In Hincmar, *De praedestinatione*, ch. 25: “yet these insults to cohabitation”; from a reading of that kind the corrupt text in the printed editions, “yet from the saint’s habitation,” was produced.] yet it does not endure these insults to its dwelling so as to remain perpetually within us. If, however, these vices which have been mentioned are always in us, it will not even deign to enter the polluted dwellings of our bodies.

5. God’s word is at hand for everyone. Like the sun, it enters the open and refuses the closed. — It is near to each person, [Note: [Col. 0578D] In Par.: “nearest.” Shortly after, in Hincmar: “before the door,” for “at the door.”] as has been said; for God’s word stands at the door and knocks at the door of our soul, saying: “Behold, I stand before the door and knock; if anyone opens the door to me, I shall enter in to him” (Rev. 3:20). Therefore it always wishes to enter; but we exclude it, so that it may not enter. [Col. 0578C] For through these bodily vices we close the entrance of our soul.

[Note: [Col. 0578D] The printed editions read “who.” But Hincmar and our manuscripts have “which,” namely the soul. Slightly earlier the manuscripts read *cludimus*, “we shut,” not *claudimus*, “we close.”]

If the soul begins to lie open after all things have been cleansed, God’s word will enter at once, in the manner of the sun: when the shutters of a window are closed, the sun is prevented from entering; when they are open, it pours itself in whole.

[Note: [Col. 0578D] Thus our manuscripts agree with Hincmar. The printed editions read: “It indeed … is ready.”]

It is always ready to give light; but the house itself, through barred entrances, excludes its light. For the word of God is the sun of righteousness, standing beside each person in order to enter; and, when it finds open entrances, it does not delay to pour in its light.

[Note: [Col. 0578D] The printed editions read “opened,” against Hincmar and the manuscripts.]

Therefore this word of God remains in the heavens through the tireless [Note: [Col. 0578D] The Regius manuscript with Albinus: “through the tireless obedience of ministries. Also in those who are heavenly,” etc. The reading of the other manuscripts appears more complete. Hilary calls “heavenly things” the yearly course of the sun, the monthly return of the moon, and the other matters explained in no. 2. Having offered that literal understanding, he then adds another, spiritual one, with which Augustine agrees in *Exposition 2 on Psalm 18*, no. 3: “The heavens are the saints, suspended from the earth, bearing God, thundering with commandments, flashing with wisdom.” Likewise Ambrose, Sermon 11 on Psalm 118, no. 12: “By heaven, which is my throne, I understand the disposition of the righteous more than an element.”] obedience of heavenly things. By this example, we must believe that God’s word also remains in the saints who are heavenly according to the image of the heavenly one (1 Cor. 15:49).

6. As in heaven, so it remains in the saints. The two generations in which alone God’s truth exists. — Then follows, VERSE 90: [Note: [Col. 0579D] “From generation to generation.”] *In generation [Note: [Col. 0579D] Par. here and below: “from generation to generation.” Other editions: “into generation and generation.” The Greek favors these. But the manuscripts consistently read “in generation and generation,” after which Hilary, as is clear from what follows, understands “remains.” “The truth of God,” therefore, he says, “remains in these two generations alone.”] and generation is your truth.* The verse which follows confirms this twofold interpretation by which we judge that God’s word remains in saints as in heaven. For he does not say, [Note: [Col. 0579D] “In the generation of generation,” or “from generations.”] “in the generation of generation,” nor “in generations [Note: [Col. 0579D] The printed editions read “in the generation of generation, or from generations,” against the manuscripts. Before “generations,” “in” is understood.] of generations,” but “in generation and generation is your truth.” He mentions each generation with a simple expression.

Therefore we recognize two generations in two peoples: one is that of the Law and the prophets; the other, that of the Gospels and the Apostles. Thus God’s truth remains in these two generations alone. But when the former generation possessed God’s truth within itself, no other then possessed it. For there were many generations of nations and peoples. And now that this same generation has proved unworthy to contain God’s truth, no other generation possesses that same truth of God except the one that has believed the Gospels.

7. The founded and enduring earth: the earthly mass, more properly the human body. — He continues: *You founded the earth, and it will remain.* The sequence called for earth to be named after heaven; but I think that the intervening phrase, “In generation and generation is your truth,” was inserted for the purpose of confirming that twofold understanding of heaven, in which God’s word remains. Now, therefore, the complete sequence is preserved: after heaven, in which God’s word remains, comes the founded earth which will remain.

This may perhaps be understood also of this earth which remains because it has been founded, and which, according to Solomon, God founded by wisdom. Although it is laid over the fluid nature of waters and floats upon an unstable element beneath it, it has nevertheless been so founded by the wisdom, power, and Spirit of God that it remains. But to me the prophetic utterance also seems to speak of the earth of the human body, which has been so founded that God’s word may remain in it as in heaven. For heaven and earth will pass away (Matt. 24:35); and how will [Col. 0580A] this founded earth remain? Unless it remains founded only in this age—that is, unless it too remains according to the constitution of this age.

But if it is to remain permanently—[Note: [Col. 0579D] In two manuscripts: “in what way?” We must certainly retain “by what word,” namely, *permanet*, “it remains.” The phrase “by what word” is not interrogative, as in the earlier printed editions.] a permanence signified by the word *permanet*—then the earth of those generations must be believed to be founded and enduring, for whom, because God’s truth remains in them, glory is prepared for these bodies, now earthly but destined to be heavenly.

[Note: [Col. 0580D] Lipsius and Parisiensis read “the generation,” not “the earth,” incorrectly and contrary to the manuscripts. The following word *necesse est* must be understood adverbially: “necessarily” or “of necessity.” This manner of speaking occurs in Psalm 68, no. 16: “one will desire necessarily to be rescued from evils, lest one be afflicted by evils”; and in Psalm 121, no. 1: “he will necessarily cry out after the Prophet’s example.” Here the bodies of righteous persons, for whom a glorious resurrection is prepared, are called “the earth of the generations.”]

And this may be understood thus when the following verse is completed.

8. The day: the light of the saints. At present, not all things serve God. — For he says, VERSE 91: *By your ordinance the day endures, because all things serve you.* This present day does not endure, being removed by the intervention of night.

[Note: [Col. 0580D] Two manuscripts: *exeptus*. At first we thought *exceptus*, “excepted,” should be read; but then judged that *exemptus*, “removed,” as though taken away, could properly be accepted.]

Or, if he had spoken of the times of this day, it would have been appropriate to mention night also, which endures by God’s ordinance equally with day. But because day is light, and every saint is light in this world, the day of this light is unambiguously believed to endure by God’s ordinance. And it will endure because all things shall serve God. For now all things do not serve God. Do sinners serve God? Do those who still must be subjected beneath the footstool of the Lord’s feet also serve Him? Yet David said: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109:1). And according to the Apostle: “He must reign until he has placed his enemies beneath [Note: [Col. 0580D] His.] his feet” (1 Cor. 15:25). Therefore then the day—that is, the light of the saints—will remain, when all things begin to serve God.

[Col. 0580C]

9. In the foregoing, what the letter itself says is also true. — These matters, indeed, have been set forth by us according to prophetic and apostolic teaching. Thus, although in the present words we understand the time of future goods to be signified—a time in which a new heaven, a new earth, the blessed transformation of bodies, and the eternal day of our light, after the nights of earthly vices have been [Note: [Col. 0580D] The printed editions read “forgotten.” The manuscripts more correctly read “abolished.”] abolished, are prepared for our hope and expectation—nevertheless all the creations of this world also bear witness to God’s majesty through the unchangeable ordering of their functions. For all things are so firmly established, [Note: [Col. 0580D] We have added “founded” on the authority of the Mic. manuscript.] founded, and fixed that they persevere in the enduring courses established for them from the beginning of time.

10. Meditation on the Law must not be abandoned amid temptations and sufferings. — But the Prophet prays that he may endure as the day does, and remembers that he is already the servant of his Lord, saying, VERSE 92: *Unless your law is my meditation, then perhaps I would have perished [Note: [Col. 0581D] “Into my humiliation.” But below: “in my humiliation.”] in my humiliation [Note: [Col. 0581D] Our manuscripts read “in lowliness,” as below.].* We have often pointed out that “humiliation” signifies the state in which the soul is subjected to temptations and, left to its own weakness, is made lowly.

Therefore the Law is his meditation; and unless it had been his meditation, perhaps he would have perished in humiliation. Therefore meditation upon God’s Law is not to be abandoned when we are troubled and distressed. Rather, when we are afflicted with the various weaknesses of the body, when we are harassed amid the wars of persecutions, meditation on the Law must remain constant within us. Though fires burn toward the destruction of faith, though scourges tear us toward peril to our salvation, though claws pierce bodies redeemed by God in order to force out a confession of impiety, we must nevertheless remember the prophetic saying, so that we may share in it. Let us also say, patient and victorious: “Unless your law is my meditation, then perhaps I would have perished in my humiliation.”

The Prophet recalls the blessedness of this meditation at the beginning of the Psalms, saying: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence. But his will was in the law of the Lord, and in His law he shall meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:1–2). And truly blessed will be whoever meditates on God’s Law, [Note: [Col. 0581D] “By which meditation itself.”] because by that meditation he will be preserved even in the very [Col. 0581C] humiliation of tribulations.

11. The Law is the beginning of life. — Then follows, VERSE 93: *For the age I shall not forget your ordinances, because in them you gave me life.* The Prophet knows, according to the Apostle, that Christ is the end of the Law (Rom. 10:4), [Note: [Col. 0581D] Par.: “in whom.” More correctly, the other books read “in which,” namely, in the Law.] in which observance of the ordinances is established. He knows too that the Law is a pedagogue for those who will believe in the Gospel; he knows that the righteous person lives by faith (Gal. 3:24, 11); he knows that the Law is spiritual (Rom. 7:14); he knows that whoever does what is contained in the Law shall live (Rom. 10:5). Therefore he says: “For the age I shall not forget your ordinances, because in them you gave me life,” so that, although evangelical faith must be preached when the works of the Law have ended, he may nevertheless not forget the ordinances of the Law, which are for him the beginning of life; because the Law’s justification is the pedagogue of evangelical justification and faith.

[Note: [Col. 0581D] According to Paul’s statement in Galatians 3:24, cited in the *Tractate on Psalm 91*, no. 1: “The Law became our pedagogue in Christ, that we might be justified by faith.”]

12. He belongs to God who serves Him alone; he belongs to the vices to which he submits.---Firmly, then, since no forgetfulness of God’s ordinances can steal upon him, he has professed what follows [Col. 0582A], saying, VERS. 94: *I am yours; save me, for I have sought out your ordinances.* This voice of profession does not suit everyone; rare indeed is the person who would dare to call himself God’s. Yet he will dare who said: “For me, to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21); and: “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). Those who resemble this faith will not shamelessly confess that they are God’s.

This is the voice of a soul ever intent upon God; this is the work of tireless mercy, unwavering self-control, habitual fasting, unrepented generosity. For how shall one who burns with lust, is quick to anger, is anxious for wealth, thirsts for drunkenness, and is vainly devoted to worldly glory profess himself to be God’s? Such a person will belong rather to these things than to God. For in whom these vicious passions [Col. 0582B] abound, how will he not belong to those whom he serves? There are many gods among the Gentiles (1 Cor. 8:6); but for Paul there is one God, from whom are all things, and one Lord, our Lord Jesus, through whom are all things. Therefore the Prophet firmly confesses himself to belong to Him alone whom he serves; and because he is His, he prays to be saved. But he is His because he seeks out His ordinances. While others seek worldly glory, others fields, houses, or money, he seeks God’s righteousnesses and glories in belonging to God.

13. The devil’s contest against the righteous; the righteous person’s weapons.---There is, however, immense hatred on the part of irreligious persons toward pious and devout men of this kind. And the Prophet knows that the one who professes himself God’s is hateful either to the people of the world or to the devil and his ministers.

[Note: With the preceding words, *weary of*. Immediately after: “who says, ‘I am hated; they waited for me.’”]

[Note: In the printed editions, *pertaesum*, “weary of.” We restore *perosum*, “hated,” from the royal manuscripts and the Albinus manuscript. Similar is Letter 3, §20: “He knows that all the truth of prophecy is hated by the rulers of this world.”]

This is also taught by the following verse [Col. 0582C], in which he says, VERS. 95: *Sinners waited for me, to destroy me; O Lord, I understood your testimonies.* The devil and his ministers wage war in order to strip the faithful man of all glory, and not to allow him to remain God’s portion, but to draw him into partnership with their own condemnation. Thus a long and protracted battle is fought against the Prophet’s faith. But, mindful of God’s commandments and understanding His testimonies, he resisted and stood firm. Nor did he frustrate the hope of those who awaited his destruction in any other way than by understanding that the teaching of life for him was contained in God’s testimonies.

Yet it is arduous and difficult to understand God’s testimonies; their understanding advances beyond the knowledge of present perception. We have already discussed the testimonies at the beginning of the Psalm. Through these present testimonies of the Law [Col. 0582D], knowledge of the eternal testimonies is bestowed. Finally, the following statement itself demonstrates this.

[Note: Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius: “His concern is battle and all glory.” Paris: “His concern is all glory”; the manuscripts oppose this reading.]

14. What *peras* means; what “end” means; the manifold consummation, and the kingdom of Christ before judgment, not unknown to the Prophet.---For it follows, VERS. 96: *I have seen the end of every consummation.*

[Note: In our manuscripts: “of every consummation.”]

We have frequently warned that satisfactory understanding cannot be obtained from the Latin translation. For the Greek expression has another force; it reads: *pásēs synteléias eîdon péras*—“I have seen the πέρας (*peras*) of every consummation.” What the Greeks call *peras* is beyond the end of established things and is not bounded by anything so as to cease; rather, under an unbounded signification, it transcends every limit. But what is written among us, “unto the end,” will be thought to be contained within that end by which the matter in question is signified.

[Note: “Which is signified”: it is supposed to mean the matter under discussion.]

[Note: The printed editions: “which is signified.”]

But the Prophet, who understands not bodily or earthly testimonies of the Law, beholds, according to the Greek sense, beyond every consummation. He knows that there is a consummation of the times [Col. 0583B] of the Law, when, after the fullness of times, God is to be contemplated in the body; but beyond this consummation he sees further. He sees also the time of evangelical hope. Yet even its consummation is not unknown to him; for beyond it he extends the eyes of his understanding. For he sees also the consummation of the resurrection; he knows that an order of transformation has been appointed, the Apostle saying: “Each in his own order” (1 Cor. 15:23); and again: “All indeed shall rise, but not all shall be changed” (ibid., v. 51). He knows also the day of the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, from which we are advanced into the kingdom of God the Father and transferred into those unsearched-out and unsearchable judgments of God. He knows also that there is a time of judgment. And he was enabled to know these things from the breadth of God’s commandments, because the divine discourse has spread itself out for him into the instruction of boundless [Col. 0583C] knowledge.

[Note: “of the Law” is absent from the royal and Albinus manuscripts.]

[Note: “Exquisite,” i.e. searched out.]

15. Why God’s commandment is broad; God’s precepts are not difficult.---For he says: *Your commandment is exceedingly broad.* It is broad indeed, whether because it extends human ignorance’s knowledge into infinity, or because there are many ways in which one may obey God’s precepts:

[Note: Thus Bad., Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Lipsius, however, rashly substituted *excedit*, “surpasses,” for *extendit*, “extends”; later editions retained it.]

[Note: In the common editions, “and may please [God]”; less aptly, since one does not “please” God’s precepts. The manuscripts more fittingly read “and may obey”; this repetition is habitual with Hilary whenever he wishes to impress how something must be performed.]

—and obey them according to the divisions and gifts of graces. For not everything is expected of all, nor can everyone fulfill every kind of service to the fullness of pleasing God. One pleases Him by fasting; another earns merit by simplicity of faith; another redeems vices by almsgiving; another makes himself complete in charity. Thus to some the power of healings has been granted; to others, knowledge of prophecy bestowed; to others, firmness of faith given; to others, wisdom and knowledge donated.

[Note: Another “completes charity”: the verb *consummo* is frequent in Hilary in the sense of “fulfill” or “perfect.”]

God’s commandment, therefore, is broad [Col. 0583D] and extends through every kind of our hope, so that, if the will is present, it is not difficult to obey God’s commandment, since it is broad and widely extended for pleasing Him through the variety of dutiful religion [Col. 0584A]. Nor is it merely broad, but exceedingly broad: the infinity of its breadth is shown by this very superlative addition.

## LETTER XIII. Mem

*How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day. By your commandment you have made me wiser than my enemies, because it is mine for ever. I have understood more than all who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation. I have understood more than the elders, because I have sought out your commandments. From every evil way I have restrained my feet, that I may keep your word. I have not turned aside from your judgments, because you have set the law before me. How sweet are your utterances to my throat! More than honey [Col. 0584B] and the honeycomb to my mouth. From your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I have hated every way of iniquity.*

[Note: Although “and the honeycomb” does not occur below in the exposition of these words, it may be inferred from the exposition at Letter 17, §7 that this reading was not unknown to Hilary.]

1. The usefulness of this Psalm.---This work of the Prophet is useful and necessary for us, by which we are taught perfect knowledge of God and obedience to Him. He instructs us especially in two matters suited to our weakness: that we may know the God whom we did not know, and that we may obey His commandments in accordance with the will of His decree. For throughout the whole body of this Psalm the Prophet forms the perfect man of Law, Prophets, and Gospels, either in his own person or in that of another whom he is instructing, who may confidently declare of himself the things set down here.

[Note: In the printed editions, *instituti*, omitting the preceding *nos*, “us.”]

[Note: Thus the Mic. manuscript with the Vatican manuscript, as also frequently above. Others read “confirms.”]

It is worthy of consideration with what care of words and what completeness of understanding the Prophet confirms us in every kind of saying [Col. 0584C].

2. The difference between doing and loving; the greatness of David’s love for the Law.---For in the verse of the thirteenth letter he says, VERS. 97: *How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day.* He might readily have said: “How I have done your law!” But because it is a greater merit to act from love than from fear, he therefore says: “How I have loved your law.” For the obedience of love differs greatly from the service rendered by fear; and action compelled by necessity has none of the grace of free will. For those things do not suffice for themselves unto the perfection of complete obedience which, although they fulfill their task, nevertheless, because [they are compelled], lack the merit of full grace.

[Note: That is, they are destitute.]

Therefore the Prophet wishes his work to arise from love rather than terror, and his obedience to be undertaken from charity [Col. 0584D], not fear. Many fast because they fear our rebuke. Many provide something for the use of the needy because they fear that the irreligious [Col. 0585A] avarice and useless covetousness of their own will be reproached. Many attend church because they are ashamed that their absence and negligence may be censured. But not all love what they do.

Necessity of compliance, therefore, cannot enter into love, because no one who loves something is unwilling toward it. But love may be absent from an act when what is done is something that fear or shame might have caused one not to do. The Prophet, however, is weak in nothing. What he loves he does, and what he does he practices without failing. For the Law which he loves he meditates upon every day and without interruption. No other pursuits of occupations steal in; no varied storms of worldly cares intervene; nor does forgetfulness overtake him through the intrusion of some new thought. He is always the same and remains in the same state. As great as the entire day is in duration, so great is he in meditation upon the Law beloved by him [Col. 0585B].

3. It is no great thing to be wiser than idolaters.---VERS. 98. And because, as we have mentioned above, the Prophet displays in himself the man of Law, Prophets, and Gospels, he says in the following verse: *By your commandment you have made me wiser than my enemies, because it is mine for ever.* The Prophet understands God’s commandments more wisely than his enemies do. But what do we and our enemies have in common concerning God’s precepts, when they have not merely acquired even a moderate knowledge of them, but do not even pursue the beginning of knowing them? And what is great if the Prophet is wiser than his enemies concerning God’s commandments? For when could those who worship lifeless stones, metals, or pieces of wood attain anything of the knowledge of the living and eternal God [Col. 0585C], so that the Prophet might become wiser by comparison with them?

[Note: “By comparison with these.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “that, by comparison with these”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

But this whole error of the impious rejects, repudiates, and shudders at the very name itself—namely, that of the eternal God—together with the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles.

[Note: “Reconsiders” or “rejects.”]

4. Heretics and Jews, the enemies surpassed by wisdom.---But this holy Prophet has other enemies, whom he surpasses in wiser understanding of God’s commandments. Heretics possess God’s commandment in the Prophets and in the Law, but through the ignorance of their irreligious will they make no use of any of it. Jews claim the commandment of the Law as their own and hereditary possession; but if they do not possess the author of spiritual circumcision, what good will circumcision, now established merely as a sign, do them? What help will the observance of the Sabbath bring to those who do not know the Lord [Col. 0585D] of the Sabbath? What assistance will the paschal lamb, the blood upon the doorposts, and the feast of unleavened bread render to those ignorant of the Lamb of God, the unleavened bread of sincerity, and the blood of salvation?

They practice the commandments, but they do not know the efficacy and the appointed time of the commandments. They read the Law; but the Christian understands it, while the Jew reads and does not understand. This person is plainly an enemy of the Prophet: he lays parricidal hands upon the only-begotten Son of God and, so far as lies in him, condemns to death the Savior of the human race and giver of eternal life. Above all these, therefore, the Prophet is wiser in God’s commandment.

5. Those teachers who are enemies; David’s knowledge from God.---And so that it might be understood that he had absolutely meant these persons by “enemies,” he added what follows, VERS. 99: *I have understood more than all who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation.* You, David, learned the Law from Moses; Aaron is your teacher in all sacrifices; Joshua is the master of renewed circumcision; Samuel showed you in yourself the mystery of the One to be anointed—both prophet and king. What then is this that you have dared to say: that you have understood more than all who teach you?

[Note: “Of anointing,” as often in ancient books.]

[Note: Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius read “in anointing you,” which the final Paris edition adopted. The manuscripts rightly read “of anointing,” that is, of Him who is to be anointed, namely Christ, of whom David bore the type; Moses foretold Him as prophet, Isaiah as the king to come.]

[Col. 0586A]

But the preceding verse shows above whom he understands more than all who teach him: namely, above his enemies. And again, this verse now under consideration declares who the enemies are: namely, all who teach. For they profess that they possess the keys of heaven and glory in being teachers of the Law. Yet although all the testimonies of the Law testify to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Prophet understands more than his teachers, because, meditating upon those testimonies, he continually awaits the only-begotten Son of God as one who is to come in the flesh. O blessed understanding of the disciple! O marvelous ignorance of the teachers! The teachers do not know, while those who are taught understand.

The Prophet, however, is free from the vice of boasting, for he shows from whom he obtained the excellence of his understanding. For above he said that he had been made wiser by God than his enemies in His commandments [Col. 0586C]. Every understanding comes from Him who made him wiser. Therefore he understands more than those who teach him.

6. It is given to one who seeks; “elder” means the earlier people.---And because it can sometimes happen from a difference of natural ability that a disciple is wiser than his teacher, he nevertheless shows that this very thing is due to his own diligence and earnestness. For he says, VERS. 100: *I have understood more than the elders, because I have sought out your commandments.* He understands more both than teachers and than elders, showing the service of his instruction and understanding by the very antiquity of time—that is, indicating the age of the people earlier than himself.

[Note: “He understood.”]

[Note: “More ancient.”]

In this person both things coincide: he is older, and he considers himself to be a teacher.

[Note: The printed editions read “more learned,” wrongly. The reference is to the older people, who are declared to be a teacher, not more learned. The manuscripts correct the text and are supported by what follows.]

Yet he understands more than the one who is both taught and younger [Col. 0586D]. He understands because he has sought out God’s commandments, which the teacher, while believing that he teaches, does not know.

7. The fruit of knowledge.---It follows that one who understands more than elders and teachers should yield the fruit of his understanding: namely, that he should practice the things which he has begun to possess in knowledge and perfection. Let us see whether this very point occurs in what follows [Col. 0587A]. For he says, VERS. 101: *From every evil way I have restrained my feet, that I may keep your word.* This is the perfect voice of the evangelical man: to abstain from every path of wickedness and, though paths of error meet him everywhere, to walk in none of them by which wickedness may be approached.

8. Vices must be kept away so that God’s word may be guarded.---But the Prophet signifies something deeper when he says, *I have restrained my feet.*

[Note: Lipsius and Paris read “I know not what else,” without any authority.]

Our bodily nature carries us into every course of sin, and the impulse of human desires compels us along this path. But the one who understands more than elders and teachers has restrained himself through the teaching of understanding, and has recalled himself as he went forth and rushed ahead.

[Note: The nature of our body carries us.]

Therefore we must resist and strive, first to keep ourselves from every evil way [Col. 0587B], and then, if some impulse begins to carry us that way, to draw ourselves back.

[Note: “By that impulse.”]

[Note: In three manuscripts: “if his own impulse begins to carry us”; this is not approved.]

[Note: The printed editions read “ourselves, and by his power”; the manuscripts oppose this.]

We ourselves must first be checked by our own power, so that afterward we may keep God’s word. First there is need of self-restraint, if the guarding of God’s word is to be possible. For no one will first keep the word and then be able to restrain himself.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “will first keep [it], than be able to restrain,” etc.]

For restraint properly occurs when what was being done is prevented from being done; but guarding is then firm when one, restraining oneself from evils, observes good things without interruption of vigilance.

9. The true keeping of God’s word.---The following verse teaches what the keeping of God’s word ought to be. For it follows, VERS. 102: *I have not turned aside from your judgments, because you have set the law before me.* This, then, is true guarding: not to turn aside in any direction from God’s judgments, not even to deviate by the slightest departure, but always to remain attentive and ever unmoved in that upon which one has taken one’s stand.

10. The evangelical Law is contained in Moses’ Law and gives humanity hope of God’s glory.---He does not turn aside because the Lord has established a law for him. Moses indeed established a law; but this same Prophet had prayed in another Psalm, saying: “O Lord, appoint a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are human” (Ps. 9:21). For the Law which Moses wrote was our pedagogue unto Christ; and therefore he understood more than those who taught him and than the elders, because he understands the evangelical Law contained in Moses’ Law. This Law, therefore, was given through our Lord [Col. 0588A]; it instructed every human being in the knowledge of God.

[Note: “In the knowledge of God,” without “in.”]

And therefore, to what he had said, “Appoint a lawgiver over them,” he added: “Let the nations know that they are human”; that is, born from the earth and formed from clay into the knowledge of God. What they formerly did not know through ignorance of Moses’ Law, they now know through the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: The word “Law,” deleted by Lipsius, is lacking also in Paris. Then, instead of “did not know,” Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius wrongly read “foreknew,” although the passage concerns Gentiles who had never foreknown the blessedness of the Gospel.]

And as in the new giver of the Law they recognize their origin—that is, the nature of their body—so they await the glory of this new giver of the Law, having already at their beginning been established in the image and likeness of God.

[Note: Again here the word “Law,” omitted in the common editions, is restored from the manuscripts, which shortly afterward read “established,” not “established [feminine].”]

[Note: “Established.”]

11. God’s utterances are sweet, if they penetrate the soul.---And in what follows the Prophet testifies to the sweetness of this evangelical preaching. For he says, VERS. 103: *How sweet are your utterances to my throat, more than honey to my mouth!* Honey is sweet in the mouth, but not also in the throat. For beyond the region of the mouth there is no sensation of bodily flavors. But God’s utterances are sweet in the throat: they flow into the soul and penetrate within. They are not merely pleasant as food in the mouth, but sweet there where the faculty of knowledge, wisdom, and understanding is. Therefore the utterances are sweeter in the throat and in the mouth than honey [Col. 0588B].

[Note: The royal manuscript with the Albinus manuscript reads “in my mouth.” The ensuing discussion supports this reading, as does Letter 17, §6: “The evil one snatches God’s word from the heart, though it delights more than honey and the honeycomb in the mouth,” not “to the mouth.”]

[Note: “Honey is sweet.”]

[Note: Thus the royal, Vatican, and Albinus manuscripts, whereas the common editions have “honey is sweet.” But: “more sweet than honey,” etc.]

But as honey lessens the bitterness in the mouth caused by sickness and the burning heat of fevers, so God’s utterances, when received, soothe the soul’s bitternesses and the grievous fevers of harmful desires—provided only that they are not kept in the mouth, but swallowed by the throat.

12. The precepts instruct those who perform them; knowledge is not given by God to those who do not desire it.---Then follows, VERS. 104: *From your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I have hated every way [Col. 0588C] of iniquity.* The precepts make us understanding—but precepts fulfilled in fact and deed; that is, we fulfill, insofar as we can, the things contained in them.

[Note: “You” in place of “we,” just as elsewhere in this same Psalm the Verona manuscript gives “your” in place of “our.”]

[Note: The Albinus and royal manuscripts: “Those who understand do not perform precepts alone, but precepts completed in fact and deed.” Even if these words perhaps do not preserve Hilary’s exact wording, they certainly help one grasp his meaning more readily.]

Therefore the precepts must be performed if we are to be understanding.

[Note: From the manuscripts we restore the words: “Therefore the precepts must be performed if we are to be understanding,” which were absent from earlier common editions.]

Although perfect understanding comes from God, nevertheless we must make a beginning ourselves, so that we may merit perfect understanding. For to those who do not initiate this in themselves, all things are closed by God. The prophetic discourse itself teaches this through Isaiah, who says: “Do not say of my commandments that you have known them; neither have you known nor believed them, nor from the beginning have I opened your ears. For I knew that you would utterly despise, [Col. 0589A] and that you would still be called iniquitous from the womb” (Isa. 48:7–8).

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “whom you opened your ears to know. For I knew,” etc.; it looks like a gloss. A little earlier, the words “of my commandments” occur neither in the Vulgate nor in the Greek Septuagint.]

Knowledge, therefore, is not granted to those who do not seek it. And because God searches hearts, those who would reject it have dull ears and a blunt understanding. But the Prophet gains understanding from God’s precepts: by practicing the precepts, he obtains understanding; and, having understanding, he hates every way of iniquity.

13. The right use of human affections.---All movements of diverse affections belong to human nature, such as hatreds and loves.

[Note: “Of hatred and love.”]

But love must be directed toward affection for good things, and hatred must be assumed from offense at evil things. It is ours, therefore, to tune our bodies, like a useful instrument, to fitting and harmonious modes: not to love vices, not to hate good virtues, but to adapt ourselves fittingly and beneficially to each kind [Col. 0589B].

[Note: Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and two manuscripts: “Therefore it is good.” The same two manuscripts shortly afterward read “to tune our hearts to fitting and harmonious modes,” etc.]

The Prophet loves God’s commandments; and he who loves God’s commandments hates paths of iniquity. For just as it belongs to the service of perfect faith to love obedience, to fulfill from charitable affection what one does, and to anticipate the necessity of action by the will of one who loves, so it is also the mark of great innocence not merely not to commit iniquities but to hate them; for sometimes fear and terror keep us from them.

[Note: “And service.”]

[Note: The common editions read “and service”; we have deleted “and” on the authority of the manuscripts.]

[Note: The Paris edition alone reads “not by these.”]

But hatred of them instills in us the judgment of a true and perfect opinion concerning them. Let us therefore love righteousness, moderation, frugality, and mercy; and let us hate quarrels, drunkenness, murders, pride, and fornications—along with which we must necessarily hate the devil. But loving peace, truth, and righteousness, we shall love Him who is peace, righteousness, and truth: our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER XIV. Nun

*Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths. I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness. I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord; give me life according to your word. Make the free offerings of my mouth acceptable, O Lord, and teach me your judgments. My soul is always in your hands, and I have not forgotten your law. Sinners set a snare for me, and I have not strayed from your commandments. I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance for ever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart. I have inclined my heart to perform your ordinances for ever because of the recompense.*

[Note: The word “O Lord” is absent not only here but also below, in §2. Neither the Septuagint nor the Hebrew sources includes it.]

1. Human darkness; eternity; God as guide to it.---Human life and perception remain in error—or rather, in the night of ignorance—while, infected by carnal contagion, they are held fast in the depth of ignorance by the weight of the nature with which they are mingled. For when will a person, by oneself, know the cause and reason of one’s origin? When will one know what fruit belongs to one’s life, what is the condition of hope, what path leads to the future state that must be attained?

[Note: The printed editions: “when, if there is any fruit”; corrected by the manuscripts.]

[Note: In two manuscripts, “power.” Perhaps read: “of future eternity”? Certainly this is not a matter of attaining some worldly favor from descendants, but of blessed eternity, to which human beings are here proved to have been born by the same argument as in *On the Trinity*, Book I, §9.]

For no one is so mad or lacking in understanding as to think that, when one did not exist, one was born in order that, after being born, one should again not exist; since one undoubtedly remembers that one’s birth proceeded from God’s goodness, and it cannot belong to His goodness to destroy in us this gift of His by which we are born [Col. 0590B].

[Note: “That we are born.”]

But the Prophet, worthy of the knowledge of heavenly things and placed by God’s gift and utterance in the light of knowledge, follows as guide for good and innocent living Him who is the true light and who enlightens every human being (John 1:9).

2. The light of God’s word must be used in every action.---He directs this ignorance of his life toward understanding by setting before it a certain light, saying, VERS. 105: *Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet.* He knows that unless he is illuminated by God’s word, he cannot escape these bodily shadows and this night of the world.

[Note: “Cannot endure.”]

[Note: The printed editions: “cannot endure.”]

He knows that stones of stumbling, snares of cords, and pits of traps are everywhere present. For as one who goes out by night carries a lamp before oneself, sees where to place one’s foot, and is watchful at every step with the light going before, so each of us, keeping God’s word within oneself, holds it out like a lamp in every course of action [Col. 0590C]. For all heavenly teaching is our guide upon the path of life; like a lamp, it must be carried before us in this night of the world whenever we act, think, or speak, so that we may use it in every advance of whatever action we undertake.

3. Let the lamp’s light not be useless within us; let it burn continually.---In the Gospels the Lord commands that this lamp of His precepts not be hidden away idle and useless, saying: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel” (Matt. 5:15).

[Note: The common editions: “and useful to the eyes.” More correctly in the manuscripts: “and uselessly hidden,” that is, hidden so as to become useless.]

For what use is a lamp if it is covered by a bushel? It expends its usefulness only within that by which it is covered. He therefore commands it to be placed on a lampstand [Col. 0590D], that is, established in the seat of its function. Thus, having received this teaching and this word of God within us, let us not conceal it as though under a bushel, idle and useless; but let us provide this light first for ourselves and then, from ourselves, for all nations [Col. 0591A].

The Lord likewise admonished us by the following command, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35).

[Note: “By this command.”]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “command.”]

He commands, therefore, that we do nothing in darkness; for everyone who does evil hates the light and loves darkness (John 3:20). He wishes our lamps always to be lit, lest at some point we be left in the night of this world. For the Jews a lamp is lit in the tabernacle of testimony, and it burns throughout the whole time of their feast (Exod. 27:20–21). They do not know what they are doing. But let us always have burning lamps in these tabernacles of ours—that is, in our bodies—and celebrate the feast of our hope [Col. 0591B] by their light.

4. The Apostles are the Church’s eyes; John is a lamp; the prudent virgins.---The Lord also calls the Apostles the salt of the earth and the light of the world (Matt. 5:14), and by this signification shows that they are also lamps of the Church, saying: “The lamp of your body is your eye” (Matt. 6:22)—that is, of the body of the Church, which is one body in Christ and of which we are members one of another. First, God’s word is an eye or lamp for each of us; then an apostolic man is a lamp for his whole body—that is, the Church.

[Note: “A lamp for itself.”]

[Note: The Paris edition inserts “for itself” here.]

For the whole body is not all foot, eye, or hand. Therefore, if the eyes, the brightest part of the whole body and for that reason preeminent over the other members, become darkness (ibid., v. 23)—that is, if the lamps of the Apostles do not burn—then, when the very light is in darkness, how great a night will remain for the whole body [Col. 0591C]! John, preacher of repentance, was a lamp both to Jews and Gentiles, the Lord saying: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35), “and you wished to rejoice in his light for an hour.” We have, therefore, the light of teaching: let us rejoice in it, not for an hour but always; not temporarily but for eternity.

Those blessed virgins, prudent and industrious buyers of oil, alone entered the bridal chamber with the bridegroom in the light of their lamps; the others, being negligent and asleep, were shut out from entrance into the bridal chamber (Matt. 25).

[Note: That is, industrious. For “useful” here is opposed to “useless,” “idle,” and “free from the duty of work.]

5. God’s word as lamp and light.---Let us therefore use God’s word as a lamp for every step of our soul, but let the lamp always burn, always be prepared by our care for its function [Col. 0591D].

[Note: The printed editions read “prudence.”]

But the word which is a lamp to the feet is also itself a light to the paths. Those proceeding gently and near home need a lamp; but those embarking upon a foreign and public road need rather a light, lest a robber lie in ambush or the uncertainty of the roads bring error. For by stages one ascends from lesser things to greater [Col. 0592A].

[Note: “One advances.”]

[Note: The printed editions: “one approaches.”]

Thus for the one to whom God’s word is first a lamp to the feet, that same word becomes a light to the paths.

[Note: “To the paths.”]

But lamp for the feet and light for the paths ought to yield beneficial progress. Let us see whether the Prophet has added something worthy.

6. What is sworn and determined.---For he says, VERS. 106: *I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness.* He no longer wanders in the night of the world, nor fears that his foot may stumble. For every oath is a matter of established knowledge, and the sacred obligation of swearing is undertaken from knowledge of the truth. The Prophet therefore swears; nor does he merely swear, but also determines, because the bond of an oath is the firmness of determinations. Thus, swearing, he determines to keep the judgments of God’s righteousness. Determinations are difficult to overthrow, and it is best to make sworn determinations.

7. God’s judgments are just.---But he remembers that there is nothing unjust in God’s judgments. If human judgments are truly considered judgments when they are established by the decision of a just judgment, how can there be any doubt that there is nothing unjust in God’s judgments?

[Note: The royal and Albinus manuscripts read “are brought about.” Then Mic. and Vatican: “how much less should it now be doubted.”]

[Note: “How much less should there be doubt.”]

We lose children and consider this judgment unjust. Did God unjustly give the devil power over Job’s children? We grieve at our losses as though they happened unjustly. Did God permit that perfect man to be reduced to poverty without a reason of justice? We are tortured by pains and reproach God with the complaints of our impatience. Was Job, consumed by worms, flowing with pus, and pierced with ulcers, afflicted by an uncertain plan? Certainly all these things served for the proof of faith and the reward of glorious patience. Our weakness makes us think that what we suffer is evil [Col. 0592C]. Yet God’s will is always that we be tested by the patience of sufferings; but we reject the justice of divine judgment because we wish it to remain hidden without the proof of faith.

### 8. Christ gave both the precept and the example of humility.

But he who above both swore and determined that he would keep the judgments of God’s righteousness ought, in observing those judgments, to render something worthy of his oath and resolution. For what he resolved under oath to keep is no slight matter. And what that is, the following verse declares. For he says, verse 107: “I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord; give me life according to thy word.”

The only-begotten Son of God, assuming to himself from the Virgin a body of our nature, and having presented in himself a true and perfect pattern of human wisdom, must be considered in respect of what he wished to be learned from him as an example of doctrine. For he says: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29). He himself—perfect, alone without sin, and the one in whose mouth no deceit was found—willed that this should especially be taken from him as an example of instruction: namely, meekness and humility, through which rest is found for souls.

### 9. He removed grounds for pride.

He knows that the weakness of our nature is insolent and incapable of bearing prosperity. Some become insolent through riches, not knowing that it was said concerning the bestowal of wealth: “For almsgiving conceals sin” [note: In two manuscripts: “cuts off sin.” Compare Ecclesiasticus 3:33, “Almsgiving will expiate sins”; Tobit 12:9, “It cleanses every sin.” Whether these or other passages are intended here is uncertain.]; and again: “He hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor; his righteousness remaineth for ever” (Ps. 111:9) [note: “For ever and ever,” in accordance with the Greek.]. And God himself said to those who had fed him when hungry, given him drink when thirsty, received him as a stranger into their home, clothed him when naked, visited him when sick, and comforted him when shut in prison: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

Others swell with the glory of this world, not knowing that this was the chief saying of the heavenly blessing: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Others are lifted up to eminence by carnal nobility [note: The Regius manuscript reads “into arrogance”; this might be preferable, were it not that below, §12, all books read “the swelling of eminence.” Yet we conjecture that here *fastidium* and there *fastidii* should be restored, from Book 3, §14: “O unhappy pride, which disdains to live under heavenly precepts, which in the swelling of an unbelieving mind scorns the divine commandments!”], not considering that it was said to those reborn in Christ: “But ye are an elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Pet. 2:9) [note: “Holy race.” Others are kings of this world.].

The laws of this world are one thing; the gifts of God another. When the devil dared to tempt the Lord, he boasts that the world belongs to himself (Matt. 4:1). But the Lord commands us to die to the world, that we may live to him. [Note: *Cum* may be understood as a conjunction connecting and confirming what precedes, so that the following word *Domino* is in the dative case. Yet it seems truer to be a preposition having the same force as *secundum*, “according to.” Thus above we have more than once read *cum Graecis*, “according to the Greeks.”] With the Lord, contempt for riches is wealth; with the Lord, contempt for earthly honour is the kingdom of heaven; with the Lord, humility of heart is the adornment of noble and royal birth. This, therefore, he wished to be learned from himself, because it is the greatest of all virtues.

### 10. The reward of Christ’s humility.

The Apostle also, teaching us humility, exhorts us in these words: “Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:6 ff.).

We have from the only-begotten God an example of humility; but let us also look at its reward. “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9–11) [notes: “Every knee should bend.” “Is in glory.”].

This was the reward of humility: that the assumed body should remain in the glory of God the Father, and that heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings should bow their knees at his name. For, remaining in the form of God, he did not think that what he was—namely, equality with God—was to be claimed for himself by any force or seizure. For he was in God’s form, and nothing of the glory of him in whose form he remained was lacking to him. Yet he took the form of a servant through humility [note: We have removed the interpolated word *sui* on the authority of our oldest manuscript; likewise, we have removed *sui* on the authority of the manuscripts.], and was found in appearance as a man, humbling himself through obedience unto death—and not merely unto death, but unto death on a cross.

He himself established the heavens by God’s command [note: The printed editions read “formed”; the manuscripts more correctly read “established,” in accordance with Psalm 32:6: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.”], adorned the world by the Father’s command in this form of such great beauty, and created the earth and the things in it [note: “Which are in these.”]. But did he merit, by those deeds, to place the assumed man in the glory of the eternal Father? This is humility’s reward; this is humility’s recompense: that he who formerly remained in the form of God should thereafter be made in the form of a servant [note: That is: not merely according to that which remains in the form of God, but also according to that which is in the form of a servant, he should be known to be in the glory of God the Father—the servant-form advancing into the glory of him in whose form he formerly remained; as explained on Psalm 138, §19. See the exposition of Psalm 143, §7.]; and that, remaining in the form of God and made in the form of a servant, he should be known, by the confession of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, to be in the glory of God the Father.

[Note: The editions of Lyons and Paris read, “so that, remaining”; they express less clearly the reason why Christ merited glory.]

### 11. Paul guards his own people against self-exaltation; God calls him away from it.

The same Apostle, fearing also lest the very grace of divine gifts should make some persons insolent, says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness” (1 Cor. 12:7). In saying “for usefulness,” he taught that it must be used humbly [notes: “To be used usefully.” The Regius manuscript, with Albinus, reads “humbly.” Others read “to be used usefully,” but this does not convey Hilary’s point: from Paul’s words “for usefulness” he shrewdly concludes that God’s gifts must be used humbly, because without humility they become idle and useless.], lest perhaps confidence in spiritual gifts should make anyone insolent and the grace of God should, through the fault of insolence, become idle.

From his own case he shows that he too received this grace from God: that, through confidence in the many graces bestowed upon him, he might not be raised into some swelling of pride. He says: “And because of the greatness of the revelations, there was given me a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me, lest I should be exalted” (2 Cor. 12:7). Even that vessel of election and teacher of the Gentiles feared lest, through confidence in spiritual gifts within him, he should be lifted above the nature of human weakness into pride [note: The two manuscripts mentioned above read, “be lifted up by grace.”].

Scripture praises King Hezekiah because he “did what was right and good in the sight of God” (2 Kings 18:3); but this praise could not endure to the end. For it is written in the second book of Chronicles: “And Hezekiah fell from the height of his heart” (2 Chron. 32:26) [note: The editions of Basle and Erasmus read *Paralipomenum*; Lyons and the final Paris edition, *Paralipomenon*. With the first edition and the manuscript of Mic., we prefer *Praeteritorum*, “of Things Past,” as a reading less open to suspicion of alteration and confirmed in the exposition of Psalm 113, §11.]. When he lifted his heart on high, when through confidence in praise he raised himself into pride, he lost, through the sin of pride, the grace of his past deeds.

### 12. David was most humble, though he had many grounds for pride.

Therefore the Prophet, determining by oath that he would keep God’s righteous judgments, undertook this first work: to become humble; and not merely humble, but exceedingly humble—teaching, by this addition, the modesty of humility brought to perfection in himself.

And he had many causes for pride. His descent from Judah offered grounds for insolence, and in him the authority of royal blessing was first begun. For the family of royal power remained for some time in the tribe of David, from which, according to the flesh, the eternal King came forth. He was also exceedingly wise. For he says: “Thou hast made known to me the invisible and hidden things of thy wisdom” (Ps. 50:8). He also merited to be a prophet, as is said: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter hidden things from the foundation of the world” (Ps. 77:2). He likewise abounded in the resources of human wealth. He himself says: “Behold, from my poverty I have gathered a hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand of silver, and brass and iron beyond number” (1 Chron. 22:14) [note: The printed editions read: “so many thousand talents, and other amounts of silver, brass, etc.” This conflicts with our manuscripts as well as with the sacred Greek and Latin text.].

Thus, nobility of family, royal power, confidence in wisdom, prophetic merit, and abundance of resources did not raise him into pride or lift him into any swelling of eminence. He therefore safely asks, saying: “Give me life according to thy word”; that is, that, as one not yet living, he may merit the life of eternal life according to God’s word, because the modesty of humility kept him within the discipline and teaching of Gospel preaching.

### 13. David willingly performs more than the Law commands.

Next follows, verse 108: “Make the freewill offerings of my mouth acceptable, O Lord, and teach me thy judgments.” [Note: The Regius and Albinus manuscripts: “The Prophet worthily carries out his oath.”]

The Prophet worthily carries out the oath [note: “By his oath.”] of his resolution. For first he became exceedingly humble; next he prays that the voluntary offerings of his mouth may be pleasing. He is not content to be confined even by the prescribed requirements of the Law, nor merely to be subject to the necessity of obedience. [Note: In the printed editions: “next,” and shortly thereafter: “not content with the things already prescribed … the Law had commanded him to be subject to the necessity of obedience.” For understanding this and what follows, recall Hilary’s statement on Psalm 53, §13, that the sacrifices of the Law do not contain in themselves a profession of free will. He therefore concludes: “What was done had to be done, because the addition of a curse did not allow neglect of the sacrifice,” etc.]

The Law commanded that evil be returned for evil. Yet when this David had often taken and trapped Saul, who pursued him with all the forces of his kingdom, he not only did not kill him, but even dismissed him with honour, saying: “I will not lay my hand upon him, because he is the Lord’s anointed” (1 Sam. 24:11). When he learned that Saul had been slain in battle, he wept and avenged him (2 Sam. 1:15, 17).

His son Absalom [note: In the Regius manuscript, here and below, “Absolon.”] also seizes the kingdom, gathers an army, and pursues his father in parricidal war. But David says to his soldiers: “Spare the boy Absalom” (2 Sam. 18:5). Necessity indeed was imposed upon them to resist, because he was king; but affection and goodness were present to spare him, because he was a prophet. He also mourned the dead man with paternal affection and grief. These acts are voluntary, not legal; and obedience to them is an office of freedom rather than necessity.

### 14. Works of voluntary devotion commended by Paul.

The Apostle follows this practice of voluntary, and not merely legal, instruction when he says: “Now concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord; but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:25). Or when he praises the glory of widowhood and continence, he does not forbid the power to marry, but proclaims the merit of celibacy (ibid. 7:38) [note: Our manuscript agrees almost with earlier editions: “not by forbidding the power of marrying, but as a preacher of celibacy’s merit, he establishes something beyond the Law.”].

He establishes beyond the Law and exhorts beyond commandment, setting voluntary acts before legal requirements. Again he says: “Have we not power to eat and drink? Have we not power to lead about women, as also the other apostles, and the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas? Or have only I and Barnabas no power to do this work? But we do not use this power” [notes: “Not to work,” in accordance with the Greek, *τοῦ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι*. The Regius manuscript and Albinus read “we use the power.” Power is for unlawful things. Power is in what is lawful.] (1 Cor. 9:4–6).

There is freedom in what is lawful, when the Law—that is, the Gospel—spares our unbelief and does not burden us with severe prescriptions. But the profession of free will comes from the growth of faith, when, in matters in which the Law is moderate toward us, we restrain ourselves by zealous voluntary devotion.

### 15. David performs the Law’s judgments without understanding them.

Therefore the Prophet prays that these voluntary acts may be pleasing to God, because those things which are done according to the prescription of the Law are performed by the necessity of its service. [Note: “Are done.”] Yet he always gives a reason for his prayer. For after praying that the voluntary offerings of his mouth might be acceptable, he added: “And teach me thy judgments.”

He performs the judgments of the Law and, so far as lies in him, practices them in deeds and works; but he does not yet understand them. [Note: The printed editions read “says”; the manuscripts more correctly read “performs,” since, as was said just before, he performs what is done according to the prescription of the Law.] For he knows that the Law is spiritual, and hastens to know that which lies hidden beneath the appearance of present acts. For a person must necessarily ask to be taught those things which he does not know.

### 16. He hands himself over wholly to God.

But the Prophet, according to the resolution of his oath, gave himself wholly to God. He was humbled exceedingly; the voluntary offerings of his mouth are acceptable; now his soul is always in God’s hands, and he does not forget God’s Law, saying, verse 109: “My soul is always in thy hands, and I have not forgotten thy Law.”

All that he lives, he lives to God. All his thought and spirit are in God. No moment is allowed in which forgetfulness of the Law may creep in. In all his works and thoughts God is considered. The Law is in his memory; the soul of the living man is always in God’s hands.

### 17. How necessary this is for everyone. Snares everywhere.

He also knows how beneficial and necessary it is daily to commit himself to God’s hands, in his deeds and works and through unfailing remembrance of the Law. For he says, verse 110: “Sinners have set a snare for me, and I have not wandered from thy commandments.”

He knows that in this forest of the world many snares are spread and many traps are laid for his life. Our speech, thought, and action always have snares lying near them: when there arises, at one time, an occasion for anger, an impulse of grief, a necessity for complaint, or an opportunity for evil desire. The devil and his angels—transgressors from the beginning and sinners from the outset—always spread these snares.

But he whose soul is in God’s hands and who is never forgetful of God’s Law, though surrounded on every side by such cast snares, will nevertheless not wander from the commandments. For, always thinking on God, he escapes from them, as he says in another psalm: “Like a sparrow, delivered from the snare of hunters” (Ps. 123:7) [note: “Another.”]. And the Lord himself says through the Prophet: “Deliver yourselves from the snare of hunters and from the word of disturbance” (Ps. 90:3) [note: The editions of Basle and Erasmus, with the manuscripts, read “Deliver yourselves.” Ambrose, on this same passage, also has this reading in all manuscripts and printed books except one Roman edition, which substituted “He delivered thee from the snare.” Lipsius restored that latter reading here on his own authority, and it subsequently prevailed.].

### 18. How destructive the world is to those who have renounced it.

“For nets are not spread unjustly for birds” (Prov. 1:17, according to the Septuagint). You have been instructed in heavenly knowledge: what have you to do with earthly works and concerns? You have become a bird: why do you not remain in the element proper to your nature? For they are called birds of heaven; therefore snares are not unjustly laid for them within the possession of an earthly dwelling.

You have renounced the world: what have you to do with the world’s affairs? Why do you complain when caught in the world? Why complain of the wrong of a snare in a country that is not yours? Rather say, and yourself use, the words of the Psalmist: “Who will give me wings like a dove? And I shall fly and be at rest” (Ps. 54:7) [note: “Thus,” in place of “these words.”].

It is the nature of birds not to rest when they wish [note: The printed editions read “so that they rest only when they wish.” One Vatican manuscript reads “so that when they do not wish.” We prefer, with Regius and Albinus, “so that they do not rest when they wish,” so that spiritual birds may here be shown to excel bodily birds in that the former rest by flying, whereas the latter do not.]. But you, now made a dove, find rest by flying; that is, by raising yourself through the flight of a faithful soul into the heavenly abode and knowledge, away from earthly snares.

### 19. David desires to be God’s witness and to suffer for his cause. Testimonies acquired as an inheritance.

Then follows, verse 111: “I have inherited thy testimonies for ever, because they are the joy of my heart.” According to human custom, an heir possesses all that belongs to the person of whom he is heir. But the Prophet disdains human inheritances, having inherited God’s testimonies. It is pleasing to him if he himself becomes God’s witness [note: “Of God.”], because it is the joy of his heart if he bears witness to God amid the battles of persecutions.

Thus we remember that the Apostles rejoiced in these testimonies, when, leaving the assembly of their persecutors, they rejoiced that they had been judged worthy of insults for God’s name (Acts 5:41). Therefore his testimonies were the joy of their hearts.

But the Prophet, like the Apostles, retains amid many persecutions these testimonies of God—that is, the act of testifying concerning him—with joy of heart as an inheritance. Yet he also holds as an inheritance those testimonies of God which were spoken under witnesses. Moses gave the Law with heaven and earth as witnesses (Deut. 4:26); Isaiah rebuked with heaven and earth as witnesses (Isa. 1:2); the Apostle, as a preacher of the Gospel, used still loftier witnesses, saying: “I charge thee before God and Christ Jesus and his angels” (1 Tim. 5:21).

These testimonies, therefore—written under these witnesses, testified under them, and testified in them—he takes possession of as heir of a new inheritance; not partially, but wholly. For the right of inheritance belongs in full. Although an inheritance is divided among several persons according to human succession, nevertheless the inheritance itself belongs in full under the name of heir.

### 20. Perseverance is from God; beginning is in some sense from ourselves. The defect of our origin.

And lest what is often said by many should appear to have any rational authority—when they assert that it is God’s own gift for a person to be occupied in God’s matters and works, excusing their own unbelief on the ground that they remain unbelieving because God’s will toward them has ceased—although remaining in faith is indeed God’s gift, the beginning is from ourselves. [Note: “And our will must have this as its own from itself: that it should will.”]

And our will must have this as its own from itself, that it should will [note: In two manuscripts: “has from itself that it should will.” These first words of Hilary are subject to a sound interpretation. Augustine truly says, *City of God* III.10: “We do many things which, if we did not will them, we certainly would not do”; and to this belongs first of all willing itself: for if we will, it exists; if we do not will, it does not exist. For we would not will if we did not will. And in *On Free Choice of the Will* III.3.8: “Our will, therefore, would not be a will unless it were in our power.” Yet Augustine must be added from *On Grace and Free Will* 16: “It is certain that we will when we will; but God makes us will”—lest Hilary’s following words seem to imply that our will can by itself, without God’s grace, accomplish some good. See above, Letter 5, §12.].

God will give increase to one who begins, because our weakness does not obtain completion by itself; nevertheless, the merit of attaining completion comes from the beginning of the will. Therefore the Prophet concluded the psalm thus, verse 112: “I have inclined my heart to perform thy justifications for ever, because of the recompense.”

He himself inclines his heart and bends it from the sins of human nature toward obedience to God. The nature and origin of his flesh indeed held him fast; but will and religion incline his heart away from the defect of origin in which it remained, toward the works of justifications. And he inclines it throughout all the time of his life: not within a fixed limit of time, but throughout every age of his life. He inclines it because of the recompense, being assured, namely, that these things are reserved for the merits of faith [note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “being assured that he is reserved for the merit of faith”; this has every appearance of interpolation.], and that his recompense lies in those things “which eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God hath prepared for those who love him in Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 2:9), to whom be glory now and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER XV. Samech

“I have hated the lawless, and loved thy law. Thou art my helper and protector” (Hilary adds, “art thou”); “and I have hoped” (or, “I hope”) “in thy word. Depart from me, ye malicious ones; and I will search out the commandments of my God. Receive me according to thy word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation. Help me, and I shall be saved; and I will meditate always on thy justifications. Thou hast despised all who depart from thy justices” (below, “justifications”), “because their knowledge” (or, “thought”) “is unjust. I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I have loved thy testimonies” (below, “thy justifications, without ‘always’”) “always. Pierce my flesh with thy fear; for I have feared thy judgments.”

### 1. To love enemies is a commandment.

The teaching of the evangelical precept is that we should love our enemies (Matt. 5:44), and that we owe love not only to those who love us but also to those who hate us. Therefore this profession of the Prophet seems opposed to the Lord’s commandments: though love of enemies is enjoined upon us, he presents as a good work his hatred of the lawless, saying, verse 113: “I have hated the lawless.”

[Note: The Regius manuscript: “The commandment of evangelical teaching is … that we should return love to those who love us, but also love those who hate us.”]

### 2. Hatred of father, mother, and so forth is commanded when they call one away from martyrdom or God’s service.

But the reason for this very saying must be learned from the Gospels themselves. For the Lord, who commanded enemies to be loved and decreed that those who cursed father or mother were guilty of death (Lev. 20:9), again elsewhere gave this command: “If any man come to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yea, and even his own soul, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26).

These things therefore seem contrary to one another: that he whose command makes not merely hatred of parents, but even a curse, worthy of death, should himself again say that no one can be his disciple unless he hates father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and his own soul. This is a hard saying and a grievous commandment: that impiety should be made necessary for the fulfilment of religion.

### 3. Yet nothing harsh, impious, or contrary to earlier commands is commanded by God.

But these names so dear to us—father, mother, wife, and children—cannot be angry because we are commanded to hate them, when we are commanded to hate our own soul as well. For the Lord knows that many have such unwise love that, when they see their children persisting in the glory of martyrdom, they beg them to yield to the times and pray them to change their resolve. They employ toward them the affection of an impious piety [note: “Employ,” for “may employ.”].

An aged mother and an old father display before their son, in the very contest of martyrdom, their pitiable grey hairs, reproaching the excessive harshness of his resolve. Then his wife is present, eager in the company of their children, praying that he may rather live for her and them. Then brothers and sisters entreat him by the tender familiarity of their names. Even his own soul, long captivated by the enticements of life, creeps in with certain silent counsels, seeking to incline his resolve toward compromise.

At such a time, therefore, the Lord commanded us to hate father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even our own soul. For he ended this same saying, after the hatred of all these, by declaring: “And whosoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:27). They are therefore to be hated when they do not wish us to carry the cross of martyrdom, when they dissuade us from following God through the example of suffering. This hatred is honourable and useful: to hate those who try to draw us away from the love of Christ.

### 4. By hating the lawless, David does not contradict the Gospel.
