Thus the Prophet now appears to have said nothing contrary to the Gospel commands by which we are commanded to love enemies, when he says: “I have hated the lawless.” [Note: “I hated.”] For he does not speak of his enemies [note: The earlier printed editions read “hates.”], but of the lawless: that is, transgressors of the Law.

The Greek uses a more exact term here, saying *paranomous* (παρανόμους), that is, persons acting outside the Law. [Note: The Albinus manuscript with the Regius: “Greek expresses this word in a more precise sense, saying …”] But one who hates transgressors of the Law cannot fail to love that whose neglect he hates; and therefore he says: “And I loved thy Law.” It is fitting that, because he loves the Law, he should hate those who are enemies of the Law.

### 5. We greatly need God’s help. Hope obtains it. All merit comes from hope and faith in Christ.

Then follows, verse 114: “Thou art my helper and protector, and I hope in thy word.” We greatly need God’s help in so great and unceasing a battle in this world. For, according to the Apostle, our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against spiritual wickednesses in heavenly places (Eph. 6:12). These, therefore, are our enemies; against them God must be entreated as our helper, that he may receive us into his protection.

Yet this prayer ought not to arise so much from fear as from merit. For fear arises from the trembling of the human condition; but the Prophet hopes in God’s word. Hope does not possess present things, but future ones. Therefore he hopes for the things contained in God’s word—that is, in prophetic sayings. He hopes either for the rewards of faith unto spiritual life, or he awaits the coming of that Lord of ours who is the Word of God. Such hope merits God’s aid and help.

Neither we nor any before us have otherwise merited than by hoping that the Word of God, God, would dwell in the flesh of our nature, or by believing that he had dwelt in it. [Notes: The editions of Basle, Erasmus, and Lipsius read, “either would indwell or had indwelt”; Paris and the manuscripts read “would indwell,” etc. Nestorius indeed expressed his heresy by this word, against whom Leo, *Sermon 3 on the Nativity of the Lord*, ch. 1, says: “Nor was the creature so assumed into fellowship with its Creator that he should be an indweller and it a dwelling, but so that one nature might be mingled with the other.” Yet Hilary is far removed from Nestorius. In *On the Trinity* I.11 he says: “And lest the Word made flesh should be anything other than God the Word, or should not be flesh of our body, he dwelt in us: so that, while he dwelt, he remained nothing other than God, but while he dwelt in us, he was made nothing other than flesh of our flesh … perfect in his own things and true in ours.” He also repeatedly teaches, with Leo, a mingling of the two natures—an expression afterwards abused by Eutyches to assert confusion of the divine and human natures. He cuts off the heresies of both Nestorius and Eutyches, germs of Arian heresy, by the words cited above and elsewhere, especially in *On the Trinity* X.16 ff. and on Psalm 53, §11.

The Vatican manuscript reads “they hoped … they believed.” Augustine held the same truth. In Letter 157, §14, he teaches that whatever righteous persons there may have been in ancient times were liberated only through the same faith by which we are liberated, namely faith in Christ’s Incarnation, which was foretold to them and is proclaimed to us as accomplished. “Since,” he says in Letter 190, §6, “all the righteous—that is, true worshippers of God—whether before or after Christ’s Incarnation, neither lived nor live except by faith in Christ’s Incarnation.” Hence Ignatius, *Letter to the Magnesians* §§8–9, says that the most divine Prophets lived according to Christ Jesus, being taught by him and therefore called his disciples. Hence Leo, *Sermon 3 on the Nativity of the Lord*, ch. 4, replying to those who complained that this grace of God was too broadly extended, says: “What has always been believed was not fulfilled late.”]

### 6. Malice exists in everyone. The heart contains manifold malice.

But the Prophet remembers that many things are in him which strive to oppose his hope; and therefore he adds, verse 115: “Depart from me, ye malicious ones, and I will search out the commandments of my God.” The logic of heavenly teaching instructs us to understand this saying as referring to persons in whom malice resides. For the Prophet, who teaches the nations and preaches God’s word, commands all malicious persons to depart from him, because the assembly of saints is unworthy of workers of malice. [Note: The printed editions read “the holy assembly.” Here is a figure of speech signifying that workers of malice are unworthy of the assembly or company of saints. The printed editions read “and may not know,” as though the word referred to “assembly”; this is altogether wrong. They also omit “malice lies near” below and “the Lord” before “saying”; the manuscripts restore these readings.]

And I do not know whom he can except. For by the choice of our changeable nature, malice lies near to all; and the Lord taught that even the Apostles—though already cleansed and holy through the word of faith—were not free from malice by reason of the condition of our common origin, when he said: “If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children” (Luke 11:13). [Note: Augustine cites this in *Against Julian* II.8.26.]

But it is our duty to love the evil and teach the good toward goodness [note: The editions of Lipsius and Paris read “to love both the good and the evil and to teach the evil toward goodness,” against Basle, Erasmus, and the manuscripts, with which Hincmar, *On Predestination* ch. 25, agrees. Hilary raises an objection: “We must love the evil; therefore we must not repel them.” He then resolves it: “But he knows,” etc. As Ambrose explains on the same passage, Christ repels the malicious but calls those who labour; those invited are burdened, certainly not with malice of mind but with weakness of flesh.], according to him who instead invites all to himself, saying: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

But the Prophet knows that there are many forms of malice hidden in the human heart. For according to the Lord’s saying, “From within proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, falsehoods, blasphemies” (Matt. 15:19). These are what make a person common, or defiled. He therefore asks that such things, which oppose his faith, may depart from him [note: “That” was absent from the printed editions.]. For they hinder efforts toward innocence and hinder spiritual teaching; and when they intrude through continual familiarity with their counsels, the mind is not free to search out God’s commandments, because the presence of malicious persons greatly hinders one who wishes to search out God’s commandments.

### 7. Slanders against Christian hope. A prayer against them.

And because mercy is God’s work, so that, received into his household, we may be freed from the dominion of these evil powers, the prophet prays, saying, VERSE 116: “Uphold me according to your word, and [p. 374] I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.” The prophet waits and hopes: he pursues nothing present, nothing temporary. Yet many accuse and ridicule this expectation of our faith, saying [Col. 0602C]: “What benefit will fasting, self-restraint, chastity, and the loss of property bring—or take away [Note: [Col. 0602C] “Bring.”] [Note: [Col. 0602D] The printed editions read “bring.” The manuscripts more fittingly read “take away,” that is, from this world.]? Where is your hope, O Christians? Death rules all alike; it has a common right over the bodily nature of all. Indeed, we enjoy every good thing of this world, and use the freedom of the real life; and wherein, finally, do you surpass us by the expectation of your hope?” [Note: [Col. 0603C] The printed editions read “of our hope”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

Therefore the prophet prays that he may not be put to shame in this hope, but may remain confident and receive the fruit of that true life which he awaits. For he knows that he does not yet live, although he is alive. For our life, according to the Apostle, “is hidden with Christ” (Col. 3:3). And therefore he says: “Uphold me according to your word, and I shall live,” because he is held fast by expectation and hope of that true and unfailing life. He hopes for eternity; he hopes for the kingdom of heaven; he hopes for the kingdom of God; he hopes for spiritual blessings in the heavenly places in Christ. In this hope, in which he will not be put to shame, he asks to be upheld and to live.

### 8. A prayer not that adversaries may be absent, but that they may be overcome.

[Col. 0603B] Then follows, VERSE 117: “Help me, and I shall be saved; and I shall meditate always upon your justifications.” [Note: [Col. 0603C] “Your justifications.”] Above he had said, “My helper and my upholder”; but now he asks for the reality denoted by these names: that he who is the upholder may uphold him, and he who is helper may help him. He prays that the assistance of his helper may not be absent from him. He does not pray that he may have no evil opponents, because faith is proved through endurance of sufferings [Note: [Col. 0603C] In two manuscripts: “is effected.”]; rather, he prays to be helped against them, because help must always be sought from the Lord. But just as, in the preceding verse, he will live when upheld, so here he will be saved when helped.

[Note: [Col. 0603C] Here the Royal manuscript adds, “when, from bodily and earthly nature,” etc., omitting the remainder. Augustine, in Epistle 164, §7, and in *On Genesis according to the Letter*, II.33.63, testifies that he could find nowhere in Scripture that the lower regions (*inferi*) were called good, and he does not wish them to be endured by holy persons. Hilary, however, maintains even of David himself, whose holiness he often praises, that the lower regions had to be endured—not as a place of punishments, but as a peaceful abode where he waited until Christ opened the barriers of paradise. For, as Jerome says in Epistle III: “Abraham, though in different places, is seen with Lazarus by the rich man in the lower regions,” thereby teaching that the condition of those who lived after Christ was better; and this follows Origen, whose notable discussion of the matter, in *On the Witch of Endor*, is found in Huet, vol. I, p. 36. Hilary seems chiefly to have imitated him at this point. Accordingly, the prophet David here should be understood, insofar as he preceded Christ, to declare that the lower regions must be endured; but concerning the righteous who followed Christ, he holds an altogether different view.]

For he must still undergo death; he must still endure the lower regions. Then he will be saved, when, transformed from bodily and earthly [p. 375] nature into spiritual glory, he fears no danger from an opposing enemy, lives among the chosen angels, becomes an inhabitant of paradise [Note: [Col. 0604C] It is clear from the surrounding words that heaven is here meant by “paradise.”], and, corruption having been swallowed up, passes from mortality into immortality.

### 9. Eternal meditation upon the justifications.

But when he says that he will meditate upon God’s justifications—and will meditate always—does he not meditate, who has hoped in meditation? [Note: [Col. 0604C] The printed editions read: “how does he say that he will meditate upon God’s justifications?” against the manuscripts; if permissible, we would prefer *what* to *how*.] This may indeed be understood as a work of the present life: that, so long as he is in the body, he may always meditate upon the justifications. Yet the discourse nonetheless extends into the future. He knows that in heaven all angels are engaged in meditation upon God’s justifications. Nothing there is idle, nothing inactive: all the heavenly powers [Col. 0604A] [Note: [Col. 0604C–D] Hilary clearly understands “heavenly powers” here to mean angels. This illuminates the statement in his exposition of Psalm 91, §7: “Heaven would collapse . . . if the ordering of the powers were inactive under the law of the Sabbath,” although there “powers” may mean the stars. Other similar passages are also clarified.] remain occupied in the work of their ministry. And since we shall then live the life of angels, there may likewise be for us, after the pattern of those who always work, an eternal meditation upon the justifications.

### 10. The distinction between a sinner and an apostate.

Then follows, VERSE 118: “You have despised all who depart from your justifications, because their thought is unjust.” The prophet prays for help and support in order that he himself may not be despised together with those who depart from God’s justifications. But this distinction is preserved: it is not said, “You have despised all sinners,” but, “You have despised all who depart.” [Note: [Col. 0604D] Augustine employs this against Pelagius, *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 62.]

For if he despised sinners, he would certainly despise all, since no one is without sin. But he despises those who depart from him, whom people call apostates. Nor does it matter whether anyone had at some time been in God’s justifications. Whoever has departed must be despised by God, because the completion of remaining preserves the merit of one who remains. [Note: [Col. 0604D] The printed editions read “the completion of despising”; corrected with the help of the manuscripts.]

Departure differs from sin [Note: [Col. 0604C] “From a sinner.”] [Note: [Col. 0604D] In Hincmar, *On Predestination*, ch. 25: “from a sinner”—which Hilary’s editions also display here—“departure.” For pardon is reserved for the sinner through repentance; but departure condemns itself by the very departure from repentance, not by departure from *penance*. This is erroneous.]: for pardon is reserved for sin through repentance, whereas departure condemns itself by departing from repentance itself. This arises when the will of those who are about to depart is unjust.

### 11. Those commonly called transgressors. How all are such. The natural law.

Then follows, VERSE 119: “I accounted all the sinners of the earth transgressors; therefore I loved your justifications.” [Note: [Col. 0604D] In earlier editions the word “always” was wrongly printed as though part of the sacred text.] The prophet’s discourse always extends far beyond ordinary understanding. We think those to be transgressors who abandon the faith they have received and the knowledge of God they have attained, having promised one thing [Col. 0604C] and now doing another. But here all sinners of the earth are held to be transgressors: none is excepted; the designation of transgression is applied generally to all.

For there is, as it were, a natural law: to injure [p. 376] no one, to seize nothing belonging to another, to abstain from deceit and perjury, and not to lie in wait for another’s spouse. The Apostle also knows this law, saying: “For when the nations, which do not have the law, by nature do the things of the law, such persons, though they do not have the law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts” [Col. 0605A] (Rom. 2:14). Therefore those are accounted transgressors who abandon what they receive from the natural law. [Note: [Col. 0605D] “From the nature of the law.”] [Note: [Col. 0605D] Vatican manuscript: “from the law of nature.” Others: “from natural law.” The printed editions: “from the nature of the law.”] One may accuse a detected thief, adulterer, or murderer by the law of nature. But if he himself is engaged in such things, he is a transgressor of the law.

### 12. Sinners of heaven.

He also knows, when he says “sinners of the earth,” that there are other sinners—sinners of heaven. Let us hear the prodigal son of evangelical preaching, lost and dead, confessing his sin to his father: “Father,” he says, “I have sinned against heaven [Note: [Col. 0605D] “In heaven.”] and before you” (Luke 15:22). Whoever, having become a participant in heavenly teaching and spiritual grace, persists in sin, is not a sinner of earth but of heaven. For our Lord Jesus Christ has raised up with himself all who believe in him and seated them in heavenly places; and whoever departs from these [Col. 0605B] is charged as a sinner of heaven.

Therefore, since the prophet regards sinners of earth as transgressors because through sin they have broken the law of nature, he loves God’s testimonies for this reason: although transgression consists in departing from the law of nature, departure from the heavenly law is now without pardon.

### 13. The vices of the flesh must be nailed to the cross.

He concludes thus, VERSE 120: “Nail my flesh with your fear; for I have feared your judgments.” [Note: [Col. 0605D] “With fear.”] The prophet’s prayer is new and unusual: that his flesh may be nailed by the fear of God. But he remembers that those who wish to reign with Christ must suffer and die with him. And the Latin rendering has expressed this with less force than the original saying. [Note: [Col. 0605D] One Vatican manuscript: “this saying, by the force of the Latin translation,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0606D] “The Latin translation.”] For where we have *confige*, “nail fast,” the Greek has **κατήλωσον**, meaning that he should nail it fast with nails [Col. 0605C] (Rom. 6:4).

We must therefore die, and all the vices of our flesh must be nailed to the Lord’s cross. For according to the Apostle we die with Christ and are buried with him in baptism. And although the prophet possesses this in his own will, he nevertheless asks that he may attain it through God’s mercy. For he prays that his flesh may be nailed through fear of God because he fears God’s judgments. He fears the sentence of eternal judgment; he fears that he may not be nailed, die, and be buried with Christ, understanding that he will not become the new man unless he has put off the old man with his vices and desires [p. 377].

## LETTER XVI. Ain

[Col. 0605D] “I have performed judgment and justice: do not deliver me to those who persecute me” (Hilary: “injure me”). “Receive your servant for good: let not the proud falsely accuse me. My eyes have failed [Col. 0606A] for your salvation and for the word of your justice. Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your justifications. I am your servant: give me understanding, and I shall know your commandments” (“that I may know your testimonies”). “It is time for the Lord to act” (“for the Lord”): “they have scattered your law. Therefore I loved your commandments above gold and topaz” (*topazion*). “Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every wicked way.”

### 1. How much this octave teaches us together with the earlier ones.

Both at the beginning of the psalm and frequently afterwards, we have mentioned that by these individual letters, as by certain rudiments of learning, we are instructed in the teaching of piety, self-restraint, understanding, faith, and fear; and that we are trained by the very beginnings of human speech from unformed infancy toward the knowledge of speaking, which is followed also by the teaching of acting [Col. 0606B]. This may be understood from the eight verses now before us, under the sixteenth letter. [Two manuscripts: “must.”]

For the prophet, speaking in his own person, teaches everyone what, in view of the weakness and nature of each one’s conscience, it is useful to will, to do, and to profess; likewise what must be feared, avoided, and cleansed away. The same blessed prophet is, through God’s mercy, a teacher, guardian, cleanser, and judge both for himself and for all. [Note: [Col. 0605D] In the Royal, Vatican, and Albinus manuscripts: “cleansed,” and shortly afterward, “cleanser.” The verb *emundo*, “to cleanse,” is more familiar to Hilary than *emendo*, “to correct.”] [Note: [Col. 0605D–0606D] The word “who” is absent from the Micy manuscript. In the printed editions the words “and teacher of all” were missing. The Royal and Albinus manuscripts omit the following words, “and guardian” (in the Vatican manuscript, “watcher”), “and cleanser and judge.” The *et* before *universis* has the force of “also.”] And certainly it most fittingly accords with his dignity that one who speaks by God’s Spirit should speak what concerns human beings and eternal salvation.

### 2. Work must precede prayer.

For he says, VERSE 121: “I have performed judgment and justice: do not deliver me to those who injure me.” [Note: [Col. 0606D] The manuscripts read “performs,” and then in the Micy manuscript alone, “and because he performs.”] He performed works pleasing to God; and because he performed them, he prays that he may not be delivered to those who injure him. The work by which one merits comes first; afterward the reward of merit is sought. First, what is pleasing is done; then the favor of him whom one pleases by the work is requested [p. 378].

But we neither act nor please God; indeed, we offend him by impious and irreligious deeds. And because, being such, we do not please him, we become angry. Yet it is fitting to consider what sort of deeds they are which the prophet performs when he prays not to be delivered to those who injure him.

### 3. David’s virtues are useful to himself alone.

Everything that anyone does in the fear of God is useful and beautiful for that person. One who cultivates chastity brings a glorious and shining light to the flesh of his body, foul with defilement. [Note: [Col. 0606D] *Sordenti*, “foul,” is lacking in the first Paris edition. The other editions read, “glorious and fearing the defilement of his body,” etc., against the manuscripts.] One who embraces contempt for money preserves himself free from earthly dominations. [Note: [Col. 0606D] “Has preserved.”] [Note: [Col. 0606D] The Royal and Albinus manuscripts: “has preserved.”] One who loves moderation [Col. 0606D] and frugality does not leave the nobility of his heavenly soul captive to drunkenness.

But although these things are great and splendid, nevertheless, because they are peculiar to the prophet [Col. 0607A] and useful to him alone, they do not count toward merit.

### 4. Judgment and justice, however, benefit others too.

But what has he done, that he prays not to be delivered to those who injure him? Judgment and justice, surely: doing nothing rashly, nothing unjustly. He first performs judgment, examining all things by reason, measure, and truth, so that whatever he does toward another, having first weighed and considered it, he may carry out in accordance with the decision of his counsel.

Yet he does not entrust the sentence of judgment merely to his own counsel, but with judgment performs justice. And this is the greatest work of one who judges with deliberation: that what he judges should be just. For justice is the harmony of friendship, the bond of unanimity, the foundation of peace, and the working of divine and human reason. [Note: [Col. 0607D] Thus five manuscripts agree with the ancient editions; the reading “friendly harmony” in the Paris edition from the Micy manuscript ought not to have been substituted.] These, then, the prophet performed. Though the work is his own, it is also beneficial to those for whom he performed judgment and justice [Col. 0607B].

### 5. The sinner is the devil’s house. To him the sinner is delivered by God. To be cut off from the Church is to be delivered to the devil.

He asks not to be delivered to those who injure him. For everyone in whom the will to sin exists is empty of God; and where God is not, there is the devil’s place. Lying in wait and besieging, whenever he has an opportunity to enter, he occupies it like an empty house, delivered to him because God has abandoned it (see *Exposition of Psalm 120*, §8). [Note: [Col. 0607D] Incorrectly in the Paris edition: “where there is an opportunity to depart.”]

The prophet, indeed, because he spoke in the person of all, prays that he may not be delivered by God. The Apostle, however, already has within himself such confidence that he himself delivers sinners to the devil. Writing to the Corinthians concerning the man who, surpassing every form of sexual immorality, had taken his father’s wife, he says: “For I, absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as though present, him who has done this: when you and my spirit are assembled with the power of my Lord [Col. 0607C] Jesus, to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5:3 ff.). [Note: [Col. 0607C] *Mei*, “my,” is lacking in the Verona copy.] [Note: [Col. 0607D] We have added “my” on the authority of the Royal and Albinus manuscripts. In the sacred texts we now read “our.”]

But although the Apostle delivers him, he knows that he will deliver him both in Christ’s power and in his own spirit. In another epistle he says of Phygelus and Hermogenes: “I have delivered them to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20). [Note: [Col. 0607D] The Royal manuscript, with the Albinus, reads “Philetus.” But the subsequent words of 1 Tim. 1:20 concern Hymenaeus and Alexander, not Philetus or Phygelus, nor Hermogenes. The Apostle does say in 2 Tim. 2:17 that Hymenaeus and Philetus had departed from the faith together; and he recounts the defection from the faith of Phygelus and Hermogenes in 2 Tim. 1:15. Yet in both places he says nothing of delivery to Satan, so Hilary seems to have spoken from memory.]

For those rejected from the body of the Church, which is Christ’s body, are delivered to the devil’s dominion as strangers and aliens from God’s body.

### 6. The various temptations of demons. They prevail only over those whom God abandons.

[Col. 0608A] But the prophet prays that he may not be delivered to those who injure him. For hostile and threatening powers are present: powers which disturb the purpose of faith, erase the fear of God, entice toward earthly covetousness and desires, and rouse the weak nature of the body to vices by certain stings of seductive pleasure. The Apostle also knows this multitude of ruling powers, saying: “In which you also once walked according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the children of unbelief” (Eph. 2:2).

Therefore the prophet performed judgment and justice and asks that he may not be delivered to those who injure him: those who injure when they drive one into sin, puff one up with glory, kindle one to anger, inflame one to hatred, lure one to sensuality, or provoke one [Col. 0608B] to greed. But although they hasten to injure by such means, they cannot prevail over those who are innocent unless they have been delivered to them by God’s withdrawal. [Note: [Col. 0607C] “They will not be able to overcome those whom they have harmed.”] [Note: [Col. 0607D–0608D] In the Micy manuscript: “who are harmful, unless to themselves,” etc.; then in three others, “by God’s concession.” “By withdrawal” should be retained, as is indicated by §5: “The devil occupies it like an empty house, delivered to him because God has abandoned it”; and also by *Exposition of Psalm 120*, §8: “Its desolation is therefore delivery, because the devil cannot obtain sinners unless God departs from them.”]

### 7. The proud: the devil and his ministers. Those who falsely accuse.

Then follows, VERSE 122: “Receive your servant for good; let not the proud falsely accuse me.” [Note: [Col. 0608D] The Vatican manuscript, with the Royal and Albinus, reads “he has advanced in his hope.”] The prophet advances in his hopes [Note: [Col. 0607C] “In his hope.”] and now ascends to a higher stage of supplication. For he who had prayed not to be delivered to those who injure him now asks to be received as God’s own servant, praying that God’s blessed dominion may come upon him through this favorable reception. And he asks to be received for good for no slight reason: namely, so that the proud may not falsely accuse him.

And who are the proud? Surely those whose prince Isaiah introduces as speaking thus [Col. 0608C]: “By my strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of nations and their power, and I will move inhabited cities, and I will seize the whole world in my hand as young birds, and as broken eggs I will carry it away” (Isa. 10:13–14). [Note: [Col. 0608D] The Royal and Albinus manuscripts read: “I will act by strength and by the wisdom of understanding. I will remove,” etc.; and shortly afterward omit “I will seize in my hand as young birds, and as broken eggs I will carry away.”] [Note: [Col. 0608C] “Their powers.”] [Note: [Col. 0608D] The word *inhabitabiles* does not seem here to be understood negatively, as it sounds, especially since the Greek has κατοικουμένας, “inhabited.” Thus *inhabitabiles* here is equivalent to *habitables*, “inhabited,” deriving from *inhabito*, which often has the same sense as *habito*.]

This is the voice [p. 380] of one who boasts—namely, the devil—who dared also to say to God and our Lord Jesus Christ, after showing him the glory of earthly kingdoms: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9). That he is not alone, but has many ministers of spiritual wickedness with him, we learn from him who says: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire [Col. 0609A] which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). [Note: [Col. 0608C] “Subordinate ministers.”]

He therefore prays that he may be free from the false accusation of these proud powers. For they falsely accuse: since they themselves supply incentives to sin, they lay before the Lord against us the accusation of the sin we have committed through them. [Note: [Col. 0609D] “They bring [the accusation].”] They turn the cause of sin into a charge and intensify the odium of the charge by false accusation, as Scripture testifies in the Apocalypse that he is the accuser (Rev. 12:10).

### 8. David’s mental eyes fail in longing for Jesus.

But now the prophet extends himself into a higher advance, saying, VERSE 123: “My eyes have failed for your salvation and for the word of your justice.” Eyes fail when sight, fixed upon some expectation, grows weary. The prophet, therefore, fixed the eyes of his soul upon God’s salvation. [Col. 0609B] And we have often explained what must be understood by “salvation”: namely, Jesus, who will save his people from their sins.

While others occupy their eyes with worldly desires and direct them toward the pleasures of present things, the prophet has fixed them on God’s salvation. [Note: [Col. 0609D] Earlier editions read: “and lest, through bodily eyes, he should fail.”] And lest we suppose that his bodily eyes fail through this intentness of contemplation, they fail not only for God’s salvation but also for the word of justice.

### 9. God’s words and deeds are just, though hidden.

He therefore confesses that God’s words are just. He knows that certain things are thought by the ignorant and impious to have the appearance of unjust speech: [Note: [Col. 0609D] That is, according to the ignorant. For such is the force in Hilary of the preposition *cum*, as noted above. Then, where the printed editions have “Pharaoh’s heart,” “Pharaoh” has been restored on manuscript authority, though the word may be taken in the genitive case; see the notes on Psalm 67, §25.] when Pharaoh is hardened in heart unto obstinacy (Exod. 4:21) and attached to the stubbornness [Note: [Col. 0609D] Thus we read from our manuscript. Earlier: “to him of obstinacy.”] of his irreligious will [Note: [Col. 0609D] In the Paris edition: “religious.”]; when, of two nations still in the womb, the greater is to serve the lesser, and, although neither nation has earned any good, slavery is imposed on the one and dominion granted to the other (Rom. 9:11 ff.); [Col. 0609C] [Note: [Col. 0609D] The printed editions have “neither” in the neuter; more correctly the manuscripts have the feminine, referring to “nation.”] when Adam is expelled from paradise lest he touch the tree of life (Gen. 3:22). Since people unable to grasp divine power, goodness, and justice cannot understand these things, they judge them unjust [p. 381].

But the eyes of this prophet fail for such a word of justice [Note: [Col. 0609D] The printed editions read “justly”; corrected from the manuscripts.], because he knows that nothing in these sayings of God is unjust, but that all these words of justice are both to be fulfilled and to be understood through the coming of God’s salvation. [Note: [Col. 0609D–0610D] Supply here: “as they truly are, words.” Shortly above our manuscripts read “of the Savior” instead of “of salvation.”] Through this intent expectation, which brings his eyes to failure, he proceeds so far that he dares to ask something further.

### 10. Whence David’s confidence comes. A person needs God’s help to accomplish good.

Having confessed the word of justice, he adds, VERSE 124: “Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your justifications.” Perhaps the words, “Deal with your servant,” would seem presumptuous. For “Deal” seems to claim with a certain confidence the right to ask. Yet he would not say it shamelessly who had performed judgment and justice, who had prayed to be received as a servant, and whose eyes had failed for God’s salvation and for the word of justice.

Yet even in these things the prophet is not presumptuous. For in saying, “Deal,” he added, “with your servant.” And because our servitude itself, in order to remain faithful to the commitment of servitude, needs the Lord’s mercy, he further added, “according to your mercy.” For we need his compassion if we are to remain [Col. 0610B] in this profession of our servitude. Human weakness is too feeble of itself to obtain anything; and this alone is the office of its nature: to will and begin to join itself to God’s household. [Note: [Col. 0610D] “But it belongs to divine mercy.” Then: “that she,” not “that he.”]

It belongs to divine mercy to help those who are willing, strengthen those who begin, and receive those who approach; but the beginning belongs to us, [Note: [Col. 0610D] We restore from the manuscripts “he,” namely God, where previously “she” stood, which could have been referred to mercy.] so that he may bring it to completion.

### 11. Something great lies hidden in the rites of the old law.

But what, finally, does he ask God to do with his servant according to his mercy? Surely, to teach him his justifications. He knows that in the justifications which Moses was commanded to establish there is contained some great thing, unknown and incomprehensible to human intelligence. He also wishes to know who that purchased Hebrew boy is, as we have often said, who is to serve only six years [Col. 0610C] (Exod. 21:2). [Note: [Col. 0610D] We have also supplied “he.”]

He reads these things, certainly; but what is read is not at once understood. He wishes to know what that servitude is (ibid.), what the freedom of the seventh year is (ibid., v. 6), what the piercing of the ear with an awl means if he does not wish to be free, what that Hebrew’s woman is [Note: [Col. 0610D] Namely, the slave’s woman: if his master had given him a wife, after six years of servitude he went out without children and without the woman, or wife, according to Exod. 21:4. Hence the printed editions wrongly read “Hebrew woman” here, and still worse afterward, “that he should go in without a woman.” These are corrected from the manuscripts.], and what it means that he himself should go out without the woman (ibid., v. 4); then what patterning of future mysteries belongs to the second justification, the third, and those that follow. [Note: [Col. 0610D] The printed editions read “prefigurations.” The manuscripts more correctly read “of prefiguration”: as though, “what prefiguration of future mysteries the second, third, and following justifications, or commands there given, possess.”]

Human intelligence cannot attain these things: a heavenly teacher is needed [p. 382], and many merits of our faith are necessary if we are to deserve to be taught them.

### 12. Nothing in David’s words is low or commonplace. No one denies verbally that he is God’s servant; many deny it in deed.

We should know that in all the prophet’s words there is nothing low [Col. 0611A], nothing shared with the rest; rather, something proper either to himself or to those like him is declared. Under familiar words lies the greatest profession of conscience and faith, as we understand in what follows. For he says, VERSE 125: “I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may know your testimonies.” [Note: [Col. 0611D] “And I may know,” in agreement with the Greek.]

There is none of us who does not confess himself God’s servant, whether in the prayer of petition or in ordinary conversation. And what great thing did the prophet do by professing himself a servant, which no one has dared to deny? But the profession of the rest is false: though it bears the obligation of conscience, it does not possess the truth of confession.

This is peculiar to the prophet: that he professes himself God’s servant, fulfilling the service proper to his condition in every kind of life—whether walking [Col. 0611B], sitting, waking, or sleeping; whether in eating or fasting, he is hungry or satisfied for God; and at no time does he cease from the duties of his servitude. Such a man freely says, “I am your servant.” But one who sleeps in sexual vice, wakes for robbery, travels for gain, and rests for luxury—if he says, “I am your servant,” he indeed professes what he is, but does not do what he is. [Note: [Col. 0611D] The printed editions read, “does what he is not”: a faulty placement of the negative particle which reverses Hilary’s meaning.]

### 13. Understanding comes from God; false understanding is introduced by the devil.

Although the prophet confesses the condition of his duty by his very service, he remembers his weakness and asks that understanding may be given to him. For understanding is stored in a certain treasury of spiritual graces; yet the devil sometimes insinuates it into unguarded minds under the error of false opinion [Col. 0611C]. But the prophet asks God for understanding, lest empty understanding creep in upon him, such as belongs to the Gentiles, the Jews, and heretics. He asks for it in order that he may know God’s testimonies: those given under witnesses, those which are reproached as having been neglected and violated under witnesses, and those which, at his coming—for whose testimony they were spoken—will be vindicated as neglected and despised. [Note: [Col. 0611D] The printed editions read “at his coming.” Then the first Paris edition has “for which testified”; the Micy manuscript, “for whom testified”; and shortly afterward, “will be judged,” rather than “will be vindicated,” omitting the earlier verb “to be,” which is likewise omitted in the printed editions.]

### 14. The law having been scattered, it is the time of the Gospel.

The prophet does not ignore the time of these testimonies, saying, VERSE 126: “It is time for the Lord to act: they have scattered your law.” [Note: [Col. 0611D] “The wicked have scattered,” according to the Roman Psalter.] The law was given to the people under witnesses; when it was scattered and cast aside by the Jews [Col. 0611D], then came the time for the Lord to do the things contained in the law [p. 383].

For in the law he promised that he would give salvation to the nations; that he himself would assume the body of man, who was made according to the image and likeness of God; and that, the law having been scattered, he would grant the grace of faith. He recalls this time through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49:8). The Apostle, interpreter of this saying, writes: “Behold, now is the very acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). [Note: [Col. 0611D] “Acceptable.”] [Note: [Col. 0611D] The Royal and Albinus manuscripts read “accepted.”] That is: the law having been scattered, the time of evangelical preaching has arrived.

### 15. Why David loves God’s commandments. To love is more than to do.

But while they scatter the law, the prophet has another work. What it is, we learn from the following words. For he says, VERSE 127: “Therefore I loved your commandments [Col. 0612B] above gold and topaz.” [Note: [Col. 0612D] Here and below, consistently, *topazon*.] By “therefore” he refers back to what he had said: “It is time for the Lord to act,” because he knew that the time for the Lord to act would come when they had scattered the law.

He loved the commandments because they contained the time for the Lord to act. For the whole law bore witness to the Lord’s coming, as he himself said: “If you believed Moses, you would certainly believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). [Note: [Col. 0611D] The printed editions, except Paris, as well as the two aforementioned manuscripts, read: “If you believe Moses, you believe,” etc.]

The prophet therefore loved God’s commandments because in them he understood the coming of the Lord’s embodiment. And in the fact that he loves, he signifies something greater. To do something is less than to love it, because often what we do is done from necessity, whereas love is the affection of one’s own will.

16. Perfect Love.—But that love is finally perfect which is greatest and is not equalled by comparison with anything similar. He loves the commandments of God above gold and topaz. Human error considers nothing more precious than gold and gems; and these are the things to which human desires have submitted themselves through the dominion of their value and distinction. Among men, the honour of chastity can be bought with gold [Note: [Col. 0611D] In the Paris edition: “For men, law, honourableness, and chastity are saleable for gold”; but neither the other books nor what follows supports that reading.]; while by means of gems the supposedly superior appearance of the human body is polished, to nature’s insult [Note: [Col. 0612D] “Is sought after”; a little later, “more beautiful” in place of “more precious.”] [Note: [Col. 0612D] The Micy codex, with one Vatican manuscript, reads “is sought after.” The others more correctly read “is polished”: that is, “the superior appearance of the human body.” The words that follow leave no doubt that the female sex is meant by this expression. Hilary says that women employ the adornment of jewels to nature’s insult because, as Cyprian teaches in *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*, “what God formed is covered, and that which the devil devised over it is made visible.” Hence his general judgment concerning women’s adornment: “What you think to be adornment, what you think to be beautification, is an attack upon the work of God, a violation of truth.”].

Therefore neither sex has anything more precious: men wish to be able to do everything by means of gold, while women suppose that gems make them more beautiful. But as gold surpasses other metals, so topaz surpasses other stones. For it is itself the rarest, most beautiful, and largest of all.

It is usually found in a place of the Thebaid called Alabastrum [Note: [Col. 0613C] *Alabastrane.*] [Note: [Col. 0613C] The Micy manuscript has *Alabastrans*; but in Ambrose and Pliny this place is called Alabastrum. Ambrose, on this same verse, Sermon 16, §41, says: “We find it written in the history of Xenocrates that it is produced near the Thebaid city of Alabastrum.” Pliny, *Natural History* XXXVII.8, says: “The most recent writers say that it is also produced near the Thebaid town of Alabastrum.”]. Secular historical writings likewise report that it was discovered on the island of Topazos by its inhabitants, that is, the Arab Troglodytes [Note: [Col. 0613D] The Regius codex with Albinus reads “in Taparius”; the Micy codex, “in Topharia.” Juba, cited by Pliny in the passage named, states that the island of Topazos lies in the Red Sea, one day’s voyage from the mainland. Archelaus, however, cited by the same Pliny, judges that it was discovered on an Arabian island called Cytis by Troglodyte raiders.] [Note: [Col. 0613D] The royal manuscripts and Albinus read *Troglotides*, contrary to the other books, and also to Pliny and Ambrose.], and was brought as a gift to the mother [Note: [Col. 0613D] In the passages cited from Ambrose and Pliny she is called Berenice; to this pertains Juvenal, *Satire* VI, v. 155:

“. . . . A diamond already most renowned,
And made more precious on Berenice’s finger.”] of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, under whom the Scriptures of the Law were translated from Hebrew into Greek [Note: [Col. 0613D] Namely, by Philemon, the king’s prefect, as Pliny testifies; or, if one prefers to trust Ambrose, by Philo, who bought this stone from Arab merchants arriving there, who had bought it from the Troglodytes. Hilary relates all this, “as secular historical writings report.” Sacred Scripture establishes that topaz was discovered long before Ptolemy. For in Exodus 28:10 Moses was commanded to place a topaz in the first row of the breastpiece, and Exodus 39:10 declares that he actually placed it there. Nor does David, who was several centuries earlier than Ptolemy, here mention a thing unknown to him. Perhaps this stone, though not unknown in the age of Moses and David, subsequently lay hidden for a long time, until it was rediscovered by the Troglodytes and was regarded as though it had never before been known.].

This stone alone contains within itself the appearance of the other finest and most precious gems; in this single stone is contained a blending of very different colours. Therefore the Prophet loved the commandments of God above this topaz and above gold, signifying that he was held fast not by earthly but by heavenly desires.

17. He Cuts Off Every Desire.—Having despised the desire for worldly riches, he cuts off from himself every occasion of perverse and corrupt will. For, loving the commandments of God above gold and topaz, he then says, verse 128: “Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every way of iniquity.” He is not turned aside or diverted by earthly desires, but is directed toward all God’s commandments; things encountered on the way do not occupy him. He saw gold and knew it to be mud of the earth; he saw gems and remembered that they are pebbles either of mountains or of the sea; he saw a face enticing to lust [Note: [Col. 0614D] One Vatican codex reads “enticing.”], and knew that, as from snares set for birds of heaven, he must escape from these.

Therefore he resists the vices grown together with his nature and hates every way of iniquity. Accordingly, he is directed toward all the commandments [Note: [Col. 0613C] “In all the commandments.”] because he loves them above earthly desires; and he is directed lest he become a participant in those to whom it is said: “O perverse and crooked generation” (Luke 9:41). And he hates every way of iniquity, that he may be in him who is the Way—namely, our Lord, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER XVII. Phe

“Wonderful are your testimonies, O Lord; therefore my soul loved you” (Hilary: “has searched them out”). “The unfolding of your words gives me light” (“me” is absent below), “and gives understanding to little ones.” “I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I desired your commandments. Look upon me and have mercy on me according to the judgment of those who love your name. Direct my steps according to your word, and let no injustice rule over me. Redeem me from the calumnies of men, and I shall keep your commandments” (“that I may keep your precepts”). “Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your ordinances. Streams of waters passed over my eyes, because they did not keep your law.”

1. Wonder Is Not of What Is Unknown. Why God’s Testimonies Are Wonderful; Why They Are Unknown.—Such is the nature of human perception that it regards as wonderful what it has first come to know. For the judgment of admiration arises from things known; no one can marvel at what is unknown. These matters have accordingly been mentioned beforehand, so that the meaning of the prophetic saying might be sought more carefully. For in verse 129 he seems to say something contrary to the judgment of common sense: “Wonderful are your testimonies, O Lord; therefore my soul has searched them out” [Note: [Col. 0614C] “My soul searched them out.”].

For according to human custom one must first search and find, and then marvel at what has been found. But for him the testimonies of the Lord are wonderful beforehand and are therefore worthy of searching out [Note: [Col. 0614D] We have added “for him” on the authority of the Micy and Vatican manuscripts.].

The explanation of this perfect and most beautiful saying is as follows. The testimonies of God—that is, those things written under witnesses—even though by observance of the Law they train human weakness for the knowledge and service of God, since chastity, piety, purity, charity, truth, innocence, frugality, and religion are commanded, and since the duty of divine worship is prescribed through certain religious observances and varieties of sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0614D] The printed editions, except the Badian, read “varieties of histories,” corruptly and against the authority of the manuscripts.]—in all these there is indeed great wonder: a victim offered for sins, a gift given for the redemption of the soul, and a lamb slain in the sacrament of Passover. Yet in these is contained a greater ground of wonder arising from the hope and instruction of future things.

These, then, are wonderful to the Prophet. But because, through present objects of wonder [Note: [Col. 0614C] “Through present admiration.”] [Note: [Col. 0614D] The Badian, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions, with two manuscripts, read “present admirations,” without *through*; the Paris edition reads “through present admiration.” The word *admiratio* is familiar to Hilary in the plural; examples have appeared above, p. 267, note. What is said here more compactly may be explained more clearly thus: because the things performed in the Law are wonderful insofar as they are figures of future and eternal goods, which contain within themselves many grounds for wonder, he searches them out.], they are wonderful as patterns of future and eternal goods, he searches them out. He does not merely inquire, which is the diligent investigation of hidden matters; he searches them out, displaying by this addition the labour of a more careful inquiry in his searching. Nor does he merely search them out, but searches them out from the soul, joining the soul’s intention to the service of the will.

2. God’s Words, the Sayings of the Prophets, Are Obscure.—He then continues, verse 130: “The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to little ones.” This saying too may perhaps seem at variance with the custom of our nature. For one must first understand and then use the light of understanding, since he calls the light acquired by understanding the illumination of the night of ignorance. Yet the Prophet says that the unfolding of God’s words first gives light and, after illumination, supplies understanding.

But we must first learn what God’s words are; then we must provide an account of illumination, and afterwards of understanding. The words of God are whatever the prophets spoke. For though Moses announced observance of the Law to the Hebrew people in his own words, nevertheless it is written in the book of the Law itself: “And the Lord said to Moses, Say to the children of Israel” (Exodus 3:14). Thus the lawgiver used those words which he had been commanded to use. Therefore the words of God are those which, though heard through the ministry of a human mouth, are God’s words.

Likewise, that great prophet, approved as having spoken well by the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, after saying, “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth,” added: “for the Lord has spoken” (Isaiah 1:2); and, after several matters were reproved with the strongest complaints, he said: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (ibid. 20). Therefore all these are words of God.

3. But the Unfolding of the Words Is Especially Necessary.—For they are proclaimed under the veil of another meaning; they are, according to the Apostle, *allegoroumena* (ἀλληγορούμενα, “allegorically spoken,” Galatians 4:24); they are ambiguous through comparative meanings (Matthew 13:14). The Lord bears witness, reproaching unbelieving Jews, that these very words were spoken through Isaiah: “Hearing you shall hear and shall not understand” (Isaiah 6:9). For all things are sealed and must be unsealed only through spiritual teaching.

Thus it was said to Daniel, the man of desires: “Go, Daniel, for the words are shut up and sealed” (Daniel 12:9) [Note: [Col. 0615D] “To Daniel,” with the remaining manuscripts; and so everywhere.] [Note: [Col. 0615D] The manuscripts read “to Daniel.”]. Isaiah also says: “This book shall be given into the hands of a man who knows letters, and he shall be told, ‘Read these’; and he shall answer, ‘I cannot read, for it is sealed’” (Isaiah 29:11).

4. Through the Gospels They Are Unfolded. Who the Little Ones Are.—But the unfolding of mystical words is supplied through the Gospels, where, while the Lord remains in the body, the hidden and concealed matters of the Law and the prophetic commandments [Note: [Col. 0615D] The Micy manuscript reads “and the prophetic commandments.”] are disclosed; from them faith is first learned. For there the things spoken by the prophets are fulfilled by him in events and deeds. When a virgin gives birth; when the Lord is the Word, and the Word becomes flesh and dwells among us; when the mute speak, the deaf hear, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the blind see, demoniacs are healed, and the dead rise: this unfolding of God’s words illuminates this darkness of our nature with the light of faith [Note: [Col. 0615D] “Makes bright.” Then follows:]. For now we understand the glory of resurrection, the power of judgment, and the honour of eternity.

And we understand these things as little ones: either reborn into innocence or unlearned through ignorance. The Lord shows in the Gospels the time and age to which this unfolding of God’s words and this understanding granted to little ones belonged [Note: [Col. 0615D] Thus the Micy codex. The others read, “of this time and age, that the Lord,” etc.], saying: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and have revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 18:25) [Note: [Col. 0616D] “Father” is absent; shortly afterwards, “wise” replaces “understanding.”].

Behold the time of unfolding, illumination, and understanding. For things hidden until these days are unfolded [Note: [Col. 0615D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “until this point, namely into these days”; another, “until this point, namely in these days.” The Badian, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions read “have been hidden until this point.” In these days these things are unfolded.]; when unfolded, they illuminate; and, by illuminating [Note: [Col. 0616D] The printed editions read “having been illuminated”; corrected from the Micy manuscript.], they supply understanding to little ones, who through this understanding become capable already of the Holy Spirit.

5. Let the Mouth of the Heart Be Open to the Spirit. It Receives Food for the Soul’s Life.—Finally, the following saying added this very point, verse 131: “I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I desired your commandments.” He certainly did not speak of the mouth of the human body, which is shut and opened by the lips. For we draw breath through the function of the nostrils rather than the mouth. It is conveyed into the soul more laboriously through the passage of the mouth, but travels more freely by its natural course through the service and function of the nostrils [Note: [Col. 0616D] The printed editions read “by the hearing of the ear”: a double error, one corrected from a Vatican manuscript, the other from the Regius and Albinus manuscripts.].

But Scripture is accustomed to call not only the lips’ opening, but also that of the heart, a mouth. For when the heart is opened through faith and gapes through desire to draw in, understanding of heavenly teaching is received. This is not the soul’s function, but the heart’s. For the Apostle says: “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:14), for they are foolishness to him. And the same teacher of the Gentiles says: “The Law is written not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3).

Therefore, opening this mouth of his, the Prophet drew in the Spirit. For it does not rush in of itself (*ingruit*, perhaps *inruit*, “rushes in”). It must be sought, drawn in, and, like innocent milk by infants, drunk in. The Prophet opened his mouth because he remembered that in another psalm it had been said to him: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11); and because he knew that it is written in the Law: “Write these things in the breadth of your heart” (Proverbs 7:3, according to the Septuagint). For God’s preaching is received by the heart, not by the mouth. And according to Gospel preaching, the evil one snatches the word of God from the heart (Matthew 13:19), though it delights the mouth beyond honey and the honeycomb. As through the mouth we receive foods for the nourishment of the body, so through the heart we receive the foods of heavenly teaching for giving life to the soul; unless they have somehow been drawn in by a heart enlarged and open, they will not enter [Note: [Col. 0617D] The Paris edition reads “they will not help,” which Lipsius wrongly introduced without authority.].

6. God Looks in Order to Punish, Frighten, and Have Mercy.—He then continues, verse 132: “Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name.” Immediately after saying, “Look upon me,” he added, “and have mercy.” For he knows that the Lord also looks upon the wicked for vengeance and punishment. For, as it is written, he looked upon the camp of the Egyptians and bound the wheels of their chariots (Exodus 14:24–25). And again: “The Lord looked upon Sodom and Gomorrah” (Genesis 18:16). He looks not only for punishment but also for terror, as it is said: “You look upon the earth and make it tremble” (Psalm 103:32).

Therefore the Prophet does not pray merely that God may look upon him, but that he may look upon him with mercy; nor merely with mercy, but according to the judgment of those who love his name.

7. This Look Must Be Earned by Innocence.—Mercy indeed comes from God’s goodness, but it must be earned by our pursuit of innocence: that he may look upon us as he looked upon Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Job, and Moses. For he knows that God is accustomed to look down for these works of his mercy, when it is said: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the earth, to hear the groaning of prisoners and to loose the children of those put to death” (Psalm 101:20–21); and again: “He looked upon the children of the poor and did not despise their supplication” (ibid. 18).

Therefore, according to this judgment of those who fear the Lord, he prays that God may look upon him and have mercy: so that if he sees him fasting, observes him showing mercy, and beholds him pious and devout in every deed, then he too may be worthy of God’s mercy according to the judgment of those who love his name.

8. A Human Being Does Not Suffice by His Own Strength for Doing Good.—He then continues, verse 133: “Direct my steps according to your word, and no injustice shall rule over me” (“and let no injustice rule over me”).” The Prophet indeed walks in steps of righteousness by his own will, but he knows that dominations of injustice threaten on every side. Above he had prayed that God might look upon him and have mercy according to those who love his name. He recognizes this as the fruit of the mercy for which he prays: that his steps be directed not according to the ways of the world, not according to human glory, not according to bodily pleasures, but according to God’s word.

If no obstacle met him anywhere, if adversaries did not stand against him on every side, he would be strengthened by his own powers in the things he wished to do. But where there are snares, where there is war, the help of one stronger is needed, lest all injustice rule within him.

9. The Usefulness of Temptations. We Must Pray That They Do Not Conquer.—He prays not that injustice may be absent from him, but that it may not rule him. He knows that glory is attained through temptations. He remembers Abraham’s trial by the wrong of exile, by fear of losing his wife, and by the grief of being required to sacrifice his son. He knows that Job completed every campaign of temptations. He recalls that Joseph, when sold by his brothers, when compelled to adultery by his master’s wife, and when held in prison for punishment, earned the glory of the greatest faith through these trials of injustice.

The Prophet fears the domination of injustice, but does not refuse its temptation. He remembers that his steps must be directed by the Lord according to his words, lest the iniquity that is to tempt him [Note: [Col. 0618D] Thus the manuscripts, more smoothly than the printed editions, which read “by which he is tempted.”] should have power to rule him.

10. What Calumny Is. It Is Hard to Avoid. The Saints Were Attacked by It.—After this follows, verse 134: “Redeem me from the calumnies of men, that I may keep your precepts.” Human temptation is not grievous, as the Apostle says: “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human” (1 Corinthians 10:13) [Note: [Col. 0617D] “Has not yet overtaken,” agreeing with the Greek *eilēphen* (εἴληφεν).]; but calumny is grievous.

Calumny is either when a good deed is given the name of an evil crime, or when the poison of inward malice is concealed beneath a flattering appearance. It does not need open malevolence; rather, it works destructively by deceit and craft, under the appearance of goodwill. It is difficult to guard against such people, who are enemies under the name of brothers, foes under the name of friends, parricides under the appearance of children, and, under the appearance of unanimity [Note: [Col. 0618D] “Under unanimity.”] [Note: [Col. 0618D] The Paris edition reads “under the unanimity of spouses.”], the unavoidable evil of spouses.

Wicked Cain killed righteous Abel through the familiarity of brotherhood. Ham, his son, mocked Noah, whom God had approved. Esau made Jacob an exile from his paternal home. Job, the devil’s strongest combatant, was tempted to yield by his wife alone. What calumnies of men deceived this holy Prophet himself? How often was he betrayed to Saul? How often was Saul told in what places he acted? Everywhere the snares of calumniators were at hand against him.

11. How It Is to Be Avoided.—The Lord knows that the scandals of domestic calumny are accustomed to bring the gravest destruction of faith, saying: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, and if your right foot or hand causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cut it off from you” (Matthew 18:8). He did not speak these words of bodily members, since neither foot nor hand can bring scandals; rather, he commands this concerning those members most closely joined to us and most necessary, because we are all one body in Christ. Thus, lest domestic calumnies and scandals remaining among us should cause some stain of vices to cling to us [Note: [Col. 0619D] “On the day of judgment” is inserted, then “might cling.”] [Note: [Col. 0619D] On the authority of the manuscripts and old editions we have removed “on the day of judgment” here, where it seems superfluous in the Paris edition.], he commands their removal.

Therefore the Prophet promises that, if redeemed from these, he will keep God’s precepts, because all these calumnies of household members frequently bring an impediment to faith.

12. May We Receive the Light of God Who Looks upon Us.—He then continues, verse 135: “Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your ordinances.” The face of the Lord is indeed against those who do evil, “to destroy the memory of them from the earth” (Psalm 33:17). But just as God looks both for punishment and for mercy, so he turns his face to both ends. The Prophet prays for this face of the Lord for his illumination. For from the majesty and countenance of God looking upon us [Note: [Col. 0619D] “Of God who deigns to look upon us.”] [Note: [Col. 0619D] The Paris edition, following the Micy manuscript, reads “of God who deigns us,” contrary to the other books.], we receive light; and the countenance of his mercy, turned toward us, shines upon us with the grace of spiritual power.

Or certainly, when the day of judgment comes, when Christ stands before us visibly in the glory of paternal majesty [Note: [Col. 0619D] The printed editions read “the day will come”; the manuscripts more smoothly read “when the day comes,” namely, Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0619D] One Vatican codex reads “the Father of majesty”; it is not to be accepted.], then he will illuminate us with the light of his face. For as certain metals and gems reflect the radiance of their nature upon things near them [Note: [Col. 0619D] In place of “they reflect upon things which are near them,” the following is then supplied: “from the proximity of their appearance.”], and communicate an imitative appearance through the neighbouring brilliance of their own appearance [Note: [Col. 0619D] Thus our manuscripts. The printed editions read “from the proximity of their appearance.”]; and as Moses received light from contemplating God’s glory, so that the people could not behold the honour of his glory; so too the Prophet, confessing himself God’s servant, prays to be illuminated, to be made conformable, according to the Apostle, to God’s glory (Philippians 3:21), and to be taught God’s ordinances, so that he may behold him not in part, nor through the shadow of the Law, but face to face and by spiritual contemplation.

13. Repentance Must Not Cease. What It Is.—He then continues, verse 136: “Streams of waters passed over my eyes, because they did not keep your law.” Though, as history itself teaches, he was conscious of former sins and had directed himself to God with his whole heart, yet, since he had already written in an earlier psalm of the grief for his sin [Note: [Col. 0620D] The Badian, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions, with two manuscripts, read “he had already written in fact of the grief of his sin.” Psalm 50 is indicated here.]—when, rebuked by the prophet Nathan, he acknowledged his crime and wept—he does not now cease to wash away the crime of his former deed with the tears of true repentance, saying: “Streams of waters passed over my eyes”: that is, the fountains of his tears surpassed fountains of rivers.

For this is the voice of repentance: to pray with tears, to groan with tears, and with this confidence to say: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Psalm 6:7). This is forgiveness of sin: to weep with a fountain of tears and be soaked by a plentiful shower of tears. Yet he preserved the measure of his most restrained statement with regard to the proper time and the now immovable firmness of faith [Note: [Col. 0620D] Thus the Micy and Vatican manuscripts, except that the Micy manuscript has “firmness,” not “of firmness.” The other books read: “but according to the proper time, and the even now—much better, “now”—immovable firmness of faith, he moderated the measure of his statement.”].

For he said concerning the past: “Because they did not keep your law.” Confession of sin is always timely, because repentance for sin ought never to cease; but the ending of a former sin belongs to the past. For true confession of sin is to repent without interruption of time; repentance for sin, however, is to have ceased from that which one has understood must be repented of [Note: [Col. 0620D] That is, although we ought to cease from sins, we ought not to cease from confession. The same matters are explained more clearly in Psalm 135, §5.]. Therefore the Prophet neither ceases to confess sin nor fails to confess it as belonging to the past.

## LETTER XVIII. Zade

“Righteous are you, O Lord, and your judgment is upright [Note: [Col. 0620D] “And upright.”]. You commanded righteousness—your testimonies—and your truth exceedingly” (Hilary: “greatly”). “Zeal for your house caused me to waste away” (“your zeal made me waste away”), “because my enemies forgot your words. Your word is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant loved it. I am younger and despised; I have not forgotten your ordinances. Your righteousness is righteousness for ever” (“your righteousnesses are for ever”), “and your law is truth. Tribulation and distress have found me, but your commandments are my meditation. The equity of your testimonies is for ever; give me understanding, and I shall live” (“of them, and I shall be given life”).

1. Faith Confesses God to Be Righteous Even When He Punishes.—With tireless and persevering faith it is necessary that our confession remain fixed and unshaken, lest, stirred by some injury of circumstances or pain of persecutions, we relax the zeal of devotion. Rather, if diseases trouble us, sufferings and bodily tortures rage, losses exhaust us, griefs and bereavements afflict us, we must always use the words now used by the Prophet, who says in verses 137–138: “Righteous are you, O Lord, and your judgment is upright. You commanded righteousness—your testimonies—and your truth greatly.”

For we must remember first that he who is Lord of all is righteous and that his judgments are upright. Why should he be unjust to his own? Why should he be unjust to those whom he himself brought forth? The immensity of his goodness does not permit such a thought about him. He brought us forth not for injury, not for the pain inherent in the nature of our origin. Whatever we suffer comes through the judgment of his goodness. He delights that the devil is conquered by the powers of our endurance, and he desires us to be tested through griefs, pains, and losses, so that the power of the world may understand that it has no right or authority of condemnation over his servants. Whatever he commanded is righteous, attested, and true, with an added intensification; for it is exceedingly true.

2. Impatience Under Afflictions Insults God. The Cause of Zeal. Days of Fasting.—Because it is rare to observe these things, and difficult to preserve unshaken faith amid these storms of the world and these shipwrecks of human vices, whenever adversity occurs complaint against God is ready at hand. The greedy person accuses God amid his losses. One bereaved is angry with God through resentment at his own tears. One who is tested by persecutions for the glory of confession reproaches God with injustice. This is the most foolish complaint of all: by impatience under ungodly grief they accuse God of injustice.

Therefore the Prophet added, saying, verse 139: “Your zeal caused me to waste away, because my enemies forgot your words.” Through zeal for God the Prophet is consumed at all our vices and crimes. Human nature too has this habit: if we see anyone opposing the will of those whom we love, we are zealous for the one who is not obeyed. How great is our pain when we see someone of God’s people made a servant of the world, a worker of the devil [Note: [Col. 0621D] The Regius and Albinus manuscripts read “a worker of the devil”; this is also the reading of the Badian, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions.], a vessel of death, and material for Gehenna! Therefore whoever sees a Christian giving himself to luxurious feasting on a fast day is angry with zeal for God. Whoever observes one acting arrogantly toward brothers and ministers is angry with zeal for God. Whoever rebukes a body already sanctified in Christ for turning aside to sexual debauchery is angry with zeal for God.

3. Examples of Zeal.—We learn that the Apostles remembered this zeal when the Lord entered the temple and drove out with a whip of cords all who were selling and buying (John 2:17); it was the zeal of which it is written: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68:10). For we sometimes make ourselves either a temple of God, a house of commerce, or a den of thieves. According to the Apostle, bodies sanctified in Christ are God’s temple (1 Corinthians 6:19). When we think and do acts of sexual immorality, murder, theft, deceit, and robbery, we make these same bodies a den of thieves. But when we labour in worldly business and commercial dealings [Note: [Col. 0621D] “Of merchants.”], we make the house of God into a house of commerce. Thus what should have been the seat of prayer becomes either a hiding-place for robbers or a house of business. The Lord is moved by this zeal in order to cast such persons out of the temple.

Men approved and accepted by God also exercised this zeal. Phinehas deserved the judgment of eternal peace because of it. For when the children of Israel had committed fornication, and he had been moved by zeal for God to punish them, the Lord said: “Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, in that the agitation of my soul subsided, because he was zealous with my zeal” (Numbers 25:11) [Note: [Col. 0621D] “Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron rests the agitation of the soul, because he was zealous with my zeal.”] [Note: [Col. 0621D–0622D] In the Micy manuscript, from which a version of this kind passed into the first Paris edition, there occurs “from the children of Jeharhe,” corruptly, as may be inferred here from the Greek and Ambrose; we therefore retain the alteration made in the later Paris edition. The passage is read differently in the Badian, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions and in the Vatican, Regius, and Albinus manuscripts: “Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, made the agitation of my soul rest, because he was zealous with my zeal.” Greek: *Phinees huios Eleazar, huiou Aarōn tou hiereōs, katepause ton thymon mou apo huiōn Israēl en tō zēlōsai mou ton zēlon* (Φινεὲς υἱὸς Ἐλεάζαρ, υἱοῦ Ἀαρὼν τοῦ ἱερέως, κατέπαυσε τὸν θυμόν μου ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ ἐν τῷ ζηλῶσαί μου τὸν ζῆλον): “Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, calmed my wrath from the children of Israel when he was zealous with my zeal.”].

That holy prophet Elijah, who was taken up bodily into the heavenly dwelling, said: “I have been exceedingly zealous, because the children of Israel have forsaken you and killed your prophets; and I alone am left” (3 Kings 19:10).

4. Those Forgetful of God’s Word Are Worthy of Hatred.—This zeal also possesses the Prophet. For he sees irreligious complaints about loss, ungodly tears of grief, and profane forgetfulness of God’s Law; therefore those who do these things are his enemies. For devout people can have no bond of friendship with such persons, when the irreligious must be shunned and abhorred with hatred. This is also taught in another psalm: “Those who hate you, O Lord, I hated, and I wasted away over your enemies; with perfect hatred I hated them” (Psalm 138:21). The Lord also said to Abraham: “Whoever curses you shall be cursed, and I shall be an enemy to your enemies and oppose those who oppose you” (Genesis 12:3). If Abraham’s enemies are enemies of God, what sort of people ought those to be for us whom we see to be enemies of God? [Note: [Col. 0622D] “What sort of people ought they to be for us?”]

5. In God’s Words Nothing Is Empty or Untrue.—He then gives the reason why he hated those who had forgotten God’s words: they are not empty, earthly, or trivial. For he says, verse 140: “Your word is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant loved it.” The Latin translation does not explain the precise sense of this word. What is *ignitum* (“made fiery,” “refined by fire”) in Latin is written in Greek *pepyromenon* (πεπυρωμένον). *Pepyromenon* signifies that which has been purified as though smelted by fire.

Whatever metals are smelted by fire contain no foreign and useless dross [Note: [Col. 0622D] The Badian, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions read “dross”; the Regius and Albinus manuscripts read “seat.”]; all that remains in them is true, perfect, and cleansed from every contamination of faults. Such is the word of God, containing in itself the assurance of eternal goods [Note: [Col. 0622D] The Paris edition, from the Micy manuscript, reads “bearing witness to assurance.”]. Hence the Lord says in the Gospels: “Not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the Law until all these things are fulfilled” (Matthew 5:18).

For all God’s words are true and established neither idly nor uselessly; they are refined by fire beyond every ambiguity of superfluous emptiness, and exceedingly refined by fire, lest anyone suppose that anything there is not perfect and proper. Therefore his servant loves these things. He does not merely do them, but loves them, because the work of love surpasses the work of obedience. Obedience alone is often a matter of fear; love, however, proceeds only from the devoted will of the mind [Note: [Col. 0622D] “From a devoted [will].”].

[Col. 0623A] 6. David, younger and despised, was chosen as king. — He then says, VERSE 141: “I am younger and despised; I have not forgotten your ordinances.” The prophet indeed speaks these words in his own person; yet they also apply to the people of our time. And in what sense David may be believed to have said this of himself is plainly shown. For the prophet Samuel was commanded by God to come to the house of Jesse, in order to anoint one of his sons as king. [Note: When he had come to Jesse, he orders all Jesse’s sons to be brought.] When he came, he ordered all Jesse’s sons to be present. He then saw the eldest, handsome in appearance, eminent in bearing and stature; but he was instructed by this reply: “Do not look upon his beauty or his great stature, because God does not see as man sees. For man sees the face, but God sees the heart” (1 Kingdoms [1 Samuel] 6:7). The second was present, the third was present, [Col. 0623B] and all whom Jesse then had with him were present; yet none of those present proved pleasing.

But because the prophet Samuel knew that he who had ordered him to come was not deceptive, and understood from those who were present that none had been [Note: Beloved.] chosen by God [Note: The Paris edition preferred “beloved.” Yet “chosen,” with the other books, is more satisfactory.], he said to Jesse, “Have you still a son?” (ibid., 11). He replied: “I have a little one, whom I left in the pasture.” Therefore he was chosen by the Holy Spirit and anointed king; and, though younger and despised, he received the glory both of prophet and king.

7. The younger people purchases the birthright. — These words likewise apply to the people who are both younger and formerly despised.
