For it was amid the vices of the age, in the night of ignorance, in the uncultivated, rustic, and ruinous dwelling of the earthly body, that it lived. Yet this people does not forget God’s ordinances; when the elder people is rejected, the younger is chosen for the inheritance of the household. For Jacob bought Esau’s birthright, which Esau, as though about to die, considered useless to himself (Gen. 25:32). The younger people knows that these firstfruits of its birth are eternal and cannot be cut off by death. Therefore it does not forget them—those things which the elder both despaired of and sold.

8. By faith it purchases what the elder lost through unbelief. The Law now made truth. — VERSE 142. Finally, it teaches the same point in the following verse: “Your righteousness [Note: “Your righteousness,” to which the Greek bears witness.] is for ever, and your law is truth.” The people that came forth from Egypt did not ponder these acts of righteousness: the sea dried up for it; a pillar of cloud served it by day, and a pillar of fire by night; heaven supplied it with morning manna [Note: “Morning manna,” as also a little below “heavenly manna” for “manna of heaven.” These readings seem preferable to us as more genuine, and manuscripts of better quality elsewhere frequently prefer them; thus, in Matthew, ch. 12, no. 22, the learned Benedictine editor preferred to read “manna serving the hungry” with those same manuscripts. On the same principle Psalm 139 reads, “Passover will go before,” which, etc.]; [Col. 0624A] twenty-seven kingdoms yielded to it; the Jordan stood dry for it; and the walls of Jericho fell at the sound of the army and the circuit of the ark of the covenant [Note: In the royal manuscript, “circuit.” A similar phrase occurs in Psalm 5, no. 19: “When the Jordan flowed back, when the great city fell to the ground at the circuit of the ark of the covenant” (again, “circuit” in another royal manuscript).].

The people which is younger knows that these acts of God’s righteousness are eternal. Since it knew them to be eternal, it bought them by faith; because the elder believed itself destined to die, it sold them through unbelief. For to the younger people the Law is truth. For now truly, through Jesus, circumcision of the heart is repeated for it unto life; truly it crosses through the sea of this age into the land promised to it; truly, being eternal, it receives heavenly manna [Note: Bad., Er., Lips., and three manuscripts: “eternal”]; truly, reborn in the Jordan, it rejoices; truly it sacrifices the Passover, to be delivered by the blood of the Lamb; truly it feasts upon unleavened bread of sincerity and is cleansed from the leaven of ancient malice [Note: From the manuscript of Mic., the Paris edition first added the word “ancient.” Above, Letter 3, no. 7, we read of the prophet: “He hastens to cast out the leaven of the old nature.”]. The Law is no longer a shadow to it, but truth.

9. The speech and conduct of those suffering for truth’s sake. — This younger people knows that, for the confession of this truth, it is hard pressed by many persecutions. Hence, throughout the whole world, come the blessed faithful confessors and holy martyrdoms. Hence many have been stripped of their property, scattered into exile, bound, beaten, burned, and killed; but, [Note: The Paris edition: “but happily.”] by a faithful and continual meditation on the commandments, they have always overcome whatever assailed them through the strength of confirmed faith. Therefore he says, VERSE 143: “Tribulation and [Note: “Distress.” Thus this manuscript and below; the Greek ἡ ἀνάγκη also supports it.] distress have found me; but your commandments are my meditation.”

Though battles press upon us, [Note: “May assaults be made.”] though exile is threatened, proscriptions imposed, and deaths—not merely inflicted, but devised with fresh instruments of punishment (see Tractate on Psalm 65, no. 21)—nevertheless this should always be the voice of a faithful person: “Tribulation and distress have found me; but your commandments are my meditation.” Neither violence overwhelming us [Col. 0624C] nor the oblivion that creeps in with time should cause the meditation on God’s commandments to be absent from us.

10. Understanding, a pre-eminent gift. — He then says, VERSE 144: “Your testimonies are righteous for ever; give me understanding [Note: Thus the royal and Albinian manuscripts and the ancient editions, as the words that follow also seem to require. But the Paris edition, omitting “of them” before, reads here “that you may give life”; and, if it then added “to me,” it would agree with many Greek copies, in which, according to Nobilio, ζῆσόν με, “give me life,” occurs. Yet he himself prefers ζήσομαι, “I shall live,” from more corrected copies.] of them, [Note: “And I shall live.”] and I shall live.”

He is not content merely to judge and expect God’s testimonies to be righteous for the present. He hopes for their righteousness for ever, and through the preceding tribulations and distresses strives to obtain what is eternal. The rich man in the Gospel, considering that nothing was eternal, exchanged his present happiness [Note: “His life,” perhaps also “and life.”] for a death of punishment (Luke 16:25). But poor Lazarus [Note: “Eliazer” for Lazarus.], expecting God’s eternal testimonies, is contained in Abraham’s bosom [Col. 0625A] and exchanges the misery of his laborious life for the honor of blessed rest. The prophet prays for understanding of these things: a gift, namely, pre-eminent among the many gifts of spiritual graces; and through it he asks that he may be made alive. For just as he now meditates on God’s testimonies and commandments in the present, so he awaits what is eternal; and just as he lives the life of the body, so he requests that, through the understanding he receives from God, he may live with eternal glory.

LETTER XIX. Koph.

“I cried [Note: Coc.: “I cried with my whole heart, O Lord, hear me; [Col. 0626D] I shall seek your ordinances.”] with my whole heart (Hil.: “my”), hear me, O Lord; I shall seek your ordinances. I cried to you: save me, and I will keep your commandments. I came before the dawn, and cried; in (and in) your words I hoped [Col. 0625B] (Hil. adds “always”). My eyes came before the morning light, that I might meditate on your utterances. Hear my voice, O Lord, according to your abundant (below, “abundant” is absent) mercy; according to your judgment give me life. Those pursuing me drew near to iniquity; but they have gone far from your law. You are near, O Lord, and all your commandments are truth. From (in) the beginnings I knew concerning your testimonies that you founded them for ever.”

397. 1. Crying of the mouth, not of the heart, forbidden in prayer. — Among the many precepts of evangelical teaching, the Lord required of us silence in prayer (Matt. 6:6): that we should pray silently and from the secret place of the heart, and that in prayer the function should belong to the mind rather than to the voice, since God hears the secrets of our prayer because he is the inspector of secrets [Note: Royal manuscript with Albin.: “the secret place,” and shortly afterwards “hearing,” not “heard.”]. Therefore what the Prophet says seems contrary to the Gospel’s ordinances when he declares, VERSE 145: “I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord; I shall seek your ordinances.”

But the Prophet knows that the cry should be of the heart, not of the voice; and therefore he cries from the heart. This is no sound of a raised voice, nor bodily hearing, but the cry of faith, the cry of the mind, to be lifted to the throne of God not by the exertion of the voice but by the spirit of faith. For that person cries to God with his whole heart who asks for great things, who prays for heavenly things [Note: In the two manuscripts mentioned above: “who despises earthly things.”], who hopes for eternal things, who lives by the duties of innocent fear.

2. Abel, slain, cries out. Moses silently cries by faith. The Spirit’s cry. — Thus, at the beginning of this world, righteous Abel, even after being slain, speaks and [Col. 0625D] cries out mightily. For it is written: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me” (Gen. 4:10). The complaint of the saints is not lowly, nor the prayer of the faithful depressed. What it asks is lofty, what it awaits is exalted, and what it prays is resonant with crying.

Pharaoh pressed God’s people with hostile forces; the Red Sea obstructed their flight; Israel, hemmed in on every side, seemed already doomed to death [Note: In the printed editions, “was being pressed.” In two manuscripts, “feared.” With Mic., we prefer “seemed.” On Moses’ silence while crying, Ambrose, *On Duties*, I.41.211, represents one of the Maccabees as saying: “The Lord does not hear only those who speak; he heard Moses when he was silent. He hears the silent thoughts of his own more than the voices of all.”], with the enemy close and the sea confronting them. Scripture testifies that amid these events Moses uttered no voice to God: he stood sorrowful, he stood silent, yet resounding in the secret of his heart and crying out through the faith of his prayer. For the divine voice testifies to this, saying: “And the Lord said to Moses, Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. 14:15). He was silent, but the prayer of his faith was a cry to God. The Apostle too knows that this cry of the Spirit is in faithful people when he says: “For the Spirit cries in our hearts, Abba, Father” (Gal. 4:6).

This cry of silence penetrates even to God’s ears; yet those ears hear not the cry but faith: faith which does not ask for earthly wealth, does not desire empty and passing glory, and does not pray for pleasures of the body that must die. The Apostle writes his letters indeed in small characters, [Col. 0626B] 398 and this is the ordinary form of letters and strokes for him; yet he knows that his letters are great, saying: “See in what large letters I have written to you with my own hand” (Gal. 6:11), comprehending in such letters the greatness of his meanings and the usefulness of his precepts.

The Prophet therefore cries with his whole heart. And because he cries from the heart, he prays to be heard; and, once heard, he asks this—that he may seek out God’s ordinances. He knows that they are hidden and concealed and covered by the shadow of the Law. He desires to investigate them; for this task requires many and great things: the cry of the heart, the merit of being heard, and the duty of inquiry.

3. The order in which salvation must be sought. Prayer of the lips. The reward of salvation. — VERSE 146: But he who cried that he might be heard and seek God’s ordinances now [Col. 0626C] cries that he may be saved and keep God’s testimonies [Note: The Vatican manuscript alone here prefixes “he says.” For it reads, “I cried to you: save me.” Up to this point Hilary has not expounded a verse without first placing the sacred text before it; nevertheless that manuscript is suspect of interpolation.]. How great was the modesty of the order he followed! He did not immediately dare to hope that his cry would result in salvation. First, he had to be worthy of being heard; first, he had to seek the ordinances. Being heard had to be earned; inquiry had to be undertaken; only after these could salvation be hoped for.

But we ask for salvation as though it were owed to us; and, as though God must necessarily grant it, we ask for it in our first prayers. If only we spoke with the cry of the heart! Our lips alone murmur words they do not know while our mind wanders elsewhere; and the mind, occupied with other matters, does not follow the body’s act. But after praying in so many preceding prayers that he might be saved, the Prophet teaches the reward of salvation, saying: “And I will keep your commandments.” This is the service of our faith: to keep the commandments and, as though under a most faithful seal, to preserve this treasure of the precept entrusted and committed to us.

4. Youthful years should be dedicated to God. — He who had cried out and professed that he would keep God’s testimonies—written under heaven, earth, and angels as witnesses—[Col. 0627A] added yet another [Note: Two manuscripts: “for the merit.”] merit for attaining salvation, saying, VERSE 147: “I came before the dawn, and cried, and I have always [Note: “Always” is absent from our manuscript. Shortly afterwards: “from vices.”] hoped in your words.”

He did not wait for old age, weak [Note: Printed editions: “from vices.” More correctly, the royal and Albinian manuscripts read “for vices.” For David is commended because, at an age strong and prone to vices, he chose to serve God.] for vices; nor did he choose the season of a cold age, when the heat of luxury had cooled through its long practice [Note: In the manuscript of Mic.: “through ages of long practice and luxury.”]. [Note: The Albinian manuscript with the royal manuscript reads “but immaturity,” perhaps more truly. From this we conjecture that above one should read “I came before in immaturity,” from the Greek προέφθασα ἐν ἀωρίᾳ, since the syllable *in* before the following word was perhaps dropped by the copyist. For the ancients, joining the particle *in* with a word beginning with *m*, did not always change it to *im*. This is clear from Augustine on this same Psalm, Sermon 30, no. 3: “What was said in Greek, ἐν ἀωρίᾳ, not in one word but in two—that is, a preposition and noun—some of our translators rendered ‘in the untimely night’; most, ‘in immaturity’ [thus it must be read with the old Corbie manuscript, not ‘immaturity’; otherwise Augustine would not add what follows], not in two words but one, whose nominative is *inmaturitas*; while some rendered it in two words, as the Greek has it, ‘in immaturity,’ etc.”]

Rather, he forestalled all maturity by faith and devotion, conquering youth through self-restraint, checking the wanton years, and forestalling the maturity of old age by the tranquillity of a modest and chaste adolescence. The Prophet’s cry is that of one hoping in God’s words—not sometimes, but always. For our hope has no end: it always stretches forth toward heavenly things and advances toward God’s eternal promises. It has no vacant time, none spent in idleness.

[Col. 0627B] 5. Watches of pre-dawn meditation. — Finally comes what follows, VERSE 148: “My eyes came before the morning light, that I might meditate on your utterances.” He who had forestalled the dawn with crying [Note: Printed editions: “had forestalled the cry”; corrected with the aid of manuscripts.] [Note: In the earlier edition: “to cry.”] now forestalls the days themselves with meditations. He keeps watch before dawn; he does not wait for the rising light to disturb eyes heavy with sleep. He keeps watch and covers the very returning dawn of light with prayers: now occupied with the sayings of the prophets, now intent on the hymns of the Psalms, now diligently engaged with the deeds of patriarchs and saints, meditating on every utterance of God [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “every utterance of God at every time.”] at every time and with constancy.

6. Trust in God’s mercy, not one’s own merits. — He next says, VERSE 149: “Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life.” Let us learn modesty from the Prophet’s [Col. 0627C] utterances: from all the things above [Note: “The cry of the heart, the ordinances, [Col. 0628C] observance,” etc., “self-restraint, watches.”], the cry of the heart, the seeking of ordinances, the keeping of God’s testimonies, self-restraint in youth, and watches of pre-dawn meditation [Note: Vatican manuscript with Mic.: “the cry of the heart, the inquiry into ordinances, observance,” etc. In the accusative case, less correctly. Before these words the preposition *ex* is understood.]. Through these he places all his hope in God’s mercy [Col. 0628A]; at last he asks that his voice may be heard according to mercy [Note: “And he asks for mercy according to God’s judgment.”], and he seeks mercy according to God’s judgment.

We, if we fast once, think we have done enough; if we give some small thing from the abundance of our household resources [Note: In the printed editions: “from the granary”; and above, “we have satisfied,” one word.], we believe that we have fulfilled righteousness. We fast either that we may please people or refresh bodies wearied by food; and amid the very fasts we contemplate fornications, [Note: “Murders,” adds the Verona manuscript.] murders, injuries, and hatreds [Note: In the Paris edition: “thoughts of hatred,” corruptly.]. We give some trifling gift while we do not support the poor person knocking at our door [Note: Royal manuscript with Albin.: “knocking,” and shortly afterward “delays,” in place of “poor.”], or while we pursue a reputation for goodness in the empty and idle opinion of people; and we suppose that we deserve to be heard. But the Prophet hopes for everything from God and expects everything from his mercy. Though he himself is perfect in every work of goodness [Note: Three manuscripts: “he himself wholly,” etc.], he does not think this sufficient for salvation unless, in accordance with God’s compassions and judgments, he receives mercy.

7. Whoever approaches in order to harass the faithful withdraws from God’s Law. — Yet he is never idle; those who harass and persecute are never far away: his whole life, according to the witness of Scripture, was spent in ambushes. And whoever now wishes to please God must necessarily displease the ungodly. Therefore he says, VERSE 150: “Those who persecute me have drawn near to [Note: Manuscript: “the wicked.” Thus the Roman Psalter.] iniquity; but they have gone far from your law.”

This is indeed believed to have been said of himself, whose life was attacked from every side. But he who sets forth in this Psalm an order of human instruction has adapted everything to our education, so that we might know that those who become near to the injury of the faithful are far from [Col. 0628C] God’s Law. For the more one advances toward inflicting injury upon the saints, the farther one withdraws from God’s Law [Note: Printed editions: “in the saints.” More correctly, the manuscripts read “upon the saints”: that is, the nearer one comes to inflicting injury upon saints, the farther one recedes from God’s Law.]. We must take care, therefore, lest anger at any time move us against our brothers, lest envy sting us, [Col. 0629A] lest rivalry provoke us, so that we act toward them in a manner irreligious or contemptuous; for when we join in their injury, we depart from God’s Law.

8. God is wholly everywhere, as the soul is wholly in all the members. When a decayed member is cut off, the soul remains unharmed. — He then says, VERSE 151: “You are near, O Lord, and all your commandments [Note: “Are truth.”] are truth.” Elsewhere we read: “I am a God who is near, and not a God far away, says the Lord” (Jer. 23:23). God is not contained by bodily places, nor is the immensity of the divine power restricted by boundaries or spaces. He is present everywhere, and wholly wherever he is; he is not anywhere in part, but in all things he is wholly present.

The blessed Apostle, replying in an address to Athenians made ridiculous by the emptiness of philosophy, says: “We do not seek God as one dwelling far from us; for in him we live and move [Col. 0629B] and are” (Acts 17:28). And the Spirit of God, according to the prophet, “has filled the whole world” (Wisdom 1:7). And again: “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jer. 23:24). Nothing is devoid of God; nothing lacks him. He is everywhere, in the manner of the bodily soul [Note: The printed editions have “of the incorporeal soul.” We prefer, with the royal, Vatican, and Albinian manuscripts, “of the bodily soul”; yet this is said not because the soul’s nature is bodily, but because it is joined to the body—much as we call the Word, joined to flesh, incarnate and embodied. Thus above, Letter 3, no. 9, Hilary calls a commandment concerning the life we live in the body “a commandment of bodily life.” He needed to mention the soul joined to the body because there is also an angelic nature, which may properly be called a soul free from a body, whose example would contribute nothing to illustrating God’s presence in all places. This passage also makes it quite clear that Hilary was far from holding our soul’s nature to be bodily. For how could he have thought it bodily if he taught that it exists, after God’s manner, in all the body’s members at once and that no part of it is cut away even when a member of the body is amputated? It would indeed be vain for him to advance from knowledge of the soul to understanding that God is wholly in the entire world and in every part, unless he believed the soul also to be commonly understood as wholly in the whole body and wholly in each part—and therefore indivisible and incorporeal.], which is diffused throughout all the members and absent from none of the individual parts. Even though it has a certain private and royal seat in the whole body, it is nevertheless infused into the marrow, fingers, and limbs.

Now, if it becomes necessary to remove by cutting certain corrupted members of the body, because those members, dead through their defects, no longer have their proper use, whatever is decayed [Note: “And perishable flesh.”] and falling away belongs to the perishable flesh [Note: Thus our manuscripts. The printed editions read, “and whatever belongs to perishable flesh.”] and is cut off without injury to the soul. For the soul itself is united to the sound and whole members of our body; and when those same members have become both rotten and fit to be cut off, it does not follow [Col. 0629C] that the soul is cut off with them.

9. Though God is everywhere, he is not present in the vicious. — These comparisons are indeed applied to the divine nature beyond what is proper, because whatever is eternal is incomparable and the exception of unoriginated divinity admits no form of created truth configured to it. [Col. 0630A] Yet an example of this kind is fitted to our understanding, so that, by it and according to the authority of heavenly sayings, we may understand the incorporeal and immeasurable God as joined to this bounded and bodily world, but not as present in those made dead by their vices and deeds. [Note: Namely, by the grace of indwelling, as Augustine says in Epistle 187, no. 16, although he is present to them by the presence of his divinity. Yet he is farther from them in proportion as they are more obstinate in vice, just as eyes are rightly said to be farther from this light in proportion as they are blinder—even though the light is at hand, as he adds in the same epistle, no. 17. Here the printed editions add: “Indeed, still further, when,” etc. We have removed this on the authority of the manuscripts, from which shortly afterward we restored *sects*, where previously *we follow* stood.]

Moreover, the understanding of divine and invisible things is still pursued through the contemplation of bodily things and their natures. We see the sun remaining in a particular region of heaven according to its course; yet it surely stretches everywhere, is present everywhere, and, as great as it is throughout all things, so [Note: The printed editions read “wherever it is.” The word “is” is absent from the royal, Vatican, and Albinian manuscripts. For demonstrating the same point, Augustine, no. 17 of the aforementioned Epistle 187 on God’s presence, prefers the example of sound to that of light.] it is infused everywhere in its full greatness. But if it falls upon the shut windows of houses, its light is indeed at hand, but the things that are closed deny themselves its light.

[Col. 0630B] 10. God’s presence should make us cautious. — Therefore, in every action of our life, we must be watchful and open to God: first, so that he may deign to pour his light into hearts free and open through innocence; and then, so that we may believe ourselves to act in the bosom of his divinity and not suppose him absent when we become angry, when we strike, [Note: “When we contend.”] when we despise [Note: Vatican manuscript: “when we contend.”], when we curse, when we become drunk, when we act lustfully, when we neglect divine and human obligations—sinning with the greater insult against him within whom we do these things.

11. To this is added also that his commandments are truth. Nothing there is uncertain, nothing doubtful; everything is perfect in the completeness of truth. They are neglected with the greater danger because they are more fully established as [Col. 0630C] precepts [Note: “As a precept.”] of truth [Note: Five manuscripts read “as a precept.”].

12. God’s testimonies from the beginning of the world onward. — How the Prophet learned what he adds, saying, VERSE 152, “From the beginnings I knew concerning your testimonies that you founded them for ever,” may be understood as follows. Although the Prophet speaks this of himself, knowing God’s Law from the beginning, these words nevertheless apply to the whole age [Note: In the royal and Albinian manuscript: “yet to the whole Church”; in the Vatican manuscript: “yet to the whole age of the Church.” These readings are not to be despised. Similar are the words in Letter 5, no. 8, by which Hilary shows that the way of the commandments had been trodden from the very beginning of the world and thereafter, because the path of God’s commandments had been followed from the beginning of the age. On this path Abel also ran, Seth stood firm, etc.] [Col. 0631A] that has been instructed by God’s teachings from the creation of the world.

For whoever remembers the law of free will established for Adam [Note: This law appears to be meant in the words of the Tractate on Psalm 2, no. 16: “Goodness was therefore entrusted to the will, so that the will might acquire for itself the reward of goodness and that the progress and exercise of this eternal blessedness might come to us from merit, not from an indiscriminate necessity imposed by law.”]; whoever has learned of Eve’s very creation; whoever has heard the serpent’s curse; whoever has read that the tree of life was closed off by a Cherub with a flaming and turning sword; whoever knows that Abel’s slain blood cried out; whoever reckons the measure of punishment in Cain and Lamech [Note: Printed editions: “in Ham”; corrected from manuscripts.] (Gen. 4:24); whoever has examined Enoch taken away, Noah preserved, the blessing of Shem and Japheth, and the curse of Ham [Note: The printed editions lack the words “has examined … Melchizedek the priest, who.” They occur with great agreement in the manuscripts.]; whoever has examined Melchizedek the priest, Abraham chosen, Isaac promised, Jacob preferred, Joseph sold, Judah sanctified, Moses nourished and instructed—and, after the mighty mysteries of the Law had been given, dead in the word of God—and Jesus [Col. 0631B] the divider of the promised land [Note: “Promised” is absent from the royal and Albinian manuscripts.] and author of the renewed circumcision: such a person can rightly use the Prophet’s words: “From the beginning I knew concerning your testimonies that you founded them for ever.”

For in the life and deeds of all the men named above is contained the hope of eternal blessings; and through them we are instructed toward the teaching of Gospel preaching. [Note: Royal manuscript: “But when they have been founded.”] But things founded are prepared for the building of the house to come. For, according to blessed Paul, we are built upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles (Eph. 2:20), in whom God’s testimonies have been founded for ever, where that heavenly and royal city, the holy Jerusalem, will be built: that dwelling of thronging angels [Note: Printed editions: “a throng of angels,” against the manuscripts.] and of the elect firstborn, whose foundations are living stones [Note: “Divine stones.”] and precious gems, living, rising, and reigning in Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

403. LETTER XX. Resch.

“See my humility and deliver me, for I have not forgotten your Law. Judge my cause and redeem me; for the sake of your utterance give me life. Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your ordinances. Your compassions are exceedingly many [below: “are very great, O Lord”], O Lord; according to your judgments [“your judgment”] give me life. Many are they who persecute and afflict me; I have not turned aside from your judgments [“from your testimonies”]. I saw those who do not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, [Col. 0631D] because they did not keep your utterances. See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; in your mercy give me life. The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your righteousness are for ever.”

1. In humility is the head and sum of all commandments, all titles and rewards of faith. — Throughout the whole Psalm the holy Prophet has set before us many great examples of his faith and confession. By them he has established in himself for others a pattern of believing, acting, understanding, not knowing, hoping, and praying, perfecting the evangelical person by perfect observance of the Law. Although he either does, testifies to, preserves [Note: In two manuscripts: “or preserves.”], or hopes for all things pleasing to the divine will or proposed to human hope, he nevertheless remembers in what kind of observance lies the head and sum of all commandments; and he knows what would be required by his Lord even of the Apostles to whom the keys of heaven were to be entrusted.

For when they disagreed among themselves in opinions and ambitions, and each claimed precedence for himself through human rivalry [Col. 0632B], since each either desired or sought to be superior to the others, the Lord, showing from where the reward of such merit and title must be sought, said: “Whoever among you wishes to be greater, let him become the least of all” (Luke 22:26); “for everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted, and whoever exalts himself shall be humbled” (Matt. 23:12). Thus he taught that in humility are contained all titles and rewards of faith. It is therefore most useful for those obedient to the divine precepts to keep within themselves, broken and crushed, every empty form of human arrogance and insolence, and, considering themselves dependent upon God’s [Note: Vatican manuscript with the royal and Albinian manuscripts: “God’s magnificence and mercy, considered”; and a little above, “intruding,” instead of “obedient.”] magnificence and mercy, to contain themselves within the moderation of humility.

2. David displays humility alone. He reserves his vindication for God. — Accordingly, this holy king and prophet—also counted, according to the flesh, as ancestor of his God and Lord in the lineage of his seed—amid these assaults of the age and battles of spiritual wickedness, cries out to God with the sole and such ambition of his prayer, VERSE 153: “See my humility and deliver me, for I have not forgotten your Law.” He prays that God may behold in him not the riches of a kingdom, not the spirit of prophecy, nor any other titles of human boasting, but humility. For he does not resist those persecuting him with weapons of war, nor, impatient with human indignation, seize the occasion both for his own vengeance and for royal power. But, knowing this decree of the divine will: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12:19), he does not forget God’s Law, which must be maintained in humility [Note: “To be maintained.”] [Note: Thus three manuscripts; the printed editions read “maintained.”]; but he prays for deliverance because [Col. 0632D] he is humble, declaring that remembrance of God’s Law consists in preserving humility.

3. His judgment is just. — Therefore, entrusting all things to divine judgment and seeking deliverance for the merit of humility, since he was stirred in no way against God’s ordinances, against [Col. 0633A] human hatreds, or against the suffering of present troubles [Note: Royal and Albinian manuscripts: “impatience.” Here *patientia* means suffering.], and determined that nothing concerning these matters was to be judged [Note: “Avenged.”] by himself [Note: Vatican manuscripts: “avenged.”] in this present age, he consequently adds, VERSE 154: “Judge my cause and redeem me; for the sake of your utterance give me life.”

It is the voice of a great and secure conscience to seek the judgment of one’s own judgment [Note: Paris edition: “of his judge,” corruptly.], so that one desires the scrutiny of the divine verdict even concerning that which one has determined and approved for oneself. He does not here depart into the opinion of corrupted judgment by judging either others or himself; nor does anger, favor, hatred, or love turn him aside from true judgment. He is not ignorant of this Gospel commandment: “For with the judgment with which you have judged, you shall be judged” (Matt. 7:2).

4. He Awaits Redemption through Christ. — [Col. 0633B] But not even he fears the judgment of his own judgment who says: “But I judged myself to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). Therefore, secure in this judgment upon his own judgment, the Prophet awaits the time of redemption and prays that he may be redeemed and quickened for the sake of God’s utterances. For, having been sold under sin,

> [Note: Col. 0633D: The printed editions, omitting “for,” presently read: “through redemption and justification … we are set free.”]

we shall be set free through redemption and justification in the blood of the Lord.

> [Note: Col. 0633D: “We are set free through redemption and justification.”]

This is what the giving of the Law, the whole spirit of prophecy, the hope of the patriarchs, the voices of angels, and the word of God’s utterance throughout the whole course of the age have testified; and therefore he prays that he may be redeemed and quickened.

5. Voluntary Ignorance Has No Pardon. — But these same utterances of God, while they proclaim [p. 405] life and redemption to pious hopes, leave none to the impious. [Col. 0633C] The Prophet’s expectation is immediately followed by these words concerning sinners:

> V. 155: Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought out thy justifications.

Ignorance of the will has no pardon; for the capacity to know, yet not to know, is guilt for knowledge rejected rather than not discovered. Salvation is therefore far from sinners because they have not sought God’s justifications, since they certainly remain recorded in writing for no other purpose than that they might spread to the knowledge and understanding of all. But the Prophet knows that, though salvation is far from sinners who do not seek God’s justifications, yet the Lord is near to those who are upright of heart (Ps. 33:19); and likewise, according to the Apostle: “You who were far off have been made near” (Eph. 2:13). Therefore, lest both he himself and salvation [Col. 0633D] be far from Him,

> [Note: Col. 0634D: From the manuscript of Micy; we have added “he too,” to which the immediately preceding words of the Apostle refer.]

he seeks knowledge of God’s justifications.

6. Eternal Realities Were Prefigured in the Mysteries of the Law. — He is not unaware how great a mystery of our salvation is expressed in them, through certain indications [Col. 0634A] in present things of eternal prefigurations: namely, in the Hebrew servant’s serving only six years; then, after the same period of six years, in the whole land’s being left at rest and its produce being allotted even to beasts;

> [Note: Col. 0634D: In the earlier printed editions the word “its” was lacking.]

and also in the law of the Jubilee year, that is, the fiftieth year, through which, when debts are released and all fields return to the rights of their owners, if they had perhaps passed into other hands, a new and heavenly remission and renewal of all things is foretold.

And since salvation is far from those who have not sought these things, the Prophet, wholly occupied in seeking them and contemplating in a mirror the justifications of divine and eternal mercy, adds:

> V. 156: Thy mercies are very many, O Lord; according to thy judgment quicken me.

> [Note: Col. 0633D: “According to thy judgments.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0634D: The printed editions read “according to thy judgments,” agreeing with Aquila but differing from the Septuagint and our manuscripts.]

God’s mercies, then, are exceedingly many; [Col. 0634B] for they surpass the measure of human estimation.

7. David Is Not Moved from God amid Afflictions. — But although the Prophet is confident in these things and hopes that he will be quickened by God’s judgments, many hatreds and persecutions from without wear him down. Yet, not forgetful of God’s mercies, of which—according to the same Prophet—there is no number, he did not turn aside from his testimonies. For it follows:

> V. 157: Many are they that persecute me and afflict me; from thy testimonies I have not declined.

> [Note: Cols. 0633D–0634D: “And afflict me” has been supplied on the authority of our manuscript and of the Septuagint, nearly all books of the Psalms adding their confirmation.]

He is not impelled;

> [Note: Col. 0634D: “He is not driven away.”]

he is not moved.

> [Note: Col. 0634D: The editions of Badius and Erasmus read “he is not driven away”; two manuscripts, “he is not repelled.”]

Though many persecute him, he does not even turn aside.

8. His Zeal for God’s Law. — Yet he who so remains in God’s commandments that he cannot be driven or deflected by persecutors has something that [p. 406] troubles him with grievous sorrow, and even dissolves him, as it were, into the wasting away [Col. 0634C] of a melting soul: others depart from God’s law

> [Note: Col. 0634D: “From the fear of God.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0634D: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions instead read, “from the fear of God.”]

and violate the faith and covenant of the Law which they had undertaken, while he himself does not turn aside from God’s testimonies. These are the burning agitations, these the only wearinesses, which the Prophet feels when he says:

> V. 158: I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, because they did not keep thy utterances.

Israel was called heir of the sealed covenant, and, when he heard the voice of the Lord from the mountain, he answered: “All that God has spoken we will hear and do” (Exod. 24:7). But when he worshipped strange gods, when he defiled himself with the vices of every crime, he forfeited the covenant both of the designation he had heard and of the observance he had professed. For they did not keep the utterances of God, which they answered that they would hear and do.

Nor is this wasting away of the Prophet over the transgression [Col. 0634D] of the people something new; for we know that the Lord himself wept over Jerusalem because of its impiety (Luke 19:41), that the Apostle likewise weeps in the same teaching over the impenitent (Phil. 3:17), and further that [Col. 0635A] he himself burns if anyone is caused to stumble (2 Cor. 11:29).

9. He Fulfils the Law through Love, Not Fear. — But he who grieves over those who do not keep the covenant and wastes away does not decline the test of God’s commandments in himself. For he says:

> V. 159: See that I have loved thy commandments, O Lord; in thy mercy quicken me.

It is too little for the Prophet to fulfil the commandments through fear; rather, he loves them, because the work of love lies outside the compulsion of fear. And although love of the Law is superior to fear, he is nevertheless not so confident in himself that he does not rather pray to be quickened through God’s mercy. He does not now think that he lives; rather, he awaits life when this mortal body has been removed and swallowed up in the glory of immortality.

10. God’s First Word Concerning Man. — For he knows that [Col. 0635B] this was already promised him at the beginning of his creation, when God says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). This is God’s first utterance concerning man, when the beginning of our origin was created in the image of unbounded eternity.

> [Note: Col. 0635D: The Royal manuscript, with the Albinus manuscript, reads: “when our origin was established as a beginning.”]

Therefore, certain that he will live by that life and image of God, he says:

> V. 160: The beginning of thy words is truth, and all the judgments of thy righteousness are for ever.

The words of God do not pass away though heaven and earth pass away (Matt. 24:35). Whatever has flowed from his lips is not void. His justifications are eternal, and his righteousness is eternal. Truth, therefore, is the beginning of God’s words; and he knows no earlier utterance of God concerning himself—that is, concerning the creation of man—than that man should be made according to the image [Col. 0635C] of God

> [Note: Col. 0635D: In the printed editions the word “God” was missing.]

and likeness. This, [p. 407] then, is the ordinance of unchangeable truth: thus truth is in the beginning of God’s words, so that the new man, regenerated in Christ, may henceforth live eternally according to the image of the eternal God—that is, of the heavenly Adam.

> [Note: Col. 0635D: In the Royal and Albinus manuscripts the words “that is, of the heavenly Adam” are omitted.]

## LETTER XXI. Sin

> Princes have persecuted me without cause, and my heart has feared thy words.  
> I will rejoice over thy utterances, as one who finds abundant spoils.  
> I have hated and abhorred iniquity; but I myself have loved thy law [below, “I myself” is absent].  
> Seven times in the day I have spoken praise to thee for the judgments of thy righteousness.  
> Much peace is for those who love thy name, and there is no stumbling-block for them.  
> I awaited thy salvation, [Col. 0635D] O Lord, and I performed thy commandments.  
> My soul kept thy testimonies and loved them exceedingly.  
> I kept thy commandments [and thy testimonies], because all my ways are before thee.

1. God Must Not Be Denied amid the Hatred of Princes. — The prophet David indeed endured the grievous hatreds and persecutions of King Saul and the princes [Col. 0636A] of the people, because professed impiety could not bear the constancy of a devout conscience.

> [Note: Col. 0635D: Three manuscripts read: “but he confirms the Lord’s evangelical saying to the Apostles. For he is not unaware,” etc.]

But, conforming himself to the evangelical and apostolic man, he is not unaware of the evangelical saying:

> [Note: Col. 0635D: “Which says.”]

> “For they will hand you over and scourge you in their synagogues, and you will stand before kings and authorities as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles” (Matt. 10:17–18).

Indeed, teaching steadfastness in preaching and the glory of confession, he had previously exhorted them, saying:

> “Everyone who confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I too will deny before my Father who is in heaven” (ibid. 32–33).

Therefore, whether consecrated under the Law or prepared for the glory of the Gospel, he who had left Saul [Col. 0636B] and his people no cause for persecuting him, and knew through the many hatreds of rulers and nations that the world must be renounced for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,

> [Note: Col. 0636D: The printed editions read “the kingdom of heaven to be proclaimed to the world,” omitting the preceding *propter* (“for the sake of”); the manuscripts restore the text.]

confidently says these things to God:

> V. 161: Princes have persecuted me without cause, [p. 408] and my heart has feared thy words.

For he fears that he will be denied if he denies.

2. The Voice of Conquering Faith. — But since he does not ignore the rewards of this blessed persecution, the Lord saying:

> “Blessed are you when they persecute you and say every evil thing against you for righteousness’ sake; rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 5:11–12),

after the hatred of princes he moderates his fear of God’s words by what follows:

> V. 162: I will rejoice over thy utterances, as one who finds abundant spoils.

His fear, then, was lest he either be subjected undeservedly to the persecutions of princes

> [Note: Col. 0636D: In two manuscripts “undeservedly” occurs without “or.” What follows appears to require “or be subjected deservedly,” for example, after he had furnished the cause of their hatreds.]

[Col. 0636C] or give way; for it is not the mark of a holy person to have furnished the cause of hatreds, and it is without pardon to have lost God’s grace through fear of the world. Yet to find spoils is the mark of a victor;

> [Note: Col. 0635D: “To find.”]

certainly, to have offered them from oneself is already the mark of one defeated. Therefore, since the Prophet is not broken by these persecutions and overcomes the hatred of princes through faith, he carries away certain spoils of impiety from the defeated.

For he knows from the Gospels that the strong man is bound in his house, stripped of the weapons of his power, and has now offered spoils from himself to be plundered by the faithful (Matt. 12:29). Therefore he now rejoices in God’s utterances as one who finds many spoils, since, after the power of the impious has been broken and he remains victorious through faith, he has stripped them of every weapon either of impiety or of cruelty.

> [Note: Col. 0636D: The Vatican manuscripts read “unbelief”; two others, “craftiness,” a reading not to be despised.]

3. This Befits Only Those Who Love the Law. — But this [Col. 0636D] disposition of joy

> [Note: Col. 0636D: “Does not exist”; afterwards, “pursuit” in place of “detestation.”]

does not exist unless there is both love of the divine Law and detestation of iniquity. For no one will wish to flee what he does not hate, nor strive to obtain what he does not love. Rejoicing, therefore, as over abundant spoils, he adds:

> V. 163: I have hated and abhorred iniquity; but I have [Col. 0637A] loved thy law.

Therefore he hates iniquity and loves God’s Law.

4. The Law Says Something Other Than What It Commands. — But one who loves God’s Law is not occupied only with those things fulfilled through obedience to the Law; by the work of the Law he must extend himself to something else. Let us hear, then, what further duty he has:

> V. 164: Seven times in the day I have spoken praise to thee for the judgments of thy righteousness.

The holy Prophet first loves what he does: namely, the work of the Law,

> [Note: Col. 0637D: The Albinus manuscript reads *qua vitiorum*, as does the Royal manuscript after correction. *Quia* must certainly be retained, with *ab eo* (“by it”) understood. For the Law does not cut off the will together with the practice of vices; love does so.]

because both the practice and the desire of every vice are cut off. But afterward he praises the judgments of God’s righteousness. For these, as we have often observed, signify more than they enact, since the deeds themselves

> [Note: Col. 0637C: “The deeds themselves [give] knowledge.”]

suggest to us knowledge of the eternal dispensation: such as the Sabbath rest, the Hebrew child, the land lying fallow, and the fiftieth year, which [p. 409] are understood under the significances of the mysteries of the image.

> [Note: Col. 0637D: The old edition reads: “are understood to be of no slight import under the mystery of the image”; four manuscripts have the same, except that three have “little” in place of “slight.” We would prefer: “under the mystery of the image, they are understood to be anticipatory indications of future things,” or something similar; for, as is said in Letter IV, §5, the Law is established as a mirror of future goods, and shortly before: the things established in the Law are a way for those whose example is prefigured in them.]

[Col. 0637B] This, therefore, is what is praised seven times in the day.

5. The Number Seven. — Nor is it uncertain why the number here belongs to praise. For these same things—whether in the day, the child, the land, or the year and years—are contained under the sanctification of this number, since the number seven is completed up to that eternal rest of the fiftieth year, which is the Sabbath of Sabbaths (see Prologue, §§11–12). Much is known concerning the sanctification of this number: the very ordering of the days, the election of angels standing by God’s throne, and the fullness in the Lord of spiritual powers and resting graces. Certainly the judgments of God’s righteousness are fittingly praised by the Prophet in this number, through which and in which the power and order of those same justifications are contained.

[Col. 0637C] 6. Love of One’s Neighbour; the Disposition of Charity. — The present order of prophetic proclamation is no different from that of faith.

> [Note: Col. 0637D: The Royal manuscript reads, incorrectly, “and fear of the words for endurance of sufferings,” etc. Hilary’s point here is the same as Paul’s in Romans 13: all virtues and all commandments are comprised and recapitulated in the one love of neighbour.]

For endurance of persecutions, fear of the words, joy in the utterance, hatred of iniquity, love of the Law, praise of righteousness, and absolutely everything else—if there is any other commandment in the Law—is summed up in the observance of this one commandment:

> “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Rom. 13:9).

This is greater than burnt offerings and all sacrifices: to remember that one is one and the same body with another who belongs to Christ, and to love one’s neighbour as one’s own body, that is, [Col. 0638A] as oneself.

> [Note: Col. 0637D: The Vatican manuscript reads “which is Christ”; the Albinus and Royal manuscripts, “to be one body with others, which is Christ.” The former reading relates *which is Christ* to “with another.”]

For it follows:

> V. 165: Much peace is for those who love thy name, and there is no stumbling-block for them.

> [Note: Col. 0638D: The Royal and Albinus manuscripts insert the particle “in” here.]

The Apostle, considering not his own interests but those of others, declared that he would abstain from flesh for ever lest he cause his brother to stumble (1 Cor. 8:13). So fully did he hold the disposition of perfect charity and peace that he restrained himself even from the ordinary use of life, provided that he might cut off a cause of offence. Peace, therefore, must be maintained; and one must seek not what suits each individual but what accords with the whole community.

> [Note: Col. 0638D: The printed editions read “must be weighed,” against the manuscripts.]

For, according to the Gospel, it is more advantageous never to have entered life than to have inflicted a stumbling-block upon the little ones (Matt. 18:9).

7. Remaining in these precepts of peace and charity, the Prophet [Col. 0638B] is held fast by longing for evangelical hope. For he knows in whom, or what, is the end of the Law

> [Note: Col. 0637C: “Fire,” where he says.]  
> [Note: Col. 0638D: Thus the manuscripts, except that Micy has “fire,” not “Law”; in the printed editions “witness” stood in its place.]

when he says:

> V. 166: I awaited thy salvation, O Lord, and I performed thy commandments.

Jesus is the Saviour. This is the Hebrew meaning of the name; this is what the Angel said to Joseph; this is what Simeon, when about to depart in peace, recognized; and this is what the salvation restored to us through him teaches. [p. 410] He professes that he has performed God’s commandments in awaiting the Lord’s salvation, declaring that all the commandments of the Law contain the advent

> [Note: Col. 0638C: “To be contained by the advent of the only-begotten God.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0638D: The printed editions read: “to be contained by the advent of the only-begotten God.” The reading of the Royal and Albinus manuscripts, “to contain the advent …,” is preferable. Thus in Prologue §5, Christ’s advent is said to be the work preached by the prophets; and for one who does not know or denies it, the Scriptures are altogether closed and sealed, because faith in the bodily advent, when denied, shuts out knowledge of the Law which proclaims the Lord’s bodily advent.]

of the only-begotten God.

8. God’s Presence. — He also kept and loved God’s testimonies exceedingly, saying:

> VV. 167–168: My soul kept thy testimonies and loved them exceedingly. I kept thy commandments and thy testimonies, because all my ways are before thee.

[Col. 0638C] The Prophet acts under God, the Judge and Searcher of hearts, and remains in keeping God’s commandments and testimonies. He does not walk in the ways of the world, nor in the ways of vices and impiety. For whatever course of life he pursues, he pursues it so commendably and innocently that it is worthy of God’s sight; for God knows the thoughts and movements of hearts, and no one who is unclean in heart is worthy of his sight. [The transmitted syntax here is uncertain.]

> [Note: Col. 0638D: That is, before God. By a similar manner of speaking above, the assembly of saints is declared unworthy in relation to workers of malice.]

For this was spoken by our Lord Jesus Christ, the faithful witness in heaven, who is blessed unto ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER XXII. Tau

> [Col. 0639A] Let my prayer draw near before thee, O Lord; according to thy utterance, O Lord, give me understanding.  
> Let my petition enter before thee, O Lord; according to thy utterance deliver me.  
> My lips shall utter a hymn [below: “uttered”]; when thou hast taught me thy justifications.  
> My tongue proclaimed [below: “shall proclaim”] thy utterances, because all thy commandments are equity.  
> Let thy hand be made ready to save me, because I have chosen thy commandments.  
> I have longed for thy salvation, O Lord, and thy law is my meditation.  
> My soul lives [below: “shall live”] and shall praise thee, and thy judgments shall help me.  
> I have gone astray like a lost sheep; quicken thy servant, because I have not forgotten thy commandments.

[Col. 0639B] [p. 411] 1. The Obscurity of God’s Utterances; Stages of Prayer. — The Psalm comes to its conclusion according to the letters.

> [Note: Col. 0639C: “According to the letter”; then, “For in all these things.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0639D: The printed editions read “according to the letter.” More correctly the Royal and Albinus manuscripts read “according to the letters,” namely the Hebrew letters, in which are included all things proper to the holy man.]

For, since all those things which belonged to the holy man have been comprehended according to the order of the Hebrew letters, the Prophet now prays that his prayer may draw near to God:

> V. 169: Let my prayer draw near before thee, O Lord; according to thy utterance, O Lord, give me understanding.

> [Note: Col. 0639C: Our manuscript, the Hebrew text, and the Greek lack “O Lord” at the second occurrence.]

He has prayed to the Lord for many things throughout the whole Psalm. But because God’s utterances contain very much obscurity in themselves through the mysteries of heavenly realities, he now especially prays that he may be worthy of understanding this utterance of God. And first he observed the proper order of his modest hope, when he asked that his prayer might become near to the sight of God. Then his petition is repeated at a higher stage of progress, [Col. 0639C] when he says:

> V. 170: Let my petition enter before thee, O Lord; according to thy utterance deliver me.

This was the order by which prayer, drawing near to the sight of God, should enter: having begun to be near, it should enter; and now, having understood God’s utterance, he prays to be delivered according to that same utterance. For it is not the case that salvation is first where understanding is found;

> [Note: Col. 0639D: The editions read, “where understanding is, there salvation is,” contrary to Hilary’s meaning and to the manuscript evidence.]

rather, after understanding has been attained, salvation is to be obtained.

2. The Difference between Common and Prophetic Speech; What an “Uttered Forth” Word Is. — And because these things were expressed through the spirit of prophecy, whether beneath the shadow of future things, [Col. 0640A] beneath some image of reality set before us as in a mirror,

> [Note: Cols. 0639C–0640C: In the earlier edition: “beneath reality, as though imagining from a mirror,” etc. Yet the earlier received reading ought not to be altered on the authority of our manuscript.]  
> [Note: Col. 0639D: The printed editions read “under some image of reality presented as in a mirror,” etc.; we alter that reading on the authority of the Royal, Vatican, and Albinus manuscripts.]

or beneath the hidden and profound sense of divine words—being uttered more through the spirit of prophecy than through the understanding of the human mind—he adds:

> VV. 171–172: My lips uttered forth a hymn. When thou hast taught me thy justifications, my tongue shall proclaim thy utterances, because all thy commandments are equity.

> [Note: Col. 0639D: Leipzig and Paris read “shall utter forth.” The other books more correctly read “uttered forth,” supported by the Greek ἐξερεύξαιντο (*exereuxainto*, “may they utter forth”), although Hilary seems to have read ἐξερεύξαντο (*exereuxanto*, “they uttered forth”); §3 also requires it: “Although the lips have uttered forth a hymn.” In manuscripts it is commonly written *eructuaverint*, *eructuaverunt*, *eructuabo*, and so forth.]

We remember every prophetic utterance to be indicated by the expression “to utter forth,” as when it is said: “My heart has uttered forth a good word” (Ps. 44:2); or: “I will utter forth things hidden from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 13:35); or: “Day utters forth speech to day” (Ps. 18:3).

> [Note: Col. 0639D: Paris, following Leipzig, retained “of the prophet”; this is good if the discussion concerns David’s utterance alone, not every prophetic utterance.]

Every human utterance, however, begins from the perception and movement of thought: when our mind is moved to declare something, it makes known in words [Col. 0640B] what has settled within its disposition. [p. 412] But when, outside the prompting of the human mind, the tongue serves not the soul’s own intention, but, through the incoming Spirit, divine meaning is poured forth through the ministry of our mouth, then what is spoken seems to have been uttered forth: the mind does not speak that to which it has been moved,

> [Note: Col. 0640D: The editions read “to that to which it has been impelled”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

after first apprehending it by thought and movement, but the Spirit, while the conscious mind remains unaware, distinguishes its voice into words.

3. In What Order God Grants Understanding of the Commandments; Their Aim. — Now, although the lips have uttered forth a hymn, yet after being taught God’s justifications the tongue shall proclaim what it speaks, so that, when knowledge of the things spoken has been received, the declaration of that knowledge may then follow.

> [Note: Col. 0640C: “Proclaimed.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0640D: The printed editions read “proclaimed.” More correctly the manuscripts read “shall proclaim”; for God’s instruction must be awaited before his utterances are proclaimed. This passage makes clear that the preceding words, “when thou hast taught me,” etc., are joined to what follows, “my tongue shall proclaim,” not, as in the earlier printed editions, to the preceding “my lips uttered forth,” etc.]

God’s commandments are not so distinct from equity [Col. 0640C] that it would not be worthy of God first to grant their understanding to one who is prophesying,

> [Note: Col. 0640D: Paris reads “to the prophet”; Badius and Erasmus, “of prophesying”: erroneously.]

then to make that understanding clear to public knowledge through the confession of preaching. For it would be foreign to God’s goodness either to conceal what he wills to be proclaimed, or to have commanded anything other than in equity.

> [Note: Col. 0640D: The editions read “if outside goodness”; and Leipzig, in order to complete the sentence, substituted “yet equity” for “the equity.” The text is better restored from the manuscripts.]

The sum of the equity of God’s commandments is that they are salutary for all;

> [Note: Col. 0640D: The printed editions prefixed “in” here. We have deleted it on the authority of the Royal, Vatican, and Albinus manuscripts, especially since in the Prologue to the Songs of Ascents, §4, we read: “The word of God has provided for all who would come into life.”]

so that our entrance into this life may be undertaken with advancement toward eternity. For to be born for death is not the cause of life, but of death.

4. Free Will. — [Col. 0641A] The Prophet immediately adds his confidence in this hope, saying:

> V. 173: Let thy hand be made ready to save me, because I have chosen thy commandments.

While some choose the glory of the world, others embrace reverence for the elements and demons, and others seek earthly wealth, this holy man chose God’s commandments. He chose them, moreover, not by natural necessity but by the will of piety, because for each person there is set before him a way of life according to what he wills, and freedom is permitted to desire and act (Deut. 30:19). Consequently, each person’s choice will be visited either with punishment or with rewards.

> [Note: Col. 0641C: The Royal and Albinus manuscripts read “each person,” omitting the following word “choice.”]

5. The End of the Law. — But he shows what is the end

> [Note: Col. 0641C: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions wrongly had “what the source was.”]

of the Lord’s commandments, saying:

> V. 174: I have longed for thy salvation, O Lord, and thy law is my meditation.

[Col. 0641B] He directs his whole self toward the advent of Jesus, that is, the Saviour.

> [Note: Col. 0641C: “He shows [himself directed] toward Jesus the Saviour.”]

And he longs with impatient desires for that which it was especially granted to the blessed Apostles to see. Yet he indicates that this very activity [p. 413] in the Law

> [Note: Col. 0641D: The printed editions read “says”; the same fault was corrected above from the manuscripts. Hilary repeatedly insists that the Prophet not only does what the Law commands, but by doing it meditates upon what is shadowed forth in those things. Hence, in the preceding Letter, §4, he says: “These, as we have often reminded you, signify more than they enact, since the deeds themselves suggest to us knowledge of the future dispensation.”]

is meditation upon future hope, because all meditation is understood to be undertaken not for the effect of present things but for progress toward things to come.

6. The Reward of This Meditation. — And he shows what the reward of this meditation will be:

> V. 175: My soul shall live and praise thee, and thy judgments shall help me.

> [Note: Col. 0641D: After Augustine had quoted these words of Hilary against Julian, Book I, ch. 3, he adds: “Do you perceive what you hear? Do you ask what you are to say? Dare, if you have any effrontery, to bring an accusation against this man concerning original sin—a man so illustrious in renown among Catholic bishops, so conspicuous in reputation and fame.” Then, in Book VII, §32, he summarizes the same words: “Saint Hilary says that he whose voice says, ‘I was conceived in iniquity,’ was born under the origin of sin and under the law of sin.”]

He does not count himself as living in this life, since he said: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. 50:7). He knows that he was born under the origin and law of sin; therefore he chose meditation upon God’s Law, in order that he might live. In the preceding Psalm he exhorted his soul toward the joys of [Col. 0641C] that life, saying:

> “Return, my soul, unto thy rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with thee; for he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:7 ff.).

> [Note: Col. 0641C: “Of the living.”]

He hastens to render these praises to God, helped by God’s judgments toward advancement to eternity after the weakness of earthly corruption has been swallowed up: [Col. 0642A] namely because he chose the commandments, longed for the Lord’s salvation, and always meditates upon God’s Law.

7. With a fitting end he concludes all things in the mystery of the Gospel, saying:

> V. 176: I have gone astray like a lost sheep; quicken thy servant, because I have not forgotten thy commandments.

For he hastens, as a wandering and lost sheep, to be borne back upon his shepherd’s shoulders, so that, received again, he may provide eternal joys in heaven to the angels through his Saviour and eternal Shepherd

> [Note: Col. 0641D: Although with the manuscripts we prefer “when he has been received,” referring to the Prophet, the received reading “when she has been received,” referring to the sheep, does not displease, since it gives the same sense. But Hincmar, *On Predestination*, ch. 25, has entirely perversely: “that he may bear witness to the angels that he has been received into eternal joys.”]  
> [Note: Col. 0641C: “When she has been received.”]

(Luke 15:10). For the Son of Man came to save that which was lost (Matt. 18:11), being sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel: the Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed unto all ages of ages. Amen.

> [Note: Col. 0641C: “Unto ages. The one hundred and eighteenth Psalm ends. The one hundred and twenty-fifth Psalm begins happily. A Song of Ascents. ‘When the Lord turned back captivity,’ etc. It is apparent that the manuscript was formerly deprived of several leaves; for what follows is: ‘Although it is reverent to suppose the change of the future captivity,’ etc. By those words we leap to the exposition of Psalm 125.”]

[p. 414] ## PROLOGUE TO THE FIFTEEN SONGS OF ASCENTS

> [Note: Col. 0642D: In the Micy manuscript the whole of Psalm 119 is prefixed here without any title. In the first Paris edition it is placed there under the title, *Commentaries on the Song of Ascents. Preface.* In the final edition the text of the Psalm was moved back to the place in which we have now taken care that it be printed. The other editions and the Royal manuscript do not have it in either place; the latter bears this inscription: “Exposition of the fifteen ascents by blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers,” and then, “the titles of the Psalms,” etc. The manuscript of Marmoutier at Tours lacks both title and Psalm.]

[Col. 0642B] 1. Titles of the Psalms. — As we have shown in many places, the titles of the Psalms have their own proper meanings and briefly contain the rationale and subject of the writings beneath them; they direct us, by a kind of indication of teaching, onto the path of understanding. There is no need now to discuss them, for this must be done when each individual Psalm is treated. Since Psalm and title mutually lend authority to one another, discussion of either apart from the other will be weak.

We now take up the Songs of Ascents, whose inscription is continuous and uniform; and therefore, because the meaning of the titles is congruent, [Col. 0642C] the explanation of them all will be shown under the judgment

> [Note: Col. 0642D: Thus the Royal and Tours manuscripts; the printed editions read “under the undertaking.”]

of a single exposition.

2. A Historical Inscription Does Not Exclude an Allegorical Sense. — In the superscriptions of many Psalms, we read that much is set forth in accordance with the order of history: as, “when David fled from the face of his son Absalom,” “when he changed his countenance before Abimelech,” “when, after Bathsheba, he was admonished by Nathan,”

> [Note: Col. 0642D: Badius, Erasmus, and Leipzig read “because of Bathsheba”; Paris, “because of Bersabeth.” The reading of the Tours and Royal manuscripts is preferable: “after Bathsheba,” that is, as the title of Psalm 50 has it, “after he went in to Bathsheba.”]

[Col. 0643A] and elsewhere wherever the truth of events is contained in the titles of the Psalms themselves. But we must remember that these same Psalms are not all to be understood bodily or literally merely because an indication of bodily events is set before them. Rather, we ought to pursue spiritual understanding beneath this commemoration, as it were, of events that occurred. This is not the time to speak of it; but, with regard for the simplicity of readers, it was appropriate to remind the reader.

We must therefore consider whether, like the titles just mentioned among many others, these Psalms of Ascents also contain something historical.

3. The Ten Steps in Hezekiah’s House. — In the book of Isaiah, when Hezekiah prayed, a sign of his prolonged life was given to him in the steps (Isa. 38:7–8, [Col. 0643B] according to the Septuagint). There were ten steps in his house, which the sun ascended when its light advanced beyond the course of its time; and it descended again, [p. 415] on the day of his death, as its light withdrew from the boundary of its allotted time.

> [Note: Col. 0643D: Leipzig and Paris read: “on the day of his death, descended as its own light descended.” Older editions read: “on the day of death it descended as it withdrew from the light of its time.” The text is restored with manuscript assistance. The scribe of the Tours manuscript wrote in the margin, “or beginning the day,” evidently in place of “on the day of death.” These words indicate not the day on which Hezekiah died, but the day on which he would have died without God’s aid. A little earlier that manuscript has “the granted prolongation of life,” not “the prolonged life”; this may also rightly be said, because he had first asked for it. Earlier, from the same manuscript, we restored “was given to him,” in place of “and was given.”]

But this history has no similarity to the Psalms, since not even the number of steps agrees.

Yet this sign given to Hezekiah clearly shows that God’s light advances toward those to whom, on account of the merits of their worldly affairs, the blessedness of the future life is granted; but withdraws from those to whom it is denied.

#### 4. Whether the fifteen steps in the Temple, constructed after these psalms, are referred to here

History has told us that there were fifteen steps in the Temple, and that the ranks of those standing there were arranged, so that a certain precedence was held by those before them: first the Levites stood, then the Israelites, then the proselytes, and afterwards the rest. [Note: In the royal and Tours manuscripts: “of Leviticus.”] But why do we infer from a later history something concerning psalms written earlier, when, if anything is to be taken from that history, it ought to be taken in such a way that the psalms follow the history—unless, indeed, something had been prophesied concerning that future history?

Yet, contemplating that very construction of the Temple and altar, we should understand it to be a shadow of the incorruptible Temple and an image of the sanctified altar, [Note: In the editions of Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius: “a holy image,” which was restored in the final Paris edition against the witness of the manuscripts.] unless authority for this were to be drawn from the psalms, by means of those things which were bodily prefigured in it. [Note: The printed texts read “is presumed.” We restore “were presumed” from the royal and Tours manuscripts. Yet the sentence is not fully complete unless, above, “for those things which were in it” is supplied. The copyist of the Tours codex thought that something was missing here. Immediately after the words “image of the altar”—or, as it has there and a little earlier, “of the altar”—he left the space of one line blank.]

The psalms, however, do not declare events only of their own age, nor are they suited only to the generations in which they were written; rather, the word of God has provided for all who would come into life, itself most fitting for the advancement of every age.

#### 5. Christ, the true Priest, ascended into the Holy of Holies

For such was the law of the priesthood which Luke carefully set out in the Gospel, in connection with the birth of John the Baptist, according to the observance of the Law: that no one was to enter the Holy of Holies except the chief priest, and he only once on a single day in the whole year (Lev. 16:17; Luke 1:8). All these things, formerly done as types, have been fulfilled in the one Lord Jesus Christ, as both our faith and the Lord himself assure us in the Gospel, saying: “I came not to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5:17). The Apostle too testifies that the whole fulfilment of the Law is in our Lord Jesus Christ: “For Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. 10:4).

And this same prophet David teaches that he is an eternal priest, saying: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109[110]:4). This chief priest, therefore, having entered the heavens, sitting at the right hand of God, and praying to the Father that where he was we too might be, [Note: In the royal manuscript: “will raise and will seat us.” Both readings are sound. For we have already been raised in the person of Christ, though we shall at some time be raised in our own persons.] he who raised and seated us in the heavenly places (John 17:24), had already through the prophet instructed us by what ways and works of life it is possible to ascend to him.

Thus through Isaiah he says [Note: The word *ait* (“he says”) is absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts, as likewise above the particle *sed* (“but”), in whose place one Vatican manuscript has *cum* (“when”)]: “Wash yourselves; be clean; remove your wickednesses from your souls before my eyes. Cease from your wickednesses; learn to do good; seek judgment; rescue the one who suffers wrong; judge for the orphan and vindicate the widow; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord Almighty” (Isa. 1:16 ff.). [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “deliver.”] These, then, are the steps of that perfect and eternal Temple, which the chief priest transcended after making propitiation for our sins through his blood—surpassing the manner of the earthly priest under the Law, whether ascending by steps into the Holy of Holies or offering a sacrificial victim for the people.

#### 6. The mystery of the number fifteen. What the fifteen Songs of Ascents teach

We have already, at the beginning of the psalms, when discussion arose concerning numbers and superscriptions, treated to some extent of the fifteen steps [Note: The printed editions read “from the superscription”; and shortly after, “of the week and the octave.”] and the superscription of the song: namely, from the two numbers of the week and the octave. One belongs to the Sabbath of the Law; the other, to the eighth day added to the Sabbath, which is also the first day and belongs to the Gospels. [Note: The printed text reads: “which is also the first of the Gospels: that this number is fitting, through which their song, as it were, of the Law, etc.”—a very confused text. It is corrected from the Tours manuscript, supported by the royal manuscript.] This number is fitting (Prologue, no. 16). By the steps of these songs, as it were of Law and Gospel, we ascend to heavenly and eternal things, knowing that we shall be seated in the heavenly places with the supreme Priest, if only, according to the Apostle, our citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3:20).

Let us seek these steps of the songs, by which we may climb to the places that are the Holy of Holies. For the ascent to them is steep and the path narrow. We know that there were fifteen steps in the Temple; we also read fifteen psalms of ascents. Numerous is this ascent to that desired dwelling. Perhaps, just as in the Temple one ascended gradually and by individual steps to the holy places, so by the successive progress offered in the psalms, after ascending these steps which are sung, we shall be taught that we can be placed in the heights, the holy places, and the eternal realities.

#### 7.

There are many, however, who think that these psalms prophesy only the captivity of the people, during which they were held in Babylon for seventy years, [Note: Paris reads “the whole,” not “only”; and shortly after, together with the other editions, “which,” for “which captivity.”] and also the return of the same people with the rebuilding of their lost city. [Note: “Now” is absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts.] We do not now dispute with them. For there is no doubt that the prophet could have known the things threatening this people because of its impiety. But the psalms themselves will tell us what captivity of the people, and what building of what city, the Prophet recalls, [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “because they began thus.” The text of the whole psalm was then transferred to this place in the final Paris edition, and it does not seem that it could have been placed more suitably. In other codices only the first verse of the psalm is prefixed here: “To you, Lord, when I was troubled I cried, and you heard me.”] since they began thus:

### PSALM 119. SONG OF ASCENTS

“To the Lord [Hilary: *to you, Lord*] I cried when I was troubled, and he heard [*you heard*] me. Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue. What shall be given to you, or what shall be added for you against a deceitful tongue? Sharp arrows of the mighty [*mighty arrows*], with desolating [*of desolation*] coals. Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; [*and*] I have dwelt with the dwellers of Kedar. My soul has long been a sojourner. With those who hated [*with those hating*] peace, I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.”

### TREATISE ON THE PSALM

#### 1. Tribulations are not to be feared by the Christian

Although prophetic discourse uses the common usage of human speech, it does not contain the same meaning that lies near to common understanding. For, although it has adapted the declaration of heavenly matters to the measure of our understanding, it has nevertheless preserved the force of its meaning even through a restrained choice of words.

It began thus, verse 1: “To you, Lord, when I was troubled I cried, and you heard me.” This cry to God by the Prophet might perhaps, from ordinary custom and in accordance with human feeling, be supposed to arise from indiscriminate sorrow—so that he prays to God even with loud outcry. For fear of danger or terror of death, anxiety over loss and grief for money, or the blow of bereavement and the wounds of sorrows compel many to raise their voice to God, [Note: We have added *enim* (“for”) on the authority of the royal and Tours manuscripts.] as though not everything that happens to them were most fitting for good hopes. [Note: In Paris, *tamquam non* (“as though not”) is absent, in whose place the other editions have *quamquam non* (“although not”). The sense would then be clearer: “all things that happen are most fitting for their good hopes,” etc.]
