The Apostle testifies that it is better for him to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23); he condemns care for money as the root of all evil (1 Tim. 6:10); and the Gospels say that it is rather the living who should be wept for (Luke 23:28). And, once the purpose of our faith has been established against these things, what room will be left for the world against us, [Note: The word *loci* is absent from the royal manuscript; the Tours manuscript has *dilectissimi* (“beloved”) in its place.] when death gains us fellowship with Christ, lack of money provides lack of sin, [Note: This outstanding passage was gradually more and more corrupted. Erasmus first substituted “sins” for “sin,” to agree with the following “our.” Then Lipsius substituted “abundance” for “lack.” Finally, when the first Paris edition lacked “provides lack of sin,” the final edition restored: “provides abundance: the cutting off of our sins,” etc. The passage is restored from Badius and the manuscripts. By this threefold clause Hilary shows that none of the things commonly feared is to be feared: not our death, through which we obtain fellowship with Christ; not the loss of wealth, through which the root of sin is cut off; nor, finally, the departure from this life of our own people—that is, relatives or any righteous persons—whose departure hastens the coming of judgment and thus of the heavenly kingdom. Below, at no. 11, he teaches that the hastening of this kingdom should be prayed for, and therefore desired. By it he signifies beatitude consummated in the recovery of bodies, while he expressly teaches that the blessedness of the saints begins immediately after death through fellowship with Christ, so that death is a cause of joy to them.] and the departure of our own is a hastened advance toward the common hope?

#### 2. What tribulations are to be guarded against. They are guarded against by prayer

But if these are not the tribulations, what then are the tribulations for which one should cry to the Lord? They certainly exist, and are very great: those which draw us down into the depth of sin. For the Prophet, portraying in his own person a human being ascending by steps to eternal things, teaches from what evils he must especially guard himself. [Note: “Man” is absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts.] These are the evils which plunge us into hell through the authority of counsels, the force of exhortations, and the enticements of flatteries: one urges us toward honors; another holds us to the present life by leisure, sleep, gluttony, and luxury; another leads us into the superstition of false religions; another exhorts us toward schisms; another solicits us toward heresy. Of these it is written: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33). [Note: The Micy codex reads “evil counsels.”]

For the nature of our mind is weak against all these things. They run about us on every side and prick us with the various stings of their enticements. And the first hope of life is this: that, when they burst upon our mind by force, fraud, and domination, we may cry to the Lord as though from the midst of tribulation; so that our turning to him, amid conflicting calamities, may be heard with all the strength of faithful crying. Indeed, this very cry to him will be our rest, and this very turning in prayer is the greatest part and hope of salvation. [Note: The Tours and royal manuscripts read “our,” a word which we would gladly add while retaining “our own.”] Therefore he says: “To you, Lord, when I was troubled I cried, and you heard me.” For he is accustomed to say to those who pray: “Behold, I am present” (Isa. 52:6).

#### 3. Unjust lips: Epicureans. The deceitful tongue

And because he is present, he must be asked concerning what follows, verse 2: “Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips, from a deceitful tongue.” For this alone is dangerous tribulation for the righteous: companionship in evil exhortation and familiarity with destructive counsel. From these the mind must be turned back, [Note: That is, from these evils. Above we have seen that *namque* is commonly used in the sense of *nempe* (“namely”).] [Note: The printed texts read “restrained,” a word less characteristic of Hilary. We have: “The heart is undoubtedly turned back from those things which are judged useful by human judgment,” and “from this way of faith, by religious devotion.” See Treatise on Psalm 123, no. 8.] and the ears must be stopped.

He distinguished unjust lips from a deceitful tongue. Injustice is shameless: it dares openly, plots openly, and accomplishes openly. Such are those who deny God and maintain that no progress in religion toward God remains for human affairs, but that their sole good is to live for luxury and the body, taking from God care, providence, judgment, and power. Their lips, therefore, are unjust.

But the work of deceitful tongues is fraudulent and harmful through pretence: under the name of religion it overturns religion, and under the hope of life it leads into death. Such too are the lies of heretics, who, concealing the words of the prophets, the power of the Gospels, and the authoritative teaching of the Apostles by falsehood, hand down and teach everything otherwise than it is written. [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “and harmful through the injury of pretence”; another, together with Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius, “and harmful through harmful pretence.” We retain, with Paris and the older royal, Micy, and Tours manuscripts, “and harmful through pretence.” From the same manuscripts we restore “which under the name of religion,” where the editions alone read “under the light of religion,” omitting the preceding “which.”] From these, therefore, we who pray are delivered by God’s mercy; and amid their tribulations, crying to God, we shall be heard.

#### 4. Why God asks questions. The fruit of confession

It follows, verse 3: “What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you against a deceitful tongue?” It is well that to what was said—“To you, Lord, when I was troubled I cried, and you heard me; Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips, from a deceitful tongue”—there is added: “What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you against a deceitful tongue?” Thus there is fulfilled through the Prophet what the Lord said: “Behold, I am present to you” (Isa. 52:6); as though, at the very moment of the imprecation, this voice of the Lord is uttered: “And what shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you against a deceitful tongue?” [Note: The editions read “intercession”; the Micy manuscript, “interpretation”; more correctly the Tours manuscript, “imprecation.” Thus in no. 6: “the Prophet may invoke a curse.”]

We frequently read in both the New and Old Testaments of the Lord speaking as one who asks questions: to Adam, “Where are you, Adam?” (Gen. 3:10); to Cain, “Where is your brother?” (Gen. 4:9); to the crowds, when the woman touched the hem of his garment, “Who touched me?” (Luke 8:45); to the disciples, “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13), and “But whom do you say that I am?” (ibid., 15). [Note: The Tours manuscript reads: “Whom do men say that I am? But what do you say?”]

He who is God, searching hearts and reins and examining our thoughts, does not wish to be taught. Rather, he asks in order, through the confession of those questioned, to grant either forgiveness for sins or honor for faith. Thus Adam, having confessed, was preserved for forgiveness and glorified in Christ; [Note: Chrysostom says almost the same in his Sermon on the Fall of the First Man: “They, Adam and Eve, receive garments of skin, so that, having already confessed their sin, they might receive forgiveness through the humility of their clothing.” Tertullian speaks no differently, concluding his book *On Repentance* with these words: “Adam himself, the first father of the human race and of offense against the Lord, restored to his paradise by confession, does not keep repentance silent.” Indeed, in *Prescription against Heretics*, no. 52, he counts Tatian among heretics because Tatian taught that Adam could not attain salvation. Likewise, after Epiphanius, Augustine in *On Heresies*, 25, lists among the errors of the Encratites their denial of the salvation of the first man. Irenaeus vigorously refutes them in book 3, chapter 30, and following him most of the Fathers; our Hilary here openly agrees with them, supported by Wisdom 10:2, which says of Adam: “And he brought him out from his transgression.” See Philip, Abbot of Good Hope, whose book is entitled *On the Salvation of the First Man*. We observe in passing that Hilary proclaims Adam to have attained not merely forgiveness but also glory, so that those of whom above, no. 1, death gains fellowship with Christ may be understood already to be glorified in Christ.] Cain, denying, was made equal to the accursed devil; for the devil has already from the beginning been designated a murderer (John 8:44). The woman who confessed was healed by faith; Peter, answering in faith, received the keys of heaven.

Thus the whole reward of our hope consists in confession: we testify that we shall obtain those things which we have believed ourselves able to obtain.

#### 5. The Lord’s arrows and the coals of desolation: the word of God

For this reason the Prophet’s question has been transformed in a certain way; but a response worthy of faith follows it. To the question, “What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you against a deceitful tongue?”—that is, “What protection shall be brought to you against this falsehood?”—the answer is given, verse 4: “Sharp mighty arrows, with desolating coals.” For only the Lord’s arrows are mighty and sharp, able to pierce the deceitful tongue, containing the power to burn away and lay waste its fraud. Of them he says in the seventh psalm: “He made his arrows for those who burn” (Ps. 7:14). [Note: Thus here and below in the Tours manuscript, as the following words also require. The printed texts, however, read “of the mighty.”]

Both descriptions suit them. For the word of God pierces every wickedness, wounds every impulse of wantonness, and pricks even that most violent sting of death itself. When the sinner hears of God eternal, God the creator of the world, God the judge, and understands himself to be a human being owing to God the fact that he was born, how greatly will his conscience and error be pierced by the dart of God’s teaching, [Note: Paris reads “when,” erroneously. The Tours manuscript reads “by the dart of teaching, or by the word of God”: not badly. The Micy manuscript reads foolishly “by the zeal of God’s teaching”; and again below, “by zeal of teaching.”] when he knows that he is to be burned in unquenchable fire, separated as chaff from wheat, and deprived of fellowship in good fruits?

He mentions in another psalm the revelation of this teaching through the Apostles: “The arrows of little children became their wounds” (Ps. 63[64]:1). Every faithful person prays that these mighty arrows and these coals of desolation may be given to him and applied against the deceitful tongue, for the correction of those who trouble him, whether by the weapon of teaching or fear of punishment.

#### 6. Torments of the flesh

The blessed Job too, not knowing by whom his enemy had pierced him, called his bodily torments and pains the arrows of the Lord: “For the arrows of the Lord are in my body, whose wrath drinks my blood” (Job 6:4). [Note: The editions read “drinks my spirit as blood”; they are corrected from the Tours manuscript, supported by the Greek: *hōn ho thymos autōn ekpinei mou to haima*—“whose wrath drinks my blood.”] Perhaps the Prophet also invokes these arrows of avenging punishments against unjust lips and the deceitful tongue, so that when the deceitful tongue has been pierced, all unjust lips may be burned away with it. [Note: We have supplied “unjust” from the Tours manuscript.]

#### 7. The coal of desolation: cleansing from sins

Yet there are many who would understand the commandments of heavenly teaching, spiritually received by the faithful, to be the arrows, and the coals of desolation to be cleansing from sins. [Note: Thus the Tours manuscript. The Micy manuscript reads “of those desolated”; the printed texts, “of desolations.”] They think the phrase “coals of desolation” should be understood thus because the Lord said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will, if it is already kindled?” (Luke 12:49).

There is no doubt that he brought cleansing and forgiveness of sins—this fire which he said was already kindled, because through it there comes a purification from every vice and stain. [Note: The editions read “in which fire”; the Micy manuscript, “with fire”; the Tours manuscript, “which fire.” We had first conjectured that *but* should be prefixed to these readings; but the latter reading was subsequently seen to be complete without an addition, signifying that cleansing from sins is now called by the name of fire.] They apply to this also what was said to Isaiah, when his lips were touched with a coal taken in tongs: “Behold, I have removed your injustices and cleansed your sins” (Isa. 6:7). [Note: Thus the Tours manuscript, which corresponds better to the Greek. The printed texts read: “Behold, I have removed your sins and cleansed your iniquities.”]

#### 8. The arrow is Christ

We remember that the Lord himself was called an arrow in the same Isaiah, in this way: “He made me like a chosen arrow and hid me in his quiver, and said: It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. 49:2). We therefore understand this too to be a useful and mighty arrow, [Note: The printed texts and the Tours manuscript read “this”; we prefer, with the Micy manuscript, “him,” referring to the Lord.] which, piercing the stings of our vices, penetrates us with a saving and beneficial wound. Of this arrow that bride in the Song of Songs said: “I am wounded with love” (Song 2:5, according to the Septuagint).

#### 9. Why the arrows are to be desired

Let these arrows, then, be expected in both ways: either piercing the unjust and deceitful as punishment for their conscience, or wounding sins and vices in the bodies of those whom he loves. Let the coal either lay waste or cleanse, provided that it consumes those who deny God by punishment, but purifies those who confess him unto perfect innocence.

#### 10. By our actions we show what we judge good. The Prophet desires the kingdom of God

But what is the Prophet’s following response to the foregoing words? Verse 5: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged.” We cannot be judged truly to regard good things as good unless we desire them. [Note: The word “to be seen” is absent from the Tours manuscript. Yet it should be retained, since it indicates judgment not our own but another’s concerning us.] For how shall we establish the credibility of our judgment except by bringing about those things which we have judged good? We consider chastity good: what fruit, then, will there be from our opinion except in the very pursuit of chastity? Innocence is good; but unless we hasten toward it and practice it, we shall not be understood to think it truly so.

For the judgments of minds are not to be expressed by words but fulfilled by deeds. [Note: The Tours manuscript reads “For of those who love”; it is not to be followed here.] It is therefore fitting that the Prophet, awaiting after the Lord’s arrows and those coals of desolation the glory of that blessed kingdom and eternal age, should desire what he awaits. And he does indeed desire it. Nor does he merely desire it: he hates delay, and grieves that the deferment of so great a desire prevents his already obtaining it, saying: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged.”

#### 11. For its sake, death was desired by many saints

We have often heard this kind of complaint from many saints, lamenting the slow fulfilment of their hope and the lingering dissolution of their bodies. [Note: Paris reads “the slowness of their hope and the lingering,” etc.; the other editions, “concerning the slowness of their hope and the lingering dissolution of their bodies.” The Micy manuscript reads “the slowness of their hope and, or perhaps from, the lingering dissolution of their bodies.” We follow the Tours manuscript.] The Lord taught in his Gospels that the hastening of the heavenly kingdom should be prayed for. Love must fittingly be impatient for those things which it loves; [Note: The printed texts read “which love.” More correctly the manuscripts: “which it may love” or “which it loves,” that is, love is impatient to obtain those goods which it loves.] and therefore we must say what we are commanded by the Lord to say: “May your kingdom come; may your will be done” (Matt. 6:10).

The blessed Paul laments his bodily dwelling, complaining that through his sojourn in the flesh he is away from God (Rom. 7:24). [Note: Thus the Tours manuscript, and below, no. 12: “he laments the sojourn of this body,” with the ablative case. The printed editions read “in the dwelling,” an expression which also occurs below.] Conversely, he knows that he must be absent from God while he dwells in the flesh; yet it is better for him to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1:22–23). Ecclesiastes also says: “And I praised all who have died above all who are alive until now” (Eccl. 4:2), because, when the soul is freed through the dissolution of the body, it is stripped of the burden and fellowship of this weak and dangerous flesh. [Note: The printed editions read “and even the weak things of this … stripped off”; they are corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.]

Thus the Prophet laments his excessively prolonged sojourn in the body, hastening to depart from earthly things and to dwell in heavenly things, so that, leaving behind corruptible and present things, he may attain invisible and eternal ones.

#### 12. Why Job and Jeremiah curse the day of their birth

Holy Job, worthy of God’s testimony, not only laments the sojourning of this body, but curses even the very day of his birth: “Let that day perish in which I was born, and the night in which they said, ‘Behold, a male child has been born’” (Job 3:3). [Note: The Tours manuscript omits “has been born.”] Jeremiah likewise says: “Cursed be the day on which I was begotten; cursed be the one who announced it to my father, saying, ‘A male child has been born to you’” (Jer. 20:14).

Yet this same man had heard from the Lord: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you.” What then? Does one whom God knew before he existed and sanctified before he existed curse his own existence? [Note: The printed texts read “he curses that he began to exist.”] Far be it. He does not hate in himself what has been sanctified; rather, he curses the things that followed upon his sanctification: namely, that he advanced through the growth of the body into these troubles of bodily sojourning. [Note: The first Paris edition, following the Micy manuscript, has “in sanctification”; other books omit *in*, which may be omitted. Here it may well be understood as “against.” Hilary’s point is certainly that the soul is created clean and holy by God, but is polluted and corrupted by association with the body. On the contagion of flesh see book 3, Treatise on Psalm 118, nos. 3 and 4.]

For, formed within his mother’s womb and shaped through the power of his Creator, in the substance of his soul, according to God’s image, [Note: The printed editions read “into substance.” More correctly the Tours manuscript reads “in substance.” Hilary frequently insists that the image of God is impressed in the human soul.] he laments not his conception nor the beginning of his formation, but the condition that came with the growth of his developed body, in which he must live amid the evils of the world, the weaknesses of the flesh, and vices.

Yet, once formed in the womb and sanctified in the womb, having in himself an eternal form of heavenly origin, it is beyond doubt that through God’s sanctification he would remain eternal after the law of this death. [Note: The first Paris edition, from the Micy manuscript, read “confirmed,” which the second correctly changed from the other books, since reference is made to Jeremiah’s words, “Before I formed you.” The meaning of “the eternal form in himself of heavenly origin” must be recalled from Treatise on Psalm 62, no. 3: “Each person’s mind is borne by a kind of natural instinct toward knowledge and hope of eternity, because it is as though there were implanted and impressed upon all of us the fact that our souls have a divine origin, since the mind itself recognizes in itself no small kinship with a heavenly race.” Whoever considers Hilary’s words will observe that for him “heavenly origin,” “divine origin,” “heavenly race,” and “heavenly nature” differ little or not at all. The soul’s origin is called divine and heavenly because, unlike the body, it comes not from earth but from God, who is expressly declared to dwell in heaven. Again, the soul’s race, form, and nature are divine, or at least closely akin to the divine, because it too, like God, is spiritual. This is relevant to the fact that Hilary designates Christ’s divine nature by the name “heavenly nature”; see above, pp. 216 and 228.] [Note: The editions, except Paris, read “from God’s designation,” wrongly, since the reference is to the preceding words of Jeremiah. Here, so far as we understand, the soul’s immortality is demonstrated both from the reason of its origin, which it has from God alone and therefore can be destroyed by God alone, and from the relation by which it was made in the image and likeness of the eternal God.]

#### 13. Kedar, a people of Ishmaelites. Saracens

The Prophet’s disposition, however, is not far different from that of Job and Jeremiah. For he complains not of his sojourning but of its prolongation. After his complaint of this long sojourning follows upon his words, “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged,” the statement: “And I have dwelt with the dwellers of Kedar.”

Kedar is a people of Ishmaelites dwelling in the desert, [Note: In the royal and Tours manuscripts: “inhabitants.”] whose borders extend as far as the Medes and Persians. For Kedar was a son of Ishmael, as Genesis testifies: “The firstborn of Ishmael,” it says, “were Nebaioth and Kedar” (1 Chron. 1:29). These are now called Saracens.

Those, therefore, who think these psalms should be understood in an earthly sense wish the Prophet, speaking in the person of the captive people, to have complained that he had a long sojourning among the dwellings of Kedar. But, failing to understand the force of the word or to perceive the Prophet’s Spirit, they use the authority of the name to confirm a foolish opinion, although the psalm contains absolutely nothing fitting the people’s captivity.

#### 14. Kedar: darkness. The body, the soul’s dark prison

For in the Hebrew language Kedar means what we pronounce as *obscuratio*, “darkness.” Within this dark and shadowy dwelling of bodies, the invisible formation of our souls is confined; [Note: The printed texts read “confirmation.” More correctly the manuscripts read “formation.” Shortly above, the Tours manuscript reads “for this,” without “in.”] and the noble nature of heavenly origin, held captive, has this prison of its contaminating sojourning.

That bride in the Song of Songs recalls this tent, saying: “I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tent of Kedar” (Song 1:5). [Note: The printed editions read “but beautiful,” contrary to the royal and Tours manuscripts and the Greek Septuagint.] She confesses herself black because of the darkness of this tent, yet does not deny that, because she is Christ’s bride, she is beautiful. [Note: The royal and Tours manuscripts read “like the tent of Kedar.” The printed texts read “like the tents of Kedar.” Whoever prefers that reading should subsequently, with the royal and Micy manuscripts, read “from the tents of this darkness.” Moreover, the printed texts alone add “she confessed herself black.” Shortly afterward the Tours and royal manuscripts read “which are Christ’s,” not “because she is Christ’s.”]

For everyone who pledges herself to Christ already stands in the eternal form. [Note: The printed texts read “in hope.” On the authority of the manuscripts we restore “in form,” that is, in appearance, in view of which the bride calls herself beautiful. Above also, no. 12, Jeremiah, sanctified, is said to remain eternal “in the eternal form in himself of heavenly origin,” through God’s sanctification.] The Lord commanded us to be enlightened in these tents, saying: “The lamp of your body is your eye” (Matt. 6:22); and, “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness itself!” (ibid., 23). [Note: Paris reads: “But if your eye is dark, darkness,” etc.] And again: “You are children of light, not children of darkness” (1 Thess. 5:5).

#### 15. The saints are with the flesh, not in the flesh

The Prophet also preserved this distinction: he dwelt *with* the dwellings of Kedar, not *in* the dwellings. [Note: Thus the royal and Tours manuscripts, agreeing with the Hebrew text, from which Jerome translated “with the tents”; Augustine also read it, and it was not unknown to Hilary himself, since he shortly adds, “they shall dwell with the tents of Kedar.” The Greek also supports it: *meta tōn skēnōmatōn*, “with the tents.” We nevertheless retain above “with the dwellers of Kedar,” which the printed editions also have here: first, because there is no authority for changing it there; and second, because below we read “he dwelt with dwellers.”] For although the saints live in the flesh, nevertheless, if they have weapons of warfare not fleshly but mighty through God, they will dwell with the tents of Kedar; they will not inhabit them. [Note: Paris reads “in the tents,” which conflicts with Hilary’s meaning.]

For, being absent from the body, they will hear from the Apostle, as dwellers with God: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. 8:9). Thus he dwelt in such a way as to dwell with those who dwell there, showing that in the sojourning which he lamented he was a stranger. [Note: The Tours manuscript reads “contemplating.”] And because he hated the society of the wicked and cohabitation with those dwelling in darkness, although he had already complained concerning the future, he now also says concerning the past, verse 6: “My soul has long been a sojourner”—that is, amid the many tribulations of unjust lips and the deceitful tongue, because of which he cried aloud to the Lord.

16. But he shows what kind of sojourning it was for him, when he says, VERSE 7: “With those who hated peace I was peaceable.” This is proper and worthy of a Prophet: to restrain by the peace of his own will the quarrels and agitations of a foreign nature, and to contain every faithless, turbulent affection of minds by all the moderation of gentleness. And this the Lord taught, himself making peace in himself between the things that are in heaven and on earth, praying for persecutors, hating no one, loving enemies (Matt. 5:44). And the Apostle exhorts: “If it be possible, have peace with all” (Rom. 12:18). [Note: The royal and Tours manuscripts have more briefly: “have peace with every person.” And the Lord, etc.] And the Lord seals this as though it were the sum of the commandments: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (John 14:27). This, therefore, will keep our hearts in Christ; this will make us equal to the patriarchs; this will keep even those who hate peace, when they obey through peace, in peace.

17. But another duty remains for the Prophet as well: namely, steadfastly to impart the teaching of God to all, and continually to preach the word of eternal life. Nor was he unmindful of this ministry; for he says: “When I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.” He was indeed peaceable with the enemies of peace; but the enemies of peace hated the preaching of peace itself, and were stirred against the teaching of God—those whom, through the Prophet’s gentleness, his silence restrained in peace. [Col. 0653D–0654A] Thus the Prophet is peaceable with the enemies of peace, and yet the Prophet does not cease to preach peace; but the enemies of peace attack the preacher of peace.

## Psalm 120. A Song of Ascents.

“I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me” (below: “aid”). “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. May he not give your foot into disturbance” (“lest he give [it] into disturbance”), “nor may he slumber who guards you. Behold, he who guards Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep. May the Lord guard you” (“will guard you”); “the Lord is your protection above the hand of your right hand. By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night. The Lord shall guard [Col. 0654B] you from every evil.” [Note: We restore here from the manuscript of Micy the words, “thus above the hand of your right hand,” previously omitted; from this manuscript the complete psalms were first copied at the head of each Treatise. Hilary nevertheless does not read those words below.] “Thus may the Lord guard your soul above the hand of your right hand. May the Lord guard your entrance and your departure, from now and for ever” (“will guard your departure and your entrance from now,” etc.).

## Treatise on the Psalm

1. Some apply this psalm to Christ.—According to this psalm [Note: Thus the Tours manuscripts; others read, “song,” where the printed editions have “of the song.”] of the songs of ascents, some think that it should be referred to the person of our Lord and Savior, applying especially to him this saying: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.” For they think that this prophecy was fulfilled at the time when, during the Lord’s Passion, night intervened after the sun was darkened. But we take nothing away from their judgment. For we do not criticize this interpretation; each person may choose what he prefers to follow from what he has read or understood. Yet I could not adapt my discourse otherwise than to what I understood.

2. The power of the eyes of the mind, or of thought.—VERSE 1. “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains.” It belongs to the nature of the human mind that, if we contemplate something in thought, each form presents itself to us such as we ourselves form it by thinking. For wherever we direct the eyes of our mind, they bring to awareness the very object on which they are fixed. To make what has been said clearer, let us offer an example. If someone on a winter day should think of spring, and behold its beauty with the light of his mind, then, with the winter in which he is and feels cold forgotten, spring in all its appearance and adornment will stand wholly before his awareness. So greatly do the eyes of the mind surpass the eyes of the body, that, when forgetfulness of present things comes upon us, a certain anticipated experience of absent things takes possession of us wholly, as it were, in the mind. We shall presently see, therefore, at what this gaze is directed.

3. Here the eyes of the mind are lifted up.—The Prophet lifts his eyes to the mountains. What eyes? Surely those of which it is written: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall know the wonders from your law” (Ps. 118:18); and again: “The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18:9). Were not these our eyes kindled by bodily light for seeing? Have they not received the faculty of sight? What illumination or unveiling, then, would be needed? Moreover, what wonders would they see in the law? Unless perhaps they are to see the festival booths of leafy branches, the blood of animals in the temple, the sacrificial victim of the lamb at Passover, [Note: The royal manuscript reads, “in the sum of religion.”] the rest of the Sabbath as the sum of religion? [Note: The printed editions read, “and, as I think, it is done.” Owing to faulty punctuation, Hilary’s meaning is not understood by those who read “these [things] by those who are spectators,” etc. The natural order of his words is: “But, as I think, since these things were enacted sensibly, they were seen being done by those present as observers.” Some words have been altered on manuscript authority.] But, I think, these things were seen being done by those present as observers. Therefore the eyes are not to be unveiled for what was seen, but for what was desired to be understood in the law.

4. The mountains are the prophetic books; also angelic ministries.—The Prophet therefore lifted the eyes of his mind to the mountains. To what mountains? Certainly not to these mountains, defiled by profane lights and altars and impious gatherings; nor to those grim with woods, bare with rocks, impassable through precipices, frozen with snow. For what of admiration or hope is situated in them? Rather, we understand the mountains to be the prophetic books, raised from earth on high, through which there is an ascent to the things above and a step into eternity. We may also understand the mountains as angelic ministries, and the powers and authorities of heaven, by whose ministry ascent to the heights is granted to us. For if, according to [Note: Tours manuscript: “Daniel.”] Daniel, the Lord himself is the great mountain (Dan. 2:35), there is no doubt that those are called mountains who are ministers of his command and will, and of the blessedness to be shared with us.

5. The eyes are lifted to these, but help is not expected from them.—Therefore the Prophet, lifting the eyes [Note: “Of the heart” is absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts.] of his heart to these mountains, contemplating within himself all their counsels, ministries, offices, and gifts, and directing upon them the light of his understanding, gave his awareness a complete and perfect apprehension of the form he had contemplated, and held in his mind all that he had seen in thought. Knowing whence help would come to him, he said, VERSE 2: “Whence shall help come to me?” And immediately he answered himself with blessed confession: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” The eyes are indeed lifted to the mountains, because through them there is the ministry of teaching, an advancing ascent. [Note: Only the Paris edition reads “a perfect approach.” Other books read “an advancing approach,” except the Tours manuscript, from which we restore “an advancing ascent.” The whole passage might also be restored thus: “because through them—whether prophetic books or angels—is an advancing ascent through the ministry of teaching,” namely, the ascent of the mind to things above and eternal.] But since one must confess whence help comes: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” This is blessed faith; this is true confession; this is eternal hope and worthy of the gifts of heavenly blessing.

6. Whose verse this is, concerning whom, and to whom.—Finally, because every prophecy is in the Spirit, immediately upon this blessed confession of his there followed the blessing of the Holy Spirit, in the person [Note: The printed editions read “to the person.” More correctly, the Tours manuscript has “in the person,” namely, of the Prophet speaking here.] of the Prophet: VERSE 3: “May he not give your foot into disturbance, nor may he slumber who guards you.” The sense itself shows that a change of speaker has taken place. For the speech is addressed to the one who spoke above: “May he not give.” Who? Surely he who made heaven and earth. “Your foot.” Whose? We ask: for it is the foot of the one who lifted his eyes to the mountains and confessed that his help was from the Lord. And the phrase “may he not give” is the expression of one praying and blessing. [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “And who prayed? Surely he prayed who is for us another advocate besides God.” The phrase “besides God” is ill-sounding, as if the Holy Spirit, who is the other Advocate, were not God.] And who prays? Surely he who is for us, besides the Lord, another Advocate, of whom he says: “And he will send you another Advocate,” who also speaks in the prophets (John 14:16). [Note: The editions of Baden, Erasmus, and Leipzig read “I will send”; Paris, “I will send.” With the royal and Tours manuscripts we prefer “he will send,” as it is again read in Psalm 125, no. 7.] What, then, does this Advocate say? He blesses the confessor of this faith and hope: “May he not give your foot into disturbance, nor may he slumber who guards you.” But both of these are unworthy of God: both that he should give someone over to disturbance, and that he should slumber and, after the watchfulness of guarding, rest through some continuance of labor. But before we touch on this, we must consider what the foot signifies.

7. The foot of the flesh and the foot of the soul.—The foot is a part of the body, carrying the whole body about for accomplishing and performing things. And because Scripture teaches spiritual things through bodily things, and shows invisible things through visible things, under the name of “foot” it signifies the movements and course of our mind, as in this same Prophet: “But my feet were almost moved” (Ps. 72:2). Certainly these fleshly feet are always moved in the body; how, then, is it a danger that they were almost moved, when their proper function is always to be moving? And in the Gospels also, signifying other feet, the Lord commanded that the right foot causing offense be cut off, saying: “And if your right foot causes you to stumble, cut it off” (Matt. 5:30; Mark 9:44; Matt. 18:8). If there is an offense in the right foot, will the left cause less offense? Or what temptation can that part of the body bring, when, without any inclination of desire itself, it has only the ministry of necessary service in accomplishing a thing [Note: The editions read “in itself.” More correctly, the royal and Tours manuscripts read “in the thing,” that is, in accomplishing, not in seeking, the thing.]? Therefore, just as there are eyes of the mind, so feet also must be understood: possessing in themselves both the sight of understanding and the movement of will.

8. Why God is said to hand people over, though he does not hand them over to vices.—It must not be understood that this blessing, “May he not give your foot into disturbance,” means that God hands some over to vices, into which we are carried by the feet of a corrupted mind. He does not hand us over; rather, when we depart from him, abandonment follows. [Note: Here “being handed over” is understood: unless, with the Tours and royal manuscripts, one reads “and our departure from him follows,” because we depart from him, etc., omitting the five intervening lines.] For when we are carried along by the feet of a corrupted mind, he does not hand us over; rather, we revolt from him through sins. And since he does not dwell in sinners, our departure from him is followed by his departure from us, because we depart from him through sins. And when he departs from us, we fall into every pit of transgression and run along the broad road of death, subject to the dominion of demons, to whom God’s departure from us leaves us (Literal Interpretation 16, Psalm 118, nos. 5–6). And his desertion is therefore “handing over,” because the devil cannot possess sinners unless God departs from them. [Note: The preposition *a* (“from”) is wrongly prefixed here in the Paris edition, since *obtinere* here means “to possess,” not “to permit.” The devil possesses us when God departs; God departs when we sin.]

9. Who sleeps and who keeps watch; the holy person and the perverse person.—But while we remain with him, or he remains in us, there is sleepless protection and untiring defense. Yet if we sleep through lukewarmness of faith, he himself sleeps in us. [Note: The editions read: “Does he too sleep with us? By no means. For there is no,” etc.; corrected on manuscript authority.] For in eternal Power there is no sleep or rest; his angels are watchers both in name and in nature. These things are necessary to earthly bodies. But because, in accordance with our faith, God’s help with us either keeps watch or sleeps according as we keep watch or sleep, the Lord is therefore frequently signified as both watching and sleeping. An example is the saying in this same Prophet: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverse” (Ps. 17:26). Is God not always holy, so that at some time he is also perverse? Certainly not. For nothing exists in him except what is good and eternal. But because God attends to each person according to that person’s character and disposition, he is therefore turned away from the perverse and holy in the holy.

10. God is free from sleep. Who Israel is. For whom God keeps watch.—And to show that the sleep of protection arises rather from our own sleep away from faith, and that the rest of sleep is incompatible with the nature of heavenly guardianship, because it is untiring and eternal, he immediately continues: VERSE 4: “Behold, he who guards Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.” [Col. 0657D] Above, he prayed that he might not slumber; now he says that he neither slumbers nor sleeps—above signifying slumber through our departure from him, but now showing, by saying “neither slumbers nor sleeps,” that eternity is untiring. But who is this who neither slumbers nor sleeps? Surely he who guards Israel. Genesis explains Israel to be the one who has seen God (Gen. 32). For the patriarch Jacob received this name after the struggle which he had with God. Beholding God beyond human nature with the eyes of his faith, he was worthy of this name. And he saw God so truly that he begged to be blessed by him. Paul also remembers that Israel is now among the people of the Gentiles—that is, among the people of the Church—when he says: “Peace be upon him and upon the Israel of God” (Gal. 6:16), lest this name be thought to have belonged only to that ancient people. Therefore, if he who guards Israel does not sleep, and if Israel is properly the name of the one seeing God, then the one who lifted his eyes to the mountains, saw, and said, “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth,” must be guarded. Heavenly protection is therefore bestowed upon this faith, and this confession obtains the defense of eternal watchfulness. It must be followed, attained, and retained perfectly, [Note: “Perfectly” is absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts.] with the guardianship of him whom we thus confess never sleeping toward us.

11. The hand of the right hand; what the right hand is; the hand.—And lest it should be thought that some other sleepless guardianship is being indicated, it is added: “The Lord shall guard you”—surely he who made heaven and earth. Then the nature of his guardianship is specified: VERSE 5: “The Lord is your protection above the hand of your right hand.” We have already said that incorporeal things are signified through corporeal ones. For the weakness of our understanding cannot grasp invisible things except by comparison with visible things; and so what is said here does not enter our understanding except through the terms “hand” and “right hand.” Yet here “hand” and “right hand” are used contrary to ordinary understanding of nature. For it is said: “The Lord is your protection above the hand [Note: Erasmus wrote in the margin: “Yet even now the Greeks read ‘right hand,’ not ‘of the right hand.’ Hilary was not alone in reading it thus. Augustine follows the same reading. It appears in the old psalters: Roman, Milanese, Chartres, and Germanensis.”] of your right hand.” The expression would be complete if it said: “above your right hand.” But since it says, “above the hand of your right hand,” the “right hand” appears to be signified as having a right and a left hand. This neither human nature nor reason admits. Yet Scripture always shows the right side as the better and more useful. Indeed, the Gospels will show the significance of the two sides through those who are on the right and on the left (Matt. 25:33). We understand “hand” as the effect of every work. Thus this same Prophet says: “Deliver my only one from the mouth of the lion and from the hand of the dog” (Ps. 21:21–22). Certainly that barking and rabid animal was not a part of this body; [Note: Baden and Erasmus, with the manuscripts, read “of this body.”] rather, he prays that he may be delivered from works of evil. Therefore, because the demonic powers opposing us strive to weaken and wound the best and strongest works of our faith, God’s ever-watchful protection is promised above the hand of the right hand, so that the works of good will may remain unimpaired in us. While these remain, we shall enjoy the kingdom of that eternal and blessed time, with every weakness of bodily frailty wiped away. [Note: The editions read “we shall be enslaved.” More correctly, the manuscripts read “we shall enjoy”; Hilary commonly uses *uti* in the sense of “enjoy,” as may be seen in Psalm 2, nos. 15–16.]

12. The character of the sun and moon.—For the Spirit of the Prophet promises us this in what follows, saying: VERSE 6: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.” The nature of these elements has this effect in itself: each, in its own season, weakens the strength of human bodies through the alteration of the frail substance within us—the sun by heat, the moon by cold. And their cycle through the year is such that in winter the sun does not burn, while the moon burns, but rather melts; [Note: On the authority of the royal and Tours manuscripts, we remove here the words “the moon, turning away, burns when the sun does,” which have the character of a gloss.] while again in the summer months the sun burns and the moon melts.

13. These psalms are not to be understood bodily.—Therefore, to those who think these things are to be understood bodily, I ask what they maintain the Prophet promises to the person who has lifted his eyes to the mountains in the saying: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.” For while the nature of our body remains, the mutable nature of the elements will not also be changed, so as not to persist in its customary relation of its own nature to our nature. Or will anyone dare to hope in this age for such soundness of body that he cannot be burned by night or day, when the blessed patriarch Jacob complained that he had been scorched by daytime heat and nighttime cold, saying: “By day I was scorched with heat, and with frost by night” (Gen. 31:40)?

14. The blessedness of eternal rest.—But the Prophet now—or the Spirit through the Prophet—knows that blessedness of times in which every alteration of bodily weakness departs from us, in which there is neither cold nor heat, neither night nor change, but eternal day and blessed mildness, with the sun of righteousness ruling over us. Prefiguring the rest of that time already in the wilderness, the Lord tempered for his people the heat of day with a pillar of cloud, and the cold and darkness of night with a pillar of fire. Therefore, in this eternal and blessed mildness of times, whoever has deserved the Lord’s protection shall remain: lest the nature of the body be burned by the moon’s frost and the sun’s heat; but, freed from the evils and injuries of this age, resting amid eternal, blessed, and temperate things, he shall receive the solid and unchangeable nature of his glorified body.

15. Supposed evils; the true evils that must really be avoided.—Then follows, VERSE 7: “The Lord shall guard you from every evil.” And from what evils will the Lord guard? Not, I think, from those which are considered evils. For these are due to our weakness and to the body: dying, being ill, being in need. If these were evils, [Note: Thus the royal manuscript with the Tours manuscript. The printed editions read: “and Abel would live.”] neither would Abel have died, nor Job have been afflicted, nor Peter have lacked the money requested for almsgiving. Therefore the Lord guards the faithful soul from every evil: that the moth of the devil may not corrupt it; that the thief may not creep in; that the dog may not bark; that the wolf may not tear it; that the bear may not rage; that the leopard may not leap upon it; that the tiger may not swoop down; that the lion may not lay it waste. For these are now the ministries of the devil; these are all his functions in the time of this age: to consume through vices, to creep in through flatteries, to tear apart through pleasures, to leap upon through ambition, to swoop down through wantonness, [Note: The printed editions read “to entice.” More correctly, the manuscripts read “to swoop down,” in accordance with the preceding “lest the tiger swoop down.”] and to lay waste with the whole power of his strength. From all this evil, therefore, God’s protection must be awaited. And because he rages especially against the soul—[Note: The Tours manuscript reads “nor is it due”; perhaps more correctly. Yet we suspect that something is missing here, such as: “nor is it due to us that we be guarded against him in the body” (for, as said above, dying, being ill, and being in need are due to the body), “but only that we fight in the body,” etc. A little later, from the same manuscript, we restore “will guard” for “may guard [the] soul.”] for it is due to us to fight against him in the body, and there is no victory except through contest—therefore it follows: “The Lord will guard your soul,” so that none of all those many and great evils mentioned above may have power over it.

16. The righteous, kept in Abraham’s bosom for the kingdom of heaven.—The prophetic discourse has maintained its order, saying: “The Lord shall guard your departure and your entrance from now and for ever.” [Note: The editions read, “your entrance and your departure.” We alter this order on the authority of the manuscripts, as the following exposition requires: for we first depart from the body before we are admitted into the eternal kingdom.] For this protection—not to be burned by sun and moon, and to be preserved from every evil—belongs not to this time and age, but is the expectation of future good: when, departing from the body, all the faithful shall be kept through the Lord’s guardianship for that entrance into the heavenly kingdom, being meanwhile placed in Abraham’s bosom, to which the intervening chasm prevents the wicked from coming, until the time arrives for entering once again into the heavenly kingdom (Luke 16:26). [Note: The Tours codex, in the first hand, reads: “The Lord will therefore guard the departure from the body, so that, departing”; but after the deletion of “so that,” it was replaced with “while,” following the royal manuscript. The printed editions here read “guards,” and afterwards “they rest.”] Therefore the Lord will guard the departure, while, departing from the body, they rest, separated from the wicked by the intervening chasm. [Note: Thus the Tours manuscript, supported by the royal manuscript. The editions read: “He guards also the entrance, while he introduces us into the eternal …”] The Lord will guard the entrance, introducing them into that eternal and blessed kingdom. For he himself says: “I am the door” (John 10:7); and, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6): that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Psalm 121. A Song of Ascents of David.

“I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’ Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem. Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same thing. For there” (“for” is absent below) “the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony of Israel, to confess the name of the Lord; because there sat seats for judgment, seats over the house of David. Ask for the things that belong to the peace of Jerusalem; and abundance for those who love you. Let there be peace in your strength, and abundance in your towers” (Hilary adds: “weighty [towers]”). “For my brothers I spoke indeed” (Hilary does not have “indeed”) “peace concerning you. For the house of the Lord our God” (“of the Lord my God”) “I sought good things for you.”

## Treatise on the Psalm

1. One who longs for heaven understands this psalm; our hope.—Whoever is held by heavenly longing will find nothing obscure in the psalm. For from his own inward sense he will attain an understanding of prophetic grandeur. Since he remembers that it is written that he is a co-heir of God and a sharer in eternal goods, that through resurrection he is to be renewed into likeness with angels, that, corruption having been laid aside, he is to be conformed to the glory of the body of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that he will become an inhabitant of the heavenly city built of living stones—of which it is written in the Gospel, when the Lord had forbidden swearing by heaven, that he added: “Nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King” (Matt. 5:35)—he understands that this does not mean the city which killed and stoned the prophets, but the one of which blessed Paul thus speaks: “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2:19–20). And when he has read that the things which now exist are partial, that for the present we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but that when the perfect comes what is now partial will be destroyed, and that face to face, as though by bodily sight, we shall contemplate what is now invisible to us, where there is neither sickness, death, sorrow, nor fear (1 Cor. 13:12)—when anyone recognizes that these things were announced by angels, prefigured in the law, expounded by prophets, presented by the Lord in examples, preached by Apostles, and made possible for himself by faith, he must cry out in the Prophet’s words: VERSE 1: “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me.”

2. Joy over entry into the house of God.—But what are the things that were said, from which joy was received? Surely what follows: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.” Here is the cause of joy, here is the cause of exultation: because these things were said, that we must go into the house of the Lord. What the house of the Lord is, he taught in another psalm, saying: “For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has chosen it beforehand for his dwelling. This is my rest [Note: Two manuscripts read “for ages of ages”: certainly not, etc.] for age upon age; here I shall dwell, because I have chosen it beforehand” (Ps. 131:13). Certainly, as we have said, this does not mean the earthly and perishable city suffering the penalties of its impiety, but the free and heavenly Jerusalem, because it is also Zion. Through dwelling there, because it is God’s house, we too are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household. Here, therefore, is the joy: that it was said that we shall go into the house of the Lord.

3. The Apostles are the feet standing in the courts.—But those who said these things neither fail to know them nor are strangers to the very house into which they announce that we shall go. Rather, they say, VERSE 2: “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem.” They do not announce uncertainties or promise unknown things. We have recognized this desirable house, beloved by many. For Scripture says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see [Note: The royal codex originally reads “will”; in a second hand, “delights.” Greek: *tēn terpnotēta*, “pleasantness.”] the delights of the Lord and visit his temple” (Ps. 26:4). And again: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place [Note: The Tours manuscript, with the royal manuscript, reads “of the tabernacle”; this agrees with the Greek, *tou skēnōmatos*. Later it reads “joyful entry” instead of “joyful hearing.”] of the dwelling of your glory” (Ps. 25:8). This house is desirable; this hearing is joyful: living stones are built upon a foundation of twelve living gems, first cut out for the work of building by Moses in the law, by the prophets in their sufferings, by the Lord in the body, by the Apostles in martyrdoms, and by the Holy Spirit in miracles. These are the builders; these the structures; this the city. [Note: Thus the Tours codex. Others read “hence standing.” Then Paris: “feet in its courts.” Subsequently other editions omit the word “guardians,” namely those to whom the keys were entrusted, etc.] These feet stand in its courts: they are the guardians to whom the keys of this house were given, for it was said: “I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” Blessed feet announce the form of the house to those who do not know it, and are deservedly praised by the Prophet: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Isa. 52:7).

4. The heavenly Jerusalem is built day by day.—And lest any of these things be thought applicable to the Jerusalem which was earthly, there follows, VERSE 3: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city.” Not “a city,” but “as a city,” because the building of that earthly city, the construction of the temple, and the establishment of the tabernacle prefigured the form of that eternal and heavenly city. And because the building of this heavenly city must be completed throughout all time, until the consummation of the age, and through the duration of all generations, he signifies that it is being built without assigning a time, saying: “It is built as a city,” [Note: The word “until” is absent from the royal manuscript and does not occur in the Tours manuscript; instead: “so that, as the Apostle says.”] until, as the Apostle says, “the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and then what remains of Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

5. We are joined to it in unity.—But because the Church is one body, not mingled together in some confusion of bodies, nor formed by uniting individuals into an undifferentiated heap and shapeless mass, but one through unity of faith, fellowship of charity, harmony of works and will, and the one gift of the sacrament in all of us, we are all one. Paul exhorts us to this, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, that you all think the same thing, exercising the same charity” (1 Cor. 1:10). And when it comes to pass, as is written, “The heart and soul of all who believed were one” (Acts 4:32), then we shall be the city of God, then holy Jerusalem; because “Jerusalem is built as a city, whose participation is in the same thing.” But those who dissent from the assembly of the saints and separate themselves from the body of the Church, being cast down by their sins, [Note: Paris reads “separating themselves by sins, pride, and quarrels,” more elegant than accurate. Sins cast people down when they separate them from the Jerusalem above.] have no participation in this holy house, because the participation of this city is in the same thing. For those united in fellowship with the perfect city cannot have participation in what is diverse, but in the same thing. Therefore all who shall be one will be in it, as the psalm bears witness; for it says, VERSE 4: “There went up tribes, tribes”—not one tribe, but many.

6. Only those who belong to the Lord build it.—But perhaps the city will seem to be built by all without exception, since no exception is made among the tribes named; and will peoples who do not know the Lord have common entrance into this house? But Scripture does not permit that interpretation, adding to what it had said, VERSE 5: “There went up tribes, tribes of the Lord.” [Note: The printed editions add here, pointlessly, “a testimony of Israel.” Hilary means only that not every tribe is signified by the Prophet’s words, but only the tribe that belongs to the Lord; and therefore Scripture, after saying “tribes,” added “tribes of the Lord.” Then, lest carnal Israel claim this for itself because it was called the Lord’s portion and people, he shows from what follows that another Israel must be understood.] For there are those who are not the Lord’s, to whom it was said: “You are of the devil” (John 8:44); and again: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). Therefore the tribes which belong to the Lord will go up.

7. Nothing here belongs to carnal Israel.—But perhaps Israel claimed this as due to itself—that is, Israel according to the letter and not according to the Spirit, carnal and not heavenly, crucifying the Lord and not worshiping him? But it is driven back from this hope. For “there went up tribes, tribes of the Lord, a testimony [Note: The word “to that [Israel]” was missing in the printed editions; the meaning of what follows depends upon it.] to that Israel.” Not tribes of Israel as a testimony to the Gentiles, but tribes of the Lord as a testimony to Israel. For we are the tribes of the Lord, and we shall enter the house of the God of Jacob; and he will announce his way to us, and we shall walk in it. For the tribes of the Lord said: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will announce his way to us, and we shall walk in it. For from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3). For the word of the Lord, going forth from Jerusalem, came to the Gentiles. These enter the holy city as a testimony to Israel.

8. Prerogatives of the Israelite people; testimony against its crimes. — Testimony to what end? “To confess,” he says, “the name of the Lord.” For the tribes of the Lord confess the Lord’s name. And this is the testimony concerning Israel. [Note: From the royal and Tours manuscripts we have restored here the word *Israel*, which had previously been omitted.] That Israel—avenged by the Lord upon Pharaoh, washed in the sea [Note: In Hincmar, as in the royal and Tours manuscripts: *ablatus*, “taken away”; a reading refuted by the following passage, *Tractate on Psalm* LXV, §11: “For through these waters of the Jordan there was, by the steps of bodies to be washed, a passage—and one is passed—into those good things of the land which were promised by the prophets.”], fed in the wilderness with the food of angels, instructed in the Law, rebuked by the prophets, received by the Lord at his birth through fellowship in the body, saved on the cross if he had believed, glorified in the resurrection if he had confessed—believed none of these things to be his own, and wished none of them to remain his own.

Though possessing manna, he longed for the cucumbers of Egypt; while awaiting from God the law of life, he worshipped the calf; though hearing the prophets, he killed them. He slandered as shameful the birth from the Virgin that had been prophesied for him; he did not believe that God was in the flesh; he falsely accused the forgiver of sin of being guilty of sin [Note: We restore *falso*, “falsely,” from the Tours manuscript, in place of *falsi*, “of false [sin].”]; he bought him for death and lifted him upon the cross. [Note: Only the Paris edition reads: “if he should believe . . . if he should confess.”] He bribed the witnesses of the resurrection into silence and put the Apostles to death.

As testimony to this crime of his, the tribes of the Lord ascend. What was promised to him, they obtain. The covenant is his, but the inheritance is theirs. [Note: The royal and Micy manuscripts read *illi*, “to him.” With the Tours manuscript we retain *illius*, “his,” on account of Romans 9:4: “whose are the adoption as sons, the glory, and the covenant.”] Him whom he judged worthy of the cross, the tribes confess as their God. [Note: Erasmus reads *cruciarum*; the Leuven edition, *cruciatum*, which was also restored in the final Paris edition. Yet Bade is more correct with the manuscripts: *cruciarium*, that is, him whom carnal Israel judged worthy of the cross.] In this testimony, therefore, Israel recognizes him whom it pierced, and is barred from access to him whose resurrection it did not believe. The archangels worship him; all the heavenly powers minister to him; he makes his tribes conformed to the glory of his body. They therefore confess the name of the Lord: because he is God, because he is the only-begotten Son of the unbegotten One. Thus, as testimony against Israel, the tribes of the Lord ascend into the house of the Lord, confessing the name of the Lord.

9. Judgment of carnal Israel; a type of the Church. — But this confession is a judgment. For Israel is judged by those to whom it was said: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Not only these shall judge, but the queen of the South shall also condemn, and the Ninevites shall condemn (Matt. 12:41–42), because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, and she came from the furthest parts of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. In them is a prefiguration of the Church, which, though foreign and unknown, both believed repentance and desired to hear wisdom.

10. Where the seats of judgment are; Christ as man is called David; the prophets speak future things as accomplished. — [Note: The printed editions read “this therefore.” Shortly afterward Paris reads “ascended” for “shall ascend,” and later “the Church, namely, the city of saints.” Other editions read “the Church, namely, the city of holy stones.” We follow the manuscripts.] Therefore, this will be the seat of judgment: where, as testimony against Israel, the tribes of the Lord shall ascend to confess the name of the Lord—namely, in the Church, the city of holy stones, which is the house of the Lord. For he says, v. 5: “For there sat seats for judgment, seats over the house of David.” [Note: Thus the Tours manuscript, following the Greek. Others read: “in judgment.”]

Here too, as elsewhere, David is the Lord’s name taken from his bodily descent. [Note: The printed editions read “of the Lord.” On the authority of the Tours and royal manuscripts, we restore “to the Lord,” so that the preceding word *David* is understood in the genitive case. Moreover, that Christ is called David because of the flesh of his body is again found in *Psalm* CXXXI, §17.] Wherever Scripture mentions his assumption of a body, it customarily calls him David, taking his name from the parent of the flesh. Nor should understanding be disturbed because the prophets have spoken some things in the past tense. We have already frequently set out the explanation of this matter in many places. For to God, who embraces all things within himself, future things are as accomplished. [Note: The manuscripts read “presence” here.] His foreknowledge is so trustworthy that things not yet done are nevertheless regarded by him as already completed and as past and accomplished. [Note: The words “completed and” are absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts and appear superfluous.] Indeed, the Prophet immediately shows that he is speaking of an event still future.

11. The Church is built by peace. — For although he had spoken as of the past, recalling that the tribes of the Lord had ascended there and had sat upon the seats of David’s house, he now, in the manner of public teaching and exhortation, gave instruction concerning the future, saying, v. 6: “Ask for the things that belong to the peace of Jerusalem,” so that he might demonstrate the reliability of his foreknowledge in what he had said had occurred, while preserving the order of times in events yet to occur. [Note: In the Paris edition: “that [he might show] the reliability of foreknowledge.” In the other editions: “that [he might show] the reliability of foreknowledge.” In the Micy manuscript: “that [he might show] the reliability of presence.” With the Tours and royal manuscripts we prefer “that [he might show] the reliability of presence,” that is, that he might show himself to be foreknowing.]

Its construction, therefore, is in peace; its participation is in the same thing; that house is one in mind, faith, and love. Therefore the teaching of peace must be learned. For here “ask” (*ἐρωτήσατε*, *erōtēsate*) means, according to the idiom of Greek, not “pray” but “inquire.” But learning peace depends upon the will of those who hear. For when they have inquired concerning its peace, then they will rejoice to be told: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.”

12. The fruit of peace. — Nor is the fruit of the peace for which one inquires insignificant, for what follows is: “And abundance for those who love you.” The love of peace awaits perfect fruits and hopes for an abundant store of happy increase. This very thing was signified beforehand in Jacob’s blessing as a hope set before believers. For, having secured his brother’s blessing, he was blessed thus: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which God has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). A field full and fruitful, yielding a hundredfold fruit, shall abound for this Jacob in eternal riches. [Note: Bade, Erasmus, and Leuven read “hence”; Paris reads “here.” The manuscripts more rightly read “for this one,” namely Jacob.]

And meanwhile, indeed, we abound in blessed fruits, which the sacrament of the Church and the unity of peace supply to us as an image of eternal fruits. [Note: The printed editions read “in hope,” contrary to the manuscripts.] But this sacrament of common hope has been shown by the names of bodily and shared things; those who know will understand. For the same Prophet mentions this abundance and plenty in another psalm, saying: “You have given joy into my heart; from the time when their grain and wine and oil were multiplied, they were multiplied together into one and the same thing” (Ps. 4:7–8). This, therefore, is the abundance “in the same thing.” For through this abundance of peace and sacraments, that blessed peace and unfailing, eternal abundance of heavenly goods is prepared.

13. The strength of the Lord’s house is not without peace. — Then follows, v. 7: “Let there be peace in your strength, and abundance in your weighty towers” (*ἐν πυργοβάρεσί σου*, *en pyrgobaresi sou*). The peace and strength of this house are joined together. For it cannot accomplish anything except from peace, because its participation is in the same thing; and being in the same thing results from peace alone. Perfect and peaceful strength, however, belongs only to those gathered into the same thing. [Note: We add only *tantum*, “only,” on the authority of the manuscripts. Shortly before, the Tours manuscript reads “peaceful strength,” without “perfect”; the latter word occurs in Micy, but not “peaceful.”] Therefore he says: “Let there be peace in your strength.” [Note: The editions here read only “in your strengths”; the Tours manuscript, which we follow, is more internally consistent.]

14. The towers of the Church are its leaders; their abundant blessedness. — A city must necessarily consist of various kinds of buildings. Not everything is wall, gate, or tower; neither is everything street, portico, shop; nor house, forum, temple, or palace. And according to the differing magnificence of houses, the ranks of their inhabitants also differ. Yet in every kind of city, nothing is firmer, more useful, or higher than towers.

Scripture customarily calls things “weighty” (*gravia*) when it means firm and immovable, as when it says: “I shall praise you among a weighty people” (Ps. 34:18). Having now spoken of the peace of strength, it assigns the abundance of the perfect and eternal blessedness of this city to its leaders, as though to the firmest towers, saying: “And abundance in your weighty towers.” Above it had said: “And abundance for those who love you.” Therefore abundance does not belong to all, but to those who love God. It then added: “Let there be peace in your strength.” For the peace and unity of the Church grant us strength and firmness, according to the Apostle’s saying: “And the peace of God, which surpasses every thought of understanding, shall guard your hearts in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 4:7). [Note: Thus the manuscripts according to the Greek; the printed editions read “shall guard.” The royal and Micy manuscripts lack the following word, “understanding.”]

Now too it declares that this abundance, which it had promised to those who love, belongs properly to the weighty towers. By “weighty towers” it signifies all who have loved. Thus it must be understood that this abundance is not indiscriminate, nor belongs to the whole city without distinction, but only to those holy and faithful persons who provide for the building of the rest of this city with the firmness of towers.

15. The distinction between the city of God and the house of God. — There follows the Prophet’s great affection and the concern of his pious exhortation for every human being who believes. For he says, v. 8: “For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors, I spoke peace concerning you; for the sake of the house of the Lord my God, I sought good things for you.” By his brothers and neighbors he signifies the multitude of this city, for whose sake he spoke peace concerning it—that is, the city—so that, hearing him, they might fit themselves into the building of this city as it is brought to completion. [Note: In the royal and Tours manuscripts, “that” is omitted here; shortly afterward they have “to fit” for “that they might fit”; and Tours has “daring” for “hearing.”]

But he who speaks peace concerning it for the sake of his brothers and neighbors seeks good things for that same city for the sake of God’s house, saying, v. 9: “For the sake of the house of the Lord my God, I sought good things for you.” Thus good things are sought for the city on account of the house of the Lord. For he distinguishes the glory of God’s house from the totality of the city, since the adornment of the royal house must necessarily be preferred to the building of the whole city; and so he sought good things for that city. [Note: At Paris, from the Micy manuscript, “the royal house of God.” The word “God” seems to have crept into the text from the margin, since here the house of God is understood in fact under the name “royal house.”]

First, through the preaching of peace, his brothers and neighbors became the Lord’s city. Second, the city itself, now constituted from his neighbors and brothers, upon hearing of the dignity of God’s house, hastened to become itself the whole house of God. [Note: Bade, Erasmus, and Leuven read “the house of God itself prepared itself”; they are corrected from Paris and the manuscripts, which differ only in that some have “will hasten,” others “has hastened.” Here the word “whole” refers to the city, not to the house.] Thus good things are sought for this city while it advances from being the Lord’s city into God’s house, according to the Apostle’s saying: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of the Lord dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3:16). For faithful is he who says: “Father, I ask you for these, that we may all be one; I in them, and you in me”: our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Psalm CXXII. A Song of Ascents

To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven. Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands [Below: “the hands”] of their masters, as [Below: “and as”] the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands [Below: “hands”] of her mistress, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us. Have mercy upon us, O Lord, have mercy upon us, for we are greatly filled with contempt [Below: “scorn”]; for our soul has been greatly filled [Col. 0668A] with reproach from the prosperous and disdain [Below: “scorn”] from the proud.

## Treatise on the Psalm

1. The various ascents in the preceding psalms. — What the title announces is accomplished in the subject matter: for by the steps of the song one ascends, as it were, from low things to high. Thus, in the first Song of Ascents, the cry was made to the Lord from tribulation. [Note: In the royal and Tours manuscripts, “in the first of the song,” which is not bad if after “in the first” one understands “psalm.”] Afterward the eyes were lifted up to the mountains, and it was asked whence help would come. Then, because instruction of prophetic teaching attends one who lifts up his eyes and seeks whence help may come, he rejoiced in the things said to him.

But now, because he has reached as far as the teaching’s instruction led, the Prophet sings from a certain stage, as it were, of his progress, v. 1: “To you who dwell in heaven I have lifted up my eyes.” Through suitable stages in the contemplation of God, he has been prepared—after much blindness—by small and measured intervals of admitted light, for the habitual enjoyment of the whole light. [Note: The royal manuscript with Tours reads “through the Lord’s [things] and measured [intervals].” Then Tours alone reads “of lost [light].” Paris reads: “is prepared for the habitual enjoyment of the whole light.” The other editions: “is prepared by habit.” They are corrected according to the manuscripts, of which Tours has “has been restored.”]

For God, first invoked in tribulation, was sought through the prophets, and he gave them joy through the hearing of prophecy. [Note: The printed editions read “heard, and now”; the Tours manuscript more suitably reads “by hearing”—that is, “God gave joy”—but now.] But now he who dwells in heaven must be contemplated with the eyes of the mind through the confidence of faith.

2. The visible heaven is not God’s dwelling, but the Son is. — Yet this heaven, which lies before our eyes in its material substance, which has received both the nature and the name of firmament as though solidified smoke, shall pass away and cease to be; but the Lord’s throne remains for ever. A dwelling must be worthy of its inhabitant, lest we confine what is infinite and incorruptible within a corruptible place by believing that God dwells in this heaven. [Note: The editions read, “and if [we confine it] in a corruptible place,” and shortly afterward, “and if [we believe] God in this heaven,” etc. We owe the correction to the Tours manuscript. Yet “in a corruptible place” would not be displeasing, in the sense of an unworthy place: “we confine what is infinite and incorruptible, if we believe God dwells in this heaven”—as the royal manuscript has, except for “if.” See *On the Trinity*, I.6.]

Let us therefore inquire what God’s dwelling is. Surely it is he who said: “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (John 10:38); and again: “I and the Father are one” (ibid. 10:30); and of whom it was said: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). The Father dwells in the worthy and sufficient Son through the same power of nature; and the Father does not separate from himself the Son whom he has begotten from himself through any difference of divinity. [Note: Thus the manuscripts, with Bade agreeing, except that it mistakenly reads “Father” in place of “the Father.” From this other editions produced: “But the Father does not separate the Son from himself,” etc., less well. For the reciprocal indwelling of the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father is explained here.
