From the Father’s indwelling in the Son their equality is demonstrated thus in *On the Trinity* IV.38: “For God is not in the dwelling-place of a nature different and alien from himself, but abides in his own and in one begotten from himself—God in God—because God is from God.”]

But the present discourse is not about the inseparable power of Father and Son. For God begotten from God is not, by nature, absent from him from whom he must be confessed to have been begotten; and the unbegotten God, begetting the only-begotten God, remains, by the property of begetting, in him whom he begot. Our whole hope is in knowing the only-begotten God. For of the unbegotten God, no one is so mad as not to perceive, by looking upon heaven, that there is a God (*Treatise on Psalm* LII, §2). Therefore God dwells in this heaven—in a dwelling worthy of his majesty and divinity.

3. Through Christ God dwells in us. — Yet there is another dwelling pleasing to God and chosen by him: namely, those of whom it was said, “I shall dwell in them and walk among them, and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God” (2 Cor. 4:16); and concerning whom the Apostle says: “You are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3:16). The same Apostle also says: “As is the earthly man, such also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly man, such also are the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:48).

Therefore the second Adam is heavenly, and heavenly because the Word was made flesh: that is, a man born from the Spirit and from God. [Note: The printed editions read “was born”; *was* is superfluous. The second Adam is heavenly because the Word was in heaven before becoming flesh upon earth. Thus, to use Athanasius’s words, *On the Saving Advent of Jesus Christ*, p. 647, “the Lord was a heavenly man, not because he brought flesh with him from heaven, but because he made heavenly him who was from earth.” Immediately following: “from the Spirit, that is, from God, since he was previously Spirit and God”; here “Spirit” signifies little or nothing other than God. See *On the Trinity* X.16–17.]

Therefore, in this Word—not in an empty sound of speech, but in God the Word; not in a substance discordant from and different from himself, but in God’s Word—God dwells as in heaven, abiding in that which is from himself and is his own. Through him he also dwells in those who are heavenly, as he himself says to the Father: “That they may all be one, I in them, and you in me” (John 17:21, 23). Thus, if we were clay in Adam, we are now heavenly in Christ; Christ dwells in us, and through Christ dwelling in us, he also—that is, the Father—dwells in us, he whose dwelling in us is Christ dwelling in us.

4. The common opinion concerning God’s seat is not excluded. — And because, according to bodily understanding, we are inclined to suppose that God dwells in the heaven beyond the nature of this firmament [Note: The royal manuscript reads “the firmament of heaven.” See *Treatise on Psalm* CXXXV, §8.], we do not exclude the common opinion concerning God’s seat, namely, that the heaven of heavens is his throne. Yet we believe that this dwelling worthy of God is also signified in his heavenly Adam, Christ. Therefore God must be recognized as dwelling also in that heaven, while through him he dwells also in those whom he has made heavenly in him.

5. A mind devoted to God must not be diverted. — Those who have raised the eyes of their mind to God must not turn them back or divert them. For, as it is said in the Gospels, “No one looking back after putting his hand to the plough is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:6). [Note: The printed editions mistakenly read “and holding the plough,” whereas in the Gospels no one both looks back and holds the plough. With *and* removed on manuscript authority, and since “having put [his hand]” has the force of “when he has put,” in accordance with Greek *ἐπιβαλών* (*epibalōn*), the sacred words are clear.]

Having left temples, altars, greed, sensual indulgence, and every depth of vices, we ought to persist with tireless and unvanquished gaze. If the nations, blinded by their error, are held by unchangeable obstinacy in false religions, so that they cannot be turned from their superstitions by the reasoning of truth, serving various gods, as they call them, with persistent folly; and if the soul of sinners, captured by the allurements of vices, most devotedly serves a body as though it were its master—how much more ought we, who know God as the creator of heaven and earth, worship without any turning aside or wandering religion, and never divert the steadfastness of our fixed faith? He who was able to give life to man from lifeless earth is also able to raise to fellowship in eternity the man who, once given life, has died.

6. Hands mean works; servants of sin; the works on which they fix their attention. — The Prophet teaches that these eyes of the mind must always remain fixed upon God with unchanging gaze, saying, v. 2: “Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us.” [Note: The editions here and subsequently, though not consistently, read “in the hands.” But the manuscripts here and immediately afterward read “upon the hand”; subsequently, however, “upon the hands,” which we think should consistently be read in accordance with Greek *εἰς χεῖρας* (*eis cheiras*), with “fixed” understood. What follows, together with the next two treatises and part of the treatise on Psalm CXXV, is absent from the Tours manuscripts.]

The Prophet gave this comparison as an example, so that as servants’ eyes are upon the hands of their masters, so the eyes of his faith might be fixed upon God. For a faithful servant ought to be attentive to every act of obedience to his master’s will and always keep his eyes fixed without turning aside.

But if the discourse concerned bodily servants and masters, it would have been said that servants’ eyes are in the eyes, tongue, presence, or nod of their masters: for commands are given by these, either through gesture or through speech. But Scripture frequently uses “hands” to signify works. There are some who are servants neither of human beings nor of God, but are servants of sin, as the Lord says: “Everyone who commits sin is the servant of sin” (John 7:34). These servants of the spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places keep the eyes of their mind always fixed on the works of those wickednesses, as upon the hands of their masters, held fast by longing for and admiration of vices. [Note: The royal manuscript omits “in the heavenly places, in their works as though.”]

These are the works of the devil—that is, of the gods of the Gentiles—signified by “hands”: gluttony, idleness, extravagance, lust, pride, avarice, ambition. Upon these works of the wills to whose dominion they are subject, they fix the eyes of their understanding, looking toward them. [Note: The printed editions read “pleasures.” With the royal manuscript we prefer “wills,” namely those of the wickednesses or gods of the Gentiles, whose promptings they obey. In the same manuscript, then, “whose” rather than “of which,” as above, “their works”; and shortly afterwards, in the old manner, “awaiting” for “looking.”] To them there are many and countless gods and masters, according as each person’s disposition and nature has chosen for itself an author of religion. [Note: All editions except the first Paris edition read “and numerous masters,” against the manuscripts.]

7. God is one for us, but not solitary. — But for us there is one God; yet we do not deny to our Lord Jesus Christ that he is God by a unification which abolishes plurality. [Note: What the Greeks call *μονάς* (*monas*), Hilary calls *unio*, “unity”: by this term plurality not only of natures but also of persons is excluded.] Rather, following the Law, the prophets, the Gospels, and the Apostles, we confess with faith and truth the unity of divinity in the unbegotten God and in the only-begotten God, according to property and nature.

For prophetic discourse nowhere calls either gods or lords by a plural term, but names each in his proper order. Thus Genesis says: “The Lord rained sulphur and fire from the Lord” (Gen. 19:25); and the Prophet: “God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. 44:8); and, “The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. 110:1); and the Gospels: “The Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1); and the Apostle: “One God, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6); and again: “From whom is Christ, who is God over all” (Rom. 9:5).

This, then, was said because of the Lord: that we might understand that, because the unbegotten God is one, what belongs to God cannot be taken away from the only-begotten God. For both are one God: not because, as Hierax held, one has been divided into two; nor because both are himself, as Sabellius thought, so that a mere naming made Father and Son, rather than the nature of begetting. But God is one because there are neither two unbegotten Gods nor two only-begotten Gods; there is one from one, and both are one—not, of course, through any dissimilar or differing substance of divinity in the two.

8. Why there are many servants and masters, but one maidservant and mistress. — He then continues: “And as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress.” The Prophet preserves the same order by mentioning also, as an example for the comparison, the eyes of a maidservant fixed upon the hands of her mistress, thereby teaching that these desires of servants are fixed rather upon the effects of works. But since many servants of many masters have been set forward as the example, one must ask why one maidservant of one mistress is mentioned.

For, as we said above, the many servants belong to many gods. [Note: The printed editions read “masters,” against the manuscripts; yet at the end of §6 those servants are described to whom there are many gods.] But now there is one maidservant and one mistress, because human soul has one nature, just as earthly flesh has one nature. And because the present discourse concerns sinners, who are servants of sin, this maidservant—the soul—is devoted to her mistress, the flesh, and subjected through the enticements of bodily things and vices. [Note: The printed editions read, “and is subjected through the blandishments of bodily vices.” With the royal manuscript we prefer “through [the enticements] of bodily things and of vices,” by which Hilary commonly means the incitements of the flesh or fleshly desires.]

Through incentives to pleasure, it is under the dominion of what is inferior to itself, gazing at the fruits of its works. Thus, as their vices hold these servants and this maidservant unchangeably, so that they persist in them with a kind of religious dedication to their own folly [Note: The printed editions with the royal manuscript read “religious”; Micy more plausibly reads “religiously.”], so faith must remain not temporary or unstable, nor wearied by assaults of temptations, but immovable and unchanging until the completion of God’s mercy. [Note: The editions add here, “ought to be,” which we remove on the authority of the royal manuscript. In their place one may perhaps more rightly understand: “holds fast to virtues,” or something similar.]

9. The Prophet’s steadfast hope. — Therefore the Prophet displays the constancy of his hope until the end, when mercy is received, saying: “So our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us.” He does not cease or desist, even if the Lord delays his mercy in order to test faith; for faith ought to provide a steadfast expectation of its confidence, and every despair is a confession of distrust. [Note: Bade, Erasmus, and the final Paris edition with the royal manuscript read “delays”; Leuven reads “is delayed”; they are corrected from the Micy manuscript.]

But the Prophet is not uncertain of God’s mercy, for his eyes are fixed upon him until he has mercy. Indeed, they are so fixed that a doubled prayer follows their attention. For after this he says, v. 3: “Have mercy upon us, O Lord, have mercy upon us.” He is fixed upon God, and, being fixed upon him, he prays: that is, with the same perseverance by which servants of vices remain in the vices that rule them, he perseveres in the most certain hope of eternal goods and in confidence in mercy made perfect within him.

10. The faithful, afflicted by injuries, grieve both for their injuries and for the sins of those who afflict them; their relief comes from God alone. — There follows, as we have often learned, this grievous disparagement of the faithful by the wicked and troublesome persecution by the malicious. The wicked man hates righteousness preached by us; if we praise chastity, the impure man is offended; drunkenness abhors fasting in us. When we exhort people to generosity, the miser charges us with folly. When we preach Christ, crucified, as God, the Jew and every persecutor from among the Gentiles reproaches our religion. [Note: The royal manuscript reads “crucified.”]

When we await God’s judgment, the kings of the world are offended and reject God as the judge of every life that has been lived. When we announce the resurrection, the bodies of unbelievers, dead with their vices, object. All the falsehoods of heretics also accuse our faith, received from the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, and the Apostles. We are beaten, cursed, driven away, killed by sword, flames, and the deep; violence is exercised against our honour, violence against our bodies. [Note: The royal manuscript omits: “violence is exercised against our honour.”]

We feel grief because of our injuries. And because our injuries are death to those who inflict them, we grieve out of pity for those who perish. Therefore, after the double prayer in which he had said, “Have mercy upon us, O Lord, have mercy upon us,” he added: “For we are greatly filled with scorn.” Verse 4: “For our soul has been greatly filled”—God alone being able to help against these things, so as to deliver from scorn and contempt the person who remains always fixed upon him until the end of receiving mercy.

And therefore he remains fixed upon God until God has mercy upon him; therefore he entreats God’s mercy for himself with a double prayer, because he and his soul have been greatly filled with scorn. As we have said, God alone is able to show mercy amid great scorn; nor is he only able to do that, but he is also able to turn everything to the contrary and provide a certain reversal for the sufferer. [Note: The printed editions read “into the verse.” The manuscripts more correctly read “to the contrary.” In what follows, “for the sufferer,” rather than “suffering,” may conveniently refer to those who injured the saints.]

11. The reversal of poor Lazarus and the rich man. — We have as witnesses both the poor man resting in Abraham’s bosom and the rich man burning in punishment. For the former sat upon a heap of dung before the rich man’s door, wasted with hunger, flowing with the discharge of ulcers, while dogs licked his open wounds. [Note: The royal manuscript reads “bosom” here.] [Note: The royal manuscript reads: “For he, placed in a heap of dung at the rich man’s door, was wasted with hunger,” which Bade, Erasmus, and Leuven also have, adding “poor” after “wasted.”]

But these things were the warfare of the body, the battle against the world. Within, however, his soul was invulnerable through faith and inaccessible to every weapon of pleasure and vice. [Note: The Micy manuscript reads “to the vices of pleasure”; the royal manuscript “to the vices of will.” Perhaps the text is: “invulnerable against every heel”—which can do nothing to the soul—“inaccessible to the vices of will.” For “inaccessible,” Bade, Erasmus, and Leuven read “unconquered.”] Therefore, after the dissolution of the flesh, blessed by angels, it is carried into Abraham’s bosom.

But the other man, whose every garment was purple, to whom the nobility of the whole city rendered service in subjection to his oppressive rule, for whose banquet the resources of air, earth, and sea were amassed, with all the elements serving the needs of his one belly—he who had shut his door against that poor man, denied him the crumbs falling from his table, and reproached his appearance as though it were an affront to himself—when he departed from the body which he had abused, was separated from the saints by an impassable chaos. He was received into every ministry of punishments; he suffers pain, is tormented, burns, and begs that he be moistened and cooled by the smallest finger of the poor man resting in Abraham’s bosom.

Abraham answered him: “Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented” (Luke 16:25). A reciprocal reversal takes place: joy is changed into sorrow, and sorrow into joy. Let us see, then, whether the Prophet now also signifies what the Gospel has set forth.

### 12. The end of the rich and of the humble or needy

For he says: “Reproach to those who abound, and contempt to the proud.” After the persecutions already mentioned—those of kings, Jewish peoples, heretics, and often even our own people—there is here likewise an evangelical reversal: abundance becomes reproach, and pride contempt. Pride is changed into contempt, and plenty into want; again, contempt into pride, and want is changed into plenty. The Prophet shows both by the same words when he says: “Reproach to those who abound, and contempt to the proud”: either because those who now bear reproach will afterwards abound in the kingdom of the Lord, and those who are now held in contempt will afterwards be proud through the confidence of faith; or because, at the time of judgment, reproach and contempt will return upon those who now abound and are proud in the world.

[Note: Thus the royal manuscript, supported by the manuscript of Micy, which reads *superius* above. The printed editions instead give *superbas*, “proud women.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “in the kingdom of God.” The manuscripts more correctly read “in the kingdom of the Lord.” It is known from elsewhere that Hilary distinguishes the kingdom of God from the kingdom of the Lord, and that he places the righteous immediately after death in the kingdom of the Lord, while deferring for them the kingdom of God.]

[Note: The printed editions read *superbiant*, “may be proud”; the Micy manuscript reads *superbiunt*, “are proud.” We would write *superbiunt* with the royal manuscript, if grammar allowed it, or if the same verb occurred more frequently.]

### 13. Examples of humility

Paul glories in his weaknesses and distresses. He also commanded that judges should be chosen for the powerful from among the contemptible members of the Church (1 Cor. 6:4). He and Peter establish a mutual obligation for themselves, that they should remember the poor and diligently care for them. The angels of the least daily see God (Matt. 18:10); the humble shall be exalted (Matt. 23:12); and the best sacrifice to God is a troubled heart (*cor contribulatum*) (Ps. 50:19).

Therefore let us not reject the humble, despise the poor, or pass by the needy, lest we be separated from them by a deep chasm, lest they disdain to refresh us with their little finger—because there is reproach for those who abound and contempt for the proud. This is a changeable reversal, and a fitting exchange for good and evil alike, which he showed in the Gospels when he said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5); and again: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke 6:25), says our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: The printed editions read “a contrite and humbled heart.” From the royal manuscript we restore “a troubled heart,” since we later read, in Psalm 125, §9: “Since, therefore, the best sacrifice to God is a troubled heart.”]

## Psalm 123. A Song of Ascents. Of David.

“Had the Lord not been in us,” let Israel now say, “had the Lord not been in us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. When (below: *in eo cum*) their minds grew angry against us, perhaps the water would have engulfed us. Our soul passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through the immense water. Blessed is the Lord God, who did not give us as prey to their teeth. Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of hunters. The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered. Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

## Treatise on the Psalm

[Col. 0675A]

### 1. The voice of Israel, following the Prophet’s example

The preceding psalm brought us great benefit, for from it one ascends to this psalm. For the eyes of our mind were fixed upon God until the end of mercy, while contempt and reproach surrounded us on every side. After receiving mercy, and being placed from reproach into abundance and from contempt into pride, the Prophet shows what we ought to do and say, declaring:

> Verse 1. “Had the Lord not been in us,” let Israel now say, “had the Lord not been in us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”

The expression itself is indeed such that it is understood to be spoken by the Prophet, instructing what the rest ought to say. First, the statement itself is made; then it is shown how it is to be spoken. This was the order: what was to be done was first shown, and then the measure in which it was to be done. “Had the Lord not been in us,” let Israel now say. Thus it was stated what Israel ought to say.

We have often reminded you that Israel is to be understood as the person who has contemplated God with the eyes of the mind. Now, therefore, Israel, having learned from the prophetic teaching what it ought to say, speaks:

> Verse 2. “Had the Lord not been in us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”

Thus Israel, taking its example from the Prophet, says this because it heard: “Had the Lord not been in us,” let Israel now say.

### 2. Human beings have no ground for glorying in themselves

This command is not a slight one; it had to be displayed through a preceding proclamation of the Prophet. In difficult matters, an example is needed. For all human nature is insolent in prosperity and forgetful of its own weakness, recklessly boasting in favorable circumstances. Such boasting ought to be absent from a person instructed by the teaching of God.

For what place is left to us for glorying, if we remember that all things are from God? If we have given life to ourselves, let us also claim that we owe to ourselves the beauty of our bodies. If we ourselves regulate rains and heat, let us glory that the yield of fruits is our own. If we do not need God’s mercy in all things, then let us also claim all things as though they were our own.

Will the strong person glory in being strong, when bodily illness may make him weak? Will the rich person glory in wealth, when perhaps a thief, robber, or tyrant will carry all of it away? Will nobility glory, when it sometimes becomes an unworthy and pitiable slavery? Will the wise person glory, being uncertain what may happen to him from moment to moment?

[Note: The royal manuscript reads *incertis*, “uncertain”; nor is this kind of expression new in Hilary, since we have already seen *sincerīs* and *infirmīs* in the nominative case.]

But if we enjoy any of these things without interruption by some affliction, we delight and are carried away. And if we return from some sorrow to joy, scarcely able to contain the joy we have gained, we are exalted beyond all awareness of human weakness, forgetting this saying:

> “Let not the wise glory in his wisdom, nor the strong in his strength, nor the rich in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows that I am the Lord” (Jer. 9:23–24).

Therefore, because we are made insolent by the fault of our habitual disposition, the Prophet has formed us by a prescribed confession, and by the example of his exhortation has instructed us both to render honor to God and to glory in him, saying: “Had the Lord not been in us,” let Israel now say.

[Note: Thus the royal manuscript, more elegantly than the printed editions, which read “we ought to owe.” If we do not owe ourselves even the appearance of our bodies, how much less do we owe ourselves that of our souls? The Second Council of Milevis, canon 4, reasons very aptly: “Since the Apostle says, ‘Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up,’ it is most impious to believe that we have Christ’s grace for what puffs us up and do not have it for what builds us up; when both are God’s gifts: both knowing what we ought to do and loving to do it, so that, as love builds up, knowledge may not puff us up.” Thus Hilary, showing that even those things toward which our own effort seems to contribute something are gifts of God, leaves us no place for glorying, and rightly concludes that all things are from God and that in all things we need God’s mercy.]

[Note: In the royal manuscript, corrected by a second hand: “we rejoice, we are lifted up”; by the first hand: “joyful, and we are borne along.” Perhaps one should read: “we are lifted up by joy.” For excessive joy is here criticized.]

### 3. All good things are to be ascribed to God, from whom they come

Having therefore heard from the Prophet what we ought to say, let us also say: “Had the Lord not been in us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (v. 3). For though we have endured human persecutions, the impious decrees of kings, and the seductive exhortations of counsellors, yet, while we remain in faith, abide in the fear of God, and dwell upon hope in eternal goods, helped by God’s mercy and knowing him faithful who said, “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20), let us refer our joys to him who dwells in us.

Let us acknowledge that whatever is in us is owed to him, taught by blessed Paul that nothing is to be considered our own, when he says: “For what have you that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Let us learn from the holy patriarch Jacob the humility of rendering thanks, when he says: “God who has nourished me from my youth, and the angel rescuing me from all evils” (Gen. 48:15).

[Note: The first edition follows the Micy manuscript: “impious constitutions.” The Paris edition has “thoughts.”]

[Note: The printed editions here read “dwelling in us,” and in §4 “remaining in us,” but in §9 read “dwelling in us.” We retain the consistent manuscript reading in these three places.]

### 4. The death of the living

It is not human practice for some people to devour others alive, nor does hatred proceed so far as to swallow flesh. Nor is there now joy over a body rescued from death, but over a soul freed from the fellowship of sinners. Therefore he says that they perhaps would have swallowed us alive: that is, while we were still placed in the body, we would have been overtaken by death and consumed by sin. For this is the death of the living: to live for luxury, sleep, sacrilege, adultery, and murder.

Therefore thanks must be given to God who remains in us, because, living through faith in him and his teaching, we are not swallowed by these things. Thus the order in this thanksgiving follows the order of evils. First, we shall not be swallowed by those rising up against us; nor afterwards, when their minds are enraged, shall we be engulfed by water, the Lord protecting us.

[Note: In the royal manuscript: “separated.” Immediately afterwards: “that is, those still placed in the body would have been overtaken by death,” etc.]

[Note: The manuscript reads *nam qui*, “for he who,” in place of *namque*, “for.”]

### 5. The different kinds of waters and what they signify

For he says:

> Verse 4. “At the time when (*in eo cum*) their minds grew angry against us, perhaps the water would have engulfed us.”

But what is this? Human minds grow angry, and water engulfs us? Do avenging waters stand ready at the agitated movements of excited minds, or are they living creatures so as to engulf? Those submerged may indeed be drowned in water; but that which is inanimate cannot engulf. We must therefore inquire what ought to be understood here, and we must recall those passages in which waters are mentioned.

At the beginning of Genesis it is written: “And darkness was upon the deep, and the Spirit of God was borne over the water” (Gen. 1:2). Again: “God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water” (Gen. 1:6). Again: “Let the water which is above the heavens praise the Lord” (Ps. 148:5–6). Again: “The waters saw you, O God; they saw and were afraid” (Ps. 76:17).

Therefore, since the law is spiritual, and faith in the historical narrative is not endangered if we suppose that events have meaning within them and a related significance beyond them, we see that there are waters over which the Spirit of God is borne; waters above the heavens; waters on earth; waters that praise; and waters that fear. Hence we rightly understand waters to signify peoples: among whom some are spiritual and some dark; some heavenly and some earthly; some will praise the glorious coming of the Lord, and others will fear.

These, then, are the fearful, earthly, dark waters that seek to engulf us: their minds stirred to anger and moved with the full violence of diabolical rage, like torrents in the greatest winter storm, rushing headlong down.

[Note: Thus the royal manuscript according to the Septuagint. The printed editions read: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters”; and again: “Behold, darkness was upon the face of the deep.”]

[Note: The printed editions read: “between the water which is under the firmament and the water which is above the firmament.” They are corrected from the royal manuscript, in which, however, “and water” was omitted. In the Greek Septuagint we read: *kai estō diachōrizon ana meson hydatos kai hydatos*, “and let it divide between water and water.” This is translated by our Hilary; by Augustine, *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, unfinished work, book 1, chapter 8, “and let it divide between water and water”; and by Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book 2, chapter 2, “and let it distinguish between water and water.”]

### 6. What the devil’s attacks do to those full of God and to those empty of him

And so, in the order of our confession to the Lord, the Prophet adds:

> Verse 5. “Our soul passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through the immense water.”

Behold the rushing assaults of the devil and his followers, their violent courses stirred up and raging by turbulent movements, and the torrents of a passing storm. But this unbearable water did not pass over the soul in which God dwells. It is unbearable to those empty of God; but for those in whom God is, it is a sudden torrent, shortly afterwards dry and exhausted, so that it can be passed through.

[Note: In the royal manuscript, “for the ability to pass through” is absent. From this exposition Hilary seems to have read “unbearable water,” not “immense water.”]

### 7. The devil’s teeth

And lest anyone suppose that the passage concerns literal waters, there follows:

> Verse 6. “Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth.”

And what are the teeth of these torrents? Certainly those powerful forces for tearing and seizing: anger, desire, lust, hatred, gluttony, and avarice. These are evil and clinging teeth. Through them they rule us when we are captured and torn apart, making us either servants or companions of their vices. By these, not our flesh but our souls would have been devoured, had God not been in us.

[Note: The royal manuscript reads “into capture.” Shortly afterward we add from the manuscripts “of these torrents.”]

### 8. Snares of souls

For he says:

> Verse 7. “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of hunters.”

Those who hunt set snares secretly and deceptively: hidden in valleys, covered with grass, baited with food, or matching the color of clouds. Such snares are for beasts and other birds; but these are prepared against our soul. For us there is a snare in leisure, money, ambition, and lust. These are set before us, flatter us, and deceive us; but our will must be turned away from them all.

For these snares have been set for everyone, as it is written: “For nets are not spread unjustly upon the earth for birds” (Prov. 1:17, according to the Septuagint). Perfect glory consists in flying free from the snares that have been set.

[Note: The printed editions here and below read “of those hunting,” although below Hilary expressly rejects that reading and explains that *venatorum*, “of hunters,” restored from the manuscripts, must be understood passively.]

[Note: Lipsius corrected the earlier editions, which, like the Micy manuscript, read “effaced by food”; the royal manuscript reads “effaced by foods.”]

[Note: Bade, Erasmus, and the royal manuscript read “in leisure, money, ambition,” etc. Lipsius, then deleting *in*, read “leisure, money, ambition,” which the Paris edition eventually adopted from the Micy manuscript.]

[Note: Here too the printed reading was “must be restrained”; the manuscripts support “must be turned away.”]

### 9. One must remain steadfast in the Church

Finally, the psalm says: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of hunters”—not, certainly, “of those hunting,” but of those for whom snares have been stretched in hunting. For a person does not become a sinner only when he falls into a snare. Rather, although snares are spread for all, only the person who is already a sinner is in the snare, as it is written: “The eye of a harlot is the snare of a sinner.”

Therefore we must abstain from every sin, lest we fall into the snare. For we are spiritual, and we fly like sparrows. The sparrow is a domestic bird and dwells in buildings: it is not seasonal or temporary, but remains without change or regard to seasons. Therefore, dwelling in the Church without alternation of seasons, let us abstain from sins so that we may fly free from snares.

For the snare is broken by God dwelling in us, because it follows: “The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered.”

> Verse 8. “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

By this help the snare is broken; by this help we are delivered: in the name of the Lord who made heaven and earth. This is, of course, the name above every name, in which every knee bends—of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings—and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: The ancient editions read *ille autem*, “but that one”; the Paris edition reads *ille tamen*, “that one nevertheless.” A little earlier, after “he becomes a sinner,” *first* is understood after *then*. Hilary means that no one is in the devil’s snare and power except through sin, and thus that one is a sinner before being in the snare. He confirms the same point in his exposition of Psalm 140, §14.]

[Note: This same passage, cited again in the same words in the exposition of Psalm 139, §3, could nowhere be found by us. It nevertheless seems to be a summary statement drawn from Ecclesiastes 7:27: “I found woman more bitter than death, who is a hunter’s snare . . . but the sinner will be caught by her.”]

[Note: Here the sparrow is contrasted with birds that inhabit our regions only temporarily, such as the swallow, the quail (*ortyx*), and the like.]

## Psalm 124. A Song of Ascents.

[Col. 0679B]

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever. Mountains are round about it, and the Lord is round about his people, from this time forth and for ever. For he will not leave the rod of sinners over the inheritance of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity. Do good, O Lord, to the good and to the upright in heart. But those who turn aside to their bonds the Lord will lead away with workers of iniquity. Peace be upon Israel.”

## Treatise on the Psalm

### 1. Against those who follow the letter alone

Many people create obscurity for us because they wish to evaluate prophetic Scriptures solely by the hearing of the ears and to understand in them nothing other than what is heard under the individual names of particular things. When they insist on this, they leave us nothing to understand, and make the Prophets speak neither heavenly matters nor even earthly matters rationally.

For what can we suitably expound, or what can be thought rightly spoken by them, when we hear of waters praising, seeing, fearing, and clapping their hands, unless we demonstrate from the authority of those very Scriptures that under the name of waters something else, of another kind, is signified: namely, something living and sentient, which moves itself by its own motion and perception toward the judgment of each thing? This is understood to be a human being: praising, seeing, fearing, clapping, judging.

For the prophetic utterance has attributed these kinds of human affections to waters. Since such things do not accord with the nature of waters, neither did the Prophet speak of waters, nor should we understand the utterance to concern waters. This must be reconsidered because of what occurs in the present psalm, whose words are such as these.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “from the authorities.”]

### 2. The literal sense does not cohere here

> Verses 1–2. “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever. Mountains are round about it.”

If the name Mount Zion, Jerusalem’s habitation, and the mountains around it have no basis for inward understanding, the psalm is empty, and the Prophet false—though the Holy Spirit is believed to have spoken in him. Mount Zion does indeed overlook the city Jerusalem; and that city itself has several mountains around it externally.

What benefit, then, will one who trusts in the Lord obtain by becoming like Mount Zion? Is a rational human being to become a rock, tree, or turf, and be transferred from an animate to an inanimate nature? Further, how can this statement be trustworthy—that one who dwells in Jerusalem will never be moved? Did Jerusalem itself bring sanctification to its inhabitants, so that dwelling there gave eternal stability? From there came the sacrilegious slaughter of the Prophets, the judgment of death against God, the flight of the Apostles, and the scandal of the cross.

How often were its inhabitants taken captive? How often slain? Finally, the city itself was utterly destroyed, and those who remained amid its devastation were captured and scattered. The Prophet had previously announced this destruction for its impiety:

> “Your land is desolate; your cities are burned with fire; foreigners devour your country before your eyes. The daughter of Zion shall be left desolate and overthrown by foreign peoples, like a hut in a vineyard and like a watchman’s shelter in a cucumber field” (Isa. 1:7–8).

The statement is therefore empty, the prophecy empty, if it adds: “Mountains are round about it, and the Lord is round about his people, from this time forth and for ever.” Jerusalem has been overthrown, its people exterminated, its remnant scattered. Today no one dwells in it: no priest, prophet, or ruler. It has been trampled down, deserted, and fruitless. How then shall its inhabitant not be moved for ever? Or how is the Lord round about its people from this time forth and for ever?

Therefore the prophecy cannot appear to concern that city, since the truth of prophecy contradicts it. It follows that we must seek those to whom the meaning of these words applies.

[Note: The printed editions read “there were sacrileges”; they are corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.]

[Note: The royal manuscript reads “how often redeemed.”]

[Note: In the royal manuscript *now* does not occur here, nor below except once in §5.]

### 3. The Church is the mountain of the Lord; Christ became from mountain a stone, and from stone a mountain

First we must observe that no mountain other than Zion is mentioned. For we read that Horeb is the mountain of the Lord, to which Moses first came after passing through much (Exod. 3:1); and Sinai is the mountain of the Lord, on which the law was written for the people. Zion also is a mountain overlooking Jerusalem. But since prophecy finds no fulfillment in this mountain, we must see what is to be understood by “mountain.”

Isaiah provides an excellent guide to understanding. For after he had signified above the high mountain of the Lord, to which the nations would come (Isa. 2:2), he says: “Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a splendid, chosen, precious cornerstone; and he who believes in him shall not be confounded” (Isa. 28:16).

It is not doubtful that the Apostle identified Christ as the foundation. Hence the blessed Church of the Lord’s body, whose foundation is Christ, appears to be signified in the mountain. The same Apostle calls it Jerusalem, saying: “The Jerusalem which now is serves with her children; but the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:25–26).

Thus we have Mount Zion of the Lord, and we have Jerusalem, the city of God; and the interpretation of the name Zion is “watching” or “contemplation” (*speculatio*). Thus we understand the mountain of the Lord in Daniel: from mountain into a stone, and again from stone into a mountain (Dan. 2:34–35). For though existing in the form of God, he emptied himself and took the form of a servant; and when, through his passion, the world with its superstitions and terrors had been overthrown, he is in the glory of God the Father and is God over all.

Through the weakness of the flesh he was emptied from mountain into stone; through the glory of the passion he was again made from stone into mountain: an overhanging and lofty mountain, in whom we ourselves behold ourselves through the assumption of our flesh and body.

[Note: The royal manuscript reads “and Horeb.” The particle “and” seems superfluous. Neither Horeb, nor Choreb according to the Greeks, is called “the mountain of the Lord” in the sacred text, but “the mountain of God.”]

[Note: Bade, Erasmus, Lipsius, and the royal manuscript read “of Christ.” More correctly, the Paris edition from the Micy manuscript reads “Christ,” since Paul’s words at 1 Corinthians 3:11 are in view: “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ.” Then “through which,” that is, “for which reason.”]

[Note: The royal manuscript reads “in Daniel,” a manner of expression consistently found in the Tours manuscript, etc.]

[Note: In the royal manuscript: “with its substitutions and errors.”]

### 4. We contemplate our resurrection in Christ; the present Church is the form of the future one

For in him we contemplate our resurrection in the resurrection of our body; for Mount Zion is contemplation. Let the Hebrew language speak this interpretation, in which it is said: “Mount Zion is the mountain of contemplation.” Let Paul speak and say: “But our citizenship is in heaven, from which also we await our Savior, our Lord Jesus, who will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21). Let him say again: “Even when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ, and raised us together, and seated us in heavenly places” (Eph. 2:5–6). Let the Gospel say: “But to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

Let the Prophet therefore now say: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever.” Let us follow the Apostle, the Gospel, and the Prophet. Let us trust in the Lord, so that we may be conformed to the body of God’s glory. Let us now inhabit the Church, the heavenly Jerusalem, so that we may not be moved for ever. For by dwelling in this Jerusalem, we shall dwell also in that one, because this is the form of that one:

> “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:9, 12).

Yet this too is heavenly, and that one heavenly; this too is Jerusalem. That one is indeed the Church of the multitude of assembled angels; but there is also the Church of the firstborn and the Church of spirits established in the Lord (Heb. 12:22–23). Therefore we must be established in the Spirit, and stand with those who dwell there, not roam about, as was said to Moses: “But you, stand with me” (Deut. 5:31). Let us not be wandering runners, uncertain in our paths, or blown away by the wind of empty teaching. For we must remain for ever, if we stand without being moved.

[Note: The Micy manuscript reads: “For in him we are [contemplating] our resurrection in the resurrection of his body; in him we have contemplation through the contemplation of the body,” etc.]

[Note: Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “he speaks,” as does the royal manuscript, which then has “this interpretation … Mount Zion is a mountain of contemplation.”]

[Note: The royal manuscript omits “our Lord Jesus,” and, with Micy, adds “who transformed.”]

[Note: What follows immediately seems to require “the heavenly Jerusalem,” so that we may not be moved. Yet Hilary, because we are already heavenly in Christ—as he says in his exposition of Psalm 122, §3—seems below, as also in his exposition of Psalm 121, §2, to teach that the title “heavenly Jerusalem” applies to the Church militant.]

[Note: We add “is” from the manuscript. It might be preferable to read, “Both this and that are Jerusalem.” The printed editions have “the multitude of those assembled,” against the manuscripts. For what seems difficult here, compare the Apostle’s words to the Hebrews.]

[Note: The royal manuscript reads “forward-runners.”]

### 5. The mountains around us: saints and angels

[Col. 0682B]

Nor do those wishing to stand lack the guardianship of saints or the protection of angels. For it is said: “Mountains are round about it, and the Lord is round about his people from this time forth and for ever.” In accordance with the preceding examples, we understand these to be mountains: surpassing the lowliness of earth, firm, lofty, and immovable.

For since we read that the Church—that is, the Lord in the body—is signified by a mountain, and since we find that the mountains of God leap and rejoice—it is written, “The mountains leapt like rams” (Ps. 113:4)—how can we fail to understand mountains to signify those who, already glorious beyond earthly nature, rejoice in the things of God?

[Note: The printed editions read “therefore these”; the manuscripts’ “for these” is preferable, namely saints and angels. Hilary therefore thought that these provided us with help.]

### 6. We need Christ’s help; our perils; God is everywhere

And lest we should believe that the assistance found in apostles, patriarchs, prophets, or rather angels—who surround the Church with a certain guard—is slight, it is added: “And the Lord is round about his people from this time forth and for ever.”

Perhaps, however, the guard of apostles or angels may be judged sufficient. It is indeed good; but let us also hear Moses. For when the Lord said to him, “Behold, my angel will go before you” (Exod. 32:34), Moses replied, “Unless you yourself are going to walk with me, do not send me away from here” (Exod. 33:15). The protection of an angel is good, but the Lord’s is better.

Our soul is assailed by many snares; many weapons wage war against us. Neither land, sea, nor air is free from danger to our faith. The rare pearls of an unknown sea seize our eyes; the gold of the earth occupies the mind; spiritual wickednesses and the powers of this air fly around with every allurement of our death, lying in wait through the troubles of the present life, through the habits and lust of another’s will, in order that we may become angry, hate, or love. We are awaited and assailed on every side.

Knowing, therefore, that our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against the rulers of this world and spiritual wickednesses, the Lord says at the conclusion of the Gospels: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:26). For he is present; and when faithfully invoked, he is present through his nature. For he is the Spirit penetrating and containing all things. He is not bodily in our manner, so that when he is present in one place he is absent from another; rather, by his present power, and extending himself wherever anything extends itself, while his Spirit fills all things and is in all things, he nevertheless stands by the one who believes in him. For he will be present where three or two are gathered in his name (Matt. 18:20), and he is round about his people from this time forth and for ever.

[Note: We add “something” from the manuscripts, which thereafter read “extending,” not “to one extending.” A little earlier, “bodily in our manner” means in the likeness of us, who are bodily according to the body and bound to the body according to the soul. Similar is the statement in the exposition of Psalm 134, §16: “And this is so in the Lord, who is not seen as bodily in places, but as coming everywhere.”]

### 7. The rod as an emblem of power; our tribulations are brief; the work must be both right and voluntary

But what does it mean that he is round about his people from this time forth and for ever?

> Verse 3. “For he will not leave the rod of sinners over the inheritance of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity.”

By “rod” we must understand power; for it is an emblem of power. Moses received a rod by which he could do all things; Aaron too had a rod. But Pharaoh had a rod, and Nebuchadnezzar had a rod. Therefore the Lord guards us round about, lest the rod of sinners be left over our inheritance.

Tribulations do come, but they do not remain. Persecutions come, but they do not persist. Many want to reduce the freedom of our faith to captivity; but no one rules over the confidence which we have in Christ. For the rod of the sinner will not be left over our inheritance. The Lord is indeed round about his people for ever, lest, conquered and exhausted by the rod’s power, we stretch our hands out to iniquity.

But when the rod falls upon us, it will be removed; and when the sinner presses upon us, he will not be left in place. Whatever we suffer from God’s adversaries is brief. It has the reward of victory, though it does not have the labor of a long battle. The Lord is present. Even if some force compels us, let us keep our hands from iniquities; let us not stretch out our works toward sins. For since the Lord stands round about us, the sinner’s rod will not be left to remain.

[Note: The printed editions read “confession”; they are corrected with the help of the royal manuscript.]

### 8. The Prophet’s prayer for recompense

After this the Prophet turns to praying that the Lord may recompense the person who has kept his hands from iniquity:

> Verse 4. “Do good, O Lord, to the good and to the upright in heart.”

In both expressions he signifies the soundness both of deed and of will. For often a deed is good either for the sake of human favor or because of danger and fear. But unless we are good by will, even if we appear good to people, we are not good before God; because perfect goodness consists in the disposition of an upright heart.

[Note: Only the Paris edition reads “after which”; the others read “and after.” They are corrected from the manuscripts.]

9. The worker of iniquity, turning aside from the Law. — As recompense is present for the good, so it is not absent for the evil. For it follows, verse 5: “But those who turn aside to their bonds the Lord will bring with those who work iniquity.” Here too the expression has a double meaning: “those who turn aside to bonds,” and “those who work iniquities.” Those who turn aside turn from one thing to another—that is, from the good works of an upright heart to bonds. And what bonds are we to suppose these to be? Certainly those which the prophet commanded to be loosed, saying, “Is not this the fast [Col. 0684B] [Note: Thus the Regius manuscript, following the Septuagint. The printed editions: “which the Lord has chosen.” Then the Paris edition from the Micy manuscript: “but loose every knot” (the Micy manuscript here adds “of yours”) “of iniquity.” Other editions: “but loose every bond; undo the knot of iniquity.”] I have chosen, says the Lord? But loose every bond of iniquity; undo the bonds of violent exchanges” (Isa. 58:6). Therefore, if anyone, turning away from God’s commandments, has bound himself with these bonds, he shall be brought with those who work iniquity, that is, into the same punishment of condemnation, becoming a transgressor and unrighteous. For the person who works iniquity is alien to the observance of the Law; and the one who turns aside from the Law transgresses the Law in which he formerly remained.

10. Bonds that hinder faith. — We must not, therefore, turn aside to bonds; nor must our freedom be entangled in the chains of the age and the fetters of worldly affairs. Blessed Paul knows that those who are free ought not to be bound, when he says, “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek to be bound” (1 Cor. 7:27). And he did not understand this merely of the criminal [Col. 0684C] bond of a necessary marriage-tie. There are, moreover, other bonds which impede and bind our faith, fastening it to themselves: above all, the toil of increasing wealth and the insincere pursuit of trade. These bind us by sins, pledges, and transactions, so as to hold us captive and possessed by themselves. Therefore mind, will, and zeal must be freed from them, because those who turn aside to bonds will be brought together with those who work iniquity.

11. But Israel shall be at peace, for the rod of the sinner is not left over it; rather, abiding in perfect faith and everlasting hope, it shall hear said as its allotted portion: “Peace be upon Israel.” For he is our peace, “who made both one” (Eph. 2:14): our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

457

## Psalm CXXV. A Song of Ascents.

[Col. 0684D]

“When the Lord turned back [Note: [Col. 0683D] “In turning back,” which the book again has where it repeats the verse.] (below, “when he turned back”) the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted. Then our mouth [Col. 0685A] was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation. Then they shall say among the nations, ‘The Lord has magnificently dealt with us’” (below, “The Lord has magnificently dealt with them”); “we are” (below, “we became like”) “joyful. Turn back, O Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south” (below, “like a torrent in the south” is not read). “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (below, “sows … shall reap”). “Going, they went and wept, scattering their seed. But coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.”

## Exposition of the Psalm

1. The spiritual understanding of the Psalms cannot wholly be rejected. — If there were not in the Psalms certain prophecies of such a kind that they did not fit the events and persons of the times in which they were written, many would indeed dare to think that nothing in the Psalms is spoken spiritually. They would imagine that we seek certain fabricated assertions and fictitious interpretations, by which we might seem to have understood something loftier and deeper than others; as though we fitted what is written to our own understanding, rather than deriving from what is written the meaning attained by careful and diligent interpretation. For the Scripture of the Law remains, and was completed by prophets in times before the Lord was present—[Note: [Col. 0685D] Bad. and Er.: “entered into”; from which Lipsius made “heard,” not badly, if he had done so with manuscript authority. Yet the reference here is more probably to the publication of the Law by the seventy Jews at the command of King Ptolemy. Hence it came to be discussed by kings and received by nations.] published by Jews, examined by kings, received by nations; but understood and approved by Christians.

2. Understanding of the Law granted to Christians by God. — Perhaps this will seem presumptuous. Certainly it is presumptuous if we claim this glory for ourselves, if we wish to allow our weakness so much that we—fools in the eyes of the world, refuse of the world, and madness to its wise men—should boast of understanding things hidden through so many ages and obscure to so many generations of humankind, things in understanding which kings labored in vain and the very teachers and masters of the Law erred. [Note: [Col. 0685D] Printed editions: “of their understanding,” against the manuscripts.] Yet we understand, because he who says, “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7), is not false. And it is written that he who said, “It was necessary that all things written concerning me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44), then opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures; and said to them, “Thus it is written: that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance [Col. 0685D] and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations” (ibid., vv. 45–46). Therefore, what we understand is not from ourselves, [Col. 0686A] but from him who [Note: [Col. 0685D] Thus the first Paris edition with the manuscripts. The later edition with Bad., Er., and Lips.: “made known things that were unknowable.”] made intelligible what had been unknowable. Understanding, therefore, must be hoped for from him: he will open to those who knock, show to those who seek, and not deny to those who ask. [Note: [Col. 0685D] Regius manuscript: “he will open … show … not deny.”]

3. This Psalm does not narrate a bodily captivity. Subject of the Psalm. — For how can this Psalm be understood, when it disagrees with the history of events? Nowhere is a captivity of this people recorded down to the time of David; rather, long afterward, when his son Solomon had obtained the kingdom, Israel was taken captive and served the Assyrians, and then Judah the Babylonians. How, then, does David pray in this Psalm as though captive? Or how does he rejoice that captivity has been turned away from him, saying, verses 1–3: [Note: [Col. 0686D] Micy manuscript: “when the Lord turned back.” Paris: “when the Lord turned toward.” Other printed editions here: “when turning back”; below, however, “when he turned back,” a reading consistently preserved by the Regius manuscript.] “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became as those comforted. Then our mouth [Col. 0686B] was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation. Then they shall say among the nations, ‘The Lord has magnificently dealt with them’”? Although it is reverent to suppose that the reversal of the future captivity was foretold through the prophet’s knowledge of prophecy, and that things certainly to be done were, through faith in their future accomplishment, recounted as accomplished; nevertheless, the reasoning of the statements and force of the words do not now permit us to understand this as rejoicing in the return granted after the Babylonian captivity. Especially since that same return was afterward followed by a more grievous captivity, and it would be unworthy of the prophet, as though ignorant, [Note: [Col. 0685D] “With all disgrace of that captivity removed.” Thereafter, “with” in place of “for.”] to rejoice as though every reproach of captivity had been removed, when captivity, renewed with an unchangeable reproach, followed again. Rather, the entire Psalm is rejoicing, as we shall show by expounding each point, by the soul that returns from captivity to vices into the freedom of the knowledge of God.

4. Captivity of the soul is more grievous than that of the body. — Bodily captivity is indeed grievous: once the right of freedom has been lost, it is subjected to the rule of conquerors. Bodies then serve, certainly, but the liberty of the faithful soul is by no means taken captive. The three youths singing amid the flames are my witnesses; Daniel, fed by the prophet’s meal amid the hunger of lions, is my witness; Eleazar, free under the laws of his masters through adherence to his ancestral laws, is my witness (2 Macc. 6); [Note: [Col. 0686D] “With their old woman.”] the seven martyrs with their mother are witnesses, giving thanks to God amid unprecedented torments of death (ibid. 7). [Note: [Col. 0686D] In Vatican and Regius manuscripts, “with their old woman.” Three mothers of the seven martyrs are read of as encouraging them to martyrdom; but Hilary here seems especially to have had in view the mother of the Maccabees. A little earlier the Paris edition, as is found in the Regius manuscript, has “by the laws of his father,” for “by his ancestral laws.”] But how much more unhappy is the captivity of the soul! If avarice has seized it, it commits robbery and [Note: [Col. 0686D] “And commits violence” is absent from the manuscript.] violence through the body. If lust has conquered, it shares its slavery with the body. If luxury, anger, hatred, rashness, drunkenness, or envy [Col. 0687A] has subdued it, then soul and body alike serve together under these masters who rule them; and so captivity of the soul is followed by captivity of the body. But the noble character of a devout soul despises the condition of the body. Its service is indeed harsh, but not altogether pitiable for a human being, because [Note: [Col. 0687C] “Although.” Then: “because slaves serve.”] slaves serve as slaves. [Note: [Col. 0687D] We have removed the particle *ei*, inserted here in the Paris edition. This may be explained thus: it is not pitiable that slaves should serve, from which one must understand: nor consequently that bodies should be captive, since they are made to serve. But how pitiable is the captivity of the soul, whose nature is free!] But how unhappy is captivity of the soul!

5. Enslavement to avarice, lust, drunkenness, and other vices. — The miser, who is soon to lose himself, fears losing money. The man of business is sorrowful, anxious, and never at rest, continually detained by fear of loss; forgetful of honor, disregarding friendships, fleeing [Note: [Col. 0687D] Regius manuscript: “flight.”] human kindness, ignorant of religion, and utterly hating goodness. But the person whose mistress is lust—in what mire of disgrace does he wallow! He hangs upon opportunities for adultery; anxious over the stealth of his wantonness, with eyes, mind, and body wholly among prostitutes. Though daily seeing and hearing the human laws against adulterers, [Note: [Col. 0687D] What these laws are will be explained more conveniently in Psalm CXLIV, §9.] he thinks of adultery in the very lawcourt. He fears what he does, yet does not flee what he fears. And what is more miserable than the dominion of drunkenness? To pour into the belly beyond its capacity; [Note: [Col. 0687C] The manuscript supplies what had dropped out of the earlier edition: “to deny the body its proper function.”] to deny the body its proper function; to take reason away from perception; neither to speak, nor remember, nor stand; and to impose a kind of death while nature is still sound. How shameful, too, is the movement of those who rage, the onset of rashness, the spur of hatreds, the anxiety of envy! How great, then, is the disorder and how great the misery of those who serve the evils just named!

6. The voices of those delivered from vices. — But if, having come to know the teaching of wisdom, God’s proclamation, remission [Note: [Col. 0687C] “Of all these sins.”] of sins, [Note: [Col. 0687D] In the printed texts: “of all these sins.” The first two words are deleted on the authority of the Regius manuscript.] resurrection of bodies, fellowship in eternity, and the heavenly kingdom, we pass from the ruling vices—supply, “vices”—from avarice to generosity, migrate from lusts to continence, return from drunkenness to fasts, and rise from fury, rashness, hatred, and envy to [Col. 0688A] placability, reason, mercy, and kindness; learning all these things from the Law and Prophets, the Gospels and Apostles; and singing from the Law: [Note: Above, p. 10, note, we showed from this passage that Hilary also reckons the Book of Judith among the books of the Law. Strictly speaking, the Pentateuch alone is called the Law. But since Hilary divides all Scripture into Law, Prophets, Gospels, and Apostles—so that the first two divisions contain the Old Testament, the latter two the New—it is clear that he calls “Law” everything in the Old Testament that does not belong to the Prophets. Indeed, in Psalm LXIV, §7, he indicates that all Scripture delivered to the Jewish people is called Law, saying: “This prayer does not pertain to the Jew. And although this book, namely the Psalms, belongs to the Law, its prophecy is not of one people.” There you see both the name of Law and of prophecy applied to the Psalter. Thus in Psalm CXVIII, letter 17, §5, when about to cite a passage from Proverbs, he simply says that it is written in the Law.] “The Lord breaks wars; the Lord is his name” (Jdt. 16:3); recognizing from the prophet: “I am he who made heaven and earth from nothing” (Isa. 48:13); [Note: Earlier: “believing.” The reading of our manuscript is supported by what follows: “proclaiming,” etc.] responding from the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1); proclaiming from the Apostle: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things in heaven and on earth were established” (Col. 1:15–16). And when the nations marvel at our conversion from vices to virtues, from ignorance of God to confession of him, then we shall testify that the prophecy of the Psalm can be understood [Note: [Col. 0688C] “We shall testify it to be intelligible.”] by us, saying: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became as those comforted. Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation. Then they shall say among the nations, ‘The Lord has magnificently dealt with them.’” For the Lord turned back our captivity through remission of sins. He freed the soul from the dominion of vices, not reckoning its former offenses, renewing us into new life, and transforming us into the new man, [Col. 0688B] establishing us in the body of his flesh. For he is the Church, containing her entire self in himself through the sacrament of his body. [Note: [Col. 0688D] Thus the Regius manuscript; printed editions, however, have “reforming.”] [Note: [Col. 0688D] In the Regius manuscript, in a second ancient hand: “containing all members,” more ingenious than true. We have already seen several similar expressions, as when in Psalm LI, §16, Christ is said to have assumed in himself the nature of all flesh. What is here stated more compactly is explained there more fully. Thus in *On the Trinity*, II.23, we shall hear that Christ, by assuming one body of flesh, dwells inwardly in all flesh.] Zion did not exist before she was delivered; but Zion is that which has been delivered. The name accords with freedom. For this name belongs not to captivity remaining, but to captivity turned away.

7. At present we have some consolation, but not its fullness. [Col. 0688C] — And when he says, “We became [Note: [Col. 0688C] “As those comforted.” Hilary repeats it in interpretation as “as one comforted.”] as those comforted,” the Apostle too remembers that he was meanwhile comforted as one who was comforted, saying, “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). He who now knows in part and prophesies in part (1 Cor. 13:9), who knows that Jerusalem is laid up for us in heaven, [Note: [Col. 0688D] Instead of “Jerusalem,” “hope” seems to be the reading, from Paul, Col. 1:5: “because of the hope laid up for you in heaven.”] and who says, “To depart is better for me, and to remain with Christ” (Phil. 1:23)—we are now indeed comforted, because the Lord says, “He will send you [Note: [Col. 0689D] The word “Father,” added here in the printed editions, is absent from the manuscripts, as above in Psalm CXX, §6. Soon after “remain,” *se* seems to be deleted. These words nevertheless appear to refer to Christ’s final coming, of which Paul says in Phil. 3:20: “We await a Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation,” etc.] another Comforter” (John 14:16). By saying “another,” he teaches that he himself remains. For he remains: indeed, all creation awaits the revelation of the children of God. That revelation is consummate consolation. But now it is as consolation; [Note: [Col. 0689D] Printed editions: “consolation itself”; corrected from the manuscripts. After “not lacking,” understand “we are.”] though we do not lack it even now, its perfection is still reserved for our consummation.

8. Our conversion is God’s gift. The state of the converted is far better than that of sinners. — Our mouth also is filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation: for the services of our tongue and mouth are not sufficient to render praise to God. [Note: [Col. 0689D] Printed editions: “For it is filled”; soon after, “to render praise to God.” Then Regius manuscript: “For we have changed the services of our tongue and mouth. We have changed crimes,” etc. The same manuscript above adds “our mouth and tongue” after “are not sufficient.”] We have changed crimes into innocence, vices into virtues, ignorance into knowledge, destruction into immortality; [Col. 0689B] and this by God, who grants the grace of things to be repented of and gives the beginnings of new good things. [Note: [Col. 0689D] Bad.: “by God’s grace causing things to be repented of.” Erasmus then added on his own, after “things to be repented of,” the word “end”; and this interpolated reading afterward prevailed. From the Regius manuscript, which reads, “by God, grace bringing repentance,” one might form: “by God, grace bringing the sinner’s mind to repentance.” But the reading presented from the Micy manuscript is complete in itself and makes an entire sentence; the Tours manuscript agrees entirely, except that it has “bringing” for “causing.” God grants the grace of things that must be repented of when he forgives sins; they must be repented of because they must be followed by repentance that is never to cease.] For what time is more desirable for us: the time when we committed adultery, or that in which we would rather have been virgins? When we were drunk, or when we rejoice in fasts? When we served money, or when our money is employed in kindness? When we worshiped demons, or when we rule demons? When we eagerly wished to please the age, or when we overcome the age? When we did not know God, or when we are prepared as heirs for God?

9. As the nations behold this faith of our hope, they say: “The Lord has magnificently dealt with them.” Seeing this change of vices into virtues, they marvel at God’s greatness toward us. We too, from our experience of this blessedness, confess the same thing in the joy of our mouth and exultation of our tongue: “The Lord has magnificently dealt with us; we have become [Note: [Col. 0690D] Printed editions: “as those rejoicing.” The word “as” is absent from the Regius and Tours manuscripts, and also from the Greek and Latin sacred text.] joyful.” For we rejoice that we have now been washed clean from the deep and wretched mire and made new from all the vices of our former life.

10. Why what precedes is in the past, and what follows in the future. — Since the prophet was speaking of the joys of future hope, although, according to the custom of Scripture, he rejoiced as though over things past, yet by his ensuing prayer he makes clear that these are not events of his own time, saying, verse 4: “Turn back, O Lord, our captivity.” If he became as one comforted when captivity was turned away, [Col. 0690A] how does he now pray for it to be turned away from him? In what precedes, the utterance was that of prophetic knowledge announcing future joys as though past; but now the prayer concerning things to be turned away—supply, “evils” or “vices”—is common, and the prophet associates himself with it, [Note: [Col. 0689C] “Announcing.”] although he himself is not captive, [Note: [Col. 0690C] “As though he himself were captive.”] as though he knew himself still to be among those things. [Note: [Col. 0690D] Thus the Tours manuscript, with the agreement of the Regius except that it lacks “not” at this point. But the printed editions have: “he associates himself as though he himself were captive.”] For it is written: “The righteous man, at the beginning of his speech, is his own accuser” (Prov. 18:17); and again: “First confess your sins, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26); and: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). The prophet knows indeed that he is free; but he is subject to God as though captive, either through the discipline of his own confession—because where there is confession of sin, there too is justification from God, as the Lord testified in the case of the publican and the Pharisee. When the Pharisee boasted that he was righteous, while the publican prayed for his sins, he said: “Amen, I say to you, the publican went down more justified than the Pharisee” (Luke 18:14). Therefore the prophet prays that captivity be turned back for all in common, [Note: [Col. 0690D] Printed editions: “common”; more correctly Regius and Tours manuscripts: “in common.” Thus above: “now the prayer concerning things to be turned away is common.”] either for this reason, or because he knew that the whole people had been taken captive by sins. And just as, with—or according to—the Apostle, the whole body suffers together with one member (1 Cor. 12:26), so the prophet is taken captive together with a people captive through sins.

11. Two sowings. — Yet he shows that it is good for himself to pray concerning his captivity, saying, verses 5–6: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. Going, they went and wept, scattering their seed. But coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.” [Col. 0690C] What speech here is directed to the Jews, so that their captivity may seem to be prophesied in this Psalm? What corresponds to the common experience of humankind? Who ever wept while sowing? Or does the Law prescribe for the Jews any practice of this lamentable sowing? By no means, therefore, is this either written or recorded as done anywhere; rather, it is a prophecy connected with what has been said above. The holy Apostle Paul teaches that there are two sowings, of flesh and spirit (Gal. 6:8). He sets forth and enumerates the seeds of each sowing: the flesh sows adulteries, sorceries, revelries, drunkenness, avarice, [Col. 0691A] idolatry, and other things like these (Gal. 5:19); while the spirit sows peace, joy, continence, charity, sobriety, gentleness, and the things consequent upon these (ibid., v. 22); and each person shall reap what he has sown. [Note: [Col. 0691D] “Each person shall reap.”] Since, therefore, a contrite heart is the best sacrifice to God (Ps. 50:19), those who mourn are blessed because they shall be comforted (Matt. 5:5), and each shall reap what he has sown, bearing the fruits of his deeds to judgment as sheaves: we must sow with confession of sins, with mourning over bodily weakness, with lamentation and sorrow of our conscience that we cannot at all worthily fulfill God’s commands according to the purpose of our will. Then what we have sown in tears we shall reap in joy; and, going forth weeping, we shall return with exultation, filled with our fruits [Col. 0691B] and laden with the sheaves of the harvest we have labored for, comforted through Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Notice Concerning the Following Five Expositions

The next exposition, apart from its opening, together with the four following, appears in its entirety among the sermons commonly published under the name of Saint Zeno of Verona. Thus some doubt their authorship. Among them Theophilus Raynaud, in *Erotemata de bonis ac malis libris*, p. 142, says: “The exposition of Psalm CXXVII, which is found in Saint Hilary, is ascribed by others to Zeno of Verona.” There he fails to notice that other expositions too are attributed to each author. Raphael Bagata considers these expositions sufficiently established as Zeno’s on the basis of the antiquity of the manuscript he used. He does not, however, deny that they differ in style from the other sermons. [Col. 0691C] Nor do we deny that this collection of Zeno’s sermons is ancient. In a manuscript which Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, gave to the library of Saint Remigius, we saw it divided into two books, prefaced by: “The discourse of the venerable notary Coronatus on the life of Saint Zeno, bishop and confessor.” In that discourse Zeno is proclaimed to have been sanctified from his mother’s womb and afterward ordained a pastor; to have lived in a monastery until, sought at the command of Emperor Gallienus to deliver an only daughter from a demon, he entered Verona; there not long afterward he died in peace; and thereafter a basilica was built in honor of God and of this holy bishop, not far from the river Adige, where his holy body now rests. This title follows the discourse of Coronatus: [Col. 0691D] “Expositions of Saint Zeno, Bishop of Verona.” Then follows an index of the expositions, which, as we said, are divided into two books and arranged in a far different order from that in which they appear in the *Library of the Fathers*. These points having been noted in passing, it is not at all difficult to demonstrate that the aforesaid expositions were inserted not from Zeno’s sermons among Hilary’s writings, but from Hilary’s writings among Zeno’s sermons.

First, against the antiquity of the manuscript that attributes them to Zeno, we set the Regius and Micy manuscripts, not inferior in antiquity, which attribute the same works to Hilary of Poitiers. Next, their dissimilarity of style from the other Zenonian works, and their similarity to Hilarian works, leave no room for doubt as to their true author. Finally, since they are asserted to be Zeno’s by no testimony of the ancients, while Jerome, in Epistle CXLI to Marcella, attributes the first and second among them to Hilary, and Hincmar, in book *On Predestination*, ch. 25, attributes the third and fourth to Hilary, I do not know whether one may safely refuse to yield to such great authority.

But even if such weighty testimonies in favor of Hilary were lacking, it would be ready at hand to establish the same point by reasoning no less certain and evident.
