Those expositions on the Songs of Ascents, as they stand in Hilary, cannot be regarded as several separate little works wholly without mutual connection, capable both of being detached by others and conveniently attached to Hilary. All form one work, joined together by a preface, which chiefly refutes those who maintained that the Babylonian captivity and the return from it are foretold in those Songs. Thus, if five are assigned to Zeno, the other ten along with their prologue must likewise undoubtedly be assigned to him. Moreover, once these are so assigned to Zeno, the general preface to the Book of Psalms must also be attributed to him, since the author of the prologue to these expositions, §6, acknowledges it as his own. Consequently Zeno must be declared author of the expositions on Psalm CXVIII. For whoever composed them refers more than once to the aforesaid general preface as his own. Cassiodorus, then, was mistaken in praising this preface under Hilary’s name. Augustine too was mistaken in attributing the expositions [Col. 0692C] on Psalm CXVIII—so often in both *On Nature and Grace* and *Against Julian*—not to Zeno but to Hilary. Hincmar was mistaken, as were all others who believed that they used Hilary’s testimony on the Psalms when they brought forward Zeno’s words. It is fairer to suppose that the collection of sermons circulated under Zeno’s name, though ancient, is later than Hilary’s age. Or if anyone maintains that it belongs to that Zeno who lived under Gallienus, he must surely grant that it was afterward enlarged with works by other authors, since no prudent person will deny that it includes several expositions not only by Hilary but also by Basil.

465

## Psalm CXXVI. A Song of Ascents of Solomon.

[Col. 0692D]

[Note: [Col. 0691D] Here also, in the first verse of the Psalm, which alone is prefixed, according to custom, as the subject of the exposition, the reading is: “Unless the Lord has built a house for himself.” Then “in vain” occurs in place of “to no purpose.” Solomon’s name does not appear in the heading of the title, nor in the Greek text; but it is evident from what Hilary says concerning Solomon in §3—namely, “the heading placed before shows him to be the author,” etc.—that Hilary read it.] “Unless the Lord builds [below, “for himself”] the house, in vain have those who build it labored. Unless the Lord guards the city, in vain has he watched who guards it” (below, “those who guard have watched”). “It is vain for you to rise before dawn” (below, “at daybreak”): “rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow. When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, sons are the inheritance of the Lord, the fruit of the womb a reward. As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the sons of those cast forth. Blessed is the man who has filled his desire [Col. 0693A] from them; they shall not be ashamed when they speak with their enemies in the gate.”

## Exposition of the Psalm

1. The understanding of this Psalm is not that which first presents itself. Hilary does not forbid understanding it of earthly captivity. — Both the circumstances of time and the purpose of prophecy demand diligent and attentive care in understanding this Psalm, lest perhaps the mere apparent completeness of its words and the very sequence of physical events move us toward a vain interpretation. This is especially so because many, ignorant of the inward reasons of prophetic teaching, suppose in a Jewish sense [Note: [Col. 0693D] Those times are called past in relation to us, for the Babylonian captivity is already past; or rather in contrast to eternal things, which we hope for but have not yet attained—not in relation to the prophecy. For whether David or Solomon is held to be the author of this Psalm, the captivity occurring under Jeremiah was future in relation to either.] that the prophecies in these Songs of Ascents concern times past: that the captivity of Jerusalem which occurred in the days of Jeremiah was foretold, and that rejoicing over the removal of that captivity was likewise prophesied; [Col. 0693B] and that the things uttered in these Psalms are either the sorrow of servitude or the joy of return. [Note: [Col. 0693D] Paris: “professes”; other printed editions and Regius manuscript: “professes rejoicing.” Tours: “they profess”; corrected from the Micy manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0693D] “And that it is of those times which are proclaimed in these Psalms.”] [Note: [Col. 0693D] In the Paris edition: “and that it is from those.” The word “those” appears able to refer only to the past times.] We do not reject this interpretation or refute their understanding. For it is fitting that the Spirit of prophecy should speak beforehand, according to foreknowledge of providence, of the people’s miserable fall, the punishment due to its impiety, its sufficient satisfaction after long servitude for grave sins, and God’s merciful will in granting them return. [Note: [Col. 0694D] “The Spirit of prophecy”; below, “the grief of prophecy.”] [Note: [Col. 0693D] Regius and Tours manuscripts: “the Spirit of prophecy”; and below, “the grief of prophecy.”]

466

2. He maintains that eternal things are foretold in it. — But since a more grievous and unremitted captivity followed the return from that captivity, and since the building of the restored city was followed by a miserable devastation that remained and was not to be changed; and since they know—or perhaps, “and since I know”—that the glory of spiritual return is reserved for the remnant of Israel, and that the building of the heavenly and holy Jerusalem is prepared until the times of the blessed kingdom of the Lord; especially since the hopes and realities of those days bear witness to the force and kinds of all these Psalms: I do not understand why they wish the prophet’s sorrow to concern only fleeting and changeable evils, and not eternal things as well; or why they understand joy to have been shown more concerning temporal blessings—and things later to be changed into most grievous calamities—than concerning unchangeable and eternal blessings, when it is more worthy of prophetic magnificence to have proclaimed blessed, eternal, and heavenly things. [Note: [Col. 0694D] Lipsius, followed by Paris: “Since, therefore,” and shortly after “also here,” in place of “yet also here”; this would be less objectionable had they adopted it with authority and not against the manuscripts.] Although, therefore, the preceding Psalms have been shown to contain not merely bodily and earthly captivity, just as they contain freedom that is not fleeting, present, or worldly, [Note: [Col. 0694D] Printed editions: “but just as.” More correctly, the Regius and Tours manuscripts have “just as,” without “but.”] so also this Psalm is understood to contain nothing earthly, lowly, or suited to past times. Rather, according to prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic authority, it foretells all those hopes toward which the desire of the patriarchs, the expectation of the saints, the faith of the apostles, the confession of the martyrs, and the course of all believers stretches: that is, toward holy times, citizenship and assembly in the eternal city, the blessedness of the Lord’s kingdom, the new glory of spiritual freedom, fellowship in divine eternity and kingdom. And that this may be understood more fully, let us examine the force and particular meanings of the very words.

[Col. 0694B] **3. Those who interpret this as concerning the destruction and restoration of Solomon’s temple are refuted.**—**VV. 1–2.** Unless the Lord builds a house for himself, those who build it have laboured in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it have kept watch in vain. It is in vain for you to rise early.

Many maintain that holy Solomon, while intent on building the city and the temple, prophesied at that very time of his undertaking the overthrow of the city and temple which he was establishing, since the prefixed title also shows him to be the author of this psalm. For with great energy and all the resources of his kingdom he attempted to accomplish something magnificent and worthy of God. Thus, as it is written, one hundred and fifty thousand men were employed in the various tasks and services of the building work. [Col. 0694C] (2 Chron. 2:17.) And although, according to the practice he had instituted, when everything had been completed the greatest care should be devoted to guarding the city and the temple [Note: “Guarding.”]: nevertheless, since he knew that the operation of so great a labour would prove fruitless, because that same city was to be destroyed by the Babylonians on account of the people’s sins, he said: “Unless the Lord builds a house for himself, those building it have laboured to no purpose.”

They further suppose that this prophecy was fulfilled at the time when, after the people’s captivity, King Darius granted their return and the city was rebuilt through Zerubbabel and [Note: In Zeno, where this treatise begins only with the opening words of section 3, the text here reads “and Joshua son of Josedec”; not badly. Yet the Greek text which Hilary usually follows has *Jesus*, not Joshua.] Josedec (Hag. 2:3; Ezra 5:2).

**4. The very outcome of the building might convict their impoverished interpretation.**—For through the prophet Haggai the Lord spoke thus to these same [Note: The printed editions have “restorers.” The word we substitute from the royal and Tours manuscripts is more suitable; in these, shortly afterward, the reading is “I move heaven,” not “I shall move,” as also in the Greek.] rebuilders [Col. 0695A] of Jerusalem: “Yet once more, I shall move heaven and earth and sea and dry land; and I shall overthrow the thrones of kings” (Hag. 2:7). Therefore the force of the psalm must be understood as applying not only to Solomon’s time but also to Haggai’s. For the labour of both buildings is vain. The city built through Zerubbabel now offers from itself only the ashes of its conflagration and the hideousness of disfiguring ruins. And those thrones of kings, which its rebuilders believed they were restoring [Note: “For the glory of the kingdom.”] [Note: The printed editions here prefix the preposition *ad* (“for”), which is more elegantly absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts and from Zeno.] for the glory of an eternal kingdom, a repeated devastation has overthrown—while the thrones of the remaining kingdoms still await overthrow.

**5. Human works are empty.**—The prophet rightly prophesied that the works of human effort are empty. He knows the watches of human guards to be useless; he knows that the early anxieties of those who rise are futile. The city, both originally founded by him and restored by others, is now no more: neither its first nor its subsequent building accomplished anything. And rightly is he who had been the author of constructing the city also the prophet of its coming overthrow.

Therefore the house which is to endure must be built by God, because unless it is built by the Lord it will not endure. The city must be guarded by God so that it does not perish, because unless the city is guarded by God, it will be destroyed. Let us first understand what the house of God is, so that through this it may be known in what sense it is to be built by him and endure.

**6. What the house of God is in common usage. God is not confined to places.**—A house is the dwelling of one who inhabits it. For the divine discourse accommodates itself to the habit and nature of our understanding, adapting common names for things [Col. 0695C] to express its teaching and instruction. It speaks for us, not for itself; and therefore in speaking it uses our terms.

Our customary usage is accustomed to call either “the house of God” or “the temple” the assemblies of churches—or, as they were then called, temples [Note: We restore here from the manuscripts the particle *then*, absent from the printed editions; Hilary indicates that what we now call a church was customarily called a temple when this psalm was written.]—which the enclosing boundaries of buildings shut in for the hidden religious rite of the sacraments [Note: The royal manuscript with the Tours manuscript reads “for the sacred.”]. Prophetic and apostolic Scripture also has used these names in designating places. Yet we are taught by God’s own words that the house which is thus named by us and among us is not the house of God. For he says: “Heaven is my throne, and earth the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, or what is the place of my rest? Did not my hand make all these things?” (Isa. 66:1–2).

Thus the infinite God is not enclosed in houses made of buildings, nor is immeasurable power contained in any places—he who made all things [Col. 0695D] [Note: The reading is “which made all things.”] [Col. 0696A] [Note: In the two aforementioned manuscripts, “which made all things”; Zeno adds “has wrought.”]—as the Apostle likewise testifies: “God, who made the world and all things in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by hands” (Acts 17:24).

**7. What the true house of God is.**—Then does God have no rest and no dwelling? Perhaps it would not at all be believed that he exists, if he were nowhere. Let us therefore hear him himself testifying concerning his rest and dwelling [Note: “Testifying.” This is also the reading in the edition of our Zeno. From this point: “for ever and ever.”]: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here I shall dwell, because I have chosen it” (Ps. 132:14). He chooses Zion. But is it that Zion concerning which the present complaint of the prophecy says, “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have laboured in vain”? Zion in which the temple stood has been destroyed. Where, then, is the Lord’s eternal seat? Where his everlasting rest? What temple is fit for habitation?

Surely it is that of which it was said: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3:16). This is the house and temple of God: filled with God’s teachings and powers, and capable, through holiness of heart, of the divine inhabitant. Concerning it this same prophet has testified: “Your holy temple, wonderful in righteousness” (Ps. 65:5–6). Human holiness, righteousness, and self-restraint are God’s temple.

**8. The structure of God’s house.**—This house, then, must be built by God. For a house built by human works does not remain; nor does one established by worldly doctrines stand; nor will it be protected by the care of our empty labour and anxiety. It must be built in another manner [Note: The words “it must be guarded in another manner” are absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts and do not appear necessary.]; it must be guarded in another manner: it must not be begun upon the earth, nor upon shifting and crumbling sand [Note: The words “not upon the earth” occur neither in the manuscript nor in St Zeno.]; rather, [Col. 0696C] its foundation must be laid upon the Prophets and Apostles. It must be enlarged with living stones, held together by the cornerstone [Note: “It must be held together by mutual,” etc.; shortly afterward Zeno has “it must be built.” This repetition is very familiar to Hilary.], and built up through the growth of mutual joining into a perfect man and into the measure of Christ’s body; it must also be adorned with the appearance and beauty of spiritual graces.

Built in this way by God—that is, by his teachings—it will not fall. Captive Israel will now attain the building of this house after the fullness of the Gentiles. This house will grow into many houses through the varied edification of believers, in each one of us, for the adornment and [Note: The Vatican manuscript, with the royal manuscript, reads “and fullness.” By the same reasoning, both one and many houses of God are proclaimed here, just as in Psalm 14, section 3, one and many churches are simultaneously spoken of: for although the Church is one throughout the world, each city has its own church; it is one in all, yet there are many, because the one exists in many.] enlargement of that blessed city.

**9. That the Lord may provide for it from the beginning.**—The Lord has long kept watch as guardian of this city: when he protects Abraham in his pilgrimage; when he preserves Isaac, who was to be sacrificed; when he enriches Jacob in servitude; when he sets Joseph, sold into Egypt, over Egypt [Col. 0697A]; when he strengthens Moses against Pharaoh; when he chooses Jesus [Joshua] as leader in wars; when he rescues David from every danger; when he endows Solomon with the gift of wisdom; when he is present with the prophets; when he takes Elijah away; when he chooses Elisha; when he feeds Daniel; when he sprinkles dew upon the children in the furnace; when, as the fourth, he stands beside the three; when, in bringing himself to birth [Note: “To be born.” In the Paris edition, from the manuscript of Micy, “bringing himself to birth.” In the Vatican manuscript, “to be born”; in others, “in bringing himself to birth,” that is, “as he was about to be born.”] from a virgin, he instructs Joseph through an angel, strengthens Mary, and sends John beforehand; when he chooses the Apostles; when he prays to the Father, saying, “Holy Father, keep them; while I was with them, I kept them in your name” [Note: The words “in your name” are absent from the royal manuscript.] (John 17:11–12); and finally, when after his passion he himself promises the perpetual watchfulness of his protection over us, saying: “Behold, I am with you always, until the end of the age” (Matt. [Col. 0697B] 28:20).

This is the eternal protection of that blessed and holy city, which is God’s city through the many who come together into one and through each one of us. For it is a possession pleasing to him: the holy body and the faithful soul.

**10. It must be built by the Lord.**—[Note: The editions of Bad. [Badius], Erasmus, and Lipsius read: “Which house he himself testifies in the Gospel must be built”; wrongly, since the discussion is now no longer of the house but of the city. The Paris edition, from the Micy manuscript, has “but which,” and then omits “is.” Zeno reads “that which.” The royal manuscript in its second corrections reads “but when,” a reading favoured by what immediately follows. Yet we retain “but which,” as it appears in the same manuscript in the first hand and in the Tours manuscript. The purpose of this section is to show Christ as the builder and perfecter of this city, while the occasion also declares the time when this work is to be completed.] But that it is to be built by the Lord, he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying: “Amen I say to you, you will not complete the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes” (Matt. 10:23). The blessed Apostle also recalls this time and building, saying: “But when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then what remains of Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

[Note: The Paris edition from the Micy manuscript has here “of the city,” and shortly afterward “one.” Other books more correctly read: “These cities”—of which, plainly, it had just been said, “you will not complete the cities.”] These cities, then—that is, the dwelling and assembly pleasing to God of the body and soul of each holy person—have this one [Col. 0697C] maker of their perfect [Note: We have removed the word “blessedness,” on the authority of our manuscripts and others, and of Zeno’s edition.] building [Note: The royal and Tours manuscripts read “maker of this perfect building.”]. Therefore this city must be built by the Lord, so that it may grow toward the increase of its completion. For a building already begun is not perfection; rather, through building, the completion of perfection is attained.

**11. Here human skill fails.**—But in building these houses of bodies and cities of souls, human skills are idle. All the watchings of philosophers are empty, their anxieties unproductive, and their pursuit frustrated in investigating nature’s secrets and searching out the works of the world. Such labour builds a house soon to fall. Their early rising, too, will be vain: though it is appointed for all bodies that have come into the light [Col. 0698A], nevertheless those which have not been built by the Lord will by no means attain the glory of that early resurrection which has already begun in the Lord rising from the dead.

**12. How there is here no discourse concerning an earthly building.**—And lest the psalm admit any notion of an earthly and bodily interpretation, it teaches, by the very sequence of its words, both the time of this perfection and what is to be built. For after rejecting human buildings, earthly protections, and the early risings [Note: In the Tours manuscript a contemporary hand has written above this word, “their.”] of those people, it says: “Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow. When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold: children are the Lord’s inheritance, the fruit of the womb is a reward.”

No room for doubt is left in these words; only the faith of understanding is needed, for the words state the matter itself. For subsequent events fulfil the truth of prophecy, while evangelical and apostolic teaching furnishes knowledge of those events. Thus the city which endures must be built by God, because human building is weak and perishable. And lest we suppose this city to be stones, mortar, and timbers, he teaches what this city is and when it will be complete, saying: “Rise after you have sat down.” Sitting is the rest of those at rest; and those who are to be made ready for this perfect city are commanded to rise from it.

**13. Those eat the bread of sorrow who know what is good but cannot attain it by their own effort.**—And who, then, are these who are commanded to rise after they have sat down? Surely, those who [Col. 0698C] [Note: So the royal and Tours manuscripts. Other books read, “who eat.” Jerome’s Letter 141 to Marcella should be consulted; after citing various readings, he appears to prefer, from the fifth edition and Theodotion, “bread of idols,” not “bread of sorrow.”] “eat the bread of sorrow.” Whoever remembers that he was born and lives a human being amid vices eats the bread of sorrow.

For while our will, through fear of God and hope of eternal things, strives toward the perfect works of innocence [Note: The royal manuscript with the Tours manuscript reads “toward the hope of eternal things and the works of perfect innocence.”], a certain natural habit of vices holds us back precisely amid those things from which we struggle to emerge. We thus receive the sorrow of life from the weakness of a failing will [Note: The manuscripts just mentioned read “and weakness.” We would prefer “from weakness.” Here Hilary explicitly teaches that knowledge of truth alone is insufficient for accomplishing a good work.], according to the prophet’s saying: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18).

For when knowledge of truth urges our will toward the progress of attaining what is beneficial, while the habit of nature restrains a will which knows that it ought to advance, progress in knowledge is progress in sorrow [Col. 0699A]: inasmuch as one grieves to be held fast by nature to the degree that one understands through knowledge that nature must be abandoned. Thus comes sorrow in life; thus comes the bread of sorrow. This same prophet recalls this life and sorrow, saying: “You shall feed us with the bread of tears, and give us tears to drink by measure” (Ps. 80:6).

Yet one must always strive and never cease; nor should one fail to press toward perfection because one grieves that what one seeks cannot be reached. But in the very persistence of striving, one must grieve that we cannot attain what we seek. The Lord recalls this sorrow when he says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5), granting the blessedness of consolation in return for grief and sorrow at a perfection not attained.

**14. Because prophecy is certain, what is promised in the future is stated in the present.**—The very order of the words, arranged according to their times, preserves prophetic force: “Rise after you have sat down.” One part of this is in the present—“rise”—so that faith might not hesitate as though concerning uncertain and doubtful matters; for prophetic truth offers, as it were, the present effectiveness of its exhortation and implants in us, while we live, a confidence of hope that does not [Note: In Zeno, “does not hesitate.”] hesitate. But it defers into the future the time of this present command in saying, “after you have sat down.” Thus, in commands not to be doubted, there is the truth of the present; but in attaining them, the ordering of an awaited time is reserved.

**15. The time of the resurrection; the death of the saints is sleep.**—[Col. 0699C] So that they may know when they must rise after sitting down, the fullness of that very time is shown: “When,” he says, [the Lord] “gives sleep to his beloved.” God very frequently calls the death of the saints sleep [Note: Zeno reads, “as to the prophet David.” This removes the difficulty arising from the words “to this same David.” For these words indicate David as author of this psalm, although, by the rules in the preface, section 2, it should be called Solomon’s, since Solomon’s name is written in the title. Yet above, in section 13, with Zeno’s copies agreeing, it again reads: “This same prophet recalls this life and sorrow,” etc. So strong was the habit by which those psalms were generally called Davidic that our Hilary sometimes forgot his own received rules concerning the authors of the psalms—if indeed he can be said to have forgotten here, when in section 3 he recalls that the prefixed title shows Solomon to be the author of this psalm.]: as [God says] to that same David, “When you have slept and rested with your fathers, then I shall raise up one from your seed, who shall be my son, [Note: “And I shall be his father.”] and I shall be his father” (2 Sam. 7:12 ff.); and the Lord says of Lazarus, “Lazarus is asleep” (John 11:11); and the Apostle says concerning those who shall rise: “We who are alive shall not precede those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thess. 4:14).

Therefore, when the fullness of the Gentiles has been received after the sleep of death [Col. 0700A] [Note: “Into sleep.”], and the remnant of Israel saved, then, after this sitting and sleep, comes the time of resurrection. And because, while the fullness of times is being brought to completion, the fullness also of the Gentiles who are to believe will, according to the Apostle, be completed (Rom. 11:25–26), he therefore says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved.” He thereby shows that this is the time of those sitting down rising [Note: The Tours manuscript reads “rising from sitting.” The royal manuscript, “those rising to sit.”], and also the time when sleep is given to the beloved—that is, when every fullness has already been received.

**16. The Lord’s inheritance and reward are the nations whom he begets as sons.**—**V. 3.** He immediately shows, with a certain indication of present reality, who the beloved sleepers and those sitting down who are to rise are [Note: The words “beloved” and “those sitting down who are to rise” are omitted in the royal and Tours manuscripts; we have supplied them from Zeno’s copies, where the earlier reading was “the beloved and those who are to sit, rising.”], saying: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord.” The holy sleepers, that is, and those sitting down who are to rise, are the Lord’s inheritance—not that carnal Jacob or earthly Israel which, through the division of the nations, became a portion and [Col. 0700B] [Note: The noun *funiculus*, “measuring-line,” is consistently neuter.] measuring-line of inheritance, according to Moses’ saying: “When the Most High divided the nations according to the number of the angels of God, Jacob became the Lord’s portion, Israel the measuring-line of his inheritance” (Deut. 32:8).

And because this Israel no longer deserves, on account of its impiety, to be the inheritance, he shows what inheritance there would be, saying: “Behold, children (*huioi*, υἱοὶ) are the Lord’s inheritance; the fruit of the womb is a reward.” Therefore the inheritance consists in the Lord’s children, which he has received as the reward of the fruit of the womb. For this is not an empty fruit, since God, who existed beforehand [Note: The printed editions, including Zeno’s, read “by which, when.” The word “by which” is correctly absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts. Then: “God existing beforehand,” that is, God who existed beforehand. Hilary likes the word *manet*, “remains,” to signify God’s existence, which has neither beginning nor end. This passage is illuminated by these words from the common edition of Jerome: “The Lord himself, born of the Virgin, became the fruit of the womb; his assumed humanity received this reward, that the nations called in his sons should be his inheritance.”], is born from the virginal womb [Col. 0700C]. For his reward is an inheritance, [Note: “And this inheritance.”] and the inheritance is children. “As many as received him,” he says, “he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12); and again: “Little children, I am with you yet a little while” (John 13:33).

These children, therefore, are the inheritance, and this inheritance is the reward [Note: “Is the fruit,” as in Zeno.] of the fruit of the womb. The Lord, then, is the fruit of the womb, whom the Virgin, bringing forth from herself for the fruit of our life [Note: Many passages in Book 10 *On the Trinity* persuade us that “from herself” refers to the Word, not to the Virgin; such as section 15: “But if, by taking flesh to himself from the Virgin through himself, he adapted to himself from himself also the soul of the body conceived through himself”; and shortly afterward: “if the powerful Word God was not able to take flesh from himself within the Virgin.” He expressly notes that the Word was conceived from the Virgin’s womb “from himself,” in order to show conception without a man’s agency. Shortly afterward the Tours manuscript reads “he willed to be the fruit of the womb.”], brought forth. And this is his reward: he who, in being born from the Virgin, [Col. 0701A] willed to be the fruit of the womb, so that the nations whom he would beget through faith as sons might be his inheritance.

**17. He earned a reward because he became human.**—That, because he became the fruit of the womb, he received this reward of inheritance, another psalm testifies, saying: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2:8). The Apostle also testifies:

“He who, being in the form of God [Note: The royal and Tours manuscripts read “being established.”], did not regard equality with God as a thing to be grasped; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:6 ff.).

This, then, is the reward of the fruit of the womb: bestowed in the Name, rendered in honour, granted in glory. And the birth which assumed human weakness receives this recompense from his immortal nature: that because he himself [Note: “Himself” is absent even from Zeno’s edition.] became the fruit of the womb, the inheritance of the nations may also become his reward, and that inheritance may itself be children.

**18. The arrows are prophetic and apostolic teaching.**—Then follows **V. 4**: “As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the children of those cast out.” Arrows serve here in that, once shot, they travel in swift flight and are directed in a straight course toward their respective targets. We read that there are arrows which the Lord employs when he says: “He sent forth his arrows and scattered them” (Ps. 18:15).

Isaiah also writes thus, which may be understood [Col. 0701C] to be said [Note: Perhaps “said.” The Vatican and Micy manuscripts read “perhaps said.” Hilary interprets the same words absolutely of the Lord in Psalm 119, section 8: “We recall that in the same Isaiah the Lord himself is called an arrow in this way: ‘He made me like an arrow.’”] even of the Lord himself: “He made me like a chosen arrow, hid me in his quiver, and said to me: It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. 49:2).

Such, then, are God’s swift-flying arrows, faithful in their strike [Note: This is also the reading in Zeno and in the royal and Tours manuscripts. Other books read “in their cast.” What “faithful in their strike” means is explained by the final words of the following section: “wounding unbelieving hearts with the weapon of doctrine,” etc.]. As spiritual reasoning shows, they must be understood to signify the prophetic and apostolic teachings, in which the word of God is sent forth everywhere—piercing, rebuking, flying.

**19. The children of those cast out: prophets or apostles.**—Although in many places we remember also deadly and lethal arrows, concerning which it is written: “He made his arrows for those who burn” (Ps. 7:14). Yet nothing can here be understood as said about avenging arrows, because it now says: “As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the children of those cast out.”

Pharaoh was cast out into destruction in the Red Sea because of the crime of his impiety (Ps. 136:15). [Note: Jerome, in Letter 141 to Marcella, thought that Hilary cited this passage in order to show the Apostles as “children of those cast out,” since they were commanded to shake the dust from their feet. Since he did not approve this interpretation—because on that reasoning the Apostles would more properly be called those shaking out, or shakers, rather than those cast out—and since he did not dare criticize Hilary out of reverence, he attributed the error to the presbyter Heliodorus, with whom, he says, Hilary was intimate. Hilary, he says, had consulted him; and Heliodorus, having nothing from Origen to answer, preferred to insinuate his own opinion rather than confess ignorance. But, with deference to so great a man, we say that Hilary understands *excussorum*, “of those cast out,” not actively but passively: “children of those cast out” means the same as children of the accursed, or of those who are accursed. He introduced the passage about dust shaken out, as also that about Pharaoh cast out, solely to show that *excussus* in Scripture denotes a curse. Finally, Hilary’s interpretation is precisely the one which so greatly pleased Jerome in the aforementioned letter. For after giving various interpretations from Hebrew, he adds: “I read the book of a certain man and found in it an elegant interpretation: the Jews are called cast out from the temple, Law, and grace of the Lord—that is, rejected; and the Apostles are their children, begotten from their seed and held in the Lord’s hand in the likeness of arrows.” But, as Jerome himself says, writing his work hurriedly and oppressed by severe stomach pain, he did not sufficiently attend to Hilary’s meaning in this somewhat difficult passage.]

We know likewise that dust shaken out by apostolic feet is a pronouncement of curse (Matt. 10:14). And because either the prophets themselves, who, being children of those cast out—that is, of sinners and accursed persons—were sent forth as flying and faithful arrows of heavenly teaching; or the Apostles and teachers of churches, who believed from nations cast out into curse through their own impiety [Note: “Born” is understood here. Thus the preceding word “Apostles” does not mean only the Twelve, who were not born from the Gentiles, but apostolic men and teachers of churches, who preached Christ far and wide. The same sense must be understood in Psalm 14, section 3, where the Apostles are said to have prepared many dwellings for God throughout all parts of the world that can be reached, even on islands in the Ocean. Or, if it is referred to the Twelve, “from nations cast out” means from peoples and nations under a curse.]—therefore he says: “As arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the children of those cast out”: traversing the world in flight, wounding unbelieving hearts with the weapon of doctrine, and piercing all inducements to sin with the saving dart.

**20. And so that it might be understood that this had been said of those whom God was then sending forth from among the children of those cast out as arrows for the teaching of salvation, the following words ensue: V. 5.** “Blessed is the man who has filled his desire from them; they shall not be put to shame when they speak with their enemies [Col. 0702C] in the gate.”

Blessed, then, is the one who can fill his desire from them—that is, either from the arrows or from the children of those cast out: who fills himself with the desirable words of teaching, and is satisfied from the proclaimed [Note: The printed editions read “hoped-for.” The Vatican manuscript with the royal manuscript reads “prayed-for.” We restore from Zeno’s copies and the Tours manuscript “proclaimed”—that is, proclaimed by the Apostles and prophets, who above were understood as the children of those cast out.] fruits of future goods which are awaited. And in order to show that these are builders through God’s teaching [Col. 0703A] of the city he mentioned above, he therefore concluded thus: “From them they shall not be put to shame when they speak with their enemies in the gate.”

The phrase “from them” either refers to the blessed man who filled his desire from them, or belongs properly to the children of those cast out themselves, because from them they are not put to shame when they speak with their enemies in the gate.

**21. The confidence of the righteous against their enemies.**—There is no uncertainty about who will speak in the gate of the city built by the Lord through their preaching. We recall that another psalm says: “You raise me up from the gates of death, that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9:15). Here there are indeed many gates in which the prophet, raised from the gates of death, [Col. 0703B] proclaims all God’s praises. But we know there is one royal, lordly, heavenly gate, of which it was said: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” [Note: “Into it,” with the Greek.] (Ps. 118:20).

And when these children of those cast out are not put to shame as they speak with their enemies in the gate [Note: Zeno has “they shall not be put to shame” here, not “these.” Shortly afterward, the word “not” before “shall be put to shame” has been erased in the royal manuscript. That “not” must be retained, as above “these.” For Hilary’s reasoning is this: since the reference is not to gates in the plural but to a gate in the singular, the passage must be understood of the gate through which the righteous enter, and of those enemies who will be driven in shame from access to that gate.], it follows that they speak without shame to those enemies of theirs who will not deserve to enter with the righteous. They reproach them with impiety toward God, disobedience toward those preaching, unbelief in eternal promises, hatred toward the innocent, and cruelty toward the very members of the Church. They themselves are confident and tremble with no uncertainty in their faith and religion, but bar these enemies from access and entrance to him who says, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6): [Note: So the Tours manuscript. Other books read, “that is, through our Lord,” etc.] our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever and ever. [Col. 0703C] Amen.

## PSALM 127. A Song of Ascents.

Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. You shall eat the labours of your fruits; you are blessed, and it shall go well with you. Your wife is like an abundant vine at the sides of your house. Your children are like young olive plants around your table. Behold, thus shall every person who fears the Lord be blessed. May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things [below: “may you see the good”] of Jerusalem all the days of your life. And may you see your children’s children: peace [below: “and may you see peace”] upon Israel.

476 **TREATISE ON THE PSALM**

**1. The distinction between fear of God and human fear.**—Whenever Scripture speaks of fear of the Lord, it must be observed that it is never left alone as though sufficient for bringing faith to perfection [Col. 0704A]. Rather, many things are added or set before it, from which the nature and perfection of fear of the Lord may be understood. We learn this from what was said through Solomon [Note: The printed editions read “in Proverbs,” against the manuscripts, which with great agreement read “in the *Prooemia* [Prefaces].” From this we judge that *Paraemiis* should be restored, especially since Cyprian, in Book 3 to Quirinus, repeatedly cites “Solomon in the *Paraemiae*,” and Tertullian attests the use of the same term in *On Modesty*, section 18, where he says, “Solomon in the Proverbs, which we call *Paraemiae*.”] in the Proverbs: “For if you call upon wisdom and raise your voice to understanding, if you seek it as silver and search for it as treasures, then you shall understand the fear of the Lord” (Prov. 2:3 ff.).

We see, then, through how many stages one arrives at the fear of the Lord. Wisdom must first be invoked, the entire duty of reading assigned to understanding, and wisdom sought out and thoroughly investigated; then the fear of the Lord is to be understood.

But so far as the common judgment of human opinion goes, fear is not understood in this way. Fear is the trembling of human weakness, dreading to undergo what it does not wish to happen to itself. It arises and is stirred in us by consciousness of guilt, by the authority of a superior, by the attack of a stronger power, by the occurrence of illness [Col. 0704B] [Note: The Paris edition reads “cause.” Shortly afterward the royal and Tours manuscripts have “recurs” rather than “occurs.”], by encountering a wild beast, and by the experience of every evil. This fear, therefore, is not taught; it arises from the nature of weakness. Nor do we learn what ought to be feared; rather, the very things feared instil their terror into us.

2. The fear of God is not natural. It lies in obedience and love. — But concerning the fear of the Lord it is written: “Come, children, listen to me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12). Therefore the fear of God must be learned, because it is taught. For it consists not in terror but in the rationality of instruction; nor is it to be entered upon through the trembling of nature, but through the observance of the commandments, the works of an innocent life, and the knowledge of truth. For if God is to be feared because many things have been burned by lightning, struck down by thunder, or have now collapsed in an earthquake, now been swallowed in a chasm, then fear that is stirred by terror at such occurrences has no merit of faith. But for us, the whole fear of God is in love: perfect love brings His fear to completion. The proper duty of our love toward Him is to obey His warnings, submit to His ordinances, and trust His promises. Let us therefore hear Scripture saying: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all His ways, love Him, and keep His commandments with all your heart and with all your soul, that it may be well with you?” (Deut. 10:12–13). In words fitting and corresponding to these, the prophet spoke at the opening of the psalm, saying:

> Verse 1. Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in His ways.

He shows that those who fear are blessed, not because of our trembling—for in other matters trembling is the cause of fear [Note: The royal manuscript, together with the Tours manuscript, reads “on earth.” The reading in the other manuscripts must certainly be retained: that is, trembling is the cause of fear of other things, apart from God. Shortly afterward the same manuscripts read, “not in the fear of obedience, but the evidence of fear,” etc. Nor should anything be changed here. Only after “in obedience,” understand: “not in obedience alone, but in the obedience of love”; for, as stated above, p. 394, “the activity of love takes precedence over the activity of obedience.” Obedience alone is often the effect of terror, etc.]—nor because of terror before One who is terrible, but because they walk in God’s ways. For fear, as we have said, lies not in dread but in obedience; and the evidence of fear is compliance. Otherwise, if someone fears and yet does not obey, he will indeed be fearful through natural trembling, but he will not be blessed through the duties of fear.

3. The ways of the Lord are many, and one. — There are many ways of the Lord, although He Himself is the Way (see the literal exposition of Ps. 118, §10). But when He speaks of Himself, He calls Himself the Way, and He shows why He called Himself the Way, saying: “For no one can come to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). Yet when the discourse concerns the prophets and their writings, through which one proceeds toward Christ, then there are many ways converging from every side into the one Way. Both points are indicated in the same passage by the prophet Jeremiah, who says: “Stand in the ways of the Lord, inquire concerning the eternal paths of God, see which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jer. 6:16). Thus many ways must be sought out, and one must persist in many, so that we may find the one which is good: through the instruction of many, that is, we shall discover the one way of eternal life. For there are ways in the Law, ways in the Prophets, ways in the Gospels, and ways in the Apostles; there are also ways in the various works commanded. Those who walk in them through the fear of God are blessed—the persons addressed here.

4. All are one in Christ. — Verse 2. “You shall eat the labors of your fruits.” A discourse begun in the plural is referred to one person, teaching us [Note: “Us, all who have believed in Christ,” thus also in the Zeno copies.] that all of us who have believed in Christ are one, as the Apostle confirms: “For you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. 3:28). Therefore, whether He speaks to one or to many, what is signified in one is also signified in many.

5. The labors of fruits are not ordinarily eaten. — We should observe that this prophetic saying differs from ordinary usage. For in the course of this life, those who eat eat the fruits of their labors, taking them from the returns of work accomplished. But the prophet says [Note: Jerome, again in the same Epistle 141 to Marcella, criticizes this passage of Hilary because he preferred “the labors of fruits” to “the labors of hands,” and again lays the blame of the error upon Heliodorus. Yet there is no reason why Heliodorus should be judged to have been consulted by Hilary on this matter, much less to have erred. Hilary had not adopted the new translation, but was interpreting the Latin text. The Latins, however, as Jerome himself observes in the passage mentioned, were deceived by the ambiguity of the Greek word, translating καρπούς (*karpous*) as “fruits” rather than “hands,” although καρποί (*karpoi*) also means “hands.” In fact Augustine, and the expositor of the Psalms found among Jerome’s works, read “labors of fruits” with our Hilary; nor do the old Roman, Milanese, German, Chartres, and other Psalters give another reading. Nevertheless, we do not dispute Jerome’s preference for “labors of hands.”] that “the labors of fruits” are to be eaten. Human reason does not grasp the meaning of this statement. For fruit comes from labors, not labor from fruits. Further, labor is a service of the body, while fruit is the reward of labor. But bodily service is incorporeal, although it is performed by the body. Yet we can eat nothing except what is bodily.

6. Here labor is the food of the soul; afterward come fruits. — But the prophet treats of nothing earthly or present. His discourse concerns the blessedness of those who fear the Lord and walk in His ways. Those who walk in the ways of the Lord will eat the labors of their fruits. For this is not bodily eating, since what is to be eaten is not bodily. Rather, we have here spiritual food, nourishing our soul unto life [Note: The printed editions read “in life.” The reading “unto life,” found in the royal and Tours manuscripts, is preferable, since it signifies that the soul’s life is sustained by this food. Where the duration of this present life is indicated below, the text reads “in this bodily life.” From the royal manuscript we have also added the word “chastity.”]: namely, good works of goodness, chastity, mercy, patience, and tranquility, in which we must labor against the vices of our bodies. The fruit of these labors lies in eternity; but here the labor for eternal fruits must first be eaten [Note: In Zeno: “because”; incorrectly.], and in this bodily life our soul must thereby be nourished [Note: The Paris edition alone reads, “through the food of good labors.” Then, in Zeno, “obtaining.” Hilary uses *obtinentes* (“obtaining”), as though he had previously read, “we ought to nourish our life.” Here *obtinentes* signifies not possession but merit. For shortly afterward he calls Him the living bread whom we shall taste in heaven, and of whom we receive a pledge in the sacrament of the Eucharist, although he then turns his discourse to that venerable sacrament when he says, “whoever receives Him unworthily,” etc.; because Christ is one and the same, the one bread whom we taste on earth and in heaven.], through the food of these labors, obtaining the living bread, the heavenly bread, from Him who said: “I am the living bread [Note: In the Mic. manuscript: “who came down from heaven.”] from heaven” (John 6:41). Whoever receives Him unworthily, according to the Apostle’s command, incurs judgment upon himself (1 Cor. 11:29). These, then, are the labors of fruits which must be eaten: the labors, that is, of those fruits which shall be reaped in heaven. Now, while we are on earth, works must be undertaken. For these now satisfy the soul; these will follow it to heaven with their fruits [Note: Thus the royal and Tours manuscripts. But the printed editions continue: “less aptly for Hilary’s meaning, who is explaining the present and future fruits of good works.”]. Finally, in the following verse the prophet sets forth the blessedness of each of these times, saying: “You are blessed, and it shall be well with you.” Of these, one is obtained in the present—“you are blessed”; while “it shall be well with you” is reserved for the future, because [Note: Thus we emend from the manuscripts and the Zeno copies, where the earlier reading was: “because again the labor of future fruits will be eaten.”] for the time being the labor of future fruits is eaten.

7. A temporal blessing is not promised to the righteous. — Verses 3 and 4. “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine along the sides of your house. Your children shall be like young olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall every man who fears the Lord be blessed.” This saying may perhaps seem to many suited to the joy of a present blessing: that by God’s mercy there may be peaceful and beneficial well-being in the household of one’s wife [Note: “Peaceful.”], and a most delightful gathering of children about the meal. But if these things were perfectly good—though they are good, they are nevertheless not heavenly goods—and if blessedness in the fear of God consisted in them, then Abraham, the foremost man of faith and of the fear of God, would certainly have possessed them. Yet his wife was barren for a long time and twice carried away; his one son from the promise was commanded to be offered as a victim and, brought to sacrifice, caused him the sorrow of childlessness. Isaac himself then had two sons at variance, enemies even to murderous hatred. Jacob, unexpectedly husband of an unknown wife, forced by deceit into another marriage, mourning the funeral of a living son because of the fratricidal lie of his brothers, lacked the blessings of those who fear God. Shall sanctification through faith not be found among those in whom and from whom faith exists? And how many sinners do we see flourishing in household, spouse, and children! Furthermore, will that happy and blessed virginity be deprived of God’s blessings, leaving it no ground for its blessedness? And where then will Paul’s saying be: “I wish that all people were as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:7)? I do not know, then, how the prophet could have made that a perfect blessedness which is denied to saints, common among sinners, and not to be hoped for by virgins.

8. What is promised them is spiritual. Who the bridegroom Christ is. — Therefore, since according to human understanding the wording of this saying does not explain a proper and perfect blessedness, minds and ears must be raised to spiritual instruction. For, according to the Apostle, “the whole Law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14); and he himself pursued not a lowly or earthly blessedness but a spiritual one, saying: “Blessed is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Eph. 1:3). Since, therefore, he shows that we are blessed in spiritual and heavenly things [Note: The royal manuscript reads, “shows that they are blessed.”], that perfect blessedness of the saints is not to be expected in these earthly and bodily things. Rather, we must understand that, through the naming of bodily and earthly things, an understanding of heavenly goods is to be attained. When the Lord is the bridegroom according to the Gospels, and according to John has a bride (Matt. 9:15; John 3:29), should we suppose that earthly and bodily spouses are meant? Certainly not. Rather, through this customary manner of speech we are taught that He is the One promised to the nations, to whom the Church was betrothed by the Father as an inheritance, through the adoption of the body which He would take from the Virgin [Note: In the earlier printed text: “through acquisition.” More correctly, in Zeno and the royal and Tours manuscripts: “through adoption,” with nearly the sense in *On the Trinity*, II.27: “The dignity of power is not lost when the lowliness of flesh is adopted,” that is, through the assumption of a body. Thus, because He Himself became the fruit of the womb, the nations might also become His reward and inheritance, as stated in the preceding exposition, §17.].

9. The wife of the righteous is wisdom. What a proverb is. — To learn now what should be understood under the designation “wife,” we must consider what is treated elsewhere under this same name of wife. Solomon therefore says: “I sought to bring Wisdom as a bride to myself” [Note: The printed editions read, “Solomon thus says: Because I sought…” They are corrected from the Tours manuscript, supported by the royal manuscript.] (Wis. 8:2). And because whoever seeks a bride seeks a wealthy one, he recalls the riches of this bride of his, saying: “She glorifies nobility, having companionship with God, and the Lord of all loved her” (Wis. 8:3); and, “if anyone desires much knowledge, she knows the things which are from the beginning, and foresees the things that are to come” (Wis. 8:8). Again: “Who shall find a valiant wife? She is more precious than stones of great value [Note: “Precious.” Shortly afterward: “because proverbs,” as in Zeno, which then explain and announce the matter coherently.] of this kind” [Note: This expression refers to the woman, in accordance with the Greek, ἡ τοιαύτη πολυτελῶν (*hē toiautē polytelōn*), “such a woman [is more precious] than costly things.” In the printed editions, however, it was wrongly placed after the words “and these,” which follow immediately.] (Prov. 31:10). These things are said in Proverbs, because a proverb does not explain what merely sounds forth in its words, but communicates the force of its sayings through the use of ordinary words. The Lord teaches in the Gospels what is to be understood by proverbs, saying: “The hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but shall openly declare the Father to you” (John 16:25). Therefore, according to the principle of proverbs, we must recognize the valiant wife: namely, the one whom Solomon wished to take as his bride. Of her he again says: “I therefore resolved to bring her to live with me [Note: In Zeno, as in the royal manuscript: “to feast with me”; this is refuted no less by the Greek text, εἰς συμβίωσιν (*eis symbiosin*, “for life together”), than by the Latin.], and I became a lover of her beauty” (Wis. 8:9). This Wisdom, then, taken as a wife, is valiant: accomplishing all things, bringing them under her control, and strong in the labor of useful works. She is pleasing to God, worthy through her teaching [the reading is uncertain], perfected by knowledge of past things and awareness of things to come.

10. Wisdom is fruitful in children, that is, good works. — This is the wife of the one who fears God; like a fruitful vine spreading over all the sides of her house, she extends herself through every aspect of our works. There is no doubt that the house is the dwelling-place of our soul, which each person cleanses, by entering upon the fear of God and His ways, as a habitation for Wisdom. The children who come from her will be like young olive shoots around our table. He does not say that they will be around the feast, but around the table. [Note: It is noteworthy, first, that for Hilary the table of the Lord and the table of sacrifices are one and the same, as is clear from his exposition of Ps. 68, §19: “The Apostle has testified that there is a table of sacrifices—to say nothing of the Law, which contained within itself the figure of what was to come—when he says: ‘You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons.’” Second, he understands it as the Lord’s table from which we receive the food of living bread. Finally, he calls that bread living not merely because it has the power to give life to those who receive it, but rather because it itself lives and, from the life it has in itself, has power to give life to others.] For the table of the Lord is that from which we receive food, namely, the living bread, whose power is such that, being itself living, it gives life also to those who receive it. There is also the table of the Lord’s readings, at which we are nourished with the food of spiritual instruction. [Note: The Paris edition reads: “we are nourished, who follow the teaching of God,” apparently in imitation of Lipsius, who on private authority had substituted “they are nourished, who follow the teaching of God.” Here, after the table of the Lord’s sacrifice, the table of the Lord’s readings is mentioned, which is celebrated in the Church at the beginning of that same sacrifice. In Zeno, however, the words “but those who follow the teaching of God” are wrongly omitted. After them Lipsius, with still less prudent boldness, added—and the Paris edition retained—“but there is a table,” as though the following words, “of which it is written in another psalm, ‘Let…,’” referred to some third table rather than to the same table of the Lord’s readings, or table of teaching. Hilary shows in his exposition of Ps. 68, §19, on the authority of the Apostle in Rom. 11:9, that this table of teaching is signified in the cited psalm passage.] But those who follow the teaching of God—of which it is written in another psalm, “Let their table before them become a snare, a trap, a recompense, and a stumbling-block” (Ps. 68:23); for every reading of prophecy, rightly understood, serves them as a trap and stumbling-block—[Note: The Tours manuscript lacks the words “but those who follow the teaching of God.” Yet they are appropriately repeated because of the intervening parenthesis.] but those who follow the teaching of God, unless they are engaged in the service of good works, will gain no benefit from the food of that table. For as children come from a wife, so works of good will are begotten from wisdom. These, then, like young olive shoots, will surround our table; that is, they will shade the knowledge of our teaching with the fruits of the finest branches. The prophet also preserved this principle by calling the olive “newly planted” (*neophyta*), that is, recently planted: because through Wisdom, taken as a wife, whose children are faithful works, this same olive is planted in the soil of our bodily existence. [Note: “Is planted.”] This, then, is the wife who, like a fruitful vine, is spread along the sides of our house. These are the children: works begotten from such a wife, standing [Note: In Zeno: “standing by.”] like planted olive trees around our table. And because this is the blessedness of those who fear God, the prophet added: “Behold, thus shall every man who fears the Lord be blessed.”

11. Blessedness is not of this age; what is meanwhile granted to us. Wisdom is the parent of innocence; innocence, of blessedness. — To the merit of the one who fears God is joined also the prophet’s prayer: “May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem.” We have already spoken often in the preceding psalms of Jerusalem and Zion, from which, or in which, the fulfillment of every good thing is to be hoped for. For although we now enjoy heavenly goods, still greater things are reserved for us in Zion and Jerusalem in hope for the times to come. This present age cannot contain the promised goods. For “woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7): in it the devil has sown tares; it is a realm of corruption, a place of iniquity, and a valley of weeping; in it are the world-rulers of this darkness. Yet in the meantime we possess the light of the goods promised to us, in which we behold, as through a mirror and in a riddle [Note: Hilary’s printed editions read only “through a mirror”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.], an image of blessed realities. Then we shall see face to face, and rejoice in the true and visible contemplation of our blessedness—not with a cloud of obscurity interposed, nor with the mirror’s reflected brilliance competing with our sight—beholding the fruits of our works and seeing the reward of an innocent life. For just as works are begotten from wisdom, so recompense is born from works. Wisdom, therefore, is the mother of innocence; and innocence in turn bears the fruit of recompense. We shall attain these things when the devil has been crushed, the sting of death blunted, and every ruler and power of this age removed; when peace is within us, the enemy defeated and slain. The prophet testifies to this in the conclusion of the psalm itself, saying:

> Verses 5 and 6. May the Lord bless you from Zion; may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life; may you see your children’s children; and may you see peace upon Israel.

Let us therefore hope for the good things of heavenly Jerusalem, of Mount Zion, and of the peace of Israel (Ps. 75:3), because the Lord’s dwelling is in peace—in our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed unto ages of ages. Amen.

483. PSALM 128. A Song of Ascents.

“They have often assailed me from my youth,” let Israel now say. “They have often assailed me from my youth; yet they could not prevail against me. Sinners built [Hilary: “were building”] upon my back; they prolonged their iniquity. The righteous Lord will cut down [Hilary: “cut down”] their necks [Hilary: “the necks of sinners”]. Let all who hate Zion be confounded and turned backward in shame. Let them become like grass upon buildings [roofs], which withers [Hilary: “has withered”] before it is pulled up; with it the reaper will not fill his hand, nor the gatherer of sheaves his bosom. And those who passed by did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we bless you in the name of the Lord.’”

## Exposition of the Psalm

1. This psalm teaches patience. The godly often face conflict from their earliest years. — By prophetic sayings we are instructed to endure present sufferings; and the weakness of our nature, always impatient against the injuries of the world, receives instruction in patience [Note: In the Paris edition and in Zeno: “the instruction of wisdom.”] from him who says in the present psalm: “They have often assailed me from my youth.” The life of a religious person is not idle, nor does he seek a quiet life. From the very years of his youth he is assailed, and he is assailed often. Thus the hatreds of his assailants are neither recent nor rare, but have been hostile even from the first beginnings of life. For this reason they test faith, bear witness to patience, and earn the crown of unconquered virtue. The blessed Apostle Paul knew this crown of a long contest, saying: “No one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully.” Contest alone is not enough for the crown: one must contend lawfully, that is, one must undergo all the wars of suffering. It is not enough to have served in battle once, or in the war of one contest. Let us hear this lawful contest itself [Note: “This very one who competes lawfully.”] when he says of himself: “In labors more abundantly, in stripes beyond measure, in prisons more frequently, in deaths often; from the Jews five times I received forty [Note: In the royal and Tours manuscripts: “minus one.” Greek: παρὰ μίαν, *para mian*, “one short.”] lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, [Note: Hilary’s printed editions read: “three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was in the depths of the sea.” We prefer the reading of the other books, which agrees more closely with the Greek: τρὶς ἐναυάγησα, νυχθήμερον ἐν τῷ βυθῷ πεποίηκα, “three times I was shipwrecked; I have spent a night and a day in the deep.”] three times I suffered shipwreck, I spent a night and a day in the deep” (2 Cor. 11:24). Rightly, having passed through so many and such great battles, he dared say: “Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4:8), because no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully.

2. The devil is the author of human injuries; a human being is his instrument. — This prophetic utterance also applies to him:

> Verse 1. They have often assailed me from my youth.

It is a matter for the greatest exultation of confidence to remember wars so great and so numerous. Yet now the name of the assailants is left unstated, and only the assault itself is mentioned. We must understand why the authors of the assault are passed over in silence. All human wrongs inflicted upon religious people do not have the same authors as they have instruments. The actual execution is human, but the prompting is the devil’s. The Apostle gives us this understanding when he says: “For our contest is not against flesh and blood, but against the powerful rulers of this world, of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). [Note: Baden, Erasmus, and Lipsius, as in Zeno: “the powers of this world, the powers of this darkness.” The Paris edition, from the Mic. manuscript: “the powers of the world, the powerful ones of this darkness.” Hilary often reads *mundipotentes* (“world-rulers”) as one word, translating the Greek κοσμοκράτορας, as above in §11 of the preceding exposition: “the world-rulers of this darkness.” Yet he sometimes renders the word separately; an example is found in Ps. 124, §6: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the powerful ones of this world and spiritual wickednesses.” Therefore the reading of the royal and Tours manuscripts is the truer one, reconciling the two preceding forms: the first has “of this world,” and the second “powerful ones.” See the literal exposition, Ps. 118, §5. Then, in place of “spiritual wickedness,” the Tours manuscript has written above it “spiritual wickednesses.”] And again: “According to the prince of this air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience” (Eph. 2:2). These spiritual wickednesses therefore work in those who are disobedient to God’s law; they choose them as workers of their will, intending to employ them in their own affairs through the service of another’s intervention [Hilary: “to employ”].

3. We understand this not only from the Apostle’s words, but are also taught by the book of Job. For when the devil sought authority to tempt Job (Job 1), intending first to rage through the plundering of his property, he stirred up men [Note: In Zeno: “men who would serve.”] for the slaughter of the shepherds and the seizure of the livestock, and inflamed them with this desire for robbery. Thus he accomplished what he wished through the activity of human agency. Judas likewise was an instrument of the devil in the Lord’s Passion, and through him the devil carried out the effect of his own will, as the Evangelist testifies: “Satan,” he says, “entered into Judas, who was called Iscariot” (Luke 22:3).

4. One who inflicts injury deserves pity, not anger. — Therefore, in every injury which we suffer, the deed belongs to one, the prompting to another; and no one accomplishes something for himself when he acts under the impulse of a turbulent will. We should not, then, be angry with those from whom we suffer anything. Rather, whenever insults provoke us to anger, whenever abuse stirs us to quarrels, whenever robbery and theft compel us to grief and an impious complaint over loss, or whenever seductive encouragement moves us by its prompting toward bodily pleasures [Note: In Zeno: “nourishing,” in place of “seductive.”], we must recognize that enemy through whom these incentives to deeds and words are offered. We should not be angry at people, who are workers under another’s instigation [Royal manuscript: “of another’s work”]; rather, we should pity the shameful intervention of their detestable service, because they are vessels of the devil, servants of Satan, weapons of robbers, and bearers [Note: “Attendants.”] of another’s warfare and wickedness. [Note: Thus the royal manuscript together with the Tours manuscript. The printed editions have *paritores* (“attendants”), a word which, had it been in established Latin use, we would not have changed; for whether it derived from *pareo* (“obey”) or *pario* (“bring forth”), it would not be at variance with Hilary’s meaning.] On account of this understanding, therefore, the prophet mentions only those who assail him, without distinguishing names, speaking indiscriminately of these and those, because through men there was being done to him what belonged to spiritual wickednesses.

5. What those often but vainly assailed ought to say. — The Prophet began, therefore, as though speaking in his own person; but he first speaks beforehand, by an example of confession, what we ought to say. For the order of the words is this: “They have often assailed me from my youth; let Israel now say.” Israel is therefore first taught what it should say; then, as taught and imbued with the example of prophetic confession, Israel itself speaks:

> Verse 2. They have often assailed me from my youth; yet they could not prevail against me.

Such should be the confession of religious people. This is the true proof of faith: that those who assail often and from youth should nevertheless never prove stronger than those whom they have assailed both often and long ago [Note: In Hilary’s printed editions, here and below, “from youth” is added after “long ago” without effect.]. The battle against stronger persons is both long and frequent; and for this reason hostile spiritual powers test men who are strong in faith and the fear of God both long and often: what is carried on long and never succeeds must necessarily be repeated. Let us therefore stand firm, so that we may often be assailed; and, often assailed, let us have this glory, that we never yield. Let the constancy of our being assailed arise from the fact that the strength of those who assail us is not victorious.

6. Against such persons enemies continually lay snares from behind. — It is the custom of those who do not prevail in long and sustained battles to approach from behind a victorious army advancing in firm ranks; wherever it has already passed, they devise ambushes at its rear, fashion plots there, and exercise there every artifice of treachery. Thus sinners also approach from behind faithful people whom they have vainly tempted and who are now proceeding in the way of truth; from behind they lie in wait, and from behind they contrive deceit. Therefore he says:

> Verse 3. Sinners were building upon my back.

The Apostle runs (Phil. 3:13), forgetting what lies behind and stretching himself toward what lies ahead. The Law spoke thus to the faithful [Note: The Paris edition alone reads “to unbelievers.” See Deut. 28:7.]: “Your enemies will pursue you and will not overtake you.” He teaches that they did not overtake him when he says, “were building,” for this is the force of the indefinite tense. They were always building, never attaining the effect of their construction; while he ran on in an untiring course of faith, he against whose back battles were built every day [Note: In Zeno, with “he” omitted here, “those running” is then found in place of “as he ran”; wrongly. Nor is the reading in the other editions better, where *eo* is marked as an adverb of place, followed in Baden, Erasmus, and Lipsius by “where daily.” The sense is clear in itself: “as he ran on, against whom battles were being built every day.” In the Tours manuscript one reads, uncertainly: “he to whom … was building, as battles ran.”].

7. The rope of sinners. — The following verse explains this persistent wickedness of the assailants: “They prolonged their iniquity.” [Note: “Their iniquity.”] The prophecy of Isaiah says: “Woe to those who draw their sins like a long rope” (Isa. 5:18). For they do not cease to link sins to sins [Note: “And, like a rope, always extend them intertwined to great length.”], and to extend them perpetually intertwined like a long rope. For while the saint runs and sinners build upon his back, and while there is no limit either to his running toward the appointed goal or to their continual building, there results a drawn-out succession and manifold length of sins.

8. God’s patience. A stiff neck signifies obstinacy. — But we must learn at last what awaits this lengthening of iniquities [Col. 0714B]. For it follows, VERSE 4: “The righteous Lord will cut down the necks of sinners.”

> [Note: Col. 0714D. *He cuts down*: shortly after, “in vengeance.”]

> [Note: Col. 0714D. In the royal manuscript, here and shortly after, the reading is *cut down*, supported by the Greek συνέκοψεν, “he cut down.” The standard Jerome also supports it: observing that in Hebrew “bonds” stands in place of “necks,” he interprets the words of the Psalm thus: “Those who had surrounded me on every side with their snares also held me bound; but, with the Lord’s aid, all the knots have been loosed.” He does not say “will be loosed,” but “have been loosed.” The Tours manuscript nevertheless has the received reading, and the following words seem to confirm it.]

The Lord is righteous: patient, that is, in inflicting punishment; delaying until there is time for repentance; not swift to punish at the first beginnings of human wickedness, but waiting even for the sinner’s late willingness to abandon crimes.

> [Note: Col. 0714B. The Hilarian editions read *late, that is*; they are corrected from the manuscripts, Zeno’s edition, and Hincmar, who cites this passage under Hilary’s name in *On Predestination*, chapter 25. We have already corrected a similar error above.]

Yet he will cut down their necks when they go on building without any prospect of ceasing, when sins are stretched out to length, when every period of the mercy of him who has been patient has now been excluded. We remember that the law always reproaches the obstinate for being stiff-necked: Moses charges before God that the people are stiff-necked (Exod. 32:9); the prophet reproaches the daughters of Zion because they walk with uplifted necks (Isa. 3:16)—that is, with a neck [p. 487] scorning the yoke, insolent toward works of faith, abusing God’s patience to extend the length of their sins [Col. 0714C]. The neck, however, must be submitted to the gentle yoke to which the Lord invites us, saying: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). The neck that submits itself to this yoke is not to be cut down. For this is the yoke of humility and gentleness: it does not continually attack, does not build upon the back, does not prolong sins; rather, by humility and patience it cherishes the submitted neck, while that proud and insolent neck is to be cut down by the decree of righteous judgment.

9. Mount Zion. It means “contemplation.” It signifies Christ’s glorious body. Christ’s body is the Church. Whoever hates it hates Christ. The penalty of the crime. — Then follows [Col. 0714D; 0715A], VERSE 5: “Let all who hate Zion be confounded and turn backward.”

> [Note: Col. 0715D. Thus in Zeno and in the Tours manuscript, as the following exposition supports. In other books, “let them reverence.”]

We have often observed that Mount Zion lies near Jerusalem. But when the prophets speak of the King of Zion, the daughter of Zion, or the gates of Zion, we must first understand that under the very name Zion something else is signified. For Zion means “contemplation”: what is called *contemplatio* among us is called *Sion* in Hebrew. Next, we ought to recall the apostolic saying that, by believing in our Lord Jesus Christ, we have come to Mount Zion and the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb. 12:22). In his glorified body, transformed into heavenly glory, we contemplate the dignity of our hope, our body of humiliation being conformed to the glory of his body.

The Apostle testifies that the Church is Christ’s body, of which we are mutually members (Eph. 1:23) [Col. 0715B].

> [Note: Col. 0715D. In the previously published Hilary editions, *saying* is added here; then, with the verb *is* omitted, *is* is supplied after “built,” as though the following words, “which itself,” etc., were Paul’s words, to which “the Apostle testifies” should be referred. The manuscripts give this sense: the Apostle (Eph. 1:22–23) testifies that the Church is the body of Christ, of which we are mutually members, which itself is Zion, etc. Zeno has *because it itself is*, less well.]

It itself is Mount Zion of the Lord, the daughter of the King, the holy city, built with living stones upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles. Whoever therefore hates this Zion hates him whose body it is. For unbelievers bear a particular hatred against the faithful. Those who hate Zion, then, will be confounded; they will turn backward, not running toward heavenly things or reaching forward to those to come, but returning to their earthly and original things.
