At the time of judgment they will feel shame for their iniquity and unbelief and, losing the transformation of resurrection, will return to a penal bodily consciousness.

10. The empty labours of the wicked; buildings, some firm and some unstable. — The sequel of the Psalm teaches the same thing [Col. 0715C]. VERSES 6–8: “Let them be like the grass of buildings, which withered before it was plucked up; with which the reaper does not fill his hand, nor he who gathers sheaves his bosom. And those who passed by did not say: ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you.’”

I think that, according to a merely bodily understanding [p. 488], there is no grass of buildings [Col. 0715C–D]; grass belongs to a field, and indeed to a highly fruitful one. Therefore nothing here is to be considered or understood according to the sound of the words. According to the authority of Scripture, there are firm buildings and unstable ones. Firm are those built upon faithful foundations, cast upon the rock, which are not moved by rivers, winds, and floods (Matt. 7:25). There are also unstable ones, built upon a sandy foundation, which, when storms arise, suffer a great fall (Matt. 7:27).

> [Note: Col. 0715D. The royal and Tours manuscripts read “great falls.”]

There are likewise, according to the Apostle, two sowings: that of the Spirit and that of the flesh. He who sows spiritual things will reap spiritual things; and he who sows fleshly things will reap fleshly things (Gal. 6:8).

> [Note: Col. 0715D. In Zeno, *will have sown* occurs a second time, and shortly afterward the reading is “attack.”]

Therefore those who often and long ago attacked, who built upon the back, who prolonged their iniquities, whose necks will be cut down, who hate Zion—these will be like the useless grass of buildings [Col. 0716A], yielding the vain and empty fruit of this bodily and present life.

> [Note: Col. 0716D. In the Tours manuscript: “useless and bodily.”]

For, according to the evangelical comparison, buildings and roofs are human bodies, either firm by faith or about to fall through unbelief. In the same way, when persecution is at hand, the Lord forbade anyone to come down from the roof of the building, saying: “Let him who is upon the roof not come down to take anything out of his house” (Matt. 24:17). Certainly in persecution one must flee. How, then, did he forbid descent from the roof, unless bodily care is to be abandoned?

> [Note: Col. 0716D. The published editions read “unless because bodily care”; we have deleted *because*, on the authority of the Tours manuscript and with the agreement also of Zeno’s copies.]

For one standing upon the roof—that is, remaining above earthly nature [Col. 0716B]—is forbidden to seek low things again and descend to what is beneath. But the wicked are grass upon buildings, for they have sown emptiness. And this grass withers even before it is plucked up: the reaper will neither fill his hand from it nor will he who gathers sheaves load his bosom, nor will a passer-by bless its fruit with rejoicing.

> [Note: Col. 0716D. “Filled … loaded,” etc.; thereafter, “of fruits.”]

> [Note: Col. 0716D. Thus in Zeno, as in the royal and Tours manuscripts. Other books read: “filled … loaded … with rejoicing over fruits.”]

Empty, void, useless they are; for they have sown what is empty and useless. O unhappy labours, and unfruitful works of the flesh, compared with the unfruitful grass of buildings, dry before it is uprooted—that is, dead even before the very time of its useless harvest.

11. The distinction between deeds and good will. — But since we have explained the grass of these buildings as the fruit of fleshly works, we must consider what difference there is between him who fills his hand and him who gathers sheaves into his bosom [Col. 0716C]. For they are not the same, nor is Scripture accustomed to repeat identical matters in double expressions. It is greater to gather into the bosom than to fill the hand. Those who fill their hands seem rightly to receive the fruit of deeds well done, because in the divine discourse “hands” signify works [p. 489]; whereas in the bosom is shown the disposition of conscience, faith, and perfect will. For conscience reaps more than deeds: deeds fill the hand, but conscience gathers the sheaves.

> [Note: Col. 0716D. The previous editions read “gathers in the bosom.” More correctly, *in the bosom* is absent in the royal and Tours manuscripts and in Zeno.]

The Lord regards the two coins of the poor widow as more acceptable than the abundant coins of the rich (Luke 21:3). To such an extent does will surpass deeds.

> [Note: Col. 0716D. In the royal manuscript and Zeno: “and deeds indeed fill the hand.” In Tours: “and deeds indeed fill hands.”]

Deeds indeed fill the hand.

> [Note: Col. 0716D. “Are filled by the hand.”]

But bosoms can contain sheaves. Therefore this grass of the building will fill neither the hand of the reaper [Col. 0716D] nor the bosom of him who gathers sheaves.

12. Those who pass by: persons exalted in mind above earthly things. — Nor will those who pass by say, “The blessing of the Lord be upon you” [Col. 0717A]. Who are those who pass by, except those who, as pilgrims, pass through the age of bodily life:

> [Note: Col. 0717D. In the previously published editions, “as though pilgrims.” Then in the Tours manuscript: “of the bodily way.”]

who do not remain among things that are nothing, but reach toward eternal things; who do not linger over what lies before the eyes, but proceed toward invisible things? To understand fully who those who pass by are—

> [Note: Col. 0717D. “Are.” Shortly afterward, “Moses speaking.”]

—let us hear Moses when he saw fire burning in the bush without harm to the bush in which it burned. He said: “I will pass over and see this vision” (Exod. 3:3). What is this, “I will pass over”? No intervals of place separated him:

> [Note: Col. 0717D. “Had separated.”]

he both spoke and saw in the same place. What, then, does he pass over? Clearly, he passes beyond bodily and fleshly cares. While feeding his father-in-law’s sheep, he rises, leaving earthly works behind, into heavenly knowledge. The same is true of him who says in the preceding Psalm: “I saw the wicked exceedingly exalted, and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not” (Ps. 36:35–36) [Col. 0717B].

> [Note: Col. 0717D. Thus the royal manuscript with Tours. The printed editions have “in bodily concerns,” words which should be referred to the one who sees, not the one seen. A little before, the Tours manuscript has *superaltatum* for *superexaltatum*, “exceedingly exalted.”]

He had admired him in worldly circumstances; while remaining amid bodily concerns, he had seen him lofty and exalted. But passing by—that is, becoming a pilgrim to the world and rising from earthly and perishable things into heavenly and spiritual knowledge—he regarded him as nothing, said that he was not, and judged him dead.

> [Note: Col. 0717D. In Zeno: “as nothing,” etc. In our printed editions: “he regarded him as nothing, and already …” We prefer, with the manuscripts, “he regarded him as nothing,” since this refers to “and behold, he was not.” The standard Jerome interprets the same words of the Psalm more concisely in accordance with Hilary’s thought: “The saints of God, who regarded the world as nothing and passed through [Col. 0718D] to heavenly and eternal things, did not bless them.”]

Thus those who pass by deny God’s blessing to the grass of buildings, knowing that the favour of the divine gift is denied to fruits that are dry and perishable [Col. 0717B; 0718D].

13. The Prophet does not utter an imprecation. — Yet the Prophet’s wishes may be thought harsh and severe, for his whole expression seemed to be that of one wishing when he said: “Let them be like the grass of buildings” [Col. 0717C]. But far be it that the Prophet should be thought to have uttered an imprecation. He spoke these things with prophetic knowledge; this was speech of recognition, not of desire, so that fear might at the same time come upon sinners who would come to know the emptiness of their withering fruits.

[p. 490]

14. He prays a blessing for the repentant. — He then shows the disposition of his wishes, saying: “We bless you in the name of the Lord.”

> [Note: Col. 0718D. The ancient editions, with the royal and Tours manuscripts, read “I will bless you.”]

The blessing is ready, if those who sowed grass upon buildings begin to sow that which will fill the reaper’s hand and the bosom of the gatherer of sheaves.

> [Note: Col. 0718D. The royal manuscript with Tours reads “begin to bear.” The received reading is supported by Jerome’s words: “We have blessed you, so that, abandoning unfruitful and dry works, you may sow those things which will fill both the reapers’ hand and the bosom of those gathering sheaves.”]

Therefore the Prophet showed their fruits, dead through dry works, to be in the grass of buildings, by denying blessings; but in regard to the salvation of the repentant he showed his wishes, on account of their return to good works, by desiring again the blessings which he had denied [Col. 0717D; 0718A]. Let us therefore sow usefully and prepare our labours to fill hands and bosoms, so that we may share in God’s blessings in our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 129. A Song of Ascents.

“Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord. Lord, hear my voice. Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my prayer. If you observe iniquities [*if you will observe*], O Lord, who shall endure you [“O Lord,” with *you* omitted]? For with you is propitiation; and because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord. My soul has waited upon your word; my soul has hoped in the Lord. From the morning watch until night let Israel hope in the Lord, because with the Lord is mercy, and with him abundant redemption. And he himself will redeem Israel from all their iniquities” [Col. 0718B].

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. Man does not penetrate God’s secrets; how far it is pious to investigate them. — Among the many splendid things which the Apostle writes to the Romans, after speaking of the faith of the Gentiles and the unbelief of the Jews, and after treating at length of the judgments and decrees of God, he says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and untraceable [p. 491] his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? Because all things are from him, through him, and in him. To him be glory for ages of ages” (Rom. 11:33 ff.).

> [Note: Col. 0718D. “Of judgment”; then, “unsearchable.”]

> [Note: Col. 0718D. The Tours manuscript has here and below “unsearchable.”]

It is the devout confession of human weakness to know this alone concerning God: that God is. But the earthly mind does not penetrate those secret and profound decrees of inscrutable judgment [Col. 0718C]. It is indeed pious to seek and investigate them; but we must confess that they are unsearchable and beyond investigation. The former belongs to a devout will; the latter, to their impenetrable nature. Who will know the causes and natures of this heaven, of the higher heaven, and of the rest? Who has comprehended the offices and reasons of angels, powers, dominions, thrones, and principalities? Who will understand the unceasing voices and eternal utterances of Cherubim and Seraphim? Who will know the waters above the heavens that praise God? Who will boast that the lights of sun, moon, and stars are known to him? Who will measure this fullness of air, empty, as we think, to us?

> [Note: Col. 0718D. We have removed *here* as spurious, following the manuscripts and Zeno’s edition. Shortly after, we have supplied the word “who” from the Tours manuscript, where it was formerly absent.]

Further, who will attain full knowledge of the arrangement of the world, the powers of the elements [Col. 0718D], the changes of seasons, the courses of rivers [Col. 0719A], the bounds of the sea, the changes of the Ocean, the blowing of winds, the natures of animals, the ferocity of beasts, the kinds of trees, the powers of roots, the origins of souls, the growth of bodies, the deaths of children, the life of old people, the labours of the age, the glorious afflictions of the saints, the unhappy prosperity of the irreligious, and the books of the Law, Prophets, Gospels, and Apostles consecrated by a heavenly mystery?

> [Note: Col. 0719D. In Zeno: “mysteries consecrated in a heavenly book”; this does not commend itself to us.]

2. The voice of one ignorant, suffering, or praying. — In all these matters, then, held fast and detained, the Prophet also cries from the inward secret of his heart, according to the Apostle’s utterance, saying, VERSE 1: “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord.”

> [Note: Col. 0719C. “Cries aloud,” with Zeno.]

Place him, according to the Apostle, abiding in the depth of God’s unsearchable and untraceable riches [Col. 0719B] (Rom. 11:33); set him praying from the deep surge of human calamities, according to the Lord’s saying in the preceding Psalm: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me” (Ps. 63:3); suppose him to pray not with his lips but, as commanded, in the secret of his heart (Matt. 6:6). This saying, “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord,” is suited either to ignorance, suffering, or prayer: whether he does not know, suffers, or prays. And because he cries from the depths, he says confidently: “Lord, hear my voice,” VERSE 2: “Let your ears be attentive [p. 492] to the voice of my prayer.”

3. The difference between God’s hearing and his ears’ being attentive to prayer. What it means to ascribe members to an incorporeal God. — We must ask whether “hear my voice” is the same thing as, VERSE 2, “Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my prayer.” For he prays from the depths, and whatever he prays is profound [Col. 0719C]. First, we must understand that God is incorporeal and does not consist of certain parts and functions of limbs which together make one body. For we read in the Gospel: “God is spirit” (John 4:24), that is, an invisible, immeasurable, self-contained, and eternal nature. It is also written: “A spirit does not have flesh and bones” (Luke 24:39). Bodily members consist of these, and God’s substance has no need of them.

But God, who is everywhere and in all things, wholly hears, wholly sees, wholly acts, wholly moves [Col. 0720A]. We are taught this from Scripture when it says: “I am God near at hand, and not from afar” (Jer. 23:23); and again: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). Therefore God’s power, equal and undivided—

> [Note: Col. 0719C. “Uniform,” together with Zeno.]

—bears the names of functions and limbs: the power by which he sees is called eyes; the power by which he hears, ears; the power by which he acts, hands; the power by which he is present, feet. The distinct functions are performed by the power of this virtue. God therefore is everywhere, and everywhere is present, hears, sees, and acts. Yet we must pray to him that, according to our prayer, he may be present, hear, see, and act. It belongs to his nature to hear; but it belongs to our faith to pray that we may be heard. He hears those who revile; he hears those who curse; he hears even those speaking within the secrets of their hearts. Yet faith performs its duty [Col. 0720B] by asking for God’s hearing, so that he who hears by his own nature may deign, in answer to the prayer of the petitioner, to hear.

4. Against the Anthropomorphites. Man consists of body and soul. God is not composite. — If anyone perhaps thinks that God is bodily, possessed of a form, and differentiated into limbs—because the eye is not the same as the hand—and imagines this to follow from the words, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26), he must first remember that the constitution of human beings contains two natures—

> [Note: Col. 0720C. “Constitutions,” likewise.]

—soul and body: the one spiritual, the other earthly; and that this lower material, the body, has been fitted for the effectiveness and operation of that higher nature, the soul. Therefore, whoever wishes to believe that God is bodily because man was made in his image will posit a composite God [Col. 0720C], composed of a higher and lower nature, since man consists of such elements. But whatever is composite necessarily has not been eternal, because composition has a beginning by which it is embodied in order to [p. 493] remain.

> [Note: Col. 0719D. Thus the Vatican manuscript. In Zeno: “by which it is compared.” Other editions read: “by which it is composed.” The Tours manuscript has *comparatorum quo maneat*; the royal manuscript, *quo comparatorum maneat*. From this reading one might make: “by which it obtains, or reaches, that it may remain whole”; or perhaps rather, “by which it remains embodied.” Gregory of Nazianzus similarly excludes composition from God, *Oration* 34, §13: “For composition is the beginning of conflict; conflict, of dissension; dissension, of dissolution. Dissolution, however, can in no way belong to God and that first nature.”]

Yet these are the ravings of unbelief, when, through ignorance of heavenly—

> [Note: Col. 0719D. That is, as we have elsewhere shown, of the divine, or even spiritual, nature. In the latter sense man is immediately afterward declared composite of a lowly and a heavenly nature, namely soul and body. Nor need we point out that the soul’s heavenly nature is declared, not because it was created out of some heavenly matter—Hilary expressly teaches in Psalm 118, §7, that it does not possess in itself an origin of another nature assumed from elsewhere, and therefore consists neither of earthly nor heavenly matter—but because it owes its origin to the power of God alone, who dwells in heaven.]

—nature, the mind is confined within these narrow limits of opinion through the fault of a degraded intellect.

5. In creating man, God did three things. — But God, always remaining and everywhere the same in all things, himself nowhere absent in his entirety, when he began the most beautiful work after the world had already been completed—namely, making man in his own image—composed him of a lowly and a heavenly nature, that is, soul and body.

> [Note: Col. 0720D. What remains of this section is omitted in Zeno, doubtless because the person who subscribed Hilary’s Treatises in other respects did not wish to adopt his singular opinion concerning the first man’s formation. It may be asked whether Hilary in fact thought that the creation of soul and body, and their union, took place at distinct intervals of time, or whether he intended only to indicate from Moses’ words a certain order, or quasi-order, of God’s operations in creating man. Scultetus’s observation cannot stand: among Hilary’s singular opinions he lists the view that Adam’s soul was formed before his body and that God created all things at once and simultaneously. For if Hilary did not think Adam was created at once and simultaneously, he did not think all things were created by God at once and simultaneously. See Psalm 118, §6.]

First, he constituted the soul by that divine and incomprehensible work of his power [Col. 0721A]. For when he made man in God’s image, he did not then also make the body. Genesis teaches that long afterward, once man had been made in God’s image, dust was taken and the body fashioned from it (Gen. 2:7); then again it was made into a living soul through God’s breath—the earthly and heavenly natures being joined by a kind of covenant of inspiration.

6. The image of God in man according to the soul. — The blessed Apostle Paul knows himself to be divided between the inward and the outward person. Through the inward person he delights in the law—

> [Note: Col. 0721D. In Zeno, *law* is absent. Other editions read “he delights together in the law.” We restore from the manuscripts “he delights in the law,” with the preposition *in* understood; in Psalm 118, §8, it is also expressed.]

—through the outward he does what he does not wish. The inward person desires the works of the Spirit, while the outward desires the pleasures of the body [Col. 0721B] (Rom. 7:22–23). Thus the inward person was made in the image of God: rational, mobile, moving, swift, incorporeal, subtle, eternal. So far as lies in itself, it imitates the form of the supreme divine nature: it traverses, it flies around, and more swiftly than speech is now beyond the ocean, now soaring into the heavens, now in the depths, now surveying east and west. It is never abolished so as not to exist—God’s nature, indeed, is in all these things—nor does it depart from one place in order to be elsewhere.

But the human soul, in this mobility of its consciousness, was made in the image of its Maker.

> [Note: Two manuscripts read: “the human mind … was made.”]

The soul’s perpetual mobility imitates God’s nature—

> [Note: Supply *while*, unless you prefer the Tours manuscript’s *having*.]

—and has nothing bodily, nothing earthly, nothing heavy, nothing perishable in itself [Col. 0721C]. Let us hear Paul still further teaching this: “Putting off the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new, who is renewed unto knowledge according to the image of the Creator” (Col. 3:9–10). Do we put on anything bodily when we are renewed [p. 494] unto knowledge? Nothing, I think. Rather, we put on knowledge of God, faith in eternity, the purity of innocence, and dispositions of goodness. These are garments of the soul rather than of the body, and all are proper to God.

> [Note: Col. 0721D. Thus in Zeno and in the manuscripts: that is, “made new unto knowledge,” in accordance with Paul’s preceding words, “who is renewed unto knowledge,” etc. Thus the word *man* was formerly supplied wrongly after *new*.]

We, made new unto knowledge, put these on, so that in every service of our soul we may be according to the image of the Creator, perfected in the knowledge of goodness, holiness, and love. These matters have been treated briefly because of God’s ears, lest he be thought bodily.

7. God’s members may be called angelic powers. God does not need them, but we do. — Although these things stand as stated [Col. 0721D; 0722A], still we remember that there are many spiritual powers called angels, or presiding over churches. For according to John, the Asian churches have angels (Rev. 1:20). According to Moses, the boundaries of the nations were established for Adam’s sons according to the number of angels (Deut. 32:8). According to the Lord, the angels of the little ones see God daily (Matt. 18:10). According to Raphael speaking to Tobias, there are angels who stand before God’s glory and carry the prayers of petitioners to God (Tob. 12:12, 15). This has been mentioned so that, if perhaps we wish to understand these as God’s eyes, ears, hands, or feet, we may have the authority of an interpretation that is not implausible [Col. 0722B]—especially since it is written: “For they are active spirits, sent in ministry for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. 1:14). God’s nature, therefore, has no need of their intercession; our weakness does. For they are sent for those who will inherit salvation. God is ignorant of none of the things we do; rather, our weakness needs the ministry of spiritual intercession in order to ask and obtain.

8. The distinction between sin and iniquity. — Then follows, VERSE 3: “If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?”

> [Note: Col. 0721D. In our text the word *Lord* is not repeated, in agreement with the Greek.]

The meaning of this saying must not be treated carelessly. For he does not say, “If you observe sins,” but, “If you observe iniquities.”

> [Note: Col. 0722D. Our text also rejects the reading, “but if you observe iniquities.”]

> [Note: Col. 0722D. These words, “but if you observe iniquities,” are omitted in Zeno, as in the royal and Tours manuscripts.]

Iniquity differs from sin. Will God not observe sins? Will there be no remembrance of crimes? Certainly there will be [Col. 0722C].

> [Note: Col. 0722D. The royal manuscript with Tours: “because even.”]

Indeed, every person will render an account for an idle word (Matt. 12:36), and everyone cast into prison will pay the last farthing (Matt. 5:26). But we are taught that iniquity and sin differ when it is said [p. 495]: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31:1); and again: “I acknowledged my iniquity, and I did not conceal my sin” (Ps. 31:5).

> [Note: Col. 0722D. Only the Paris edition reads “I know.” The Greek has ἐγνώρισα, “I made known.” After “I did not conceal,” the royal and Tours manuscripts add: “which the Apostle himself [distinguishes], omitting other instances.”]

Every iniquity is a transgression of God’s law, and is more serious than sin. The Apostle made this very distinction most plainly, saying: “Those who sinned unlawfully shall perish unlawfully; but those who sinned under the law shall be judged by the law” (Rom. 2:12).

> [Note: Col. 0722D. The Hilarian editions’ “Those who sinned without the law shall perish without the law” offers nothing from which the distinction between sin and iniquity may be established. The reading we provide from the manuscripts is therefore truer, although the Greek, ὅσοι γὰρ ἀνόμως ἥμαρτον, ἀνόμως καὶ ἀπολοῦνται, “for as many as sinned lawlessly will also perish lawlessly,” permits either.]

Thus the sin of iniquity has already perished; but sin under the law will be judged. The sin of iniquity is every offence committed outside the law, such as the crimes of the Gentiles [Col. 0722D; 0723A]—

> [Note: Two manuscripts: “of the nations.”]

—which have already been condemned together with their ignorance of the law.

> [Note: Col. 0723D. Thus in the royal and Tours manuscripts and in Zeno; other books read: “Sins under the law, however, do not perish, but are to be judged.”]

But sins under the law are to be judged, because, though they are sins, they are sins under the law. Therefore, if God remembers iniquities, who will endure thefts, murders, false testimonies, fornications, and perjuries? For these are crimes committed unlawfully, that is, outside God’s law, and they are washed away by the sacrament of the new birth.

9. The Son, our redemption, who is one with the Father. — But God no longer remembers these things at all; and in the following verse the Prophet shows why he does not remember them, saying, VERSE 4: “Because with you is propitiation.” For the only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, is our redemption and our peace; in his blood we have been reconciled to God. He is the one who came to take away the sins of the world; fastening the handwriting of the law to the cross—

> [Note: Col. 0723D. What law is meant is explained in *On the Trinity*, book IX, §10, where we read: “Blotting out the handwriting of the law of sin, which by its earlier sentences was contrary to us.”]

—he erased the decree of the former condemnation (Col. 2:14) [Col. 0723B].

Whether the Prophet’s prayer is understood to be addressed to the Father or to the Son—for both are one, and whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father; in the likeness of glory each is glorious in the other: the Son is glorious because he is worthy of fellowship with the Father; the Father is glorious because he has a Son worthy of fellowship with him—

> [Note: Col. 0723C. We have restored to the text the reading of our manuscript as superior to the others. The earlier edition read, “the Son worthy of fellowship with himself.”]

> [Note: Col. 0723D. The previously published editions read “worthy of fellowship with his Son,” which does not suit Hilary’s manner of speech. He is accustomed to defend the Son’s equality by words that do not detract from the Father’s dignity. This manner is especially preserved by the reading of the royal and Tours manuscripts: “the Father is glorious because he has a Son worthy of fellowship with himself.” By this way of speaking, in Psalm 122, §2, he teaches that the Father is in the Son, “in a Son worthy and sufficient, in whom the Father dwells through the same power of nature.” Nor is the Vatican manuscript and Zeno’s reading displeasing: “the Father is glorious by reason of his Son worthy of fellowship with him.”]

—whichever of the two you choose, the Prophet will rightly be thought to have said: “Because with you is propitiation.”

> [Note: Col. 0723D. The royal manuscript with Tours reads: “to whom the Father may rightly be thought, if you choose, to have spoken through the Prophet”; Bad., Erasmus, and Leipzig followed this reading, omitting the first word, “to whom.” Paris, from the Mic. manuscript, reads: “the Father may rightly be thought to have spoken through the Prophet to whom he chooses.” More elegant is the reading restored here from Zeno’s copies.]

For in the Father, according to the likeness of glory, is the Son; and the Son himself is propitiation, redemption, and intercession for our sins, and, because he is their propitiation, does not remember our iniquities [Col. 0723C].

10. For the Prophet who observes the law, Christ is hope—and this throughout life. — The Prophet knows that it is a matter of great danger [p. 496] to sin unlawfully, that is, without law, because destruction belongs to sin without law—

> [Note: Col. 0723C. “Destruction belongs to the sinner”: apparently a gloss. Yet this may perhaps account for the reading in Zeno’s copies: “for destruction belongs to the sinner; but judgment belongs to the sinner under the law.”]

—whereas judgment belongs to sin under the law. Therefore he says: “Because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.” The law is holy and spiritual, and in it are the words of life; and Christ is the end of the law. This is shown in the following verse: “My soul has waited upon your word.” The Prophet indeed performs the bodily observances of the law—sacrifices, burnt offerings, new moons, and sabbaths—all of which are a shadow of things to come [Col. 0724A]. Yet his soul has waited upon God’s Word. Because of the law he waits—that is, as I said, he bodily performs the offices of the law. But in God’s Word his soul waits: with spiritual faith he expects the coming of the Son of God, who is both the Word of God and God the Word. How he waits, he shows by saying, VERSES 5–6: “My soul has hoped in the Lord, from the morning watch until night.” Let us recall the form of the Gospel comparison and remember that some labourers spend the whole day in the vineyard’s work. From the morning watch until night the Prophet hopes: he has no idle time; he is an untiring labourer throughout the whole day [Col. 0724B].

### 11. One who has not spent his whole day in hope of the Lord must not despair.

[Note: [Col. 0724C] “Not every life [spends] its own day”; then, “spends.” This reading is also found in Zeno.]

[Note: [Col. 0724D] Mic. manuscript: “as in Zeno, not every life”; Regius manuscript: “not in every life.”]

But what, then, will become of hope? Not every life spends its whole day in hope of the Lord; for there are laborers of the third hour, of the sixth, of the ninth, and also of the eleventh. And the Prophet, who hoped from the morning watch until night, seems to cut us off from hope of the Gospel’s reward. He certainly does not cut us off. For he says: “Let Israel hope in the Lord.” This exhortation to hope sets no time-limit. He indeed, as a perfect laborer, hoped from the morning watch until night. But every time is open to hope; and the laborers of the eleventh hour will receive a reward not of work but of mercy (Matt. 20:9).

For thus he says: “Let Israel hope in the Lord,” vv. 7–8: “For with the Lord is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption. And he himself will redeem Israel from all their iniquities.” Good is he in whom hope is placed; and one must hope in him, because he is merciful, because abundant redemption is with him, because he has redeemed all from all their iniquities.

[Note: “He will redeem”; then, “from iniquities.”]

It is the eleventh hour; the times of day are closed. Let us all run; let us hasten lest night be upon us, lest the hour pass by. We are old; the night of death presses upon us, and we have not even advanced to the eleventh hour of our life.

[Note: Regius manuscript, with the Tours manuscript: “lest the works pass by.” This whole section commends works. Yet Erasmus wrote somewhat earlier in the margin: “Where are the good works of N. Ecmondanus?” We do not concern ourselves with what Ecmondanus said, but with preventing Hilary from being misunderstood. For although he says that the laborers of the eleventh hour will receive a reward not of work but of mercy, he does not deny that their works are good, but only denies them a right to demand the reward. Since their works neither merit the denarius in themselves nor by agreement with the master of the house, he says that they must await it solely from his mercy. But he implies that the other laborers, for whom a wage was stipulated, possess by agreement a right to demand it [Col. 0725D], and therefore do not await it from mere mercy. Nevertheless, since the reward of eternal life has been promised to us through God’s mercy, Hilary more than once teaches, in this respect, that it is granted to all by God’s mercy.]

Blessed indeed is he who, laboring from morning until night, claims the stipulated denarius as a debt. But because the Lord is good, because he is merciful, let us hope in him, so that, although laborers of the eleventh hour, we may receive the denarius of the day’s labor through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Psalm 130. A Song of Ascents.

Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up. Nor have I walked in great things, nor in wonders beyond me. If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul: as one weaned upon his mother, so you will repay unto my soul. Let Israel [Col. 0725B] hope in the Lord, from this time forth and forever.

## Treatise on the Psalm

### 1. The teaching of this Psalm. Humility, the greatest work of our faith.

This is a short psalm, to be explained more by divisions than by a treatise; teaching us humility and gentleness.

[Note: Thus in Zeno and in the manuscripts, as also below in the next Psalm, no. 1: “teaching us unto the knowledge of the Son of God,” and very often elsewhere. In other books, however: “introducing.”]

Since we have dealt with certain points concerning humility in many other places, it is idle to repeat the same things. Certainly we must remember that humility is the greatest work of our faith, since the Prophet mentions it as the consciousness of an excellent work, saying, v. 1: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted.” For the best sacrifice to God is a contrite heart (Ps. 50:19). Therefore the heart must not be lifted up by prosperity, but must be restrained, through fear of God, within the bounds of gentleness [Col. 0725C] by humility.

### 2. The eyes must be raised to God, not to something else.

“Nor have my eyes been lifted up.” The Greek expresses this with another nuance, saying: οὐδὲ ἐμετεωρίσθησαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοί μου, that is, “nor have my eyes been raised from one thing to another.”

But according to the Prophet’s words, the eyes are to be raised: “Raise your eyes and see who displays all these things” (Isa. 40:26). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Raise your eyes and behold the fields, for they are white for harvest” (John 4:35). Therefore the eyes must be raised, but not in turn raised to something else, so that they may persist in that to which they have once been raised.

[Note: In the Hilary editions, “from one thing to another”: “from one thing” is superfluous; it is found neither in Zeno nor in the manuscripts.]

### 3. David, raised toward God, is not made arrogant by his own glory.

Then follows: “Nor have I walked in great things, [Col. 0726A] nor in wonders beyond me.” It is a matter of great danger if we walk in modest things and do not dwell among wonders. Great are the utterances of God; he himself is wonderful in the heights. How, then, does the Prophet set forth as a good work of his own that he does not walk in great and wonderful things?

But when he added, “beyond me,” he does not walk in those things which are regarded as humanly wonderful and great.

[Note: The Hilary editions read perversely: “things great to man,” etc.; for divine things appear wonderful and great to human beings, and the Prophet is not said to deny walking in them. More correctly the manuscripts, as in Zeno: “those things which are human,” that is, things found in human beings. Thus Hilary understands the words “beyond me” not as “above me,” but as “in me,” so that David says: “The power of king, prophet, and so forth, seems great and wonderful in me; but I have not exercised that power.” The same exposition is treated more clearly in Zeno in the form of a sermon delivered to the people; instead of “those things which are humanly great,” etc., it has: “those things which people consider great in this world.”]

For David, both prophet and king, had formerly been humble and lowly, not even worthy of his father’s table. Yet he pleased God, was anointed king, and inspired as a prophet. He is not arrogant in his kingdom, nor stirred by hatred.

[Note: “He loves those who persecute him.”]

He loves the one persecuting him, honors the deaths of his enemies, and spares his incestuous and parricidal sons. The ruler is despised, the father injured, the prophet harassed: he does not pray for revenge as prophet [Col. 0726B], does not exact vengeance as father, does not pursue the insult as ruler. Thus he does not walk in those great and wonderful things which are beyond him.

### 4. He is humble in heart, not in understanding.

But let us consider what follows. Verse 2: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul.” What is this contrast in the Prophet? He does not exalt his heart; he exalts his soul. He does not walk in great and wonderful things beyond him; yet he does not think humbly. He is lofty in mind and lowly in heart. He is humble in what belongs to himself; but he is not humble in understanding. For his understanding is in heaven [Mic. manuscript: “into heaven”]; his soul is on high.

[Note: “But the heart”; thereafter: “is humble . . . is subject.”]

But in heart—from which, according to the Gospel, proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, and blasphemies (Matt. 15:19)—[Col. 0726C] he is humble, subject to that sweet yoke of gentleness. Therefore the measure of humility and loftiness must be maintained: we should be humble in heart, but lofty in understanding and soul.

### 5. He hungers for the living bread.

Then follows: “As one weaned upon his mother, so you will repay unto my soul.” When Isaac was weaned, we learn that Abraham made a feast (Gen. 21:8), because, being weaned, he was now passing beyond food of milk, appropriate to childish age.

[Note: In Bad., Erasmus, Zeno, and the Regius and Mic. manuscripts: “childish age.” Then, in the Regius manuscript in the first hand and in Zeno: “nearest.” Perhaps: “because, now beyond the drinking of milk appropriate to childish age, he would receive more substantial food.”]

And the Apostle gives milk to all who are untrained in faith and still infantile in their knowledge of divine things (Heb. 5:12).

[Note: In the printed texts: “untrained in faith, and infantile.” The reading of the Tours manuscript is preferred: “untrained in faith and infantile,” namely, in knowledge. The Regius manuscript also has “and infantile.”]

Therefore it is the greatest progress no longer to need milk. For Abraham’s joyful feast testified that his son had passed on to stronger food; and the Apostle denies bread to those who are carnal and little children in Christ (1 Cor. 3:2). The Prophet therefore prays that, because he has not exalted his heart, because he has not walked in his own great and wonderful things, because he has not thought humble thoughts but exalted his soul, his soul may be repaid as to one weaned upon his mother: that is, that it may be worthy of the recompense of perfect, heavenly, living bread, because through the works previously mentioned it has now passed beyond food of milk.

[Note: “Food of milk”: the verb was previously lacking in the editions.]

### 6.

Nor does he ask this living bread from heaven for himself alone; rather, he exhorts all to hope for it, saying, v. 3: “Let Israel hope in the Lord, from this time forth and unto age of age.” He bounds our hope by no limit of time; he stretches the faith of our expectation into immensity. One must hope unto age of age [Col. 0727B], because through hope in the present age we shall attain hope in the future age, in our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: “Because even” is absent from the Verona manuscript.]

[Note: “Because” is absent from the manuscripts and from Zeno, who then reads “will attain”; the manuscripts read “attaining,” not “will attain.”]

## Psalm 131. A Song of Ascents.

Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness. As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob: “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house; if I go up upon the bed of my couch” (Hilary: “of my couch”); “if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.” Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah (Ephrata); we found it in the fields of the forest. “We entered” (Hilary: “we shall enter”) [Col. 0727C] into his tabernacles; “we shall worship in the place where his feet stood.” “Arise” (“rise up”), Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification. Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints exult (“rejoice”). For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Anointed. The Lord swore truth to David and will not disappoint him: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Hilary: “my throne”). “If your sons keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine which I shall teach them, their sons also shall sit upon your throne forever.” For the Lord chose Zion; he chose it beforehand as his dwelling. “This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, because I chose it beforehand. I will richly bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread. I will clothe her priests with salvation; [Col. 0727D] and her saints shall exult with exultation. There I will cause David’s horn to spring forth; I have prepared a lamp for my Anointed. [Col. 0728A] I will clothe his enemies with shame; but upon him shall my sanctification flourish” (“shall flourish”).

## Treatise on the Psalm

### 1. This Psalm sings of Christ. The Jews wrongly refer it to David. Their reverence for the sacred books.

All the preceding Songs of Ascents raise us toward progress in a loftier hope, and by the teaching of faith, hope, confession, humility, and action lead us upward by their steps.

[Note: Only the Paris edition: “prayer.”]

But this Psalm especially teaches us unto knowledge of the Son of God and instructs us concerning the mystery of the flesh assumed by him.

[Note: The printed texts read: “teaches us also knowledge”; this produces a faulty sense, as though this Psalm also sang of us. The manuscripts correctly read “unto,” as above, no. 1, where the Psalm is said to teach us unto humility and gentleness; and in Psalm 118, no. 1: “by which we are taught unto perfect knowledge and obedience to God,” etc.]

For it begins thus, v. 1: “Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness.” The Jews, denying the coming of our Lord by which he restored salvation to humankind in the body, dare to refer this Psalm to David. Thus, impious in the Lord’s passion, they are likewise ignorant in prophetic knowledge: reading yet not understanding, possessing yet not knowing, venerating yet not obeying.

[Note: In the Tours and Regius manuscripts the words “possessing yet not knowing, venerating yet not obeying” are absent. A little later, only the Tours manuscript has “they spread linen beneath”; but subsequently both manuscripts have “they employ witnesses,” omitting “them.”]

Many know with what appearance of religious observance they venerate the books of the Prophets. They dare not touch them with the hand when reading; they spread linen beneath them; they use them as witnesses to establish the mystery. Yet this results in their incurring the greater guilt of irreligion: they either despise, disregard, or do not know the sayings of those to whom so great an honor is due.

This has been said because they have the following written in the Prophets, long after David had departed bodily, in Jeremiah: “In that day, says the Lord, I will crush the yoke from their neck, and I will break their bonds; and they shall no longer serve other gods, but they shall serve the Lord [Col. 0728C] their God; and I will raise up David their king for them” (Jer. 30; in the LXX, 37:8–9). And again: “I will raise up for them David, a righteous rising king; and the king shall reign and understand, and shall perform righteousness and judgment upon the earth: in his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell in confidence” (Jer. 23:5).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek. But the printed texts: “in those days Judah shall be saved.”]

Likewise in Isaiah:

[Note: This passage, sought in vain in Isaiah, is found in Ezekiel. There, after “one,” “high” is absent even in the LXX, with which the Vulgate adds: “and he shall feed them, my servant David,” not “my servant shall feed them.”]

“And I will raise over them one high shepherd; my servant David shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd, and I will be their God, and David shall be prince in their midst, I the Lord have spoken; and I will establish for David a covenant of peace” (Ezek. 34:23 ff.). They refuse to believe what they are taught and do not trust those to whom they acknowledge reverence is due.

[Note: Only the Regius codex: “those whose brief veneration they acknowledge.”]

And how will they be religious when they deny authority to religion?

### 2. The true David is Christ.

David rested with the fathers; he himself had known the covenant of the Law given through Moses. So long afterward God spoke through the Prophets of a David who was to be raised up: shepherd, king, rising one, righteous one, in whose days Israel would be saved, and for whom God would establish a covenant of peace. Therefore there is a David—not this son of Jesse, partial author of the Psalms—but David as shepherd because of his guarding of his flock; for “the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:11); king because of the glory of the eternal kingdom, to whom it was said: “Rabbi, you are the king of Israel” (John 1:49); righteous because of judgment—for “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22); rising one because of the light of the world—for “he was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9); and heir of the covenant of peace because of the dignity of the Son: “All things have been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18), and, “I leave you my peace” (John 14:27).

[Note: The printed texts read “because of God’s judgment.” The word “God” has been removed on the authority of the manuscripts.]

[Note: “Gives light.”]

[Note: The Regius manuscript and the Tours manuscript read “gives light”; this is likewise the reading in Psalm 118, no. 1, and Psalm 138, no. 35. But we read “enlightens” in *On the Trinity*, book I, no. 10.]

The Jews must therefore confess that these things were foretold long after David’s time. This David is the one who received the name of his ancestor according to the origin of the flesh: taking the name of him from whose line he also took his body. Yet everything contained in the Psalm differs both from the deeds of the prophet David, from the condition of human weakness, and from the times of life.

[Note: “From the blessed.”]

[Note: The printed texts: “from his.” The Regius manuscript: “from the blessed.” In the margin of the Tours manuscript is written “you have”; but the text reads “from things past.” We restore from Mic.: “from the times of life,” to be understood from no. 20 below: “The discourse is not of the present age,” etc.]

Because neither event, condition, nor time fits him, whereas these things fit the David whom God afterwards promised through the Prophets, there is no doubt that this eminent and great prophet also spoke, by God’s Spirit and in the office of prophet, concerning that David who appeared later.

[Note: “This prophet . . . who is eminent and great.”]

### 3. Christ’s prayer, asking God to remember his own human being.

For he says: “Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness.” He does not say, “Remember me,” but, “Remember, Lord, David,” thereby showing another person to be speaking. The entire prayer must be understood as that of the only-begotten Son of God speaking through the Prophet, beseeching God the Father to remember that human being whom he was about to assume.

[Note: Regius codex with Tours: “through the Prophets.”]

For Jesus is now, according to the Apostle, in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:11), and every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bends to him. Therefore the firstborn Son of God, God the Word, now calls himself David, taking through the Prophet the name of the human being who was to be placed with him in the Father’s glory, according to the privilege of his divinity. “Remember, Lord, David and all [Col. 0730A] his gentleness”; for he himself says: “I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). And the Father’s testimony concerning him is: “Behold my servant whom I chose, my beloved in whom my soul was well pleased; I will put my Spirit upon him, and he shall announce judgment to the nations. He shall not contend, nor cry out, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets” (Matt. 12:18–19).

[Note: The printed texts read “my soul”; corrected from the manuscripts and the Greek: εἰς ὃν εὐδόκησεν ἡ ψυχή μου, “in whom my soul was well pleased.”]

He therefore prays that the Father may remember all his gentleness, through the modesty of which gentleness he vowed to God the Father the service of his humility.

### 4. He is said to have sworn because he fulfilled all things as though he had sworn. Peter’s prerogatives.

Verse 2: “As,” he says, “he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” Mention of an oath is employed to signify a profession of will. And I do not know whether the Only-Begotten swore. Certainly he both did and said everything in such a manner [Col. 0730B] as to seem to fulfill the obligation of an oath.

[Note: Thus the Vatican and Mic. manuscripts; whereas the printed texts and the Regius and Tours manuscripts read: “the religious obligation of an oath.”]

For when he had spoken to his disciples about certain matters concerning his passion, and Peter, as though this were unworthy of the Son of God, had rejected it, he addressed Peter—whom he had earlier given the keys of the kingdom of heaven, upon whom he was going to build the Church against which the gates of hell would have no power, and whose acts of binding or loosing on earth would remain bound or loosed in heaven—with this rebuke, when he rejected this mystery of the passion: “Get behind me [Note: “Go back.”] Satan; you are a stumbling block to me” (Matt. 16:23).

[Note: “Would have no power”; then, “or loosed.”]

[Note: “For” is absent from the Regius and Tours manuscripts. It is noteworthy that Hilary not only here but also in Psalm 138, no. 6, expressly declares that Peter was called by the rebuke “Satan.” Yet, since in his Commentary on Matthew, chapter 16, he indicates that these same words of Christ were spoken to Satan himself, he can—and indeed must—be reconciled with himself as follows: Christ is said there to have rebuked Satan himself as the author of Peter’s unbelief, but here Peter as consenting to Satan’s suggestion; and Peter was therefore “Satan,” because through Satan he had become unbelieving. For, as is taught in Psalm 142, no. 2, each person receives the name of those through whom he has become such.]

For his religious commitment to suffer for the salvation of humankind was so great that he called Peter—the first confessor of the Son of God, foundation of the Church, gatekeeper of the heavenly kingdom, and judge of heaven in earthly judgment—by the rebuke “Satan.”

Moreover, in that disturbance when he had offered himself to be handed over to the passion, when the same Peter cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant with a sword, he said: “Put your sword back into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” (John 18:11), teaching it to be impious and profane if he did not accomplish everything which he had vowed to the Father concerning human salvation.

[Note: “He had willed to suffer.”]

And he showed absolutely the devoted commitment of his passion when, after the draught of vinegar, he was about to give up his spirit. For, when all things had been completed, he said: “It is finished”; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30). He had gone through every duty of the mystery; and where completion brings joy, there is joy in the perfection of the work undertaken. Therefore, because in accordance with this devotion in his deeds everything was so done as to appear to have been completed zealously in observance of religion, as though these things had been sworn, it follows that we should see what this David both swore and vowed.

[Note: The Tours manuscript with the Regius: “as though these things had been sworn,” omitting what follows.]

### 5. These are not the words of a human being, who cannot lawfully swear such things and cannot find a place worthy of God.

Verses 3–5: “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house, if I go up upon the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes, and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

These cannot be vows of human nature; the requirement of this oath exceeds the weakness of earthly necessity. One must not enter the tabernacle of one’s house, one must abstain from the bed of one’s couch, one must give neither sleep to the eyes, nor slumber to the eyelids, [Col. 0731B] nor rest to the temples, until a place is found for the Lord and a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. Thus one would have to stand beneath the sky night and day; the body would never lie down in rest; the eyes would always toil in wakefulness; and even the eyelids would not be permitted the closing of slumber by blinking.

[Note: “Night and day.”]

[Note: Thus the Regius and Tours manuscripts; the printed texts read: “the closing in slumber by blinking.”]

The temples, moreover, which in the whole head and body are especially subject to the injury of sleeplessness and standing, would have no rest. A human being is not permitted to swear such things concerning himself; however much he may wish it, he will nonetheless violate the terms of this vow through the very necessity of his nature. Though the mind may keep watch and hold the body upright, still, with the weakness of nature prevailing, it must collapse, sleep, and rest against its will.

[Note: In two manuscripts: “to pray.”]

Furthermore, what place will a human being find for God? In what kind of tabernacle will he contain the incomprehensible and infinite nature? God himself has spoken of himself through the Prophet, saying: “Heaven is my throne and earth the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, or what is the place of my rest? For my hand made all these things, and all these things are mine” (Isa. 66:1–2).

[Note: “Had spoken.”]

The Prophet, however, is not ignorant of this divine utterance, and knows that a house produced by human and earthly work cannot be for God; he testifies to this very point in the preceding Psalm, when he says: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain” (Ps. 126:1). Therefore, since neither human nature can accept the terms of this vow, nor can human effort seek out—or perhaps, find—a place and tabernacle for God, we must learn through the authority of the heavenly Scriptures what this vow is, by whose fulfillment a place for the Lord and a tabernacle for the God of Jacob have been found.

### 6. Christ’s work: making the human being worthy of God’s dwelling. What kind of God dwells in a human being.

For our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who fulfilled all the mysteries of human salvation as though sworn to them, and whom we have shown to be signified by David in the Prophets, had this as his greatest work: to render a human being instructed in divine knowledge worthy to be God’s dwelling-place.

[Note: The printed texts read “a dwelling for God.” Shortly afterward the Tours manuscript reads “I shall walk among them,” not “in them.”]

And we are taught that the human being is the seat and dwelling of God, when God himself speaks through the Prophet: “For I will dwell in them, and walk in them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people” (Lev. 26:12; 2 Cor. 6:16); and again: “They shall rejoice forever, and I will dwell in them” (Ps. 5:12).

[Note: “I shall dwell,” ἐνοικήσω.]

The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, [Col. 0732B] and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

[Note: Tours codex: “My Father will love him, and we shall come and make a dwelling,” etc.]

The Apostle likewise says: “You are God’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3:16). God dwells in religious minds, not through bodily access nor by the entrance of a more weighty nature, as though he departed from elsewhere and remained only where he had entered; but by spiritual power he allows himself into hearts empty of earthly corruptions, and, like light, pours himself in to illuminate minds open through the gates of innocence.

[Note: The printed texts read: “as though not dwelling elsewhere”; corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.]

[Note: The printed texts read “in open places.” The manuscripts more aptly read “into open minds,” that is, he pours himself into minds. How the Word refuses himself to no one except the person who refuses him access is likewise illustrated by the likeness of the sun in Psalm 118, no. 5.]

Therefore, having assumed a body, the only-begotten God swears that he will not enter before his human being into the tabernacle of his house—that is, return into his heavenly dwelling—until he finds these places of a devout heart for the Lord.

[Note: “God.”]

### 7. He will not resume rest until the human being has become God’s seat.

Nor does he vow that he will ascend the bed of his couch. A bed is rest after human labors and refreshment for weary bodies. But because there is always rest in heaven, and that tireless nature knows no labor, he is always upon the bed—that is, always in rest.

[Note: “Because” is absent from the Regius and Tours manuscripts.]

Our Lord, remaining in the form of God, took the form of a servant and became obedient unto death, even death of the cross, in order to suffer something beyond death itself.

[Note: That is, because the cross brought not death alone, but also torment and disgrace.]

But for this reason alone was he obedient unto death on the cross: that he might make us worthy of God’s dwelling. Therefore he who is life willed to die, and tireless power did not refuse to make itself weak for the dwelling of the body, so that, remaining in the form of God, he might take the form of a servant. He therefore departed from the bed of his eternal blessedness.

And the fortieth Psalm bears witness for us, declaring in the person of the Lord the whole mystery of the passion: “You have turned his whole bed in his weakness” (Ps. 40:4). When, through obedience to the Father’s will, he who was God became human, the powerful became weak, the life-giving became dead, and the eternal judge of ages was called guilty of the cross, then his bed is changed in weakness.

[Note: “Of eternal things”; then, “into weakness.”]

[Note: Regius manuscript with Tours: “eternal.”]

[Note: The printed texts read “into weakness.” The manuscripts more correctly read “in weakness”: first, because this refers to “you have turned [it] in weakness”; secondly, because it removes any suspicion that the divine nature, which is incapable of change, is said to have undergone a transformation.]

He therefore vows not to return to that bed of eternal and blessed rest until God’s tabernacle has been found; nor will he first give sleep to his eyes.

### 8. Jacob’s prophecy of Christ under the name of Judah. The lion secure in sleep: Christ, God, fearless in death.

What is this sleep? Surely that of which he says: “I slept and began to sleep, and I rose, because the Lord will sustain me” (Ps. 3:6). This is the sleep of death, which he will not give to his eyes before he finds a place of habitation.

The blessed patriarch Jacob also remembers this sleep in his blessing of Judah, who became the leader of that tribe, saying: “Judah, a lion’s cub; from the shoot, my son, you have gone up. Falling down, you slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub. Who will rouse him?” (Gen. 49:9). Both the preceding and the following blessing suit neither Judah’s age nor his deeds, but him who is from Judah’s shoot as from Jesse’s root, who is both a lion’s cub and Jacob’s son. For Mary, who was mother of our Lord according to the flesh, came from this tribe of Judah.

[Note: “Of our Lord.”]

He therefore, falling down, slept as a lion. The lion is a terror to all wild beasts, and is as though ruler over the other animals; and he alone, through confidence and security, sleeps fearless. He is the terror of all when awake, but is himself secure in sleep. Therefore he added: “Who will rouse him?” because no fear of external terror troubles the security of a fearless and overwhelmingly powerful nature.

[Note: Regius codex and Tours: “from death.” You see that wherever Christ is proclaimed impassible, this is affirmed of him only according to his divine nature; this is especially clear from these words and from the opening words of the following section.]

Thus, lest we should suppose that in the death which he underwent the impassible substance of the only-begotten God had experienced anything lowly or capable of suffering, the example of this beast sleeping fearlessly is adduced to make us understand the security of that death: so that it might be shown that he was free in that sleep from the disturbance of human fear, since by the power of his own kind and nature, even while sleeping, he could not fear.

The reasoning is, however, very carefully preserved, so that in the only-begotten God might be recognized the glory of the eternal God who begot him, when it is said: “Like a lion and like a lion’s cub.” In respect of his subsistence from God, he is a lion’s cub; but in respect of being a lion, the undifferentiated nobility of the Father’s majesty in him is proclaimed. That the two may be one, he is a lion; that he may not be one and the same person, he is a lion’s cub.

[Note: In the Regius manuscript: “was born.”]

### 9. In what sense Christ did not die as God.

The continuation of the Psalm itself also teaches this.

[Note: In two manuscripts: “shows.”]

For lest that tireless power and impassible nature of the only-begotten God should be thought to sleep the sleep of death, he referred the entire matter to the function of the body, for which the departure of the immortal soul is death, saying: “If I give sleep to my eyes, and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

By the sense of the translation, he denies rest to the temples not as periods of life, but as parts of the head. These are bodily affections, agitated by prolonged labor and the anxiety of life. But he rested, for whom death is sleep; and what is for us a penal change became rest for the only-begotten God, who remained in the body.

### 10. Those who through Christ became God’s house.

But before this rest the Apostles are chosen; they receive the right of loosing and binding both on earth and in heaven; they receive power against every opposing force; they are God’s temple; and, coming themselves from the Law, they are found to be a tabernacle worthy of the God of Jacob.

And lest anyone perhaps suppose that, by manifold interpretations of human ingenuity, we force the truth by transferring through many subtle allegories to our Lord and Savior what was spoken in David’s person, we must consider what follows, so that from these things we may press the truth upon even the unwilling and resistant. For he says, vv. 6–7: “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of the forest; we shall enter into his tabernacles; we shall worship in the place where his feet stood.”

Above, where he swears and vows, we taught that the vow’s solemn obligation does not suit human nature, because bodily labor could not sustain wakefulness for so long a time. Now, too, when the very places and their names are mentioned, lest anything be capable of being referred to David [Col. 0734C], the truth itself and the evidence of the region still existing today contradict it.

For David, having in his kingdom a scattered people who had no seat of worship, bought a threshing-floor in Jerusalem for the site of the temple, so that they might gather there to fulfill the observances of the Law (2 Sam. 24:24). But his son Solomon built this temple, adorned it, and dedicated it for worship.

11. The Jews are refuted who understand these words as spoken of David, not of Christ. — The Jews, then, maintain that David, the purchaser of this threshing-floor, vowed separation from his house, the deprivation of sleep, and bodily toil, until he should be able to find for God of Jacob this place and this tabernacle. But neither does the history of Kings or Chronicles, in which David’s deeds are contained, say this; nor does the Psalm allow it. Why it does not allow it is plain. David bought a threshing-floor; the site of the Temple was the site of a threshing-floor, where grain is heaped, threshed, and where chaff is separated from wheat. But the Lord’s rest is in Ephrathah: first it was heard of in Ephrathah, and afterwards found in the fields of the forest. And what has Jerusalem in common with Ephrathah? What has a threshing-floor in common with the fields of a forest? Nothing here agrees; nothing is not discordant.

The threshing-floor in which the God of Jacob is supposed to have rested, the Lord in the last times cleanses with the winnowing-fan: He gathers His wheat into barns, but burns the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. 3:12). He considers men proved by the Law worthy of storehouses; the useless and unfruitful He assigns to the fire of judgment. That Temple no longer exists today: it has been burned, destroyed, and rendered shapeless by ruins. Where, then, is God’s rest? Has the Prophet lied, and is the vow of his very oath void? Has God lost the rest which He vowed on oath that He would find for Himself? Therefore, because these fabrications of irreligious opinions accord neither with God’s dignity, nor with human nature, nor with the truth of places, nor with the change of times, it must now be demonstrated from the very authorities of the heavenly Scriptures that the Psalm is to be referred to the person of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the sanctification of the Church.

[Note: The word “forest” is added here from the Tours manuscript, which a little earlier reads: “the chaff has been separated from the wheat.”]

508

12. Why the preceding speech is singular, but this one plural. — We said above that this prophet also prophesied in this Psalm concerning that righteous David, shepherd, king, and rising one, and spoke in his person when he said: “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house, if I ascend the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

But now, in order that the Prophet might show himself neither ignorant nor unskilled concerning this vow, he speaks in his own person, saying: “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of the forest.” Above, where the sacred character of the oath is mentioned, one person swore and vowed. For one who remained in the form of God took the form of a servant; and there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and one God the Father, from whom are all things (1 Cor. 8:6). But now, where knowledge of prophetic understanding is displayed, the statement is made in the person of many: “We heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of the forest,” because the Lord’s rest was prophesied by many.

[Note: The printed editions read “one God the Father,” which is less to the point and opposed by the manuscripts. Hence Christ is shown to be one because He is from one Father.]

13. The Church begins in Bethlehem and is found among the Gentiles. — It is therefore heard of in Ephrathah. Ephrathah is the same as Bethlehem, where the Lord was born of Mary. The Prophet bears witness for us, saying: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are not least among the thousands of Judah; for from you shall come forth one who shall be king of Israel” (Mic. 5:2); and again: “And you, Bethlehem of Judah, are not least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth one who shall rule my people Israel” (Matt. 2:6).

[Note: “Shall rule.”]

For there God’s rest is first heard, where the only-begotten God first inhabited a body of human flesh; and what is heard in Ephrathah is found in the fields of the forest. Thus the beginning of the Church is heard in Bethlehem, for it began from Christ; but it is found among the Gentiles, who are fields out of forests: bright out of what was bristling, fruitful out of barrenness; a region of life-giving food out of fuel for fire; God’s rest, house, temple, and possession out of the dens of wild beasts.

That the Gentiles were like a forest, the lair of the devil, Psalm 79 bears witness for us, saying: “The boar out of the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it” (Ps. 79:14). There the discourse is about the vine—that is, about the people of God, as it was then thought—which the devil, dwelling among the Gentiles, had devastated as unbelieving and impious. Therefore, in these fields of the forest is found the rest of God that was heard in Ephrathah.

[Note: In the received text: “from the fields of the forest.” But in the royal and Tours manuscripts: “the fields out of forests,” much more suitably indicating the conversion of the Gentiles.]

14. Blessedness is not here except in hope. The Church is one and many. The Church’s unchangeable standing. — The sequence of times is preserved, so that “we heard” and “we found” signify a past age, while what follows teaches the hope of the future time, when he says, verse 7: “We shall enter into His tabernacles; we shall worship in the place where His feet stood.”

The Prophet, despairing of this benefit of entering the tabernacles of God as an office belonging to the present bodily life, presumes by faith and Spirit that he will enter the tabernacles of God’s rest, because he both saw and heard them. But above there was an oath concerning only one tabernacle; now, however, they will enter many tabernacles. For from the one Church of the Apostles, concerning which the vow above was made, there are many churches and many tabernacles; but the same rest of God is in many. Into these tabernacles of God’s rest, therefore, they shall enter. Nor shall they only enter, but they shall also worship where His feet stood.

When one stands in one place, from which one ought not depart, one remains fixed; but where one stands with the feet, there one is established by the whole service of the body. The Law has passed away; prophecy is closed; Christ is their end; there is no place for another change. One must stand forever in this, where the Lord has now taken His stand after the course of the Law and the Prophets. The preaching indeed ranges abroad through the Apostles, whom we have often remembered to be denoted by “feet”; but in the Gospels it stands firm. There, therefore, worship shall be offered where the Lord’s feet—that is, the final stage of preaching—have stood without any transgression into a change.

[Note: The printed editions read “of this life.” More correctly, the manuscripts read “this,” namely, the benefit of entering God’s tabernacles. A little earlier the royal and Tours manuscripts read simply “we shall worship,” without “in the place.”]

[Note: The Paris edition omits the preposition “from.” In other editions the words “for from the one … but the same” are missing. On the Church as one in many, see Tractate on Psalm 14, no. 3.]

[Note: The royal and Tours manuscripts read “could not.”]

[Note: In the received text: “the final preachings.” We restore from the manuscripts: “the final stage of preaching,” so that, as the feet are the final parts of the body, the Gospels are the final stage of preaching. Hence, by the preceding word “Apostles,” we think all those sent by God to preach God’s word, even before Christ’s advent, are to be understood.]

[Note: The royal manuscript, with the Tours manuscript and early editions, reads “transgression.”]

15. God’s desire. — Because we read in the Gospels that it was said: “Many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear” (Matt. 13:17), the holy Prophet cannot endure this desire. For after he heard and found God’s rest, after he believed that he would enter and worship, he prays to become now a participant in so great a hope, saying, verse 8: “Arise, O Lord, into Your rest”—the rest which Your David vowed that he would find; which we heard in Ephrathah; which we found in the fields of the forest; into whose tabernacles we shall enter, to worship there where Your feet stood.

Arise, then, into that rest which was sought by the sacramental pledge of a vow; which was heard in a place through prophetic knowledge; which was found in the fruitful cultivation of the Gentiles; which is frequented by those entering it; which is unchangeable in its place; and which is venerable through the worship of those who adore it.

[Note: The editions read “in the fruitful fruitfulness of the Gentiles”; corrected from the royal and Tours manuscripts. The editor conjectured that the author intended *frugifera*, “fruit-bearing.”]

[Note: “Those entering.”]

510

16. The ark of sanctification is Christ. — But not only, Lord, arise into Your rest; rather, both You and the ark of Your sanctification. Not the ark of the covenant, not the ark of the Law, but the ark of Your sanctification. We remember indeed that there was an ark of the covenant, golden within and without, in which were the tablets of stone, the holy writings, the book of the Covenant, and a *gomor* of manna. But all these are a figure of that body which the Lord assumed, containing in itself every mystery of the Law.

Now, united in the Spirit of deity and the origin of flesh, it is golden within and without; for our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. Containing within itself eternal manna—for He Himself is the living bread; preserving within itself the tablets of the Covenant and the book of the Law—for in Him are the words of life. Therefore the Prophet prays that this ark of sanctification too may arise with the Lord into rest: “For this Lord, according to the Gospels, the Father both sanctified and sealed” (John 6:27).

But that earthly ark was often captured by the Philistines and defiled by kings; and today, with Temple and city overthrown, it no longer exists. Let us see what follows.

[Note: For “now,” the Tours manuscript reads “for this.”]

[Note: The royal codex, together with the Tours manuscript and received text, has “fortified.” More correctly, the manuscripts of Micy and the Vatican have “united”: that is, Christ, now glorious in flesh as in divinity, is golden within and without, since, being both man and God, He is now wholly God, as Hilary says in *On the Trinity*, book 11, no. 41. We have explained this manner of speaking more fully elsewhere. It is enough to observe here that he says Christ’s body—or rather Christ Himself—is united in human and divine nature only when, after the resurrection, He received again the glory which He had before the ages; because before the glory of the flesh, the lowly and inglorious form of a servant in some manner stood apart from the glorious form of God. To that extent Christ had lost, according to the assumed manhood, unity with the nature of God; nor did the Word made flesh return, even according to His humanity, to unity with the paternal nature, except when the assumed flesh possessed the glory of the Word, as he explains in *On the Trinity*, book 9, no. 38. Nor should it be thought from this that he preached the abolition of the body, as though in Christ there were now nothing but the gold of divinity. It appears that there is nothing else, yet there is something else. Hence Cyril, in Facundus of Hermiane, book 11, chapter 7: “The wood indeed was adorned with the splendour of gold; nevertheless, it did not cease to be wood.” He says this of the ark, concerning which he adds: “That the ark is to be understood as an image of Christ can be shown by many proofs.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “containing eternal manna within itself,” perhaps the more genuine reading. In the same way, in the exposition of Psalm 139, no. 12, we read “the Passover which goes before.” Yet in the exposition of Psalm 134, no. 24, *manna* appears in the accusative.]

[Note: Thus the Tours manuscript. But Bade, with the royal manuscript, has “For this Lord.” Erasmus, however, substituted “For this [ark]” for “For this Lord,” removing the following word “Lord”; this reading subsequently prevailed. The Micy manuscript reads: “For this one, as God, etc.”]

17. Why the saints have joy, and the priests must be clothed with righteousness. — Verses 9 and 10. For he says: “Let Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let Your saints rejoice.” The priests are clothed for God with righteousness when the ark of His sanctification rises into rest, with that most powerful breastplate of which the Apostle says: “Putting on the breastplate of righteousness” (Eph. 6:14), so that they may receive the enemy’s darts and protect the earthly human being. But let the saints rejoice.

Let us see why both the priests put on righteousness and the saints rejoice. For he says: “For the sake of David Your servant, do not turn away the face of Your Christ.” He refers “Christ” to the Spirit of deity, David to the flesh of the body. For He who remained in the form of God took the form of a servant.
