Therefore he prays that Christ may not turn His face away from the priests and saints, so that He may illumine with the glory of His divinity those who rejoice for David’s sake—that is, for the mystery of the body assumed by Him.

[Note: The editions read “the eternal human being,” which we alter on the authority of the manuscripts.]

[Note: That is, He takes the name from the parent of His flesh, as stated in the exposition of Psalm 121, no. 9. This understanding of the name Christ must be retained. By its help Hilary will be recognized in many passages in which he was thought to preach Christ as absolutely incapable of suffering: he protected Him from the experience of pain only according to the divine nature. This understanding of the name Christ is confirmed by Justin near the beginning of his *First Apology*, where he says: “He is called Christ because God through Him anointed and adorned all things”; and this name too has an unknown significance, just as the name God … But Jesus comprises both the name and significance of man and Savior.]

511

18. These things cannot be understood literally. — Verses 11–14. And why, for the sake of David His servant, He should not turn away the face of His Christ, he shows by saying: “The Lord swore truth to David, and He will not disappoint him.” The Lord swears, and swears truth; and lest we doubt, He confirms the reliability of His word by an oath. Therefore He will not defraud His David of the truth He has sworn. It is fitting to consider what He swore to him: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon My throne. If your children keep My covenant and these testimonies of Mine which I shall teach them, their children also shall sit upon your throne for ever. For the Lord has chosen Zion; He has chosen it beforehand as a dwelling for Himself. This is My rest for ages upon ages; here will I dwell, because I chose it beforehand.”

What is contained here that is peculiar to David? That city, which was the royal city of his race, was captured by the Babylonians and overthrown; it did not retain royal dignity under the power of its rulers. Afterwards also it was captured and burned by the Romans, and now it no longer exists. Where, then, is God’s eternal rest? Where are kings from the fruit of his womb upon God’s throne? Today they are servants, exiles, deprived of their country and scattered throughout the whole world. Where is that truth which was sworn? Where is that which was not to be disappointed in truth? Where is the everlasting throne of eternal rule for David’s children? Zion, which is called chosen, is dreadful with ruins and empty of inhabitants; and how is it God’s rest for ages upon ages? Time runs on, and only this present age of our life remains; therefore God is without rest.

[Note: In the first Paris edition: “that He not turn away the face of His Christ.” The other editions agree, except that they do not have the particle “not.” The manuscripts have it without “not”: that is, why he prays that, for David’s sake, He not turn away the face of His Christ. Shortly afterward, the royal and Tours manuscripts read “will not disappoint” for “will not be disappointed.”]

[Note: The editions read “your throne”; corrected with the help of the manuscripts, since no. 22 plainly refutes their reading. Erasmus noted in the margin: “Everywhere he demolishes the historical sense. Thus he indeed pursues the spiritual sense, so that he seems to reject history.” Yet Hilary explicitly declares in many places, especially in the immediately following exposition of Psalm 134, nos. 13 and 18, that he willingly grants truth to history, but that history is expressed in words not sufficiently suited to the events, in order to warn us that spiritual matters are signified by them. Nor will Erasmus deny that the words at hand concern especially Christ and the Church.]

[Note: “Under the power of rulers.”]

[Note: The Vatican codex’s reading “does not remain” has an appearance of truth, but is false. Misled by it, Lipsius substituted *manat*, “flows,” for *manet*, “remains”; whether this word occurs anywhere in Hilary, we doubt. As far as we understand, the meaning is this: only the present time remains; past things do not remain. Therefore God lacks a rest that extends through ages upon ages.]

19. They are elucidated by a similar passage. — But let those who believe this under the influence of so unfortunate an error hear to which David the oath was sworn. Namely, to Him of whom it is said: “I have placed My help upon one who is mighty, and have exalted one chosen from My people. I have found David My servant; with My holy oil I have anointed Him. For My hand shall assist Him, and My arm shall strengthen Him. The enemy shall gain nothing against Him, and the son of iniquity shall not add to afflict Him. I will crush His enemies before His face and turn those who hate Him to flight. My truth and My mercy shall be with Him, and in My name His horn shall be exalted. I will set His hand upon the sea and His right hand upon the rivers. He shall call upon Me: ‘You are My Father, My God, and the defender of My salvation.’ And I will make Him firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth. For ever I will preserve My mercy for Him, and My covenant shall be faithful to Him. I will set His seed for the age of ages, and His throne as the days of heaven. If His children forsake My Law and do not walk in My judgments, if they profane My ordinances and do not keep My commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes; but I will not scatter My mercy away from Him, nor deal falsely in My truth, nor profane My covenant, nor make void what proceeds from My lips. Once have I sworn by My holy one: if I lie to David, His seed shall remain for ever, and His throne as the sun before Me, and as the perfect moon it remains for ever, and as a faithful witness in heaven” (Ps. 88:20 ff.).

These are the promises of that David who was chosen as a help against the mighty one; whose hand is upon the sea and whose right hand is upon the rivers; who dares to call God Father because He is His Father; who Himself is firstborn, who is exalted above the kings of the earth; whose seed is for the age of ages; for whom what has been said is not void; to whom an oath is once sworn in holiness without falsehood; whose throne is as the sun before God and remains as the perfect moon for ever. Therefore, from the fruit of His womb they shall be placed upon God’s throne.

[Note: “With oil.” Then: “shall assist Him.”]

[Note: “Above kings.”]

[Note: The royal manuscript, with the Tours manuscript, reads “above kings.”]

[Note: Thus the royal codex, in agreement with the Greek word *ta dikaiōmata*, “the ordinances.” Others read “righteousnesses.”]

[Note: The word “remains” is absent from the royal manuscript, which afterwards, together with the Tours manuscript, also omits “and as a faithful witness in heaven.”]

[Note: “As the days of heaven, and remains.”]

512

20. The sons of God are to be placed upon God’s throne. — But how we are the fruit of His womb, let us hear the prophet Jeremiah teach: “Have you then heard such a thing? Has a male given birth?” (Jer. 30:6). This sex does not admit childbirth; but the generation which is from God has obtained the character of childbirth. Let us hear Paul also travailing in the begetting of children when he says: “My children, for whom I am again in travail” (Gal. 4:19).

The Lord Himself bears witness in the Gospel that all of us are His children, saying: “Child, your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9:2); and again: “Children, I am still with you” (John 13:33). Therefore His children are to be placed upon the Lord’s throne.

[Note: The editions read “which is from Him”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

[Note: “Little children,” according to the Greek *teknia*.]

513

21. Which children, and on what condition of hope. — And the condition of hope is set forth: “If,” He says, “your children keep My covenant and these testimonies of Mine which I shall teach them.” Moses wrote the Law in which God’s testimonies are contained; this same prophet is entirely occupied with the Law. How, then, are the children of that David still to be instructed in testimonies? The discourse is not about the present age, but belongs to those of whom it was said: “I confess to You, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because You hid these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little children” (Matt. 11:25).

But what shall those taught and remaining in the things which will be taught receive? “For ever,” He says, “they shall sit upon Your throne.” And who are these who will sit? Surely those of whom it was said: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

22. The Father’s and Son’s throne is one, because their substance is one. — We must not overlook what is said above and below. Above it was said: “I will set upon My throne”; but now it is said: “They shall sit upon your throne.” What can this be? Surely what is said: “All things that the Father has are Mine” (John 16:15). The throne itself is the Father’s throne and the Son’s throne, because “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

But how can “I will set upon My throne” and “They shall sit upon your throne” be understood, except because, through the harmonious and not dissimilar nature of the unbegotten and the only-begotten, the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, the substance of deity in each being at variance neither in kind nor in will, since the glory of paternal majesty is connate with the Only-begotten? For this reason the Father calls the Son’s throne His own throne: because the only-begotten and true God was born both from Him and in the glory of His unchangeable divinity; nor does He consider the thrones shared with Him a dishonour, since for Him who was begotten from Himself in likeness of nature there is no diversity.

[Note: The royal manuscript reads “substance with the paternal glory and majesty known to the Only-begotten”: incorrectly. The Tours manuscript reads “with the paternal substance and glory of majesty known to the Only-begotten”: a less bad grammatical construction, but less genuine.]

[Note: The received editions connect this with the following words thus: “there is no diversity of dignity. Then their dwelling, who …,” against the manuscripts. Here you have *homoiousion*, or likeness of nature. Hilary judged that this term should not be rejected, but proclaimed with the greatest caution, holding no difference between confessing consubstantiality and confessing complete likeness, as the books *On Synods* and *To Constantius* show. “For my part,” he says in *To Constantius*, no. 22, “likeness is holy, lest an occasion be given for union.”]

23. What Zion is the true rest of God. — Next, the dignity of those who shall sit upon the throne for ever is shown thus: “For the Lord chose Zion; He chose it beforehand as a dwelling for Himself. This is My rest for the age of ages; here will I dwell, because I chose it beforehand.”

He did not choose, that is, the deserted and useless mountain Zion, nor a city demolished and overthrown. For God is not contained by places; nor does the omnipotent and eternal substance rest either in the empty solitudes of mountains or in the names of cities now made unsightly by ruin. Rather, He chose the rest of those concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one comes to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him” (John 6:44).

He chose that holy Zion and heavenly Jerusalem: namely, the concordant assembly of believers and souls sanctified by the sacraments of the Church, in which the ineffable nature of divinity, rational and intelligent and unstained and eternal, rests as in a rational, intelligent, cleansed, and eternal house through the glory of resurrection. This does not mean that He ceases from the infinity in which He exists by His immensity, so as to be confined within the narrow limits of human minds; but rather that He who is everywhere, the same, whole, and always, rests by the dwelling-place of a habitation made worthy for Him in holy and approved persons—where there is no alteration through offenses, but a dwelling worthy and pleasing is chosen for the age of ages, that is, for eternal times.

[Note: We restore here from the Micy and Vatican manuscripts the word “names,” omitted in the editions. It signifies cities which retain nothing of their former splendour except their names. A little earlier the royal codex reads “separated” rather than “deserted.”]

[Note: The editions read “from His infinity.” The royal and Tours manuscripts more suitably read “from that infinity in which He is”—that is, He does not cease from that immensity in which His infinity consists. The interpretation of this passage is to be drawn from the exposition of Psalm 122, nos. 2–3, where it is taught that the Son alone is indeed worthy in Himself to be God’s dwelling-place, yet that this is granted also to the saints through the Son dwelling in them.]

[Note: The editions read “who also is everywhere,” and shortly afterward, “where there is no offense, no change.” Better are the manuscripts: “who is everywhere,” without “also”; and then the Tours manuscript: “where there is no alteration through offenses,” which the royal manuscript has corruptly rendered, “where there is no offense, not change.” The reading of the Tours manuscript is evidently to be preferred from the exposition of Psalm 52, no. 12, where one finds the expression familiar to Hilary’s version, “the offenses of changes having been rebuked.” The same tractate, no. 11, teaches what that alteration through offenses consists in, to which we are now subject and from which we shall be freed after this life.]

24. Among variant translations, the Seventy are preferred. The dignity of widows. The Church, widow of the Law. — Next follows, verse 15: “Blessing I will bless her widow.” One of the translators is found to have rendered it: “Blessing I will bless her capture,” as though, since the Apostles became hunters and fishers of human beings, this capture of theirs were blessed—especially because Bethsaida, from which the Apostles came, is called in the interpretation of the Hebrew language “house of hunters.”

But we must follow that first authority of translation which, under the Jews before the Lord’s coming, was authenticated for the teaching of the Church: “Blessing I will bless her widow.” How great is the dignity of widows: the honourable consciousness of one marriage-bed, and the unchanging constancy of blessed continence! For she is blessed and is blessed by blessing: that is, through the judgment of the one blessing, she is made worthy of blessing.

But the Apostle, teacher of the Gentiles, exhorts us to think something further about the widow who is to be blessed. He teaches that the Church which has been made from the Synagogue is a widow, since the Law has died not through the power of spiritual efficacy but through the termination of its observance. He says: “Do you not know, brethren—for I speak to those who know the Law—that the Law has dominion over a person as long as he lives? For the woman who is under a husband is bound by law to her living husband. But if her husband has died, she is discharged from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband is living, she shall be called an adulteress if she is joined to another man. But if her husband dies, she is freed from the Law, so that she is not held to be an adulteress when joined to another man. Therefore, my brethren, you also have been put to death to the Law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to Him who rose from the dead.”

By comparison with a widow, who when her husband has died is free to marry whom she wishes, he shows that, now that the Law has ceased, the Church is the widow of the Law, to be lawfully joined to Christ. Therefore He will bless by blessing this widow of the Law.

[Note: Undoubtedly the Septuagint, although the author of the commentary on the Psalms reports through Jerome that they have *thēran*, “capture.” He adds: “But because of the novelty of the word, it gradually came to pass that *chēran*, ‘widow,’ was read instead of *thēran*, especially because ‘the poor’ followed in the next verse.” He adds that Symmachus and Aquila rendered it “provisions,” which Jerome testifies is signified by the Hebrew word in *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 45, where he also observes that in many Greek copies *chēran*, “widow,” occurs. In his Psalter, however, Jerome translated it “hunting.”]

[Note: “Blessing.”]

[Note: The received editions read “joined”; more correctly, the manuscripts read “bound,” in accordance with the Greek *dedetai*. Then the royal and Tours manuscripts read: “But if her husband has died.”]

[Note: “If he dies first.”]

[Note: “May be joined in marriage.”]

[Note: In place of “is joined,” the received editions read “may be.”]

515

25. Christ satisfies the poor by inviting them to be fed. — Then He says: “I will satisfy her poor with bread.” It is good that the poor in the Church should not hunger, for when a needy person is fed, a thirsty person given drink, a naked person clothed, a sick person visited, or one shut in prison sought out, these services of duty are offered to Him who in each of us hungers, thirsts, is cold, sick, and imprisoned, and who says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: what you did to one of the least of these, you did to Me” (Matt. 25:40).

Therefore, through this faithful declaration of His words, He satisfies her poor with bread. He also satisfies with bread those who, through humility of heart and contempt for the world, place themselves in poverty: He will fill them with the food of eternal life, as was said elsewhere: “The rich have lacked and hungered; but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.”

[Note: “Amen” only once.]

[Note: Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “promise.” The Paris edition and manuscripts rightly retain “declaration,” by which Christ announces that what is done for the poor is rendered to Himself.]

26. The glory of the priests and the perfected joy of the saints. — Next follows, verse 16: “I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her saints shall rejoice with rejoicing.” Above the priests are clothed with righteousness, but they receive the increase of their honour: namely, they are clothed with salvation, having been made conformed to the glory of the Savior. For, according to the Apostle, we await our Savior from heaven, who is able, by the operation of His power, to conform the body of our humiliation to the body of His glory (Phil. 3:20–21).

With this salvation the priests are clothed; and the saints shall rejoice with rejoicing. Above they merely rejoice, still placed in the body of humiliation and joyful only in the hope of eternity. But now they rejoice with perfected rejoicing: not in hope but in reality, not in an image but in the body. For often there is a rejoicing that is subject to change through accident, weakness, or time; but this is the rejoicing of the saints: that they rejoice with the rejoicing of rejoicing consummated in themselves.

[Note: “Salvation.” Shortly afterward: “they shall rejoice with His rejoicing.”]

[Note: That is, of the Savior; nor should the Paris edition, against the other witnesses, have substituted “salvation.” Shortly afterward, “from heaven” is absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts.]

[Note: “They shall be clothed.”]

[Note: The Paris edition incorrectly reads “in the humiliation of the body,” although the reference is to Paul’s words, “He will transform the body of our humiliation.”]

[Note: The received editions read “then.” With the royal and Tours manuscripts one should read “now,” that is, in the verse currently being expounded. This particle is opposed to “above,” which indicates verse 9. The meaning is: in verse 9 we have “let Your saints rejoice,” but no “rejoicing” is added; thus is expressed the begun joy of saints who rejoice in this age only in hope. But now we do not read merely “they shall rejoice,” but, with the added word “with rejoicing,” the saints’ consummated joy is signified.]

27. Christ’s kingdom. — The cause of the rejoicing is shown, verse 17: “There I will bring forth the horn of David.” The horn is the insignia of kingship; for through it royal anointing was poured upon those about to reign. When “there” is said, the rest is signified of which it was said: “This is My rest for the age of ages.” In this rest God brings forth the horn of David—that is, the kingdom of that David concerning whom prophecy is made: not a human kingdom, nor corruptible, nor transitory, but that which, according to God’s rest, is for the age of ages.

And whose will the kingdom of heaven be? Surely those of whom it was said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3): that is, those in whom the eternal King, whose kingdom according to Daniel has no end, will reign (Dan. 7:27).

[Note: The manuscripts read “insignia.”]

[Note: The received editions read “prophesies.” The manuscripts’ “is prophesied” is preferable, for the following word “David” is in the genitive: “the kingdom of that David concerning whom prophecy is made.”]

[Note: “Will bring forth.”]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts, whereas the received editions read “according to the kingdom of God.”]

[Note: The royal manuscript, with the Tours manuscript, reads “in whom.” In this way Daniel’s expression is consistently rendered, as noted above.]

28. Not hidden. Every prophecy, Christ’s lamp.---Therefore this king is not concealed: the Law proclaims him, the Prophets promise him, John, preacher of repentance, points him out. For he is, according to the Lord’s saying in the Gospel, “a burning lamp,” revealing Christ amid the darkness of this world (John 5:35). Every prophecy concerning him, therefore, is his lamp: it displays to the night of our ignorance the light of knowledge, confounds unbelievers and the impious by the light of truth, and teaches the glory of the Father’s majesty in the Only-Begotten. And this is what follows: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.”

[Col. 0744C] VERSE 18. “I will clothe his enemies with confusion; but upon him [Note: Bad., Er., and Lips. read *florebit*, “will flower.” In Paris, in accordance with the manuscripts, *floriet*, “will flourish,” has been restored. Concerning this word, Augustine’s statement is well known, *On Christian Doctrine*, II.13: “What we can no longer remove from the mouths of the singing peoples.” [Col. 0744D] “But upon him my sanctification will flourish” plainly detracts nothing from the sense; nevertheless, a more learned hearer would prefer it corrected to read not *floriet* but *florebit*, “will flower.” In the old psalter which St Germanus of Paris is said to have used, *floriet* is found.] my sanctification will flourish.” The lamp has been prepared so that the night of ignorance may not hinder the knowing of him. His enemies will be clothed with confusion; for they shall see the Son of Man in the majesty of his Father. They shall be clothed not with salvation but with confusion, [Note: Bad., Er., and Lips. read “in an earthly, that is, an unseemly body.” Paris, from the Mic. manuscript, reads “in an earthly, that is, in a body of unseemliness.” Reg. and Turon. read “in a body of earthly disgrace.” From these two readings the true text is established. Moreover, after the resurrection the impious are called earthly, because they will plainly not be changed, and consequently will, as before, belong to the first man, of whom the Apostle says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly.” They are also said to be in a body of disgrace, because they are not conformed to Christ’s body of glory.] namely, rising again [Col. 0745A] earthly and in a body of disgrace. “But upon him my sanctification will flourish.” “God,” he says, “exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those beneath the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9–10), who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: He thus concludes his exposition of this Psalm: “Psalm CXXXI is ended.” Here the manuscript of the Church of Verona, worn out beneath the burden of so many centuries, leaves us; its final leaves have been cut away. [Col. 0746D]]

## PSALM CXXXII. A Song of Ascents.

Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. It is like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon Aaron’s beard, which runs down to the edge of his garment; like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion: [Col. 0745B] for there the Lord commanded blessing, and life unto the ages.

## EXPOSITION OF THE PSALM.

### 1. Many good things are not pleasant, and pleasant things are not good.

Throughout the entire order of instruction one ascends by steps, for by steps we are carried upward. Since the Prophet began in this way, VERSE 1, “Behold, how good and how pleasant,” we are taught what is good and pleasant, so that, through knowing them, we may remain among things good and pleasant. The Prophet deliberately preserved the principle of joining good and pleasant together, because not everything good is pleasant, nor is everything pleasant good. Luxury is pleasant, but it is not good; for that very delight of bodily wantonness brings harm both to health and reputation. [Col. 0745C] Enduring injury is good—especially when, in order to compel us into irreligion, we are subjected to the punishments of hunger, thirst, cold, vigils, insults, and pains—but it is not pleasant; there the duty of perfect virtue is burdensome. Thus, through such things, goodness sometimes lacks pleasantness, and pleasantness lacks that which is good.

### 2. The good and pleasant thing is brotherly unity; where it is real.

Let us consider what it is that the Prophet declares to be good and pleasant: namely, for brothers to dwell together in unity. The prophet David does not mean human cohabitations or the sharing of earthly houses. For we see brothers quarrelling beneath the very same roofs, and the dwelling of the same home often contains enemies; and sometimes the very indignation of having to live together supplies fuel for hatreds. But the Apostle knew the common and religious house, saying: “That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, [Note: Paris erroneously reads “be preserved.” Other editions read “conduct yourself.” We restore from the manuscripts *diversari*, “to dwell,” as Hilary also reads it in Psalm LXIV, §6, and elsewhere.] which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and [Col. 0746A] foundation of the truth” (1 Tim. 3:15). Thus it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell in unity. When they dwell in unity, [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “They assemble the gathering of the Church.”] they are gathered in the assembly of the Church; when they are called brothers, they are harmonious in the love of a single will.

### 3. The character of unanimity.

For we read that this was the chief glory of the believers at the first preaching of the Apostles: “For the heart and soul of all who believed were one”—one in assent, undivided in will, united in faith, perfected by unanimity of love and judgment (Acts 4:32). The Teacher of the Gentiles also testifies to this, saying: “That you may all be perfect, of the same mind and the same judgment” (1 Cor. 1:10). And again: “Complete my joy, that you think the same thing, having the same love, being unanimous, thinking one thing, [Col. 0746B] doing nothing through rivalry or vain glory, but in humility each considering the other superior to himself, each of you looking not to his own interests but to those of others” (Phil. 2:2 ff.). This is the Apostle’s joy: that we think the same thing, are held together by the same love, remain unanimous through the judgment of one mind, are not divided by rivalry or estranged through the pursuit of vain glory, and that each must think not of his own concerns but of those of others, in order that we may consider those things by which the wills of others are to be held in concord. This he urges elsewhere when he says: “If it is possible, as far as it depends upon you, having peace with all” (Rom. 12:18). He wishes it to depend upon us, so that, if possible, peace may exist with all. Let our will be devoted to friendship with everyone, [Note: The printed editions read, “even if the nature of the rest does not possess,” etc.; this is also found in the Turon. manuscript. We prefer, with Reg., “if the nature of the rest also has,” etc., by which the Apostle’s words, “if possible,” are explained more fittingly.] if the nature of others also has an inclination toward peace, [Col. 0746C] provided that the cause either of interrupted peace or of peace not preserved does not arise from us.

This, therefore, befits God’s people: under one Father to be brothers, under one Spirit to be one, under one house to walk unanimously, under one Head to be members of one body. For the eye does not hate the ear, nor do the nostrils abhor the mouth, nor does the hand despise the foot. These are bound closely together [Note: In Paris, *distracta*, “separated,” erroneously; but *destricta*, that is, strictly joined together, as *distringit* is read in this sense in Matthew X, §23.] both by their mutual services and by love. This is pleasant and good: for brothers to dwell in unity, to be in the same place, to be the same, and to differ neither in assembly nor in love.

### 4. What anointing is prefigured by Aaron’s anointing.

The Prophet establishes a comparison for this good and pleasant thing, saying, VERSE 2: “Like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, [Note: The word “beard,” not repeated in the earlier printed editions, is added on the authority of the Turon. manuscript, which shortly before reads “from the head,” not “upon the head.”] Aaron’s beard; [Col. 0746D] which runs down to the edge of his garment.” Aaron was anointed priest with ointment whose composition and blending consist of fragrant substances (Lev. 8:12). [Col. 0747A] God was pleased that this should be the consecration of his first priest.

We have also learned that our Lord was anointed invisibly and incorporeally, when it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation” (Ps. 45:8). This anointing is not earthly; it is incorporeal and invisible. He is anointed not with oil as priest and prophet, nor with a horn as king, but with the oil of exultation. This is a work of spiritual joy, and the fruit of exultation is employed for the mystery of heavenly anointing; it is not the material of a created thing. Because bodily beings required bodily things, Aaron is anointed with compounded ointment; but the bodily thing, imbued through the efficacy of spiritual power, imitates the appearance of heavenly oil. Accordingly, after this anointing Aaron is called Christ according to the Law, after the compounded anointing—through what was shown to have been compounded by God—has been consecrated into the likeness of invisible anointing.

Therefore, as this ointment extinguishes, wherever it is poured, every foul odor and the unclean spirits of hearts, and pours this fragrance of sweetness into everything to which it is applied, so through the mystery of this poured-out anointing, and with every foulness of our earthly and sordid vices cleansed away by it, we now breathe forth what is sweet to God. The blessed Apostle Paul knew this spirit of sweet fragrance, saying: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God in every place, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; to the latter indeed a fragrance from death unto death, but to the former a fragrance from life unto life” (2 Cor. 2:15–16). Thus he shows that we are a fragrance of life to the living, and a fragrance of death to those [Col. 0747C] who were dying in their sins. Yet Christ’s fragrance from us is good to God. Therefore, as this ointment was pleasing to God in the first priest, Aaron—by which he was anointed as an image of the oil of exultation, [Note: Thus the Turon. manuscript, supported by Reg. The printed editions read: “and offers to God from itself a grateful fragrance of faith and innocence.”] offering from itself to God a pleasing fragrance of faith and innocence—so it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell in unity, through which the unanimity of a single will is compared with the first and greatest mysteries of heavenly goods.

### 5. Christ’s anointing flows from him into the man of perfected faith.

The ointment runs down from the head to the beard. The beard is the ornament of manly age. We ought not to be children in Christ, except only in what has been said: “Children in malice, not in understanding” (1 Cor. 14:20). The same Apostle rebukes all unbelievers as children, [Col. 0748A] because, weak and still unable to take solid food, they need milk, saying: “I fed you with milk, not with food; [Note: Reg. and Turon. read, “for not yet.”] for you were not yet able, nor indeed are you yet able” (1 Cor. 3:2). But of himself he says: “When I became a man, I put away the things of a child” (1 Cor. 13:11). He hastens to attain “a perfect man, to the measure of the age [Note: The word “fullness” is absent from the Reg. and Turon. manuscripts.] of the body of Christ” (Eph. 4:13). Therefore this ointment descends from the head into Aaron’s beard, that is, into the man of consummate faith. According to the Apostle, “Christ is the head of the man” (1 Cor. 11:3). Moses compounded and blended this ointment; but God taught that it was to be compounded and blended, and God is mediator in the Law.

It therefore descends from the Head, that is, from Christ, into the beard; and it descends from him to whom it was said: [Col. 0748B] “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song 1:2). It descends into one who, through the steadfastness of age, would remain unchangeable in steadfast faith. It also descends to the edge of the garment. The edge of the garment consists of those parts which hang down to the feet; by this, the fragrance of the ointment descends from the head into the beard, and then to the edge of the garment, over the whole body.

In those women who anointed the Lord and presented in the Gospel a type of the Church, we are taught that one [Note: Namely, the woman of Matt. 26:7: “A woman came to him having an alabaster flask of precious ointment, and poured it upon his head.” But the woman who anointed his feet is she of Luke 7:38: “She kissed his feet and anointed them with ointment,” or the woman of John 12:3: “Mary therefore took a pound of costly pure nard ointment and anointed Jesus’ feet.” Thus, for Hilary, there was not one woman who anointed the Lord; though Ambrose, *On Luke*, VII.14, was uncertain on the point, very many Greek Fathers asserted the distinction more certainly.] anointed the head and another the feet; by this each of them is shown to have anointed the whole body in her respective part. The middle portions of the body have therefore been omitted. For when the edge of the garment and the beard are mentioned, the whole body is indicated in them.

### 6. Zion is the Church. Mount Hermon in Phoenicia is interpreted “anathema”; it is worshipped by the Gentiles with profane religion.

A second comparison is also added when it is said, VERSE 3: “Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.” Dew does not descend from Hermon upon Zion, for these mountains are separated from one another by a great distance. Nor indeed does nature permit dew to descend from one place to another. But Zion, according to heavenly teaching, is the Church, whether that now existing or that of the saints which shall be, thronged through the resurrection by the assembly of glorified saints and rejoicing angels. Hermon, however, is a mountain in Phoenicia, [Note: “Which the Phoenicians call Sanior,” says Jerome, *On Hebrew Places.*] whose interpretation is “anathema”; for what [Note: The printed text reads “to us,” without the particle *cum*, which here has the same force as “according to.” Jerome, and the author of the Commentary on the Psalms attributed to him, interpret Hermon as “anathema,” as does our Hilary. Augustine, however, on this Psalm, §11, on the testimony of those who know Hebrew, interprets it “exalted light.”] is called *anathema* among us is called Hermon in Hebrew.

There is said to be a book—of unknown authorship [Note: This is the book commonly circulated under Enoch’s name, a fragment of which is reported by George Syncellus, *Chronographia*, p. 11. Jerome, in his comment on this passage, mentions it without the author’s name and rejects it as manifestly apocryphal, because it openly favors the Manichaean doctrine that souls desired human bodies. He adds that he had read a book of someone confirming his heresy from it. Augustine also counts it among the apocrypha, *City of God*, XV.23.4. Tertullian, *On Women’s Dress*, I.3, says: “I know that Enoch’s Scripture is not accepted by some.” Yet in the same place he defends its authority as far as he can; and from that book, in *On Idolatry*, 9, he calls the angels lovers of women, who, he says in *On Women’s Dress*, I.2, “fell from heaven to the daughters of men.” From the same source Cyprian says in *On the Singular Dress of Clerics*: “We know also that angels fell with women.” Justin, at the beginning of his *First Apology*, and Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, II.15, borrowed the same opinion from that book. Yet that ancient opinion concerning angels’ intercourse with women also arose from the words of Gen. 6:2, “The sons of God, seeing the daughters of men,” etc., because many codices read, “The angels of God, seeing the daughters of men,” etc. Hence Ambrose, on Psalm CXVIII, Sermon 8.58: “Finally, it is written that angels loved the daughters of men,” etc.; though, wavering in this opinion, in Sermon 4.8 he suggests that “angels” may mean people who imitate angelic grace by excellence of life. So also Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, I.3: “It is asked how angels could have lain with the daughters of men,” although some Latin and Greek codices have not “angels” but “sons of God.” He discusses the same question more carefully in *City of God*, XV.23. Josephus, *Antiquities*, I.4, writes that angels had intercourse with women; but Zonaras, I.4, judges that by “angels” Josephus understood the sons of Seth.]—which states that angels, desiring the daughters of men, [Col. 0749A] when they descended from heaven assembled upon this exceedingly high mountain. [Note: Lips. and Paris read, “assembled upon the exceedingly high mountain.” Even in Bad. and Er. the adverb *maxime*, “exceedingly,” is placed before *convenerint*, “assembled,” contrary to the manuscripts. The meaning is explained by the fragment of Enoch copied by George, in which it is told that the Egregori burned with love for the daughters of men and bound themselves by an oath to take them as companions. They were two hundred in number, who in the days of Jared went to Mount Ermonim. They called the mountain Ermon because of the oath by which they bound one another and the curses to which they voluntarily subjected themselves. See more in the cited fragment.] But let us pass these things over. For what is not contained in the book of the Law, we ought not even to know. They have been mentioned only because the Prophet’s declaration concerning this mountain moved us to speak of it. Certainly, even today Gentiles venerate this mountain with profane religion, and by that very seat of impious superstition testify to the interpretation of its name, namely, “anathema.”

### 7. Dew from Hermon to Zion: passage from curse to blessing.

Dew, however, is from heaven, and we remember that it is desired among the gifts of blessing when Isaac says to Jacob: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and the abundance of earth in plenty” (Gen. 27:28). Therefore, because God’s gifts and blessings—by which he first blessed all things when they were created and made, but which afterward, through Adam’s sin, came under anathema—are pleasing to God when they return and descend again to the seat of sanctification. For man was blessed; but after his blessing he sinned, and immediately became impious. Yet he who prefers the repentance of the sinner to his death wishes the dew of his blessing to descend from Hermon to Zion, that is, to pass from the seat of impiety to the place of sanctification. For by dew all things grow green, are nourished, and increase; so by that primal blessing of God man is born, breathes, and grows.

It is therefore good and pleasant that one should descend from Gentile error—that is, from the profane veneration of Hermon—and pass to Zion, that is, to the dwelling of eternal blessedness, and delight him who rejoices in the salvation of all, for this reason: “For [Col. 0749C] there [Note: “Lord” is absent from the Reg. and Turon. manuscripts.] the Lord commanded blessing and life unto the ages”: namely, in Zion, or also in the unanimity of brothers dwelling together. For the Church alone bestows blessings; unanimity gains eternal life. For he who, opening the way of eternal life, said, “Love one another as I have loved you,” is not false (John 13:34). For he is Truth, Way, Life—our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM CXXXIII. A Song of Ascents.

[Col. 0750A]

Behold, now bless the Lord, all his servants, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. In the nights lift up your hands in holy things, and bless the Lord. May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth.

## EXPOSITION OF THE PSALM.

### 1. To whom blessing belongs.

The Songs of Ascents reach their end, but an end worthy of their ascents. For since through them one ascends to the knowledge of the heavenly mystery, it is necessary that afterward blessing be rendered to him to whom one has ascended. Therefore the Prophet calls all to bless the Lord; and, as though all things had been completed, he gathers all together for the acknowledgment of due honor, saying, VERSE 1: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all his servants.” In saying “Behold, now,” he signifies that the work of the laboriously achieved ascent is perfect and complete: they are now to bless, because by advancing they have ascended. He is to be blessed because he has brought us upward, because he has raised us by the steps of faith to the height of his house. But the mouth of a sinner is unworthy to bless God; and therefore he says, “all his servants.” Not everyone’s blessing is acceptable to God; nor should anyone indiscriminately suppose that he can please him. This belongs only to God’s servant, not to the servant of sin or of the world. “For everyone,” he says, “who commits sin is the servant of sin” (John 8:34). It belongs, therefore, to God’s servant to bless his Lord with a reverent [Col. 0750C] mouth.

### 2.

Nor will this even belong to the servant who professes himself a servant in name alone, who even now, hesitating and wavering, is driven about by the uncertain wind of faith, [Note: The printed editions read “by the vow of faith”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.] whose thought and will roam among the recollection of sins and the cares of pleasures. Therefore, after saying, “Behold, now bless the Lord, all his servants,” he adds: “Who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts [Note: The Regius codex with Turon. reads “in the courts of the house of the Lord,” without “our.”] of the house of our God.” One who stands does not move from his place. [Note: The printed editions read “he now runs”: they express a contradiction. Hilary’s point is that one who formerly ran now stands at rest.] He has already run; he has already ascended; he now [Col. 0751A] remains unmoved; he now eagerly drinks in that blessed saying of the Prophet: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. 40:3); and again: “You have exalted me upon a rock” (Ps. 27:6). And he will hear spoken to him, as to Moses: “But you, stand here with me” (Exod. 34:2). But concerning sinners we read: “They loved to move their feet” (Jer. 14:10). Therefore one must stand in the house of the Lord, because the blessing of those who stand is pleasing: those who stand in that holy, heavenly Jerusalem, [Note: The Turon. manuscript reads “the throng of angels.”] thronged by angels, to which one ascends through this house of the Church and our assembly.

### 3. The distinction between God’s court and house.

And because “there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house” (John 14:2), they bless the Lord not only while standing in his house but also in his courts. Not every part of the house is a court. Whatever lies outside the court is also house; but the court is a more inward and familiar place of dwelling. Therefore those in the court will stand more inwardly; for though it is an honor to stand in the house, he who stands in the court surpasses the other. The Prophet shows elsewhere that those in the house and those in the court are distinct, saying: “Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall [Note: The printed editions read “flourish”; corrected from the manuscript. See above, p. 516, note.] flourish in the courts of our God” (Ps. 92:14). To have flowered is a greater fruit. And though planting has dignity, the honor of those flowering is higher; for as the beginning is in planting, so the joy of good work is in flower.

### 4. Whether an addition has been made here to the Hebrew text.

I have found some who were uncertain about the phrase, “in the courts of the house of the Lord,” saying that it was added here by the first translators because [Note: In the Turon. manuscript, “under the same verses,” and in the margin, “lines.” Hilary undoubtedly meant the Seventy by “the first translators.” Yet the commentator on the Psalms found among Jerome’s works, while maintaining that these words were added, attributes the addition not to the Seventy but to some unknown person who, because they occurred in the following Psalm, thought they ought also to be added here. They are absent, indeed, from Jerome’s Psalter translated from Hebrew; but Nobilius testifies that he found them in all the Greek and Latin codices he collated.] they are contained under the same verses [Col. 0751C] in the following Psalm, supposing that through a scribal fault they had been omitted in Hebrew books. But let new interpreters debate whatever they please; for our part, we must submit both to the authority of the translations and to antiquity.

### 5. Prayers bare of works are nothing. Let works be cheerful and accompanied by praise of God.

The Prophet urges us toward this hope of standing in the house and courts of the Lord, saying, VERSE 2: “In the nights lift up your hands in holy things, and bless the Lord.” For, according to the Apostle, we live under the rulers of these darknesses (Eph. 6:12), and the night of this world holds us, though through the Gospel preaching it has now [Note: The Regius codex with Turon. reads “has advanced into light. For the night has now advanced.”] passed into light. “For the night is far advanced; walk becomingly as in the day” (Rom. 13:12–13). Therefore, in this night of ignorance, [Col. 0751D] snares, weaknesses, desires, and vices, hands must be lifted up in holy things—not merely [Note: The printed editions read “for preaching”; corrected from the manuscripts.] for praying and entreating, but also for working. Bare prayers do not avail. [Col. 0752A] Our works must be raised up into God’s holy things: that is, in clothing the naked, feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, consoling the afflicted, helping the oppressed, and loving all people. These things sanctify us amid the weakness of this body; these are holy and pleasing to God. The Prophet knew this too, saying: “The lifting up of my hands is the evening sacrifice” (Ps. 141:2). For now, at the consummation of the age, which is evening, the sacrifice to God is not bulls and goats, but good works. Moses taught us by example: while he stood with his hands raised, he prevailed; but when they were lowered to the earth, he caused the people to be overcome by the enemy (Exod. 17:11). Through this figure he showed that our enemy prevails if our works are earthly, but is overcome if they are exalted. Therefore our hands must be raised in the nights, so that we may be planted in the house and flower in the courts.

And the Lord must be blessed: that is, we must always work with God’s blessing, [Note: Thus the Turonensis codex. The others read “we must pray.”] lest, when you give bread to one in need, you be sad through fear of hunger; lest, when you offer expenses to the needy, you think it a loss; lest, when you clothe the naked, you imagine yourself stripped. For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7).

### 6. Their reward.

What cheerful and blessing works of uplifted hands merit, he shows in saying, VERSE 3: “May the Lord bless you from Zion”—that is, the Lord of the Church, holy Jerusalem, and the city built from living precious stones. [Col. 0752C] And, so that we might know that all our hope is placed in the true and eternal God, he adds: “Who made heaven and earth,” showing that he who made heaven and earth is the God of the Churches: through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM CXXXIV. Alleluia.

Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, you his servants, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. Praise the Lord, because the Lord is gracious; sing to his name, because it is sweet. For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel for his own possession. For I know that the Lord is great, and that our God is above all gods. Whatever he willed (below: “whatever he willed”) he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the [Col. 0752D] abysses. Bringing clouds from the end of the earth, he made lightnings for rain. He brings forth winds from his treasuries; he struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man even to beast. He sent forth (*Hil.*: “and sent”) signs and wonders in the midst [Col. 0753A] of you, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants. He struck many nations and killed mighty kings: Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan he killed; and he gave their land as an inheritance (the word “inheritance” is repeated) to Israel his people. O Lord, your name endures for the age, and your memorial from generation (below: “generation”) to generation. For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be comforted in his servants. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, works of human hands. They have a mouth and shall not speak; they have eyes and shall not see; they have ears and shall not hear; they have nostrils and shall not smell; they have hands and shall not touch; feet, and shall not walk; nor is there breath in their mouth; they shall not cry out from their throat. Let those who make them become like them, [Col. 0753B] and all who trust in them. House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless him.

## EXPOSITION OF THE PSALM.

### 1. Scripture, full of mysteries, requires a learned and devout reader. Comparison. This Psalm discloses a deeper meaning through bodily acts. Who should expound it.

The Psalm appears straightforward according to the capacity of its hearers. For it contains, for the most part, matters recorded in the book of Exodus: the plagues of Egypt, Pharaoh’s punishment, the deaths of kings, and possession of the inheritance of an enemy land. But, according to the Apostle, the things in the Law are a shadow of things to come; the acts performed in it [Note: The printed editions read, “the acts performed are allegorical,” afterward omitting “are.”] are [Col. 0753C] allegorical and must not be heard carelessly, because beneath the truth of bodily acts they are established as types of spiritual works.

It is a matter requiring great diligence to weigh the force of the words as arranged, and to know what properly belongs to each matter under the signification of the things that are said. For it is not everyone’s ability to know the kinds and properties of herbs. If an unskilled or ignorant person comes into a field rich in these health-giving herbs, he will pass everything by, judging them all useless and merely growing indiscriminately. But if an experienced and learned person enters this precious field of grasses [or: shoots], he will harvest everything that others had passed over and marvel at what the ignorant had neglected. He knows when is the proper time for harvesting them, for which kinds of illnesses they should be used, how much of them should be applied, and to what extent. So too the divine Scriptures must be understood in such a way that, if an impious ear and an uncultivated mind hear them, they neglect them as idle and unnecessary; but if a hearer or reader devoted to the knowledge of God approaches them, one to whom frequent reading and the gift of spiritual grace have supplied the knowledge to distinguish and understand each thing, he will marvel at all of them and use them according to their natural properties and effects. He will know when one thing or another is to be employed and for what cure it is to be chosen: when it grants healing to the body, when remedy to the soul; so that nothing may be premature, ill-timed, or delayed. Rather, comparing their properties, times, and subjects, he will use intelligently those things which he has discovered.

This is especially to be understood as true in this Psalm. For words have been set beneath the events in such an incredible manner that, while they faithfully report what was done, their arrangement nevertheless affords a greater advance in inward and spiritual understanding. Nor was this principle observed merely so that the events themselves, bodily performed, might be recalled to display God’s magnificence; rather, through knowledge of the events and the powers of names, they might furnish, in what has been done, an example for what ought to be done. It is therefore necessary to distinguish all these things by persons, times, and powers, [Col. 0754B] so that the very things which careless ears may perhaps have lost as unnecessary may be applied to the remedy and healing of human unbelief. We shall teach this from the matters themselves in the Psalm, which begins as follows.

### 2. Praise surpasses blessing. God’s names are worthy of praise.

VERSES 1–3. “Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, you his servants, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. Praise the Lord, because the Lord is gracious; sing to his name, because it is sweet.”

At the beginning of the Psalm it must be observed that it calls us to God’s praise, whereas in the preceding Psalm it exhorted us to blessing alone. That [Col. 0754C] praise surpasses blessing is beyond doubt. [Note: Reg. and Turon. manuscripts: “Praise [surpasses] blessing.”] For the first order is placed in blessing, but it is completed in praise. Praise, however, must not be begun indiscriminately; it must be offered with order and measure. For this is first: “Praise the name of the Lord.” We are therefore first admonished to praise the Lord’s name: because he is God of heaven, because he is God of earth, because he is God of the world, because he is—what is proper to our faith and hope—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. In these things is our first praise of God.

3. The order by which one comes to the praise of God. — The next command is: “Praise the Lord, you servants.” Through knowledge of God’s name we advance to knowledge of him. For we now praise not merely the name of the Lord, but the Lord himself, knowing why he is God of heaven, why God of earth, why God of the world, why God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob [Col. 0754D]. For, having passed beyond these first rudiments of childish instruction, we praise God no longer merely through the obedience of subjects, but through the majesty of his immeasurable power; and we praise him as his servants—not servants named only by the bare title of our profession, but those “standing in his house”: no longer wandering or straying, but established in the steadfastness of those who stand; and not merely standing, but also in the court of the Lord our God, received into the inner, indeed the middle, dwelling-place of the house.

[Note: The printed editions read “only in the house.” The manuscripts more correctly read “merely.” Here what had been said is taken only as a step toward something higher.]

Thus, by this order, praise begins from servants and from those standing in the house and in the court.

4. We need God’s kindness. What it is to sing psalms. — God is to be praised because he is kind. For that he is almighty belongs to the power of his nature; but that he is kind is necessary for us, whom bodily weakness and the condition of our origin hold fast in sins. What hope is there for human offenses if kindness be absent from God?

[Note: The printed editions read “if God be absent,” a reading also found after correction in the royal manuscript, which previously, with the Tours manuscript, had “if kindness be absent from God,” that is, if kindness is not present with God.]

But the logic of the words must be considered. For he who is to be praised because he is kind is to have psalms sung to his name because it is sweet: “Sing psalms to his name, because it is sweet.” Where “sing psalms” is said, it refers to bodily acts: so that, through the manifold activity of our instrument—that is, our body—praise harmonious with and fitting for God may arise (see Preface, no. 19). We are therefore commanded to sing psalms to his name [Col. 0755B], because it is sweet. For it is sweet to God that our bodies serve him with willing ministry and approved service; or rather, that very name of the Lord is sweet.

5. Why Jacob and Israel are mentioned, not Abraham. — And what sweetness there is either in his name or in singing psalms to him, he immediately added by saying, V. 4: “For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel for his possession.” The beginning of Jewish descent, in respect of the consecration of the race, is Abraham; for to him God first spoke.

[Note: *First* was absent from the earlier printed editions. It is restored from the manuscripts.]

Why, then, did the Lord choose Jacob rather than Abraham? Further, since the same person is Israel and Jacob according to the differing form of designation, why is it added again: “Israel for his possession”? The order required that Abraham, the first in election, be mentioned—not Jacob, who is already third in the election. Reason also suggested that the meaning of Israel should be understood in Jacob [Col. 0755C]. Moreover, this is added: Jacob is chosen, Israel is possessed.

6. Jacob as a type of the Church. — But we have already pointed out at the beginning of the discourse that the Psalm recalls things performed bodily, in which the image of the future shines out as in a mirror; and that words were likewise fitted to the events, so that, while declaring what had happened, they nevertheless furnish us a fuller understanding of those things spiritually prefigured in the events. The name of God is sweet not for one people only—and that an irreligious people—but now for all nations and tongues.

For he chose Jacob: one who supplanted his elder brother, who bought the birthright with food and the despair of a seller, who seized the blessing, who was unyielding after servitude, then, after the wrestling, beheld God and was called Israel.

[Note: Erasmus, Lipsius, and the Paris edition read “saleable,” which would not be objectionable had it been altered with authority to “of the seller,” as is supported in Bade’s edition from the manuscripts, with “brother” understood. This relates to Psalm CXVIII, no. 7, where Jacob is said to have bought the birthright which the elder both despaired of and sold; and a little earlier: “For Jacob bought Esau’s birthright, which he, as though about to die, considered useless to himself.”]

[Note: That is, because even then he stubbornly demanded the blessing from the angel. If the particle *and* were placed before “after the wrestling,” and the punctuation altered, “unyielding” could be referred to the blessing, which would be called unyielding because Isaac would not revoke it even at Esau’s entreaty.]

For he is first Jacob, and then Israel. Let us look upon the body of the Church, which has in itself, through its differing condition of faith, both Jacob and Israel.

[Note: With the word *itself* restored from the manuscripts, the meaning of this passage presents itself: the Church manifests itself as both Jacob and Israel through different dispositions of faith—Jacob when it supplants the Synagogue; Israel when it beholds God with the eyes of faith.]

This assembly supplants the people of the Law through faith; it receives its birthright and snatches away its blessing, according to the Lord’s saying: “From the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and men of violence seize it” (Matt. 11:12). Jacob, then, is the one chosen, as the Lord says: “I chose you; you did not choose me” (John 15:16). Israel is the one possessed: recognized in the former birthrights and blessings, faithful in the servitude of long duration, mighty in the mystery of wrestling, persistent in winning blessings anew [Col. 0756B], and Israel in the knowledge and sight of God.

[Note: The printed editions read “recognized in former birthright,” then Lipsius and the Paris edition, “recognized in blessings.” They are corrected from the manuscripts. This may be understood either as meaning that the people of the nations were foreshadowed in the Jews and their blessings; or that, once the Jews, who were the firstborn, had been passed over, that people was preferred.]

7. It belongs properly to the Son to know the Father. — The Spirit of prophecy knew the surpassing sweetness of God’s name in gathering the nations and possessing the faithful, saying, V. 5: “For I know how great the Lord is.” The prophet indeed speaks by the office of his mouth, but not by his own knowledge.

[Note: The printed editions read “but by his own knowledge,” omitting *not*; the manuscripts correct this.]

This voice belongs to him who says: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). The Son will indeed reveal the Father to whom he chooses; but no one knows his greatness, as the prophet says: “There is no end to his magnificence” (Ps. 144:3). Knowledge, therefore, of this infinity belongs properly to him alone who, according to the perfect fullness of his origin, is himself the image of the infinite.

8. The Church’s one God. — “For I have known how great the Lord is; and our God is above all gods” [Col. 0756C].

[Note: Although elsewhere in the manuscripts the preposition *prae* is joined to the accusative, here the manuscripts agree with the printed editions, though not consistently below.]

He is not above all those gods of whom he says below: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands; they have mouths and do not speak” (Ps. 113:4–5). For it is no great thing if he is preferred to metals, stones, and wood. And because those are not gods, we must ask whom he calls gods. For the Church does not acknowledge a multitude of gods. It is the error of the nations either to invent or to believe in unions, conceptions, births, and successions of gods.

But for us, according to the Apostle, there is one God, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him [Col. 0757A] (1 Cor. 8:6). One from one, God from God. The Unbegotten does not admit another Unbegotten, lest there be two; nor does he deny that the Only-begotten is one, lest he not be God. There are not two Unbegottens, nor are there two Only-begottens. Each is one in that which he is, since the Only-begotten has no equal and the Unbegotten admits none; nor does the Only-begotten God subsist from any other than the Unbegotten God.

9. Men are gods by designation. — We must see above which gods our God is. I find that the prophet calls gods thus: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he judges gods” (Ps. 81:1). This seems ambiguous and does not state with sufficient definiteness whom it means by gods.

[Note: The printed editions read “to declare an absolute necessity.” The Tours manuscript supplies the genuine reading.]

But in the Gospels the Lord freed us from error concerning this designation, saying: “I said, You are gods, and all are sons of the Most High” [Col. 0757B] (John 10:34). He added: “If, then, he called those gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken” (ibid., 35). The word of God, which calls human beings gods, is unbreakable. I also find Moses called God, when it is said to him: “I have made you God to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1).

The Apostle too taught that others are called gods, when he says: “For although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:5–6). For us there is indeed one God and one Lord; but many are called gods, in heaven and on earth. And if this name of gods belongs to human beings by the judgment of God, it is much more fitting for angels, archangels, thrones [Col. 0757C], dominions, principalities, and powers, whom the Apostle shows to be called gods in heaven.

10. How God surpasses these. Whatever is made cannot do all things. — Therefore there are those who are called gods; but our God is above all: not by comparison, for he surpasses all comparison, but by power he is above the rest. And he immediately shows how he is above the rest, saying, V. 6: “All things whatsoever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the depths.” It belongs to God alone to do all that he wills. For perfect power alone is hindered in nothing from doing what it wills; and for him from whom all things are, no difficulty arises.

It belongs to a nature inferior to him not to do all that it wills. For while another owes its existence not to itself, it lacks the power of omnipotence, because it has another author for the very fact that it subsists [Col. 0757D]. And one who does not owe himself to himself cannot do all things, because he subsists from one greater than himself. But let us see what it is that God’s omnipotence has done according to his will in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the depths.

[Note: The word *itself* is absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts.]

11. God’s diverse wonders in the world. — It is indeed great, if we contemplate the unchangeable stability of heaven; the sun, regulated by its yearly and unwearied courses, moderating the seasons of the year by fixed bounds; the perpetual changes of the moon; and the undisturbed risings, settings, and revolutions of the constellations. Great too are the riches of the earth and its fruitful produce for the life of human beings, birds, cattle, and beasts; then the seas, filled with their inhabitants, and the life of fish breathing within the waves.

Moreover, because Greek speaks of “seas” in the plural, ἐν ταῖς θαλάσσαις (“in the seas”), there are the immeasurable movements of the ocean and the inscrutable nature of the capacious abyss, by which the tide, poured out upon the land, is drawn back again. Yet, though these things are full of wonders according to human judgment, and though it may rightly be said of them, “All things whatsoever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the depths,” let us see what all these things are which he willed and did.

12. A higher meaning lies hidden beneath the letter. — V. 7: “Bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth, he made lightnings for the rain; he brings winds out of his treasuries.” Passing over the wonder of thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, cherubim and seraphim, angels and archangels, heaven, earth, sea, and abyss: in these God did all that he willed, in heaven and on earth, in sea and abyss—bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth, making lightnings for the rain, bringing winds out of his treasuries.

[Note: The royal manuscript reads *Thrones*, though in Psalm CXXIX, no. 2, it has “of Thrones.”]

Is this alone the omnipotence of perfect will in God: that lands exhale clouds, lightning flashes when rain is at hand, and winds blow by alternating currents? But the force of the words and the nature of the kinds mentioned challenge this opinion of ours.

[Note: Contrary to the authority of the ancient books, Lipsius rashly substituted “the powers of herbs and the nature of gems,” and was not later corrected. Hilary means nothing other than that the force of the sacred text and the nature of the kinds or things expressed in it by no means permit excessive adherence to the letter. In Lipsius’ mind there had lodged too deeply the comparison made at the beginning of this Treatise concerning a field rich in health-giving herbs; but he had heard nothing yet about gems.]

“Bringing forth clouds,” he says, “from the end of the earth”: what does it mean that clouds are led forth and brought forth from the end of the earth [Col. 0758C]? Damp valleys do indeed exhale mists; but valleys are neither the ends of the earth, nor has anyone judged mist to be the same thing as a cloud.

[Note: In Pliny, Book II, chapter 60, mist differs from cloud because it is vapor rising from earth and waters, which either immediately vanishes or, rising on high, becomes a cloud.]

Then, “He made lightnings for the rain.” What meaning of ordinary human understanding is there here? We sometimes see lightnings without rain, and rain often without lightning. Rains do not bring lightning, nor, conversely, does lightning pour down rain. There follows also: “He brings winds out of his treasuries.” What meaning of ordinary human understanding is there here? Shall we suppose that winds are stored in some hollow and fortified place of treasure, from which they are brought out as though the most precious portion of a treasury? And, when changes of winds are commonly frequent, uncertain, and often opposed [Col. 0758D], does God busily bring out those very winds from the secret place of his riches as often as they are to change and contend with one another?

13. Yet the literal sense is preserved. — But I have mentioned these things in order to show the force and rationale of the statements, while nevertheless it must be understood that it belongs to invisible and almighty power [Col. 0759A] to bring clouds forth from the sea, which is the end of the earth; to make lightnings flash amid rains; and to cause winds to blow from the hidden abodes of its spirits.

[Note: One wonders why Erasmus had just before noted, “He destroys the history,” against so explicit a declaration here and at the beginning of the Treatise by our interpreter, that he can scarcely be excused from a certain itch for finding fault.]

But since the omnipotence of God lies not only in these things, nor did he do only in these the things that he willed in heaven and on earth, in sea and in the depths; and since we remember that spiritual things are signified in those things recorded as having been performed bodily, we must now show what we ought to understand beneath these sayings through the power of prophecy.

14. The prerogatives of humankind. — In God’s doing all things that he willed in heaven and on earth, in sea and in the depths, so far as knowledge is permitted us, nothing is dearer to God than the human being. There is a reason why this creature is peculiarly his. The world stands by a word; but the human being is made with counsel—not by a word, but by considered action. The human being is also made in the image of God; and, through the inspiration of God, is perfected as a living soul.

[Note: So the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “He is also made in the image of God through inspiration, and is perfected as a living soul by that of God”; wrongly and contrary to Hilary’s meaning. For Hilary does not hold that by God’s inspiration the human being is made in God’s image; rather, the soul made in God’s image is joined with the body into a living soul. See this explained more fully in the Treatise on Psalm CXVIII, nos. 7 and 8, and on Psalm CXXX, no. 5.]

The human being receives law; is entrusted to his own will; is established free, lord over the whole world; is an inhabitant of paradise; is worthy of the devil’s envy; after sin is preserved for mercy (see p. 402, a, b); is instructed throughout every age of this world toward the knowledge of God; and is prepared as a judge of angels. Creation awaits his revelation, itself subjected to vanity in hope; because of his repentance after sin, there is the greatest joy among the angels in heaven.

This same human being has been assumed into Jesus Christ through the mystery of his birth according to humanity. Now he who was formerly irreligious teaches religion everywhere with his mouth; now the body once defiled by sexual impurity is pure through continence [Col. 0759C]; now the mind once blind to the knowledge of God has become Israel. Now envy has advanced into imitation of good; now drunkenness has flamed into fasting; now hatred has been transformed into love; now vices have been slain into the life of virtues.

[Note: The printed editions omit the particle *now*: “has advanced into transformation of good.” The Tours manuscript reads, “now envy has advanced by imitation of good.” The reading “into imitation of good,” with the royal manuscript, is preferable, for it expresses the transition from perverse rivalry to holy emulation.]

[Note: The printed editions read *life*. The manuscripts correctly read “into life,” declaring the mind’s progress from vices to virtues.]

15. The clouds are doctrine, given from the end of the earth—that is, through humble apostles. — Therefore the Lord did all things that he willed in heaven and on earth, in sea and in the depths. For among all these things he held nothing dearer than his human being, for whose sake even his Only-begotten God became human; and he did this by “bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth” [Col. 0760A].

The Lord commanded the clouds not to rain upon the thorny and unfruitful vineyard (see Origen, Homily 5 on Jeremiah): “I will command,” he says, “the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6).

[Note: The Tours manuscript reads “my clouds.” Above, in Psalm LXVII, no. 10, this command is said to have been given to certain clouds.]

I have also learned of the cloud in which God spoke: “He spoke to them,” he says, “in a pillar of cloud” (Ps. 98:7). And Paul testifies to me that in this cloud one must not understand only what is read literally, when he says: “Do you not know that our fathers were under the cloud and were baptized into Moses?” (1 Cor. 10:1–2).

This cloud, therefore, signifies apostolic teaching. By giving shade and defending from heat, it excludes every burning heat of the future judgment. And that these clouds are from the last of the earth, let us hear the Apostle saying: “I think God has displayed us apostles as the last, like abortive births” (1 Cor. 4:9).

[Note: Hilary refers the word “are” equally to the apostles, as if above he had written “the teaching of the apostles,” rather than “apostolic teaching.”]

The Lord himself, when there was discussion among the disciples concerning place and dignity, said: “Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be last of all” (Mark 10:44). Therefore God, doing all things that he wills, brings forth these clouds from the last of the earth; and the lowly places of the earth exhale this teaching that gives shade.

16. Lightnings: those who flash with knowledge. They become rains while pouring out doctrine. — “He made lightnings into rains.” Lightning is the recognition of heavenly power; and the Lord himself testifies to this, saying: “For as lightning comes forth from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24:27). This is so in the Lord, who is seen as coming not locally like a bodily thing, but everywhere.

[Note: The printed editions read “not in bodily places . . . is seen”; the manuscripts correct this. Yet “bodily things” might be preferable. For is Christ not present in places in the manner of bodily things, though he plainly is not without a body? Hilary seems to be considering Christ insofar as he is everywhere present by divine power, not insofar as he shares our body. We have noted a similar passage in Psalm CXXIV, no. 6, where, explaining Christ’s words to the apostles, “Behold, I am with you,” etc., he adds: “For he is Spirit, penetrating and containing all things. He is not bodily according to our manner, so that when he is present somewhere, he is absent elsewhere,” etc.]

But today, in each individual who proclaims God’s power and gives knowledge of him through teaching, lightnings have become rains: first flashing with the lightning of knowledge itself, then pouring forth a rain of words [Col. 0760C].

[Note: The printed editions awkwardly read “among rains,” against the manuscripts. Then, from the Tours manuscript, we restore “first flashing with the lightning of knowledge itself,” where previously “lightnings first of knowledge itself” was read.]

Moses recalls this rain which was to be poured forth from himself, not now shining spiritually through doctrine but bodily through glory: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words from my mouth. Let my speech be awaited as rain, and let my words descend as dew, as rain upon grass, and as snow upon hay” (Deut. 32:1–2). Those lightnings were made into these rains: that is, life-giving words, watering those who drink.

[Note: The Tours manuscripts read “watering powerfully.”]

17. Winds. Angels, our guardians. — The order has been preserved: after the clouds gathered from the last of the earth, after the lightnings made into rains, he brings forth winds from his treasuries.

[Note: On manuscript authority we restore “into rains,” which was absent from the printed editions.]

What winds he brings forth is not doubtful: namely, those of whom he says, “Making his angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4). For there are angels of little ones who daily behold God. These spirits, then, have been sent for the salvation of humankind; for our weakness could not withstand so many and such great spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places unless angels had been given for our protection. Help from a superior nature was needed; and that this is so we learn from the words by which the Lord strengthens Moses when he is afraid and trembling: “Behold, my angel shall go before you” (Exod. 23:23).

[Note: By “superior nature” nothing is meant here except angelic nature. Yet Hilary does not seem consistent with himself, since in Psalm CXX, no. 5, he teaches that help comes to us from the Lord, not from angels.
