Nevertheless, as there he does not deny, indeed implies, that God’s help comes to us through them, so here too he declares that not angels by themselves, but the Lord in angels, gives us aid in the words, “granting in them help to human weakness.”]

Thus he brings forth these winds from his treasuries [Col. 0761B], granting in them help to human weakness, so that these divine protections may guard us against the world-rulers (πρὸς κοσμοκράτορας) of this darkness, for the salvation that is our inheritance.

18. These great deeds of God are now performed spiritually in us. — The following order of statements comes next, Vv. 8–12: “He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from human being to beast; and he sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, upon Pharaoh and all his servants. He struck many nations and slew mighty kings: Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan; he slew all the kingdoms of Canaan, and gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.”

Divine speech frequently teaches that the God of heaven and earth, the creator of the universe, is to be understood as he who struck Egypt, divided the sea, drowned the Egyptians, led out his people by great and wonderful powers, fed them with manna in the wilderness, and, after driving out the nations, brought them into the land of promise [Col. 0761C]. All these works indeed are magnificent and splendid, and testify that he is God. For performing such things does not belong to a modest or limited power: he must be understood as admirable in them.

But the Apostle teaches us, together with reverence for the deeds, to recognize in them a prefiguration of spiritual teaching and operation: because the Law is spiritual; because its deeds are allegorical; because the fathers were under the cloud; because they were baptized into Moses; because they drank from the spiritual rock; because the rock was Christ; and because, finally, the Lord was to be lifted up according to the form of the serpent lifted up in the wilderness. Therefore, though these things were done bodily in Egypt, they are now done spiritually in us.

19. Egypt struck: the powers of the world crucified. Christ’s wonders in the midst of Egypt, that is, the world. Pharaoh, that is, the devil, is killed with the vices in baptism. — Egypt, in which there is the form of the world, is struck by God’s powers and plagues, and terrified by signs and portents. It is struck by God’s plagues when it hears its judgment, when it recognizes its condemnation, when it is daily judged in the guilt of its own conscience, when the Lord has nailed its ruling and original powers to his cross.

He also spoke as though to Egypt, living and animate—not to an inanimate territory devoid of earth, but, as one must suppose, to its inhabitants, whom he had made rational and animate: “He sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, upon Pharaoh and all his servants.”

[Note: The printed editions read “as not having earth,” corruptly.]

What is “in your midst”? We learn from what has been said: “But the Lord God, our king, king before the ages, worked salvation in the midst of the earth.” Thus, in the midst of the earth—that place where the Lord suffered while working salvation for us—he sent signs and wonders: while in the hours of his cross the sun fled, the earth trembled, rocks were split, tombs opened, and the dead arose [Col. 0762B]. These signs were performed in your midst, O Egypt.

Your Pharaoh, that is, the devil, is killed in the waters when the people are baptized, he himself overwhelmed together with his army. Then many nations are struck: that is, the countless indwelling vices within us are destroyed. Mighty kings also are slain—mighty indeed.

20. Why only a few are mentioned among the many kingdoms destroyed. Sihon the Amorite, Og of Bashan, and Canaan. — “He slew Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan.” What is this? So many kingdoms were overthrown and so many kings destroyed, yet only these are mentioned [Col. 0762C]. In accordance with the truth of the events, indeed, a few are remembered out of many; but these alone are named because, though the event itself was certainly recognized in them, yet through the conditions and meanings of their names a spiritual condition was woven into them.

For Sihon means “an unfruitful tree”; for what an unfruitful tree is among us is called Sihon in Hebrew. But Amorite means “one who provokes.”

[Note: Here “interpretation” is understood. Earlier printed editions read “provoking”; and the royal and Tours manuscripts, “but the Amorites, those who provoke.”]

Thus, beneath the meaning of these names, he destroyed in us the unfruitful powers that provoke: namely, unfruitful rulers who held us while we were provoking the Lord; and for that reason they were cut down according to the Gospel saying, by the example of the unfruitful tree.

[Note: The Paris edition alone reads “of one who provokes.”]

[Note: The royal manuscript, with the Tours manuscript, reads “by whom we provoked.” Then the printed editions omit *in* before “the Lord.”]

But Og the king has the meaning “wall” or “rampart”; Bashan, “confusion” or “shame” [Col. 0762D]. Therefore he destroyed this king of our confusion and shame, dissolving, according to the Apostle, the dividing wall (Eph. 2:14), or rampart—that is, overthrowing the obstacle by which we were kept from the knowledge of God.

[Note: The printed editions read “which [kept us] to the knowledge of God”; corrected from the Tours manuscript.]

Then he slew all the kingdoms of Canaan. Genesis teaches that Canaan was cursed (9:25) and made the servant of his brothers because of his insulting outrage against his father. The interpretation of the name Canaan is “movement.” Therefore the Lord destroyed those powers which moved us into vices and into cursed impiety, and which reigned over us by their force and power.

[Note: The Tours manuscript reads “which moved [us] into cursed impiety, and within us.”]

But hear the Apostle concerning the various powers which operate in children of obedience, so that sins may not reign in us: “Let not sin therefore reign any longer in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12). These kingdoms, therefore, have been killed: for they no longer rule in us.

[Note: Thus the Tours manuscript with the royal manuscript, though in the latter the first hand wrote “let them not reign,” and then, after the *c* was erased, “let them not reign” remains. But the printed editions read, “the powers which operate in children of disobedience: these sins reign,” which conflicts with what follows. The powers in question are not those of the devil, who now works in the children of unbelief, Eph. 2:2, but those of the Lord, of whom Eph. 3:20 says: “To him who is able to do all things . . . according to the power that works in us,” etc.]

21. The faithful are promised the eternal possession of their bodies. — But after these have been killed, what follows? “He gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people” [Col. 0763B]. The land of the kings and nations mentioned above was indeed given, but it was later lost again. Today it is inhabited by nations; Israel is everywhere in exile. How, then, is the land that was given an inheritance?

The same order remains: beneath the things that were bodily done, those things which were to be spiritually done were set forth beforehand. Thus, the land of our bodies has been given as an inheritance. Formerly it was Canaan, cursed and mobile toward vices; Bashan, full of confusion and shame; Amorite, provoking and irritating; Og, the wall of unbelief, possessed it; Sihon, the unfruitful tree, occupied it. This land, therefore, once the rampart of unbelief has been broken down and the unfruitful tree cut out from it, has been given as an inheritance—given to Israel his people.

What this land of inheritance is, and who this Israel is, let us hear the apostle Paul saying: “As we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:49). This is the Israel to whom the inheritance of this blessed land will fall: the one to whom, glorified together in the Lord, there will be eternal possession of his earthly body [Col. 0763C]. This belongs properly to Christians who preserve this name uninjured in themselves, through the heavenly image, unto the end.

22. What we seem to ask for God, we ask for ourselves. — Thus he says, V. 13: “O Lord, your name is forever.” Must we ask this for God? Or does eternal power need our prayer in order to remain forever? Rather, we must pray that it may remain in us. So too, when we say, “Hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matt. 6:9–10), we certainly do not pray that these things may accrue to God: that he who is holy may be sanctified, or that the will of him whose deed lies in his will may be done.

These are rather prayers concerning our own condition: that through the excellent works of our faith his name may be sanctified in us [Col. 0764A]. For he says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 11:44); that his kingdom may come into us, and that through the substance of eternity granted us we may be worthy of the eternal kingdom. For the hope of life is to confess his kingdom; and to the thief saying to him, “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom,” he answered: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43).

And just as his will is obeyed in heaven by the tireless heavenly powers, so may it be obeyed by us upon earth, lest bodily weakness turn us aside from carrying out his will. For in heaven it is daily said with tireless voices: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of Sabaoth; heaven and earth are full of your glory” (Isa. 6:3). So may we also have nothing else in our activity by which his name is sanctified; nothing else in our hope by which we hope that his kingdom may come into us; nothing else in our will by which eternal praises are to be offered to him by us.

[Note: In the printed editions, here and below, *unless* is inserted before “by which,” against the manuscripts. In place of this particle one may understand: “than that which is sung without interruption in heaven.” Then “by which” means “by means of which it comes about that.”]

This progress of our prayer is a matter of need: that his name may remain with us forever.

23. God’s memorial. It passed from the Jews to Christians. — Then follows: “And your memorial in generation and into generation.”

[Note: The printed editions read “into generation.” The royal manuscript more correctly reads “in generation,” with “remained” understood, just as after “and generation” one understands “passed.” The Tours manuscript has “in generation and generation.”]

Not “from age to age,” as often occurs, nor “from generations to generations,” but “in generation and generation.” And this concerns not the name, but the memorial. For the memorial is the remembrance of God’s works, which are contained in the book of the Law. Since the Law and God’s memorial remained in the first generation—that is, the Jews—until the fullness of times [Col. 0764C], just as punishment was delayed for the people of Sodom and Gomorrah until the fullness of their sin, so, when the first generation had filled up the measure of all impieties, God’s memorial and the remembrance of all his works passed into the second generation: namely, to Christians, with whom today are the reverence of the Law, prophecy, and the name of the Lord.

[Note: The royal and Tours manuscripts read “prophecy.” Then the Tours manuscript omits “and the name of the Lord,” while the royal manuscript omits the whole particle *and*.]

24. God’s consolation over lost Israel; the faithful people. — He maintained the same order in what follows, saying, VERSE 14: “For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be consoled in his servants.” To be judged differs from being consoled; and people differs from servant. Consolation, however, is in the servants, but judgment in the people. Who does not know that Israel according to the flesh was called God’s people? Yet the Apostle said: “Those who sinned under the law shall be judged by the law” (Rom. 2:12). Therefore God will judge his people; but he will be consoled in his servants—namely, those of whom the Lord said: “He who believes in me shall not be judged, but shall pass from death into life; but he who does not believe has already been judged” (John 5:24).

But, once Israel has been judged, the Lord will find consolation in his servants. For among all the faithful of the earth he will have consolation for the loss.

> [Note: The printed editions, along with the royal manuscript, read *terra* (“earth”): wrongly, since the immediately following word, *habebit* (“he will have”), is to be referred to the Lord, who, having lost the single region of the Israelite nation, consoles his loss by gaining the whole world, in which he has faithful servants. The manuscript of Tours therefore reads better: *terrae* (“of the earth”).]

25. God’s kindness and benefits toward the Israelites; how ungrateful they were, unlike the nations. — For he had wished that his people, whom he had chosen in their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, should not be judged: for their sake he had afflicted Egypt with diverse plagues; for their sake he had stood by in a pillar of fire and cloud; for their sake he had divided the sea, brought water out of the rock, sent manna from heaven, given the Law, pardoned such great sacrileges, overthrown so many kingdoms of the irreligious, sent prophets, and willed his Only-begotten Son to be born as a human being. Yet this people, ungrateful despite benefits so many and so great, though first chosen as the tenant of the vineyard, laid parricidal hands upon the Lord of the vineyard himself (Matt. 21:38), killing in a human being the God whom, so far as lay in them, they crucified.

But servants were chosen, to whom the vineyard might be entrusted as they rendered its fruit; and in them, once his people had been judged, the Lord might console the loss sustained by his loving-kindness. Thus the nations console him, repaying in their martyrs, confessors, and faithful the fruits of the grace entrusted to them. Nor is this a new utterance, nor one belonging to this prophet alone.

> [Note: In the Paris edition. Immediately afterward, “in that famous song of Deuteronomy”: incorrectly. Then the royal manuscript has “in the song of Exodus.” But the words cited are taken from Deuteronomy, not Exodus.]

Moses, in that famous song of Deuteronomy, when he foretold this people’s sins, their final impieties, and the faith of another generation, said: “For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be consoled in his servants” (Deut. 32:36). Holy Eleazar also, when the leaders of his people compelled him to feign that he had eaten what had been sacrificed, consummated the glory of martyrdom under this same declaration, knowing that, after the people had been judged, the Lord would be consoled in his servants who do his will.

> [Note: Erasmus, following Badius, reads “sacrificed to those who lie,” and conjectures in the margin that one should read “from a Gentile sacrifice.” Lipsius introduced this conjecture into the text. The royal and Tours manuscripts preserve the authentic reading, in accord with 2 Maccabees 6:20: “They urged that meat which he was permitted to eat should be brought, so that he might pretend to have eaten, as the king had commanded, meat from the sacrifice.” What Hilary adds—that Eleazar completed martyrdom with the aforesaid words from Deuteronomy—is not related by the sacred text concerning Eleazar, but concerning the seven brothers, who together with their mother encouraged one another to endure the tortures courageously with these same words (2 Macc. 7:6).]

26. Against idolaters. — He then turns, in prophetic speech, to drive away the error of the Gentiles, so that from the very grounds of their superstitions he may convict their foolish and irreligious practices, saying, VERSES 15–18: “The idols of the Gentiles are silver and gold, the works of human hands. They have a mouth, and shall not speak; they have eyes, and shall not see; they have ears, and shall not hear;

> [Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the Vulgate and seem to have been inserted from Psalm 113; nevertheless, they occur in the ancient Roman, Milanese, Chartres, and German psalters, as well as in our manuscripts, and Hilary’s exposition requires them.]

[they have nostrils, and shall not smell; they have hands, and shall not touch; they have feet, and shall not walk;

> [Note: In the printed editions the following sentence, namely, “nor is there breath in their mouth,” is placed before this.]

they shall not cry out through their throat]; nor is there breath in their mouth. Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.”

> [Note: The royal codex and the Tours manuscript read, “who trust in these things.”]

The same thing has often been said of the idols of the Gentiles in other psalms also; and all prophecy labors to turn human error away from these utterly foolish pursuits of irreligion. For many add authority to these impieties of theirs, seeking honor for gods whom they have made for themselves by the price of metals, fashioning them in gold and silver. Yet they confer only what they are capable of conferring: an image of mouth, eyes, ears, nostrils, hands, and feet. They worship their gods in the form of a dead body, whose mouth, once its spirit has departed, is mute; whose eyes are dull, ears deaf, nostrils lifeless, hands limp, feet stiff, and whole body motionless.

> [Note: Badius and Erasmus read “whose spirit exists without will”: a false reading, since a dead body is no less devoid of spirit than of will. Lipsius substituted *species* (“appearance”) for *spiritus* (“spirit”), and this was retained in the Paris edition. The royal manuscript wrongly reads, “whose spirit [is] from will.” This passage has been restored from the Tours codex.]

But what they do not even dare to hope is reckoned to their error: that they may become like those whom they worship; that the worshipers may share the condition of the things worshiped; that they themselves, like idols, may be left as lifeless bodies, without the spirit of life.

> [Note: The printed editions read “in a dead body”; they are corrected from the Tours manuscript, supported by the royal manuscript, which also reads “dead bodies.”]

27. The fourfold order of the faithful; the most excellent of all. — Having exposed Gentile error, prophetic discourse returned to the order of doctrine, saying, VERSES 19–20: “House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless him.” In these distinctions of names and offices it has encompassed the whole people of the Church; yet through the significance of the designations and their proper characteristics, it has distinguished the merits belonging to the offices themselves. For by saying “house of Israel,” “house of Aaron,” “house of Levi,” and “you who fear the Lord,” it indicates that one is distinct from another.

> [Note: The word “to be” is absent from the Tours manuscript.]

Thus, according to the Apostle writing to the Corinthians, a distinction is made in the names when he says: “To those called, to the saints, together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 1:2), so as to signify that those called, the saints, and those invoking the Lord’s name are different.

> [Note: The printed edition reads “is in persons”; the royal manuscript, “is made in all.” With the Tours manuscript one should read “is made in the names,” which agrees with what was just said: “In these distinctions of names and offices,” etc. The preceding conjunction *ut* is used in the sense of *sicut* (“just as”). Below, the word “says” is restored from the royal manuscript.]

Now we see Israel named first, Aaron second, Levi third, and those who fear the Lord fourth. That priests are signified in Aaron is beyond doubt: Aaron was the first priest in the Law, and afterward the honor of the priesthood remained in his succession. In Levi, moreover, ministers are clearly indicated, for this tribe was chosen for service. The remaining people, whose duty is neither priesthood nor ministry but fear, is designated by “those who fear the Lord.”

But the Apostle teaches us that Israel stands above all these, when he says: “And upon as many as shall follow this rule, peace be upon them and mercy, and upon Israel” (Gal. 6:16).

> [Note: The royal and Tours manuscripts read “above all,” a reading that more aptly signifies Israel’s superiority to the other three orders.]

Priests and ministers are confined by the rule of their office to what they do; but to act voluntarily beyond what the Law requires is far superior. And it is best, through the order of ministry, not merely to satisfy the demands of ministry, but through knowledge of doctrine and fervor of faith to strive toward knowledge and contemplation of God. Therefore he placed first in the order of those blessing God the person who understands and sees God—which is Israel’s proper characteristic—because such a person surpasses the office in which he stands and the honor of priesthood through the very power of knowing by faith and contemplating God. For though there are many Aarons—that is, priests—few Israels, that is, persons who shall contemplate God through knowledge of the mind, will be found. These, therefore, are first summoned to bless; all the others after them will bless in the office which they too possess.

But the house of Israel, the house of Aaron, the house of Levi, and all who fear the Lord bless God: namely, him who is God blessed from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem—the holy mountain Zion and the heavenly city, the Church of the first, who abide and are enrolled in heaven—in our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 135. Alleluia.

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ages. Give thanks to the God of gods, for his mercy is for ages. Who alone has done wonders” (Hilary adds, “great”), “for his mercy is for ages. Who made the heavens in understanding, for his mercy is for ages. Who established the earth upon the water” (Hilary: “waters”), “for his mercy is for ages. Who alone made the great lights, for his mercy is for ages. The sun for rule over the day,

> [Col. 0767D]

for his mercy is for ages. Who struck Egypt with their firstborn, for his mercy is for ages. And brought Israel out from among them, for his mercy is for ages. With a mighty hand and an uplifted arm, for his mercy is for ages. Who divided the Red Sea into divisions, for his mercy is for ages. And led Israel through the midst of it, for his mercy is for ages. And cast Pharaoh and his force into the Red Sea,

> [Col. 0768A]

for his mercy is for ages. Who led his people through the wilderness, for his mercy is for ages. Who brought water from the rock of the cliff, for his mercy is for ages. Who struck great kings, for his mercy is for ages. Sihon, king of the Amorites, for his mercy is for ages. And Og, king of Bashan, for his mercy is for ages. And gave their land as an inheritance, for his mercy is for ages. For he remembered us in our lowliness” (Hilary adds, “the Lord”), “for his mercy is for ages. And redeemed us from our enemies” (Hilary: “from the hand of our enemies”), “for his mercy is for ages. Who gives food to all flesh, for his mercy is for ages. Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his mercy is for ages.”

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. The dignity of Scripture; it is cheapened through inattentiveness. — Prophetic discourse is not idle, nor is spiritual speech produced by empty and superfluous causes. For if in prudent persons we especially expect that what they say should be worthy of their seriousness and learning, and that every utterance should not be accidental and wandering, but proceed from rational causes, be useful to the expectation of hearers, and accord with the authority of those speaking—

> [Note: The printed editions read “author”; we restore “authority” from the royal and Tours manuscripts, which earlier read “desire” rather than “expectation.”]

—how much more must we judge that in heavenly utterances whatever is lofty, divine, rational, and perfect should be so regarded.

> [Note: The printed editions read, “whatever is lofty in these,” a transposition that renders Hilary’s sense wholly confused. For *excelsum* (“lofty”) must be referred with the other predicates to the verb *esse existimetur* (“should be considered to be”).]

Yet it often—indeed always—happens through our own fault that we neglect what we hear read in church, while our ears and minds are far away from it; and through carelessness in hearing the dignity of heavenly sayings becomes cheap in our estimation. While the reading is taking place, we calculate accounts, conceive anger, brood over injuries, recall acts of luxury. Then, occupied with such things, our ears are deaf and our mind dull; and if perhaps something of what is read reaches our ears, the mind, overwhelmed by the cares of the world, does not perceive the power of the sayings. What it does not attain in understanding, it will judge to have little authority.

2. Scripture’s manifold teaching; why its books are numerous and varied. — Everything contained in the prophetic books holds within itself the greatest advancement of humankind, both in salvation and in instruction; and everything was written for our sake: now to bring us instruction in innocent living, now to impart knowledge of God, now to grant knowledge of our origin and nature, now to provide understanding of things to come not by hope alone but by reason, now to set forth the causes of this universe and its beginning, and to stretch the human mind—which is incapable of understanding such great matters—toward grasping this knowledge through various kinds of instruction.

For certain sections and divisions were necessary, through which, little by little and by continual practice, at least some apprehension of this understanding, incomprehensible to us, might make its way into us. There are many prophets,

> [Note: The royal manuscript, together with the Tours manuscript, reads: “and their sayings are abundant—the things which have been said. There are many,” etc.]

and their utterances are great and abundant. There are also many psalms, and in each many and varied matters are gathered. Although all contain within themselves one and the same pattern of doctrine, they nevertheless direct us by diverse methods into the same path of knowledge. They do not heap everything together into one place—for we are incapable of receiving everything—but unfold parts through parts, so that through knowing individual things we may advance to many.

In this psalm, however, because its successive arguments concern different instances of the same matter, this is contained: that we may understand, from the goodness and mercy of God, the cause of this whole universe—that is, why heaven exists, why earth, why human beings, why the rest—through what is said in VERSE 1: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ages.”

3. The twofold meaning of confession; what confession of sin is. It entails a profession of ceasing. — VERSE 1. First, in the opening, “Give thanks to the Lord,” a twofold sense is conveyed: either that we praise God in confession, because he is good and because his mercy is for ages; or that we confess our sins to him, to be forgiven by him because he is good and his mercy never fails.

> [Note: The word “to him” is absent from the printed editions; after it, the royal and Tours manuscripts continue, “because he is good,” omitting the words “to be forgiven by him.”]

Both are fitting to our nature: that we should praise him whom we are born to know, and that we should confess our sins, in recognition that they are sins, to him who is good and merciful for ages.

> [Note: The printed editions read: “For confession to God, who is ignorant of nothing, is not necessary, that you should confess what you have done. Since God does not need this profession,” etc.—an interpolated and corrupt reading. Nor is the royal manuscript’s reading better: “For confession is not for God, who is ignorant of nothing, but it is proper to a human being to confess what one has done.” Those intermediate words, “but it is proper to a human being,” also occur in the Tours manuscript; the rest agrees with the Micy manuscript, whose reading is preferred as more authentic. Hilary here certainly does not explain the necessity of confession but its nature: he teaches that it does not consist in making one’s sins known to God, but in oneself recognizing those sins as such, and as things to be avoided which one formerly pursued. Thus he had just said that sins are to be confessed not in any manner whatever, but “in recognition that they are sins.”]

For confession is not to tell God, who is ignorant of nothing, what you have done. God has no need of this confession: nothing is hidden from his knowledge, nothing is inaccessible to his approach,

> [Note: Lipsius and Paris, following Erasmus, read “hearing”: against the evidence of the ancient books and Hilary’s manner of expression. Then the royal manuscript reads, “whose power leaves nothing unprovided for.”]

nothing remains beyond his power, and outside him there is no place. Rather, confession is the acknowledged knowledge of a thing previously unknown, openly professed: it advances from the opinion of one judgment to the conviction of another understanding.

> [Note: The Paris edition reads “which is unknown,” with manuscript support; from the manuscripts the particle *scilicet* (“namely”) has just been added. Here again Hilary explains that confession is the declared change of a previously conceived false judgment about some matter. For no one, he says in his exposition of Psalm 137, §2, undertakes an action without either the delight of some fruit or the judgment that it is good: one either thinks it right or takes pleasure in it. But in confession each person recognizes and declares that what he had thought right, pleasant, and useful is unjust, evil, and destructive; thus he changes and corrects his former judgment.]

A person had previously believed it beneficial and pleasant to seize, kill, steal, be proud, drink to excess, and fornicate. But once he has learned that all these acts are liable to eternal condemnation, he confesses, now that he knows them, his error. Confession of error is a profession of ceasing from it. (So below, in Psalm 137, §3.) Therefore sin must be ceased from, since the begun confession of sin concerns it. Otherwise, the person who has recognized sin yet does not confess what he has recognized is beyond pardon.

4. It must not be interrupted even by those already justified. — Confession must always be made—not because one must always sin, so that one must always confess, but because unwearied confession of ancient, former sin is beneficial.

> [Note: The royal codex and Tours manuscript read, “may be safe for oneself.” This kind of confession is called true in Psalm 118, §13, because true confession of sin is repentance without interruption of time. This passage, together with the exposition of Psalm 144, §18, confirms the observation that Hilary often uses the name “confession” to signify the whole of repentance, not merely one part of it.]

The Holy Spirit teaches that confession must always be made, when he says through the Prophet: “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17). The righteous person accuses himself not on account of the present but of the past; for present accusation removes the name of righteous. Let us hear the Apostle Paul himself reproving himself for the past when he says: “For I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:9–10). This is the true confession of a righteous person, which commends present righteousness through awareness and confession of the past. We are also admonished to it elsewhere through the prophet: “Confess your sins first, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26). To this confession, then, we are summoned in the psalm: “for he is good, for his mercy is for ages”; with especially earnest faith—or confidence of faith—we invoke him to whom we confess, because he is good and does not know how to cease being merciful.

5. The God of gods, that is, of the blessed; God’s mercy, the greatest cause of eternal glory. — VERSE 2. “Give thanks to the God of gods, for his mercy is for ages.” As we are taught in the Gospels by the Lord’s answer to the Sadducees, he is not God of the dead but of the living (Matt. 22:32); and through him it was said: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (John 10:34). God does not deign to be God of corruptible and mortal beings.

> [Note: The printed editions read “mortal”: a false reading.]

Rather, he is God of those who will be transformed into heavenly glory, who, having put off the old earthly human being, have put on the new one who is in heaven, and who will be conformed to the body of God’s glory. And although these are made gods in accordance with the merit of their faith, the greatest cause of this is that “his mercy is for ages.”

> [Note: The Tours codex reads, “and that he may make these persons gods.” Then, after “although,” the words “and that” have been adopted from the royal manuscript, since they are absent from the others. Hilary teaches three points here: first, merit is granted for eternal glory; second, that glory is measured according to the merit of faith; and finally, the chief and greatest cause of obtaining it is God’s mercy. As Augustine teaches, Letter 194 to Sixtus, §19: “No good merit is produced in us except by grace; and when God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing other than his own gifts.” Hence Hilary, in Psalm 62, §7 and Psalm 118, §15, calls eternal life “mercy.” Augustine further illustrates this in *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 13: “It must without any doubt be confessed that grace is called eternal life because it is rendered for those merits which grace has bestowed upon a human being.”]

God had no need to be called the God of gods; rather, it belongs to his goodness and mercy to make gods, granting the honor of his own name out of merciful and benevolent affection.

6. Kings and lords are those who do not serve the flesh; their God is Lord. — VERSE 3. “Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is for ages.” The Apostle teaches that many are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, so that this designation may appear fitting not only to human nature but also to spiritual nature—that is, angelic nature, according to the preceding treatise, §9—when he says: “Even if there are those who are called gods in heaven and on earth” (1 Cor. 8:5). By the designation of heaven and earth he shows this name to be applicable to each nature alike.

The same Apostle also signifies that he is Lord of lords when he says: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Tim. 6:15). Dominion over the base and degenerate is unworthy of God. He is King of kings and Lord of lords, as he is God of gods. The gods he means are not uncertain: they are those of whom he said, “God stood in the assembly of gods” (Ps. 81:1). The same Apostle also plainly shows who the kings are, saying: “Already you reign without us; and would that you did reign” (1 Cor. 4:8). Kings are those in whom sin does not reign, who rule their bodies, and whose flesh is subjected and made subject to their rightful authority.

> [Note: Badius reads “in the authority of this one.” Erasmus then deleted the particle “in,” which was later restored in the Paris edition. The royal manuscript reads “in these.” From the Tours manuscript we restore *in jus*, “into rightful authority,” by which expression the authority of one ruling is denoted. See the exposition of Psalm 2, §42, where, among other things, Christ is proclaimed to reign in us when through him we ourselves rule by the right of lords over ourselves. A little earlier in the same manuscript: “Kings are those in whom,” not “upon whom”; and above: “dominion over the base and degenerate is unworthy of God,” etc.]

These, then, are kings, and their God is King. They are also lords, who will not be slaves of sin: “for whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). Therefore one must rule sin, not serve it. Lords are those who bring these bodies of sin under their own dominion by subjugating their vices and sins. The Apostle knows himself to be lord of his body when he says: “For I subject my body to myself and bring it into slavery” (1 Cor. 9:27). Whoever brings another into slavery must necessarily bring the one who is to serve into slavery by the right of a lord.

Therefore God is Lord of such lords, calling them through the hope of eternity so that they may be lords and God may be Lord in these lords. And this is for no other reason than that his mercy is for ages: through the kindness of his eternal mercy he grants that, having become lords, we may be worthy to have him himself as our Lord.

> [Note: The royal codex together with the Tours manuscript reads, “through eternity,” etc., “of whose hope he—not they—may be Lord.”]

7. Whatever wonderful thing is accomplished through human beings belongs to God. — VERSE 4. “Who alone has done great wonders.” In many achievements of human actions, many great and wonderful things have indeed occurred; yet whatever was accomplished in them is referred to him whose power accomplished it. Moses performed many wonders in Egypt; but the magicians and enchanters bear witness that in those works was the finger of God, as it is written: “Then the enchanters said to Pharaoh, ‘This is the finger of God’” (Exod. 8:19). From this it is shown that God’s power was at work through Moses, whose ministry was then the means by which those things were done.

Also a great miracle was that which occurred when, at the word of Jesus son of Nave, the sun stood still opposite Gibeon and the moon opposite the valley of Haylon (Josh. 10:12).

> [Note: The latest Paris edition, following the Vulgate, reads “Ajalon.” The Micy manuscript reads “Helloim”; the royal and Tours manuscripts, as in Origen, “Elom”; Greek: αἰλών (*ailōn*).]

I do not know what more wonderful thing could be accomplished: at a human being’s word, the sun and moon were held back from the law of their course for the delay of a single day. But Scripture immediately added the author of this power, saying: “There was no day like it, neither before nor afterward, in that the Lord so heard a human being; for the Lord fought for Israel.” For in that Jesus was heard and God fought for Israel (ibid., v. 14), the power of him who both fought and heard was displayed in these deeds.

8. The first heaven and the dwelling-place of the angels. — VERSE 5. “Who made the heavens in understanding, for his mercy is for ages.” The sole cause of things made is his mercy; for he had no need that they should be made.

> [Note: In the printed editions the word “heavens” is inserted here; it seems better absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts, so that this proposition applies to all created things.]

But because he is good, he made all things in order that more beings might enjoy the abundance of his goodness. He made the heavens in understanding: not irrational, not formless, not confused and disordered.

> [Note: That is, he formed them not irrationally, but ordered by wisdom and reason governing them; or, as stated below, tempered through stages of rational arrangements. This should be noted, lest Hilary be thought to have held, with Origen and other ancients, that the heavens are animate. It is sufficiently clear from his exposition of Psalm 122, §§2–3, that he was alien to that opinion. Nor does he say here that the heavens are endowed with knowledge, but that they are the region of those who would know God; neither does he call them thrones, dominions, and so forth, but the dwelling places of those beings.]

But when the One who is infinite established a region for his knowledge,

> [Note: The printed editions read “for knowledge of himself.” More correctly the royal and Tours manuscripts read “for his knowledge”: that is, either a region in which he offers himself to be known, or one destined for powers created to know him. Nor is God here called infinite without reason: lest he be thought confined by place while a finite place is assigned in which he offers himself to be known.]

he set the highest and first heaven in a circle, and enclosed within it as a certain boundary those Powers which would first be created to know him.

> [Note: Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius agree with the royal and Tours manuscripts, which use “Powers.” It has already been observed that Hilary first calls angels “Powers”; and from what follows it is evident that he here includes under the general name of Powers thrones, dominions, authorities, and so forth. From this one might easily conclude that he thought that first and highest heaven created before the angels, unless in *Against Auxentius*, §5, he had explicitly affirmed that the angels were created before absolutely all ages and times. His view on this question may perhaps be considered more suitably in that place.]

For created beings would not have been able to endure the power of the unseen God unless they inhabited this dwelling, regulated to the weakness of their condition by the interposition of a more tempered nature. For, by waters set on high, he tempered the very nature of the first heaven, which, kindled by the power of God surrounding it,

> [Note: The printed editions read “of the heavenly God.” More fittingly the royal and Tours manuscripts read “of the surrounding God.” Perhaps they called that first heaven “empyrean” from this fire surrounding it through God’s presence.]

could not be endured by lower natures.

9. The lower heaven is manifold and is called the firmament. — But he stretched out the lower heaven, not uniform but manifold; naming the whole of it the firmament, he solidified it with a strength sufficient to sustain the upper waters and to moderate our air. Accordingly prophetic teaching has declared several heavens, because it was necessary for our nature that, through certain stages and advances of rational arrangements, this region of the habitation granted us for the present should be tempered.

10. The number of the heavens is not established. — Concerning the number of the heavens, human doctrine should presume nothing rashly. The Apostle understands that he himself was caught up only as far as the third heaven. He enumerates many thrones, dominions, powers, and principalities (2 Cor. 12:2), to which appropriate dwelling-places must be assigned.

> [Note: The royal codex alone reads “to be changed.” Then, with support also from the Tours manuscript: “but he also signifies that there are other things, the knowledge of which he promises for future times.” Afterward, before the word “is,” the particle “and” is written above the line in the Tours manuscript.]

But he also indicates that there are other things, the knowledge of which he promises for future times, when he says: “And above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come” (Eph. 1:21).

> [Note: The word “name” is absent from the royal and Tours manuscripts.]

Yet the Apostle taught nothing concerning their number, and I do not know whether he was silent or ignorant. For he has now also declared that he knows in part; and yet, when caught up to the heavens, he testifies that he heard things not to be spoken (1 Cor. 13:9). It is enough for us to know that there are several heavens, since “the heavens of heavens” and “the waters above the heavens” praise the Lord.

### 11. The Situation of the Earth, and God’s Immensity

> [Note: Thus the Royal and Tours manuscripts. In the printed editions, however, these words circulated as follows: *ita manendi sede moderatus est, ut paribus undique mensuris ponderibusque librata et substrata consisteret: ut is qui infinitus est Deus, primo illi superioris coeli circulo circumfuse supereminens aequalibus ex omni transfusione sua spatiis omnia virtutis suae spiritu, etc.*—“he so ordered its abiding place that, balanced and supported by equal measures and weights on every side, it should stand firm; so that the infinite God, diffusely rising above that first circle of the higher heaven, by equal spaces from every outpouring of himself, should reach all things by the Spirit of his power,” etc. In these words we have a kind of system of the whole world, by which Hilary seems chiefly to intend to demonstrate both the order of the heavens and the divine immensity that penetrates all things equally. To this end he represents the world as a sphere and God as fire spread around it. He teaches that the first circle, or heaven, of the sphere is kindled by that power of God which no created thing can bear. Beneath it he places the abodes of angels, moderated by intervening waters and diverse according to their different orders; he seems to permit these also to be called different heavens. Below these he sets the lower heaven, which, though not uniform but manifold, is nevertheless comprehended under the single name of firmament. Finally, with air intervening, he places the earth in the centre of the sphere. From this he concludes that God is equally spread around the whole sphere, reaching and penetrating it alike from every side. Here one must resist carnal imagination, lest we conceive in the mind a bodily surrounding and diffusion of God. How greatly Hilary recoils from asserting such a thing is clear from his exposition of Psalm CXXIX, sections 4 and 6; Psalm CXVIII, section 8; and Psalm CXXIX, section 3. But because, as he teaches in Psalm CXX, section 11, the weakness of our understanding cannot apprehend invisible things except through comparison with visible things, he tries to give us some knowledge of divine realities through such comparison. Yet, as he warns in Psalm CXVIII, section 9, these things are superfluously applied to the divine nature by way of likeness, because whatever is eternal is incomparable, etc.]

Beneath the heaven of the higher circle, which he has called the firmament, he placed the earth below. Suspending and establishing it in the middle, he so ordered its position that it should occupy, by equal measures on every side, the centre of the circle by which it is enclosed: so that he who is infinite, surrounding that first circle of the higher heaven by equal lines of his encompassing presence on every side, might reach all things by the Spirit of his power, tempered for the use and nature of living creatures.

> [Note: Thus, he does not reach things part by part, but is wholly present at once by the Spirit of his power. What is meant by “tempered for the use and nature of living creatures” must be learned from Psalm CXVIII, section 8, where, by comparison with the human soul, it is shown how God is wholly present everywhere. Thus God is said to touch the individual parts of the world in much the same way as the soul touches the individual members of its body. Moreover, those familiar with the ancient Fathers know that *temperari* (“to be tempered”) is almost the same as *misceri* (“to be mingled”). Philo the Jew explains both the agreement and the difference between the two terms in *On the Confusion of Tongues*, p. 347. The comparison of the soul’s presence in each part of its body is employed only so that it may be perceived, in some measure, how God is wholly present everywhere; not so that, just as the soul joined to the body makes one living creature, God may be understood to animate the world by being mingled with it. See Book I *On the Trinity*, section 6.]

For the Apostle says: “For in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). By this it is shown that the earth stands in his midst, as within the circuit of the diffused Spirit, since in God we all live and move and are.

> [Note: Printed editions read “in his Spirit.” We restore “in his midst” from the Royal and Tours manuscripts; the former later reads “thus surrounded,” while the Tours manuscript reads “yet surrounded.”]

But that he is diffused through and penetrates all things by the Spirit of his ordering is taught by the Prophet when he says: “The Spirit of God has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7). By this he is shown both within and without, both encompassing and entering—both surrounding and diffused through all things.

> [Note: The Royal and Tours manuscripts omit the particle “in”; on their authority we have added *suae* after “ordering.” We then restore “by which within,” where printed editions had “Therefore within.”]

### 12. That the Earth Is Not Submerged in One Region

The Holy Spirit next shows that the earth is not submerged in one region, saying, verse 6: “Who established the earth upon the waters, for his mercy endures for ever.” The method and subject of the present exposition do not permit us to inquire more deeply. It is enough that we have learned on prophetic authority that the earth stands securely, though suspended upon the waters, overshadowed by the covering of the heaven’s ordering—by that firmament which, stretched out like a skin and solidified like smoke, separates the upper from the lower waters.

> [Note: Printed editions read “this firmament,” wrongly. Still worse, Lipsius had formerly substituted *umbratum* (“overshadowed,” masculine) for *umbratam* (“overshadowed,” feminine) without any authority. Hilary says that the earth is overshadowed by the milder heaven, which he had earlier taught to be called the firmament.]

Certainly, that it is held suspended upon the waters—and in this, as in all things—has this cause: “for his mercy endures for ever.”

### 13. The Father Works Alone, Yet Not Without the Son

In the words which follow, verse 7, “Who alone made the great lights, for his mercy endures for ever,” we must not understand that he made them apart from Wisdom, Word, and Power—that is, apart from the only-begotten God, our Lord Jesus Christ. For he spoke in the person of Wisdom: “I was beside him, ordering [all things]” (Proverbs 8:30).

> [Note: Printed editions read “ordering all things.” *All things* is absent from the manuscripts, as also from the Septuagint and from Book XII *On the Trinity*, section 35.]

But he who ordered was both begotten and born from him with whom he ordered. Since the works of the Son are the works of the Father, and the Father works in the Son, as he says: “The Father who is in me, he does his own works” (John 14:10), and again: “I do the works of the Father” (John 10:37), he works alone by working in and through him whom he begot.

> [Note: Thus our manuscripts; printed editions instead read, “and by that, indeed, which he says.”]

### 14. Why “Divisions” of the Red Sea Rather Than “Division.” Many Paths Lead to Heaven

In the remaining verses there is a complete teaching concerning the manifestation of God’s mercy: we are to know that all things were accomplished for no other reason than that God is always merciful. The exposition of the preceding psalm has treated, so far as we were able, those matters connected with Egypt which must be understood spiritually. In confirmation of that exposition there is also this statement in the present psalm, verse 13: “Who divided the Red Sea into divisions, for his mercy endures for ever.”

The Book of Exodus teaches one division of the Red Sea, saying: “And he made the sea dry land, and the water was divided” (Exodus 14:21). How, then, is the Red Sea now divided into divisions? Unless, as I think, the account of these events contains an ordered spiritual teaching. For those escaping Egypt, which is the image of the world, and journeying to the land of promise which, according to the Gospel, the blessed will inherit, will pass through the Red Sea—that is, through the stormy surges and fluctuating motions of this very world. In it there are many divisions, or paths, for the journey. For some, the path is through fastings; for others, through chastity; for others, through almsgiving, faith, hope, and love. And all these must necessarily have their different divisions for crossing this sea; yet through these divisions of the ways all will make their passage through the world.

### 15. What Redemption Is Sung Here

The conclusion of the psalm establishes with greater faith that all these things are to be understood of the future, when it says, verses 23–26: “The Lord remembered us in our lowliness, for his mercy endures for ever. And he redeemed us from the hand of our enemies, for his mercy endures for ever. He gives food to all flesh, for his mercy endures for ever. Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his mercy endures for ever.”

> [Note: In the Royal and Tours manuscripts the following verse appears neither here nor below.]

For God did not remember human lowliness only then, when he chose Moses as leader to free the people from Egypt. Rather, he remembered our lowliness more perfectly when, being born in the body, he took our very lowliness upon himself, when he absorbed this lowly earthly body into himself by the glory of his heavenly nature. Nor did he redeem us from the hand of our enemies merely when he removed them from Egyptian rule; for afterward they were subjected to enemies, and even today they are held under the legal restraint of a foreign power. Rather, he redeemed us when he gave himself for our sins; he redeemed us through his blood, through his passion, through his death, through his resurrection. These are the great prices of our life. For the Apostle says: “You were bought at a great price” (1 Corinthians 6:20); and we were redeemed from enemies—from the devil, from his angels, from the son of perdition, from the rulers of the air, from the powers of the world, from hostile death.

> [Note: “Price” is absent from the Royal manuscripts, which, shortly before, together with the Tours manuscript, omit “through his death.”]

And he redeemed us by giving food to all flesh: “He gives food to all flesh.” To all flesh—that is, to the flesh which has been redeemed—he gives incorruptible and eternal food: the bread of life, the heavenly bread.

> [Note: The manuscripts read thus; printed editions read “from the powers of the world.” In them, shortly afterward, “all flesh” was not repeated.]

In each of these matters—that he remembers our lowliness, that we have been redeemed, that all flesh of the redeemed receives food—the cause is this: “for his mercy endures for ever”; and for this reason we must give him thanks: “Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his mercy endures for ever.”

> [Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the Royal and Tours manuscripts, though the sense remains sound and complete.]

Whatever heaven is, whatever earth is, whatever the other things are, and even this—that we are who once were not, and that we shall be what we are not—has no other cause than the mercy of God, because he who is good willed that we should be born into the fellowship of his good things.

> [Note: Printed editions read “who,” not “because.” Shortly afterward the Royal and Tours manuscripts omit: “For one is good, he says.”]

“For one is good,” says our Lord Jesus Christ (Matthew 19:17), who is blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXXXVI

> Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion.  
> [Below, *you* is absent.]  
> Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments. For there those who led us captive asked us for words of songs; and those who carried us away said: “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.” How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land? If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten.  
> [Below: “let my right hand forget me.”]  
> Let my tongue cleave to my jaws  
> [Hilary: “to my throat”]  
> if I do not remember you. If I do not set Jerusalem before  
> [Hilary: “prefer”]  
> the beginning of my joy. Remember, Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say: “Empty her out, empty her out, even to her foundation.” Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who repays you the repayment which you rendered to us. Blessed is he who seizes and dashes your little ones against the rock.

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

### 1. This Psalm May Apply to the Babylonian Captivity. It Is Ascribed by Some to Jeremiah

It is well known that, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy, the Jews were taken captive and carried into Babylon. Nor is there any doubt that the captivity of the people could have been foretold through this same book of Psalms.

> [Note: The Royal manuscript reads: “that the people might be prophesied.”]

For in another psalm it is evident that the overthrow of this nation and city was plainly foretold, when it is said: “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem like a watch-post for fruit” (Psalm 78:1).

> [Note: The manuscripts read *custodiarium*, “watch-post” or “guard-house.”]

The same thing seems to be signified also in the present psalm, especially since some have thought fit to inscribe it as if with Jeremiah’s title, because the captivity was announced by him before it occurred. Certainly, among the Hebrew elders, according to the information which we have received from them, this psalm has no such title of inscription.

> [Note: The word “elders” is absent from the Royal and Tours manuscripts. This is supported by the fact that, when Hilary speaks of “Hebrew elders,” he ordinarily means the Septuagint; in that version alone the present reading is found: τῷ Δαβὶδ Ιερεμίου, “Of David, [through] Jeremiah.” Nevertheless, we have retained this word, both because Hilary here, as he usually does in doubtful cases, follows the Septuagint reading, and because, according to Nobilius, this psalm in ancient Greek copies bears only the title ψαλμὸς Δαβὶδ, “A Psalm of David.” The Roman Psalter, published in the fivefold edition, and the German Psalter also bear no other title. Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew has no title. Theodoret likewise supports this view in his commentary on this psalm: “Among the Hebrews this psalm is without a title; but some ventured upon a bold act and wrote, ‘Of David through Jeremiah,’ adding, ‘Without a title among the Hebrews.’” Nevertheless, in Jerome, as in the Vulgate, the title “A Psalm of David, on account of Jeremiah” has already prevailed.]

### 2. All Events in the Law Are Shadows of Future Things

There is no doubt that all things done to our fathers or through our fathers bore, in the events themselves, the form of things to come. This same book of Psalms also witnesses that this is so. For when, in the seventy-seventh psalm, all the events in Egypt, the wilderness, and the other places thereafter were recounted, it was shown that these very things were parabolic: “Give heed, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter propositions from the beginning” (Psalm 77:1–2). For in being both parables and propositions, they are compared with the realizations of future things.

The Apostle likewise teaches that those same events occurred as prefigurations: “For the law has a shadow of good things to come, and all things happened to them as a prefiguration; but they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Thus the events themselves occurred as examples and were written for instruction.

### 3. The Captivity of the Mind, Treated in This Psalm, Rather Than Bodily Captivity

Therefore, this bodily captivity of the people must also be referred to as an example of spiritual captivity. For our minds have been taken captive by the dominion of the body and of the world; they have been taken captive by demons through the law of vices, which exercise their rule over us through various kinds of service: while drunkenness possesses us, luxury subdues us, greed binds us, ambition occupies us, malice holds us, anger usurps us, and all these incentives to vice reign within us.

> [Note: Thus the Tours manuscript; others read “by the law of the more powerful.”]

For the Lord came, according to the Prophet, “to turn away captivity” (Isaiah 61:1), when it is said: “To proclaim release to captives” (Luke 4:19). He came to loose those who are bound, when he said: “This daughter of Abraham, whom Satan bound for eighteen years, ought she not to have been loosed on the Sabbath day?” (Luke 13:16). He came to lead slaves into freedom, saying: “Amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin. But the slave does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever. If, therefore, the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:34 ff.).

We are therefore taken captive, bound, and enslaved not so much in body as in mind. In the present psalm, all the force and meaning of the words seem to me to concern not bodily captivity so much as spiritual captivity.

> [Note: Printed editions read, “Behold, for even in complaints and places,” contrary to the manuscripts. Then “in matters and names,” with the Tours manuscript, is preferred to the reading of other books, “in matters and in all things.” Shortly afterward the word “lamentable” is absent from the same manuscript as well as from the Royal manuscript.]

For there is such significance in its complaints, its inhabitants, its things, and its names that this lamentable complaint of the Prophet signifies spiritual captivity more particularly.

### 4. The Captivity of the Jews Worthy of Mourning

Verses 1–2: “Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion. Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.”

It is an instinct of human feeling that amid the injuries of present calamities one groans at the remembrance of former blessings. Let us contemplate in thought Jerusalem captured; kings serving victorious masters; priests subjected to overseers of Gentile impieties; every right of marriage taken away; the modesty of captive virginity subjected to Babylonian lust. From the groaning of those who were to suffer these things, we shall judge that the Prophet rightly cried: “Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion.”

> [Note: Printed editions read “Jerusalem captured”; more elegantly, the Tours manuscript reads simply “captured.”]

### 5. The Fallen Condition of Humanity Also to Be Mourned. What Was Lost Through Adam’s Sin

But because that Zion is the dwelling-place of eternal blessedness, and the heavenly Jerusalem is our mother, the holy city of the innumerable angels and of the firstborn enrolled in heaven; and because Babylon is the city turbulent with irrational motion, which, as Genesis teaches, was called Babylon by people whose languages had been confused—for there they began to speak the languages of all nations when there had been one speech for all—and because the very name Babylon has the interpretation “confusion”: whoever remembers that, through the sin of the first parent Adam, he has been made an exile from that Zion in which there is life without desire, pain, fear, or sin, and remembers that he has been delivered over to the world of this confusion as it were to Babylon—delivered over to the body confused by the disturbance of vices, cravings, and desires—will rightly cry out, himself also a spiritual captive: “Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion. Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.”

> [Note: Printed editions read “Babylonian”; they are corrected from the Micy manuscript. Nor is the reading “Babylon” in the Royal and Tours manuscripts displeasing: thus each person laments that, after Babylon’s pattern, he has been delivered over to the world of confusion.]

### 6. Against Those Excessively Attached to the Letter. The Works of the World and Flesh Are Rivers

I would ask those who think that all things must be understood according to the letter: What rivers flow past Babylon, so that the captive people sat there, rather than mourning their captivity in streets, gates, towers, or houses? Further, with what drums, lyres, or instruments were they captured? What history has said that Israel served its conquerors with every musical apparatus? Finally, what willows ever put forth leaves in the middle of the city, so that instruments hung there suspended as though in a public storehouse of musicians?

If all these things are empty when applied to the literal events of bodily affairs, we must follow that interpretation which, from prophetic authorities, exhorts us to spiritual understanding. All who perceive themselves to be captives in Babylon weep and sit by rivers. For all works of the world and the body flow past, after the manner of rivers, without any pause in their course: they run, slip away, and pass on. What bodily pleasure is not already past? [The text is uncertain; perhaps: “does it pass, or is it already nothing?”] What earthly joy does not pass away with the very fleeting awareness of its present enjoyment?

> [Note: The Micy manuscript reads “with a stealthy sensation,” a reading wrongly adopted by the Paris editor. Hilary means that the fruit of earthly joy is scarcely perceived, since the joy itself and awareness of it flee away.]

Therefore, sitting beside these rivers of worldly captivities and weeping at the remembrance of Zion, they groan both from longing for what they have lost and from the calamity of the present.

### 7. Willows: Saints and Believers. Instruments: Human Bodies

They not only sit and weep, but also hang their instruments upon willows in Babylon’s midst. The nature of willow trees is such that, though dried out, if they are watered they become green; then, when cut off and planted in moist ground, they sink down roots of their own. Under the image of this tree, prophetic authority signifies saints and believers, Isaiah saying: “They shall spring up like grass in the midst of waters, and like a willow beside flowing water” (Isaiah 44:4).

For each person who was formerly dry, dead in sins, rises again; cut off from the root of his former life, he now lives again through the life-giving waters of God’s word and the sacrament of baptism.

> [Note: The Paris edition reads “of the inner life,” wrongly. Hilary calls the former sinful life “the earlier life,” from which a person is cut off by conversion and restored to life through baptism and the word of God as through living waters.]

Moreover, when the Jews were given the Feast of Tabernacles in a bodily observance—when a leafy tabernacle was made from the branches of chosen trees as an image of future joy and of the future tabernacle—it was commanded that branches of the willow growing by streams should also be used, because the perfect joy of the heavenly tabernacle was to arise from the assembly of holy men.

Scripture indicates that instruments are human bodies, by whose worthy movements and harmonious actions we sing what is pleasing to God.

> [Note: Printed editions, together with the Royal and Tours manuscripts, read “the psalm.” More correctly, the Micy manuscript reads “we sing psalms”; that is, Scripture signifies that human bodies are instruments, whose … The Royal and Tours manuscripts read “agreeing” for “harmonious.” See the Prologue, section 20.]

Therefore, amid this captivity of worldly confusions, those who remember the Zion they have lost, who remember that in Adam they became exiles from the heavenly Jerusalem, and who feel themselves to be captives in Babylon—these sit and weep, and hang their bodies in the form and manner of holy men, lifting themselves above earthly desires.

### 8. When One Draws Back from Vices, the Memory of Vices Intrudes

Yet although our bodies have been hung upon willows by the pursuit of self-restraint, the things which make us captives do not remain inactive. For it follows, verse 3: “For there those who led us captive asked us for words of songs; and those who carried us away: ‘Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.’”

Anyone who reflects on the habitual conduct of human nature will fully understand the point. Those who labour to abandon vices and wish to forget what they have done impiously are nevertheless troubled by the incentive of a habit which dies only with difficulty.

> [Note: The adverb “with difficulty” is absent from the Royal and Tours manuscripts.]

The vices hidden within us try to mingle themselves with and insert themselves into the sacraments of faith, so that, amid divine hymns and sacred readings, thought of these hostile desires which hold us captive may creep in. There are certainly very many clear examples of this. We see many wicked persons reading and discussing, yet discover that they are always distracted again by debaucheries and impieties.

> [Note: The Micy manuscript reads “whom we see,” a reading not to be rejected. It then reads, “and these again are found distracted.” Printed editions read, “and it happens that these again are distracted.” The example of the wicked seems less appropriate for showing that many who labour to abandon vices are drawn in mind to former desires while reading and singing. Yet Hilary gradually descends to these persons and, by their example, shows that the mind can be joined simultaneously to reading and sexual vice: for, he says, we daily see wicked people who, while engaged in debaucheries, are nevertheless always found distracted in mind so long as they read.]

But every holy person, and one who has hung up his instrument upon willows, denies the fellowship of Zion’s song to those who led him captive and does not communicate words of holy song to hostile powers.

> [Note: The scribe of the Tours manuscript conjecturally preferred “captive”; but, to preserve the integrity of his exemplar, he added *-os* to the final syllable—a practice he followed elsewhere also.]

### 9. Demons Try Through the Flesh to Subject the Mind to Themselves. The Flesh Must Not Be Yielded to Them

The Apostle teaches us what the things are that lead us captive, saying: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans 7:25).

> [Note: The Royal and Tours manuscripts read “into the law.” Shortly afterward the Royal manuscript alone reads “and the battle is of the spirit.”]

Therefore, when there is conflict between the desire of the flesh and that of the spirit, those things which try to subject us to captivity attempt to occupy the body and rule it; they seek to insert themselves into spiritual teachings so that, by habitual association, they may deprive them of their authority. But they must be resisted, and we must answer in the Prophet’s words, verse 4: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

Our own land must be retained and guarded in freedom. For bodies polluted in their earthly state can hear nothing of the songs of Zion; and, although they are ours, they will be alien from God if they begin to be captive under the law of sin.

> [Note: The following word, “captive,” refers no less to “will be” than to “are,” with which it is most closely joined.]

### 10. What Punishments the Prophet Invokes for Forgetfulness of Heaven. The Right Hand: the Place of the Elect

But the memory of that heavenly Jerusalem and holy Zion must always be maintained, whether while one hopes to be restored or mourns her loss. For this follows, verse 5: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget me. Let my tongue cleave to my throat, if I do not remember you, if I do not prefer Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy.”

> [Note: The words “me” after “forget” are absent from the Royal and Tours manuscripts. Here and below they might easily be thought removable, were they not found also in Augustine and in ancient copies of the Psalms.]

In the promise of memory is contained the punishment for forgetfulness. But the words, “Let my right hand forget me,” are obscure because of the nature of Latin expression. According to the Greek idiom, in which it is written, ἐπιλησθείη ἡ δεξία μου, this does not mean that the right hand itself should forget, but that there should be a forgetting of it. It is a matter of great danger if our right hand should be forgotten. For all who are full of good hope are assigned to the right hand; sinners are to be placed on the left.

Therefore he has made the condition that his own right hand, which he claims for himself through faith and expectation, be forgotten—the penalty for not remembering Jerusalem—so that he might fall away from the remembrance of his right hand, that is, from being placed at the right hand, if he did not retain the memory of Jerusalem.

### 11. How Great a Punishment It Is to Be Mute in God’s Praises. Each Person Rejoices in What Affects Him. The Prophet’s Whole Affection Is Directed toward Heaven

He added another punishment for forgetfulness, saying, verse 6: “Let my tongue cleave to my throat if I do not remember you.” He knows that his mouth would be miserable if it were mute in the praises of God.

> [Note: The Royal manuscript reads: “He knows it is miserable for his mouth to become mute in God’s praises.” The Tours manuscript is so obliterated here that it cannot be read.]

He knows that those blessed and eternal Powers standing beside God’s throne remain continually in God’s praises, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth; heaven and earth are full of your glory” (Isaiah 6:3). He knows, too, that it has been said of those who, silent like the dead, lived without God’s praises: “Their throat is an open grave” (Psalm 5:11), because in their throat, as in an open grave, a voice dead to the praises of God lies silent.

Therefore he subjected himself to this punishment of silence, on the condition of forgetfulness, if he did not remember Jerusalem. He adds also: “If I do not prefer Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy.” For each of us, according to the judgment of his will, has a cause of joy set before him; and each derives the beginning of gladness from the inclination of his mind: the drinker from drunkenness, the glutton from food, the greedy person from money, the ambitious person from honours, the seditious person from tumults, the lustful person from debauchery. These things, then, bring each person a cause for joy according as he delights in them.

But the Prophet sets Jerusalem before himself as the beginning of joy. From this he takes the origin of gladness: that, received into Jerusalem, he will become immortal from mortal; that he will be joined to the assembly of innumerable angels; that he will be received into the kingdom of God; that he will be made conformable to Christ’s glory. He knows no other joys and has nothing else from which to rejoice, setting Jerusalem alone before himself as the beginning of joy.

### 12. The Destruction Wrought by Desires. Christ Is Our Foundation

And because he remembers that he must come there through many weaknesses of the body, many distresses of the spirit, and many incentives of creeping vices, he fears lest something from the vices of bodily nature cling to him. Therefore, after this, he prays to the Lord, saying, verse 7: “Remember, Lord, the children of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who say: ‘Empty her out, empty her out, even to her foundation.’”

> [Note: The Tours manuscript reads “on the day.” In Greek, “day” appears without the preposition “on.”]

> [Note: The Royal and Tours manuscripts read *quousque*, “until.” Augustine has *usque dum*, “until.” We retain *quoad usque*, which is also found in the old German and Chartres Psalters. Above, in Psalm CXXII, section 9, *quoad usque* occurs in the sense of *donec*, “until”; here it means “up to,” as though: “up to the foundation which is in her.” In Greek: ἕως τῶν θεμελίων αὐτῆς, “unto her foundations.”]

Edom is interpreted “earthly.”

> [Note: The Tours manuscript reads “earthly.” In Jerome’s *On Hebrew Names*, from Genesis, Edom is interpreted “red” or “earthly”; in Augustine, “blood,” which he further says is signified by the Punic word *Edom*; in the exposition of the Psalms attributed to Jerome, “earthly” or “bloody.”]

Therefore the vices of our earthly body, which are called children of Edom because they arise from the nature of the body, rule over these Babylonians—that is, over the confusions and disturbances of our mind—so that they may empty us of the fullness with which we have been filled.

> [Note: The word “which,” earlier omitted here, is supplied from the manuscripts. The vices do not arise from the nature of the soul, whose origin is repeatedly affirmed to be holy and heavenly, but from the body, which is earthly because it is from the earth.]

For it is written: “For from his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). Whoever is capable of the Lord has also been filled from his fullness. Yet such is the nature of a mind made turbulent and confused by the vices of the body that, if it once draws us into every willing and habitual practice of sin, it empties us of every pursuit of good virtues.

Therefore these vices command the turbulent confusions of our mind to empty us even to the foundation itself.

> [Note: Printed editions read “so that they may empty us”; corrected with the aid of the manuscripts.]

For whoever is holy is himself a part of Jerusalem, because Jerusalem will be the city of living and precious stones, made from the assembly of blessed men and those worthy of heavenly fellowship. These earthly vices strive to empty it even to its foundation. The Apostle teaches what the foundation in us is, saying: “But no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

> [Note: The Royal manuscript together with the Tours manuscript reads: “But no one can lay another foundation besides that which is Christ.”]

They therefore attempt to destroy every beginning of religion and every foundation of our hope, so that no memory or remembrance of God may remain in us and no hope of any good be left. For once the foundation of faith, which is Christ, has been dug up and overthrown, not even the consolation of pardon, to be built for us through repentance, will remain.

### 13. The daughter of Babylon is the flesh. It must be subjected to the soul whose rule it had usurped.

Having recalled the captivity of Jerusalem [Col. 0783C], and the exhortation of the sons of Edom to strip us bare even to the foundation, it follows that the Prophet should show how we must guard ourselves against these things. And he does indeed show it, not leaving us helpless or untrained, when he says, Vv. 8–9: “Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you the repayment which you repaid to us. Blessed is he who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock.”

I would ask those who consider the spiritual interpretations of the Psalms idle: whom do they understand the Prophet here to call the daughter of Babylon? And [Note: [Col. 0784D] Thus the Tours manuscript, supported by the royal manuscript.
