But in the printed editions: “And since above one sat and wept by the rivers of Babylon, why is the daughter of Babylon now wretched?” This is a gloss which does not even cohere with itself. “Above, the daughter of Babylon, proud,” where she proudly asks, “Sing a hymn,” etc.] how, though above she was proud, is the daughter of Babylon now wretched? But because the reader’s understanding lacks a merely bodily interpretation, a spiritual explanation must be considered.

For the entire discourse returns to that unhappy flesh of our confusion and disturbance [Col. 0783D], which, according to the historical account, was born from the fathers of confusion; for all flesh is daughter of an earlier flesh. [Col. 0784A] From those who first founded the city of confusion, Babylon, when languages had been confused, the origins of all nations were dispersed. This, therefore, is the wretched daughter of Babylon—that is, the flesh of all people. Blessed is the one who repays her her repayments, [Note: [Col. 0784D] In the printed editions: “if anyone has subjected his flesh to the dominion of the soul. And whoever has subjected it to the spirit, he will have subdued under all … all those who are untrained in and ignorant of God, and will rule.” A passage corrupted in many places is restored with the aid of the manuscripts.] namely, one who has subjected his flesh to the dominion of the soul and placed it under the spirit.

For she had subjected to all her pleasures and desires all those who were untrained in and ignorant of God, and, ruling the captive mind, exercised dominion. But when, through the knowledge of divinity, her vices are destroyed—not, I say, by abolition, but by death—when religion, chastity, generosity, sobriety, and love have consumed impiety, lust, greed, drunkenness, rivalry, and hatreds, and the conquered flesh serves all the works of the spirit: then blessed is he [Col. 0784B] who repays her her repayment—that is, who changes into dominion of the spirit over her the domination which she herself had formerly exercised over the spirit.

### 14. Desires must be destroyed at their first arising.

Nor is only the repayer of repayment blessed; blessed also is he “who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock.” Bodily vices must not be allowed to grow together and become strong; they must be killed at once in their beginnings. For desires, once robust, are dangerous; and whatever has grown to maturity is destroyed only with difficulty. It is easier to tear them away as they break forth, to cut them off while tender, to bend them back while pliant.

Blessed, therefore, is whoever, at their first beginning, first restrains within the authority of his patience and virtue every shameful pursuit of desires arising from the will of the flesh; then crushes and kills them against faith [Col. 0784C] and the fear of God. For everyone who passes from sins to religion crushes and shatters all sins upon the religion to which he has departed. In the fact that he seizes the little ones of the wretched daughter of Babylon and dashes them against the rock, both the virtue by which he restrains them at birth and the faith by which he dashes them down lest they grow up are shown.

And he dashes them against the rock. Now the rock, according to the Apostle, is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4). Blessed is the one who dashes and crushes against him the little ones of the daughter of Babylon—that is, the still tender vices of the flesh. To the same only-begotten God and our Lord be glory and praise for ages of ages. Amen.

## Psalm 137

“I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, because you have heard the words of my mouth. And in the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you; I will worship toward your holy temple, and [Col. 0784D] confess to your name because of your mercy and your truth, because you have magnified your holy name above all. In whatever day I call upon [Col. 0785] you, hear me; you will multiply your strength in my soul. Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, O Lord, because they have heard the words of your mouth. And let them sing in the ways of the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord; because the Lord is exalted, and looks upon the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar. If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will give me life. You have stretched out your hand over the anger of your enemies, and your right hand has saved me. O Lord, you will repay for me. O Lord, your mercy endures for ages; do not forsake the works of your hands.”

*Variants:* “above all” (below: “all things”); “you will multiply **me**” (Hilary adds *me*); “in your strength” (Hilary); “they have heard **all**” (below); “your enemies” (Hilary: “my enemies”); “the Lord will repay” (Hilary).

## Treatise on the Psalm

### 1. The twofold meaning of confession.

We have shown in many places that “confession” has a twofold meaning [Col. 0785B]: either confession of our sin or praise of God. That this is so can readily be known from statements in the Gospels. For when the Lord says: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent of the age and revealed them to little children” (Matt. 11:25), he confesses praise to God the Father because things unknown to the prudent were revealed to little children. He teaches that they were hidden from those who seemed wise because they had not believed the evangelical commands in accordance with the innocence of little children.

But where it is said in the same Gospels, “And all were baptized in the Jordan, confessing their sins” (Matt. 3:6), there confession of sins is contained without ambiguity of another meaning.

### 2. Confession of sin is most beneficial: what it is.

The greatest and most useful remedy for the diseases of deadly vices [Col. 0785C] lies in their confession. But confession of sin is not a declaration of matters unknown to others, as when a thief questioned about theft or a murderer about killing confesses (see Psalm 135, §3). Nor does God, who searches hearts and reins, need your confession in order to come to knowledge of his own [556; Note: [Col. 0785D] We conjectured that *your* should be read; but *his own*, meaning “his own knowledge,” should be retained, and the old editions also have it, though not the manuscripts.]: he is ready to perceive not only [Note: [Col. 0785D] Royal manuscript and Tours: “things not thought,” which is not displeasing in place of “things not yet thought,” especially since what follows is “but things to be thought,” not “but also” or “and.”] things thought, but things to be thought.

Rather, confession of sin is this: that, through recognition of sin, you confess that what you have done is sin. For no one undertakes to do what he does without either the pleasure of some profit or a judgment that it is good; for he either thinks it right or delights in it. But when, through God’s teaching and the reasoning of truth, he understands that what he chose under the appearance either of usefulness [Col. 0785D] or pleasure [Note: [Col. 0785D] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions: “did.”] is sin, then through understanding the sin he confesses that what he has done is sin.

### 3. Having confessed sins, one must cease from them. Confession and conversion must be whole. This must be sought from God.

No one should thereafter commit what he has confessed to be sin [Note: [Col. 0785D] The manuscript of Micy: “thereafter admits pardon.”], because confession of sin is a profession of ceasing from it. Otherwise, to remain in sins understood and confessed, this knowledge of sin, long possessed, loses the pardon of confession. [Note: [Col. 0785D] For *haec* we would prefer *ex*. Then after *jam pridem* “possessed” must be understood. Here, but especially in Psalm 140, §7, Hilary seems to grant the pardon of confession only to those who have sinned through weakness and error.] For one cannot confess as though newly recognized what one has done while knowing it to be sin.

Therefore, after sin has been recognized in confession, one must cease from sins; and one must confess, as the Prophet teaches, with the whole heart—not partially, nor while any practice of sins still known remains with us.

For what if someone repents of theft but increases his money by unjust and shameful gain? He will indeed not be a thief, but he will be greedy and a plunderer. Or if someone ceases from fornication but ruins himself with excessive wine, he will not defile his body, but he will contaminate his soul. And if someone abstains from killing but persists in abusive speech, he will not have a murderous hand, but he will have a murderous tongue. How, then, can anyone confess with his whole heart while no small portion of sin remains within him?

Therefore, when all vices have been cleansed by confession, there is need of ceasing from them; and God must always be prayed to, that in restraining sins and extinguishing their incentives he may strengthen the wavering efforts of our will.

### 4.

For this reason, now [Note: [Col. 0786D] Bad., Er., Lips., and the royal and Tours manuscripts: “confessing.” Immediately afterward, the Tours manuscript alone, with Lips. and Paris, places *when he says*. We prefer, with Paris and the Micy manuscript, “trusting”; and then, with the same manuscript as well as the royal manuscript and the editions of Bad. and Er., the placement “he says.”] trusting that through his confession and prayer the Prophet has been placed in the harbor of innocence, he says, v. 1: “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, because you have heard the words of my mouth.”

This understanding has a twofold sense, as we said above. For either he confesses praise to God because the words of his mouth have been heard; or, aided by God’s mercy after he had prayed long [Note: [Col. 0786D] In the last Paris edition: “heard,” a reading preferred by the scribe of the Tours manuscript, who relegated “aided” to the margin.], he now confesses as all sins cease. Both suit our faith: that we should praise the Lord and confess sins that have been understood.

### 5. Angels are everywhere present with the faithful.

Then follows: “And in the sight of angels I will sing psalms to you.” The Prophet thinks it too little to sing psalms only when human beings are present, [557] because human beings observe only the duties of bodily affairs. For in singing psalms he displays the movement of action pleasing to God. Therefore, he does not desire what is seen in the body to be observed, but hastens to perform what spiritual natures [Col. 0786D] spiritually behold.

For he knows that he conducts his whole life and conduct beneath the watch of angels, and that these aids of divine ministries [Note: [Col. 0786D] The printed editions read “mysteries.” More correctly, the Tours manuscript reads “ministries.” Angels are called divine ministries, because, as Psalm 65, §14 teaches: “The incorporeal God protects nations with the eyes of his mercy and, as it were, by the ministry of serving angels.” Hence Psalm 120, §4: “We may also understand the mountains as angelic ministries and the powers of heaven, by whose ministry ascent to the heights is granted us,” etc. Their ministry toward us is again explained in Psalm 129, §7.] attend all the faithful everywhere, as it is written: “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him” [Col. 0787A] (Ps. 33:8).

The Apostle also teaches that the law of Moses was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator (Gal. 3:19). Elisha, too, taught most clearly that human weakness is defended by angelic help and that, in every danger, provided faith remains in us, the protection of spiritual powers is present. For when the king of Syria was preparing to seize the city of Geth, in which the prophet Elisha was, and had sent out his army on night marches so that it might besiege the city before dawn, Elisha’s servant, seeing the siege, said: “O Lord, what shall we do?” And Elisha said: “Do not be afraid, for there are more with us than with them.” And Elisha prayed to the Lord and said: “Open, O Lord, the eyes of this boy, that he may see.” And the Lord opened the boy’s eyes, and he saw—and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots all around Elisha; and they came down to them [Col. 0787B] (4 Kings 6:15 ff.).

So great and distinguished a prophet alone was worthy to behold spiritual aids; but his prayer to the Lord won for his servant also the sight of incorporeal beings. Therefore, in the sight of these angels, who stand by with assistance to human beings, the Prophet will sing psalms, so as to please through the spiritual contemplation of spiritual works.

### 6. Why the Prophet will worship toward the temple, rather than in it.

But he will not only sing psalms before angels; he will also perform what follows, v. 2: “I will worship toward your holy temple.” Not “in the temple,” lest, if he worshiped in the temple, he should seem to speak bodily in accordance with Jewish custom; but “toward the temple,” that is, near the temple, worshiping in spirit and body.

The Apostle teaches that all holy persons are God’s temple, saying: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Cor. 6:16). Thus the dwelling [Col. 0787C] which is worthy of God from among us is God’s temple. [Note: [Col. 0787D] Royal manuscript: “from us”; Tours: “in us”; and immediately afterward, “God’s holy temple”; and below, “because of your mercy and truth.”]

### 7. How many heresies this destroys. Names of God.

At this holy temple of God, therefore, he will worship, not without the perfect rationale of doctrine, lest the disorderly confusion of speech offer heretics an occasion for their irreligious pursuits. For he says: “And I will confess to your name because of your mercy and your truth.”

When he confesses to God’s name, he holds the faith appropriate to the Gospels and the law. For the Lord showed in the same evangelical [558; Col. 0787D] and legal saying what name God wished to be known by, when answering the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection of bodies. For he said: “Concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken to you by God, saying: ‘I [Note: [Col. 0787D] In the Tours manuscript: “by the Lord.” It is clear from *On the Trinity*, book IV, §30, and book V, §21, that Hilary refers the following words to the Son.] am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’” [Col. 0788A] (Matt. 22:31–32)? “He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Exod. 3:6).

Therefore the error of the heretics—namely, the Manichaeans—is wholly exposed: they maintain that the God of the Gospels is one and the God of the law another, although the Lord recalls what is foundational in the law to confirm evangelical hope.

There is also another name of God which we learn in the Gospels, when the Lord says: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). And after many other words follows: “I have made your name known to men” (ibid. 6). And he showed above what that name was when he said: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.” Therefore, the one worships this name [Note: [Col. 0788D] Tours manuscript: “worships the name,” which the royal manuscript also had in its first hand. Thus Bad. on Matthew, chap. 19, §5: “He had worshiped foreign gods.”] who is, according to the law, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob [Col. 0788B], and, according to the Gospels, the Father of the only-begotten God.

### 8. Against the Novatians.

He also extinguishes the arrogant profession of those who, forgetful of human nature and weakness and preaching a merciless God, leave no pardon or consolation for the sins of those who repent. Yet the teaching of the law, prophets, Gospels, and apostles exhorts those who have sinned to repentance, through which one ceases from sins, so that by it some consolation may be found for hope now desperate: so that, though we have lost things blessed, great, and [Note: [Col. 0788D] The royal manuscript with Tours omits “and near to God”; then, with Micy, adds: “lest we at least be deprived forthwith,” not “lest we be deprived even of these things that are second to such things.” A similar manner of speaking occurs when Flavian says of Eutyches in Leo, Epistle 2, chap. 2: “When by the latter acts he ought to have saved the former”—that is, repaired his evil deeds through repentance.] near to God, we may not at least lack those things which are second to such goods.

### 9. Against Marcion, the Manichaeans, and others.

He also removes the utterly foolish presumption of those who contend that the Lord appeared in flesh with a deceptive and unreal body: as though the Father had displayed him in the appearance of false flesh by a fabricated truth. They do not recall that, after the resurrection, when the apostles believed that they saw a spirit, it was said: “Why are you troubled, and why have thoughts arisen in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:38–39).

The Prophet therefore distinguishes his own confession from theirs, maintaining the order of perfect faith: when in the name he confesses the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; in mercy, one merciful toward penitents; and in truth [Col. 0788D], [Note: [Col. 0788D] The particle *that*, and then the verb *is*, missing in the printed editions, are supplied from the Tours manuscript; the royal manuscript and Bad. also have *is*. A little above, Bad., Er., and Lips. have “merciful to the penitent,” rather than “to penitents,” which means the same as “toward penitents.”] that the Word became flesh.

### 10. God’s name is great everywhere.

The reason for confession is also taken from this: “Because you have magnified your holy name above [Col. 0789A] all things.” God’s name is not known to one nation alone [Note: [Col. 0789D] In Hincmar, *On Predestination*, chap. 25, as also in the Tours manuscript: “not only of the only-begotten God,” a reading not to be despised. In the royal manuscript: “not only to the only-begotten God.”]; rather, it has been magnified above all, [559] and the greatness of holiness extends to everyone. Neither barbarian nor Scythian, neither slave nor free, neither woman nor man, nor any age is excluded; for the name of God has been magnified above all.

The temples have collapsed; the mute images have been altered [Note: [Col. 0789D] The scribe of the Tours codex, preferring *muta* in the text, added the syllable *ta* in the margin, as well as *vel minutata*, clearly indicating that he was following conjecture. This does not displease us.]; diviners are silent at the intervention of the saints [Note: [Col. 0789D] Micy manuscript: “omens.” Royal and Tours: “the omen.”]; the trustworthiness of augurs fails. The one name of God is holy among all nations. For he is always present to his saints who hope in him; and wherever he is invoked, he supplies present help.

### 11. The righteous person is never without fear; he always trusts in God.

For he says, v. 3: “In whatever day I call upon you, hear me.” No righteous person passes any day without fear [Col. 0789B], nor does faith, always anxious for itself, accept the leisure of a secure time. He knows that every day is full of snares for him, since the devil and his angels are always plotting his destruction. [Note: [Col. 0789D] In the manuscripts: “plotting.”] He knows that that day of the Lord is hidden, unforeseen, and suddenly coming like a thief in the night.

Therefore he prays that God may hear him whenever he calls upon him. Nor does the Prophet doubt what he will obtain when heard on whatever day. For it follows: “You will multiply me in my soul by your strength.” That is, through God’s abundant care he himself will be multiplied in the strength of his soul, so that no weakness may lie open in him to tribulations or terrors; but when temptations press upon him and fear comes, all may be endured through the multiplied strength of the soul.

### 12. The kings of the earth.

And because this is a certain hope—that the strength of the soul is multiplied by the help of divine mercy—he declares that God is therefore owed confession by all, saying, vv. 4–6: “Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, O Lord, because they have heard all the words of your mouth. And let them sing in the ways of the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord; because the Lord is exalted, and looks upon the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar.”

Who the kings of the earth signified by the Prophet are has already been shown in many Psalms. They are kings not of nations but of the earth—that is, kings each of his own body, once the reign of sin in himself has ceased. For we have been called into the kingdom of heaven, when the reign of death has been overthrown; for “death reigned from Adam until Moses” (Rom. 5:14). And now, according to the Apostle, each is his own king: “Already you reign without us” (1 Cor. 4:8). The confession of these persons is therefore worthy of God [Col. 0789D], for they have heard all the words of God’s mouth and know that they have been constituted kings.

### 13. Great glory.

They should not only confess, but also sing in the ways of the Lord—not transgressing [Col. 0790A] God’s ways, but proceeding in them. Now all the prophets and apostles are God’s ways, each directing by his own way toward the one Way. The Prophet demonstrates that all converge into one, saying: “Stand in the ways of the Lord, ask for the eternal paths of God, and see which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jer. 6:16). For the ways of the Lord are eternal.

Therefore one must sing in these ways of the Lord and join in harmony with prophetic hymns, [560] because God’s glory is great: there is no end to his magnificence. For his works testify to the greatness of his glory: heaven, earth, seas, ether, and humankind itself, endowed with reason [Note: [Col. 0789D] Printed editions: “made perfect by knowledge of these things”; corrected from the Micy and Tours manuscripts.], made perfect for the knowledge of these things, so that through visible things it might behold the invisible glory of God.

### 14. God looks upon the humble; the proud are far removed from God.

God’s glory is not only great; he is also exalted and looks upon the lowly. The greatest wonder at the loftiness of his eminent height is that he, who is exalted, looks upon the lowly. But upon which lowly does he look? Surely upon these: “God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19); and again: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

But because the exalted One looks upon the lowly, there is another wonder in him as well: he knows the lofty from afar. Proud and insolent thoughts do not escape God; he knows all things, and nothing is impenetrable to his knowledge. God, as it is written, is near to those who are troubled in heart (Ps. 33:19); but he does not mingle with the arrogant, nor is he near to the insolent. To each one of us, according to the difference in faith, he is either near or remote, abiding through spiritual power where he judges himself worthy.

And therefore [Note: [Col. 0789D] In the printed editions, “the lowly from near,” or “the lowly in body,” had been inserted here without purpose. Immediately afterward, the royal and Tours manuscripts have “who also,” rather than “because also.”] he knows the lofty from afar: because through unworthiness he is absent from the insolent, and through power [Col. 0790C], [Note: [Col. 0790D] In the printed editions: “the lofty things which nevertheless are far away,” confusedly. Here it is shown that the proud are far from God because of their unworthiness, yet are reached by his knowledge because of his supreme power.] he knows, though they are far away, those who are proud.

### 15. The usefulness of tribulation. It cannot be endured without God’s help. God’s right hand is power.

V. 7: “If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will give me life.” This righteous person does not refuse to walk amid tribulations. For he knows that tribulation, according to the Apostle, produces endurance (Rom. 5:3). He knows that an untested person does not please; he knows that a soldier cannot become victorious without war; he knows that faith not put to the test grows weak; he knows that, according to the Apostle, one must glory in tribulations (ibid.).

He knows himself unequal to tribulations without God’s help [Col. 0790D], and therefore is certain through God of his salvation. Though he walks amid tribulations, [Note: [Col. 0790D] Bad., Er., Lips., and the royal and Tours manuscripts: “through the same [tribulations].”] he trusts that through God he will be given life. For he says, v. 8: “You have stretched out your hand [Col. 0791A] over the anger of my enemies, and your right hand has saved me. The Lord will repay for me.”

God’s outstretched hand protects us when enemies rage. For enemies bring tribulations, raging against our faith and hope, because, according to the Apostle, our adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion seeking to devour us (1 Pet. 5:8). But over the anger of enemies, through whom the devil always works, the Lord’s hand is stretched out; and his right hand makes safe those who hope in him.

Power is signified by the right hand. Therefore the Lord, who is God’s power and God’s wisdom, is sometimes called God’s right hand; through him we are protected against every enemy in the warfare of all tribulations.

### 16. Vengeance must be left to God.

The Prophet has preserved the principle of evangelical gentleness [561], by which we are forbidden to return injury to those who persecute us, saying, v. 8: “The Lord will repay for me.” For vengeance must be reserved for him who, when someone seeks by lawsuit to take one’s garment [Col. 0791B; Note: [Col. 0791D] The printed editions read “garments.” More correctly the manuscripts read “in a suit concerning a garment,” that is, where someone, having brought suit, attempts to take a garment. See Cange’s *Glossary*. In *On the Trinity*, book X, §28, we have: “in the very assault upon the trunk of the body”; these words indicate the very moment in which Malchus’ ear was cut off.], commanded that the cloak also be surrendered; who, after the injury of one slap, willed that the other cheek too be offered; who forbade returning evil for evil. Those will obtain the greater vengeance who reserve revenge for a present injury to the eternal Judge.

### 17. A human being was made not by God’s hand, but by God’s hands.

He then concludes in a statement of utterly faithful hope: “O Lord, your mercy is for ages; do not forsake the works of your hands.” Since God’s mercy is for ages, may he who stretches out his hand over the anger of enemies, protects his faithful by his right hand, and repays on their behalf, not forsake the works of his hands: namely, the human being who says, “Your hands made me,” etc. [Col. 0791C] (Ps. 118:73).

Things made by God’s hand are sometimes mentioned; but a human being is always said to have been made by God’s hands, an allusion to his more noble workmanship in the mention of hands being thereby displayed. [Note: [Col. 0791D] Royal manuscript: “enumeration”; then, “through him and in him.” See *On the Letter*, 10, §5.] He therefore prays that God may not forsake this human being, but may be his constant helper through him and in him who says: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). Our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Psalm 138

“O Lord, you have tested me and known me. You have known my sitting down and my rising up. You have understood my thoughts from afar; you have searched out my paths and my direction. And you have foreseen all my ways, because there is no deceit on my tongue. Behold, O Lord, you have known all things, both last and first; you formed me and placed your hand upon me. Your knowledge is wonderful beyond me; it has been strengthened—I cannot attain to it. Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings before dawn and dwell in the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand, O Lord, will hold me. And I said: ‘Perhaps darkness will tread me down, and night will be my illumination in my delights.’ For darkness will not be darkened from you, and night will be illuminated as day: as is its darkness, so also is its light. For you, O Lord, possessed my reins; you took me up from my mother’s womb. [562] I will confess to you because I have been made wondrously and fearfully; wonderful are your works, and my soul knows it exceedingly. My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret; and my substance in the lower parts of the earth. Your imperfect work—my eyes saw it—and in your book all shall be written; they shall be filled in a day [reading uncertain], and none among them. But your friends have been greatly honored by me, O God; their dominion has been greatly strengthened. I shall count them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand; I arose, and I am still with you. If you kill the sinner, O God, men of blood, depart from me. For there are disputes in thought; they will receive your cities in vain. Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? I hated them with a perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me. Test me, O God, and know my heart; question me and know my paths. And see whether the way of iniquity is in me, and lead me in the eternal way.”

*Variants:* “all [my thoughts]” (below); “my path and my direction” (below); “O Lord” absent below; “O Lord” rather than “you”; “wonderful” rather than “wondrous”; “very greatly” rather than “exceedingly”; “what you made” rather than “you made”; “my unfinished work … your eyes saw” rather than “your unfinished work … my eyes saw”; “their dominions have been greatly strengthened”; “the sinner”; “because you say in thought, ‘They will receive their cities in vanity’”; “those hating you, O Lord, I hated”; “the eternal way.”

## Treatise on the Psalm

### 1. The Holy Spirit is the author of the Psalms, all of which concern Christ.

It is not obscure that every prophetic utterance proceeds from the inspiration of the divine Spirit. For we read, “Thus says the Lord”; and again, “Hear the words of the Lord” (Jer. 31:2); and again, “For the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 24:37); and in the same prophet, “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isa. 58:14).

The Lord himself confirms this concerning the Psalms in the Gospels, when, speaking of himself, he says: “If David calls him Lord in the Spirit, how do you say that he is his son?” (Matt. 22:45). He thus teaches that David spoke all things by the prophetic Spirit. Although in this very passage he showed that David spoke of himself, by saying that David had called him Lord in the Spirit, he nevertheless more fully showed that every mystery of his bodily advent is contained in the Psalms, saying: “These are my words [Col. 0792D] which I spoke to you while I was still with you: that all things written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). [Note: [Col. 0792D] Bad., Er., and Lips., with the royal and Tours manuscripts, read “in the book of Moses”; yet in Psalm 125, §2, all alike have “in the law.”]

It is therefore not doubtful that the Psalms contain writings concerning him. For although [Note: [Col. 0792D] Thus our manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “for the most part.”] there are often such things in them as ought to be referred to the person of patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, [Note: [Col. 0792D] The Micy and royal manuscripts read “the first generations and the succeeding generations,” wrongly. By “the first generation” and “the succeeding generation,” Hilary means Jews and Christians respectively, as he himself explains in Psalm 134, §22. To this pertains what he says in the treatise on Psalm 63, §3, where he teaches that in the Psalms one must observe when the faith of the Gentiles is announced and when the sins of the former people are rebuked.] the first generation [Col. 0793A] and the succeeding generation: nevertheless, because all things are in Christ and through Christ, whatever is prophesied in the Psalms under the persons of different individuals is entirely about him. For all teaching, though manifold through diverse kinds of precepts, accomplishes this through diverse persons: that he may be known.

These matters had necessarily to be recalled because of the present Psalm, lest perhaps we should be thought to have presumed without credible authority [Note: [Col. 0793D] Printed editions: “without probable”; against the manuscripts, which immediately afterward have “presumed” rather than “assumed.” Thus on p. 480, line 6, the Lord is said to be “about to assume a body from a virgin.”] in referring this entire prophecy to the person of Christ.

### 2. Christ’s two natures must not be confused. In assuming humanity, God remained what he was.

The principle must be carefully observed that whatever appears fitting and appropriate to that human being whom he assumed from the womb of the holy Virgin, and in whom he who was God willed to be born as a human being [Col. 0793B], must be treated with the dignity due to his heavenly—that is, divine—nature. We must not adapt the mystery of our salvation, by which, remaining in the form of God, he took the form of a servant, so as to dishonor his unchangeable, invisible, incorporeal, and impassible substance.

That he was human benefited us; it took nothing away from him. For he emptied himself while remaining in the form of God [Note: [Col. 0793D] Paris: “so that he might be in the form of a human being, not so that the form of God,” etc. Other editions: “so that he might be in the form of a human being, not so that the form of God,” etc. We follow the royal and Tours manuscripts, whose reading is more easily understood if what precedes is expressed thus: “He so emptied himself that he remained in the form of God.”], not so that he might be in the form of a servant and cease to be in the form of God.

For he himself says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does in the same manner” (John 5:19). Did he, while remaining in the form of God, lose the power and divinity in which he remained in the form of God? Since, in the body of our humility, he himself likewise does whatever the Father does, he does not decline from the power of paternal divinity through partnership with flesh. Nor did the body which he assumed abolish the power of the previously abiding nature [Col. 0793C; Note: [Col. 0792D] The royal and Tours manuscripts read “destroys.” Similar is *On the Trinity*, book IX, §14: “The change of condition in the body and the assumption of nature did not destroy the nature of abiding divinity.”], since in that body which he assumed the power of the previously abiding nature works.

### 3. Whatever in Him is weak must be referred to the man.

Therefore, if anything said from His person is found to be weak, it must be referred to the man through whom He dwelt among us. For “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). This must be referred to the man for the reason that He did not assume a human being of an alien or simulated nature. For the Word, having become flesh, dwelt among us: not falling, through the power of the Word, into the vices and weaknesses of the flesh, but, being born man, taking upon Himself the weaknesses of our nature.

Yet the assumption of weakness did not make Him weak, since it is one thing to be a nature and another to have assumed a nature. Moreover, beyond the necessity of His kind, there is the addition of will. For He was not a sinner, but He took sins upon Himself. Nor was He weak, but He bore weaknesses. For, according to the prophet, “He took up our sins and bore our weaknesses” (Isa. 53:4). And lest anyone should suppose that weakness had come upon the impassible and unchangeable divinity, he added: “And we thought him to be in pains.” [Note: In the royal manuscript, “we think.” In *On the Trinity*, book X, §46, one reads “we thought,” which agrees with the Greek and Latin copies of Scripture. See the aforementioned passage of *On the Trinity.*] He therefore took weaknesses upon Himself because He is born man; and He is thought to suffer pain because He suffers; but He Himself is free from pains because He is God.

And while He dwells among us, while He takes up our weaknesses, and while, with the weaknesses assumed, He does not suffer pain, He cannot fail to be He who dwells; nor can He who assumes them have fallen away from Himself; nor can God, who does not suffer pain, have been abolished. [Note: The royal manuscript has “have been lacking,” and shortly afterwards “have fallen away” instead of “have departed.” We have already observed, on Psalm 63, §3, that where the person of the man is mentioned, only the nature is to be understood; and this is clear from §5 below: but the person of the divinity and that of the body must not be confused, especially since Hilary repeatedly affirms that God and man in Christ are one and the same.] These matters have been mentioned briefly because of the present psalm, since it seems at once to have begun from the person of the man; lest, because He speaks as a man, He should seem to have departed from the glory of the Father’s divinity.

[Note: The printed editions read, “dwelt … took up.” The present tense in the royal manuscript states more fittingly the distinction of the two natures in Christ and the continuance of the divine nature even after the human had been assumed. For those of whom one dwells and the other is dwelt in, one assumes and the other is assumed, are different; finally, one suffers from the weaknesses assumed, whereas the other neither suffers nor feels pain from them. In all these cases divine nature alone is exempt from pain.]

### 4. The righteous are proved through tribulations.

For he says, verse 1: “Lord, you have tested me and known me.” The Apostle, instructing us in the doctrine of patience and hope, says: “Tribulation produces patience; patience, proof; proof, hope; and hope does not put to shame” (Rom. 5:3). We know that this was so in the lives and works of all the saints: shaken by many sufferings and tribulations, they became approved before God.

For if anyone remembers that Abraham remained always faithful while an exile, amid fear of parricide and childlessness and the injuries of his other sufferings; if anyone recalls Jacob’s flight and, besides the toil of summer days, his wakefulness through winter nights while guarding sheep; if anyone recounts Moses’ forty years of servitude, the bitter reproaches of the people during it, and the rival powers of the magicians against him—he will understand that they were proved by patience and steadfast hope, and not without deserving thereby received this reward: that in Abraham’s seed the nations should be blessed; that from Jacob Israel should arise; and that Moses should become a god to Pharaoh.

[Note: The royal codex has “name”; then it was preferred to read “from Jacob” rather than, with the common editions, “and Jacob.” These statements are to be understood more closely as though it read: Abraham indeed, that the nations might be blessed in his seed; Jacob, however, that, his name and condition being changed, he might be Israel; and so on—not undeservedly receiving these things.]

It would be lengthy to recall the sufferings of the other patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, and those blessed and unconquered demonstrations of faith shown by Paul at sea, in rivers, on land, in wildernesses, in cities, among his own people, among strangers, under blows, in chains, in prisons, and in theatres. [Manuscripts: “demonstrations,” *decimenta*.] Certainly, patience rendered all these approved, and by it they proved the confidence of their hope, which was not to be ashamed. But these matters should be treated more suitably and fully in their proper places [royal manuscript: “should be treated”]; for now we must return to Him from whose person we have said the psalm proceeds.

### 5. Christ, as man, first tested and then known.

The person of the divinity and that of the body must not be confused. For at this beginning the whole discourse proceeds from the person of that man whom He assumed: “You have tested me and known me.” He was tested in order that He might be known, since knowledge follows testing.

Let us see, then, according to the Gospel teaching, how the Son of God was both tested and known. His humility, through which He deserved to be worshipped by every heavenly, earthly, and infernal being and to be in the glory of God the Father, was His testing. For thus the Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name, that at His name every knee should bend, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:8 ff.).

Therefore, because of this obedience unto death, even death on a cross, the weakness of assumed flesh is placed in the name and honour of immortality and in the glory of God the Father. [Note: In the Micy manuscript, “and the honour of nature”; this was also printed in the first Paris edition. “Of nature” is absent from the other books, nor do the following words require it.] For the name of God is given, and the name is not given without honour. But the honour given can be none other than that of the name; and the name of the honour bestowed is none other than the Father’s glory. Thus He who, remaining in the form of God, took the form of a servant, might, because of the obedience of His servile form assumed with death upon the cross, be in the glory of God the Father, in whose form He had previously remained.

But the Apostle has already spoken of these perfected matters—namely, the mysteries of assumed flesh after the resurrection. [Note: This is to be understood as supplied.] We must instead show from the Gospels where He was tested and known.

### 6. He was tested and known in baptism and in the wilderness. Peter tested and knew Him.

His humility, then, is His testing. For the only-begotten God, the forgiver of sins and Lord of the eternal kingdom, demands baptism as though He were a sinner. The Baptist declines this office, recognizing Him who ought rather to have forgiven his sins. But He fulfilled even in the sacrament of baptism the righteousness of the man assumed into Himself; and though Himself ignorant of sin, He did not refuse to become a participant in our sin. Taking into Himself all the humility of perishable flesh, He entered the Jordan mingled with crowds of sinners.

In all these things, while they occurred, He was tested. But let us see whether, once tested, He was recognized. For the Evangelist says: “When Jesus had been baptized, immediately He went up from the water. And behold, the heavens were opened, and He saw the Spirit of God descending from heaven, coming upon Him like a dove; and behold, a voice from heaven saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:16–17). [Note: In the Paris edition, “saying to Him.” Hilary recalls other words of the Father addressed to the baptized Son in his exposition of Psalm 2, §29.] Knowledge immediately followed testing: the One whom humility had rendered worthy of approval was shown by the Father’s voice, once tested, to be the Son well pleasing to Him.

There is also a testing immediately followed by recognition. He lives in the wilderness, is subjected to the devil’s temptation, and permits Himself now to be carried to the pinnacle of the Temple, now to a high mountain. Thus, while He is in the wilderness, while He is mocked under the condition of temptation, while He can be lifted to the Temple and mountain, He submits Himself to the affront of so grave an injury. Yet the proof furnished by the temptations did not lack the testimony of One who recognized Him. For Scripture says: “Then the devil left Him, and behold, angels ministered to Him” (Matt. 4:11). The man is tempted; the man is carried about; but after this angels minister to Him. Through testing He is known; through knowledge He is worthy of angelic ministry.

Moreover, as often as He was tested in other cases, so often was He known. Peter recoiled from His passion, unable, through love and through his knowledge of the divinity he had already confessed, to endure the scandal of the cross in Him (Matt. 16:23). But because Christ had called him Satan on account of his unbelief concerning the cross, not long afterwards, when He stood upon the mountain in the appearance of His glory, He was recognized by this voice from the Father: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear Him” (Matt. 17:5). The recognition conveyed by the Father’s voice followed the testing caused by the Apostle’s temptation.

### 7. Sitting is teaching; rising is action.

Then follows, verse 2: “You have known my sitting down and my rising up.” Gospel authority establishes that teaching is signified by sitting. The seats among us are those called by the Greeks *cathedrae*, “chairs.” Moses had a chair, according to the Lord’s saying: “The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ chair. Therefore do and observe everything they tell you; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:2–3). Since the teaching of the Pharisees is taught to be worthy of approval on the ground that they sit in Moses’ chair, teaching is necessarily signified in a chair.

Thus He knew His sitting when He proclaimed His dignity in all things, when He carried out the will of Him who sent Him, when, asking glory for the humility of His body, He heard from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it” (John 12:28). Yet teaching is known in His sitting no less than action in His rising. [Note: The printed editions read, “His teaching is known no less in His sitting than in His resurrection [Paris: rising].” They are corrected from the Tours manuscript.] For just as sitting is the act of teaching, so rising is the accomplishment of action.

Jesus taught while sitting on the mountain; but after His teaching He descended to works. For it is written: “When He had come down from the mountain, crowds followed Him. And behold, a leper came and worshipped Him, saying: Lord, if You will, You can make me clean. And Jesus stretched out His hand, touched him, and said: I will; be clean” (Matt. 8:1–2). [Note: The word “coming” is absent from the Basel, Erasmus, Leipzig editions and the royal and Tours manuscripts.]

He also rose to heal the synagogue-ruler’s daughter; for it is written: “And Jesus, rising, followed him with His disciples” (Matt. 9:19). [Note: The royal codex with the Tours manuscript reads “the centurion’s daughter.” The prevailing reading is deservedly suspect. Hilary here recalls Matthew’s Gospel, in which he is simply called a ruler, not a synagogue-ruler, as in Mark 5:35. Nor does the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 9, assign him any title other than ruler.] When He fulfilled that perfect service of humility in washing the apostles’ feet, we read: “He rose from supper, laid aside His garments, and, taking a towel, girded Himself” (John 13:4–5). Thus teaching and action are known in His sitting and rising, because by word and deed He proclaimed in Himself the Father’s glory.

[Note: In the Tours manuscript, “in Himself” is absent; in the royal manuscript only the preposition “in” is absent.]

### 8. God knew Christ’s thoughts long beforehand.

Verse 3: “You have understood all my thoughts from afar.” God searches hearts and reins; how, then, were His thoughts understood “from afar”? “From afar” refers not to place, but to time. He does not say, “You have understood from afar,” so that it might be thought a matter of location, as though He were far from human actions while, by the sight of His power and knowledge, He understands what is thought. [Note: The printed editions read, “He says that He understood from afar, so that the meaning of place, etc.” They are corrected from the manuscripts.] Rather, He says, “You understood from afar,” signifying a period of past time.

And where shall we find that His thoughts were known long beforehand? Surely where it is said: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon Him, and He will proclaim judgment to the nations. He will not cry out or contend, nor will anyone hear His voice in the streets” (Matt. 12:18–19). The Evangelist recalled this prophecy when He commanded those whom He healed to be silent about Him. Therefore, His thoughts of humility and patience were understood long beforehand, because God had testified to them through the mouths of the prophets.

### 9. What “path” and “course” mean.

“You have searched out my path and my course.” Before treating path and course themselves, something must first be said. For what is for us a *path* has among the Greeks another force and meaning. They call it *tribos* (τρίβος), that is, a way worn down by frequent going and passing, through which one travels not once, nor occasionally, but continually. [Note: Thus the Tours manuscript, agreeing with the royal manuscript except that it has *tribu* for τρίβον. The printed editions read: “for they call it worn, that is, frequently by walking and passing … it must always be entered.” See Psalm 118, §7.]

But what our translators rendered “course,” the Greeks interpret from the Hebrew as *schoinion* (σχοινίον). [Note: The Tours manuscript has, as do the common editions here and below, σχοῖνον. If Hilary had used this word, he would subsequently have written σχοῖνος, not σχοῖνον. The Micy and royal manuscripts more correctly have σχοινίον, agreeing with the Vulgate, which gives not “rope” but “little cord.” Genebrard conjectures that the Seventy wrote κοῖτον instead of σχοῖνον. Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew, “my lying down,” favours this conjecture. Nor is Hilary’s exposition far from such an interpretation.] Now *schoinion*, according to the usage of certain peoples, signifies a fixed and appointed measure of a journey: thus what we call miles, they call *schoinion*.

[Note: The printed editions read “a mile,” against the manuscripts. Indeed, if σχοινίον corresponds to the Hebrew word meaning a place appointed for a traveller’s lodging or resting-place—commonly, a *gîte*—that is, a day’s journey, this measure should be defined not by one mile but by several. Thus Origen, cited by Corderius in the Greek Catena of the Fathers: “The *schoinos* (σχοῖνος) is a measure of a journey among Egyptians and Persians; it is also said in the Psalms, ‘You have searched out my path and my *schoinos*’” (Ἡ σχοῖνος ὁδοῦ μέτρον ἐστὶ παρ’ Αἰγυπτίοις καὶ Πέρσαις, εἴρητο καὶ ἐν ψαλμοῖς, τὸν τρίβον μου καὶ τὸν σχοῖνόν μου σὺ ἐξιχνίασας).]

### 10. Christ traverses the way which He Himself had previously passed through and which the prophets had worn.

Our Lord, then, in the body which He assumed, traversed the path which He had already passed through Himself and which had been worn in the prophets; and He completed the fixed and appointed end of His journey. [Note: That is, when He was seen with the patriarchs in the appearance of a man or angel; these appearances are the subject of books IV and V of *On the Trinity*.]

Let us hear Him Himself say that He walked along the worn path of preaching: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks, and you would not!” (Matt. 23:37). By saying “how often,” He indicates the frequency implied by a great number. Therefore He did and suffered nothing new when, in the prophets, He was so often heard and dishonoured by Jerusalem, unwilling that her children should be gathered.

### 11. He completed the journey prescribed for Him.

That He was to complete a defined and prescribed journey is shown when He says: “I have glorified You upon earth; I have completed the work which You gave Me” (John 17:4). [Note: We have added “journey,” on the authority of the manuscripts.] He who completes the work given to Him fulfils the measure of the operation prescribed to Him.

He knows that what He ought to do has been appointed for Him when He says to Peter, who was resisting with the sword those who had come to seize Him: “Shall I not drink the cup which my Father gave Me?” (John 18:11). [Note: Thus the manuscript here and in *On the Trinity*, book X, §30. The printed editions read: “Do you not wish that I should drink it?”] By this He teaches that He would drink the cup of the passion prescribed to Him by the Father.

He also knows that He has completed His path and course, when, after drinking vinegar, and about to yield up His spirit, He says: “It is finished”; and immediately He yielded up His spirit (John 19:30). [Manuscript: “having drunk.”]

### 12. The Father foreknew what Christ did and suffered.

Therefore the Father searched out this path and course of His. He searched it out through the prophet when He prophesied concerning the lot for His garment, as it is written: “They cast lots upon my garment” (Ps. 21:19). And again, when the prophecy was recognized in His being delivered over among criminals and suspended, saying: “And He was numbered with the wicked” (Isa. 53:12). [Note: The printed editions read, “the prophet was recognized,” awkwardly and against the manuscripts.] Or when it was foretold beforehand concerning His unbroken bone and pierced wound: “You shall not break a bone of Him” (Exod. 12:46), and “They shall look upon Him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10).

These things, therefore—all prescribed for Him in His passion—were searched out by God, as they had been prophesied by Him. [Note: The common editions read, “as they had been prophesied.” This wrongly makes God’s knowledge subsequent to prophecy; rather, it is shown from this that God foreknew all Christ’s future sufferings because they were prophesied by His agency. The reading is corrected with the help of the royal manuscript.] And lest anything He did or suffered should be thought unknown to the Father, He embraced everything generally, saying, verse 4: “And You have foreseen all my ways.”

But He who foresaw saw before the thing existed. He also foresaw this: “there is no deceit in my tongue.” For He is, according to His own confession, truth, way, and life (John 14:6). [Note: Royal manuscript: “your way,” not “way and life”; and shortly afterwards, “deceived in speech.”] Truth does not admit deceit; for He neither lied nor deceived. All His speech performed the office of truth, He who said: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). He proclaims God the Father, and confesses Himself to be both Son of Man and Son of God. This proclamation contained no deceit, since it declared both Himself and the honour of Him who sent Him.

### 13. God’s knowledge was handed down to us not by a prophet or by Moses, but by Christ.

The discourse begun from the man then gradually advances and rises to signify the heavenly—divine—nature in Him, when He says, verses 5–6: “Behold, You, Lord, have known all things, last and first; You formed me and placed Your hand upon me. Your knowledge has become wonderful from me; it has been strengthened, and I shall not attain to it.”

This does not suit the person of a prophet, so that he might seem to have said of himself, “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me,” as though God’s knowledge had become wonderful through him, when Moses had previously made God known to us through the books of the Law. [Note: The printed editions read, “speaking in the book of the Law”; they are corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.]

Nor can this be proper even to Moses, who did not know God before seeing the burning bush, though he was religious by repute as one of the people of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, chosen by God; nevertheless, before that time he had not attained a familiar knowledge of God except from God. [Note: The words following were wrongly separated from the preceding words by a full stop, although they refer to Moses. Although he is thought by his people to have been devoted to God’s worship before the vision of the bush, he is nevertheless denied to have attained a familiar knowledge of God before then.]

But all this discourse belongs to Him who says: “Father, I have made Your name known to men” (John 17:6), and who says: “This is eternal life: that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent” (ibid. 3). These matters we shall pursue more fully in their proper place.

### 14. What in Christ is “last” and what is “first.”

We must proceed in the order of the words: “Behold, You, Lord, have known all things, last and first.” The “last” things are: “You have tested,” “You have known,” and the rest that belongs properly to that man whom He assumed. The “first” things are those without measure, those signifying the antiquity of unbounded time. For “in the beginning was the Word, and all things were made through Him” (John 1:1).

### 15. As God, He says, “You formed me”; as man, “You placed,” and so forth.

Then, as God knew things last and first, so in what follows—“You formed me and placed Your hand upon me”—He signifies both: what He formed is first; what He placed His hand upon is last. For the Apostle teaches that He was formed according to the nature of divinity when he says: “Who, being in the form of God” (Phil. 2:6). For what is in a form is formed into form, indeed into the form of the Father’s nature and divinity.

[Note: “He was formed into” must be supplied here. The reading of the royal manuscript seems mutilated and corrupt: “for what is formed, in form and to it is of the Father’s nature and divinity,” so that it may be referred to the Father and be formed by Him. But when Hilary says that he does not know whether Christ’s being formed in the form of a servant can be referred to the Father, understand this in a certain proper sense. He does not deny that the works of the Son and Father are inseparable, since he repeatedly insists that the Son’s works are the Father’s works. That proper sense is that, by the Holy Spirit coming upon the Virgin according to the angel’s word, he understood the Son Himself, who formed and fitted a body for Himself from the Virgin, as has been fully shown in the General Preface, §1.]

Yet I do not know whether the fact that He was formed in the form of a servant can be referred to the Father, so that He was formed by Him. For Wisdom herself built a house for herself (Prov. 9:1). But this is neither the time nor the question for further discussion.

That “You placed Your hand upon me” ought properly to be referred to bodily birth is taught to us from the person of the Father: “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him. For my hand shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him. The enemy shall not prevail against him, and the son of iniquity shall not add to harm him” (Ps. 88:21 ff.). There is no doubt that this whole psalm must be referred to the person of the Lord, because all its contents are proper to His divinity and differ from the weakness of our nature.

### 16. Why God’s knowledge is wonderful.

And because in both times—that is, the last and the first—He made knowledge of God wonderful from Himself, whether preaching in person or speaking in the apostles and prophets, He says: “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me.” But how is it wonderful? Surely because all things are taught to be within God, because God is proclaimed to be in all things, because His immeasurable and incomprehensible nature, abiding within and without, exceeds all places in which it could be contained.

It is wonderful that God is everywhere and absent nowhere; that He is in all things and wholly present; and that, beyond places and times, He always is according to His infinity and eternity. This is wonderful; this is strengthened—that is, made firm without any weak opinion of understanding.

### 17. In what sense the Son, equal to the Father by nature, cannot be made equal to Him.

But what is meant by the saying, “I shall not attain to it”? The Only-Begotten says: “All things that are the Father’s are mine” (John 16:15); “As the Father has life in Himself, so He gave the Son also to have life in Himself” (John 5:26); “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wills” (John 5:21); and, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). There is no distinction of power in these words, nor any difference of power in these works.

Many of the irreligious have referred “we are one” only to agreement of will. [Reference: Against these people the whole of book VIII of *On the Trinity* is directed.] But when He says, “Believe because of my works, that the Father is in me and I in the Father” (John 14:11), not only unity of will but also unity of divine power is shown. Therefore, since the Son does all the things that the Father does—for He does the same things in the same manner—we must ask what was meant by: “I shall not attain to it.”

But when I hear: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), and again: “The Son can do nothing of Himself, except what He sees the Father doing” (John 5:19), these words give me the meaning of the saying, “I shall not attain to it.” For the Father is greater than the Son, but as father to son: by generation, not by kind. For He is Son and came forth from Him. And although the proper designation of fatherhood differs, nature does not differ: God born from God is not unlike the substance of Him who begot Him.

Therefore He cannot be made equal to Him from whom He is. [Note: Royal manuscript: “cannot be made equal,” which is sound if this sentence is referred to what precedes rather than to what follows.] For although each remains in the other by the uniform and like glory of the same nature, nevertheless He who was begotten cannot seem capable of being made equal, in that respect, to Him who begot Him. [Note: The word “and” is erased in the royal manuscript according to ancient practice; “but” would not be unwelcome in its place. Shortly after, the same manuscript has “therefore” for “in Him.” Here the Son is declared, as begotten, incapable of being made equal to the Father insofar as the Father begot Him.]

### 18. The Father’s immensity.

Let us see whether “I shall not attain to it” refers to the dignity of the Father’s confession. [Note: In the Paris edition the word “begot” had wrongly been inserted here.] For it follows, verses 7–10: “Where shall I go from Your Spirit, and where shall I flee from Your face? If I ascend into heaven, You are there; if I descend into hell, You are present. If I take up my wings before dawn and dwell in the furthest parts of the sea, even there Your hand will lead me and Your right hand will hold me.”

The Son does not exceed the Father’s infinity; nor does He who is in the bosom of the Father (John 1:18) pass beyond the nature that is beyond all places. Though He be in heaven, though He be in the lower world, though He fly beyond the furthest reaches of the sea, yet He who is everywhere is present wherever He may be. Nor can He escape Him within whom all things are and who is in all things.

### 19. Christ’s threefold state must be distinguished.

And lest, from the words “Where shall I flee from Your face?” we should irreligiously suppose something dishonouring to the unchangeable and impassible substance—as though He had contemplated flight from fear of suffering—the logic of the words must be understood, so that we may see that these matters have necessarily been mentioned without harm to His dignity.

[Note: The Paris edition lacks “logic,” having “power” instead in the other printed editions. Then, after establishing Christ’s threefold state—before man, that is, before He assumed flesh; in man, namely from the time He assumed flesh; and after man, or after He had put off by death flesh weak in nature and received it through resurrection as glorious and free from weakness—it may cause difficulty that He is said to have been God and man only while He was “in man,” as though after the resurrection He were not also God and man. But Hilary means only that Christ was at once God and man while He had the power of divinity united with our weakness: that is, as long as He left the man in the weakness of his nature. This is treated at length in the Preface, §5. See a similar passage in *On the Trinity*, book IX, §6.]

No one who devotes himself to the study of heavenly doctrine can doubt that our Lord Jesus Christ must be confessed as God and man: man indeed in time, but God always, both before man and after man; yet both God and man only while He was in man. For He was in the form of God and took the form of man; and again He is in the glory of God the Father, the servile form advancing into the glory of Him in whose form He had previously remained—namely, the nature of corruption being swallowed up by its advance into incorruption.

### 20. What belongs to each nature.

Since, therefore, we remember that this psalm began from the person of the man whom He assumed, we must consider carefully in order to understand what is to be assigned to His divinity and what to the man. We must adapt our understanding to the words rather than, through an erroneous interpretation, subject the words to our preconceived understanding. [Note: According to the rule delivered in *On the Trinity*, book I, §18: “The best reader is one who expects the understanding of the words from the words themselves rather than imposes it upon them, and who conveys rather than imports it; who does not compel the words to seem to contain what, before reading, he presumed they should be understood to mean.”]

For He says: “Where shall I go from Your Spirit, or where shall I flee from Your face?” The meaning of “Spirit” is different from that of “face.” From the Spirit, indeed, “I shall go”; but from the face, “I shall flee.” Then follows: “If I ascend into heaven, You are there; if I descend into hell, You are present.” Ascending into heaven is not the same as descending into hell.

Then there is a third statement: “If I take up my wings before dawn and dwell in the furthest parts of the sea, even there Your hand will lead me and Your right hand will hold me.” These are no longer the words of man: to take wings, to take his own wings, to dwell across the Ocean, to be led there by God’s hand, to be held by God’s right hand. This belongs to a higher nature. The logic of the words themselves will show who it is that says these things confidently.

### 21. As God, He is nowhere absent from God’s Spirit; as man, He cannot flee from God’s face.

Therefore the only-begotten God, setting forth the confession of the Father’s wondrous greatness—made wondrous through Himself and beyond His attainment—indicates both times and both natures in Himself: namely, that by which He taught while abiding both in the Spirit and in the body. [Note: The Micy manuscript has “where,” which could be referred to time were the word “nature” not closer. Christ taught knowledge in the Spirit when, before assuming man, He appeared to the patriarchs and spoke in the prophets; and He taught also in the body, personally preaching through the man He had assumed.]

For when He says, “Where shall I go from Your Spirit?” He shows that time in which He Himself, who is Spirit, remained in the Spirit of the Father’s glory before assuming man. For He who is Spirit cannot be absent anywhere from the Spirit, since neither can this One be deceived nor that One deceive. [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “could be from the Spirit,” and shortly afterwards, “nor can that One fail,” in place of “nor can that One deceive.”]

But when He says, “Or where shall I flee from Your face?” He teaches the period of the weakness which He assumed. Human weakness cannot endure an encounter with the face of God, because it was said to Moses: “What man is there who will see my face and live?” (Exod. 33:20). What we cannot endure, we flee, because it belongs to human weakness to flee an encounter with the unseeable nature.

It flees indeed insofar as it cannot bear the vision. [Note: The particle “to” is absent from the royal manuscript, in which the following word cannot be read because the letters have faded. “Unable to bear the vision” would be acceptable: that is, unable to endure the sight.] Yet because, according to the Prophet, “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 33:17), it also belongs to human nature not to be able to flee God’s judgment, which is signified by the face.

For He who knows no sin did not speak as a sinner, as though He were fleeing; rather, having previously taught in the Spirit that the Father’s infinity remains beyond all things, He now also shows, from the person of the man who could flee God nowhere, that God cannot be escaped.

22. As God he ascends into heaven; as man he descends into hell.---There follows also the order of the statements: “If I ascend into heaven, thou art there”: this belongs properly to his divinity. For “no one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:3). The nature of an earthly body cannot attain this ascent unless it has been transformed into heavenly glory. “If I descend into hell, thou art present”: this is the law of human necessity, that when bodies are buried together, souls descend to the regions below. The Lord did not refuse this descent, in order to bring to completion the reality of the human being. But the words, “Where shall I go, or where shall I flee?” and there, “thou art” and “thou art present,” concern the meaning of his teaching, which became wondrous through him: by it God was known to exist everywhere and in all things. Thus, though a man flees God’s face because he cannot endure it, though by the law of death he descends from the heights to the regions below, God is nevertheless always everywhere and in all things.

[Note: The Micy manuscript reads *narratio*; the Royal manuscript, *paratio*. Perhaps *par ratio*, “an equal argument.”]

[Note: Tertullian refers to this law in *On the Soul*, §55: “If Christ is God, yet also man, dead according to the Scriptures and buried according to those same Scriptures, he also satisfied this law, undergoing in the lower regions the form of human death,” etc.]

23. Matters concerning Christ’s glorious state.---Since in these preceding words he had separately proclaimed, from each of the two kinds of nature in which he existed, namely God’s and man’s, he now shows, thirdly, the unity of the nature advancing into itself, saying: “If I take up my wings before dawn and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there thy hand will lead me, and thy right hand will hold me.”

When he takes up wings, he is no longer weighed down by the body (*On Psalm* 54, §7). When he takes up his own wings, he teaches that this power of flight had always belonged to him. When he takes them up before dawn, he indicates the time of the resurrection. When he is in the uttermost parts of the sea, as God he surpasses the places of human sojourn. When he is led by the hand, he does not fear. When he is held by God’s right hand, he is not changed or brought low: “For God gave him the name which is above every name, that at his name every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9 ff.). For in being given the name above every name, the man in him is received and assumed into his glory by the hand and power of God the Father.

[Note: In the Paris edition, the particle *in* had dropped out. “Into himself,” that is, into God. Here is touched on Christ’s third state, in which, through the resurrection—as Hilary says elsewhere—he becomes wholly God, not because human nature is abolished, but because it is assumed into the unity and fellowship of God’s glory.]

24. Wings signify the power to fly into heaven after the resurrection.---Prophetic authority applies wings to the transformation of earthly bodies into a spiritual and eternal nature, when it says to one poor in faith and impoverished in good works: “Do not stretch yourself out, being poor, toward a rich man; but restrain yourself by your understanding; for he has prepared wings for himself like an eagle, and he will return to the house of the one who rules him” (Prov. 23:5).

The poor man stretching himself toward the hopes of the rich is rebuked because he would match the poverty of his unbelief to the abundance of the faithful. For the rich man prepares wings for himself, not through human resources but through heavenly treasures, by which he may return to the house of the one who rules him. He will return to the place from which he fell, from which he was expelled through the sin of the first man. And who is this one whose house it is and who rules it? Surely he who said: “Amen, I say to thee, today thou shalt be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Elsewhere also, when discussing the now tireless eternity of spiritual beings, he says: “They shall put forth wings like eagles” (Isa. 40:31), meaning that in the transformation of the resurrection they will receive the nature capable of flying to heaven. But here he takes wings in order to fly—not another’s, not new ones, but wings claimed by the prerogative of his own possession—because, after the mystery of his voluntary Passion, he possessed the wings both of nature and of power by which to raise himself to heaven.

[Note: The printed editions read “and ethereal nature”; this is corrected from the Micy manuscript. In these treatises Hilary frequently calls the nature of bodies eternal after their transformation in the resurrection, but never ethereal. When he occasionally calls it heavenly, he gives it this name because heaven is its region, not because it is composed of some heavenly material. “For,” he says in *On Psalm* 55, §12, “at the resurrection a body is not acquired by all from external matter,” etc.; and in *On Psalm* 2, §41: “The Lord will restore broken bodies, not from some other substance, but from their old matter, the very matter of their origin,” etc. These points should be noted in passing, lest anyone suppose that we have corrected this passage without cause, or imagine that Hilary agreed with Origen concerning the doctrine of the resurrection. He differs even more widely from him in *On Psalm* 67, §35, when he attributes to restored bodies the form and solidity of limbs.]

[Note: Bad., Er., and Lips. read *in opes*, “toward riches,” which the first Paris edition rightly changed from the Micy manuscript, but the later edition wrongly restored. For the poor man is not blamed for aspiring to a rich man’s wealth, or for acquiring treasures of virtues; rather, though lacking those resources by which alone we are raised to hope of heavenly goods, he stretches himself toward that hope. Those who substituted *in opes* wished to imitate the Vulgate, which Hilary does not follow.]

25. Here Christ’s alarm is not indicated, but the supposition of alarm.---The same order of statements continues, and the discourse proceeds from the understanding of each nature, namely man’s and God’s. For he says, verse 11: “And I said, Perhaps the darkness will trample me.” This voice is thought to be that of a man because some irreligious or uninstructed persons suppose that, beneath the fearfulness of the Passion, he trembled in fear. Yet this statement does not now contain an avowal of any fear; rather, it signifies the willingness with which he undertook death, without any fear or terror being set before it.

For he does not say, “The darkness will trample me,” but, “Perhaps the darkness will trample me.” By adding “perhaps,” he mocked the error of uncertain human opinion concerning himself, by which he was believed to fear the lower regions. For no one who is certain that he is being trampled can at the same time be uncertain whether he is trampled.

[Note: Thus the Micy manuscript. The printed editions read “human.” Since this voice is denied to be a man’s where alarm is subsequently denied to be fitting for Christ, it must necessarily be denied to him as God, not as man. Nor need we inquire further why, suppressing what was fitting to him as man, Hilary hastens toward the one point of showing that in Christ there is a nature exempt from the infirmity of alarm: any prudent person will readily judge that this was more useful and salutary for that period.]

26. Why the Passion was a delight to him. The Father is with the Son in power and nature. Darkness touches neither.---In order that the words, “Perhaps darkness will trample me,” might not be understood as alarm in his own nature but as the uncertainty of an impious understanding concerning him, he immediately added: “And the night is illumination in my delights.” For how can one be trampled by darkness when death will be an illumination in his delights?

Therefore this Passion is a delight to the Lord: as he breaks the brazen gates, crushes the iron bars, strips every power, triumphs over them in himself, redeems the one whom he made in his own image, and restores him to the delights of paradise. Amid these enjoyments and delights of the Passion, then, night is illumination to him; and it is illumination because “darkness shall not be darkened by thee.”

By the unity of nature, the Father is in the Son in the unchangeable likeness of divinity; and, as the works themselves bear witness that the Father is in him, he confidently says, “They shall not be darkened by thee.” For we remember that it was said in the Psalms in the Father’s person: “I am with him in tribulation” (Ps. 90:15). And the Lord himself in the Gospels, speaking of the apostles’ alarm, says: “Behold, the hour comes when each of you will be scattered and leave me alone; but I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32).

Whether in power, by which he can do things like the Father; or in nature, kind, and divinity, by which he is God born from God, the Father is with him. He therefore says confidently, verse 12: “For darkness shall not be darkened by thee.” Unchangeable power does not experience darkness, and true light does not endure the night of hell. For it follows: “And night shall be illuminated as day; as its darkness, so also its light.” All this refers to what was said: “Darkness shall not be darkened by thee, and night shall be illuminated as day by thee, and as its darkness, so its light is by thee.” The one occurrence of “by thee” is carried over to many expressions.

Night is a delight because it shall be illuminated as day. It shall be illuminated because, just as darkness, so light is from God, who has power, as the creator of darkness, to create light amid darkness.
