Let us hear the Evangelist teach this in these words: “And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5): he had power for light to be in darkness, while darkness had no power to comprehend, by the night of its own obscurity, the light of unfailing brightness.

[Note: Lipsius preferred “night”; Bad., Er., and the manuscripts oppose this. As the term “darkness” in the preceding section, so the word “night” here indicates that death is to be understood.]

[Note: The reading should perhaps be *ac*, “and,” rather than *ad*, “to”: “By unity of nature and unchangeable likeness of divinity, the Father is in the Son.”]

27. So that each of Christ’s natures may be proclaimed. The office of Christ as man. Whence he was made terribly wondrous.---Then follows, verses 13 and 14: “For thou, Lord, hast possessed my reins; thou didst receive me from my mother’s womb. I will confess to thee, because I have been made terribly wondrous.” He still preserves the order that signifies both, so as to teach that he is both man and God.

For when his reins are possessed by God and he is received from his mother’s womb, his bodily condition is shown. For the source of pleasure is in the reins. But the reins of one possessed by God do not issue into the incitements of bodily wantonness. And one received from his mother’s womb does not depart, having been received by God, for the works of the world. Therefore all his will and labour are to proclaim the Father, fulfil the Father’s will, and drink the cup received from the Father. These are the offices of the man whom he assumed.

But when he says, “I will confess to thee, because I have been made terribly wondrous,” he renders every confession of terrible wonder concerning himself to the glory of his divine substance. For he was made wondrous because God possessed his reins and because he was received from his mother’s womb. By this—that his will and activity were devoted to God—he deserved to be made terribly wondrous. And he was made terribly wondrous when there was darkness during the hours of the cross; when the earth trembled; when rocks were split; when tombs stood open; when the dead rose; when he was seen in the same body; when, with doors closed, he stood present by an entrance open to himself alone; when he was lifted up to heaven; when the apostles spoke in the languages of the nations; when their shadows healed diseases; when the power of walking was granted to a lame man asking for a coin; when one dead was restored through alms given to the poor; when persecutors became preachers; when, chains having been loosened, songs were sung in prison; when in martyrdom he is seen in heaven by the martyr; and finally, when in the body in which he was raised he sits at the right hand of God, in whose glory he both was and remains.

[Note: We restore *incentiva*, “incitements,” in place of *incentivae*, since the adjective *incentivus* is nowhere read in Hilary, whereas he frequently uses *incentiva* whenever speaking of bodily pleasures.]

[Note: The Vulgate editions read “at the hour of the cross.” The manuscript more suitably reads “during the hours,” namely from the sixth to the ninth hour, Mark 15:33.]

[Note: “Dead” would be more pleasing as feminine, referring to Tabitha, who, after her death, was restored through the tears of the widows and poor persons whom she had aided (Acts 9:36).]

28. Though not unequal to the Father in power, the Son ascribes all that is his to the Father.---But he attributes to the work of him whose will he obeyed all the dignity by which he was made terribly wondrous, saying: “Thy works are wonderful, and my soul knows them exceedingly well.” For, he says, my being made terribly wondrous is thy work.

The same principle is preserved in the Gospels: though, to demonstrate his power, he said, “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19), and again, “As the Father raises the dead, so the Son gives life to whom he wills” (ibid., 21), nevertheless, assigning the dignity of all his works to the Father, when he says, “The Son can do nothing from himself except what he sees the Father doing” (ibid., 19), he subjected the power affirmed concerning himself, in the honour of reverence, to him to whom he remembered that all things must be confessed. He did not take from himself the ability to do things like the Father, but showed him through whom he could do them.

Therefore, although these things by which he was made terribly wondrous belonged to his own power because he could do them, he ascribed them all to the Father’s works, saying: “Thy works are wonderful, and my soul knows them exceedingly well.” This is not the voice of human weakness, boasting that it knows God’s wonderful works exceedingly well. This belongs to him alone who says: “No one knows the Father except the Son” (Matt. 11:27). For he knows—not in any ordinary or superficial way—but exceedingly well, through the confidence by which he says: “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (John 10:38). For in saying “exceedingly,” he shows the perfect knowledge of innermost cognition.

[Note: The first Paris edition, from the Micy manuscript, reads “of innermost cognition.”]

29. The Church is Christ’s bone. Mysteries have been revealed to the Church.---Since his soul knows all God’s wonderful works exceedingly well, he recalls the instruction of his doctrine to us, by which the mysteries of the Father’s operation are no longer hidden from us, saying, verse 15: “My bone, which thou didst make in secret, is not hidden from thee.”

That Christ’s bone is the Church rests upon both prophetic and apostolic authority. For when the Apostle was discussing Adam and Eve according to what is said in Genesis, he said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23); and in explaining this saying he added: “This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32).

The Lord himself testified in the Gospel that these things were not hidden from the Church through the mercy of God the Father, when he said: “I confess to thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because so it was pleasing before thee” (Matt. 11:25–26). Therefore those things which were made in secret are not hidden from us by him. They are not hidden from us, certainly, but they were made in secret from the wise persons of this world.

[Note: The Micy codex reads “saying in the Church.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “because to us”; corrected from the Micy manuscript.]

30. They were formerly hidden.---The Apostle also testifies that all the mysteries of ecclesial hope were hidden, saying: “As you are able to understand my insight into the mystery of Christ, which in other ages was not made known to the children of men as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles should be fellow-heirs, fellow-members of the body, and fellow-partakers of his promise in Christ” (Eph. 3:4).

And again: “According to the dispensation of God which was given to me for you, to fulfil the word of God: the mystery which was hidden from ages and from generations, but now has been manifested to his saints, to whom he willed to show the riches of the glory of God’s mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Col. 1:25 ff.).

Thus it was a hidden mystery, now revealed, that the Gentiles are to God fellow-heirs, fellow-members of the body, and fellow-partakers of his promise in Christ. It is also a hidden mystery that he willed to show to them the riches of the glory of God’s mystery among the Gentiles, namely, “Christ in you, the hope of glory.”

[Note: The word “my” was absent in the Vulgate editions; we supply it from the manuscript, as required by the sacred text.]

31. The Father revealed these things to the lowliest of the earth.---Therefore this mystery—that Christ should be in us—was hidden; the Father revealed it. For it was said to Peter: “Neither flesh nor blood revealed this to thee, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17).

But it was revealed that Christ is in us: in the poor in spirit, the afflicted in heart, the humble of the earth, the refuse of the world, the lowliest members of the Church. For “the lowliest of the Church” means those brought low by every kind of humility. Therefore this hidden mystery was revealed: “Christ in us.” The Lord says these things not only through the Apostle but also in this same Psalm: “My bone, which thou didst make in secret, is not hidden from thee; and my substance is in the lower parts of the earth.”

This is not in hell, as above when he treated of the Passion; it is in the lower parts of the earth when he proclaims those things formerly hidden that were revealed by the Father. For what had been hidden was “Christ in us,” that is, “my substance in the lower parts of the earth”: in the lowermost offices of every humility.

32. “Unwrought,” according to the force of the Greek expression, belongs to God alone.---Then, as the Psalm’s discourse proceeds in evangelical advancement, it says, verse 16: “Thine eyes saw my imperfect thing, and all shall be written in thy book; they shall be filled in the day, and none among them.” In order that we may understand everything according to heavenly teaching, we must resolve what creates difficulty.

What the Latin translators rendered *imperfectum*, “imperfect,” is written in Greek books as ἀκατέργαστον (*akatergaston*, “unwrought,” “unworked”). We do not complain of the translators, for I fear that they could not have expressed it otherwise. The Greek ἀκατέργαστον signifies that which remains without operation, yet exists although it has not been made. But *imperfectum* in our usage signifies something begun but not completed. Still, if we examine more deeply the force of this word, it may not in fact differ from the proper force of Greek.

It can belong to God alone to be and yet to be unmade; for that which is need not be made, and that which exists is not something that comes to be. But he who is eternal remains and has not been made. Therefore his eyes saw this “imperfect” or, to speak boldly for the advancement of understanding, “unwrought” nature of God.

[Note: The Micy manuscript reads: “not sufficiently according to the property of Greek.”]

33. “My eyes saw thine imperfect thing.” But what eyes, after all? Surely not those spiritual—or divine—eyes by which the Only-begotten alone sees God the Father? For those eyes do not require what follows: “And all shall be written in thy book; they shall be filled in the day, and none among them.” The unchangeable nature of the only-begotten God does not seek advancement. What advancement could there be for him, that all his eyes should be written in a book and filled in the day, so that none should be among them? To suppose all this is insulting and shameless.

34. The eyes of Christ’s body are apostles and priests. Against those occupied in worldly affairs.---But just as those things that were hidden were not hidden from his bone, in which the body of the Church is shown, so his eyes saw that which is God’s “imperfect thing.” We have explained above that bone refers to the Church, which is Christ’s body. Now no one doubts that the eyes hold the chief office and power in the body. Since the eyes are more excellent than the other members, there can be no doubt that the apostles are signified in them: through them the light of the Church and the mysteries of divine operation are supplied.

The Lord clearly shows this in the Gospels. Having called the apostles “salt of the earth,” “light of the world,” and the lamp of a house upon its lampstand, because of the outstanding and conspicuous works of their faith—as an illustration for comparison—he again calls them away from earthly and perishable treasures and from the gains of the world, and says that they are the eyes of the body: “The lamp of thy body is thine eye. If thine eye is single, thy whole body will be full of light; but if thine eye is evil, thy whole body will be dark. Therefore if the light that is in thee is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be!” (Matt. 6:22–23).

This passage lies beyond a bodily interpretation and must therefore be understood spiritually. Accordingly, the apostles, who are the eyes of the Church—that is, of Christ’s body—are commanded to be bright and single, so that the whole body may remain bright through those single eyes. But if they are evil, the whole body must necessarily become dark; that is, no hope of light remains in darkness if light itself is in darkness.

Hence priests, who are the eyes of the Church, incur grave danger when they are occupied with worldly business, anxiety over money, enlarging their households’ possessions, and the excesses of banquets. For they are the Church’s light, that is, the eyes of the body. And if light itself is darkened by the night of avarice and self-indulgence, how great an additional darkness will be brought upon the body—that is, the Church, which by its nature has darkness—from the example of darkened light?

These, therefore, are his eyes which saw God’s “imperfect thing.” By God’s “imperfect thing,” we have meant that which has not been made and yet remains, in which the eternity of unmade divinity is shown.

[Note: The first Paris edition with the Micy manuscript reads “eyes”; earlier editions, “eye.” We prefer “eyes” with the later edition.]

[Note: The Micy manuscript reads, perhaps: “and ministries of divine operation.”]

[Note: Here “body” is understood by the word Church as separated from the head, and especially from the eyes. Just as in our body light belongs by nature only to the eyes, while darkness belongs to the other members, so also in the Church, which otherwise, considered with its head and members, should by its own nature be called not dark but very luminous.]

35. The apostles saw the Father in the Son—not by contemplation of nature but of works.---Perhaps it seems bold to assert that the apostles saw that unbegun eternity of God the Father, especially since it has been said: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18). Yet we say nothing of ourselves and proclaim nothing boldly. Let him say it who said: “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), not thereby signifying that he himself is the Father.

For when Philip asked him to show the Father, he did not answer, “I am the Father,” but said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father.” By the power of an undiffering nature, he answered that the Father whom Philip sought was seen in him and exists in him. He then added this still more plainly: “How do you say, Show us the Father? Do you not believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself; but the Father who remains in me, he himself does his works. Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father in me; or else believe because of the works” (John 14:9 ff.).

He rebukes one who does not understand and still asks about the Father, not perceiving through the efficacy of the works the Father’s power in the Only-begotten. For the Father remains in him. He is begotten from the Father; he does not have in himself an alien nature produced by a new creation. He is Son in power, Son in divinity, Son in substance, Son in generation. The works bear witness, the powers speak: by the descent of nature the Father is in the Son, and by the substance of legitimate origin the Son is in the Father. The nobility born from the Unbegotten does not differ from him; both are one.

The Father is seen in the Son, but he is seen not by contemplation of the nature invisible to us, but through wonder at the works. For the Son’s works are the Father’s works, not because the Son is too weak to perform them, nor because his power of nature differs, but because the Son performs whatever he from whom he is begotten performs. Therefore, because the Son is contemplated in the majesty of his works, the Father also is seen in the Son.

[Note: The printed editions read “that initial”; corrected from the manuscript.]

[Note: We add *is* on the authority of the manuscript.]

[Note: Here one must add “in him.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “from the only-begotten,” a serious error corrected with the manuscript’s aid.]

[Note: The printed editions read “nor by a different power”; the manuscript more correctly reads “nor by a Son differing in the power of nature.”]

36. God’s book is eternal remembrance. It is better to be written in God’s book than in the book of the living.---For these eyes, which behold in the Son the eternity of the Father’s power—that is, for the apostles—he prays that they may be written in God’s book, that they may remain in eternal remembrance. For them he prayed in the Gospel with this prayer: “Father, I have made known thy name to the men whom thou gavest me from the world. They were thine, and thou gavest them to me, and they have kept thy word. Now they have known that all things which thou gavest me, I gave to them; and they received them and truly knew that I came forth from thee, and believed that thou sentest me. I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom thou gavest me” (John 17:6 ff.).

He therefore prays for them that they may be written in God’s book. And if anyone perhaps wonders why they are not written in the book of the living, it seems to me a greater dignity to be written in God’s book, because sinners are erased from the book of the living, while the righteous are written in God’s book (*On Psalm* 68, §24). Both points are signified by these words: “Let them be erased from the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68:29).

For because of the difference in resurrection—for star differs from star in glory (1 Cor. 15:41)—many will be in the book of the living. But the righteous will be written in God’s book, since sinners will not merely fail to be written with the righteous; they will not even remain in the book of the living.

37. For those written in God’s book, day is perpetual and without night.---But we must consider what advancement belongs to those who are written in God’s book. Surely, “they shall be filled in the day, and none among them.” In some manuscripts we read: “They shall be formed in the day.” There is not much difference between being filled and being formed. For we are formed in order to be conformed to the glory of God’s body. And the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I labour again until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). But we are filled according to the Prophet’s saying: “We shall be filled from the abundance of thy house” (Ps. 64:5).

Therefore they shall be filled in the day, that is, with the true light—for Christ is light (John 1:9): “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world.” They will no longer be held in the night of ignorance or blinded by the darkness of this world, but enlightened by truth’s light and filled with day. What has been filled receives nothing beyond that by which it is full. Night does not enter one who is filled with day, according to the Apostle’s words: “What participation has light with darkness?” (2 Cor. 6:14). Nor does the spirit of the world approach the dwelling-place of Christ’s Spirit, as it is written: “For you have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Cor. 2:12). Nor does one who has died to the world live to himself, as the Apostle teaches: “For I now live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

One who is filled with day has only day within himself; and therefore he says: “They shall be filled in the day, and none among them.” No one will be in them except the day with which they are filled: no fever of money, no spur of pleasures, no burning ambition, no malice of hatreds, no sting of envy, no fury of insults, no madness of pride, nor any other weapons and powers of the devil. Rather, there will be the true light, the day alone with which they are filled; they have now become incapable of all other things. Those who are full of day alone rightly receive this testimony.

[Note: The author of the *Commentary on the Psalms* attributed to Jerome indicates that, according to the Septuagint interpreters, the reading should be “they shall be formed in the day.” Augustine, however, has “they shall wander by day.” In Greek exemplars one now finds ἡμέρας πλασθήσονται (*hēmeras plasthēsontai*, “they shall be formed in the day”); in place of this word Hilary’s translator must have read πλησθήσονται (*plēsthēsontai*, “they shall be filled”). The translator followed by Augustine took πλασθήσονται from πλάνομαι, “to wander.”]

38. “Exceedingly,” that is, “very.” Abraham and Moses, God’s friends, are properly Christ’s disciples. Their principalities.---For it follows, verses 17–18: “But to me thy friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured; their principalities have been exceedingly strengthened. I will number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand.”

What has a human being in common with these words, that he should number those who will be multiplied beyond the sand? This belongs only to one whose knowledge of an innumerable multitude is without reckoning and calculation. His friends, then, are exceedingly honoured. When “exceedingly” is used, it must not be understood according to customary Latin usage. For *nimis*, “exceedingly,” commonly means for us that which uselessly exceeds a necessary measure; but the Greeks interpret what our translators rendered *nimis* by λίαν (*lian*), in which “very” is contained more than “exceedingly.” Therefore his friends are very highly honoured.

We know that Abraham was God’s friend. The Law says that Moses also was God’s friend. But the Gospels show that many are now God’s friends, the Lord saying: “I no longer call you servants, because the servant does not know what his master wills; but I call you friends, because you have remained with me in all my temptations” (John 15:15). Therefore those whom he now calls friends, as we showed above, he has confessed both to have been given to him by the Father and to belong to the Father; and, according to his saying, “All mine are thine, and thine are mine” (John 17:10), he calls them the Father’s friends.

Nor are they alone honoured; their principalities also are strengthened—namely, the churches begun by them and receiving their beginnings from them, churches established throughout the whole world upon the earth and standing firm by strong foundations.

[Note: The Vulgate editions read “has been strengthened.” But the manuscript, as also Augustine, reads “have been strengthened,” corresponding to the Greek and to the explanation which follows. Old Psalters of Chartres and Germany read “have been confirmed.”]

39. The number of the elect is certain. Some refer “beyond the sand” to angels.---And in order that this must be understood as referring to the peoples of the Church, he added: “I will number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand.” Is the number of those written in God’s book uncertain? Therefore there is no difficulty regarding the number of those whose reality remains in writing.

But some have thought that the statement, “They shall be multiplied beyond the sand,” should not refer to human beings alone. Since it was said to Abraham, “Thy seed shall be as the sand of the sea,” they suppose that, in the words “they shall be multiplied beyond the sand,” a multitude of angels is added to God’s friends. For they thought that “like the sand of the sea” and “beyond the sand of the sea” could agree only if an abundance of angels were numbered together with the multitude of human beings. But we do not restrict anyone’s understanding. What, however, we ourselves have understood according to the gift of spiritual grace, we shall discuss without insulting anyone.

40. He indicates that the Gentiles will believe and the Jews will fall away.---We learn from Genesis that two promises were made to Abraham. One was before Ishmael’s birth, when God said: “All the land which thou seest I will give to thee and to thy seed for ever; and I will make thy seed as the sand of the sea. If anyone can number the sand of the sea, so also shall thy seed be numbered” (Gen. 13:15–16). But after Isaac was born and, so far as Abraham was concerned, offered as a burnt offering, the following promise was made: “Unless I bless thee with blessing and multiply thy seed with multiplication as the stars of heaven and as the sand which is upon the shore of the sea” (Gen. 22:17).

And if, according to the Apostle, these are the two Testaments—one, according to Ishmael, begetting into slavery; the other, according to Isaac, leading forth into the freedom of our mother Jerusalem which is in heaven (Gal. 4:24)—then the multitude of two seeds must be proclaimed in the stars and in the sands. Therefore God’s friends are numbered beyond the sand of the sea. For who can doubt that, according to the Church numerous throughout the whole world, the multitude of the Jewish people is surpassed by the abundance of those believing in Christ? Therefore they shall be multiplied beyond the sand, because they will be more numerous than those who, as belonging to the impious people of the Law, are signified by the sand as earthly and dry.

[Note: In Bad., Er., and Lips., “before” was absent. Then in the Paris edition “Ishmael’s birth” was wrongly placed.]

41. Christ’s future resurrection is foretold as though already accomplished. — Then follows: “I have risen, and I am still with thee.” “I have risen” refers to the glory of the resurrection; but according to God’s foreknowledge, he speaks of what is future as though it were past, because for God, by reason of his knowledge and power, things future are accomplished—just as we ourselves regard as accomplished those things which we confidently expect to come. But the words, “And I am still with thee,” indicate that the time for his resurrection had not yet come, because the time of the Passion had not yet arrived, while he professes that he is still with God. For he himself says: “I came forth from God, and came” (John 16:28). “I am still with thee,” therefore, because it is not yet time “that I should come from thee, and come into the world,” in order to fulfil what has been prophesied.

[Note: Col. 0813D. Up to this point the reading had been: “that I should come before thee.” We could not refrain from restoring: “that I should come from thee,” since Hilary refers to the words, “I came forth from God”; where, because “and came” follows, he here also adds with a certain emphasis, “and I shall come into the world.”]

42. Christ kills in order to make alive. — But when he says, verse 19, “If thou wilt kill the sinner, O God,” does he who came to save what was lost and to redeem the sinner pray that the sinner may be killed? Far be it that he should wish him killed. But the sinner is killed when he dies to the world, when he dies with Christ, so that he may live in Christ. The blessed Apostle says: “I die daily” (1 Cor. 15:31). And again: “I died to the law, that I might live to Christ” (Gal. 2:19). We die in this way when sins, put to death in us through faith, die. Let us hear further how God kills sinners, through what is said: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and covetousness” (Col. 3:5). Thus the sinner is killed when, by the death of all vices and sins, he is renewed into a generation of spiritual life.

[Note: Col. 0813D. For “thus,” which belongs to the phrase “we die in this manner of death,” Lipsius had substituted “he says,” and this was subsequently retained without any authority.]

43. “Contentions” is preferable to “thou shalt say.” — There follows: “Men of blood, depart from me; because thou shalt say in thought: They shall receive their cities in vain.” The Latin translation, failing to understand the force of the expression, has introduced great obscurity, since it did not distinguish the proper meaning of an ambiguous word. For what is written among us, “Because thou shalt say in thought,” is in Greek: ὅτι ἐρεῖς εἰς διαλογισμόν, *hoti ereis eis dialogismon*, “because thou shalt say into a thought”; and the word ἐρεῖς (*ereis*) is not distinguished in pronunciation, so that it may be understood either as “thou shalt say” or as “contentions.” For both meanings are denoted by the same sound. But those who have acquired knowledge of the Hebrew language have reported that “contentions,” not “thou shalt say,” is conveyed by what has been translated ἐρεῖς. And reason and interpretation will show that this is indeed so.

[Note: Col. 0814D. In earlier printed editions the negative particle was lacking. The logic of the statements demands it so clearly that we thought ourselves permitted to add it, especially since here and subsequently we have only the Micy manuscript, preserved at Rome and not easily consulted.]

[Note: Col. 0814D. Jerome translates from the Hebrew: “who wickedly contradict thee.” Most Greeks read: “you who are contentious.” With them the Milan Psalter has: “you who are contentious in thoughts.” The Heracleotian, cited by Corderius, says that one reads, “because they are quarrelsome”; another, “who spoke a thought against thee”; another, “because they provoked thee by an evil counsel.”]

44. Men of blood: those whose teaching is flattering or deceitful. — “Men,” he says, “of blood, depart from me.” I recall that in Ezekiel bishops are said to be liable for blood when, through flattering silence, many have fallen into destruction:

> “Son of man, I have given thee as a watchman to the house of Israel; and thou shalt hear the word from my mouth, and shalt warn them. And if thou hast not warned nor spoken, so as to warn the wicked man that he should turn from his ways and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at thy hand” (Ezek. 3:17–18).

And I find another bloody man, of whom it is said: “God shall abhor the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. 5:8). Therefore, just as men of blood are those whose doctrine is flattering, so also men of blood are those whose doctrine is deceitful.

45. Heretics are men of blood. — The doctrine of heretics is deceitful: blasphemous under the name of God, impious under the pretext of religion, deceptive beneath an appearance of truth. In their mind and thought there persists only an eagerness for contention. They labour in nothing for human salvation; they gain nothing for hope; they think nothing peaceful. Thus all their labour lies in disputes, and they meditate battle. These unhappy men extinguish souls and gather churches for themselves in vain—churches which, according to prophetic and evangelical usage, are very frequently called “cities of God.” This, then, is signified by the words:

> “Men of blood, depart from me,” verse 20, “because they have contentions in thought; they shall receive their cities in vain.”

They are men of blood because they bear the guilt of souls destroyed; they are commanded to depart because contentions occupy their thoughts. They receive the cities of God in vain, rendering congregations of churches unfruitful through the divisions of schisms.

46. Pious hatred. — Yet, because peace, justice, and truth are plainly at issue, he displays his feeling toward them, saying, verses 21–22:

> “Have I not hated them that hate thee, O Lord, and pined away because of thine enemies? With perfect hatred I hated them; they became enemies to me.”

Hatred is religious whenever the man who hates God is hateful to us. We are indeed commanded to love our own enemies (Matt. 5:44), but our enemies, not also God’s. For, in relation to God, it is devout to hate father, mother, wife, children, brothers (Luke 14:26). Therefore he hates those who hate God; he wastes away with hatred of his enemies; he hates with perfect hatred; and they have become his enemies. For the Son is not different from the Father, so that one who is enemy to one should not become enemy to both.

47. These are Christ’s words. — He then concludes with the confidence of his freedom; and, at the same time, in order that he might now show in temporal manifestation the things which he had recalled as already accomplished through foreknowledge, he said, verses 23–24:

> “Prove me, O God, and know my heart; question me, and know my paths. And see whether there be a way of iniquity in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.”

This is not the confidence of human nature: to wish to be tested, to ask that one’s heart be known, to await the knowing of one’s paths, not to fear inspection lest a way of iniquity be found in oneself, and by that knowledge to be led into the everlasting way. This voice can belong only to him who said: “Behold, the prince of this world cometh, and findeth nothing in me” (John 14). For our Lord Jesus Christ alone is without sin, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

[Note: Col. 0815D. The latest Paris edition, with Bad., Er., and Lips., reads “through presence.” From the first edition and the Micy manuscript we restore “through foreknowledge,” that is, through certain knowledge of events to be done, by which, ordering all things, he foreknew them and, by foreknowing, disposed them—as Tertullian says, *Against Marcion*, book II, no. 5. There he also says of the same foreknowledge: “It has as many witnesses as it has prophets.”]

## Psalm CXXXIX

> Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; free me from the unjust man.  
> For they devised wickedness [below: “who devised wickednesses”] in their heart; all day long they prepared battles.  
> They sharpened their tongues like serpents; the venom of asps is under their lips. Diapsalma.  
> Keep me, O Lord, from the hand of the sinner; and [“and from”] unjust men deliver me, who have devised to trip up my steps.  
> The proud have hidden a snare for me, and stretched cords as a trap [“into a trap”] for my feet; they have set stumbling-blocks continuously along the paths for me. Diapsalma.  
> I said to the Lord: Thou art my God; hear [“give ear”], O Lord, the voice of my prayer.  
> O Lord, the strength of my salvation, thou hast overshadowed my head.  
> Deliver me not [below adds: “in the day of battle”] to the sinner from my desire; they have devised [“against me. Then: do not deliver without me”]; do not deliver me, O Lord, lest they ever be exalted. Diapsalma.  
> The head of their encircling band—the labour of their lips—shall cover them.  
> Coals of fire shall fall upon them, and thou shalt cast them down; they shall not stand in miseries.  
> A talkative man shall not be established upon the earth; evils shall seize the unjust man unto destruction [“in destruction”].  
> I have known that [“because”] the Lord has wrought [“will work”] judgment for the needy and vindication for the poor.  
> Nevertheless the righteous shall confess thy name, and the upright shall dwell with thy face.

## Treatise on the Psalm

1. The psalm may apply to David; or it is the prayer of the faithful. — The psalm begins in the person of a man anxious amid many assaults of enemies, against whom there are many snares and abundant deceits. All this appears capable of applying to the person of the prophet David, whose life was harassed on every side and always full of dangers. Saul pursued him in the wilderness, in cities, by war and by stratagems; his own son Absalom also pursued him, devising and daring many things against his kingdom and life. Besides, he was continually exposed to many other domestic and foreign plots. Yet the psalm contains nothing special from all these matters that would make it credible that it is a prayer peculiar to his own person. Rather, it is perhaps known to be a general psalm, proceeding from the spirit of prophecy and teaching each of us, by an example of prayer, with what prayer we ought to entreat God when we are tossed amid the hatreds of those who assail us.

2. It suits Christ more, without excluding the faithful. As man he says some things, as God others. — But as I consider more deeply certain powers and peculiarities of the words, which speak something loftier and more exalted beyond the ordinary usage of human speech, this psalm is found to require interpretation rather in reference to that man in whom the only-begotten Son of God was born of the Virgin for the sacrament of human salvation. According to the twofold nature which was in him—the nature, namely, of God and of man—he spoke not only in the Gospels but also in the Prophets with sayings fitted to each nature. Thus, while he teaches the impassible and unchangeable power of his divinity, he does not pass over the weakness of bodily nature either (see *On the Trinity*, book IX, nos. 5–6); and again, when his speech concerns weakness arising from his assumption of flesh, there immediately stands beside it the proclamation of a divinity that cannot be weakened by anything. That he is God belongs to his own nature; that he was man belongs to the assumption of our nature. Therefore in the psalm he speaks from the condition of our weakness which he assumed: when he knows his betrayer; when he foresees plans laid against him; when he endures the battles of accusations and the poisons of slanders; when he avoids the stumbling-blocks of temptations and traps of words; when he confesses to the Father; when he prays to him; when all strength belongs to him from the Father; when, though anxious from bodily weakness, he nevertheless remembers that he is not to be abandoned in the day of the Passion. We are therefore taught that all these things are contained in the psalm in his person, yet in such a way that, in those matters which fellowship in human nature permits, the prayer may in some degree also be understood as belonging to our own persons.

3. The prayer of the faithful, who entreat against occasions of sin; and of Christ, who searches hearts. — For the opening, verse 2, “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; free me from the unjust man,” also pertains to the common prayer of all believers. For every snare which spiritual wickednesses spread for us is especially contrived through human beings, and the perversity of another nature supplies occasions for our vices. The unjust man drives us into quarrels; fear of adversaries and plotters impels us into anxieties. A place which offers itself for such a purpose invites us into lust. “For the eye of a harlot is a snare of the sinner” (see Treatise on Ps. CXXIII, no. 9). Therefore, placed amid these evils, we pray, saying: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; free me from the unjust man.”

But that this is properly the Lord’s prayer is shown by what follows, when he says, verse 3: “Who devised wickednesses in their heart.” To know the thoughts of the heart does not belong to us, but to him of whom it is said: “God searches hearts and reins” (Ps. 7:10); and to him who, knowing their thoughts, said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4). By the penetrating and unhindered access of his powerful nature, he beholds every hidden intention of malicious hearts.

[Note: Col. 0817D. Earlier editions: “by impenetrable and inaccessible approaches.”]

4. The unjust man is the betrayer. Christ’s life, and that of the godly, wholly harassed by the hatreds of the ungodly. The evil are instruments of demons. — But he who prayed to be delivered from one evil and unjust man, in whom he is understood to signify his betrayer, now speaks of many who devise evil in their hearts:

> “Who devised wickednesses in their heart; all day long they prepared battles. They sharpened their tongues like serpents; the venom of asps is under their lips,” verse 4.

There was not warfare with arms against David throughout every whole day, nor were battles continually arrayed. But against the Lord, according to the evangelical narratives concerning his deeds, we find no time free from the hatred of persecutors. He heals a paralytic (Matt. 9:3): immediately poisonous mouths argue that he grants forgiveness of sins unlawfully, as they suppose. He restores a withered hand (Matt. 12:10): at once he is charged with violating the law. He heals demoniacs (Luke 11:15): immediately he is accused of doing this through Beelzebul, prince of demons. Nothing exists for him that is not continually full of snares, nothing that is not exposed to the venom of a viper’s tongue.

The life of all of us also—and especially of those devoted to religion—endures the wars of hostile powers and receives the poisoned darts of slander. Whom does the venom of fraudulent flattery not attack? And all these things arise through human beings in whom spiritual wickednesses operate. For it is written: “The Lord raised up Satan against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite” (3 Kings 2:14). Hadad opposed Solomon not as a man, but as Satan, throughout all the days of his life. Hadad was raised up by God as a Satan against Solomon because Solomon deserved it; but through persons of this kind the manifold hatreds of those who assail us rage against us, and hostile powers pursue their attacks through their ministry.

[Note: Col. 0818D. In the Micy manuscript: “his works”; a reading not to be despised.]

5. Above the complaint concerned words; now it concerns deeds. — The insertion of the diapsalma appears to have brought either a change of person or a change of sense. The same prayer is repeated, but in such a way that the matters previously added in a confused form are now recounted more fully, and the complaint which above concerned words now concerns deeds:

> “Keep me, O Lord, from the hand of the sinner, and deliver me from unjust men, who have devised to trip up my steps,” verse 5.

The prayer, having begun with one person, is transferred to many, in order to signify that in the one the betrayer and in the many the people may be recognized. To the one man, both here and above, he attributes malice, sin, and injustice; but in the many he censures contemplated tripping-up, hidden snares, stretched cords for capture, and stumbling-blocks set continuously along the paths, saying:

6. Plans to trip up Christ. Snares hidden for him. Cords stretched into a trap for him. — “Who have devised to trip up my steps. The proud have hidden a snare for me, and stretched cords as a trap for my feet; they have set stumbling-blocks continuously along the paths for me,” verse 6. The rulers of the synagogue devised to trip up his steps when, after Lazarus had been raised from death, they planned to kill him (John 12:10); when they reviled the man blind from birth because his eyes had been opened (John 9:28); when they determined that men should be silent concerning him; when they threatened death to his confessors (ibid. 22). Thus they devised to trip up the distinguished course and progress of his divine works.

The proud hid snares when the Sadducees concealed the fraud of their feigned question about the resurrection (Matt. 22:23), when they held out a snare for an answer through crafty speech (ibid. 15). They were proud when they disdained to associate with sinners, when they reproached him—the forgiver of sins—for the banquets of tax collectors (Matt. 9:11). They also stretched cords as a trap for his feet when tribute was demanded, when he was questioned about giving tribute to Caesar (Matt. 22:17). The snare above was hidden, but now cords are stretched into a snare, so that the trap of questioning might be recognized as stronger in the cords: through the extended snare of their question they sought from him an answer that could be treacherously alleged against the name of Caesar.

[Note: Col. 0819D. First Paris edition and Micy manuscript: “of one continuing.”]

They set stumbling-blocks continuously along his paths when he was questioned about the commandments of the law; when the rich man, supposedly satisfying the law, asks what he still lacks (Luke 18:18); when the condition of divorce is discussed with him. For they set these stumbling-blocks of questioning continuously along the path of his teaching and law, so that, under the appearance and familiarity of questions written in the law, the paths of those continually questioning him might everywhere set before him stumbling-blocks of questions and answers.

[Note: Col. 0819D. Micy manuscript: “along the path of his teaching and law.”]

7. Snares are prepared for us everywhere. The necessity of prayer. — We also know and remember that everywhere in our life cords, stumbling-blocks, and snares confront us, and that there is nowhere where traps are not continually spread before us. It is now difficult to free the belly from the snare, because confusion belongs to those whose god is their belly (Phil. 3:19). It is likewise rare now to free the eye from the snare, because whoever looks with lust has already committed adultery in his heart (Matt. 5:28). It is also arduous to remove the tongue from the snare, because an account will be given on the day of judgment for every idle word (Matt. 12:36). It is an exceedingly great labour, too, to withdraw the heart from the snare, for evil thoughts come forth from the heart (Matt. 15:19). These snares are spread everywhere for all of us; and the Lord must be entreated that, by the wings of faith and the Spirit, we may fly away from all these snares.

8. Here the prayer changes. It is for saints to say, “Thou art my God.” — Then follow verses 7–9:

> “I said to the Lord: Thou art my God; give ear, O Lord, to the voice of my prayer. O Lord, the strength of my salvation, thou hast overshadowed my head in the day of battle. Deliver me not, O Lord, to the sinner from my desire; they have devised against me. Do not deliver me, O Lord, lest they ever be exalted.”

Here too the intervening diapsalma appears to have introduced some change, and indeed no slight one. For whereas above all the speech had concerned conceived tripping-up, hidden snares, stretched traps, and set stumbling-blocks, now the prayer is directed to God: “I said to the Lord: Thou art my God.” It is not a light or insignificant confidence to have said to the Lord: “Thou art my God.” The lustful, avaricious, insolent, drunken mind cannot say this faithfully. All these things must be renounced, and one must cease from their slavery and service, so that, having ceased from them, we may dare to say: “I said to the Lord: Thou art my God.” These words are fitted to our own person, insofar as we may properly mingle it with the psalm.

9. It is also proper to the Son of God. — But it is also customary, frequent, and proper for the Lord, as we have said, to say: “I said to the Lord: Thou art my God.” He never refused the honour of this confession (see *On the Trinity*, book XI, no. 10 and following), confessing both Lord and God when he said: “I confess to thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11:25); and again: “To my God and your God” (John 20:17). His whole prayer, too, was always directed to God. When he is about to raise Lazarus, he prays (John 11:41); when about to bless the loaves and fishes, he prays by lifting his eyes to heaven (Matt. 14:19); when about to drink the cup, he prays through the night. Therefore after the confession of his Lord and God follows: “Give ear, O Lord, to the voice of my prayer.” The confession of honour has preceded, when he calls him his Lord and God. Then follows the request that his prayer be heard, when he prays that he himself may be heard.

10. It belongs to us to pray for the salvation of our strength; to Christ, for the strength of his salvation. — But in what follows, “O Lord, the strength of my salvation,” the confession is not one of ordinary confidence. For he does not say: “The salvation of my strength.” It belongs to human desire to pray for salvation for our strength, that God may give health to those capacities in which we are strong. But this prayer is the opposite: not that salvation may belong to his strength, but that strength may belong to his salvation from God. He who prays for strength for salvation no longer doubts salvation, and is certain that there is nothing perishable or mortal in himself.

But he prays through the body which the Lord bore in himself that strength may be granted to that which he assumed, being weak. Though it was subject to death in the same manner as ourselves, it was nevertheless not liable to corruption, as he himself speaks through the Prophet: “For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, nor wilt thou give thy Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10).

[Note: Col. 0820D. Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions: “but also that which he assumed.”]

[Note: Col. 0820D. That is, it had to die after our likeness. The preposition *secundum*, “according to,” has the same force above, p. 455b.]

11. Why Christ has supreme confidence along with the condition of fear. — Therefore he is not uncertain about the salvation of this nature, weak though it is in itself. He asks from God only strength for the salvation that is in him; and he asks it with the confidence by which he says: “Thou hast overshadowed my head in the day of battle.” If this whole psalm belongs to the person of every human being, how can such contrary things agree in him? For, after it has been said, “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man,” and “Keep me, O Lord, from the hand of the sinner,” he now says again, secure in every respect: “Thou hast overshadowed my head in the day of battle.” And whereas above the prayer arose from fear, now there is rejoicing from security.

But all this can reasonably be said by him who, bearing the nature both of man and of God, had both the feeling of fear from human weakness and the confidence of security from consciousness of divinity. He knows that, on that day of glorious battle in which he will destroy death, conquer the devil, and nail every hostile power to the triumph of his cross, he will be overshadowed and protected. For since it had previously been said of him in the person of God the Father, “I am with him in tribulation” (Ps. 90:15), and again, “For my hand shall aid him, and my arm shall strengthen him; the enemy shall profit nothing against him, and the son of iniquity shall not add to harm him” (Ps. 88:22–23), what did the enemy gain by inspiring Judas with the purpose of betrayal? The body was indeed surrendered to the Passion, but death, though permitted to act upon it, did not gain dominion over it: for the Holy One did not see corruption. And when the son of iniquity betrayed him, what did he add in order to harm him? Not only did the body return from death to life, but, the nature of corruption having been swallowed up, it also hastened into the glory of divinity.

[Note: Col. 0821D. The printed editions: “but of the body surrendered to it”; we suspect an interpolation and correct it from the manuscript.]

12. Obedient to the Father, he nevertheless has a will. He desires that what was foretold concerning his Passion be fulfilled and hindered in nothing. — Secure and confident that he is overshadowed in the day of battle, he also prays this: “Deliver me not, O Lord, to the sinner from my desire.” He who says, “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38), hastens to fulfil the work undertaken even in the service of obedience; yet we must remember that in him there is the function of will.

[Note: Col. 0821D. Not so that he should be without freedom of will and weakness of nature should impose necessity upon him, as is discussed at length in *On the Trinity*, book IX, nos. 48–49.]

For he wills what the Father willed. What he says, “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me,” shows him to obey the one by whom he was sent; nevertheless, it does not deprive him of will. Therefore he desires to accomplish everything pleasing to the Father and hastens to carry out everything desirable to himself in his Passion, lest the sinner, intervening beforehand, hinder anything of these things.

He “earnestly desired” to eat the Passover with the disciples (Luke 22:15), and hastened to celebrate the supper of the Passover. He desired to drink the cup of the Passion, saying: “The cup which my Father has given me, shall I not drink it?” (John 18:11). When those who had come to seize him sought him and asked who Jesus was, he presented himself to them unbidden (ibid. 4). He knew that he was to drink the cup of vinegar and asked for it in order to drink it. Receiving the great fruit of his own will when he had drunk it, he said: “It is accomplished” (John 19:30); in that word is contained rejoicing at the fulfilment of a desired prayer.

He had frequently prayed in the psalms that his soul might be delivered from the sword (Ps. 21:21); he had signified that no bone was to be broken (Exod. 12:46); he had declared that lots would be cast for his garment (Ps. 21:19). He prays that all these things which belong to his desire may be fulfilled for the truth of prophecy: lest the sinner have any power concerning them; lest he hinder the Passover which is earnestly desired; lest he not dare to offer the cup of the Passion—for at the Lord’s first answer every sinner who came to seize him fell down; lest the vinegar which was to be drunk not be ready; lest, before he gives up the spirit, a soldier pierce his side with a spear; lest, while the spirit still remains, an opportunity be available to break a bone; lest anything of the prophecy fail; lest anything of his desires be delivered to the sinner. Rather, may all things which were both desired by him and prophesied be fulfilled in him. He prays about these things, not because they were not going to be fulfilled, but that they may be understood to have been prophesied concerning him.

[Note: Col. 0821D. From the manuscript we restore *pascham*, “the Passover,” for *pascha*, especially since *quae*, not *quod*, follows. We also think *praepediat*, “hinder,” should be read, not *praeveniat*, “forestall.”]

[Note: Col. 0821D. Printed editions: “give up”; corrected from the manuscript.]

13. His enemies fell short of their designs. — “They devised,” he says, “against me; do not abandon me, lest they ever be exalted.” Many things were devised against him, but especially this: that money having been given to the soldiers, they should spread abroad the report that the body had been stolen by them. But when he again stood present in that body, this scheme of impious thought was futile. No opportunity was left to sinners for exalting themselves: prophecy is fulfilled. Their life hangs upon the wood; he is given vinegar and gall to drink; his soul is delivered from the sword; no bone is broken; lots are cast over his garment. Nothing of the desires of the only-begotten Son of God is delivered to the sinner. On the third day he rises; he is not left in hell, nor does the Holy One see corruption. And all things done in the Lord possess both a wonderful efficacy in present events and the unchangeable truth of prophecy, for the confounding and overthrow of impious designs.

14. Their punishment. The encircling band against Christ. — Then follows, verses 10–11:

> “The head of their encircling band, the labour of their lips, shall cover them. Coals of fire shall fall upon them, and thou shalt cast them down; they shall not stand in miseries.”

After the preceding discourse, in which the entire prayer concerning himself had been addressed to God, he now changes the order of thought also through the intervention of the diapsalma. For he turns to the most just punishment of sinners: first, the very head of their assembly; then the labour of their lips and every work of cursing shall cover them. For just as Christ is head of all saints, so the devil is head of all the wicked. The Lord frequently testifies to these encircling bands of the ungodly around himself when he says: “The sorrows of death surrounded me” (Ps. 18:5); and again: “Fat bulls besieged me” (Ps. 21:13); and again: “Surrounding, they surrounded me” (Ps. 117:11); and immediately: “They surrounded me like bees” (ibid. 12).

That these things occurred with the devil as leader is testified by the Gospels when they say: “And the devil put it into the heart of Judas to betray him” (John 13:2). The people laboured with much shouting when they cried: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:21). Therefore the head of their encircling band and the labour of their lips shall cover them, so that, while others are clothed with the glory of immortality, they may be covered with the shame of their impiety and the condemnation of the devil. And what that condemnation was by which they would be covered, he added: “Coals of fire shall fall upon them; thou shalt cast them down upon the earth; they shall not stand in miseries.” These are the coverings of the ungodly; this is the eternal garment of the irreligious: that, unable to stand against falling coals and impending miseries, they may be pressed down under such a burden of condemnation with the very head of their encircling band and the labour of their lips.

[Note: Col. 0822D. Thus Paris and the Micy manuscript, supported by the very ancient German Psalter, except that it has “and he shall cast them down.” Jerome likewise translates from the Hebrew, omitting “and.” Bad. and Er.: “thou shalt cast them down into fire.” Lips.: “thou shalt cast them down into the fire.” The Greek text is: ἄνθρακες πυρὸς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, καὶ καταβαλεῖς αὐτούς, “coals of fire upon the earth, and thou shalt cast them down”; accordingly Augustine has: “coals of fire upon the earth, and thou shalt cast them down.” Hilary below agrees with the same reading.]

[Note: Col. 0822D. The printed editions omit “himself.” It is supplied from the Micy manuscript.]

[Note: Col. 0822D. The printed editions omit “these.” Then Paris after Lipsius has “of the ungodly,” against the evidence of the other books.]

15. The wickedness of Judas the betrayer. — He has maintained even now the order used above: while he shows the people in the many, he now appears to signify Judas in the one, saying, verse 12: “A talkative man shall not be established upon the earth; evils shall seize the unjust man unto destruction.” In the talkative man is shown the equivocal, dubious, and deceitful mouth of the betrayer. When he discovered too late the wickedness of his crime, he hanged himself with a noose, fleeing from life and faith. Nothing in him was upright, nothing simple, nothing whole: first a thief, then a betrayer, finally his own worthy avenger (Job 12:4); now accusing the woman who poured ointment on the Lord’s head of useless waste, now reporting to the Jews all the Lord’s entrances and departures, now bargaining for the price of righteous blood (Matt. 26:15). Ever talkative, ever engaged in words, so that the prophet’s saying may fittingly be applied to him: “In much speaking thou shalt not escape sin” (Prov. 10:19). Therefore, as a sinner in his excessive speech, he was not set upright into life, nor did he hold the straight way of faith; but, as was fitting, evils seized him in destruction. Having been impious toward God, he afterward remained impious even toward himself: a thief of money, seller of righteous blood, betrayer of God, and—so far as lay in him—a parricide. He could obtain neither pardon of life nor pardon of death.

16. Christ’s poverty. Vindication does not properly suit Christ, but his servants. — Therefore the only-begotten God is not ignorant of this vindication of his own, for he says, verse 13: “I have known that the Lord will perform judgment for the needy and vindication for the poor.” The Lord is poor according to his humanity. For according to the Apostle he made himself poor, that we might become rich; in the things of this world he had nothing but a body (2 Cor. 8:9). For the sake of this salvation he chose to be born poor from a virgin; the Lord did not choose money, a field, or the livestock of heaven. Thus he was poor only in his humanity; yet the Lord will perform not only judgment for the needy, but also vindication for the poor.

Judgment for the needy must be referred to the condemnation of those who were unjust toward the Lord. For it is fitting that they be judged according to judgment, not according to vindication. It belongs to an inferior nature to require vindication. The other poor are vindicated—that is, those who followed the Lord by the example of his Passion, those who were poor through contempt for the world and money. Judgment for the needy therefore occurs when, on account of the Lord’s Passion, the ungodly are judged. But the poor are vindicated: those whose blood, slain beneath the altar, cries out and asks vindication upon the ungodly (Rev. 6:9), who, continuing daily in the glory of martyrdom, confess the name of God.

[Note: Col. 0823D. Micy manuscript: “which ought to be vindicated.”]

17. The very statement with which the psalm closes speaks thus, verse 14: “Nevertheless the righteous shall confess thy name, and the upright shall dwell with thy face.” The confession of the righteous may also appear bodily, because many, though still placed in the flesh, confess the name of God. But the upright who dwell with the face of God are understood to retain nothing bodily in themselves. For the nature of flesh does not endure the sight of God, he himself saying: “No man shall see my face and live” (Exod. 33:20). This belongs now to those who are heavenly, transformed, and exchanging earthly corruption for heavenly incorruption. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself will deliver them, already glorious in the honour of divinity and destined to reign with God the Father, into the kingdom; he is blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

[Note: Col. 0823D. That is, it may be referred to those who still dwell in the earthly body—frail, weak, corruptible, and not yet renewed through the glorious resurrection. From this it is understood what follows: those who dwell with the face of God ought to retain nothing bodily in themselves.]

[Note: Col. 0824D. The printed editions: “to God himself.” With the Micy manuscript we prefer “he himself,” namely the Lord.]

## Psalm CXL

[Col. 0824B]

Lord, I have cried to you: hear me; give heed to the voice of my prayer when I cry to you. *(Below: while I cry.)* Let my prayer be directed like incense before you. *(Prefaced here: Lord.)* The lifting up *(alleviation)* of my hands is an evening sacrifice. Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of enclosure upon my lips. Do not incline my heart to evil words *(of malice)*, to devising excuses for sins, together with men who work iniquity; and I will not join company with their chosen ones. The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat. For still *(and)* my prayer is among their things pleasing to them; their judges, joined to the Rock, have been swallowed up. [Col. 0824C] My words shall be heard *(will hear)*, because they prevailed: as the richness of earth has burst forth upon the ground. Our bones have been scattered beside hell; for my eyes are toward you, O Lord; in you have I hoped: do not take away my soul. Keep me from the snare which they have laid for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity. Sinners shall fall into his net: I am alone until I pass over.

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. **Prayer, though silent, cries out through faith.**—The faithful prayer of all saints is a cry to God; for one cries to him by faith, not by the loudness of one’s voice (Ps. CXVIII, §§1–2). Moses stood sorrowfully on the shore while the king of Egypt pressed upon him; yet, although he was silent, the Lord heard the faithful prayer of his exalted mind, saying: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV, 15). The blood of the martyrs likewise has no bodily voice; yet the outrage of their death is a cry to God, as the Lord himself said concerning Abel to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me” (Gen. IV, 10). Thus too the souls of the martyrs beneath God’s altar are written to cry aloud, saying: “How long, holy and true Lord, do you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell upon the earth?” (Apoc. VI, 10).

If, therefore, we pray in the spirit of faith—not lowly, earthly, or bodily things—our prayer, though silent, is a cry to God. Therefore the Prophet, [Col. 0825A] wholly intent upon God in the spirit of prayer, began thus, V. 1: “Lord, I have cried to you: hear me.” And, to teach that this cry was one of faith rather than voice, he added: “Give heed to the voice of my prayer, while I cry to you.” Even against our will, a cry penetrates the hearing and, by the force of its utterance, thrusts itself of its own accord into our ears. But because the Prophet does not cry with such a cry, he prays that, while he cries, God may give heed to the voice of his prayer. For in that to which attention is given lies the inspection of faith, not the hearing of a cry. That which is inward is attended to; whereas there is no need for bodily crying to receive attention, since of itself it occupies every faculty of hearing.

[Note: Thus the manuscript; but Bad. has “intent upon God in spirit,” and then, with Er. and Lips., “upon prayer.” Then in Par. *intent* is lacking.]

[Col. 0825B] 2. **Pure prayer. The nature and composition of incense. It signifies either four kinds of prayer, or a sacrifice of praise offered to God from the four elements.**—There follows, V. 2: “Lord, let my prayer be directed like incense before you.” Those whose prayer is pure, upright, and sincere may say, “Let my prayer be directed”; but if it is corrupted by the intrusion of external thoughts, it will not be directed. Yet when he says, “Let it be directed like incense,” we must understand the meaning of the proposed comparison with incense.

First, the nature of incense is such that it rises from low places to on high, gives forth an excellent fragrance, and communicates to our senses the perception of sweetness. Hence it is composed from four most fragrant substances, ground into the finest powder: stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense. That all these were constituted as a figure of the prayers of the faithful is shown by the Apocalypse of blessed John, when he says: “And the twenty-four elders indeed fell down before the Lamb, each having a harp and golden bowls full of perfumes, which *(or: which things)* are the prayers of the saints.”

The Apostle indicates that there are four kinds of prayer when he writes to Timothy:

[Note: The printed editions, except Par., have “I beseech therefore.” In Par., from the Mic. manuscript, “I exhort therefore” has been restored. We should prefer “I exhort,” in accordance with the Greek, παρακαλῶ.]

“I exhort, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings be made” (I Tim. II, 1). Supplication belongs to our lowliness; prayer, to the magnificence of God; petition, to faith; thanksgiving, to confession and praise. Perhaps those four kinds of perfumes, compounded from their finest parts into one incense-offering, may also be fitted individually to the four kinds required for perfect prayer.

Although the nature and appearance of these four perfumes seem to signify the form of the four elements: frankincense, which is translucent, being compared to spirit; stacte, to waters; galbanum and onycha, to earth and fire. Thus through them a prayer of praise may be offered to God like incense on behalf of all things that are in heaven, beneath heaven, on earth, and in the waters. But let us leave these matters to those who delight in the knowledge of deeper learning. For us, the prophetic and apostolic authority is sufficient: it indicates both that incense is prayer, and that prayers are to be directed like incense.

[Col. 0826A] 3. **The difference between lifting and stretching out the hands.**—But he who prayed that his prayer might be directed like incense also says afterwards: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.” In many places (On Ps. LXII, §7) we have treated of how the lifting up of hands signifies the service of exalted work: thus Moses was commanded to stand with uplifted hands, while the people were victorious or defeated according as his hands were lifted or lowered. The Apostle likewise commands those who pray to lift up pure hands (I Tim. II, 8). And when he says, “without anger and disputing” (ibid.), he does not prescribe an outward posture of prayer, but adds a rule of divine action.

Finally, the Lord, through the prophet Isaiah (Isa. I, 15), rejecting the prayers of the ungodly, spoke thus: “If you stretch out your hands, I will turn away my eyes from you”—not, surely, if you lift up your hands, but if you stretch them out. For the posture of prayer consists in stretching forth the hands; the accomplishment of perfect work consists in lifting them up.

[Col. 0826B] 4. **What the evening sacrifice is.**—The lifting up of hands, then, is the evening sacrifice. For we, upon whom the consummation of the ages has come, do not sacrifice to God by blood and burnt offerings. But let us hear what evening sacrifice is pleasing, as the Lord says in the Gospels: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you received me; I was sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you set me free” (Matt. XXV, 34 ff.). And when they answered that he had never lacked these offices of human necessity, he said: “Amen, I say to you: so long as you did it [Col. 0826C] to one of these least brothers, you did it to me” (ibid., 40).

This is the evening sacrifice—that is, the sacrifice of the last times. In this sacrifice the hands must be lifted up, because by prayers of this kind the possession of the heavenly kingdom has been prepared, from the beginning of the world, for those blessed by God.

5. **Slips of the tongue and their remedies.**—But the Prophet remembers that, beyond the cry of faith, beyond the prayer which must be directed like incense, and beyond the lifting up of hands in which lies the evening sacrifice, he has still another work to desire for the completion of righteousness within himself. Remembering, of course, that evangelical saying, “By your words you will be justified, or by your words you will be condemned” (Matt. XII, 37), and recalling also that he will render an account on the day of judgment for every idle word (ibid., 36), he necessarily prayed, saying, [Col. 0826D] V. 3: “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of enclosure upon my lips.”

He does not pray that a slight guard may be set upon his mouth, but a door of enclosure: that this guard may not be merely some watchfulness, but a barrier. For the tongue’s fall is dangerous and exceedingly ready; from it curse, falsehood, perjury, slander issue forth with easy motion and open access. Let us therefore pray for a door of enclosure for ourselves.

For in that book which among us is entitled *Solomon’s*, but among Greeks and Hebrews is regarded as the *Wisdom of Sirach*, [Col. 0827A] we are admonished thus: “Behold, surround your possession with thorns; secure your silver and gold; and make for your mouth a door and bolt, and for your words a yoke and measure” (Ecclus. XXVIII, 28–29). He commanded both a door and a bolt to be placed upon the mouth, lest words should have an easy exit. He also imposed a yoke and measure upon words, so that, subjected to the yoke of reason, they might be weighed by the balance of moderation.

[Note: That is, among the Latins. This title frequently occurs in Cyprian, for example *To Quirinus*, book III, §§95, 96, 100, etc. The same book is called “divine Scripture” by the same writer in *On Mortality*. Pamelius, in his note 2 on Cyprian’s book II *To Quirinus*, lists ancient writers who ascribe the same book to Solomon and attribute divine authority to it.]

6. **A perverse heart that seeks excuses for sins, especially in heresy.**—The Prophet still strives toward the perfection of righteousness. For after the cry of faith, prayer, works, and the door of the mouth, he prays that he may be made complete also in the office of the heart, saying, V. 4: “Do not incline my heart to evil words, to devising excuses for sins, together with men who work [Col. 0827B] iniquity.” When we fall from the pursuit of innocence and righteousness into a vicious will, then our heart inclines to evil words—not that we may excuse sin, for every sin is inexcusable, but that we may excuse excuses.

For the crime of murder, adultery, and other such deeds is inexcusable by the nature and enormity of the act. But one caught in such a deed will not say, “Adultery or murder is no crime.” Rather, he will say: “An importunate, uncontrolled, seductive woman enticed me and compelled me to pleasure.” Another will say: “He provoked my anger with insults, armed my grief with injuries; the accident of a quarrel brought about the killing.” After one has sinned, the heart inclines to such words, so that by excuses for the sin it may excuse itself for what it has committed.

[Note: The printed editions read “will”; corrected from the manuscript.]

[Note: Thus the printed editions except Par., where there appears: “that by excuse for sin,” after which *itself* is omitted. “That it may excuse excuses for sin,” without *itself*, would not be displeasing.]

But an upright and [Col. 0827C] pure heart does not incline to these words of excuse. It remains uninjured and steadfast, without the anxious search for words by which excuses may be devised; since the innocence of its life has no need of an excuse for sin. These things are indeed so in bodily matters. Yet in matters considered spiritual—that is, in the teaching of heresy—it is incredible with what labor of heart and searching of words heretics excuse their excuses. The righteous man prays that his heart may not incline to all these things, lest through this necessity of an inclined heart to devise excuses he should join company with their chosen ones.

7. **The number two has an evil connotation.**—“And I will not join company,” he says, “with their chosen ones.” The Prophet does not wish to join company with the chosen ones of the wicked. For he remembers that this number was assigned to unclean things when the command was given to Noah concerning the animals to be shut up in the ark (Gen. VII, 2): “But of clean cattle you shall bring in to yourself seven and seven, and of unclean cattle two and two.” There is also a greater and more complete illustration of the uselessness of this number.

[Note: Bad., Er., and Lips. read *combinabor*, “I shall be joined,” supported by Hilary’s explanation below. Yet in Par., from the Mic. manuscript, *combinabo*, “I will join,” has not wrongly been restored. For this is the reading in Augustine and in the old German Psalter, supported by most Greek manuscripts, which write συνδυάσω, “I will join,” where others prefer συνδιάσω, “I will have fellowship.” Hilary, however, assigns a passive force to the word.]

For our Lord Jesus Christ, taking away all our uncleannesses and sins, “made both one,” according to the Apostle (Eph. II, 14); and, according to the same Apostle, “that he might create the two in himself [Col. 0828A] into one new man, making peace, that he might reconcile both to God in one body,” he made the inner and outer human being one (ibid., 15). We therefore are not paired, but made one; for unity belongs to faith, whereas pairing [Col. 0828B] is partnership in faction.

[Note: We restore the particle *in*, omitted hitherto, on the authority of the manuscript and the apostolic text. Moreover, Hilary understands the outer human being as the body and the inner as the soul in Ps. CXVIII, §§6–7, and Ps. CXXIX, §6.]

8. **Mercy should be exercised toward offenders, but justly.**—The Prophet not only does not wish to join company with the chosen ones of the wicked; but also, because it is due to humanity to err, if perhaps he should do anything amiss through human weakness, he prefers to be corrected and rebuked by a righteous person in mercy. In himself he sets forth the pattern of our nature and frailty. For many of us, when we have fallen or gone astray, disdain to be corrected by the rebuke of just mercy; and they prefer to join company with sinners rather than be turned toward repentance by the correction of the righteous.

[Note: Who these are is explained by the common Jerome on the same verse: “As the Lord has chosen saints, so the devil too has his chosen ones.”]

[Note: Here “it is due to humanity to err” is said in the same way as above in Ps. CXXX, §15: “These things are due to our weakness and body: to die, to be sick, to be in need.” It refers to fallen humanity.]

The prophetic utterance admirably maintained the principle of truth, saying, V. 5: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me.” For there is a measure of mercy, and justice must be applied in showing mercy. [Col. 0828C]

[Note: Thus the manuscript and the first Paris edition; it ought not to have been altered in the last edition to the reading falsely found in Bad., Er., and Lips.: “Alas, what can there be toward those,” etc. We have only just heard Hilary argue against the impious doctrine of the Novatians, for example in Ps. CXXXVII, §7, so that one cannot even suspect that he intended here to support them.]

There may indeed be grief concerning those whose crimes are grievous, but there is no place for mercy. For mercy turns itself toward asking God for forgiveness for what has been done; whereas granting pardon to unlawful deeds is not to exercise mercy, but to fail to preserve the justice of mercy. The Apostle John most carefully preserved this principle when he said: “If anyone knows his brother to sin, but not unto death, let him ask, and God will give him life. There is sin unto death; but I do not speak concerning that” (I John V, 16).

Blessed Paul teaches that the righteous ought to correct and rebuke in mercy one who has fallen, saying: “Brothers, even if a person has been overtaken in some fault, you who are [Col. 0829A] spiritual, restore him in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. V, 1). But he too did not forget the principle of just mercy; for he commands that a person overtaken in a fault, not one sinning deliberately, be restored through rebuke.

[Note: That is, one whose will is so hardened in sin that, though he knows it is sin, he refuses to depart from it; or, as Hilary himself explains in Ps. CXLIV, §19: one who persists in sin by will, whom habitual vice delights, who does not repent of what he has committed. Hence, when he says in Ps. CXXXV, §4, “Outside forgiveness is the one who has known sin and does not confess what he has known,” he seems here to use “confess” in the sense of “repent,” and thus to deny forgiveness only to the unrepentant. For the phrase “does not confess what he has known” may be understood from “who does not repent of what he has committed.” Indeed, when in Ps. CXXXV, §4, and CXXXVII, §3, he says, “Confession is a profession of ceasing,” and again in Ps. CXLIV, §18, “Repentance is the author of ceasing,” he sufficiently indicates that he often means the same thing by the terms repentance and confession. Therefore, since in Hilary those who sin deliberately are contrasted with the repentant—because in the latter the disposition is involuntary—whom should we understand by those sinning deliberately but the unrepentant?
