Denying forgiveness to these, he grants it to the rest in Ps. CXLIV, §19: “For there is with God the consolation of forgiveness: to have repented of one’s deeds; nor is it unworthy of the moderation of severity when, through grief for the act committed, one thus professes an unwilling disposition.” Although in many places he seems to teach that forgiveness is to be granted only to those who have fallen through error, weakness of the flesh, or the temptation of the devil, but denied to those who have sinned knowingly and willingly. This is the tenor of that passage in book VI *On the Trinity*, §45, addressed to certain notable Arians, whom, as he says, “the will of irreligion fixed in heresy”: “All avenues to salvation are now closed to you, who deny what you can no longer be ignorant of. For you do not fail to know that there is [Col. 0830C] a Son of God,” etc. See similar passages there, §1, and elsewhere.]

Therefore, when the Prophet says, “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me,” mindful both of his faith and of human frailty, he says that he is to be corrected in those matters which deserve the rebuke of just mercy.

9. **As correction, so also teaching is to be sought from a holy man.**—He further prays for another thing: namely, that he may not be imbued with the teachings of sinners, nor fall even as far as the mercy of those who sin: “But let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat.” He wishes the one who teaches and rebukes us to be of pure conscience.

[Note: In the printed editions: “even to the practice of sin through mercy,” an interpolated reading. The reading we give from the manuscript is more authentic. It should further be observed that in certain Psalters, for example the German, “But the mercy of the sinner” occurs in place of “But the oil of the sinner,” evidently because the translator read ἔλεος, “mercy,” for ἔλαιον, “oil.” Hilary, however, embraces both translations and supplies an interpretation suited to each, as is clear not only from the opening but also from the closing words of this section.]

[Col. 0829B] The Lord in the Gospels, speaking of the purity of fasting, said: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face” (Matt. VI, 17). In washing the face, he required the brightness of a pure conscience, lest anything dirty or stained should cling to us; in anointing the head, he commanded that we be perfected by the teachings and works of spiritual instruction. For oil is nourishment for light, and teaching and spiritual work are the cause for us of heavenly glory. As light derives its source from oil, so teaching and action enable us to retain the light of spiritual glory, so that our head—the seat, that is, of life, prudence, and all the senses—may be made rich by the oil of action and teaching.

But this oil must not be received from a sinner; and God must be prayed to, that he may not pour in this oil of sinners. For just as it is prudent to wish to be rebuked by a holy and faithful man, since for diseased minds and those weakened by the sickness of sin, the medicine of stern rebuke under a reputable author is useful; so it is miserable, through compassion for sin, to have fallen as far as compassion for sinners themselves. The Prophet therefore rejects both of these things in his own case.

10. **One remains in sins because they are pleasing.**—There follows: “For still my prayer is among their things pleasing to them; [Col. 0830A] their judges, joined to the Rock, have been swallowed up.” He gives as the reason why those joined to the Rock are swallowed up that his prayer is still among their things pleasing to them. The Prophet prays, as in the preceding words, that the oil of the sinner may not make his head fat. This is what the Prophet prays. But sinners are not frightened even by this prayer of the Prophet into desisting from what pleases them. For no one persists in sins except because he delights in them; and the pleasure of enjoyment supplies the reason for remaining in each matter.

[Note: In the manuscript: “the same.”]

Therefore, because even while he prays they remain in their things pleasing to them—that is, because what they are is not changed, through their continuing will to sin, and they persist in being sinners—his prayer does not come to an end. For his prayer is among their things pleasing to them as long as it pleases them to sin.

[Note: Thus the manuscript and first Paris edition. The other editions read “who.” Thus below we have restored “because still,” where “who still” had prevailed.]

11. **The wicked are to be swallowed up at Christ’s coming.**—For this reason their judges, joined to the Rock, have been swallowed up. We know no Rock except Christ, because it was said of him: “And the Rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). When he comes, when these chosen ones of sinners and their judges join themselves to him, they are swallowed up. For then death, corruption, and sin will be swallowed up, as it is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory. Where is your sting? Where is your victory? For the sting of death is sin” (I Cor. XV, 54–55).

[Note: Thus the manuscript. The printed editions read: “when these will be joined to him . . .”]

But their judges, joined to the Rock, are swallowed up together with their prince, concerning whom it was said: “And then that wicked one shall be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the spirit of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation [Col. 0830C] of his coming” (II Thess. II, 8). Therefore, through this manifestation of the Lord’s coming, those who are swallowed up shall be destroyed—and swallowed up by the judgment of the saints. For it follows: “They shall hear my words, because they prevailed.” They prevailed either to swallow up or to hear.

[Note: The Micy manuscript reads “to be heard.” “To hear” is preferable. Yet “to be swallowed up” first would not be displeasing.]

For in the Lord’s presence they are swallowed up by the rebuke of prophetic truth and the reproach of their own impious falsehood.

12. **Grossness as companion or cause of vices. Vices do not allow a human being to be restrained within the laws of nature.**—Not only shall they hear words which they are able to hear, but what follows will also happen to them, V. 7: “Like the richness of earth, it has burst forth upon the ground.”

[Note: Thus the manuscript here and below, with the Chartres and German Psalters agreeing. The printed editions have “it was burst forth.” The Greek verb διερράγη permits either. By the example of earth—which, when dug out, is in a certain manner enlarged and swells, so that it cannot be contained within the pits from which it was excavated—Hilary shows that flesh, when vices burst forth, has passed beyond the laws of nature and can no longer be restrained within them.]

That richness is either the companion or the cause of impiety and vices is attested by the Prophet, who says: “The heart of this people has grown fat.” Moses too, declaring the irreligion of an insolent people, says: “Jacob ate and drank and was filled, and grew fat, and the beloved one kicked” (Deut. XXXII, 15).

We shall understand the force of this saying more fully from the nature of the earth itself. For we know that richer and fattier soils do not return as a solid mass into the pits from which they have been dug, because, as their richness bursts forth, those pits are again incapable of containing them. Therefore, by saying, “Like the richness of earth it has burst forth upon the ground,” he taught by an example [Col. 0831B] that all the grossness of our earth—that is, of the body—when excavated by vices, bursts forth from the law of its own nature and, swelling for its own destruction, is incapable of containing itself, so that it cannot be restored within itself.

13. **Love for another mourns evils as though they were its own.**—As this grossness bursts forth upon itself, the Prophet grieves, saying: “Our bones have been scattered beside hell.” In the calamity of sinners he considers himself scattered, dispersed, and driven beside hell. For “if one member suffers, all suffer with it” (I Cor. XII, 26). We are all members of one body in relation to one another; as he says also in another psalm: “All my bones were scattered” (Ps. XXI, 15). He does not mean, surely, those bones through which our body is held together in this strength of its power; rather, because we are all one body and members in relation to one another, the rest are the bones of our body.

[Col. 0831C] 14. **The Prophet directs the eyes of body and mind toward God.**—He would rather that the grossness of their earth should not burst forth, nor that the bones should be scattered beside hell; rather, that all might use the voice of this subsequent desire: VV. 8–9: “For my eyes are toward you, O Lord; in you have I hoped; do not take away my soul. Keep me from the snare which they have laid for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity.”

The Prophet’s eyes, fixed on the Lord, are not turned aside toward the admiration of superfluous things. They do not gaze upon the attractive forms of human bodies so as to dishonor chastity. They are not captured by the craftsmanship of costly clothing, the alluring gleam of silver, the seductive glitter of gold, the empty splendor of gems, the partisan contest of a theatrical spectacle, or the ambitious pomp of worldly powers. Rather, they attend to all God’s magnificent works, in admiration of him who has wrought them. Nor is he intent only with his eyes, but always also with his mind, saying: [Col. 0832A] “In you have I hoped; do not take away my soul.” The taking away of the soul is not its annihilation; rather, it occurs when it is removed from the glory of the honor appointed for it, when *(perhaps: then when)* it falls away from the expectation and love of its hope.

15. **The whole world is full of snares. The difference between a snare and a stumbling-block.**—He does not fail to know that there are many perils to his hope, when he says: “Keep me from the snare which they have laid for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity.” Everywhere are snares, everywhere stumbling-blocks; the whole world is full of traps—whether through the prince of this air, through the spiritual powers in the heavenly places, or through the children of disobedience in whom the spirit of error works.

For we have snares in people: evil exhortation, dangerous example, and [Col. 0832B] necessity drawn out.

[Note: What those “snares of drawn-out necessity” are may be understood from Ps. CXVIII, §17: “When at times an occasion for anger arises, an impulse of grief, the necessity of complaint, an opportunity for evil desire.” Again, in Ps. CXLII, §4, necessity is described as joined through the nature of the body or through the motion of the ever-fluctuating soul.]

They urge us toward pleasures; in their prosperity the ungodly are hostile to God; through insults and injuries they stir us into an agitation of troubled will. Yet a snare differs from a stumbling-block. A snare is the exhortation of pleasures and an incentive to shameful desire, which captures deceitfully in the manner of a noose. A stumbling-block is an irreligious wife, an iniquitous son, and thereafter all the names of the household, and every brother from the Church who is insulting, greedy, drunken, or shameful.

[Note: That is, what in Ps. CXVIII, §3 and elsewhere he calls “the names most dear to us.” How they are a stumbling-block is explained there.]

For in these things there is a stumbling-block for us whenever we are provoked, out of the gentleness of our tranquil faith, to the necessity of anger, rebuke, restraint, or punishment.

16. **The devil is the one author of all iniquities.**—But he knows that there is one being who himself works continually in all those who work iniquity through these snares, saying, V. 10: “Sinners shall fall into his net”—that is, into the net of him who works in the many. For whatever iniquities people commit are suggested by the devil. Him he now indicates in the singular number, though above in the plural he had signified his agencies in the many. He signifies many in him, and him in many. Therefore the wicked spread snares, and sinners shall fall into his net, because the wicked spread the snares of their net—namely, the devil’s own net.

[Col. 0832C] But sinners shall fall—not made sinners when they have fallen, but falling because they are sinners, made liable to the capture of the net because they are sinners.

[Note: A similar passage is Ps. CXXIII, §9. Hilary means only this: sin always pre-exists, by which a human being becomes a sinner, before he falls into the snares of the devil, or is handed over to his power.]

17. **Good singleness.**—But the Prophet, secure through his hope and faith, confidently says of himself: “I am alone until I pass over.” He knows, as we have shown above, that joining in pairs is impious. Given to God and occupied by no other affairs of the world, he is single until he passes over. And what is that which he passes over? Clearly, stumbling-blocks, nets, and snares. And where he passes over to must be asked. Assuredly, to that of which it has been said; for faithful, holy, and true is he who says: “Whoever believes in me shall not be judged, but shall pass from death into life” (John V, 24): our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM CXLI

**An understanding of David, when he was in the cave: a prayer.**

With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to the Lord. I pour out before him *(below adds: my prayer and)* my tribulation; before him I declare it, when my spirit fails within me. And you have known my paths. In this way in which I walked, they hid a snare for me. I looked [Col. 0833B] to the right and saw that there was no one who knew me. *(There is no one who knows me.)* Escape has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul. I cried to you, O Lord; I said: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living. Give heed to *(below lacks: to)* my prayer, for I have been brought very low. Deliver me from those who pursue me, for they have grown strong against me. Bring my soul out of prison, to confess your name, O Lord. The righteous awaited *(await)* me, until you repay me.

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. **This psalm concerns Christ foreshadowed in David; by his deeds David prophesied Christ.**—The meaning of this psalm is contained in its title, but by a spiritual rather than a bodily [Col. 0833C] understanding; and therefore the prayer in the title is an “understanding.” For if its meaning were simple, according to David’s deeds, “prayer” alone would have been inscribed as the title of the psalm. But because spiritual understanding is required for knowledge of the prayer, “a prayer of understanding”—because it must be understood—is prescribed.

For we know also that David whose fallen tabernacle was raised up, the righteous one, the rising one, the reigning one—namely, our Lord, the Son of God—often fled, often hid, often prayed; and in the very time of his Passion both wept and cried to God in tribulation. This was not through a natural fear, as it were, of suffering, but in order to show the human affection which he bore, so that by this prayer both the Son of God to whom he prayed and he himself might be understood—not as an apparent human being but as a true [Col. 0833D] human being.

[Note: If he assumed human affection for this purpose, that he might be understood not as an apparent man but as a true one, that affection too had to be real: real sorrow, real pain, real fear of suffering. Yet because it was assumed, it is rightly described as not natural to the Word who assumed it, as explained in Ps. LXVIII, §18. See the treatise on Ps. LIV, §6. Nor without reason does he say in Ps. CXXXIX, §11: “Bearing the nature of man and God, he had from human weakness the affection of trembling, and from consciousness of divinity the confidence of security.”]

This, therefore, is understood to be his prayer. David indeed speaks in a cave, but he prophesies in Christ. David flees, but by his flight he prophesies his Lord’s flight no less by deed than by words. David’s spirit fails, but the Lord’s soul too is sorrowful even unto death. God knows David’s paths, but no one knows the Son except the Father. Snares were hidden in the paths of David’s faith; everywhere too snares are prepared for the Lord in the course of his preaching. [Col. 0834A] The one prays in a cave; the other prays in the body. The servant prophesies the Lord Christ: this David prophesies that David by the example of all his sufferings. Therefore this prayer is to be understood as spoken not so much by David concerning himself as concerning the Lord through David.

2. Various stages of perfect prayer.—VERS. 2–4. “With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to the Lord. I pour out my prayer before Him, and declare my tribulation before Him, when my spirit fails within me.” The sequence of the words is excellently arranged. First there is a cry with the voice: for every silent and spiritual expectation of a faithful person is a cry to God. Then there is prayer with the voice; that is, the petition of desire and faith is expressed in audible words, according to the Apostle’s saying: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the voice” (1 Cor. 14:15). Third, prayer is poured out in God’s sight—not, that is, in words merely falling from the tongue, but from the deep and inward spring of faith the prayer of the suppliant is poured forth. And it is poured out in God’s sight, not carelessly or with self-assurance, but as though the Lord were present: for He who is prayed to that He may hear must be believed present; and He who is deemed present must be reverenced, not with the disregard shown to one absent, but with the honour due to one present. Fourthly, he declares his tribulation. Even when afflicted, he is not prevented from continually referring to God all the distress and suffering of his troubles. Nor indeed are the tribulations slight which he declares before God after pouring out his prayer: rather, he declares them when his spirit fails within him. Yet it is only slight temptations that hinder us from constancy in prayer; and any sudden agitation caused by a small difficulty turns even the little steadfastness of our minds—which exists only in favourable circumstances—away from the duty of devotion. But he, even while his spirit fails, does not cease to declare his tribulation, to pour out prayer, to pray with the very voice, and to cry with the voice of spiritual faith.

3. How psalms concerning Christ are recognized. Certain things here suit no one else.—“Thou hast known my paths. In this way wherein I walked, they hid a snare for me.” This prayer may be thought to belong both to that David and to this David; for, as we have said, by the faith of the servant and the example of the prophet, all the Lord’s words and deeds were prefigured. Yet whenever the prophecy of the Psalms is uttered in the person of the Lord, it always adds something peculiar and proper to Him, which cannot be shared in common by another. Thus, because much that is recalled in the person of the man whom He assumed was common to human persons and natures, the prophecy of the Psalms might show itself to concern Him by those things which were said properly in His own person. So here, VERS. 5: “I looked to the right hand, and saw that there was no one who knew me. Escape has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul.” Although David fled, he was nevertheless not unknown; nor did he look only to the right, but the view to his left also lay open before him. But how can this be fitted to his person: “Escape has perished from me”; then, “There is no one who seeks my soul”; and finally, the words with which the Psalm concludes: “The righteous wait for me, until Thou repayest me”? Understood in the person of a man, these things contradict one another. For if righteous persons are waiting, how does no one know him? How does no one seek his soul? For no one seeks his soul and no one knows his soul because, while he looks to the right, no righteous person is seen.

4. They apply to Christ.—But all these things were fulfilled in the Lord at the time of His Passion, when no one accompanied Him as He went to the cross—those whom, according to the Gospel arrangement, He was preparing, separated from the left, for the possession of the kingdom of heaven at the right [Note: [Col. 0835D] Thus the manuscript. The printed editions read, “at the right.”], and for whose sake He had also been born a man; when, amid so many and such great signs of the cross itself, no one recognized God; when He had often previously hidden Himself, and had both disclosed and presented Himself to those seeking Him. And by the offering of His voluntary will, escape perished from Him, when no one sought the power of His life [Note: [Col. 0835D] Manuscript: “the truth of His life.”], which is signified in the soul. For while they looked upon the body which they had fastened to the cross, no one sought the power of the soul [Note: [Col. 0835D] It might be preferable to read “which.” Yet “which” may refer to the power, or rather to the soul insofar as it signifies divinity; and thus there is no difficulty here. But if anyone should refer it to the soul properly so called, it must be understood that it proved itself God by its deeds only insofar as it showed itself to belong to God, to whom it was substantially joined in unity of person. For as the Word is called flesh because He assumed flesh, so the soul is proclaimed God because it too was assumed by God together with the flesh. Since, however, most Fathers, enumerated by Petavius, book IV, *On the Incarnation*, ch. 13, hold that the Word was united directly with the soul, while the soul was united with the body only through that mediation, it may rightly be thought that the soul especially displayed the signs of divine power.], which had proved itself God by signs and deeds.

5. What Paradise is.—The following words, though they appear common to others, were nevertheless all spoken and done through Him at the time of the Passion: “I cried to Thee, O Lord; I said: Thou art my hope, my portion in the land of the living.” Crying out, He said, “Thou art my hope,” when He said: “Father, into Thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). His portion is in the land of the living when He promises the thief, that very day, residence in Paradise (ibid., v. 43), that is, the lot and kingdom of His inheritance; so that, though He should go down to the lower regions, He nevertheless taught by His spiritual—divine—power that He was not absent from Paradise.

6. Why Christ ascribes His resurrection to the Father.—Then He returns to the humility of His worship, saying, VERS. 7: “Attend to my prayer, for I am greatly humbled.” For He was humbled by taking the form of a servant, and becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8). “Deliver me from those who persecute me, for they have grown strong against me. Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess Thy name, O Lord.” Although He had power to lay down His life and to take it up again, yet, out of filial reverence, He always reserved honour for the Father’s majesty [Note: [Col. 0835D] The printed editions read “majesty”; the manuscript more suitably reads “to majesty.” Thus Hilary observes, *On the Trinity*, IX.12, that Christ ascribes to the Father’s command the power of taking up His life; and in XI.10, as also in his exposition of Psalm 138, §10, that He declares He came to do not His own will but that of Him who sent Him. Finally, in *On the Synods*, §54, and on Psalm 138, §29, he says that He can do nothing from Himself. He speaks these and similar things not only insofar as He is man, but also insofar as He is the only-begotten God, who, in words expressing reverence, signifies Himself equal to the Father while at the same time declaring that He is born from Him. For this reason Hilary does not hesitate, in his exposition of Psalm 138, §17, to refer “The Father is greater than I” to Christ as God. See similar expressions in *On the Synods*, §51.], when He prays, “Father, glorify Me” (John 17:5), and when He cries, “My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?” (Ps. 21:2). In these words there is no confession of His weakness, but a proclamation of the Father’s power. Thus He now likewise prays to be delivered from His persecutors because they have grown strong. For they grew strong when they dared to crucify Him, when through the flesh they failed to know God, when the clothing of humility and the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0836D] The printed editions read “form”; the manuscript’s “clothing and form” is preferable.] encouraged them against Him.

7. Then He asks that His soul be brought out of prison. If the Lord, according to blessed Peter, preached resurrection to those placed in prison even before Noah’s time (1 Pet. 3:19–20) [Note: [Col. 0836D] In the exposition of Psalm 118, §3, we read “exhortation,” not “resurrection.” Compare the passage.], then prison is the infernal region; from it He asks to be brought out, as He had prayed in another Psalm: “Let not the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16). This whole prayer, as we have said, is for confession of the Father’s power. But He also adds the reason why He asks to be brought out of prison: “That I may confess Thy name.” His resurrection is a proclamation of the Father’s power in Him, because all power belongs to Him from the Father.

8. The Apostles’ faith wavered before Christ’s resurrection and was established afterwards.—But He goes on to say through whom God’s name is to be confessed: “The righteous wait for me, until Thou repayest me.” Until the time of the resurrection, the faith of all the Apostles was fearful; beholding His resurrection, they were strengthened by the assurance of their expectation. Hence the Lord said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38). He did not say, “because of death”; for though He gave Himself up to the Passion, eternal Power did not undergo the pain of suffering. But because the fear of the Apostles arose from the humiliation of the Passion—so that even the firm rock upon which the Church was to be built trembled—and would cease to remain in that fear after the Lord’s death and resurrection, He is sorrowful unto death, since after it those of trembling faith were to be strengthened in assurance. The righteous therefore wait until He is repaid by God. And what is repaid to Him by God, the Apostle teaches, saying: “For this reason God exalted Him and gave Him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9–10). This is His recompense from God: that to the body which He assumed may be granted the eternity of the Father’s glory. And what the expectation of the righteous is, the same Apostle teaches, saying: “But our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await our Saviour [Note: [Col. 0837D] Manuscript: “Saviour.”] Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation so that it may be conformed to the body of His glory” (Phil. 3:20–21). The righteous therefore await Him while He is repaid: namely, that they may be made conformed to the glory of His body, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 142

Of David himself, when Absalom pursued him.

“O Lord [Below: God], hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication. In Thy truth hear me; in Thy righteousness. And enter not into judgments [judgment] with Thy servant, for no living person shall be justified in Thy sight. For the enemy has persecuted my soul; he has humbled my life to the earth; he has placed me in darkness, like those dead from ages past. And my spirit has been distressed within me; my heart has been troubled within me. I remembered the days of old, [‘and’ omitted] and meditated on all Thy works; I meditated [below: ‘I shall meditate’] on the works of Thy hands. I stretched out my hands to Thee; my soul is to Thee like land without water. DIAPSALM. Hear me swiftly, O Lord; my spirit has failed. Turn not Thy face away from me, lest I be like those who go down into the pit. Make me hear Thy mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in Thee, O Lord [‘O Lord’ absent]. Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for to Thee I have lifted up my soul. Deliver me from my enemies, O Lord; to Thee I have fled. Teach me to do Thy will, for Thou art my God. Thy good Spirit will lead me into a straight land for Thy name’s sake, O Lord. Thou wilt quicken me in Thy righteousness. Thou wilt bring my soul out of tribulation, and in Thy mercy Thou wilt destroy my enemies. And Thou wilt destroy all who afflict [below: all enemies who persecute] my soul, for I am Thy servant.”

### Exposition of the Psalm

1. The Psalm’s superscription was added by the Septuagint.—According to the Hebrews, the Psalm appears to have no superscription; this is handed down by those learned in both languages. [Note: [Col. 0837D] The reading in Bad. is “and the other translators.” In other editions, “the translators and the rest.” The manuscripts more correctly read “the translators and the others,” namely, all who besides the Seventy translated the Psalter from Hebrew, as is clear from the discussion that follows, §1. Thus Theodoret, speaking of the title, says: “I find this addition neither in the Hebrew nor among the other interpreters.” In Jerome it is simply entitled “A Psalm of David.”] Nor did the other translators write anything at all about the historical events—namely, Absalom’s pursuit of his father David. But those seventy elders, possessing knowledge of the Law and Prophets beyond the prescribed limits and ambiguity of the letter, judged that this should be added to the Psalm (see *Exposition of Psalm 2*, §§2–3). We have explained the reason for this judgment in the introduction to the Psalms (Preface, §5): we ought to recognize that nothing but prophecy is to be treated in the Psalms. Since neither the wording agrees with the events nor the order with the times [Note: [Col. 0838D] “Order” is absent from the royal manuscripts and the Albinus manuscript.], it remains that we should be taught that all David’s deeds, and all that is understood from them, are for an example and instruction in things to be done. The superscription has therefore now been affixed to the Psalm though it does not stand in the book, so that where it does stand—that is, as in the third Psalm, in which David is written to have fled from the face of him who is now said to persecute him—we might be summoned to an understanding of prophecy.

2. Who speaks throughout this Psalm, and under what name.—David therefore now prophesies the Lord’s sufferings by his own sufferings: not complaining about Absalom, but about those who inflamed Absalom to the crime of impiety. For, according to the Apostle, the devil’s darts are fiery (Eph. 6:16); these cast themselves into Judas’s heart so that the Lord might be betrayed, and now work in the children of disobedience. For this reason the Lord, having assumed the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh through sin. We shall therefore expound the Psalm in the person of the Prophet, understanding himself to be placed in a body of sin and, through man, wearied amid many grave temptations of the devil. For just as the Lord knew that the prince of this world had accomplished these things against Him through the Jews and Judas, when He says to the Apostles, “Behold, one of you is Satan” (John 6:71)—for Judas is shown to be wholly that because he was animated by him—so David understands in Absalom those through whom Absalom is such. And because the discussion of this was fuller in the third Psalm (*This exposition is not extant*), let us now expound the words of the Psalm itself, remembering that all things said under the Prophet’s name must also be referred to the person of the Lord, who, emptying Himself from the form of God and assuming the form of a servant, professed Himself a man subject to the weakness of our nature, even to the point of being said not to know the day and hour that were His own.

3. An example of prayer. God is not an envious or unduly harsh judge.—VERS. 1: “God, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication. In Thy truth hear me, in Thy righteousness.” First he asks that his prayer be heard, because it belongs to human humility to desire that God give a hearing to what he prays. Then secondly, according to prophetic knowledge, he requests to be heard in God’s truth. For this faithful man, God is not one of the elements of the world, nor one made from the names of kings, nor one resulting from the world’s error in stones, metals, and wood; rather, his God is true, eternal, almighty, and the Maker of all things. The third request also is that he be heard in God’s righteousness. [Note: [Col. 0838D] In the aforesaid manuscripts there is no “God of an envious will”—or perhaps “hearer”?] God is not an arbiter of tyrannical will, nor of excessively harsh and unjust obstinacy; rather, He takes account of human weakness. He does not measure the most ready falls of our changeable nature according to the inflexible constancy of His unchangeable substance; rather, being righteous and moderate, He expects from man only as much as He remembers human nature can accomplish.

4. How many things lie in wait for human innocence.—And therefore, in connection with his prayer to be heard in God’s righteousness, he adds, VERS. 2: “Enter not into judgment with Thy servant, for no living person shall be justified in Thy sight.” For what hope is there if God should wish to judge us by His own standard, if He should require the innocence of our life in comparison with Himself? Which living person can be justified in God’s sight—one to whom anger, pain, desire, ignorance, forgetfulness, mischance, and necessity are continually joined, whether through the nature of the body or through the motion of the ever-fluctuating soul; and over whom, moreover, the most grievous enemy daily hangs, namely the devil, lying in wait for the faithful person’s soul and pursuing it to destruction? For he teaches that this is why no living person can be justified in God’s sight. VERS. 3: “For the enemy has persecuted my soul; he has humbled my life to the earth; he has placed me in darkness, like those dead from ages past.” Darkness is poured forth through the body’s vices; and when we fall through the devil’s snares into the desires of the flesh, driven from the light of knowledge we are placed in darkness, submerged in the gloom of the Gentiles and held fast in the night of worldly works.

5. Whom the spiritual man calls darkened.—But however much the enemy persecutes the soul and humbles it in the body, placing it in darkness as one dead from ages past, the distress of the spiritual man is not held by these bodily darknesses [Note: [Col. 0839D] In Paris: “is contained.”]. His heart is troubled at this very weakness of his nature; resisting vices, he turns his human self toward remembrance of its original constitution and meditation on God’s works. For the enemy has not placed him in darkness dead from ages past, but as one dead from ages past; thereby the freedom of the ever-distressed spirit is preserved within him.

6. Matter for meditation. Man is the work of God’s hands.—For this follows, VERS. 3–4: “And my spirit has been distressed over me; my heart has been troubled within me. I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all Thy works; I meditated on the works of Thy hands.” [Note: [Col. 0839D] Mic. manuscript: “within me.”] He knows that Adam was captured by the devil, and therefore remembers the days of old. He knows that through transgression of the law established for him, Adam fell both from God’s promises and from residence in Paradise, and therefore remembers God’s works. He knows that innocence in the past does not suffice, but that blessed is the person who has remained innocent unto the end; and therefore he will meditate on the works of God’s hands. Man himself is the work of God’s hands; after he sinned, he became a slave of sin. He therefore meditates on being such as that man was before sin who was made by God. [Note: [Col. 0839D] Bad. and Er. read: “such as he whom God made was,” while Paris adds “who,” omitting “is,” which we supply from the manuscripts.] Since he has been placed in darkness not dead from ages past, but as one dead from ages past, he will always meditate; and he will always meditate because, remembering the days of old, he knows [Note: [Col. 0840D] The printed texts have “may know”; the manuscript’s “knows” is much better.] that through transgression of the law the death of sin entered.

7. Without God’s grace man is barren.—Although in remembering the days of old, meditating on God’s works, and continuing to meditate, he began by his own faith, yet, lest he should be thought presumptuous, he shows that this is not his own possession but granted through the help of God to whom he prayed, saying, VERS. 6: “I stretched out my hands to Thee; my soul is like land without water.” Land without water is dry and unfruitful, and always awaits to be watered with the shower of heavenly rain. So too the soul of the saint, conscious of its own nature, desires to be moistened by the gift of the divine word, concerning which Moses says: “Let my utterance be awaited as rain, and let my words descend as dew, as rain upon grass and as snow upon hay” (Deut. 32:2). Thus the dry and thirsty soul is drenched with such a rain of prophetic teaching, so that, dead and barren through the drought of nature, it may grow green again into rich fruits through knowledge of God’s commandments.

8. The Prophet desires quickly to be dissolved and to be with Christ.—In the words that follow is a confession of human faith and consciousness, while the interposition of the diapsalm reveals the impatience of prophetic desire. VERS. 7: “Hear me swiftly, O Lord; my spirit has failed.” The Prophet cannot endure the delay of his body; and, according to the Apostle’s saying, “To be dissolved and to be with Christ is better for me” (Phil. 1:23), and “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24), and “For in this old tent we groan, desiring to be clothed over” (2 Cor. 5:2), he endures weariness in this body of death. Yet he seeks the swift aid for which he prays because of the failure of his spirit, together with the fulfilment in himself of the grace of the divine gift. For what would it profit him to be heard swiftly unless he departed from the body as faithful, pleasing to God, and destined to rest in blessed places?

9. The pit, a place of punishment.—And therefore he says: “Turn not Thy face away from me, lest I be like those who go down into the pit.” Scripture calls the penal place of the lower world a pit, as in the Psalms: “Thou, O Lord, hast drawn my soul out of hell; Thou hast preserved me” [manuscripts: “saved me”] “from those who go down into the pit” (Ps. 29:4). Therefore, unless the face of God—who is certainly Christ, the image of the invisible God—be present to every saint, that person will be like those assigned to the punishment of hell, who depart this life without hope of rest.

10. The Prophet hopes for resurrection.—But the Prophet does not doubt concerning his hope, nor is he outside the confidence of Gospel assurance. Though earlier in time, he shares in spirit in apostolic joy [Note: [Col. 0840D] Paris reads “sharers.” Other books read “sharer,” namely the Prophet; what follows is then referred to the Apostles, as though “the Apostles’ joy,” not “apostolic joy,” had first been given.]; beholding the Lord’s resurrection, they believed in the eternity of perishable bodies. For he says in what follows, VERS. 8: “Make me hear Thy mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in Thee.” The joy of this morning mercy is shown in many passages, as where he says: “Weeping will tarry at evening, and joy at morning” (Ps. 29:6). For this is the time of resurrection, in which the power of death was broken through God’s mercy. Since the Prophet hoped in this mercy, he desires to hear it.

11. Conscious of ignorance, he asks God for light. He desires to return to man’s first condition.—Then follows: “Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to Thee.” The Apostle sees through a mirror and in an enigma, knows in part and prophesies in part (1 Cor. 13:12, 9). Likewise the Prophet, as one ignorant through the nature of human frailty, prays that the paths in which he is to walk may be made known to him. For these worldly paths are not useful; he desires to know spiritual and heavenly ones. This is what he says: “For I have lifted up my soul to Thee.” His soul is not among low things but among those on high; and therefore he asks to know the lofty paths. For he knows that he has enemies who would draw him away into other paths and lead him into another will. The Apostle has often spoken at length concerning these spiritual enemies. He therefore prays to be delivered from them, asks to know the afflicted path which leads to heaven [Note: [Col. 0841D] “Afflicted” is absent from two manuscripts. Yet this passage treats the path mentioned in the exposition of Psalm 118, §11: “The way which leads to life is both narrow and afflicted.”], to be taught the Lord’s will, and to be led by His Spirit into a straight land: that is, to be established as a person not twisted by vices. For how could he desire to be led into a straight land if this were understood of the creation of this element [Note: [Col. 0841D] Bad., Er., and Lips. read: “if it be thought he spoke of the nature of this element.” Paris: “if it be thought he desired this from the elements of this nature.” The passage, corrupted, is restored with the aid of the royal and Albinus manuscripts.], unless, in accordance with the nature of the first man, to whom after sin it was said, “Thou art earth, and into earth thou shalt go” (Gen. 3:19), he desires to be established as a straight and unbending man? [Note: [Col. 0841D] Thus in the manuscripts; the printed texts wrongly read “to establish man.”] This is contained in the words: “Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to Thee.” VERS. 9–11: “Deliver me from my enemies, O Lord; to Thee I have fled. Teach me to do Thy will, for Thou art my God. Thy good Spirit will lead me into a straight land for Thy name’s sake, O Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0841D] We have deleted here, on manuscript authority, “Thou wilt quicken me in Thy righteousness.”]

12. Not by one’s own merits, but by God’s goodness.—The Apostle’s confession corresponds with his words, “Teach me to do Thy will”: “He who thinks he knows does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2). And if we do not yet even know how to pray, nor know how to speak our desires, while the Spirit Himself instead intercedes for us with unutterable groanings and compensates for our ignorance by the hidden affection of conscience [Note: [Col. 0841D] Thus the royal manuscript and Albinus. The printed editions read “of hidden knowledge”; then Bad., Er., and Lips. read “by effect,” Paris “by affection.”], according to the Apostle’s saying, “For we do not know what we ought to pray for; but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8:26), the Prophet is not thought to pray incongruously that he may be taught to fulfil God’s will. It is also a fitting profession of human modesty that, when he is to be led by God’s Spirit into a straight land, he should not claim this as his own merit or demand it for himself through satisfaction rendered by his own service [Note: [Col. 0842D] The printed editions read “of pious service”; the manuscripts’ “of his own” is preferable.], but should await all of it for the glorification of God’s name within him, so that for the honour of God’s name he may be established in a straight land.

13. Blessedness comes from God’s mercy, without excluding the duty of meriting.—And because he knows that this straight land cannot be granted him in the body of this death—since the stain of human flesh, through the habit of vices mixed into it, cannot be entirely abolished except when nature is changed—he asks to be quickened, as though he did not yet live, saying: “Thou wilt quicken me in Thy righteousness. Thou wilt bring my soul out of tribulation,” VERS. 12, “and in Thy mercy Thou wilt destroy my enemies. And Thou wilt destroy all enemies who persecute my soul, for I am Thy servant.” [Note: [Col. 0842D] We have added “enemies” on manuscript authority. Then only the Paris edition has “who afflict,” not “who persecute.”] He had indeed, as we have said, this righteousness of modesty: whatever blessedness he hopes for himself, he asks it rather for the magnificence of God—because it is fitting to ascribe blessedness, eternity, and goodness to God—than for his own merit. Yet, while setting forth God’s honour and mercy, he did not exclude the duty of earning it on his own part. For although he is to be quickened, he is to be quickened in righteousness, because it is just that life be repaid as the reward of holiness. And although, by God’s mercy, after he is brought out of tribulation his enemies are to be destroyed, this is no longer mercy of indiscriminate and confused judgment [Note: [Col. 0842D] The royal and Albinus manuscripts: “by which He both brings him out of tribulation and destroys his enemies”; “by which,” etc.], since the same judgment which brings one out of tribulation destroys the enemies: because, according to the diversity of merits, judgment is apportioned either to punishment or to mercy [Note: [Col. 0842D] The printed editions read “or to the judgment of mercy it is apportioned.” The manuscripts are better: “or to mercy,” etc.].

14. What belongs to God’s grace and what to merit in victory over temptations.—The Prophet shows that his enemies are not slight, but such as even pursue the soul—not that it can be killed together with the body, but that he is so wearied by diabolical assaults and so burned under the fires of vices cast upon him [Note: [Col. 0842D] The printed editions read “is accused by inducements”; corrected from the manuscripts, from which the following particle *verum* (“but”) is absent, though it may be present or absent without affecting the sense.] that he might deserve to be slain by the Lord. But although it is chiefly God’s name and mercy that his enemies should perish, yet this too is a cause: that he is God’s servant whose soul they pursue. Thus generosity—from God’s side—and merit—from man’s side—are joined; and to the Lord’s mercy are added the servant’s faith and name. Hence, although God’s mercy is ready for all, it is understood to assist those who are His servants, through Him and in Him who says: “I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20), our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed now and always and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 143

A Psalm of David against Goliath.

“Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for war and my fingers for battle. My mercy and my refuge, my supporter and my deliverer [below: “art Thou” added]. My protector, and in Him I have hoped; who will subject [below: subjecting] my people under me. O Lord, what is man, that Thou hast made Thyself known to him? Or the son of man, that Thou dost account him?” Man has become like vanity; his days pass like a shadow. O Lord, bow down Thy heavens and descend; touch the mountains, and they shall smoke. Flash forth lightnings [below: flashes], and Thou shalt scatter them; send forth Thy arrows, and Thou shalt trouble them. Send [below: Thou shalt send] Thy hand from on high; deliver me and free me [“and free me” absent] from many waters and from the hand [below: the unjust hand] of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity. O God, I will sing to Thee a new song; upon a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing praise to Thee. Who gives [below: Thou givest] salvation to kings; who deliverest Thy servant [below: deliverest David Thy servant] from the wicked sword, deliver [below: rescue] me. And deliver me from the hand of the foreign son [These words do not occur below], whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity. Their sons are like young plants, established [below: a young plant established] in their youth. Their daughters adorned [below: fashioned], and embellished like the likeness of a temple. Their storehouses full, pouring forth from one thing into another. Their sheep fruitful, abundant in their paths [below: in their goings forth]; their oxen fat [below: fat, feminine]. There is no breach in the wall, no passage through, no cry in their streets. They called blessed the people to whom these things belong; blessed is the people whose Lord is its God.”

### Exposition of the Psalm

1. The title added by the Septuagint indicates concerning whom the Psalm is to be understood.—VERS. 1–7. The Septuagint also considered this superscription to be added to this Psalm: “A Psalm of David against Goliath,” although it occurs neither in the Hebrew books [Note: [Col. 0843D] Indeed, according to Theodoret, neither does it occur in all Septuagint copies. He writes: “In certain copies I find added to the title, *pros ton Goliath* [‘against Goliath’]. But I have found it neither in the Hebrew, nor among the other interpreters, nor even in the Septuagint within the Hexapla.”] nor did the other translators prefix anything other than the simple title, namely “David.” That this was not done without a spiritual reason is shown by the text of the Psalm itself. This Psalm contains nothing peculiar that can be referred to celebration of Goliath’s death; on the contrary, many things there conflict both with the event and with the time. For when it says, “Subjecting my people under me,” was David then king? Or what people was subject to him, if the people of the Philistines was not his own? Nor indeed could Israel itself, while Saul still reigned, have been subject to him. Again, what sort of prayer could these words be at the time of a human war: “O Lord, bow down Thy heavens and descend; touch the mountains, and they shall smoke; flash forth lightnings, and Thou shalt scatter them”? Or, when according to the title Goliath had been killed, what do these prayers mean: “Deliver me and free me from many waters and from the hand of foreign sons”? Or, when there was only one king in Israel, what is meant by the words, V. 10: “Thou who givest salvation to kings”? The plural number excludes an interpretation confined to that time, when there was only one king. But since the title is not so given in the Hebrew books, nor have the other translators added any of these things, we understand that those seventy elders left us the meaning of spiritual knowledge: so that we might know that in David and Goliath the battle of Satan and the Lord was prefigured, since neither did the superscription occur in the books nor did the prophetic discourse accord with the historical events.

2. Whether the psalms are David’s own, or are about David, Latin usage does not make clear. This psalm concerns Christ.---The character of Latin often creates difficulty for our understanding, since it is not accustomed to prefix pronouns to names, as occurs with the name David. For when the pronoun is absent, it is uncertain whether a psalm was produced concerning him or through him. When “a psalm of David” is written, the bare inscription of the name leaves ambiguous whether it was spoken by him or for his sake. Greek, however, when it signifies that the psalm was written through David, inscribes the title thus: *ψαλμὸς τοῦ Δαβίδ*, “a psalm of David”; but when it intends the psalm to be understood as written about David, it writes: *τῷ Δαβίδ*, “for David.” By the particular force of each pronoun it distinguishes whether David is the author or the subject of the written psalm. Thus the heading of this psalm reads, *τῷ Δαβίδ*—that is, it was written on his account, or rather for him, not by him. From this heading it is further shown that this psalm was sung, through the power of the Spirit and the mouth of the Prophet, concerning that man whom the Lord assumed by being born in him, and whom, as we have often taught, David designates.

3. “Blessed be the Lord my God, who trains my hands for war and my fingers for battle.” If this psalm is assigned to the rejoicing over Goliath’s death because it says, “Who trains my hands for war,” let them accept this as an example that the passage is more fitting to the person of the Lord. For in the seventeenth psalm, which throughout proceeds in the person of the Lord, we remember this same statement: “Who trains my hands for battle, and has made my arms like a bronze bow” (Ps. 17:35).

That nothing can be referred to David himself is shown throughout that psalm, but especially by these words: “He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry entered his ears before him. And the earth was shaken and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were disturbed” (ibid. 7–8). And again: “They cried out, but there was none to save them; to the Lord, but he did not hear them. And I shall grind them like dust before the face of the wind; I shall destroy them like the mud of the streets. You shall deliver me from the contentions of the people; you shall set me as head of the nations. A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (ibid. 42 ff.). The facts themselves refute the foolish interpretation of those who maintain that David spoke these words about himself, since all things agree, in spiritual meaning and in the events themselves, with that man whom the Lord assumed by being born in him.

4. Christ equipped for the warfare of the Passion.---His hands, therefore, were trained for war when he conquered the world: “For I,” he says, “have conquered the world” (John 16:33); when, stretched out upon the cross, he was equipped with the unconquerable weapons of his own Passion: “You have made my arms like a bronze bow”; when he triumphs in himself, in the trophy of the glorious cross, over every power and authority. “For he stripped principalities and powers, triumphing over them confidently in himself” (Col. 2:15); when he reconciles things heavenly and earthly, which were at variance with one another: “And through him,” he says, “to reconcile all things to him, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (Col. 1:20).

For this warfare his hands were trained: a warfare in which the bronze bow is overcome in the contest [a word appears to be missing here]; the powerful are conquered by humiliation; enemies are reconciled by peace. But after the warfare of the hands comes also the battle of the fingers. For in him every posture and struggle of the Passion is displayed. His hands are stretched out, and his fingers are fastened in his palms; thus, according to the Apostle, blotting out the old written bond and fastening it to the cross (Col. 2:14), he mentions even those parts of the hands in the battle by which all the sins of ancient crimes were nailed fast.

5. Then follows: “You are my mercy and my refuge, my supporter and my deliverer; my protector, and in him I have hoped.” These words present no difficulty. For all these things were both done and spoken by him in the Gospels, so that by the confession of our humility—the condition which he had assumed—he might proclaim the honor of his Father’s majesty.

6. Christ’s people are not the Jews alone.---But the words, “Subjecting my people beneath me,” must not be thought to have been spoken in the person of the Jewish people alone. For in another psalm he called the whole body of the Church one people, saying: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. 17:45). That even here the one who did not know him is nevertheless his own, the Gospels teach when they say: “He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:11, 10).

[Note: Col. 0845D: The manuscript has “did not know.” Hilary nevertheless usually reads otherwise.]

But lest anyone suppose that this people, which did not know him and served him, was not his own because it had not known him, that divine song of Moses removes every error of this ambiguity: “When the Most High divided the nations, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of his angels; and Jacob became the Lord’s portion, Israel the line of his inheritance” (Deut. 32:8–9; see *Treatise on Psalm 2*, no. 31). This Israel had been chosen for an eternal inheritance; and therefore, because it was the Lord’s portion, the rest were regarded as though unknown, because they were selected by the privilege of that portion. Yet all are his own, because they owe to him, as their author, what they are.

7. When, why, and to what extent all things were given to Christ.---They are subjected to him when it is said: “Just as you gave him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you gave him” (John 17:2); and again: “All things have been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). But they were not then given to him for the first time, since he was already in the world through whom the world had been made, and since he asks again for the glory which he had with the Father before the foundation of the world. Rather, they were given after the assumption of humanity, because it is written: “Though he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant; for which reason God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:7, 9).

What, then, is given, and to whom? Certainly it is not given to him who was in the form of God that he may have the form of God; for he already was so, and because he was so he did not need this gift. But the reason for giving was that he who was in the form of God took the form of a servant; emptying himself of the form of God and assuming the form of a servant, he became obedient unto death. Therefore, to that obedience through which the servile condition was assumed, and to that servile condition itself, it is granted that it may be what it was—namely, that it may be in the form of God.

[Note: Col. 0845D: That is, that what it was according to divinity might also be so according to the flesh; then, “the form of God,” that is, the glory of God.]

For the emptying of the form of God does not know loss to its own detriment; rather, it acquires again the form of God for the servile assumption.

[Note: Col. 0845D: The printed editions read “of the emptied form,” but the manuscript has “the emptying of the form,” more correctly, as is clear from *On the Trinity*, book IX, no. 14, with which this passage should be compared. Arnobius, book II *On the Conflict with Serapion*, explains how the form of God is acquired by the servile assumption in a fragment quoted from Hilary: “For the greatness of the Lord overcame the smallness of the servile form, so that the servile form itself which he assumed ceased to be servile through the Lord who assumed it.” Perhaps someone will understand this to mean that the Word did not degenerate into the subsistence of the assumed man, but rather that the man advanced into the subsistence of the Word. In this sense Leporius seems to have said in his book of correction: “The flesh therefore advanced into the Word; the Word did not advance into the flesh; and yet truly the Word became flesh.” Yet since the discussion here concerns the advancement which Christ acquired through obedience unto death, it appears to be understood of glory rather than subsistence. The servile form ceases to be servile not through destruction but through a change of nature, insofar as, from being mortal, corruptible, and weak, it becomes eternal, incorruptible, and glorious—qualities which are not human but divine.]

Thus Power, though restraining itself in humility, did not fail from itself, since it remained what it was.

[Note: Col. 0847D: Manuscript Mic. reads “in humility.”]

And humility, restrained in itself and taken up by Power, when it began to be what it was not, received the advancement of that Power which had not failed from itself. This, indeed, is the truth of the evangelical mystery and of human hope: human nature and corruptible flesh have, by this transformation of glory, been transformed into an eternal substance.

8. Humanity unworthy of knowledge of God. What it means to be “appointed.” Everything transient is vain. To what extent man may know God, and for what he is appointed.---But the prophetic utterance also bears witness in this present psalm to the wonder of this event, as though most difficult, and to the gift of this greatest and most beautiful hope. To the words, “Subjecting my people beneath me,” it adds: “Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him? Or the son of man, that you appoint him? Man has been made like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow.”

In the eighth psalm also the Holy Spirit cries out in like manner: “What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you visit him?” This is a most beautiful confession: man himself declares that he is unworthy of so great a gift. And when he confesses himself unworthy, he extols the grace of him who grants him these things. For what merit has man that God should make himself knowable to him, that the unknowable nature should submit itself to our knowledge? Or what dignity has the son of man that he should be appointed?

Now whatever is destined from the state in which it is into something else is “appointed.” The force of the words expresses the nature of the thing. Man, made like vanity, and whose days pass like a shadow, is appointed through the knowledge of God granted to him. Vanity is the world, whose condition and form shall be removed. For before God, whatever exists but does not endure as abiding is empty; and every shadow, although it exists, yet does not truly exist, because when it comes into being it is removed when that by which it was produced departs.

[Note: Col. 0847D: Thus the first Paris edition with the manuscript. The later edition, with the editions of Bad., Er., and Lips., reads “is emptied.” The verb “is removed” will recur below, no. 15, with the same force.]

Man, therefore, is not a shadow but is like a shadow; nor is he vanity, but is made like vanity through the intervention of death. Yet through the knowledge of God granted to him he is appointed. And the granted knowledge shows to what he is appointed. For if God could not become known to man except by assuming man, because our nature could not know the unknowable except through our nature; and if through this knowledge man is appointed, he must be appointed to that in which he himself knew God—namely, that he may become conformed to God, because this is the appointment involved in granted knowledge.

[Note: Col. 0847D: It seems one should read, “to what is man appointed?” and then, “he must be appointed to that to which, not in which—that is, for the sake of which—he knew God.”]

9. The very powerful enemies are demons; they are also the mountains.---And because this whole prayer is spoken in the person of that man whom the Lord assumed, he knows with what dignity God releases him from the laws of death and snatches him from the hands of the wicked through the glory of the resurrection, saying: “Lord, bow your heavens and come down; touch the mountains and they shall smoke; flash forth lightnings and you shall scatter them; send forth your arrows and you shall trouble them. Stretch forth your hand from on high.”

Similar words occur in the psalm mentioned above: “He bowed the heaven and came down” (Ps. 17:10); “coals were kindled by him, and fire shall blaze from before him, and smoke rose in his wrath” (ibid. 9); “He sent arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and troubled them” (ibid. 15). “He sent from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters. He delivered me from my strongest enemies” (ibid. 17–18).

[Note: Col. 0847D: Here the text had “blazes.” That Hilary regularly read “shall blaze” is clear from his *Treatise on Psalm 64*, nos. 8–9.]

When he called them “strongest,” we may understand whom he meant: namely those of whom the Apostle says, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the world, against spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12), Satan himself entering Judas’s heart so that he might betray the Lord (Luke 22:3).

But in this psalm we should also observe: “Flash forth lightnings and you shall scatter them; send forth your arrows and you shall trouble them.” Above, he did not identify those whom he meant by “them”; therefore the pronoun must be referred to these mountains, which will smoke at the mere touch of God.

[Note: Col. 0847D: Thus manuscript Mic., which shortly above has *nullos* instead of *non illos*. The Paris edition has *memorabat*; other editions, *memorarat*. Hilary means that in the preceding words the psalmist had not shown to whom the pronoun *eos* refers in “you shall scatter them” and “you shall trouble them,” unless it is referred to the mountains.]

And lest we think the words refer to earthly mountains, another psalm admonishes us when it says: “Why have you received curdled mountains?” And, so far as understanding is permitted, we think that “mountains” sometimes signify demonic powers, as here: having transgressed the ordinances of the divine law, they have curdled, as it were, from the purity of milk into the defective corruption of curdling. These are the strongest enemies of whom the earlier psalm, Psalm 17, spoke.

[Note: Col. 0848D: Thus the manuscript, as also in Psalm 67, no. 16, where it has been restored from the manuscripts. The printed texts read, “Why do you receive?” That demons are meant by “mountains” has already been shown in Psalm 64, no. 8.]

10. What the descent of God and the bowing of heaven mean.---The Lord came down, therefore, when his heaven was bowed, not by bodily movement, as though heaven was physically lowered when he descended. Rather, through the bodily expression a spiritual meaning is taught: when sleep, wakefulness, remembrance, forgetfulness, departure, and approach are attributed to God, this is because, according to the differing character of our merits, he is for each of us either sleeping or awake, forgetful or mindful, absent or present.

[Note: Col. 0848D: What is expressed here as “according to the difference of our merits” is expressed in Psalm 120, no. 9: “According to the character and earnestness of each person, God is present to each”; and shortly before: “According to our faith, whether wakeful or sleeping, God’s help will be wakeful or sleeping with us.”]

Thus heaven was bowed when he descended, because when he came down to assume humanity, the heavenly ministry stood by him: when the annunciation was made to Mary; when the shepherds saw and heard the heavenly assembly and sound; when angels ministered after the devil’s temptation; when he himself, though wholly in the form of a servant, nevertheless acted in the power of his Father’s majesty.

[Note: Col. 0849D: Here *cum* has the force not of a conjunction, as the printed editions represented it, but of a preposition: as though “together with Christ’s descent”; thereafter the construction is different.]

[Note: Col. 0849D: For the form of God was hidden so completely that bodily eyes saw only the form of a servant. Hence one may understand how, in many passages, Christ is proclaimed as wholly endowed with glory in the form of God, while the substance of his flesh is preserved.]

Thus heaven is bowed when the Power—namely, the Son of God—and honor of heavenly things are brought down to earth.

11. The devil’s power is broken, though still very great. He smokes; he is not yet wholly burned.---That the touched mountains smoke rather than burn—

[Note: Col. 0849D: The latest Paris edition preferred the reading in Bad., Er., and Lips.: “although what smokes is burned; then,” etc. We prefer the manuscript’s reading: “although it indicates that what smokes is being burned.” Since smoke is an indication of burning, and since fire, when it is being prepared, also smokes before it burns, Hilary thinks this comparison shows that the punishment of demons has begun, while their lawful retribution is meanwhile being prepared. “For smoke is meanwhile a preparation for fire which will one day burn,” he says in Psalm 64, no. 9.]

—and that they are scattered rather than illuminated by flashing lightnings, and troubled rather than pierced by arrows sent forth, is said in this way for a most weighty reason of spiritual interpretation. Another psalm indeed signifies parallel things when it says: “Preparing the mountains in your strength, girded with power” (Ps. 64:7).

By the Lord’s coming the devil’s power was shattered and crushed when it was subjected to the faith of holy people. This does not mean that it does not still possess very great strength; but insofar as it has in some measure been subjected, by the condition of its present subjection it is prepared for lawful retribution and punishment. Thus, now touched by God’s power through this same subjection, it smokes, although it is not yet wholly burned; but because it can meanwhile smoke, it must be recognized as capable also of burning. Nor is he alone burned, but all his followers as well. This fire was not prepared for him alone; for the Lord says: “Depart into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). These mountains, then, when touched by the Lord, shall smoke.

12. God’s teaching scatters them.---They will also be scattered by flashing lightnings:

[Note: Col. 0850D: The manuscript reads “by flashed lightning,” which may be referred to Christ in this sense: those who now cannot endure the light of the apostles will much less endure Christ’s light when he appears like lightning.]

that is, they cannot bear the light of those of whom it was said, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). For the Lord’s coming will be understood as lightning appearing from east to west (Matt. 24:27). But meanwhile there are many flashes—that is, the apostolic proclamations and the brightness of God’s teaching—which scatter by the light of their flashing that dense and united power of demons.

[Note: Col. 0850D: The printed texts read “will scatter.” We prefer with the manuscript “scatters,” because the discussion concerns what happens now, until Christ’s flashing light succeeds it.]

13. By believers’ teaching, the devil is driven from his kingdom.---The arrows sent forth will also trouble them. This same prophecy elsewhere recalls these arrows: “The arrows of little children became their wounds” (Ps. 63:8)—little children in malice, as the Apostle says, but not in understanding (1 Cor. 14:20). Thus the words of those who have been reborn to innocence—that is, of the faithful—are sent out like arrows and trouble those smoking mountains, when the blessedness and eternity of the heavenly kingdom are preached; when worldly honor is despised and Christ’s glory is hoped for; when luxury and drunkenness are abandoned and the body is purified by fasts; when avarice is conquered and generosity practiced; when virgins hate their own bodies; when widows wish that they had remained virgins; when confessors despise their lives; when it is desirable for martyrs to die.

All this is accomplished by those arrows—that is, by words of teaching and exhortation—which, when sent forth, trouble those who oppose them, while expectation of Christ’s kingdom is proclaimed and their kingdom comes to an end.

14. The hand of God is Christ.---But the hand of the Lord is also sent from on high. That the hand of God signifies our Lord Jesus Christ in the Spirit is no obscure teaching. For through him all things were made. And we read: “For my hand,” he says, “shall help him” (Ps. 88:22). For through the Son of God the assumed man is delivered, through the glory of the resurrection, from the snares of death and the judgment of unjust condemnation.

15. The waters are peoples destined to perish.---For it follows: “Deliver me from many waters.” That waters mean peoples is familiar knowledge, as Isaiah also teaches when he says: “Therefore, behold, the Lord will bring upon you the strong and abundant water of the river, even the king of the Assyrians” (Isa. 8:7). Their strength and life slip away toward a final destruction, after the pattern of flowing water. As this same Prophet says: “They perished like water flowing past” (Ps. 57:8), because their nature is removed when the increase of the sea into which they are borne ceases.

[Note: Col. 0850D: Namely, because they are carried as far as the seas only for their own destruction, as stated in Psalm 57, no. 4.]

“And from the wicked hand of alien sons.” For those of whom it was said, “Alien sons have grown old” (Ps. 17:46), and to whom it was said, “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44), had ceased to be God’s own.

16. Their right hand is wicked.---They are not alien sons merely by not receiving their Lord, but also by what follows:

“Verse 8: Whose mouth has spoken vanity.” The vanity of their mouth and confession was that by which they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15).

[Note: Col. 0850D: Thus the manuscript. The printed texts read “confusion.”]

For the people chosen for an eternal kingdom chose as king the king of the world—that is, of vanity. “And their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” The right hand is wicked when it strikes with palms, tears with rods, beats with a reed, places the crown of thorns, fastens hands and feet with nails, mixes gall with vinegar, and completes every work of iniquity.

17. A new song: for the nations, because of their new knowledge of God.---After these mighty acts, done and completed by the Lord, we must sing a new song of glorious victory. For he says, “Verse 9: O God, I shall sing a new song to you; upon a ten-stringed psaltery I shall make music to you.” We must consider what this new song is. Many psalms are found that sing a new song. For the ninetieth and ninety-fifth psalm begins thus: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.” And again: “Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among every people.” And again: “Let all the earth be moved before his face; say among the nations, ‘The Lord shall reign.’”

This is the new song which all the earth sings: that knowledge of him who created all things is no longer celebrated only within the boundaries and limits of Judaea; that the glory of the invisible God is now proclaimed among the nations; that all lands of the nations confess the praise due to his honor; that God is shown to be about to reign among the nations.

[Note: Col. 0851D: The manuscript reads “boundaries and limits.”]

This is a new song amid the many errors of the world, an unexpected hymn for nations previously wandering astray: a song by which God is proclaimed to be invisible, incorporeal, eternal, judge of righteous judgment, and king of blessed eternity.

18. Another new song: because of Christ’s wondrous resurrection.---The ninety-seventh psalm also sings a new song: “Sing to the Lord a new song, because the Lord has done wondrous things.” But I do not know whether a new song is to be sung merely because God has done wonders. From earliest and ancient times heaven has remained most beautiful and immovable; from earliest times the stars in it continue their unwearied courses and offices; from earliest times the seasons are ordered by their alternating and unchanging recurrence; from earliest times the earth is rich in yearly fruits; from earliest times man, the most wondrous work of God, is born. If God added no wonder after he created these things, I ask why a new song should be sung because of the wonders accomplished.

[Note: Col. 0852D: That is, from ancient and earliest times.]

But the psalm does not permit us to wander long. It shows for what wonders it sings the new song, saying: “His right hand and his holy arm delivered him. The Lord made known his salvation before the sight of the nations” (Ps. 97:1–2). This is the new song; this is the wonder of God: that his right hand delivered him, that his own power bestowed salvation upon himself. “For I have power,” he says, “to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

The only-begotten Son of God did not require external assistance to save the man in whom he chose to be born; rather, remaining in the glory of his Father’s majesty, he exercised his own power in himself. Through the glory of the resurrection he made his salvation known to the nations, when they recognize that, in him, the flesh of his nature has been transformed into the substance of eternal salvation.

19. Another new song: because authority to judge is granted to the saints.---The one hundred forty-ninth psalm also sings a new song. The Prophet immediately adds why this song is new, saying: “He shall exalt the meek unto salvation. The saints shall rejoice in glory; they shall exult in their resting places. The exaltations of God shall be in their throats, and two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples; to bind their kings in manacles and fetters, and their nobles in iron chains; to execute upon them the judgment that is written. This glory is for all his saints” (Ps. 149:4 ff.).

This is the new song: God’s saints receive the power of eternal judgment. For, according to the Apostle, “the saints shall judge the world” (1 Cor. 6:2). Therefore we sing this new song: vengeance among the nations, rebuke among the peoples, manacles and fetters for kings, iron chains for nobles, and the sentence of the written judgment against them.

20. The ten-stringed psaltery. Kings as partners in God’s kingdom.---A similar song is sung in the new song of this psalm: “O God, I shall sing a new song to you; upon a ten-stringed psaltery I shall make music to you, who give salvation to kings.” The ten-stringed psaltery may mean either that the instrument has ten strings, or that this new song is sung through an instrument of ten utterances and deeds; or that man himself, stretched out upon ten strings—his hands and feet—thus makes music in the perfect action and movement of his spiritual works, so as to sing this new song.

“Verse 10: Who give salvation to kings”—to those kings to whom it was said: “Come, blessed of my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34); who will bind nobles, bind kings in manacles and fetters, judge, rebuke, and execute vengeance.

21. Christ’s deliverance is the salvation of kings.---He shows how salvation is given to kings: “Who,” he says, “deliver David your servant”—that David, namely, concerning whom this same book elsewhere prophesies in the person of God the Father: “I have laid help upon one who is mighty; I have exalted one chosen from among my people.
