I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him. For my hand shall help him. He shall call upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, the defender of my salvation.’ And I shall make him my firstborn, exalted above all kings of the earth. And his throne shall be like the sun before me, and like the moon perfect forever, and a faithful witness in heaven” (Ps. 88:20 ff.).

And again, in the same psalm, in his own person addressing the Father: “Remember, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth, the reproach of your servant, which I have held in my bosom, from many nations; with which your enemies reproached you, O Lord, with which they reproached the change of your Anointed” (ibid. 50 ff.). This one David received into his bosom the reproaches of many nations. “For he bore our sins and carried our infirmities; by his wound we were healed” (Isa. 53:5).

Thus, when this David is delivered and removed from the law of death, salvation is also given to kings. For he is “the firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18). And as in Adam we all die, so also in Christ we shall all rise again (1 Cor. VIII, 22). His deliverance, therefore, is the salvation of kings. For they shall reign, conformed to his glory, through his assumption of our nature into union with himself, and shall in turn all remain in participation in his nature.

[Note: Col. 0853D: Bad., Er., and Lips. read “condition,” which the latest Paris edition also preferred. With the first edition and the manuscript we retain “union,” that is, fellowship; for Psalm 67, no. 37, reads: “God is therefore wonderful in his saints, whom, having made them conformed to the glory of his body, he, who is mediator, will also through himself assume into the unity of the Father’s majesty: since the Father is in him by nature, and he in turn is in us through fellowship in the flesh.”]

22. Therefore this David is delivered from the sword of the wicked. For Jesus laid down his spirit when he willed; he did not wait for the wound inflicted to cause his life to depart. The irreligious hand had no right over his life. For he says: “Rescue me from the evil sword.” Although, after his body was already lifeless, the soldier pierced his side (John 19:34), he employed the service of cruelty; but the power to send forth his spirit left no occasion for his life to be violated.

23. The opinion of false happiness is rejected.---He then completes the new song with a hymn of new confession, condemning as false the judgments of earth and the joys of worldly goods, when he says: “Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity. Verses 12–15: Whose sons are like a young plantation firmly established in their youth; whose daughters are adorned and embellished like the likeness of a temple; whose storehouses are full, pouring forth from one into another; whose sheep are fruitful and abundant in their goings forth; whose oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no passage through, no outcry in their streets. They called the people blessed to whom these things belong; blessed is the people whose Lord is its God.”

These, I think, are the goods of this world which the common judgment of all calls blessed: to speak and act in worldly ways; to seize or buy honors; to grow rich at a fraudulent price; to boast in children of mature age, whose flourishing years are confidently established in the vigor of youthful delight; to desire daughters of beautiful appearance and adorn them like a temple by the useless outlay of great wealth; to burst granaries with multiplied produce, so that other storehouses, too narrow for what they contain, pour out the amassed riches; to desire doubled offspring among the sheep, whose departure no encounter with a wild beast diminishes; to delight in the fattening of one’s oxen; even to furnish strong enclosures around one’s houses so that no one may pass through them; not to weep, mourn, or groan, but to be hindered by no affliction of adverse calamity in the prosperous course of one’s happiness.

They called blessed the people to whom these things belonged. But the Prophet knows that this judgment of blessedness is false. For what can all these many and great goods of the world gain for a life that death will cut short? He therefore shows which people is blessed, saying: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is its God”—that God who, although he grants these earthly things mentioned above, will nevertheless bestow eternity upon those who use them rightly; who chose us in his Son before the foundation of the world to be co-heirs; who will be God all in all. To him be glory, praise, honor, power, dominion—to the Father in the Son, to the Son in the Father and in the Holy Spirit—now and always and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: Col. 0854D: This conclusion is unique in its doxology of the whole Trinity, whereas the other treatises usually end with a blessing of the Son alone.]

## PSALM 144

**A praise: to David himself.**

“I shall exalt you, my God and my King, and I shall bless your name for ever and ever. Every day I shall bless you, and I shall praise your name for ever and ever. Great is the Lord, and exceedingly praiseworthy; and there is no end to his greatness. Generation after generation shall praise your works, and they shall proclaim your power. They shall speak of the magnificence of your majesty and of your holiness, and they shall recount your wonders. They shall declare the might of your awesome deeds, and they shall recount your greatness. They shall pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness, and they shall exult in your righteousness. [Below: ‘your righteousness they shall exult.’] The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and of great mercy. [Below, *and* is absent.] The Lord is kind to all, and his mercies are over all his works. Let all your works confess you, O Lord, and let your saints bless you. [Below: ‘let them confess you.’] Let them confess you; they shall speak of the glory of your kingdom and proclaim your power, so that they may make known to the children of men your power and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom. Your kingdom is a kingdom [below, ‘kingdom’ is not repeated] of all ages, and your dominion is in every generation and descent. The Lord is faithful in his words and holy in all [below, ‘works’ is added] his works. The Lord supports all who fall [below: ‘supports,’ ‘fall’], and sets upright [below: ‘raises’] all who are cast down. The eyes of all hope in you, and you give [below: ‘O Lord, and you give’] them their food in due season. You open your hand and fill every living soul with good pleasure. The Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works. The Lord is near to all [below, ‘all’ is absent] who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth. He does [below: ‘will do’] the will of those who fear him; he shall hear their prayer and save them. The Lord preserves all who love [below: ‘God preserves those who love’] him, and he shall destroy all sinners. My mouth shall speak the praise of God [below: ‘of the Lord’], and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever.”

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM
1. Christ is praised in this psalm under the name of David. — The psalm is complete, being occupied solely with the praises of God. Its very title also teaches that the psalm contains only the proclamation of God. Yet, by adding the pronoun, according to Greek usage, here as in the other psalms, it shows that he is praised by this David as David praises him. And who this one is whom this psalm praises, all prophecies of every age proclaim, as this Prophet himself often testified concerning him:

“Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you” (Ps. 44 [45]:7–8).

And again:

“All kings shall worship him, and all nations shall serve him. His name shall be blessed for ages; his name endures before the sun. In him all tribes of the earth shall be blessed; all nations shall magnify him” (Ps. 71 [72]:11, 17).

Therefore this psalm sings the praise of him in whose person we remember it was said: “But I have been established by him as king upon Sion, his holy mountain. The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession. You shall rule them with a rod of iron” (Ps. 2:6 ff.).

Daniel bore witness to the perpetuity of this kingdom, saying:

“In the days of those kingdoms the God of heaven will raise up another kingdom which shall never be destroyed for ever; and his kingdom shall not be left to another people. It shall crush and scatter all kingdoms, and this kingdom shall stand for ever” (Dan. 2:14).

And again:

“And behold, coming with the clouds of heaven, one like a son of man came and reached the Ancient of Days; and he was presented before him, and dominion and honour and a kingdom were given to him. All peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him; his power is an everlasting power which shall never pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. 7:13–14).

This king, then, is praised by the words contained in this psalm: “I will exalt you, my God and my king”; and by these: “Your saints shall confess you; they shall declare the glory of your kingdom and speak of your power, that they may make known to the children of men your power and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom. Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion endures through every generation and descent.”

2. We are instructed to marvel at God. — Although here, because of the glory of the eternal kingdom, in which he himself shall reign while the saints reign with him, praise is sung to God in the Prophet’s confession, still the reasoning and order of the praise itself are so arranged that what is said of him is proclaimed according to the understanding common to all: so that, as far as ordinary human speech permits, it may instruct us concerning that immense and incomprehensible nature of God—not indeed unto the perfect truth of knowledge, but unto admiration [Col. 0855D] of that mighty power which is his. For we can admire him as greatly as lies within us; but we cannot know how great he himself is.

3. The praise of Father and Son is mutual. — Yet since throughout the psalm there is a simple and absolute praise of God, we must remember that the Father is praised in the Son and the Son in the Father. Since, through likeness of substance and property of nature, each is in the other, both are one, and he who has seen the Father sees the Son, we must remember that it makes no difference which of the two one supposes to be praised. For both the likeness of power and works which they have reciprocally, and the divinity of the Father who is God and of the Son who is God—begotten from the Father and born in an undiffering nature—testify that they are one.

4. Against those who deny God’s providence or the immortality of the soul. — Thus the psalm begins, verses 1 and 2:

“I will exalt you, my God and my king, and I will bless your name for ever and ever and ever. Every day I will bless you, and I will praise your name for ever and ever and ever.”

The meaning and force of prophetic lofty speech must be understood through attentive diligence in hearing. For he says: “I will exalt you, my God and my king.” Many magnify God through those things which, in the works of the world established by him, are subjected to our knowledge; but few are those willing to believe that he will be their king. For they either deny that God has care for human affairs, or, to console the conscience of deeds impiously committed, presume the annihilation of soul and body, and refuse to acknowledge that divine judgment has been appointed over good and evil persons.

[Note: Col. 0855D] Cicero appears to have been disposed to wish this were true when, after setting out Strato’s view in Book IV of the *Academic Questions*—“Surveying the individual parts of the world, he teaches that whatever exists or comes to pass comes to pass, or has come to pass, through natural weights and motions”—he adds: “Thus he frees God from a great task, and me from fear. For who, if he thinks himself cared for by God, can fail to dread the divine power day and night?” If this pagan was uncertain concerning God’s providence, what ought the Christian to think, for whom the contrary judgment is certain?

But the Prophet takes his starting-point for proclaiming God from the fact that God is his king. And now he blesses the name of him who is his king and God, because of expectation of the kingdom, saying: “I will bless your name for ever.” Yet because he knows that he will owe gratitude to God and his king even when he remains in that kingdom—when the weakness of his perishable body has been changed and the dominion of hostile death driven away, and he stands before his king conformed to him and coeternal with him—he adds, “and for ever and ever,” that is, in that age in which, when the condition of this present age has been put off, it will now be renewed as an age of ages by the succession of eternity.

[Note: Col. 0856D] In the printed editions: “now for ever.” The manuscript more correctly has: “now as an age.” Thus in Psalm 118, no. 7: “He says ‘age of ages,’ as it were a time of time, because through a certain succeeding change the age of this age is to come.”

5. The distinction between blessing and praise. We owe both to God always. — In this present age, someone blessing God may be unable always to remain in the office of blessing, while he is hindered by grief, occupied by fear, held in anxious sickness; and, whether his mind has grown numb or ungrateful, he is silent in God’s blessings.

[Note: Col. 0856D] In the manuscript: “or is hindered by place.”

But the perfection of prophetic faith is free from changes of infirmities of this kind, saying: “Every day I will bless you.” It has no vacant time and no day idle to it, without being always occupied in the confession of blessings.

It often happens, however, that we may speak well of persons whom we cannot praise. To abstain from evil is worthy of blessing. But merely to admit no evil has no praise unless the abstinence from evil is also followed by the glory of good work. We may indeed bless a benefit done to us, because nature requires that we not speak ill of those by whose goodwill we are sustained. But if they are bespattered with other vices, they are blessed on account of our advantage, but are not commended by a true judgment.

The perfection of God, however, permits nothing partial in itself. For as he is blessed, so also is he praiseworthy: he has both the confession of our blessing arising from those things by which we enjoy his beneficence toward us, and the proclamation arising from admiration of the virtues perfect in himself. Therefore the Prophet, who was to bless him every day, added also: “And I will praise your name for ever and ever and ever.”

[Note: Col. 0857D] The manuscript of Micy and the first Paris edition read: “When he blesses, when he praises for ever,” etc.

When he praises the Blessed One and praises him for ever and ever, the Prophet’s office is deficient in nothing: neither in blessing, nor in praise, nor in time.

6. The first ground for praising God: his infinity. — Then follows verse 3:

“Great is the Lord, and exceedingly praiseworthy; and there is no end of his greatness.”

This is the first and chief praise of God: that he has nothing mediocre in himself, nothing bounded, nothing measured, whether in his greatness or in his praise. His power is not enclosed by opinion, contained by places, expressed by names, or subjected to times. Our perception is too narrow for it, our intellect dull, our speech mute. His magnificence knows no end; and his immense greatness does not permit any opinion that might measure him. Extended everywhere, it is extended always, having this praise of its infinity; for it surpasses all understanding of this infinite quality in itself.

7. By whom he is to be praised. — Since neither this knowledge of immeasurable greatness nor the praise of God’s works belongs to all nations—to whom life and perception were given from the creation of the world and would be given thereafter—he consequently adds, verse 4:

“Generation and generation shall praise your works.”

Certainly not generations and generations which are many and contrary in both time and peoples; but the generation that began from Abraham, which through the sign of circumcision is reckoned into the Law; and the generation renewed in Christ, which is instructed from prophetic teaching unto faith in evangelical justification. To these generations, therefore, it belongs peculiarly to praise God’s works.

[Note: Col. 0857D] Hilary does not mean that before Abraham there were none who praised God’s works, since he repeatedly teaches that obedience to God’s commandments extended from the establishment of the age. Explaining this explicitly in Psalm 118, no. 8, he adds: “In this path Abel also ran, Seth persevered, Enoch pleased God, Noah deserved preservation, and Melchizedek,” etc. Nor did they please God except by praising God and his works. His point is only that the distinct generation and people which praised God began to be set apart in Abraham’s age.

8. God is to be praised because he is mighty in his deeds. — No other reason urges us to praise God’s works than that all things were powerfully wrought by him: for the proclamation is not that he did something, but that he did it powerfully. Therefore he adds: “And they shall proclaim your power.”

[Note: Col. 0858D] The printed editions read “who”; the manuscript more correctly reads “because.”

9. Magnificent. — But the power of his works must be proclaimed only when it is equal to the magnificence of the worker, so that the operation may be understood to be powerful in accordance with the magnificence of the Powerful One. Therefore follows, verse 5: “The magnificence of your majesty.”

[Note: Col. 0858D] The editions read: “which corresponds to the magnificence of the worker”; corrected from the manuscript.

10. Holy, or beneficent. — But magnificence, if it retains only what it has in itself for itself, has admiration but not praise; and the operation of the powerful one is idle for others unless, through the holiness of the worker, it imparts from itself some benefit to those who will praise and admire it. Hence this fittingly follows: “And they shall speak of your holiness.”

Holiness is already good, nor does it profit itself alone; it does not consume what it has from itself within the use of its own advantage. For, in order to draw others toward beneficence, it commends itself by offices of holiness. Yet it would display nothing worthy of admiration from itself if it existed for itself alone. But this is the distinctive and admirable quality of holiness: that it grants to the use of others that which is holy in itself—being itself in need of nothing, except perhaps through goodwill, only that another may make use of it. Therefore, after the words, “And they shall speak of your holiness,” he fittingly adds: “And they shall recount your wonders.”

[Note: Col. 0858D] Origen, in Corderius, interpreting “wonders” as miracles performed for the benefit of some persons, sheds considerable light upon this passage of Hilary. The peoples speak of holiness which has become known to them through miracles.

11. Terrible to the wicked. — It is wonderful that holiness, profiting nothing to itself, overflows for the benefit of another’s blessedness; but it is more wonderful that holiness is full of terror, lest, if it makes itself indiscriminately available to those who use or abuse it—being common alike to good and evil persons, and supplying itself as though by necessity of nature—it should have no admiration as holiness. Therefore he immediately adds, verse 6: “And they shall declare the power of your terrible deeds”; so that, while speaking of holiness and recounting wonders, they may also declare the power of terrible things, with admiration positioned between holiness and terror. Thus sweet terror and terrible sweetness make terror admirable and sweetness terrible.

[Note: Col. 0858D] In the editions of Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig, “of error” is corruptly printed in place of “lest it should not,” etc. This whole passage is now corrected from the manuscript. The later Paris edition still retained “lest it should not.”

12. Great without measure; always and abundantly good. — Understanding this great magnitude of admirable balance, the Prophet adds: “And they shall recount your greatness.” For it belongs to infinite greatness that, in God, what is terrible should be sweet and what is sweet should be terrible. But greatness has no measure; for if it were measured, it would no longer be greatness, because it would not lack measure. Therefore, so that the admiration proper to holiness and terror may consist in the infinity of its greatness, it shall remain both always and abundant, defined neither by time nor by supply. Therefore he joins to it, verse 7: “They shall utter the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness,” because neither is remembrance interrupted by forgetfulness nor abundance diminished by want.

[Note: Col. 0858D] Thus the first Paris edition with the manuscript. The other editions read “measure,” which cannot stand with the words immediately preceding: “it has no measure,” etc.

13. God’s goodness is regulated by justice. — The Prophet preserved the order of his discourse, tempering the remembrance and abundance of sweetness by the condition of greatness both regulated and preserved, saying: “And they shall exult in your justice.”

[Note: Col. 0859C] The editions read “your righteousness,” against both the Greek text and the manuscript.

The remembrance and abundance of sweetness are indeed infinite, because God neither forgets to be sweet nor ceases to be so. Yet justice, interposed, regulates the infinity of remembrance and abundance. It regulates not merely the manner of giving, but the manner of using: while that which is always open equally to all through God’s abundance and remembrance is not received by the wicked because of their unworthiness in using it.

God’s holiness gave his people a way when the sea was divided (Exod. 14:22 ff.); but the same holiness was also terrible power when the ungodly entered that very way. Where there had been salvation for the devout, there punishment came upon the ungodly. Waves solidified with the firmness of a wall surround some; those same waves which had stood still, flowing back, engulf others. For the one group the sea does not know its own nature; the other it punishes by its nature. For the one group, land comes from the sea; for the other, what was sea remains sea. For these, holiness is salvation; for those, terror is death.

Or again, while the three boys sing in the furnace, those standing around are burned by flames which the boys do not feel. For them the fire is tempered into the moisture of dew; these are scorched by blazing fire. The flames are the same within and without; yet according to the diversity of merits, their nature both fails and does not fail. For it remains fire toward those whom it burns; and what is not fire must necessarily be present in those for whom there is dew.

[Note: Col. 0859C] The words “is not” are lacking in the earlier printed editions and are supplied from the manuscript. After these words, namely “dew” must be understood. The whole phrase may also be inverted: “And what is, must necessarily not be in those for whom there is dew.” For, as is said in Book X *On the Trinity*, no. 44: “Both the bodies and the fire lose their nature in them; for the bodies are not burned, nor does the fire burn. Yet in the others both fire and body remain in their nature; for those standing around are burned.”

Thus justice alone regulates the greatness of God’s remembrance and holiness, since through God’s justice holiness gives terror to the wicked and terror tempers holiness toward the righteous.

14. God’s justice is merciful, and his mercy just; unlike those of men. God’s patience toward sinners. — Human justice is indeed upright and useful; yet it is sometimes itself too harsh, so that it is not permitted to use goodness, because in deciding what is just according to the diversity of judgment, it becomes severe. But God’s justice is not equal to human justice. For it is not subject to the law of nature, by which the law of nature itself was established; consequently, when it is just, it is not under necessity not to be good. God’s justice possesses the will to show mercy; yet through the will to show mercy it will not so change from itself that it ceases to be justice.

Human justice, however, tends to become not merciful; and mercy tends to present itself in such a way that it is not just. Mercy will not exist if you begrudge the right of the wealthier person to a needy man who brings a false accusation; if you prefer a woman’s tears to a man’s injury; if you think the insults of a blind man should not be reproved. On the other hand, justice will not retain mercy if you punish the thief of one coin as the thief of an immense treasure—even though the person who lost it had a treasure in that one coin; or if you harass with the examination of punishments a young man entangled in one and the same disgraceful adultery, with a death equal to that imposed on one practised in many adulteries, though the crime is capital in both cases.

[Note: Col. 0859C–0860D] Here “just” must either be added or understood. Shortly afterward the editions of Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig read: “if you prefer a woman’s tears to a man’s injuries,” which is less apt. The editions read “punishment,” not “examination”; corrected from the Micy manuscript, whose reading is confirmed by *Codex Theodosianus* IX.4, “On Appeals,” where it is decreed that the crime of adultery be proved by judicial examinations, and that the judge ought to sew up alive in a sack or burn those guilty of violating marriage, as manifest parricides. The celebrated Letter XLIX of Jerome, concerning a woman beaten seven times, supports this: an innocent woman, accused with a young man of adultery, was beaten so many times, while the young man, preferring to confess himself guilty rather than endure the prolonged torments of a most bitter examination, was beheaded. Ambrose also, *On the Fall of Consecrated Virgins*, Book I, chapter 5, no. 20, indicates that the penalty of death had been decreed for adulterers. Finally, Justinian, Novella 134, chapter 10, approves and confirms Constantine’s constitution concerning punishment for adulterers. Many consider him the first author of this severe law. Yet no one who has read in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 17, Valois edition, will deny that it was in force before Constantine: “When Urbicius had ordered Ptolemy led away to execution, Lucius addressed Urbicius thus: ‘Why have you condemned a man who was convicted neither of adultery nor of fornication, nor of homicide nor theft…?’” Ptolemy suffered under Marcus Aurelius; adulterers were therefore already punished by death. Likewise the author of the Passion of St Vincent, in the *Acts of the Sincere Martyrs*, p. 392, no. 5, lists adultery among crimes liable to capital punishment. In the same Acts, p. 141, Achatius replies to Martianus, consular governor under the emperor Decius, when ordered, “Either sacrifice or die”: “Public law punishes the fornicator, adulterer, thief, corrupter of the male sex, sorcerer, and murderer. If I am guilty of these, before you speak I condemn myself.” Arnobius also, Book IV *Against the Nations*, reproaching the adulteries of pagan gods, says: “Men avenge adulteries by laws and inflict capital punishments upon those whom they have caught overthrowing another’s marriage covenant by assault upon the marriage bed.” Finally, Augustine, *City of God*, Book III, chapter 5, where he says, “The ancient Romans punished adulterous women with some penalty, though not with death,” seems to mean that a different custom prevailed among later Romans. Nor need we mention that the ancient law, Deuteronomy 22:22, provided that the adulterer and adulteress should be punished by death.

These things and others of this kind make human mercy and justice imperfect. But God’s justice is made merciful by the patience granted before the punishments of criminals. Since, contrary to the custom of human impatience, he does not hasten to punish, he has shown mercy. He retains justice in punishment when patience, after mercy, does not produce improvement; he has mercy in punishment when, after patience, he exercises justice.

[Note: Col. 0860D] Here, as elsewhere, the printed editions had substituted “by exercising.”

For God does not seize upon occasions of human sins, nor, as though ignorant of our weakness and nature, does he attack at once with punishment the very time of our error and sin. Rather, he overlooks and delays, and by deferring vengeance awaits the comfort of repentance; showing himself sweet to all, while through the balance of mercy and justice he reserves indulgence as the moderation of severity.

[Note: Col. 0861D] That is, he does not punish immediately when we err or sin; or, as in Psalm 128, no. 8: “He is not swift to punish at the beginnings of human wickedness, but waits for the sinner’s will—even if late—to cease from crimes.”

15. Mercy is God’s chief work. — This is God’s chief excellence; this is what is praiseworthy in the Powerful One: not that he made heaven, because he is powerful; not that he founded the earth, because he is strength; not that he regulated the year by the stars, because he is wise; not that he gave life to man, because he is life; not that he set the sea in motion toward ebb and flow, because he is spirit; but that he is merciful, though just; that he pities, though king; that he overlooks, though God.

Therefore after the words, “They shall exult in your justice,” there follows as though necessarily, verses 8 and 9:

“The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and of great mercy. The Lord is sweet to all, and his compassions are over all his works.”

For his being powerful is the strength of his nature; but his being merciful is the advancement of our salvation. And it is greater not to use one’s own things for oneself, but to confer upon others what is one’s own. Therefore mercy surpasses God’s other works, because his magnificent operation is a matter of his own power, whereas his mercy is for the use of another.

16. Proof of our immortality. — Therefore the Prophet, standing as it were on the summit of divine praises because of mercy, displays the honour owed to God as a public confession, saying, verses 10–13:

“Let all your works confess you, O Lord, and let your saints confess you. They shall declare the glory of your kingdom and speak of your power, that they may make known to the children of men your power and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom. Your kingdom is of all ages, and your dominion is through generation and generation.”

The order of these utterances is worthy of prophetic loftiness. The works confess God: for the magnificence of his works and creation confesses how magnificent he is. But the saints also confess him, for whom he deigns to be king. They speak of the glory of his kingdom, lest, being unknown, it should not be desired for its benefits. They also proclaim the magnificence of the glory of God’s kingdom, lest eternity be despaired of. His dominion also is shown to be through generation and generation, so that the generation may understand itself to be coeternal with his dominion. Thus knowledge of God is in works, the saints’ office lies in teaching, the use of prophecy lies in proclamation, the kingdom’s glory lies in eternity of dominion; and the eternity of dominion must include those over whom it is eternally exercised.

[Note: Col. 0861D] The editions read: “so that it may subject itself to coeternal dominion”; corrected from the Micy manuscript, except that it corruptly has *dominatu*. Hilary reasons thus: the eternity of dominion must necessarily include in eternity those over whom it is eternally exercised; but it is exercised eternally through generation and generation; therefore that generation must necessarily be coeternal. It does not appear to what it refers itself as coeternal except to generation. The same argument is repeated in the final words of this treatise, from which it is clear that *dominatui*, not *dominatu*, should be read here.

17. The holiness of God’s works confirms faith in his words. — And immediately the Prophet adds an exhortation that we should seek this with faithful hopes:

“The Lord is faithful in his words and holy in all his works.”

Faith in his words might perhaps waver unless holiness were joined to his works. Thus holiness in works confirms faith in words, so that you do not doubt the faithfulness in promises of one whose holiness you experience in things. For if we understand God to be holy because we are born, live, are nourished, and abound in every provision suited to human nature, such holiness cannot be unfaithful in its utterances.

18. God upholds the penitent. — But the Prophet knows also another work of God’s holiness, in what follows:

“The Lord upholds all who are falling, and raises up all who are cast down.”

God’s holiness is present to all and does not withdraw itself from human assistance. Yet the Prophet still preserves the principle of justice and mercy. For the Lord upholds not those who have collapsed, but those who are falling. Though the downward tendency of nature may draw them into a fall, repentance—which is the author of ceasing—will nevertheless stop them so that they do not fall utterly; and God upholds them in their fall. For “to be falling,” not “to have fallen,” can be established in this sense: that one has not fallen.

[Note: Col. 0861D] The manuscript reads “raises up.” We do indeed have at the beginning of no. 20: “Why he upholds those who are falling and restores those cast down”; but the preceding section also begins from these words: “But those who are cast down are raised.”

[Note: Col. 0862D] Thus the manuscript and first Paris edition. The latest edition wrongly preferred “prophecy,” which had prevailed in the editions of Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig.

[Note: Col. 0862D] The printed editions read “has fallen,” and then “if he stands,” in two words. The manuscript more correctly reads “have fallen, will stop”: that is, those whom repentance will stop, God upholds in their fall. These are the two principal propositions; the remainder are only appendages. Incidentally, observe that repentance is here called “the author of ceasing,” just as confession is called “the profession of ceasing” in Psalm 135, no. 4, and Psalm 137, no. 3.

19. He raises those cast down through frailty or error. — But those who are cast down are also raised. There is a difference, however, between being struck down by an external force and falling by one’s own fall. He is cast down whom youthful heat, through the devil’s prompting, has precipitated into a fall; whom ignorance has driven into error; whom the weakness of nature, employing deceitful enticements, has led into sin. Such a person is more properly struck down than one who has persisted by his own will, whom the practice of vices delights, and who does not repent of what he has done. For repentance for deeds done has consolation of pardon with God; nor is it unworthy of the moderation of severity when, through sorrow for the deed, one thus acknowledges an unwilling disposition.

[Note: Col. 0862D] The editions read “whom vicious practice,” or “whom the practice of vice”; then, “for he has pardon also with God,” etc.; and shortly afterward, “he acknowledges an unwilling disposition,” without “thus.” These are corrected on the authority of the manuscript. On the sinner who does not deserve pardon, see the notes on Psalm 140, no. 8.

20. Every good of body and soul must be expected from God. — Why he upholds those falling and restores those cast down, he teaches in the words that follow, verses 15 and 16:

“The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them their food in due season. You open your hand and fill every soul with blessing.”

Therefore those who are cast down and those who are falling should look toward God with all their eyes. Let no one be so confident in himself that he does not always fear falling and always fear being struck down. From him we must hope that we may not be endangered by a fall or struck down through the weakness of nature. All the aids of life come to us from him: when we live upon foods granted in the seasonableness of their fruits; when, by opening his hand, he fills our souls with spiritual gifts; and when, from the fountain of his power, the abundance of those things pleasing to himself overflows into us.

He distinguishes these two matters in what follows, verse 17:

“The Lord is just in all his ways, and holy in all his works.”

He is just in his ways when he leads our frailty, strengthened by the fellowship of spiritual gifts, into his eternal kingdom; but he is holy in his works when he supplies fruits to all in the fitting seasons, showing his holiness in the nourishment of all and preserving his justice in filling souls with what is pleasing to him.

21. God is wholly everywhere; with what disposition he must be invoked. — After this follows, verse 18:

“The Lord is near to those who invoke him.”

He is not far away who, by the power of his nature, both is himself always everywhere and is always wholly and everywhere, according to the Apostle’s saying: “For in him we are, and in him we live and move” (Acts 17:28). He is near, therefore, to those who invoke him, since there is nothing that exists without him. But the following words teach to which invokers he is near: “To all who invoke him in truth.” Not to those who invoke him idly, nor in the uncertainty of faithless hesitation, but to those who invoke the true God in faithful truth.

22. With what result. — And when he is near, he shows what he gives to those who invoke him in truth, saying:

“He will fulfil the will of those who fear him.”

God will not fulfil shameful wills or vicious desires, but the wills of those who fear him—innocent through fear, honourable through faith, modest through reverence; and wills not idle, not mute, nor disdainfully refusing by a sort of silent contempt to hope anything from him, but wills which prayer expresses and petitions attest. Therefore he adds: “And he will hear their prayer.” The will, then, which God fulfils is that which he hears in the voice of prayer. But what will of those who pray shall be fulfilled? “And he will save them,” he says.

This is what those who fear God will; this is why they pray to be heard: that eternal death may not rule over them, that they may not be assigned to the destruction of perpetual judgment, but may be safe under God’s protection. For it follows, verse 20: “God guards those who love him.” Therefore he will save them by guarding them—that is, by preserving as participants in the eternal kingdom those who fear, pray, and love. Then follows: “And he will destroy all sinners,” who have neither feared as human beings, nor prayed as subjects, nor loved as persons endowed with life and the world.

[Note: Col. 0863D] These things are explained more clearly in Psalm 120, no. 16: “For this guardianship is not of this time and age . . . but is the expectation of future good, when, upon departing from the body, all believers will be kept through the Lord’s guardianship until that entrance into the heavenly kingdom, being meanwhile placed in Abraham’s bosom . . . until the time arrives to enter the kingdom of heaven again.” Hence, immediately above, we would prefer “the Lord” to “God guards,” as the psalm text prefixed to the treatise reads.

23. God must always be praised. The Prophet desires this from all. — The Prophet concludes the confession of honour due to God, saying, verse 21:

“My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord.”

It is not enough for him to have praised, unless he also does not cease praising. For he will still praise while already praising. But while he praises, he also exhorts the whole human race to God’s blessing: “And let all flesh bless his holy name.” By the constancy of his office and faith, he himself will indeed always praise; but the Prophet both takes care that all may bless God and desires it.

[Note: Col. 0864D] The editions of Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig read “that praiseworthy one,” wrongly. Then the same editions read, “but the Prophet takes care of these things”; the Paris edition, “but the Prophet’s care.” The manuscript’s reading is more elegant.

For he does not say, “They shall bless,” as though certain that it will happen in the future; rather, from the affection of his desire, he says, “Let them bless.” He adds this so that he may be understood to desire it rather than be confident that it will so happen. Then he asks that the blessing be not temporary but eternal: “for ever and ever and ever.” We ought rather to desire that we may eternally bless the Eternal One; for one who blesses eternally must necessarily remain coeternal with that Eternal One—namely, our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten and firstborn Son of God, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: Col. 0864D] The editions, with the manuscript, read “so that that…” Then the editions of Basel, Erasmus, Leipzig, and the latest Paris edition remove the following *ut* (“so that”). We prefer to replace the first *ut* with *et* (“and”), especially since such interchange is not rare in old books. On this reading, after “and that,” “he said” must be understood. Shortly afterward, “rather than he should be confident” is preferable to “rather than he should be confident.”

## Psalm 145

A Psalm of David. Alleluia. Of Haggai and Zechariah.

“Praise the Lord, O my soul. I will praise God [the Lord] during my life; I will sing to my God as long as I exist. Do not put your trust in princes, nor [below: ‘nor’ is absent] in sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. His spirit has gone forth, and he shall return [below: ‘their spirits … and they shall return’] to his earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish. Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, and [below: ‘and’ is absent] whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them; who preserves truth for ever, executes judgment for those suffering wrong [below: ‘for those who suffer wrong’], and gives [Col. 0864D] food to the hungry. The Lord frees those in bonds; the Lord gives wisdom to the blind. The Lord raises up those cast down [below: ‘struck down’]; the Lord loves the righteous. The Lord protects strangers [below: ‘the proselyte’]; he shall take up the orphan and widow, and he has destroyed [below: ‘he shall destroy the way of sinners’] the ways of sinners. The Lord your God, O Sion, shall reign for ever [below: ‘unto eternity’], through generation and generation.”

### Treatise on the Psalm
1. Why the addition to the title was made. The wretched life which is not our life.—The translators thought fit to add something to this psalm also. For whereas the Hebrews prefix only “Alleluia” [Note: [Col. 0865D] Thus the manuscript. The printed editions, however, have “of Alleluia” only. “Of Alleluia” might indeed be tolerated, as not inconsistent with Hilary’s usage; but not “of” alone, since that pertains to “confession.” As for the names Haggai and Zechariah, Theodoret testifies that he found them neither in the Hebrew nor in other translators, nor even in the Septuagint of the Hexapla.], they chose to put Haggai and Zechariah first in the title, in order that we might recognize the psalm as prophetic: because through these prophets, under whom Jerusalem was rebuilt, the building of the eternal Jerusalem was being proclaimed at that very time. The Gospel also bears witness, when the Lord was about to enter the Temple and overturn the tables of the money-changers [Col. 0865B] and the business of buyers and sellers (Matt. 21:4–5): “This happened, that what was spoken through Zechariah the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: ‘Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, meek, sitting upon an ass and upon a young colt under the yoke’” (Zech. 9:9).

2. And, I think, the psalm shows rather the King of this Jerusalem and Zion, when it begins thus, v. 2: “Praise the Lord, O my soul; I shall praise the Lord in my life; I shall sing to my God as long as I am.” Deliberately it also retained the order of the Prophet’s teaching. First, it exhorts that soul to praise which has been established in such a nature as to remain eternal. Then, because through the gift of resurrection it will remember that, with its body glorified, it is wholly coeternal with Him [Col. 0865C]—that is, the body together with the soul—it says confidently of the future: “I shall praise the Lord in my life.” For this life which now exists amid the infirmities of the body is not its own life. This life began from that Adam; it was not begun with Adam—the life which the Apostle knows to be not life but death when he says: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). [Note: [Col. 0865D] The printed editions read, “thus began.” The manuscript more rightly reads “this,” that is, a life wretchedly subjected to bodily desires and infirmities. Augustine aptly says, *Retractations*, I.10.3: “For that alone is truly and properly called the nature of man which was originally created without fault.”] Therefore in that life of its own, in which man was first established [Note: [Col. 0865D] The printed editions read “constituted.” The manuscript’s “instituted” is more elegant; namely, the life which, as is explained in the exposition of Psalm 136, no. 5, is without desire, pain, fear, or sin. Here life is blessed in a certain respect, not in every respect, when compared with the life of the first man. [Col. 0866D] For elsewhere Hilary commonly attributes to our bodies after the resurrection endowments which Adam lacked. Yet his meaning here is that of Augustine, *Retractations*, I.11.3, where he says: “What I said—‘That health will then be most firm and certain, when this body has been restored, at its appointed time and in its proper order, to its original stability’—must not be understood as though bodies after the resurrection will not be better than those of the first human beings in paradise. Those bodies will no longer need bodily food, as these are fed; but ‘original stability’ must be understood only insofar as those bodies will suffer no sickness, just as these could not have suffered it before sin.”], it will praise God. Thirdly, lest he be thought irreligious in this present body itself, he added: “I shall sing to my God as long as I am”—supply, “in this wretched life” (see Prologue, no. 19). Throughout this entire book of Psalms, we remember that “to sing psalms” signifies the religious actions of the body: actions intended to please God through fitting and harmonious varieties of bodily movement.

3. One must not hope in kings whom antiquity fashioned into gods.—After this he rebukes the foolish opinions of men and the vain religious devotion attached to the names of kings, whom antiquity fashioned into gods for itself, saying: “Do not put your trust in princes,” vv. 3–4, “nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. Their spirit shall go forth, and they shall return to their earth; on that day all their thoughts shall perish.” He forbade trust in kings. And in what kings? He adds: “And in the sons of men.” And in what sons of men? Those “in whom there is no salvation.” And why is there no salvation? He shows it: “Their spirit shall go forth, and all shall return to their earth.” And what shall befall those who return to earth? “On that day all their thoughts shall perish.” They are themselves of corrupt origin, since they remained sons of men and would not become sons of God; they are also devoid of all salvation, because, when the spirit has gone forth [Col. 0866B] and their bodies have been dissolved into earth, their bodily and earthly thoughts will perish with the earthly body.

4. How much more rightly hope is placed in the Maker of the world.—But lest you place confidence in such kings, he shows in whom hope should be placed, vv. 5–7: “Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob; his hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them; who keeps truth for ever, and executes judgment for those who suffer wrong.” It is no transient thought to hope in such a King; nor does that hope perish which reaches out to the Creator of heaven, earth, sea, and this whole universe. He is the Helper in whom one must hope, in whom there is no deceit. For although, according to prophecy, every human being is a liar [Col. 0866C], He alone keeps truth for ever; and, keeping truth, He executes judgment on behalf of those who suffer wrong. Blessed is the one whom, by helping, He will make Israel out of Jacob [Note: [Col. 0866D] Thus the manuscript. The printed editions read, “makes Israel,” and shortly afterward, “who in the Creator.”]. His hope is eternal because he trusts in the Creator of heaven, earth, and sea. The Creator of all these things is both true and judge: true in keeping truth, and judge in executing judgment.

5. God satisfies hunger for the word. He looses spiritual fetters. He dispels the blindness of the age.—Nor does He merely execute judgment, but also does what follows: “He gives food to the hungry. The Lord looses those in fetters,” vv. 8–9; “the Lord gives wisdom to the blind; the Lord raises up the crushed; the Lord loves the righteous. The Lord guards the proselyte; He will receive the orphan and widow, and He will destroy the way of sinners.” It is not unprofitable indeed to understand these things bodily [Col. 0866D]; but the passage embraces something deeper and greater [Col. 0867A]. “He gives,” it says, “food to the hungry.” Let us see what food, and to what hungry persons. Bodily food is not always supplied by God precisely when we hunger for it [Note: [Col. 0867D] The printed editions read “not nevertheless.” The manuscript more rightly reads “not then.”]. Its provision is annual, and thus it is supplied within a period of time, so that none may hunger within that time. There is, then, another hunger and there are hungry persons of another kind, to whom food is supplied when they hunger. For it is written in the prophet Amos (8:11): “Behold, I shall bring a famine upon the earth—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine that the word of God may be heard.” The Lord therefore bestows upon the hungry this food of preaching. Once it has been received as food, the bonds of the devil are undone. For, according to the Gospels, he bound the daughter of Abraham for eighteen years (Luke 13:16). Such food also releases the fetters [Col. 0867B] of greed, lust, and drunkenness. And, once the fetters have been loosed, it grants wisdom to the blind. Had the Prophet been speaking of bodily gifts, he would rather have mentioned light bestowed on the blind [Note: [Col. 0867D] From this passage it is clear that Hilary did not know the reading of our Vulgate: “The Lord enlightens the blind.”]. But because, through the food [Note: [Col. 0867D] “Of the word” is absent from the manuscript.] of the word, hunger is expelled and the fetters of the age are loosed, the blindness of the age is likewise driven away through the imparting of wisdom. For after a great famine of divine knowledge we are nourished with spiritual food; and when the fetters by which we are not permitted to run toward eternal things have been loosed [Note: [Col. 0867D] The manuscript reads “are now permitted”; perhaps more correctly, for the reason that “the word” may refer not only to “fetters loosed,” but also to the relative “by which,” as though, “when those by which … have been loosed.”], and blindness has been scattered by wisdom granted to us, we behold our Creator with the eyes of understanding. Thus the long famine, grievous fetters, and foolish blindness cease, and what follows succeeds.

6. The orphan.—The crushed are raised, the righteous are loved, [Col. 0867C] strangers or proselytes are guarded, the orphan and widow are received, and the way of sinners is destroyed. Whoever he may be who now belongs to God, though he does not have the same gift as another, nevertheless has a gift proper to himself: so that, though crushed [Note: [Col. 0867D] The printed editions read: “although he is, he now hungers; if he is now fettered and foolish,” etc., very confusedly. The confusion is now removed with the aid of the manuscript. Moreover, in this and the preceding passages “hunger” means not a holy desire for the word, but lack and deprivation of it; and those whom Hilary here calls hungry he calls below, in the exposition of Psalm 146, no. 9, dry and unfruitful [Col. 0868D], and this because of unbelief and impiety, as is suggested there in no. 8.], even if he does not hunger, is not fettered, and is not foolish, he may nonetheless be raised, lest he lie fallen for ever; so that the righteous person may be loved because of righteousness; so that the stranger, though not loved as a righteous person, may at least be preserved because he has come; so that the orphan, because he has renounced the devil as his father, may not be left orphaned, following the example of the Apostles; and so that the widow may be received as a bride, after this world has been crucified to her in Christ (see Exposition of Psalm 131, no. 24). For the Apostle called all the faith of believers a widow, since through the fulfillment of the times the Law, like her first husband, had died to her [Col. 0867D] (Rom. 7:4). Yet not only is the widow received, but [Col. 0868A] also the way of sinners is destroyed. When they have been plunged into destruction, the city Jerusalem of that holy King will be inhabited—not, certainly, this Jerusalem which, desolate and overthrown, pays the penalty for its profane parricide.

7. Which Zion is the seat of God’s kingdom.—For he concludes thus, v. 10: “The Lord shall reign for ever, your God, O Zion, from generation to generation.” Where is that Zion in which the Lord shall reign? Surely not in that—understand, “He shall reign”—which killed the Prophets and stoned those sent to it? That city plainly no longer exists today; and how will the Lord reign for ever when the seat of His kingdom has been overthrown? Rather, He will reign in that Zion which is the heavenly mother, which, built from living stones, and filled with holy citizens [Note: [Col. 0868D] In the manuscript of Mic., “filled through the generation of faith,” with the intervening words omitted. Some may judge the omitted words interpolated in fact, since the generation of the Law seems to belong to that Zion which killed the Prophets and which is immediately denied to be the seat of God’s kingdom. But for Hilary the generation of the Law included two kinds of people: those who fulfilled the Law carnally and those who fulfilled it spiritually. And just as in Psalm 144, no. 7, he declares that it belongs properly both to the generation of the Law and to the generation of faith, in the persons of the latter, to praise the works of God, so here he declares both to be the seat of God’s kingdom. Conversely, in Psalm 134, no. 22, considering only the carnal, he states that the memory of God’s works passed from the Jewish generation to the generation of Christians.], will be thronged through the generation of the Law and through the generation of faith [Col. 0868B] by the household of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXLVI

Alleluia. Of Haggai and Zechariah.

Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good; let praise be pleasing to our God. The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersions of Israel. He heals those broken in heart and binds up their wounds. He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name. Great is our Lord, and great is His power; and His wisdom has no number. The Lord receives the meek, but humbles sinners down to the earth. Begin [below: “Begin anew”] unto the Lord in confession; [Col. 0868C] sing psalms to our God upon the harp: He who covers heaven with clouds and prepares [below: “who prepares”] rain for the earth; who brings forth grass on the mountains and herb for the service of humankind; who gives [below: “who gives”] food to their beasts and to the young ravens that call upon Him. He has not taken pleasure [below: “will take pleasure”] in the strength of a horse, nor is His good pleasure in the dwellings of a man. The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear Him and in those who hope in [below: “all who hope upon”] His mercy.

## Exposition of the Psalm

1. The temporal rebuilding of Jerusalem is not sung in this psalm.—After Jerusalem’s first overthrow and the people’s captivity and removal to Babylon, the history of Kings and the books of Ezra relate that the same city was rebuilt. But the evidence of events teaches that today it no longer exists. We have said this beforehand [Col. 0868D; 0869A], lest, because the translators thought fit to place the title “Of Haggai and Zechariah” upon this psalm and the preceding one, we should suppose that the foreknowledge of this prophecy applies to the people of that period. For the Prophet, not ignorant of the heavenly mystery, had said that human building was vain in the building of God’s city, since a city could not be eternal unless built by God Himself. He would not now exhort us to rejoice at Jerusalem’s rebuilding by God, when he had previously foretold that it was vainly built by human beings.

If anyone perhaps thinks that what is said in another psalm—“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 126:1)—was said because the Prophet foresaw the overthrow of the city in which the Temple was to be built, such a person should remember, if he understands this passage thus, that this same Prophet could not have been ignorant that the building renewed a second time by Zerubbabel would be vain and perishable. Nor did he say that the building begun by Solomon was not established by God merely because it would be destroyed by the king of Babylon—Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chron. 36:26)—when after seventy years it was rebuilt, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy (Jer. 29:10). Yet he proclaims that the work carried out by Zerubbabel was a building of God, although afterwards it was ruined and dissolved without any restoration; and he proclaims that the former, though its destruction was followed by renewal, was nevertheless vain and human, while this latter destruction, which occurred without hope of rebuilding, is renewed by the perpetuity of divine work. All such modes of interpretation are foolish and ridiculous.

2. The spiritual Jerusalem is invited to praise God through good works.—The Prophet praises the Lord as builder of that Jerusalem which, according to the Gospels, is the city of the holy King (Matt. 5:35), in which the saints rising through the Lord are shown [Note: [Col. 0869D] The printed editions read “dwell.” We judge “are shown,” with the manuscript, preferable; it alludes here to Matthew 27:53: “and, coming out of the tombs after His resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many.” Thus “are shown” corresponds to “appeared.”], and which joyfully received the Lord entering on the colt of an ass [Note: [Col. 0869D] The printed editions read “in hope”; they are corrected from the manuscript.] in the hope of the saints. Bodily, indeed, the Lord entered by such a riding into that Jerusalem which kills the Prophets and stones the Apostles (Matt. 21:9); but that joy belonged to another city [Note: [Col. 0870D] Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read “will be.”]. Therefore on account of the building of that city the Prophet calls us, saying, v. 1: “Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good; let praise be pleasing to our God.” The praise whose psalm is good is not a matter of slight rejoicing. And, as we have often said, a psalm generally signifies not so much an activity of the voice as an office of bodily action. For we praise God not so much by speech as by deed and acts of obedience, just as sea, earth, and heaven praise God not so much by voice as by the alternation [Col. 0870A] and observance of their functions. The Prophet therefore calls us to God’s praise because the psalm is good, and desires that from this good psalm pleasing praise may be rendered to our God: that is, that our works may please God, through which He is praised by the obedience of our actions.

3. Israel is built here, to be gathered at the end of time.—Verses 2–4: “The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersions of Israel; He heals those broken in heart and binds up their wounds; He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name.” Under King Darius, the Jews returning from Babylon to Jerusalem were given permission to return by edict [Note: [Col. 0870D] This authority was first given by Cyrus in 1 Ezra 1:2, and then confirmed by Darius, his successor, in 1 Ezra 6:14.]. At that time they were held nowhere except within the bounds of the Babylonian kingdom. From what dispersion, then, is Israel gathered? Clearly from that of which the Lord says: “He will send His angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather His elect from the four corners of the winds” (Matt. 24:31). Their gathering will form the assembly of the holy city, which today is being built in us through the work of hope and faith. And therefore building precedes gathering [Note: [Col. 0870D] The printed editions read “gathering does not”; they are corrected with the help of the manuscript.], because through the grace of justification God’s mercy builds us for the gathering of the future city. Otherwise, had He been speaking of earthly construction, gathering should have been proclaimed first, since Israel could not build Jerusalem after its overthrow unless Israel had first been gathered.

4. Its healing has now begun; then it will be perfect.—He then preserves the fitting order, saying, v. 3: “He heals those broken in heart and binds up their wounds.” For when Israel has been gathered and collected into the one city that is being built, all human weaknesses and bodily defects will be removed. When corruption has been swallowed up and all defects of human nature consumed, eternal incorruption will take its place, never to be crushed by any deaths of anxiety. For, according to the Gospels, the Lord came “to heal the broken in heart, to preach release to captives and sight to the blind, to send the broken away into rest, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense” (Luke 4:18–19). These things have indeed already begun in part, because, according to the Apostle, we still abide through a mirror, in an enigma, and in an image of future things (1 Cor. 13:12). Yet we do not yet possess the fruit of that time in which, having obtained the consummation of hope, we may say with the Prophet [Col. 0870D]: “Return, my soul, into your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you [Note: [Col. 0870D] Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read “with me.”]. For He has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling; I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:7 ff.). For when every breaking of heart has been healed and bound up lest it recur for ever, and we have been freed from all these weaknesses of human passions [Col. 0871A], we shall please God in the land of the living, as our soul returns to its rest, from which it was cast out through the transgression of its first parent Adam (see Exposition of Psalm 145, no. 2).

5. The stars: the elect whom God calls and numbers.—But after the proclamation of the healed heart, this too is added to the praise of divine goodness: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name.” If praise is offered to God for the bodily building of Jerusalem, why are the number of stars and names given to all of them advanced here as a chief object of praise for God’s work? Or is it more praiseworthy for God to have numbered and named the stars than to have created them, when creation gave them both number and names, and distinguished names and number by their appellations? But the stars numbered here are those which Abraham beheld in heaven, which Isaac received in his seed, and which Paul distinguished in glory. That they are called by their own names, let us hear from Him who will call them. For He says in the Gospels: “Do not wonder at this, for the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs shall hear His voice and shall come forth” (John 5:28–29). Thus they are called, and they shall come forth. Indeed, they are so numbered by God that even the hairs, thought innumerable in each of us, are numbered, as the same Lord says: “Are not even the hairs of your head numbered?” (Luke 12:7). This is more worthy of the Lord, this is more to be celebrated in His mercy: that those whom He has healed when broken in heart, whose wounds He has bound, He may call by name, number individually, and glorify with heavenly light [Col. 0871C].

6. For these marvelous and glorious works, He says, vv. 5–6: “Great is our Lord, and great is His power; and His wisdom has no number. The Lord receives the meek, but humbles sinners down to the earth.” This belongs properly to the meek—because, according to the Gospels, “the meek shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4)—that they should be worthy before God of being called, numbered, and made bright. The Lord is great when He gathers the dispersions. His power is great when He makes the broken bright. His wisdom is innumerable when He distinguishes all alike by names and by number. But He who receives the meek also humbles sinners down to the earth. After the reward of holiness comes the punishment of impiety: when the meek have been received into the brightness of stars, sinners, humbled down to the earth, are assigned by the judgment [Col. 0871D] of the infernal law [Note: [Col. 0871D] The printed editions read “excepting the internal law.”].

7. The Creator of all things is not one God and the God of the Law another.—For these reasons the Prophet, as though we hesitated and wavered, exhorts us to praise, saying, vv. 7–8: “Begin unto the Lord in confession; sing psalms to our God upon the harp—He who covers heaven with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who brings forth grass upon the mountains, who gives food to their beasts and to the young ravens that call upon Him.” Prophetic discourse frequently warns us to believe that He is Lord of this universe whom the whole Law has called God, who wished to be called the God [Col. 0872A] of Israel. Thus in this same psalm, after saying, “The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersions of Israel,” and exhorting us to His praise, it adds, “He who covers heaven with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth,” so that the God of the Law and the God of this creation might not be understood as different beings.

The reasoning of this teaching is so proportioned that the names and kinds of the enumerated creation are recalled in such a way as both to show that the God of the promulgated Law is Creator and to contain within themselves the significance of a typical and prophetic institution. We are now urged to confess God because He covers heaven with clouds, prepares rain for earth, produces grass on mountains, gives food to beasts, herb for the service of humankind, and food to young ravens that call upon Him. In all these things God’s providence and goodness are signified: He covers heaven with clouds and pours rains upon the lands; clothes hilltops with grass; provides pasture for beasts and food for birds, because everything He has created awaits nourishment from Him [Col. 0872B]. But when carefully examined, all these things contain the force of another meaning.

8. The several meanings of clouds. The teaching of saints is signified by them.—For we know of clouds to which God commands that they should not rain upon the vineyard, as is said through Isaiah: “And I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it; for the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:6). We know clouds which pass before the Lord’s face because of His brightness: “Because of His brightness,” it says, “clouds passed before Him” (Ps. 17:12). We know clouds which God made His ascent: “And He made the cloud His ascent” (Ps. 103:3). We know clouds to which God’s truth reaches: “And Your truth reaches unto the clouds” (Ps. 56:11). Sound reasoning establishes that in several passages these clouds signify the teaching of saints. Forbidden to rain upon unbelievers [Note: [Col. 0871D] The manuscript reads “to rain utterances.”], they do not moisten the hearts of the impious, dry for want of the word. When the Lord is present, they will cease to exist: just as, perhaps, when the sun rises the light of the stars grows dim, so the teaching of the clouds will pass away when the Lord Himself shines directly. By these clouds also we ascend to the Lord, because divine preaching shows us the way of the heavenly kingdom; and therefore these clouds have been set for us as an ascent. God’s truth likewise extends to these same clouds, because this prophetic teaching contains within itself the true knowledge of God.

9. God’s rain is His utterances. Fruitful mountains are eminent men.—These kinds of creatures, therefore, were selected for recounting God’s praises: while they displayed within themselves the Creator’s glory, they nevertheless supplied, through their very mention, a parabolic teaching—or, as the Apostle says, an allegorical one (*allegoroumena*, Gal. 4:24) [Col. 0872D]. Heaven, then, is covered with clouds—that is, prophetic teaching is made subject to divine realities. Rain is poured upon the earth—that is, the utterances of these covering clouds are poured forth, through which we ourselves, unfruitful and dry, are moistened by the gift of divine rain so that fruits may be drawn from us [Note: [Col. 0872D] The manuscript reads “to draw out [fruits].”]. Moses testifies that these divine utterances are to be understood as rain, saying: “Let my utterance be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew, as rain upon grass” (Deut. 32:2). This rain is therefore prepared for the earth [Col. 0873A], through which grass is produced upon the mountains and supplied as the appropriate food of beasts.

I think valleys are more fruitful than mountains, for they are enriched by the moisture that flows down into their hollow slope from the surrounding hills; and what reason is there for praising grass as produced on mountains for food of beasts? Although many mountains have fruitful summits and are grassy, nevertheless spiritual teaching is woven together under the names of bodily things. Mountains, then, produce grass for beasts as their food—but those mountains which “leaped like rams” (Ps. 113:4), to which the Prophet frequently lifted his eyes, saying: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. 120:1). These mountains—the exalted persons of patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs—produce grass for the cattle. But for what cattle? Let us hear Isaiah: “The ox,” he says, “has known its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known Me” (Isa. 1:5). Since human beings were called cattle because of the irreligious ignorance of a dull nature, their food is likewise signified by grass. Thus this grass is supplied to these beasts on the mountains.

10. A verse added. What “herb for the service of humankind” means.—In many manuscripts we find this verse inserted [Note: [Col. 0873D] It is absent even now from the Hebrew text, though not from the common copies of the Septuagint.]: “And herb for the service of humankind,” in order that the matters mentioned above might be understood to have been said of human beings through the designation of “humankind” itself. But we have no need of this interpretation. For although the addition does no harm, we do not embrace it as though we could not use other means for confirming this interpretation [Note: [Col. 0873D] In the Paris edition, “not in others.”]. The order of the words is this, vv. 8–9: “He who covers heaven with clouds, and prepares rain for the earth; who produces grass on the mountains, gives their beasts food, and herb for the service of humankind, and food to the young ravens that call upon Him.” [Note: [Col. 0873D] The editions of Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig read “if therefore,” etc., erroneously.]

Whether, then, this herb is supplied for the service of humankind when grass has been produced for beasts upon mountains through the rain of the clouds—so that allegorical teaching may be understood—namely, for people who have laid aside brutish ignorance and at last have rationally discovered God; or whether, in a more complete interpretation, the fruits supplied for human food are taught by “herb,” because all fruits are sustained through herb until harvest: in either case it is praise to God that He has supplied our weakness either with bodily food from fruits [Note: [Col. 0873D] From the manuscript we restore “into fruits,” which was absent from the printed editions. We would nevertheless prefer “in fruits,” or “bodily fruits into foods.” Thus above “fruits supplied for human food” means supplied as bodily nourishment.], or with spiritual food for life in the Prophets.

11. The nature of ravens.—But how should what follows be understood: “And to the young ravens that call upon Him”? To call upon God is the proper office of a human being [Col. 0874A], who alone among all living creatures has been made a participant in reason. But how do young ravens call upon God? And why young ravens rather than ravens, whose nature is dull, wicked [Note: [Col. 0874D] We have added “wicked” on the authority of the manuscript.], improvident, and endowed with no knowledge of God? Or what food is supplied? Is it that, just as grass is supplied to beasts and herb to human beings, God should grant to young ravens calling upon Him the foul filth of decaying corpses and the deaths of animals as food for this present life? To understand these things thus is not, I say, the height of error, but the height of irreligion. What, then, must be understood? We shall speak according to the gift of heavenly grace which we ourselves have received.

12. The raven is a figure of sinners. The raven feeding Elijah prefigures the conversion of the Gentiles.—We remember that the raven was made a figure of the sinner when, sent out from the ark, it did not return. For when no place to stand was anywhere to be found, since waters had spread over all things, it did not return, whereas the dove later returned when it found no rest (Gen. 8:7). Since the ark there bore the figure of the Church, the one who abandons the Church, though he can stand nowhere else, is made an example of the sinner: though he has no rest in the world except that of the Church, he nevertheless prefers to linger amid the vanities of the world.

We also read that this bird was appointed to feed Elijah and was accustomed always to bring him food (1 Kings 17:6), and this at the time when the whole people lived most impiously and irreligiously. This bird, therefore, which had been made a figure of the sinner, was chosen for the service of so great a Prophet [Col. 0874C]. For when the former people was found reprobate, then God’s preaching—which is food and hunger for the Prophets—is carried out through the services of those who were sinners. For we, or others before us [Note: [Col. 0874D] “Before” was lacking in the Paris edition. Augustine sheds light upon Hilary’s words: “Truly,” he says on this same psalm, no. 18, “all nations were in sin, in idolatry, in the worship of stones and wood; but did they remain so? Though our fathers themselves were not ravens, yet we ourselves, their young, call upon God.”], begotten and born from the shameless, insolent, unclean, and bloodstained, call upon God as young ravens through recognition, confession, and service. Thus, from beasts and cattle, through the knowledge of God, we become human beings—that is, participants in reason, from those ignorant of reason—and daily receive from God the nourishment of heavenly food, as He produces the preaching of doctrine in the Prophets, like grass upon mountains.

13. From these points it is established that the foregoing must be understood allegorically.—That all these things which have been set forth allegorically are to be understood as occurring for the advancement of human salvation is confirmed by the conclusion of the psalm. For it says thus, vv. 10–11: “He will not take pleasure in the strength of a horse, nor is His good pleasure in the dwellings of a man. The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear Him and [Note: [Col. 0874D] Thus the manuscript. The Greek, however, has *en tois pasin* [“in all”]. The printed editions read “and all,” without “in.”] in all who hope upon His mercy.” These statements are contrary to one another if understood bodily. For how does God produce grass upon mountains for beasts when He takes no pleasure in horses? To provide food for what does not please Him would be a service of necessity, not the kindness of providence. But because all God’s mercy has care for human salvation, He completes the preceding allegorical statements by the explanation given in the conclusion: it is not the appearance or strength of beasts, nor the adornments of costly houses, that please God—though possessing noble horses and beautiful houses is the chief ambition of human opinion—but only the one who fears, hopes, and testifies through hope and fear both to God’s power and to His mercy. For He is merciful and powerful, who said: “Whoever believes in Me shall not be judged, but shall pass from death into life” [Col. 0875B] (John 5:24). Our Lord Jesus Christ is powerful to change death into life, and merciful to remove the terror of judgment; He is blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXLVII

Alleluia, of Haggai and Zechariah.

Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion, because He has strengthened the bars of your gates and blessed your children [Hilary: “your sons”] within you. He has made your borders peace [and] satisfies you with the fat of wheat. He sends His utterance to the earth; swiftly His word runs. He gives snow like wool; He scatters mist like ashes. He sends [Hilary: “casts”] His ice like fragments [Hilary: “morsels”] of bread: who can stand [Hilary: “endure”] before His cold? He will send forth His word and melt them; His spirit has blown, and the waters shall flow. He declares [Hilary: “who declares”] His word to Jacob, His righteousness [Hilary: “righteousnesses”] and His judgments to Israel. He has not done thus to every nation, and He will not make known [Hilary: “has not made known”] His judgments to them.

## Exposition of the Psalm
1.
