The eternal kingdom of God is sung here. — To this psalm, as to the preceding one, the names of Haggai and Zechariah are appended, although they do not occur in the Hebrew text, so that through this psalm and through them, as we have shown above, the prophecy of the eternal Jerusalem might be understood.

2. Why it is called Jerusalem. — VERSE 12. Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion. Jerusalem does not differ from Zion; for, according to the names of places, the site of the city itself is one and the same. But the interpretation of the names required this twofold mention of the same city. For Jerusalem is the city of peace. And because the kingdom of our Lord is in the peace and unanimity of the saints—and, it says, “His place was made in peace” (Ps. 75:3)—that assembly of the blessed, which is the kingdom of God [perhaps: of the Lord], is called Jerusalem, as the city of peace. This city, moreover, built, as the Apostle says, of living stones, is brought to completion by the assembly of the saints, conformed through the resurrection to the glory of God (1 Pet. 2:5). It has already beheld itself by faith in the body of the Lord, such as it will be; and for this reason it is also called Zion.

> [Note: In it, indeed, as is explained in Psalm 124, §4: “We ourselves behold ourselves in the assumption of our flesh and body. For we are in Him, contemplating our resurrection in the resurrection of our body in Him; for Zion is the mountain of contemplation.”]

The Lord’s body, indeed, by the force of the interpretation, is thought to be called Zion throughout the Scriptures, because in it we behold our hope by faith: for Zion means “contemplation.” But that city which is Jerusalem, which is the city of peace because of unanimity, is also called Zion because of its conformity within itself to the body of God, in which it has beforehand contemplated itself; and, having attained that body’s glory, it has also received its name. Therefore both that peaceful assembly and that glory of transformed bodies are denoted by the names Jerusalem and Zion—which are one and the same—not as lifeless stones or insensible buildings, but as a rational living being: foundations and living stones of gems, citizens of holiness, and the city of God’s rule over His own household.

> [Note: Thus the manuscript. The printed editions read “assigning” (*deputans*) in place of “rule” (*dominatus*).]

From the consciousness of its blessedness and the confession of praise, this city is called to praise.

641 3. The blessedness and security of eternal life. — And the Prophet added the reason for praise, VERSES 13–14: “For He has strengthened the bars of your gates; He has blessed your children within you. He who has made your borders peace, and satisfies you with the fat of wheat.”

> [Note: Manuscript: “He has blessed your children in peace, and satisfies you with the fat of wheat.”]

This is that inheritance of the blessed land which the Lord promised to the meek in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matt. 5:4). In many places the prophets proclaimed the time of this blessedness and the firmness of this eternal city. Its gates and bars have been so strengthened that it remains impenetrable, inaccessible, and indissoluble to our adversaries and hostile powers: needing nothing for the sustenance of body and soul; firm in eternity; blessed in its inhabitants; peaceful in will; abundant in the substance of life.

4. The swiftness of God’s Word in building God’s city. — But to this proclamation of God is also joined the following, VERSE 15: “He sends forth His utterance to the earth; swiftly His word runs.” The advance of the proclamation of God’s kingdom was not slow; rather, it passed through the whole earth with tireless movement and speed. For where did not the course of apostolic and prophetic teaching go forth at once when the Lord, born in the body, displayed the glory of His kingdom?

> [Note: The printed texts lacked “of His kingdom.” It is supplied from the manuscript.]

For through this swift passage the building of this blessed city was begun. Hearing of the abundance of its riches, it is daily built everywhere with the living stones of believers, and is being prepared until the fullness of its inhabitants is attained. The swift word ran beforehand for gathering all from the four quarters of the world, and again for gathering them into the completed fullness of the assembly, to fill this city of the blessed kingdom.

> [Note: Thus the manuscript. Paris reads *percurrit*, “runs through”; other editions, *percurreret*, “would run through.” At first sight one might think something missing. Yet the sentence is complete: namely, the word of prophetic and apostolic teaching ran beforehand to gather those who would begin here the building of the heavenly Jerusalem and who would again have to be gathered in order to complete it. All obscurity disappears if, after “again,” one adds “for the same purpose.”]

5. On the way of life there is severe labor, but it is temporary. — Another proclamation is also connected with it, VERSES 16–18: “He gives snow like wool; He scatters mist like ashes. He sends forth His ice like morsels; who can endure before His cold? He will send forth His word and melt them; His spirit will blow, and the waters shall flow.”

> [Note: Manuscript: “like pieces of bread,” agreeing with Augustine and with the old German, Chartres, Milanese, and Roman Psalters. The words of the exposition also appear to support “solidified into pieces.” But if “pieces” is read, the same exposition nevertheless does not allow “bread” after that word.]

The way of life, as the Lord says in the Gospels, is narrow and afflicted (Matt. 7:14); and only through the greatest difficulties and troubles does one proceed by this way toward the kingdom of heaven. This must be understood to have been said of the troubles of this age; for through present afflictions one enters eternal rest. And although we are scorched by the toils of present things, as by a certain violence of a most bitter winter, nevertheless, after the rigors of these present bitter things, once God has dissolved them, we shall rest in calm, tranquil, and serene conditions.

For according to prophetic language and the customary allegorical interpretation, snow, mist, and ice—things which by their nature burn and kill—must here be understood to signify the nocturnal cold of worldly troubles, calamities, and pains directed against us.

> [Note: The printed editions, except Paris, read “and allegorical custom.”]

This same Prophet knows that one who shares in this blessed city will no longer be scorched by this cold of worldly injury, saying: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120:6). For all these things by which we are scorched amid present calamities are in turn dissolved and melted by God’s goodness.

> [Note: Baden, Erasmus, and Leipzig read, “being dissolved, we melt.”]

For snow, flowing down with the softness of wool, covers and holds everything within itself; frost too, scattered like the ash of descending mist, constricts; and ice, hardened beyond the ordinary nature of hail and solidified into pieces, contains both violence and severity.

> [Note: Where the Vulgate now reads, “He scatters mist like ashes,” the commentator on the Psalms attributed to Jerome observes that the Hebrew requires “frost,” not “mist.” Jerome himself translates “frosts.” Hilary seems both to have seen and approved each reading, combining them here, just as we observed in this edition, col. 391, note a, that he reads “death swallowed up in victory’s contest,” whereas elsewhere he read only “into contest,” and elsewhere “into victory.”]

And if these things remained forever, would not everything always be scorched and dried up by their cold? For who could bear eternal bodily calamities that never fail, if the succession of our evils were prolonged forever?

6. Eternal blessedness. — But once the infirmities of the body have been dissolved, the time of this blessed kingdom is eternal, where there is no weeping, no grief, no slipping through the changeability of bodily desire; rather, there one lives in those things which, it says, “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:8).

In the future blessings, the hearing and sight of understanding cease: whatever blessed and eternal thing is promised to the eternally blessed is neither subjected to sight, grasped by hearing, nor perceived by mind. Therefore all these colds of snow, frost, and ice will be dissolved, as though by a warm breath, when, after the rigors of this worldly night, the Spirit of God shall temper those times of the eternal kingdom into one unchanging tranquility.

7. Who is the true Jacob; his prerogatives. — And so that we might recognize that, beneath the cold of snow, mist, and ice—intolerable if it remained, yet dissolved into melting by God’s Spirit—the Prophet had signified that blessed temperateness of the eternal kingdom for the eternal people, he concluded the Psalm with this confession: “Who can endure before His cold? He will send forth His word and melt them; His spirit will blow, and the waters shall flow.” VERSES 19–20: “He declares His word to Jacob, His righteousnesses and His judgments to Israel. He has not done thus to every nation, nor has He made His judgments known to them.”

This is God’s peculiar purpose in Jacob and Israel: not in that Israel or Jacob who embraces this bodily name as the consolation, as it were, of a noble stock within himself, but in that Jacob who supplanted the elder, who bought the birthright in hope of eternity, to whom Israel is a surname from seeing God; who is himself Jerusalem and the city of peace; who, built upon the rock of faith, with the bars of its gates strengthened, will possess gates stronger than the gates of hell; who is gathered in the Word of God; who does not suffer want and will not be scorched by the cold of worldly severity; but, when all things have been melted and set free by God’s Spirit, will enjoy the temperateness of eternal serenity.

> [Note: Paris incorrectly reads, following Leipzig, “time.”]

To this Jacob the Word is proclaimed; he awaits these righteousnesses and judgments of God through spiritual understanding. No other nation shares in this good, nor does irreligious unbelief know this glory of judgment. “He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. But to as many as received Him, He gave power to become children of God” (John 1:11–12): our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 148

Alleluia.

“Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise Him in the heights. Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His powers. Praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all stars and light. Praise Him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters which are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. For He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created. He established them for ever”

> [Below: “and He established them for an age”]

“and for age upon age; He gave a command, and it shall not pass away. Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps. Fire, hail, snow, ice, storm-wind, which do His word”

> [Below: “ice, storm-winds which do His words”]

“mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars, beasts and all cattle”

> [Below: “all livestock”]

“creeping things and winged birds, kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth, young men and maidens, old men with the younger: let them praise the name of the Lord. For His name alone is exalted. His confession is above heaven and earth. He has exalted”

> [Below: “and He has exalted”]

“the horn of His people: a hymn for all His saints, for the children of Israel, the people drawing near to Him.”

## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. The preceding three Psalms, in which prophecy calls us to praise the Lord, have followed, in the very order of their arrangement, the distribution of that blessed hope of ours. The first of them was sung because of the hope of eternity and expectation of the heavenly kingdom. The second followed because of the building of the holy city and the gathering of the saints who are to assemble for the fullness of this holy city. This third Psalm has now been composed as a hymn because of the rejoicing over the city built up, founded in eternal peace, and tempered by the heavenly Spirit after the scorching and drying cold of this age.

Thus the order of doctrine is the same as the order of events. For according to prophetic and apostolic proclamation, the sequence of that blessed kingdom and eternal city is set forth in these things: in the transformation of the resurrection; in the gathering of the saints; and in the dwelling of the assembled citizens of the Lord.

> [Note: Baden, Erasmus, and Leipzig read “with the thronging together”; this is contrary to Hilary’s usual manner. Compare §4 of the preceding treatise.]

2. Every created thing awaits our blessedness. — After this, when all things have been established in eternal blessedness, the choir of heavenly virtues and powers is summoned by this following Psalm to sing God’s praises. The purpose is that, with the vanity of the age driven away, every creature, released from the great labors of its duties and at last breathing freely in the blessed kingdom of eternity, may proclaim its God joyfully and at rest; and that it too, according to the Apostle, may be assumed into the glory of blessed eternity:

“For the eager expectation of the creation awaits the revelation of the children of God. For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it in hope; because creation itself also will be liberated from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:19 ff.).

> [Note: Thus the manuscript, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions read, “who subjected it”; and shortly before, “not voluntarily,” for “not willing.”]

Therefore this is a hymn for freedom granted: the elements of creation, released from the necessity of their functions and formerly subjected to the uses of human servitude, now at last conformed to the glory of the children of God in eternal blessedness, come to rest. They had long been held in desire for this blessedness, according to the Apostle Peter, when he says: “These things which have now been announced to you through those who preached the Gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven—into which things angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12).

Thus the blessedness of things on earth—or of earthly beings—is the expectation of heavenly beings; and the transformation of our corruption delays the elements of divine creation, which desire to behold this hope of Gospel preaching and will receive their own glory from conformity to our glory. Having now obtained this, according to the prophecy of the Psalm, they are called to a harmonious praise for the blessedness received.

3. The world is neither accidental nor God. No part of the world is to be worshiped with divine honor. — VERSES 1–6. “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise Him in the heights. Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His powers. Praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all stars and light. Praise Him, heavens of heavens; and let the water above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. For He commanded, and they were created; He spoke, and they were made; and He established them for age and for age upon age. He gave a command, and it shall not pass away.”

The meaning being clear, the Prophet exhorts all the heavenly powers to praise, yet not without a fully reasoned doctrine. First, he removes that error of human ignorance by which some have dared to suppose that this ordered form of the world came together by accidental collisions, and thus, from disorder, was established in order. Then he rejects the view of others who suppose that this world itself is God, moving and agitating itself and regulating itself into the yearly temperateness of an ordered course. Finally, he rejects the practice by which each person chooses from these very elements—heaven, sun, water, or air—something to which he offers divine honor in vain and impious worship.

He therefore excludes every error of ignorance, saying: “For He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created.” Thus no accidental concurrence, no power of an independent nature, no substance possessing eternity from itself, is admitted in things which are taught to be created.

4. The Son stood with the Father in the creation of the world. — This saying also teaches what Genesis distinguished, the Gospels testified, and the Apostle proclaimed: that all things were made by God’s command; that they did not arise by themselves, as though matter itself possessed the living capacity for obedience and merely received the command to exist and subsist.

> [Note: The printed texts have *vitalis*, “living,” as one word, which we have judged should be divided. Thus, as far as we understand, a view is here refuted which would maintain that matter existed of itself and received from God’s command only the form in which it existed.]

Rather, all things were created by command, and the command was spoken by Him who said that they should be made.

> [Note: The printed editions read “that it should be made.” The manuscript more correctly reads “that they should be made,” namely all things. The Father spoke, and the Son acted, as is explained in *On the Trinity*, book IV, §16.]

For Genesis speaks thus: “And God said … and God made” (Gen. 1:6–7). And now the Prophet says: “He spoke, and they were made.” He did not command Himself that they should be made; rather, they were made when He spoke. And they were made through Him of whom the Evangelist testified: “All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” (John 1:3). The Apostle also says: “Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in Him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible—whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers—all things were created through Him and in Him” (Col. 1:15–16). And Wisdom speaks thus of herself: “I was with Him, arranging all things; I rejoiced with Him when He rejoiced in the completed world” (Prov. 8:30).

Therefore uncertainty of understanding ceases: convicted by the authority of the New and Old Testaments, one recognizes that the Son, abiding with the Father before the ages, stood present at the beginning of the world’s creation.

5. Creatures that will not be dissolved are invited to praise God. Their permanence is due to God’s command, not their own nature. — The Prophet also added another reason for praise: “For He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created; He established them for age upon age.” For, having been established from nothing, they remain; and they owe to their Creator the grace of their existence, perceiving His goodness and power through the awareness of their life, by which they began to perceive that they live.

> [Note: The printed editions read, in a very confused form: “with the sense of their life, His goodness and power and knowledge, through which they began to live or to perceive.” The confusion is removed with the help of the manuscript, in which, however, the copyist wrongly wrote *sententiae* (“of opinions”) instead of *sentientia* (“by perception”).]

Indeed, they live in such a way that they remain for age upon age and, according to the Apostle, await the revelation of the children of God, to be freed from the slavery of corruption into conformity with their glory. But one should observe that, among these creatures established for age upon age, neither this heaven which is called the firmament nor the earth which was called dry land has been included.

> [Note: Thus the manuscript. Baden and Erasmus read “numbered together”; Leipzig, “mentioned”; Paris, “mentioned.”]

For it is said in the Prophets, “Behold, I make a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. 65:17), and the Lord said in the Gospel, “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). These are not the subject of the present passage. We have mentioned this only as a reminder: the creations now numbered for God’s praise are not those that are to be dissolved, but those established for eternal subsistence.

> [Note: The printed editions read, “are in the substance of eternity.” The manuscript more correctly reads, “established for the substance of eternity,” that is, for an eternal substance or endless subsistence. Since this relates to what was mentioned at the beginning of §3, where sun, moon, stars, and so forth are called to praise God, one may ask whether Hilary thought the specified created things animate. Licinius, writing to Pope St. Gregory about Hilary’s books on Job, says in *Spicilegium*, II, p. 369: “I greatly wonder, in my barbarous manner of speaking, that a most learned and holy man transferred Origen’s follies about the stars.” But regarding that passage of Licinius, it is not established that he encountered genuine treatises of Hilary on Job. Either what Hilary writes on Job must be judged free from the stated error, or—heaven forbid—weight must be assigned to Jerome’s judgment as well. Jerome, who teaches that Hilary’s books should generally be read without stumbling, says specifically of Origen’s treatises on Job, in Epistle 75: “I come to you yourself, Vigilantius: why do you possess copies of his treatises on Job, in which, disputing against the devil and concerning the stars and heaven, he spoke certain things which the Church does not receive?” Why reproach a man merely for retaining copies of Origen’s treatises, while advising a woman not merely to retain but also to read Hilary’s books, unless he found in Hilary’s works none of the error concerning the stars which he judged rejectable in the other?

Nor can that same error be rashly criticized in this very treatise. First, Hilary does not say that only animate creations were numbered, but those not to be dissolved. Secondly, if by the names of sun, moon, stars, and the water above the heavens he understood living substances, he must have understood them not literally but spiritually. Anyone who considers his words in the treatise on Psalm 123, §5, will not deny this. There he first says that it appears absurd for waters to be animate; then he assumes that waters above the heavens praise the Lord and therefore are animate; finally, he concludes that peoples are signified by the name “waters,” among whom some are heavenly and others earthly, and so forth.

He seems to understand those waters more literally in Psalm 135, §8, when he calls them a more temperate nature, by whose interposition the abode of God, surrounded by the power of the first heaven and excessively inflamed, is tempered so as to be endurable by lower natures. Nor is there doubt about which stars Hilary considered animate in the treatise on Psalm 146, §5, where, explaining “He counts the multitude of the stars,” he first rejects the literal sense and then says: “Here the stars are counted which Abraham beheld in heaven, which Isaac received in seed, which Paul distinguished in glory.” For it is clear that by “stars” he interprets the elect and the children of Abraham.

Nor indeed could anyone say that heaven and earth, spiritually understood, might likewise have been adapted to things not to be dissolved. For the statement “Heaven and earth shall pass away” forbids this, and nothing similar is found concerning the creations mentioned above. Finally, Jerome, in Epistle 62 to Theophilus, explaining how far Hilary imitated Origen, says: “Cutting away everything harmful, he transferred what was useful.” This clearly indicates that Hilary by no means transferred Origen’s follies about the stars, to use Licinius’s phrase, or, in Jerome’s own words, those things which the Church does not receive.]

And lest perhaps they should believe that their perpetual permanence belongs to them naturally because of the blessedness of their substance, he added: “He gave a command, and it shall not pass away,” so that they may understand that what they are—that is, their remaining eternally—does not belong to their nature but to the command of Him who can bestow the nature of eternity upon things established from nothing. For, it says, “the command shall not pass away,” that is, His injunction will not come to an end.

> [Note: The manuscript reads: “that they may remain forever.”]

For they remain forever because the Power of eternity has granted eternity to them.

6. How inanimate things praise God. — After this the remaining earthly things are again called to praise. Though not all share in these heavenly and blessed goods—some because of irrational perception, some because of inanimate nature, some because of the offense of impiety—yet, by the fact that they were so constituted, they proclaim God through the providence displayed in the constitution they possess. Thus he says, VERSES 7–12:

“Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps; fire, hail, snow, ice, storm-wind, which do His words; mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds; kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth, young men and maidens, old men with the younger: let them praise the name of the Lord.”

All things sing God’s praise, although some lack the faculty of praise; nevertheless, through the order of their constitution and the character of their generation, they show forth the proclamation of the Creator. Dragons are confined upon earth, and many of them are plunged in the deeps, in order that, while they themselves are bound within abyss and earth and prepared for the penalties of their impiety, they might restrain us within fear and reverence. The nature of fire, the whiteness of snow, the icy cold of ice, the breath of storms, the height of mountains, the distinction of hills, the fruit of trees, the variety of beasts, the usefulness of cattle, the motion of serpents, the flight of birds, the power of kings, the service of peoples, the rank of princes, the justice of judges, the characters, pursuits, and virtues of every age and sex: all these things, formed, distinguished, animated, and completed for diverse and ineffable uses, praise the Creator’s providence.

> [Note: As in the preceding treatise, §5, “frost” and “mist,” and in Psalm 59, §14, “victory in contest,” so here not merely “ice” or “frost” is stated, but “icy frost,” the two modes of reading thus being adopted.]

And he showed what praise belongs to things inanimate or irrational by saying, “which do His words,” so that from their being established in this order of their functions they bear witness to the proclamation of Him by whom they were so constituted.

7. The reason rational beings should praise God; the seat of the blessed kingdom. — To kings and the other beings who share in reason, however, this reason for praise is proposed, VERSE 13: “For His name alone is exalted; His confession is above heaven and earth.” God is praiseworthy indeed in this constitution of kings, peoples, princes, judges, and all ages, because He sustains the course of human life by such a balanced arrangement of diverse functions.

> [Note: The manuscript reads “by which” (*quo*) rather than “because” (*quia*).]

Nevertheless, because the whole preceding praise indicates the time of that blessed kingdom, he added this reason for praise: “For His name alone is exalted.” For then God alone is both understood and seen, even by the unwilling: when the devil has been bound; when his angels have been assigned with him to the punishment of eternal fire; when every power of spiritual wickedness has been removed; when sin no longer exists, nor death, nor this earthly world.

> [Note: Thus the manuscript. The printed editions read “will be seen.”]

For he says, VERSE 14: “His confession is above heaven and earth, and He has exalted the horn of His people.” That is, in that age of the blessed city, where the Lord will exalt the horn of His people and, through the honor of immortality, confer upon it incorruption, which is signified by the horn. Then there will be a new heaven and a new earth, when these present things have been dissolved and those new and eternal things succeed. Therefore His confession will be rendered above heaven and earth, because the seat of that blessed kingdom is established not in this age nor in this air, but in higher places.

8. The people drawing near: already in the kingdom of the Son, not yet in the kingdom of the Father. — And because it is the kingdom of the saints, through which, under the Lord’s reign, they shall ascend to the blessed kingdom of God the Father, the Prophet concluded the Psalm thus: “A hymn for all His saints, for the children of Israel, the people drawing near to Him.”

This hymn belongs wholly to the saints. They praise God not, like the other kings, princes, or judges, from admiration for power and confession, but from joy in the blessedness fulfilled within them and from the rejoicing of those who sing: namely, the saints who are children of Israel and draw near to God. They are certainly not those of whom it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15:8); rather, they are those who will deserve to hear: “The Lord is near to all who call upon Him” (Ps. 144:18).

Therefore this hymn belongs especially to those who will draw near to God; through this blessed kingdom of holy Jerusalem, they are near to the eternal kingdom. After the kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ, when the Lord gathers them, they shall pass into the kingdom of God the Father, as the Apostle says:

“When He shall hand over the kingdom to God the Father, when He has abolished every rule and every authority and power. For He must reign until He has placed all enemies beneath His feet.”

> [Note: Baden, Erasmus, and Leipzig read: “For He will subject all things beneath His feet. For death shall be abolished last.” See *On the Trinity*, book XI, §22.]

“For when all things have been subjected beneath His feet, death is abolished last. When He says, ‘All things are subjected, except Him who subjected all things to Him,’ then the Son Himself also shall be subjected to Him who subjected all things to Him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:24 ff.).

Thus this is the people drawing near, made near to the kingdom of God the Father through the kingdom of the Son of God. The Lord reigns, therefore, in order to hand the kingdom over to God the Father—not because He will be deprived of the power of His kingdom, but because He will hand us over, who are His kingdom, to God the Father in His kingdom.

> [See *On the Trinity*, book XI, §39.]

The handing over of the kingdom is our advancement: so that we who shall be in the Son’s kingdom may also be in the Father’s kingdom; worthy of the Father’s kingdom because we shall be worthy also of the Son’s kingdom; then near to the Father’s kingdom, when we shall be the Son’s kingdom.

> [Note: The printed editions read, “we shall be the kingdom”; corrected from the manuscript.]

He is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 149

Alleluia.

“Sing to the Lord a new song; His praise”

> [Below: “His praise-song”]

“in the church of the saints. Let Israel rejoice in Him who made him, and let the children of Zion exult over their king. Let them praise His name in the choir; let them sing psalms to Him with tambourine and psaltery. For the Lord has taken pleasure in His people; He has exalted”

> [Below: “He will exalt”]

“the meek unto salvation. The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting places. The exaltations of God are in their throats”

> [Below: “in their gullet”]

“and a two-edged sword”

> [Below: “a sword sharpened on both sides”]

“in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes”

> [Below: “reproofs”]

“among the peoples; to bind their kings in manacles and”

> [Below: “manacles and” is absent]

“fetters, and their nobles in iron bonds; to execute upon them the written judgment. This glory belongs to all His saints.”

649 ## TREATISE ON THE PSALM

1. Recapitulation of the preceding Psalm. — The preceding Psalm exhorted every diversity of created things to praise God the Creator. Beginning with heavenly things, its sequence ranges through all creatures of earth, sea, and air; and every class of ages, sexes, and powers is admonished to render the honor of due confession, so that a devout word of thanksgiving might celebrate the glory of Him who had given them life, established, and adorned them.

After the Prophet had fittingly fulfilled the proper task of his ministry at the end of that Psalm—having exhorted all things to divine praise—he showed that the hymn belongs only to God’s saints, namely, the children of Israel, the people who would become near to God. Thus, although the whole universe praised God from consciousness and rejoicing in its life, Israel alone, drawing near to Him, might sing a hymn out of the intimacy of divine knowledge and favor.

> [Note: Paris reads “His alone”; corrected from the manuscript.]

After this we are now urged to sing a new song to God.

> [Note: What follows was first published from the manuscript of Micy in the Paris edition of 1605; previously Hilary’s Commentary ended here.]

Perhaps the preceding Psalm may seem to have left nothing further of novelty and wonder, since whatever belongs to our rejoicing and understanding seems itself to have been prescribed as belonging in praise. Yet our mind is not capable of raising itself beyond the heavenly seat.

> [Note: In Paris, as in the manuscript, the reading is “the measure is insufficient,” corruptly. The following words confirm that it should be “our mind”; experts know that there is little difference in old books between the two readings. Shortly afterward the manuscript has “they are admonished,” whereas the common reading everywhere was “we are admonished.”]

Nevertheless, those things above the heavens are commanded to praise God. Again, the conception of our understanding cannot extend itself beyond the immensity of the abyss; yet the things within it are called to the duty of praise. The very nature of air, in hail, snow, ice, and the spirit of storm, is commanded to sing the glory of so great a praise. Further, the entire human race—in kings, princes, judges, in every flower of age and maturity of old age—has been commanded to sing God’s praise, because all these things remain in an undisturbed and regulated course, and all things flow according to the law prescribed to their nature in such a way that they are not permitted to depart from the constitution in which they were created.

## 2. To whom this “new song” properly belongs

Since, then, no knowledge or praise of knowledge seems to have been granted to humankind apart from these decrees concerning divine and heavenly things, let us see to what new song we are now summoned, when it is said:

**VERSE 1.** *Sing to the Lord a new song.*

It is indeed a new song. We have already shown, in the preceding psalms in which a new song is sung, what rejoicing belongs to this new song: when the Lord is shown to be about to reign among the nations (Ps. 95:10); when his right hand will save him unto the glory of kingship (Ps. 97:1); when, taking up his own soul from hell, he took us up with himself to be kings. Therefore this new song properly belongs to his saints. For what follows is: *His praise is in the Church of the saints.*

**VERSES 2–3.** *Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, and let the sons of Zion exult over their king. Let them praise his name in the choir; let them sing psalms to him with tambourine and psaltery.*

That is, in him who, according to the new song of the ninety-fifth psalm, will reign among the nations, and whom, in the following new song, his right hand will save as Lord in his wondrous deeds. Therefore Israel and the sons of Zion rejoice over this king: namely, the sons of that Zion which is the mother in heaven, the city of the enrolled firstborn and of the assembled angels; and that Israel which is according to the Spirit, not the letter—over which is the Apostle’s peace (Gal. 6:16).

Thus those sons who, receiving and confessing the king, have become sons of God, and those who have recognized God in the body with the eyes of the mind, shall rejoice while singing psalms in choir, with tambourine and psaltery. This, however, is the cause of joy in the tents of the righteous; and the sound of the symphony is heard at the return of the repentant son.

> **Note:** This was in some fashion shown in Psalm 143, no. 19. But since Hilary says “in the preceding psalms,” not “in the preceding psalm,” and adds, “in which a new song is sung,” he plainly indicates that he had expounded Psalms 95 and 97, whose treatments are now missing.

> **Note:** In the Paris edition: “the same in him.” We prefer “that is,” since in manuscripts *idem* and *id est* are commonly written alike. This particle indicates the meaning of “Let Israel rejoice in him.”

> **Note:** We restore *whom* in place of *which*, as the sense plainly requires. Shortly afterward, the first Paris edition lacked “the Lord,” and the final edition substituted “the Lord” for it, omitting the words “his right hand”: contrary to the authority of the manuscript exemplar. “Has saved” would not be unsuitable in place of “will save,” just as earlier “has reigned” might stand for “will reign.”

## 3. Man, pleasing to God in creation, displeasing through sin, became well-pleasing in Christ

What, then, is now the particular reason for this new song, after the praise of created things and the preceding new songs? He shows it in saying:

**VERSES 4–5.** *For the Lord has taken pleasure in his people; he will exalt the meek unto salvation. The saints shall exult in glory.*

Certainly, when all things were created, they pleased God, as Genesis testifies when it says: *And God saw that they were good* (Gen. 1:31). Yet we know that he takes pleasure in his people. The creation of man is good, since it received the beginning of creation according to origin and the likeness of God. Yet God, who is unchangeable in judgment, adapting his judgment to the changeableness of human will and choice, testified at that time—because men had sinned and were doing deeds requiring repentance—that he repented of having made man.

But when those very persons were reshaped from sin unto life, and the complaint of repentance had been removed, the affection of his good pleasure toward them is now shown. For through the body and blood of Christ we have been reconciled to God, changed from enemies into sons, since he had promised us the propitiation of the eternal priest by the sacrament of irrevocability, the Prophet saying: *The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek* (Ps. 110:4).

Therefore that which was sworn to be irrevocable for him has found acceptance; and while he reigns according to the order of Melchizedek—that is, as both king and priest of the nations—salvation belongs first to the meek, and then splendor to the saints exulting over their king.

> **Note:** In the manuscript, *because* appears in place of *as*. Perhaps it should be retained. Then “according to origin,” that is, because man has no other cause of his being than God—at least according to his higher part, the soul, from whose creation man is said to have taken his beginning in Psalm 129, no. 5, and Psalm 118, no. 7.

> **Note:** Up to this point the text read, with variants, “adapting, since they had sinned,” or “had sinned.” No one will fail to see that *adapting* is preferable; it is expressed differently in Psalm 120, no. 9: “According to each person’s character and pursuit, God disposes himself toward each; and thus he is turned away from the perverse and holy among the holy.” Then we judge that *at that time* should be restored for *while*: as though he had testified then, at that time, and so forth.

> **Note:** That is, after changing his judgment, God says that he no longer repents. From the particle “now,” it is clear that above *at that time*, not *while*, must be read.

> **Note:** The Paris edition reads “in the sacrament of repentance,” a reading contradicted by what follows. More plainly one might say “in the sacrament of non-repentance”; but a studied play on words seems intended, since “the complaint of repentance” had just been mentioned.

> **Note:** The Paris edition has “sworn,” to which follows “reigning according to the order of Melchizedek,” that is, “king and priest of the nations,” etc.

## 4. Privileges of the saints. What “throat” signifies; what the sword signifies. The use of the two-edged swords for the saints

But after the glory of the saints, we must understand what follows for the fullness of the new song:

*They shall rejoice in their beds.*

**VERSE 6.** *The exaltations of God are in their throat, and two-edged swords in their hands.*

No longer shall the couch be watered with tears, nor shall the bed of those who dwell in this body of death be washed every night because of the necessity and sorrow of sin. For the saints shall now rejoice in glory in their own resting places; and therefore the exaltations of God shall always be in their throat. By “throat” he signifies the disposition of the inward conscience.

Yet the exaltation of God is not only in their throat; their hands also shall be armed with two-edged swords. This knowledge the king grants to the sons of Zion, for whom salvation, glory, joy, exultation, and power are prepared as they sing psalms in choirs and with tambourines. For we are taught, both in many places and by what follows, that power is signified by the sword.

Why, indeed, are two-edged swords in their hands? The Prophet immediately explains:

**VERSES 7–9.** *To execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples; to bind their kings in fetters, and their nobles in iron manacles; to execute upon them the written judgment: this is glory for all his saints.*

This, then, is the new song: when the humble of the earth and the troubled in heart are established as kings; when those considered the refuse of the world and, as it were, the miscarried offspring of the nations, become the light of the world and avengers upon the nations (1 Cor. 4:13).

For two-edged swords are in their hands because the holy one in the Apocalypse has a two-edged sword from his mouth, exercising judicial power on every side (Rev. 19:15). The Lord also came to cast a sword upon the earth (Matt. 10:34); and, according to the Apostle, the saints shall judge the world, and in them the world shall be judged (1 Cor. 6:2). For it is said: *Do you not know that you are to judge angels?*

Thus vengeance is executed upon the nations through them; for God is the God of avengings in us. Then rebuke is exercised against peoples. For faithful is he who says: *I will rebuke you and set these things before your face* (Ps. 50:21). But the result of this rebuke is that the kings of the nations and their nobles are bound in manacles and fetters. For, according to the Gospels, those bound hand and foot are assigned to outer darkness (Matt. 22:13).

And because there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth there, the written judgment shall be executed: that is, the judgment prescribed by the Law, announced by the Prophets, and testified by every divine utterance. This is the reward possessed by faith, devotion, self-restraint, and confession; this is the gift received by contempt for the world: that those who endured hatreds for Christ’s name may become kings over kings; that nobles may be bound who had confined us in chains and prisons; that written judgment may be executed upon those whose swords and authority raged against us.

Thus all the glory of the saints is from God, when after the sufferings of this life and body they exercise power. Thus the hymn of the new song is fulfilled, when, after the reproach of the nations and the torments inflicted by kings, they decree written judgment against the nations and kings, for whom the Lord Jesus Christ is the only-begotten God, Lord, and King, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

> **Note:** I think no one will oppose this correction, although the Paris edition, following the manuscript, prints “signifying in many places.”

> **Note:** Here also we restore *because*, where *who* had prevailed. Shortly thereafter, the word “exercising” — though “putting forth” would be more customary for Hilary — is referred, by a certain figure, to the two-edged sword.

> **Note:** The Paris edition reads “the rebuke of avengings.” Then the punctuation is defective.

> **Note:** Presumably, the power of binding kings and of decreeing written judgment; for “these things” is to be understood as plural accusative. Shortly afterward, “the immediately preceding” is used adverbially in the Paris edition; for Hilary’s *superior proximus* means what is commonly called the antepenultimate, namely Psalm 147.

# PSALM 150

*Praise the Lord in his saints; praise him in the firmament of his power. Praise him in his powers; praise him according to the multitude of his greatness. Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with psaltery and harp. Praise him with tambourine and choir; praise him with strings and organ. Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation. Let every spirit praise the Lord.*

# TREATISE ON THE PSALM

## 1. The psalms are filled with mysteries. Why they are divided into three fifties

We have often treated of the Book of Psalms as filled with the great mysteries of heavenly realities: whether because the arrangement of the individual psalms has received an order and number contrary to the sequence of times and events; or because certain superscriptions have been added differently from the form in which they are contained in the Hebrew books; or because several titles are prefixed where there are none.

Since, therefore, the book has been arranged according to a meaning of higher understanding beyond the literal sense, it was fitting that it should be concluded with a worthy end: so that, in accordance with the glorious perfection of our hope, the book of so great a Prophet might likewise be brought to completion. For it was first distributed into a number that was to be completed from a threefold fifty, although among the Hebrews the number is not attached to each individual psalm, and many of their psalms are joined together, preventing the number here from fitting the threefold fifty.

The translators, therefore, showed this spiritual understanding by dividing into a number this accumulated and continuous sequence existing in many psalms, so that both the order and the number of all the psalms might be completed in this one, which is the one hundred and fiftieth. Thus the entire book might attain the same kind of state that belongs to faith—as we treated in the fiftieth and hundredth psalms. One of these, according to the prescriptions of the Law, embraced confession and forgiveness of sin after sabbaths of sabbaths; the other, under the fullness of the same number, comprehended not forgiveness of sin but the fruit and duty of righteousness.

After this, when the city of God had been built again for eternity, and all had been summoned to rejoice and praise him, under the power of the same number the hope of the saints was again brought to completion, all now renewed unto spiritual glory and nature. Thus one comes step by step to fellowship with God: forgiveness of sins deserves innocence of life and firmness in judgment; and innocence of life and firmness in judgment receive the dignity of spiritual glory.

And so baptism, resurrection, and transformation are all contained here: the first fifty of this book regenerates us unto innocence; resurrection, following the judgment of innocence, brings us onward; the third establishes us in the nature and praise of the Spirit. For after the kings bound in fetters, the nobles bound in manacles, and the written judgment of the saints—when glory had been established in all these things—the completion of that very glory followed.

> **Note:** Here too *threefold fifty* seems to be required, and below “three fifties,” in place of the word *trisquinquagesimus* (“one hundred and fiftieth”).

> **Note:** We restore “after which,” where previously “after” stood, having discovered that the same corruption must be corrected above.

> **Note:** The Paris edition reads “resurrection brings [us] forth.” “By resurrection” would not be unsuitable, except that the manuscript resists it; for “the following” seems to refer to the word “fifty,” which should be retained.

## 2.

The psalm immediately preceding summoned us to praise God because of the magnificence of creation. But after the hymn of the new song, God is no longer to be praised in his works, but in the saints, whom, after the written judgment, he will have placed in the glory of eternity and endowed, now unchangeable, with heavenly honor. In them he is to be praised in the firmament of his power, because he will have brought them into the firmament of eternal power, death having been swallowed up in victory, when incorruption has devoured corruption.

And therefore praise in the firmament of power follows praise of powers, because immortality has consumed death, granting what eye has not seen, nor heart conceived, nor ear heard.

*(Five verses could not be read here, because the manuscript letters had faded.)*

… in the saints and unto praise … his … God, according to the Apostle, blessed us before the foundation of the world in the heavenly places with spiritual blessing (Eph. 1:3), to the glory of whose praise all duties both of voice and of works are incited by the diversity and splendor of their dwellings.

Therefore we praise him with well-sounding cymbals; in cymbals of exultation this praise is perfected. This entire praise is in the saints: because he has driven away from them the corruption of flesh and blood; because they have been re-formed according to the image of their Creator; because they have already begun to be conformed to the glory of God’s body; because they are filled unto all the fullness of God; because, though God is Spirit, God will no longer be praised by flesh, but by spirit.

# COMMENTARY ON PSALMS 15, 31, AND 41

## Notice concerning the Commentary on Psalms 15, 31, and 41

*(From the Library of Galland.)*

How greatly Saint Hilary excelled in letters and learning is sufficiently clear from the praises with which the ancient writers of the Church celebrated his merits. Jerome, the greatest Doctor, calls him a pillar of the Church. Moreover, he calls him a most eloquent man and, against the Arians, the trumpet of the Latin tongue. Elsewhere he calls him a great man and the most eloquent of his age, renowned wherever the Roman name extends for the merit of his confession, the industry of his life, and the brilliance of his eloquence. Writing to Laeta, he exhorts her daughter to run through Hilary’s books with unimpeded step.

Indeed, Jerome thought so highly of Hilary’s writings that he himself copied in his own hand Hilary’s interpretation of the Davidic Psalms and his very lengthy book *On the Synods*. Augustine too praises Hilary as a most vigorous defender of the Catholic Church against heretics, as a venerable Catholic disputant and distinguished Doctor of the churches, a man of no slight authority in the treatment of the Scriptures and the defense of the faith. After these doctors of great name, there is no need to bring forward the remaining judgments on our Bishop of Poitiers known to have been delivered by Rufinus, Sozomen, Cassian, Cassiodorus, and others.

“Wherefore,” says Martène, “we cannot sufficiently lament that very many monuments of so great a Doctor have either perished altogether or lie somewhere forgotten, covered with dust. In the most recent recension of his works, prepared by our own Peter Coustant of pious memory, no diligence was omitted to ensure that all should come to light, both purified of errors and complete. Nor was his labor altogether fruitless: he enlarged his edition with several treatises on the Psalms and with the apologetic replies to critics of the book *On the Synods*. Yet not a few works still remain hidden.

“Accordingly, when by order of our superiors we undertook a journey to Germany, a most learned man urged us, while examining libraries, to turn over Hilary’s manuscripts with special care, in case we might recover his treatise on Job, his preface to Matthew, and expositions of several psalms. For he was persuaded that the whole Psalter had been expounded by the blessed Doctor. And behold, while we were examining the handwritten books of the monastery of Aquicinctum, a codex elegantly written about six hundred years ago fortunately came into our hands. At its beginning was read this heading:

> ‘This volume contains the twelve books of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, *On the Trinity against All Heresies*, and other works of the same author: namely, the book *On the Synods against All Heresies*; the book *Against Constantius*; the treatise addressed to him; the book addressed to him, which he issued at Constantinople while he was still alive; the blasphemy of Auxentius, bishop of the Arians; the book against the same. On the Psalms.’

“Having consulted the index of Psalms whose expositions are lacking in the published works of Hilary, we found in that codex unpublished expositions of Psalms 15, 31, and 41. Reading them diligently, we observed in them Hilary’s method of writing, his style, the very ancient version of Scripture customarily cited before Jerome’s Vulgate had been produced; and we judged that there was no objection to attributing them to Hilary.”

> **Notes:** Jerome, *Against Rufinus*, book 1, §11, *Works*, vol. II, p. 459, Verona edition.

# SAINT HILARY’S INTERPRETATION OF PSALMS 15, 31, AND 41, hitherto lacking from the published editions

*(From the same source.) (C, G, S)\**

# TREATISE ON PSALM 15

## 1.

This psalm is marked by an inscription of a title; but we do not find in the historical record what David’s inscription of a title was. Nevertheless, we recognize that the inscription of a title was made in the Lord’s Passion; and it cannot be denied, according to the interpretation, that this psalm appears to have prophesied concerning Christ’s Passion and resurrection. This is clear where it says:

**VERSE 10.** *For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you give your Holy One to see corruption.*

For David died and was buried; but Christ’s flesh alone did not see corruption, nor could his soul be held in hell. Therefore the psalm, which was to speak both of his Passion and resurrection and of his inheritance, was appropriately marked with the inscription of a title.

For what did the inscription which Pilate affixed to his cross contain? “Jesus,” it says, “King of the Jews.” And he himself confessed that name when Pilate questioned him: *Are you King of the Jews?* (Mark 15:26). “For this,” he says, “I came, and for this I was born.”

## 2.

But is he king of the carnal Jews, [set] by him over Zion, his holy mountain? (The verb is absent from the supplied source.) Certainly I do not think that the Lord received kingship from the Father on that earthly mountain in Judea, since the Apostle teaches that his kingdom is heavenly. Likewise he shows that Christ’s Jerusalem is not this one which now is in bondage with her children, but that Jerusalem above, our free mother, the heavenly Jerusalem.

So too, Jesus is not king of those Jews circumcised with circumcision made by hand, but—as the Apostle teaches, saying that he is not a Jew who appears outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is in the flesh, but circumcision is of the heart, whose praise is not from human beings but from God—he is not king of those Jews who glory before human beings in works, but of those whose glory is before God because of hope in his grace.

See, indeed, the Apostle saying whose glory is before God: *For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory before human beings* (Rom. 4:2). Why then does he believe in him who can justify the ungodly and hope for the gratuitous mercy of God? He has glory, but not before God.

## 3.

Therefore Christ is king of those Jews whose glory is not from human beings but from God. Accordingly this psalm also says significantly:

**VERSES 5–6.** *The Lord is the portion of my inheritance. The measuring-lines have fallen to me among the very mighty; indeed, my inheritance is exceedingly great.*

What, then, is the Lord’s inheritance, except that of which it is written: *Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance* (Ps. 2:8)? But sinners from among the nations believe in him who can justify the ungodly. And if their glory is not from human beings but from God, Christ is also king of these Jews.

For he is not a Jew who appears outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is openly performed in the flesh. But what does he say? Did not very many from that circumcision believe? It is true that they believed; yet they too were brought back to the example of the nations, so that they first confessed themselves sinners and thus deserved mercy. Paul teaches this in writing to the Galatians: *If you, though you are a Jew, live as a Gentile, how do you compel the nations to Judaize? We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the nations, knowing that no flesh is justified by the law* (Gal. 2:14).

Thus, wishing to gain Christ, he was found a sinner, because Christ came not to call the justified but sinners. Therefore those also who believed from the circumcision made by hand believed after being humbled to the confession of sinful nations, so that all might be Christ’s inheritance: not those who are to be justified by their own works, but those who are justified through God’s gratuitous grace.

And this is the inscription of the title: that he himself is king of the Jews. Thus this psalm sets forth the Jews of whom Christ appears to be king, and the meaning of the inscription of the title: he is king not of those Jews who appear outwardly and whose circumcision is manifest in the flesh, but rather of those Jews who are Jews in secret, who possess circumcision of heart, and whose glory is not from human beings but from God. Let us now see whether the text of the psalm concerns the matters we have stated.

## 4.

**VERSE 1.** *Keep me, Lord, for I have hoped in you.*

One who asks for what is owed does not hope; for if something is owed to me, I demand it by right. But if someone grants me something freely, not from obligation, I shall hope for his goodwill from this customary benevolence of his.

Therefore, he who did not magnify righteousness from works but introduced the gratuitous grace of God said: *Keep me, Lord, because I have hoped in you. I shall say to the Lord: You are my God.*

For the Lord’s power consists in his doing to a servant what he wills, not what he must. But if payment is owed for works, he will repay me what he must, not what he wills. For if I have worked, whether he wills it or not, payment is owed to me; and by this the grace of God will be emptied, as the Apostle says: *To the one who works, wages are credited as a debt, not as grace.* But one who wishes to be saved not by his own works but by God’s grace—as all of us ought to believe—will, by hoping in God, appoint for himself as good what God wills, not what God must. Thus he significantly says:

**VERSE 2.** *I said to the Lord: You are my God.*

For the Lord never gives thanks to a servant if he has done what he was commanded. Rather, in all these matters he expects his own goodwill and grace, just as the Lord teaches, saying: *Which of you has a servant ploughing or feeding sheep? When he comes home, does he say to him, “Come and recline at table”? Rather he says, “Come and serve me, and then you shall eat.” Does the master thank that servant because he has done so? Amen, I say to you, he does not. So you also, when you have done everything I command you, say: “We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do”* (Luke 17:7).

Therefore one who acknowledges that he has God ought to exhibit such humility of service. Yet this confession is not one of works but of faith. Hence the noble herald of the New Testament says: *I said to my Lord: You are my God.* And what does he say after this?

## 5.

*For you have no need of my goods.*

**VERSE 3.** *To the saints who are on earth.*

What could be more consistent than his saying that his goods are not necessary to the saints of the earth, nor are the Lord’s goods for the use of saints who inhabit the earth? What are Christ’s goods, the goods of the New Testament, if not gratuitous grace, if not forgiveness of sins? These goods are not necessary for the saints of the earth. *Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill* (Mark 2:17).

And he aptly calls those who justify themselves by their own works saints not of heaven but of earth; for their praise is from human beings, not from God. The Lord identifies them as such when they reproached him for dining with tax collectors: *I have not come to save the righteous, but sinners* (ibid.).

Therefore gratuitous grace and forgiveness of sins are not necessary for the righteous—but, certainly, for those righteous persons who think themselves righteous. For the truly righteous person lives by faith. Thus these saints do not need their Son’s goods. Therefore he says below: *I will not gather their assemblies from my blood.* For redemption through my blood is not necessary for people such as these, who consider themselves righteous.

## 6.

But why does he say: *They made your wills wonderful in themselves; their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they hastened*?

The Apostle treats this passage very fully in Romans: the Law entered so that sin might be increased; but where sin was increased, grace abounded (Rom. 5:20). For after those who rejected God’s grace were found in the works of the Law, God’s wills, by which he was summoning them to his grace, became wonderful to the weak.

Therefore whoever wishes to be saved must wish to be delivered by God’s grace. Thus the psalm rightly says: *They made your wills wonderful in themselves; their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they hastened.* For when the infirmities of those wishing to be justified by works were multiplied, the wills of God that called them to faith in grace became wonderful.

Of these, therefore, he says: *I will not gather their assemblies from my blood*—that is, I will not redeem those who do not seek the redemption of my grace. *Nor will I remember their names with my lips.* For one who wishes to be saved by his own works does not confess my benefit; and *whoever has not confessed me before human beings, neither will I confess him before my Father who is in heaven* (Matt. 10:32).

Since he was not going to gather persons of this sort, it remained for him to show whom he would receive as his inheritance. Accordingly he adds in order:

## 7.

**VERSE 5.** *The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you are he who has preserved my inheritance for me.*

For if he rejected those justified by works, he preferred to possess those whom God saved by grace. Thus he significantly says: *The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.* For when the Lord saves by his grace those whom he gave to the Son as an inheritance, the Lord is truly the portion of his inheritance.

The Son, however, maintained dutiful submission, so that he might not proclaim his inheritance as sought by his own blood, but might say that it had been given him by God through God; and so that he might confess that the Lord was the portion also of his cup, that is, his Passion. For although the nations were redeemed from sin by the Lord’s Passion, that Passion of the Lord was nevertheless the will of the Father, as he testifies in the Gospel when speaking as the man whom he assumed: *Father, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will* (Matt. 26:39).

Therefore, if you consider the Lord’s will, he himself confessed it when he said: *If it is possible, let this cup pass from me.* Hence the redemption of the nations must also be received as belonging not to the will of the Son but to the will of the Father. For he says: *Not what I will, but what you will.* Thus the Son assigns to the Father, not to himself, that very grace by which the nations were redeemed through his death. Therefore he declares the Lord to be the portion both of his inheritance and of his cup.

## 8.

**VERSE 6.** *The measuring-lines have fallen to me among the mighty; indeed, my inheritance is great for me.*

For it was an ancient custom to measure the boundaries of possessions by a line. Therefore, since he was speaking here of the portion of his inheritance, he says: *The measuring-lines have fallen to me among the very mighty.*

We receive testimony concerning this from the Song of Moses, where it is written: *When God scattered the sons of Adam and established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, the Lord’s portion became his people; Jacob, the measuring-line of his inheritance* (Deut. 32:8).

And rightly, he who had said that God was the portion of his inheritance said that the measuring-lines of his possession had fallen among the very mighty. For who are mighty, if not those whom the Lord justifies and honors? *Who will accuse God’s elect? God is the one who justifies; who has condemned?* (Rom. 8:33).

Therefore, since he said that his inheritance would be among such people, he rightly says: *The measuring-lines have fallen to me among the very mighty.* Yet no one should understand “have fallen” as though he meant that his inheritance had become worse, since everything which falls becomes worse. Rather, he used a proper and necessary word. For where one is chosen not according to merit, there a kind of lot of grace falls, as is written concerning the choice of the apostle substituted in Judas’s place: *The lot fell upon Matthias* (Acts 1:26).

Thus, because such an inheritance befell him only by the Lord’s grace, he significantly says: *The measuring-lines have fallen to me among the very mighty; indeed, my inheritance is great for me.*

Here the new Adam speaks.

## 9.

**VERSE 7.** *I will bless the Lord who made me understand.*

For the Son knows nothing except what he has seen and heard from the Father. Therefore he blesses him who made him understand. And truly this understanding is not from man but from God. For what human being, when two inheritances are set before him—one splendid and rich in works, the other poor and needy—would choose the one that needs another’s mercy?

But the Son, instructed by the Father, prefers an inheritance among those who hope in God to one among those justified by their own works. Thus he beautifully says: *I will bless the Lord who made me understand; moreover, even as if in the night, my reins instructed me.*

What did his reins instruct him? They made him understand, that it is better to hope in the Lord than to be justified in one’s own work. Did not even the Lord himself, as if in the night, have his reins instruct him to hope in God? For his soul was sorrowful unto death. He learned to hope in God; and this is what he means when he says that he was instructed by his reins in this understanding, as if in the night.

For what follows also shows that he is speaking of his Passion, when he adds:

10. VERS. 8–10. “I kept the Lord always before my sight, because he is at my right hand, so that I shall not be moved. Therefore my heart was made glad and my tongue rejoiced; moreover, my flesh also shall dwell in hope: because thou wilt not abandon my soul to hell, nor wilt thou give thy Holy One to see corruption.”

The text and its sequence are clear; but, lest what he said about the “reins,” namely that “they instructed me as though in the night,” seem rather obscure, let us inquire into it. God is said to search the reins and the heart, as though the secrets of the human being were held in these two places. In the heart is the secret of the soul, while in the reins is the secret of the flesh. The Apostle likewise teaches the distinction between the inward and outward human being when he says: “I consent to the law according to the inward man; but I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind” (Rom. VII, 12). And elsewhere: “Thus I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin” (ibid. 25).

Our Lord Jesus himself reports that he experienced a certain such dissension when he says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” For according to the inward man he consented to the law of the Father, to suffer; but according to the outward man, as he himself testifies, he trembled in the flesh. Therefore, because the reins contain the secrets of the flesh, which was weak in the time of the Passion, he says that he was instructed by his reins, so that he might understand—even though he was the Son—to hope in God. The Epistle written to the Hebrews similarly understands this concerning him: “Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things which he suffered; and, having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him” (Heb. V, 8).

Thus his reins instructed him, so that he might keep the Lord always before his sight, because he is at his right hand and he should not be moved. That is, in will the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. And he rightly says that he was instructed by his reins “as though in the night”: he did not say “in the night,” but “as though in the night.” For his perceptions were not wholly darkened by fear of death, he who said: “Yet not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Matt. XXXVI [probably XXVI], 39). Nevertheless, he was not without a certain disturbance, he who confessed weakness and sorrow. For if David says elsewhere, “The fear of death fell upon me; fear and trembling seized me, and darkness covered me” (Ps. LIV, 6), rightly this darkness arising from fear of death—which it is fitting to regard as exceedingly slight in the Son of God—is called not night, but as though night. Thus it is said significantly: “Moreover, as though in the night, my reins instructed me.” And what did they instruct him? Surely what follows below: that he might keep God always before his sight, because he is at his right hand, so that he should not be moved.

11. “For this,” he says, “my heart was made glad, and my tongue rejoiced; moreover, my flesh also shall dwell in hope: because thou wilt not abandon my soul to hell, nor wilt thou give thy Holy One to see corruption. Thou hast made known to me the ways of life; thou wilt fill me with joy with thy countenance: delights are at thy right hand.”

Thus there are also joys at God’s right hand, with all of which the Son has been filled. For he had God at his right hand: “I kept the Lord,” he says, “always before my sight, because he is at my right hand.” Yet when he ascended into heaven, he himself was made to be at the Father’s right hand.

Let us ask what, in relation to this right hand, is the left hand. The Apostle, in one passage, speaks of “the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left”—of glory indeed and dishonour. I understand the right hand as the form of righteousness, but dishonour and disgrace as the left. Nevertheless, both are weapons of righteousness. But in order to reach the weapons of righteousness on the right, we must first serve as soldiers amid those on the left. In this world one must undergo dishonour, disgrace, weakness, folly, and the like, so that one may attain nobility, glory, strength, and wisdom. We shall receive all these when we arrive where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. We are sown in dishonour, that we may rise in glory; we are sown in mortality, that we may rise in eternity.

Therefore our Lord, when in the time of his Passion he endured the mockery of scourges and of spitting, when he was accused as though a blasphemer, when he was reckoned among thieves—being placed in such great dishonour and disgrace—what else was he doing but serving as a soldier amid the weapons of righteousness on the left? Therefore, then placed at God’s left hand, he kept him at his right hand, so that he should not be moved. But after he rose again and ascended into heaven, arriving at the right hand, at the palm of righteousness, at glory and nobility, he is filled with joy in God’s presence and has delights at his right hand.

To these the Apostle exhorts us in hope, saying: “The sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with those good things that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18). Therefore let us too more gladly glory in our weaknesses, that God’s power may protect us. And now let the Father himself be at our right hand so that we may not be moved, he who will afterwards transfer us to his own right hand, into the riches of our Lord Jesus Christ: to whom be glory. Amen.

## TREATISE ON PSALM XXXI

1. The designation “understanding” in this Psalm of David indicates the prophecy it contains. The Apostle taught that it announced the New Testament through the calling of the Gentiles. In it faith was to be justified without works, and remission of iniquities and the forgetting of sins were promised through God’s gratuitous grace; and the reason for this is clear. But it is worthwhile to follow the entire text of the psalm, in which the dispositions of the singer may be discerned.

Whoever looks according to the flesh sees the temptations that enter into faith. For he saw that those were blessed whose righteousness was not reckoned from works. “The law entered so that sins might be increased”; and “the law produces wrath”; and “where there is no law, neither is there transgression.” Therefore not without reason will that person be called blessed who has not been under law, but rather under grace.

2. But the Psalmist indicated what kind of faith is required when he said, VERS. 2: “Nor was guile found in his mouth.” I believe that he seeks precisely such a man as the Lord praised when Nathanael came to him; unlike those in Israel whom God rebuked through the prophets: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX, 13). There is no doubt that this is guile: to have one thing on the lips and another in the heart.

Thus David says well in another psalm: “I believed; therefore I spoke” (Ps. CXV, 10). And the Apostle explains: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10). Thus, if one believes in the heart what the lips confess, no guile will be found in his mouth. But if someone honours God with his lips while his heart is found far from him, guile is in his mouth. By this we are especially marked in the time when, rejecting God’s commandments, we follow human teachings and our own counsels. For it is written: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX, 13). “They worship me, following the commandments and teachings of men” (Matt. XV, 7).

So too, in the Gospel, the Lord calls the teachers of the law hypocrites, because they pass over God’s will and establish their own counsels. Every hypocrite is a pretender and deceitful. And plainly it is guile to promise faith to God while trusting human counsels. Such persons can neither have their iniquities remitted nor their sins covered, because they place their salvation more in human counsels than in God’s help.

Accordingly, the prophet at once describes, as it were, his own temptation in the wavering of faith; and, chastising himself, he warns what others ought to avoid. When God’s hand was heavy upon him—that is, persistent amid many temptations—he had indeed cried out to God, but had not persevered in crying out. At last he fell silent, and through that silence his bones immediately grew old.

3. We have often noted what we should understand spiritually by “bones.” As bones are the support and strength of the body, so patience is the support and strength of our mind. Thus this man, unable to persevere toward God under the hand that weighed heavily upon him, but failing and falling silent, rightly says that his bones “grew old”: that is, that his patience became aged. Every old age brings weakness. It is therefore clear that his patience was weakened.

He properly used the phrase “grew old,” that is, returned to the old impatience. For the new human being and the new birth possess enduring patience. Hence the Apostle says: “Tribulation produces patience; patience, proof; proof, hope; and hope does not bring confusion, because the love of God has been poured out into our hearts” (Rom. V, 3). Therefore, because in the new human being the love of God has been poured into the heart through the Holy Spirit, who cries, “Abba, Father,” that person’s patience endures, so that he can say: “Who shall separate me from the love of God? Tribulation, distress, nakedness, famine, or the sword?” (Rom. VIII, 35). But one who fails in crying out and hoping in God declares that his bones have grown old: that is, they have returned to the old impatience, the love of the new birth having failed—that love which never despairs of the Father.

4. What, then, does he teach? That this is our sure promise: if there is iniquity or the working of sin, even if the hand of the Lord has become heavy upon us and burdens us with many temptations, our cry to God ought not to fail. What if we fall silent? We return to old thoughts, seeking remedy in our own counsels, applying cares and anxieties, and through our own wisdom abandoning the hope that is from God, which is firmer than all our thoughts.

Marking this, as it were, in temptation, the prophet sings, VERS. 3 and 4: “Because I kept silence, all my bones grew old; while I cried out all day and night, thy hand was heavy upon me.” And what does he finally say? “I was turned unto misery, while a thorn was fixed in me.” He clearly signifies that, because he had ceased to cry out to God and hope in him when temptations came upon him, and silence and stillness had followed, he had taken into his thoughts the cares and anxieties of his life. Through this he had been turned to misery, having abandoned the hope of God’s aid; and significantly he says that a thorn had been fixed in him.

For in the Gospel the Lord teaches that thorns are the cares and anxieties of sustenance, by which the word is choked. Or rather, the prophet here says that a thorn—that is, the care and anxiety of life—was fixed in him after he fell silent and ceased to cry out to God; and through this he confesses that he was turned to misery. And because these secular cares and anxieties often creep into our minds, even when they are unnoticed, “Make my sin known to me,” he says.

5. And he distinguishes iniquity from sin, because iniquity cannot possibly be unknown. The significance of this word is more fitting in Greek.
