For in Greek they call it *anomian* (lawlessness), by which is signified the time in which the world lived without law, when it did not yet know God in its Gentile way of life. All who are converted to the Lord must confess that the life of the earlier time was blameworthy.

But because we define the name “sin” as that by which a person enters into cares, anxieties, and thoughts about sustenance—these being very many and varied, and their images occurring very frequently even to the unwilling good person—who can detect them in his own watchfulness? Therefore the prophet properly seeks help from God concerning this, saying, VERS. 5: “Make my sin known to me, Lord.”

And we plainly find that the name of sin has been held from the beginning of the world, if we distinguish the transgression of the first-created human being himself. But it would take long to pursue this; nevertheless, to those who pursue the matter, distinguishing the senses of “sin” and “iniquity,” the distinction is made clear. Concerning sin he asks that it be made known to him; but he says that he did not hide his iniquity from himself. For that, since it was not without the person’s knowledge, had remaining in it the remedy of humility: that he should declare it and confess it to the Lord. But concerning sin, whose variety could creep in even without one’s knowledge, whose multitude could deceive and remain hidden, he prayed that it might be made known to him.

Finally, he remained consistent in the meaning of the word; and because he distinguished iniquity from sin, he said: “I will declare against myself my iniquity, Lord.” Thus even here he does not say, “I will declare my sin, Lord,” but “my iniquity.” For he could not declare the sin whose knowledge he sought from the Lord. But his iniquity, which he possessed in his conscience, “I will declare,” he says, “against myself before the Lord.”

For iniquity has no other remedy than confession to God. We do unknowingly what the Lord makes known, once conversion has brought about its recognition; and repentance must follow. Thus, after this iniquity, if one has confessed before the Lord and declared it against oneself—that is, has become one’s own accuser—one will redeem the impiety of one’s heart. And here he speaks with prudent reasoning: “I said: I will declare against myself my iniquity, Lord; and thou hast forgiven the impiety of my heart.” For one who does not confess iniquity to the Lord embraces pride against the Lord and thus acquires impiety. Such a person does not acknowledge the Lord as Father of all creation. Conversely, the prophet calls humble the one who confesses and thereby begs pardon for the charge of impiety; and humility is, of course, the opposite of pride.

6. “For this,” he says, “the humble and righteous person will pray to thee at the right time.” Thus there is a time when it is not right for the righteous person to approach the Lord. The prophet himself teaches this in what follows, saying, VERS. 6: “Yet in the flood of many waters they shall not draw near to him.” Therefore, amid a flood of many waters, it is not the right time for the righteous person to draw near to the Lord. For it is not the part of a righteous person to give boldness to his own soul, as the law says: “You shall not give boldness to your soul.”

If anyone seeks the Lord as profound and most exalted in mysteries, searching all his judgments, and perhaps thinks himself able to endure all his waves [the text has *fructus*, perhaps *fluctus*], that person will not be righteous, nor will he profitably attempt to approach and seek the Lord amid the flood of many waters; for in the exaltation of his wisdom he will have attempted to knock at the hidden depths.

So also the Apostle Paul: “And lest I be exalted by the abundance of revelations, a thorn was given to my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me. On account of this I asked the Lord three times; and it was said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness’” (II Cor. XII, 7–9). Thus the prophet here, having said that the righteous and humble do not approach the Lord in the flood of many waters, shows instead at what time the Lord is especially to be sought by him: VERS. 7: “Thou art my refuge from the tribulation surrounding me.”

Here too, therefore, he glories rather in weaknesses, so that God’s power may protect him, as Paul says: “Therefore I will more gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may protect me” (ibid. 9). Finally he adds: “My exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me.” He calls the Lord his exultation, because “let not the wise person glory in his wisdom, nor the strong person in his strength”; rather, let each person glory in this, that he has known and fears the Lord. “My exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me.”

7. VERS. 8. “I shall understand and be joined to thee in this way by which thou shalt walk; I shall fix my eyes upon thee.” The commandment follows: “You shall walk after the Lord your God.” And this is the faithful person: not choosing a way for oneself, but following the way which the Lord shows, and judging right what he commands.

Finally he says: “I shall fix my eyes upon thee,” so that they may see no other path except that which the Lord directs. He says this more plainly in another psalm: “As the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God” (Ps. CXXII, 2). That is, we are directed not because we ourselves aim at what is true, but because the Lord turns our eyes, which ought to be in his hands; and because it lies within his power where he opens our sight and where he closes it.

8. If anyone does not willingly come to this refuge of God, let us learn how the prophet chastises such a person, to what he compares him, and what he forbids. “Do not become,” he says, VERS. 9, “like horse and mule, which have no understanding.” A human being obeys the word and gives heed to a voice. But those to whom it may be said, “I sought and there was no human being; I called and there was none to hear” (Isa. LXIII, 5)—such are horse and mule: with bit and bridle they must be compelled to go where they do not wish.

Accordingly, the righteous person asks that their stiff neck and hard jaws be softened by punishment and force. The prophet mercifully does not wish those who do not voluntarily draw near to the Lord to be abandoned to their hardness; rather, he asks that they be dragged by whatever punishments may be necessary, provided that they are saved. Thus he says: “With bit and bridle draw their jaws, those who do not draw near to thee.”

9. VERS. 9. “Many are the scourges of the sinner.” By these the Lord fashions salvation for sinners: by inflicting blows and tribulations, he instructs the sinners’ pride to become accustomed to fear. “But mercy shall surround the one who hopes in the Lord.” Such a person need not be led with bit or bridle, nor corrected by the scourge in order to draw near, since his hope is always in God’s help. Therefore God’s mercy is close to this person.

Wherefore, as the prophet says, VERS. 11: “Be glad in the Lord and rejoice, you righteous; and be joyful, all you upright in heart.” Through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom is glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## TREATISE ON PSALM XLI

1. I think that, in expounding all psalms generally, we should keep the method of first examining the title and then fitting the whole psalm to it. For no one is so foolish that, having promised to speak about a cedar, he would describe an oak. Still less would the Spirit of God, whom we believe spoke through the prophet, have marked one thing in the title and said another in the song of the psalm.

Thus in the present case David sang those things which ought to be an understanding for the sons of Korah (Num. XVI, 8); for such is the superscription of the psalm. We read that Korah’s assembly, in the time of Moses, murmured against God’s ordinance, striving to usurp and seize for themselves the supreme ministry of the priesthood which Aaron and his sons had received according to God’s will.

The Apostle points out this fault of covetous ambition and, in a manner, reproves it: “I say to you through the grace given to me, to all of you, not to think above measure beyond what you ought to think” (Rom. XII, 3); but let each of you think according to the measure of faith which the Lord has distributed. “For as we have many members in one body, but all members do not have the same functions, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another, having diverse gifts” (ibid. 4–6). Thus to one is given ministry, to another prophecy, to another power, to another a word of teaching.

If anyone, wishing to think above measure, goes beyond the measure of the Lord’s distribution, that person is found in Korah’s folly and will spiritually be called a son of Korah. To such persons will be sung this psalm of understanding which he teaches.

2. VERS. 2. “As the stag longs for springs of waters, so my soul longs for the living God.” I judge that “springs of waters” have not been inserted without reason, when it would have been near at hand simply to say, “as the stag longs for waters.” But he preferred to name “springs of waters,” that is, the source and beginning of waters, knowing through spiritual wisdom—which alone knows the roots of trees and the natures of beasts—that even this dumb animal longs not for any waters nearby, but for the very springs of waters, seeking the cleaner and purer beginnings of streams.

By this example he wishes us to be admonished that we too should long for the Lord himself, the fountain of life and wisdom, who is the head of all. For there is one fountain from which many distributions of spiritual waters arise: healings, prophecies, kinds of tongues, ministries, the word of knowledge, and the word of teaching. But neither should the respective gifts of those near us be so sought through rivalry, contention, and dissensions that we neglect longing for the fountain itself. For we neglect him whenever we refuse to preserve, in peace and love, the measure of his distribution and ordering.

Thus all who, after the likeness of the sons of Korah, are found in this pride will be admonished by this psalm to understand what their desire ought rather to seek, as the righteous person says: “As the stag longs for springs of waters, so my soul longs for the living God.”

3. VERS. 3. “When shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears became bread for me by day and by night, while it is said to me daily: ‘Where is your God?’” By the very words “When shall I come and appear?” we are shown that this is not something easily obtained; and unless our tears become our bread day and night, we shall by no means attain the face of the Lord.

The understanding of the sons of Korah ought to follow the order of instruction, so as to know that one reaches the house of God through many tribulations, afflictions, and reproaches [the text has *imperia*, probably *impropería*]; lest it be exalted in its pride, knowing that strength is more proved in weakness, and lest it seize dignity for itself. For the Apostle says: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized; but humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in appearance as a human being. He emptied himself unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II, 5–8). While fastened to it, he heard these reproaches: “Where is your God?” as they said to him in reproach: “Let him come and deliver him” (Matt. XXVII, 43).

Therefore, as I said, Korah’s assembly is taught through how many tribulations and tears one comes to the house. The prophet aptly says that these tears were his bread, that is, food unto eternal life. And in sequence he proceeds to say:

4. VERS. 5. “I remember these things, and I poured out my soul within me, because I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.”

Here I think something should first be said about the force of the word: what “I poured out” means. He says that he poured himself out because he was going to pass into the place of the tabernacle, even to the house of God. The passage into God’s house is a good thing of the Spirit. Therefore to pour out one’s soul is an act of good hope. Yet what do we know of its ordinary meaning? Whatever is poured out is thrown away and lost, and is not as secure as when it is retained in a vessel. For to pour out is to pour forth outside something which one had enclosed somewhere.

Thus, one who says, “I poured out my soul,” should be understood as saying nothing other than, “I cast it away, lost it, and regarded it as worthless.” How then did he cast it away and lose it because he was to pass into the place of the tabernacle, even to the house of God? Unless perhaps he makes clear the commandment of God, who says to his disciples: “Whoever saves his soul will lose it, and whoever loses it will save it” (Luke XVII, 33).

And indeed he maintained the sequence. For after speaking beforehand of tribulations—because his tears had become his bread day and night while it was daily said to him, “Where is your God?”—he says: “I remember these things, and I poured out my soul within me.” By this he should be understood to have said nothing other than: “I cast it away, lost it, and regarded it as worthless.”

How then did he cast away his soul for God? The righteous person knows that whenever tribulations, persecutions, and reproaches arise because of God’s name, the soul must be lost, cast away, and held worthless, so that it may be saved on the day of the Lord. Therefore here too he significantly shows that he poured out his soul not because he despaired of hope in the life to come, but because he was to pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.

Being taught by this psalm, therefore, whenever the enemy persecutes us and reproaches the name of the Lord, let us pour out our souls for him, prepared to lose them so that we may save them. Let us not pour them out as though we despaired of confidence in God’s help, but because we are certain that they will be restored to us, and that we shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.

5. But what is this place of the wondrous tabernacle, through which there will be passage even to the house of God? Let us now begin to ask. In the ancient books we find that Moses made a tabernacle for the God of Israel, in which the ark of the covenant was kept (Exod. XXVI, 1); in it all the mysteries were celebrated, and there those offering sacrifices first appeared before the face of God. Until Solomon built the house of God, the ark passed from the tent of skins into a temple constructed of stones. But that tabernacle in the wilderness, and those skins which formerly covered the roof of the temple, were wondrous in their ministry.

Thus in the Song of Songs the bride praises her beginnings in this way: “I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tent of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Cant. I, 4). And in another psalm, although David longs for the courts of the Lord, he nevertheless praises his tabernacles, saying: “How wondrous are thy tabernacles, O Lord; my soul longs for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII, 2). God’s tabernacle is indeed wondrous, but the house of God is more to be desired.

Thus David himself, once Israel’s kingdom was at peace, when the ark of God remained in Shiloh under the skins [the text has *sub pedibus*, apparently *sub pellibus*] of the tabernacle, longed to build God’s house. But what did the prophet say to him? “You shall not build me a house” (II Reg. VII, 7). Not everyone is able to build God’s house. Therefore, as though toward greater ascents, we must make our passage through the place of the tabernacle so that we may arrive at the house of God.

We are admonished by Jerusalem’s example that the Lord’s house is not built until the enemy and sin have been conquered. Yet we remain in the tabernacle until the wilderness is crossed and one enters the land beyond the Jordan, the beginning of the promised inheritance, and every Canaanite enemy is overcome.

6. The difference between the dignity of the tabernacle and of the house is that one does not remain always in the tabernacle, whereas one remains always in the house, as David signifies in the Songs of Ascents when he says: “The Lord has chosen Zion; he has been pleased with it as a dwelling for himself: ‘This is my rest for age upon age’” (Ps. CXXXI, 13).

But in the tabernacle one does not have rest: it must be moved in the time of war, when the cloud that signified God’s presence also withdrew from it. This is rightly comparable to our own condition: while we are pilgrims in this body, we must in this steadfastness overcome all its vices, so that no enemy remains alive or vigorous. For God will visit us even in the tabernacle, and in a time of rest. But whenever battle against vices arises, our tabernacle must be folded up and prepared for the campaign of war; it cannot be spread out or delight in God’s rest while the vices make their assault.

God will indeed go before you in battle, so that, if you walk after him, you may easily conquer your enemies; but at that time he cannot dwell in you. Therefore, although you conquer and overcome the vices of the flesh, you nevertheless stain your hands in your own blood by the conflict itself. You will not be fit at that time to build the Lord’s house, just as David, who acted amid bloodshed, is rejected.

But the one who builds the Lord’s house is the one who enters into rest, who is troubled by no vices, whose every enemy has been destroyed, who can say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14); with whom all old things have passed away and all things have become new. Such is the kingdom of Solomon, set forth as a figure of our own.

But if, in the course of this life, no one is found so perfect that, clean from every assault of sin, he can arrive at the house of God, I may nevertheless say: “I shall pass into the place of the tabernacle, even to the house of God.” That is, in this present life, while I am in this world, I shall pass into the place of the tabernacle, since daily battle must be waged against flesh and blood, against the spiritual powers of wickedness. But when the dwelling of this tabernacle has been dissolved, as the Apostle says, and I receive a house not made by hands but eternal in the heavens; when the body of our humiliation has been transformed into the likeness of the body of the Son of God—then I shall arrive at the house of God, at the time when he may dwell in me for eternity. And rightly I shall sing: “I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.”

7. But this passage of mine will be “with the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting.” Nor is it surprising that the shadow of future good things contained an image of this joy: whether when David, transferring the ark of God from the tabernacle at Shiloh, entered Jerusalem with choir and timbrels, celebrating a feast day; or when Solomon, after building the temple, brought in all the sacred ministry amid great exultation of those singing and making melody to God.

It is not surprising, I say, that when each one of us exchanges this tabernacle of the body for that house not made by hands but eternal in the heavens, the passage will be with the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting.

8. Therefore, one who has received this hope rightly interrupts the sadness of his soul by saying, **VERSE 6:** “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess him: the salvation of my countenance and my God.” See whether this accords with the interpretation we have followed: that, in a time of persecution and reproach directed against God’s name, the righteous person consoles his soul with such hope. “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess him.”

But since it cannot happen that one who casts his soul into death is not disturbed by some sorrow—for the Lord himself of all virtues, the prince of faith himself, the Son of God himself, who before he came to the time of the cross spoke with confidence, saying, “No one takes my life from me; I have power to lay it down and power to take it up again” (John 10:18)—yet he, at the very hour close to death, said, “My soul is troubled unto death” (Mark 14:34); and, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39); and in his final cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46)—so this Psalm, setting forth in sequence an image of persecution and showing what conflicts and afflictions the righteous person must endure, through which his faith is to be tested and proved, says: **VERSE 7:** “My God, my soul is troubled within me.”

For whose soul is not troubled in the time of those who persecute the name of God? Besides the necessity arising from human frailty, besides bodily terrors, there is a particular disturbance of faith when the persecutors of God’s name seem to grow and prevail, while God neither vindicates his servants, nor comes to their aid in their afflictions, nor stretches forth his mighty right hand against their enemies. And therefore, because at such a time no one retains an understanding of God’s judgments, that exclamation of the Lord is beautiful: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (ibid.). By it he shows that he does not understand the reason why he has been forsaken. And if he, the teacher of wisdom and expounder of the Father, the Son, is so troubled that he asks the Father why he has forsaken him, what will the rest, however righteous, do when the depths of God’s judgments come upon them?

Nevertheless, the Psalm teaches what we ought to retain and what alone we ought to do amid these disturbances. For every righteous person, when tested, afflicted, distressed, and brought into a disturbance of soul, even though he does not understand why these things happen to him, ought nevertheless not to abandon faith or condemn the belief which the prophet taught, saying: “Therefore I shall remember you, O Lord, from the land of Jordan and Hermon, from the little mountain.” For because “my soul is troubled within me,” he says, “therefore I shall remember you from the land of Jordan and Hermon.”

For the land of Jordan signifies the entrance of the people Israel into the promised inheritance. And since we compare spiritual things with spiritual things, for us faith is regarded as the entrance into the inheritance. For this is the gate of our promises. Therefore, when the Prophet wished to indicate the beginning of our faith, he named there the land of Jordan and Mount Hermon. So also in the Song of Songs, where the Church’s first calling is made: “Come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon” (Song 4:8): “You shall pass over and pass over from the beginning of faith, from the summit of Hermon.”

Nor should anyone be troubled because Sanir is also named in that passage, since Mount Sanir is the same as Hermon, which Moses in Deuteronomy teaches history to have been situated in the land of Jordan: “And at that time we took the land from the hands of the two kings of the Amorites who were beside Jordan, from the torrent as far as Hermon Sanir” (Deut. 3:8). “The Amorite called it Sanir.” Therefore the summit of Hermon, which is in the land of Jordan, is called the beginning of faith. For this reason John, the first forerunner, is heard there, and Christ is first manifested to John there; there the Lord is filled with the Holy Spirit, there the testimony of the Father’s voice is given: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). Here he begins the first stages of virtues; here the first signs by which the Son of God is believed to have worked.

9. Mount Hermon’s summit is therefore rightly called the beginning of faith. From it we ought to remember God, who is the salvation of our countenance, whenever our soul is troubled in temptations. For the beginning of faith is the simple, first belief by which we enter upon the way toward faith in God through Jesus Christ. But wisdom is sought among the perfect (1 Cor. 2:6): namely, what the varieties of God’s judgments are, and what the depths of his thoughts.

Thus, even if wisdom fails in times of persecution, amid the disturbance of imminent death, the beginning of faith must not be abandoned. At least by that simple and bare belief, let us remember God, knowing that the enemy has no power over us except insofar as it is permitted him. Yet let us not misuse the boast of the foolish woman, by which it was said: “Where are the works of God’s righteousness? Job, what profit was there in fearing the Lord?” (Job 22:3). But whenever this thought comes into such disturbance, it will be right, according to the teaching of this Psalm, to say: “My God, my soul is troubled; therefore I shall remember you from the land of Jordan and Hermon, from the little mountain.”

Thus he also significantly adds the designation “little” to Mount Hermon. For the beginning of faith is a little mountain, with many ascents to the kingdom of heaven: to believe in God through reproaches, injuries, afflictions, and death on the cross is the first ascent. Whenever, therefore, my soul is troubled upon that most bitter height of the cross, from the beginning of faith, from the little mountain, I shall remember you, O Lord, who are the salvation of my countenance.

10. “For deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts,” that is, at the surge of God’s temptation which the earth endures; for who knows the depths of his thoughts and judgments? The Lord’s understanding is a flood. The righteous man, wishing to show its magnitude because he was speaking of his afflictions, says: “Deep calls to deep, **VERSE 8**, at the sound of his cataracts.”

11. “All your heights and your waves have passed over me.” He gives the reason why his soul was troubled: for “deep calls to deep at the sound of the cataracts.” We have already said what we consider the deep to be; nevertheless, we shall explain what the Prophet himself says concerning it: “Your judgments, O Lord, are a great deep” (Ps. 35:7). For there is a great profundity in the depths of God’s judgments: when judgments so frequently follow judgments upon us, what flesh can emerge, what flesh can endure?

See the Apostle: although he was discoursing in peace, yet, contemplating God’s mystery, he cried out in distress: “O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). This depth of God’s heart is therefore rightly called an abyss, whose profundity no one knows; for there are many depths where there is no end. And rightly does “deep call to deep at the sound of your cataracts” come upon us here.

Let us set out certain examples of these abysses, so that the exposition may become clearer. Behold, the Son of God comes in many signs and powers, heals the various diseases of many people, and is accused because he brings healing. Who has ever been reviled for doing good? Yet the Father permits so impious an insult to his Son: behold one abyss. God’s judgments are arranged; false witnesses are assembled against him as though he were a blasphemer and irreligious, though he alone was the true witness of God; and the wicked give testimony and prevail in their case: behold, a second abyss follows the first. He is struck, scourged, clothed in mocking attire; the enemy exults and derides; every prolonged impiety is directed against the Son of God: behold, now a third abyss is called upon. The Lord of glory is condemned to the cross and reckoned among robbers and the impious. See how many judgments, how many abysses, follow one another, so that he may rightly say: “All your heights and your waves have passed over me.”

12. I think enough has now been said about this. But lest anyone should inquire and think that we have passed over out of negligence what is meant by “Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts,” let us briefly return to the sound of the cataracts.

These visible cataracts of waters certainly have their own sounds, since the outpourings of rivers must necessarily resound and roar. And whenever rivers rise in their course from the inexhaustible eruption of an infinite lake, pool, or spring, whose depth cannot at all fail or be drained, it is well said of them: “Deep calls to deep at the sound of the cataracts.” But we must remember of what abysses the Prophet speaks, which we have also discussed already. And thus we must know the cataracts belonging to them. We find that all the outpourings of God’s judgments have sounded through the voices of the prophets, and I think these are called “cataracts” here.

“Deep calls to deep at the sound of the cataracts.” After the prophets’ preaching, God’s judgments followed, and as though they called themselves into that sound which had gone before, in order that they might follow it. One cataract’s voice was: “Let us oppress the righteous man, because he is useless to us and contrary to our works, and calls himself the Son of God” (Wis. 2:12). Another cataract’s voice is: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). There is also another voice: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21:17). And another: “They divided my garments, and cast lots for my clothing” (ibid., 19); “and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22).

Why need we now recount every voice of the cataracts, when the books of the prophets are full of the Lord’s reproaches and passion? Since, therefore, faith in the deeds accomplished followed all the prophecies, deep called to deep at this sound of the cataracts, in order, that is, to supply their sounds with their fulfilment. Therefore, because the Prophet was speaking of such abysses, he fittingly adds:

13. **VERSES 9 and 10.** “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he made it manifest; with me is my prayer to the God of my life. I shall say to God, ‘You are my protector; why have you forgotten me?’”

He plainly gives teaching and consolation to all righteous persons: if, overwhelmed by the many waves of temptations, they suffer a disturbance of mind—which is called the night of darkness to the eyes—they should remember that God’s mighty mercy is always made manifest in this night, provided only that the time for mercy has come.

But when we have come into danger, and the disturbance arising from despair of life has made a kind of night in our heart, then, if we can say, “With me is prayer to my God; I shall say, ‘You are my protector; why have you forsaken me?’” this, then, must be retained in the night. And although the other faculties are disturbed, this must not fail: that we cry to the Lord, “Why have you forsaken me?”—a saying we discussed earlier. For even if we do not understand the reason for God’s judgments, why he leaves us amid certain temptations, we ought not therefore to fail to entreat mercy from him.

14. “Why,” he says, “do I go about sad, while the enemy afflicts me, **VERSE 11**, and breaks my bones?” This, therefore, will always be the righteous person’s prayer, even in the night. When he says, “He breaks my bones,” he surely does not mean that imminent death is to be understood. Rather, because in tribulation his patience was being broken—patience which is the support and strength of our mind, just as bones are of the body—he calls patience “bones.” When it is broken by continual afflictions, “while he breaks my bones,” he says, “those who afflicted me reproached me, saying every day, ‘Where is your God?’”

But although the righteous person feels this grievous hand, the Psalm teaches what must nevertheless be done and what remedy must be sought in persecutions, saying, **VERSE 12:** “Why are you sad, O my soul? Why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess him: the salvation of my countenance and my God.” With this purpose and example set before us, if any vexation, pressure, or reproach directed against God’s name comes upon us, if our soul is sad or troubled, let us say: “Hope in God, for I shall confess him,” through the protection of Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

# COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

[Col. 0909]

# NOTICE CONCERNING THE COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF SAINT MATTHEW

[Col. 0909A]

I. **Hilary’s rank among Latin interpreters of Scripture; his judgment of Tertullian’s writings.**—When Jerome sent a translation of Origen’s homilies on Luke to certain persons who had requested it of him, he also sent them this Commentary of Hilary together with another by Victorinus, rejoicing that Latin writers themselves had long before devoted labor to expounding the Scriptures. “After a few days,” he says in the preface prefixed to his explanation of Origen on Luke, “I have decided to send you the commentaries of the most eloquent man Hilary and of the blessed martyr Victorinus, which they published on Matthew in differing styles but with the one grace of the Spirit, so that you may not be unaware how great an interest in the holy Scriptures our own countrymen—that is, Latin writers—once had.”

By these words Jerome indicates in some measure that the understanding of the sacred writings had hitherto been sought from Greeks, and that those Latins who had undertaken the same pursuit were not yet well known. In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, apart from Victorinus—who knew Greek no less well than Latin—he mentions no one before Hilary as having labored on the Scriptures, except Rhæticus, bishop of the Aedui, on the Song of Songs, and Fortunatianus of Aquileia, on the four Gospels in a brief and unpolished style. Since Hilary was contemporary with these men, even if he may not be assigned first place among Latin interpreters of Scripture, he may certainly be counted among the foremost.

It may also be doubted whether he knew that any Latin writer before him had expounded Matthew’s Gospel. For he does not seem likely to have undertaken an exposition of it if he had known that it had already been completed in Latin; since, as he himself testifies in chapter 5, he refrained from writing on the Lord’s Prayer solely because Cyprian had explained it. In that place he does not pass over in silence Tertullian’s very suitable work on the same prayer; but, because of that man’s subsequent error, he says that the authority of his otherwise commendable writings had been diminished.

It would indeed be difficult to suppose that he was ignorant of Victorinus’s works, if, along with Mariano in Jerome’s edition of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, the same Victorinus were to be written “of Poitiers,” rather than, as the manuscripts have it, “of Petovio,” “of Petabio,” “of Poetabio,” or finally, as a German manuscript written in Merovingian letters has it, “of Pectabio,” bishop in Upper Pannonia. Yet we have already heard from Jerome that the commentaries of the two were composed in different styles. Thus, when Hilary brings forward the opinions of others in these writings, he should be understood to mean Latin writers rather than Greeks.

II. **Whether he borrowed anything from Origen in this work.**—There are some who think that, just as in the Psalms, so here in Matthew, he borrowed the senses of Scripture from Origen. Jerome’s words in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* are ambiguous. In enumerating Hilary’s works, he says: “Also a book of hymns, another of mysteries, commentaries on Matthew, and treatises on Job, which he translated in sense from Origen’s Greek.” For it is uncertain whether he means only the treatises on Job to have been translated from Origen’s Greek, or the commentaries on Matthew as well.

But Jerome himself resolves the ambiguity in Letter 75, against Vigilantius. Accused by Vigilantius of being familiar with Origen’s reading, he replies among the first points: “If this is a crime, let the confessor Hilary also be accused, who translated the interpretation of the Psalms and the homilies on Job from his books, that is, from Greek into Latin.” He would not there, in defense of his case, have passed over the Commentary on Matthew in silence if he had also believed it translated from Origen.

This is still clearer from the beginning of his own *Apology against Rufinus*, where, enumerating ancient translators of Origen, he immediately puts forward Hilary the confessor, who translated almost forty thousand lines of Origen on Job and the Psalms. Certainly it was more readily available to him to mention an entire commentary than so many thousands of lines. Or if he thought his case aided by the number of lines, why not by the number of works? Moreover, when he promises this work of Hilary to persons asking for Origen’s homilies, he does not describe it as filled with Origen’s opinions, but with the grace of the Spirit.

III. **Style.**—Nor does this Commentary show very frequent agreement with those writings which we possess from Origen on Matthew. Its chief difference is that scriptural testimonies are rarely introduced to prove the matters narrated. Nor does the discourse ever wander at length; rather, its language is almost always concise and embraces much in few words. This is far removed from Origen’s method of instruction. Yet, while striving for brevity, Hilary here and there omits words and is not always bound by exact grammatical rules. He also touches some passages of Scripture so lightly that sometimes his meaning does not occur to the mind unless one has first read the portion of the Gospel that he expounds. For the most part, he rapidly runs through Gospel sayings and events and fixes them in the mind. Then he sometimes indicates the literal sense in few words. But his chief, indeed almost his whole, labor lies in investigating spiritual and hidden meanings.

IV. **His method of interpretation.**—For he believed that not only the Old Testament, but also the New, besides its plain meaning, was filled with another, loftier, inward, and spiritual sense. “The word of God,” he says in chapter 12, section 9, “is rich; and, placed before the inquiry of understanding, it supplies from itself a very abundant store of examples. Whether understood simply or examined inwardly, it is necessary for every advancement. But leaving aside those matters which lie open to common understanding, let us dwell upon the inward reasons.”

By these words he declares that this twofold understanding is useful and necessary, but that he himself especially adheres to the inward and spiritual sense—because the simple sense, obvious in itself to everyone, does not surpass ordinary comprehension.

V. **Drawn from the innermost meanings of Scripture itself.**—Having undertaken this method of interpretation, he professes in chapter 7, section 8, that he followed not a private opinion of his own mind, nor adapted the Scriptures to preconceived thoughts, but adapted his thoughts to the Scriptures: “We do not invent an interpretation; rather, the events themselves impart the interpretation. For events do not follow interpretation; interpretation follows the event.”

Indeed, in chapter 19, section 4, as also very frequently elsewhere, he acknowledges that all the things written in the Gospel were done and accomplished. Yet he immediately warns that those things which were done under God—that is, under Christ—had, in their present fulfilments, set forth the pattern of future things; and that the language of the heavenly Scriptures had always been so framed as to accord no less with the things being done than with the likeness of things yet to be done.

VI. **How he investigates what the Holy Spirit secretly signified.**—In order to attain those things which he was persuaded were prefigured in the writings and sayings of the Gospels, he habitually observes the order of the events, the precise force of the words, and also the circumstances of places, times, and persons. Having carefully weighed and considered all these, he sometimes maintains that it could scarcely have happened otherwise than that the Holy Spirit intended to signify to us some spiritual sense beyond the literal meaning.

For this reason, he thinks, something is sometimes lacking for a complete treatment of present events. “As we have warned in other cases,” he says in chapter 21, section 13, “so here also we ought to remember that, under this condition, something sometimes falls short of the rationale of present things, so that the figure of future things may be fulfilled without detriment to its prefiguring efficacy.”

VII. **He always preserves the truth of history.**—Sometimes he expresses the necessity of this spiritual understanding, taking account of surrounding circumstances, in such a way that, if he had not very often protested that he wished to leave the literal sense untouched, he might seem altogether to reject it. For example, one might think him, in chapter 10, section 17, to deny that the words, “For I came to set a son against his father,” and so forth, command any separation from fleshly relatives, unless he had already taught in chapter 4, section 19, on the authority of the same words, that such separation is wholly necessary when they are an occasion of stumbling.

Whatever words, therefore, he uses to declare that something in Scripture is to be understood differently from what it sounds like, must be taken in this sense: as he warns in chapter 2, section 2, we should remember that truth is not corrupted because the principle of an inward meaning is subordinate to events that are to be accomplished. He conveyed the same point in other words in Psalm 123, section 5: “Faith in history is not endangered if we hold that an outward signification is inherent in and joined to accomplished events.”

While he diligently seeks what lies hidden beneath Gospel sayings and events, nothing is more familiar to him than the respective conditions of the Law and the Gospel, the Church and the Synagogue, Jews and Gentiles—or Christians—which he explains as prefigured in those sayings and events. Among these, his distinction concerning the Jews is especially prominent: namely, between the comparatively few who obeyed the Gospel and the far greater number who resisted it.

VIII. **The title of this work.**—Whether he delivered these discourses to the people is uncertain. Indeed, since in chapter 19, section 11, he himself calls this work a “book,” it is certain that it was not published in the form of sermons. In some manuscripts it is entitled *Treatises on Matthew*; in others, *Exposition on Matthew*; in the rest, *Commentary on Matthew*. Jerome consistently calls it by the latter name, with Hilary himself supporting this designation in chapter 5, section 1, where he recalls that blessed Cyprian had freed him from the necessity of commenting on the Lord’s Prayer.

IX. **It is unquestionably Hilary’s work.**—There is no reason to dwell longer on establishing these commentaries as Hilary’s. For not only did the ancients hand down that he published commentaries on Matthew; but the excerpts from them preserved by Hincmar in chapter 25 of *On Predestination*, by Augustine, after Pelagius, in chapter 62 of *On Nature and Grace*, and by Jerome in Letter 145 agree with those we now have before us. We have already heard at the beginning of this notice how highly Jerome valued them.

It may also be said that Ambrose profited greatly from them. Certainly, in expounding Luke, in those places where that Evangelist agrees with Matthew, he generally either imitates or cites the interpretations which our Hilary recorded in these commentaries.

X. **The preface which he published is missing.**—John Cassian saw these commentaries enlarged by a preface. For in book 7, chapter 24, of *On the Incarnation*, after reporting several excerpts from Hilary’s books *On the Trinity*, he adds: “Likewise, by the same author in the prologue of the exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew: ‘For it was first necessary for us that the only-begotten God, for our sake, should be born as man—something which he then was not.’ Likewise in the same work: ‘Next, it was fitting that, since God, born as man in the world,’” and so forth.

Alcuin also saw the same preface. Although we strongly suspect that he saw in it nothing other than what he had read in Cassian. For, copying Cassian’s words after the middle of book 4 *Against Felix of Urgel*, he says: “Hilary, a man eminent in every virtue and ornament, and distinguished alike in life and eloquence, in the second book *On Faith*,” and so forth. “Likewise in the prologue of the exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew: ‘For it was first necessary for us that the only-begotten God, for our sake, should be known as man.’”

Moreover, from Hilary’s own words at the beginning of section 2 in chapter 1, it is apparent that something is missing for us, in which he had prefaced a discussion of Christ’s generation.

XI. **On the list of subject headings.**—In place of the preface, there is now a list of headings, or subjects, distributed into thirty-three chapters. In earlier printed editions this list is entitled “List of Canons,” and from it the whole Commentary was divided into canons. Since the reason for this inscription and designation is not obvious to everyone, it will not be beside the point to inquire whence it came and whether it is to be approved. We hope that this will become apparent of itself once we have considered what authority is due to those headings.

XII. **Its author.**—It may be questioned whether Hilary should be regarded as their author, since their list seems arranged somewhat barbarously and not quite accurately, omitting certain matters discussed at considerable length while containing others that are scarcely touched upon afterward. For example, chapter 15 is headed: “On washing hands, and on the fact that things entering the mouth do not defile, but things coming out of the mouth do”; yet nothing is treated that openly corresponds to this heading.

We add also chapter 13, in which headings are prefixed concerning the sower of good seed, tares, and wheat, although not a word is said about these parables in the exposition. Yet I do not know whether this consideration should not have more weight in assigning the list to Hilary than in denying it to him. For he himself could at the beginning have proposed certain matters upon which he afterwards judged that he need not dwell; another person, however, could not have gathered from his writings anything but the subjects actually treated.

From this arises a strong suspicion that those headings had already been prefixed in copies of the Gospels in Hilary’s own age and that he selected from them those whose explanation he deemed more useful. For although he ranges over the whole Gospel of Matthew, he does not expound every word of it, but only selected headings from each chapter. It is clear that Origen had done the same before him from the commentaries of Origen published by Huet, in which Matthew’s Gospel is elucidated under definite headings. Jerome confirms that this was customary in that age in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he recalls that Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, wrote commentaries on the Gospels in a brief and unpolished style, arranged by headings.

This being so, one may suppose that Hilary was author, if not of the headings themselves, at least of their collection or preliminary index. Certainly no one is permitted to think it later than Hilary, since even the more ancient manuscripts present it under this inscription: “The chapters of Saint Hilary on Matthew begin.” Accordingly, we judged that this same index, complete with its headings, should be reproduced according to the authority of those manuscripts, with nothing altered, even if something might perhaps have been prepared more accurately.

XIII. **Lists placed by the ancients at the beginning of books.**—Certainly the ancient practice of placing a list of such headings at the beginning of books will be demonstrated by the Canon of Hebrew Truth composed by Jerome himself and at last intended for publication. There one may see, at the very beginning of each book, an index of headings divided by various numbers, which presents in summary whatever is contained in the book that follows.

These indexes are entitled interchangeably *Capitula* (“chapters”) and *Tituli* (“headings”): for example, “The chapters of the book of Exodus begin”; “The headings of the book of Leviticus begin”; “The headings of the book of Deuteronomy begin”; “The chapters of the book of Joshua begin,” and so forth. Likewise, in the older manuscript copies of Augustine’s *City of God*, an index distinguished merely by various numbers is placed before the books themselves; later these divisions were called chapters. It contains the summary of what each book includes. Moreover, in a Corbie manuscript written a thousand years ago, this index is called a *canon*. It is inscribed thus: “The first book of Aurelius Augustine, bishop, against the Pagans, *On the City of God*, begins, with a canon placed before it, indicating what each book contains”; and at the end of the list or index: “The canon of ten books ends.”

XIV. **This work is incorrectly divided into canons; the origin of this practice.**—From these facts anyone may now readily observe how the word *canon* came to prevail in these commentaries of Hilary and whether it has prevailed rightly. Certainly we have seen no manuscript in which this word *canon* occurs. Yet we concede that it may be possible that where our manuscripts read, “The chapters of the book of Saint Hilary begin,” some have instead: “The canon of the book of Saint Hilary begins.” And we believe this to have existed in the manuscript once belonging to Saint Benignus of Dijon, from which this Commentary was first published.

But since Jerome calls the canon of Hebrew Truth what we would call a compendium of all the books which the Hebrews receive into the true Scriptures, and since the canon of Augustine’s books is what for us is an index or list of the matters contained in those books, it is clear that the title printed at the beginning of the index—namely, “List of Canons”—is not to be approved, much less that the name “canon” should be repeated for individual sections of the Commentary.

Accordingly, in place of *canon* we shall substitute the more customary and accepted term *chapter*, and, for convenience, append its headings to each chapter, as has already been done, although in the manuscripts they occur only in the index prefixed to the work. For in those manuscripts the entire Commentary proceeds in a single continuous sequence, unbroken by the addition of chapters or headings. Only in some manuscripts, and those not the best, numbers are marked at about the places where formerly canons and now chapters are set down.

XV. **Date of this work.**—Something should be said concerning the date of this work. There is, however, no indication by which it can be asserted with certainty. Yet, insofar as may be gathered from comparison with Hilary’s other writings, we judge that it was composed before his other works and before his exile, and therefore before the year 356.

For it does not savor of a man already trained by many battles waged against the Arians. Certainly, in the expositions of the Psalms he lets no opportunity slip for asserting Christ’s divinity. But in this Commentary, to say nothing of other instances, he touches upon the Father’s testimony concerning his Son in chapter 2, section 6, and even Peter’s illustrious confession in chapter 16, section 6, as though he did not know the Arians. At least, from chapter 31, section 3, it plainly appears that he was not yet fully instructed in their sophistries. There he writes, soundly enough in meaning but less cautiously in wording, that the Son was born from him who existed, and that in the one who was born is that which the one possessed with whom he was before he was born; namely, that the begetter and the begotten have the same eternity.

No one will deny that this was written before the books *On the Trinity*, in which—especially in the twelfth book—it is argued with great care and with many arguments that the phrase “before he was born” has absolutely no place in the eternal generation of the Son. How much more must it be granted that the treatises on the Psalms, in which the books *On the Trinity* are mentioned, are later than this same Commentary?

Yet it is clear that the aforesaid heretics were not unknown to him even then, not only from the final chapters but also from chapter 15, section 12. Since, however, the Arian heresy came later to the knowledge of the Gauls—so much so that Hilary himself testifies in book *On the Synods*, section 91, that he had never heard the Nicene faith until he was about to go into exile—it may in some way be inferred that this Commentary was composed not long before his exile.

But if he wrote it even before he heard the Nicene creed, then, since in this work he repeatedly declares the Son to be of one substance with the Father, he does not testify in vain, in the cited passage *On the Synods*, that he learned that faith from the Gospels and Apostles: “Long since regenerated,” he says, “and having remained for some time in the episcopate, I never heard the Nicene faith until I was about to go into exile; but the Gospels and Apostles had made known to me the meaning of *homoousios* and *homoiousios*.”

XVI. **On the unity of the Trinity.**—Since an occasion presents itself to conclude this little study with a confession of the most holy Trinity, we shall close it with that illustrious testimony from chapter 13, section 6: that in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, without the necessity of an externally admixed leaven, all things in Christ are one.

Here the reader also has an example of passages in this Commentary that have been restored to their former purity by the aid and authority of manuscript copies. For formerly the whole statement was transmitted in a corrupt and confused form: “In the Father and Son and Holy Spirit, in the necessity of leaven externally admixed, all things in Christ are one.” Those who seek in Hilary an explicit statement concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit may for the present hold to this, until fuller satisfaction is given them in the books *On the Trinity*.

Moreover, anyone may observe in Jerome, Augustine, and other Fathers that any proposition drawn from Scripture is called a *capitulum* (“chapter”); in this sense the same word is still used in ecclesiastical offices.

XXXI. When Jesus came to the estate called Gethsemane, and says to his disciples, “Sit here while I go over there to pray”; [Note: [Col. 0918C] Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions instead: “and his soul was sorrowful unto death. And concerning the cup of death, when he said, ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.’ Concerning the spirit,” etc. Then the manuscripts have *promptu* (“ready”), not *prompto*.] concerning his soul sorrowful unto death; the cup, if possible, passing from him; the spirit ready and the flesh weak; and again, [Note: [Col. 0918C] Printed editions add here: “concerning what he said.”] “Father, this cup cannot pass unless I drink it; let your will be done.”

XXXII. Concerning Judas, who was one of the twelve disciples, coming to Jesus with a great crowd in order to betray him; and the sword which he ordered Peter to return to [Col. 0918C] its place.

XXXIII. Concerning Pilate: while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man.” Concerning those passing by the cross, who shook their heads and said, “This is the man who destroyed the temple and rebuilt it in three days.”

[Col. 0917]

*(WRITTEN ABOUT THE YEAR 355.)*  
**668. COMMENTARY OF SAINT HILARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.** *(C)*

# CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the birth of Christ, the Magi with their gifts, and the slaughtered infants.

## 1. Christ’s birth from royal and priestly stock.

[Col. 0918C] [Note: [Col. 0917C] In the printed editions the following was here uselessly prefixed: “The book of the generation [Col. 0918C] of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham,” etc., [Col. 0919B] without the authority of any manuscript. Moreover, it is remarkable how greatly the printed texts disagree with the manuscripts. For the edition printed by Badius Ascensius, together with Erasmus, who revised that same edition, begins thus: “The course which Matthew and Luke set forth in the order of royal succession: while each enumerates it, each both indicates in the Lord the kinship of the two tribes and sets forth the step of direct descent: because priestly,” etc. Lipsius, however, under the name Martinus, and after him the Paris edition, has: “The course which Matthew set forth in the order of royal succession, Luke set forth through the priestly order: while each,” with the remainder as in Badius, except that they shortly afterward have *agnationem* (“relationship by birth”) in place of *agnitionem* (“recognition”). Three manuscripts—the Michaelinus, that of the monastery of La Sauve-Majeure, and the Bec manuscript—have: “The course which Matthew set forth in the order of royal succession, Luke also follows up; while each,” agreeing in the remainder with Badius, except that they subsequently add, “and the step of direct descent is rightly set forth.” The codex of Marmoutier at Tours and that of Vendôme have: “The course which Matthew set forth in the order of royal succession, while each,” etc., as in the preceding manuscripts. The Vatican manuscript has: “The course which Matthew sets forth in the order of royal succession, and which Luke enumerates through the priestly order, each indicates the recognition in the Lord [Col. 0919D] of the two tribes,” etc.

We have preferred to all these the reading presented complete in every respect by the manuscript Germanense lectionary; the sole Colbert manuscript does not differ from it, except that at the beginning it has *gressum* (“course”) for *gradum* (“step”), and *agnitionem* for *cognationem* (“kinship”). We were nevertheless strongly inclined toward the reading exhibited by the manuscripts of St. Peter at Chartres and another Colbert manuscript, if only it had been permissible to add a word: “The lineage which Matthew and Luke set forth in the order of royal (here “and priestly” seems to be missing) succession, while each enumerates it and indicates the recognition in the Lord of the two tribes, the step of direct descent is rightly set forth.” But it is clear from chapter 11, section 6, that *cognationem* with the lectionary, or *agnationem* with the Paris edition, is to be preferred to *agnitionem*. It is quite probable that this first portion belongs to the preface, and that so great a disagreement among the codices arose because, when the preceding material had disappeared after a leaf fell out of the archetypal copies, [Col. 0920B] and thus the beginning of this commentary was defective, many people labored according to their own understanding to obtain a full and complete sense by removing or adding several words.]

The step of descent which Matthew set forth in the order of royal succession, Luke calculates in priestly descent. While each enumerates it, each indicates in the Lord the kinship of the two tribes. And the [Col. 0919A] step of generation is rightly set forth: because the alliance of the priestly and royal tribes, entered into through marriage in David, is now confirmed in the lineage from Salathiel to Zerubbabel. Thus, while Matthew recounts the paternal descent proceeding from Judah, but Luke teaches the lineage received through Nathan from the tribe of Levi (Luke 3:24), they established for our Lord Jesus Christ, 669 who is eternal, king, and priest, the glory of each lineage even in his fleshly birth.

[Note: [Col. 0920C] Printed editions read *uterque* (“each”), though not a single manuscript supports it; most manuscripts read *quisque* (“each one”), while three read *quibusque* (“to each”). Then, with the Paris edition and the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, which we shall call Roman, we retain *patribus* (“fathers”), whereas other books have *partibus* (“parts”).]

That Joseph’s birth rather than Mary’s is recounted makes no difference: for the whole tribe has the same single kinship. Matthew and Luke also supplied an example by calling fathers one another, not so much by lineage as by people; because a tribe begun from one person is contained within the family of a single succession and origin. For since he had to be shown to be the son of David and Abraham—as Matthew began in this way: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1)—[Note: [Col. 0920C] The printed editions read “must be shown,” against the manuscripts; they then omit *because*, in place of which the Germanense lectionary has “wherefore.”] it does not matter who is placed at what point or in what order in the genealogy, provided it is understood that the family of them all began from one person.

[Note: [Col. 0920C] Printed editions read “it makes no difference,” against the manuscripts. Then the Chartres and Colbert manuscripts have “who at what point in the genealogy.” Chrysostom, *Homilies on Matthew* 2, is relevant: “It was not lawful to contract marriages not only from another tribe, but not even from another family.” Thus, when it is said that someone is from the house and family of David, the statement will hold whether it is applied to the Virgin or rather to Joseph; the same conclusion results.]

Accordingly, since Joseph and Mary belong to the same tribe, when Joseph is shown to have proceeded from Abraham’s lineage, Mary too is shown to have proceeded from it. For this arrangement was preserved in the Law: if the head of a family had died without sons, a later brother of the same kinship would take the deceased man’s wife and assign the sons born to him to the family of the man who had died (Deut. 25:5); and thus the order of succession would remain [Col. 0920A] among the firstborn, when they were accounted fathers of those who were subsequently born, either in name or in lineage.

[Note: [Col. 0920C] The Roman manuscript has “in the succession of the offspring.” The Chartres and Colbert manuscripts have “in the firstborn”; shortly afterwards, with the Paris edition, “those born after them,” whereas the Bec manuscript has “those born before.” Nothing should be altered: for the firstborn are here said to be regarded as fathers [Col. 0920D] of those born after them.]

## 2. Why certain generations are omitted; why fourteen are stated where only thirteen are enumerated.

The next point is that, since [Note: [Col. 0920D] The word “we have said” was struck out in the Bec manuscript; yet Hilary certainly recalls what he proposed in the preface.] we have said that, according to the factual record, the order of this genealogy is consistent neither in number nor in succession, an explanation of this matter must also be supplied. For there is no slight reason why one thing should appear in the narrative, another have occurred in the events, and one thing be given in the total while another is retained in the number.

For fourteen generations are enumerated from Abraham to David, [Note: [Col. 0920D] We restore this passage from the Germanense lectionary. But the Chartres manuscripts and one Colbert manuscript immediately add here, “whereas in the books of Kings.” In Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius, after “to the Babylonian deportation,” there follows: “seventeen are found in certain books.” The reading is even more curtailed in seven manuscripts, which after “are enumerated” have only, “and are found in other books.” “In this, therefore, there is no,” etc.] and fourteen generations from David to the [Col. 0920B] Babylonian deportation, whereas seventeen are found in the books of Kings. But this involves no fault of falsehood or negligence. For three are omitted for a reason. Joram begot Ahaziah; Ahaziah begot Joash; Joash then Amaziah; and Amaziah Uzziah (2 Kings 8:25). Yet in Matthew Joram is written to have begotten Uzziah, although Uzziah is the fourth from him. This happened because Joram begot Ahaziah by a Gentile woman, [Note: [Col. 0920D] Thus four manuscripts of better quality. Others read: “namely from Ahab.” “For the Lord had foretold through the prophet.” But the printed editions have: “namely from Ahab, who had Jezebel as his wife. Finally, through the prophet . . . is said to sit”: a perverse interpolation by an editor. For “Gentile woman” does not here signify Jezebel, but Ahab’s daughter, whom Joram took as his wife and by whom he begot Ahaziah. Hilary refers to 2 Kings 8:18 and 2 Chronicles 21:6, where, when Joram is said to have done evil in God’s sight, the reason is given: “For Ahab’s daughter was his wife.” Elijah’s prophecy is uttered in 1 Kings 21:21 and confirmed in 2 Kings 9:8, not only against four generations but against Ahab’s entire house; its fulfillment is recorded in 2 Kings 10:30.] namely, one of Ahab’s house; and it had been declared through the prophet that no one of Ahab’s house should sit on the throne of the kingdom of [Col. 0921A] Israel until the fourth generation. Therefore, once Ahab’s Gentile family had been purged and three generations passed over, the royal descent is counted in the fourth of the succeeding generations.

[Note: [Col. 0921C] In some manuscripts and printed editions: “therefore, the stain of the Gentile family having been purged,” a reading not to be despised so far. But in the printed editions alone there is then perversely added: “tribe,” which violates the preceding rules. Then Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius read: “is counted in the sequence of four generations,” in place of “in the fourth.” Some manuscripts have “in the fourth [feminine],” with no different sense.]

But why fourteen generations are written as extending to Mary, when thirteen are found in the number, [Note: [Col. 0921C] Printed editions read “seventeen are found,” falsely and against the manuscripts. Chrysostom, *Homilies on Matthew* 1; Jerome; and the author of the homily attributed to Hilary, which we may perhaps publish in the Appendix, observe with Hilary that only thirteen generations, from Jeconiah to Joseph, are included.] can involve no error for those who know that our Lord Jesus Christ has not only the descent which began from Mary, but that in his bodily procreation the signification of his eternal birth is also contained.

[Note: [Col. 0921D] Thus most manuscripts. But printed editions read: “the eternal significance of bodily birth.”]

## 3. Against those who deny that Mary remained a virgin.

The rationale of the genealogy [Note: [Col. 0921D] In the Germanense lectionary: “The rationale is not simple.” The genealogy is here said to have a simple rationale because it is from one Virgin, not from a man and woman.] is simple. For his conception from the Holy Spirit and birth from the Virgin Mary are the work of all the prophets. But many [Note: [Col. 0921D] Epiphanius seems to have marked out the same people in *Heresies* 78.7, where he says: “I have learned with certainty from an authority that some have dared to assert this about her, that after she bore the Savior she had intercourse with a husband.” Unless, perhaps, these words of Epiphanius should be referred to Helvidius or Jovinian, who were later than Hilary. But Hilary may have had in view the disciples of Ebion. Certainly Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins* 6, maintains Mary’s virginity against their teacher: “She was, of course, certainly a virgin, although Ebion resists.”] irreligious persons, very far removed from spiritual teaching, take occasion shamefully to form opinions about Mary because it was said, “Before they came together, she was found to be with child” (Matt. 1:18); and, “Do not fear to take Mary your wife” (ibid., 20); and, “He did not know her until she gave birth” (ibid., 25). They do not recall that she was betrothed, and that this was said to Joseph when he wished to put her away, because he himself, being righteous, would not wish judgment to be pronounced against her under the Law.

Thus, lest any doubt concerning her giving birth should arise, Joseph himself is taken as witness to Christ conceived from the Holy Spirit. Then, because she was betrothed, [Note: [Col. 0922C] Badius, Erasmus, and Lipsius, with several manuscripts, read “she was received as a wife” or “into marriage”: a reading not to be despised. Hilary first reproves those who do not recall that she was betrothed; then he adds a double reason why Joseph was told, “Do not fear to take Mary your wife”: namely, both that he might be witness to Christ conceived from the Holy Spirit and that Mary, who until then had merely been betrothed, might thereafter also be received into marriage. The rules of grammar are admittedly not observed here; but do not demand them too scrupulously in what follows. For they are very often neglected out of a concern for brevity.] she is received into marriage. She is therefore “known” after giving birth—that is, she passes into the designation of wife. For she is “known,” not sexually joined. Finally, when Joseph is instructed to go into Egypt, it is said: “Take the child and his mother,” and, “Return with the child and his mother” [Col. 0922A] (Matt. 2:13 and 20); and again in Luke (Luke 2:33, according to the Greek): “And Joseph and his mother were [there].” Whenever there is mention of both, she is called Christ’s mother, because that is what she was; she is not called Joseph’s wife, because she was not. But the angel too observed this rationale: when he indicated that she was betrothed to the righteous Joseph, he called her wife. For he says: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife.” Therefore, the betrothed woman received the designation of wife; and after giving birth she is recognized [Note: [Col. 0922C] The Chartres and Colbert manuscripts merely read “that she might be shown to be Jesus’ mother”; they are not to be followed.] only as Jesus’ mother: so that, just as her marriage in virginity to the righteous Joseph might be reckoned to Mary’s credit, so her venerable virginity in being Jesus’ mother might be shown.

## 4. Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage.

But most depraved people [Col. 0922B] draw support for their opinion from the tradition that our Lord had several brothers. If these had been Mary’s sons, and not rather sons of Joseph [Note: [Col. 0922C] The Germanense lectionary reads: “from an earlier wife. They relate that Joseph fathered sons and daughters in an earlier marriage.” Epiphanius, *Heresies* 78.7; Theophylact on Matthew 13; and others whom Origen, *On Matthew*, in Huet’s edition, p. 223, observes were led to this view by the tradition of the Gospel entitled *According to Peter* or of the book of James. Origen himself adds that he considers it consistent with reason that Jesus was the first-fruits of male chastity and Mary of female chastity. Jerome, however, in *Against Helvidius*, considers it much more consistent that Joseph himself was a virgin, so that from a virginal marriage a virgin son might be born.] by a previous marriage, she would never, at the time of the Passion, have been entrusted as mother to the apostle John, when the Lord said to each: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26–27); and to John: “Behold your mother,” 672 unless, for the consolation of one left desolate, he was leaving a son’s affection in the disciple.

[Note: [Col. 0922D] The Paris edition alone reads “to the disciple,” without “in.” Chrysostom, *Homilies on Matthew* 5; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 78.9; and Ambrose, *On Luke* II.4, use the same argument against the same heresy, although Ambrose, by supposing Joseph still alive at the time of the Passion, uses it differently.]

## 5. What the Magi’s faith and gifts signify.

The rising of the star, first understood by the Magi, indicates that the Gentiles would immediately believe in Christ, and that people whose vocation was far removed from knowledge of divine understanding [Note: [Col. 0922D] The Bec manuscript reads “turned away,” which the Michaelinus also has in a second hand. The other manuscripts are more correct: “of a vocation turned away,” that is, from divine knowledge. Hilary plainly teaches that the Magi, as their name indicates, were devoted to magical art; he teaches this again in *On the Trinity* II.27 and IV.36, and agrees in this with Ignatius, *Letter to the Ephesians*; Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*; Origen, *Against Celsus* I; Ambrose, *On Luke* II.47–48; and Jerome, on Isaiah 19 and 47. Jerome nevertheless seems to depart from this opinion in Daniel 2, where he says: “Common custom and speech understands Magi as sorcerers, though they are regarded differently among their own people, because they are philosophers of the Chaldeans, and even their kings and princes of the same people do everything according to the knowledge of this art.”] would recognize the light that appeared at his very birth.

[Col. 0923A] Finally, the offering of gifts expressed recognition of his whole [Note: [Col. 0923D] Three manuscripts read “of his whole equality.”] nature: confessing him as king in the gold, God in the incense, and man in the myrrh. Thus, through their reverence, the knowledge of the entire mystery is brought to completion: in the man, the mystery of death; in God, of resurrection; in the king, of judgment. And in that they are forbidden to repeat their journey and return to Herod in Judaea (Matt. 2:12), we are taught that nothing of knowledge and understanding is to be sought from Judaea; but, placing all salvation and hope in Christ, we are admonished to abstain from the pathway of our former life.

## 6. What Christ’s flight into Egypt signifies. The Innocents: martyrs.

But while Herod prepared the death of the child, [Note: [Col. 0923D] Two manuscripts have “the little child”; four others, “the little children”; and shortly afterwards, “Jesus” in place of “him.” The Gospel words, “for Herod is going to seek the child in order to destroy him,” require either “the little child” or “the little children.” Chapter II begins in the manuscripts with the preceding words, “But while [Herod] was preparing,” etc.] Joseph is warned through an angel to take him into Egypt (ibid., 13): Egypt, full of idols and worshiping monstrous gods of every kind. After the Jews’ persecution and the profane people’s agreement in destroying him, Christ passes to the Gentiles given over to utterly empty religions. Leaving Judaea, he is brought to be worshiped by a world ignorant of him, Bethlehem—that is, Judaea—overflowing with martyrs’ blood.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] Printed editions read: “leaving Jewish ignorance to the world,” [Col. 0924D] etc.; they are corrected with the help of the manuscripts, in most of which “the ignorant world” is corruptly transmitted. Here “world” is a name for a people alienated from God, just as in Psalm 1, section 6, “a worldly man” means a man who does not belong to Christ.]

Herod’s fury and the slaughter of the infants are a figure of the Jewish people raging against Christians, imagining that by killing blessed martyrs it can extinguish Christ’s name in the faith and confession of all.

## 7. The Church grieves for the Jews’ destruction.

But through the prophet a glorious honor is rendered to their death, when he says: “A voice was heard in Ramah, much weeping and lamentation: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, [Col. 0923C] because they are not” (Jer. 31:15; Matt. 2:18). Rachel, Jacob’s wife, was barren for a long time, but she lost none of those to whom she gave birth. Yet in Genesis she presented a type of the Church. Therefore it is not her voice and weeping that are heard—she who had no grief over lost children—but those of this Church, long barren but now fruitful. Her weeping for her children is heard, not because she grieved that they had been killed, but because they were being killed by those whom she had wished to keep as her firstborn children. Therefore, she who grieved refused to be comforted.

[Note: [Col. 0924D] Erasmus testifies that he found in one manuscript: “For they were not those who,” etc.; he does not reject it in the sense, “For those thought dead were not dead,” though it is less relevant. Hilary’s point is that the words “because they are not” do not fit those who suffered persecution, who, far from not being, are better off; they fit those who, by stirring it up, fell away from the Church’s bosom and were so lost that they truly no longer are.]

For those who were thought dead were not non-existent; through the glory of martyrdom they were borne onward into the gain of eternity. Consolation should have been offered for a thing lost, not for one increased.

[Col. 0924A]

# 673. CHAPTER II. Concerning Jesus’ return from Egypt, John’s preaching and baptism, and the Lord’s baptism.

## 1. Joseph as a type of the apostles.

After this, Herod having died, Joseph is warned through an angel to return to Judaea with the child and his mother (Matt. 2:20). On returning, when he heard that Archelaus, Herod’s son, reigned, he was afraid to go there (ibid., 21); and through an angel he is warned to go into Galilee and dwell in Nazareth, a city of that region. He is thus commanded to return to Judaea, and he returns but is afraid. Again he is warned in a vision and commanded to go over into the region of the Gentiles. Yet either one who had been so warned ought not to have been afraid, [Col. 0924B] or the instruction given through an angel should not immediately have required alteration. But a typological rationale is preserved.

For Joseph represents the apostles, to whom Christ was entrusted to be carried abroad. As though Herod were dead—that is, as though his people had perished in the Lord’s Passion—they were commanded to preach to the Jews, for they had been sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. But, with the dominion of inherited unbelief still remaining, they are afraid and withdraw. Warned through a vision—that is, beholding among the Gentiles the gift of the Holy Spirit—they carry over to them Christ, who was sent to Judaea but designated the life and salvation of the Gentiles.

## 2. John’s place, preaching, clothing, and food.

“In those days John came preaching in the wilderness of Judaea, saying, ‘Repent, for the kingdom of [Col. 0924C] heaven has drawn near,’” etc. (Matt. 3:1). In John his place, preaching, clothing, and food must be considered; and this in such a way that we remember that the truth of the events is not thereby impaired [Note: [Col. 0924D] The Bec manuscript reads “but for things to be done.” This warning of Hilary’s should be carefully retained, lest hereafter, when he unfolds the hidden meanings of Scripture, he seem to violate the truth of the events.] if the rationale of an inner understanding is subordinated to the things done. For the preacher had a more suitable place, more useful clothing, and more fitting food; yet an example lies beneath the events, and in it action itself is meditation.
