For he comes to a deserted Judaea, [Note: [Col. 0924D] The Paris edition has “he comes,” and shortly afterward, “to the empty dwelling of the Holy Spirit”: incorrectly.] deserted of God’s visitation, not of people; empty of the Holy Spirit’s dwelling, not of human beings; so that the place of preaching might declare the desolation of those to whom the preaching was sent. He also proclaims repentance as the kingdom of heaven draws near; through repentance there is [Col. 0925A] a return from error and a retreat from sin, and, after shame for vices, the profession of ceasing from them.

[Note: [Col. 0925C] Here confession is indicated from its effect.]

Thus deserted Judaea might remember that she would receive him in whom the kingdom of heaven exists, and that she would not thereafter remain empty if she cleansed herself from her former vices by the confession of repentance. His garment woven of camel hair likewise signifies the foreign character of this prophetic preaching: since the preacher of Christ is clothed with the cast-off skins of unclean beasts, to which [Note: [Col. 0925C] Namely, the Gentiles. Hence below, chapter 19, section 11: “At the beginning of the book we observed, under John’s clothing, that the Gentiles are signified in the camel.”] we are reckoned akin; and whatever in us had previously been either useless or filthy becomes sanctified in prophetic attire.

The girding of the belt is effective preparation for every good work, so that we may be girded by willingness for every ministry of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0925C] Printed editions read “by the girdle of willingness.” Four manuscripts have “of willingness,” the rest “by willingness”; but none has the word “girdle.”]

Locusts are also chosen for food: creatures that flee from human beings and fly away at every perception [Col. 0925B] of our approach—meaning ourselves, who were carried away, by certain bodily leaps, from every word and association of the prophets.

[Note: [Col. 0925C] Erasmus, Lipsius, and the Paris edition read “by certain impious persons,” against Badius and the manuscripts, which agree strongly.]

Wandering in will, useless in works, querulous in words, [Note: [Col. 0925D] Printed editions and most manuscripts read “in seat.” The Colbert and Chartres manuscripts’ reading “in faith” is preferable.] strangers to faith, we are now chosen as the food and satisfaction of holy prophets, together with wild honey: we shall provide from ourselves most sweet food, not from the hives of the Law but from the trunks of wild trees.

## 3. Faith or unbelief makes people children of Abraham or of the devil.

John, then, preaching in such attire, calls the Pharisees and Sadducees coming for baptism a brood of vipers. He warns them to produce fruit worthy of repentance and not to boast that they have Abraham for their father, because God is able to raise up children for Abraham from stones (Matt. 3:7–9). For fleshly succession is not sought, but the inheritance of faith. Therefore, the dignity of origin consists in examples of deeds, and the glory of ancestry is retained through imitation of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] Since it is not established from the manuscripts that Hilary pronounced this word for a reason different from that of the other Fathers—the oldest manuscripts read *diabulus*, some *zabulus*, and others *diabolus*—we have consistently taken care to write it in the latter form, though *diabolus* sometimes, but *zabulus* more often, prevailed in the earlier printed editions.]

The devil is unbelieving; Abraham believing. For the former was faithless in humanity’s transgression, while the latter was justified by faith. Thus each person’s character and life acquire the closeness of kinship: those who believe become Abraham’s offspring through faith; but those who do not believe are transformed through unbelief into the devil’s offspring. For the Pharisees too are called a brood of vipers; they are forbidden to glory in their sanctified ancestor; children of Abraham are raised from stones and rocks; and they are admonished to bear fruits worthy of repentance. Thus those who had begun to have the devil as father may again become Abraham’s children through faith, together with those raised from stones.

#### 4. Christ our Savior and Judge

But the axe laid to the roots of the trees testifies (Matt. 3:10) to the right of present power in Christ, signifying, by the cutting down and burning of fruitless trees, that the destruction of useless unbelief is being prepared for the conflagration of judgment.

> [Note: Thus MS Carnotensis together with Colbertinus. But the Paris edition alone prefers “force” rather than “right.” In other books, “testifies to the right of present power in Christ” is absent. Shortly afterward some of them have “signifies” instead of “signifying.”]

> [Note: MS Beccensis has “by breaking”; five others, “by conflagration”: wrongly. Hilary means that unbelievers, while they are already being cut down, are being prepared for the fire in which they will burn at the judgment. Not dissimilar is the passage in his exposition of Psalm 143, §11, where he first declares that at the Lord’s coming the devil’s power was restrained and crushed, and then adds: “By the condition of its present subjection it is being prepared for lawful vengeance and punishment.”]

And because the work of the Law was now ineffective for salvation,

> [Note: The Carnotensis codex, with Colbertinus, reads “was also ineffective.” The other manuscripts more correctly read “was now.” Again Hilary declares the Law now useless and ineffective in ch. 7, §1. Let the heretics of our time see whether he does not make a great distinction between Christ’s baptism and John’s.]

and John had appeared as the herald calling those to be baptized to repentance—for it was the office of the prophets to call people back from sins, whereas Christ’s own proper office is to save believers—he says that he himself baptizes unto repentance, but that one stronger than he is to come, for whose sandals he is unworthy to perform the service of carrying them (Matt. 3:11). He leaves to the apostles the glory of carrying abroad the preaching, whose beautiful feet were bound to proclaim the peace of God (Isa. 52:7).

> [Note: The printed editions here add “and unfastening them,” which neither the manuscripts contain nor the text of Matthew or Hilary’s exposition requires. For he interprets carrying Christ’s sandals as carrying abroad the glory of preaching, and says nothing that pertains to unfastening them.]

Thus he marks out in the Lord the time of our salvation and judgment, saying: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire”; because, once we have been baptized in the Holy Spirit, it remains for us to be perfected by the fire of judgment.

> [Note: As is taught in the exposition of Psalm 118, §5: “A cleansing of perfect purity is still reserved even after the waters of baptism … which will refine us by the fire of judgment.”]

“He has the winnowing fan in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. 3:12). The function of the winnowing fan is to distinguish fruitful things from fruitless. Its being in the Lord’s hand indicates the discretion of his power: he stores up his wheat, that is, the perfect fruits of believers, in barns; but he burns the chaff—that is, the emptiness of useless and fruitless people—with the fire of judgment.

> [Note: The words “that is” do not occur in the manuscripts. Above, Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius read “to be stored up” instead of “storing up”; and below, “those to be burned” instead of “burning,” which was also restored in the last Paris edition.]

#### 5. By assuming humanity, he sanctified the waters by the washing

Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him (Matt. 3:13), and what follows.

> [Note: The printed editions read “into Galilee,” against the manuscripts and the sacred text.]

There was in Christ Jesus the whole human being; and therefore the body, assumed into the service of the Spirit, fulfilled in himself the entire mystery of our salvation.

> [Note: That is, every human being. This passage is illuminated by the following from the exposition of Psalm 13, §4: “Because these infirmities of our body were to be removed only by the assumption of our flesh, by the assumption of the saving flesh all flesh is in the Lord,” etc.; and also by these words from *On the Trinity*, II.25: “He did not need to become human … but we needed God to become flesh and dwell in us; that is, by the assumption of the flesh of one man, to dwell inwardly in all flesh.” This was so that in him the body of the entire human race might be sanctified, as he explains there in §24. Hence below, ch. 4, §12, Christ’s flesh is called a city, because in him, through the nature of the body assumed, there is contained a certain gathering of the whole human race. Once this principle is laid down, it rightly follows that certain things are predicated of Christ which apply only to us.]

> [Note: That is, into the service of the Word. The body is assumed into the Word’s service, since through its union it is so subject to him that whatever it does is attributed to the person of the Word. Thus there is little difference between the body’s being assumed into the service of the Spirit and its subsisting in the Word, or being assumed into the unity of the Word’s person.]

Therefore, born of a woman, made under the Law, and made flesh through the Word, he came to John.

> [Note: In most manuscripts: “to the Jordan.”]

> [Note: Not “through a man.” It has already been observed that Hilary understood the angel’s words to Mary, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” as said of the Word himself. Hence in *On the Trinity*, II.24: “The Son of God was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit, the Spirit himself serving him in this operation, and his own—that is, God’s—power overshadowing her, and sowing for himself the beginnings of a body.”]

He himself had no need of washing, because it is written of him, “He committed no sin” (1 Pet. 2:22); and where there is no sin, remission is also idle. But both the body and the name of our created nature had been assumed by him. Thus it was not he who had a need to be washed; rather, through him the cleansing of our washing was to be sanctified in the waters.

> [Note: Two manuscripts read “for him.” What else can “our created nature” mean except the flesh first created in Adam and propagated from him down to us? Numerous passages of this kind refute those who wish to maintain that Hilary held Christ to have received nothing from Mary.]

Finally, John forbids him to be baptized, as God (Matt. 3:14); and he teaches, as man, that it is fitting for this to be done in him (Matt. 3:15). For through him all righteousness had to be fulfilled, since the Law could be fulfilled through him alone. Thus, by the testimony of the prophet, he has no need of washing; yet by the authority of his example he completes the mysteries of human salvation, sanctifying humanity both by assumption and by washing.

#### 6. The effects of our baptism prefigured in Christ’s baptism

In this also the order of the heavenly mystery is expressed. For when he had been baptized, the entrances of heaven were opened, the Holy Spirit was sent forth and visibly recognized in the form of a dove, and he was anointed with a manifestation of paternal loving-kindness of this kind. Then a voice from heaven spoke thus: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Matt. 3:17).

> [Note: It has been observed at col. 278, note i, that Justin Martyr also read the passage this way.]

The Son of God is shown by hearing and sight; and testimony, both of vision and voice, concerning their Lord is sent to a faithless people disobedient to the prophets. At the same time, from what was accomplished in Christ, we learn that after the washing of water the Holy Spirit flies upon us from the heavenly gates, that we are anointed with the glory of heaven, and that by adoption through the Father’s voice we become sons of God. Thus the truth, by the actual effects of things, has prefigured in us the image of the mystery arranged in this way.

[Col. 0928A]

## CHAPTER III. On the devil the tempter; on Jesus’ forty-day fast; and on Peter and Andrew the fishermen

#### 1. “Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matt. 4:1), and what follows

His being led into the wilderness, his fast of forty days, his hunger after the fast, Satan’s temptation, and the Lord’s answer are full of the effects of a great and heavenly plan. For in his being led into the wilderness is signified the freedom of the Holy Spirit, who now offers his own human being to the devil and permits the occasion for tempting and assailing him—an occasion which the tempter would not have had unless it had been granted.

> [Note: That is, the freedom of the divine nature of the Word. This freedom is considered so that no one may suppose that Christ was tempted by necessity rather than voluntarily, and thus possessed nothing above humanity, to whom temptation comes, even if that person does not yield, without that person’s own will. Shortly afterward MS Mich. reads “which he would not have had unless granted,” omitting “not.”]

Thus there was in the devil a suspicion arising from fear, not knowledge arising from suspicion. For he was moved by the forty-day fast. He knew that for an equal number of days the waters of the abyss had poured forth (Gen. 7:17), that the land of promise had been explored, that the Law had been written by God for Moses, and that this number had been completed also in the years during which the people remained in the wilderness with the life and manner of angels.

> [Note: Several manuscripts read “the abysses poured out.”]

Therefore, fearing this period, he took the bold step of tempting him whom he saw as human. For he had seduced Adam and, by deceiving him, brought him over into death. But it was fitting to his wickedness and crime that he should be conquered in the human being whose death and miseries he gloried in; and that he who had envied God’s benefits to humanity should be unable, before the temptation, to recognize God in that human being.

Therefore the Lord is tempted immediately after baptism, indicating by his temptation that the devil’s temptations rage most fiercely against us when we have been sanctified, because victory over the holy is more desired by him.

#### 2. What kind of hunger Christ had

Nor did he hunger for human food, but for salvation. For after forty days—not during the forty days—he hungered (Matt. 4:2), whereas Moses and Elijah did not hunger during the same time of fasting. Therefore, when the Lord hungered, the working of deprivation did not creep upon him; rather, that power, unmoved by the forty-day fast, left the human being to his own nature.

> [Note: In one Colbert manuscript: “but as though unmoved by that forty-day fast.” In the Roman manuscript: “but as though that …,” as in Colbert. In five others, as in Bad.: “but he wishes that, unmoved by the forty-day fast …” The reading preferred here, with Erasmus, Lipsius, and Paris, must certainly be retained. In a few words Hilary here indicates that there was in Christ a certain nature not itself subject to hunger, and capable of ensuring that even the human nature did not hunger. Hunger, therefore, did not overtake him unwillingly; but when he wished, he left his human nature to itself.  
>   
> When he adds that the human being was left to its own nature because the devil was to be conquered by flesh, not by God, he expressly declares that by the “power” which withdraws he means the divine nature of the Word. Similarly, in the preceding section he shows that Christ was tempted only when he wished, since the Holy Spirit—that is, the Word—permitted his own human being to be tempted by the devil, so that the devil might be conquered in humanity. Thus, from the very passages by which either the Ebionites and their followers Paul of Samosata and Photinus, who asserted that there was nothing in Christ beyond a human being, or the Arians, who refused to confess a divine nature in him, attempted to defend their heresy—from these passages, I say—Hilary habitually demonstrates with care both that there was in Christ something beyond and above humanity, and that this very thing was God.  
>   
> Hence everyone may see why he preferred to call that singular nature of Christ, which he himself understands as divine, not by the proper name of God but by the more general terms “spirit” and “power”: namely, to accommodate himself to the language of the heretics. Certainly, when Hilary is speaking of Christ, we have nowhere observed the term “power” not to refer to his divine nature. Anyone who considers even chapter 9, §7 will not doubt its force.  
>   
> This passage also seemed so well suited to elucidating this doctor’s view both of Christ’s passion and of his death that we judged it should not be passed over carelessly. For it makes clear that he attributes to Christ a real bodily hunger, though on the occasion of it he proclaims a certain spiritual hunger. Why indeed was the human being, after fasting, left by God to his own nature except that he might suffer what human nature commonly suffers from fasting? This is especially so since that spiritual hunger for human salvation does not befit God. Nor can his statement that the devil, through the weakness of hunger, recognized in Christ the human being the things belonging to humanity refer to anything except bodily hunger.]

For the devil was not to be conquered by God, but by flesh; and indeed he would not have dared to tempt the flesh unless he had recognized in it, through the weakness of hunger, what belongs to humanity. Perceiving this in him, he began thus: “If you are the Son of God” (Matt. 4:3). “If you are the Son of God” is an ambiguous utterance. Although he saw him hungry, he nevertheless feared his forty-day fast.

By this arrangement of events Christ indicates that, after the forty days during which he was to remain in the world after the Passion, he would have a hunger for human salvation. At that time he brought back to God the Father the expected gift: the human being whom he had assumed.

#### 3. Why the devil seeks to probe Christ’s divinity or to break his endurance: Christ, God and human being

We must now consider what questions he finally used. He said: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” The devil is deceitful and exceedingly skillful in the art of leading astray. He knew that Christ could do all things, and from the very period of fasting he perceived hunger in the human being; yet he did not know what it was that he hungered for. Therefore, in tempting him, he proposed a condition of action through which he might recognize in God the power of authority, by the transformation of stones into bread; and in the human being might mock the endurance of hunger through the pleasure of food.

> [Note: In several manuscripts: “the hungry person’s endurance.” Here again Hilary acknowledges bodily hunger in Christ’s human nature, so real that through it he attains an endurance worthy of the devil’s envy.]

But the Lord, hungering not so much for bread as for human salvation, said: “A human being does not live by bread alone” (Matt. 4:4). For he was not only human but also God. Although until the day of temptation he had abstained from human food, he was nevertheless nourished by the Spirit of God, showing that hope for the nourishment of eternity rests not in bread alone, but in the Word of God.

#### 4. The devil is silent about what is against himself; boasting must be avoided

The next question too was of this kind. When he had placed him on the pinnacle of the temple, he said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down,” and what follows (Matt. 4:6). By the temptation he strives to bring the Lord down from the heights to the lower regions; and to confine in lowly things one placed on the summit of the temple—that is, one exalted above the Law and the prophets.

He knew indeed that the ministries of angels stood ready for the Son of God, and that he could not stumble against a stone of offense (Ps. 91:12–13), since he was to walk upon the asp and basilisk and tread down the lion and dragon. But he kept silent about the things said concerning Christ himself. By recalling the earlier words, he seeks somehow to draw obedience from the one tempted, intending to win glory from this if the Lord of majesty should obey him, even in the confidence proper to his nature.

> [Note: Four manuscripts read “the tempter.” Then, “through confidence,” that is, as Lord of all things: he had not forgotten the confidence of Christ’s nature, which he did not lack even in assuming humanity, as Hilary says in his exposition of Psalm 54, §2.]

But no opportunity for such great deceit came to the devil. The Lord himself testified to this later when he said: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has found nothing in me” (John 14:30). Thus the Lord’s response fittingly followed this insolence: “You shall not tempt God and your Lord” (Matt. 4:7). Crushing the devil’s efforts and temptations, he both declares himself God and Lord, teaching that boasting must be absent from believers, because although all things are possible to God, nothing ought to be dared in order to tempt him.

> [Note: The Carnotensis, Roman, and Colbert manuscripts read “despising.”]

#### 5. Christ’s temptations follow the same order as Adam’s: worldly honor is the devil’s work

But now, for the third time, the whole ambition of the devil’s power is stirred. So, having placed the Lord on a high mountain, he offered him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, if only he himself might be worshiped (Matt. 4:8–9). By two answers already, Christ had surpassed the devil’s conjectural suspicion.

The devil had seduced Adam by food and brought him from the glory of paradise into the place of sin, that is, into the region of the forbidden tree. Thirdly, he had corrupted him by ambition for the divine name, promising that he would become like gods. Therefore the Lord is now attacked by the whole power of the world, and possession of this entire universe is offered to its Creator, so that, following the order of his ancient deception, he might now corrupt by ambition the one whom he had neither seduced by food nor moved by place.

But the Lord’s answer fittingly advanced beyond the previous ones. For he said: “Depart, Satan. For it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (Matt. 4:10).

> [Note: The Carnotensis manuscript reads, “Go back behind me, Satan.”]

He received a fitting outcome for such boldness: he heard himself called Satan because of his crimes, and he recognized in the human being the Lord his God whom he was to worship. By the effect of this answer the Lord also offered us a great example: that, despising the glory of human power and setting aside worldly ambition, we should remember that God and Lord alone is to be worshiped, because every worldly honor is the devil’s business.

> [Note: Three manuscripts read “having contemplated.”]

After this flight of the devil, angels minister to Christ (Matt. 4:11), showing that after the devil’s head has been conquered and trampled down by us, neither the ministries of angels nor the services of heavenly powers toward us will be lacking.

> [Note: The better manuscripts read “showing,” a barbarous but perhaps more genuine reading, in place of “which is an indication.”]

#### 6. What the calling of the first apostles signifies

When Jesus heard that John had been delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee (Matt. 4:12). The journey into Capernaum and the prophecy of Isaiah are the sequence of events.

> [Note: In some manuscripts, “calling” (*allectione*).]

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts, which briefly recall Matthew’s statement: “Leaving the city of Nazareth, he dwelt in Capernaum … that what was spoken through Isaiah might be fulfilled,” etc. Therefore Bad. and some manuscripts wrongly read “betrayed in Capernaum and the prophet Isaiah.” Nor is the reading in other printed editions any better: “passing into Capernaum and the prophet,” etc.]

But in the choice of fishermen, the work of their future office is revealed by their human trade: just as fish are drawn from the sea, so people were thereafter to be drawn from the world into a higher place, that is, into the light of the heavenly dwelling. Since they leave their trade, their homelands, and their houses, we are taught that, if we are to follow Christ, we must not be held by the anxieties of secular life or by attachment to our father’s house.

Moreover, in the first choice of four apostles, besides the truth of events—for it happened thus—the number of the future evangelists is prefigured. He therefore goes about Galilee and preaches the Gospel of the kingdom in the synagogues; and by healing the infirmities of every sickness, he makes himself known through deeds, so that those accustomed to read of him in the scrolls of the prophets might behold him present in his works.

[Col. 0931C]

## CHAPTER IV. On blessedness and commandments; reconciliation of brothers; adultery; plucking out the eye and hand; oaths and almsgiving

#### 1. What Christ is on the mountain

When great crowds had gathered, he went up the mountain and taught them (Matt. 5:1). Set, that is, in the height of paternal majesty, he established the precepts of heavenly life. For he would not have delivered the ordinances of eternity unless he were situated in eternity.

Accordingly, it is written: “He opened his mouth and taught them” (Matt. 5:2). It would have been more straightforward simply to say that he spoke. But because he was established in the glory of the Father’s majesty and taught eternity, it is shown that the office of the human mouth obeyed the movement of the Spirit who spoke.

> [Note: The Beccensis manuscript reads “had established.” The other manuscripts more correctly read “was established,” that is, “was situated,” to be supplied, and did not depart from that glory.]

#### 2. The grounds and reward of humility

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). By example the Lord had taught that the glory of human ambition must be abandoned, saying: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4:10). And since through the prophets he had foretold that he would choose a people humble and trembling at his words (Isa. 66:2), he placed the beginning of perfect blessedness in humility of spirit.

> [Note: The printed editions read “had warned that he would choose”; they are corrected from the better manuscripts.]

Therefore, those who think humbly—that is, remember that they are human—are established in possession of the heavenly kingdom. They know that they have grown together from mean and very slight beginnings into this form of a perfected body; that they advance, with God supplying the increase, toward this capacity for perception, contemplation, judgment, and action; that nothing is anyone’s own or private; that the same beginnings of coming into life are granted to all by the gift of the one Father, and the means of using that life are supplied to them.

> [Note: The Paris edition reads “established, conscious.” The Colbert manuscript less wrongly adds “conscious” after “established.”]

> [Note: The printed editions read “the same.” The manuscripts more correctly read “these things,” namely, life.]

We ought, by the example of that best One who has bestowed these things upon us, to be imitators of his goodness fulfilled toward us: that we may be good to all, consider all things common to all, and allow neither the arrogant insolence of worldly pride, nor greed for riches, nor the ambition of empty glory to corrupt us. Rather, we should be subject to God and be bound, through the fellowship of living, in the love of a common life toward all. We should also reckon that even in our birth there will be a great result of divine goodness, whose reward and honor must be earned by the works of this present life.

> [Note: The same matters are explained more clearly in the exposition of Psalm 118, §1: “For no one is so insane or lacking in understanding as to suppose that, when he did not exist, he was born in order that, after being born, he should again not exist. For without doubt we remember that it was by God’s goodness that he came to be born; nor can such malice belong to that goodness as to destroy in us this gift of his by which we are born.”]

Thus through this humility of spirit—by which we remember that all things have been granted to us by God and that greater things are still to be hoped for—the kingdom of heaven will be ours.

#### 3. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matt. 5:4)

He promises the inheritance of the earth to the meek: that is, the inheritance of that body which the Lord himself assumed as a dwelling place (see below, §12). For since Christ will dwell in us through the meekness of our minds, we too, glorified with the glory of his body, shall be clothed with it.

#### 4. Whose mourning will be comforted

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). He promises the comforts of eternal consolation to those who mourn. This constant consolation in heaven is prepared not for those who grieve over bereavements, insults, or losses, but for those who weep for former sins and are burdened by consciousness of the crimes through which we are defiled.

#### 5. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6)

He grants blessedness to those who thirst and hunger for righteousness, indicating that the longing of the saints extended toward God’s teaching will be fulfilled by the good things of perfect satisfaction in heaven.

#### 6. “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matt. 5:7)

He prepares the gifts of mercy for the merciful. For God so delights in the disposition of our goodwill toward all that he will grant his mercy only to the merciful.

> [Note: “Only” is absent from four manuscripts of no inferior authority; and it should be absent if only the Gospel words of this chapter are considered. Yet we have not deleted it, lest there perhaps be a reference to Christ’s words in Matthew 25:35.]

#### 7. The impure cannot endure the sight of God

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). He promises the sight of God to the pure in heart. For nothing polluted or defiled can stand before the encounter of divine brightness, and the gaze of a mind dulled by long disuse is blunted for the sight of God. Those, namely, are able to endure both the sight and encounter of God who, through brightness of soul and purity of life, possess the power of contemplation.

> [Note: Several manuscripts read “from afar, by an obsolete mind”: corruptly. The prophet was free from this defect of an unpracticed mind, of whom it is said in the exposition of Psalm 122, §1: “Through fitting degrees of increase in the exercise of contemplating God, prepared by the small and measured intervals of light admitted to him, he was prepared for familiarity with the whole light.”]

> [Note: Thus MS Beccensis with the early editions. Other manuscripts read “enduring,” which would not be displeasing if joined with the second case. For in the exposition of Psalm 138, §21, human weakness is said to flee the encounter of God because it cannot endure the vision. The Paris edition indeed reads “able to endure the sight and encounter of God,” but without authority. The verb *patere*, “to be able to endure,” is familiar to Hilary, as may be seen in Psalm 118 and Psalm 131, §6.]

For only those perfected in spirit and transformed by immortality—which is appointed for the pure in heart alone—will behold that which is immortal in God.

> [Note: The printed editions read “and now transformed by mortality.” Several manuscripts more correctly read “and by immortality,” as Pelagius once read it in Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 62. Pelagius attempted to twist these words of Hilary into support for his heresy. Augustine replies there: “What has Hilary said against what we maintain, or how does it help this man [Pelagius], I do not know, unless because he has testified that a human being can be pure in heart. Who denies this? Yet it is by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, not by freedom of choice alone.”  
>   
> Hilary in fact rejects Pelagian purity and self-confidence in countless places, repeatedly emphasizing the corruption, ignorance, and weakness of human nature. The statement in Psalm 136, §5 and Psalm 145, §2—that humanity fell from the endowments implanted in its nature through sin—does not favor Pelagius at all. Nor is Pelagius aided when Hilary teaches not only in Psalm 52, §11 that perfect goodness exists in no human being, but also, explaining this teaching in Psalm 118, §6, says: “There are many stumbling blocks which prevent us from keeping the commandments perfectly. I say nothing of the natures of bodies, which for the present compel us to be imperfect through incentives to vices.” And in §3: “We still have mingled with us matter subject to the law of death and sin,” etc. Or in §1, urging that no one fails to need God’s mercy: “For if there should be recompense according to our works, we shall remain in the punishments for our sins and offenses.”  
>   
> What further help can Pelagius derive from the statement in Psalm 146, §4 that human healing begins in this life but is not completed except in the next? Nor is this statement from the exposition of Psalm 144, §20 more favorable to his teaching: “With eyes wholly fixed and falling upon God, let them look; and let no one be so confident in himself as not always to fear falling, always to fear being struck down.” Indeed, in this very passage Hilary asserts something wholly different from what Pelagius wishes to prove from it. Hilary affirms here that, so long as a person remains mortal, the sight of God cannot be granted, since that person will not yet be undefiled. Pelagius, by contrast, contends that this passage proves that some people, even in this life, possess that brightness of soul and purity of life which Hilary grants only to those endowed with immortality. These remarks have been made briefly to show the character of heresy, which seeks not so much to illustrate truth from the testimonies of the ancients as to practice deception.]

#### 8. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9)

The blessedness of peacemakers is the reward of adoption, so that they may remain sons of God; for the one God is Father of all. Nor can we otherwise enter into the designation of his household unless, forgetting the things by which we might be offended, we live in the peace of mutual brotherly love.

#### 9. “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” and what follows (Matt. 5:10)

Finally, he rewards with perfect blessedness those whose disposition is ready to suffer everything for Christ, because he himself is righteousness.

> [Note: Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius read “a ready disposition.” Yet below, §25, they have: “they ought to be inclined toward the office of dispensing grace.”]

For them the kingdom is reserved, and an abundant reward in heaven is promised: those who, despising the world, are poor in spirit; who are disgraced by losses and the forfeiture of present possessions; who are confessors of heavenly righteousness against human curses; and finally glorious martyrs of God’s promises, having expended every use of life in testimony to his eternity.

> [Note: The printed editions read “truth.” The manuscripts more truly read “eternity”: that is, they were prodigal of temporal life in order to testify that it is eternal. On this account the apostles are shortly afterward called, as it were, sowers of eternity.]

#### 10. The apostles, salt of the earth

“You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has lost its savor, that which is salted is good for nothing” (Matt. 5:12). There is, I think, no salt of the earth; how then did he call the apostles salt of the earth? We must seek the proper meaning of the words, which both the apostles’ office and the nature of salt will show.

> [Note: Lipsius and Paris read “has become foolish.” The Colbert and Carnotensis manuscripts read “has vanished.” Shortly afterward one might read “that by which it is salted”; but the final words of this section fit the received reading no less well, declaring that those who have salted others are to be cast out and trampled along with those whom they have salted.]

Salt contains within itself the elements of water and fire, and from the two is one. Thus, made into one service for the human race, it gives incorruption to the bodies on which it is sprinkled and is most suited to impart flavor to every sense.

> [Note: The printed editions with seven manuscripts read “into every [use].” With the Roman, Vatican, Colbert, and Carnotensis manuscripts we prefer “into one [use],” since it responds more closely to the Gospel words, “is good for nothing,” etc.]

But the apostles are preachers of heavenly things and, as it were, sowers of eternity. They confer immortality on all bodies upon which their word has been sprinkled, and, as John above bears witness, are perfected by the mystery of water and fire.

> [Note: Thus most manuscripts. Other books read “conferring.” Then, in Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and the final Paris edition: “And … perfected by the mystery of perfect water and fire,” where “perfect” refers to the mystery, not to the apostles. In the first Paris edition: “so that … they might be perfected by the mystery of water and fire.” In most manuscripts: “and … perfected by the mystery of fire.” From these readings we conjecture that “water” should be restored: “as John above bears witness, perfected by the mysteries of water and fire.” This conjecture is further supported below in §26, where the mysteries of baptism and the Spirit are again mentioned. We follow three manuscripts, except that we print “and so that,” where they have “but indeed.”]

> [Note: The printed editions had inserted here, “when he says: ‘He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire,’” although not one of our manuscripts supports it. Incidentally, it should be observed that Hilary, though above in ch. 2, §4 interprets baptism by fire as the fire of the final judgment, does not exclude another interpretation of this baptism; for here he declares that the apostles were perfected by this baptism of fire before the judgment.]

They are therefore deservedly called salt of the earth, preserving bodies for eternity through the power of their teaching, after the manner of salt. Yet salt’s nature is always the same and can never be changed. But because a human being is subject to change, and only the person is blessed who remains to the end in all God’s works, he therefore warns those called salt of the earth to persist in the power entrusted to them, lest, having lost their savor, they salt nothing; lest, losing their capacity for the flavor received, they be unable to restore corrupt things to life; and lest, cast out from the storehouses of the Church, they be trampled under the feet of passers-by along with those whom they have salted.

#### 11. They drive away the world’s darkness

“You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). It is the nature of light to emit brightness wherever it is carried, and, when brought into a house, to destroy darkness by the dominance of light. Thus the world, placed outside the knowledge of God, was darkened by the shadows of ignorance. Through the apostles the light of knowledge is brought to it, the knowledge of God shines forth, and from their small bodies, wherever they go, light is supplied against darkness.

> [Note: Several manuscripts read “was held in dark darkness.” Shortly afterward three read “comes” instead of “is brought in.”]

#### 12. The city is the flesh assumed by Christ; the citizens are human beings

“A city built upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel,” and what follows (Matt. 5:15). He calls the flesh which he assumed a city, because, just as a city consists of a diversity and multitude of inhabitants, so in him, through the nature of the body assumed, there is contained a certain gathering of the whole human race. Thus he becomes a city from our gathering into himself, and through participation in his flesh we are the dwelling-place of that city. It can therefore no longer be hidden, because, set on the height of God’s exaltation, he is raised up for all to behold and understand through the wonder of his works.

13. The Synagogue, the Measure That Conceals the Light; Christ the Lamp.—“Nor is a lamp lighted in order to be hidden under a measure.” For what benefit is there in confining, shut up, the abundance of light?

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Thus with the great agreement of the manuscripts, that is, “secretly and covertly.” So in Book III, *On the Trinity*, §20: “The disciples were shut in and had assembled together in secret after the Lord’s passion.” But the first Paris edition has *clausam*; the others, *clausi*.]

The Lord aptly compared the Synagogue to a measure: receiving the fruits entrusted to it only within itself, it contained a fixed measure of prescribed observance. Yet now, with the coming of Christ, it has been emptied of every fruit; nevertheless, it is no longer able to conceal the light.

[Note: [Col. 0936C–D] Thus four manuscripts. Others have *vacuata sit* (“has been emptied”). But the printed editions wrongly have *vacuavit* (“emptied”). Worse still, shortly before, Lipsius substituted *nunc tametsi* for *nunc tamen*, and afterward, separating *se* from *adveniente* by a comma, joined it with *vacuavit*, although it refers to Christ, by whose coming the Synagogue’s worship became empty and unfruitful.]

Therefore the lamp of Christ is no longer to be placed under the measure, nor hidden beneath the covering of the Synagogue; but, suspended in the passion of the wood—that is, upon the cross—it will supply eternal light to those dwelling in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] We would prefer, with several manuscripts, *in ligno passione* (“in the passion on the wood”), as though meaning “at the time of the passion,” unless we had found that Hilary is familiar with inversions of words of this kind, so that he says *in ligni passione* for *in ligno passionis* (“in the passion on the wood”).]

He likewise commands the Apostles to shine with an equal light (Matt. 5:16), so that through admiration of their work praise may be rendered to God. This is not because glory ought to be sought from human beings, since all things must be done for the honour of God; but so that, although we ourselves may not seek notice, our work may shine forth among those with whom we live.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] Bad., with most manuscripts, reads *in ordine in honorem* (“in order for the honour”).]

14. The Law Foretells Christ.—“Do not suppose that I have come to destroy the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to destroy, but to fulfil” (Matt. 5:17). The power and force of the heavenly words embrace great significance within themselves. For the Law was established for works, and enclosed everything within faith in those things which were to be revealed in Christ; and both his teaching and his passion are the great and profound purpose of the Father’s will.

Now the Law, under the veil of spiritual words, spoke of the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, his bodily nature, his passion, and his resurrection. That these things had been ordained before the ages for fulfilment in the time of our own age is attested frequently by both prophetic and apostolic authority. Therefore, after the fast of forty days, Satan, troubled by such great suspicions, burst forth even into the boldness of temptation, greatly fearing in Jesus the secret of a heavenly undertaking. For “Jesus” is a name of our Lord derived from the body.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] Thus the better manuscripts. Others read: “For Jesus is not a name of the Lord derived from the body”; these are opposed by the exposition of Psalm 65, §12: “For Jesus is the designation of that man who was born from Mary.”]

Thus both his bodily nature and his passion are the will of God and the salvation of the world. And it surpasses the power of human speech that God from God, the Son from the substance of the Father and abiding within the substance of the Father, should first be embodied as a human being, then be subjected to death according to the condition of humankind, and finally, after three days, return from death to life, carrying back to heaven the material of the assumed body, united to the eternity of his Spirit and substance.

[Note: The clearer arrangement would be: “he carried back to heaven the material of the assumed body, united to the eternity of his Spirit and substance”—that is, his divine nature, which belongs to the Son of God by propriety, whereas human nature belongs to him only by assumption. This passage removes every suspicion that might arise from others, that Hilary considered the flesh of the glorified Christ to have been abolished.]

15. What Was Fulfilled by Christ; Christ’s Cross Is Not to Be Ashamed Of.—Therefore, lest we should suppose that there was anything in his works other than what was contained in the Law, he declared that he had come not to destroy the Law but to fulfil it. Heaven and earth—and especially, as we suppose, the elements—are indeed to be dissolved; but not even the least of the commandments of the Law can remain unfulfilled, for in him all Law and prophecy are fulfilled.

In his passion, and when he was now about to yield up the spirit, certain of this great mystery within himself, he declared, after drinking vinegar, that all things were completed: for then all the sayings of the prophets attained the fulfilment of the deeds accomplished. Therefore he ordained that not even the least of God’s commandments could be annulled without guilt before God (Matt. 5:19), declaring that those who annul the least commandments will be least—that is, last and almost nothing.

But nothing can be less than what is least. Now least of all is the Lord’s passion and death on the cross. Whoever does not confess it, as though it were something of which to be ashamed, shall be least; but to the one who confesses it he promises the glory of a great calling in heaven.

[Note: Some books read *poto* (“having drunk”); others, *potato aceto* (“having drunk vinegar”); some, *potu aceti* (“with a drink of vinegar”); in Psalm 131, §4, “after the cup of vinegar.” Then, instead of “for the truth of the deeds,” we would much prefer “for the completion of the deeds,” namely, Christ’s deeds. For, when all had been completed, as is said in Psalm 131, §4, he said: “It is finished.” He had run through all the offices of the mystery; and where there is joy at completion, there is gladness at the perfection of the work undertaken. Thus, when Christ said, “It is finished,” and immediately yielded up the spirit, all the prophets’ sayings—and, in the Paris edition and one Colbert manuscript, “deeds”—reached their end: first, because death is the end and final point of those things which the prophets had foretold that he would undergo in the flesh; and also because prophecy reaches its end when whatever it predicted has been brought to fulfilment.]

16. The Gospel, Which Surpasses the Law.—“But I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20). With a most excellent beginning, the work of the Law began to be surpassed—not so as to destroy it, but to go beyond it by a fuller advance. He declared that the Apostles would have no entrance into heaven unless they surpassed the righteousness of the Pharisees by equity. Thus, after setting forth what was prescribed in the Law, he goes beyond it by advancement, not by abolition.

17. Anger Without Cause Is Guilty of Murder.—The Law forbade killing, to expiate the guilt of homicide by the severity of judgment (Matt. 5:21). But the emotion of a mind wrongly stirred against another incurs the same punishment in the Gospels; and by the commandment of faith, anger undertaken without reason is no less guilty than homicide in the works of the Law.

“And whoever says to his brother, *Racha*, shall be liable to the council” (Matt. 5:22). *Racha* is an insult denoting emptiness. Whoever accuses one filled with the Holy Spirit of emptiness becomes liable to the council of the saints, and must atone, under their judgment, for an insult against the Holy Spirit. “But whoever says, ‘You fool,’ shall be liable to the Gehenna of fire.” It is perilous guilt to assail with the insult of a senseless mind one whom God has called salt; and to aggravate by a curse, as though with foolish understanding, the understanding that gives savour to fools—that is, the one who salts them. Such a person, therefore, shall be fuel for eternal fire.

Thus, what the Law did not condemn even in the actual deeds, the faith of the Gospels condemns merely for the reckless offensiveness of words.

[Note: [Col. 0938D] The expression *idem poenae* (“the same of punishment”) is singular, in place of *eamdem poenam* (“the same punishment”). Next, it should be noted that the term *fides* (“faith”) is set in opposition to the Law, and the commandment of faith to the commandment of the Law.]

[Note: The negative particle *ne* is absent from the printed editions. It occurs in the manuscripts and is added here on their authority, especially since the Law is said to condemn homicide actually committed not to Gehenna, but only to judgment.]

18. Peace with Brothers Must Precede Peace with God.—Binding all together, therefore, by mutual charity, he allows no prayer made in a state of discord. Rather, when those offering gifts at the altar remember that they have some disagreement with their brothers, he commands them first to be reconciled in human peace and then to return to divine peace, passing into the love of God from love toward human beings (Matt. 5:23–24).

19. Reconciliation Must Be Undertaken Quickly.—And since he permits no time to be without the disposition of reconciliation, he commanded that throughout the whole course of our life we should promptly be reconciled to an adversary in goodwill, lest, slow in returning to grace, we come to the time of death without having made peace; lest our adversary hand us over to the judge, the judge to the officer, and we be thrown into prison, from which we shall not leave until we have paid the last quadrans (Matt. 5:25–26).

In the commands of the Lord’s Prayer, we pray that our sins may be forgiven us by the example and condition of the forgiveness we grant to our adversaries; and we ask for his forgiveness (Matt. 6:12). This forgiveness will therefore be denied us if it is denied by us to others; and by our own judgment we are guilty if we pass into the time of judgment without having forgiven our disputes. For the adversary hands us over to the judge because our continuing anger of contention against him accuses us. And because charity covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8) and is an eager advocate to God for our errors, we shall pay the last quadrans of punishment unless the fault of certain sins is redeemed by the price of that charity.

I have not thought it necessary to discuss the sense given to this passage by many. For they have referred the command to be reconciled to one’s adversary in goodwill to the concord of body and spirit, which oppose each other. But we, preserving the sequence of the teaching and the Gospel’s surpassing of the work of the Law, have not thought that the continuity of the interpretation should be broken.

[Note: When Hilary here says “be reconciled by goodwill,” and above, “be reconciled by kindness,” he expresses the force of the Greek expression. For, as Jerome notes on this passage, where Latin copies have *consentiens* (“agreeing”), the Greek reads εὐνοῶν, interpreted “well-disposed” and “kind.”]

20. “You Have Heard That It Was Said to the Ancients, ‘You Shall Not Commit Adultery,’” etc. (Matt. 5:27).—The sequence of the command proceeds in its own course. Passing beyond the works of the Law, the Gospel now equates adultery with the mere movement of the eye that falls upon another; and the seductive inclination of a roaming gaze is punished as the act of fornication.

21. Members to Be Cut Off: Near Relations Who Cause Offence. It Is Useless to Cut the Body Rather Than the Heart.—“If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you,” etc. (Matt. 5:29). The degree of innocence becomes higher, and faith makes progress. For we are warned not merely to lack our own vices, but also to avoid those which arise externally.

The command does not prescribe injury to the body because sinful members are its causes. For the left eye would err no less than the right. Certainly a foot, lacking the faculty of desire, is uselessly mutilated: the ground for punishment does not fall upon it.

[Note: [Col. 0939C] In some manuscripts the negative particle is omitted. It may be retained, so that Hilary’s reasoning is this: the ground of punishment is sin; but there is no sin where there is no movement of evil desire; therefore the ground of punishment does not fall upon that bodily part which, without any movement of desire, has only the service of necessary subjection in the matter itself, as he says in Psalm 120, §7. Thus, since the foot or such a member is not the cause of fault, and consequently not of punishment, it would be cut off to no purpose while desire nevertheless remained. The preceding particle may also be deleted, and the foot called the ground of punishment, as sinful members are called above, in this sense: a foot upon which punishment is inflicted, since it lacks the faculty of desire and desire is therefore not cut off with it, is cut off to no purpose.]

But because our different members are nevertheless all one body, we are warned to cast away from ourselves—or rather, to pluck out—the ties designated by the most beloved names, if we perceive anything of this kind in them, lest intimacy bring us into partnership in their sin. It is better to lack things useful and even most necessary, like the members of an eye or foot, than to be held by affection for a corrupt relationship even into fellowship with Gehenna.

The cutting off of members would be useful if the heart also could be cut away. But since desire is reckoned equivalent to accomplishment, bodily mutilation is futile when the impulse of the will remains.

[Note: Some printed editions, with not a few manuscripts, read “of most beloved persons.” The Vatican manuscript, with the Roman and Colbert manuscripts, more correctly reads “of most beloved names.” Hence below, chapter 18, §4, this very passage is mentioned in these terms: “Above, in the cutting off of hand or foot, we explained that the names of relatives are included.” And in chapter 10, §24, those are condemned who preferred the household affections denoted by such names to love of God. These most beloved names are listed in Psalm 118, §3: “These most beloved names—father, mother, wife, and children—cannot be angry with us because we are commanded to hate them,” etc. When Jerome, in Epistle 29, *On Death*, says that death divides brothers and cruelly and divinely separates most beloved names from one another, he adds that he has borrowed these words from prophetic utterance.]

[Note: That is, evil desire is condemned no less than the deed. There is no discussion here of the movements of concupiscence called “first first movements.”]

22. “It Was Also Said: Whoever Dismisses His Wife, Let Him Give Her a Certificate of Divorce,” etc. (Matt. 5:31).—Reconciling equity among all, he commanded that it should remain especially in the peace of marriages: adding much to the Law, taking nothing away. Nor can such progress rightly be criticized. For whereas the Law granted freedom to give a divorce on the authority of a written document, now Gospel faith enjoins on the husband not only the desire for peace, but also imposes upon him responsibility for the wife’s adultery if, compelled by separation, she must marry another. It prescribes no other cause for ending the marriage than that which would defile the husband by continuing association with a prostituted wife.

[Note: [Col. 0939D–0940C] Three manuscripts read “no cause of wickedness.”]

[Note: Three manuscripts read “no cause of wickedness.” Those who wish to infer from this passage that Hilary grants a man permission not only to dismiss an adulterous wife but also to marry another attribute to him something other than what he says or thinks, since he frees the husband of an adulterous wife only from association with her.]

23. The Practice and Necessity of Swearing Removed for Christians.—“Again, you have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely,’” etc. (Matt. 5:33). The Law imposed punishment for perjury, so that the religious force of an oath might restrain the deceitfulness of those who lied; and so that a rude and untrained people might, through the familiarity of swearing, make frequent mention of their God.

[Note: [Col. 0940C] The printed editions read *fraudulentiam mentium* (“the deceitfulness of minds”); the manuscripts correct this to *fraudulentiam mentientium* (“the deceitfulness of those who lie”).]

But faith removes the practice of oaths, establishing the affairs of our life in truth, casting aside the disposition to deceive, and prescribing simplicity in speaking and hearing: so that what is, should be “is,” and what is not should be “not,” because between “is” and “not” there would otherwise lie an open opportunity for deception; and whatever is beyond this is from evil (Matt. 5:37). For what is has this as its own property, always to be; but what is not has by nature not to be. Therefore those who live in simplicity have no need of the religious obligation of swearing, since with them what is, is; what is not, is not; and in this both all their action and all their speech are in truth.

[Note: In some manuscripts: “the obligation of swearing.” The Colbert manuscript has “the religious force of swearing,” so that the word *opus* may be expressed adjectivally as “necessary.” Here Hilary teaches that the necessity of swearing, above its habitual use, and below its superstition—not its permissibility—is removed for Christians. Indeed, in *On the Trinity* V, §§26 and 29, in showing that Isaiah’s prophecy, “And those who swear on earth shall swear by the true God,” applies to Gospel times, he approves an oath as sometimes pious and praiseworthy even for Christians. This is still clearer in his exposition of Psalm 62, §1: “Whoever swears by him will be praised for the religious force of this oath.” Thus, when he adds below that he does not permit us to render oaths to God, this must be understood as excluding necessity. Scultetus therefore wrongly counts among Hilary’s distinctive opinions, on the basis of this one passage on Matthew, the view that oaths are altogether forbidden to Christians—although this was once the opinion of very eminent men.]

24. The Superstition of the Jews Is Condemned.—“Nor shall you swear by heaven, because it is God’s throne,” and the rest (Matt. 5:34). He not only forbids us to render oaths to God, because the whole truth of God must be maintained in the simplicity of our speech and deeds; he also condemns the superstition of ancient obstinacy. For among the Jews there was a religious practice of swearing by the names of the elements: by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and even one’s own head. In so doing they rendered to created things, by oath, a reverence that dishonoured God.

For what weight was there in swearing by heaven, God’s throne; by earth, the footstool of his feet; or by Jerusalem, a city soon to be destroyed because of the insolence and sins of its inhabitants? Especially when it had been established as a prefiguration of the Church—that is, Christ’s body—which is the city of the great King. Why, moreover, would they swear by their head? Did one taking such an oath have power even to alter the colour of a single hair, when nature, coming from God, supplies everyone’s colour? Thus he shows that these pledges of oaths were among them full of guilt, since, ignorant of or neglecting their Maker, they bestowed religious devotion upon his works.

[Note: Many manuscripts read “the reverence of an oath.” The better manuscripts, with the printed editions, read “by oath.” Jerome’s comment on the same passage supports this: “The Jews, swearing by angels, the city Jerusalem, the temple, and the elements, venerated creatures and material things with the honour and service due to God.”]

25. The Desire for Revenge Is Restrained.—“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth,’” and the rest (Matt. 5:38). The Lord wills that the hope of our faith, extended into eternity, be demonstrated by the things themselves, so that the very endurance of overlooking injury may be a witness to the judgment to come. The Law restrained unbelieving Israel within fear, and checked the desire to inflict injury by the prospect of reciprocal injury.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] *Metu* (“by fear”) is absent from Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and several manuscripts.] But faith does not allow any injury to cause pain so grave that it seeks revenge, or that anyone should avenge the insult done to himself. For in the judgment of God there is greater consolation for those who have endured injury, and harsher punishment for those who inflict it.

Thus the Gospels command us not merely to refrain from injustices, but require us also to disregard injuries for which revenge might be sought. For when struck on the cheek, we are commanded to offer the other cheek (Matt. 5:39); and after carrying a burden for a thousand paces, to go forward for the distance of two thousand paces. By the increase of the injury we shall obtain an advance in revenge, since the Lord himself of the heavenly powers offered both his cheeks to blows and his shoulders to scourges for the increase of glory.

26. Grounds for Litigation Are Removed; Generosity Is Commanded; God’s Grace Must Be Dispensed Freely.—He commands not only that the judgments of human courts be avoided, but that they be avoided even at the cost of loss: so that, when someone wishes through legal action to take our tunic, we should also surrender our cloak (Matt. 5:40). And, through hope in future goods, despising worldly possessions, we should expose the empty greed of the nations and the vanity of unfruitful avarice.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] Bad., with the manuscripts, reads *eruere* (“to tear away” or “strip off”). The printed editions then have *per spem bonam* (“through good hope”); the better manuscripts restore *per spem bonorum futurorum* (“through hope in future goods”).]

He also commands that all be given what they ask, and that we not turn away face or mind from those who wish to borrow: so that through our generosity they may be supplied with what they need, and that we may ward off their thirst with drink, their hunger with food, and their nakedness with clothing granted to them. Thus we may be found worthy of the good things which we need from God, since the habit of granting obtains the merit of receiving.

He also shows that we ought to be ready in the duty of dispensing the grace we have received:

[Note: [Col. 0941D] Several manuscripts, with Bad. and Erasmus, read *dispendendae* (“to be expended”).]

so that the dispensing of a free good may itself be free, and we may not refuse to those who wish to borrow what we borrow from God, ever performing the ministry of giving without loss to our own possession.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] The Bec manuscript reads *fruituri* (“being about to enjoy”).]

27. Love of Enemies.—“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy,’” and the rest (Matt. 5:43). He brought all things to their conclusion in perfect goodness. For the Law required one’s neighbour to be loved and allowed freedom to hate an enemy. But faith commands enemies to be loved and breaks the insolent movements of human minds by the disposition of public charity (Matt. 5:44): not only driving anger away from revenge, but softening the wrongdoer into love. For it belongs to Gentiles to love those who love them, and loving those who love them is common to all.

Therefore he calls us not only into God’s inheritance but also into his imitation: for God gives sun and rain, through the coming of his Christ, to both good and unjust people in the sacraments of baptism and the Spirit (Matt. 5:45). Thus, through this concord of universal goodness, he instructs us toward the perfect life, because our Father in heaven is perfect and must be imitated.

[Note: The editions of Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius, with some manuscripts, read “sacrament.” We judge that “sacraments” should be retained with the Paris edition and better manuscripts. For two sacraments appear to be distinguished here, one likened to rain and the other to sun; the latter is granted to the good for growth in faith and charity, the former to the unjust for forgiveness of sins and fruitfulness in good works. We are confirmed in this view by Psalm 118, §5: “There is therefore, as far as one may suppose, reserved even after the waters of baptism a cleansing of that perfect purity which sanctifies us by the coming of the Holy Spirit,” etc. We consider these to be called here the sacraments of baptism and Spirit, and above, §10, the sacraments of water and fire.]

28. Boasting Must Be Avoided.—“Take care not to perform your righteousness before people,” etc. (Matt. 6:1). He removes every concern for present things and commands us to be attentive only to hope in what is to come. We must seek neither human approval through display of goodness nor the vainglory of religion through an abundance of public prayer; rather, the fruit of good work must be kept within the conscience of faith. For the pursuit of human praise shall receive only the reward it seeks from human beings; but expectation of pleasing God shall obtain the reward of long patience.

He also commands that the left hand should not know the work of the right hand (Matt. 6:3). But does the nature of the body permit this? Or do the functions of the hands possess the faculty of understanding? Rather, he means that our works should remain within God’s knowledge, so that, under the names of bodily members, the awareness of those things which are ours and are with us may be excluded from what we do.

## Chapter V. On Prayer and Fasting; Treasure in Heaven; the Lamp of the Body; Two Masters; Food and Clothing; the Birds, Lilies of the Field, and Grass; Anxiety for the Day; and the Speck and Beam in the Eye

1. The Place of Prayer Is the Heart.—We are commanded to pray with the door of the chamber shut, and are taught to pour out prayer in every place (Matt. 6:6). The prayer of the saints has been offered among wild beasts, in prisons, in flames, from the depths of the sea, and from the belly of a beast (Jonah 2:2). Therefore we are instructed to enter not a hidden house but the chamber of our heart, and, with the secret place of our mind shut, to pray to God not with much speaking but with conscience, because the whole work surpasses the words that are spoken.

Cyprian, a man of holy memory, has spared us the necessity of commenting upon the mystery of prayer. Tertullian also wrote a most suitable work on this subject; but the subsequent error of the man deprived his commendable writings of authority.

[Note: Only here in the manuscripts does Chapter 5 begin. Like Hilary here, Ambrose, in expounding Luke, passed over the Lord’s Prayer.]

2. The Fasting Person Must Have a Pure Conscience and Good Works.—“But when you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites; for they disfigure their faces, so that they may appear to people to be fasting,” etc. (Matt. 6:16–17). He teaches that the profit of fasting ought to lie outside the ostentation of an exhausted body, and that popular approval should not be sought through display of injury; rather, every fast must be placed within the beauty of holy action.

For heavenly and prophetic Scripture teaches that oil is the fruit of mercy. Therefore our head—that is, the understanding of our life—must be adorned with works of goodness, because all understanding is in the head. The filth must be washed from the face, so that there may be no ugliness arising from vices, but rather the grace of brightness in our encounter with God. Thus, washed into the splendour of a good conscience and anointed with the grace of merciful action, may we commend our fasts to God. Otherwise, while in fasting we flee human awareness with anointed heads, we shall be all the more ridiculous—and recognized.

[Note: The editions of Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius read “of hunger.” But the Paris edition, with all manuscripts, has “of suffering,” which we believe was corruptly written in place of “of negligence.”]

[Note: Supply here the word “God.” For we have already read in chapter 4, §7, that those are open to the sight and encounter of God who, through brightness of mind and purity of life, have the power to behold. In both places Hilary seems to refer to the parable of the virgins, to whom it is said: “Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him.” This is also illuminated by his exposition of Psalm 140, §9: “In washing the face, he required the brightness of a pure conscience, lest anything filthy or stained should cling to us; but in anointing the head, he commanded that we be perfected in the teachings and works of spiritual instruction.”]

[Note: The Chartres manuscript reads “with well-arranged heads.” Jerome notes that Christ speaks here according to the custom of Palestine, where people customarily anoint their heads on feast days.]

3. Where the Heart Is Here, There It Will Be After This Life.—“Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth,” and the rest (Matt. 6:19). Therefore, having set aside concern for human glory and wealth, he shows that every care must be directed toward pleasing God. For bodily weakness or the detraction of the envious corrupts human praise; and treasure of money here is endangered either by loss or by theft. But heavenly praise is eternal, neither liable to be stolen away by stealth nor consumed by the moth or rust of envy. Our heart will have the seat of treasure according as it follows either the harmful light of understanding joined to money or the everlasting light joined to God.

[Note: The printed editions read *secutus*, a solecism corrected by the manuscripts. Before it, some have *utrum* instead of *utram*, which is more rightly referred to the seat possessed either in God or in money. Afterwards, some have *damnoso* (“harmful”), which may be referred to the light of understanding: harmful in money, everlasting in God.]

4. The Body’s Brightness or Eternal Darkness According to the Different Condition of Minds.—“The lamp of your body is your eye” (Matt. 6:22). This is a coherent meaning. For from the function of the eye’s light he expressed the light of the heart. If that light remains simple and clear, it will impart to the body the brightness of eternal light and infuse into the corruptibility of the flesh the splendour of its own origin. But if it is darkened by sins and its will becomes wicked, the nature of the body will be subject to the vices of the mind.

“And if the light that is in you is darkness, how great must the darkness itself be!” (Matt. 6:23). For the corrupt origin of earthly flesh is already wont dangerously to dominate the nobility of the soul; and the sins of bodies are far more heavily aggravated if they are aided even by the desires of minds. Thus our bodies become dark beyond their own nature if the light of the mind within them is extinguished. But if we retain that light through simplicity of spirit, it must also illuminate the body with its own light.

[Note: The Paris edition reads *fuerit*, corruptly. Then “beyond their own nature” means more than they are by their own nature—as though, beyond their natural darkness, they take on a new darkness through the extinguishing of the light of their minds. If we retain this light, however, etc.]

5. God and the World Cannot Both Be Served.—“No one can serve two masters,” etc. (Matt. 6:24). Service to two masters is faithless, and equal concern for the world and for God cannot exist. For there must be hatred toward one and love toward the other, since one and the same work cannot accord with the differing wills of masters, nor can those poor in spirit who please God be suited to the ambitious vainglory of this world.

6. In Contempt for the World, Let the Soul Yearn for Heaven Alone.—“Therefore I say to you: do not be anxious in your heart about what you shall eat, nor for your body about what you shall wear. Is not your soul worth more than food, and the body more than clothing?” (Matt. 6:25). Throughout the preceding discourse he had commanded contempt for the world and confidence in future things. For when he bids us be ready for injury, willing to suffer loss, indifferent to revenge, impartial in loving, and unconcerned for human glory, he seeks to establish us in hope for eternal goods.

[Note: [Col. 0944D] That is, he commands us to be indiscriminate in loving friends or enemies, those who treat us well or ill.] For the love of present things and despair of future things make many uncertain: the former ensnares them through allurements, the latter confounds them through unbelief.

Therefore he wishes the kingdom of heaven, which the prophets announced, John preached, and our Lord declared to be established in himself, to be hoped for without any uncertainty of wavering will. Otherwise, there is no justification from faith if faith itself becomes uncertain. Thus he commands there to be no concern about clothing and food, saying that the soul is more precious than food, and the body than clothing.

[Note: That is, although in the words, “Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious,” the word “therefore” indicates a connection of what follows with what precedes, still the matters following that “therefore” do not sufficiently accord with the preceding ones.]

7. A Higher Meaning Lies Hidden in the Foregoing.—It is indeed beautiful, through contempt for present things, to bestow care only on divine matters. But the discourse descends more deeply, and the reasoning expressed in the words extends to an understanding of the heavenly saying. The Lord commanded treasure to be laid up in heaven; he promised that the body too would receive brightness from the light of the eye; he declared that no one can please two masters. After these things he says: “Therefore I say to you: do not be anxious in your heart about what you shall eat, nor for your body about what you shall wear.” What follows does not sufficiently agree with the propositions. Can even the servant of one master not be anxious about clothing and food? Will the body become dark because the light of the eye is weakened by ill health? Or how can the body have light from the eye? Can laying up treasure in heaven be achieved by nakedness or hunger alone?

### 8. Certain doubts concerning the resurrection are resolved.

But because the thinking of unbelievers concerning the care of future things is corrupted—men who cavil at what form bodies will have in the resurrection, and what sustenance will preserve them in the substance of eternity—and because from the difficulties of useless questions a rationale has been sought for indulging present pleasures, they linger in a useless fear regarding reverence for God and pass over into the joys of the world. Thus it comes about that, for two masters, there is the faithless service of one. Therefore, after first declaring the gravest danger of unbelief, he thus admonishes us out of the highest affection of piety: “Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” (Matt. 6:25).

[Note: [Col. 0945B] The printed editions read “in substance.” The better manuscripts more correctly read “into substance”; that is, by what they may be able to subsist and be preserved eternally. Then, in place of “and when,” we would prefer “so that when,” especially because in the Colbert manuscript, after “follows,” it has: “they pass over into the joys of the world.”]

There is truth in God’s utterances, and every power of creating things is in the Word. Thus neither is what he has promised uncertain, nor is what he has spoken ineffective. Nothing is not bodily in its substance and creation; and the elements of all things, whether in heaven or on earth, visible or invisible, have been formed. For even the kinds of souls—whether possessing bodies or exiled from bodies—nevertheless receive a bodily substance proper to their nature, because everything created must exist in some place.

[Note: [Col. 0945B–C] That is: when, having cast away hope in eternity, they remain in worship and fear of God in such a way that they expect no benefit from their worship and fear. For everyone cast down or shaken from the rank of hope which he had received from the Creator is now readily inclined toward the author of another hope, as Tertullian says in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, no. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0945C] The printed editions have “and most grave”; the superfluous particle is removed on the authority of the Colbert manuscript. Nor should five other witnesses be followed, which present the passage thus: “therefore, from the highest affection of impiety and most grave unbelief, the preaching thus admonishes.” But the Lord admonishes out of an affection of piety, after he has foretold the danger of unbelief.]

[Note: [Col. 0945C–0946C] What Hilary means here by “bodily” is not entirely clear. Yet, since in his exposition of Psalm 129, no. 3, when explaining John’s statement “God is spirit,” he adds that the divine nature is invisible, immeasurable, self-contained, and eternal, he indicates that whatever lacks immeasurability or eternity and does not remain within itself is body. The same appears confirmed in Psalm 124, no. 6, where he teaches that God is present to all things because he is Spirit, penetrating and containing all things: “For he is not bodily as we are, so that, when he is present somewhere, he is absent elsewhere,” etc. There “bodily” plainly denotes that which, being somewhere, is absent elsewhere.

Thus, since he here maintains that nothing is not bodily in its substance and creation, and supports this by the one reason that everything created must be in some place, nothing prevents us from understanding him to call bodily that which exists only in some place, not in every time or place; or which remains in something else, not within itself. He may also call bodily that which, composed by nature of parts or qualities, lacks nothing belonging to its integrity. This is the point of Psalm 129, no. 4: “Whatever is composite … has a beginning by which it is embodied so as to remain.”
