Indeed, Phoebadius, Hilary’s contemporary, contrasts body with what is void, empty, and not full. For he calls the Son of God the Word of God—not a sound of voice, but a substantive reality, bodily through substance. He continues: “For what he made from so great a substance did not subsist without substance” [perhaps: “was”]. “Therefore nothing empty comes from the full, nothing void from the solid; because Christ, the Word of God, is the Spirit of God furnished forth; and, to speak more plainly, he is the body of the Word. For Spirit has a body, but a body of its own kind. For Spirit is invisible and incomprehensible; but is God therefore an empty and void thing?” [perhaps “a void reality” or “a void thing.”]

In this sense Tertullian seems to have said, in *On the Flesh of Christ*, no. 12: “Everything which exists is a body of its own kind. Nothing is incorporeal except what does not exist.” Cicero likewise says in *On Ends*, book IV: “Others, as though a human being had no body, care for nothing besides the mind; whereas the mind itself is not some empty thing—I cannot indeed understand it so—but belongs to a certain kind of body.” Finally, one may call bodily that which is not without some relation to body; and thus the saying of Evodius in Augustine, *Letter* 158, no. 11, may conveniently be understood: “That the soul cannot be entirely devoid of every body is, I think, shown by the fact that God alone is always devoid of every body.” Let these remarks be prefixed for the moment to the following note.]

[Note: [Col. 0946C–0948C] It is difficult to reconcile this passage with several others, for example Psalm 52, no. 7; Psalm 118, no. 8; and Psalm 129, nos. 4, 5, and 6, where the soul is expressly affirmed to be not only spiritual but also incorporeal. If one were permitted to read “fitting” in place of “bodily,” no difficulty would remain. But who would presume to alter a reading already received by the age of Claudianus Mamertus?

Yet it may be reconciled otherwise if Hilary’s purpose is considered. He is not speaking about the inward substance of souls, but about something external, or quasi-external, required for preserving their life in the manner of clothing or nourishment. His entire argument is against those who, though they hear of the resurrection from God, nevertheless distrust it because they cannot grasp what sustenance there will then be.

First, therefore, he establishes the resurrection, concerning which it would be foolish to doubt, since God—truthful in his words and powerful in his works—has promised it. Then, having established the truth of the resurrection, he shows that it is no less vain to be anxious about nourishment, since experience teaches us that God creates nothing half-full, incomplete, unformed, or in some manner unembodied, but grants all things whatever is necessary for preserving a substance once created. He adds that God, who has promised the greater things—namely soul and body—will not deny the lesser, namely nourishment and clothing.

Finally, he illuminates all this by the example of unclean spirits, to whom the power of the eternal counsel grants a means of life, without any toil of seeking or gathering. Hence a little later he concludes: “He has confirmed faith in our vital substance by the example of spirits.” Therefore, when he says, “The kinds of souls receive a bodily substance proper to their nature,” he means nothing else than that souls do not perish, but receive that from which they may be preserved and subsist in their life. What he here calls “bodily substance” he calls, in the following section, “a substance for living,” and in no. 10, more plainly, “vital substance.”

He silently indicates in no. 11 that human beings will derive this vital substance from themselves and not from elsewhere, where he teaches that angels receive from the lot of their origin that they may always exist, and that human beings after the resurrection will not be like them. He declares this expressly in Psalm 147, no. 3, where the assembly of the blessed is proclaimed to need nothing for the substance of body and soul.

Finally, since Hilary here refutes those concerned about both the nourishment and the clothing of souls after the resurrection, and since below, in chapter 11, no. 4, when explaining “a man clothed in soft garments,” he interprets the soul’s clothing as the body by which it is surrounded and circumscribed—“Clothing,” he says, “signifies the circumference of the body with which the soul is clothed”—what can “they receive a bodily substance proper to their nature” mean except: “They do not lack clothing, since they are never not encompassed by bodies”?

At most, therefore, he held here that souls never exist outside every body, since the entire question concerns not the substance of the soul but its mode of subsistence. Let each interpret these matters as he wishes, provided he does not believe that Hilary intended by these words to make the soul bodily in itself; for it is established that he thought otherwise, as was shown at length in the general preface by a special dissertation.

We note in passing that some think the words “the kinds of souls, whether possessing bodies or exiled from bodies” signify human souls and angels. But to us they seem rather to refer to differing conditions of human souls.]

And therefore, while God refutes the folly of this utterly useless question, he does not allow our hope, when soul and body are to be placed in the substance of eternity, to linger over anxiety about future food and clothing in the resurrection—lest an insult be offered to him who restores such precious things, namely body and soul, as though he could not accomplish lesser things.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Thus the better Paris manuscripts. Many others, with the editions of Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius, read “sloth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0948D] The Paris edition reads “so much more precious,” which the earlier Lipsius transferred from Erasmus’s margin into the text; but the manuscripts resist it, some reading “such great things,” others “things so precious.”]

### 9. Demons do not labor to obtain their livelihood.

“Look at the birds of heaven, for they neither sow nor gather into barns; and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?” (Matt. 6:26). Under the name of birds he exhorts us by the example of unclean spirits. To them, without any toil of seeking or gathering, a means of living is nevertheless granted by the power of the eternal counsel. And to show that this must be referred to unclean spirits, he added: “Are you not worth much more than they?” By the superiority of the comparison he indicates the distinction between wickedness and holiness.

### 10. Bodies will be raised in the stature of a perfect man.

“But which of you can add one cubit to his stature? And why are you anxious about clothing?” (Matt. 6:27–28). He has confirmed faith in our vital substance by the example of spirits; but he has left our opinion about the future condition to the judgment of common understanding. Since he is to raise the diversity of all bodies which have received life into one consummate and perfect man, and since he alone has power to add a cubit, or a second or third cubit, to each person’s stature, with what great insult to him do we doubt concerning clothing—that is, concerning the appearance of bodies? (Eph. 4:13). For, in order to make every human being equal and uniform, he will add so much measure to human bodies.

### 11. The lilies that do not labor are angels. Why angels are compared with lilies.

“Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither labor nor spin. Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of them,” etc. (Matt. 6:29). The lilies neither labor nor spin, and Solomon—the great prophet, beloved by God because of his rightly cherished wisdom—was not clothed in their glory. But lilies are born rather than clothed. Clothing, however, is a covering of the body, not the body itself. If this is referred to ordinary human understanding, the whiteness of a covering might have rivaled the color of the lily.

But the lilies, which neither labor nor spin, must be understood to signify the brightnesses of the heavenly angels. Apart from the learning of human knowledge and the reward of their own work, brightness of glory has been granted them by God, lest they be thought to have possessed anything through their own labor or skill. And since human beings at the resurrection will be like angels, he has willed us to hope for the covering of heavenly glory through the example of angelic brightness.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] The printed editions read “as of angels”; *as* is redundant and does not occur in the manuscripts.]

Moreover, the nature of this plant is such that it is most suitably compared with the heavenly substances of angels. When it blossoms, after being torn from the root held fast in the soil, it conceals the power of its nature, although that power may be thought to have withered; and when the season returns, it is again clothed in the honor of its lily. For it blossoms and is restored from itself; and what it is cannot be owed either to the root or to the earth, since the sap that pervades it comes from itself. Thus, by the example of this yearly greenness, it imitates the power of its own heavenly substance, since it is nourished into blossom only from what it has received within itself.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] The printed editions read “therefore”; the manuscripts more aptly read “for.” By the example of a lily whose stem, cut from its root, once it has put forth its calyxes, nourishes and cherishes them so that they blossom completely, it is shown that the life of angels is sustained from its own, not an external, substance.]

Therefore the lilies neither labor nor spin, because the angelic Powers, from the lot of their origin which they have received, receive that they may always exist.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] From several manuscripts the word “its own” is restored here. It refers not to the lily but to the heavenly substance, which is its own—that is, which has from its own nature the power to exist always.]

### 12. The grass: the nations. They will rise for eternal fire. The resurrection of the righteous is far less doubtful.

“For if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is cast into the fire, how much more you, people of little faith?” (Matt. 6:30). He confirms the inviolable confidence of our faith by the authority of examples, so that it may be a matter of so much greater danger to doubt as he has removed every occasion for unbelief with more lavish care.

Grass does not grow in order to be given to the fire; nor is God’s special care in clothing it directed to its burning. Yet we frequently find that the nations are denoted by God under the name of grass. It is that growth which, after the flower of its strength has fallen away, withers under the heat of the sun. Therefore the nations will have no rest, nor will rest be given them by the short expedient of death, as they suppose. Rather, bodily eternity will also be appointed for them, so that in them there may be eternal material for eternal fire, and everlasting punishment may be inflicted upon all the everlasting.

If, then, bodily eternity is granted to the nations only that they may soon be appointed to the fire of judgment, how profane it is to doubt the saints’ glory of eternity, when the work of eternity is bestowed upon the wicked for punishment. Therefore he demands that all our expectation be placed in faith in his promises and in the power of his might, so that, leaving aside anxiety for the things we need, we may expect all things rather from him from whom we ourselves received the beginning of life, and seek the kingdom of God by the service of our life.

And this is the reward of those who live rightly and perfectly: that they may be transferred from this material of a corruptible body into a new and heavenly substance, and that earthly corruption may be changed into heavenly incorruption. Therefore it belongs to the nations to be distressed by this anxious unbelief: held fast by love of the world and occupied with bodily pleasures, they neither seek nor desire, by faith and confession of God, any path into the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] In seven manuscripts: “to the fire the judge”; this reading should not be despised, so that the fire may be called judge, as avenging fire. Yet the other reading is confirmed by the exposition of Psalm 13, no. 11, where we read that the useless and unfruitful are assigned to the fire of judgment.]

### 13. What “day” means. Anxiety does not belong to a day. The things around which all human concern ought to turn.

“Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34). The common judgment is that a day is the course of passing times illuminated by the light of the sun, distinguished by intervening night, which by its arrival substitutes one day for another. But the meaning of future time is contained in “tomorrow.” Therefore God forbade us to be anxious about the future.

But this release from anxiety is a matter not of negligence but of faith. For why should we be anxious about tomorrow, when tomorrow itself will be anxious for itself? Thus the day itself, being anxious on our behalf, drives away our anxiety. But anxiety, I think, is properly a human affection: for the uneasiness of care, fear, or pain arouses it. A day, however, is a course of time; and only after acquiring foresight can it receive the affection of anxiety. Therefore a day would have to be established as a living creature that guards, foresees, and cares, one for whom its own evil is sufficient and to whom sin arising from outside need not be added.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] The printed editions read “foresight alone”; they are corrected from the Roman, Colbert, and Carnot manuscripts. Hilary calls *providentia* the faculty of foreseeing and looking ahead.]

But the nature of the matter does not allow us to assign a mental affection to a day. Therefore both the statement that it is anxious for itself, that its own evil is sufficient for it, and that we are forbidden to be anxious about tomorrow—all this is contained under the significance of a heavenly saying.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] Thus the better manuscripts: that is, all this is said spiritually. Others, with the printed editions, read “under the significance of the heavenly saying.”]

We are therefore commanded not to doubt about future things. For the evil of our life and the sins of the days we live are sufficiently grave, so that all the meditation and labor of our life should be directed toward purging and atoning for these, lest an inexpiable irreligion also be incurred through distrust of future things. For when our care ceases, future things themselves are attentive to their duty, and, through God’s provident goodness, the advance of eternal brightness is prepared for us who are no longer anxious.

### 14. It is unlawful to judge God’s promises. Why.

“Do not judge, lest you be judged. For with the judgment with which you judge, judgment will be made concerning you” (Matt. 7:1–2). God entirely removes every function of judgment and allows none at all to be undertaken. Yet what follows seems to conflict with the preceding commands when he says: “With the judgment with which you judge, judgment will be made concerning you.” But above he said: “Do not judge, lest you be judged.” Must one then not undertake the discernment of good judgment? Yet he declares that people will be judged according to the condition of their judgment, and that all will be measured by the kind of measure with which they measured. Therefore one will never judge well if one is never to judge at all.

But, as was recognized above, nothing in God’s words is treated as trivial or empty; and this whole discourse is beyond the understanding of Gentile ears. For he forbade judgment about his promises. Just as judgments among human beings are formed from uncertain matters, so also this judgment against God arises from the ambiguity of feeling and opinion. He wholly repels it from us, so that steadfast faith may rather be retained. For in other matters it may be a sin to have judged wrongly; but in these matters, judgment concerning God itself is the beginning of guilt.

[Note: [Col. 0950D] The Paris edition reads “in matters,” omitting the pronoun “these,” by which God’s promises are indicated. Soon after, Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “undertaken,” whereas the other books more correctly read “beginning.”]

### 15. The nature and magnitude of unbelief as sin. One who is uncorrected corrects others in vain.

“But why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye and do not see the beam in your own eye?” and the rest (Matt. 7:3). In what follows he taught that blasphemy against the Spirit alone will be beyond forgiveness, while God grants pardon for all other sins. Sin against the Spirit is to deny God the power of might and to take from Christ the substance of eternity. For through him, because God came to be human, the human being in turn will be made God.

Therefore, as great as the difference between a speck and a beam, so great does he show the sin against the Spirit to exceed the condition of other offenses. Thus, when unbelievers reproach others with bodily sins, they do not first see in themselves the burden of sin by which they doubt God’s promises: the beam of unbelief resting in the eye, as it were, in the faculty of the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0950D–0951D] The Paris edition reads “which [they doubt] concerning promises.” It may help here to summarize briefly Hilary’s whole argument, which is not equally clear to everyone. He reasons as follows: Whoever doubts God’s promises doubts that he himself will pass into God. Being uncertain on this point, he does not believe that Christ is God; for this was why he, though God, became human: that the human being might become God. Whoever does not believe Christ to be God sins against the Holy Spirit—that is, against Christ’s divinity; and this sin is the beam of unbelief in the eye of the mind.]

It often happens that, without any example of our own correction, we assume the authority to accuse others and display boastfulness in healing another’s blindness, though we ourselves stand in darkness because our own light has been corrupted. Yet it is difficult for anyone to provide what he lacks, and it is best to teach by example rather than by words. Care must be directed toward one’s own blindness, because it belongs to the nature of things that no one can first become a fit teacher for removing the speck from a brother’s eye until he has cast out the beam of faithlessness weighing upon the light of his own mind.

[Note: [Col. 0951D] The printed editions, omitting the words “beam of unbelief,” add “in either eye”; the omitted words are restored from the manuscripts, though in some the word “unbelief” is absent.]

## CHAPTER VI. On pearls before swine, the false prophet, and the house built on the rock.

### 1. The mysteries of Christ must be disclosed cautiously to Gentiles and heretics.

“Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine,” and the rest (Matt. 7:6). Nothing is more precious or holy than God’s commands and promises, which grant to those sanctified by them the treasure of immortality. We are therefore not permitted to bring their sacraments and powers before the nations or to debate them with heretics. For the nations are called dogs because of their rabid barking against God. Heretics bear the name of swine because, although they have cloven hoofs, they do not order by rumination the knowledge of God which they have received.

Therefore it is fitting that we not handle indiscriminately the embodiment (*concorporatio*) of the Word of God, the mystery of the Passion, and the power of the resurrection, nor bring them forth ignorantly and carelessly—lest they trample and crush our ignorance, if it lacks the equipment of perfect knowledge, mock the weakness in God’s Passion, and, turning against us, tear apart our ignorance and faith with the stings of contradiction.

[Note: [Col. 0952D] Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “incorporation”; other books read “concorporation.” Hilary is accustomed to say *corporatio* in the Prologue to the Psalms, nos. 5–6, and elsewhere.]

### 2. The power of prayer against ignorance. The law of charity.

But in matters which we do not know, a way of attaining truth is opened to us; and it is only by perseverance in prayers that this may be obtained. Therefore, in order that we may understand and believe all things, and may not be delayed by any uncertainty of wavering will, we must pray, seek, and knock (Matt. 7:7): through prayer we shall find mercy, through inquiry progress, through testing an entrance.

[Note: [Col. 0952D] The Roman manuscript reads: “mercy, through inquiry a perfect entrance found by testing”; this is false under an appearance of truth, although elsewhere also “mercy,” “inquiry,” and “progress” occur, and then in two manuscripts “testing.”]

Moreover, we are taught to hope for receiving by the example of human feeling. For when our children ask us for fish or bread, we do not give them a serpent or a stone. How much more will God, the best and most excellent Father, grant us who pray the gifts of perfect faith (Matt. 7:9 ff.); nor will he give, in place of the food of life, the stone of Gentile hardness, or, in place of the preservation of baptism, the serpent of heretical poison?

Then he completed everything by an example of goodness, joining all people in the peace of mutual love. In this he established the commandments of the Law and the Prophets: as we desire all people to be good toward us, so we ourselves should be good to all.

### 3. The road to heaven trodden by few, and the contrary road.

“Enter through the narrow gate. How broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction!” The human journey to heaven is arduous, and its entrance narrow and confined; but the road to destruction is broad. The many take that road; only a few find the other. For few count losses of present things dear, and for them it is the greatest gain of heavenly hope to overcome the desires of mind and body, to break the body’s impulses, and to pass beyond the enticements of every allurement, laid openly before them by all the powers of the world. But for those whose only good is sexual vice, feasting, ambition, arrogance, disdain, hatred, and plunder, that way is thronged by a very large company.

### 4. God’s servant is known not by words but by deeds.

And because few would find the narrow way, he exposes the deceitfulness of those who falsely claim to seek it, saying: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing,” etc. (Matt. 7:15). He warns that blandishments of speech and a pretended gentleness must be weighed by the fruit of conduct, so that we look not at what a person represents himself to be in words, but at what he makes himself in deeds. For in many, wolfish rage is concealed beneath sheep’s clothing.

Therefore, just as thorns do not produce grapes, thistles figs, and evil trees useful fruit (Matt. 7:16), he teaches that the result of good work cannot exist in such persons either, and that all must therefore be known by their fruits. For the kingdom of heaven is not gained by services of words alone, nor will the one who has said, “Lord, Lord,” be its heir (Matt. 7:21). What merit is there in saying to the Lord, “Lord, Lord”? Will he not be Lord unless he has been called so by us? And what holiness of service lies in uttering the name, when the path to the heavenly kingdom is found rather by obedience of the will, not by naming God?

[Note: [Col. 0952D] The printed editions read “the will of God,” against the manuscripts. Again, the particle “rather” is not joined below, chapter 8, no. 8.]

### 5. Heaven is granted not for miracles but for good works.

“Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?’” and the rest (Matt. 7:22). He still condemns the deceitfulness of false prophets and the pretenses of hypocrites, who take glory to themselves from the power of speech—in prophetic teaching, the expulsion of demons, and powers of works of this kind—and promise themselves the kingdom of heaven on that account. As though anything they say or do were their own, rather than everything being accomplished by the invoked power of God: for reading supplies knowledge of teaching, and Christ’s name drives away demons.

[Note: [Col. 0953C] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “the demons of Christ,” etc.]

Therefore that blessed eternity must be earned from what is ours. We must contribute something of our own: we must will what is good, avoid every evil, and obey heavenly commands with our whole affection. Let us thus become known to God by such services, and do what he wills rather than boast of what he can do. He rejects and drives away those whom works of wickedness have turned away from his knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0953C–D] Some manuscripts read “we prefer.” Hilary means that blessedness is to be earned from what is ours without denying that the work of our salvation belongs to God. Appropriately, he says in Psalm 142, no. 12: “That is the confession of human modesty: that a person who is to be led by the Spirit of God into a right land should not claim this as his own merit.” Then in no. 13 he splendidly reconciles merit with God’s glory: “Justice possessed this modesty indeed: that whatever blessedness it hopes for itself, it asks rather from God’s magnificence—because it is fitting to ascribe blessed, eternal, and good things to God—than from its own merit. Yet while preferring God’s honor and mercy, it did not exclude the duty of earning this also through itself,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0953D] The Paris edition reads “what is profitable.” Other books more correctly read “what he can do,” that is, what is freely granted through God’s power and without any merit.]

### 6. The progression of temptations.

“Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house upon a rock,” and the rest (Matt. 7:24). The sense is connected with what precedes. For, rebuking the boasting of false prophets and the fabrications of hypocrites, he sets forth by a comparative example the person of perfect faith in himself: the one who both hears and does his words is built upon the rock and stands on a stable and firm foundation, incapable of being destroyed by the force of storms which fall upon it. By the rock the Lord signifies himself, the strong foundation of the building.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] In most manuscripts: “rebuking.”]

[Note: [Col. 0953D] Thus the Colbert manuscript, supported by others. But Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius, with some manuscripts, omit “and him,” as well as the following word “stands,” and then add: “cannot be destroyed … the Lord signifies.” We would prefer: “and cannot be destroyed by the force of storms which fall upon it.”]

But the person who has grown by his own effort into a lofty work cannot be moved either by rains, rivers, or winds. By rains he signifies the enticements of flattering pleasures that creep in gradually, through which faith first becomes damp as open cracks admit them. After these comes the rush of torrents, that is, the onset of stronger desires. Then the whole violence of surrounding winds rages: namely, the entire spirit of diabolical power attacks. But the human being built upon the foundation of the rock will stand firm and cannot be moved from his place.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] The printed editions read, “but he cannot be moved.”]

The fool, however, who disregards what he has heard, has expended the work of building, as it were, upon sand. He stands faithlessly, soon to be undermined by falling rains, driven by rivers, and scattered by winds, according to the nature of the sands upon which he was built, and to be dissolved in the heavy wreckage of his ruin (Matt. 7:25).

[Note: [Col. 0954C–D] The printed editions read “to be overthrown.” The manuscripts more correctly read “to be undermined.” For a house is not overthrown by rains, but prepared for overthrow. Thus in *On the Trinity*, book II, no. 22, a foundation “not to be undermined by floods” is praised; and in Psalm 68, no. 3: “There are also waters undermining a sandy house.”]

### 7. The purpose of the foregoing.

Thus, by the example of the foregoing comparisons, the Lord willed us both to do what he commanded and to believe what he promised. When everything had been completed, the crowds marveled at his teaching, because he had not taught as the scribes and Pharisees did (Matt. 7:28–29). For in the power of his words they measured the effects of his powers.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] The printed editions read “by the example of disturbances”; they are corrected from the better manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER VII. On the leper whom he healed, the centurion’s paralyzed servant, Peter’s mother-in-law, and many diverse healings.

### 1. The allegorical sense takes nothing away from the truth of the letter. The Law is now useless.

“And when he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a certain leper came and worshiped him, saying, ‘Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,’” and the rest (Matt. 8:1–2). At the beginning of this discourse we warned against anyone perhaps thinking that something must be taken away from faith in the events themselves if we taught that the events contained within themselves the advance of subsequent realities. For truth suffers no loss when it is followed by a corresponding representation.

In the whole preceding discourse, therefore, the Lord had handed down the commands of faith. He had gone beyond the Law, signifying by going beyond it that it was now useless and ineffective. He had required the observance of the commandments and had first commanded the most steadfast hope in his promises. We must therefore consider what he first did after this.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] Namely chapter 2, no. 2.]

### 2. Christ supplies the Law’s weakness.

A leper is present; he asks to be cleansed and is purified by the power of the Word together with touch. He is commanded to be silent (Matt. 8:3–4), yet to show himself to the priest and offer the gift which Moses commanded to be offered as a testimony.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] The printed editions read “he is commanded to be silent after being touched.” The manuscripts agree better with the Gospel words, “he touched him, saying, ‘I will; be cleansed.’”]

Thus the healing of the obedient and believing crowd which had come down from the mountain with the Lord is displayed in the leper. Contaminated by the diseased stain of the body, and having heard the preaching of the kingdom of heaven, it asks to be healed; it is visited with the touch of the body, healed by the power of the Word, and commanded to be silent, lest this salvation seem to have been offered rather than sought. It is commanded to show itself to the priests, so that he who was foretold in the Law may be seen in deeds and works, and so that where the Law was weak, the power of the Word may be understood.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] The better manuscripts read “of the obedient and believing crowd”; other books have “of the obedient,” and add after “coming”: “worship.”]

[Note: [Col. 0954D] The printed editions read “by touch.” The manuscripts more correctly read “together with touch.” Thus the time of the bestowed healing is also indicated: when the people were visited by flesh assumed by the Word, and the power of the Word is joined with the body’s touch, just as above: “he is purified by the power of the Word together with touch.”]

[Note: [Col. 0954D] The word “Word” is absent from Bade, Erasmus, Lipsius, and certain manuscripts.]

The one who has been cleansed must also offer to God the reward of received salvation; but the gift must not be from birds. Rather, the human being, cleansed from the defilements of the body of sin, must pass into God’s sacrifice (Lev. 14:4), because what Moses commanded in the Law was a testimony, not an accomplishment.

[Note: [Col. 0955D] “He is commanded” must be supplied here. Then the particle “but” has been wrongly deleted in the Paris edition.]

### 3. The tribune: ruler of the Gentiles who would believe

After this, when he had entered Capernaum, a certain tribune approached him, begging him and saying: “My servant lies at home paralyzed,” etc. (Matt. 7:5–6). The healing of the paralyzed servant follows the cleansing of the leper. But what does it mean that the tribune, the servant’s master, declares himself unworthy that Christ should enter his house, see his servant, and, being present, bring aid to one present; and that he has soldiers, commands what he wishes, and has many under his authority who obey him—while likewise the Lord is able to grant healing by a word?

Let it suffice for me to say concerning the tribune that he is the ruler of the Gentiles who would believe. Whoever wishes to know who this ruler is, to whom many are subject, should read the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy (Deut. 32), and the book of Ecclesiasticus by Solomon, where they have spoken in some fashion of the dispersion of the nations. Let our discussion concern only the servant.

### 4. The Gentiles’ salvation is from faith

Then, in this servant, after the healing from paralysis, there succeeds the salvation of the Gentiles after the cure of the people descending from the mountain.

> [Note: Lipsius and Paris: “the healing of the people”: wrongly. More plainly one might say this: To the healing, signified in the leper, of the people descending from the mountain, there succeeds the salvation of the Gentiles, prefigured in the servant after the healing from paralysis. Nevertheless, we have restored *paralysis*, especially since the Turonian manuscript has *paralyticis*, where the editions and other manuscripts have *paralytici*.]

For the servant lay disabled in a lowly, perishable house, unworthy of the entrance of the Savior—though he needed that entrance. And the tribune knows that the servant can be healed by a word, because the whole salvation of the Gentiles is from faith, and in the Lord’s commandments is life for all.

Therefore the nations lying in the world, disabled by the diseases of sins, must be understood: their limbs everywhere weakened and incapable of the function of standing and walking. The mystery of their salvation is fulfilled in the tribune’s servant, yet Christ does not enter the house. For although he dwelt in the world, he did not take upon himself the vices and sins of the world.

### 5. The tribune was not from the Gentiles

Then, marveling at the faith, he says: “I have not found such great faith in Israel” (ibid. 10).

> [Note: The Beccensis manuscript has “for he was not”; it is inconsistent with itself, since it immediately adds that he was an Israelite because he believed.]

This tribune was not from the Gentiles; and how was such faith not found in Israel, when the one who believed was an Israelite? But, so that this very historical truth might imitate the likeness of what was to come, the phrase was accordingly added: that so great a faith as belongs to the Gentiles would not be found in Israel, and that men from the farthest Gentiles would rest with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (ibid. 11).

The reality of healing is indeed perfectly accomplished in the servant according to the believer’s faith. Yet the efficacy of present events is shown also to serve as an image of future things: when the tribune believes and the servant is saved, no such faith is found in Israel, and fellowship in the kingdom of heaven with Abraham is assigned to the Gentiles.

### 6. Peter’s mother-in-law: the disposition of unbelief. Peter, chief in faith and apostleship

When Jesus came into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying ill with fever, and the rest (ibid. 14). In Peter’s mother-in-law is understood the corrupt disposition of unbelief, beside which lies freedom of will, joined to us by a kind of marital association. Therefore, by the Lord’s entrance, unbelief—burning with the heat of sins and sick under the domination of vices—is healed in Peter’s house, that is, in the body.

> [Note: The editions read, “into Peter’s house, that is, the body.”]

Then, immediately healed, she ministers in the service of her duty. For he was the first to believe and was chief of the apostleship.

> [Note: The Roman manuscript reads “apostleship.” The meaning of Hilary is illustrated by Innocent’s letter to Victricius, speaking of Peter: “through whom apostleship and episcopacy received their beginning in Christ.”]

What had formerly languished in him, strengthened by God’s word, performed the ministry of public salvation.

> [Note: The Carnotensis, Colbertine, Vatican, and Roman manuscripts read: “performed ministries.”]

We shall discuss in the passage that follows concerning the daughter-in-law and mother-in-law (chapter 10, §18) why this analogy from Peter’s mother-in-law is properly applied to the disposition of unbelief. For now she is called Peter’s mother-in-law of unbelief because, until she believed, she was held in the service of her own will.

### 7. Christ healed our infirmities by his passion

When evening came, they brought to him many who had demons; and he cast out unclean spirits, etc. (ibid. 16). In the indiscriminate healing at the evening hours, we recognize the gathering of those whom he instructed after the Passion: forgiving the sins of all, removing the infirmities of all, driving away the incentives of evil pleasures that assail them, and, by the passion of his body, according to the words of the prophets, absorbing the infirmities of human weakness (ibid. 17).

### 8. The method by which these things must be explained

Jesus, seeing great crowds around him, commanded his disciples to cross the sea. And a certain scribe approached him and said, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go,” and the rest (ibid. 18–19). Many things occur here that can disturb ordinary understanding.

> [Note: Lipsius and Paris read “but not we”; Bade and Erasmus, “to which not we,” contrary to the manuscripts.]

Yet we do not invent an interpretation; the deeds themselves impart their interpretation to us. For it is not the reality that follows interpretation, but interpretation that follows the reality.

There are many crowds, and the Lord commands his disciples to cross the sea. I do not think it accords with the Savior’s goodness that he should have wished to leave behind those running about him and choose some secret dispensation of salvation.

> [Note: Bade and Erasmus read “of salvation to be commanded.”]

Then the scribe follows, saying that he will follow the teacher wherever he goes. Yet nothing is recorded as said or done by the scribe that could give offense. The Lord answered that foxes have dens and birds of the air nests in which to rest, but that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (ibid. 20). And a disciple asked that time be granted him for burying his father; this was denied, and the observance of a pious and humane duty was forbidden (ibid. 21–22).

Therefore the rationale of matters so great and so diverse must be brought forth, so that, according to the connected order of events and the weightiest grounds of truth itself, the understanding of their inner significance may be explained.

### 9. A type of the election of believers. The ship of the Church

The designation “disciples” must not be thought confined to the twelve Apostles. For we read that, besides the Apostles, there were many disciples. Thus an election is commanded to be made from the whole crowd:

> [Note: The printed editions read “is seen”; but the manuscripts read “is commanded,” as also in the sacred text: “He commanded his disciples to cross the sea.”]

namely, of those who would follow the Lord through the many dangers and storms of this world. For the Church is like a ship, and in many places it is so called. Having received a passenger of every kind and nation, it is exposed to all the blasts of winds and motions of the sea.

> [Note: Here, as below in chapter 21, §2, *vector*, “passenger,” is used passively.]

Thus it is harassed by the assaults both of the world and of unclean spirits. For, with every movement of dangers set before us, we enter Christ’s ship, that is, the Church, knowing that we shall be tossed by sea and wind. Therefore, in order that the sequence of the typical meaning might hold together and that the portion of believers embarking upon the ship and the crowd of unbelievers remaining behind might be understood, the person of the scribe and of the disciple is added.

### 10. The scribe, a teacher of the Law, represents unbelievers. Foxes: false prophets. Birds of the air: demons. Christ’s head is God. All are invited into the Church

The scribe, indeed, who is one of the teachers of the Law, asks whether he is to follow. As though the Law did not contain that this was the Christ whom it was beneficial to follow. He thus expressed a disposition of unbelief beneath the hesitation of his question, because the acceptance of faith is not to be questioned but followed.

And so that that same question of unbelief might be punished by judgment, the Lord answered that foxes have dens and birds of the air nests in which they rest, but that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

> [Note: The manuscripts unanimously read “the fox.”]

The fox is a crafty animal, hiding itself in holes near houses and lying in wait for domestic birds; and we read in several places that false prophets are called by this name. The birds of the air, moreover, we have often learned to be called unclean spirits.

Therefore the Son of God, observing the small number of those who followed him and the hesitation of the teacher of the Law whether he would follow him, reproaches them: false prophets have dens and unclean spirits nests in which to rest, because, left outside the ship—that is, placed outside the Church—they have become a dwelling-place of false prophets and a habitation of demons. But the Son of Man, that is, he whose head is God, finds none in whom he may rest when the knowledge of God has been placed in them. All have been invited into the ship, and thus into the Church; but few will follow because of fear of the sea, that is, the world.

### 11. Whether an unbelieving father has a claim upon a believing son

After this a disciple appears, not asking whether he should follow—for he had already believed that he ought to follow—but begging that he be permitted to bury his father. We have received in the opening of the Lord’s Prayer that we must first pray thus: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). Therefore, because the disciple represents the believing people, he is admonished to remember that his living Father is in heaven.

> [Note: The editions read “one is in heaven.” The manuscripts more correctly read “living,” in place of “dead”; this is because, through faith in God, the living ought to cleave to the Living One, as is added below.]

He is commanded to follow the Lord, because he wished to do so, so that the dead may bury the dead. But I do not think that any duty can be expected from the dead. How, therefore, shall the dead bury the dead?

First, then, he shows that perfect faith in oneself is bound by no religious obligation of a worldly duty toward another. Next, he shows that between a believing son and an unbelieving father no claim remains from the title of fatherhood. He did not, therefore, forbid the service of burying his father; but by adding, “Let the dead bury their own dead,” he warned that dead unbelievers are not to be joined to the memorials of the saints. He also teaches that those who live apart from God are dead. Mutual duties must therefore be left to the dead, so that the dead may be buried by the dead, because by faith in God the living ought to cleave to the Living One.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the disciples in the ship awakening Jesus; on the two demoniacs in the land of the Gerasenes; and on the paralytic healed and carrying away his bed

### 1. When and by what danger Christ sleeps within us

When he had entered the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, a great storm arose on the sea, and the rest (Matt. 8:23 ff.). After the disciples had entered the ship, a storm arises, the sea is stirred, and the voyagers are troubled. But he, lulled to sleep, is awakened by the fear of those who are afraid and is asked to bring aid.

> [Note: The Carnotensis manuscript, together with one Colbertine manuscript, reads “lulled to sleep.”]

Having rebuked them because they were of little faith, he commanded the wind and sea to become calm, while people marveled that the wind and sea obeyed his commands.

> [Note: The phrase “while people marveled” has the same force as “with people marveling.”]

Accordingly, churches in which the Word of God has not remained awake are shipwrecked—not because Christ is given over to sleep, but because through our sleep he is lulled to sleep within us. Above all, it happens that in fear and distress of danger we look especially to God for help.

> [Note: The manuscripts do not support Latinius’s conjecture that *praesidium*, “help,” should be read.]

Would that even late hope might trust that it can escape danger, while Christ’s power is awake within it.

> [Note: The printed editions read “while slavery is awake within us”; they are corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.]

He left us an enduring reminder of his rebuke, saying: “O you of little faith, why are you afraid?” (ibid. 26). That is, there ought to be no fear of worldly disturbances while faith in Christ is awake.

> [Note: Six manuscripts read “while Christ is awake,” with no other sense: according to our faith, God and Christ are awake or asleep within us, as is explained in Psalm 120, §9. Yet the term “faith” is more correctly expressed in the other books, because of the words “of little faith.”]

### 2. Why the disciples are now called “men,” not “disciples”

Then follows the amazement of the men, who say: “What sort of man is this, that the winds and sea obey him?” (ibid. 27). This is not the speech of the disciples but of the Gentiles. For although above he had said that only the disciples entered the ship and that he was awakened only by the disciples, he now indicates that men were amazed:

> [Note: We restore the word “men,” omitted in the printed editions, from the manuscripts, while retaining the following word, namely “man,” although it is lacking in them.]

men calling him “man” in the very act of amazement. By this interchange of names it is understood that all Christ’s works and all his powers must be praised as God’s. For it displays the folly of the most wretched error and guilt of the Gentiles: that from the humility of his Passion they call him man rather than, from his powers, God.

### 3. “And when he had crossed the sea into the country of the Gerasenes, two men possessed by demons came to meet him, coming out from the tombs, exceedingly dangerous,” and the rest (ibid. 28)

The meeting with two men; the long possession of the two men by demons; the road dangerous to passersby; the request to flee into the swine; the headlong plunge of the whole herd into the sea after the men were cleansed; then the flight of the herdsmen to the town; the people’s departure from the city; their embassy that the Lord should not enter their city; his return to his own country; there the bringing forward of the paralytic lying in bed; the remission of sins then and there in return for faith; the murmuring of the scribes; the confession of his power; the paralytic’s return home even under the burden of his bed; and the amazement of the people—all these have one meaning.

### 4. Demons expelled from the Gentiles possess heretics. Christ, rejected by the Jews, goes to the Gentiles

At the beginning of the human race there was a division of humankind among Noah’s three sons, from whom, according to the prophecy of Genesis, Shem was chosen for God’s possession. But outside the city—that is, outside the synagogue of the Law and the prophets—demons held two men among the tombs. They had occupied the origins of two Gentile peoples amid the abodes of the dead and the remains of corpses, making the path of this present life dangerous to those passing by.

Therefore, so that there might be in these actions a complete forethought of the future, two men meet the Lord as he comes, so that their meeting might signify a will running together toward salvation. But in the men the demons cry out, asking why he begrudges them their dwelling, why he harasses them before the time of judgment.

Beside these two Gentile peoples was the people of the Sadducees, from the line of Shem, whose heresy is the sin, arising from the Jews, of denying the resurrection.

> [Note: In certain manuscripts, “from the stock,” with the word “Shem” omitted; it must certainly be retained with the other books. For Hilary means that heresy, especially the kind that denies the resurrection, is close to Gentile unbelief; it corrupted the portion of God’s people, or of the race of Shem. By these words he explains: “Now there was not far from them [the two demoniacs] a herd of many swine”; for by the swine he understands heretics here and below, as also above in chapter 6, §1.]

The demons, therefore, seeing that no place was now left for them among the Gentiles, beg that he allow them to dwell in heretics. Once these were possessed, the whole herd, driven headlong by a rapid rush, was forced into the sea. That is, by the demons’ prompting, they are driven into worldly desire, to perish in many waters—that is, amid the unbelief of the other Gentile peoples.

> [Note: The printed editions read “worldly [desires],” contrary to the manuscripts, with which we prefer the following: “they are driven … to perish,” namely, the heretics, rather than the printed reading, “it is driven … to perish.”]

The typical meaning is preserved also in this: it was not enough to say that they were cast into the sea unless it were also added, “And they died in many waters.” Their leaders and shepherds, troubled by wonder at such events, come to the city and report what happened (ibid. 32–33). That city represents the Jewish people.

> [Note: The printed editions read “who”; the manuscripts better read “which,” namely, the city. Hence shortly afterward the text reads “by which,” not “by whom.”]

When it hears of Christ’s works, it goes out to meet its Lord and prevents him from touching its borders and city. For the Law does not accept the Gospels.

> [Note: In many manuscripts, “law” is absent; if that word were suppressed, it would be permissible to refer “receives” to the Jewish people. In their place, Bade reads, “the evangelical law commanded”; Erasmus, “the evangelical law commands”; Lipsius, “it received the evangelical law.”]

Rejected by it, he returns to his own city (Matt. 9:1).

> [Note: The editions read “the city of God,” without support from the manuscripts; three of them immediately add: “Therefore, he entered this dwelling by ship,” etc.]

The city of God is the faithful people. Into this city, therefore, he entered by ship—that is, by the Church.

> [Note: Thus read most manuscripts, as Latinius also conjectured. But the editions read, “that is, the Church.” Hilary himself observes above, chapter 7, §9, that the Church is called a ship in many places.]

### 5. Adam obtained forgiveness

And now, in the paralytic, the whole body of the Gentiles is brought forward to be healed. But the words of the healing themselves must be considered. The paralytic is not told, “Be well”; he is not told, “Rise and walk”; but he is told, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (ibid. 2).

In the one Adam, sins are forgiven to all the Gentiles. He, therefore, is brought to be healed while angels minister; he is called “son,” because he is God’s first work.

> [Note: The printed editions read “who.” The better manuscripts read “because,” which gives the reason Adam is called son of God, following Luke 3:38: “who was Enos, who was Seth, who was Adam, who was God.” A little earlier Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius, together with several manuscripts, read “is brought to be ministered to by angels”: wrongly. On Adam’s salvation, see note g, column 647 of this edition.]

The sins of his soul are forgiven, and forgiveness of the first transgression comes through pardon. For we have not learned that the paralytic committed any sin—especially since elsewhere the same Lord said that blindness from birth had not been incurred through either one’s own sin or that of one’s father (John 9:3).

### 6. Christ is God

> [Note: In some manuscripts: “truth”; this is unsatisfactory. Here, as often elsewhere, *truth* is contrasted with the image of what is to come; thus “the order of truth” means the order of events that truly occurred.]

Then, in the events, the order of historical reality follows, although in the words the image of the future is fulfilled. The scribes are disturbed that sin has been forgiven by a man (Matt. 9:3), for they saw only a man in Jesus Christ. Yet what the Law could not release was released by him, for faith alone justifies.

Then the Lord sees their murmuring within and says that it is easy for the Son of Man to forgive sins on earth (ibid. 4–5).

> [Note: In the Roman, Vatican, Colbertine, and Carnotensis manuscripts the following words occur in a different order: “And he says: No one can forgive sins except God alone; therefore, he who forgave is God; it is easy [the Colbertine has ‘is’] for the Son of Man to forgive sins on earth.” For the Word of God dwelling in a man, etc.]

Indeed, no one can forgive sins except God alone; therefore, he who forgives is God. Since none forgives except God, God dwelling in a man was granting healing to the man. And there was no difficulty for him in acting or speaking, since all power belongs to him whose word he speaks.

### 7. How much is taught by the healing of the paralytic

Moreover, so that it might be understood that he himself, being placed in a body, was the one who both forgave sins to souls and granted resurrection to bodies, he said: “That you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins,” he said to the paralytic, “Rise, and take up your bed” (ibid. 6).

> [Note: Bade reads “was.” Erasmus then moved the word “to be” after “could,” somewhat distorting Hilary’s meaning, which is that Christ declares that he is now seen embodied in himself—the one to whom it belongs to forgive sins.]

It would have been enough to say, “Rise.” But because the whole rationale of the work being accomplished had to be unfolded, he added, “Take up your bed and go to your house.” First he grants forgiveness of sin; then he shows the power of resurrection; then, by the lifting of the bed, he teaches that weakness and pain will be absent from bodies; finally, by the return to his own house, he teaches that believers must be restored to the way into Paradise, from which Adam, the parent of all, had departed when disabled by the stain of sin.

### 8. All need forgiveness. Christ’s power to forgive sins is not astonishing

But when the crowds saw it, they were afraid (ibid. 8). This work ought rather to have produced amazement than fear. Yet the sequence of the mystery remains even now: alongside the historical reality of present events, the image of future things is added. The crowds fear the power of the Lord’s words and deeds.

> [Note: Paris, together with the Colbertine manuscript, reads “attached.” The other books read more suitably “added,” namely, beyond the reality of present events. Moreover, in other editions a full stop was placed after the words “words and deeds,” whereas in §6 Hilary says that the image of the future is fulfilled in the words, not in the deeds.]

For it is a matter of great fear to be delivered over to death with sins not forgiven by Christ, because there can be no return to the eternal home if pardon of offenses has not been granted. And they glorified God, who had given such power to human beings.

All things have been brought to their conclusion in due order. Now that fear of despair has ceased, honor is rendered to God because he has given such power to human beings. But this belonged to Christ alone; it belonged solely to one sharing the Father’s substance to perform these things. Therefore it is not astonishing that he could do them—for what will be believed impossible for God? Otherwise the praise would have been offered on account of one man, not of many. Rather, the reason for the honor paid to God is that power and a way have been given to human beings through his Word: power and a way both for forgiveness of sins, resurrection of bodies, and return to heaven.

> [Note: The printed editions read “by this way.” The reading “and a way” in four manuscripts is preferable, especially since the discussion shortly turns to the return to heaven.]

## CHAPTER IX. On Matthew the tax collector; the fasting of the Pharisees and John’s disciples; the unshrunk patch; the issue of blood in the woman; the ruler’s daughter raised from the dead; the two blind men; and the deaf and mute man

### 1. “And as Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax office, and he said to him, ‘Follow me,’” and the rest (Matt. 9:9)

He commands Matthew the tax collector, sitting at the tax office, to follow him. Matthew consents, prepares a banquet in his house, and a crowd of tax collectors and sinners reclines with him. The Pharisees rebuke the disciples because their teacher was eating with tax collectors. He answers them that the healthy have no need of a physician, but the sick need healing; and he commands them to go and learn what this means: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice.”

### 2. Tax collectors. Matthew’s calling. Salvation necessary for all, supplied by the Law to none

The name “tax collectors” is derived from their way of life: they are those who, abandoning the works of the Law, preferred to conduct themselves according to common and public custom. Therefore, from the house—that is, from the sins of the body—the Lord called Matthew, and, entering into his mind, reclines there.

For this is the same writer of this Gospel. Going forth from the house of his sin, he himself received the Lord within himself, illumined by his inward dwelling. Within him a banquet of evangelical food is prepared in rich abundance for sinners and tax collectors.

Then envy stirs the Jews because the Lord associates with tax collectors and sinners (ibid. 11). To them he brought forth the words of the Law, hidden beneath the veil of unbelief: that he brings help to the sick and gives medicine to those who need it, but that those who think themselves healthy have no need of healing. Yet, in order that they might understand that none of their own were healthy, he warned them to learn what this means: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (ibid. 13). That is, the Law, bound to the observance of sacrifices, cannot bring help; but salvation is reserved for all in the forgiveness of mercy.

“For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” He had come for all; how then does he say that he had not come for the righteous? Were there, then, people for whom it was unnecessary that he come? But no one is righteous by the Law. He therefore shows the boast of righteousness to be empty, because, since sacrifices were weak for salvation, mercy was necessary for all who were placed under the Law. For if righteousness had been from the Law, pardon through grace would not have been necessary.

### 3. Christ the bridegroom. The food of life, by whose presence no one hungers

Then John’s disciples came to him, saying: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?” (ibid. 14). The Pharisees and John’s disciples were fasting, while the Apostles were not fasting. But he answers them spiritually and shows himself to John’s disciples as the bridegroom.

For John pledged that every hope of life was laid up in Christ; and his disciples could not be received by the Lord while John was still preaching. For the Law and the prophets are until him, and, unless the Law came to its end, no one of them would enter evangelical faith.

When he answers that the disciples have no need to fast while the bridegroom is present (ibid. 15), he teaches the joy of his presence and the mystery of the holy food. No one in whose mental vision Christ is present—that is, no one who holds Christ within the mind—will need another food while Christ is present.

> [Note: Six manuscripts read “needed,” which is unsatisfactory. These words indeed appear to mean only that no one will need this holy food while Christ is present; but what follows makes clear that they should rather be understood thus: by that holy food Christ is made present, and when he is present no one will need another food.]

But he says that they will fast after he has been taken away, because all who do not believe that Christ has risen will lack the food of life.

> [Note: Three manuscripts read “into faith.” We receive the Eucharist in faith in the resurrection, since by receiving it we believe that we receive the living bread and the body of the living, not dead, Christ. We receive it also unto faith in the resurrection, since we confess that it contains not merely living bread but life-giving bread, in which some Fathers have rightly taught that the seed of immortality is granted to us. Hence Athanasius, Letter 4 to Serapion, vol. 1, p. 379, Paris edition of 1627, represents Christ as saying: “My body, which is shown and given for the world, will be given as food, so that it may be spiritually bestowed upon each person and become for each a defense and preservation unto the resurrection of eternal life.”]

For the sacrament of heavenly bread is received in faith in the resurrection; and whoever is without Christ will remain fasting from the food of life.

> [Note: Latinius, from the Vatican manuscript, would have expressed Hilary’s meaning more clearly as “fasting from the food of life,” rather than “fasting in the food of life.”]

### 4. The old person does not receive this food

So that they might understand that these perfect mysteries of salvation could not be entrusted to them while they remained in their old state, he set forth an example by comparison. A raw patch is not sewn onto an old garment, because the strength of the new patch tears apart the weakness of the old garment; nor is new wine poured into old wineskins, for the heat of fermenting must bursts old wineskins (ibid. 16–17).

> [Note: Thus read Bade, Erasmus, and Lipsius, supported by Paris and four manuscripts, which have “of the patch sewn on.” Other manuscripts have “of the patch sewn to.”]

That is, souls and bodies weakened by the age of sins cannot receive the mysteries of new grace. For the tear will be worse, and, once the wine has been spilled, the old wineskins will perish. Such persons will have a double guilt: beyond the oldness of their sins, they will not sustain the power of new grace. Therefore neither the Pharisees nor John’s disciples will receive the new unless they become new.

### 5. The ruler begging life for his daughter: a type of the Law

While he was speaking these things, behold, a certain ruler came and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, my daughter has just died; come and lay your hand upon her,” etc. (ibid. 18). The ruler’s prayer, the woman’s faith, the crowd assembled in the house, the cry of the two blind men, and the bringing forward of the mute, deaf, and demoniac maintain an order of meanings connected with the matters previously discussed.

This ruler is understood to be the Law, which prays to the Lord on behalf of the people whom its own proclamation of Christ had nourished by expectation of his coming, that he might restore life to the dead girl.

> [Note: The editions read, “the people prays, whom Christ’s own proclamation of his coming,” etc.; corrected from the manuscripts.]

For we read of no ruler who believed. Hence the person of this praying ruler is rightly applied as a type of the Law. The Lord indeed promised help to it and set out to grant it.

### 6. The Gentiles seize the salvation prepared for the Jews

But first the crowd of sinners is saved with the Apostles. And although the election appointed from the Law ought first to have lived, yet, under the figure of the woman, salvation is first restored to tax collectors and sinners.

This woman, meeting the Lord as he passes, trusts that by touching his garment she will be healed of her issue of blood. Polluted, that is, by the defilements of her body and weakened by the impurities of inward vice, she hastens in faith to touch the hem of the Lord’s garment. She touches the gift of the Holy Spirit, proceeding as it were in the hem from Christ’s body and associating with the Apostles; and immediately she is healed (ibid. 22).

> [Note: That the term “Holy Spirit” signifies the divinity of the Word is clear from what follows. For what can “the gift of the Holy Spirit, proceeding as it were in the hem from Christ’s body” mean here, except the divine activity extending even to the hems of clothing, or the power remaining within the body and imparting effectiveness of healing to perishable things? Nor is it less clear that the name “Power” shortly afterward is taken in the same sense. Christ’s divinity went out from the body when it revealed itself through divine works. It is rightly said to have gone out, since it was not confined by the body.]

Thus salvation is given to one while it is delayed for another. The Lord immediately praised her faith and constancy, because the people of the Gentiles seized what was being prepared for Israel.

### 7. Christ’s power is infinite

Yet even in the literal interpretation there is great wonder at the Lord’s power: that power remaining within the body added the efficacy of healing to perishable things, and divine activity extended even to the hems of his garments. For God was not divisible or comprehensible, so as to be enclosed by a body. He himself distributes gifts in the Spirit, yet is not divided among the gifts. Faith attains his power wherever it is, because he is everywhere and absent nowhere.

The assumption of a body did not confine the nature of Power; rather, Power assumed the frailty of the body for its redemption.

> [Note: “Its” refers not to Power but to the body; by “body” is understood human nature. Thus the meaning is that Power assumed weak human nature for its redemption.]

That Power is so infinite and so free that the working of human salvation was contained even in the hems of his garments.

> [Note: In Bade, Erasmus, Lipsius, and certain manuscripts, the final words of this section are lacking; in their place many words from the following section have been inserted, as will shortly be stated.]

### 8. The Jews mock the resurrection. Few of them will believe

Then the Lord enters the ruler’s house, namely the synagogue, in which, in the songs of the Law, the lamentation-hymn was sounding (ibid. 23), and he is mocked by many. For they never believed God to be in a man; indeed, they mocked the proclamation of resurrection from the dead.

Taking the girl by the hand, for whom death was sleep in his presence, he brought her back to life (ibid. 25). And so that it might be understood that the number of those chosen from the Law who would believe was small, the entire crowd was expelled. The Lord would certainly have wished to save it, but by mocking his words and deeds it was not worthy to share in the resurrection.

And when the report went out through all that land (ibid. 26), after the salvation of the election, Christ’s gift and works are proclaimed.

> [Note: The editions, except Paris, read “unto the salvation of the election.” The other books correctly read “after the salvation of the election”: that is, after the chosen portion of the Jews, represented in the ruler’s daughter, was healed. For here, as shortly before and at the beginning of §6, Hilary calls the Jews “the election,” those for whom salvation was appointed by God, following Paul in Romans 11:5, 7: “A remnant according to the election of grace has been saved … What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it”; and again verse 28: “According to the Gospel, indeed, enemies for your sake; but according to election, beloved for the fathers’ sake.”]

9. Faith prerequisite to salvation.—Accordingly, as the Lord went out, two blind men immediately followed Him (ibid. 27). But how could blind men have known both the Lord’s departure and His name? Indeed, they call Him Son of David and ask to be saved. In the two blind men the entire meaning of the preceding prefiguration is brought to completion. For by them the ruler’s daughter is shown to be, that is, the Pharisees and the disciples of John, who had previously joined together in testing the Lord.

> [Note: The manuscript of Bec, with the Tours manuscript in its second recension agreeing with it, reads: “namely, the Pharisees and the disciples of John.” Nothing seems to require alteration. Above, the ruler—the father of the daughter—was understood as the Law; the daughter, as the people subject to the Law. Thus, in the ruler’s daughter the Pharisees and disciples of John are shown as children of the Law, blind in themselves, yet learning Christ as Savior through the ministry of the Law.]

They did not know from whom to seek salvation; but the Law pointed Him out to them, and showed them in the body their Savior, descended from David’s line. Blind through their ancient sin—since they did not see Christ unless admonished—it implanted in them the light of the mind. The Lord, showing that faith is not to be expected from salvation, but salvation through faith—for the blind saw because they had believed, not believed because they had seen (ibid. 28), whence we must understand that what is asked must be merited by faith, not that faith is to be derived from things obtained—promises sight if they believe, grants it to those who believe, and commands silence (ibid. 30), because preaching was the Apostles’ particular office.

> [Note: The following six lines, namely through “if they had believed,” omitted here in the ancient editions and in seven manuscripts, formed the end of section 8. They stand much better here in the Paris edition and four manuscripts—unless one suspects that they slipped from the margin into the text.]

10. The Gentiles are represented by the demoniac.—Moreover, after these things, in the mute, deaf, and demoniac man (ibid. 32), the Gentile people, needy of all salvation, is presented.

> [Note: The Paris edition has *indigna* (“unworthy”); then other printed editions also have “with the ailments of the whole body.” They are corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.]

For, beset on every side by every evil, it was entangled in the ailments of the whole body. And in this the order of events is preserved. For first the demon is cast out, and then the remaining functions of the body return. Once the madness of every superstition has been driven away through the knowledge of God, sight, hearing, and speech of salvation are brought in.

> [Note: Printed editions read “For God, by knowledge …”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

The confession of so great a crowd followed in amazement at this deed: “Never has anything like this appeared in Israel” (ibid. 33): namely, that one to whom no help could be brought through the Law should be saved by the power of the Word; and that a man mute and deaf should speak the praises of God. But once salvation had been given to the Gentiles, all cities and all villages are enlightened by Christ’s power and coming, and escape every infirmity of their lethargic sickness.

## CHAPTER X

> [Col. 0966B] In which He sends forth the twelve disciples with instruction.

1. “But seeing the crowds, He had compassion on them, because they were harassed and lying down,” and the rest (Matt. 9:36).—We ought to examine the force of the words no less than that of the events, because, as we have said, the same weight of meaning resides in sayings and deeds alike. The Lord has compassion on the crowds, harassed and lying down, as upon a scattered flock without a shepherd. And He says that the harvest is plentiful, the laborers few, and that the Lord of the harvest should be asked to send more laborers into the harvest (ibid. 37). Having summoned His disciples, He gave them power to cast out unclean spirits and to heal every weakness and every disease (Matt. 10:1). Although these things were then done in the present, we must nevertheless consider what they signify for the future.

2. The harvest: the gift of the Holy Spirit; its abundance; its power is granted through prayer.—No assailant had rushed upon the crowds, nor were they lying down, struck by some accident or commotion. Why, then, does He have compassion on them as lying down and harassed? Clearly, the Lord has compassion on the people harassed by the dominating violence of unclean spirits and sick beneath the burden of the Law, because as yet they had no shepherd to restore to them the guardianship of the Holy Spirit.

> [Note: Three manuscripts read “no one.”]

The fruit of this gift was exceedingly abundant, but had not yet been harvested by anyone.

> [Note: Six manuscripts read “not yet a harvest”; the others, with the editions of Basel and Erasmus, read “not yet sent.”]

For its abundance surpasses in itself the multitude of those who draw from it.

> [Note: The words *de se* (“in itself”), omitted in the editions of Lipsius and Paris, are supplied from the Roman and Colbert manuscripts. When these words were wrongly connected with the following word, the editions of Basel and Erasmus produced “dissimilarity” in place of “multitude,” while most manuscripts produced “dissimulation.”]

For however much is taken by all, it nevertheless always overflows for further giving. And because it is useful that there be many through whom it may be ministered, He commands the Lord of the harvest to be asked to send more laborers into the harvest: that is, that God may provide an abundance of reapers to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit that was being prepared. For through prayer and supplication this gift is poured out upon us by God.

> [Note: Basel, Erasmus, and Lipsius read “will be poured out”; the other books, “is poured out.” This passage may again be referred to the sacrament of confirmation. See below, chapter 19, section 3, where the gift of the Holy Spirit is declared to be bestowed through laying on of hands and prayer. The same editions, with the Paris edition and the Colbert and Chartres manuscripts, read: “and that He might indicate that numerous reapers were to be sent into that harvest, first from these twelve Apostles”; the two manuscripts just mentioned add after this: “from these, twelve Apostles first.” We follow the others.]

And, to indicate that numerous reapers were to be dispersed into that harvest, first from these twelve Apostles, having summoned them He gave power to cast out spirits and heal every infirmity. By the powers of this gift both the disturber could be expelled and the sick healed.

> [Note: Two manuscripts read “by this power they could.” Then, in Latinius, the Vatican manuscript reads “and troubled,” wrongly, since the power given is signified as directed against the disturber, the devil.]

It is fitting to examine the meaning of each command.

3. Christ’s commands concerning the apostolic office.—They are warned to keep away from the ways of the Gentiles (ibid. 5), not because they were not also to be sent for the salvation of the Gentiles, but in order that they might abstain in conduct and life from Gentile ignorance. They were forbidden to enter cities of the Samaritans. Did He not rather Himself heal the Samaritan woman (John 4)? But they are warned not to approach the churches of heretics. For perversity differs in no respect from ignorance. They are then sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 10:6). Yet against Him—Christ—they raged with the tongues and jaws of wolves and vipers. But the legislation of the Law ought to receive the privilege of the Gospel, so that Israel might have the less excuse for its crime, the more diligence it had experienced in being warned.

> [Note: The Tours manuscripts, in the first hand, read “but more properly, the reading”; in the second hand, “but the reading of the Law,” which five others also have.]

4. The perfect image of Christ in the Apostles.—Then the entire power of the Lord’s virtue is transferred to the Apostles. Those who in Adam had been formed in the image and likeness of God now receive the perfect image and likeness of Christ, differing in nothing from their Lord’s powers; and those who had formerly been earthly now become heavenly.

> [Note: Printed editions read: “so that those who … may receive … may become,” contrary to the manuscripts. Then before the word “preach,” the words “they are commanded to” have been omitted.]

They are to preach that the kingdom of heaven is at hand (ibid. 7): that is, that the image and likeness of God are now admitted into fellowship with truth, so that all the saints, who are called heavens, may reign with the Lord.

> [Note: Here again supply “they are commanded to.” In the earlier printed editions the continuation was wrongly referred to the saints to whom the kingdom of heaven is preached, whereas the words concern the Apostles who preach.]

They are to heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, and cast out demons (ibid. 8): whatever evils Satan’s instigation had inflicted upon Adam’s body, they in turn are to cleanse away by their participation in the Lord’s power. And, that they may wholly attain the likeness of God according to the prophecy of Genesis (Gen. 1:26), they are commanded to give freely what they received freely: so that the ministry of a free gift may itself be without charge.

5. Nothing for sale in apostolic ministry.—They are forbidden to possess gold, silver, or money in their belts, to carry a bag on the road, or to take two tunics, sandals, or a staff in their hands; “for the laborer is worthy of his wages” (ibid. 9–10). The treasure in the belt is not, I think, an object of envy; and what does this forbidden possession of gold, silver, and copper in the belt mean? The belt is the equipment of ministry and the girding-up for effective work. Therefore we are warned that nothing in our ministry should be for sale, and that the possession of gold, silver, and copper should not be the purpose of our apostolate.

> [Note: Many manuscripts read “nor in the apostolate.”]

Nor should we carry a bag on the road: that is, we must abandon concern for worldly property, because every treasure is harmful on earth, our heart being where our treasure is stored. Not two tunics: for Christ, once put on, is sufficient for us; and we must not afterwards, through perversity of understanding, clothe ourselves in another garment, whether of heresy or of the Law. No sandals. Is the weakness of human feet able to endure being bare?
