But, since we are to stand barefoot upon holy ground, not occupied by thorns and briars of sins, as was said to Moses (Exod. 3:5), we are warned to have no equipment for our entry other than that which we received from Christ. Nor a staff in our hands: that is, we are not to seek the claims of alien power, having the rod from the root of Jesse; for whatever other rod there may be will not be Christ’s.

> [Note: In the Paris edition the word *indigi* (“to need”) has been deleted. Other editions, reading “not to need by right of external power,” subsequently omit the word “to seek.” We follow the manuscripts, some of which have *externae* (“external”) in place of *extraneae* (“alien”).]

Furnished by all the preceding teaching for completing the journey of this age—with grace, provision, garment, sandal, and power—we shall be found worthy of our wage when we work in these things: that is, through observing them we shall receive the rewards of heavenly hope.

6. “Into whatever city you enter, inquire who in it is worthy,” and the rest (ibid. 11).—Perhaps the Lord will be thought to have given the Apostles trifling commands, since He has descended even to directions about entering, dwelling, staying, and departing. Understood simply, these suit the modesty of the saints: hospitality should be with one worthy, lest through carelessness or ignorance they be polluted by living with a disgraceful household. But He commands them, upon entering a city, to inquire for one worthy and remain with him until departure. He also commands that the house be greeted peacefully by those entering it; if it is worthy, it is to be worthy also of the fellowship of peace; if unworthy, the peace is to return to them. But upon those who do not receive them and their words, after the dust is shaken from their feet, seeds of eternal curse are to be left (ibid. 13–14).

7. The worthy house is the Church; the worthy host is one in whom Christ dwells.—These matters strongly stir the understanding. For if they are not to receive hospitality unless they have first inquired who is worthy, how can a house afterwards be found unworthy? And how will one neither hear their words nor receive them?

> [Note: Three manuscripts read: “not hearing their words and not receiving them.”]

Either this is not to be feared in one who is righteous; or, if he is found unworthy, no fellowship of dwelling is to be undertaken. And what advantage will there have been in inquiring and seeking for one worthy, if both observance and punishment are prescribed in relation to an unworthy host? But the Lord instructs them not to associate with the homes and acquaintances of those who either persecute Christ or do not know Him; and, in whatever city they may be, to inquire whose dwelling is worthy—that is, where the Church is and Christ dwells—and not to go elsewhere, because there is the worthy house and the righteous host.

8. How the peace that is spoken may return.—He commanded those entering to greet the house aloud, saying, “Say: ‘Peace to this house’”; and, if the house were found worthy, peace ought to come upon it, but if unworthy, the peace should return to them. Yet if peace has already been spoken at the first entry in the act of greeting, how will it afterwards come, or how will it afterwards return? Either peace ought not to have been spoken before it was proved whether the house was worthy; or, if it was worthy and greeted with peace, the condition of peace both coming and returning cannot logically cohere with what precedes. We must therefore show the proper meaning of these words.

9. The various deceit of Jews professing faith; peace wished for the unworthy, not given.—There would be many Jews whose attachment to the Law would be so great that, although through admiration of Christ’s works they had believed in Him, they would nevertheless remain in the works of the Law. Others, curious to investigate the freedom that is in Christ, would pretend that they had passed from the Law to the Gospels.

> [Note: The Roman manuscript reads *exprobrandae* (“to be reproached”). It is evident that this thought is expressly drawn from Paul’s words in Galatians 2:4: “because of false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our freedom.”]

Many, moreover, would be led over into heresy through perversity of understanding. Since all persons of this kind deceive, flatter their hearers, and falsely claim that catholic truth resides with them, He had therefore previously warned that one worthy to live with should be sought. But because the ignorant might, through verbal deceit, fall in with such a host, they must use with caution and diligence the house itself which is called worthy—that is, the Church called catholic. It is indeed to be greeted with the disposition of peace, but so that the peace is spoken rather than given. For thus He commanded: “Greet it, saying: ‘Peace to this house.’” Therefore the peace of greeting is to be bestowed in words and in the language of prayer. But one’s own peace, which consists in the inward affections of compassion, ought not to come upon it unless it is worthy; and if it is found unworthy, the sacrament of heavenly peace must be retained within their own conscience.

10. Fellowship in dwelling.—But upon those who, after hearing the preaching of the heavenly kingdom, reject the Apostles’ commands, an eternal curse is left at their departure and by the sign of dust shaken from their feet (ibid. 14). For there appears to be some fellowship between one standing upon a place and the place upon which he stands, and there arises between them a kind of union of body and ground.

> [Note: The Paris edition, with the Colbert manuscript, reads *insistentis* (“standing upon”), with the same sense.]

Therefore every sin of that house and dwelling is left within it when the dust of the feet is shaken off, and it borrows nothing of holiness from the tracks of the Apostles who stood there. Thus those whose coming and entering remove the sins of earthly origin bear witness that unbelief, together with all the dust of its earth, is judged. It will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrhites than for that city (ibid. 15), because it was a lighter thing for them to err without knowing Christ; but for these it is inexpiable either not to receive Him when preached, or not to preach Him, once received, in a holy and catholic manner.

11. In what respect, according to some, the serpent’s prudence is to be imitated.—He signifies that there will be many who are to rage against the Apostles with mad fury, when He says that He sends them as sheep among wolves, declaring that they must be simple as doves and prudent as serpents (ibid. 16). But the dove’s simplicity is self-evident; we must consider what the serpent’s prudence is. I do not know what prudence or counsel exists in it, although some have committed to memory this account:

> [Note: This very account of the serpent was handed down after Theophilus of Antioch by Chrysostom, Homily 34; Jerome on this passage; Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book 3, §131; Augustine, *Questions on Matthew*, question 17, book 8; and others.]

When it realizes that it has fallen into human hands, it withdraws its head from the blow by every means, either covering it with its body coiled into a circle or plunging it into a hole, and leaves the remaining part to be struck. By this example, we are said to be bound, if any persecutions occur, to conceal our head, which is Christ, so that, when we are exposed to every torture, we may preserve uninjured the faith received from Him at the cost of our body.

12. But this whole discourse of the Lord concerns Jews and heretics: “Brother will deliver up brother, father son, and children will rise against parents” (ibid. 21); that is, members of the same kindred household will be divided against one another.

> [Note: Printed editions, except Paris, and most manuscripts read “of the same house.” They have a certain appearance of truth; nor should the manuscript reading “of the same kind,” found in the Colbert and Chartres manuscripts—where Paris has *ejusmodi*—be preferred unless Hilary were pursuing a spiritual sense here.]

For under the names of parents and kindred is indicated the people’s former unity, now made diverse through mutual hostile hatred; and they are to be brought before governors and kings of the earth (ibid. 18), while these attempt to compel either our silence or our connivance.

> [Note: The final Paris edition wrongly and without authority reads “men.” Then six manuscripts read “a certain unity of the people.” Thereafter the printed editions read: “is indicated. Now by mutual hostile hatred, and by diverse judges, and even kings”; the reading is corrupt and the punctuation confused. A sounder, clearer text is supplied from the manuscripts. Their sense is this: by the example of a household first joined by kinship and later divided by hatreds, the people is indicated which, once united, is now divided by hostile hatred.]

For we are to be witnesses to them and to the Gentiles: by this testimony the excuse of unrecognized divinity is to be removed from the persecutors, while for the Gentiles the way of believing Christ is to be opened, as He is preached by the voices of confessors steadfast amid the penalties inflicted by raging men.

> [Note: Thus the better manuscripts. Printed editions read “witnesses also to them.” The word “are” has been omitted after “to be,” just as earlier “or the discourse is” was omitted after “warns,” and after “brought before.”]

Accordingly, He warns that we must be equipped with the serpent’s prudence.

13. The serpent is to be imitated by preachers.—Before it deceived Adam, Genesis already called it wise (Gen. 3:1), and taught its prudence by the sequence of its malicious plan. First it attacked the mind of the weaker sex; then it enticed it by hope; it promised participation in immortality; and through such great rewards it accomplished the work of its counsel and will. With like timeliness, after examining each person’s nature and disposition, prudence in speech must be employed. The hope of future goods must be disclosed, and then the heavenly rewards of perfect faith must be set forth.

> [Note: We have added the particle *sic* (“thus”) on the authority of the Roman, Colbert, and Chartres manuscripts, which immediately afterwards read *promerenda* (“to be earned”) in place of *proferenda* (“to be set forth”).]

Thus what the serpent falsely promised, we may preach in truth: according to God’s promise, those who believe will become like angels. Thus, though wolves and heretics rage around us, we may gain over the receptive and unencumbered minds of peoples by promises of heavenly kingdoms, and deliver the truth of realities with the serpent’s prudence and the dove’s simplicity.

14. When the Gentiles will believe, and when the Jews.—He also warns those handed over not to be concerned about their answer, but rather to await what the Spirit of God may suggest (Matt. 10:19), because our faith, intent upon all the commands of the divine will, will be instructed in the knowledge of how to answer.

> [Note: Printed editions read “for the answer of knowledge.” We prefer, with the three manuscripts just mentioned, “for the knowledge of answering,” that is, that one may know what answer must be made. Then six manuscripts have “having authority to set before us an example” in place of “having,” which we prefer to retain with the sounder texts.]

We have Abraham as an example: when Isaac was demanded for sacrifice, a ram for the victim was not lacking to him (Gen. 22:13). Then He advises flight from one city into two (Matt. 10:23). For His preaching, first driven from Judaea, passes to Greece; then, wearied by the sufferings of the Apostles in different cities of Greece, it remains a third time among all the Gentiles.

> [Note: Lipsius, and Paris after him, read *fugata* (“put to flight”), contrary to the authority of the old books. Here an abstract noun is used for a concrete one: “preaching” in place of “preachers,” to whom suffering and weariness properly belong.]

But to show that the Gentiles would indeed believe the Apostles’ preaching, while the remnant of Israel must believe at His coming, He says: “You will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes” (ibid.). That is, after the fullness of the Gentiles, what remains of Israel is to be placed in the Church at His coming in glory, to complete the number of the saints.

> [Note: Printed editions read “to be summoned into the Church”; several manuscripts, “to be summoned in the Church.” More truly the Roman, Vatican, Colbert, and Chartres manuscripts read “to be placed” or “settled in the Church.” For being summoned applies also to unbelievers; but being placed in Christ’s body, which is the Church, applies only to believers. Thus, in chapter 7, section 11, all are said to be invited into the Church, but few to enter.]

15. It consoles us in sufferings that through them we are made like the Lord.—“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord” (ibid. 24). Knowledge of coming events greatly advances one’s undertaking to endure them, especially if willingness for patience is supported by example.

> [Note: Six manuscripts read “continuance,” especially if the pleasure of wisdom is assumed. Then three read “pleasure.”]

Our Lord, eternal light, guide of believers, and parent of immortality, first sent before His disciples consolations for their future sufferings, lest any disciple should think himself better than his teacher, or a servant above his lord. If through envy they added the name of demon to the master of the household, how much more will they inflict every kind of injury and insult upon His household servants (ibid. 25)? But let these things not terrify us. Rather, let us embrace as glory the fact that we are made equal to our Lord even in the conditions of suffering.

16. Hidden things will be disclosed on the day of judgment.—“There is nothing hidden that will not be revealed” (ibid. 26). He points to the day of judgment, which will disclose the concealed awareness of our will and expose by the light of public knowledge those things we now consider hidden. Therefore He warns that threats, plans, and powers of persecutors are not to be feared, because the day of judgment will reveal them all as nothing and vain.

17. The knowledge of God must be proclaimed steadfastly.—“What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (ibid. 27). We do not read that the Lord customarily spoke at night or delivered teaching in darkness. But because all His discourse is darkness to carnal persons, and His word is night to unbelievers, and because each one must speak what has been said by Him with the freedom of faith and confession, He therefore commanded that what had been spoken in darkness be preached in light, and what had been entrusted to the privacy of ears be proclaimed from elevated places, so that it may be heard by the heralding voice of speakers.

> [Note: Printed editions read: “Therefore He wishes that what has been said by Himself should be spoken with the freedom of faith”; they are corrected from the manuscripts.]

> [Note: Basel and Erasmus read “to speak loftily, so that by proclamation,” etc.; Lipsius and Paris, with the Tours manuscript, “of those speaking loftily”; four others, “in the loftiness of those speaking.” We follow the Chartres, Vatican, and Colbert manuscripts.]

For the knowledge of God must be asserted steadfastly, and the deep secret of evangelical teaching disclosed by the light of apostolic preaching. We must not fear those who have license over bodies but have no right at all over the soul (ibid. 28); rather, we must fear God, who has power to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.

> [Note: The Colbert manuscript, with the Roman, reads: “over the body, but no right over its soul.”]

18. Two sparrows for an *as*: body and soul sold to sin.—“Are not two sparrows sold for an *as*, and does not one of them fall to the earth without the will of your Father?” (ibid. 29). I think bird-catching is not a crime, nor does the sale of sparrows involve guilt. And His saying, “One of them does not fall upon the earth without the will of your Father,” seems contrary to the apostolic statement, “God does not care for cattle” (1 Cor. 9:9). His authority would be greatly diminished if He were found to have meant otherwise than what is delivered in the Gospels. Nor would much dignity be granted to the Apostles if they were ranked before sparrows.

This passage proceeds from the preceding meaning. For the iniquities are aggravated of those who will hand believers over, persecute them, compel them to flee, and make us hateful because of the Lord’s name—those who exercise all their authority over bodies alone, possessing no power over the soul. These, therefore, sell two sparrows for an *as*.

> [Note: Thus all manuscripts. Therefore the pronoun “these” must necessarily refer to the persecutors. That Hilary habitually used *veneunt* actively (“sell”) is plainly established by what follows. The editors of the earlier editions, failing to observe this, placed here “two sparrows are sold,” and below allowed themselves many alterations.]

Now what was sold under sin Christ redeemed from the Law. Therefore what is sold is body and soul; and that to which it is sold is sin, because Christ redeemed from sin and is redeemer of both soul and body.

> [Note: Erasmus reads, “What then are the two sparrows,” etc.; Basel, “Who then are the two sparrows that are sold?” Paris also has *esse* (“to be”) instead of *asse* (“for an as”). Lipsius substituted *vendunt* (“sell”) for *veneunt*; other editions also have that word shortly afterwards, contrary to the manuscripts.]

Those, therefore, who sell two sparrows for an *as* sell themselves to the slightest sin—beings born to fly and be borne up to heaven on spiritual wings. But captured by the prices of present pleasures and offered for sale to the luxury of the world, they market their whole selves for such actions.

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts, supported by Psalm 118, section 18: “You have been trained in heavenly knowledge: what have you to do with earthly works and deeds? You have become a bird,” etc. There it is beautifully shown that human beings born for things above rightly suffer snares amid earthly things. Printed editions here read “they are traded at auctions.”]

19. Body and soul are born to become one in heaven; those who fall become one upon earth.—But we must ask how that “one of them” is which will not fall without the will of God.

> [Note: Lipsius, deleting the verb *est* (“is”) with the following relative *quod* (“which”), placed immediately before and after it “one of them,” contrary to the manuscripts, as though “one” referred to the sparrows rather than to the unity of body and soul. Hilary commonly teaches that soul and body, now two because neither is wholly and perfectly subject to the other, will after the resurrection become one either in glory or punishment. Either the body will follow the soul, so as to fly with it into heaven as a participant in spiritual subtlety; or the soul will be drawn downward by the body, so as to fall with it to earth, or earthly heaviness. Thus he understands by the words “one of them” this unity consisting of body and soul.]

God’s will is that this one should rather fly upward, but the law proceeding from God’s ordinance determines that this one should rather fall.

> [Note: The Roman, Vatican, Colbert, and Chartres manuscripts read: “God’s will would rather have one of them fly upward; but the prophet determines, from God’s ordinance, that one of them should rather fall”—corruptly. Hilary’s meaning is that God, so far as He is concerned and without regard to us, wills that the body rise into the nature of the soul; but, by the requirement of the law of justice on account of our sins, determines that the soul fall into the earthly nature of the body. Hilary elsewhere also affirms this general will of God, by which He wills all to be saved: for example, in Psalm 134, §24, “He would have willed that His people, whom He had chosen in their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, should not be judged”; or above, chapter 9, §8: “The whole crowd was cast out, whom the Lord would certainly have wished to save; but by mocking His words and deeds, it was not worthy of sharing in the resurrection.” This is explained at length in Psalm 2, §§16–18, where it is further declared that this secondary law and will of God is nothing other than the punishment established for those who act unjustly, since vengeance has been appointed for those to whom, by free choice, the malice of freedom was more pleasing.]

For just as, if they flew upward, they would be one—that is, the body would pass into the nature of the soul, the heaviness of earthly matter would be abolished into the advancement and substance of the soul, and the body itself would become spiritual—so, when sold for the price of sins, the subtlety of the soul is made heavy into the nature of bodies, draws earthly matter from the filth of vices, and becomes that one of them which is delivered over to the earth.

> [Note: The Roman manuscript reads *avolaret* (“would fly away”), a reading not to be despised. Nor should Hilary be thought to assert the abolition of bodily matter. He means only that earthly heaviness and similar qualities, naturally belonging to bodies and burdensome and troublesome to souls, will be absent after the resurrection; so that resurrection of corruptible bodies into the glory of incorruption does not destroy nature by annihilation, but transforms it by a change of condition. For it is not a different body, though it rises into another condition, as he himself says in Psalm 2, §41. The preceding statements—that the body passes into the nature of the soul or is abolished into the substance of the soul—must therefore be understood otherwise than we usually understand them, as is clear also from what immediately follows: the soul of sinners is made heavy into the nature of bodies. Thus we may meanwhile moderate what is read below in §24, that baptism grants us that the body itself becomes the nature of the soul which comes from God’s breath.]

When He says that they stand before many sparrows, He shows that the election of believers is set above the multitude of unbelievers: for the latter fall to earth, while the former fly to heaven.

20. Hope of a better life removes fear of death.—To be gathered into a number is a matter of attentive and solicitous care; for it is not a worthy task to count what will perish. Therefore, that we might know that nothing of us will perish, since we are much better than sparrows, the very number of our hairs, which are counted, indicates that we shall remain wholly safe (ibid. 30–31), since what is innumerable in us is numbered by both the affection and the power of Him who preserves it.

> [Note: The Colbert manuscript, with the Chartres manuscript, reads “to be preserved.”]

Therefore no loss of our bodies is to be feared, nor should any grief at the destruction of flesh be admitted, since, dissolved according to the condition of its nature and origin, it is poured back into the substance of the spiritual soul.

21. And because those strengthened by such teachings ought to possess a free steadfastness in confessing God, He added also the condition by which we were bound: that He would deny before the Father in heaven the one who had denied Him before human beings on earth (ibid. 32); but that He would Himself confess in heaven the one who had confessed Him before human beings—so that whatever witnesses of His name we had been among human beings, by such testimony of His we should be upheld before God the Father.

22. Various questions are proposed.—“Do not think that I came to send peace upon the earth. I came not to send peace, but a sword. For I came to divide son against father, daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s household members shall be his enemies” (ibid. 34–36). What is this division? For among the first precepts of the Law we received: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:12). And the Lord Himself says: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave with you” (John 14:27). What is meant by the sword sent upon the earth, the son separated from his father, the daughter from her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man’s household members as enemies? Public authority will henceforth be brought forth for impiety.

> [Note: Three manuscripts read: “public authority will be extended for impiety.”]

Everywhere there will be hatreds, everywhere wars, and the Lord’s sword raging between father and son, and between daughter and mother. In Luke, indeed, this is said of the matter: “From this time there will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three” (Luke 12:52).

> [Note: All manuscripts consistently read “three against two”; then six of them likewise consistently read “and two against three.” The particles *in* and *super* are expressed in Greek by the same word, ἐπί (*epi*, “against/upon”).]

Can a household family not extend into a larger number of domestic relations? Or was it confined by a prescribed period, that from this point there should be only five in one house, and these divided? We must therefore consider what the sword upon earth is; what is the proper significance of the names; what the meaning of the number five; how three are to be divided against two and two against three; and in what sense a man’s household members are his enemies.

### 23. The Nature of the Sword: It Signifies the Word of God. Three Elements in Adam before Sin, Five in His Descendants

The nature both of each individual matter and of the entire question must first be explained; and both the preceding and the following sense will no less assist our understanding. The sword is the sharpest weapon of all weapons; in it reside the right of authority, the severity of judgment, and the punishment of sins. The prophets frequently attest that the preaching of the new Gospel is designated by the name of this weapon. Let us therefore remember that the word of God is called a sword: this sword was sent into the earth, that is, his preaching was infused into human bodies. [Note: Thus the manuscripts, except one suspicious Colbert manuscript, which reads: “infused into bodies or hearts.” Paris: “infused into hearts.” Hence: “his preaching infused into human hearts.” These words correspond to “sent into the earth.” Whenever Hilary finds “earth” in Scripture, however, he usually understands by it the body, which was taken from the earth; see chapter 4, no. 3; Tractate on Psalm 118, nos. 7, 8, 9; and many other places. But he nowhere interprets “earth” as the heart.]

This sword therefore divides the five dwelling in one house, and divides three against two and two against three. Yet we find only three things in a human being: body, soul, and will. For just as a soul was given to the body, so power to use themselves as it wished was granted to both; and for that reason a law was set before the will. [Note: Printed editions: “placed before.” Some manuscripts more suitably read “set before.” The law was set before the will for this purpose: he who had created us in the kindness of granting us the use of his blessedness established that we should advance toward it through the merit of an innocent and honorable life; see Psalm II, no. 16.]

But this is found in those who were first formed by God, in whom the effect of the arising original beginning existed, not something transmitted from elsewhere. But because of the sin and unbelief of the first parent, in succeeding generations sin began to be the father of our body and unbelief the mother of the soul; for from these we received our origin through the transgression of the first parent. [Note: Bad., Er., and four manuscripts read “death.” Other books more correctly read “origin,” namely, from sin and unbelief. Then: “for the will is likewise,” and “furthermore, the will.”] For each person’s own will is present beside him.

Thus there are now five in one house: sin, father of the body; unbelief, mother of the soul; and the added free choice of the will, which binds the whole person to itself by a certain marital right. [Note: Printed editions read “entering in”; some manuscripts, “advancing”; the better ones, “being added.” The will is added, so that sin, unbelief, body, and soul become five.] Unbelief is mother-in-law to this will, [Note: By omitting the relative “which,” the printed editions corrupt Hilary’s meaning. He intends that we, born from unbelief, are taken into a kind of marriage by the freedom of the will; thus unbelief is mother-in-law to the will.] which, receiving us as born from itself and estranged from faith and the fear of God, holds us possessed between unbelief and pleasure, [Note: Five manuscripts read “and will,” incorrectly. Earlier the corresponding terms are sin, later delight in vices, and here pleasure.] in ignorance of God and in delight in every vice.

### 24. The Effect of Regeneration: The Struggle against Desire in Those Regenerated

Therefore, when we are renewed by the washing of baptism through the power of the word, we are separated from the sins and authors of our origin; [Note: In Bad., Er., Lips., and several manuscripts, the word “word” is absent. It must be retained with Paris and the better manuscripts, as is clear from the immediate comparison with the sword. Paris alone then reads “and thus,” for “and cut off.”] and, cut off by a kind of severing sword of God, we are at variance with the attachments of father and mother. Putting off the old human being with its sins and unbelief, and renewed in soul and body through the Spirit, we must hate the habit of the innate and ancient work.

And because the body itself, mortified through faith, passes into the nature of the soul—which comes from the breath of God—although it still remains in its own material; and because through the word a fellowship between them is reconciled, it therefore begins to will one and the same thing with the soul. That is: since the soul is spiritual, the freedom of the will, divided from its mother-in-law—that is, from unbelief—cedes all its right to them, soul and body reconciled by the word; [Note: That is, to the soul and body, now reconciled through the word.] so that what had been the freedom of the will may henceforth be the power of the soul.

And a grievous dissension arises in the one house, and the members of his household will be enemies to the new human being. For the person divided from them by the word of God will rejoice to remain both inward and outward—that is, in the newness of the Spirit, both body and soul. But those things which are innate and derived from a certain antiquity of lineage desire to remain in those things in which they took delight. [Note: Four manuscripts read “undertaken”; “implanted” would not be displeasing. Here “innate,” as above, means inborn; this denotes unbelief and sin, or pleasure.]

The origin of flesh, the origin of soul, and freedom of power are divided against the two—namely, the soul and body of the new human being—which have begun to will one and the same thing. [Note: The Colbert manuscript reads “because [they are] one,” supported by several others reading “since [they are] one.” Soul, body, and will are now reduced to two because the will has yielded its own right to the soul. Then unbelief, sin, and will are divided from body and soul and subjected to them, since through the power of the Spirit soul and body rule and exercise dominion over them.] And the three, divided, will be subject to the two, who are stronger through the newness of the Spirit.

For this reason, those who have preferred the household affections denoted by these names [Note: That is, love of father, mother, and spouse; as already observed in chapter 4, no. 19, where, as also in Psalm 118, no. 3, matters understood literally are here explained spiritually.] to love of him will be unworthy of the inheritance of future goods.

### 25. The Cross, the Sacrament of Faith

He next continues in the same course of precepts and interpretation. For after commanding that all things most dear in the world must be left behind, he added: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:38), because those who belong to Christ have crucified the body with its vices and desires.

And one is unworthy of Christ who, unless he takes up his own cross—in which we suffer with him, abide with him, are buried with him, and rise with him—does not follow the Lord, so as to live in the newness of the Spirit in this sacrament of faith.

### 26. It Brings Death to Vices and Removes Fear of Death

“Whoever finds his life shall lose it; and whoever loses his life for my sake shall find it” (Matt. 10:39). By the power of the word and the division from former vices, gain to the soul will issue in death, and loss in salvation. [Note: Paris, following Lipsius, reads “dismissal,” less fittingly with the preceding context and contrary to the authority of the older books.]

Therefore death must be embraced in the newness of life, and vices must be nailed to the Lord’s cross. Against persecutors, through contempt for present things, the freedom of glorious confession must be preserved; the gain that harms the soul must be avoided. We know that no one retains any right over the soul, and that by the loss of a brief life, the interest of immortality is acquired.

### 27. Christ as Mediator

“Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (Matt. 10:40). He bestows upon all the affection of doctrine and the diligence of precepts. Having declared, by the testimony of shaken-off dust, the danger faced by those who do not receive the apostles, he commends to those who receive them a reward surpassing the grace of hoped-for service. [Note: The Bec manuscript reads “of prepared service.” By this manner of speaking, he understands hoped-for grace as service.]

He also teaches his office as mediator: when he has been received by us, and since he has proceeded from God, God is poured through him into us. [Note: Although “in us” occurs in many manuscripts, “into us” must be retained, as is clear from chapter 12, no. 12, where the same office of mediator is explained on the same principle.] Thus whoever receives the apostles receives Christ; whoever receives Christ receives God the Father. For one receives in the apostles nothing other than what is in Christ, nor is there in Christ anything other than what is in God. Through this order of graces, therefore, to have received the apostles is nothing other than to have received God, because Christ dwells in them and God in Christ.

### 28. Many Occasions for Attaining Eternity

“Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. 10:41). Whoever receives a prophet receives the one dwelling in the prophet; and, receiving a prophet in the prophet’s name, becomes worthy of a prophet’s reward. Likewise, a reward is reckoned for receiving a righteous person, and one becomes righteous through the honor paid to righteousness.

Thus righteousness is completed through faith and service gains its reward. God gives many occasions for attaining eternity, since, in receiving a righteous person and a prophet, the very disposition of reverence receives both the honor of the righteous person and that of the prophet.

### 29. Service Rendered to an Unworthy Person under the Appearance of Religion Is Not Deprived of Its Reward

“And whoever gives to one of these little ones only a cup of cold water to drink,” and the rest (Matt. 10:42). He taught that the work of a good conscience is not empty, nor does the hope of faith suffer because of another’s unbelief. For he foresaw that many would be glorious only in the name of apostleship, while reprehensible in every work of their lives; that they would deceive and lie for a long time. Yet he does not deprive of the reward of its deed and hope the service rendered to such persons under the appearance of religion.

For even if they themselves were least—that is, the last of all sinners, for the least of all is that below which there is nothing else—he nevertheless determines that even slight acts of service toward them, represented by the cup of cold water, are not empty. Honor is paid not to the human being’s sins, but to the name of disciple. Thus the integrity of the one rendering service is not harmed by the disgrace of the one who deceives concerning himself, since the former obtains his reward through the faith of the giver, not through the falsehood of the one who receives.

## CHAPTER XI. John Sends from Prison to Jesus, and Jesus Speaks to the Crowds concerning John. Likewise, Jesus’ Confession to the Father

### 1. John Did Not Fail to Know Christ

When John had heard in prison of Christ’s works, he sent his disciples to him and said: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect another?” (Matt. 11:2–3). Did John, held in prison, not know the Lord? Did so great a prophet not know his God? On the contrary, he announced him as coming, as the forerunner; he recognized him as present, as a prophet; he revered him as approaching, as a confessor. [Note: Vatican and Bec manuscripts: “in chains.”]

Whence had error crept into knowledge so varied and so abundant? But the Lord’s subsequent testimony concerning him does not allow this to be understood so. Nor can it reasonably be believed that, when John was placed in prison, the glory of the Holy Spirit failed him, since that Spirit was to furnish to the apostles, when they were placed in prison, the light of his power.

### 2. He Was a Figure of the Law: The Work of the Law, and Why John Sent to Christ

But in what was done to John a fuller interpretation is offered, and, together with the efficacy of the event, the grace expressed in him is perceived: the prophet himself, by the very kind of his condition, prophesied, because in him the form of the Law was set forth. For the Law announced Christ, preached forgiveness of sins, and promised the kingdom of heaven; and John fulfilled this whole work of the Law.

Therefore, now that the Law had ceased—the Law which was enclosed by the sins of the people and bound by the people’s vices, so that Christ could not be understood, being held in chains and prison—[Note: That is, hidden because of the people’s sins, or concealed from the people’s unbelief, according to Prologue to the Psalms, no. 5: “All prophecies are shut up and sealed against worldly understanding and the wisdom of the age.”] the Law sends to behold the Gospels, so that unbelief may contemplate in deeds the faithfulness of its sayings; and so that what within it is bound by the deceit of sins may be released through the understanding of evangelical freedom. [Note: Four manuscripts read “washed away,” which must by no means be followed. Compare the cited Prologue, no. 6: Christ alone releases, through the sacrament of his embodiment and divinity, the seals by which the closed book is bound. Shortly afterward: “By believing the things fulfilled through him, all those things which are sealed and closed will be opened and released.”]

Thus, by John’s example, he provides not for his own ignorance but for that of his disciples. For he himself preached the one who was to come for the forgiveness of sins. But, so that they might know that he had proclaimed no other, he sent his disciples to observe Christ’s works, that they might compare his works with the authority of his words and that no Christ other than the one whose works bore testimony to him might be expected.

### 3. Christ Foretells the Scandal of the Cross

When the Lord had revealed himself wholly through the miracles of his deeds—by sight for the blind, movement for the lame, healing for lepers, hearing for the deaf, speech for the mute, life for the dead, and preaching to the poor—he said: “Blessed is anyone who is not scandalized in me” (Matt. 11:6). [Note: Paris alone reads “walking” for “movement.” To be consistent, it would have needed to change no. 10 above: “the lame run about.”]

Had anything yet occurred in Christ that might scandalize John? Certainly not. For he was still engaged in the course of his teaching and work. But the force and exact meaning of the preceding statement must be considered: what it means that good news is proclaimed to the poor—that is, those who have lost their lives, taken up their crosses, and follow; those who become poor in spirit, for whom a kingdom is prepared in heaven.

Therefore, because this whole array of sufferings would be fulfilled in the Lord, and because his coming cross would be a scandal to many, he pronounced blessed those whose faith would receive no temptation from the cross, death, and burial. Thus he showed the danger against which John had guarded, saying that blessed were those for whom there would be no cause of scandal in him. [Note: The word *rei*, “thing,” is absent from the Colbert and Carnot manuscripts. It denotes the scandal of the cross, which John feared for his disciples.] For through fear of this John had sent his disciples to hear and see Christ.

### 4. What the Reed Signifies

And lest this be referred to John, as though he had been scandalized by something in Christ, after they had departed he spoke to the crowds concerning him: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. 11:7). [Note: Paris here and below reads “moved by the wind,” against the other books.]

The wilderness is to be understood as empty of the Holy Spirit, where there is no dwelling of God. In the reed is displayed a person who, through the vanity of his life, is showy in worldly glory but hollow within, lacking the fruit of truth; pleasing outwardly but inwardly nothing; liable to be moved by every motion of the winds—that is, by the breath of unclean spirits—unable to stand firm, and empty in the very marrow of the mind. [Note: It had occurred to us that the reading should be: “a person puffed up by worldly glory is shown,” etc. But nothing should be altered, since the word *talis*, “such,” indicates a person like a reed.]

Therefore, when he says, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” he means: “Did you go out to see a person empty of the knowledge of God and wandering at the breath of unclean spirits?” For he speaks this more with the tone of rebuke than of confirmation, showing that in John one does not see someone empty and unstable.

### 5. Bodies Dissolved by Luxury Are Houses of Demons

“But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11:8). [Note: Paris reads “garment,” and then, after Lipsius, “the covering of the body,” against the manuscripts, some of which subsequently read “with which one is clothed.” The body, in which the soul is surrounded and girded as by a garment, may appropriately be understood as the soul’s clothing.]

The garment signifies the covering of the body in which the soul is clothed, a body softened by luxury and sensual indulgence. But those clothed in soft garments are in kings’ houses. “Kings” is the designation of transgressing angels; for they are the powers of this age and rulers of the world.

Therefore, those clothed in soft garments are in kings’ houses: that is, people whose bodies have become loose and undisciplined through luxury are a dwelling-place of demons, who choose a habitation suited to their purposes and deeds. [Note: “It signifies” is here omitted. The preceding words, “are in kings’ houses,” are to be taken passively, meaning those frequented by kings and constituting their houses, not those who frequent royal residences.]

### 6. John’s Glory

“But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet,” and so forth (Matt. 11:9 ff.). The Lord displays all John’s glory, declaring him more than a prophet because he alone was permitted both to prophesy Christ and to see him.

How, then, can he be thought ignorant of Christ, when he was sent under an angel’s power to prepare the way for the coming one, and when no greater prophet has arisen among those born of women, unless the one who is less than he—that is, the one questioned, the one not believed, the one to whom not even his own works bear testimony—is greater in the kingdom of heaven? [Note: Printed editions, with fewer manuscripts, read “arose.” Paris alone reads: “except that the lesser one who is questioned”; and later, with three manuscripts, “will be greater,” rather than “is greater.” As Chrysostom explains in Homily XI, Christ is understood as lesser in age and in many persons’ opinion.]

### 7. The Gentiles Seize the Kingdom of Heaven from the Jews

“From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use violence seize it” (Matt. 11:12). As the nature of things requires, the stronger inflicts violence; and the one upon whom violence is inflicted is weaker. We must therefore consider what it is that seizes and what it is that suffers violence.

The Lord had observed the unbelief of John’s disciples; he had also understood the crowd’s opinion about John’s message; he perceived a great danger to faith in the scandal of the cross. He had commanded the apostles to go rather to the lost sheep of Israel: they ought to have been established in the kingdom and retained in the family and recognition of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. [Note: The Bec manuscript reads “to the lost sheep of the house of Israel he had commanded [them to go].” Then, with five others, it reads “they themselves immediately,” rather than “them to be established”; this less suitably refers “themselves” to the apostles rather than the Jews. Bad., Er., and Lips. read “and nation”; Paris, “and recognition,” which the manuscripts also have, except that in the Carnot manuscript “and kinship” was restored on second revision. The manuscripts agree in the same error in chapter 10, no. 22.]

But all this preaching brought advancement to tax collectors and sinners. From them came believers, from them apostles, and from them—Matthew, for example—the kingdom of heaven. Conversely, the people do not believe John; Christ’s works do not obtain authority; the future cross was to be a scandal. Prophecy has now ceased, the Law has now been fulfilled, all preaching has now been enclosed, and Elijah’s spirit is sent ahead in John’s voice.

Christ is preached to some and recognized by others; born for some and loved by others. His own reject him; strangers receive him. His own people persecute him; enemies embrace him. Adoption claims the inheritance; the family rejects it. Sons repudiate the testament; servants acknowledge it. [Note: Roman, Colbert, and Carnot manuscripts: “His own reject him; strangers receive him.”] Thus the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those bringing violence seize it: because the glory of Israel, owed from the fathers, proclaimed by the prophets, and offered by Christ, is occupied and seized by the faith of the Gentiles. [Note: We restore the preposition *a*, “from,” which Lipsius wrongly deleted, from Bad., Er., and the manuscripts. Moreover, *Israel* is expressed in the dative; therefore “from the fathers” means “by the name and right of promises made to the fathers,” according to Romans 11:28: “beloved for the sake of the fathers.”]

### 8. The Jews, Rejected by Law and Gospel, Have Fallen Away

“To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another,” and so forth (Matt. 11:16). This entire discourse is a reproach for unbelief and proceeds from the feeling of the preceding complaint, because the insolent people were not instructed by the varied forms of preaching. By “children” he means the prophets, who in the midst of the synagogue—as in the public gathering-place of the marketplace—rebuke the people because they did not respond with bodily action when they sang to them; that is, because they did not obey their words. For movements of dancers are adapted to the rhythm of singers. [Note: Three manuscripts of good authority read “rhythm.”]

In the simplicity of their understanding, like children, they preached and summoned them to confess God by singing psalms, as is required by the song of Moses, by Isaiah, David, and the other prophets. Again, neither John’s preaching moved them to repentance for sins and to sorrow and mourning for former offenses. [Note: Here and below, “they rebuke because” must be supplied. Paris reads “and cleansing of former [sins],” etc. One Colbert manuscript, with the Carnot manuscript, reads “and cleansed by sorrow from former [sins],” etc. We restore the reading of Bad., Er., and Lips., found in most manuscripts.]

For the Law seemed to them burdensome, difficult, and troublesome because of prescribed food and drink; it had sin within itself, which he calls a demon (Matt. 11:18), because the difficulty of its observance made it necessary for them to sin within the Law. [Note: Some manuscripts read “prescribed foods and drinks.” We would then prefer “they call [it] a demon.” A little later printed editions read “to sin against the Law,” against the manuscripts. These remarks illuminate: “John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’” Under John’s name this is understood as said concerning the Law.]

Again, the Gospel’s preaching in Christ did not please them because of its freedom of life, through which the difficulties and burdens of the Law were relaxed and tax collectors and sinners had now believed (Matt. 11:19). Thus, after so many and such great forms of admonition had been employed in vain, they are neither justified by grace nor rejected by the Law.

### 9. They Were Justly Rejected: Christ Is Wisdom Itself, Not Merely Wisdom’s Work

“And Wisdom has been justified by her children”: namely, by those who, doing violence to the kingdom of heaven, seize it by the justification of faith itself, confessing that Wisdom’s work is just because it transferred its gift from obstinate and unbelieving persons to faithful and obedient ones.

It is not idle to consider here the force of the saying. “And Wisdom has been justified”: he plainly spoke of himself. For he is Wisdom not by effects, but by nature; for he possesses the power of every reality. Every operation, however, is an effect of power; and the work of power is not the same as power itself, while an efficient cause differs from its effect.

Many habitually evade the apostolic statement in which he calls Christ “the wisdom of God and the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:24) in this way: they say that in his creation from the virgin there existed an effective wisdom and power of God, and that in his birth the work of divine wisdom and power is to be understood; thus, they hold that in him there is efficacy rather than the nature of wisdom. [Note: Leontius, *On Sects*, act 3, attributes this very opinion to Paul of Samosata: “Paul of Samosata did not say that God’s Word subsisting in itself was in Christ; rather, he wished the Word to be a certain command and injunction—that is, as he himself said, God commanded that what he willed should be done through that man, and did it through him.”]

Lest anything of this kind be understood, he called himself Wisdom, showing in himself Wisdom itself, not merely what belongs to it. For faith, hope, love, chastity, fasting, self-control, humility, and kindness are works of Wisdom; [Note: The Carnot manuscript, with Colbert, reads “prudence, fasting.” Hilary seems here to have in view Galatians 5:22–23, where Paul lists the fruits of the Spirit, and thus treats the names Wisdom and Spirit as referring to one and the same reality, although he mentions other things and not all those named by Paul.] but these are works of its nature, not nature itself. The reality which acts does not consist in the things it makes. [Note: One Colbert manuscript lacks the end of this section. Here Lipsius substituted “when” for “why,” and Paris retained it, against the other books. The following proposition is omitted here: “If the reality which acts does not consist in the things it makes.” From it this follows most aptly: Why does the apostle attribute the name of the efficient cause to the thing effected?]

Why, then, did the apostle call Christ “God’s power and God’s wisdom”? Because from that Wisdom which he was, created wisdom came into being?

### 10. How Guilty the Jews’ Unbelief Was

“Woe to you, Chorazin and Bethsaida! For if the miracles done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon,” and so forth (Matt. 11:21). The curse of disobedience is determined together with the blessing of obedience. For the Jews ought first to have received the preaching; but the privilege of preaching increases the odium of their unbelief when they are reproved by the example of believers, to whom, without any displayed wonder of deeds, all salvation belongs through faith.

For in Bethsaida and Capernaum the mute praise the Lord, the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame run about, and the dead have perception; yet no wonder at such great events moved anyone to the willingness of faith, although the mere report of these deeds ought to have summoned them to fear and carried them away to faith. [Note: Printed editions read “none”; four manuscripts more correctly read “no one.” Six others read “no willingness of faith,” and “no one toward willingness of faith” would not be displeasing: that is, no one was moved to obey faith even after seeing so many and such great miracles, though they should have believed merely by hearing of them. The Silva Major manuscript reads “to the physician,” also found in the Michaelinus manuscript in a second hand. The first reading is truer. Thus in chapter 10, no. 23, people alienated from God through original sin are called estranged from faith and fear of God. Throughout Hilary, the fear of God is the same as the worship, religion, and love of God.]

But not Tyre and Sidon alone: even Sodom and Gomorrah will make their sins seem light, because perhaps they would have had a disposition to believe if the sight of such miracles had been granted them.

### 11. Christ’s Joy over the Faith of the Gentiles

“At that time Jesus answered and said: ‘I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones,’” and so forth (Matt. 11:25). Such a confession is fittingly joined to what was said above. For although Israel’s salvation was desirable, the faith of the Gentiles, preached of old, was not outside the Lord’s joy.

For the mysteries and powers of heavenly words are hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones: little ones in malice, not in understanding; but wise in the presumption of their folly, not by reason of true prudence. The Lord confirms the justice of this act by the judgment of the Father’s will (Matt. 11:26): those who disdain to become little ones in God may thereafter become fools in their own wisdom.

### 12. The Father and Son Are of One Substance

And lest anything in him be thought less than what is in God, he says that all things have been handed over to him by the Father; that he alone is known to the Father, and the Father to him alone, or to whomever he has wished to reveal him (Matt. 11:27)—revealing him to the person by whom he is asked that he may wish to reveal him.

Through this revelation he teaches that both possess the same substance in their mutual knowledge, since whoever knows the Son will also know the Father in the Son, because all things have been handed over to him by the Father. But the things handed over are none other than those which are known only to the Father in the Son. And those things which belong to the Father are known only to the Son. [Note: The word “only” is absent from most manuscripts. Then “to be” refers to the preceding verb “teaches.”]

Thus, in this secret of mutual knowledge, it is understood that nothing existed in the Son other than what is unknowable in the Father.

### 13. Why Christ’s Yoke Is Sweet

He then calls to himself those burdened by the difficulties of the Law and weighed down by the sins of the world (Matt. 11:28). He promises to remove their labor and burden, provided only that they take up his yoke—that is, receive the commands of his precepts and approach him through the sacrament of the cross. For he is humble and gentle in heart, and they will find rest in their souls (Matt. 11:29).

He offers the attractions of a sweet yoke and light burden, so that he may grant believers knowledge of his goodness, which he alone knows in the Father. What is sweeter than his yoke, or lighter than his burden? To become approved; to abstain from crime; to will what is good and refuse what is evil; to love everyone and hate no one; to attain eternal things without being captured by present things; and not to wish to inflict upon another what one finds painful to suffer oneself.

## CHAPTER XII. The Disciples Pluck Ears of Grain. Jesus Heals the Man with a Withered Hand on the Sabbath. He Heals a Blind and Demoniac Man. On Blasphemy against the Spirit; on the Fruit of the Good and Bad Tree; on Every Idle Word; on the Ninevites and the Queen of the South; on Seven Spirits and an Eighth; on the Mother and Brothers of Jesus

### 1. Christ’s Deeds Foreshadow Something Else

“At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the sabbath; and his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat” (Matt. 12:1). His going out into the grainfield, the sabbath day, the disciples’ hunger, the plucking of ears, the Pharisees’ accusation, and the Lord’s reply all possess—as do the other matters—a meaning underlying the inward cause.

For, as we have said, all realities of deeds attain, in the very results of events, an image resembling and intelligible from themselves of the future reality.

### 2. The Faith of the Gentiles and the Unbelief of the Jews Are Foretold

At the outset, it must be observed that this discourse begins thus: “At that time Jesus went through the grainfields”—that is, at the time when he gave thanks to God the Father for salvation granted to the Gentiles—so that one meaning might encompass both what precedes and what follows.

Let us therefore proceed through the remainder. The field is the world; [Note: Colbert and Carnot manuscripts read “on sabbaths.”] the sabbath is rest; the grainfield is the growing crop of those who will believe, destined for harvest. Therefore, when he goes into the field on the sabbath, the Lord’s advance into this world occurs in the rest of the Law, as he visits that grainfield—that is, the sowing of the human race.

And since hunger is a hunger for human salvation, the disciples hasten to pluck and gather ears of grain—that is, to satisfy themselves with the salvation of the saints. For an ear of grain is not fitting food for a human being, nor is eating plucked heads of grain useful; but the outward appearance of the deed unfolds faith in the future, and the force enclosed in the words discloses the mystery both of hunger and of satisfaction.

### 3. The Pharisees, who thought that the key of heaven belonged to them, accuse the disciples of doing what is unlawful (Matt. 12:2). The Lord reminded them of the deed of David, in which, under the factual event, the meaning of prophecy is contained: David, hungry together with those who were with him, was filled with unlawful bread (Matt. 12:3). [Note: The same manuscripts, together with the Roman and Vatican manuscripts, read “had been an example.”]

For if it had not been lawful to do this, David would not have been believed to have done it without guilt. Rather, a prophet prophesies in the Law through deeds performed without the expiation of guilt: he himself, together with the others, was filled with the loaves of the Presence, thereby showing that Christ with the apostles would be satisfied by the salvation of the Gentiles, although this would seem unlawful to the Jews. [Note: Paris, with the four manuscripts mentioned, reads “understand the deeds of the prophet.”]

### 4. He Also Reminds Them of Another Prophecy, so that they might recognize that everything previously said in the Law was being fulfilled in him: that priests in the temple violate the sabbath without guilt (Matt. 12:5). [Note: Printed editions and most manuscripts read “violate.” Colbert and Carnot more suitably read “to violate”; supply the verb “he reminds,” to which the construction subsequently refers.]

He indicates, of course, that he himself is the temple, in which salvation is given to the Gentiles through apostolic teaching while the people of the Law rest in unbelief. [Note: Six manuscripts read “praying,” which must not be followed.] For he is greater than the sabbath, and evangelical faith works in Christ without the guilt of violating the Law.

### 5. When the Law Has Ceased, We Are Saved by God’s Goodness

And, to show that the entire effectiveness of events contains this image of the future work, he added: “If you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned the innocent” (Matt. 12:7).

The work of our salvation lies not in sacrifice but in mercy; and, when the Law has ceased, we are saved by God’s goodness. Had they understood the gift of this matter, they would never have condemned the innocent—that is, the apostles—whom they were going to accuse with the charge of transgressing the Law, while the antiquity of sacrifices was ceasing and the newness of mercy was coming to the aid of all through them. Nor would they have supposed that the Lord of the sabbath was confined by the prescription of the sabbath.

These things were spoken and done in the field.

6. Healing of the man with the withered hand. — After this, on entering the synagogue, they brought him a man with a withered hand, asking [Col. 0986A] whether it was lawful to heal on the sabbath (ibid., 9), seeking from his answer an occasion to accuse him. He refuted them by the example of a sheep falling into a pit, which they are concerned to draw out on the sabbath without blame [Note: [Col. 0985D] In the vulgate editions: “are accustomed.” That the manuscript reading “are concerned” is to be preferred is suggested by what follows: “concern for the sheep.” Then, in the Carnotensis and Colbertinus, and more commonly—but not more correctly—another reading.], (ibid., 11); and showed that it was more right to heal a human being, who is superior to a sheep. Nor should the sabbath be thought capable of being violated by the ministry of human salvation, when concern to draw a sheep from a pit does not violate it.

7. He signifies those to whom Christ gave the power of works. — Such a healing by the Lord appropriately follows. For, after his return from the grainfield, from which the apostles had already received the fruit of the sowing, he came to the synagogue, intending to prepare workers there also for his harvest—those who later became many, together with the apostles. Thus these [Note: [Col. 0986D] The printed editions read “are healed.” They are corrected from the better manuscripts: “in the withered man,” etc.] are healed in the man with the withered hand. For they lacked the capacity [Col. 0986B] for giving salvation; the office of the hand was inactive, and the bodily ministry by which something is done and [Note: [Col. 0986D] Bad. and Erasmus read “is commanded.” Shortly afterward Lipsius and Paris read “when he commanded,” instead of “he commanded him.” A little later three manuscripts read “into the ministry of the apostles.” Other books more correctly have “by the ministry,” in the ablative, after “giving.”] bestowed had withered away. Therefore the Lord commanded him to stretch out his hand, and it was restored to him like the other one (ibid., 13). Every healing lies in the word; and the hand is restored like the other—that is, it is made like the ministry of the apostles for the task of giving salvation. He teaches the Pharisees that they ought not to resent [Note: [Col. 0986D] In Paris, “healings on the sabbath” is inserted here; it also occurs in the Roman, Colbertine, and Carnotensis manuscripts, but does not appear relevant to the sense.] the work of human salvation in the apostles, since their own hand must be refashioned for the ministry of the same office, if they believe.

8. But envy at the deed moves the Pharisees, and they take counsel against him (ibid., 14), because, seeing the man in his body, they did not understand God in his works. Knowing their counsels, he withdrew (ibid., 15), so that he might be known to remain far away from the counsels of the malicious. [Col. 0986C] And great crowds followed him: as he withdrew from unbelievers, the company of believers attended him.

9. Why Christ commands those healed to be silent about him. — But he commanded silence to those whom he healed (ibid., 16). Was silence concerning the healing then being commanded? Certainly not; for the salvation restored to each person was itself its own witness. Rather, by commanding secrecy, he avoids boastful self-display, yet nevertheless makes himself known precisely when he orders silence concerning himself; for the observance of silence arises from the matter that is to be kept silent.

10. He shall not break the bruised reed; he shall not quench the smoking flax. — Indeed, by this wish that there be silence concerning him, the fulfillment of the words spoken through Isaiah is accomplished [Col. 0986D] (ibid., 17; Isa. 42:1 ff.). From that prophecy we now note only this: that he is beloved of God; that in him is the Father’s well-pleasing will; that the Spirit of God is upon him; that judgment is proclaimed by him to the nations; that the bruised reed [Col. 0987A] is not broken, nor the smoking flax quenched. That is, the frail and shaken bodies of the nations were not crushed, but rather preserved for salvation; nor was the small flame now only smoking in the flax quenched—[Note: [Col. 0987D] The printed editions read: “the small Israel from Zion and from the remnant.” They are corrected from four manuscripts, where Hilary interprets the unquenched small flame as the small spirit of the old grace not removed from Israel.] the small remnant of Israel, the spirit of the old grace, was not taken away—because at the time of repentance there is an opportunity to recover the whole light. But this is prescribed within the limits of a fixed time, until, when he brings forth judgment unto victory (Matt. 12:20), having removed the power of death, he introduces the judgment of his splendor by his return, for the nations who shall believe in his name through faith.

11. Healing of the demoniac, blind and mute: the salvation of the nations. — “Then a man possessed by a demon, blind and mute, was brought to him,” and the rest (ibid., 22). The fitting healing of the demoniac, [Col. 0987B] blind, and mute follows. For it is not without reason that, after saying in general that all the crowds had been healed, he now has brought before him from without a man possessed by a demon, blind and mute: the same sequence of interpretation is thereby to be followed without any ambiguity. The Pharisees accused the apostles of plucking ears of grain—that is, of gathering in the people of the world; mercy was being proclaimed above sacrifice; a man with a withered hand was brought into the synagogue and healed. Yet these things not only accomplish nothing toward Israel’s conversion, but the Pharisees even take counsel for murder. It was therefore necessary that after these things the salvation of the nations should be accomplished in the figure of this one man: so that he who was the dwelling-place of a demon, and blind and mute, might be made capable of God; might behold God in Christ; and might praise Christ’s works by confessing God. The crowds were astonished at the work of this deed [Col. 0987C]; but the Pharisees’ envy grows heavier. Since his works so greatly surpassed human weakness, they avoided the shame of confession by the greater crime of unbelief: because they could not judge these works to be those of a man, they refused to confess them to be God’s, and said that all this power over demons came to him from Beelzebub, prince of demons (ibid., 24).

12. How rich is the Word of God. — But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste” (ibid., 25). The Word of God is rich; when set forth as an argument for understanding, it supplies an abundant store of examples from itself. Whether understood simply or examined inwardly, it is necessary for every advance. But leaving aside those matters open to common [Col. 0987D] understanding, let us dwell upon the inward reasons.

13. The loss of Israel’s kingdom foretold. — “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste.” In answering what had been said about Beelzebub, he turned the force of his answer back upon those very persons [Col. 0988A] to whom he replied. For the Law is from God; the promise of Israel’s kingdom is from the Law; and Christ’s birth and coming are from the Law. If the kingdom of the Law is divided against itself, it must be destroyed [Note: [Col. 0987D] The better manuscripts read: “must necessarily be laid waste,” perhaps more authentically. We have already encountered this manner of expression in Psalm 118, no. 7: “must necessarily be believed”; and where Psalm 121, no. 1, has “must necessarily be proclaimed,” the manuscripts have “will necessarily proclaim.”]. All power is weakened by division, and the strength of a kingdom, divided against itself, is consumed. Thus Israel lost its kingdom from the Law when the people of the Law attacked the fulfillment of the Law in Christ.

14. The destruction of Jerusalem. — “And a city or house divided against itself shall not stand” (ibid.). The same principle applies to a house and a city as to a kingdom. But the city indicated here is Jerusalem, [Note: [Col. 0987D] In several manuscripts: “is said.” Shortly afterward, the Beccensis and Romanus read “the people grew furious.” The word “grew furious” must be referred to Jerusalem.] always glorious through dominion over the nations. Now, after it had grown furious in the rage of its people against its Lord, and had driven out his apostles together with the crowds of believers [Col. 0988B], it shall not stand because of the division caused by those departing from it. And so the destruction of that city, which soon afterward followed through this division, is foretold.

15. Christ casts out demons by divine power. — “If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself” (ibid., 26). By the very form of their words, in which they said that he acted in Beelzebub, he condemns the malice of their earlier statement. They did not understand that they had confessed Beelzebub to be divided; and if he was compelled to his own division, so that one demon might drive out demons and division itself stand against him, it must also be judged from this that greater power resides in him who divided than in those who were divided. Therefore he is already divided, compelled to act against himself, and his kingdom has been destroyed by such division. [Col. 0988C] But if Christ casts out demons by the power of Beelzebub, by whose name do their sons—that is, the apostles—cast them out (ibid., 27)? For this reason they are rightly appointed judges over them: Christ will be found to have given them power against demons which he himself is denied to possess. Therefore, if the disciples work in Christ, and Christ works by the Spirit of God, the kingdom of God is present, already transmitted to the apostles through the office of the Mediator. [Note: [Col. 0988D] The word “Spirit” denotes the divine nature manifested in Christ’s works, not the third person of the Trinity. Hilary’s reasoning is as follows: if God is in Christ, as his divine works prove, and Christ is in the apostles who work by his power, then the kingdom of God has already been transferred to them through Christ as mediator.] But when Christ is accused of acting through Beelzebub, God is blasphemed in Christ; and so, in the name of Beelzebub, the Pharisees commit an inexpiable outrage of abuse against God.

16. “How can anyone enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods?” and the rest (ibid., 29). He declares that in the first temptation he had crushed all the devil’s power, [Col. 0988D] because no one can enter the strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he has first bound the strong man; then he will plunder his house. And the one doing this must necessarily be stronger than that strong man. Therefore he was bound when Satan, being named by the Lord, was constrained by the very designation of his wickedness [Col. 0989A] (Matt. 4:10). Having bound him thus, Christ stripped him of his spoils and took away his house: that is, he brought us, once his weapons and soldiers of his kingdom, back under his own rightful authority; and, after overcoming and binding him, made from us a house empty for himself and fit for use. He also shows that he is far from having borrowed any power from him, since whoever is not with him is against him, and whoever does not gather with him scatters (Matt. 12:30). From this we understand that it is exceedingly perilous to think wrongly of him with whom not to be is itself to be against him; and not to gather is to scatter.

17. Blasphemy against the Spirit: denying to Christ the divinity which his works disclose. — “Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven to men; but blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven” (ibid., 31). [Note: [Col. 0989C] Only the Paris edition reads “blasphemy shall not be forgiven.” Then also the other editions read “the opinion of the Pharisees.”] He condemns, by a most severe definition, the judgment of the Pharisees [Col. 0989B] and the perversity of those who think with them: promising pardon for every sin, yet denying indulgence for blasphemy against the Spirit (ibid., 32). For while all other words and deeds are remitted by generous pardon, there is no mercy if God is denied in Christ. And concerning the sinner who is without pardon [Note: [Col. 0989C] Lipsius and Paris read “sins”; Bad. and Erasmus, with all the manuscripts, read “sinner”—supply “is.”], he gives the kindly warning a second time: sins of every kind are altogether to be forgiven, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is not to be forgiven. For what is so far beyond pardon as [Note: [Col. 0989C] The Carnotensis manuscript reads “to deny Christ,” without *in*; the Colbertinus and Romanus, “to deny Christ.” Then Mich., Vind., the other Colbertinus, Turonensis, Beccensis, and Silv., with Bad. and Erasmus, read “that he is of God.” The reading of the other books, “that he is God,” is preferable. Why it is without pardon to deny Christ to be God, Athanasius, in Letter IV to Serapion—whence a treatise on this same passage was detached and printed separately on p. 970, vol. I of the Paris edition of 1627—gives this reason at the end: “For one who denies the Son, whom can he entreat in order to find propitiation? Or what life or restoration can he expect, when he rejects him who says, ‘I am life’?” In that place Athanasius explains clearly why blasphemy against the Holy Spirit here means blasphemy against Christ’s divinity. Neither Hilary nor Athanasius, however, holds that all who have denied Christ’s divinity lack pardon, but those who have denied a divinity proved and known to them by his works. For, as Athanasius says, by these words Christ shows that the Pharisees fastened themselves upon this inescapable blasphemy not through ignorance but willingly, and were restrained by no shame, though they knew that works of this kind were God’s and, like madmen, attributed them to Beelzebub, asserting that they were done through an unclean spirit. In agreement with this, our Hilary affirms that they are beyond pardon because they take away the substance of the paternal nature, even though Christ accomplishes every work in the Spirit of God—that is, in the very power and nature of divinity. Moreover, the author who, in Athanasius, assembled testimonies to the common essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, interpreting blasphemy against the Holy Spirit on no other ground, observes that Christ did not say that forgiveness is not to be given to one who blasphemes and repents, but to one who blasphemes and remains in blasphemy. It is probable that Hilary held no other view, since below, chapter 18, no. 10, we read that God grants us pardon for absolutely every sin, [Col. 0990D] and in fact granted it to those who not only denied Christ to be God, but even killed him or caused his death; pardon was not delayed when they returned to him through faith.] to deny in Christ that he is God, and to take away from him the substance of the Father’s Spirit which abides in him—when he accomplishes every work in the Spirit of God, is himself the kingdom of heaven, and in him God is reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19)? Therefore every reproach [Col. 0989C] directed against Christ is directed wholly against God, because God is in Christ and Christ is in God.

18. Against the Jews and Arians. Those who worship Christ but deny that he is God are worse than those who do not know him. — “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad,” and the rest [Col. 0990A] (Matt. 12:33). The saying has force both for the present and for the future. In the present it refutes the Jews, who, although they understood that Christ’s works exceeded human power, nevertheless refused to confess that they were God’s. For the future it rebukes every perversion of faith: namely, those who, taking from the Lord his divinity and communion in the Father’s substance, have burned with various heretical zeal. [Note: [Col. 0990D] The Carnotensis and Colbertinus manuscripts read “dignity”; and shortly afterward “engaging in,” instead of “dwelling in.”] They do neither: they neither dwell among the nations under the pardon accorded to ignorance nor remain in the knowledge of truth. By the tree he signifies himself as existing in the body, because by the inward fruitfulness of his power every abundance comes forth into fruit. Therefore either the tree must be made good with good fruits, or established as bad with bad fruits; for the tree itself will bear witness concerning itself from its fruits. This is not because, according to the nature of trees, a bad tree which is good can be made, or because that same tree can be good with its branches if it is bad. Rather, through this figure we are to understand that Christ must either be left as useless or retained as good through the usefulness of good fruits. For words spoken against the Son of Man receive pardon, whereas blasphemy against the Spirit lacks pardon. But to adopt an intermediate position, to give Christ some honor while denying what is greatest, to venerate him as God while stripping him of communion with God—this is blasphemy against the Spirit.
