Thus, although awe at such great works prevents you from daring to withhold the name of God, you nevertheless, through malevolence of mind and judgment, cut away his nobility—which you are compelled to confess in his name—by denying his communion in the Father’s substance. [Note: [Col. 0990D] Six manuscripts read “in man”: wrongly. Here the Arians are refuted, who denied Christ the nature of God while according him the divine name and worship.] [Col. 0990C] Therefore the Lord also extends to this case the gift of his goodness, saying that either a bad tree with bad fruits or a good tree with good fruits must be made. For in the judgment that the tree is bad, while its goodness remains hidden [Note: [Col. 0990D] That is, so long as his goodness is hidden and concealed from us.], the pardon of God’s indulgence is reserved—because every [Note: [Col. 0990D] The printed editions, with one Colbertine manuscript, read “because every.” Then only the Paris edition, with the same manuscript, has “in good confession”; the Beccensis manuscript has “in the confession, that is, of the good tree,” which would suitably have a place in the margin to clarify the text, with “and” prefixed before “in good.”] sin is to be forgiven. But in confession that the tree is good there is eternal fruit, lest, advancing [perhaps: “falling”] [Col. 0991A] upon a position midway between the two judgments—when we do not dare to declare it bad but refuse to confess it good—we be left under the irreversible judgment of our corrupted opinion concerning it.

19. He taught that every corruption of such thinking arises from a defect of nature, saying that from an evil treasury only evil things can be brought forth, and that an account must be rendered to God for every idle—that is, foolish and useless—word (Matt. 12:35). For by the words of our confession we shall either be condemned or justified, receiving such favor in the future judgment as the opinion we have held concerning the Lord of heavenly glory.

20. Jewish unbelief reproved by the faith of the nations. — A sign is then requested of him; he answers that he will give the sign of Jonah [Col. 0991B] (ibid., 38), and that, as Jonah was held in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and as many nights, so he himself would remain within the depths of the earth for an equal time. But he shows that the faith of the nations will be greater. For when Jonah preached, the Ninevites repented and deserved pardon from God through the confession of their repentance. Likewise, the Queen of the South, now taken as a figure of the Church, admiring Solomon’s wisdom, came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom she had admired (ibid., 41–42). The comparison therefore compounds their disgrace, and the faith of the nations leaves the Jews without excuse: for while the former believed the prophets—that is, Jonah and Solomon—the latter do not believe Christ, who is greater than Jonah and Solomon. Therefore the former will judge them at the resurrection, because the fear of God was found in persons [Col. 0991C] to whom the Law had not been preached. Those are all the more unworthy of pardon [Note: [Col. 0991D] The vulgate editions read “because.” The manuscripts more correctly read “who”; that is, the people of the Law who are unbelieving are more unworthy of pardon.] who are unbelieving despite belonging to the Law, insofar as greater faith has been found in those who did not know the Law.

21. “But when the unclean spirit has gone out from a man, it wanders through dry places, seeking rest and not finding it,” and the rest (ibid., 43). The passage is continuous and, from the very beginning of the sentence, [Note: [Col. 0991D] The printed editions read “and from the sense”; they are corrected from the manuscripts. That is, the beginning itself of the discourse—“But when the unclean spirit,” etc.—shows that this passage proceeds from, and continues, the preceding sense.] is shown to proceed from the preceding thought; for it begins with a conjunction. But the meaning of the whole comparison proposed must be considered. The unclean spirit, leaving a human being, wanders through dry and waterless places, in which no fountain of life flowed. When it finds no rest, it then says within itself that it is fitting to return to its house whence it came; it will find it empty, swept clean and adorned; and it will take with itself 733 seven [Col. 0991D] spirits more wicked than itself, which enter and dwell there, and the last condition of that person will be worse than the first. [Col. 0992A] The Lord concludes: “So shall it be for this most wicked generation” (ibid., 45).

22. The foregoing applies to the Jews. Before the Law, the demon possessed the Israelites; expelled by the Law, it invaded the nations. — We therefore cannot doubt that all this must be referred to the person of this people; but we must consider how each element proposed corresponds to particular times and circumstances. Above, [Note: [Col. 0991D] In the more authentic manuscripts, *namque*, a word familiar to Hilary in the sense of “namely.”] namely, in the case of the Ninevites and the Queen of the South, the faith of the nations was justified. Yet long before this, after many and grievous sins against God, the Law was given to the Jews. Their sins indeed are contained in [Note: [Col. 0991D] Only the Turonensis manuscript, with the printed editions, reads “the book of Moses.” Below, chapter 14, no. 11, the five books of the Law are mentioned.] the books of Moses. But after so many demonstrations of divine power—Egypt struck with ten plagues; the pillar of cloud and light serving them night and day; a passage opened through the Red Sea [Col. 0992B]; springs flowing when rocks were split; [Note: [Col. 0991D] The Vatican manuscript cited by Latinus reads “manna supplied to the hungry,” without support from any other witness. We noted, note d, col. 737 of this edition, that the manuscripts have “eternal manna.”] manna supplied to the hungry; and finally, throughout forty years, a people living in the life and dress of angels—[Note: [Col. 0992D] The Colbertine manuscript has “afterward worshiping beasts with stones,” with the Carnotensis agreeing except that it has “worshiping” only as a later correction. In other manuscripts too, “and offering supplication” is absent; we suspect it has been added without authority, especially since elsewhere in Hilary the verb *adoro* is found with the accusative. Paris has “worshiping and offering supplication,” etc. Before “worshiped,” understand: “the books of Moses contain.”] they afterward worshiped and supplicated beasts and stones; they danced around them with choirs and songs; and called metals gods. Therefore the Law, subsequently given, drove out by its intervention the unclean spirit that occupied the hearts of this people, and excluded it by a kind of guard formed by its surrounding power. Departing from there, it wandered about the deserted and dry nations, leaving its old house, so that it might rest there in an undisturbed dwelling until the day of judgment.

23. Grace granted to the nations returned to the Jews. Why it takes seven spirits with it. — But when God’s grace was again imparted [Col. 0992C] to the nations, after the living fountain flowed in the washing of water, there was no place to dwell among them. Since it now had no rest in them, reflecting within itself, it judged it best to return to the house from which it had departed. This house—cleansed by the Law, adorned by the proclamations of the prophets, and prepared for Christ’s coming—is found empty, since the guard of the Law had departed from it, for all the Law is until John (Matt. 11:13), and Christ had not been received to dwell there. Thus it is empty of an inhabitant and deserted by its guards, although, [Note: [Col. 0992D] The vulgate editions read “for the coming inhabitant.” We prefer the better manuscripts’ “when the inhabitant came,” namely the devil, against whom neither the Law nor the prophets had provided vigilant protection, as the earlier reading suggests.] when its inhabitant came, it had been cleansed and adorned through the care of those who went before. Seven more wicked spirits are therefore taken along, because so many gifts of grace had been appointed [Note: [Col. 0992D] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “in Christ.”] with Christ, which the manifold wisdom of God had placed in him in sevenfold glory: so that the possession of wickedness might be as great as the grace that was to have been. Thus the last condition of that person will be worse [Col. 0993A] than the former, because [Note: [Col. 0993D] In the Colbertine and Carnotensis manuscripts: “from him”; in the others: “from them.”] the unclean spirit had departed from the Jews through fear of the Law, but now will return to them with vengeance for the grace they rejected.

24. Whence the bond of kinship must now be drawn. Christ’s relatives standing outside: the Synagogue. — And because he spoke all this in the power of the Father’s majesty, when it was reported to him that his mother and brothers were waiting outside, he stretched out his hand toward the disciples and answered that they were his brothers and mother; and that whoever obeyed the Father’s will was his brother, sister, and mother. Thus he made himself the pattern for all in action and thought: the claim and name of every kinship must henceforth be retained, not from the condition of birth, but from communion with the Church. [Col. 0993B] Yet he must not be thought to have held his mother in contempt, since, during his Passion, he showed her the affection of greatest concern (John 19:26–27). A typological meaning is also preserved in the fact that his mother and brothers stood outside, though they certainly had, like the others, power to enter to him. But because he came unto his own and his own [Note: [Col. 0993D] Two manuscripts: “did not know him.”] did not receive him, his mother and brothers prefigure the Synagogue and the Israelites, refraining from entrance and access to him.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0993C] Jesus, sitting in a boat, speaks parables to the crowds: concerning the sower of good seed; the tares and wheat; the mustard seed; the leaven hidden in meal; the explanation of the tares; the treasure in the field; the good pearl; and the net cast into the sea.

1. Those outside the Church do not receive the Word of God. — “On that day Jesus went out and sat beside the sea; and crowds gathered to him, so that he went up into a boat” (Matt. 13:1–2). The reason why the Lord sat in the boat and the crowds stood outside is evident from what follows. For he was about to speak in parables; and by the nature of this event he signifies that those who are outside the Church can receive no understanding of the divine word. For the boat represents the type of the Church: those outside it, lying about barren and useless like sand, cannot understand the word of life set and preached within it. It is unnecessary to speak of the parables already explained by the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0993D] Such are the parables proposed among the headings: that of the sower of good seed, and that of the tares and wheat. From this everyone can see that those headings do not wrongly hold their present place above, although Hilary deals with them so briefly.]

2. The Jews lost the Law through lack of faith. — [Col. 0993D] “For to the one who has, more shall be given, and he shall abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away” (ibid., 12). Faith receives the mysteries of the kingdom. Those in whom it exists will advance and abound through the increase of their progress; but from those in whom it does not exist, even what they have will be taken away [Col. 0994A]. He thus declares that the loss of the Law arises from lack of faith: [Note: [Col. 0993D] In several manuscripts: “because they had not faith.”] because the Jews, not having faith, lost also the Law which they had possessed. Therefore evangelical faith has the perfect gift, because when received it enriches with new fruits, but when rejected it removes even the wealth of the former substance.

3. “But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear” (ibid., 16). He teaches the blessedness of the apostolic age, whose eyes and ears were granted to see and hear God’s Salvation; whereas prophets and righteous persons desired to see and hear the Salvation appointed for the fullness of times [Note: [Col. 0993D] The Turonensis manuscript, in a second ancient hand, reads “appointed,” which five others also have, and which can suitably be referred to “Salvation.” Nevertheless, we do not alter the received reading, confirmed by manuscripts no less authentic. Lipsius, on his own authority, had deleted the preposition *in* before “the fullness.”], and the joy of this expectation was reserved for the apostles.

4. The mustard seed is the Lord; the herbs are the words of the prophets; how the apostles are branches. — “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed,” and the rest (ibid., 31). The Lord compares himself to the mustard seed, exceedingly pungent and the least of all seeds, whose force and power are kindled by afflictions and pressures. When this seed was sown in the field—that is, when, seized by the people and handed over to death, he was buried in the ground, as it were, by a sowing of the body—it grew beyond the measure of all herbs and surpassed all the glory of the prophets. For the preaching of the prophets was given to Israel, as herbs are given to one who is sick. But now the birds of heaven dwell in the branches of the tree raised from the ground to the heights. We understand the apostles, stretched forth by Christ’s power and overshadowing the world, as the branches; to them the nations will fly in hope of life and, tossed by the storm of winds—that is, by the breath and blast of the devil’s spirit—will rest as in the branches of a tree.

5. Christ in the Law, the prophets, and the Gospels. — “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened” (ibid., 33). Leaven comes from meal and imparts to the mass of its own kind the power it has received. The Lord compares himself to this leaven: the woman, namely the Synagogue, received and hid it through the judgment of death, accusing the Law and prophets of being dissolved by the Gospels [Note: [Col. 0994D] Only the Paris edition reads “by the Gospels”; then the other editions, with several manuscripts, read “dissolved.”]. Yet this leaven, covered by the three equal measures of meal—that is, the Law, the prophets, and the Gospels—makes all things one: so that what the Law established, the prophets proclaimed, and the progress of the Gospels fulfills. All are brought about through the Spirit of God, with the same [Col. 0994D] power and meaning; and nothing leavened in equal measures will be found to differ from another.

6. The foregoing must not rightly be referred to the unity of the Trinity or to the calling of the three races. — Although I remember that many have held the three measures of meal to refer to the mystery of faith [Note: [Col. 0994D] Incidentally, it may be noted that Hilary calls the mystery of the Trinity the sacrament of faith; thus the books he wrote concerning this mystery could fittingly be entitled, some “On Faith,” and others “On the Trinity.”]—that is, to the unity of Father, Son, [Col. 0995A] and Holy Spirit—and also to the calling of the three races descending from Shem, Ham, and Japheth, I do not know whether reason allows this opinion. For although the calling of all nations is equal [Note: [Col. 0995C] *Aeque* (“equally”) is absent from several manuscripts of good authority. In Shem, Ham, and Japheth, all human beings, whether Gentiles or Jews, are expressly said to be included in chapter 8, no. 4.], Christ has not been hidden in them but revealed; nor has the whole been leavened within such a multitude of unbelievers. But in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0995C] The printed editions read: “in the necessity of leaven mixed in from outside, all things are one in Christ.” They are corrected from the often-cited Carnotensis, Romanus, Vaticanus, and Colbertinus manuscripts. Erasmus had observed that Hilary had restrained himself from calling the Holy Spirit God, by words allegedly adequate to show his doubtful belief in the Holy Spirit’s divinity. Yet even this one passage refutes him abundantly. For if the Holy Spirit is one with the Father and Son in all things, he must be one with both not only in the name of God but also in power, dignity, honor, nature, and substance. One who asserted this without hesitation surely did not fear that, by calling the Holy Spirit God, he would attribute more to him than was fitting. What else does one teach who asserts that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one through themselves, and not figuratively one in Christ through leaven mixed in from outside? It follows that the words “in Christ” in the earlier printed editions were wrongly referred to “are one.”] all things are one in Christ without the need of leaven mixed in from without.

7. The treasure in the field: Christ in the flesh. — “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field,” and the rest (Matt. 13:44). Through the likeness of a treasure in a field, he shows the riches of our hope placed within himself: because God is found in a human being, for whose price all the resources of the world [Col. 0995B] must be sold, so that by clothing, feeding, and giving drink to those in need, we may acquire the eternal riches of the heavenly treasure. But it must be considered [Note: [Col. 0995D] That is, why the treasure, once found, was hidden rather than immediately taken away; for the finder could have removed it secretly, and the time during which it was hidden would have sufficed for this.] that the treasure was found and hidden, although the person who found it could have taken it away secretly, at the time when he hid it, and by taking it away would not have needed to buy it. But the meaning of the thing, as also of the saying, must be explained. The treasure was hidden because the field also had to be bought. For the treasure in the field, as we have said, signifies Christ in the flesh; to have found him [Note: [Col. 0995D] Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and six manuscripts read “is pleasing,” a reading supported by: “the man who finds it hides it, and for joy over it goes away.” Nevertheless, the Paris edition and four manuscripts’ “is free of charge” is preferable, as the following explanation suggests: “For the preaching of the Gospels is in the open,” that is, public and accessible to all; in much the same sense chapter 14, no. 17, says: “The confession of all will then be unrestricted and public.”] is free of charge. For the preaching of the Gospels is in the open; but the power to use and possess this treasure together with the field cannot be had without a price, because heavenly riches are possessed only through loss of worldly goods.

8. The merchant passing from the Law to the Gospel. — [Col. 0995C] The same reasoning applies to the pearl (ibid., 45). But this saying is now directed to the merchant long occupied in the Law, who by long and sustained labor has arrived at knowledge of the pearl and abandons what he had acquired under the burden of the Law. For he has traded for a long time and at last found the pearl he desired; and the cost of this one desired stone must be reckoned as the loss of all his other labor.

9. Preaching is like a net.—“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea,” and the rest (ibid. 47). Rightly did he compare his preaching to a net: coming into the world, it gathered together within the world those who dwell in it without injury to the world; after the manner of a net which, penetrating the sea, is drawn from the deep in such a way that, passing through the whole body of that element, it draws out those enclosed within its circumference. Thus it brings us out of the world into the light of the true sun, displaying the scrutiny of the future judgment in the choosing of the good and the rejection of the evil.

737 CHAPTER XIV. On the scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven; on the Lord’s brothers and sisters; on John’s head on a platter; on the five loaves and two fish; on his walking upon the sea, and raising Peter when he sank.

[Col. 0996B] 1. “Have you understood all these things?” They say to him, “Certainly.” And he said to them, “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven,” etc. (Matt. XIII, 51–52). He spoke not to the crowds but to the disciples; and he gives fitting testimony to those who understood the parables, comparing them to himself under the name of the householder, since they had gained doctrine concerning things new and old from his treasure. [Note: [Col. 0996D] The expression “of the Holy Spirit” has here been wrongly inserted in Bad., Er., Lips., and several manuscripts; for Hilary interprets “the doctrine of things new and old” as the doctrine of the Law and the Gospels, and the Law is no less the work of the Holy Spirit than the Gospel. For the treasure is Christ; doctrine from the treasure is doctrine concerning Christ, which is contained alike in the Law and in the Gospel.] He calls them scribes because of their knowledge, since they understood those things which he had set forth as new and old—that is, in the Gospels and in the Law—[Note: [Col. 0996D] That is, the things contained in the Law and the Gospel, which belong to the same householder and concern one treasure. The statements in the preceding chapter, no. 5, shed light upon this.] and which belong to the same householder and to one and the same treasure.

2. “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these parables, that he departed from there and came into his own country,” and the rest (ibid. 53). The Lord is dishonoured by his own people. Although both the wisdom of his teaching [Col. 0996C] and the power of his works aroused amazement, yet their unbelief did not receive the truth of judgment. For they do not believe that God performs these things in a man; indeed, they name his father, mother, and brothers, and taunt him with the supposed disgrace of his father’s trade (ibid. 55). Yet plainly he was the son of a smith: one who conquers iron by fire, who melts down in judgment every power of the world, [Note: [Col. 0996D] Here Hilary alludes to the fire of judgment, which he mentions in chapter 2, no. 4, and chapter 5, no. 12. By “the power of the world” he means the devil and his ministers, whom he is accustomed to call the powerful ones of the world. Those who are to be melted down in judgment are identified in Psalm CXLIII, no. 11. Hence it is concluded that, for Hilary, Joseph was an ironworker. Theophilus of Antioch seems to hold the same view in his commentary on Matthew, teaching that those Gospel words indicate that God the Father softens the hardness of minds with the fire of the Spirit. Ambrose agrees in *On Luke*, book III, no. 2, where he transcribes the words of Theophilus. Bede takes the same view in his commentary on Mark, chapter VI. There was therefore no reason for Scultetus to mark this opinion of Hilary’s as a blemish for which he could in no way be excused. For although others have called Joseph a carpenter, it was equally permissible to call him a smith, since the Gospel defines neither trade. Indeed, Hilary does not deny that he was a carpenter. Ambrose, in the passage cited, suggests both. But the common opinion that Joseph practised carpentry had so deeply rooted itself in Scultetus’ mind that he readily persuaded himself that Scripture mentions carpentry and that Hilary contradicts it.] and who moulds the unformed material [Col. 0997A] of our bodies for every work of human usefulness, shaping it into the diverse services of the limbs and for all the works of eternal life. [Note: [Col. 0998D] Bad., Er., Lips., and six manuscripts read: “namely, the form of our bodies and their material.”] Therefore all took offence at him; and amid so many [Note: [Col. 0998D] The more reliable manuscripts read: “so great and magnificent.”] and such magnificent things which he did, they were disturbed by consideration of his body. To these the Lord replied that a prophet is without honour in his own country (Matt. XIII, 57), because in Judaea he was to be despised even unto the sentence of the cross. And because the power of God belongs only to believers, on account of their unbelief he abstained from all works of divine power.

3. The Gospels also have an inward meaning.—“At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report of Jesus, and said to his servants,” and the rest (Matt. XIV, 1–2). We have frequently [Col. 0997B] warned that every care must be brought to the reading of the Gospels, because in the events which they narrate there is found an underlying rationale of inward meaning. For the narration of all the deeds has its own sequence; yet, through the effects of the deeds, the form of the underlying cause is prefigured, as is understood in Herod and John. For Herod was ruler of the people, and by the right of his authority had taken into marriage Herodias, the wife of Philip his brother. And this Herodias had a daughter, who, when she pleased him by dancing on his birthday, received, by the oath which he swore, authority to choose whatever reward she wished. At her mother’s prompting she asked that the head of John, who had long been kept in prison, be brought to her on a platter. [Note: [Col. 0998D] In some manuscripts: “who had long dwelt in prison.” It should rather be translated: “who had by then long been kept in prison.”] And Herod, though grieved, fulfilled his oath and presented the girl’s gift to her mother; and [Col. 0997C] after John had been buried, his disciples came to the Lord (ibid. 6–11).

4. On hearing these things, the Lord withdrew in a boat to deserted places. He had compassion on the distress of the crowds that followed him; and the Apostles urged that they be dismissed into the villages to buy food. But the Lord replied that they had no need to return there, and commanded that food be given them. They pleaded that they had only five loaves and two fish. He ordered these to be offered to him, and the crowd to recline upon the spread grass. He blessed the offerings, broke them for the crowd to eat, and gave them to the disciples to distribute. When all had been satisfied, twelve basketfuls of fragments remained, although, apart from women and children, five thousand men had been fed [Col. 0997D] (ibid. 13–21).

5. He then commands the disciples to embark in the boat and go ahead across the strait; and, having dismissed the crowd, he himself went up alone into the mountain to pray. When evening came, he was alone [Col. 0998A]; and the boat, in the midst of the sea, was being tossed by the waves because the wind was contrary. In the fourth watch the Lord came walking upon the sea. When they saw him they were troubled and, believing the empty appearance to be a phantom, cried out in fear. The Lord at once spoke to them and commanded them to be steadfast. Then Peter, answering out of the many, asked to be allowed to come to the Lord upon the waters. Having descended from the boat and advanced a little, he began to fear and sink as the wind grew stronger. The Lord seized him and rebuked him for being of little faith; and, when he entered the boat, stillness returned as wind and sea became calm (ibid. 22–32).

6. Therefore these events occurred as we have recalled them; yet beneath all these persons, effects, causes, and numbers lies a pattern, so that, beyond the office and impulse of acting which each received from his own nature, they did all these things outwardly as an example. This view should be held with all the greater reverence if one and the same interpretation follows the efficacy of such diverse causes. Therefore the discourse must be referred back to the origin of the proposition.

7. John, the Law; Herod and his brother, the Jews and the Gentiles; the Gentile wife, unbelief; the daughter, pleasure.—As we have frequently observed, John bore the figure of the Law: for the Law preached Christ, and John came forth from the Law, announcing Christ beforehand from the Law. Herod, however, is the ruler of the people; and the ruler of the people comprehends in himself the name and condition of the whole community subject to him. John therefore warned Herod not to unite to himself his brother’s wife (ibid. 4). For there are and were [Col. 0998C] two peoples: that of the circumcision and that of the Gentiles. But the Law warned Israel not to join to itself the works and unbelief of the Gentiles. For unbelief is the companion of the Gentiles, joined to them as though by the bond of marital love. These brothers, then, derive from the same parent of the human race. Because of the truth of this severe warning, John, as the Law, was held in prison. But on the birthday—that is, amid the delights of bodily things—the daughter of Herodias danced (ibid. 6): for pleasure, as though born of unbelief, was carried throughout all Israel’s joys in the full course of its allurements. The people committed themselves wholly to her, even under oath and as saleable property; for under sins and worldly pleasures the Israelites sold the gifts of eternal life. At the prompting of her mother—that is, of unbelief—she asked that John’s head, that is, the glory of the Law, be brought to her (ibid. 8), because the Law reproved incestuous Israel by the authority of divine commandments.

8. The Law perished through unbelief and pleasure.—[Col. 0999A] But above Herod was represented as wishing to kill John and delaying through fear of the people, because John was regarded as a prophet (Matt. XIV, 5). How, then, when his death was requested, especially since he was bound by the religious obligation of an oath, is he now made sorrowful (ibid. 9)? It is plainly contradictory that he should then have wished it and now not wished it; and the present distress does not accord with the earlier will. But in the former passage there is the sequence of the event; here, however, the form of the consequent cause is now expounded. Pleasure, born from unbelief, seized the glory of the Law. Yet the people, conscious of the good that was in the Law, [Note: [Col. 0999D] Bad., Er., and Lips. read *voluntatis*, “of will”: wrongly.] with some sorrow over the certain danger to itself, does not willingly close its eyes to the conditions imposed by pleasure. [Note: [Col. 0999D] Editions except Par. with some manuscripts read *concedit*, “yields.” Other books more correctly read *connivet*, “closes its eyes”; that is, although not willingly, it nevertheless consents.] And it knows that it ought not to have abandoned such glory of the commandments; [Note: [Col. 0999D] Six manuscripts read: “such glory of the commandments”; the reading is not to be approved. Here *concedere* signifies abandonment and is equivalent to withdrawing; above, *oportuisse* has the force of “ought to have.”] but compelled by sins as if by an oath, and corrupted, overcome, by the fear and example of neighbouring rulers, it obeys even sorrowfully the enticements of pleasure. Thus, amid the other delights of a dissolute people, John’s head is brought upon a platter (ibid. 11): that is, bodily pleasure and worldly indulgence are increased through the loss of the Law; and so it is conveyed by the girl to her mother. Thus shameful Israel consigned the glory of the Law to both pleasure and the unbelief of its household—that is, formerly of the Gentiles. Therefore, when the times of the Law were ended and John had been buried with them, his disciples report these events to the Lord, coming, that is, from the Law to the Gospels (ibid. 12).

9. 740 The end of the Law; the beginning of the Church.—Therefore, when the Law was ended, the Word of God embarked in a boat and came to the Church, and withdrew into the desert (ibid. 13): leaving behind [Col. 0999C] the manner of life of Israel, he was about to pass into hearts empty of divine knowledge. Hearing this, the crowd follows the Lord on foot from the city into the desert: that is, it passes from the Synagogue to the Church. Seeing it, he had compassion and healed all its languor and weakness (ibid. 14): that is, he cleanses minds and bodies oppressed by the lethargy of unbelief for the understanding of the new preaching.

10. The food of legal doctrine; what the five loaves and two fish signify.—When the disciples urged that the crowds be dismissed into the nearby villages to buy food (ibid. 15), he replied, “They have no need to go” (ibid. 16), showing that those whom he was healing did not need the food of legal doctrine [Note: [Col. 0999D] The common editions and several manuscripts read “the doctrine of pardon,” a reading which has an appearance of truth. But the reading now presented from the Carnotensis and Colbertinus manuscripts appeared more authentic, especially because it is less likely to occur to those who correct—or corrupt—ancient books by their own ingenuity.]; nor did they need to return to Judaea and purchase food. [Col. 1000A] He commands the Apostles to give them food. Did he not know that there was nothing which could be given? Did he, who saw the inward things of human minds, not know the measure of the food stored with the Apostles? But the whole typological meaning had to be unfolded. For it had not yet been granted to the Apostles to prepare and minister the heavenly bread as food for eternal life. Their answer follows the order of spiritual interpretation. They answered that they had only five loaves and two fish (ibid. 17), because they were still contained under the five loaves—that is, the five books of the Law—and were fed by the preaching of the two fish, that is, of the prophets and John. [Note: [Col. 0999D] The printed editions read, “the five loaves, the five books of the Law,” etc.; they are corrected from the manuscripts.] For life was in the works of the Law as though in bread; but the preaching of John and the prophets, in the power of water, nourished the hope of human life. These, therefore, the Apostles first offered, because they were still in them; but from these sources the preaching of the Gospels is shown to have gone forth and, having issued from these beginnings, to grow into a greater abundance of its power. [Note: [Col. 0999D] The Colbertinus and Carnotensis manuscripts read *propheta*, “prophet.” From this kind of corrupt reading the reading *prophetata* gained currency in Par.]

11. Christ transformed into food; why the loaves are given to the Apostles, verse 20; why five thousand are fed by them; why twelve baskets are reserved.—Having received the loaves and fish, the Lord looked up to heaven, blessed them, and broke them, giving thanks to the Father that, after the times of the Law and the prophets, he was being transformed into Gospel food. [Note: [Col. 1000D] Against all manuscripts, the printed editions add here *significans*, “signifying.” Without this word the reading is complete: “giving thanks that he was transformed,” etc.] After this, the people are commanded to recline upon the grass: no longer lying upon the ground, but supported by the Law; and each person is spread beneath himself like the grass of the earth, by the fruits of his own work. The loaves are then given to the Apostles, because through them the gifts of divine grace were to be bestowed. [Note: [Col. 1000D] Thus the ancient editions, with most manuscripts; likewise no. 12, as in no. 4: “He then gives the loaves to the disciples.” But Par. reads, “They are also placed beneath the Apostles”; and the Carnotensis and Colbertinus manuscripts: “They are also placed beneath by the Apostles.”] [Col. 1000C] The people are then fed and filled with the five loaves and two fish; and, after those reclining had been satisfied, fragments of bread and fish abounded to the full measure of twelve baskets. That is, the multitude is satisfied by the word of God proceeding from the doctrine of the Law and prophets; and, reserved for the people of the Gentiles from the ministry of eternal food, [Note: [Col. 1000D] Bad. and Er., with manuscripts, read “and eternal.” But in the Tours manuscript, in a second revision but by the same hand, *et* has been deleted and *reservato*, “reserved,” substituted earlier in place of *reservata*. We judge that this should not be changed, but referred to *copia*, “abundance.”] an abundance of divine power overflows into the full number of the twelve Apostles. The number of those who ate is also found to be the number of those who were to believe. For, as the Book of Acts records, out of the innumerable people of Israel five thousand men believed (Acts IV, 4). [Note: [Col. 1000D] Hilary often uses the word *admiratio*, but particularly in this place, not to mean the act of admiring but the miracle itself by which admiration is aroused.] The wonder of the events extends to the measure of the underlying cause. And the loaves, broken together with the fish, when the people had been satisfied, were thereafter piled up in an increase equal to the number both of the people who would believe and of the Apostles who were to be filled with heavenly grace: so that measure obeyed number and number measure, while the reasoning enclosed within its own limits was held, by the very ordering of divine power, to the condition of the consequent effect.

12. Why Christ looked to heaven; by this deed the maker of the world is made known.—The work accomplished surpasses human understanding. Although there are often things conceived by the mind which speech cannot explain, in these instances the very subtlety of thought becomes burdensome and, because of the difficulty of such an invisible matter, is struck dumb in the contemplation of the thing. For when the Lord received the five loaves, he looked up to heaven, confessing the honour of him from whom he was; not because it was necessary to behold the Father with bodily eyes, but in order that those present might understand from whom he had received the efficacy of so great a power. [Col. 1001B] He then gives the loaves to the disciples. The five are not multiplied into more, but fragments follow upon fragments, and continually deceive those breaking them by the breaking already done. [Note: [Col. 1001D] The ancient editions, with several manuscripts, read *praefracta*, “already broken.” This is relevant to the passage in *On the Trinity*, book III, no. 6: “The fragments of one ever breaking occupy the hand; they deceive the sight moment by moment, while you follow a hand full of fragments.”] The material then increases: [Note: [Col. 1001D] The Roman, Colbertinus, Vatican, and Carnotensis manuscripts read: “I do not know whether in the place of the tables.”] I do not know whether in the place of the tables, or in the hands of those taking them, or in the mouths of those eating. [Note: [Col. 1002D] One Colbertinus manuscript reads “of those believing”; this is not pleasing. In the cited passage from *On the Trinity*, those breaking are engaged in ministry, those eating in the action itself, and the hungry are satisfied.] Do not be astonished that springs flow, grapes are present upon vines, wine is poured out from grapes, and all the resources of the world flow forth in an annual, unwearied course. For so great an increase of loaves shows the maker of this universe, through whom a measure was added by such increase to the material being dealt with. For in a visible work an invisible operation is carried on; and the Lord of heavenly mysteries works the mystery of the present act. The power of the worker surpasses all nature; the rationale of his power exceeds understanding of the deed; and there remains only astonishment at his might. [Col. 1001C] The sequence of causes and works also follows.

13. Israel will have salvation through the remnant.—After this he commanded the disciples to embark in the boat until he himself had dismissed the crowds; and, after dismissing the crowd, he went up into the mountain to pray, and when evening came he was alone (Matt. XIV, 22–23). The meaning of these things must be distinguished by their times. His being alone in the evening signifies his solitude at the time of the Passion, when the rest fled in terror. But his commanding the disciples to embark in the boat and cross the strait while he dismisses the crowds, and his ascending the mountain after dismissing them, commands them to remain within the Church and to be carried over the strait—that is, through the world—until the time when, returning in the advent of his glory, he himself shall grant salvation to all the people who remain from Israel and forgive their sins. Then, when they have been dismissed—or rather admitted—into the heavenly kingdom, he shall give thanks to God the Father and stand in his glory and majesty.

14. The four watches of God over the Church; the terror of Antichrist.—Meanwhile the disciples are driven about by wind and sea, and are tossed by all the disturbances of the world while the unclean spirit opposes them (ibid. 24). But the Lord comes in the fourth watch: for in the fourth age he will then return to the wandering and shipwrecked Church. For in the fourth watch of the night is found the corresponding number of his periods of watchfulness [Col. 1002A] (ibid. 25). The first watch was that of the Law; the second, of the prophets; the third, of the bodily advent; [Note: [Col. 1002D] Four manuscripts of no inferior quality read “of the bodily advent.”] and the fourth will be at the return of glory. But he will find it weary, beset by the spirit of Antichrist and by all the disturbances of the world. For he will come especially to those who are anxious and afflicted. And because, owing to their experience of Antichrist, they will be apprehensive at every new movement of temptations, [Note: [Col. 1002D] The Bec manuscript reads “movement.”] they will even be frightened at the Lord’s coming, fearing false appearances of things and deceptive images creeping before their eyes. But the good Lord will immediately speak and drive away their fear, saying, “It is I” (ibid. 27), and by faith in his coming drive away the fear of the impending shipwreck.

15. Peter’s ardour, fall, and repentance.—That Peter alone [Col. 1002B], from among all those standing in the boat, dared to answer and asked that he be commanded to come to the Lord over the waters (ibid. 28), signifies the disposition of his own will at the time of the Passion. Then, coming back alone and clinging to the Lord’s footsteps, he accompanied him with equal courage in despising death, having despised the movements of the world as of the sea. Yet his fearfulness shows the weakness of the temptation to come. For though he dared to walk, nevertheless he was sinking (ibid. 30): through the weakness of the flesh and fear of death, he was compelled even to the necessity of denial. But he cries out and asks salvation from the Lord. This cry was born of his repentance. For before the Lord had suffered, he returned to confession and obtained pardon for his denial in due time, [Col. 1002C] Christ being afterwards to suffer for the redemption of all.

16. Why he was not freed from fear; Christ the redemption of all.—The Lord did not grant him, in his fearfulness, the power of coming to him; rather, he stretched out his hand and, having seized him, supported him. The reason is this. Peter was not unworthy of access to his Lord, for he both attempted to approach him; but a typological order was also preserved in him. For while the Lord alone was treading upon the disturbances and storms of the world, no one could be a participant in his Passion. For he alone, about to suffer for all, was paying the debt of the sins of all; and he does not admit a partner in what is bestowed upon the whole human race by one. Thus, although he himself was the redemption of all, Peter too had first to be redeemed, being then reserved for faith in this redemption unto martyrdom for Christ. [Note: [Col. 1002D] The printed editions read “unto martyrdom with Christ,” and thereafter—except Bad.—“is reserved.” They are corrected by the authority of the manuscripts.]

17. Peter surpassed the rest in faith.—[Col. 1002D] This also must be considered in Peter: that he preceded the rest in faith. For while the others were ignorant, he was the first to answer, “You are the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 17). He was the first to reject the Passion, because he thought it evil (ibid. 22). He was first also to promise both that he would die and that he would not deny (Matt. [Col. 1003A] XXVI, 33). He was the first to refuse to allow his feet to be washed (John XIII, 8). He also drew the sword against those who were arresting the Lord (John XVIII, 10).

18. But by his entering the boat, wind and sea are calmed: after the return of his glory, eternal peace and tranquillity for the Church are signified. [Note: [Col. 1003D] Bad., Er., and the manuscripts read “of the eternal Church.” The preceding words should be translated thus: “But that the sea was calmed,” etc.] And because he will then come manifestly, all rightly spoke in amazement: “Truly, he is the Son of God” (Matt. XIV, 33). For the confession of all will then be both unqualified and public: they will confess that the Son of God has restored peace to the Church, not now in bodily humility but in heavenly glory. [Note: [Col. 1003D] Par., like the Colbertinus and Carnotensis manuscripts, reads *redisse*, “has returned.” That reading may also be retained, so that the glorious return of Christ, who is the Church’s peace, may be proclaimed. Then those same manuscripts read *cum transfretasset*, “when he had crossed the strait.” We restore from the Mich. manuscript *Gennesar*, which is closer to the Greek Γεννεσαρέθ; some have *Gennasar*, Bad. and Er. *Gennassar*. The remaining manuscripts, like the Vulgate, have *Genesar*.]

19. The Apostles’ power proceeds from Christ.—“And when they had crossed over, they came into the land of Gennesar; and when the men of that place recognized him, they worshipped him” (ibid. 34–35). [Note: [Col. 1003D] Several manuscripts read “many things in between.”] Many intervening matters have occurred, which have delayed us [Col. 1003B], after the gathering and feeding of the five thousand men, through concern to give an account; yet the meaning remains the same down to this point. For when the times of the Law had ended, and five thousand men from Israel had been placed within the Church, the people of Israelites who already believe comes to meet him: already saved from the Law through faith, it brings to the Lord its remaining sick and infirm members, and those presented desired to touch the fringes of his garment, so as to become whole through faith. But as fringes come from the whole garment, so the power of the Holy Spirit came forth from our Lord Jesus Christ. Given to the Apostles, who likewise go forth as if from the same body, it supplies salvation to those who desire to touch it.

CHAPTER XV. On washing hands; on how not the things entering the mouth, but [Col. 1003C] the things proceeding from the mouth, defile; on the daughter of the Canaanite woman; on the seven loaves and a few fish.

1. [Note: [Col. 1004D] The printed editions begin this fifteenth chapter from the words of no. 2, against the manuscripts and contrary to the sacred text; moreover, the first part of the headings, “on washing hands,” etc., can refer only to no. 1.] “Then scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem came to him, saying,” etc. (Matt. XV, 1). The connection of both sayings and deeds in what follows is complete. For in response to the things which had been proposed, he himself said that every planting not of the Father must be uprooted (ibid. 13): that is, the tradition of men must be eradicated, through whose favour they transgressed the commandments of the Law. Therefore they are blind guides, promising the way of eternal life which they do not see; and the fall into the pit is shared alike by the blind and by the blind guides.

2. (otherwise, CANON XV) “And Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the districts of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman, coming out from those borders, cried out,” and the rest (ibid. 21–22). Different kinds of cures contain different effects of causes; but the event and the discourse take their sequence from [Col. 1004A] what precedes. For he rebuked and condemned the unbelief of the Pharisees by reproaching them as blind guides, and he condemned the superstitions of human traditions. [Note: [Col. 1004D] The common editions read “and reproach.” More correctly, the better manuscripts read *opprobrio*, “by reproach”; that is, he rebukes and condemns the unbelief of the Pharisees. Then Bad. and Er. read, “and the superstitions of human traditions”; Lips. and Par., “from human,” etc.; in the Tours manuscript, in a second hand: “and the superstition of human tradition.”] After this he came to the regions of Tyre and Sidon; and a Canaanite woman, coming out from those borders, cries and prays, confesses the Lord to be David’s Son, and asks help for her daughter. The Lord is silent; the disciples plead for her; and he replies to them that he was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. But she worships and asks to be helped; to her the Lord says that it is unlawful to give the children’s bread to dogs. In return she answers that puppies are accustomed to be fed by crumbs falling from their masters’ table. After this the Lord praises her faith, and at that very moment health is restored to the girl (ibid. 23–28).

3. The Canaanite woman as a figure of proselytes; who the Canaanites were.—[Col. 1004B] Therefore, in order that the inward meaning may follow the events which occurred, we must consider from the force of the words themselves what person the Canaanite woman represents. It is certainly established by faith that there were, and still are, among Israel a people of proselytes, who passed from the Gentiles into the works of the Law and, having left the region of their former life, were held, as though in a home, by the foreign and ruling Law. The Canaanites, moreover, were inhabitants of the lands in which Judaea now lies; having either been destroyed by war, scattered into neighbouring regions, or subjected to servitude as the condition of the conquered, they bear only their name, without a homeland or settled place. Therefore this people, intermingled with the Jews, is from the Gentiles. Since it is beyond doubt that among the crowd which believed there was some portion of proselytes, this Canaanite woman, bearing the figure of the proselytes, will rightly be understood to have gone out from her own borders, passing from the Gentiles into the name of another people; and she prays for her daughter, that is, for the people of the Gentiles. Because she knew the Lord from the Law, she calls him David’s Son. For the Law contains the rod from the root of Jesse (Isa. XI, 1), and David’s Son as king of an everlasting and heavenly kingdom (Jer. XXIII, 5).

4. The Canaanite woman’s daughter bears the type of the Church; the firstfruits of faith are from Israel.—She herself has no need of healing, since she confesses Christ as both Lord and David’s Son; but she asks help for her daughter—that is, the people of the Gentiles—occupied under the dominion of unclean spirits. The Lord is silent, preserving by the endurance of his silence the privilege of salvation for Israel. [Note: [Col. 1004D] The printed editions read “the repentance of silence”; corrected from the manuscripts.] And the disciples, moved to compassion, join their petitions; but he, preserving the mystery of the Father’s will, [Col. 1004D] replies that he was sent to the lost sheep of Israel, so that it might plainly appear that the Canaanite woman’s daughter contains the type of the Church, since she sought [Col. 1005A] what was being bestowed upon others—not because salvation was not also to be imparted to the Gentiles, but because the Lord had come to his own and among his own, awaiting from those from whom he had sprung the firstfruits of faith, [Note: [Col. 1005D] The particle *ergo*, “therefore,” is absent from Bad., Er., Lips., and most manuscripts.] and afterwards intending that the rest be saved through the Apostles’ preaching. [Note: [Col. 1005D] The Vendôme manuscript reads *explicandus*, “to be explained”; five others with Bad., *explicans*, “explaining”; Er. and Lips., *explicat*, “explains.” The word *exspectans*, “awaiting,” found in Par. and the better manuscripts, better accords with what precedes, especially with “the endurance of silence.”] Therefore he says: “It is not lawful to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs” (ibid. 26). The honour bestowed upon Israel heaps jealousy upon God’s affection for it; [Note: [Col. 1005D] The relative *quem* refers either to the affection or to Israel. [Col. 1006D] Hence neither *juxta quod*, with one manuscript, nor *juxta quam*, with two others, is satisfactory.] beside it the people of the Gentiles received the name of dogs. But the Canaanite woman, already herself saved by faith and assured of the inward mystery, replies that puppies are fed from the crumbs which fall from the table, the reproach “dogs” now softened by the endearing diminutive designation.

5. Then the Gentiles are called to faith.—In order that we might understand that the Lord’s silence proceeded from the order of time, not from reluctance of will, he added: [Col. 1005B] “O woman, great is your faith” (ibid. 28): that is, she herself, already certain of her own salvation, is confident even regarding the gathering of the Gentiles. At the time when they believe in this way, they will immediately, like the girl, be liberated from every dominion of unclean spirits. The fact immediately follows the faith. For after the people of the Gentiles had been prefigured in the daughter of the Canaanite woman, those afflicted by various kinds of disease are immediately brought from the crowds to the Lord on the mountain (ibid. 29–30): that is, unbelievers and the sick are instructed by believers to worship and fall down; and salvation is restored to them, while every faculty of mind and body is renewed for perceiving, beholding, praising, and following God.

6. “But Jesus, having called his disciples, said: ‘I have compassion on this crowd, because it has now remained with me for three days,’” and the rest (ibid. 32). He preserves the order of the course of his works, and in the same works a corresponding rationale of the sayings follows. For in the daughter of the Canaanite woman we have recalled that the figure of the Church was established; and we have maintained that the consequent healing of the people is the gathering of sick Gentiles. Now, therefore, both the Lord’s words and deeds must be carefully considered, in order that we may see [Note: [Col. 1006D] The printed editions read, “whether the discourse of the preceding treatment and of this one”; against all manuscripts. For the same reason, at the beginning of no. 2 we have: “But the event and discourse take their sequence from what precedes.” Although these words may seem to indicate a miracle like that narrated in the preceding chapter, they chiefly signify the Lord’s preceding sayings and deeds expounded in this very chapter, whose connection with what follows is being examined.] whether the preceding event and discourse, as we have handed down its interpretation, receives confirmation of the same interpretation from what follows. The Lord has compassion on the crowd because it has remained with him for three days. He does not wish to dismiss it fasting, lest it faint from hunger on the way. The disciples plead that there are not enough loaves to fill and satisfy it (ibid. 33). The Lord asks how many loaves they have. They answer that there are seven loaves and a few fish. The crowds are commanded to recline upon the ground; and the Lord, taking the loaves and fish, gave thanks, broke them, and gave the broken pieces to the disciples to distribute (ibid. 34–36). But the fragments of the seven loaves and few [Col. 1006A] fish filled four thousand men, so that, after all had been satisfied, the broken bread overflowed to fill seven baskets (ibid. 37).

7. Above the faith of Israelites, now that of Gentiles, is expressed.—There are indeed many new features when this is compared with what has been narrated in Matthew XIV and XV, etc. The disciples, having compassion on a single day’s fast, wished the five thousand men to be sent away into the villages to buy food; now they are silent for the entire three days. Further, the earlier crowd reclines upon grass; this one reclines upon the ground. There five loaves are offered; here, seven. There two fish; here, an indefinite number, though marked as few. There are five thousand men; here, four thousand. There, twelve baskets; here, seven full hampers. I think that the former matters have indeed been answered, and that all were set forth suitably in accordance with the character of that people. Let us now likewise attempt to give an explanation appropriate to the matter and its cause, so that, just as those things correspond to the Jewish people who believe, these may be compared with the people of the Gentiles.

8. Profession of faith by those to be baptized. Fasting during the time of the Lord’s Passion.---The order, therefore, in the Lord’s discourse is the same as that which remains in obtaining grace. For those who are to come to baptism first confess that they believe in the Son of God and in His Passion and Resurrection; and faith is pledged to this sacrament of profession. And so that a certain reality of the things themselves may follow this verbal promise, by remaining in fasts throughout the whole time of the Lord’s Passion, they are joined to the Lord in a kind of fellowship of compassion. Thus, whether through the sacrament of the promise [Col. 1006C] or through fasting, they pass with the Lord through that whole period of the Lord’s Passion.

9. The Apostles’ concern for the salvation of Israel.---And the Lord, having pity on this hope and companionship, says that they have been with Him for three days. Lest exhaustion should weaken them in the course of secular life—that is, in the work of the way—He wishes to feed them with His food and to strengthen them by the power of His bread for completing the whole journey, while the disciples complain that there are no loaves in the wilderness. Yet in the preceding events they had taken their example, that nothing is impossible with God. But the causes of the deeds call for an inward understanding. For the letters of the most blessed Paul teach how great was the Apostles’ goodwill in saving Israel (Rom. 9:3); and therefore, while He remains for the same period, there is now introduced both the assembling of the Gentiles and discussion of bread, [Col. 1006D] while fasting is passed over in silence.

10. The seven loaves: the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The unspecified fish: diverse charisms. The Gentiles to be called from the four parts of the world.---Seven loaves, therefore, are offered. [Col. 1007A] For the Gentiles derive no salvation from the Law and the Prophets, but live through the grace of the Spirit, whose sevenfold gift is, as Isaiah teaches, [thus]: therefore the Spirit is salvation to the Gentiles through faith (Isa. 11:2).

[Note: [Col. 1007D] The Chartres manuscript, with Colbertinus, reads “Spirit.”]

They recline upon the ground; for previously they had not been laid upon the works of the Law, but, clinging to the origin of their sins and their bodies, they are called to the gift of the sevenfold Spirit. The unspecified number of fish signifies the distributions and ministrations of diverse gifts and charisms,

[Note: [Col. 1007D] In the Roman manuscript: “participations.”]

by which the faith of the Gentiles is satisfied through a diversity of graces. But the filling of seven baskets indicates the overflowing and multiplied abundance of the sevenfold Spirit, whose bounty exceeds all measure; and thus, when we have been satisfied, it is always richer and fuller. And the gathering of four thousand men [Col. 1007B] signifies the multitude of the innumerable persons from the four quarters of the world. For, as a figure of what was to come, the people are counted in so many thousands according to the divisions, because as many thousands of believers were believed to be about to assemble from the several regions for the gift of heavenly food. Therefore the crowd is dismissed, satisfied and filled. And because the Lord remains with us throughout all the days of our life, He enters the ship—that is, the Church—in the company of the multitude of believers.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the sign of the prophet Jonah; the leaven of the Pharisees; Peter’s confession and the Lord’s blessing; and self-denial by one who would follow Christ.

1. The mark by which Christ is recognized: the power of His works.---“And the Pharisees and Sadducees came to Him, testing Him, and asked Him to show them a sign from heaven,” and the rest (Matt. 16:1). [Col. 1007C] The Pharisees and Sadducees are present, presumptuous in their confidence in the Law and scorning the works of faith’s powers; they ask that a sign from heaven be shown them. Seeing the humility of flesh and body in Christ, they disdain to receive instruction from what He did under the appearance of a man. Mocking their presumption and emptiness, He answers that they are accustomed to infer many things from the nature of the sky, when, at either sunrise or sunset, its redness leads them to predict fair or stormy weather (ibid., v. 2); but that they do not know the signs of the times (ibid., v. 4), although the whole Law and the Prophets signify the tokens of His coming through the wonder of the works that He performed:

[Note: [Col. 1007D] In the Paris edition, “all the Law.” More correctly in the other books, “the whole Law.” So also in chapter 12, §2: “because the whole Law [was] until John.”]

so that, just as the redness of the morning [Col. 1007D] or evening sky gives assurance regarding the weather, so the signs of powers and works ought to furnish a manifest knowledge of the times.

2. Jonah as a figure of Christ.---But, in place of a sign arising from heaven, He appoints for them an earthly sign, in order to keep them within the confession of bodily humility, saying that the sign of Jonah would be given. The Lord compares Himself to Jonah, whom, in a like figure, He had sent beforehand to the Ninevites for preaching repentance, in preparation for the accomplishment of the Passion to come. For Jonah, when the winds raged, was cast from the ship and swallowed by a sea-monster; and after three days he was sent forth alive, neither held by the monster nor consumed by the condition of its food, but, contrary to the nature of the human body, whole and unharmed, he escaped into the upper air through the power of the Lord’s prefiguration.

[Note: [Col. 1007D] Latinius, from the Vatican manuscript, reads “of the Incarnation”; it is not to be accepted.]

Therefore He shows that this sign of His power has been appointed: He Himself preaching remission of sins through repentance, to be cast out from Jerusalem, or the Synagogue, by the prevailing blast of unclean spirits, and delivered to the power of Pilate—that is, to the judgment of the world—and swallowed by death as by a monster belonging to the same element; and, after three days, emerging from it alive and incorrupt, [Col. 1008B] not held by it contrary to the condition of the man whom He had assumed. Thus He wished that those things in the man assumed from the Virgin’s conception which were full of divine powers should be recognized and understood concerning Himself, both by the prophet’s sign and by the example of a man.

[Note: [Col. 1007D] Six manuscripts read “in Himself remission,” not “He Himself.”]

3. There is no hope in works of the Law where the truth has arrived.---“And leaving them, He went away” (ibid., v. 4). It is not written, as in other places, that He went away after dismissing the crowds; but because the error of unbelief held the minds of these presumptuous men, He is written not to have dismissed them but to have left them. And when they had crossed the sea, His disciples forgot to take loaves. But Jesus said to them: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (ibid., vv. 5–6). Every obscurity concerning the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees is removed. In commanding the Apostles to refrain from it, He warns them not to mingle with the teaching of the Jews, [Col. 1008C] because the works of the Law were established for the result of faith and as a prefiguration of things to follow; so that, when the truth had come in the time and age to which they belonged, they might not think that any hope remained placed in a likeness of the truth, lest the teaching of the Pharisees, ignorant of Christ, should corrupt the effects of Gospel truth.

[Note: [Col. 1008D] The Roman manuscript reads, “in whose time and age,” with no different sense. Then “the truth is silent,” supported by Colbertinus and Chartres, in which “will be silent” is read: wrongly. Here it is declared that the Law, being a figure and shadow, has no standing when the truth comes.]

4. The Son is both eternal God and born.---“And Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, and questioned His disciples,” and the rest (ibid., v. 13). In the progress of His discourse and work, He gives the disciples a fuller knowledge of Himself—that is, of His own person—and establishes a certain manner and rule for understanding Him. This is the true and inviolable faith: that from the God of eternity—who, because He has always been Father, has always also had both the right and the name of Father, lest, if the Son were not always Son, the Father also should not always be Father—God the Son has proceeded, possessing from the eternity of His begetter an eternity of His own. But His being born was His own will (see Book III *On the Trinity*, §4), since it lay within His power and authority that He should be born. Therefore the Son of God is God from God, one God in both:

[Note: [Col. 1008D] The Greek term *theoteta* [θεότητα] would be more pleasing, were the ancient editions not opposed, together with all the manuscripts, not only here but also in chapter 26, §5, where *theotetam* is again to be read. Hence Erasmus here notes in the margin: “I do not know whether he used *theoteta*, just as elsewhere he used *rheuma*, *diapsalma*, and *manna*.”]

for He received the *theoteta*—what the Latins call *deitas*, “deity”—of His eternal [Col. 1009A] begetter, from whom He proceeded by being born. Yet He received that which He was; and the Word which was always in the Father was born. And so the Son is both eternal and born, because nothing other was born in Him than that which is eternal.

5. The Son of God is also Son of Man.---Therefore the perfect confession is that He assumed a body and became man; because, just as the eternity of our nature received a body, so it must be acknowledged that the nature of our body can assume the power of eternity. Therefore, since this is the highest good in faith, He asks the disciples whom men said that He was, and adds, “the Son of Man.” For this is the rule which must be retained in confession: that, just as we remember the Son of God, so we remember also the Son of Man; because without the one [Col. 1009B] the other bestows no hope of salvation.

6. Peter’s confession in accordance with Christ’s purpose.---Having therefore set forth the differing opinions of men concerning Him, He asks what they themselves think of Him. Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., v. 17). But Peter had weighed the terms of the question. For the Lord had said: “Whom do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?” And certainly the designation “Son of Man” presented to view the body; yet by adding, “Whom do they say that I am?” He signified that, beyond what was seen in Him, something else must be understood; for He was the Son of Man. What, then, was the judgment about Himself that He sought? We do not suppose it was that which He Himself had confessed about Himself; rather, what was asked was hidden, and to this the faith of believers was required to stretch itself.

7. The reward of confession. [Col. 1009C]---And Peter’s confession plainly obtained a worthy reward, because he had seen the Son of God [Col. 1010A] in the man. Blessed is he, praised for having directed his gaze and seen beyond human eyes:

[Note: [Col. 1009C] Thus the manuscripts, for the reason stated in Book VI *On the Trinity*, §32: “The apostolic faith stretches itself beyond human understanding.” But the printed editions read, “beyond what is human.”]

not beholding what belonged to flesh and blood, but discerning the Son of God by the revelation of the heavenly Father; and he was judged worthy to be the first to recognize what was God’s in Christ. O blessed foundation of the Church in the giving of a new name, and rock worthy of its building, which would break down the laws of hell, the gates of Tartarus, and every barrier of death!

[Note: [Col. 1009C] In the margin Erasmus’ note long prevailed: “Faith is the foundation of the Church.” But there is no reason here why we should not think that Hilary commends Peter himself by this eulogy. Bellarmine perceived Erasmus’ error and rightly censured it; yet Scultetus wholly unfairly and in bad faith attempts to defend it, p. 403. Since the true judgment of Hilary ought to have convicted him from what he again heard from Hilary himself in Psalm 131, §4—“Peter, to whom earlier He had given the keys of the kingdom of heaven, upon whom He was about to build the Church . . . Peter, the first confessor of the Son of God, the foundation of the Church, the doorkeeper of the heavenly kingdom”—he cites from this passage only the statement that Peter is called the first confessor of the faith, suppressing the rest and obstinately defending a perverse opinion. Yet in vain does he contend that a most disgraceful stain of contradiction must be cast upon this most celebrated teacher if we say that Peter is called by him the foundation of the Church, because, in Book VI *On the Trinity*, he says, Hilary refers the same words to Peter’s confession. First, that conditional “if” is empty where Hilary has declared his mind in plain words. Next, what stain of contradiction is there if the eulogy which Peter earned by his faith and confession is referred now to Peter himself, now to his faith? Scultetus further asserts, with somewhat greater confidence, that Hilary consistently understood Christ by the term “rock” in the words, “And upon this rock,” etc., though he does not show that Hilary interpreted those words so even once. For the passage he brings from Book VI [Col. 1010C] *On the Trinity*, §32—“The Church was founded upon this rock of confession”—plainly calls the rock Peter’s faith, not Christ, as is clear from the beginning of §33: “This faith is the foundation of the Church; through this faith the gates of hell are powerless against it; this faith has the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” etc. Indeed, in that same Book VI Peter himself is signified to be the foundation of the Church by reason of his faith. For what else does the statement in §16 mean: “After the confession of the sacrament, blessed Simon, subject to the building of the Church, receiving the keys of the heavenly kingdom”? In what way, I ask, is he subject to the building of the Church except as its foundation? Finally, no one who considers the words of §33 will deny that a certain prerogative of Peter is there commended in the apostolate and priesthood. Nor does what is said elsewhere in this same commentary, chapter 14, §17, where his primacy is so often celebrated, sound otherwise. In these passages Hilary plainly anticipated Leo’s teaching in Letter V, chapter 2, Quesnel’s edition: “The Lord entrusted to the most blessed Apostle Peter the primacy of apostolic dignity as a reward for his faith, establishing the universal Church upon the firmness of his foundation.” These remarks are occasioned by Scultetus; we would willingly have spared his false interpretation, had bad faith not manifestly been joined to it.]

O blessed doorkeeper of heaven, to whose judgment the keys of the eternal entrance are entrusted; whose earthly judgment is an authority already ratified in heaven, so that what has been bound or loosed on earth obtains the condition of the same decree in heaven.

8. The Law and the Prophets are witnesses to Christ’s divinity; the Apostles, to the Resurrection. [Col. 1010B]---He also commands the disciples to tell no one that He is the Christ (ibid., v. 20), for others ought to be witnesses of His Spirit, namely, the Law and the Prophets.

[Note: [Col. 1010D] That is, witnesses of His divinity; with this understanding, shortly afterward, “those knowing Christ in the Spirit” means those knowing that He exists in the divine nature.]

But the testimony of the Resurrection properly belongs to the Apostles. And because the blessedness of those who know Christ in the Spirit has been shown, the danger of denying again His humility and Passion is declared.

9. Christ must be confessed as God and man.---For when He had begun to preach that He must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders of the people, the scribes and chief priests, be killed, and rise after the third day (ibid., v. 21), Peter took hold of Him and said: “Far be it from You, Lord; this shall not happen to You.”

[Note: [Col. 1010D] The Michaelinus manuscript reads, “This shall not be to You,” agreeing with the Greek and Latin copies of Scripture. In Book VI *On the Trinity*, §34, one reads: “Be gracious to Yourself, Lord; this shall not happen.”]

But He turned and said to Peter: “Go behind Me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to Me” (ibid., vv. 22–23). Just as it is God’s gift to know Christ as God in the Spirit,

[Note: [Col. 1010D] Six manuscripts read, “to know in the Spirit of God,” less elegantly but with no different meaning, since for Hilary “to be in the Spirit of God” is equivalent to “to be in the divinity of the Father.”]

so it is the devil’s work not to know Christ in the man. And it is an error of the same danger either to deny the body apart from God or to deny God apart from the body.

[Note: [Col. 1011C] The Paris edition has, “or to speak of the body without God,” to which the other editions agreeing at this point add, “or God alone without the body,” omitting the word “to deny.” We would gladly prefer their reading, were the manuscripts not opposed with great unanimity. This sentence must be understood from the preceding one, and also from Leo’s Letter 24 to Flavian, latest edition, chapter 5: “It was equally dangerous to believe the Lord Jesus Christ either to be God only without man or man only without God.” Further, where it is denied that God had a body before assuming flesh, when it is not said simply, “God has no body,” but with the addition, “the body of this flesh,” perhaps this addition was made lest something substantial should be thought denied to the Word before its assumption of flesh. For on that ground the eternal Word has been observed to be called corporeal in chapter 5, §8.]

But God has no body of this flesh in the eternity of the Spirit; nevertheless, for the sake of human salvation Christ is in the body which He assumed from man.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] In the Colbertinus and Chartres manuscripts, “from man” is omitted.]

10. The devil, author of Peter’s unbelief, is rebuked by Christ with reproach.---Therefore, after the Passion had been foretold, the devil found an opportunity—for he had withdrawn from Him only until a time—

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Namely, the devil. The words of Luke 4:13 are referred to here: “And having completed every temptation, the devil departed from Him until a time.” Hence, in the earlier printed editions, the following sentence was wrongly included within the same parenthesis.]

because it appeared sufficiently incredible to the Apostles that He in whom God was could be capable of suffering. Seizing this occasion of human unbelief, he instilled in Peter the disposition of this opinion. Finally, Peter so abhorred the Passion as to say, “Far be it”; in which expression there is an execration of things to be detested. But the Lord, knowing the prompting of the devil’s art, said to Peter: “Go behind Me”; that is, follow Me in the example of My Passion.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Origen interprets the same words in the Huet edition, p. 285, as Christ saying to Peter, “Go behind Me,” as though Peter had ceased to go after and follow Him. For, as he observes shortly afterward, to be behind Jesus is good; whereas to the devil it was said, “Go, Satan,” without the addition “behind Me.” Ambrose agrees, Book I *On Abraham*, §55. So also Eusebius, Book I *Against Marcellus*, chapter 2: “What the saying ‘Go behind Me’ means, the Savior immediately explained when He added, ‘If anyone wishes to come after Me,’ etc.; and Peter himself fulfilled this in fact when he was completed by martyrdom.” Eusebius then sharply reproves Marcellus because, not understanding how and for what purpose the words “Satan, you are a stumbling-block to Me” are said to the Apostle, he maintains that they were spoken to the devil. As regards our Hilary: though here he expounds these words as addressed to the devil, in Psalm 131, §4, and Psalm 138, §6, he expressly affirms that Peter himself was called Satan as a reproach. There we said that the two interpretations must be reconciled thus: the reproach applies both to Satan, as the author of Peter’s unbelief, and to Peter himself, as one who did not resist Satan’s suggestion; because each receives the name of those through whom he is such, as is taught in Psalm 142, §2. Jerome, in this passage of Matthew, while not denying that many hold this interpretation, nevertheless does not sufficiently approve it: “For to me,” he says, “the apostolic error arising from an affection of piety will never seem an incitement of the devil.” But those who agree with Hilary discern in Peter’s words, beyond affection of piety, a certain fault of unbelief, by which he did not believe Christ’s words concerning His coming Passion; and they do not make Satan the author of piety, but of unbelief. Yet, as Hilary teaches in Book VI *On the Trinity*, §34, this did not advance to guilt. Hence, although he seems immediately to reject the literal sense, it must nevertheless be acknowledged that this is a mode of speech also used by him elsewhere, by which he indicates that something beyond the literal truth is signified.]

But, turning toward him through whom this opinion was being suggested, He added: “Satan, you are a stumbling-block to Me.” For it is not fitting to suppose that the name “Satan” and the offence of a stumbling-block are laid to Peter’s charge after such great declarations of grace, blessedness, and power having been granted to him. But because every unbelief is the devil’s work, the Lord, offended by Peter’s answer, denounced with the reproach of this name the author of that unbelief.
