11. Blessed loss of self. The cross must at least be taken up in will.---Then Jesus said to His disciples: “If anyone wishes to come after Me, let him deny himself,” and the rest (ibid., v. 24).

[Note: [Col. 1012D] Three manuscripts: “himself to himself.”]

O blessed loss, and happy forfeiture! The Lord wished us to grow rich through the loss of soul and body, [Col. 1011C] and exhorts us to be like Himself; because He, existing in the form of God, became humble and obedient even unto death, [Col. 1012A] and received the preeminence of all the power which is in God.

[Note: [Col. 1012D] In the Roman, Colbertinus, and Chartres manuscripts, “of that [power]” stands in place of “of all.”]

Therefore He must be followed with the cross taken up; and, if not perhaps in actual event, at least in will, one must accompany Him in His Passion. For what profit is there in having gained the world and in clinging to the riches of the age through the whole dominion of earthly power, if one’s soul must be lost and life’s forfeiture incurred (ibid., v. 26)?

[Note: [Col. 1012D] The Paris edition alone reads “the works of the age.”]

And what exchange will be sought for the soul when it has been lost? For Christ will be present with the angels, repaying each person according to what they deserve. What shall we bring to life? Treasures, I suppose, prepared from earthly wealth for future transactions; ambitious titles of rank and fame; or ancestral images of a pampered nobility? All these things must be denied, that we may abound in better things; Christ must be followed by contempt for all things, [Col. 1012B] and the eternity of spiritual things must be purchased through the loss of earthly things.

## CHAPTER XVII. Where He is seen on the mountain with Moses and Elijah, and a voice is heard from heaven; where He frees the lunatic boy; concerning the faith of believers; the demanded didrachma; and the stater in the fish’s mouth.

1. The preceding commands needed to be confirmed by no slight authority; they are sweetened by the pledge of glory granted.---“Amen, amen, I say to you: there are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom” (Matt. 16:28). The Lord teaches both by deeds and by words; and speech and work alike instruct the faith of our hope. [Col. 1012C] For He had laid a heavy burden upon human weakness: that, when people had begun to derive the sense of life from the desire to live, they should lose the fruit of it which was presently pleasing to their bodies, and deny themselves—that is, should refuse to be what they had begun to be, although they had received the beginning of this awareness from the affection of their will—and then follow the uncertain and ambiguous belief of hope, when, in the things presently possessed, there were the allurements of flattering delight. Therefore the authority of a true and manifest example was necessary, so that, against the force and judgment of sense, the loss of present things might become desirable because of the thereafter unambiguous gain of future things.

[Note: [Col. 1013B] The Colbertinus manuscript, with Chartres: “that it might become desirable, through the loss of present things, to attain the thereafter unambiguous gain of future things.”]

Therefore, after He had commanded that the cross be taken up, that the soul be lost, and that eternal life be exchanged for the loss of the world, He turned to the disciples and said that some of those present would not taste death until they beheld the Son of Man in the glory of His kingdom. Now the phrase “taste death” indicates, by the nature of tasting, some slight draught of death for believers. Thus the event follows the words.

2. The Transfiguration. Why three Apostles were taken. Why among the saints only Moses and Elijah are present.---For after six days Peter, James, and John are taken apart and stand upon a high mountain (Matt. 17:1); and as they look on, the Lord is transfigured and shines around with the whole appearance of His brightness. In this manner of deed both reason, number, and pattern are preserved. For after six days the appearance of the Lord’s glory is shown: after the periods of six thousand years [Col. 1014A] have run their course, the honor of the heavenly kingdom is prefigured.

[Note: [Col. 1013B] To understand this passage, it is useful to observe that many of the ancients enclosed the entire duration of the present age within a period of six thousand years. [Col. 1013C] Irenaeus, Book V, chapter 28; Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 14; and Jerome, Letter 139 to Cyprian, explicitly favor this view. Augustine proposes it as probable in Book XX *The City of God*, chapter 7. But in Psalm 89, §5, he declares it wholly to be rejected in these words: “Men have dared to presume a knowledge of times, although the Lord said to disciples desiring to know them: ‘It is not yours to know the times,’ etc.; and they have determined that this age can end in six thousand years, as though in six days.” The ancients held this opinion because they read in Psalm 89:4 and 2 Peter 3:8 that a thousand years are with the Lord as one day, and thought that, after creating the world, God had prefigured by the Sabbath rest the time when He would grant eternal rest to His saints. Hence Irenaeus, in the passage cited: “In as many days as the world was made, in so many thousands of years is it brought to completion.” Many report that Hilary agrees with them here. Against this it may be objected, first, that below, chapter 26, §4, and elsewhere repeatedly, he declares the end of the world uncertain. This is the force of what he says in Book IX *On the Trinity*, §66: “He removed the certainty of defined knowledge, so that the mind, anxious in the uncertainty of suspended expectation,” etc., “and that very uncertainty of the time not to be doubted might keep watchful care alert.” Next, Ambrose, Book VII *On Luke*, §7, seems to observe what Hilary thinks here; that Ambrose had both read and imitated him may reasonably be judged from many passages, and especially from the beginning of the aforesaid Book VII. There he says: “Matthew and Mark record that these men were taken after six days. We could say: after six thousand years. For a thousand years are in God’s sight as one day. But more than six thousand years are counted; and we prefer to understand the six days symbolically,” etc. Yet, since Ambrose notes that one day may be understood and spoken of as a thousand years without symbolism, it follows from this interpretation only that Christ took the disciples after six thousand years from the creation of the world and was transfigured before them. This interpretation is supported by Hilary’s statement: “When the periods of six thousand years have run their course, the honor of the heavenly kingdom is prefigured”; rather than saying, as he would have needed to say if he were speaking of the consummation of the world, that the honor would be given. But because it is easily understood that the silent word “to be given” stands before “is prefigured,” nothing prevents us from understanding Hilary to be speaking of the end of the world and the time of eternal recompense. Ambrose likewise, in the words just quoted—“But more than six thousand years are counted”—sufficiently indicates that he departs from this opinion, because, although he already counted more than six thousand years, he nevertheless did not see the world brought to its end. Further, when Hilary writes here that the world is to be consummated after six thousand years, he must be understood to use a fixed and definite number in place of an uncertain and indefinite one; just as in Psalm 118, §7, he praises David for fulfilling the Law in the seventh year, but asks that the book be set free after seven thousand years of the age have elapsed. There, according to the mystical reckoning of seven years, he places the end of the world not within six thousand years, but after seven thousand have elapsed. Nor should he be thought in that latter passage to agree with the millenarians, from whom he has already been shown to be distant in the general preface, §6. Finally, that he thought Christ was born before six thousand years had elapsed will become plain from chapter 20, §6.]

And since three were taken, the future election of the people is shown from the origin of the three—Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

[Note: [Col. 1014D] That is, from the whole human race; because after the Flood, as is explained in chapter 8, §4, the human race was divided among these three.]

And Moses and Elijah stand there from the whole company of saints: Christ is in the kingdom between the Law and the Prophets; for with these witnesses, by whom He was proclaimed, He will judge Israel. At the same time it was shown that the glory of resurrection had been decreed also for human bodies, when Moses stood visibly present. But the Lord Himself becomes whiter than snow and the sun (ibid., v. 2), visible, that is, in the splendor of heavenly light beyond our conception. No answer is given to Peter when he offers to make three tents there (ibid., v. 4), for the time had not yet come for remaining in this glory.

3. Christ’s commands must be heard. Why silence is commanded to the Apostles. [Col. 1014B]---But while he was still speaking, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and they were encompassed by the Spirit of divine power (ibid., v. 5). The voice from the cloud declares: This is the Son; this is the Beloved; this is the One in whom God is well pleased; this is the One to be heard. Thus He was a fitting author of such commands, who, after the loss of the world, after the willing acceptance of the cross, after the death of bodies, had confirmed by the example of Moses—who had departed this life yet lived in glory—the glory of the heavenly kingdom resulting from the resurrection of the dead.

[Note: [Col. 1014D] The printed editions read, “after bodily death,” contrary to the manuscripts. Nor is this referred to Christ, but to those who carry out His commands. Christ is proclaimed a fitting author of the commands to leave the world, bear the cross, and undergo death of the body, because after those commands had been fulfilled He had shown beforehand the glory to be given, by the example of Moses, who had departed this life and yet lived in glory.]

Then He raised them, terrified and overwhelmed; [Col. 1015A] and they looked upon Him alone whom they had seen standing in the midst of Moses and Elijah.

[Note: [Col. 1015C] Thus the manuscripts of better authority. Others, with the printed editions: “so that they might behold Him alone.”]

For Moses and Elijah had stood upon the mountain as a figure of what was to come and for assurance of the event. He commands silence concerning the deeds they had seen until He should rise from the dead (ibid., v. 9); for this reward of faith was reserved, so that honor might be rendered to those among whom the authority of the commands alone would be found not slight.

[Note: [Col. 1015C] The particle *enim* (“for”) either refers to “He commands silence,” which Hilary says was done to allow room for faith and to render greater glory to those among whom the authority of the commands would of itself be sufficiently weighty to induce belief, without the example of the Transfiguration being presented; or it refers to the words “until He should rise from the dead,” so that the following discourse concerns the Apostles, who would then be heard with greater reverence, when among them the authority of the commands was found not bare but confirmed by the example of the Resurrection.]

For He had found them weak at the hearing of the voice, so that, when they had been filled with the Holy Spirit, they might then be witnesses of the spiritual deeds.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] Bad., Erasmus, Lipsius, and several manuscripts read “had healed.” More correctly, the better witnesses with the Paris edition read “had found” or “had experienced,” that is, He had found them weak. For it is written in v. 6: “And when the disciples heard it, they fell upon their faces and were greatly afraid.” Therefore silence is commanded until they become stronger by the power of the Holy Spirit.]

4. They inquire also with concern about the times of Elijah (ibid., v. 10). He answers that Elijah is to come and restore all things (ibid., v. 11), that is, he will bring back to the knowledge of God the remnant of Israel that he finds. [Col. 1015B] But He signifies that John came in the power and spirit of Elijah, and that in him (or, “against him”) they had exercised every grave and harsh thing; so that, as he announced the Lord’s coming, he also went before His Passion by the example of injury and affliction.

5. “And when He had come to the crowd, a man came to Him, falling on his knees and saying: Lord, have mercy on my son” (ibid., v. 14). When the Lord had returned to the crowds, a father falling at His knees presented his demon-possessed boy, who often fell both into water and into fire, and whom the disciples had been unable to cure. After they were rebuked and the demon reprimanded, the boy was made well.

6. The Apostles’ faith was at first imperfect.---The Apostles had indeed believed, but they were not yet of perfect faith. For while the Lord remained on the mountain and they sat with the crowd, a certain slackness had weakened their faith; and therefore He says: “O unbelieving and perverse generation” (ibid., v. 16), “how long shall I be with you?” (see Book VI *On the Trinity*, §23). For, in His absence, the habit of ancient unbelief had crept in. He therefore teaches that those who have departed from faith as though the Lord were absent, in the period between the Gospels and His second coming, [Col. 1016A] can bring no salvation.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] The Paris edition reads “from the Lord”: wrongly, since this is to be understood just as if one read, “having departed from faith as though the Lord were absent.”]

7. Those by whom the devil is to be cast into the depth of hell.---Finally, when they asked Him why they had been unable to cast out the demon, He answered that their inability resulted from the deficiency of faith (ibid., vv. 18–19): if it were in them like a grain of mustard seed, they would command this mountain to move from place to place, with power to accomplish it. But He had already come down from the mountain and was saying these things among the crowds. Therefore He called Himself the mustard seed, the least of all, and called the devil a mountain; because in Him spiritual wickednesses and heavenly powers are to be cast out by those whom fasting and prayer will equip for this efficacy, and are to be thrown into the depth of the sea, as into the depth of hell.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] The printed editions read “to be cast out,” and shortly afterward “to be thrown down”; and their punctuation indicated that the devil was called a mountain because spiritual wickednesses existed in him. But the words “in Him” refer to Christ, through whose power spiritual wickednesses and heavenly powers are to be cast out, etc. The devil, however, is a mountain because he exalts and raises himself against God, as is explained in Psalm 64, §9.]

8. Under the name of the Apostles, the Pharisees and Scribes are treated. [Col. 1016B] — We shall also preserve the order, so that under the name of the disciples the person of the Pharisees and Scribes may be discussed. The Law had entrusted the people to their care as to disciples, like a father entrusts his son, while the Lord was absent. But, as sins gained dominion, the people were now falling into the fire of judgment, now being submerged in the water of the daily habit of their own defilements. [Note: [Col. 1016C] The printed editions read “lasting” (*diutinarum*); but the manuscripts read “daily” (*diurnarum*), which seems more fitting also in comparison with water: for just as waters succeed one another, so daily defilements continually succeed one another. We may understand “daily defilements” as those contracted through the works of the world and of the flesh. These same works are compared, for another reason, with rivers in Psalm 136, no. 6, because, plainly, all works of the world and the body flow onward in the manner of streams, without any stopping-point in their course.] Thus these men brought no help, because, while Moses delayed with the Lord on the mountain, they had become unbelieving. [Note: [Col. 1016D] The Paris edition, with four good manuscripts, reads: “while the Lord delayed a little”: a good reading, unless this entire passage were being interpreted typologically concerning the Scribes and the people of the Law. Accordingly, the reading of the Basel, Erasmus, Leipzig editions and six manuscripts seemed truer. What was said in no. 6 concerning the disciples—that, while the Lord was absent, the habit of ancient unbelief had crept upon them—is now referred to those whom we read were unbelieving while Moses delayed on the mountain, Exodus 32:1. Thus those understood above under the name of the Scribes and Pharisees are the rulers of the people, whose duty it was to keep the people in obedience.] And, in order that the typological meaning might be fulfilled, the disciples wonder that they could not cast out the demon, although authority had been granted them not merely to drive out demons but also to raise the dead. [Note: [Col. 1016D] The printed editions read, “they became unbelieving,” so that the typological sense may be fulfilled—namely, the disciples. This is contrary to Hilary’s meaning: he does not wish the Apostles to have been unbelieving in order that the mystical meaning might be fulfilled, but, for the mystical meaning, to have been unable to cast out the demon although all power had previously been given them.]

But because the Law was not to remain with these people any longer, he says: “Faithless and perverse generation” [Matt. 17:17]—not, surely, as though he were saying this to those whom he had sanctified—“How long,” he says, “shall I be with you?” For, lacking faith, they were about to lose the Law itself which they possessed. Had they possessed that faith in themselves—since he himself is the grain of mustard seed—they would, by the power of the Word, have cast from the people offered to him this burden of sins and heavy mass of unbelief; and they would have transferred it, like a mountain into the sea, to the manner of life of the Gentiles and of the world. [Note: [Col. 1017D] The printed editions read “to the conversion of the Gentiles”; this is corrected from the manuscripts. Here, moreover, the word *conversationis* [“manner of life”] has an unfavourable sense. Hilary means that the unbelief of the world and of the Gentiles holds sway, and that the Jews were given the means to separate themselves from their practice and pass over to faith.]

9. “While they were conversing in Galilee, Jesus said: The Son of Man is about to be handed over into the hands of men” [Matt. 17:22]. Sorrow follows knowledge of the Passion; for the mystery of the cross he was about to undergo had not yet been revealed through the power of the resurrection.

10. What the payment of the didrachm ordained by the Law signifies. — “And when Jesus had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachms came to Peter” [Matt. 17:24]. The Lord is asked to pay the didrachm; for the Law had ordained this for all Israel as a ransom for soul and body, for the service of those who served in the Temple [Exod. 30:12]. [Note: [Col. 1017D] In the Tours, Mich. and Vienna manuscripts: “for those serving the Temple.” Yet the Law required this money for the uses of the Tabernacle of Testimony, not for the uses of those serving there.] But, as we know, the Law is a shadow of things to come. God did not desire the price of bronze, that by so small an expenditure some redemption from the sins of body and soul might be granted. Therefore, that we might offer ourselves in Christ—enrolled, professed, and sealed with Christ’s name—who is the true Temple of God, [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Who is the true Temple of God” is absent from the Colbert and Carnot manuscripts.] this offering of the didrachm was instituted as a testimony to the Son of God.

11. Christ, the Redeemer, has no need of the price of redemption. — Therefore, anticipating Peter, who was silent after the encounter, he addressed him thus: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax?” etc. [Matt. 17:25]. Is it doubtful that the sons of kings are not liable to tribute, and that those to whom belongs the inheritance of the kingdom are free from servitude? [Note: [Col. 1018D] The printed editions, except the Paris edition with six manuscripts, read “the reality of the kingdom,” less well. The sons of kings indeed possess the inheritance of the kingdom, but not yet its reality.] But the meaning of the discourse reaches deeper.

The didrachm was demanded from the people; for the Law is enclosed within that faith which was to be revealed through Christ. Therefore, by the custom of the Law, this same didrachm was demanded from Christ as from a man. But, to show that he was not subject to the Law and to attest in himself the glory of his Father’s dignity, he set forth an example drawn from earthly privilege: that kings’ sons are not bound by taxes or tribute. He is rather the redeemer of our soul and body than one from whom anything ought to be demanded for his own redemption; for it is fitting that the king’s son stand outside the common liability of the rest. Therefore it is preferable that he remove the offence of the rest by paying; but he is free from the Law’s obligation [Matt. 17:26]. [Note: [Col. 1018D] The printed editions read “offence,” against all manuscripts. *Solvere scandalum* means “to remove an offence,” because the offence is to be removed by paying the didrachm.]

12. Then, by the event itself, he explained both the significance of the Law and the constancy of evangelical freedom, so that it might readily be known what the didrachm prefigured in the Law. Peter is commanded to go to the sea, cast in a hook, seek the mouth of the first fish coming up, and offer the stater found in it for himself and the Lord. The didrachm—that is, two denarii—is demanded from the Lord: why, then, does Peter offer a stater, which contains four denarii? Again, when he is directed to seek the first fish, more fish are shown to be coming up. Could even the nature of fish allow a stater found by chance on the shore to be held in its mouth rather than concealed within its entrails? Therefore, an inward meaning underlies the events being enacted.

13. Peter, destined for preaching and made a fisher of men, cast the hook of doctrine into the world, so that by sweetness set before them he might draw out of that sea those who wandered and were tossed about. To this hook was fastened that blessed first martyr, who held in his mouth the fourfold denarius: [Note: [Col. 1018D] The printed editions read “from the Lord.” With the majority of manuscripts, “to the hook” is preferred.] that is, in the unity of the evangelical number, he proclaimed the glory of God and the Lord Christ, beholding him in his Passion. [Note: [Col. 1018D] The Vienna manuscript alone reads: “that is, the Gospels.” Several others: “that is, the unity of the evangelical number.” Theophilus of Antioch explains Hilary’s words by declaring that a stater contains four drachmas, by which the four Gospels are to be understood.]

Therefore Stephen came up first; Stephen held the stater in his mouth, in which there was also the didrachm of the new preaching, as it were two denarii. This the Law prefigured; it bore about the shadow of this truth as an image of the body; this redemption of soul and body was signified. Therefore he says: “Give it for me and for yourself,” because such a payment was now not a didrachm but a stater, to be paid both for Christ and for Christ’s preaching.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Concerning the children who were hindered, and the humility to be assumed from them; concerning cutting off hand, foot, and eye; concerning the lost sheep; concerning reproving brothers—first privately, then with two witnesses, finally in the presence of the Church. Forgiveness must always be granted. Concerning the servant who, after his debt had been remitted by his master, throttles his fellow-servant.

1. Believing children; the disposition of children. “At that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying: Who do you think is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” and what follows [Matt. 18:1]. The Lord teaches that no one enters the kingdom of heaven unless restored to the nature of children; that is, our soul must be brought back, in childlike simplicity, from the vices of our body.

He called all believers “children” because of the faith produced by hearing. For they follow their father, love their mother, do not know how to will evil against their neighbour, disregard concern for riches; they are not arrogant, do not hate, do not lie, believe what they are told, and regard what they hear as true. Once the practice and will of all these dispositions have been taken up in us, they make the path to heaven open. We must therefore return to the simplicity of little children, because, placed in it, we shall bear the likeness of the Lord’s humility.

2. It would have been better for the Jews to have been ignorant of God with the Gentiles than not to have received Christ. — If anyone receives such persons in Christ’s name, he shall receive the reward of receiving Christ. But “whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble”—that is, whoever brings an occasion of temptation upon him—“it is better for him that a millstone turned by an ass be hung round his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” [Matt. 18:6].

So many and such great details are not compared without purpose: the millstone, its being turned by an ass, his being drowned in the sea with it, and this being said to be better for him. By everyone’s common understanding, whatever is advantageous is useful. What usefulness, then, is there in being drowned with an ass-millstone hung from one’s neck? So grievous a death will lead to punishment; and I do not know how it can be useful to seek what is the greatest of evils. We must therefore inquire what ought to be understood.

The work of the millstone is the toil of blindness, for beasts with their eyes shut are driven round in a circle. Under the name of the ass, moreover, we frequently find the Gentiles designated. Thus the Gentiles do not know what they do; held in the work of their life, they are confined in ignorance of blind labour. But to the Jews the path of knowledge was provided in the Law. [Note: [Col. 1019D] Thus in all the manuscripts, except that one Bec manuscript reads “bestowed.” But the printed editions first had “laid beforehand,” and later “shown beforehand.”]

If they had caused Christ’s Apostles to stumble, it would have been more fitting for them to have had the ass-millstone bound round their neck and been drowned in the sea: that is, to have remained, oppressed by the labour of the Gentiles, in the ignorance of the world. For it would have been more tolerable for the former not to have known Christ than for the latter not to have received him who had been foretold.

3. The scandal of the cross is necessary, and how dangerous it is. — “Woe to this world because of scandals. For scandals must come; nevertheless, woe to that man through whom the scandal comes” [Matt. 18:7]. The humility of the Passion is a scandal to the world. For human ignorance is especially held fast by this: that it refuses to receive, under the unsightliness of the cross, the Lord of eternal glory. [Note: [Col. 1019D] On the authority of the Carnot and Colbert manuscripts, *nolit* (“refuses”) is restored, whereas previously *noluit* (“refused”) prevailed.] And what is more dangerous to the world than not to have received Christ?

Yet under the designation of “man” he identifies the Jewish people as the author of this scandal, through whom all this danger is brought upon the world: that they deny in his Passion the Christ whom the Law and Prophets proclaimed as capable of suffering. He says that scandals must come because every humiliation of his Passion had to be fulfilled for the mystery of restoring eternity to us.

4. Above, in discussing the cutting off of hand or foot, we explained that the names of relatives are included [ch. 4, no. 21]. Therefore he signifies that kinship with the Israelite race must be abandoned, as by a kind of cutting off of limbs, because through it scandals are brought into the world.

5. The angels’ care for us. — “See that you do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me” [Matt. 18:10]. He imposed a most binding bond of mutual love, especially toward those who truly believe in the Lord. For the angels of the little ones see God daily [Matt. 18:10]; because the Son of Man came to save what was lost. Thus the Son of Man saves, and the angels see God, and they are the angels of the little ones. [Note: [Col. 1019D] The printed editions and most manuscripts read: “The angels of the believing little ones preside over prayers. That angels preside,” etc. The sentence seems neither complete in its parts nor well concluded from what precedes. For from the fact that the angels of the little ones see God, it follows that they are the angels of the little ones and see God; but it does not follow that they preside over prayers. Hilary adds this latter point on the occasion of the preceding conclusion, not as inferred from it but as something plainly contained in Scripture in itself—namely, Revelation 8:3, or Tobit 12:15; to which belongs the passage in his exposition of Psalm 120, no. 7: “There are, according to Raphael speaking to Tobias, angels standing before the glory of God and carrying the prayers of those who pray to God.” Hence Tertullian also, *On Prayer*, no. 12, recognizes an angel of prayer. The reading preferred here is supplied by the Colbert and Carnot manuscripts.]

That angels preside over the prayers of the faithful is an established authority. Therefore the angels daily offer to God the prayers of those saved through Christ. He, then, whose desires and petitions are borne to the eternal and invisible God by the splendid service and ministry of angels is despised at great peril.

6. The one wandering sheep is man; the ninety-nine that did not wander are angels. Their number is completed from human beings. — To show that there is great joy in heaven at the return of human salvation, he gave the illustrative example of the man who had left ninety-nine sheep in the mountains and sought the one that had wandered; and, when he found it, had more joy than he had in the joy of preserving the ninety-nine [Matt. 18:12]. [Note: [Col. 1020D] The first Paris edition, with several manuscripts, reads “manner of life” (*conversatione*).]

The one sheep is to be understood as man, and under the one man the whole human race is to be understood. But in the error of the one Adam the whole race of mankind went astray. Therefore the ninety-nine who did not stray must be understood as the multitude of heavenly angels, among whom there is joy in heaven and concern for human salvation.

Christ, then, is the one who seeks man; and the ninety-nine left behind are the multitude of heavenly glory, to whom, with the greatest joy, wandering man has been restored in the Lord’s body. [Note: [Col. 1020D] Since Christ, of course, from the time he assumed the nature of universal flesh, holds in himself the race of all progeny, as is stated in Psalm 51, no. 15. This concerns Ambrose’s statement, *On Luke*, book VII, no. 208: “Christ bears you in his body, he who took your sins upon himself.”]

Rightly, therefore, this number is increased by the letter alpha in Abraham and completed in Sarah: for Abram is called Abraham, and Sarai receives the name Sarah. [Note: [Col. 1020D] Only in the Paris edition is “alpha” added here; it seems to be missing, though it is readily understood as suppressed.] For in the one Abraham we all are; and through us, who all are one, the number of heavenly glory must be completed. [Note: [Col. 1020D] Thus most manuscripts. But the printed editions, with the Colbert, Roman, and Carnot manuscripts, read “the heavenly Church,” which would also be approved by us if we had not read above: “the ninety-nine left behind are the multitude of heavenly glory.” A little earlier the Colbert and Carnot manuscripts read “above us,” not “through us.” In the one Abraham all believers are as in a root and parent. For he is, according to the Apostle, Romans 4:11, “the father of all believers,” and according to our Hilary, Psalm 134, no. 5, “the chief of election.”]

For this reason all creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God; and for this reason it groans and suffers, so that the number which was added to Abraham through alpha, and which was completed in Sarah through alpha, may be filled out, through the increase of believers, to the heavenly establishment. [Note: [Col. 1021C] The Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions, with the Tours and Carnot manuscripts, read “in rho.” Most other manuscripts read “in ra.” Everyone sees that the customary Greek method of reckoning is intended here, in which alpha begins the numbers and signifies unity.]

7. The order of correction observed by God toward the Jews. — “But if your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him,” and what follows [Matt. 18:15]. The Lord imposed on us that order for preserving charity which he himself had observed in preserving Israel [Lev. 19:18]. He commands that a sinning brother be reproved and rebuked by the one against whom he has sinned alone.

For he himself rebuked the Jewish people, sacrificing to alien gods, by the coming of his majesty and by the full terror of his present power. [Note: [Col. 1021D] The printed editions read “he rebuked then,” omitting the particle “and,” which we supply from six manuscripts. By it is indicated the second order which God observed in rebuking the Jews. First he terrified them by himself; then, when they could not endure him, he rebuked them through the Law and Prophets; finally, he admonished them in Christ, in whom, through the nature of the body assumed, a kind of gathering of the whole human race is contained, as stated in ch. 4, no. 12.]

Then, when that same people could not bear the coming of God drawing near—although they stood outside the mountain—he ordered that, for the disobedient person also, one or two others be brought in, so that the trustworthiness and truth of the word might stand in the mouth of two witnesses. [Note: [Col. 1021D] In the Bec manuscript: “the majesty of God drawing near to the mountain, although outside the mountain,” a gloss which gave rise to the reading of certain manuscripts that offer “to the mountain” in place of “coming.”] [Note: [Col. 1021D] The printed editions read: “could not bear disobedience, one,” etc. We prefer, with the more reliable manuscripts, “for the disobedient person also,” which corresponds to the Gospel words, “If he does not hear you.” In place of this reading the other manuscripts have “disobedience.”]

For the insolent Israel, the Law, the Prophets, and John were sent; and, summoned by these witnesses to cease sinning, it was admonished a third time by the Lord’s own coming, as though by the assembly of the Church looking on. When these rebukes had been made in vain, it is disregarded with the contempt due to a tax collector or a Gentile.

8. The power of binding and loosing given to the Apostles. — To instil the fear of the greatest terror by which all might presently be restrained, he set before them the unalterable judgment of apostolic severity: so that those whom they bound on earth—that is, left entangled in the knots of sins—and those whom they received through the confession of forgiveness into salvation, [Matt. 18:18] should, by the condition of the apostolic sentence, be either loosed or bound also in heaven. [Note: [Col. 1022C] Dallaeus, book III, *On Confession*, ch. 9, argues that “the granting of forgiveness” should here be substituted. The distinguished Jacobus Boileau objects, *History of Auricular Confession*, ch. 8: nothing should be altered; or, if anything is to be altered, *venia* (“forgiveness”) should be read in place of *veniae* (“of forgiveness”), so that confession may be called “forgiveness” because it is the cause of forgiveness, in the manner in which, in Psalm 118, no. 13, repentance is said to be “this forgiveness of sin,” etc. It cannot be denied to Dallaeus that the reading he would introduce is clearer. But the clearer it is, the less likely the other reading is to have been altered. For there is no reason to ascribe it to the rashness of pedants, since such persons usually alter only what they do not understand and substitute clearer expressions in obscure places. Still less can negligence of printers be charged, since they faithfully reproduced what they found in the manuscripts. For *confessione* occurs not only in all printed editions, but among the eleven manuscripts examined by us, not even one reads otherwise. Nor does the phrase introduced shortly afterward advise another reading: “Therefore all forgiveness is from him, since he forgives even sins committed against himself after the return of confession.” Since, therefore, it is clear that nothing should be changed, it remains to consider what Hilary means. As far as we can judge, the word *veniae* is to be referred not to the preceding word *confessione* but to the following *salutem*, so that the sense is: “whom they have received through confession into the salvation of forgiveness”; that is, into the salvation which forgiveness gives, not into its merit.]

9. By the merit of unity God refuses nothing. — He so earnestly sought the concord of human peace that he affirmed that, by the merit of unity, all things which must be asked of God are to be obtained [Matt. 18:19–20]. Where two or three are gathered in equal spirit and will, he promises that he will be in their midst. For he himself, being peace and charity, will establish his seat and dwelling in good and peaceful wills.

10. God forgives us without measure and wills that we likewise forgive others without measure. The punishment of murderers is prefigured in Cain, and that of God-killers in Lamech. — When Peter next asked whether he should forgive a brother sinning against him seven times, he replied: “Not up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times” [Matt. 18:21–22].

In every way he instructs us in likeness to his humility and goodness, and, to soften and break the stings of our turbulent emotions, confirms us by the example of his own readiness to forgive; for he grants forgiveness of all sins through faith. The vices of our nature did not deserve pardon. Therefore all forgiveness is from him, since he forgives even sins committed against himself after the return of confession.

The penalty to be paid by Cain was fixed at sevenfold [Gen. 4:24]; but that sin was against a human being, for in Abel it had been a sin against a brother, even to death. In Lamech, however, punishment was fixed at seventy-sevenfold; and in this, as we think, punishment was established for the authors of the Lord’s Passion. But the Lord grants forgiveness for this crime through the confession of believers: that is, by the gift of baptism he grants the grace of salvation to detractors and persecutors. How much more does he show that forgiveness ought to be given by us without measure or number, and that we ought not consider how often we forgive, but that we ought to cease being angry with those who sin against us whenever occasion for anger arises?

This constant forgiveness certainly teaches that there ought to be no time at all in our power for anger, since God grants us forgiveness of absolutely all sins by his own gift rather than by our merit. For it is not lawful that we should be confined, by the prescription of the Law, to a number of acts of forgiveness, when through the grace of the Gospel God has forgiven us without measure.

11. Indeed, to bring us to the disposition of perfect goodness, he gave the illustrative example in which a master remitted an entire debt to a servant who had nothing with which to repay [Matt. 18:26]. But that servant, extorting from his fellow-servant the small amount owed to himself, lost through this defect of his own will the gift of his master’s generosity and liberality. [Note: [Col. 1023C] Thus the Carnot manuscript. Others read: “and freedom.”] The meaning of this comparison, moreover, is complete and has been fully explained by the Lord himself.

## CHAPTER XIX

A wife ought not to be dismissed; concerning eunuchs; concerning children who were hindered. It is difficult for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.

1. Why Christ heals Galileans within the borders of Judaea. — “And it came to pass, when Jesus had spoken these words, that he departed from Galilee and came to the borders of Judaea,” etc. [Matt. 19:1]. He heals Galileans within the borders of Judaea. He could have spared the crowds of sick persons the trouble and brought aid to the weak within Galilee itself. But the typological meaning of the places also had to be fulfilled by these prerogatives, so that he might admit the sins of the Gentiles into the forgiveness prepared for Judaea.

2. “Then Pharisees came to him, testing him and saying: Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause?” [Matt. 19:3]. In this discourse concerning wife and divorce, the fact occurs that Genesis [2:24] is written differently from the way in which the Lord now speaks here [Matt. 19:4–5]. There the entire matter is related under Adam’s words; here the Lord indicates that all these things were said by him who both formed the man and made the woman. [Note: [Col. 1023C] The Colbert and Carnot manuscripts read “by him,” which may suitably be referred to Adam. Hilary notes that the words “A man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife” are spoken by Adam according to Genesis, but by God according to Matthew.]

But following apostolic authority, since the Apostle professed this mystery to be great and said that he understood it in Christ and in the Church [Eph. 5:32; see ch. 22, no. 3], let us leave this passage untouched as it stands. Yet we advise the reader, whenever he considers this same question, to attend carefully to the force of the words, both those by which the Lord answered and those used by the disciples; and to weigh the Apostle Paul’s judgment on this matter, whether he is silent or treats of it elsewhere.

Let our discussion and concern be about eunuchs. In one he set nature, in another necessity, in the third will [Matt. 19:12]: nature in the one born so, necessity in the one made so, and will in the one who has resolved to be so in hope of the kingdom of heaven. He admonished us to become like the latter, if indeed we can. [Note: [Col. 1023C] Scultetus, exulting and sneering, thought that these words, “if indeed we can,” sufficiently refuted what Bellarmine had cited in support of a vow of chastity from the exposition of Psalm 64, no. 3, where Hilary expressly says: “Therefore contempt of the body, the keeping of chastity, and endurance of fasting are to be vowed to God.” He wished, evidently, to suggest that a vow of this sort so exceeds human powers that no one can promise it except rashly. As though Christ had counselled something which no one could attain; or as though we could not, with God’s help, fulfil what we have vowed under his inspiration; or as though vows approved and defended by the Church had some author other than God. Here heresy shows itself alien from the Spirit of Christ, because it has none to whom his counsels are dear. On the other hand, the Church has many who, with Paul, say: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me.” Bellarmine therefore did not without reason list Hilary as a defender of vows.]

3. Children, representing the Gentiles, are hindered by the disciples because of favour toward Israel. [Col. 1024B] — “Then children were brought to him, that he might lay his hands on them and pray; but the disciples hindered them,” and what follows [Matt. 19:13]. It is remarkable that the disciples hindered the children brought to Christ from approaching him so that he might lay his hand on them and pray.

As we have said, the Gospel event, between its present occurrence and future effect, held a middle and fitting meaning for each, so that the image of the future adhered to what was being done. The children were truly brought, but they were also truly hindered. Yet they are a figure of the Gentiles, to whom salvation is restored through faith and hearing. But because of their concern that Israel should first be saved, the disciples hinder them from approaching.

The intention to hinder them does not accord with apostolic gentleness; but the prompting to hinder the children slipped in for the fulfilment of the typological meaning. [Note: [Col. 1023D–1024C] In the Vatican manuscript cited by Latinius, “into the saints” has crept in. The same concern of the Apostles toward Israel is again declared in ch. 15, no. 9. Ambrose likewise excuses the Apostles from cruelty on this ground, *On Luke*, book VIII, no. 60.] The Lord says that they ought not to be hindered, because the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these; for the gift and endowment of the Holy Spirit, through the laying on of hands and prayer, was to be granted to the Gentiles once the work of the Law had ceased. [Note: [Col. 1024C] It has already been observed in Psalm 118, no. 5, that this passage is illustrated by Tertullian’s words in *On Baptism*. After describing the rite and effect of baptism, he adds, ch. 7: “After coming out of the washing, we are anointed with blessed unction according to the ancient discipline”; and shortly afterward: “Then the hand is laid upon us by the blessing which calls and invites the Holy Spirit.” Let each judge whether these words and other passages in Hilary, ch. 4, nos. 10 and 27, concern the sacrament of confirmation. From this, certainly, the preference of our scholars was not rash when, in *On Luke*, book VIII, no. 61, they preferred to read: “When he commands children to come to him, that he might bless them either by prayer or by laying on of hands,” although, yielding to the authority of the manuscripts, they retained “by preaching.” Likewise Pope Leo, epistle now numbered 124, ch. 7, indicates that the Holy Spirit is bestowed through the laying on of hands and prayer when he says concerning those who received baptism from heretics: “They must be confirmed by the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone through the laying on of hands”; and shortly afterward: “The sanctification of the Holy Spirit alone must be invoked, so that what no one receives from heretics he may obtain from Catholic priests.”]

4. Jewish arrogance prefigured in the young man; in what respect Christ is not good. — “And behold, one came to him and said: Teacher, what good thing shall I do that I may have eternal life?” and what follows [Matt. 19:16]. Appropriately after the preceding discourse, in which children were hindered and it was answered that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such, comes this young man, asking by what good works he might have eternal life.

This young man both asked, acted arrogantly, and again became sorrowful; and all the things written were done and took place. But we have pointed out that the things done under God presented, in their present accomplishment, a form of things to follow; and that throughout the heavenly Scriptures every discourse has thus been ordered, so as to correspond no less to the likeness of things being done than to things that were to be done.

This young man, therefore, bears the figure of the Jewish people, arrogant in the Law and expecting no hope from Christ beyond the precepts of Moses. In his very answer the Lord declares the severity of the judgment he will exercise, saying: “Why do you call me good?” [Matt. 19:17; see *On the Trinity*, book IX, no. 16]. For he who must punish impious and wicked persons refrained from the title of goodness, reserving this title to God the Father alone, who, by giving the Judge, had withdrawn himself from the office of severity; not because he himself was not good, but because as Judge he would exercise the severity appropriate to him. [Note: [Col. 1025D] The printed editions, except the Paris edition with several manuscripts, read “would be.”]

5. The Jews, glorying in the Law, are convicted by the Law of having done nothing right. — Therefore he sends this man, arrogant because of the Law and concerned about salvation, back to the Law, so that in the very thing in which he gloried he might understand that he had done no righteous work from it. For the Lord answered him in the words of the Law.

But the young man, like a people arrogant and glorying in the Law, relies on the Law which he nevertheless has obeyed in no respect. He had been commanded not to kill: he had killed the Prophets. Not to commit adultery: he had corrupted the faith, committed adultery against the Law, and worshipped alien gods. [Note: [Col. 1025D] Basel and Erasmus read “he had worshipped alien gods.” Then Lipsius on his own authority substituted “he had grown up.” Above, ch. 12, no. 22, it was observed that most manuscripts read “having afterwards worshipped cattle and stones.” Hilary’s understanding of theft and adultery is supported by Turibius, among Leo’s letters, ed. Quesnel, p. 459: “Nor are those acts alone thefts which are committed by plundering another’s goods, nor those alone adulteries which are perpetrated by violating the bonds of the marriage-bed. Rather, the assertion of perverse doctrine, by withholding what is true, commits theft against the Catholic faith; and against the truth of the Word of God, seeds of tares are sown by the adultery of evil doctrines.”]

He had been commanded not to steal: before Christ restored, in faith, freedom to believe, he had by theft dissolved the precepts of the Law. Not to bear false witness: he denied Christ risen from the dead. He had been commanded to honour father and mother: he himself renounced the household of God the Father and of the Church his mother. He had been commanded to love his neighbour as himself: he persecuted Christ, who assumed the body of us all and, by the condition of the body assumed, became neighbour to each of us, even to the punishment of the cross. [Note: [Col. 1026D] The manuscripts read “becomes neighbour.”] Therefore, that he might lay aside and cut off all these vices and return to the Law, he was commanded accordingly.

6. They are urged to pass from the shadow of the Law to evangelical truth. — But he answers that he has done all these things from his youth and asks what still remains to him [Matt. 19:20]. Yet, as we have said, he had done none of the earlier things to which he is sent back; and glorying in them, he speaks as though complete.

The Lord answers him that he must sell all his goods and give them to the poor; then he will be perfect and have treasure in heaven [Matt. 19:21]. This young man is indeed answered by that most beautiful and most useful command to abandon the world, by which heavenly riches are purchased through the loss of earthly substance. But in being commanded to sell his goods and give to the poor, he is admonished to abandon confidence in the Law and exchange it in a blessed transaction; and to remember that it has the shadow of truth, which henceforth must be distributed under the body of truth itself to the poor—that is, to the Gentiles. Yet no one can accomplish this unless he begins to follow Christ.

7. What it means that the young man testifies that he has kept the Law from his youth. — But when the young man heard these things, he went away sorrowful (ibid., 22), for he had placed great confidence in wealth derived from the Law. In this too the logic of the typological operation has been preserved: although he is described as a young man, he had earlier said that from all his youth he had served the precepts contained in the Law. Yet adolescence is within youth, and a later stage of life cannot be contained within the limits of an earlier one. But this is said in order to show, by this “youth” that serves, that the people had already spent a long time in the work of the Law.

> [Note: Col. 1026D. The printed editions read “below youth,” against the manuscripts. Yet the later age is said shortly afterwards to be contained within, not below, the earlier.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1026D. The printed editions have *priores* (“earlier”); the manuscripts more suitably have *prioris*, namely, “of the earlier age.”]
>
> [Note: Col. 1026D. We restore this pronoun, by which the young man is indicated, which Lipsius deleted, on the authority of Bad., Er., and the manuscripts.]

8. Israel’s pride makes entry into heaven difficult. — Then, recognizing the young man’s sadness, the Lord answered that it is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven (ibid., 23). Israel, therefore, as we have said, gloried in being rich through confidence in the Law. Entrance into heaven is difficult for one who, under Abraham’s name, retains the ancient riches in the ambitious vanity of an empty lineage.

9. The fault lies not in possessing, but in the manner of possession. The care of riches is dangerous. — Indeed, he added that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven (ibid., 24). Possession is not a crime; rather, moderation in possessing must be maintained. For how can one distribute and share, if the material for distributing and sharing is not retained? Thus it is rather possessing harmfully, than possession itself, that becomes a fault.

But it is a dangerous concern to wish to become rich, and innocence takes upon itself a heavy burden when it is occupied with increasing wealth. The service of God does not obtain a worldly thing without the vices of that very world. Hence it is difficult for a rich man to approach the kingdom of heaven. Yet, because many might make right use of what they possess, the Lord’s saying was so framed that it did not absolutely deny that anyone could enter the kingdom of heaven; rather, the rarity of those who would enter might be understood from its difficulty. This pertains to the plain sense of the passage; but the sequence of its inner meaning must be pursued in the same course.

> [Note: Col. 1026D. After the word “possess,” the printed editions add “riches,” against the manuscripts.]

10. Why entrance into heaven is difficult for the Jews. — The young man, as we have said, is arrogant; when he is commanded to suffer the loss of the Law, he is sad and sorrowful. But for this people the cross and the Passion are a stumbling-block; therefore it derives no salvation from them. Yet it glories in the Law, despises the Gentiles as co-heirs, and refuses to pass into evangelical freedom; and therefore it will enter the kingdom of heaven only with difficulty. For few of them would believe, and, compared with the multitude of the Gentiles, they were exceedingly rare: so that it was difficult for them to bend a will hardened in the Law toward the preaching of evangelical humility.

11. It is passable for the Gentiles. The nature of the camel. — But a camel will pass more easily through the eye of a needle. A camel does not fit with the eye of a needle; nor can the huge shapelessness of so great a beast be received within the narrow confines of the tiniest opening. But at the beginning of the book (chap. 2, no. 2), under John’s clothing, we indicated that the Gentiles are signified by the camel. For this animal obeys words, is restrained by fear, endures fasting, and submits to its burden by a certain discipline. By its example, the wildness of the Gentiles is softened into obedience to heavenly commands.

Thus they enter the exceedingly narrow way of the heavenly kingdom: namely, the needle, which is the preaching of the new word, through which wounds of bodies are sewn up, rents in garments are repaired, and death itself is pierced. Therefore this is the way of the new preaching: into it the ungainliness of the Gentiles will enter more easily than the abundance of the rich man—that is, of one who glories in the Law.

> [Note: Col. 1027D. Bad. and Er.: “obeys blows.”]
>
> [Note: Col. 1027D. A Vatican manuscript cited by Latinius has “the new preaching,” in the same sense.]

## CHAPTER XX. On the hope of the apostles; on the last becoming first; where laborers are hired for the vineyard; on the sons of Zebedee; on the chief place at table; and on the two blind men sitting beside the road.

1. Summary of the sacred text. — On hearing these things, the disciples marvel and are afraid, saying that no one can be saved (vv. 25–30). The Lord replied that this is impossible with men but possible with God. Again they answer the Lord’s words by saying that they have left everything and are with him. To them the Lord promised that, when he sits upon the throne of his majesty, they will sit upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel; and that for all who leave all things for his name’s sake there is reserved the fruit of a hundredfold reward. But many who are last will be first, and those who are first will be last.

2. It must be understood spiritually. — Many things prevent us from receiving the words of the Gospel according to a merely simple understanding. For, when certain matters are introduced which seem contrary to one another from the standpoint of human reasoning, we are instructed to seek the rationale of heavenly understanding.

The apostles say both that they follow Christ and that they have left everything. How, then, do they become sad and afraid, saying that no one can be saved? For others too could have done what they had done. And then, since they had done it, why did fear arise, or whence was it received? Moreover, the Lord’s answer adds that these things are impossible with men but possible with God. Were those things impossible with men which the apostles both boast of having done and the Lord acknowledges them to have done, and which many thereafter would leave behind even unto the blessedness of martyrdom? Or does God lack anything, so that something remains for him to follow after by abandoning possessions that he has, and thus this should be possible to him alone? Therefore the whole discourse here is spiritual.

> [Note: Col. 1027D. In the manuscripts Chapter 20 begins only here.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1027D. Parisian edition with the Chartres manuscript: “which to him [is] an abandonment.”]

3. The apostles thought that there was no salvation apart from the Law. — For, hearing spiritually that no one could be saved from the Law, while they themselves were then still within the Law—for a vehement love and favor toward the Law held them fast—they had not yet fully learned the truth of the evangelical mystery and feared that no one could be saved without the Law, because even then they located all salvation in the Law.

But the Lord, by a brief and conclusive statement, dispels both their ignorance and their fear, saying: “This indeed is impossible with men, but possible with God.” For what seems so ineffectual to a Jew who expects salvation more from man and from the Law, than that, in the scandal of the cross, legislation, covenant, adoption, and inheritance should be disregarded? Yet what is so possible for God’s power as to save through faith, regenerate through water, conquer through the cross, adopt through the Gospels, and make alive from death through the resurrection?

> [Note: Col. 1027D. A German manuscript lectionary reads: “since they themselves also did not understand; for…” The apostles are said to remain under the Law in their disposition.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1027D. The printed editions read: “than that he should seek salvation more from man than from the Law,” a reading insufficiently responsive to the Gospel’s wording. Some manuscripts read: “as one who expects salvation more from man than from the Law.” A reading found in five others is not displeasing: “as for one who expects salvation more from the Law as a man”; and thus the phrase was entered as a secondary correction in the Tours manuscript, which in its first hand has “as from man … and from the Law.” This latter reading appears more complete. For the Jew, willing to hear nothing apart from Moses and his Law, expects salvation both from man and from the Law.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1028D. The first Paris edition omits the word “be disregarded.” The point is that it seems foolish to the Jew for the scandal of the cross to be preferred to the religion of the fathers, to whom, according to the Apostle in Romans 9:4, belong the legislation, covenant, and so forth.]

4. What regeneration is. The hundredfold fruit. — On hearing this, the apostles quickly believe and profess that they have left everything. But the Lord quickly rewards their obedience, resolving the entire difficulty of the previous question when he says: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, will judge the twelve tribes of Israel.” They have followed in regeneration: in the washing of baptism, in the sanctification of faith, in the adoption of inheritance, in resurrection from the dead. For this is that regeneration which the apostles followed, which the Law could not grant, and which joined them, upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel, to the glory of the twelve patriarchs.

To the rest also, who follow him in contempt of the world, he promises an abundance of a hundredfold fruit. This is the hundredfold fruit fulfilled in the hundredth sheep with heavenly joy. This is the hundredfold fruit attained by the fertility of perfect soil. This honor of the Church is already designated in Sarah’s surname (see chap. 18, no. 6), and must be earned by the loss of the Law and by evangelical faith. Thus he promises, implicitly, that the last will become first, because those who are first become last.

> [Note: Col. 1028D. It is clear from what follows that the words “in the regeneration” are wrongly connected in earlier printed editions with the following word “you will judge.”]

5. The householder. The vineyard. The denarius. The marketplace. — “The kingdom of heaven is like a man, a householder, who went out early in the morning to hire laborers,” and the rest (Matt. 20:1). The comparison as a whole is complete in itself, but it must be distinguished by persons and discerned by times.

This householder must be understood as our Lord Jesus Christ, who, having care for the whole human race, called everyone in every age to cultivate the Law. The vineyard signifies the work and obedience of the Law itself; the denarius, the reward of that obedience. We have already discussed the denarius above. We shall more suitably give an account of the vineyard in what follows. The marketplace, however, the matter itself instructs us to understand as the world: constantly tumultuous with crowds of people, contentions of lawsuits and injuries, and the difficulties of diverse affairs.

> [Note: Col. 1029C. See chap. 17, no. 12, where Hilary expressly explains the denarius as the Gospel, though the glory of evangelical hope less clearly. But in Psalm 129, no. 11, he quite plainly calls the denarius of this parable the hope of evangelical recompense.]

6. The five covenants. When Christ was born in the flesh. — Therefore, in the first hour we must recognize, from the meaning of morning, the time of the covenant established with Noah; in the third hour, Abraham; in the sixth, Moses; in the ninth, David and the prophets. For as many covenants established for the human race are found severally, so many departures into the marketplace are enumerated.

But at the eleventh hour the time of the Lord’s bodily advent is shown. For, from every number constituted within the span of the present age, his birth from Mary corresponds to that reckoning into which the time of the eleventh hour falls within the day. For, when a division is made by five hundred, throughout the entire total of six thousand years the time of his bodily birth is calculated at the eleventh reckoning of the whole division.

> [Note: Col. 1029D. The printed editions read “as many of the same,” against the manuscripts.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1029D. Bad., Er., and Lips., with all manuscripts, read “in the twelfth [hour]”; likewise below, “in which [the time] of the twelfth hour,” and shortly afterwards, “to the laborers of the twelfth hour.” We greatly doubt whether these readings were changed in these places in the Paris edition on any authority. Yet the alteration can be supported from the exposition of Psalm 129, which refers to the same parable and in one section, no. 11, mentions the eleventh hour five times and never the twelfth.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1029D. In this one place the printed editions agree with the manuscripts in reading “eleventh,” not “twelfth.” This may be confirmed by Jerome’s words on Micah 4: “At the consummation of the ages our Savior appeared; and in the eleventh hour he came to hire laborers”; and, after his Passion was completed, John says: “Little children, it is the last hour.” For if in six thousand years five hundred years are allotted to each of the day’s individual hours, the final hour consequently is the time of faith among the Gentiles. From this it follows that Christ’s birth occurred about the year 5500 of the world. But we have already warned that what is written here concerning the duration of this world, and consequently concerning the years of Christ’s birth, ought not to be pressed literally. Moreover, because Hilary believed Scripture to be fruitful in spiritual meanings, he does not adhere to this point alone; in Psalm 129, no. 11, he understands the laborers of the eleventh hour as those who begin to work out their salvation in extreme old age.]

7. The Jews envy the grace given to the Gentiles. — The address to the laborers of the eleventh hour is indeed different. To the first, and also to the others, it was said: “Go into the vineyard” (ibid., 4); but the reward of the denarius was agreed with the first. For the others, the hope of a just payment was promised; but to the last it is said: “Why do you stand here?” (ibid., 6). For though the Law had been brought to Israel, the will of the Gentiles was not excluded from the Law. They answered: “No one has hired us” (v. 7). For it was fitting that the Gospel should be preached throughout the world and that the Gentiles should be saved by the justification of faith. Therefore these are sent into the vineyard.

When evening began, the laborers of the evening hour first receive the gift of the wage established for labor during the whole day (v. 8). The reward is indeed not a gift, because it is owed for work; but God has granted free grace to all through the justification of faith. Yet, in accordance with the insolence of the people already obstinate under Moses, the laborers grumble and envy the free reward because the same recompense is rendered to workers without the hardship of prolonged labor and without long burning under the heat—that is, the heat of the devil’s incitement. But this is why what is impossible with men is possible with God: that he may grant to the last, who become first by believing through faith, as a gift of grace, the reward of the Law most excellently and blamelessly kept.

> [Note: Col. 1030D. The printed editions read “hour”; the manuscripts more correctly read “of the hour.” The sense is that the laborers of the eleventh hour are the first to receive the remuneration promised to those who had labored the whole day.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1030D. The Roman, Colbert, Vatican, and Chartres manuscripts read “justification of faith.”]
>
> [Note: Col. 1030D. The same manuscripts read “the gift of grace,” which is acceptable if the verb “may grant” is referred to God. The Paris edition, from the manuscript now Colbert, less well adds “to the first and the last.”]

8. “And as Jesus went up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples and said to them: Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem,” and the rest (ibid., 17–18). — The Lord now explains the mystery of the cross to the apostles, who are to hear it without stumbling—for indeed no sorrow follows this discourse—since they had been strengthened by the preceding discourse: through faith in the cross the last will become first, while for the rich, that is, those who put confidence in the Law and are offended by that same cross, the way into the kingdom of heaven will be impassable.

> [Note: Col. 1030D. Six manuscripts add “privately” here, in agreement with the sacred text.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1031C. The Paris edition alone reads “in the Law.” Several manuscripts read “in the Law”; then Colbert and Chartres read “who are scandalized.” From *esse* one might suppose *sese* is to be supplied, unless it were established, from chap. 30, no. 3, that Hilary understood *scandalizantibus*, although active in form, passively: “Peter, in the ardor of his faith, answered that he would never be scandalized, though the others were scandalized.” This usage of the word is habitual with him.]

9. The mother of Zebedee’s sons is the Law; her sons are believing Jews. — Then the mother of Zebedee’s sons came to him with her sons, and the rest (ibid., 20). We should not suppose without some significance that the mother of Zebedee’s sons entreated the Lord. Did not the sons themselves also have the familiarity needed to ask? But what was to be foretold lay in the significance of the events.

The apostles had already believed from the Law, which had nourished them into evangelical faith. Thus, in the mother of Zebedee’s sons, the Law is understood: relying on the privilege of its own standing, it entreats for the peoples who believe from it. Because it had heard above that the first would be last and the last first, it asks that one of its sons sit at the Lord’s right and the other at his left in the Lord’s kingdom (ibid., 21). The Lord answered her that she did not know what she was asking (ibid., 22).

There was, indeed, no uncertainty concerning the glory of the apostles, and the preceding discourse had declared that they would judge. Accordingly, in the course of the discourse he asks whether they can drink his cup. He was certainly not speaking of an ordinary kind of cup, for drinking from a cup is no labor; rather, he asks concerning the cup of the sacrament of the Passion. But they, who already possessed the freedom and constancy of martyrdom, promise that they will drink it. Commending their faith, the Lord says that they can indeed suffer martyrdom with him, but that sitting at his left and right had been appointed by God the Father for others (ibid., 23).

> [Note: Col. 1031C. Paris, with three manuscripts: “that they should sit at his left and right.”]

10. Who are appointed to sit with Christ in the kingdom. — So far as we judge, this honor is reserved for others, though the apostles will not be excluded from it, since they will sit upon the thrones of the twelve patriarchs and judge Israel. And so far as may be perceived from the Gospels themselves, Moses and Elijah will sit with him in the kingdom of heaven. For when the Lord promised that some of the apostles would see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom before tasting death, he took Peter, James, and John and appeared in the form of his glory, with Moses and Elijah accompanying him on the mountain (Matt. 16:28).

We understand these same two prophets to precede his advent, whom the Apocalypse of John says will be [killed] by Antichrist (11:7). Although many differing opinions have existed concerning Enoch or Jeremiah, on the ground that one of them must die, as Elijah does, we cannot corrupt the trustworthiness of the truth which the Lord revealed to the three foregoing witnesses by an opinion of our own reasoning; nor can we suppose that others will come than those who were seen to have come in fulfillment of the promise of faith.

And although it is unnecessary to speculate beyond evangelical truth, yet anyone who has carefully considered the condition of Moses’ death, burial, and tomb, and has attained, on the Apostle’s authority, knowledge of the hidden Scriptures, will understand that everything was so handled that Moses could already have been seen. These things have been said for instruction.

> [Note: Col. 1031C. We have added the word “burial” here on the authority of four manuscripts. Some doubt, because of this passage, whether Hilary believed that Moses truly died. Scultetus unhesitatingly lists it among Hilary’s faults: “He denies that Moses died, contrary to the plainest words of Scripture.” Ambrose seems to have denied the lawgiver’s death in more explicit words, *On Cain and Abel*, I.2.5: “We do not read of him, as of the others, that he died after failing; rather, he died by the word of God … Therefore Scripture added that no one knows his burial to this day, so that you may understand his translation rather than his destruction … He died, therefore, by the word of God, as Scripture says, not according to the Word … For who could discover his remains among earthly things, when the Son of God showed in the Gospel that he was with himself?” In the latest edition of Ambrose, however, it has been observed that he intended to express the opinion of Philo, who is known to have discussed Moses’ death in a spiritual sense, with less concern for the literal sense.
>
> Hilary is much more readily cleared of the opinion just mentioned by what he says in chap. 17, no. 2. Having asked why, among all the saints, only Moses and Elijah stood with Christ at his transfiguration, he first answers that this was done to teach that Israel must be judged by the testimonies of the Law, of which Moses was the giver, and of the prophets, whom Elijah represented. Then he gives another reason for the same event: that it might be taught that the glory of resurrection has been decreed also for human bodies, since Moses stood there visibly. What, I ask, does Moses’ being seen contribute to demonstrating the truth of resurrection unless his death is assumed to be a known and established fact? Why, in this second explanation, does Hilary mention Moses alone and not Elijah, although he had raised the question concerning both together, unless he believed that Elijah had been translated but Moses had truly died?
>
> Nor does he here deny Moses’ death or burial; rather, he observes that the condition of his death and burial deserves singular consideration, and that it is treated in Scripture as though the Scriptures intended to prepare us to believe that he could already have been seen. From his supposition that Moses is one of the two witnesses whom John says will be killed by Antichrist, it does not follow that he denied Moses’ death; it means only that he thought Moses had not yet been granted that resurrection which would no longer be subject to death. Those who maintain that Jeremiah is the other witness must likewise have thought this of Jeremiah. For no one has ever doubted Jeremiah’s death. Finally, in the words, “although many differing opinions have existed concerning Enoch or Jeremiah, on the ground that one of them must die, as Elijah does,” he sufficiently indicates that he regarded Enoch and Elijah alone as having been translated from us without death.]

11. Two callings from among the Jews; for these the apostles desire a share in their glory. — But, in order that the logic of the spiritual interpretation might be complete, the mother prayed to the Lord for two. For there are two callings from Israel: one, that of John’s disciples; the other, that of the Pharisees through the apostles. For above we read that, after John’s Passion, his disciples passed over to the Lord. Therefore prayer is made for two, because these twofold callings believed in Christ’s Gospel.

After this, the ten disciples were saddened concerning the two brothers; yet the two disciples themselves show no sadness. Reason does not permit one person to be saddened by another’s insult. The ten could certainly also have been saddened for themselves, for, under the names of the two, this seemed to have been refused to them all. But the typological order has been preserved. The apostles were confident about themselves; therefore they are saddened only concerning the two, because they desired a share in this glory also for these two callings that came from the Law. Thus the discourse orders the logic both of what is future and of what is present so that neither the ten nor the two are said to have been concerned for themselves, and so that, in the concern of the ten for the two, the typological force of the present event may be maintained.

> [Note: Col. 1033D. Thus all manuscripts. The printed editions read, “the other, of the apostles and Pharisees,” a reading contradicted by what follows shortly: “The apostles were confident about themselves; therefore they are saddened only concerning the two, because they desired a share in this glory also for these two callings that come from the Law.” See also chap. 21, no. 1: “For Israel is saved from the Law through two callings, either through the apostles or through John.”]
>
> [Note: Col. 1033D. The Bec manuscript reads “sadness,” incorrectly. For here, as must be carefully noted, Hilary does not mean that the apostles were sad because Zebedee’s sons had arrogated certain privileges to themselves, but because what was asked was not obtained. He calls them sad because of the affront suffered by their two brothers in the refusal—not a refusal endured by the two in their own names and for themselves, but one endured in the name of the two callings of their nation.]

12. Glory is attained through humility. — Therefore, wishing to show us the particular meaning of this prefiguration, and to teach those who were to come from the Law not to presume upon the prerogative of the Israelite name, the Lord teaches that they must not seek rule after the manner of the Gentiles, but that ministers and servants—not those who are served—are called to the glory of highest honor (ibid., 25): by the example of the patriarchs and prophets who served, by the example also of the apostles who ministered, and by the example of the Lord, who gave his life for the redemption of our salvation.

He also instructs them toward the glory of this humility by the example of a supper and banquet (Luke 14:8), warning that one ought not recline in the more prominent places, lest someone more distinguished arrive and, when the master of the supper assigns that place to him, he withdraw with fitting shame. But if he reclines in a humble place, then, when those more humble arrive, he will advance to the glory of a higher place. Thus one should not presume upon any honor, but earn it through works of humility.

> [Note: Col. 1034D. Supply here: “wishing to show.” Shortly after: “not in the manner of the Gentiles,” that is, “not according to the custom of the Gentiles.”]
>
> [Note: Col. 1034D. Bad.: “and in the ordinary way”; Paris: “and in the manner of a banquet,” incorrectly. Hilary may perhaps have had this parable, which is found only in Luke, joined here in his copy.]

13. The two blind men: Gentiles from Ham and Japheth.
