They proclaim Christ as God. — “And as they were leaving Jericho, a great crowd followed him; and behold, two blind men sitting by the road heard that Jesus was passing by,” and so forth (Matt. 20:30). Above, under the figure of Zebedee’s two sons, we discussed the Israelite people, which arose from the seed of Shem. Appropriately, therefore, the two blind men sit beside the road: they signify the two peoples of the Gentiles descended from Ham and Japheth, who observe his departure and journey and beg that sight be restored to them in their blindness.

The crowd rebukes them for crying out and commands them to be silent, not because silence was demanded out of respect, but because they bitterly hear from the blind what they themselves denied: that the Lord is David’s Son. For, once the minds of the blind had been enlightened, God was proclaimed in a man, so that what the Lord said might be true: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who see may not see, but the blind may receive sight” (John 9:39).

But they cry out all the more; and while the people of the Law delays, they profess the more vehement ardor of their faith. The Lord has compassion and asks what they want. They pray that their eyes may be opened. Having compassion, he touched their eyes and restored to them the sight by which God is known (Matt. 20:34). And so that the type of the Gentiles who would believe might be fulfilled, having received knowledge of heavenly grace, those who had been blind followed their Lord with sight.

> [Note: Col. 1034D. The printed editions read “besiege,” against the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XXI. On the she-ass and her colt; the money-changers cast from the temple; the cursed fig tree; the two sons sent into the vineyard; tax collectors and prostitutes.

1. In the preceding chapter two callings from Israel were prefigured; now the same number from the Gentiles is signified. — Then Jesus sent two of his disciples, saying: “Go into the village opposite you,” and so forth (Matt. 21:1–2). Two disciples are sent to the village to loose a tethered she-ass with her colt and bring them to him. If anyone asks why this is done, they are to answer that the Lord needs them and will immediately send them back.

After the preceding discourse, in which we recalled that the two sons of Zebedee signified the twofold calling from Israel, two disciples are now appropriately appointed to release the she-ass and colt, because a twofold calling from among the Gentile people was to follow. For there were—and are—the Samaritans, who once departed from the Law by separation and served under a certain custom of their own observance; there were also the untamed and savage Gentiles. Therefore two are sent, to loose those bound, fettered, and impeded by the chains of error and ignorance; and they are sent outside Jerusalem, for these two callings were found outside it.

Moreover, the mother of Zebedee’s sons prayed to the Lord within Jerusalem; for Israel is saved from the Law through two callings, whether through the apostles or through John. But Samaria likewise believed through Philip (Acts 8:5), while Cornelius was brought to Christ through Peter as the firstfruits of the Gentiles (Acts 10:5). Their instruction to answer the questioner that they are needed by the Lord and are to be sent back at once means that they themselves must be restored to their own people as preachers of evangelical faith.

Thus the prophecy was fulfilled which proclaimed that the Lord would come riding into Jerusalem on a she-ass and a new colt (Zech. 9:9). But the events themselves prophesy by their effect. For the she-ass, released from the village and presented, signifies Samaria, occupied by an alien and foreign dominion; through the apostles it is released and restored to its Lord. But the same Lord mounts the colt—new, obstinate, hard—and all these vices of Gentile ignorance hold sway; yet the wildness of so many souls became a vehicle for God.

> [Note: Col. 1034D. Thus the manuscripts here and below. But the printed editions below read “to be sent away,” which Paris also has here.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1034D. The printed editions read “equally.” With the Roman, Colbert, Vatican, and Chartres manuscripts we retain “likewise,” although “outside it,” found in six manuscripts, would especially please in place of this adverb. But the latter reading is more suspect as an interpolation than the former. Both may nevertheless be retained together thus: “But likewise outside it, Samaria believed through Philip …”]
>
> [Note: Col. 1035D. The printed editions read “the vices are tamed,” or “are subdued,” which the Tours manuscript has as a secondary correction. The Colbert and Chartres manuscripts read “they are tamed by vices.” The others read “the vices hold sway,” namely, the vices of Gentile ignorance.]

2. The garments laid beneath the Lord by patriarchs and prophets; what the branches cut by the apostles signify. — All this scene holds the pattern of what is to come; through parabolic meanings and the conditions of present things, a form of future things is set beforehand. For at the coming of his glory the Lord will possess the Gentiles; and, seated in their minds as one carried, he will be proclaimed with the whole company of his retinue—patriarchs, prophets, and apostles.

For the patriarchs spread their garments beneath the Lord in his glory: through their generations, names, and persecutions the Lord was prophesied. Yielding to him every adornment of their dignity and placing themselves beneath his seat, they teach that all their glory was laid beneath the preparation for the Lord’s coming (ibid., 8). There too the prophets lay their garments beneath the path of the one advancing. For they proclaimed that God would be borne along this way of the Gentiles; and, setting aside love of the world and offering themselves to deaths and stonings, they in a sense stripped themselves even of their bodies, offering them for the entrance of such a way.

The apostles also lay down branches cut from trees after the garments. Yet this is no reverence of human service. For branches would hinder one walking and make the path entangled for one hastening to enter. But the entire rationale of the prophecy is unfolded, and the pattern of what is to come is preserved. Therefore the branches of unfruitful Gentiles—that is, the fruits of the Gentiles once unbelieving—are laid by the apostles beneath the Lord’s path and are justified by the Savior’s entrance. He passes over them, and from branches of a barren root there arises a service most pleasing to God as he advances.

> [Note: Col. 1035D. Paris, with four manuscripts: “For the Lord will be present.”]
>
> [Note: Col. 1035D. Bad., Er., and Lips. read “conqueror.” The manuscripts, with Paris, more correctly read *vector* or *advector*, “one borne/carried,” to be understood passively, as above in chap. 7, no. 9. Thus Ambrose also, *On Luke*, IX.9: “Blessed are those who received such a rider in their inner loins.” Cicero and others likewise use the term in this sense.]
>
> [Note: Col. 1036D. Some manuscripts, with Paris, read “all.” But that edition alone then reads “the adornment of their dignity.”]
>
> [Note: Col. 1036D. The first Paris edition reads “the Lord borne along”; the final edition, after Er. and Lips., reads “the Lord about to be borne along.” The text is corrected from Bad. and the manuscripts.]

3. The conflicting dispositions of the people toward Christ. — The crowd, both going before and following, cried: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (ibid., 9). But how does the crowd praise him who is to be crucified, or how did he earn hatred from favor? The words of praise, however, express the power of redemption in him. For *hosanna*, in the Hebrew language, means “the redemption of the house of David.” Then they call him David’s Son, in whom they recognized the inheritance of the eternal kingdom. Finally, they confess: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

And yet they ought to have shouted, “Crucify the blasphemer!” But present events enact the pattern of the future. Although the dispositions of those among whom these things occurred were in conflict, and although very different things were soon to follow, the operation even of the unwilling rehearses the truth of heavenly realities. Jerusalem is then shaken, for the novelty of the events brought commotion to those who were astonished.

> [Note: Col. 1036D. Seven manuscripts read “to the Son of David.” Jerome does not approve, at the beginning of Epistle 145, Hilary’s interpretation of *hosanna*, which Ambrose, like much else, drew from Hilary in *On Luke*, IX.15.]

4. Those who sell doves—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—are driven from the Temple. — He entered the Temple, that is, the Church, by the entrance of the preaching handed down by Himself [Note: [Col. 1036D] Thus most manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “having entered,” or “is entered.”] (ibid. 12). From it, by right of His authority, He first drives out every fault of priestly ministry: for He had commanded that what they had received freely should be given freely by all (Matt. 10:8); because the freedom of the gift ought to admit neither that anything be bought through a priest’s corruption nor sold. He overturns the seats, especially of those selling doves. What dignity, indeed, belongs to the market in doves? Or what privilege is reserved in the trade of such birds, that those selling them should arrogate to themselves the honour of seats? But everywhere we are warned to consider more deeply the force of words in meanings of this sort. [Note: [Col. 1036D] Thus the Chartres manuscript with Colbert; others read “we are warned.” In imitation of Hilary, Ambrose, *On Luke*, IX.19: “Why He overturned the seats of those selling doves I do not understand according to the letter; for dealers in birds could not claim for themselves in the market the dignity of any throne,” etc.] In the dove, according to the examples of prophecy, we understand the Holy Spirit; in the seat is the chair of the priesthood. Therefore He overturns the seats of those who make the gift of the Holy Spirit a thing for sale, to whom the ministry entrusted by God is a business; recalling the authority of the warning contained in the prophet. For it is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers” (Isa. 56:7; Matt. 21:13).

But we must not suppose that the Jews were able either to buy in the Synagogue or to sell the Holy Spirit. For they had nothing by which they could sell [*venire*, “sell”], nor was there anything that anyone could buy. [Note: [Col. 1037D] Thus the Badian edition with the sounder manuscripts. Other printed editions read “they could sell”; other manuscripts, “it could be sold.” In both cases this alteration would never have been made had it been observed, in ch. 10, no. 18, that *veneo* in Hilary has an active force. Here it is said, according to John 7:30, that the Jews did not possess the Holy Spirit.] Rather, in present sayings is contained a prefiguration of things to come: that the faults of the Church were to be cleansed at the very advent of the Lord’s brightness.

5. He also healed in the Temple the infirmities of the blind and the lame (ibid. 14); and popular favour followed His public works. But the chief priests were envious at the cries of the children, and admonished Him as to why He heard these things (ibid. 15); for it was proclaimed that the house of David had come for redemption. He answered them that they had not read: “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children Thou hast perfected praise” (ibid. 16; Ps. 8:3). For, when the judgments of the wise have ceased, He declares that the glory of this confession has been prepared for Him by children and infants, whose is the kingdom of heaven; because the wise and rulers of this age rejected the wisdom of God, whereas little children and infants of regeneration are to proclaim Christ. [Note: [Col. 1037D] In six manuscripts: “the generations of little children and nursing infants are to proclaim”; less well. What is meant by the term “regeneration” is explained in ch. 20, no. 4.]

“And having said these things, He left the city and departed from them, and remained at Bethany” (ibid. 17). That is, leaving the unfaithful Synagogue, He remains in the Church of the Gentiles.

6. The fig tree lacks fruit, not leaves. The Synagogue. — “And in the morning, as He passed into the city, He was hungry; and seeing one fig tree by the way, He came to it,” and the rest [Col. 1037C] (ibid. 18–19). The same order of heavenly realities is again set forth. For in the fig tree is placed the figure of the Synagogue. Once time has been given for repentance—that is, the interval between the Passion and the return of His brightness—He will come hungering for the salvation of this people, and will find it unfruitful, clothed only with leaves: that is, glorying in empty words, but devoid of fruits, barren indeed of good works, and stripped of the expected yield. And because the time for repentance will have passed, it will wither forever under the sentence of heavenly judgment.

[Note: [Col. 1038D] Thus Bad., Erasmus, and Leipzig editions. Erroneously in the Colbert and Chartres manuscripts, “also of the number of heavenly things.” Worse still in most other witnesses: “also the number of heavenly orders.” Nor is the Paris edition better: “also the order of heavenly gifts.”]

In this, indeed, we find evidence of the Lord’s goodness. [Note: [Col. 1038D] For a fuller treatment of the evidence of God’s goodness, see Ps. 144, no. 9.] For whenever He wished to provide an example of the salvation accomplished by Himself, He exercised the power of His might upon human bodies, commending the hope of future things and the soul’s salvation through the present cares of bodily sicknesses. But now, when He established an example of severity toward the obstinate, He indicated the image of what was to come by the destruction of a tree, so that the danger of unbelief might be taught without injury to those for whose redemption He had come.

[Note: [Col. 1038D] Paris: “when He established, in the form of the obstinate, severity, He judged the image of the future by the tree’s loss”: corruptly.]

7. The condemnation of barrenness is eternal. The right conferred by faith. — The disciples marvel that the tree withered at the very moment of His word [Col. 1038A] (ibid. 20), because the efficacy of the present deed bore beforehand the image of what was to come. For when He comes in the heavenly kingdom, at the very time of His advent the barrenness of Jewish unbelief will incur the sentence of eternal condemnation. The Lord assures them—that is, the disciples—that, if they have faith, they will be able to do not only these things but even greater ones. They, indeed, were to judge Israel, according to the earlier promises; but they would also receive all authority over the devil, whom He calls a mountain. For He says: “If you have faith, you shall not only do this to the fig tree; but if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ it shall be done” (ibid. 21). O great reward of faith, by whose merit the power of believers is raised so high that, while judging all things, they may plunge the devil’s height and mass into the condemnation of the world by an equal sentence of severity!

8. Why the Synagogue is compared with the fig tree. — We must consider why the Synagogue is compared with a fig tree. For this tree flowers in a manner unlike the nature and condition of other trees. Its first flower is in its fruit, but not in those fruits which, when they emerge, attain ripeness. For common usage and prophetic authority have called these *grossa*—unripe figs. But afterwards, when the power of inward fertility abounds, fruits of the same appearance and form burst forth; and as these emerge, the earlier ones are thrust away and, their roots by which they were held having dissolved, fall off, while those others that come forth advance unto ripe fruit.

Yet if it should happen that some of those earlier ones emerge in the bosom of the shoots which spring from the same branch [Col. 1038C], they always remain; and, unlike the other unripe figs, they do not fall, but cling there alone and precede the remaining fruits in ripeness. And that tree will yield from itself these very beautiful fruits: rising along with the other unripe figs, they are produced from between the fork of the two shoots. Thus a fitting likeness of the Synagogue is offered from the particular condition of the tree.

9. The Apostles, the first fruits from the Synagogue. The unbelief of the rest prefigured in Adam and Eve. — It lost the first fruits of the people which it had produced from the beginning, under the figure of the unripe figs, because the useless people of Israel were thrust aside by the faithful and persevering people of the Gentiles, who remain until the consummation of the ages. Nevertheless, the first believers from Israel—the Apostles—clinging like the unripe figs between the Law and the Gospels, will precede the rest in the glory and time of the resurrection.

And indeed, at the beginning of Genesis (3:7), as a figure of this matter, Adam and Eve covered their shame with the leaves of this tree, when they hid themselves from the Lord calling them at His advent. For the unfaithful Synagogue, transgressing the commandments of the Law, was to cover the foulness of its shamelessness [Col. 1039A] and the confusion of its disgrace with unfruitful coverings of words, as though with fig leaves. These observations about the nature of this tree have been inserted so that the propriety of the comparison may be understood. The remaining order of events must therefore be considered.

10. The Pharisees’ true answer concerning John’s baptism. — The Pharisees had afterward seen many things more worthy of great miracles; [Note: [Col. 1039D] Erasmus divided this word into two, reading *in gentibus* (“among the Gentiles”); that reading subsequently prevailed, and the Paris edition further substituted “miracle” for “miracles.” It should be observed that Hilary commonly uses *miraculum* for an act worthy of wonder, and conversely *admiratio* for a wondrous thing.] but now they are especially troubled and ask by what authority He does these things (Matt. 21:23). For the event, in the effects of the present actions, contained a vast mystery of things to come. And therefore the impulse to question Him is found especially in connection with that event in which the prefiguration of the whole danger was set forth.

The Lord answers that He will tell them by what authority He does these things, if they first answer Him whether they think John’s baptism was from heaven or from men (ibid. 24). But they hesitate because of the danger of their answer, considering that if they professed it to be from heaven, their own confession would expose them as guilty for not believing the authority of the heavenly testimony; but if they said it was from men, they feared the crowds, for most regarded John as a prophet (ibid. 26). They therefore answered that they did not know (ibid. 27). Certainly they did not fail to know that it was from heaven, since they feared to be convicted by the truth of their own profession. Yet, even in wishing to deceive, they spoke the truth about themselves. For because of their unbelief they did not know that John’s baptism was from heaven. And they could not know that it was from men, because it was not.

11. First difficulty: which son is older, which younger? — “A certain man had two sons,” and the rest (ibid. 28). There are many grave matters here which can confuse understanding unless we maintain the order of the earlier and later meaning. For who can here be considered the older son—the one who denied that he would go to work, but, corrected through repentance, afterward went? Yet Israel did not repent; rather, it laid hands upon the Lord, and its whole body crucified its God with impious speech. And whom shall we understand as the younger son—the one who promised to go but did not go? Yet the people of the Gentiles and sinners performed what it promised. For it went and set out for the work to which it was called. How, then, will it be understood as that which did not go? [Note: [Col. 1039D] Several manuscripts read, “that it went, which did not go”; from these the Paris edition has, “that it went where it did not go.” The reading is corrected from the Badian, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions and the better manuscripts.]

12. Second difficulty: which younger son obeyed? — Next, we must ask what force the Pharisees’ own answer possesses. They say that the younger son obeyed the will. [Note: [Col. 1039D] We now read that the Pharisees gave this answer concerning the older son. Yet not only in Hilary’s time, but also in Jerome’s, the common reading gave the palm of obedience to the younger or last son. Jerome nevertheless accepts that reading and supplies an interpretation fitted to it, while warning that the authentic copies have not “the last,” but “the first.”] The logic of the matter does not allow that a pretended profession should obtain the merit of complete truth, or that it should be better to have deceived while promising than to have performed everything without promising. Who would not prefer to have what he asks denied, provided that what he asked is done, rather than have what is promised to be done not done? For the result of an act is more pleasing when it comes beyond hope, while hope disappointed causes greater pain. Unless, perhaps, the will of those asking is flattered merely by the pleasing words of those who promise.

13. The first son: those Pharisees who believed. — We must therefore remember that the proposal of this comparison follows from the discourse begun concerning John, so that it might rebuke, by such an example, their hesitation of unbelief and the consequent necessity of silence. [Note: [Col. 1040D] The Paris edition, deleting *et* (“and”), along with other editions read “it supplied from that necessity of silence.” More correctly the manuscripts have “the necessity”—namely, the necessity of keeping silent as to whence John’s baptism came.]

But, as we have noted elsewhere, here too we must remember that sometimes something is lacking from the logic of present events under such a condition that the image of future things may be fulfilled without damage to the prefiguring efficacy. [Note: [Col. 1040D] The Chartres manuscript, with Colbert, reads “the efficaciousness of what prefigures.” This would be preferable to “prefigured efficacy.”]

The first son is the people from among the Pharisees, presently admonished by God through John’s prophecy to obey His commands. This people was arrogant, disobedient, and obstinate against the words then spoken; it trusted in the Law and scorned repentance for sins because of the glory of its prerogative of descent from Abraham. But afterward, repenting after the Lord’s resurrection through the miracles of the Apostles, it believed; and, returning by the faith of its action to the will of evangelical work, it confessed through repentance the fault of its former arrogance [Col. 1040C].

14. The younger son: tax collectors and sinners. — The younger son is the people of tax collectors and sinners, later by reason of the very condition of sin in which it then remained. Through John it was commanded to await salvation from Christ, and, baptized by him, it believed. [Note: [Col. 1040D] After the conjunction *et*, *quae* is omitted; then “by him” refers to John, not to Christ. Therefore one should not accept the reading of the Vendôme manuscript, as in the Tours manuscript in its first hand: “and, baptized by him, might believe.”]

But the statement that it promised to go and did not go shows that it did indeed believe John, but that it could not receive evangelical teaching except through the Apostles after the Lord’s Passion—for then the mysteries of human salvation had to be accomplished. Thus, “it did not go” is said of it. Finally, He does not say that it refused, but that it did not go. The matter lies outside the fault of unbelief, because there was a difficulty in the accomplishment which prevented it from being done. Therefore it did not refuse immediately to go to the work commanded; but because it could not go, it did not go. In this is shown a delay of necessity without the fault of the will.

[Note: [Col. 1040D–1042C] Badian, with the Colbert and Chartres manuscripts, reads “it could not be gone to.” This whole passage must be weighed somewhat, lest anyone find an occasion for error. Hilary does not deny absolute power here, but speaks according to the order determined by God: faith was not to be preached to the Gentiles before the Lord’s Passion. This is the point of Paul’s words: “How shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?” etc. From this divine ordering comes the delay of necessity, or necessity of delay, in believing; such inversion of terms is very familiar to Hilary. And when he says, “there was a difficulty in the accomplishment which prevented it from being done,” he indicates only that the act was difficult, not altogether impossible.

Nor should it disturb us that this immediately precedes: “The matter lies outside the fault of unbelief.” By this sentence he does not excuse the Gentiles, who had not yet professed faith in Christ, from every fault, but only from the fault of unbelief—namely, that unbelief to which Christ declares the Jews would not have been liable had He not come. He means that they were free from the fault of the will: that is, of a will stubbornly resisting the faith preached to it. For in Hilary “fault of the will” means a will obstinate in evil and refusing to yield to recognized truth.

Augustine’s words may help to illustrate and confirm this. Thus he writes in Epistle 194, no. 27: “According to this excuse, Holy Scripture calls inexcusable all whom it proves to sin knowingly. Yet God’s just judgment does not spare even those who have not heard. ‘Whoever have sinned without the law shall perish without the law’ . . . because ignorance itself is undoubtedly sin in those who were unwilling to understand, but in those who could not, it is the punishment of sin.” Or perhaps Hilary excuses the Gentiles here only insofar as they had already believed John and were prepared by profession and inclination of mind to believe Christ.]

15. How these are obedient. — In the Pharisees’ answer there is, indeed, a certain necessity of prophecy. For, although unwillingly, they confess which son obeyed the will: namely, the younger son, obedient in profession, though not accomplishing it at the time, because faith alone justifies. Therefore tax collectors and prostitutes will be first in the kingdom (ibid. 3), because they believed John and, baptized for the remission of sins, confessed Christ at His advent, praised His works of healing, received the mystery of His Passion, and acknowledged the power of His resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 1042C–D] Six manuscripts read “at the advent.” “The advent” without the preposition *in* would be preferable. The Gentiles are commended because, after Christ’s Passion, when the divine mysteries had been proclaimed, they believed and confessed the advent of the Only-begotten God, praised His miracles, etc.]

But the chief priests and Pharisees, seeing these things [Note: [Col. 1042D] That is, the power of the resurrection and the works of healing. Then the Roman, Colbert, and Chartres manuscripts read, “and despising those who were not justified,” omitting “by faith.”] and despising them, since they were not justified by faith, did not return through repentance to salvation. Therefore their fruit withers forever under the curse which was prefigured in the fig tree [Col. 1041B].

## CHAPTER XXII. On the vine-growers who kill those sent to them to demand the fruits, on the indiscriminately invited guests, and on the wedding garment

1. The householder is God; the vineyard, the Israelites; the winepresses, the prophets. — “Hear another parable. There was a man, a householder, who planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a winepress in it, built a tower,” and the rest (ibid. 33). The whole question is plain. For even the chief priests and Pharisees themselves, understanding that these things were said of them, were inflamed with anger. But the identities of the persons and the comparisons of the things must be set forth.

Here we understand the householder as God the Father, who planted the people of Israel for the production of the best fruits; who enclosed them within His bounds through the sanctification of the paternal name—that is, the noble lineage of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—as if by a hedge of special protection; who also established the prophets as certain winepresses, into whom there might flow, as into vats, an abundant supply of the fervent Holy Spirit, like must; [Note: [Col. 1042D] The Roman manuscript reads “manifoldly”; the Colbert and Chartres witnesses, “in manifold fashion.”] and who built in the tower the exalted height of the Law, which rose from the earth to heaven and from which Christ’s advent could be watched for. In the tenants is represented the chief priests and Pharisees, to whom authority of teaching over the people had been entrusted. [Note: [Col. 1042D] Paris wrongly reads “promised.”]

2. The servants sent; the Son killed; the hope of the crime; the householder’s return; the cornerstone. — In the servants sent to receive the fruits (v. 34) is represented the varied and often repeated course of the prophets. The servants sent again in greater number than the former (v. 36) signify that period in which, after the preaching of individual prophets, a very great number of prophets was sent together. At different times they were beaten, stoned, and killed, demanding the fruits of the people which had been established and instructed.

In the Son sent last (v. 37) are the advent and Passion of our Lord, who was cast out beyond Jerusalem, as beyond the vineyard, into a sentence of condemnation [Col. 1042B]. The tenants’ counsel, and their expectation of inheritance upon killing the heir (v. 38), is the empty hope that the glory of the Law could be retained after Christ had been slain. In the householder’s return (v. 40) is the glory of the Father’s majesty standing with the Son at the time of judgment. [Note: [Col. 1042D] Here the manuscripts agree strongly in reading “of the householder.”] But in the answer of the chief priests and Pharisees themselves, the inheritance of the Law is more worthily rendered to the Apostles.

Yet this Son is the stone rejected by the builders, raised to the summit as the cornerstone, wonderful in the eyes of all, and the joining together of the two sides and structures—that of the Law and that of the Gentiles.

3. What the wedding is; why it is made by the Father. — “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son and sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding,” etc. (Matt. 22:2). This parable must be distinguished according to times and identified according to persons. The meaning concerning the person of the king and the son is plain. But that the Father made the wedding for the Son and then invited guests is a new consideration. For to make a wedding belongs both to the author and to the time of the wedding.

But here the wedding is the mystery of heavenly life and of the eternal glory to be received in the resurrection. It is therefore rightly made by the Father, because the betrothed union of this eternity and new body had already been perfected in Christ. [Note: [Col. 1042D–1043D] The Paris edition with some manuscripts reads “the pledged union”; we prefer “the betrothed union,” with other editions and manuscripts. Thus in Ps. 137, no. 8, Christ is explained to be called the Bridegroom because the Church has been betrothed to Him through the assumption of our body. The Colbert and Chartres manuscripts read “union,” not “joining.” The same edition alone then reads “is already perfected”; “was already perfected” would not be objectionable if authority permitted. Yet below, ch. 27, no. 4, where the same matter is treated again, one reads: “For the two were one,” not “are one.” This makes it clearer that the discourse here concerns the union which Christ’s flesh possesses with God through glory granted to it; it does not concern the unity of subsistence bestowed on His human nature by the Word’s assumption of flesh, but the unity of glory imparted to that same human nature after the glory of the resurrection.]

At this point, as also above (ch. 19, no. 2), where the condition of divorce was discussed, we shall warn readers carefully to consider what has been signified concerning the nature of the resurrection, and not carelessly to pass over the statement spoken under the person of Adam to Eve, that it is a great mystery (Eph. 5:32).

4. Those sent to invite. — Those admonished to come (Matt. 22:3) are the people of Israel, previously invited; for through the Law they were summoned to the glory of eternity. The servants sent to call the invited guests are the Apostles, for it was their particular office to remind those whom the prophets had invited. Those sent again with the condition of commandments are apostolic men and successors of the Apostles. [Note: [Col. 1043D] In all manuscripts: “They are apostolic successors of the Apostles.”]

The oxen are the glorious company of martyrs, who have been offered to the confession of God as a chosen sacrifice. The fattened beasts—supply “sacrifice”—are spiritual people, like birds fed on heavenly bread so as to take flight, destined to fill others by the abundance of the food they have received. [Note: [Col. 1044D] Thus with six manuscripts. The printed editions and some manuscripts read “birds prepared.”] Once all these have been prepared and gathered into the number of the multitude pleasing to God, the glory of the heavenly kingdom is announced as a wedding.

5. How they were rejected and punished. — Yet they so neglected this invitation that some were occupied, as it were, with a field through worldly ambition, while many more were detained by business through desire for money (ibid. 5). The rest abused and killed the servants who were sent—something fulfilled in the Apostles themselves (v. 6). But vengeance worthy of so monstrous a crime follows. The heavenly armies sent forth will burn their entire assembly by God’s judgment and set it ablaze with the flames of eternal fire (v. 7), because, contrary to the disposition of human kindness, they raged with the hatreds of murderers. [Note: [Col. 1044D] Paris reads “humility.”]

6. The calling of the Gentiles. The call, in itself, makes people good. — But since He speaks here of the time of judgment and resurrection, He turns the same discourse to the gathering of the Gentiles. For those first invited having been found unworthy, He commands that they go to the exits of the roads (v. 9). By the gift of grace, the crimes of former life are set aside. [Note: [Col. 1044D] The Roman manuscript reads “are forgiven”; most other manuscripts with the printed editions, “are remitted.” We prefer, with the sounder witnesses, “are omitted.” The force of this word may be seen in the exposition of Ps. 137, no. 17: “Do not omit the works of Thy hands.”] For we have often stated that “road” is to be understood as the time of this world. Therefore they are commanded to go to the exits of the roads, because all past things are forgiven.

He then commands that all be called to the wedding without any exception, and the evil come together with the good [Col. 1043D] (v. 10). [Note: [Col. 1044D] Several manuscripts insert *ut* (“that”) here and add “they may come.” They are not to be approved, since the king did not command that evil persons should come, for he expelled even those who had entered.] The call itself ought to have made them good, because it is holy and proceeds from the best disposition of the one inviting; but the distinction among those called comes through the fault of an uncorrected will.

7. It is not given to everyone to recognize the wicked. — Since pretence is usually highly skilled at deceiving people, and may deceive us either because another’s mind is hidden or because of the simplicity of our judgment, though it cannot escape God, therefore God, entering this assembly of the blessed resurrection and seeing a man reclining without a wedding garment, asks how he entered (v. 11). Had He specified the dress of those to be invited? Again, when He had commanded that whomeversoever should be invited, how could one garment have suited all? Or if a particular customary dress was ordinarily worn by guests at weddings, it could have been forbidden by the hosts and attendants.

But because recognizing the wicked is not granted to everyone, and human simplicity has difficulty discerning the deceit of a feigned mind, God alone finds this man wicked and unworthy of the wedding assembly. The wedding garment is the glory of the Holy Spirit and the brightness of heavenly clothing. Received through the confession of a good examination, it is to be kept spotless and whole even unto the assembly of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore this man is taken away and cast into outer darkness, because “many are called, but few are chosen” (ibid. 13–14). Thus the small number is not among those invited but the rarity among the chosen: for in the inviter is the humanity of public goodness without exception, while among the invited there is an election of uprightness according to the merit of judgment.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the tribute and image of Caesar, on the same wife of seven brothers, on the greatest commandments, and on David’s son

1. “Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel how they might entrap Him in His speech,” etc. [Col. 1044C] (Matt. 22:16). The Pharisees are frequently stirred up, yet cannot find from His former acts an opportunity to accuse Him, for fault could not attach to His deeds or words. But from a disposition of malice they extend themselves to every inquiry in search of an accusation. For He called all away from the vices of the world and the superstitions of human religions to the hope of the heavenly kingdom. They therefore test, by the terms of their proposed question, whether He would violate worldly authority—namely, whether tribute ought to be paid to Caesar (v. 17).

Knowing the hidden secrets of their thoughts—for God beholds all that is within human beings, with nothing hidden—He commanded a denarius to be brought to Him and asked whose inscription and image it bore (vv. 18–19). The Pharisees answered that it was Caesar’s. He said to them that Caesar’s things must be rendered back to Caesar, and God’s things rendered to God (vv. 20–21).

2. The freedom of minds devoted to God alone. What we owe God. — O answer full of wonder, and perfect resolution of a heavenly saying! He so moderated all things between contempt for the world and the insult of offending Caesar that He released minds devoted to God from all human cares and duties, while decreeing that Caesar’s things must be rendered to Caesar. [Note: [Col. 1045C] Six manuscripts read “and” in place of “while,” and later “decreed” in place of “decrees”; a reading not to be despised.]

For if nothing of Caesar’s remains with us, we are not bound by the condition of rendering to him what is his. But if we occupy ourselves with his things, if we make use of the right of his authority, and submit ourselves as hirelings to the management of another’s estate, then it is beyond any complaint of injury that Caesar should be given back what is Caesar’s. [Note: [Col. 1045C] Thus Leipzig with the manuscripts. Other editions read “if we devote ourselves to.”] Yet we must render to God the things that are properly His: body, soul, and will. For we possess these as proceeding and increasing from Him; and therefore it is fitting that each person should render his whole self to Him to whom he remembers that he owes both his origin and his advancement [Col. 1045B].

3. “On that day Sadducees came to Him, who say that there is no resurrection,” and the rest (ibid. 23). The Sadducees are outside faith in the resurrection. And because the Lord preached it, they frame against divine things a slander drawn from what He declared Himself willing to accomplish: namely, the case of the same woman married to seven brothers, asking to which of them she would belong in the resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 1045C–D] That is, from those things which He declared that He willed to accomplish. Above, against slanderers of this kind, we read: “In God’s sayings there is truth, and every efficacy of things to be created is in the Word.” Thus neither is what He promised concerning the resurrection doubtful, nor is what He spoke ineffectual.]

4. The authority of Scripture. In what form the female sex will rise. — Public opinion generally holds that the conditions of resurrection are contained nowhere in the prophetic Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 1045D] The first Paris edition reads “probable Scriptures”: wrongly. “The conditions of resurrection” mean those immediately discussed below: “They neither marry,” etc. On this point Origen, in Huet’s edition, p. 496, asks: “In what place of either the Law or the Prophets do we learn that those who rise again will be like the angels of heaven?” For this is not openly found in the Old Scripture. Shortly afterward he answers that it is contained there tropologically.] But the Lord says: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God” (ibid. 29). Therefore it is written; and uncertainty, condemned by so great an authority, must cease.

Many are accustomed to raise this same objection: in what form the female sex will rise, and whether it will again be restored with the functions proper to its nature and body. We indeed venture to address this passage, which nearly everyone has passed over; but we point out only this: the question put to the Lord was to which of the seven the woman ought to be assigned as wife; and the Lord rebuked them because they erred through not knowing the Scriptures and God’s power, since “they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (v. 30).

Indeed, against Sadducees holding such views, it would have sufficed for Him to remove the notion of bodily delight and to abolish these empty pleasures of bodies when their functions cease. [Note: [Col. 1045D] The Roman, Colbert, and Chartres manuscripts omit “pleasures”; then Colbert and Chartres read “to be,” and Rome “to deny,” in place of “to have abolished.”] But He added: “They shall be like the angels of God.” Therefore, since the mystery of the Scriptures and the power of God show that women will be like angels, the understanding that Scripture gives concerning angels ought likewise to govern our hope concerning women in the resurrection. [Note: [Col. 1045D–1046D] The common text reads “powers”: corruptly. Hilary thinks that women will be like angels after the resurrection on two grounds: Scripture and the divine power by which God can perform whatever He has declared in Scripture. Here he seems to agree with Tertullian, *On Women’s Dress*, I.2; Origen on Matthew, Huet edition, p. 487; and other Fathers, who on account of Christ’s words thought women would not rise in the female sex. Rufinus also reproaches Jerome with this view, on the basis of Jerome’s statements in Book III on Ephesians 5. Jerome, however, clears himself of it in *Apology*, ch. 6, and Epistle 27 to Eustochium, ch. 11. Augustine, *City of God*, II.17, says: “Defects will be removed from bodies; nature will be preserved.”] This is the answer given to the proposed question concerning the conditions of the resurrection.

5. The truth of eternal resurrection from the Law. — Against their unbelief concerning the resurrection itself, He spoke thus: “Have you not read what was spoken to you by God, saying: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead but of the living” (ibid. 31–32). This saying was addressed to Moses when these holy patriarchs had long since been at rest. Therefore those whose God He was had God. [Note: [Col. 1046D] All manuscripts omit “they had God.” But only six have earlier, “had long since been at rest”; therefore, “they had long since been.”] Yet they could have nothing if they did not exist, because it belongs to the nature of a thing that what belongs to another must necessarily exist. Thus, to have God belongs to the living; for God is eternity, and that which is eternal cannot belong to those who are dead. How, then, can those be denied to exist and to be destined always to exist, whose God Eternity declares Himself to be?

### 6. Pharisees puffed up by knowledge of the Law. Christ’s proper office.

But when the Pharisees heard that He had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together against Him; and one of them, a doctor of the Law, questioned Him, and so forth [Col. 1046C] (ibid. 34–35). The Pharisees succeed the Sadducees in testing Him. To the latter an answer concerning the resurrection had fittingly been given, so that they might be convicted that the faith of the resurrection to be hoped for was contained in that very Law from which they proceeded. But the Pharisees gloried in possessing knowledge of the Law, which, set forth beforehand as a figure of things to come, contained an image of the truth that would follow.

They ask which commandment in the Law is the greatest (v. 36), not discerning that the prefiguration of the Law was fulfilled in Christ.

> [Note: [Col. 1046D] “Meditation of the Law” is wrongly found in the Paris edition. Moreover, in Hilary *meditari* has nearly the same force as to prefigure something future. Thus, in ch. 21, no. 3: “The operation prefigures for the unwilling the faith of heavenly things.” More clearly, ch. 24, no. 1: “In all things the Law prefigured Christ’s coming”; and no. 3: “because in the Law they conceal the prefiguration of that truth which is in Christ.” In these and similar places, *meditatio* is a future reality foreshadowed by present deeds, whose meaning we attain only through this prefiguration. See *On Psalm* 118, book 2, no. 11.]

And indeed the answer to the ignorant insolence of those men is drawn from the very word of the Law: an answer containing in itself the whole doctrine of truth. For the proper office of our Lord Jesus Christ is to bring knowledge of God and to impart understanding of His name and power (see *On the Trinity*, book II, no. 22). For He had come, sent forth from eternity, and was accomplishing those things which were pleasing to God.

Therefore He answered that the first commandment is: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (v. 37). For He was accomplishing nothing other than what the Law contained, since the commandments of the Law embraced the pattern of those things which He Himself was to do. He therefore reminds them, from that knowledge which they boasted of possessing in the Law, that almighty God is to be loved with every affection of mind, heart, [Col. 1047B] and soul, so that the commandments of the Law set beforehand might confirm His admonition.

### 7. Christ is commanded to be loved under the name of neighbour.

Then He added: “This is the great and first commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (ibid. 38–39). But the following commandment, and its likeness, signify that in both there is the same obligation and the same merit—just as in ch. 4, no. 7, there is the same penalty. For love of God without Christ, or love of Christ without God, cannot be beneficial. Therefore neither, without the other, brings any gain toward our salvation.

And for this reason upon these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets (v. 40): because the whole Law and the Prophets were directed to Christ’s coming, and His coming, by fulfilling them, bestowed the understanding by which God is known. For we have frequently explained concerning “neighbour” that no one other than Christ is to be understood. For, when we are forbidden to place father, mother, or children before love of God, how is the love of one’s neighbour a commandment like that of loving God? Or will anything remain that can be made equal to the love of God? It is so only because the likeness of the commandment required an equal love for the Father and the Son.

### 8. Christ, David’s son according to the flesh, is David’s Lord.

And so that they might be refuted by the very words of the Law, and that [783] a clearer understanding of “neighbour” might be disclosed, He asks what they think concerning Christ: whose son He would be. They answered, “David’s.” To them He said: How was He called Lord by David in the Spirit, though He was to be David’s son? And how had David said: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet” (ibid. 42–44)?

It was indeed true that Christ was to be begotten from David’s seed. Yet the likeness of the name—by which Lord speaks to Lord—and His seating at the right hand until He should subject all enemies beneath His feet, signified both unity of substance through fellowship in the name, judgment through the invitation to sit, and power through the subjection of all things. Thus they might remember that He who sprang from David contained the substance of eternal power, authority, and origin, and that God would dwell in a man.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Concerning the seat of Moses upon which the scribes and Pharisees sat; concerning the kingdom of heaven shut by them; their devouring of widows’ houses; their traversing sea and land; their saying, “Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing”; their tithing mint and dill; their building the tombs of the prophets; and Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those sent to her [Col. 1048B].

### 1. The teaching of the Law commended. The Pharisees’ wickedness, ignorance, and pride.

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to His disciples, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat,” and so forth (Matt. 23:1–2). He set before them the glory of the Law which bore witness concerning Him, since it had expressed in itself an image of future truth. For in all things the Law prefigured Christ’s coming.

> [Note: [Col. 1047D] In six manuscripts, “it prefigured the coming”: less correctly, since *meditabatur* must be referred to the implicit noun “Law,” whose author, the Holy Spirit, in all its acts foresaw and prefigured the one Christ; [Col. 1048D] so that, although the Spirit of prophecy may have spoken through whatever person, the whole of it nevertheless concerns knowledge of the coming of our Lord, etc., as appears in the prologue to the book on the Psalms, no. 5.]

For whatever it contained was taken up for the advancement of making His knowledge manifest. He therefore commands obedience to the Pharisees’ precepts because they sat on Moses’ seat; He commands obedience to all the commandments of the Law, but abstention from their deeds and works, so that men’s conduct and unbelief, rather than the teaching of the Law, may be avoided.

For they lay the heaviest burdens of the Law upon the people subject to them, while not even moving a finger to touch them (ibid. v. 4). Indeed, they command that the Lord be loved with the whole heart and that one’s neighbour be loved as oneself, while they themselves, contrary to the testimony of the Law given to them, persecute God in Christ’s sufferings.

> [Note: [Col. 1048D] Thus the Paris edition, with the better manuscripts. Other books read, “God in Christ’s sufferings.”]

They also spread abroad the glory of their words like phylacteries [784] (v. 5), though God, the author of eternal life, is not understood by them in Christ. They display themselves as though fringes hanging from the garment of the Law’s honour, though ignorant of the whole Law and unable to recognize either its works or its power. They love the first reclining places at banquets, though they are assigned to eternal fire—while the Gentiles, who feast with Abraham, are preferred—and the chief seats in synagogues, though they do not know their Teacher according to the testimony of the Law and the Prophets [Col. 1048D] (v. 6). They also love greetings in the marketplace, though humility of heart and service toward all have been commanded them. They wish to be called teachers by men (v. 7), though ignorant of the Law’s teaching and rejecting the Teacher of everlasting salvation.

Since all these things were profane and perverse, they are condemned as examples not to be imitated in conduct. Yet hearing the Law and obeying its words are required, because those words spoke of Christ.

### 2. Precepts of love and humility.

[Col. 1049A] But, on the contrary, He now completes for His disciples, who knew themselves, the precepts of perfect humility: that they may remember that they are all brothers, that is, children of one parent; that by the generation of the new birth they have passed beyond the beginnings of earthly origin; that they all have one Teacher of heavenly doctrine; and that the glory of eternal honour is to be attained through consciousness of humility. For God will make arrogance lowly and raise humility into glory (ibid. vv. 8–12).

### 3. By rejecting Christ, the Pharisees shut heaven.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven” (v. 13).

> [Note: [Col. 1049D] The manuscripts read: “You shut . . . to shut.”]

He condemns their pretence by the signification of punishment. For “woe” is the voice of one grieving. He says that they shut the kingdom of heaven because in the Law they conceal the prefiguration of that truth which is in Christ, and hide beneath the pretence of teaching the bodily coming foretold by the prophets. They neither enter the way of eternity in Christ themselves, nor allow others to enter it.

### 4. Those who impose burdens upon others.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who devour widows’ houses” (v. 14). From this comes their denial of truth; from this, the hindrance of salvation for others and the closing of the kingdom of heaven: ambition is maintained through visiting widows’ houses; widows are despoiled under the pretence of lengthy prayer; from them heavenly knowledge is sought as though from a treasure of stored wealth; and the dignity of the Law persists in silence concerning grace. Therefore they will receive a greater judgment, because they will owe both the punishment for their own sin and liability for another’s ignorance [Col. 1049C].

### 5. Their hatred of the Gospel. Those to be punished doubly.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who traverse sea and land” (v. 15). By their journeying over sea and land He signifies that throughout the whole world they will disparage Christ’s Gospel and subject certain persons to the yoke of the Law against justification by faith; for proselytes are Gentiles received into the Synagogue. The rarity of those who would so become proselytes is indicated in the singular.

> [Note: [Col. 1049D] The printed editions read “is judged.” The manuscripts more correctly read “is indicated.”]

For after Christ’s preaching, faith in their teaching did not remain. But whoever has been gained for the people becomes a son of Gehenna, an offspring of punishment, and an heir of eternal judgment [785], because adoption from among the Gentiles was to make the family of Abraham. He will be a son of doubled punishment because he neither obtained the remission of sins belonging to the Gentiles nor avoided association with those who persecuted Christ [Col. 1049D].

### 6. The Law is a form of things to come; it is Christ’s seat and throne. Why it became useless when Christ came.

“Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing’” (ibid. v. 16). He reproves their reverence for human observances and their contempt for prophetic tradition: they bestowed honour upon worthless things and diminished the honour due to things worthy of honour. For He Himself had given the Law; and the Law did not contain fulfillment, but prefigured fulfillments.

For the adornment of altar and temple did not acquire dignity from worship, but fashioned from their beauty a figure of things to come. Gold, silver, bronze, electrum, pearls, and crystal each contain its proper signification according to the nature of the particular material. He therefore rebukes them for venerating the gold of the temple and the gifts of the altar for the religious significance of the mysteries, when the honour of both altar and temple was greater, since gold was dedicated to the temple and a gift to the altar as a figure of things to come.

Therefore, when Christ came, reliance on the Law became useless: for Christ was not sanctified in the Law, but the Law was sanctified in Christ, in which a seat and throne had, as it were, been set for Him.

> [Note: [Col. 1049D] That is, a seat and throne have been set for Christ. Since Christ is regarded as sacred—that is, worthy of religious reverence [Col. 1050D] (the reading “was regarded,” in the Lipsian and Paris editions, is less good)—the Law must necessarily have received religious reverence from Him who sits upon that throne of the Law. Thus we emend from six manuscripts. The other manuscripts do not differ in sense, for they read “had sat down.” But the earlier printed editions wrongly read “may sit.”]

Since He is held worthy of religious reverence, it necessarily received reverence from Him who sits in it. Thus they are foolish and blind in venerating what has been sanctified while passing over Him who sanctifies (v. 17).

### 7. External works, though not to be omitted, must yield to inward virtues.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill and every herb,” and so forth (ibid. v. 23). He rebukes the hidden mind and obscure wickedness of their wills: they perform what the Law prescribes concerning tithes of mint and dill, so that men may think they fulfill the Law, but they have abandoned mercy, justice, faith, and every disposition of goodwill, which is the proper duty of a human being.

For that tithing of herbs, useful as a prefiguration of things to come, ought not to be omitted. Yet this must be done in such a way that, fulfilling the requirements of faith, justice, and mercy, we please God by works—not through an imitation devised for display, but through the truth of a will retained. And because it would be a lesser offence to omit the tithing of herbs than the duty of goodwill, He mocks their diligence in straining out gnats, while they are careless in swallowing camels—that is, avoiding light sins and devouring grave ones [Col. 1050C] (v. 24).

A corresponding denunciation of punishment also applies to those who cleanse the outside of cups and dishes while failing to cleanse what is within them (v. 25), and who pursue the display of useless zeal but abandon the service of perfect usefulness. For the use of a cup is inward: if it has become foul, what benefit is there in having washed it outwardly? Therefore the brightness of the inward conscience must be attained, so that what belongs to the body may be cleansed outwardly (v. 26). [Col. 1050D]

He also compared them to tombs, which shine through human workmanship and adornment [786], yet inwardly are foul with the bones of the dead and the uncleanness of corpses (v. 27): that is, they set before men a comely appearance of righteousness in empty words, while within they possess the stench of their own conscience and mind.

### 8. The Jews know that the prophets were killed through hatred of truth.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets,” and so forth (v. 29). [Col. 1051A] The pattern of judgment is fixed; and from the nature of perception and the judgment of fairness, each of us is charged accordingly, so that one has less need of pardon for wickedness in proportion as equity has not been unknown.

> [Note: [Col. 1051D] “And” is lacking in many manuscripts; according to them, the word *sensus* will be understood less suitably in the genitive.]

For the people of the Law killed all the prophets. They were inflamed against them in hatred, through the bitterness of rebuke. For the prophets publicly reproved that people’s thefts, murders, adulteries, and sacrileges. Because they declared them unworthy of the heavenly kingdom on account of these deeds, and foretold that the Gentiles would become heirs of God’s covenant, they were destroyed by various forms of punishment.

But the descendants so detested their parents’ deeds that they venerate the books of prophecy, adorn their memorials, and restore their tombs; and by such reverence they testify that they stand outside the guilt of their ancestral crime.

### 9. They are all the more guilty of Christ’s murder, since He is the work of the prophets. Titles of the Apostles.

[Col. 1051B] Therefore, those who acknowledge that the prophets were killed with most grievous guilt—by what pardon will they condemn Christ, who is the work of the prophets, when they commit, with multiplied wickedness, the very deeds which they detest?

> [Note: [Col. 1051D] The printed editions read “the aim of the prophets,” contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and to Hilary’s manner of speaking. Above, in ch. 1, no. 3, we read: “Conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, He is the work of all the prophets”; and in the prologue to the book on the Psalms, no. 5, of the Pharisees: “For, in denying Christ, whose coming is the work of the prophets, they have taken away the key of knowledge.”]

Therefore they are serpents and a brood of vipers, because they will fill up the measure of their fathers’ will (v. 33). And how will they escape judgment, since they denounce the slaughter of the prophets while persecuting their Lord unto death on the cross?

> [Note: [Col. 1051D] The printed editions read “even unto death on the cross.” Three manuscripts more elegantly read “and their Lord,” etc.]

Because of the Apostles—who are prophets by revelation of things to come, wise men by knowledge of Christ, scribes by understanding of the Law—whom they would beat, stone, crucify, and drive from city to city, all the blood of the righteous, from Abel to Zechariah, fell back upon them (ibid. vv. 34–35).

> [Note: [Col. 1051D] Six manuscripts read “so that by those whom.” Since *quibus* is referred not only to “obeyed,” but also to “granted,” it is spoken both of the Apostles and of the Jews.]

Had they obeyed those Apostles, pardon would have had to be granted for their own crimes [Col. 1051C]; but because they killed these same men, punishment for their fathers’ crimes also accumulated upon those who killed them.

> [Note: [Col. 1051D] The editions of Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius read “pardon would have been granted.” The Paris edition, with four manuscripts, reads “pardon to be granted,” omitting the preceding word “would have been.” Shortly afterward Lipsius substituted *cogeretur* (“would be compelled”) for *congereretur* (“would be heaped up”); [Col. 1052D] several manuscripts support him, reading *congeretur*.]

### 10. Christ’s disposition toward the Jews.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you,” and so forth (v. 37). Amid many kinds of rebuke He continually declares the affection of His mercy; His entire complaint is that they refused to return to the salvation which He offered. For Jerusalem had killed the prophets and stoned those sent to her. In naming the city, the crime of its inhabitants is shown.

Therefore the blood of Abel and Zechariah is shown as about to come upon their descendants: [787] because Christ, already dwelling and preaching among them, had suffered. If He had been believed—when He was proclaimed by the Apostles immediately after His passion and resurrection—not only would the faith of those who believed have stood outside the punishment for the murder of the prophets, but it would also have obtained pardon for that very judgment passed concerning the Lord’s passion.

> [Note: [Col. 1052D] Thus the better manuscripts. Others, with the printed editions, read “had been.” Above, after the words “if He had been believed,” supply: “when He was proclaimed by the Apostles immediately after His passion and resurrection.”]

But since He was not believed even after His resurrection, vengeance for the blood of Abel and Zechariah will also be demanded from them.

### 11. The hen’s work. The twofold birth of chicks. What Christ offered the Jews. Their punishment.

Although He speaks these things bodily—that is, as a man made so by assuming flesh—and, found as a man, offers help to all, He nevertheless often wished to gather them through the preaching of the prophets.

> [Note: [Col. 1052D] The Roman manuscript reads “help for all”; the Colbert and Corbie manuscripts, “help for all things.” Earlier, *corporeus* means “made man by assuming flesh.” See *Exposition on Psalm* 138, no. 10.]

But He bestowed this affection fruitlessly and in vain. Like a hen gathering her chicks, He wished to keep them beneath His wings: having become, that is, a bird now earthly and domestic, granting to His chicks, through a kind of covering of His body like wings, the warmth of immortal life, and bringing them forth into flight as though by a new birth.

> [Note: [Col. 1052D] Six manuscripts read “a new generation.” This reading too may be admitted, signifying that a new kind of creature—namely, a winged animal from an egg—is produced.]

For chicks have one manner of being born and another of flying.

> [Note: [Col. 1052D] The printed editions, with three manuscripts, read “another manner of living.” This is altered on the authority of the other manuscripts, since thereafter the argument concerns the manner of flying rather than of life. Here, moreover, *to fly*, and shortly afterward *flight*, signify the capacity for flying, not the act.]

At first they are enclosed within the shell of eggs as though in a prison of the body; afterward, warmed by the parent’s care, they emerge into flight. Therefore, after the manner of this familiar and almost earthly bird, He wished to gather them within Himself, so that those already brought forth by their natural birth might now, reborn by the birth of another generation and warmed by the one who cherishes them, fly upward into the heavenly kingdom as though with winged bodies.

But because they refused, their house shall be left desolate and empty (v. 38), that is, they shall be unworthy of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. For they began to be their own house rather than God’s; [Col. 1052C] and, remaining in the obstinacy of unbelief, they shall not see Him until the time when they will bless Him returning in the Lord’s name, even by the unwilling confession of their unbelief (v. 39).

## CHAPTER XXV

Concerning the disciples’ question about the structure of the temple; those upon the roof, that they should not descend to take anything from the house; those in the field, that they should not return to take their cloak; and pregnant and nursing women.

### 1. The human being, God’s eternal temple.

“And He went out from the temple and was departing; and His disciples came to show Him the structure of the temple” (Matt. 24:1). After the threat that Jerusalem would be forsaken, the magnificence of its construction [788] [Col. 1053A] was shown Him as though He could be moved by ambition for the temple.

> [Note: [Col. 1052D] Six manuscripts read “after the warning.”]

He said that all would be destroyed and that the stones of its entire foundation would be scattered and overthrown. For the eternal temple was consecrated as a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit: namely, the human being, made worthy to become God’s dwelling-place through acknowledgment of the Son, confession of the Father, and obedience to the commandments.

> [Note: [Col. 1053D] Six manuscripts read “a worthy dwelling-place.” The wording will be less involved if arranged thus: “namely, the human being, through acknowledgment of the Son, etc., made worthy to become a dwelling-place for God,” with *habitaculum* in the dative. In *On Psalm* 131, no. 6: “This was the greatest work for our Lord: that He might render a human being, instructed in divine knowledge, worthy of God’s dwelling-place”; and no. 7: “For this reason He was obedient even unto death on a cross: that He might make us worthy of God’s habitation.”]

### 2. The time and signs of Jerusalem’s overthrow. Simon the Samaritan.

And when He had withdrawn to the mountain, the disciples approached Him privately and asked when these things would happen, and by what sign they might know His coming and the consummation of the age (v. 3). Since these three things were asked as one, they are distinguished by separate indications both of time and of meaning.

The first answer, therefore, concerns the city’s fall; and they are strengthened by the truth of doctrine, lest some deceiver steal upon the ignorant.

> [Note: [Col. 1053D] The Colbert manuscript, with the Corbie manuscript, reads “lest any deception”; and then after “for those who were to come,” they add “are foretold.” The Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius editions read “were.”]

For even in their own time people would come who would call themselves Christ. Therefore, so that faith might be withheld from destructive falsehood, warning came first. For Simon the Samaritan came, instructed by the devil in both deeds and words, and perverted many by miracles of his works. And because this applied to the Apostles’ time, He says: “The end is not yet.” But not even then will the end be, when nations rise against one another and kingdoms clash, and there are famines and earthquakes; for in these things there is not the dissolution of this whole world, but the beginning of sorrows, since all evils will thenceforth begin.

> [Note: [Col. 1054D] The word “is” is supplied by many manuscripts here; it is the work of an interpolator, who earlier substituted “dissolution” for “there is dissolution.”]

He therefore confirms them for endurance of persecution, flight, scourging, death, and the public hatred of the Gentiles directed against them because of His name. In these afflictions many will be troubled, will be scandalized by such evils rising up, and will be stirred even to mutual hatred. There will also be false prophets—such as Nicholas, one of the seven deacons—and they will pervert many by a truth falsely professed; and, as wickedness abounds, love will grow cold. But salvation is reserved for those who persevere to the end. Then, when apostolic men have been dispersed throughout every region of the world, the truth of the Gospel will be preached (ibid. vv. 4–13).

And when knowledge of the heavenly mystery has been brought to all, then Jerusalem’s fall and end will come upon her, so that the punishment and terror of the uprooted city may follow as confirmation of the preaching. These things, therefore, were fulfilled in her as had been foretold: the Apostles were stoned, driven out, and killed; and she was consumed by famine, war, and captivity. Then she proved worthy not to exist, since, by expelling Christ’s preachers, she showed herself unworthy of God’s preaching [Col. 1053D].

### 3. The sign of Christ’s coming. Why Antichrist is the abomination of desolation.

Next follows the sign [Col. 1054A] of the future coming: when they see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, then the return of glory is to be understood. Since blessed Daniel and Paul have spoken of this, I think it superfluous to add words (Dan. 9:27; 2 Thess. 2:4): for He spoke these things concerning the times of Antichrist.

He is called an abomination because, coming against God, he claims for himself the honour [789] of God; and the abomination of desolation because, through wars and slaughter, he will desolate the earth with sacrilege. Therefore, received by the Jews, he will stand in the place of sanctification, so that where God was invoked by the prayers of the saints, there he may be reverenced by unbelievers as worthy of God’s honour.

> [Note: [Col. 1054D] Some manuscripts read “will stand.”]

### 4. Why Judaea must be abandoned.

And because this will be the peculiar error of the Jews—that those who rejected truth will receive falsehood—He commands Judaea to be abandoned and that they flee to the mountains (v. 16), lest violence or contagion result from association with the people who will believe Antichrist; rather, for all who then remain faithful, the mountain wilderness will be safer than the crowded places of Judaea.

> [Note: [Col. 1054D] In the Paris edition, “violence” is absent. In other editions, the word has been corruptly joined with what follows: “seen, so that contagion.”]

> [Note: [Col. 1054D] Thus with the Colbert and Chartres manuscripts. Others read, “the crowded walls of Judaea.” The Paris edition reads “crowded Judaea.” The reading of Bad., Erasmus, and Lipsius, “crowded places of Judaea,” with *places* understood, would not be displeasing.]

### 5. Let one on the summit of perfection not descend through desire for earthly things.

But when He says, “Let him who is on the roof not descend to take anything out of his house” (v. 17), this command, understood merely humanly, admits neither the logic of the saying nor of the action. For one who is on a roof and is about to leave Judaea cannot depart unless he descends from it. Or what benefit is there in standing on the roof rather than remaining in the house?

But we have frequently warned that the particular force of words and places must be considered, so that we may grasp the import of heavenly commandments. The roof is the summit of a house and the lofty perfection of the whole dwelling. No house can be called or exist without a roof. Therefore, whoever has reached the completion of his house—that is, stands in the perfection of his body, made new by regeneration, exalted in spirit, and perfected by the completion of the divine gift—ought not to descend through desire for lower worldly things, nor, enticed by the lower pleasures of the body, withdraw from the height of his roof.

> [Note: [Col. 1054D] The printed editions and three manuscripts read “inward.”]

“And let him who is in the field not return to take his cloak” (v. 18). That is, one placed in the work of the commandment must not return to former cares, nor desire any bodily coverings, for the sake of which, if he returns, he will again put on the cloak of those old sins by which he was formerly covered [Col. 1054D].

### 6. Nothing is evil to a human being except through his own fault. Pregnant women: souls weighed down by sins.

“Woe to pregnant women and those nursing” (v. 19). In a simple sense, this may be understood because flight is delayed: those impeded by the burden of the womb find it difficult to escape the imminent ruin of the times. But what have the condition, sex, and order of generation deserved? Unless perhaps that age of women which falls into those times is uniquely destined to be cursed. But far be it that anything should become evil to a human being except through that person’s own fault.

Therefore we must not believe that, when He says, “Woe to pregnant women,” the Lord warns concerning the burden of fetuses; rather, He shows the heaviness of souls filled with sins, which, neither stationed upon the roof nor remaining in the field, cannot escape the storm of wrath laid up for them. For pain attends pregnant women by nature, and childbirth does not come forth without distress to the whole body. Whatever souls, then, are found to be such will be held in their own burden and pain [Col. 1055B].

[790] Woe also will be to those who are being nursed. Childhood after weaning is no less incapable of flight than childhood still fed with milk. And how can there be woe to one who is being nursed, since there is no difference in age or time between being nourished with milk and having left milk behind? Here likewise He indicates the weakness of souls which are still fed, as though with milk, toward the knowledge of God: they lack the strength of solid food and are imbued with a slender and feeble taste of divine knowledge. Therefore woe will be to them, because, being too weak to escape Antichrist and untrained to endure, they will neither escape sins nor receive the food of the true bread.

### 7. What flight in winter or on the Sabbath means.

For this reason we are instructed to pray that our flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath [Col. 1055C]: that is, lest we be found either in sin through coldness or in idleness from good works. For a grievous and unbearable tribulation will come upon all, unless, for the sake of God’s elect, those days are shortened, so that the shortened time permitted for the advancing force of the evils at hand may overcome them (ibid. vv. 20–21).

### 8. The attempts of false prophets. Eagles: the saints. Christ’s coming is where His passion was.

And because false prophets, appearing to those in great tribulation to point out present help in Christ, will falsely claim that Christ is present and available in many places, in order to lead down the oppressed and afflicted into Antichrist’s service—they will say now that He is in deserted places, in order to corrupt by error, and now assert that He is in inner chambers, in order to confine them under the power of the ruler—yet the Lord declares that He will not be hidden in a place nor be seen individually. Rather, He will be present everywhere and before the sight of all in the manner of lightning, which, rising in the east, spreads its light as far as the regions of the west and, flashing from any direction, is seen everywhere (ibid. vv. 22–27).

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] The printed editions read “ruling.” The manuscripts more correctly read “of the ruler,” namely Antichrist. Then, “not individually”: that is, not by persons who are private and set apart, contrasted afterward with being in the sight of all.]

And so that we might not be ignorant even of the place where He would be, He says: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (ibid. v. 28). He called the saints eagles because of the flight of their spiritual body; and He showed that, when the angels gather them, their assembly will be in the place of His passion.

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] Light is thrown upon Hilary’s interpretation by Jerome’s words on this passage: “We may understand the body—that is, πτῶμα, which in Latin is more expressively called *cadaver*, from its falling through death—to mean Christ’s passion.”]

Rightly will the coming of glory be awaited there where, through the passion of bodily humility, He wrought for us the glory of eternity.

[791]

## CHAPTER XXVI

Concerning the darkening of the sun, the moon, and the stars. (Concerning the sign of the fig tree, the uncertainty of the day of the Lord’s coming, those taken and left, and the vigilance to be maintained. These are absent from the manuscripts.)

### 1. When and what Christ’s glorious coming will be.

[Col. 1056B] “Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened,” and so forth (Matt. 24:29).
