He indicates the glory of His coming and the return of His splendor by the darkening of the sun, the failure of the moon, the falling of the stars, the shaking of the heavenly powers, the appearance of the saving sign, the lamentation of the nations as they recognize the Son of Man in God’s glory, and the sending of angels to gather the saints with a trumpet—that is, with the summons of now public liberty (vv. 30–31).

Thus the mustard seed becomes a great tree (Matt. 13:31); thus the mountain, from the stone that shattered the image, occupies the world (Dan. 2:34); thus the city is visible to all (Matt. 5:14–15); thus the light shines for all upon the wood; thus, from the humility of death, comes God’s glory.

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] Bad. and Erasmus read “in flax.” The Paris edition reads “on a lampstand,” a reading first supplied by Lipsius himself. For all manuscripts read [Col. 1056D] “upon the wood,” by which the wood of the cross is suitably understood: upon it, as upon a lampstand, Christ the true Light made Himself visible to all. Thus above, ch. 4, no. 13: “Now the lamp of Christ . . . suspended in the passion of the wood, will provide eternal light for those dwelling in the Church.”]

> [Note: [Col. 1056D] The printed editions, with most manuscripts, read “the God of glory.” With the Colbert and Corbie manuscripts we prefer “God’s glory.” For there is undoubtedly an allusion to the words of Paul in Phil. 2, in which Christ is proclaimed to be in God’s glory because He humbled Himself even to death on a cross.]

By the sign of all these things He wished us to know the time of our redemption, when we shall be transferred from the corruption of our bodies into the honour of spiritual substance [Col. 1056C].

### 2. The branch of the fig tree: Antichrist. Its putting forth leaves.

He set the sign for recognizing the time in the comparison of the fig tree (Matt. 24:32): when its branch is tender and puts forth leaves, summer is understood to be near. But the nature both of summer and of the tree is altogether otherwise. For at the beginning of spring it swells; and there is no small interval between the time when summer comes on and when the tree’s branch becomes tender into leaves. From this it must be understood that the saying is not about a tree.

Indeed, above we have already discussed the particular character of this tree (ch. 21, no. 8). We read that Adam was clothed with its leaves and covered the shame of conscience: that is, he was surrounded under the Law as though with the garment of sin. Therefore the branch of the fig tree is understood to be Antichrist, the devil’s son, the portion of sin, the champion of the Law. When he begins to become tender and put forth leaves [Col. 1057A], then summer is understood to be near—that is, the day of judgment. His putting forth leaves will be recognized by a certain green flourishing of exultant sinners: for then there will be the flower of criminals, the honour of evildoers, and favour toward the profane. Yet summer—that is, the heat of eternal fire—is near to them.

3. And so that faith in future events might be assured, he added, by saying “Amen” in a profession of truth, that our generation cannot pass away until all these things have run their course; and that those things thought firm—namely heaven and earth—will not endure, whereas his words cannot fail to be. For the former, having proceeded from the condition of their creation, that is, having come forth from nothing (manuscripts: *perfecta*, “completed”), contain within themselves the necessity of not existing; but the latter, derived from eternity, contain within themselves the power to remain (ibid., 34–35).

4. Why the end of the times was not fixed.—Concerning the end of the times, he relieved us of anxious concern by saying that that day is known to no one, and is unknown not only to the angels but also to himself (ibid., 36). O mercy beyond measure of divine goodness! Did God the Father deny knowledge of the day, with the purpose of concealing it from the Son, when the Son himself said: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. 11:27)? Then not all things are his, if there is something withheld.

But because he was to convey to us all things received from the Father, and because the Word of God contains in himself faith not so much in what is future as in what has been accomplished, the day was therefore placed outside definition: so that, although God indulgently grants us abundant time for repentance, he might nevertheless keep us continually watchful through fear of uncertainty. And, by revealing to no one his purpose in appointing this day, he might not, by any definition of what he had declared, restrain anyone’s repentance; because, as in the time of the Flood, while all are engaged in the course of this life in acting and enduring, that great day will come (Matt. 24:38).

[Note: The word “giving” is missing in the Bec manuscript. Hilary means that Christ did not disclose the time at which God decreed this day, lest he restrain anyone’s repentance. For this reason we have altered the punctuation: in earlier printed editions the words “the will of giving this day” were connected not with “by speaking,” but with “restrain.” See a fuller and clearer explanation in *On the Trinity*, book IX, §57 ff.]

[Note: The printed editions and several manuscripts read “and repenting.” But the Roman, Colbert, Carnotensis, and Vatican manuscripts read “and enduring.” In Hincmar, *On Predestination*, ch. 19, where this and the following material are inserted, the reading is “and acting.”]

5. The distinction between believers and unbelievers; between Jews who believe and those who do not; between heretics and Catholics.—Indeed, he also showed that a distinction would be made when believers are taken up: of two men in a field, one is taken and the other left; of two women grinding, one is rejected and the other chosen; and of two who are in bed, one is joined [to Christ] and the other abandoned. In leaving some and taking others, he teaches the distinction between unbelievers and believers. For when the wrath of God grows heavy, the saints, as the prophet says, will be stored away in storehouses; but the faithless will be left as fuel for the heavenly fire (Matt. 3:12).

Thus the day of the Lord will overtake two in a field—two peoples, believers and unbelievers—in the world, as in the work of this life; yet they will be separated, one left and the other taken up. The same reasoning applies to the women grinding. The mill is the work of the Law. But since one part of the Jews, as it believed through the apostles, will likewise believe through Elijah and be justified by faith, one woman will be taken through that same faith in good work; while the other will be left in the fruitless work of the Law, grinding in vain and not making bread of heavenly food.

[Note: The Carnotensis manuscript, with the Colbert manuscript, reads: “the other, however, fruitless.”]

But the two in bed are those who proclaim the same repose of the Lord’s Passion, concerning which there is one and the same confession among heretics and Catholics. Yet because Catholic truth will proclaim the unity of Father and Son, and their common *theoteta*—that is, what we call deity—while heretical falsehood will in turn assail that same truth with countless insults, one of the two in bed will be left and the other taken up. For, in taking one and leaving the other, the judgment of the divine decision will demonstrate the faith of each confession.

[Note: The Paris edition, with some manuscripts, reads “and their communion”; later, without authority, “their *theotetas*,” where Sirmond, in Hincmar’s *On Predestination*, ch. 19, printed *theoteia*, a word neither Greek nor Latin. See the observations on ch. 16, §4.]

6. The necessity of watchfulness.—And so that we might know that this silence regarding the day, kept from all, was not without the purpose of useful silence, he warned us to watch because of the coming of the thief, and, sustained by assiduous prayers, to cling to all the works of his commandments (Matt. 24:43). He shows that the devil is the thief: sleeplessly intent on stripping us of our spoils and lying in wait for the houses of our bodies, so that, when we are careless and given over to sleep, he may pierce them with the darts of his devices and enticements. Therefore we must be ready, because ignorance of the day stirs up an eager concern of suspended expectation.

## CHAPTER XXVII. [Col. 1058C] On the faithful servant whom the Lord set over his household; on the ten virgins; on the man who went abroad and entrusted his property to his servants.

1. Leaders especially must watch. The work and reward of a diligent leader.—“Who then is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord set over his household?” etc. (Matt. 24:45). Although he exhorts us all generally to the unwearied care of watchfulness, he nevertheless lays upon the leaders of the people—that is, bishops—a special vigilance in expectation of, and at, his coming. For by this faithful and prudent servant, set over the household, he signifies one who cares for the advantages and welfare of the people entrusted to him.

If he is obedient to what is said and submits to the commandments—that is, if by the aptness and truth of doctrine he strengthens the weak, restores what has been broken, corrects what is warped, and dispenses the word of life as the food of eternity for the nourishment of the household—and if he is found doing and persisting in these things, he will obtain glory from the Lord as a faithful steward and useful manager; and he will be set over all goods, that is, placed in the glory of God, because there is nothing beyond it that is better (v. 47).

[Note: Many manuscripts read “whereby,” rather than “because,” not badly. The reason is here given why one placed in glory is said to be set over all goods: namely, because that glory surpasses every good, and nothing is better than it.]

2. The vices and punishment of the negligent.—But if, observing the long patience of God, which is extended for the advancement of human salvation, he behaves arrogantly toward his fellow servants and gives himself over to the evils and vices of the world, devoting his attention only to present things in the service of his belly, the Lord will come on an unexpected day. He will separate him from the goods he had promised and assign his portion with the hypocrites in everlasting punishment: because he despaired of the coming, because he did not obey the commandments, because he pursued present things, because he lived the life of the Gentiles, because, through despair of judgment, he afflicted with hunger, thirst, and slaughter the household entrusted to him (ibid., 48–51).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the Lord’s day having been despaired of,” less well. *Desperata* here means “unhoped-for,” “unlooked-for,” or “unexpected.”]

3. Why Moses received the Decalogue on two tablets.—“Then the kingdom of heaven shall be likened to ten virgins,” and what follows (Matt. 25:1). From the preceding statements, the rationale of this discourse too may be understood. For the whole discourse concerns the great day of the Lord, when the hidden things of human thoughts will be disclosed by the knowledge of divine judgment, and true faith in the God awaited will receive the reward of unambiguous hope. For in the five prudent and five foolish virgins the division between believers and unbelievers is plainly established; and Moses received the ten words inscribed upon two tablets according to this example. For it was necessary that all of them be inscribed on each tablet; and the double page, by the distinction of right and left, marked the division of good and evil under one covenant.

4. A brief and incisive exposition of the parable of the virgins.—The bridegroom and bride are our Lord, God in the body. For as the Spirit is bridegroom to the flesh, so the flesh is bride to the Spirit. Accordingly, when the trumpet sounds, only the bridegroom goes forth to meet [the Lord]; for the two were already one, because the humility of the flesh had passed into spiritual glory. At the first going forth, by the duties of this life, we are prepared to meet the resurrection from the dead.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “they go forth,” with the same sense. The printed editions then read “for both will be”; contrary to all manuscripts and to Hilary’s meaning, which is that only the bridegroom, not the bride also, goes forth to meet him. For in Christ the flesh, which is the bride, after glorification is so united with the Spirit and deity that its distinction no longer appears. Yet this is said without prejudice to the reality of the flesh, as has repeatedly been shown. This is also evident from *Exposition of Psalm 65*, §12: “The nature of the flesh assumed from the Virgin is transferred into his eternal glory.” Nor is it doubtful that, in *Exposition of Psalm 138*, §27, he says that Christ after the resurrection is seen in the same body in which he died; and shortly afterward, that he sits at God’s right hand in the body in which he was taken up. See *Exposition of Psalm 131*, §16, note.]

The lamps, then, are the light of shining souls, which shone through the sacrament of baptism. The oil is the fruit of good work. The vessels are human bodies, within whose inward parts the treasure of a good conscience must be stored. The sellers are those who, needing the mercy of the faithful, render in exchange what is requested of them: namely, in satisfaction of their need, they sell the consciousness of our good work. For this is the abundant material of unwearied light, which must both be bought and stored by the fruits of mercy.

[Note: The Baden, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions read “buying,” against all manuscripts. Although rightly changed in the first Paris edition, this reading was wrongly restored in the last. Hilary calls the poor “sellers”: they need the alms of the faithful and, in return for the contribution that supplies their need, sell or render the consciousness of a good work. We have already seen *veneo* used actively in ch. 21, §4, and ch. 10, §18. Thus a kind of exchange takes place when the rich person gives money and receives from the poor person the consciousness of a good work.]

The wedding is the assumption into immortality and the union, through a new fellowship, between corruption and incorruption. The bridegroom’s delay is the time of repentance. The sleep of those waiting is the rest of believers, and the temporary death of all during the time of repentance. The cry at midnight is, while all are ignorant, the sound of the trumpet announcing the Lord’s coming and rousing all to go out to meet the bridegroom. The taking up of the lamps is the return of souls into bodies; and their light is the conscience made bright by good work, contained in the small vessels of bodies.

5. At Christ’s coming no one will be helped by another’s merits. There will then be no time for repentance.—The prudent virgins are those who, embracing the timely opportunity to work while in their bodies, prepared themselves for the first encounter with the Lord’s coming. The foolish, however, are those who, lax and negligent, have had concern only for present things and, forgetful of God’s promises, have extended themselves toward no hope of resurrection.

And because the foolish cannot go forth to meet him with their lamps extinguished, they entreat the prudent to lend them oil (v. 8). The prudent reply that they cannot give it, lest perhaps there not be enough for all (v. 9): that is, no one is to be assisted by the works and merits of others, because each lamp must buy its own oil. They urge them to return and buy it, so that even late, by obeying God’s commandments, they may be made worthy to meet the bridegroom with the light of their lamps.

[Note: Those who read this passage carelessly may perhaps think it favors the heterodox who reject the suffrages and intercession of the saints. Bodius in his *Collectanea* does in fact object it to Catholics. But they do not see what helps them. The question here is not whether the saints provide for us, but whether the saints can so share their merits that others, departing this life devoid of their own merits, can obtain entrance with the bridegroom into eternal glory through the assistance of another’s merits. What Catholic would deny that these merits are so proper to each person that they cannot be transferred to another? Therefore each person must buy oil for his own lamp, and no one else can suffice for one who lacks it. For salvation or condemnation will befall each person according to what he has done.

Yet though the saints are not granted the power to enrich from their own merits those who lack merits, they are granted the power to assist us while we live here, so that we may be able to act rightly and acquire merits. Indeed, Hilary here indicates, under the name of the prudent virgins, who assist the foolish by good counsel and by urging them to repentance, that the saints are concerned for our salvation. He teaches this more explicitly in *Exposition of Psalm 124*, §5: “Nor are the guardianships of the saints lacking to those who wish to stand, nor the defenses of angels”; and in §6: “And lest we should think that there is slight aid in apostles, patriarchs, prophets, or rather angels, who encircle the Church with a certain guardianship,” etc.; and shortly afterward: “But perhaps the guardianship of apostles or angels may be judged sufficient. Indeed it is.”

If the saints provide for us, what is more fitting than that we direct our minds toward them, pray that they not fail us, and finally show them some gratitude for benefits received? In these statements there seems no reason why Bellarmine, who cites Hilary as an advocate of the invocation of saints, should, as Scultetus wishes, be put to shame. Rather, Scultetus makes himself ridiculous: first he denies that Hilary is an advocate of this view; then, forgetting his own proposition, he affirms that Hilary teaches only allegorically that departed saints are guardians of the faithful. “No allegory,” he says, “establishes faith.” What does he mean by “allegorically”? Does Hilary not assert this in clear, lucid, and wholly non-allegorical words? The issue is not whether this teaching concerning the saints is contained in Scripture in some manner, but whether Hilary advocated it. There is far less room for doubt on that point when he proclaims it from Scriptures understood allegorically. For since this mode of interpretation customarily applies a truth otherwise known and clear to certain obscure passages of Scripture, it follows that Hilary thought to be known by all what he shows to be contained in Scripture understood allegorically.]

While they delay, the bridegroom enters; and the wise virgins, who are clothed in the acquired light of their lamps, enter with him into the wedding, that is, at the very coming of the Lord’s brightness they proceed into heavenly glory (v. 10). Since there is then no more time for repentance, the foolish run up and ask that the entrance be opened to them. The bridegroom replies, “I do not know you” (v. 12). For they had not been present for the service owed to the one who came; they had not run to meet the trumpet’s awakening call; nor had they joined the company entering in. Delaying and unworthy, they lost the time for entering the wedding.

6. Talents distributed according to the measure of faith.—“For it is like a man going abroad, who called his servants and entrusted his property to them,” and what follows (v. 14). The division of money is unequal; but the difference is not to be ascribed to the one who divides it. For he says that each received according to his own ability. Therefore each received insofar as he was capable; and what lay within the recipient’s capacity was outside the discretion of the one allotting it.

By the master of the household he signifies himself. The period of travel is the interval of repentance, during which, seated in heaven at the right hand of God, he permitted to the whole human race the power of faith and Gospel action. Thus each person, according to the measure of his faith, received a talent—that is, the preaching of the Gospel—from a preacher. This is the incorruptible substance; this is Christ’s inheritance reserved for eternal heirs.

7. The recipient of five talents.—But that servant who received five talents (v. 20) is the people who believe from the Law. Having come from it, this people rightly and worthily doubled its merit by the working of Gospel faith. The rendering of account is the examination of judgment, in which the use of the heavenly word and the return on the talent administered are required. Thus he to whom five talents had been entrusted, when the Lord returned, offered ten from the five: that is, he was found in faith such as he had been in the Law, having fulfilled by the grace of Gospel justification the obedience to the precepts of the ten words through the five books of Moses. He is therefore commanded to enter into the joy of the Lord; that is, he is received into the honor of Christ’s glory (v. 21).

[Note: Printed editions read “having discharged”; the better manuscripts read “having discharged,” agreeing with “people,” and some have the feminine form.]

8. The recipient of two.—But the servant entrusted with two talents (v. 22) is the people of the Gentiles, justified by faith and confession both of the Son and of the Father, and confessing our Lord Jesus Christ as God and man, both in Spirit and flesh. For faith is in the heart and confession in the mouth. These, therefore, are the two talents entrusted to this servant.

[Note: We add the particle “and” on the authority of the Colbert and Carnotensis manuscripts. By it the two talents are expressed more distinctly: the first is faith in the mystery of the Holy Trinity, the second faith in the Incarnation.]

But just as the former servant had known the whole mystery in the five talents—that is, in the Law—and doubled that same mystery by faith in the Gospel, so this one, through the increase of the two talents, and by works, gained that same thing. Though the accounting and return differ, the reward from the Lord is the same for both, so that we might recognize the faith of the Gentiles as made equal to the knowledge of those who believe from the Law. For with the same commendation he is commanded to enter into the joy of the Lord (v. 23). The doubling of the money received is that he has added the working of faith and has performed in deeds and actions what he believed in conviction.

[Note: The printed editions read “and by works”; six manuscripts read “understanding and works.” We prefer, with the better manuscripts, “and gained that same thing by works,” where “that same thing” is understood. This reading is obscure because of its brevity and may be explained thus: the people of the Gentiles are to be understood to have doubled what they received by faith through the increase of the two talents, and to have gained that same thing—namely, those two talents—by the doing of those things which faith commands. In one word: as the people of the Law, through the addition of Gospel faith, double their talents, so too the faithful people double theirs when they attest in works what they believe in heart and confess with mouth.]

9. The recipient of one talent.—He who received one talent and hid it in the earth (v. 24) is the people persisting in the Law: wholly fleshly and dull, understanding nothing spiritual, and not admitting the power of Gospel preaching. Yet, through envy at the salvation of the Gentiles, it hid the talent it had received in the earth, neither using it itself nor administering it for others to use, but thinking the Law sufficient for its salvation. Therefore, when an account was demanded of it, it said: “I was afraid of you” (v. 25), as though it abstained from the exercise of Gospel freedom out of reverence and fear for the ancient commandments, and said, “See, you have what is yours,” as though it had persisted in the things commanded by the Lord.

10. What it is to hide the talent in the earth.—To hide the talent in the earth is to conceal the glory of the new preaching beneath disparagement of bodily suffering. Though this people cannot deny that the Lord Christ was sent for the salvation of the Gentiles—for both his coming and his Passion are found in the Law—it nevertheless refuses to obey the Gospels. For it says: “I know that you are a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter” (v. 24).

The nature of present things does not permit there to be a harvest without seed, or a gathering of what has not been scattered; but the whole discourse here is spiritual. For we have said that this people is from the Law, not ignorant of the Lord’s coming and of the salvation of the Gentiles, but unbelieving. It knows that the fruits of righteousness are to be reaped where the Law has not been sown, and that those are to be gathered from the Gentiles who have not been scattered from Abraham’s stock. Therefore this man is “hard”: that is, he will justify without the Law, gather without dispersion, and reap without sowing.

11. How great is the fault, and what punishment it receives.—For this reason it will be all the more without excuse that it concealed the preaching and buried the talent entrusted to it, despite knowing that he would reap without seed and gather what he had not scattered. Rather, it ought to have given it to the bankers—that is, shared the use of the talent entrusted to it with the whole human race, occupied in the business of the world—since the Lord would demand its return from each individual.

Because of this fault, the talent is taken away from it—not so much the Gospel, which it had buried, as the Law—and given to the one who had doubled the five. For the Lord says: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away” (v. 29). One who has may indeed abound, because it is easy for a wealthy person to become richer through an increase either of generosity or labor. But how can one who does not have, have something taken away to his loss? It is because to those who possess the use of the Gospels, the honor of the Law also is restored; but from one who does not possess faith in Christ, even that honor which he seemed to possess from the Law is taken away.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the coming of the Son of Man in his majesty.

1. The separation of evil and good at judgment.—“But when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him,” and what follows (Matt. 25:31). He himself completes the entire sense of this discourse. For he speaks of the time and coming of judgment, when he will separate believers from unbelievers and fruitful from unfruitful—goats from sheep—and, placing each at the right or left, assign each a place worthy of his goodness or wickedness. He declares that he is present in his least ones: that is, in those who serve him while awaiting the recompense of their humility, and who are fed when hungry, given drink when thirsty, comforted when strangers, clothed when naked, visited when sick, and consoled when troubled (v. 40). For he is so communicated throughout the bodies and minds of all believers that these offices of humanity, when rendered, merit his favor, and when withheld, provoke his displeasure.

[Note: Printed editions read “judging”; they are corrected from the manuscripts. Then, “those who serve him while awaiting the recompense of their humility,” that is, those who serve God with all offices of humility, whose recompense they expect from him. Thus, in *Exposition of Psalm 138*, §31, the Psalm’s words “and my substance in the lower parts of the earth” are explained: namely, that Christ is in the poor in spirit, the troubled in heart, the humble of earth, the refuse of the world, and the weak of the Church. For the weak member of the Church is one humbled by every kind of humility.]

[Note: Only the Paris edition reads “humility”; the Bec manuscript reads “unanimity.” The other manuscripts read, better, “humanity.”]

2. After this discourse, in which he had shown that he would come in the return of glory, he now warns them that he is about to suffer (Matt. 26:1), so that they might recognize that the mystery of the cross is joined with the glory of eternity. Meanwhile the Jews take counsel to kill him; and, with the chief priests assembled, an opportunity for so great a crime is awaited (v. 4).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the woman who came to Jesus in the house of Simon the leper, carrying an alabaster flask of precious ointment.

1. “Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him carrying an alabaster flask of precious ointment,” and what follows (Matt. 26:6–7). At the very time of the Passion it is not without significance that a woman poured precious ointment upon the head of the reclining Lord; then that the disciples became indignant and said that it ought rather to have been sold for the use of the poor (vv. 8–9); then that the Lord both approved the woman’s deed and promised that its memory would endure forever with the preaching of the Gospel; and finally that after this Judas broke out to sell his salvation.

2. The woman anointing Christ is the people of the Gentiles. The disciples’ partiality for Israel. The poor are Jews lacking faith.—This woman prefigures the people of the Gentiles, who in Christ’s Passion rendered glory to God. For she anointed his head; and the head of Christ is God. The ointment is the fruit of good work. It is especially pleasing to the female sex because of its concern for the body. Therefore she poured forth all care for her body and the whole affection of her precious mind in honor and praise of God.

[Note: Printed editions read “is the people”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

[Note: The Carnotensis and Colbert manuscripts read “in the ointment.” Perhaps the reading is “by the ointment.”]

But the disciples, as often, are moved by favor toward Israel’s salvation: they say that this ought to have been sold for the use of the poor. Yet this woman was not carrying ointment for sale. And prophetically they called “the poor” those lacking faith. Thus they urged that this faith of the Gentiles ought rather to be bought for the salvation of this needy people.

[Note: In the manuscripts the readings are *nuncupant* (“they call”) or *nuncupaverint* (“they may have called”). After “and,” supply “they urge” or something similar.]

The Lord tells them that there would be much time in which they could care for the poor; but that salvation could be bestowed upon the Gentiles only by his command, since they had been buried with him through the ointment poured out by this woman (vv. 11–12), because regeneration is restored only to those who have died with him in the profession of baptism. Therefore, wherever this Gospel is preached, her deed will be told (v. 13), because, with Israel ceasing, the glory of the Gospel is preached through the faith of the Gentiles. Provoked by this emulation, profane Israel, in the person of Judas, is inflamed with every hatred to extinguish the Lord’s name.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the disciples came to Jesus saying, “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”

1. When the name Christian was granted.—“Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying: ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’” and what follows (Matt. 26:17). The disciples are ordered to go to a certain man and tell him that the Lord wished to celebrate the Passover with his disciples at his house. They obeyed the commandments and prepared the Passover (v. 19). But they needed to know where they were going and be informed of the man’s name. Otherwise, uncertain to whom they were sent, how could they, having been sent, carry out what had been commanded?

[Note: “Day” is missing in the Colbert and Carnotensis manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek. In the same manuscripts the word “saying” is omitted; and shortly afterward, “and they prepared the Passover” is absent.]

But the prophetic discourse is interwoven with the events present. He does not name the man with whom he was to celebrate the Passover. For the honor of the Christian name had not yet been granted to believers, who truly behold God with the eyes of mind and faith; so that we might understand that the apostles prepared the Lord’s Passover with him to whom, in the Lord’s time, a new name was to be added.

2. Judas did not receive Christ’s body.—After this Judas the betrayer is identified; without him the Passover is celebrated, after the cup has been received and the bread broken, for he was not worthy of communion in the eternal mysteries. For it is understood that he immediately left, since he is shown returning with the crowds. Nor indeed could he drink with the Lord, since he was not to drink in the kingdom, whereas the Lord promised that all who then drank from the fruit of this vine would later drink it with him (v. 29). When the hymn had been sung, they returned to the mountain (v. 30). Having completed all the powers of the divine mysteries, they are carried up, in common joy and exultation, into heavenly glory.

[Note: That the true Passover was completed while Judas was present is inferred from Luke 22:19 ff.; hence Augustine rightly said in Sermon 71, §17: “Did Judas too—the seller of his Master and impious betrayer—although he ate and drank with the other disciples the very sacrament of Christ’s flesh and blood, first instituted by Christ’s own hands, as Luke the Evangelist declares more plainly, remain in Christ, or Christ in him?”]

3. Peter’s affection for Christ.—He also warned them of their coming weakness, and that on that same night all would be disturbed by fear and unbelief (v. 31). The truth of this was contained also in the authority of ancient prophecy: when the shepherd was struck, the sheep would be scattered (Zech. 13:7). Yet he would go before them, risen, into Galilee, so that he might comfort their weakness by the promise of his return (Matt. 26:32).

But Peter, in the warmth of his faith, answered that, though the others might be scandalized, he would never be scandalized (v. 33). So greatly was he carried away in affection and love for Christ that he did not consider either the weakness of his flesh or the certainty of the Lord’s words, as though what Christ had said would not come to pass. Christ said to him: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (v. 34). But he, as well as the others, promised that not even fear of death would cause them to depart from the confession of his name; for, with fearless resolve of faith, they had strengthened themselves for every constancy of ministry.

## CHAPTER XXXI. When Jesus came into the field called Gethsemane and said to his disciples, “Sit here while I go there to pray”; concerning his soul’s sorrow even unto death; concerning the cup, “if possible, let it pass from me”; concerning the willing spirit and weak flesh; and again, “Father, this cup cannot pass unless I drink it; let your will be done.”

1. “Then Jesus came with them to the field called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples, ‘Sit here while I go there to pray,’” and what follows (Matt. 26:36). He had received the disciples’ faith and the constancy of their devotion to him; but he knew also that they would be troubled and lose confidence. He commands them to sit in that place while he goes forward to pray. And he took Peter, James, and John, the sons of Zebedee. Having taken them, he began to be sorrowful and distressed, and said that his soul was sorrowful unto death (vv. 37–38).

2. The opinion of those who attribute sorrow, fear, and the like to Christ’s divinity is refuted.—Some hold the opinion that sorrow could fall upon God himself, and that fear of the coming Passion broke him, because he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (v. 38); and, “Father, if possible, let this cup pass from me” (v. 39); and again, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (v. 41); and finally, twice, “Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (v. 42).

[Note: That is, the Arians. As Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* 51, §13; Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 19; Theodoret, at the beginning of Dialogue II; and Hilary himself, *On the Trinity*, book X, §50, testify, they taught that the Word in Christ supplied the place of a soul. Therefore they maintained that the sadness, sorrow, distress, and pain which the faithful believe affected Christ’s soul fell upon the Word itself.]

[Note: The first Paris edition reads “and upon him”; the later edition, “and the same thing.”]

They wish the misery arising from bodily weakness to adhere to the Spirit, as though the assumption of flesh had infected with its own lot of weakness that power of incorruptible substance, and eternity had taken on the nature of frailty. If it is sorrowful in relation to fear, weak in relation to pain, and trembling in relation to death, then it will also be subject to corruption and all the affections of weakness will fall upon it. It will become what it was not: sorrowful through anguish, anxious through fear, terrified through pain. Thus, if eternity is changed into fear, and can become what it was not, then that which is in it could likewise at some time cease to be.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “therefore that which it was might at some time not be.”]

But God always is, without measure of times; and as he is, so he is eternal. Eternity, abiding in infinity, extends both to things which have been and to those which will follow: always whole, incorrupt, perfect, with nothing that can exist left outside it. All things are not within something else; rather, all things are within eternity. It has power so to bestow upon us what is its own that nothing is diminished in itself by what it has bestowed.

### 3. Who Are the Authors of This Opinion?

But their whole meaning is this: those who maintain that the fear of death befell the Son of God suppose that he was not brought forth from eternity, nor had his existence from the infinity of the Father’s substance, but was made out of nothing by him who created all things; that he was taken from nothing, began from an act of workmanship, and was established in time. Thus there was in him anxiety of pain; thus the suffering of the spirit along with the suffering of the body; thus fear of death: so that he who could fear death could also die; and he who could die, although he will be eternal in the future, nevertheless is not eternal from the past through him who begot him.

[Note: Only the Paris edition reads: “but out of nothing”; then, with the Roman, Colbert, and Carnot manuscripts: “through him who created him.”]

[Note: That is, of Christ also according to that nature which assumed the body.]

But if they had been capable of the Gospels through faith and uprightness of life, they would know that the Word was God in the beginning, and that this Word was with God from the beginning; that he was born from him who was, and that there is in him who was born what belongs to the very one with whom he was before he was born: namely, that the eternity of the begetter and of the begotten is the same. Therefore nothing in God could die, nor is there any fear in God from himself. For God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19).

[Note: The Vendôme manuscript reads, “before he is born.” These words seem not to have been stated with sufficient caution, as though one might conceive a time when the Son had not yet been born and existed only with the Father. But the following words refute this erroneous sense—namely, that the eternity of begetter and begotten is the same. Nor need we repeat here what we said in the Admonition concerning this passage. Why, moreover, in discussing the generation of the Word, the phrase “before he is born” must not be admitted, Hilary himself teaches more fully in Book XII *On the Trinity*, having by then become better instructed and more cautious in expression.]

### 4. Christ’s Sorrow Arose Not from Himself but from the Disciples

But this entire discourse must be examined, so that, since we read that the Lord was sorrowful, we may discover the causes of his sorrow. Earlier he had warned that all would be scandalized. Peter, trusting in himself, had answered that, even if the others were shaken, he would not be moved; and the Lord replied that he too would deny him three times. Yet he and all the other disciples promise that they will not deny him even if they are placed in death itself. Then, going on, he commanded his disciples to sit down while he prayed. And after taking Peter, James, and John, he began to be sorrowful. Therefore he was not sorrowful before he took them; and all fear began only when they had been taken. Thus the sorrow arose not from himself, but from those whom he had taken.

[Note: The Roman manuscript, together with the Colbert and Carnot manuscripts, reads, “to be sorrowful for them.” In this passage Hilary does not deny but affirms that Christ’s sorrow was real, while explaining it in a manner not unworthy of the God-man. Ambrose and Jerome followed him. Ambrose, in Book X on Luke, §57, says: “You grieve, therefore, Lord, not for your wounds but for mine; not for your death but for our weakness,” etc. Jerome, on Matthew 26, writes: “He was sorrowful, not through fear of suffering; for this was why he had come, and he had reproved Peter for cowardice; but because of the most unhappy Judas and the scattering of the apostles,” etc.]

And it should indeed be remembered that those taken here were none other than those to whom the Son of Man, coming in his kingdom, was shown, when Moses and Elijah stood by him on the mountain and he was surrounded with all the honor of his eternal glory (Matt. 17:1 ff.). But the reason for taking them then was the same as it was now.

### 5. Christ’s Sorrow “Unto,” Not on Account of, Death. Christ Fears Blasphemy against the Spirit for His Own

Finally, he says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” Did he say, “My soul is sorrowful because of death” (see Book X *On the Trinity*, §36)? Certainly not. For if the fear concerned death, it ought surely to have been referred to death as its cause. But it is one thing to fear up to something, another to fear because of it. Whatever is at the end is not thereby made the cause, because something begun from another source is prolonged up to that end.

Earlier, therefore, he had said: “You will suffer scandal in me this night” (Matt. 26:31). He knew that they would be terrified, scattered, and deny him. But because blasphemy against the Spirit is forgiven neither here nor in eternity, he feared that they might deny him as God when they beheld him beaten, spat upon, and crucified. This principle was preserved in Peter, who, though about to deny him, denied him in this way: “I do not know the man” (ibid. 72), because something spoken against the Son of Man will be forgiven. Therefore he is sorrowful unto death. Death itself, then, is not feared, but the time of death; because after it the faith of believers would be strengthened by the power of the resurrection.

### 6

The following comes next: “Remain and watch with me. And going forward, he fell upon his face, praying” (ibid. 38–39). He admonishes them to remain awake with him. For he knew that, as the devil’s pressure increased, their faith would be lulled to sleep; and he commands them to keep watch equally with him, since the same suffering threatened them.

### 7. He Prays for the Passing of the Cup Not for Himself but for His Own

Then he prays: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will.” He asks that the cup may pass from him. Did he say, “Let this cup pass me”? That would have been the prayer of one fearing for himself. But it is one thing to pray that it may pass oneself, another to pray that it may pass away from oneself. For when it passes oneself, that person is overtaken by the affliction that passes; but one who asks that it pass away from him prays not that he himself may be passed over, but that what passes from him may proceed onward to another.

[Note: The printed editions read “passing.” The manuscripts’ reading, “of that which passes”—that is, of a punishment or any other thing—is preferable.]

Was it possible that Christ should not suffer? Yet from the foundation of the world this mystery of our salvation had already been displayed in him. Did he himself not wish to suffer? Yet earlier he had consecrated his blood, to be poured out for the remission of sins (ibid. 28). How, then, does he say, “Father, if it is possible”? And how, “Not as I will, but as you will”? His entire fear, therefore, concerns those who were to suffer. Accordingly, because it was not possible for him not to suffer, he prays for those who would suffer after him, saying, “Let the cup pass from me”—that is, as it is drunk by me, so may it be drunk by them: without despair of hope, without consciousness of pain, without fear of death.

[Note: The Beccensis manuscript reads, “Was it not possible for Christ to suffer?” The negative particle betrays the work of an interpolator. For Hilary clearly teaches here that it could by no means happen that Christ should not suffer. Yet the explanation of St. Thomas is valid: *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 46, article 2, reply to objection 2, where he raises our bishop’s words against himself and answers that this could not have happened on the presupposition of God’s foreknowledge and preordination concerning Christ’s Passion. For Hilary’s entire assertion rests on that single hypothesis.]

### 8. He Asks Strength to Suffer for Them

He says “if it is possible” because fear is heavy for their flesh and blood, and it is difficult for human bodies not to be overcome by the bitterness of such things. But when he says, “Not as I will, but as you will,” he would indeed wish them not to suffer, lest perhaps they lose faith in their suffering, and that they might merit the glory of their co-inheritance without the hardship of suffering. He therefore does not pray that they may not suffer, saying, “Not as I will”; rather, he asks that the firmness of drinking the cup may pass from himself into them, as the Father wills. For it was necessary that the devil be conquered not so much by Christ as also by his disciples.

[Note: The Roman, Colbert, and Carnot manuscripts read, “not that he may suffer”; Paris reads, “that he may not suffer.” The reading of the other books, “that they may not suffer,” seems preferable, since the discourse no longer concerns Christ but the disciples. Since the Father does not will to free them from suffering, Christ at least asks that they may be strong and steadfast in suffering.]

[Note: Six manuscripts read “to conquer by force”; the word “by force” is superfluous.]

### 9. The Cause of Christ’s Fear: Our Weakness

After this he returns to the disciples and finds them sleeping; and he rebukes Peter because he does not watch with him even for one hour (v. 41). Peter is singled out from the three because he had boasted, above the others, that he would not be scandalized. He then indicates the causes of his earlier fear, saying: “Pray that you may not enter into temptation” (v. 41). This, then, was what he wished; and therefore in prayer he had taught: “Lead us not into temptation,” lest anything be allowed against us through the weakness of the flesh (Matt. 6:13).

[Note: Many manuscripts read, “do not watch.”]

Why he had warned them to pray that they might not enter temptation, he shows when he says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak”—certainly not concerning himself, for this discourse is directed toward them. Or how could his spirit now be willing, if earlier his soul was sorrowful unto death? But he commands them to watch and pray, lest they fall into temptation and yield to bodily weakness. Therefore he prays, “if it is possible,” that the cup may pass from him, because all flesh is weak for drinking it.

### 10. Christ’s Passion Conferred upon Us the Power to Suffer

Again he withdrew and prayed, saying: “Father, this cup cannot pass unless I drink it; your will be done” (ibid. 42). For the disciples who were to suffer, he took into himself, through the justification of faith, all the weakness of our body; and with himself he fastened to the cross all that by which we were made weak. Therefore he bears our sins and suffers for us: because, when the heat of faith burns in us and battle must be waged against the devil through suffering, all the pains of our weaknesses die with his body and his Passion. Therefore the cup cannot pass from him unless he drinks it, because we cannot suffer except through his Passion.

[Note: Here, on the authority of three manuscripts, we have removed *si* (“if”), which is absent from the manuscripts also in Book X *On the Trinity*, §37.]

[Note: The Roman manuscript reads, “by which he was weakened”; six others read, “by which we are weakened.”]

[Note: St. Thomas, III, question 46, reply to objection 2, cites these words in another form: “because we cannot be restored except through his Passion”; this is less to the point.]

### 11. What the Disciples’ Sleep and Christ’s Various Addresses Signify

But when, on returning again, he found them sleeping, this shows that during his absence many would be held in a kind of sleep of faith. Yet he prayed again, repeating the same words; and when he returned, he who had commanded them to watch and rebuked them for sleeping said: “Sleep now and rest” (v. 45). After frequent prayer, after many departures and returns, he removes fear, restores confidence, urges them into rest, and, now secure concerning us, awaits the Father’s will, saying, “Your will be done”; because, by drinking the cup which was to pass into us, he would swallow up the weakness of our body, the anxiety of fear, and the very pain of death.

When he returned to them and found them sleeping, he first rebuked them at his first return, was silent at the second, and commanded them to rest at the third. The reason is this: first, after his resurrection, he will rebuke them when scattered, unbelieving, and afraid; secondly, after sending the Paraclete Spirit, he will visit them when their eyes are burdened for beholding the liberty of the Gospel. For for some time they were held fast by love of the Law and occupied by a kind of sleep of faith. Thirdly, that is, at the return of his glory, he will restore them to security and rest.

[Note: Thus the Carnot manuscript together with the Colbert manuscript. Other books read: “he found them, and immediately visited them.”]

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning Judas, One of the Twelve Disciples, Who Came to Jesus with a Great Crowd to Betray Him; and Concerning the Sword Which He Ordered Peter to Return to Its Place

### 1. No Power over Christ Except What He Gives

“And while he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great crowd” (Matt. 26:47–49). In all this there is an order of the Passion. But the purpose of Judas’s kiss was that we might be taught to love all enemies, even those whom we know will rage against us. For the Lord did not reject his kiss. And when he says to Judas, “Do what you are doing,” he permits the power of his betrayal under the condition of this expression. For he who had the right to summon against his betrayers twelve thousand legions of angels could much more easily have thwarted the designs and devices of one man (v. 53). Finally, he says to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you” (John 19:11). Therefore he gives power over himself when he says, “Do what you are doing” (John 13:27), so that the malice of his will, being reckoned as the deed, might accomplish in act what it was already doing in intention.

[Note: “Behold” has been added on the authority of the manuscripts.]

[Note: Paris, with the Colbert, Carnot, and Roman manuscripts, reads: “this was the betrayal.”]

[Note: The printed editions add “quickly” here, against the manuscripts.]

[Note: The printed editions read “more than twelve legions of angels.” The words “more than” are absent from all manuscripts. Three contain “twelve thousand legions.” See the exposition of Psalm 54, §6.]

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “what he had already done”; other books more correctly read, “what he was doing”—that is, what these words, “what you are doing,” signify he was already doing.]

### 2. He Who Uses the Sword Shall Perish by the Sword

But one of those who were with him drew a sword and cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant; and the Lord said to him: “Return your sword to its place. For all who use the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:51–52). Therefore has this very man already been judged, because, using the sword, he will perish by the sword? Yet death by the sword is not usually the fate of all who use a sword. For many who have used it either in the execution of judicial office or from necessity in resisting robbers are consumed by fever or by some other calamity.

Therefore, through the apostle, the ear of the high priest’s servant is cut off: that is, from the people serving the priesthood, disobedient hearing is removed by Christ’s disciple, and that which was incapable of hearing is cut away so that it may become capable of truth. But the whole crowd had come out armed with swords against the Lord. He commanded the sword to be sheathed because he was to destroy them not with a human sword but with the sword of his mouth. Otherwise, if according to his saying everyone who used a sword perished by a sword, the sword was rightly drawn for the death of those who employed it for crime.

### 3. The Priest’s Confession; the Rending of His Garment

The remaining events follow their historical order. False witnesses are sought out. The priest himself, ignorant of the Law in which he gloried, seeks assurance by an oath whether he is the Christ, as though the Law and the prophets spoke of him secretly. Indeed, the priest himself unwillingly confessed Christ when the Lord said: “You have said it.” On hearing his majesty, he tore his garment, breaking apart the very veil of the Law by which he was covered. And through blows of the palms and spitting, every kind of insult was inflicted upon him, to bring human humiliation to its completion (ibid. 59–67).

### 4. Peter’s Denial

But one must carefully consider under what condition Peter denied him, although this has been discussed above. For first he says that he did not understand what was being said; next, that he had not been with him; and thirdly, that he did not know the man. And indeed he was almost denying without guilt the man whose status as Son of God he had first acknowledged. Yet because, through the weakness of the flesh, he had become uncertain, he wept most bitterly, recalling the fault of this fear and that he had been unable to avoid it even after being warned (ibid. 70–75).

[Note: Thus Ambrose, Book X on Luke, §82: “And he rightly denied the man,” he says, “because he knew God.” Jerome appears to criticize this sort of interpretation in his commentary on Matthew 26: “I know,” he says, “that some, out of pious affection toward the apostle Peter, have interpreted this passage so as to say that Peter denied not God but man; and that the meaning is: ‘I do not know the man, because I know God.’ Any prudent reader sees how frivolous this is: they defend the apostle in such a way as to make God culpable.” Yet it may be questioned whether Jerome’s criticism applies to Hilary. For in saying that Christ, whom Peter had first confessed as God, could now in a sense be denied as man, Hilary does not so much excuse Peter as show an inclination to excuse him. He does not wish Peter to be without sin, but only maintains that the reason for his denial is not wholly without an appearance of truth. Nor does he make Christ guilty of falsehood, since he does not deny that Peter truly denied him and incurred guilt by denying him. See our observations on the exposition of Psalm 52, §12. As regards Ambrose, however, he admits in the cited passage, §87, that he wished to excuse Peter kindly, but that Peter himself did not excuse himself at all; rather, he freely confessed and wept over his sin.]

### 5. Judas’s Repentance Rebukes the Unbelief of Those Who Bought Him

He is then handed over to Pilate, the judge of the Gentiles. For he who was without deceit and sin could not be judged guilty under the Law. “Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned,” and the rest (Matt. 27). Judas, repenting, returned to the priests the price of Christ’s blood; so that, although he himself was the author of the sale of righteous blood, nevertheless the very confession of the seller might rebuke the unbelief of the buyers. They answered: “What is that to us? See to it yourself” (v. 4). Their confession is bold and blind. They hear that they have bought the blood of a righteous man, yet believe that they will be free of the guilt of judgment. And yet, by saying, “See to it yourself,” they locate the crime in the seller, whereas by the seller’s testimony the wickedness of the buyers is confirmed.

Accordingly, when Christ had been condemned, Judas went away and hanged himself (v. 5). Thus the time of Judas’s death was arranged so that, amid the Lord’s Passion, when all things beneath and above had been shaken and torn apart, and the administration of all the elements had been stunned into forgetfulness of its duty, he might neither be visited among the dead nor have opportunity for repentance among the living after the resurrection.

### 6. The Purchase of the Potter’s Field with Christ’s Price Is Full of Mysteries

Concerning the silver returned (ibid. 6), because it was the price of blood and could not be put into the *corbanan*, that is, the money of offerings, after consultation they buy the potter’s field and assign it for the burial of foreigners. In this is a great mystery of prophecy and a meditation full of the prodigy of iniquity in its deeds. The work of a potter is to form vessels from clay; and it lies in his hand to remake from the same clay either the same vessel or a more beautiful one. That the field is called the world is contained in the words of our Lord himself (Matt. 13:38).

Therefore the world is bought with Christ’s price—that is, its totality is acquired—and is assigned for the burial of foreigners and the poor. Nothing here belongs to Israel, and the whole use of this purchased world is for strangers: namely, those who will be buried in the price of Christ’s blood, by which all things have been purchased. For he received from the Father all things in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28:18). And therefore this is the potter’s field, because all things belong to God, in whose hand it is to remake us as he wills, like a potter. Therefore, having died and been buried with Christ in this field, we shall obtain the eternal rest of this our pilgrimage. Jeremiah’s prophecy is added in confirmation of this, so that in the working of this deed the authority of the divine utterance might be shown to have preceded it by so long a time (Matt. 27:9).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts, following the Greek κορβανᾶν; the printed editions read *corbanam*.]

[Note: The printed editions read, “and a meditation full of the miracle both in deeds and sayings,” etc., against the manuscripts.]

### 7. Why the Priest Was Answered “You Have Said,” but Pilate “You Say”

When Pilate asked whether he was King of the Jews, he answered: “You say.” But how different was the expression used to the priest! For when the priest asked whether he was the Christ, he had said: “You have said” (Matt. 26:64). This is because the whole Law had foretold the coming Christ. The priest is answered as concerning matters already declared, because the Law itself had always said that Christ would come. But to this man, ignorant of the Law, who asks whether he is King of the Jews, it is said: “You say,” because the salvation of the Gentiles lies in faith’s present confession, and he who formerly did not know may speak this of Christ, while those who formerly spoke may deny it.

[Note: The printed editions read, “he himself had learned.” The manuscripts more truly read, “it itself had said,” evidently in the person of the Law, which throughout earlier times consistently foretold Christ.]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning Pilate: While He Sat upon the Judgment Seat, His Wife Sent to Him Saying, “Have Nothing to Do with That Righteous Man”; and Concerning Those Passing by the Cross, Who Shook Their Heads and Said, “This Man Destroyed the Temple and Rebuilt It in Three Days”

### 1. Pilate’s Wife: the People of the Gentiles. Pilate’s Washing of His Hands

While Pilate was sitting upon the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man” (Matt. 27:19). In her is a figure of the people of the Gentiles. Already faithful, she summons the unbelieving people with whom she lived to faith in Christ. And because she herself suffered much on account of Christ, she invites to the same glory of future hope the man with whom she lived. Finally, Pilate washed his hands and testified to the Jewish people that he was innocent of the Lord’s blood (v. 24), because, while the Jews take upon themselves and their children the crime of the Lord’s shed blood, the people of the Gentiles, daily washed in the confession of faith, migrates (v. 25).

### 2. The Meaning of Barabbas

When Pilate offered, according to the privilege of the solemn day by which one of the accused had to be released at the people’s request, to acquit Jesus (ibid. 17), the people, urged by the priests, chose Barabbas instead (vv. 20–21). The interpretation of the name Barabbas is “son of the father.” Thus the mystery of future unbelief is already shown: in preferring the father’s son to Christ, they prefer Antichrist—the man of sin and son of the devil—and, at the urging of their leaders, choose one reserved for condemnation rather than the author of salvation.

### 3. The Scarlet and Purple Cloak; the Crown of Thorns; the Reed in His Hand and upon His Head

After the Lord has been scourged, a scarlet cloak and a purple garment are placed on him, along with a crown of thorns and a reed in his right hand; and, kneeling, they worship him in mockery. Having taken upon himself all the weaknesses of our body, he is then dyed in the scarlet color with the blood of all the martyrs, to whom the kingdom was owed together with him; and he is clothed in the precious honor of prophets and patriarchs in purple. He is also crowned with thorns—that is, with the sins of the Gentiles which once pierced—so that glory might be won from things ruinous and useless, the sins surrounding his head, that is, God. For there is a sting in thorns, from which a crown of victory is woven for Christ. In the reed, moreover, the weakness and emptiness of those same Gentiles, taken in his hand, is made firm. Indeed, it is also struck against his head. In my judgment, a blow from a reed causes no great injury to his head; but its typological meaning is preserved: the weakness of Gentile bodies, first taken in Christ’s hand, may also rest in God the Father, who is his head. In all these things Christ, while mocked, is worshiped (ibid. 28–30).

[Note: Most manuscripts read *molliuntur* (“are softened”), a reading which at first seemed more coherent. The reading *moriuntur* (“die”) also occurred to us. But we later judged that *moliuntur* should be retained: that is, the sins represented by thorns are no longer made ruinous and useless, but accomplish—namely, glory. In the Leipzig and Paris editions the word *peccatorum* is separated from *quaereretur* by a point and joined to the following *est enim*, contrary to the Basel and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts, in some of which appears *est autem aculeus*. This rather perplexing passage of Hilary is illustrated by Ambrose, Book X on Luke, §105: “What else does the crown of thorns fastened to his head show than the gift of the divine work, by which triumphant glory was sought for God from the sinners of the world, as from the thorns of the age?”]

[Note: Paris, with the Roman, Colbert, and Carnot manuscripts, reads “is placed upon.” From the other books we restore “is struck against,” especially since in the exposition of Psalm 143, §16, we read: “The right hand is iniquitous when it strikes with palms, tears with rods, strikes with a reed.”]

### 4

As they went out, they laid the wood of the Passion upon a certain man of Cyrene. For the Jew was unworthy to bear Christ’s cross, because it was left to the faith of the Gentiles both to receive the cross and to suffer with him. The place of the cross was such that, placed in the middle of the earth and standing as it were upon the summit of this universe, it might be equally accessible to all nations for attaining the knowledge of God. He also refused to drink the wine mixed with gall, for the bitterness of sins is not mixed with the incorruption of eternal glory. And his garment, divided by lot rather than torn, indicated the enduring incorruption of his body (ibid. 32–35).

[Note: Two manuscripts read “with gall”; shortly afterwards they read “incorruption,” not “to incorruption.” Then “the bitterness of sins” means the bitterness which is sin’s punishment. Hence Ambrose, Book X on Luke, §124, following Hilary’s thought: “Bitterness ought not to be mixed with purity, so that it might be shown that the immortality of those who rise again will be without bitterness.”]

### 5. What the Placement of the Thieves Represents

And so, upon the tree of life hangs the salvation and life of all; and two thieves are fixed at his left and right, so that it might be understood that the death of human beings differs from the death of the Only-Begotten. For he gave up his spirit voluntarily when he wished, whereas their legs were broken (Luke 23:33), showing that the whole human race is called to the mystery of the Lord’s Passion. But because all are divided to the right and the left by the distinction between believers and unbelievers, one of the two, placed at the right, is saved by the justification of faith (ibid. 43).

[Note: In the Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions and in five manuscripts, the words enclosed in parentheses are absent.]

That reproach is also added by which Israel itself might convict itself of unbelief, when it is said: “This is he who destroyed the temple of God and rebuilt it in three days,” and the rest (Matt. 27:40). It was not difficult for him to come down from the cross; but the mystery of the Father’s will had to be fulfilled. Yet while placed upon the cross he was performing greater works through the disturbance of all nature. Is this, then, set forth as the greatest and, as it were, the most difficult of all? What excuse, therefore, will there be when, after three days, the temple of God is seen rebuilt in the resurrection of the body? And the fact that both thieves reproach him with the condition of his Passion (v. 44) signifies that the scandal of the cross would come even to all believers.

[Note: Again, in those same editions and four manuscripts, the following four lines are absent: from “It was not difficult” to the words “this, then, is the greatest,” where they read “this, therefore, is the greatest.”]

[Note: Paris reads “of the Father’s patient will,” against the manuscripts, from which these lines were first published.]

### 6. The Three Days of Christ’s Death; Christ’s Forsaking by God; the Mystery of the Vinegar He Drank

Now night from day makes the division of the times. Thus the third number of three days and an equal number of nights is completed, and the hidden mystery of the divine operation is perceived amid the amazement of all creation. But the cry to God is the voice of the body, testifying that the Word of God was withdrawing from it. Finally, he cries out why he is forsaken, saying: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (v. 46). But he is forsaken because he was a man who had also to undergo death.

[Note: Because of this passage many think that Hilary held that Christ’s dying flesh was separated from the divinity of the Word. But since in Book VIII *On the Trinity*, §13, he affirms of Christ, “Born man, he has assumed our flesh’s nature as now inseparable from himself”; since also in Book IX, §11, he vigorously maintains that Christ who strips off flesh, strips himself of flesh, and raises his body from the dead is one and the same; and since finally in Book X, §59 ff., he disputes no less vigorously against those who divide Christ, maintaining that Christ who lies in the tomb and reigns in heaven is one and the same; it is fairer to understand him to have said these things without impairing the substantial union of the Word with the flesh. He therefore says this in the sense that, although the Word by his power could protect the body from death, he forsook it by not being present to prevent death from reaching it. Thus above, Chapter 3, §2, Christ is said to have forsaken the manhood of his nature in order to hunger; yet no one would understand this to mean a substantial separation or abandonment by the Word. Moreover, the opinion which some suppose Hilary held clashes with faith in this: the Son of God would not have truly died if he had withdrawn from the flesh before death. But how sound his faith on this point was is clear from Book III *On the Trinity*, §15: “The Son of God is crucified; but upon the cross God conquers human death. Christ the Son of God dies; but all flesh is made alive in Christ. The Son of God is in the lower regions; but man is brought back to heaven.” From this it is clear that he believed the Son of God was separated neither from the flesh in death nor from the soul in the lower regions. Moreover, in the words, “But the cry to God is the voice of the body,” “body” may be understood as the whole human being, just as in Book III *On the Trinity*, §16, concerning Christ’s words, “Glorify me, Father, with yourself,” etc., it is added: “This is the prayer of the flesh”; and the term “flesh” refers to the whole human being. But if the whole human being, even according to the soul, was forsaken by the Son of God before death, then the Son of God was not in the lower regions. It is worth noting that in the exposition of Psalm 141, §6, Hilary interprets the words “My God” not as Christ the man speaking to the Word, but as the Son speaking to the Father: “When he cries out, ‘My God, why have you forsaken me?’ these words are not a confession of his own weakness but a proclamation of the Father’s power.” Whoever wishes for more may consult the special discussion of this matter in the general preface, §4.]

Moreover, the fact that, after he had drunk the vinegar offered on a sponge by means of a reed, he cried out and gave up his spirit must be carefully considered (ibid. 48–50). Wine is both the honor and the power of immortality, but becomes sour through the fault either of neglect or of its vessel. Therefore, when it had become sour in Adam, he himself received and drank it from the Gentiles. For it is offered to him to drink from a sponge upon a reed; that is, from the bodies of the Gentiles he received the faults of corrupted immortality and transferred into himself, into communion with his immortality, the faults that were in us. Finally, in John, after he had drunk it all, he said: “It is finished” (John 19:30), because he had drained every fault of human corruption. And because there was nothing further to be done outwardly, he gave up his spirit with a cry and a loud voice (Matt. 27:50), grieving that he did not drink the sins of all.

[Note: Thus the Roman, Colbert, and Carnot manuscripts. The preposition *in* would be repeated more clearly before “immortality.” Other books read, “into that communion which was corrupted in us.” Ambrose, in the cited passage, §124, writes concerning the same words: “The fault of immortality corrupted through Adam is destroyed in the reed, so that it may be swallowed up from the human body. Let us also pour into Christ our faults, hardened through negligence of mind and body.”]

[Note: The word “every” is absent from five manuscripts. Nevertheless, we retain it with the sounder witnesses, as demanded by the words “It is finished” and supported by Ambrose, §125: “All things were completed, because every mystery of the assumed mortality had been fulfilled and, with all faults exhausted, only the joy of immortality remained.”]

[Note: That is, so that he might not lose his spirit unwillingly. Since he could not lose it through any external force, he gave it forth willingly. “For what is given forth is voluntary; what is lost is necessary,” says Ambrose, Book X on Luke, §127. Thereupon the Basel, Erasmus, and Leipzig editions and five manuscripts read, “with a cry of loud voice.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “to drink,” against the manuscripts.]

### 7. What Followed Christ’s Death

After this, the veil of the temple is torn, because from that time the people is divided into parts, and the honor of the veil, together with the guardianship of the protecting angel, is removed. The earth is shaken, for it could not contain this dead one. The rocks are split, for the Word of God and the power of eternal might, penetrating all things strong and firm, had then broken in. The tombs are opened, for the barriers of death had to be unbarred. And many bodies of sleeping saints rose, for, illuminating the darkness of death and shining light into the obscurities of the lower world, he was stripping death itself of its spoils in the resurrection of saints then appearing. And so that Israel’s crime of unbelief might be increased, the centurion and guards, beholding this disturbance of all nature, confess him to be the Son of God (ibid. 51–54).

[Note: Paris, with the Colbert, Carnot, and Roman manuscripts, reads “had to be unbarred.” On the resurrection of the saints who then appeared at Jerusalem, see the observations at column 275 of this edition, note d.]

8. Christ’s Burial.—That Joseph asked Pilate for the body, that it was wrapped in a linen cloth, laid in a new tomb hewn in rock, and that a stone was rolled against the entrance of the tomb (ibid., 58–60): [Col. 1075C] although this is the sequence of events, and it was necessary that he who was to rise from the dead should be buried, nevertheless each detail is stated with significance.

Joseph represents the apostles; and therefore, although he was not among the number of the twelve apostles, he is called a disciple of the Lord. He wraps the body in a clean linen cloth. Indeed, in this same cloth we find every kind of the 810 animals of the universe let down from heaven to Peter (Acts 10:12). From this it may perhaps not superfluously be understood that, under the name of this linen cloth, the Church is buried with Christ: because in it, as in the mixed multitude of the Church, there was gathered together a diversity of clean and unclean animals. [Col. 1076A]

Therefore the Lord’s body is brought, as it were through the apostles’ teaching, into the empty and new resting-place of the hewn rock. That is, Christ is brought into the breast of Gentile hardness, cut out by a certain work of doctrine—a breast rough and new, and previously inaccessible through any entrance of the fear of God. And because nothing besides him ought to penetrate into our breasts, the stone is rolled against the entrance: so that, since no author of divine knowledge had previously been brought into us, no one may be brought in after him apart from him.

Then the fear that the body might be stolen, together with the guarding and sealing of the tomb, is evidence of folly and unbelief: for they wished to seal the tomb of him at whose command they had seen a dead person raised from a tomb.

9. Resurrection on the Lord’s Day. Why his angel is the first herald. Why women are the first to know.—The earthquake at dawn (Matt. 28:2) is the power of the Lord’s-day resurrection: when death’s sting was crushed and its darkness illumined, and the Lord of the heavenly Powers arose, the realm of the dead [Col. 1076B] was shaken with terror.

The angel of the Lord, descending from heaven, rolling away the stone, and sitting by the tomb, is a sign of the mercy of God the Father, who sends the ministries of the heavenly Powers to his Son as he rises from the underworld. Therefore the angel himself is the first herald of the resurrection, so that the resurrection might be announced in a certain service of the Father’s will.

But immediately the Lord meets the women, encouraged by the angel, and greets them (ibid., v. 9), so that, when they were about to announce the resurrection to the disciples waiting for them, they might speak not from the mouth of an angel rather than from that of Christ. That women first see the Lord, are greeted, fall at his knees, and are commanded to announce it to the apostles, restores in reverse order the original cause: because death had begun through this sex, to it first were restored the glory, sight, fruit, and proclamation of the resurrection.

But the guards, who had seen all these things, are bought with silver to keep silent concerning Christ’s resurrection, and, through the honour of the world and greed, to spread the lie that the body was stolen; because his honour lies in money, Christ’s glory is denied [Col. 1076C] (ibid., vv. 12–13).

> [Note: Col. 1076C] In the Paris edition alone: “the resurrection of Christ.” Then “the chief priests” [Col. 1076D], with the intervening words omitted. Similar are the following passages in *Tractatus on Psalm* 68, no. 23: “that they bought with money silence concerning the resurrection . . . was known”; and on Psalm 2, no. 12: “Those who had bought from the soldiers silence concerning the resurrection and the report that the body had been stolen,” etc.

> [Note: Col. 1076D] In the Colbert and Chartres manuscripts the following words of this section are lacking.

1. > [Note: Col. 1076D] What follows was first published in the Paris edition of 1605 and, as we conjecture, from the manuscript now called Colbert, which, it is easy to understand, was then the only one collated. It also occurs at the end of the Chartres manuscript, but in a different and later hand. It has here been stitched in from Jerome’s commentary, with only the first words changed: thus “But the chief priests” has been put where Jerome has “But they.” Nor is it hidden that someone wished to carry this commentary of Hilary through to the final words of Matthew.

But the chief priests, who ought to have turned to repentance and sought Jesus risen again, persist in wickedness; and they divert money that had been given for the uses of the Temple to the purchase of a lie, just as earlier the Jews (Jerome: *Judaei*) had given thirty pieces of silver to the betrayer. Therefore all who misuse the Temple’s collection and what is contributed for the needs of the Church upon other things by which to gratify their own will are like the scribes and priests purchasing a lie and the blood of the Saviour.

2. But his eleven disciples went into Galilee, [Col. 1077A] to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them (v. 16). After the resurrection Jesus is seen on a mountain in Galilee, and there he is worshipped, although some doubt; and their doubt increases our faith.

3. Then he is shown more plainly to Thomas, displaying the side wounded by the lance and the hands fixed by nails. Jesus approached and spoke to them, saying: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (v. 18). Authority was given to him who a little before had been crucified, had been buried in the tomb, had lain dead, and afterwards rose again. Authority was given in heaven and on earth so that he who previously reigned in heaven might reign on earth through the faith of believers.

“Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (v. 19). First they teach all nations; then they immerse those who have been taught in water. For the body cannot receive the sacrament of baptism unless beforehand the soul has received the truth of faith. They are baptized in the name of the Father [Col. 1078A] and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, so that there may be one bestowal for those whose divinity is one; and the name of the Trinity is one God.

4. “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I command you” (v. 20). This is the chief order: he commanded the apostles first to teach all nations, then to baptize them in the sacrament of faith, and, after faith and baptism, to prescribe what was to be observed. And lest we suppose that the things commanded are trivial or few, he added: “all things whatsoever I have commanded you,” so that those who have believed, who have been baptized in the Trinity, may do all that has been commanded.

“And behold, I am with you” (the manuscripts add, “all days”) “until the consummation of the age.” He who promises that he will be with his disciples until the consummation of the age shows both that they will always live and that he will never depart from believers. And he who promises his presence until the consummation of the world is not ignorant of that day on which he knows that he will be with the apostles.
